speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: If I say I will not, he will kill me, I do see't writ
In his looks; and should I say I will, he'l run and tell the
King: I do not shun your friendship dear Melantius,
But this cause is weighty, give me but an hour to think.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Take it—I know this goes unto the King,
But I am arm'd.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Me thinks I feel my self
But twenty now agen; this fighting fool
Wants Policy; I shall revenge my Girl,
And make her red again; I pray, my legs
Will last that pace that I will carry them,
I shall want breath before I find the King.

speeches.speaker: MEL.
verse: Save you.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Save you sweet Brother.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: In my blunt eye methinks you look Evadne.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Come, you would make me blush.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: I would Evadne, I shall displease my ends else.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: You shall if you command me; I am bashful;
Come Sir, how do I look?

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: I would not have your women hear me
Break into commendation of you, 'tis not seemly.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Go walt me in the Gallery—now speak.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: I'le lock the door first.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Why?

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: I will not have your guilded things that dance in visitation with their Millan skins choke up my business.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: You are strangely dispos'd Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Good Madam, not to make you merry.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: No, if you praise me, 'twill make me sad.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Such a sad commendation I have for you.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Brother, the Court hath made you witty,
And learn to riddle.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: I praise the Court for't; has it learned you nothing?

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Me?

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: I Evadne, thou art young and handsom,
A Lady of a sweet complexion,
And such a flowing carriage, that it cannot
Chuse but inflame a Kingdom.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Gentle Brother!

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: 'Tis yet in thy remembrance, foolish woman,
To make me gentle.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: How is this?

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: 'Tis base,
And I could blush at these years, thorough all
My honour'd scars, to come to such a parly.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: I understand you not.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: You dare not, Fool;
They that commit thy faults, fly the remembrance.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: My faults, Sir! I would have you know I care not
If they were written here, here in my forehead.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Thy body is too little for the story,
The lusts of which would fill another woman,
Though she had Twins within her.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: This is saucy;
Look you intrude no more, there lies your way.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Thou art my way, and I will tread upon thee,
Till I find truth out.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: What truth is that you look for?

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Thy long-lost honour: would the Gods had set me
One of their loudest bolts; come tell me quickly,
Do it without enforcement, and take heed
You swell me not above my temper.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: How Sir? where got you this report?

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Where there was people in every place.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: They and the seconds of it are base people;
Believe them not, they lyed.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Do not play with mine anger, do not Wretch,
I come to know that desperate Fool that drew thee
From thy fair life; be wise, and lay him open.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Unhand me, and learn manners, such another
Forgetfulness forfeits your life.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Quench me this mighty humour, and then tell me
Whose Whore you are, for you are one, I know it.
Let all mine honours perish but I'le find him,
Though he lie lockt up in thy blood; be sudden;
There is no facing it, and be not flattered;
The burnt air, when the Dog raigns, is not fouler
Than thy contagious name, till thy repentance
(If the Gods grant thee any) purge thy sickness.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Be gone, you are my Brother, that's your safety.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: I'le be a Wolf first; 'tis to be thy Brother
An infamy below the sin of a Coward:
I am as far from being part of thee,
As thou art from thy vertue: seek a kindred
'Mongst sensual beasts, and make a Goat thy Brother,
A Goat is cooler; will you tell me yet?

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: If you stay here and rail thus, I shall tell you,
I'le ha' you whipt; get you to your command,
And there preach to your Sentinels,
And tell them what a brave man you are; I shall laugh at you.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Y'are grown a glorious Whore; where be your
Fighters? what mortal Fool durst raise thee to this daring,
And I alive? by my just Sword, h'ad safer
Bestride a Billow when the angry North
Plows up the Sea, or made Heavens fire his food;
Work me no higher; will you discover yet?

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: The Fellow's mad, sleep and speak sense.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
prose: Force my swollen heart no further; I would save thee; your great maintainers are not here, they dare not, would they were all, and armed, I would speak loud; here's one should thunder to'em: will you tell me? thou hast no hope to scape; he that dares most, and damns away his soul to do thee service, will sooner fetch meat from a hungry Lion, than come to rescue thee; thou hast death about thee: h'as undone thine honour, poyson'd thy vertue, and of a lovely rose, left thee a canker.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Let me consider.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Do, whose child thou wert,
Whose honour thou hast murdered, whose grave open'd,
And so pull'd on the Gods, that in their justice
They must restore him flesh again and life,
And raise his dry bones to revenge his scandal.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: The gods are not of my mind; they had better let 'em lie sweet still in the earth; they'l stink here.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Do you raise mirth out of my easiness?
Forsake me then all weaknesses of Nature,
That make men women: Speak you whore, speak truth,
Or by the dear soul of thy sleeping Father,
This sword shall be thy lover: tell, or I'le kill thee:
And when thou hast told all, thou wilt deserve it.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: You will not murder me!

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: No, 'tis a justice, and a noble one,
To put the light out of such base offenders.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Help!

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: By thy foul self, no humane help shall help thee,
If thou criest: when I have kill'd thee, as I have
Vow'd to do, if thou confess not, naked as thou hast left
Thine honour, will I leave thee,
That on thy branded flesh the world may read
Thy black shame, and my justice; wilt thou bend yet?

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Up and begin your story.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Oh I am miserable.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: 'Tis true, thou art, speak truth still.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: I have offended, noble Sir: forgive me.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: With what secure slave?

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Do not ask me Sir.
Mine own remembrance is a misery too mightie for me.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Do not fall back again; my sword's unsheath'd yet.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: What shall I do?

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Be true, and make your fault less.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: I dare not tell.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Tell, or I'le be this day a killing thee.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Will you forgive me then?

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Stay, I must ask mine honour first, I have too much foolish nature in me; speak.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Is there none else here?

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: None but a fearful conscience, that's too many. Who is't?

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: O hear me gently; it was the King.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: No more. My worthy father's and my services
Are liberally rewarded! King, I thank thee,
For all my dangers and my wounds, thou hast paid me
In my own metal: These are Souldiers thanks.
How long have you liv'd thus Evadne?

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Too long.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Too late you find it: can you be sorry?

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Would I were half as blameless.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Evadne, thou wilt to thy trade again.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: First to my grave.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Would gods th'hadst been so blest:
Dost thou not hate this King now? prethee hate him:
Couldst thou not curse him? I command thee curse him,
Curse till the gods hear, and deliver him
To thy just wishes: yet I fear Evadne,
You had rather play your game out.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: No, I feel
Too many sad confusions here to let in any loose flame hereafter.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Dost thou not feel amongst all those one brave anger
That breaks out nobly, and directs thine arm to kill this base King?

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: All the gods forbid it.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: No, all the gods require it, they are dishonoured in him.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: 'Tis too fearful.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Y'are valiant in his bed, and bold enough
To be a stale whore, and have your Madams name
Discourse for Grooms and Pages, and hereafter
When his cool Majestie hath laid you by,
To be at pension with some needy Sir
For meat and courser clothes, thus far you know no fear.
Come, you shall kill him.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Good Sir!

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: And 'twere to kiss him dead, thou'd smother him;
Be wise and kill him: Canst thou live and know
What noble minds shall make thee see thy self
Found out with every finger, made the shame
Of all successions, and in this great ruine
Thy brother and thy noble husband broken?
Thou shalt not live thus; kneel and swear to help me
When I shall call thee to it, or by all
Holy in heaven and earth, thou shalt not live
To breath a full hour longer, not a thought:
Come 'tis a righteous oath; give me thy hand,
And both to heaven held up, swear by that wealth
This lustful thief stole from thee, when I say it,
To let his foul soul out.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Here I swear it,
And all you spirits of abused Ladies
Help me in this performance.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Enough; this must be known to none
But you and I Evadne; not to your Lord,
Though he be wise and noble, and a fellow
Dares step as far into a worthy action,
As the most daring, I as far as Justice.
Ask me not why. Farewell.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Would I could say so to my black disgrace.
Oh where have I been all this time! how friended,
That I should lose my self thus desperately,
And none for pity shew me how I wandred?
There is not in the compass of the light
A more unhappy creature: sure I am monstrous,
For I have done those follies, those mad mischiefs,
Would dare a woman. O my loaden soul,
Be not so cruel to me, choak not up
The way to my repentance. O my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: How now?

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: My much abused Lord!

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: This cannot be.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: I do not kneel to live, I dare not hope it;
The wrongs I did are greater; look upon me
Though I appear with all my faults.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Stand up.
This is no new way to beget more sorrow;
Heaven knows I have too many; do not mock me;
Though I am tame and bred up with my wrongs,
Which are my foster-brothers, I may leap
Like a hand-wolf into my natural wilderness,
And do an out-rage: pray thee do not mock me.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: My whole life is so leprous, it infects
All my repentance: I would buy your pardon
Though at the highest set, even with my life:
That slight contrition, that's no sacrifice
For what I have committed.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Sure I dazle:
There cannot be a faith in that soul woman
That knows no God more mighty than her mischiefs:
Thou dost still worst, still number on thy faults,
To press my poor heart thus. Can I believe
There's any seed of Vertue in that woman
Left to shoot up, that dares go on in sin
Known, and so known as thine is, O Evadne!
Would there were any safety in thy sex,
That I might put a thousand sorrows off,
And credit thy repentance: but I must not;
Thou hast brought me to the dull calamity,
To that strange misbelief of all the world,
And all things that are in it, that I fear
I shall fall like a tree, and find my grave,
Only remembring that I grieve.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: My Lord,
Give me your griefs: you are an innocent,
A soul as white as heaven: let not my sins
Perish your noble youth: I do not fall here
To shadow by dissembling with my tears,
As all say women can, or to make less
What my hot will hath done, which heaven and you
Knows to be tougher than the hand of time
Can cut from mans remembrance; no I do not;
I do appear the same, the same Evadne,
Drest in the shames I liv'd in, the same monster.
But these are names of honour, to what I am;
I do present my self the foulest creature,
Most poysonous, dangerous, and despis'd of men,
Lerna e're bred, or Nilus; I am hell,
Till you, my dear Lord, shoot your light into me,
The beams of your forgiveness: I am soul-sick,
And whither with the fear of one condemn'd,
Till I have got your pardon.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Rise Evadne.
These heavenly powers that put this good into thee,
Grant a continuance of it: I forgive thee;
Make thy self worthy of it, and take heed,
Take heed Evadne this be serious;
Mock not the powers above, that can and dare
Give thee a great example of their justice
To all ensuing eyes, if thou plai'st
With thy repentance, the best sacrifice.
prose: 〈1 page duplicate〉
〈1 page duplicate〉

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: I have done nothing good to win belief,
My life hath been so faithless; all the creatures
Made for heavens honours have their ends, and good ones,
All but the cousening Crocodiles, false women;
They reign here like those plagues, those killing sores
Men pray against; and when they die, like tales
Ill told, and unbeliev'd, they pass away,
And go to dust forgotten: But my Lord,
Those short dayes I shall number to my rest,
(As many must not see me) shall though too late,
Though in my evening, yet perceive a will,
Since I can do no good because a woman,
Reach constantly at some thing that is near it;
I w ll redeem one minute of my age,
Or like another Njobe I'le weep till I am water.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: I am now dissolved:
My frozen soul melts: may each sin thou hast,
Find a new mercy: Rise, I am at peace:
Hadst thou been thus, thus excellently good,
Before that devil King tempted thy frailty,
Sure thou hadst made a star: give me thy hand;
From this time I will know thee, and as far
As honour gives me leave, be thy Amintor:
When we meet next, I will salute thee fairly,
And pray the gods to give thee happy dayes:
My charity shall go along with thee,
Though my embraces must be far from thee.
I should ha^ kill'd thee, but this sweet repentance
Looks up my vengeance, for which thus I kiss thee,
The last kiss we must take; and would to heaven
The holy Priest that gave our hands together,
Had given us equal Vertues: go, Evadne,
The gods thus part our bodies, have a care
My honour falls no farther, I am well then.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: All the dear joyes here, and above hereafter
Crown thy fair soul: thus I take leave my Lord,
And never shall you see the soul Evadne
Till sh'ave tryed all honoured means that may
Set her in rest, and wash her stains away.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: I cannot tell how I should credit this
From you that are his enemy.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I am sure he said it to me, and I'le justifie it
What way he dares oppose, but with my sword.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: But did he break without all circumstance
To you his foe, that he would have the Fort
To kill me, and then escape?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: If he deny it, I'le make him blush.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: It sounds incredibly.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I, so does every thing I say of late.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Not so Calianax.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Yes, I should fit
Mute, whilst a Rogue with strong arms cuts your throat.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Well, I will try him, and if this be true
I'le pawn my life I'le find it; if 't be false,
And that you clothe your hate in such a lie,
You shall hereafter doat in your own house, not in the Court.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Why if it be a lie,
Mine ears are false; for I'le be sworn I heard it:
Old men are good for nothing; you were best
Put me to death for hearing, and free him
For meaning of it; you would ha' trusted me
Once, but the time is altered.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: And will still where I may do with justice to the world;
You have no witness.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Yes, my self.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: No more I mean there were that heard it.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: How no more? would you have more? why am
Not I enough to hang a thousand Rogues?

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: But so you may hang honest men too if you please.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I may, 'tis like I will do so; there are a hundred will swear it for a need too, if I say it.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Such witnesses we need not.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: And 'tis hard if my Word cannot hang a boysterous knave.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Enough; where's Strato?

speeches.speaker: Stra.
verse: Sir!

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Why where's all the company? call Amintor in.
Evadne, where's my Brother, and Melantius?
Bid him come too, and Diphilus; call all
That are without there: if he should desire
The combat of you, 'tis not in the power
Of all our Laws to hinder it, unless we mean to quit 'em.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Why if you do think
'Tis sit an old Man and a Counsellor,
To sight for what he sayes, then you may grant it.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Come Sirs, Amintor thou art yet a Bridegroom,
And I will use thee so: thou shalt sit down;
Evadne sit, and you Amintor too;
This Banquet is for you, sir: Who has brought
A merry Tale about him, to raise a laughter
Amongst our wine? why Strato, where art thou?
Thou wilt chop out with them unseasonably
When I desire 'em not.

speeches.speaker: Strato.
verse: 'Tis my ill luck Sir, so to spend them then.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Reach me a boul of wine: Melantius, thou art sad.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: I should be Sir the merriest here,
But I ha' ne're a story of mine own
Worth telling at this time.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Give me the Wine.
Melantius, I am now considering
How easie 'twere for any man we trust
To poyson one of us in such a boul.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: I think it were not hard Sir, for a Knave.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Such as you are.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: I' faith 'twere easie, it becomes us well
To get plain dealing men about our selves,
Such as you all are here: Amintor, to thee
And to thy fair Evadne.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Have you thought of this Calianax?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Yes marry have I.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: And what's your resolution?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Ye shall have it soundly?

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Reach to Amintor, Strato.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Here my love,
This Wine will do thee wrong, for it will set
Blushes upon thy cheeks, and till thou dost a fault, 'twere pity.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Yet I wonder much
Of the strange desperation of these men,
That dare attempt such acts here in our State;
He could not escape that did it.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Were he known, unpossible.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: It would be known, Melantius.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: It ought to be, if he got then away
He must wear all our lives upon his sword,
He need not fly the Island, he must leave no one alive.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: No, I should think no man
Could kill me and scape clear, but that old man.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: But I! heaven bless me: I, should I my Liege?

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: I do not think thou wouldst, but yet thou might'st,
For thou hast in thy hands the means to scape,
By keeping of the Fort; he has, Melantius, and he has kept it well.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: From cobwebs Sir,
'Tis clean swept: I can find no other Art
In keeping of it now, 'twas ne're besieg'd since he commanded.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I shall be sure of your good word,
But I have kept it safe from such as you.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Keep your ill temper in,
I speak no malice; had my brother kept it I should ha' said as much.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: You are not merry, brother; drink wine,
Sit you all still! Calianax,
I cannot trust thus: I have thrown out words
That would have fetcht warm blood upon the cheeks
Of guilty men, and he is never mov'd, he knows no such thing.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Impudence may scape, when feeble vertue is accus'd.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: He must, if he were guilty, feel an alteration
At this our whisper, whilst we point at him,
You see he does not.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Let him hang himself,
What care I what he does; this he did say.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Melantius, you cannot easily conceive
What I have meant; for men that are in fault
Can subtly apprehend when others aime
At what they do amiss; but I forgive
Freely before this man; heaven do so too:
I will not touch thee so much as with shame
Of telling it, let it be so no more.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Why this is very sine.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: I cannot tell
What 'tis you mean, but I am apt enough
Rudely to thrust into ignorant fault,
But let me know it; happily 'tis nought
But misconstruction, and where I am clear
I will not take forgiveness of the gods, much less of you.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Nay if you stand so stiff, I shall call back my mercy.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: I want smoothness
To thank a man for pardoning of a crime I never knew.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Not to instruct your knowledge, but to shew you my ears are every where, you meant to kill me, and get the Fort to scape.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Pardon me Sir; my bluntness will be pardoned:
You preserve
A race of idle people here about you,
Eaters, and talkers, to defame the worth
Of those that do things worthy; the man that uttered this
Had pe^sht without food, be't who it will,
But for ^is arm that sene't him from the soe.
And if I thought you gave a faith to this,
The plainness of my nature would speak more;
^ive me a pardon (for you ought to do't)
To kill him that spake this.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I, that will be the end of all,
Then I am fairly paid for all my care and service.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: That old man who calls me enemy, and of whom I
(Though I will never match my hate so low)
Have no good thought, would yet I think excuse me,
And swear he thought me wrong'd in this.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Who I, thou shameless fellow! didst thou not speak to me of it thy self?

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: O then it came from him.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: From me! who should it come from but from me?

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Nay, I believe your malice is enough,
But I ha' lost my anger. Sir, I hope you are well satisfied.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Lisip. Chear Amintor and his Lady; there's no sound
Comes from you; I will come and do't my self.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: You have done already Sir for me, I thank you.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Melantius, I do credit this from him,
How slight so e're you mak't.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: 'Tis strange you should.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: 'Tis strange he should believe an old mans word,
That never lied in his life.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: I talk not to thee;
Shall the wild words of this distempered man,
Frantick with age and sorrow, make a breach
Betwixt your Majesty and me? 'twas wrong
To hearken to him; but to credit him
As much, at least, as I have power to bear.
But pardon me, whilst I speak only truth,
I may commend my self—I have bestow'd
My careless blood with you, and should be loth
To think an action that would make me lose
That, and my thanks too: when I was a boy,
I thrust my self into my Countries cause,
And did a deed that pluckt five years from time,
And stil'd me man then: And for you my King,
Your subjects all have fed by vertue of my arm.
This sword of mine hath plow'd the ground,
And reapt the fruit in peace;
And your self have liv'd at home in ease:
So terrible I grew, that without swords
My name hath fetcht you conquest, and my heart
And limbs are still the same; my will is great
To do you service: let me not be paid
With such a strange distrust.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Melantius, I held it great injustice to believe
Thine Enemy, and did not; if I did,
I do not, let that satisfie: what struck
With sadness all? More Wine!

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: A few fine words have overthrown my truth:
Ah th'art a Villain.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Why thou wert better let me have the Fort,
Dotard, I will disgrace thee thus for ever;
There shall no credit lie upon thy words;
Think better and deliver it.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: My Liege, he's at me now agen to do it; speak,
Deny it if thou canst; examine him
Whilst he's hot, for he'l cool agen, he will forswear it.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: This is lunacy I hope, Melantius.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: He hath lost himself
Much since his Daughter mist the happiness
My Sister gain'd; and though he call me Foe, I pity him.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Pity! a pox upon you.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Mark his disordered words, and at the Mask.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Diagoras knows he raged, and rail'd at me,
And cal'd a Lady Whore, so innocent
She understood him not; but it becomes
Both you and me too, to forgive distraction,
Pardon him as I do.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: I'le not speak for thee, for all thy cunning, if you will be safe chop off his head, for there was never known so impudent a Rascal.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Some that love him, get him to bed: Why, pity should not let age make it self contemptible; we must be all old, have him away.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Calianax, the King believes you; come, you shall go
Home, and rest; you ha' done well; you'l give it up
When I have us'd you thus a moneth I hope.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Now, now, 'tis plain Sir, he does move me still;
He sayes he knows I'le give him up the Fort,
When he had us'd me thus a moneth: I am mad,
Am I not still?

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
verse: Ha, ha, ha!

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I shall be mad indeed, if you do thus;
Why would you trust a sturdy fellow there
(That has no vertue in him, all's in his sword)
Before me? do but take his weapons from him,
And he's an Ass, and I am a very fool,
Both with him, and without him, as you use me.

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
verse: Ha, ha, ha!

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: 'Tis well Calianax; but if you use
This once again, I shall intreat some other
To see your Offices be well discharg'd.
Be merry Gentlemen, it grows somewhat late.
Amintor, thou wouldest be abed again.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Yes Sir.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Sleep soundly, it will bring thee to thy self.
prose: And you Evadne; let me take thee in my arms, Melantius, and believe thou art as thou deservest to be, my friend still, and for ever. Good Calianax,

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Sleep soundly! I sleep soundly now I hope,
I could not be thus else. How dar'st thou stay
Alone with me, knowing how thou hast used me?

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: You cannot blast me with your tongue,
And that's the strongest part you have about you.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I do look for some great punishment for this,
For I begin to forget all my hate,
And tak't unkindly that mine enemy
Should use me so extraordinarily scurvily.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: I shall melt too, if you begin to take
Unkindnesses: I never meant you hurt.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Thou'lt anger me again; thou wretched rogue,
Meant me no hurt! disgrace me with the King;
Lose all my Offices! this is no hurt.
Is it? I prethee what dost thou call hurt?

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: To poyson men because they love me not;
To call the credit of mens Wives in question;
To murder children betwixt me and land; this is all hurt.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: All this thou think'st is sport;
For mine is worse: but use thy will with me;
For betwixt grief and anger I could cry.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Be wise then, and be safe; thou may'st revenge.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I o'th'King? I would revenge of thee.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: That you must plot your self.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I am a fine plotter.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: The short is, I will hold thee with the King
In this perplexity, till peevishness
And thy disgrace have laid thee in thy grave:
But if thou wilt deliver up the Fort,
I'le take thy trembling body in my arms,
And bear thee over dangers; thou shalt hold thy wonted state.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: If I should tell the King, can'st thou deny't again?

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Try and believe.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Nay then, thou can'st bring any thing about:
Thou shalt have the Fort.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Why well, here let our hate be buried, and
This hand shall right us both; give me thy aged breast to compass.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Nay, I do not love thee yet
I cannot well endure to look on thee:
And if I thought it were a courtesie,
Thou should'st not have it: but I am disgrac'd;
My Offices are to be ta'ne away;
And if I did but hold this Fort a day,
I do believe the King would take it from me,
And give it thee, things are so strangely carried;
Nere thank me for't; but yet the King shall know
There was some such thing in't I told him of;
And that I was an honest man.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Hee'l buy that knowledge very dearly.
What news with thee?

speeches.speaker: Diph.
verse: This were a night indeed to do it in;
The King hath sent for her.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: She shall perform it then; go Diphilus,
And take from this good man, my worthy friend,
The Fort; he'l give it thee.

speeches.speaker: Diph.
verse: Ha' you got that?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Art thou of the same breed? canst thou deny
This to the King too?

speeches.speaker: Diph.
verse: With a confidence as great as his.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Faith, like enough.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Away, and use him kindly.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: Touch not me, I hate the whole strain: if thou follow me a great way off, I'le give thee up the Fort; and hang your selves.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Be gone.

speeches.speaker: Diph.
verse: He's finely wrought.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: This is a night in spite of Astronomers
To do the deed in; I will wash the slain
That tests upon our House, off with his blood.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Melantius, now assist me if thou beest
That which thou say'st, assist me: I have lost
All my distempers, and have found a rage so pleasing; help me.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Who can see him thus,
And not swear vengeance? what's the matter friend?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Out with thy sword; and hand in hand with me
Rush to the Chamber of this hated King,
And sink him with the weight of all his sins to hell for ever.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: 'Twere a ^ash attempt,
Not to be done with safety: let your reason
Plot your revenge, and not your passion.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: If thou refusest me in these extreams,
Thou art no friend: he sent for her to me;
By Heaven to me; my self; and I must tell ye
I love her as a stranger; there is worth
In that vile woman, worthy things, Melantius;
And she repents. I'le do't my self alone,
Though I be slain. Farewell.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: He'l overthrow my whole design with madness:
Amintor, think what thou doest; I dare as much as valour;
But 'tis the King, the King, the King, Amintor,
With whom thou fightest; I know he's honest,
And this will work with him.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: I cannot tell
What thou hast said; but thou hast charm'd my sword
Out of my hand, and left me shaking here defenceless.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: I will take it up for thee.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: What a wild beast is uncollected man!
The thing that we call Honour, bears us all
Headlong unto sin, and yet it self is nothing.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Alas, how variable are thy thoughts!

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Just like my fortunes: I was run to that
I purpos'd to have chid thee for.
Some Plot I did distrust thou hadst against the King
By that old fellows carriage: but take heed,
There is not the least limb growing to a King,
But carries thunder in it.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: I have none against him.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Why? come then, and still remember we may not think revenge.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: I will remember.

speeches.speaker: EVAD.
verse: Sir, is the King abed?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Madam, an hour ago.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Give me the key then, and let none be near;
'Tis the Kings pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: I understand you Madam, would 'twere mine.
I must not wish good rest unto your Ladiship.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: You talk, you talk.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: 'Tis all I dare do, Madam; but the King will wake, and then.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Saving your imagination, pray good night Sir.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: A good night be it then, and a long one Madam;
I am gone.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: The night grows horrible, and all about me
Like my black purpose: O the Conscience
Of a lost Virgin; whither wilt thou pull me?
To what things dismal, as the depth of Hell,
Wilt thou provoke me? Let no man dare
From this hour be disloyal: if her heart
Be flesh, if she have blood, and can fear, 'tis a daring
Above that desperate fool that left his peace,
And went to Sea to fight: 'tis so many sins
An age cannot prevent 'em: and so great,
The gods want mercy for: yet I must through 'em.
I have begun a slaughter on my honour,
And I must end it there: he sleeps, good heavens!
Why give you peace to this untemperate beast
That hath so long transgressed you? I must kill him,
And I will do't bravely: the meer joy
Tells me I merit in it: yet I must not
Thus tamely do it as he sleeps: that were
To rock him to another world: my vengeance
Shall take him waking, and then lay before him
The number of his wrongs and punishments.
I'le shake his sins like furies, till I waken
His evil Angel, his sick Conscience:
And then I'le strike him dead: King, by your leave:
I dare not trust your strength: your Grace and I
Must grapple upon even terms no more:
So, if he rail me not from my resolution,
I shall be strong enough.
My Lord the King, my Lord; he sleeps
As if he meant to wake no more, my Lord;
Is he not dead already? Sir, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Who's that?

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: O you sleep soundly Sir!

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: My dear Evadne,
I have been dreaming of thee; come to bed.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: I am come at length Sir, but how welcome?

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: What pretty new device is this Evadne?
What do you tie me to you by my love?
This is a quaint one: Come my dear and kiss me;
I'le be thy Mars to bed my Queen of Love:
Let us be caught together, that the Gods may see,
And envy our embraces.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Stay Sir, stay,
You are too hot, and I have brought you Physick
To temper your high veins.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Prethee to bed then; let me take it warm,
There you shall know the state of my body better.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: I know you have a surfeited soul body,
And you must bleed.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Bleed!

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: I, you shall bleed: lie still, and if the Devil,
Your lust will give you leave, repent: this steel
Comes to redeem the honour that you stole,
King, my fair name, which nothing but thy death
Can answer to the world.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: How's this Evadne?

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: I am not she: nor bear I in this breast
So much cold Spirit to be call'd a Woman:
I am a Tyger: I am any thing
That knows not pity: stir not, if thou dost,
I'le take thee unprepar'd; thy fears upon thee,
That make thy sins look double, and so send thee
(By my revenge I will) to look those torments
Prepar'd for such black souls.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Thou dost not mean this; 'tis impossible:
Thou art too sweet and gentle.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: No, I am not:
I am as foul as thou art, and can number
As many such hells here: I was once fair,
Once I was lovely, not a blowing Rose
More chastly sweet, till thou, thou, thou, soul Canker,
(Stir not) didst poyson me: I was a world of vertue,
Till your curst Court and you (hell bless you sor't)
With your temptations on temptations
Made me give up mine honour; for which (King)
I am come to kill thee.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: I am.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Thou art not.
I prethee speak not these things; thou art gentle,
And wert not meant thus rugged.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Peace and hear me.
Stir nothing but your tongue, and that for mercy
To those above us; by whose lights I vow,
Those blessed fires that shot to see our sin,
If thy hot soul had substance with thy blood,
I would kill that too, which being past my steel,
My tongue shall ^each: Thou art a shameless Villain,
A thing out of the overchange of Nature;
Sent like a thick cloud to disperse a plague
Upon weak catching women; such a tyrant
That for his Lust would sell away his Subjects,
I, all his heaven hereafter.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Hear Evadne,
Thou soul of sweetness! hear, I am thy King.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Thou art my shame; lie still, there's none about you,
Within your cries; all promises of safety
Are but deluding dreams: thus, thus, thou soul man,
Thus I begin my vengeance.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Hold Evadne!
I do command thee hold.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: I do not mean Sir,
To part so fairly with you; we must change
More of these love-tricks yet.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: What bloody villain
Provok't thee to this murther?

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Thou, thou monster.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Oh!

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Thou kept'st me brave at Court, and Whor'd me;
Then married me to a young noble Gentleman;
And Whor'd me still.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Evadne, pity me.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Hell take me then; this for my Lord Amintor;
This for my noble brother: and this stroke
For the most wrong'd of women.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Oh! I die.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Die all our faults together; I forgive thee.
Come now she's gone, let's enter, the King expects it, and will be angry.
'Tis a fine wench, we'l have a snap at her one of these nights as she goes from him.
Content: how quickly he had done with her! I see
Kings can do no more that way than other mortal people.
How fast he is! I cannot hear him breathe.
Either the Tapers give a feeble light, or he looks very pale.
And so he does, pray Heaven he be well.
Let's look: Alas! he's stiffe, wounded and dead:
Treason, Treason!
Run forth and call.
Treason, Treason!
This will be laid on us: who can believe
A Woman could do this?

speeches.speaker: Cleon.
verse: How now, where's the Traytor?
Fled, fled away; but there her woful act lies still.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Her act! a Woman!

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: Where's the body?
There.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: Farewel thou worthy man; there were two bonds
That tyed our loves, a Brother and a King;
The least of which might fetch a stood of tears:
But such the misery of greatness is,
They have no time to mourn; then pardon me.
Sirs, which way went she?

speeches.speaker: Strat.
verse: Never follow her,
For she alas! was but the instrument.
News is now brought in, that Melantius
Has got the Fort, and stands upon the wall;
And with a loud voice calls those few that pass
At this dead time of night, delivering
The innocent of this act.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: Gentlemen, I am your King.

speeches.speaker: Strat.
verse: We do acknowledge it.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: I would I were not: follow all; for this must have a sudden stop.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: If the dull people can believe I am arm'd,
Be constant Diphilus; now we have time,
Either to bring our banisht honours home,
Or create new ones in our ends.

speeches.speaker: Diph.
verse: I fear not;
My spirit lies not that way. Courage Calianax.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Would I had any, you should quickly know it.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Speak to the people; thou art eloquent.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: 'Tis a sin^ eloquence to come to the gallows;
You were born to be my end; the Devil take you.
Now must I hang for company; 'tis strange
I should be old, and neither wise nor valiant.

speeches.speaker: Lisip.
verse: See where he stands as boldly confident,
As if he had his full command about him.

speeches.speaker: Strat.
verse: He looks as if he had the beter cause; Sir,
^der your gracious pardon let me speak it;
^hough he be mighty-spirited and forward
To all great things; to all things of that danger
Worse men shake at the telling of; yet certainly
I do believe him noble, and this action
Rather pull'd on than sought; his mind was ever
As worthy as his hand.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: 'Tis my fear too;
Heaven forgive all: summon him Lord Cleon.

speeches.speaker: Cleon.
verse: Ho from the walls there.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Worthy Cleon, welcome;
We could have wisht you here Lord; you are honest.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: Well, thou art as flattering a knave, though I dare not tell you so.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: Melantius!

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: I am sorry that we meet thus; our old love
Never requir'd such distance; pray Heaven
You have not left your self, and sought this safety
More out of fear than honour; you have lost
A noble Master, which your faith Melantius,
Some think might have preserv'd; yet you know best.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: When time was I was mad; some that dares
Fight I hope will pay this Rascal.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Royal young man, whose tears look lovely on thee;
Had they been shed for a deserving one,
They had been lasting monuments. Thy Brother,
Whil'st he was good, I call'd him King, and serv'd him
With that strong faith, that most unwearied valour;
Pul'd people from the farthest Sun to seek him;
And by his friendship, I was then his souldier;
But since his hot pride drew him to disgrace me,
And brand my noble actions with his lust,
(That never cur'd dishonour of my Sister,
Base stain of Whore; and which is worse,
The joy to make it still so) like my self;
Thus have I slung him off with my allegiance,
And stand here mine own justice to revenge
What I have suffered in him; and this old man
Wrong'd almost to lunacy.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Who I? you'd draw me in: I have had no wrong,
I do disclaim ye all.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: The short is this;
'Tis no ambition to lift up my self,
Urgeth me thus; I do desire again
To be a subject, so I may be freed;
If not, I know my strength, and will unbuild
This goodly Town; be speedy, and be wise, in a reply.

speeches.speaker: Strat.
verse: Be sudden Sir to tie
All again; what's done is past recal,
And past you to revenge; and there are thousands
That wait for such a troubled hour as this;
Throw him the blank.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: Melantius, write in that thy choice,
My Seal is at it.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: It was our honour drew us to this act,
Not gain; and we will only work our pardon.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Put my name in too.

speeches.speaker: Diph.
verse: You disclaim'd us but now, Calianax.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: That's all one;
I'le not be hanged hereafter by a trick;
I'le have it in.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: You shall, you shall;
Come to the back gate, and we'l call you King,
And give you up the Fort.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: Away, away.

speeches.speaker: Asp.
verse: This is my fatal hour; heaven may forgive
My ^ash attempt, that causelesly hath laid
Griefs on me that will never let me rest:
And put a Womans heart into my brest;
It is more honour for you that I die;
For she that can endure the misery
That I have on me, and be patient too,
May live, and laugh at all that you can do.
God save you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: And you Sir; what's your business?

speeches.speaker: Asp.
verse: With you Sir now, to do me the Office
To help me to you Lord.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: What, would you serve him?

speeches.speaker: Asp.
verse: I'le do him any service; but to haste,
For my affairs are earnest, I desire to speak with him.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Sir, because you are in such haste, I would be loth delay you any longer: you cannot.

speeches.speaker: Asp.
verse: It shall become you tho' to tell your Lord.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Sir, he will speak with no body.

speeches.speaker: Asp.
prose: This is most strange: art thou gold proof? there's for thee; help me to him.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Pray be not angry Sir, I'le do my best.

speeches.speaker: Asp.
verse: How stubbornly this fellow answer'd me!
There is a vile dishonest trick in man,
More than in women: all the men I meet
Appear thus to me, are harsh and rude,
And have a subtilty in every thing,
Which love could never know; but we fond women
Harbor the easiest and smoothest thoughts,
And think all shall go so; it is unjust
That men and women should be matcht together.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Where is he!

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: There my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: What would you Sir?

speeches.speaker: Asp.
verse: Please it your Lordship to command your man
Out of the room; I shall deliver things
Worthy your hearing.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Leave us.

speeches.speaker: Asp.
verse: O that that shape should bury falshood in it.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Now your will Sir.

speeches.speaker: Asp.
verse: When you know me, my Lord, you needs must guess
My business! and I am not hard to know;
For till the change of War mark'd this smooth face
With these few blemishes, people would call me
My Sisters Picture, and her mine; in short,
I am the brother to the wrong'd Aspatia.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: The wrong'd Aspatia! would thou wert so too
Unto the wrong'd Amintor; let me kiss
That hand of thine in honour that I bear
Unto the wrong'd Aspatia: here I stand
That did it; would he could not; gentle youth,
Leave me, for there is something in thy looks
That calls my sins in a most hideous form
Into my mind; and I have grief enough
Without thy help.

speeches.speaker: Asp.
verse: I would I could with credit:
Since I was twelve years old I had not seen
My Sister till this hour; I now arriv'd;
She sent for me to see her Marriage,
A wosul one: but they that are above,
Have ends in every thing; she us'd few words,
But yet enough to make me understand
The baseness of the injury you did her;
That little training I have had, is War;
I may behave my self rudely in Peace;
I would not though; I shall not need to tell you
I am but young; and you would be loth to lose
Honour that is not easily gain'd again;
Fairly I mean to deal; the age is strict
For single combats, and we shall be stopt
If it be publish't: if you like your sword,
Use it; if mine appear a better to you,
Change; for the ground is this, and this the time
To end our difference.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Charitable youth,
If thou be'st such, think not I will maintain
So strange a wrong; and for thy Sisters sake,
Know that I could not think that desperate thing
^ durst not do; yet to enjoy this world
^ would not see her; for beholding thee,
^ am I know not what; if I have ought
^hat may content thee, take it and be gone;
For death is not so terrible as thou;
Thine eyes shoot guilt into me.

speeches.speaker: Asp.
verse: Thus she swore
Thou would'st behave thy self, and give me words
That would fetch tears into mine eyes, and so
Thou dost indeed; but yet she bade me watch,
Lest I were corsen'd, and be sure to sight ere I return'd.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: That must not be with me;
For her I'le die directly, but against her will never hazard it.

speeches.speaker: Asp.
verse: You must be urg'd; I do not deal uncivilly with those that
Dare to fight; but such a one as you
Must be us'd thus.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Prethee youth take heed;
Thy Sister is a thing to me so much
Above mine honour, that I can endute
All this; good gods— a blow I can endure;
But stay not, lest thou draw a timely death upon thy self.

speeches.speaker: Asp.
verse: Thou art some prating fellow,
One that hath studyed out a trick to talk
And move soft-hearted people; to be kickt,
Thus to be kickt— why should he be so slow
In giving me my death?

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: A man can bear
No more and keep his flesh; forgive me then;
I would endure yet if I could; now shew
The spirit thou pretendest, and understand
Thou hast no honour to live:
What dost thou mean? thou canst not fight:
The blows thou mak'st at me are quite besides;
And those I offer at thee, thou spread'st thine arms,
And tak'st upon thy breast, Alas! defenceless.

speeches.speaker: Asp.
verse: I have got enough,
And my desire; there's no place so fit for me to die as here.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Amintor; I am loaden with events
That flie to make thee happy; I have joyes
That in a moment can call back thy wrongs,
And settle thee in thy free state again;
It is Evadne still that follows thee, but not her mischiefs.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Thou canst not fool me to believe agen;
But thou hast looks and things so full of news that I am staid.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Noble Amintor, put off thy amaze;
Let thine eyes loose, and speak, am I not fair?
Looks not Evadne beauteous with these rites now?
Were those hours half so lovely in thine eyes,
When our hands met before the holy man?
I was too foul within to look fair then;
Since I knew ill, I was not free till now.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: There is presage of some important thing
About thee, which it seems thy tongue hath lost:
Thy hands are bloody, and thou hast a knife.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: In this consists thy happiness and mine;
Joy to Amintor, for the King is dead.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Those have most power to hurt us that we love,
We lay our sleeping lives within their arms.
Why thou hast rais'd up mischief to this height,
And found out one to out-name thy other faults;
Thou hast no intermission of thy sins,
But all thy life is a continuall ill;
Black is thy colour now, disease thy nature.
Joy to Amintor! thou hast touch't a life,
The very name of which had power to chain
Up all my rage, and calm my wildest wrongs.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: 'Tis done; and since I could not find a way
To meet thy love so clear, as through his life,
I cannot now repent it.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Could'st thou procure the Gods to speak to me,
To bid me love this woman, and forgive,
I think I should fall out with them; behold
Here lies a youth whose wounds bleed in my brest,
Sent by his violent Fate to fetch his death
From my slow hand: and to augment my woe,
You now are present stain'd with a Kings blood
Violently shed: this keeps night here,
And throws an unknown wilderness about me.

speeches.speaker: Asp.
verse: Oh, oh, oh!

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: No more, pursue me not.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Forgive me then, and take me to thy bed.
We may not part.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Forbear, be wise, and let my rage go this way.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: 'Tis you that I would stay, not it.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Take heed, it will return with me.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: If it must be, I shall not fear to meet it; take me home.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Thou monster of cruelty, forbear.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: For heavens sake look more calm;
Thine eyes are sharper than thou canst m^ thy sword.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Away, away, thy knees are more to me than violence.
I am worse than sick to see knees follow me
For that I must not grant; for heavens sake stand.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Receive me then.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: I dare not stay thy language;
In midst of all my anger and my grief,
Thou dost awake something that troubles me,
And sayes I lov'd thee once; I dare not stay;
There is no end of womens reasoning.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Amintor, thou shalt love me once again;
Go, I am calm; farewell; and peace for ever.
Evadne whom thou hat'st will die for thee.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: I have a little humane nature yet
That's lest for thee, that bids me stay thy hand.

speeches.speaker: Evad.
verse: Thy hand was welcome, but came too late;
Oh I am lost! the heavy sleep makes haste.

speeches.speaker: Asp.
verse: Oh, oh, oh!

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: This earth of mine doth tremble, and I feel
A stark affrighted motion in my blood;
My soul grows weary of her house, and I
All over am a trouble to my self;
There is some hidden power in these dead things
That calls my flesh into'em; I am cold;
Be resolute, and bear'em company:
There's something yet which I am loth to leave.
There's man enough in me to meet the fears
That death can bring, and yet would it were done;
I can find nothing in the whole discourse
Of death, I durst not meet the boldest way;
Yet still betwixt the reason and the act,
The wrong I to Aspatia did stands up,
I have not such a fault to answer,
Though she may justly arm with scorn
And hate of me, my soul will part less troubled,
When I have paid to her in tears my sorrow:
I will not leave this act unsatisfied,
If all that's left in me can answer it.

speeches.speaker: Asp.
verse: Was it a dream? there stands Amintor still:
Or I dream still.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: How dost thou? speak, receive my love, and help:
Thy blood climbs up to his old place again:
There's hope of thy recovery.

speeches.speaker: Asp.
verse: Did you not name Aspatia?

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: I did.

speeches.speaker: Asp.
verse: And talkt of tears and sorrow unto her?

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: 'Tis true, and till these happy signs in thee
Did stay my course, 'twas thither I was going.

speeches.speaker: Asp.
verse: Th'art there already, and these wounds are hers:
Those threats I brought with me, sought not revenge,
But came to fetch this blessing from thy hand, I am Aspatia yet.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Dare my soul ever look abroad agen?

speeches.speaker: Asp.
verse: I shall live Amintor; I am well:
A kind of healthful joy wanders within me.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: The world wants lines to excuse thy loss:
Come let me bear thee to some place of help.

speeches.speaker: Asp.
verse: Amintor thou must stay, I must rest here,
My strength begins to disobey my will.
How dost thou my best soul? I would fain live,
Now if I could: would'st thou have loved me then?

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Alas! all that I am's not worth a hair from thee.

speeches.speaker: Asp.
verse: Give me thy hand, mine hands grope up and down,
And cannot find thee; I am wondrous sick:
Have I thy hand Amintor?

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Thou greatest blessing of the world, thou hast.

speeches.speaker: Asp.
verse: I do believe thee better than my sense.
Oh! I must go, farewell.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: She swounds: Aspatia help, for Heavens sake water;
Such as may chain life for ever to this frame.
Aspatia, speak: what no help? yet I fool,
I'le chase her temples, yet there's nothing stirs;
Some hidden Power tell her that Amintor calls,
A^ let her answer me: Aspatia, speak.
I ha^e heard, if there be life, but bow
The body thus, and it will shew it self.
Oh she is gone! I will not leave her yet.
Since out of justice we must challenge nothing;
I'le call it mercy if you'l pity me,
You heavenly powers, and lend for some few years,
The blessed soul to this fair seat agen.
No comfort comes, the gods deny me too.
I'le bow the body once agen: Aspatia!
The soul is fled for ever, and I wrong
My self, so long to lose her company.
Must I talk now? Here's to be with thee love.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: This is a great grace to my Lord, to have the new King come to him; I must tell him, he is entring. O Heaven help, help;

speeches.speaker: Lys.
verse: Where's Amintor?

speeches.speaker: Sirat.
verse: O there, there.

speeches.speaker: Lys.
verse: How strange is this!

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: What should we do here?

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: These deaths are such acquainted things with me,
That yet my heart dissolves not. May I stand
Stiff here for ever; eyes, call up your tears;
This is Amintor: heart he was my friend;
Melt, now it flows; Amintor, give a word
To call me to thee.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Oh!

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Melantius calls his friend Amintor; Oh thy arms
Are kinder to me than thy tongue;
Speak, speak.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: What?

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: That little word was worth all the sounds
That ever I shall hear agen.

speeches.speaker: Diph.
verse: O brother! here lies your Sister slain,
You lose your self in sorrow there.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Why Diphilus, it is
A thing to laugh at in respect of this;
Here was my Sister, Father, Brother, Son;
All that I had; speak once again;
What youth lies slain there by thee?

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: 'Tis Aspatia.
My senses fade, let me give up my soul
Into thy bosom.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: What's that? what's that? Aspatia!

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: I never did repent the greatness of my heart till now,
It will not burst at need.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: My daughter dead here too! and you have all fine new tricks to grieve, but I ne're knew any but direct crying.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: I am a pratler, but no more.

speeches.speaker: Diph.
verse: Hold Brother.

speeches.speaker: Lysip.
verse: Stop him.

speeches.speaker: Diph.
verse: Fie; how unmanly was this offer in you!
Does this become our strain?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I know not what the mater is, but I am
Grown very kind, and am friends with you;
You have given me that among you will kill me
Quickly; but I'le go home, and live as long as I can.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: His spirit is but poor that can be kept
From death for want of weapons.
Is not my hand a weapon good enough
To stop my breath? or if you tie down those,
I vow Amintor I will never eat,
Or drink, or sleep, or have to do with that
That may preserve life; this I swear to keep.

speeches.speaker: Lysip.
verse: Look to him tho', and bear those bodies in.
May this a fair example be to me,
To rule with temper: for on lustful Kings
Unlookt for sudden deaths from heaven are sent!
But curst is he that is their instrument.

plays.play_title: PHILASTER OR, Love lies a Bleeding.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
prose: HEre's not Lords nor Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Dion.
prose: Credit me Gentlemen, I wonder at it. They receiv'd strict charge from the King to attend here: Besides it was boldly published, that no Officer should forbid any Gentlemen that desire to attend and hear.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
prose: Can you ghess the cause?

speeches.speaker: Di.
prose: Sir, it is plain about the Spanish Prince, that's come to marry our Kingdoms Heir, and be our Soveraign.

speeches.speaker: Thra.
prose: Many (that will seem to know much) say, she looks not on him like a Maid in Love.

speeches.speaker: Di.
prose: O Sir, the multitude (that seldom know any thing but their own opinions) speak that they would have; but the Prince, before his own approach, receiv'd so many confident messages from the State, that I think she's resolv'd to be rul'd.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
prose: Sir, it is thought, with her he shall enjoy both these Kingdoms of Cicilie and Calabria.

speeches.speaker: Di.
prose: Sir, it is (without controversie) so meant. But 'twill be a troublesome labour for him to enjoy both these Kingdoms, with safetie, the right Heir to one of them living, and living so vertuously, especially the people admiring the bravery of his mind, and lamenting his injuries.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
prose: Who, Philaster?

speeches.speaker: Di.
prose: Yes, whose Father we all know, was by our late King of Calabria, unrighteously deposed from his fruitful Cicilie. My self drew some blood in those Wars, which I would give my hand to be washed from.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
prose: Sir, my ignorance in State-policy, will not let me know why Philaster being Heir to one of these Kingdoms, the King should suffer him to walk abroad with such free liberty.

speeches.speaker: Di.
prose: Sir, it seems your nature is more constant than to enquire after State news. But the King (of late) made a hazard of both the Kingdoms, of Cicilie and his own, with offering but to imprison Philaster. At which the City was in arms, not to be charm'd down by any State order or Proclamation, till they saw Philaster ride through the streets pleas'd, and without a guard; at which they threw their Hats, and their arms from them; some to make bonefires, some to drink, all for his deliverance. Which (wise men say) is the cause, the King labours to bring in the power of a Foreign Nation, to aw his own with.

speeches.speaker: Thra.
prose: See, the Ladies, what's the first?

speeches.speaker: Di.
prose: A wife and modest Gentlwoman that attends the Princess.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
prose: The second?

speeches.speaker: Di.
prose: She is one that may stand still discreetly enough, and ill savour'dly Dance her Measure; simper when she is Courted by her Friend, and slight her Husband.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
prose: The last?

speeches.speaker: Di.
prose: Marry I think she is one whom the State keeps for the Agents of our confederate Princes: she'll cog and lie with a whole Army before the League shall break: her name is common through the Kingdom, and the Trophies of her dishonour, advanced beyond Hercules-pillars. She loves to try the several constitutions of mens bodies; and indeed has destroyed the worth of her own body, by making experiment upon it, for the good of the Common-wealth.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
prose: She's a profitable member.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Peace, if you love me: you shall see these Gentlemen stand their ground, and not Court us.

speeches.speaker: Gal.
prose: What if they should?

speeches.speaker: Meg.
prose: What if they should?

speeches.speaker: La.
prose:
Nay, let her alone; what if they should? why, if they should, I say, they were never abroad: what Foreigner
would do so? it writes them directly untravel'd.

speeches.speaker: Gal.
prose: Why, what if they be?

speeches.speaker: Meg.
prose: What if they be?

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Good Madam let her go on; what if they be? Why if they be I will justifie, they cannot maintain discourse with a judicious Lady, nor make a Leg, nor say Excuse me.

speeches.speaker: Gal.
prose: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Do you laugh Madam?

speeches.speaker: Di.
prose: Your desires upon you Ladies.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Then you must sit beside us.

speeches.speaker: Di.
prose: I shall sit near you then Lady.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Near me perhaps: But there's a Lady indures no stranger; and to me you appear a very strange fellow.

speeches.speaker: Meg.
prose: Me thinks he's not so strange, he would quickly be acquainted.

speeches.speaker: Thra.
prose: Peace, the King.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: To give a stranger testimony of love
Than fickly promises (which commonly
In Princes find both birth and burial
In one breath) we have drawn you worthy Sir,
To make your lair indearments to your daughter,
And worthy services known to our subjects,
Now lov'd and wondered at. Next, our intent,
To plant you deeply, our immediate Heir,
Both to our Blood and Kingdoms. For this Lady,
(The best part of your life, as you confirm me,
And I believe) though her few years and sex
Yet teach her nothing but her fears and blushes,
Desires without desire, discourse and knowledge
Only of what her sell is to her sell,
Make her feel moderate health: and when she sleeps,
In making no ill day, knows no ill dreams.
Think not (dear Sir) these undivided parts,
That must mould up a Virgin, are put on
To shew her so, as borrowed ornaments,
To speak her perfect love to you, or add
An Artificial shadow to her nature:
No Sir; I boldly dare proclaim her, yet
No Woman. But woo her still, and think her modesty
A sweeter mistress than the offer'd Language
Of any Dame, were she a Queen whose eye
Speaks common loves and comforts to her servants.
Last, noble son, (for so I now must call you)
What I have done thus publick, is not only
To add a comfort in particular
To you or me, but all; and to confirm
The Nobles, and the Gentry of these Kingdoms,
By oath to your succession, which shall be
Within this month at most.

speeches.speaker: Thra.
verse: This will be hardly done.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: It must be ill done, if it be done.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: When 'tis at best, 't will be but half done,
Whilst so brave a Gentleman's wrong'd and stung off.

speeches.speaker: Thra.
verse: I fear.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Who does not?

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: I fear not for my self, and yet I fear too:
Well, we shall see, we shall see: no more.

speeches.speaker: Pha.
verse: Kissing your white hand (Mistress) I take leave,
To thank your Royal Father: and thus far,
To be my own free Trumpet. Understand
Great King, and these your subjects, mine that must be,
(For so deserving you have spoke me Sir,
And so deserving I da^e speak my self)
To what a person, of what eminence,
Ripe expectation of what faculties,
Manners and vertues you would wed your Kingdoms?
You in me have your wishes. Oh this Country,
By more than all my hopes I hold it
Happy, in their dear memories that have been
Kings great and good, happy in yours, that is,
And from you (as a Chronicle to keep
Your Noble name from eating age) do I
Opine my self most happy. Gentlemen,
Believe me in a word, a Princes word,
There shall be nothing to make up a Kingdom
Mighty, and flourishing, defenced, fear'd,
Equall to be commanded and obey'd,
But through the travels of my life I'le find it,
And tye it to this Country. And I vow
My reign shall be so easie to the subject,
That every man shall be his Prince himself,
And his own law (yet I his Prince and law.)
And dearest Lady, to your dearest self
(Dear, in the choice of him, whose name and lustre
Must make you more and mightier) let me say,
You are the blessed'st living; for sweet Princess,
You shall enjoy a man of men, to be
Your servant; you shall make him yours, for whom
Great Queens must die.

speeches.speaker: Thra.
verse: Miraculous.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: This speech calls him Spaniard, being nothing but
A large inventory of his own commendations.

speeches.speaker: Di.
prose: I wonder what's his price? For certainly he'll tell himself he has so prais'd his shape: But here comes one more worthy those large speeches, than the large speaker of them? let me be swallowed quick, if I can find, in all the Anatomy of yon mans vertues, one sinew sound enough to promise for him, he shall be Constable. By this Sun, he'll ne're make King unless it be for trifles, in my poor judgment.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Right Noble Sir, as low as my obedience,
And with a heart as Loyal as my knee,
I beg your favour.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Rise, you have it Sir.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Mark but the King how pale he looks with fear.
Oh! this same whorson Conscience, how it jades us!

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Speak your intents Sir.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Shall I speak 'um freely?
Be still my royal Soveraign.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: As a subject
We give you freedom.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Now it heats.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Then thus I turn
My language to you Prince, you foreign man.
Ne're stare nor put on wonder, for you must
Indure me, and you shall. This earth you tread upon
(A dowry as you hope with this fair Princess,
Whose memory I bow to) was not left
By my dead Father (Oh, I had a Father)
To your inheritance, and I up and living,
Having my self about me and my sword,
The souls of all my name, and memories,
These arms and some few friends, besides the gods,
To part so calmly with it, and sit still,
And say I might have been! I tell thee Pharamond,
When thou art King, look I be dead and rotten,
And my name ashes; For, hear me Pharamond,
This very ground thou goest on, this fat earth,
My Fathers friends made fertile with their faiths,
Before that day of shame, shall gape and swallow
Thee and thy Nation, like a hungry grave,
Into her hidden bowels: Prince, it shall;
By Nemesis it shall.

speeches.speaker: Pha.
verse: He's mad beyond cure, mad.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Here's a fellow has some fire in's veins:
The outlandish Prince looks like a Tooth drawer.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Sir, Prince of Popping jayes, I'le make it well appear
To you I am not mad.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: You displease us.
You are too bold.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: No Sir, I am too tame,
Too much a Turtle, a thing born without passion,
A faint shadow, that every drunken cloud sails over,
And makes nothing.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: I do not fancy this,
Call our Physicians: sure he is somewhat tainted.

speeches.speaker: Thra.
verse: I do not think 'twill prove so.

speeches.speaker: Di.
prose: H'as given him a general purge already, for all the right he has, and now he means to let him blood: Be constant Gentlemen; by these hilts I'le run his hazard, although I run my name out of the Kingdom.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Peace, we are one soul.

speeches.speaker: Pha.
verse: What you have seen in me, to stir offence,
I cannot find, unless it be this Lady
Offer'd into mine arms, with the succession,
Which I must keep though it hath pleas'd your fury
To mutiny within you; without disputing
Your Genealogies, or taking knowledge
Whose branch you are. The King will leave it me;
And I dare make it mine; you have your answer.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: If thou wert sole inheritor to him,
That made the world his; and couldst see no sun
Shine upon any but thine: were Pharamond
As truly valiant, as I feel him cold,
And ring'd among the choicest of his friends,
Such as would blush to talk such serious follies,
Or back such bellied commendations,
And from this present, spight of all these bugs,
You should hear further from me.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Sir, you wrong the Prince:
I gave you not this freedom to brave our best friends,
You deserve our frown: go to, be better temper'd.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: It must be Sir, when I am nobler us'd.

speeches.speaker: Gal.
verse: Ladyes,
This would have been a pattern of succession,
Had he ne're met this mischief. By my life,
He is the worthiest the true name of man
This day within my knowledge.

speeches.speaker: Meg.
verse: I cannot tell what you may call your knowledge,
But the other is the man set in mine eye;
Oh! 'tis a Prince of wax.

speeches.speaker: Gal.
verse: A Dog it is.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Philaster, tell me,
The injuries you aim at in your riddles.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: If you had my eyes Sir, and sufferance,
My griefs upon you and my broken fortunes,
My want's great, and now nought but hopes and fears,
My wrongs would make ill riddles to be laught at.
Dare you be still my King and right me not?

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Give me your wrongs in private.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Take them, and ease me of a load would bow strong

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: He dares not stand the shock.

speeches.speaker: Di.
prose: I cannot blame him, there's danger in't. Every man in this age, has not a soul of Crystal for all men to read their actions through: mens hearts and faces are so far asunder, that they hold no intelligence. Do but view yon stranger well, and you shall see a Feaver through all his bravery, and feel him shake like a true Tenant; if he give not back his Crown again, upon the report of an Elder Gun, I have no augury.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Go to:
Be more your self, as you respect our favour:
You'l stir us else: Sir, I must have you know
That y'are and shall be at our pleasure, what fashion we
Will put upon you: smooth your brow, or by the gods.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: I am dead Sir, y'are my fate: it was not I
Said I was ^ wrong'd: I carry all about me,
My weak stars led me to all my weak fortunes.
Who dares in all this presence speak (that is
But man of flesh and may be mortal) tell me
I do not most intirely love this Prince,
And honour his full vertues!

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Sure he's possest.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Yes, with my Fathers spirit: It's here O King!
A dangerous spirit; now he tells me King,
I was a Kings heir, bids me be a King,
And whispers to me, these be all my Subjects.
'Tis strange, he will not let me sleep, but dives
Into my fancy, and there gives me shapes
That kneel, and do me service, cry me King:
But I'le suppress him, he's a factious spirit,
And will undo me: noble Sir, ^our hand, I am your servant.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Away, I do not like this:
I'le make you tamer, or I'le dispossess you
Both of life and spirit: For this time
I pardon your wild speech, without so much
As your imprisonment.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: I thank you Sir, you dare not for the people.

speeches.speaker: Gal.
verse: Ladies, what think you now of this brave fellow?

speeches.speaker: Meg.
prose: A pretty talking fellow, hot at hand; but eye yon stranger, is not he a fine compleat Gentleman? O these strangers, I do affect them strangely: they do the rarest home things, and please the fullest! as I live, could love all the Nation over and over for his sake,

speeches.speaker: Gal.
prose: Pride comfort your poor head-piece Lady: 'tis a weak one, and had need of a Night-cap.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: See how his fancy labours, has he not spoke
Home, and bravely? what a dangerous train
Did he give fire to! How he shook the King,
Made his soul melt within him, and his blood
Run into whay! it stood upon his brow,
Like a cold winter dew.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Gentlemen,
You have no suit to me? I am no minion:
You stand (methinks) like men that would be Courtiers,
If you could well be flatter'd at a price,
Not to undo your Children: y'are all honest:
Go get you home again, and make your Country
A vertuous Court, to which your great ones may,
In their Diseased age, retire, and live recluse.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: How do you worthy Sir?

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Well, very well;
And so well, that if the King please, I find
I may live many years.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: The King must please,
Whilst we know what you are, and who you are,
Your wrongs and juiuries: shrink not, worthy Sir,
But add your Father to you: in whose name,
We'll waken all the gods, and conjure up
The rods of vengeance, the abused people,
Who like to raging torrents shall swell high,
And so begirt the dens of these Male-dragons,
That through the strongest safety, they shall beg
For mercy at your swords point.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Friends, no more,
Our years may be corrupted: 'Tis an age
We dare not trust our wills to: do you love me?

speeches.speaker: Thra.
verse: Do we love Heaven and honour?

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: My Lord Dion, you had
A vertuous Gentlewoman, call'd you Father;
Is she yet alive?

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Most honour'd Sir, she is:
And for the penance but of an idle dream,
Has undertook a tedious Pilgrimage.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Is it to me, or any of these Gentlemen you come?

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: To you, brave Lord; the Princess would intreat
Your present company.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: The Princess send for me! y'are mistaken.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: If you be call'd Philaster, 'tis to you.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Kiss her hand, and say I will attend her.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Do you know what you do?

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Yes, go to see a woman.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: But do you weigh the danger you are in?

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Danger in a sweet face?
By Jupiter I must not fear a woman.

speeches.speaker: Thra.
verse: But are you sure it was the Princess sent?
It may be some soul train to catch your life.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: I do not think it Gentlemen: she's noble,
Her eye may shoot me dead, or those true red
And white friends in her face may steal my soul out:
There's all the danger in't: but be what may,
Her single name hath arm'd me.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Go on:
And be as truly happy as thou art fearless:
Come Gentlemen, let's make our friends acquainted,
Lest the King prove false.

speeches.speaker: Are.
verse: Comes he not?

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Madam?

speeches.speaker: Are.
verse: Will Philaster come?

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Dear Madam, you were wont
To credit me at first.

speeches.speaker: Are.
verse: But didst thou tell me so?
I am forgetful, and my womans strength
Is so o'recharg'd with danger like to grow
About my Marriage that these under-things
Dare not abide in such a troubled sea:
How look't he, when he told thee he would come?

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Why, well.

speeches.speaker: Are.
verse: And not a little fearful?

speeches.speaker: Lat.
verse: Fear Madam? sure he knows not what it is.

speeches.speaker: Are.
verse: You are all of his Faction; the whole Court
Is bold in praise of him, whilst I
May live neglected: and do noble things,
As fools in strife throw gold into the Sea,
Drown'd in the doing: but I know he fears.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Fear? Madam (me thought) his looks hid more
Of love than fear.

speeches.speaker: Are.
verse: Of love? To whom? to you?
Did you deliver those plain words I sent,
With such a winning gesture, and quick look
That you have caught him?

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Madam, I mean to you.

speeches.speaker: Arc.
verse: Of love to me? Alas! thy ignorance
Lets thee not see the crosses of our births:
Nature, that loves not to be questioned
Why she did this, or that, but has her ends,
And knows she does well; never gave the world
Two things so opposite, so contrary,
As he and I am: If a bowl of blood
Drawn from this arm of mine, would poyson thee,
