verse: Stay Sir, what are you?

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: A wretched creature wounded in these Woods
By Beasts; relieve me, if your names be men,
Or I shall perish.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: This is he my Lord,
Upon my soul that hurt her; 'tis the boy,
That wicked boy that serv'd her.

speeches.speaker: Pha.
verse: O thou damn'd in thy creation!
What cause could'st thou shape to hurt the Princess?

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: Then I am betrayed.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Betrayed! no, apprehended.

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: I confess;
Urge it no more, that big with evil thoughts
I set upon her, and did take my aim
Her death. For charity let fall at once
The punishment you mean, and do not load
This weary flesh with tortures.

speeches.speaker: Pha.
verse: I will know who hir'd thee to this deed?

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: Mine own revenge.

speeches.speaker: Pha.
verse: Revenge, for what?

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: It pleas'd her to receive
Me as her Page, and when my fortunes ebb'd,
That men strid o're them carelesly, she did showr
Her welcome graces on me, and did swell
My fortunes, till they overflow'd their banks,
Threatning the men that crost 'em; when as swift
As storms arise at sea, she turn'd her eyes
To burning Suns upon me, and did dry
The streams she had bestowed, leaving me worse
And more contemn'd than other little brooks,
Because I had been great: In short, I knew
I could not live, and therefore did desire
To die reveng'd.

speeches.speaker: Pha.
verse: If tortures can be found,
Long as thy natural life, resolve to feel
The utmost rigour.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Help to lead him hence.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Turn back you ravishers of Innocence,
Know ye the price of that you bear away so rudely?

speeches.speaker: Pha.
verse: Who's that?

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: 'Tis the Lord Philaster.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: 'Tis not the treasure of all Kings in one,
The wealth of Tagus, nor the Rocks of Pearl,
That pave the Court of Neptune, can weigh down
That vertue. It was I that hurt the Princess.
Place me, some god, upon a Piramis,
Higher than hills of earth, and lend a voice
Loud as your Thunder to me, that from thence,
I may discourse to all the under-world,
The worth that dwells in him.

speeches.speaker: Pha.
verse: How's this?

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: My Lord, some man
Weary of life, that would be glad to die.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Leave these untimely courtesies Bellario.

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: Alas he's mad, come will you lead me on?

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: By all the Oaths that men ought most to keep:
And Gods do punish most, when men do break,
He toucht her not. Take heed Bellario,
How thou dost drown the vertues thou hast shown
With perjury. By all that's good 'twas I:
You know she stood betwixt me and my right.

speeches.speaker: Pha.
verse: Thy own tongue be thy judge.

speeches.speaker: Cle
verse: It was Philaster.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Is 't not a brave boy?
Well Sirs, I fear we were all deceived.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Have I no friend here?

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Then shew it;
Some good body lend a hand to draw us nearer.
Would you have tears shed for you when you die^
Then lay me gentle on his neck that there
I may weep flouds, and breath out my spirit:
'Tis not the wealth of Plutus, nor the gold
Lockt in the heart of earth, can buy away
This arm-full from me, this had been a rans^m
To have redeem'd the great Augustus C^sar,
Had he been taken: you hard-hearted men,
More stony than these Mountains, can you see
Such clear pure bloud drop, and not cut your flesh
To stop his life? To bind whose better woun^s,
Queens ought to tear their hair, and with their tears,
Bath'em. Forgive me, thou that art the wealth of poor Phi. laster.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Is the villain ta'ne?

speeches.speaker: Pha.
verse: Sir, here be two confess the deed, but say it was Phi. laster.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Question it no more, it was.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: The fellow that did fight with him will tell us.

speeches.speaker: Are.
verse: Ay me, I know he will.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Did not you know him?

speeches.speaker: Are.
verse: Sir, if it was he, he was disguised.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: I was so. Oh my s^ars! that I should live still.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Thou ambitious fool;
Thou that hast laid a train for thy own life;
Now I do mean to do, I'le leave to talk, bear him to prison

speeches.speaker: Are.
verse: Sir, they did plot together to take hence
This harmless life; should it pass unreveng'd,
I should to earth go weeping: grant me then
(By all the love a Father bears his Child)
Their custodies, and that I may appoint
Their tortures and their death.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Death? soft, our Law will not reach that, for this fault.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: 'Tis granted, take 'em to you, with a Guard.
Come Princely Pharamond, this business past,
We may with more security go on to your intended match.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
prose: I pray that this action lose not Philaster the hearts of the people.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Fear it not, their overwise heads will think it but a trick.

speeches.speaker: Thra.
verse: HAS the King sent for him to death?

speeches.speaker: Di.
prose: Yes, but the King must know, 'tis not in his power to war with Heaven.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: We linger time; the King sent for Philaster and the Headsman an hour ago.

speeches.speaker: Thra.
verse: Are all his wounds well?

speeches.speaker: Di.
prose: All they were but scratches; but the loss of bloud made him faint.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: We dally Gentlem^n.

speeches.speaker: Thra.
verse: Away.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: We'l scuffle hard before he perish.

speeches.speaker: Are.
verse: Nay dear Philaster grieve not, we are well.

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: Nay good my Lord forbear, we are wondrous well.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Oh Arethusa! O Bellario! leave to be kind:
I shall be shot from Heaven, as now from Earth,
If you continue so; I am a man,
False to a pair of the most trusly ones
That ever earth bore, can it bear us all?
Forgive and leave me, but the King hath sent
To call me to my death, Oh shew it me,
And then forget me: And for thee my boy,
I shall deliver words will mollifie
The hearts of beasts, to spare thy innocence.

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: Alas my Lord, my life is not a thing
Worthy your noble thoughts; 'tis not a life,
'Tis but a piece of child-hood thrown away:
Should I out-live, I shall then out live
Vertu^ and honour. And when that day comes,
If ^v^ I should close these eyes but once,
May I live spotted for my perjury,
And was^ my limbs to nothing.

speeches.speaker: Are.
verse: And I (the woful'st maid as ever was,
Fo ^ with my hands to bring my Lord to death)
Do b^th honour of a Virgin swear,
To t^ll no hours beyond it.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Make me not hated so.

speeches.speaker: Are.
verse: Come from this prison, all joyful to our deaths.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: People will tear me when they find you true
To such a wretch as I; I shall die loath'd.
^ our Kingdoms peaceably, whil'st I

Fo^
^
^l^p so, gotten with my faults,
I ver^ put ^, every maid in love
Will have a piece of me if you be true.

speeches.speaker: Are.
verse: My dear Lord say not so.

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: A piece of you?
He was not born of women that can out it and look on.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Take me in tears betwixt you,
For my heart will break with shame and sorrow.

speeches.speaker: Are.
verse: Why 'tis well.

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: Lament no more.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: What would you have done
If you had wrong'd me basely, and had found
My life no price, compar'd to yours? For love Sirs,
Deal with me truly.

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: 'Twas mistaken, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Why if it were?

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: Then Sir we would have ask'd you pardon.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: And have hope to enjoy it?

speeches.speaker: Are.
verse: Injoy it? I.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Would you indeed? be plain.

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: We would my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Forgive me then.

speeches.speaker: Are.
verse: So, so.

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: 'Tis as it should be now.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Lead to my death.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Gentlemen, who saw the Prince?

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: So pl^ you Sir, he's gone to see the City,
And t^ new Platform, with some Gentlemen
Atten^ing on him.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Is the Princess ready,
To bring her prisoner out?

speeches.speaker: Thra.
verse: She waits your Grace.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Tell her we stay.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: King, you may be deceiv'd yet:
The head you a m^ cost more setting on
Than to be lost so slightly: If it must off
Like a wild overflow, that soops before him
A golden Stack, and with it shakes down Bridges,
Cracks the strong hearts of Pines, whose Cable roots
H^ld out a thousand Storms, a thousand Thunders,
And so made mightier, takes whole Villages
Upon his back, and in that heat of pride,
Charges strong Towns, Towers, Castles, Palaces,
And layes them desolate: so shall thy head,
Thy noble head, bury the lives of thousands
That must bleed with thee like a sacrifice,
In thy red ruines.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: How now, what Mask is this?

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: Right Royal Sir, I should
Sing you an Epithalamium of these lovers,
But having lost my best ayres with my fortunes,
And wanting a celestial Harp to strike
This blessed union on; thus in glad story
I give you all. These two fair Cedar-branches,
The noblest of the Mountain, where they grew
Straightest and tallest, under whose still shades
The worthie^ beasts have made their layers, and slept

Free from the
^y^a^
Sta^, and the fell Thunder-stroke,
Free from the Clouds, when they were big with humour,
And delivered in thousand spouts, their issues to the earth:
O there was none but silent quiet there!
Till never pleas'd fortune shot up shrubs,
Base under brambles to divorce these branches;
And for a while they did so, and did raign
Over the Mountain, and choakt up his beauty
With Brakes, rude Thornes and Thistles, till thy Sun
Scorcht them even to the roots, and dried them there:
And now a gentle gale hath blown again
That made these branches meet, and twine together,
Never to be divided: The god that sings
His holy numbers over marriage beds,
Hath knit their noble hearts, and here they stand
Your Children mighty King, and I have done.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: How, how?

speeches.speaker: Are.
verse: Sir, if you love it in plain truth,
For there is no Masking in't; This Gentleman
The prisoner that you gave me is become
My keeper, and through all the bitter throws
Your jealousies and his ill fate have wrought him,
Thus nobly hath he strangled, and at length
Arriv'd here my dear Husband.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Your dear Husband! call in
The Captain of the Cittadel; There you shall keep
Your Wedding. I'le provide a Mask shall make
Your Hymen turn his Saffron into a sullen Coat,
And sing sad Requiems to your departing souls:
Bloud shall put out your Torches, and instead
Of gaudy flowers about your wanton necks,
An Ax shall hang like a prodigious Meteor
Ready to crop your loves sweets. Hear you gods:
From this time do I shake all title off,
Of Father to this woman, this base woman,
And what there is of vengeance, in a Lion
Cast amongst Dogs, or rob'd of his dear young,
The same inforc't more terrible, more mighty,
Expect from me.

speeches.speaker: Are.
verse: Sir,
By that little life I have left to swear by,
There's nothing that can stir me from my self.
What I have done, I have done without repentance,
For death can be no Bug-bear unto me,
So long as Pharamond is not my headsman.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Sweet peace upon thy soul, thou worthy maid
When ere thou dyest; for this time I'le excuse thee,
Or be thy Prologue.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Sir, let me speak next,
And let my dying words be better with you
Than my dull living actions; if you aime
At the dear life of this sweet Innocent,
Y'are a Tyrant and a savage Monster;
Your memory shall be as soul behind you
As you are living, all your better deeds
Shall be in water writ, but this in Marble:
No Chronicle shall speak you, though your own,
But for the shame of men. No Monument
(Though high and big as Pelion) shall be able
To cover this base murther; make it rich
With Brass, with purest Gold, and shining Jasper,
Like the Pyramids, lay on Epitaphs,
Such as make great men gods; my little marble
(That only cloaths my ashes, not my faults)
Shall far out shine it: And for after issues
Think not so madly of the heavenly wisdoms,
That they will give you more, for your mad rage
To cut off, unless it be some Snake, or something
Like your self, that in his birth shall strangle you.
Remember, my Father, King; there was a fault,
But I forgive it: let that sin perswade you
To love this Lady. If you have a soul,
Think, save her, and be saved, for my self,
I have so long expected this glad hour,
So languisht under you, and daily withered,
That heaven knows it is my joy to dye,
I find a recreation in't.

speeches.speaker: Mess.
verse: Where's the King?

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Here.

speeches.speaker: Mess.
verse: Get you to your strength,
And rescue the Prince Pharamond from danger,
He's taken prisoner by the Citizens,
Fearing the Lord Philaster.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Oh brave followers;
Mutiny, my fine dear Country-men, mutiny,
Now my brave valiant foremen, shew your weapons
In honour of your Mistresses.

speeches.speaker: Mess.
verse: Arm, arm, arm.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: A thousand devils take 'em.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: A thousand blessing on 'em.

speeches.speaker: Mess.
verse: Arm O King, the City is in mutiny,
Led by an old Gray Ruffin, who comes on
In rescue of the Lord Philaster.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Away to the Cittadel, I'le see them safe,
And then cope with these Burgers: Let the Guard
And all the Gentlemen give strong attendance.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: The City up! this was above our wishes.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: I and the Marriage too; by my life,
prose: This noble Lady has deceiv'd us all, a plague upon my self; a thousand plagues, for having such unworthy thoughts of her dear honour: O I could beat my self, or do you beat me and I'le beat you, for we had all one thought.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: No, no, 'twill but lose time.

speeches.speaker: Di.
prose: You say true, are your swords sharp? Well my dear Country-men, what ye lack, if you continue and fall not back upon the first broken shin, I'le have you chronicled, and chronicled, and cut and chronicled and all to be prais'd, and sung in Sonnets, and bath'd in new brave Ballads, that all tongues shall troule you in Saecula Saeculorum my kind Can carriers.

speeches.speaker: Thra.
prose: What if a toy take 'em i'th' heels now, and they run all away, and cry the Devil take the hindmost?

speeches.speaker: Di.
prose: Then the same Devil take the foremost too, and fowce him for his breakfast; if they all prove Cowards, my curses fly amongst them and be speeding. May they have Murreins raign to keep the Gentlemen at home unbound in easie freez: May the Moths branch their Velvets, and their Silks only be worn before sore eyes. May their false lights undo 'em, and discover presses, holes, stains, and oldness in their Stuffs, and make them shop-rid: May they keep Whores and Horses, and break; and live mued up with necks of Beef and Turnips: May they have many children, and none like the Father: May they know no language but that gibberish they prattle to their Parcels, unless it be the goarish Latine they write in their bonds, and may they write that false, and lose their debts.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: Now the vengeance of all the gods confound them; how they swarm together! what a hum they raise; Devils choak your wilde throats; If a man had need to use their valours, he must pay a Brokage for it, and then bring 'em on, they will fight like sheep. 'Tis Philaster, none but Philaster must allay this heat: They will not hear me speak, but sling di^t at me, and call me Tyrant. Oh run dear friend, and bring the Lord Philaster: speak him fair, call him Prince, do him all the courtesie you can, commend me to him. Oh my wits, my wits!

speeches.speaker: Di.
prose: Oh my brave Countrymen! as I live, I will not buy a pin out of your walls for this; Nay, you shall cozen me, and I'le thank you; and send you Brawn and Bacon, and soil you every long vacation a brace of foremen, that at Michaelmas shall come up fat and kicking.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: What they will do with this poor Prince, the gods know, and I fear.

speeches.speaker: Di.
prose: Why Sir: they'l flea him, and make Church Buckets on's skin to squench rebellion, then clap a rivet in's sconce, and hang him up for a sign.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: O worthy Sir forgive me, do not make
Your miseries and my faults meet together,
To bring a greater danger. Be your self,
Still sound amongst Diseases, I have wrong'd you,
And though I find it last, and beaten to it,
Let first your goodness know it. Calm the people,
And be what you were born to: take your love,
And with her my repentance, and my wish^
And all my prayers, by the gods my heart speaks this:
And if the l^ast fall from me not perform'd,
May I be st^ck with Thunder.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Mighty Sir,
I will not do your greatness so much wrong,
As not to make your word truth; free the Princess,
And the poor boy, and let me stand the shock
Of this mad Sea breach, which I'le either turn
Or perish with it.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Let your own word free them.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Then thus I take my leave kissing your hand,
And hanging on your Royal word: be Kingly,
And be not moved Sir, I shall bring your peace,
Or never bring my self back.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: All the gods go with thee.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: Come my brave Mirmidons let's fall on, let our caps
Swarm my boys, and you nimble tongues forget your mothers
Gibberish, of what do you lack, and set your mouths
Up Children, till your Pallats fall frighted hal^ a
Fathom, past the cure of Bay-salt and gross P^pper.
And then cry Philaster, brave Philaster,
Let Philaster be deeper in request, my ding dongs,
My pairs of dear Indentures, King of Cl^s,
Than your cold water Chamblets o^ your paintings
Spitted with Copper; let not your hasty Silks,
Or your branch'd Cloth of Bodkin, or your Tishues,
Dearly belov'd of spiced Cake and Custard,
Your Robin-hoods scarlets and Johns, tie your affections
In darkness to your shops; no, dainty Duckers,
Up with your three pil'd spirits, your wrought valours.
And let your un-cut Coller make the King feel
The measure of your mightiness Philaster.
Cry my Rose nobles, cry.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: Philaster, Philaster.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
prose: How do you like this my Lord Prince, these are mad boys, I tell you, these are things that will not strike their top-sayles to a Foist. And let a man of war, an Argosie hull and cry Cockles.

speeches.speaker: Pha.
verse: Why you rude slave, do you know what you do?

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: My Pretty Prince of Puppets, we do know,
And give your greatness warning, that you talk
No more such Bugs-words, or that soldred Crown
Shall be scratch'd with a Musket: Dear Prince Pippen,
Down with your noble bloud; or as I live,
I'le have you codled: let him lose my spirits,
Make us a round Ring with your Bills my H^ct^s,
And let us see what this trim man dares do.
Now Sir, have at you; here I it,
And with this swashing blow, do you swear Prince;
I could hulk your Grace, and hang you up cross leg'd,
Like a Hare at a Poulters, and do this with this w^per.

speeches.speaker: Pha.
verse: You will not see me murder'd wicked V^a^s?

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
verse: Yes indeed will we Sir, we hav^ not seen one for a great while.

speeches.speaker: Capt.
verse: To make him Galoone-Laces,
I'le have a Coach-whip.
prose: He would have weapons would he? give him a Broad-side my brave boyes with your pikes, branch in his skin in Flowers like a Satin, and between every Flow ^a mortal cut, your Royalty shall ravel, jag him Gentlemen. ^'le have him cut to the kell, then down the sea^es, oh for a whip

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: O spare me Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: Hold, hold, the man begins to fear and know himself
He shall for this time only be scal'd up
With a Feather through his nose, that he may only see
Heaven, and think whither he's going,
Nay beyond Sea Sir, we will proclaim you, you would be King
Thou tender ^ir apparent to a Church-Ale,
Thou sleight Pr^nce of single Sarcenet;
Thou Royal Ring-tail, fit to fly at nothing
But poor mens Poultry, and have every Boy
Beat thee from that too with his Bread and Butter.

speeches.speaker: Pha.
verse: Gods keep me from these Hell-hounds.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
verse: Shall's g^ld him Captain?

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: No, you shall spare his dowcets my dear Donsels,
As you respect the Ladies let them flourish;
The curses of a longing woman kill as speedy as a Plague, Boys.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
verse: I'le have a Leg that's certain.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
verse: I'le have an Arm.

speeches.speaker: 3 Cit.
prose: I'le have his Nose, and at mine own charge build a Colledge, and clap't upon the Gate.

speeches.speaker: 4 Cit.
verse: I'le have his little Gut to string a Kit with,
For certainly a Royal Gut will found like silver.

speeches.speaker: Pha.
verse: Would they were in thy belly, and I past my pain once.

speeches.speaker: 5 Cit.
verse: Good Captain let me have his Liver to seed Ferrets.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: Who will have parcels else? speak.

speeches.speaker: Pha.
verse: Good gods consider me, I shall be tortur'd.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
prose: Captain, I'le give you the trimming of your hand-sword, and let me have his Skin to make false Scabbards.

verse: He had no horns Sir had he?

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: No Sir, he's a Pollard, what would'st thou do with horns?

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: O if he had, I would have made rare Hasts and Whistles of 'em, but his Shin bones if they be sound shall serve me.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: Long live Philaster, the brave Prince Philaster.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: I thank you Gentlemen, but why are these
Rude weapons brought abroad, to teach your hands
Uncivil Trades?

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: My Royal Rosiclear,
We are thy Mirmidons, thy Guard, thy Rorers,
And when thy noble body is in durance,
Thus do we clap our musty Mutrions on,
And trace the streets in terrour: Is it peace
Thou Mars of men? Is the King sociable,
And bids thee live? Art thou above thy soemen,
And free as Phoebus? Speak, if not, this stand
Of Royal blood shall be abroach, atilt, and run
Even to the lees of honour.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Hold and be satisfied, I am my self
Free as my thoughts are, by the gods I am.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: Art thou the dainty darling of the King?
Art thou the Hylas to our Hercules?
Do the Lords bow, and the regarded scarlets,
Kiss their Gumd go's, and cry, we are your servants?
Is the Court Navigable, and the presence struck
With Flags of friendship? if not, we are thy Castle
And this man sleeps.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: I am what I desire to be, your friend,
I am what I was born to be, your Prince.

speeches.speaker: Pha.
verse: Sir, there is some humanity in you,
You have a noble soul, forget my name,
And know my misery, set me safe aboard
From these wild Cambals, and as I live,
I'le quit this Land for ever: there is nothing,
Perpetual prisonment, cold, hunger, sickness
Of all sorts, all dangers, and all together
The worst company of the worst men, madness, age,
To be as many Creatures as a woman,
And do as all they do, nay to despair;
But I would rather make it a new Nature,
And live with all those than endure one hour
Amongst these wild Dogs.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: I do pity you: Friends discharge your fears,
Deliver me the Prince, I'le warrant you
I shall be old enough to find my safety.

speeches.speaker: 3 Cit.
verse: Good Si^ take heed he does not hurt you,
He's a fierce man I can tell you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: Prince, by your leave I'le have a Sursingle,
And Male you like a Hawke.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Away, away, there is no danger in him:
Alas he had rather sleep to shake his fit off.
Look you friends, how gently he leads, upon my word
He's tame enough, he need no further watching.
Good my friends go to your houses and by me have your pardons, and my love,
And know there shall be nothing in my power
You may deserve, but you shall have your wishes.
To give you more thanks were to slatter you,
Continue still your love, and for an earnest
Drink this.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: Long maist thou live brave Prince, brave Prince, brave Prince.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: Thou art the King of Courtesie:
Fall off again my sweet youths, come and every man
Trace to his house again, and hang his pewter up, then to
The Tavern and bring your wives in Musses: we will have
Musick and the red grape shall make us dance, and rise Boys

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Is it appeas'd?

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Sir, all is quiet as this dead of night,
As peaceable as sleep, my Lord Philaster
Brings on the Prince himself.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Kind Gentlemen!
I will not break the least word I have given
In promise to him, I have heap'd a world
Of grief upon his head, which yet I hope
To wash away.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: My Lord is come.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: My Son!
Blest be the time that I have leave to call
Such vertue mine; now thou art in mine arms,
Me thinks I have a salve unto my breast
For all the stings that dwell there, streams of grief
That I have wrought thee, and as much of joy
That I repent it, issue from mine eyes:
Let them appease thee, take thy right; take her,
She is thy right too, and forget to urge
My vexed soul with that I did before.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Sir, is it blotted from my memory,
Past and forgotten: For you Prince of Spain,
Whom I have thus redeem'd, you have full leave
To make an honourable voyage home.
And if you would go furnish'd to your Realm
With fair provision, I do see a Lady
Me thinks would gladly bear you company.
How like you this piece?

speeches.speaker: Meg.
verse: Sir, he likes it well,
For he hath tried it, and found it worth
His princely liking; we were ta'ne a bed,
I know your meaning, I am not the first
That Nature taught to seek a fellow forth:
Can shame remain perpetually in me,
And not in others? or have Princes salves
To cure ill names that meaner people want?

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: What mean you?

speeches.speaker: Meg.
verse: You must get another ship
To clear the Princess and the boy together.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: How now!

speeches.speaker: Meg.
verse: Others took me, and I took her and him
At that all women may be ta'ne sometimes:
Ship us all four my Lord, we can endure
Weather and wind alike.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Clear thou thy self, or know not me for Father.

speeches.speaker: Are.
verse: This earth, How false it is? what means is left for me
To clear my self? It lies in your belief,
My Lords believe me, and let all things else
Struggle together to dishonour me.

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: O stop your cars great King, that I may speak
As freedom would, then I will call this Lady
As base as be her actions, hear me Sir,
Believe hour hated bloud when it rebels
Against your reason sooner than this Lady.

speeches.speaker: Meg.
verse: By this good light he bears it hansomely.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: This Lady? I will sooner trust the wind
With Feathers, or the troubled Sea with Pearl,
Than her with any thing; believe her not!
Why think you, if I did believe her words;
I would outlive 'em: honour cannot take
Revenge on you, then what were to be known
But death?

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Forget her Sir, since all is knit
Between us: but I must request of you
One favour, and will sadly be denied.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Command what ere it be.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Swear to be true to what you promise.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: By the powers above,
Let it not be the death of her or him,
And it is granted.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Bear away the boy
To Torture, I will have her clear'd or buried.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: O let me call my words back, worthy Sir,
Ask something else, bury my life and right
In one poor grave, but do not take away my life and fame at once

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Away with him, it stands irrevocable.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Turn all your eyes on me, here stands a man
The falsest and the basest of this world:
Set swords against this breast some honest man,
For I have liv'd till I am pitied,
My former deeds are hateful, but this last
Is pitifull, for I unwillingly
Have given the dear preserver of my life
Unto his Torture: is it in the power
Of flesh and blood, to carry this and live?

speeches.speaker: Are.
verse: Dear Sir be patient yet, or stay that hand.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Sirs, strip that boy.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Come Sir, your tender flesh will try your constancie.

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: O kill me gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: No, help Sirs.

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: Will you Torture me?

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Hast there, why stay you?

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: Then I shall not break my vow,
You know just gods, though I discover all.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: How's that? Will he confess?

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Sir, so he says.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Speak then.

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: Great King if you command
This Lord to talk with me alone, my tongue
Urg'd by my heart, shall utter all the thoughts
My youth hath known, and stranger things than these
You hear not often.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Walk aside with him.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Why speak'st thou not?

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: Know you this face my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: Have you not seen it, nor the like?

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Yes, I have seen the like, but readily
I know not where.

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: I have been often told
In Court, of one Euphrasia, a Lady
And Daughter to you; betwixt whom and me
(They that would flatter my bad face would swear)
There was such strange resemblance, that we two
Could not be known asunder, drest alike.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: By Heaven and so there is.

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: For her fair sake,
Who now doth spend the spring time of her life
In holy Pilgrimage, move to the King,
That I may scape this Torture.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: But thou speak'st
As like Euphrasia as thou dost look,
How came it to thy knowledge that she lives in Pilgrimage?

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: I know it not my Lord,
But I have heard it, and do scarce believe it.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Oh my shame, is't possible? Draw near,
That I may gaze upon thee, art thou she?
Or else her Murderer? where wert thou born?

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: In Siracusa.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: What's thy name?

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: Euphrasia.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: O'tis just, 'tis she now, I do know thee, Oh that thou hadst died
And I had never seen thee nor my shame,
How shall I own thee? shall this tongue of mine
E're call thee Daughter more?

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: Would I had died indeed, I wish it too,
And so I must have done by vow, e're published
What I have told, but that there was no means
To hide it longer, yet I joy in this,
The Princess is all clear.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: What have you done?

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: All is discovered.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Why then hold you me?

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: All is discovered, pray you let me go.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Stay him.

speeches.speaker: Are.
verse: What is discovered?

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Why my shame, it is a woman, let her speak the rest.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: How! that again.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: It is a woman.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Blest be you powers that favour innocence.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Lay hold upon that Lady.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: It is a woman Sir, hark Gentlemen!
It is a woman. Arethusa take
My soul into thy breast, that would be gone
With joy: it is a woman, thou art fair,
And vertuous still to ages, in despight of malice.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Speak you, where lies his shame?

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: I am his Daughter.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: The Gods are just.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: I dare accuse none, but before you two
The vertue of our age, I bend my knee
For mercy.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Take it freely; for I know,
Though what thou didst were undiscreetly done,
'Twas meant well.

speeches.speaker: Are.
verse: And for me,
I have a power to pardon sins as oft
As any man has power to wrong me.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Noble and worthy.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: But Bellario,
(For I must call thee still so) tell me why
Thou didst conceal thy Sex, it was a fault,
A fault Bellario, though thy other deeds
Of truth outweigh'd it: All these Jealousies
Had flown to nothing, if thou hadst discovered,
What now we know.

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: My Father would oft speak
Your worth and vertue, and as I did grow
More and more apprehensive, I did thirst
To see the man so rais'd, but yet all this
Was but a Maiden longing to be lost
As soon as found, till sitting in my window,
Printing my thoughts in Lawne, I saw a God
I thought (but it was you) enter our Gates,
My bloud flew out, and back again as fast
As I had puft it forth, and suck't it in
Like breath, then was I call'd away in hast
To entertain you. Never was a man
Heav'd from a Sheep-coat to a Scepter rais'd
So high in thoughts as I, you left a kiss
Upon these lips then, which I mean to keep
From you for ever, I did hear you talk
Far above singing; after you were gone,
I grew acquainted with my heart, and search'd
What stir'd it so, Alas I found it love,
Yet far from ^ for could I have but liv'd
In presence of you, I had had my end,
For this I did delude my noble Father
With a feign'd Pilgrimage, and drest my self
In habit of a boy, and, for I knew
My birth no match for you, I was past hope
Of having you. And understanding well
That when I made discovery of my Sex,
I could not stay with you, I made a vow
By all the most religious things a Maid
Could call together, never to be known,
Whilst there was hope to hide me from mens eyes,
For other than I seem'd; that I might ever
Abide with you, then fate I by the Fount
Where first you took me up.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Search out a match
Within our Kingdom where and when thou wilt,
And I will pay thy Dowry, and thy self
Wilt well deserve him.

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: Never Sir will I
Ma^ry, it is a thing within my vow,
But if I may have leave to serve the Princess,
To see the vertues of her Lord and her,
I shall have hope to live.

speeches.speaker: Are.
verse: I Philaster,
Cannot be jealous, though you had a Lady
Drest like a Page to serve you, nor will I
Suspect her living here: come live with me,
Live free, as I do, she that loves my Lord,
Curst be the wife that hates her.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: I grieve such vertues should be laid in earth
Without an Heir; hear me my Royal Father,
Wrong not the freedom of our souls so much,
To think to take revenge of that base woman,
Her malice cannot hurt us: set her free
As she was born, saving from shame and sin.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Set her at liberty, but leave the Court,
This is no place for such: you Pharamond
Shall have free passage, and a conduct home
Worthy so great a Prince, when you come there,
Remember 'twas your faults that lost you her,
And not my purpos'd will.

speeches.speaker: Pha.
verse: I do confess,
Renowned Sir.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Last joyn your hands in one, enjoy Philaster
This Kingdom which is yours, and after me
What ever I call mine, my blessing on you,
All happy hours be at your Marriage joyes,
That you may grow your selves over all Lands,
And live to see your plenteous branches spring
Where ever there is Sun. Let Princes learn
By this to rule the passions of their blood,
For what Heaven wills, can never be withstood.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: BEssus, the King has made a fair hand on't, he has ended the Wars at a blow, would my sword had a close basket hilt to hold Wine, and the blade would make knives, for we shall have nothing but eating and drinking.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: We that are Commanders shall do well enough.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Faith Bessus, such Commanders as thou may; I had as lieve set thee Perdue for a pudding i'th' dark, as Alexander the Great.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: I love these jests exceedingly.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: I think thou lov'st'em better than quarrelling Bessus, I'le say so much i'thy behalf, and yet thou 'it valiant enough upon a retreat, I think thou wouldst kill any man that stopt thee if thou couldst.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: But was not this a brave Combate Mardonius?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Why, didst thou see't?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: You stood wi'me.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: I did so, but me thought thou wink'dst every blow they strook.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Well, I believe there are better souldiers than I, that never saw two Princes fight in lists.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: By my troth I think so too Bessus, many a thousand, but certainly all that are worse than thou have seen as much.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: 'Twas bravely done of our King.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Yes, if he had not ended the wars: I'me glad thou dar'st talk of such dangerous businesses.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: To take a Prince prisoner in the heart of's own Country in single combat.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: See how thy blood curdles at this, I think thou couldst be contented to be beaten i'this passion.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Shall I tell you truly?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: I.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: I could willingly venture for't.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Um, no venture neither Bessus.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Let me not live, if I do not think 'tis a braver piece of service than that I'me so fam'd for.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Why, art thou fam'd for any valour?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Fam'd! I, I warrant you.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: I'me e'en heartily glad on't, I have been with thee e're since thou cam'st to th'wars, and this is the first word that ever I heard on't, prethee who fames thee.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: The Christian world.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
'Tis heathenishly done of'em in my conscience, thou
deserv'st it not.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Yes, I ha' don good service.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: I do not know how thou mayst wait of a man in's Chamber, or thy agility of shifting of a Trencher, but otherwise no service good Bessus.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: You saw me do the service your self.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Not so hasty sweet Bessus, where was it, is the place vanish'd?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: At Bessus desp'rate redemption.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: At Bessus desp'rate redemption, where's that?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: There where I redeem'd the day, the place bears my name.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Pray thee, who Christened it?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: The Souldiers.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: If I were not a very merrily dispos'd man, what would become of thee? one that had but a grain of choler in the whole composition of his body, would send thee of an errand to the worms for putting thy name upon that field: did not I beat thee there i'th' head o'th' Troops with a Trunchion, because thou wouldst needs run away with thy company, when we should charge the enemy?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: True, but I did not run.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Right Bessus, I beat thee out on't.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: But came I not up when the day was gone, and redeem'd all?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Thou knowest, and so do I, thou meanedst to flie, and thy fear making thee mistake, thou ranst upon the enemy, and a hot charge thou gav'st, as I'le do thee right, thou art furious in running away, and I think, we owe thy fear for our victory; If I were the King, and were sure thou wouldst mistake alwaies and run away upon th' enemy, thou shouldst be General by this light.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: You'l never leave this till I fall foul.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: No more such words dear Bessus, for though I have ever known thee a coward, and therefore durst never strike thee, yet if thou proceedest, I will allow thee valiant, and beat thee.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Come, our King's a brave fellow.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: He is so Bessus, I wonder how thou cam'st to know it. But if thou wer't a man of understanding, I would tell thee, he is vain-glorious, and humble, and angry, and patient, and merry and dull, and joyful and sorrowful in extremity in an hour: Do not think me thy friend for this, for if I car'd who knew it, thou shouldst not hear it Bessus. Here he is with his prey in his foot.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Thy sadness brave Tigranes takes away
From my full victory, am I become
Of so small fame, that any man should grieve
When I o'recome him? They that plac'd me here,
Intended it an honour large enough,
For the most valiant living, but to dare oppose me single, though he
Lost the day. What should afflict you, you are as free as I,
To be my prisoner, is to be more free
Than you were formerly, and never think
The man I held worthy to combate me
Shall be us'd servilely: Thy ransom is
To take my only Sister to thy Wife.
A heavy one Tigranes, for she is
A Lady, that the neighbour Princes send
Blanks to fetch home. I have been too unkind
To her Tigranes, she but nine years old
I left her, and ne're saw her since, your wars
Have held me long and taught me though a youth,
The way to victory, she was a pretty child,
Then I was little better, but now fame
Cries loudly on her, and my messengers
Make me believe she is a miracle;
She'l make you shrink, as I did, with a stroak
But of her eye Tigranes.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Is't the course of Iberia to use their prisoners thus?
Had fortune thrown my name above Arbace,
I should not thus have talk'd Sir, in Armenia,
We hold it base, you should have kept your temper
Till you saw home again, where 'tis the fashion
Perhaps to brag.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Be you my witness earth, need I to brag,
Doth not this captive Prince speak
Me sufficiently, and all the acts
That I have wrought upon his suffering Land;
Should I then boast! where lies that foot of ground
Within his whole Realm, that I have not past,
Fighting and conquering; Far then from me
Be ostentation. I could tell the world
How I have laid his Kingdom desolate
By this sole Arm prop't by divinity,
Stript him out of his glories, and have sent
The pride of all his youth to people graves,
And made his Virgins languish for their Loves,
If I would brag, should I that have the power
To teach the Neighbour world humility,
Mix with vain-glory?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Indeed this is none.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Tigranes, Nay did I but take delight
To stretch my deeds as others do, on words,
I could amaze my hearers.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: So you do.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: But he shall wrong his and my modesty,
That thinks me apt to boast after any act
Fit for a good man to do upon his foe.
A little glory in a souldiers mouth
Is well-becoming, be it far from vain.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: 'Tis pity that valour should be thus drunk.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: I offer you my Sister, and you answer
I do insult, a Lady that no suite
Nor treasure, nor thy Crown could purchase thee,
But that thou fought'st with me.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Though this be worse
Than that you spake before, it strikes me not;
But that you think to overgrace me with
The marriage of your Sister, troubles me.
I would give worlds for ransoms were they mine,
Rather than have her.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: See if I insult
That am the Conquerour, and for a ransom
Offer rich treasure to the Conquered,
Which he refuses, and I bear his scorn:
It cannot be self-flattery to say,
The Daughters of your Country set by her,
Would see their shame, run home and blush to death,
At their own foulness; yet she is not fair,
Nor beautiful, those words express her not,
They say her looks have something excellent,
That wants a name: yet were she odious,
Her birth deserves the Empire of the world,
Sister to such a brother, that hath ta'ne
Victory prisoner, and throughout the earth,
Carries her bound, and should he let her loose,
She durst not leave him; Nature did her wrong,
To Print continual conquest on her cheeks,
And make no man worthy for her to taste
But me that am too near her, and as strangely
She did for me, but you will think I brag.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: I do I'le be sworn. Thy valour and thy passions sever'd, would have made two excellent fellows in their kinds: I know not whether I should be sorry thou art so valiant, or so passionate, wou'd one of 'em were away.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Do I refuse her that I doubt her worth?
Were she as vertuous as she would be thought,
So perfect that no one of her own sex
Could find a want, had she so tempting fair,
That she could wish it off for damning souls,
I would pay any ransom, twenty lives
Rather than mee^ her married in my bed.
Perhaps I have a love, where I have sixt
Mine eyes not to be mov'd, and she on me,
I am not fickle.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Is that all the cause?
Think you, you can so knit your self in love
To any other, that her searching sight
Cannot dissolve it? So before you tri'd,
You thought your self a match for me in sight,
Trust me Tigranes, she can do as much
In peace, as I in war, she'l conquer too,
You shall see if you have the power to stand
The force of her swift looks, if you dislike,
I'le send you home with love, and name your ransom
Some other way, but if she be your choice,
She frees you: To Iberia you must.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Sir, I have learn'd a prisoners sufferance,
And will obey, but give me leave to talk
In private with some friends before I go.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Some to await him forth, and see him safe,
But let him freely send for whom he please,
And none dare to disturb his conference,
I will not have him know what bondage is,
Till he be free from me. This Prince, Mardonius,
Is full of wisdom, valour, all the graces
Man can receive.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: And yet you conquer'd him.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: And yet I conquer'd him, and could have don't
Hadst thou joyn'd with him, though thy name in Arms
Be great; must all men that are vertuous
Think suddenly to match themselves with me?
I conquered him and bravely, did I not?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: And please your Majesty, I was afraid at first.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: When wert thou other?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Of what?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: That you would not have spy'd your best advantages, for your Majesty in my opinion lay too high, methinks, under favour, you should have lain thus.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Like a Taylor at a wake.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: And then, if please your Majesty to remember, at one time, by my troth I wisht my self wi'you.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: By my troth thou wouldst ha' stunk 'em both out o'th' Lists.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: What to do?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: To put your Majesty in mind of an occasion; you lay thus, and Tigranes falsified a blow at your Leg, which you by doing thus avoided; but if you had whip'd up your Leg thus, and reach'd him on the ear, you had made the Blood-Royal run down his head.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: What Country Fence-school learn'st thou at?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Pish, did not I take him nobly?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Why you did, and you have talked enough on't.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Talkt enough?
Will you confine my word? by heaven and earth,
I were much better be a King of beasts
Than such a people: if I had not patience
Above a God, I should be call'd a Tyrant
Throughout the world. They will offend to death
Each minute: Let me hear thee speak again,
And thou art earth again: why this is like
Tigranes speech that needs would say I brag'd.
Bessus, he said I brag'd.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Why dost thou laugh?
By all the world, I'm grown ridiculous
To my own Subjects: Tie me in a Chair
And jest at me, but I shall make a start,
And punish some that others may take heed
How they are haughty; who will answer me?
He said I boasted, speak Mardonius,
Did I? He will not answer, O my temper!
I give you thanks above, that taught my heart
Patience, I can endure his silence; what will none
Vouchsafe to give me answer? am I grown
To such a poor respect, or do you mean
To break my wind? Speak, speak, some one of you,
Or else by heaven.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: So please your.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Monstrous,
I cannot be heard out, they cut me off,
As if I were too saucy, I will live
In woods, and talk to trees, they will allow me
To end what I begin. The meanest Subject
Can find a freedom to discharge his soul
And not I, now it is a time to speak,
I hearken.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: May it please.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: I mean not you,
Did not I stop you once? but I am grown
To balk, but I defie, let another speak,

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: I hope your Majesty.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Thou drawest thy words,
That I must wait an hour, where other men
Can hear in instants; throw your words away,
Quick, and to purpose, I have told you this.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: And please your Majesty.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Wilt thou devour me? this is such a rudeness
As you never shew'd me, and I want
Power to command too, else Mardonius
Would speak at my request; were you my King,
I would have answered at your word Mardonius,
I pray you speak, and truely, did I boast?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Truth will offend you.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: You take all great care what will offend me,
When you dare to utter such things as these.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: You told Tigranes, you had won his Land,
With that sole arm propt by Divinity:
Was not that bragging, and a wrong to us,
That daily ventured lives?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: O that thy name
Were as great, as mine, would I had paid my wealth,
It were as great, as I might combate thee,
I would through all the Regions habitable
Search thee, and having found thee, wi'my Sword
Drive thee about the world, till I had met
Some place that yet mans curiosity
Hath mist of; there, there would I strike thee dead:
Forgotten of mankind, such Funeral rites
As beasts would give thee, thou shouldst have.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: The King rages extreamly, shall we slink away?
He'l strike us.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Content.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: There I would make you know 'twas this sole arm.
I grant you were my instruments, and did
As I commanded you, but 'twas this arm
Mov'd you like wheels, it mov'd you as it pleas'd.
Whither slip you now? what are you too good
To wait on me (puffe,) I had need have temper
That rule such people; I have nothing left
At my own choice, I would I might be private:
Mean men enjoy themselves, but 'tis our curse,
To have a tumult that out of their loves
Will wait on us, whether we will or no;
Go get you gone: Why here they stand like death,
My words move nothing.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Must we go?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: I know not.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: I pray you leave me Sirs, I'me proud of this,
That you will be intreated from my sight:
Why now the leave me all: Mardonius.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Will you leave me quite alone? me thinks
Civility should teach you more than this,
If I were but your friend: Stay here and wait.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Sir shall I speak?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Why, you would now think much
To be denied, but I can scare intreat
What I would have: do, speak.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: But will you hear me out?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: With me you Article to talk thus: well,
I will hear you out.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Sir, that I have ever lov'd you, my sword hath spoken for me; that I do, if it be doubted, I dare call an oath, a great one to my witness; and were you not my King, from amongst men, I should have chose you out to love above the rest: nor can this challenge thanks, for my own sake I should have done it, because I would have lov'd the most deserving man, for so you are.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Alas Mardonius, rise you shall not kneel,
We all are souldiers, and all venture lives:
And where there is no difference in mens worths,
Titles are jests, who can outvalue thee?
Mardonius thou hast lov'd me, and hast wrong,
Thy love is not rewarded, but believe
^t shall be better, more than friend in arms,
My Father, and my Tutor, good Mardonius.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Sir, you did promise you would hear me out.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: And so I will; speak freely, for from thee
Nothing can come but worthy things and true.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Though you have all this worth, you hold some qualities that do Eclipse your vertues.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Eclipse my vertues?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Yes, your passions, which are so manifold, that they appear even in this: when I commend you, you hug me for that truth: but when I speak your faults, you make a start, and flie the hearing but.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: When you commend me? O that I should live
To need such commendations: If my deeds
Blew not my praise themselves about the earth,
I were most wretched: spare your idle praise:
If thou didst mean to flatter, and shouldst utter
Words in my praise, that thou thoughtst impudence,
prose: My deeds should make 'em modest: when you praise I hug you? 'tis so safe, that wert thou worthy thou shouldst receive a death, a glorious death from me: but thou shalt understand thy lies, for shouldst thou praise me into Heaven, and there leave me inthron'd, I would despise thee though as much as now, which is as much as dust because I see thy envie.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: However you will use me after, yet for your own promise sake, hear me the rest.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: I will, and after call unto the winds, for they shall lend as large an ear as I to what you utter: speak.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Would you but leave these hasty tempers, which I do not say take from you all your worth, but darken 'em, then you will shine indeed.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Well.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Yet I would have you keep some passions, lest men should take you for a God, your vertues are such.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Why now you flatter.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: I never understood the word, were you no King, and free from these moods, should I choose a companion for wit and pleasure, it should be you; or for honesty to enterchange my bosom with, it should be you; or wisdom to give me counsel, I would pick out you; or valour to defend my reputation, still I should find you out; for you are fit to sight for all the world, if it could come in question: Now I have spoke, consider to your self, find out a use; if so, then what shall fall to me is not material.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Is not material? more than ten such lives, as mine, Mardonius: it was nobly said, thou hast spoke truth, and boldly such a truth as might offend another. I have been too passionate and idle, thou shalt see a swift amendment, but I want those parts you praise me for: I fight for all the world? Give me a sword, and thou wilt go as far beyond me, as thou art beyond in years, I know thou dar'st and wilt; it troubles me that I should use so rough a phrase to thee, impute it to my folly, what thou wilt, so thou wilt paron me: that thou and I should differ thus!

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Why 'tis no matter Sir.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Faith but it is, but thou dost ever take all things I do, thus patiently, for which I never can requite thee, but with love, and that thou shalt be sure of. Thou and I have not been merry lately: pray thee tell me where hadst thou that same jewel in thine ear?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Why at the taking of a Town.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: A wench upon my life, a wench Mardonius gave thee that jewel.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Wench! they respect not me, I'm old and rough, and every limb about me, but that which should, grows stiffer, I'those businesses I may swear I am truly honest: for I pay justly for what I take, and would be glad to be at a certainty.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Why, do the wenches encroach upon thee?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: I by this light do they.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Didst thou sit at an old rent with 'em?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Yes saith.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: And do they improve themselves?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: I ten shillings to me, every new young fellow they come acquainted with.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: How canst live on't?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Why I think I must petition to you.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Thou shalt take them up at my price.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Your price?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: I at the Kings price.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: That may be more than I'me worth.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
prose: Is he not merry now?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
prose: I think not.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: He is, he is: we'l shew our selves.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Bessus, I thought you had been in Iberia by this, I bad you hast; Gobrias will want entertainment for me.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: And please your Majesty I have a sute.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Is't not lousie Bessus, what is't?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: I am to carry a Lady with me.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Then thou hast two sutes.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: And if I can prefer her to the Lady Pentha your Majesties Sister, to learn fashions, as her friends term it, it will be worth something to me.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: So many nights lodgings as 'tis thither, wilt not?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: I know not that Sir, but gold I shall be sure of.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Why thou shalt bid her entertain her from me, so thou wilt resolve me one thing.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: If I can.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Faith 'tis a very disputable question, and yet I think thou canst decide it.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Your Majesty has a good opinion of my understanding.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: I have so good an opinion of it: 'tis whether thou be valiant.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Some body has traduced me to you: do you see this sword Sir?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: If I do not make my back-biters eat it to a knife within this week, say I am not valiant.

speeches.speaker: Mes.
prose: Health to your Majesty.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: From Gobrias?

speeches.speaker: Mes.
prose: Yes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: How does he, is he well?

speeches.speaker: Mes.
prose: In perfect health.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Take that for thy good news. A trustier servant to his Prince there lives not, than is good Gobrias.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
prose: The King starts back.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: His blood goes back as fast.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
prose: And now it comes again.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: He alters strangely.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: The hand of Heaven is on me, be it far from me to struggle, if my secret sins have pull'd this curse upon me, lend me tears now to wash me white, that I may feel a child-like innocence within my breast; which once perform'd, O give me leave to stand as fix'd as constancy her self, my eyes set here unmov'd, regardless of the world though thousand miseries incompass me.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: This is strange, Sir, how do you?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Mardonius, my mother.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Is she dead?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Alas she's not so happy, thou dost know how she hath laboured since my Father died to take by treason hence this loathed life, that would but be to serve her, I have pardoned, and pardoned, and by that have made her fit to practise new sins, not repent the old: she now had stirr'd a slave to come from thence, and strike me here, whom Gobrias sifting out, took and condemn'd and executed there, the carefulst servant: Heaven let me but live to pay that man; Nature is poor to me, that will not let me have as many deaths as are the times that he hath sav'd my life, that I might dye 'em over all for him.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Sir let her bear her sins on her own head,
Vex not your self.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: What will the world
Conceive of me? with what unnatural sins
Will they suppose me loaden, when my life
Is fought by her that gave it to the world?
But yet he writes me comfort here, my Sister,
He saies, is grown in beauty and in grace.
In all the innocent vertues that become
A tender spotless maid: she stains her cheeks
With morning tears to purge her mothers ill,
And 'mongst that sacred dew she mingles Prayers
Her pure Oblations for my safe return:
If I have lost the duty of a Son,
If any pomp or vanity of state
Made me forget my natural offices,
Nay farther, if I have not every night
Expostulated with my wandring thoughts,
If ought unto my parent they have err'd,
And call'd 'em back: do you direct her arm
Unto this soul dissembling heart of mine:
But if I have been just to her, send out
Your power to compass me, and hold me safe
From searching treason; I will use no means
But prayer: for rather suffer me to see
From mine own veins issue a deadly flood,
Than wash my danger off with mothers blood.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I n'ere saw such suddain extremities.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Why? wilt thou have me die Spaconia,
What should I do?

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: Nay let me stay alone,
And when you see Armenia again,
You shall behold a Tomb more worth than I;
Some friend that ever lov'd me or my cause,
Will build me something to distinguish me
From other women, many a weeping verse
He will lay on, and much lament those maids,
That plac'd their loves unfortunately high,
As I have done, where they can never reach;
But why should you go to Iberia?

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Alas, that thou wilt ask me, ask the man
That rages in a Fever why he lies
Distempered there, when all the other youths
Are coursing o're the Meadows with their Loves?
Can I resist it? am I not a slave
To him that conquer'd me?

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: That conquer'd thee Tigranes! he has won
But half of thee, thy body, but thy mind
May be as free as his, his will did never
Combate thine, and take it prisoner.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: But if he by force convey my body hence,
What helps it me or thee to be unwilling?

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: O Tigranes, I know you are to see a Lady there,
To see, and like I fear: perhaps the hope
Of her make you forget me, ere we part,
Be happier than you know to wish; farewel.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Spaconia, stay and hear me what I say:
In short, destruction meet me that I may
See it, and not avoid it, when I leave
To be thy faithful lover: part with me
Thou shalt not, there are none that know our love,
And I have given gold unto a Captain
That goes unto Iberia from the King,
That he will place a Lady of our Land
With the Kings Sister that is offered me;
Thither shall you, and being once got in
Perswade her by what subtil means you can
To be as backward in her love as I.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: Can you imagine that a longing maid
When she beholds you, can be pull'd away
With words from loving you?

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Dispraise my health, my honesty, and tell her I am jealous.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: Why, I had rather lose you: can my heart
Consent to let my tongue throw out such words,
And I that ever yet spoke what I thought,
Shall find it such a thing at first to lie?

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Yet do thy belt.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: What, is your Majesty ready?

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: There is the Lady, Captain.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Sweet Lady, by your leave, I could wish my self more full of Courtship for your fair sake.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
prose: Sir I shall feel no want of that.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Lady, you must hast, I have received new letters from the King that require more hast than I expected, he will follow me suddenly himself, and begins to call for your Majesty already.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
prose: He shall not do so long.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Sweet Lady, shall I call you my Charge hereafter?

speeches.speaker: Spa.
prose: I will not take upon me to govern your tongue Sir, you shall call me what you please.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: MY Lord Bacurius, you must have regard unto the Queen, she is your prisoner, 'tis at your peril if she make escape.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: My Lord, I know't, she is my prisoner from you committed; yet she is a woman, and so I keep her safe, you will not urge me to keep her close, I shall not shame to say I sorrow for her.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: So do I my Lord; I sorrow for her, that so little grace doth govern her: that she should stretch her arm against her King, so little womanhood and natural goodness, as to think the death of her own Son.

speeches.speaker: Ara.
prose: Thou knowst the reason why, dissembling as thou art, and wilt not speak.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: There is a Lady takes not after you,
Her Father is within her, that good man
Whose tears weigh'd down his sins, mark how she weeps,
How well it does become her, and if you
Can find no disposition in your self
To sorrow, yet by gracefulness in her
Find out the way, and by your reason weep:
All this she does for you, and more she needs
When for your self you will not lose a tear,
Think how this want of grief discredits you,
And you will weep, because you cannot weep.

speeches.speaker: Ara.
verse: You talk to me as having got a time fit for your purpose; but you know I know you speak not what you think.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: I would my heart were Stone, before my softness should be urg'd
Against my mother, a more troubled thought
No Virgin bears about; should I excuse
My Mothers fault, I should set light a life
In losing which, a brother and a King
Were taken from me, if I seek to save
That life so lov'd, I lose another life
That gave me being, I shall lose a Mother,
A word of such a sound in a childs ears
That it strikes reverence through it; may the will
Of heaven be done, and if one needs must fall,
Take a poor Virgins life to answer all.

speeches.speaker: Ara.
verse: But Gobrias let us talk, you know this fault
Is not in me as in another Mother.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: I know it is not.

speeches.speaker: Ara.
verse: Yet you make it so.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: Why, is not all that's past beyond your help?

speeches.speaker: Ara.
verse: I know it is.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: Nay should you publish it before the world,
Think you 'twould be believ'd?

speeches.speaker: Ara.
verse: I know it would not.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: Nay should I joyn with you, should we not both be torn and yet both die uncredited?

speeches.speaker: Ara.
verse: I think we should.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: Why then take you such violent courses? As for me I do but right in saving of the King from all your plots

speeches.speaker: Ara.
verse: The King?

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: I bad you rest with patience, and a time
Would come for me to reconcile all to
Your own content, but by this way you take
Away my power, and what was done unknown,
Was not by me but you: your urging being done
I must preserve my own, but time may bring
All this to light, and happily for all.

speeches.speaker: Ara.
verse: Accursed be this over curious brain
That gave that plot a birth, accurst this womb
That after did conceive to my disgrace.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: My Lord Protector, they say there are divers Letters come from Armenia, that Bessus has done good service, and brought again a day, by his particular valour, receiv'd you any to that effect?

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: Yes, 'tis most certain.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: I'm sorry for't, not that the day was won,
But that 'twas won by him: we held him here
A Coward, he did me wrong once, at which I laugh'd,
And so did all the world, for nor I,
Nor any other held him worth my sword.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: Health to my Protector; from the King
These Letters; and to your grace Madam, these.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: How does his Majesty?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: As well as conquest by his own means and his valiant Cammanders can make him; your letters will tell you all.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: I will not open mine till I do know
My Brothers health: good Captain is he well?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: As the rest of us that fought are.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: But how's that? is he hurt?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: He's a strange souldier that gets not a knock.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: I do not ask how strange that souldier is
That gets no hurt, but whether he have one.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: He had divers.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: And is he well again?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Well again, an't please your Grace: why I was run twice through the body, and shot i'th' head with a cross-arrow, and yet am well again.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: I do not care how thou do'st, is he well?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Not care how I do? Let a man out of the mightiness of his spirit, fructifie Foreign Countries with his blood for the good of his own, and thus he shall be answered: Why I may live to relieve with spear and shield, such a Lady as you distressed.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Why, I will care, I'me glad that thou art well,
I prethee is he so?

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: The King is well and will be here to morrow.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: My prayer is heard, now will I open mine.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: Bacurius, I must ease you of your charge:
Madam, the wonted mercy of the King,
That overtakes your faults, has met with this,
And struck it out, he has forgiven you freely,
Your own will is your law, be where you please.

speeches.speaker: Ara.
verse: I thank him.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: You will be ready to wait upon his Majesty to morrow?

speeches.speaker: Ara.
verse: I will.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Madam be wise hereafter; I am glad I have lost this Office.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: Good Captain Bessus, tell us the discourse betwixt Tigranes and our King, and how we got the victory.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: I prethee do, and if my Brother were
In any danger, let not thy tale make
Him abide there long before thou bring him off,
For all that while my heart will beat.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Madam let what will beat, I must tell the truth, and thus it was; they fought single in lists, but one to one; as for my own part, I was dangerously hurt but three days before, else, perhaps, we had been two to two, I cannot tell, some thought we had, and the occasion of my hurt was this, the enemy had made Trenches.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: Captain, without the manner of your hurt be much material to this business, we'l hear't some other time.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: I prethee leave it, and go on with my Brother.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: I will, but 'twould be worth your hearing: To the Lists they came, and single-sword and gantlet was their fight.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Alas!

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Without the Lists there stood some dozen Captains of either side mingled, all which were sworn, and one of those was I: and 'twas my chance to stand next a Captain o'th' enemies side, called Tiribasus; Valiant they said he was; whilst these two Kings were streaching themselves, this Tiribasus cast something a scornful look on me, and ask't me who I thought would overcome: I smil'd and told him if he would fight with me, he should perceive by the event of that whose King would win: something he answered, and a scustle was like to grow, when one Zipetus offered to help him, I—

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: All this is of thy self, I pray thee Bessus tell something of my Brother, did he nothing?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Why yes, I'le tell your Grace, they were not to sight till the word given, which for my own part, by my troth I confess I was not to give.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: See for his own part.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: I fear yet this fellow's abus'd with a good report.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: But I—

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Still of himself.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Cri'd give the word, when as some of them say, Tigranes was stooping, but the word was not given then, yet one Cosroes of the enemies part, held up his finger to me, which is as much with us Martialists, as I will sight with you: I said not a word, nor made sign during the combate, but that once done.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: He slips o're all the fight.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: I call'd him to me, Cosroes said I.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: I will hear no more.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: No, no, I lie.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: I dare be sworn thou dost.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Captain said I, so it was.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: I tell thee, I will hear no further.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: No? Your Grace will wish you had.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: I will not wish it, what is this the Lady
My brother writes to me to take?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: And please your Grace this is she: Charge, will you come near the Princess?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: You'r welcome from your Country, and this land shall shew unto you all the kindness that I can make it; what's your name?

speeches.speaker: Spa.
prose: Thalectris.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Y'are very welcome, you have got a letter to put you to me, that has power enough to place mine enemy here; then much more you that are so far from being so to me that you ne're saw me.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Madam, I dare pass my word for her truth.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
prose: My truth?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Why Captain, do you think I am afraid she'l steal?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: I cannot tell, servants are slippery, but I dare give my word for her, and for honesty, she came along with me, and many favours she did me by the way, but by this light none but what she might do with modesty, to a man of my rank.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Why Captain, here's no body thinks otherwise.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Nay, if you should, your Grace may think your pleasure; but I am sure I brought her from Armenia, and in all that way, if ever I touch'd any bare of her above her knee; I pray God I may sink where I stand.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
prose: Above my knee?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: No, you know I did not, and if any man will say, I did, this sword shall answer; Nay, I'le defend the reputation of my charge whilst I live, your Grace shall understand I am secret in these businesses, and know how to defend a Ladies honour.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
prose: I hope your Grace knows him so well already, I shall not need to tell you he's vain and foolish.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: I you may call me what you please, but I'le defend your good name against the world; and so I take my leave of your Grace, and of you my Lord Protector; I am likewise glad to see your Lordship well.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: O Captain Bessus, I thank you, I would speak with you anon.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: When you please, I will attend your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Madam, I'le take my leave too.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Good Bacurius.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: Madam what writes his Majesty to you?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: O my Lord, the kindest words, I'le keep 'em whilst I live, here in my bosom, there's no art in 'em, they lie disordered in this paper, just as hearty nature speaks 'em.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: And to me he writes what tears of joy he shed to hear how you were grown in every vertues way, and yields all thanks to me, for that dear care which I was bound to have in training you, there is no Princess living that enjoys a brother of that worth.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: My Lord, no maid longs more for any thing,
And feels more heat and cold within her breast,
Than I do now, in hopes to see him.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: Yet I wonder much
At this he writes, be brings along with him
A husband for you, that same Captive Prince,
And if he loves you as he makes a shew,
He will allow you freedom in your choice.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: And so he will my Lord, I warrant you, he will but offer and give me the power to take or leave.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: Trust me, were I a Lady, I could not like that man were bargain'd with before I choose him.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: But I am not built on such wild humours, if I find him worthy, he is not less because he's offer'd.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: 'Tis true, he is not, would he would seem less.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: I think there's no Lady can affect
Another Prince, your brother standing by;
He doth Eclipse mens vertues so with his.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: I know a Lady may, and more I fear
Another Lady will.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Would I might see him.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: Why so you shall, my businesses are great,
I will attend you when it is his pleasure to see you.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: I thank you good my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: You will be ready Madam.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: I do beseech you Madam, send away
Your other women, and receive from me
A few sad words, which set against your joyes
May make 'em shine the more.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Sirs, leave me all.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: I kneel a stranger here to beg a thing
