Unfit for me to ask, and you to grant,
'Tis such another strange ill-laid-request,
As if a begger should intreat a King
To leave his Scepter, and his Throne to him
And take his rags to wander o're the world
Hungry and cold.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: That were a strange request.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: As ill is mine.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Then do not utter it.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: Alas 'tis of that nature, that it must
Be utter'd, I, and granted, or I die:
I am asham'd to speak it; but where life
Lies at the stake, I cannot think her woman
prose: That will not take something unreasonably to hazard saying of it: I shall seem a strange Petitioner, that wish all ill to them I beg of, e're they give me ought; yet so I must: I would you were not fair, nor wise, for in your ill consists my good: if you were foolish, you would hear my prayer, if foul, you had not power to hinder me: he would not love you.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: What's the meaning of it.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: Nay, my request is more without the bounds
Of reason yet: for 'tis not in the power
Of you to do, what I would have you grant.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Why then 'tis idle, pray thee speak it out.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: Your brother brings a Prince into this land,
Of such a noble shape, so sweet a grace,
So full of worth withal, that every maid
That looks upon him, gives away her self
To him for ever; and for you to have
He brings him: and so mad is my demand
That I desire you not to have this man,
This excellent man, for whom you needs must die,
If you should miss him. I do now expect
You should laugh at me.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Trust me I could weep rather, for I have found
In all thy words a strange disjoynted sorrow.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: 'Tis by me his own desire so, that you would not love him.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: His own desire! why credit me Thalestris,
prose: I am no common wooer: if he shall wooe me, his worth may be such, that I dare not swear I will not love him; but if he will stay to have me wooe him, I will promise thee, he may keep all his graces to himself, and fear no ravishing from me.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
prose: 'Tis yet his own desire, but when he sees your face, I fear it will not be; therefore I charge you as you have pity, stop these tender ears from his enchanting voice, close up those eyes, that you may neither catch a dart from him, nor he from you; I charge you as you hope to live in quiet; for when I am dead, for certain I will walk to visit him if he break promise with me: for as fast as Oaths without a formal Ceremony can make me, I am to him.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Then be fearless;
For if he were a thing 'twixt God and man,
I could gaze on him; if I knew it sin
To love him without passion: Dry your eyes,
I swear you shall enjoy him still for me,
I will not hinder you; but I perceive
You are not what you seem, rise, rise Thalestris,
If your right name be so.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
prose: Indeed it is not, Spaconia is my name; but I desire not to be known to other.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Why, by me you shall not, I will never do you wrong, what good I can, I will, think not my birth or education such, that I should injure a stranger Virgin; you are welcome hither, in company you wish to be commanded, but when we are alone, I shall be ready to be your servant.
Come, come, run, run, run.
2 We shall out-go her.
One were better be hang'd than carry out women sidling to these shews.

speeches.speaker: Wom.
prose: Is the King hard by?
You heard he with the Bottles said, he thought we should come too late: What abundance of people here is?

speeches.speaker: Wom.
prose: But what had he in those Bottles?
I know not.
Why, Ink goodman fool.
Ink, what to do?
Why the King look you, will many times call for these Bottles, and break his mind to his friends.

speeches.speaker: Wom.
prose: Let's take our places, we shall have no room else.
The man told us he would walk o' foot through the people.
I marry did he.
Our shops are well look't to now.
'Slife, yonder's my Master, I think.
No 'tis not he.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
prose: Lord how fine the fields be, what sweet living 'tis in the Country!

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
prose: I poor souls, God help 'em; they live as contentedly as one of us.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
prose: My husbands Cousin would have had me gone into the Country last year, wert thou ever there?

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
prose: I, poor souls, I was amongst 'em once.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
prose: And what kind of creatures are they, for love of God?

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
prose: Very good people, God help 'em.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
prose: Wilt thou go down with me this Summer when I am brought to bed?

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
prose: Alas, it is no place for us.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
prose: Why, pray thee?

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
prose: Why you can have nothing there, there's no body cryes brooms.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
prose: No?

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
prose: No truly, nor milk.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
prose: Nor milk, how do they?

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
prose: They are fain to milk themselves i'th' Country.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
prose: Good Lord! but the people there, I think, will be very dutiful to one of us.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
prose:
I God knows will they, and yet they do not greatly
care for our husbands.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
prose:
Do they not? Alas! I'good faith I cannot blame ^em: for we do not greatly care for them our selves. Phi
^, I pray choose us a place.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
prose: There's the best forsooth.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
prose: By your leave good people a little.
What's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
prose: I pray you my friend, do not thrust my Mistress so, ^e's with Child.
Let her look to her self then, has she not had showing ^ough yet? if she stay shouldring here, she may haps go ^ome with a cake in her belly.
How now, goodman squitter breech, why do you lean ^n me?

speeches.speaker: Phi.
prose: Because I will.
Will you Sir sawce-box?

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
prose:
Look if one ha' not struck Philip, come hither
^hilip, why did he strike thee?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
prose: For leaning on him.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
prose: Why didst thou lean on him?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
prose: I did not think he would have struck me.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
prose: As God save me la thou'rt as wild as a Buck, there's ^o quarel but thou'rt at one end or other on't.
It's at the first end then, for he'l ne'r stay the last.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
prose: Well slip-string, I shall meet with you.
When you will.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
prose: I'le give a crown to meet with you.
At a Bawdy-house.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
prose: I you're full of your Roguery; but if I do meet you shall cost me a fall.
The King, the King, the King. Now, now, now, now.

speeches.speaker: All.
prose: God preserve your Majesty.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: I thank you all, now are my joyes at full, when I behold you safe, my loving Subjects; by you I grow, 'tis your united love that lifts me to this height: all the account ^hat I can render you for all the love you have bestowed on me, all your expences to maintain my war, is but a little word, you will imagine 'tis slender paiment, yet 'tis such a word, as is not to be bought but with your bloods, 'tis Peace.

speeches.speaker: All.
prose: God preserve your Majesty.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Now you may live securely i'your Towns,
Your Children round about you; may sit
Under your Vines, and make the miseries
Of other Kingdoms a discourse for you,
And lend them sorrows; for your selves, you may
Safely forget there are such things as tears,
And you may all whose good thoughts I have gain'd,
Hold me unworthy, where I think my life
A sacrifice too great to keep you thus
In such a calm estate.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: God bless your Majesty.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: See all good people, I have brought the man whose very name you fear'd, a captive home; behold him, 'tis Tigranes; in your heart sing songs of gladness, and deliverance.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
verse: Out upon him.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
verse: How he looks.

speeches.speaker: 3 Wom.
verse: Hang him, hang him.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: These are sweet people.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
prose: Sir, you do me wrong, to render me a scorned spectacle to common people.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: It was so far from me to mean it so: if I have ought deserv'd, my loving Subjects, let me beg of you, not to revile this Prince, in whom there dwells all worth of which the name of a man is capable, valour beyond compare, the terrour of his name has stretcht it self where ever there is sun; and yet for you I fought with him single, and won him too; I made his valour stoop, and brought that name soar'd to so unbeliev'd a height, to fall beneath mine: this inspir'd with all your loves, I did perform, and will for your content, be ever ready for a greater work.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: The Lord bless your Majesty.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
prose: So he has made me amends now with a speech in commendation of himself: I would not be so vain-glorious.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: If there be any thing in which I may
Do good to any creature, here speak out;
For I must leave you: and it troubles me,
That my occasions for the good of you,
Are such as call me from you: else, my joy
Would be to spend my days among you all.
You shew your loves in these large multitudes
That come to meet me, I will pray for you,
Heaven prosper you, that you may know old years,
And live to see your childrens children sit
At your boards with plenty: when there is
A want of any thing, let it be known
To me, and I will be a Father to you:
God keep you all.

speeches.speaker: All.
prose: God bless your Majesty, God bless your Majesty.
Come, shall we go? all's done.

speeches.speaker: Wom.
prose: I for God sake, I have not made a fire yet.
Away, away, all's done.
Content, farewel Philip.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
prose: Away you halter-sack you.
Philip will not fight, he's afraid on's face.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
prose: I marry am I afraid of my face.
Thou wouldst be Philip if thou sawst it in a glass; it looks so like a Visour.
Cit. you'l be hang'd sirra: Come Philip walk before us homewards; did not his Majesty say he had brought us home Pease for all our money?

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
prose: Yes marry did he.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
prose: They're the first I heard of this year by my troth, I longed for some of 'em: did he not say we should have some?

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
prose: Yes, and so we shall anon I warrant you have every one a peck brought home to our houses.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: MY Sister take it ill?

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: Not very ill,
Something unkindly she does take it Sir to have
Her Husband chosen to her hands.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Why Gobrias let her, I must have her know, my will and not her own must govern her: what will she marry with some slave at home?

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: O she is far from any stubbornness, you much mistake her, and no doubt will like where you would have her, but when you behold her, you will be loth to part with such a jewel.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: To part with her? why Gobrias, art thou mad? she is my Sister.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: Sir, I know she is: but it were pity to make poor our Land, with such a beauty to enrich another.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Pish will she have him?

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: I do hope she will not, I think she will Sir.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Were she my Father and my Mother too, and all the names for which we think folks friends, she should be forc't to have him when I know 'tis sit: I will not hear her say she's loth.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: Heaven bring my purpose luckily to pass, you know 'tis just, she will not need constraint she loves you so.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: How does she love me, speak?

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: She loves you more than people love their health, that live by labour; more than I could love a man that died for me, if he could live again.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: She is not like her mother then.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: O no, when you were in Armenia,
I durst not let her know when you were hurt:
For at the first on every little scratch,
She kept he^ Chamber, wept, and could not eat,
Till you were well, and many times the news
Was so long coming, that before we heard
She was as near her death, as you your health.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Alas poor soul, but yet she must be rul'd;
I know not how I shall requite her well.
I long to see her, have you sent for her,
To tell her I am ready?

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: Sir I have.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Sir, here is the Armenian King.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: He's welcome.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
prose: And the Queen mother, and the Princess wait without.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Good Gobrias bring 'em in.
Tigranes, you will think you are arriv'd
In a strange Land, where Mothers cast to poyson
Their only Sons; think you you shall be safe?

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Too safe I am Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ara.
verse: As low as this I bow to you, and would
As low as is my grave, to shew a mind
Thankful for all your mercies.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: O stand up,
And let me kneel, the light will be asham'd
To see observance done to me by you.

speeches.speaker: Ara.
verse: You are my King.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: You are my Mother, rise;
As far be all your faults from your own soul,
As from my memory; then you shall be
As white as innocence her self.

speeches.speaker: Ara.
verse: I came
Only to shew my duty, and acknowledge
My sorrows for my sins; longer to stay
Were but to draw eyes more attentively
Upon my shame, that power that kept you safe
From me, preserve you still.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Your own desires shall be your guide.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Now let me die, since I have seen my Lord the King
Return in safetie, I have seen all good that life
Can shew me; I have ne're another wish
For Heaven to grant, nor were it sit I should;
For I am bound to spend my age to come,
In giving thanks that this was granted me.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: Why does not your Majesty speak?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: To whom?

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: To the Princess.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Alas Sir, I am fearful, you do look
On me, as if I were some loathed thing
That you were finding out a way to slain.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: Sir, you should speak to her.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Ha?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: I know I am unworthy, yet not ill arm'd, with which innocence here I will kneel, till I am one with earth, but I will gain some words and kindness from you.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Will you speak Sir?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Speak, am I what I was?
What art thou that dost creep into my breast,
And dar'st not see my face? shew forth thy self:
I feel a pair of fiery wings displai'd
Hither, from hence; you shall not tarry there,
Up, and be gone, if thou beest Love be gone:
Or I will tear thee from my wounded breast,
Pull thy lov'd Down away, and with thy Quill
By this right arm drawn from thy wonted wing,
Write to thy laughing Mother i'thy bloud,
That you are powers bely'd, and all your darts
Are to be blown away, by men resolv'd,
Like dust; I know thou scar'st my words, away.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: O misery! why should he be so slow?
There can no falshood come of loving her;
Though I have given my saith; she is a thing
Both to be lov'd and serv'd beyond my faith:
I would he would present me to her quickly.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Will you not speak at all? are you so far
From kind words? yet to save my modesty,
That must talk till you answer, do not stand
As you were dumb, say something, though it be
Poyson'd with anger, that it may strike me dead.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Have you no life at all? for man-hood sake
Let her not kneel, and talk neglected thus;
A tree would find a tongue to answer her,
Did she but give it such a lov'd respect.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: You mean this Lady: list her from the earth; w^ do you let her kneel so long? Alas, Madam, your bea^ uses to command, and not to beg. What is your sute to me? it shall be granted, yet the time is short, and my affairs are great: but where's my Sister? I bade she should be brought

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: What, is he mad?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Gobrias, where is she?

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Where is she man?

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: Who, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Who, hast thou forgot my Sister?

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: Your Sister, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Your Sister, Sir? some one that hath a wit, answer, where is she?

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: Do you not see her there?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Where?

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: There.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: There, where?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: S'light, there, are you blind?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Which do you mean, that little one?

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: No Sir.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: No Sir? why, do you mock me? I can see
No other here, but that petitioning Lady.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: That's she.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Away.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: Sir, it is she.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: 'Tis false.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: Is it?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: As hell, by Heaven, as false as hell,
My Sister: is she dead? if it be so,
Speak boldly to me; for I am a man,
And dare not quarrel with Divinity;
And do not think to cozen me with this:
I see you all are mute and stand amaz'd,
Fearful to answer me; it is too true,
A decreed instant cuts off ev'ry life,
For which to mourn, is to repine; she dy'd
A Virgin, though more innocent than sheep,
As clear as her own eyes, and blessedness
Eternal waits upon her where she is:
I know she could not make a wish to change
Her state for new, and you shall see me bear
My crosses like a man; we all must die,
And she hath taught us how.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: Do not mistake,
And vex your self for nothing; for her death
Is a long life off, I hope: 'Tis she,
And if my speech deserve not faith, lay death
Upon me, and my latest words shall force
A credit from you.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Which, good Gobrias? that Lady dost thou mean?

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: That Lady Sir,
She is your Sister, and she is your Sister
That loves you so, 'tis she for whom I weep,
To see you use her thus.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: It cannot be.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Pish, this is tedious,
I cannot hold, I must present my self,
And yet the sight of my Spaconia
Touches me, as a sudden thunder-clap
Does one that is about to sin.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Away,
No more of this; here I pronounce him Traytor,
The direct plotter of my death, that names
Or thinks her for my Sister, 'tis a lie,
The most malicious of the world, invented
To mad your King; he that will say so next,
Let him draw out his sword and sheath it here.
It is a sin fully as pardonable:
She is no kin to me, nor shall she be;
If she were ever, I create her none:
And which of you can question this? My power
Is like the Sea, that is to be obey'd,
And not disputed with: I have decreed her
As far from having part of blood with me,
As the nak'd Indians; come and answer me,
He that is boldest now; is that my Sister?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: O this is fine.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: No marry, she is not, an't please your Majesty, I never thought she was, she's nothing like you.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: No 'tis true, she is not.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Thou shou'dst be hang'd.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Sir, I will speak but once; by the same power
You make my blood a stranger unto yours,
You may command me dead, and so much love
A stranger may importune, pray you do;
If this request appear too much to grant,
Adopt me of some other Family,
By your unquestion'd word; else I shall live
Like sinfull issues that are left in streets
By their regardless Mothers, and no name
Will be found for me.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: I will hear no more,
Why should there be such musick in a voyce,
And sin for me to hear it? All the world
May take delight in this, and 'tis damnation
For me to do so: You are fair and wise
And vertuous I think, and he is blest
That is so near you as my brother is;
But you are nought to me but a disease;
Continual torment without hope of ease;
Such an ungodly sickness I have got,
That he that undertakes my cure, must first
O'rethrow Divinity, all moral Laws,
And leave mankind as unconfin'd as beasts,
Allowing 'em to do all actions
As freely as they drink when they desire.
Let me not hear you speak again; yet see
I shall but langish for the want of that,
The having which, would kill me: No man here
Offer to speak for her; for I consider
As much as you can say; I will not toil
My body and my mind too, rest thou there,
Here's one within will labour for you both.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: I would I were past speaking.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: Fear not Madam,
The King will alter, 'tis some sudden rage,
And you shall see it end some other way.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Pray heaven it do.

speeches.speaker: Tig.
verse: Though she to whom I swore, be here, I cannot
Stifle my passion longer; if my father
Should rise again disquieted with this,
And charge me to forbear, yet it would out.
Madam, a stranger, and a pris'ner begs
To be bid welcome.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: You are welcome, Sir,
I think, but if you be not, 'tis past me
To make you so: for I am here a stranger,
Greater than you; we know from whence you come,
But I appear a lost thing, and by whom
Is yet uncertain, found here i'th' Court,
And onely suffer'd to walk up and down,
As one not worth the owning.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: O, I fear
Tigranes will be caught, he looks, me-thinks,
As he would change his eyes with her; some help
There is above for me, I hope.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Why do you turn away, and weep so fast,
And utter things that mis-become your looks,
Can you want owning?

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: O 'tis certain so.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Acknowledge your self mine.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: How now?

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: And then see if you want an owner.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: They are talking.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Nations shall owne you for their Queen.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Tigranes, art not thou my prisoner?

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: I am.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: And who is this?

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: She is your Sister.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: She is so.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Is she so again? that's well.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: And then how dare you offer to change words with her?

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Dare do it! Why? you brought me hither Sir,
To that intent.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Perhaps I told you so,
If I had sworn it, had you so much folly
To credit it? The least word that she speaks
Is worth a life; rule your disordered tongue,
Or I will temper it.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: Blest be the breath.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Temper my tongue! such incivilities
As these, no barbarous people ever knew:
You break the lawes of Nature, and of Nations,
You talk to me as if I were a prisoner
For theft: my tongue be temper'd? I must speak
If thunder check me, and I will.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: You will?

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: Alas my fortune.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Do not fear his frown, dear Madam, hear me.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Fear not my frown? but that 'twere base in me
To sight with one I know I can o'recome,
Again thou shouldst be conquer'd by me.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: He has one ransome with him already; me-thinks
'T were good to fight double, or quit.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Away with him to prison: Now Sir, see
If my frown be regardless; Why delay you?
Seise him Bacurius, you shall know my word
Sweeps like a wind, and all it grapples with,
Are as the chaffe before it.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Touch me not.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Help there.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Away.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: It is in vain to struggle.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: You must be forc'd.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Sir, you must pardon us, we must obey.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Why do you dally there? drag him away
By any thing.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Come Sir.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Justice, thou ought'st to give me strength enough
To shake all these off; This is tyrannie,
Arbaces, sutler than the burning Bulls,
Or that fam'd Titans bed. Thou mightst as well
Search i'th' deep of Winter through the snow
For half starv'd people, to bring home with thee,
To shew 'em fire, and send 'em back again,
As use me thus.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Let him be close, Bacurius.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: I ne're rejoyc'd at any ill to him,
But this imprisonment: what shall become
Of me forsaken?

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: You will not let your Sister
Depart thus discontented from you, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: By no means Gobrias, I have done her wrong,
And made my self believe much of my self,
That is not in me: You did kneel to me,
Whilest I stood stubborn and regardless by,
And like a god incensed, gave no ear
To all your prayers: behold, I kneel to you,
Shew a contempt as large as was my own,
And I will suffer it, yet at the last forgive me.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: O you wrong me more in this,
Than in your rage you did: you mock me now.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Never forgive me then, which is the worst
Can happen to me.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: If you be in earnest,
Stand up and give me but a gentle look,
And two kind words, and I shall be in heaven.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Rise you then to hear; I acknowledge thee
My hope, the only jewel of my life,
The best of Sisters, dearer than my breath,
A happiness as high as I could think;
And when my actions call thee otherwise,
Perdition light upon me.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: This is better
Than if you had not frown'd, it comes to me,
Like mercie at the block, and when I leave
To serve you with my life, your curse be with me.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Then thus I do salute thee, and again,
To make this knot the stronger, Paradise
Is there: It may be you are yet in doubt,
This third kiss blots it out, I wade in sin,
And foolishly intice my self along;
Take her away, see her a prisoner
In her own chamber closely, Gobrias.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Alas Sir, why?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: I must not stay the answer, doe it.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: Good Sir.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: No more, doe it I say.

speeches.speaker: Mard.
verse: This is better and better.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Yet hear me speak.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: I will not hear you speak,
Away with her, let no man think to speak
For such a creature; for she is a witch,
A prisoner, and a Traitor.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: Madam, this office grieves me.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Nay, 'tis well the king is pleased with it.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Bessus, go you along too with her; I will prove
All this that I have said, if I may live
So long; but I am desperately sick,
For she has given me poison in a kiss;
She had't betwixt her lips, and with her eyes
She witches people: go without a word.
Why should you that have made me stand in war
Like sate it self, cutting what threds I pleas'd,
Decree such an unworthy end of me,
And all my glories? What am I, alas,
That you oppose me? if my secret thoughts
Have ever harbour'd swellings against you,
They could not hurt you, and it is in you
To give me sorrow, that will render me
Apt to receive your mercy; rather so,
Let it be rather so, than punish me
With such unmanly sins: Incest is in me
Dwelling already, and it must be holy
That pulls it thence, where art Mardonius

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Here Sir.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: I pray thee bear me, if thou canst,
Am I not grown a strange weight?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: As you were.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: No heavier?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: No Sir.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Why, my legs
Refuse to bear my body; O Mardonius,
Thou hast in field beheld me, when thou knowst
I could have gone, though I could never run.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: And so I shall again.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: O no, 'tis past.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Pray you go rest your self.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Wilt thou hereafter when they talk of me,
As thou shalt hear nothing but infamy,
Remember some of those things?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Yes I will.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: I pray thee do: for thou shalt never see me so again.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: They talk of fame, I have gotten it in the wars; and will afford any man a reasonable penny-worth: some will say, they could be content to have it, but that it is to be atchiev'd with danger; but my opinion is otherwise: for if I might stand still in Cannon proof, and have same fall upon me, I would refuse it: my reputation came principally by thinking to run away, which no body knows but Mardonius, and I think he conceals it to anger me. Before I went to the warrs, I came to the Town a young fellow, without means or parts to deserve friends; and my empty guts perswaded me to lie, and abuse people for my meat, which I did, and they heat me: then would I fast two days, till my hunger cri'd out on me, rail still, then me thought I had a monstrous stomach to abuse 'em again, and did it. I, this state I continu'd till they hung me up by th' heels, and beat me wi' hatle sticks, as if they would have baked me, and have cons^n'd some body wi'me for Venison: After this I rail'd, and ^at quietly: for the whole Kingdom took notice of me for a bastl'd whipt fellow, and what I said was remembred in mirth but never in anger, of which I was glad; I would it were at that pass again. After this, heaven calls an Aunt of mine, that left two hundred pound in a cousins hand for me, who taking me to be a gallant young spirit, raised a company for me with the money and sent me into Armonia with'em: Away I would have run from them, but that I could get no company, and alone I durst not run. I was never at battail but once, and there I was running, but Mardonius cudgel'd me; yet I got loose at last, but was so fraid, that I saw no more than my shoulders doe, but fled with my whole com~pany amongst my Enemies, and overthrew'em: Now the report of my valour is come over before me, and they say I was a raw young fellow, but now I am improv'd, a Plague on their eloquence, 't will cost me many a beating; And Mardonius might help this too, if he would; for now they think to get honour on me, and all the men I have abus'd call me freshly worthily, as they call it by the way of challenge.

speeches.speaker: 3 Gent.
prose: Good morrow, Captain Bessus.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Good morrow Sir.

speeches.speaker: 3 Gent.
prose: I come to speak with you.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: You're very welcome.

speeches.speaker: 3 Gent.
prose: From one that holds himself wrong'd by you some three years since: your worth he says is fam'd, and he doth nothing doubt but you will do him right, as beseems a souldier.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: A pox on'em, so they cry all.

speeches.speaker: 3 Gent.
prose: And a slight note I have about me for you, for the delivery of which you must excuse me; it is an office that friendship calls upon me to do, and no way offensive to you; since I desire but right on both sides.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: 'Tis a challenge Sir, is it not?

speeches.speaker: 3 Gent.
prose: 'Tis an inviting to the field.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: An inviting? O Sir your Mercy, what a Complement he delivers it with? he might as agreeable to my nature present me poison with such a speech: um um um reputation, um um um call you to account, um um um forc'd to this, um um um with my Sword, um um um like a Gentleman, um um um dear to me, um um um satisfaction: 'Tis very well Sir, I do accept it, but he must await an answer this thirteen weeks.

speeches.speaker: 3 Gent.
prose: Why Sir, he would be glad to wipe off his stain as soon as he could.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Sir upon my credit I am already ingag'd to two hundred, and twelve, all which must have their stains wip'd off, if that be the word, before him.

speeches.speaker: 3 Gent.
prose: Sir, if you be truly ingag'd but to one, he shall stay a competent time.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Upon my faith Sir, to two hundred and twelve, and I have a spent body, too much bruis'd in battel, so that I cannot fight, I must be plain, above three combats a day: All the kindness I can shew him, is to set him resolvedly in my rowle, the two hundred and thirteenth man, which is something, for I tell you, I think there will be more after him, than before him, I think so; pray you commend me to him, and tell him this.

speeches.speaker: 3 Gent.
prose: I will Sir, good morrow to you.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Good morrow good Sir. Certainly my safest way were to print my self a coward, with a discovery how I came by my credit, and clap it upon every post; I have received above thirty challenges within this two hours, marry all but the first I put off with ingagement, and by good fortune, the first is no madder of fighting than I, so that that's referred, the place where it must be ended, is four days journey off, and our arbitratours are these: He has chosen a Gentleman in travel, and I have a special friend with a quartain ague, like to hold him this five years, for mine: and when his man comes home, we are to expect my friends health: If they would finde me challenges thus thick, as long as I liv'd, I would have no other living; I can make seven shillings a day o'th' paper to the Grocers: yet I learn nothing by all these but a little skill in comparing of stiles. I do finde evidently, that there is some one Scri^ener in this Town, that has a great hand in writing of Challenges, for they are all of a cut, and six of 'em in a hand; and they all end, my reputation is dear to me, and I must require satisfaction. Who's there? more paper I hope, no, 'tis my Lord Bacurius, I fear all is not well betwixt us.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Now Captain Bessus, I come about a frivolous matter, caus'd by as idle a report: you know you were a coward.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Very right.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: And wronged me.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: True my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: But now people will call you valiant, desertlesly I think, yet for their satisfaction, I will have you sight with me.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: O my good Lord, my deep Engagements.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Tell not me of your Engagements, Captain Bessus, it is not to be put off with an excuse: for my own part, I am none of the multitude that believe your conversion from Coward.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: My Lord, I seek not Quarrels, and this belongs not to me, I am not to maintain it.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Who then pray?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Bessus the Coward wrong'd you.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Right.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: And shall Bessus the Valiant, maintain what Bessus the Coward did?

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: I pray thee leave these cheating tricks, I swear thou shalt fight with me, or thou shalt be beaten extreamly, and kick'd.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Since you provoke me thus far, my Lord, I will fight with you, and by my Sword it shall cost me twenty pound, but I will have my Leg well a week sooner purposely.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Your Leg? Why, what ailes your Leg? i'le do a cure on you, stand up.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: My Lord, this is not Noble in you.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: What dost thou with such a phrase in thy mouth? I will kick thee out of all good words before I leave thee.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: My Lord, I take this as a punishment for the offence I did when I was a Coward.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: When thou wert? Confess thy self a Coward still, or by this light, I'le beat thee into Spunge.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Why I am one.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Are you so Sir? And why do you wear a Sword then? Come unbuckle.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: My Lord.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Unbuckle I say, and give it me, or as I live, thy head will ake extreamly.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: It is a pretty Hilt, and if your Lordship take an affection to it, with all my heart I present it to you for a New-years gift.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: I thank you very heartily, sweet Captain, farewel.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: One word more, I beseech your Lordship to render me my knife again.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Marry by all means Captain; cherish your self with it, and eat hard, good Captain; we cannot tell whether we shall have any more such: Adue dear Captain.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: I will make better use of this, than of my Sword: A base spirit has this vantage of a brave one, it keeps alwayes at a stay, nothing brings it down, not beating. I remember I promis'd the King in a great Audience, that I would make my back-biters eat my sword to a knife; how to get another sword I know not, nor know any means left for me to maintain my credit, but impudence: therefore I will out-swear him and all his followers, that this is all that's left uneaten of my sword.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
I'le move the King, he is most strangely alter'd; I guess the cause I fear too right, Heaven has some secret end in't, and 'tis a scourge no question justly laid upon him: he has followed me through twenty Rooms; and ever when I stay to wait his command, he blushes like a Girl, and looks upon me, as if modesty kept in his business: so turns away from me, but if I go on, he follows me again.
See, here he is. I do not use this, yet I know not how, I cannot chuse but weep to see him; his very Enemies I think, whose wounds have bred his fame, if they should see him now, would find tears i'their eyes.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: I cannot utter it, why should I keep
A breast to harbour thoughts? I dare not speak.
Darkness is in my bosom, and there lie
A thousand thoughts that cannot brook the light:
How wilt thou vex'em when this deed is done,
Conscience, that art afraid to let me name it?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: How do you Sir?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Why very well Mardonius, how dost thou do?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Better than you I fear.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: I hope thou art; for to be plain with thee,
Thou art in Hell else, secret scorching flames
That far transcend earthly material fires
Are crept into me, and there is no cure.
Is it not strange Mardonius, there's no cure?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Sir, either I mistake, or there is something hid That you would utter to me.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: So there is, but yet I cannot do it.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Out with it Sir, if it be dangerous, I will not shrink to do you service, I shall not esteem my life a weightier matter than indeed it is, I know it is subject to more chances than it has hours, and I were better lose it in my Kings cause, than with an ague, or a fall, or sleeping, to a Thief; as all these are probable enough: let me but know what I shall do for you.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: It will not out: were you with Gobrias,
And bad him give my Sister all content
The place affords, and give her leave to send
And speak to whom she please?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Yes Sir, I was.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: And did you to Bacurius say as much About Tigranes?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: That's all my business.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: O say not so,
You had an answer of this before;
Besides I think this business might
Be utter'd more carelesly.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Come thou shalt have it out, I do beseech thee
By all the love thou hast profest to me,
To see my Sister from me.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Well, and what?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: That's all.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: That's strange, I shall say nothing to her?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Not a word;
But if thou lovest me, find some subtil way
To make her understand by signs.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: But what shall I make her understand?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: O Mardonius, for that I must be pardon'd.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: You may, but I can only see her then.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: 'Tis true;
Bear her this Ring then, and
One more advice, thou shalt speak to her:
Tell her I do love My kindred all: wilt thou?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Is there no more?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: O yes and her the best;
Better than any Brother loves his Sister: That's all.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Methinks this need not have been delivered with such a caution; I'le do it.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: There is more yet,
Wilt thou be faithul to me?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Sir, if I take upon me to deliver it, after I hear it,
I'le pass through fire to do it.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: I love her better than a Brother ought;
Dost thou conceive me?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I hope you do not Sir.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: No, thou art dull, kneel down before her,
And ne'r rise again, till she will love me.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Why, I think she does.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: But better than she does, another way;
As wives love Husbands.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Why, I think there are few Wives that love their Husbands better than she does you.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Thou wilt not understand me: is it sit
This should be uttered plainly? take it then
Naked as it is: I would desire her love
Lasciviously, lewdly, incestuously,
To do a sin that needs must damn us both,
And thee too: dost thou understand me now?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Yes, there's your Ring again; what have I done
Dishonestly in my whole life, name it,
That you should put so base a business to me?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Didst thou not tell me thou wouldst do it?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Yes; if I undertook it, but if all
My hairs were lives, I would not be engag'd
In such a case to save my last life.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: O guilt! ha how poor and weak a thing art thou?
This man that is my servant, whom my breath
Might blow upon the world, might beat me here
Having this cause, whil'st I prest down with sin
Could not resist him: hear Mardonius,
It was a motion mis-beseeming man,
And I am sorry for it.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Heaven grant you may be so: you must understand, nothing that you can utter, can remove my love and service from my Prince. But otherwise, I think I shall not love you more. For you are sinful, and if you do this crime, you ought to have no Laws. For after this, it will be great injustice in you to punish any offender for any crime. For my self I find my heart too big: I feel I have not patience to look on whilst you run these forbidden courses. Means I have none but your favour, and I am rather glad that I shall lose 'em both together, than keep 'em with such conditions; I shall find a dwelling amongst some people, where though our Garments perhaps be cours^, we shall be richer far within, and harbour no such vices in 'em: the Gods preserve you, and mend.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Mardonius, stay Mardonius, for though
My present state requires nothing but knaves
To be about me, such as are prepar'd
For every wicked act, yet who does know
But that my loathed Fate may turn about,
And I have use for honest men again?
I hope I may, I prethee leave me not.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: Where is the King?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: There.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: An't please your Majesty, there's the knife.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: What knife?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: The Sword is eaten.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Away you fool, the King is serious,
And cannot now admit your vanities.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Vanities! I'me no honest man, if my enemies have not brought it to this, what, do you think I lie?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: No, no, 'tis well Bessus, 'tis very well I'm glad on't.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: If your enemies brought it to this, your enemies are Cutlers, come leave the King.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: Why, may not valour approach him?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Yes, but he has affairs, depart, or I shall be something unmannerly with you.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: No, let him stay Mardonius, let him stay,
I have occasion with him very weighty,
And I can spare you now.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Sir?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Why I can spare you now.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: Mardonius give way to these State affairs.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Indeed you are fitter for this present purpose.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Bessus, I should imploy thee, wilt thou do't?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Do't for you? by this Air I will do any thing without exception, be it a good, bad, or indifferent thing.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Do not swear.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: By this light but I will, any thing whatsoever.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: But I shall name the thing,
Thy Conscience will not suffer thee to do.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: I would fain hear that thing.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Why I would have thee get my Sister for me?
Thou understandst me, in a wicked manner.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: O you would have a bout with her?
I'le do't, I'le do't, I'saith.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Wilt thou, do'st thou make no more on't?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: More? no, why is there any thing else? if there be, it shall be done too.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Hast thou no greater sense of such a sin?
Thou art too wicked for my company,
Though I have hell within me, thou may'st yet
Corrupt me further: pray thee answer me,
How do I shew to thee after this motion?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Why your Majesty looks as well in my opinion, as ever you did since you were born.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: But thou appear'st to me after thy grant,
The ugliest, loathed detestable thing
That I ever met with. Thou hast eyes
Like the flames of Sulphur, which me thinks do dart
Infection on me, and thou hast a mouth
Enough to take me in where there do stand
Four rows of Iron Teeth.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: I feel no such thing, but 'tis no matter how I look, I'le do my business as well as they that look better, and when this is dispatch'd, if you have a mind to your Mother, tell me, and you shall see I'le set it hard.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: My Mother! Heaven forgive me to hear this,
I am inspir'd with horrour: now I hate thee
Worse than my sin, which if I could come by
Should suffer death Eternal ne're to rise
In any breast again. Know I will die
Languishing mad, as I resolve, I shall,
E're I will deal by such an instrument:
Thou art too sinful to imploy in this;
Out of the World, away.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: What do you mean, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Hung round with Curses, take thy fearful slight
Into the Desarts, where 'mongst all the Monsters
If thou find'st one so beastly as thy self,
Thou shalt be held as innocent.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: Good Sir.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: If there were no such instruments as thou,
We Kings could never act such wicked deeds:
Seek out a man that mocks Divinity,
That breaks each precept both of God and man,
And natures too, and does it without lust,
Meerly because it is a law, and good,
And live with him: for him thou canst not spoil.
Away I say, I will not do this sin.
I'le press it here, till it do break my breast,
It heaves to get out, but thou art a sin,
And spight of torture I will keep thee in.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: HAve you written Madam?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Yes, good Gobrias.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: And with a kindness, and such winning words
As may provoke him, at one instant feel
His double fault, your wrong, and his own rashness?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: I have sent words enough, if words may win him
From his displeasure; and such words I hope,
As shall gain much upon his goodness, Gobrias.
Yet fearing they are many, and a womans,
A poor belief may follow, I have woven
As many truths within 'em to speak for me,
That if he be but gracious, and receive 'em—

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: Good Lady be not fearful, though he should not
Give you your present end in this, believe it,
You shall feel, if your vertue can induce you
To labour on't, this tempest which I know,
Is but a poor proof 'gainst your patience:
All those contents, your spirit will arrive at,
Newer and sweeter to you; your Royal brother,
When he shall once collect himself, and see
How far he has been asunder from himself;
What a meer stranger to his golden temper:
Must from those roots of vertue, never dying,
Though somewhat stopt with humour, shoot again
^nto a thousand glories, bearing his fair branches
High as our hopes can look at, straight as justice,
^oaden with ripe contents; he loves you dearly,
^ know it, and I hope I need not farther
Win you to understand it.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: I believe it.
But howsoever, I am sure I love him dearly:
So dearly, that if any thing I write
For my enlarging should beget his anger,
Heaven be a witness with me and my faith,
^ had rather live intomb'd here.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: You shall not feel a worse stroke than your grief,
I am sorry 'tis so sharp, I kiss your hand,
And this night will deliver this true story,
With this hand to your Brother.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Peace go with you, you are a good man.
My Spaconia, why are you ever sad thus?

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: O dear Lady.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Prethee discover not a way to sadness,
Nearer than I have in me, our two sorrows
Work like two eager Hawks, who shall get highest;
How shall I lessen thine? for mine I fear
Is easier known than cur'd.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: Heaven comfort both,
And give you happy ends, however I
Fall in my stubborn fortunes.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: This but teaches
How to be more familiar with our sorrows,
That are too much our masters: good Spaconia
How shall I do you service?

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: Noblest Lady,
You make me more a slave still to your goodness,
And only live to purchase thanks to pay you,
For that is all the business of my life: now
I will be bold, since you will have it so,
To ask a noble favour of you.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Speak it, 'tis yours, for from so sweet a vertue,
No ill demand has issue.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: Then ever vertuous, let me beg your will
In helping me to see the Prince Tigranes,
With whom I am equal prisoner, if not more.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Reserve me to a greater end Spaconia;
Bacurius cannot want so much good manners
As to deny your gentle visitation,
Though you came only with your own command.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: I know they will deny me gracious Madam,
Being a stranger, and so little fam'd,
So utter empty of those excellencies
That tame Authority; but in you sweet Lady,
All these are natural; beside, a power
Deriv'd immediate from your Royal brother,
Whose least word in you may command the Kingdom.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: More than my word Spaconia, you shall carry,
For fear it fail you.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: Dare you trust a Token?
Madam I fear I am grown too bold a begger.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: You are a pretty one, and trust me Lady
It joyes me, I shall do a good to you,
Though to my self I never shall be happy:
Here, take this Ring, and from me as a Token
Deliver it; I think they will not stay you:
So all your own desires go with you Lady.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: And sweet peace to your Grace.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Pray Heaven I find it.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Fool that I am, I have undone my self,
And with my own hand turn'd my fortune round,
That was a fair one: I have childishly
Plaid with my hope so long, till I have broke it,
And now too late I mourn for't; O Spaconia!
Thou hast found an even way to thy revenge now,
Why didst thou follow me like a faint shadow,
To wither my desires? But wretched fool,
Why did I plant thee 'twixt the Sun and me,
To make me freeze thus? Why did I prefer her
To the fair Princess? O thou fool, thou fool,
Thou family of tools, live like a slave still,
And in thee bear thine own hell and thy torment,
Thou hast deserv'd: Couldst thou find no Lady
But she that has thy hopes to put her to,
And hazard all thy peace? None to abuse,
But she that lov'd thee ever? poor Spaconia,
And so much lov'd thee, that in honesty
And honour thou art bound to meet her vertues:
She that forgot the greatness of her grief
And miseries, that must follow such mad passions,
Endless and wild as women; she that for thee
And with thee lest her liberty, her name,
And Country, you have paid me equal, Heavens,
And sent my own rod to correct me with;
A woman: for inconstancy I'le suffer,
Lay it on justice, till my soul melt in me
For my unmanly, beastly, sudden doting
Upon a new face: after all my oaths
Many and strange ones,
I feel my old fire flame again and burn
So strong and violent, that should I see her
Again, the grief and that would kill me.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Lady, your token I acknowledge, you may pass;
There is the King.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: I thank your Lordship for it.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: She comes, she comes, shame hide me ever from her,
Would I were buried, or so far remov'd
Light might not find me out, I dare not see her.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: Nay never hide your self; or were you hid
Where earth hides all her riches, near her Center;
My wrongs without more day would light me to you:
I must speak e're I die; were all your greatness
Doubled upon you, y'are a perjur'd man,
And only mighty in your wickedness
Of wronging women. Thou art false, false Prince;
I live to see it, poor Spaconia lives
To tell thee thou art false; and then no more;
She lives to tell thee thou art more unconstant,
Than all ill women ever were together.
Thy faith is firm as raging over-flowes,
That no bank can command; as lasting
As boyes gay bubbles, blown i'th' Air and broken:
The wind is sixt to thee: and sooner shall
The beaten Mariner with his shrill whistle
Calm the loud murmur of the troubled main,
And strike it smooth again; than thy soul fall
To have peace in love with any: Thou art all
That all good men must hate; and if thy story
Shall tell succeeeding ages what thou wert,
O let it spare me in it, lest true lovers
In pity of my wrong, burn thy black Legend,
And with their curses, shake thy sleeping ashes.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Oh! oh!

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: The destinies, I hope, have pointed out
Our ends, that thou maist die for love,
Though not for me; for this assure thy self,
The Princess hates thee deadly, and will sooner
Be won to marry with a Bull, and safer
Than such a beast as thou art: I have struck,
I fear, too deep; beshrow me sor't; Sir,
This sorrow works me like a cunning friendship,
Into the same piece with it; 'tis asham'd,
Alas, I have been too rugged: Dear my Lord,
I am sorry I have spoken any thing,
Indeed I am, that may add more restraint
To that too much you have: good Sir, be pleas'd
To think it was a fault of love, not malice;
And do as I will do, forgive it Prince.
I do, and can forgive the greatest sins
To me you can repent of; pray believe.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: O my Spaconia! O thou vertuous woman!

speeches.speaker: Spa.
verse: Nay, more, the King Sir.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Have you been carefull of our noble Prisoner,
That he want nothing sitting for his greatness?

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: I hope his grace will quit me for my care Sir.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: 'Tis well, royal Tigranes, health.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: More than the strictness of this place can give Sir, I offer back again to great Arbaces.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: We thank you worthy Prince, and pray excuse us,
We have not seen you since your being here,
I hope your noble usage has been equall
With your own person: your imprisonment,
If it be any, I dare say is easie,
And shall not last too dayes.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: I thank you;
My usage here has been the same it was,
Worthy a royal Conqueror. For my restraint,
It came unkindly, because much unlook'd for;
But I must bear it.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: What Lady's that? Bacurius?

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: One of the Princess women, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: I fear'd it, why comes she hither?

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: To speak with the Prince Tigranes.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: From whom, Bacurius?

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: From the Princess, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: I knew I had seen her.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: His sit begins to take him now again,
'Tis a strange Feaver, and 'twill shake us all anon, I fear,
Would he were well cur'd of this raging folly:
Give me the warrs, where men are mad, and may talk what they list, and held the bravest fellows; This pelting prating peace is good for nothing: drinking's a vertue to't.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: I see there's truth in no man, nor obedience,
But for his own ends, why did you let her in?

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: It was your own command to barr none from him,
Besides, the Princess sent her ring Sir, for my warrant.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: A token to Tigranes, did she not?
Sir tell truth.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: I do not use to lie Sir,
'Tis no way I eat or live by, and I think,
This is no token Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: This combat has undone him: if he had been well beaten, he had been temperate; I shall never see him handsome again, till he have a Horse mans staffe yok'd thorow his shoulders, or an arm broken with a bullet.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: I am trifled with.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Sir?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: I know it, as I know thee to be false.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Now the clap comes.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: You never knew me so, Sir I dare speak it,
And durst a worse man tell me, though my better—

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: 'Tis well said, by my soul.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Sirra, you answer as you had no life.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: That I fear Sir to lose nobly.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: I say Sir, once again.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: You may say what yon please, Sir,
Would I might do so.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: I will, Sir, and say openly, this woman carries letters,
By my life I know she carries letters, this woman does it.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Would Bessus were here to take her aside and search her, He would quickly tell you what she carried Sir.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: I have found it out, this woman carries letters.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: If this hold, 'twill be an ill world for Bawdes, Chamber-maids and Post-boyes, I thank heaven I have none but his letters patents, things of his own enditing.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Prince, this cunning cannot do't.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Doe, What Sir? I reach you not.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: It shall not serve your turn, Prince.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Serve my turn Sir?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: I Sit, it shall not serve your turn.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Be plainer, good Sir.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: This woman shall carry no more letters back to your Love Pa^thea, by Heaven she shall not, I say she shall not.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: This would make a Saint swear like a souldier.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
prose: This beats me more, King, than the blow^ you gave me.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Take'em away both, and together let them prisoners be, strictly and closely kept, or Sirra, your life shall answe^ it, and let no body speak with'em hereafter.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
verse: Well, I am subject to you,
And must indure these passions:
This is the imprisonment I have look'd for always.
And the dearer place I would choose.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Sir, you have done well now.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Dare you reprove it?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: You must be crossing me.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I have no letters Sir to anger you,
But a dry sonnet of my Corporals
To an old Suttlers wife, and that I'll burn, Sir.
'Tis like to prove a fine age for the Ignorant.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: How darst thou so often forfeit thy life?
Thou know'st 'tis in my power to take it.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Yes, and I know you wo'not, or if you doe, you'll miss it quickly.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Why?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Who shall tell you of these childish sollies
When I am dead? who shall put to his power
To draw those vertues out of a flood of humors,
When they are drown'd, and make'em shine again?
No, cut my head off:
Then you may talk, and be believed, and grow worse,
And have your too self glorious temper rot
Into a deep sleep, and the Kingdom with you,
Till forraign swords be in your throats, and slaughter
Be every where about you like your slatterers.
Do, kill me.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Prethee be tamer, good Mardonius,
Thou know'st I love thee, nay I honour thee,
Believe it good old Souldier, I am thine;
But I am rack'd clean from my self, bear with me,
Woot thou bear with me my Mardonius?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: There comes a good man, love him too, he's temperate,
You may live to have need of such a vertue,
Rage is not still in fashion.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Welcome good Gobrias.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: My service and this letter to your Grace.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: From whom?

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: From the rich Mine of vertue and beauty,
Your mournfull Sister.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: She is in prison, Gobrias, is she not?

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: She is Sir, till your pleasure to enlarge her,
Which on my knees I beg. Oh 'tis not fit,
That all the sweetness of the world in one,
The youth and vertue that would tame wild Tygers,
And wilder people, that have known no manners,
Should live thus cloistred up; for your loves sake,
If there be any in that noble heart,
To her a wretched Lady, and forlorn,
Or for her love to you, which is as much
As nature and obedience ever gave,
Have pity on her beauties.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Pray thee stand up; 'Tis true, she is too fair,
And all these commendations but her own,
Would thou had'st never so commended her,
Or I nere liv'd to have heard it Gobrias;
If thou but know'st the wrong her beautie does her,
Thou wouldst in pity of her be a lyar,
Thy ignorance has drawn me wretched man,
Whither my self nor thou canst well tell: O my fate!
I think she loves me, but I fear another
Is deeper in her heart: How thinkst thou Gobrias?

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: I do beseech your Grace believe it not,
For let me perish if it be not false. Good Sir, read her Letter.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose:
This Love, or what a devil it is I know not, begets more mischief than a Wake. I had rather be well beaten, starv'd, or lowsie, than live within the Air on't. He that
had seen this brave fellow Charge through a grove of Pikes ^ut t'other day, and look upon him now, will ne'r believe ^is eyes again: if he continue thus but two days more, a Taylor may beat him with one hand tied behind him.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Alas, she would be at liberty.
And there bo a thousand reasons Gobrias,
Thousands that will deny't:
Which if she knew, she would contentedly
Be where she is: and bless her vertues for it,
And me, though she were closer, she would, Gobrias,
Good man indeed she would.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: Then good Sir, for her satisfaction,
Send for her and with reason make her know
Why she must live thus from you.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: I will; go bring her to me.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: Y'are very welcome both; some stools boy,
And reach a Table; Gentlemen o'th' Sword,
Pray sit without more complement; be gone child.
I have been curious in the searching of you,
Because I understand you wise and valiant persons.
We understand our selves Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: Nay Gentlemen, and dear friends o'th' Sword,
No complement I pray, but to the cause
I hang upon, which in few, is my honour.
You cannot hang too much Sir, for your honour,
But to your cause.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: Be wise, and speak truth, my first doubt is,
My beating by my Prince.
Stay there a little Sir, do you doubt a beating?
Or have you had a beating by your Prince?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: Gentlemen o'th' Sword, my Prince has beaten me.
Brother, what think you of this case?
If he has beaten him, the case is clear.
If he have beaten him, I grant the case;
But how? we cannot be too subtil in this business,
I say, but how?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: Even with his Royal hand.
Was it a blow of love, or indignation?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: 'Twas twenty blows of indignation, Gentlemen,
Besides two blows o'th' face.
Those blows o'th' face have made a new cause on't,
The rest were but an horrible rudeness.

prose: Two blows o'th' face, and given by a worse man, I must confess, as the Sword-men say, had turn'd the business: Mark me brother, by a worse man; but being by his Prince, had they been ten, and those ten drawn teeth, besides the hazard of his nose for ever; all this had been but favours: this is my flat opinion, which I'le die in.

The King may do much Captain, believe it; for had he crackt your Scull through, like a bottle, or broke a Rib or two with tossing of you, yet you had lost no honour: This is strange you may imagine, but this is truth now Captain.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: I will be glad to embrace it Gentlemen;
But how far may he strike me?

prose: There is another: a new cause rising from the time and distance, in which I will deliver my opinion: he may strike, beat, or cause to be beaten: for these are natural to man: your Prince, I say, may beat you, so far forth as his dominion reacheth, that's for the distance; the time, ten miles a day, I take it.

verse: Brother, you err, 'tis fifteen miles a day,
His stage is ten, his beatings are fifteen.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: 'Tis the longest, but we subjects must—
Be subject to it; you are wise and vertuous.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: Obedience ever makes that noble use on't,
To which I dedicate my beaten body;
I must trouble you a little further, Gentlemen o'th' Sword.
No trouble at all to us Sir, if we may
Profit your understanding, we are bound
By vertue of our calling to utter our opinions,
Shortly, and discreetly.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: My forest business is, I have been kick'd.
How far Sir?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Not to flatter my self in it, all over, my sword forc'd but not lost; for discreetly I rendred it to save that imputation.

verse: It shew'd discretion, the best part of valour.
Brother, this is a pretty cause, pray ponder on't;
Our friend here has been kick'd.
He has so, brother.
Sorely he saies: Now, had he set down here
Upon the meer kick, 't had been Cowardly.
I think it had been Cowardly indeed.
But our friend has redeem'd it in delivering
His sword without compulsion; and that man
That took it of him, I pronounce a weak one,
And his kicks nullities.
He should have kick'd him after the delivering
Which is the confirmation of a Coward.
Brother, I take it, you mistake the question;
For; say that I were kick'd.
I must not say so;
Nor I must not hear it spoke by the tongue of man.
You kick'd, dear brother! you're merry.
But put the case I were kick'd?

prose: Let them put it that are things weary of their lives, and know not honour; put the case you were kick'd?

verse: I do not say I was kickt.
Nor no silly creature that wears his head without a Case, his soul in a Skin-coat: You kickt dear brother?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: Nay Gentlemen, let us do what we shall do,
Truly and honesty; good Sirs to the question.
Why then I say, suppose your Boy kick't, Captain?
The Boy may be suppos'd is liable.
A foolish forward zeal Sir, in my friend;
But to the Boy, suppose the Boy were kickt.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: I do suppose it.
Has your Boy a sword?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: Surely no; I pray suppose a sword too.
I do suppose it; you grant your Boy was kick't then.

prose: By no means Captain, let it be supposed still; the word grant, makes not for us.

verse: I say this must be granted.
This must be granted brother?
I, this must be granted.
Still this must?
I say this must be granted.
I, give me the must again, brother, you palter.
I will not hear you, wasp.
But to the cause again.
prose: Brother, I say you palter, the must three times together; I wear as sharp Steel as another man, and my Fox bites as deep, musled, my dear brother.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: Nay look you Gentlemen.
In a word, I ha' done.
A tall man but intemperate, 'tis great pity;
Once more suppose the Boy kick'd.
Forward.
And being thorowly kick'd, laughs at the kicker.
So much for us; proceed.
And in this beaten scorn, as I may call it,
Delivers up his weapon; where lies the error?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: It lies i'th' beating Sir, I found it four dayes since.
The error, and a sore one as I take it,
Lies in the thing kicking.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: I understand that well, 'tis so indeed Sir.
That is according to the man that did it.
There springs a new branch, whose was the foot?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: A Lords.
The cause is mighty, but had it been two Lords,
And both had kick'd you, if you laugh, 'tis clear.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: I did laugh,
But how will that help me, Gentlemen?
Yes, it shall help you if you laught aloud.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: As loud as a kick'd man could laugh, I laught Sir.
My reason now, the valiant man is known
By suffering and contemning; you have
Enough of both, and you are valiant.
If he be sure he has been kick'd enough:
For that brave sufferance you speak of brother,
Consists not in a beating and away,
But in a endgell'd body, from eighteen
To eight and thirty; in a head rebuk'd
With pots of all size, degrees, stools, and bed-staves,
This showes a valiant man.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: Then I am valiant, as valiant as the proudest,
For these are all familiar things to me;
Familiar as my sleep, or want of money,
All my whole body's but one bruise with beating,
I think I have been endgell'd with all nations,
And almost all Religions.
Embrace him brother, this man is valiant,
I know it by my self, he's valiant.
Captain, thou art a valiant Gentleman,
To bide upon, a very valiant man.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: My equall friends o'th'Sword, I must request your hands to this.

verse: 'Tis fit it should be.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: Boy, get me some wine, and pen and Ink within:
Am I clear, Gentlemen?
Sir, the world has taken notice what we have done,
Make much of your body, for I'll pawn my steel,
Men will be cover of their legs hereafter.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: I must request you goe along and testife to the Lord Bacurius, whose foot has struck me, how you find my cause.
We will, and tell that Lord he must be rul'd,
Or there are those abroad, will rule his Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
verse: Sir, here's the Princess.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Leave us then alone,
For the main cause of her imprisonment
Must not be heard by any but her self.
You're welcome Sister, and would to heaven
I could so bid you by another name:
If you above love not such sins as these,
Circle my heart with thoughts as cold as snow
To quench these rising flames that harbour here.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Sir, does it please you I should speak?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Please me?
I, more than all the art of musick can,
Thy speech doth please me, for it ever sounds,
As thou brought'st joyfull unexpected news;
And yet it is not fit thou shouldst be heard.
I pray thee think so.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Be it so, I will.
Am I the first that ever had a wrong
So far from being sit to have redress,
That 't was unfit to hear it? I will back
To prison, rather than disquiet you,
And wait till it be fit.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: No, do not goe;
For I will hear thee with a serious thought:
I have collected all that's man about me
Together strongly, and I am resolv'd
To hear thee largely, but I do beseech thee,
Do not come nearer to me, for there is
Something in that, that will undoe us both.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: A^as Sir, am I v^nome?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Yes, to me;
Though of thy self I think thee to be
In equall degree of heat or cold,
As nature can make: yet as unfound men
Convert the sweetest and the nourishing'st meats
Into diseases, so shall I distemper'd,
Do thee, I pray thee draw no nearer to me.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Sir, this is that I would: I am of late
Shut from the world, and why it should be thus,
Is all I wish to know.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Why credit me Panthea,
Credit me that am thy brother,
Thy loving brother, that there is a cause
Sufficient, yet unsit for thee to know,
That might undoe thee everlastingly,
Only to hear, wilt thou but credit this?
By Heaven 'tis true, believe it if thou canst.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Children and fools are ever credulous,
And I am both, I think, for I believe;
If you dissemble, be it on your head;
I'le back unto my prison: yet me-thinks
I might be kept in some place where you are;
For in my self, I find I know not what
To call it, but it is a great desire
To see you often.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Fie, you come in a step, what do you mean?
Dear sister, do not so: Alas Panthea,
Where I am would you be? Why that's the cause
You are imprison'd, that you may not be
Where I am.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Then I must indure it Sir, Heaven keep you.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Nay, you shall hear the case in short Panthea,
And when thou hear'st it, thou wilt blush for me,
And hang thy head down like a Violet
Full of the mornings dew: There is a way
To gain thy freedome, but 'tis such a one
As puts thee in worse bondage, and I know,
Thou wouldst encounter fire, and make a proof
Whether the gods have care of innocence,
Rather than follow it: Know that I have lost,
The only difference betwixt man and beast,
My reason.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Heaven forbid.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Nay 'tis gone;
And I am left as far without a bound,
As the wild Ocean, that obeys the winds;
Each sodain passion throwes me where it lists,
And overwhelms all that oppose my will:
I have beheld thee with a lustfull eye;
My heart is set on wickedness to act
Such sins with thee, as I have been afraid
To think of, if thou dar'st consent to this,
Which I beseech thee do not, thou maist gain
Thy liberty, and yield me a content;
If not, thy dwelling must be dark and close,
Where I may never see thee; For heaven knows
That laid this punishment upon my pride,
Thy sight at some time will enforce my madness
To make a start e'ne to thy ravishing;
Now spit upon me, and call all reproaches
Thou canst devise together, and at once
Hurle 'em against me: for I am a sickness
As killing as the plague, ready to seize thee.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Far be it from me to revile the King:
But it is true, that I shall rather choose
To search out death, that else would search out me,
And in a grave sleep with my innocence,
Than welcome such a sin: It is my fate,
To these cross accidents I was ordain'd,
And must have patience; and but that my eyes
Have more of woman in 'em than my heart,
I would not weep: Peace enter you again.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Farwell, and good Panthea pray for me,
Thy prayers are pure, that I may find a death
However soon before my passions grow
That they forget what I desire is sin;
For thither they are tending: if that happen,
Then I shall force thee tho' thou wert a Virgin
By vow to Heaven, and shall pull a heap
Of strange yet uninvented sin upon me.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Sir, I will pray for you, yet you shall know
It is a fullen fate that governs us,
For I could wish as heartily as you
I were no sister to you, I should then
Imbrace your lawfull love, sooner than health.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Couldst thou affect me then?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: So perfectly,
That as it is, I ne're shall sway my heart,
To like another.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Then I curse my birth,
Must this be added to my miseries
That thou art willing too? is there no stop
To our full happiness, but these meer sounds
Brother and Sister?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: There is nothing else,
But these alas will separate us more
Than twenty worlds betwixt us.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: I have liv'd
To conquer men and now am overthrown
Only by words Brother and Sister: where
Have those words dwelling? I will find 'em out,
And utterly destroy 'em; but they are
Not to be grasp'd: let 'em be men or beasts,
And I will cut 'em from the Earth, or Towns,
And I will raze 'em, and them blow 'em up:
Let 'em be Seas, and I will drink 'em off,
And yet have unquencht fire left in my breast:
Let 'em be any thing but meerly voice.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: But 'tis not in the power of any force,
Or policy to conquer them.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Panthea, What shall we do?
Shall we stand firmly here, and gaze our eyes out?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Would I could do so,
But I shall weep out mine.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Accursed man,
Thou bought'st thy reason at too dear a rate,
For thou hast all thy actions bounded in
With curious rules, when every beast is free:
What is there that acknowledges a kindred
But wretched man? Who ever saw the Bull
Fearfully leave the Heifer that he lik'd
Because they had one Dam?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Sir, I disturb you and my self too;
'Twere better I were gone.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: I will not be so foolish as I was,
Stay, we will love just as becomes our births,
No otherwise: Brothers and Sisters may
Walk hand in hand together; so will we,
Come nearer: is there any hurt in this?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: I hope not.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Faith there is none at all:
And tell me truly now, is there not one
You love above me?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: No by Heaven.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: Why yet you sent unto Tigranes, Sister.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: True, but for another: for the truth —

speeches.speaker: Arb.
