verse: No more,
I'le credit thee, thou canst not lie,
Thou art all truth.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: But is there nothing else,
That we may do, but only walk? methinks
Brothers and Sisters lawfully may kiss.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: And so they may Panthea, so will we,
And kiss again too; we were too scrupulous,
And foolish, but we will be so no more.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: If you have any mercy, let me go
To prison, to my death, to any thing:
I feel a sin growing upon my blood,
Worse than all these, hotter than yours.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: That is impossible, what shou'd we do?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Flie Sir, for Heavens sake.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
verse: So we must away,
Sin grows upon us more by this delay.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: SIR, the King has seen your Commission, and believes it, and freely by this warrant gives you power to visit Prince Tigranes, your Noble Master.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: I thank his Grace and kiss his hand.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: But is the main of all you^ business ended in this?

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: I have another, but a worse, I am asham'd, it is a business.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: You serve a worthy person, and a stranger I am sure you are; you may imploy me if you please without your purse, such Offices should ever be their own rewards.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
verse: I am bound to your Nobleness.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I may have need of you, and then this courtesie,
If it be any, is not ill bestowed;
But may I civilly desire the rest?
I shall not be a hurter if no helper.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
verse: Sir you shall know I have lost a foolish Daughter,
And with her all my patience, pilfer'd away
By a mean Captain of your Kings.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Stay there Sir:
If he have reacht the Noble worth of Captain,
He may well claim a worthy Gentlewoman,
Though she were yours, and Noble.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
verse: I grant all that too: but this wretched fellow
Reaches no further than the empty name
That serves to seed him; were he valiant,
Or had but in him any noble nature
That might hereafter promise him a good man,
My cares were so much lighter, and my grave
A span yet from me.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I confess such fellows
Be in all Royal Camps, and have and must be,
To make the sin of Coward more detested
In the mean souldier that with such a foil
Sets off much valour. By description
I should now guess him to you, it was Bessus,
I dare almost with confidence pronounce it.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
verse: 'Tis such a scurvie name as Bessus, and now I think 'tis he

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Captain do you call him?
Believe me Sir, you have a misery
Too mighty for your age: A pox upon him,
For that must be the end of all his service:
Your Daughter was not mad Sir?

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
verse: No, would she had been,
The fault had had more credit: I would do something.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: I would fain counsel you, but to what I know not, he's so below a beating, that the Women find him not worthy of their Dislaves, and to hang him were to cast away a Rope; he's such an Airie, thin unbodyed Coward, that no revenge can catch him: I'le tell you Sir, and tell you truth; this Rascal fears neither God nor man, he has been so beaten: sufferance has made him Wainscot: he has had since he was first a slave, at least three hundred Daggers set in's head, as little boys do new Knives in hot meat, there's not a Rib in's body o' my Conscience that has not been thrice broken with dry beating: and now his sides look like two Wicker Targets, every way bended; Children will shortly take him for a Wall, and set their Stone-bows in his forehead, he is of so base a sense, I cannot in a week imagine what shall be done to him.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
verse: Sure I have committed some great sin
That this fellow should be made my Rod,
I would see him, but I shall have no patience.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: 'Tis no great matter if you have not: if a Laming of him, or such a toy may do you pleasure Sir, he has it for you, and I'le help you to him: 'tis no news to him to have a Leg broken, or Shoulder out, with being turn'd o'th'stones like a Tansie: draw not your Sword if you love it; for on my Conscience his head will break it: we use him i'th' Wars like a Ram to shake a wall withal. Here comes the very person of him, do as you shall find your temper, I must leave you: but if you do not break him like a Bisket, you are much to blame Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
verse: Is your name Bessus?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
verse: Men call me Captain Bessus.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose:
Then Catain Bessus, you are a rank rascall, without more exordiums, a durty frozen slave; and with the
favor of your friends here I will beat you.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sword.
verse: Pray use your pleasure Sir,
You seem to be a Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: Thus Captain Bessus, thus; thus twing your nose, thus kick, thus tread you.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: I do beseech you yield your cause Sir quickly.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: Indeed I should have told that first.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: I take it so.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sword.
prose: Captain, he should indeed, he is mistaken.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: Sir, you shall have it quickly, and more beating, you have stoln away a Lady, Captain coward, and such an one.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Hold, I beseech you, hold Sir, I never yet stole any living thing that had a tooth about it.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: I know you dare lie.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: With none but Summer Whores upon my life Sir, my means and manners never could attempt above a hedge or hay cock.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: Sirra, that quits not me, where is this Lady? do that you do not use to do; tell truth, or by my hand, I'le beat your Captains brains out, wash'em, and put 'em in again, that will I.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: There was a Lady Sir, I must confess, once in my charge: the Prince Tigranes gave her to my guard for her safety, how I us'd her, she may her self report, she's with the Prince now: I did but wait upon her like a groom, which she will testife I am sure: if not, my brains are at your service when you please Sir, and glad I have 'em for you.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: This is most likely, Sir, I ask you pardon, and am sorry I was so intemperate.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Well I can ask no more, you will think it strange not to have me beat you at first sight.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: Indeed I would, but I know your goodness can forget twenty beatings, you must forgive me.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Yes there's my hand, go where you will, I shall think you a valiant fellow for all this.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: My daughter is a Whore, I feel it now too sensible; yet I will see her, discharge my self from being father to her, and then back to my Country, and there die, farwell Captain.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Farwell Sir, farwell, commend me to the gentlewoman I pray.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sword.
prose: How now Captain? bear up man.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Gentlemen o'th'sword, your hands once more; I have been kickt agen, but the foolish fellow is penitent, has askt me Mercy, and my honour's safe.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sword.
prose: We knew that, or the foolish fellow had better have kickt his grandsir.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Confirm, confirm I pray.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sword.
prose: There be our hands agen, now let him come and say he was not sorry, and he sleeps for it.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Alas good ignorant old man, let him go, let him go, these courses will undo him.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: My Lord, your authority is good, and I am glad it is so, for my consent would never hinder you from seeing your own King, I am a Minister, but not a governor of this State, yonder is your King, I'le leave you.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: There he is indeed, and with him my disloyal child.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
prose: I do perceive my fault so much, that yet me thinks thou shouldst not have forgiven me.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: Health to your Majesty.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
prose: What? good Lygones welcome, what business brought thee hither?

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: Several businesses. My publick businesses will appear by this, I have a message to deliver, which if it please you so to authorize, is an embassage from the Armenian State, unto Arbaces for your liberty: the offer's there set down, please you to read it.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
prose: There is no alteration happened since I came thence?

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: None Sir, all is as it was.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
prose: And all our friends are well?

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: All very well.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
prose: Though I have done nothing but what was good, I dare not see my Father, it was fault enough not to acquai^ him with that good.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: Madam I should have seen you.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
prose: O good Sir forgive me.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: Forgive you, why? I am no kin to you, am I?

speeches.speaker: Spa.
prose: Should it be measur'd by my mean deserts, indeed you are not.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: Thou couldest prate unhappily ere thou couldst go, would thou couldst do as well, and how does your custome hold out here?

speeches.speaker: Spa.
prose: Sir?

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: Are you in private still, or how?

speeches.speaker: Spa.
prose: What do you mean?

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: Do you take mony? are you come to sell sin yet perhaps I can help you to liberal Clients: or has not the King cast you off yet? O thou vile creature, whose best commendation is, that thou art a young whore, I would thy Mother had liv'd to see this, or rather that I had died ere I had seen it; why didst not make me acquainted when thou wert first resolv'd to be a whore, I would have seen thy hot lust satisfied more privately: I would have kept a dancer and a whole consort of musicians in my own house only to fiddle thee.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
prose: Sir, I was never whore.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: If thou couldst not say so much for thy self, thou shouldst be carted.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
prose: Lygones, I have read it, and I like it, you shall deliver it.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: Well Sir, I will: but I have private business with you.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
prose: Speak, what is't?

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: How has my age deserv'd so ill of you, that you can pick no strumpets i'th' land, but out of my breed?

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
prose: Strumpets, good Lygones?

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: Yes, and I wish to have you know, I scorn to get a whore for any prince alive, and yet scorn will not help me-thinks: my Daughter might have been spar'd, there were enow besides.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
prose: May I not prosper but she's innocent as morning light for me, and I dare swear for all the world.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: Why is she with you then? can she wait on yor better than your man, has she a gift in plucking off your stockings, can she make Cawdles well or cut your cornes? Why do you keep her with you? For a Queen I know y^ do contemn her, so should I, and every subject else think much at it.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
prose: Let 'em think much, but 'tis more firm than earth: thou see'st thy Queen there.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: Then have I made a fair hand, I call'd her Whore If I shall speak now as her Father, I cannot chuse but greatly rejoyce that she shall be a Queen: but if I shall speak to you as a States-man, she were more fit to be your whore.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
prose: Get you about your business to Arbaces, now you talk idlely.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: Yes Sir, I will go, and shall she be a Queen? she had more wit than her old Father, when she ran away: shall she be Queen? now by my troth 'tis fine, I'le dance out of all measure at her wedding: shall I not Sir?

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
prose: Yes marry shalt thou.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: I'le make these withered kexes bear my body two hours together above ground.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
prose: Nay go, my business requires hast.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: Good Heaven preserve you, you are an excellent King.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
prose: Farwell good Father.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: Farwell sweet vertuous Daughter, I never was so joyfull in all my life, that I remember: shall she be a Queen? Now I perceive a man may weep for joy, I had thought they had lyed that said so.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
prose: Come my dear love.

speeches.speaker: Spa.
prose: But you may see another may alter that again.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
prose:
Urge it no more, I have made up a new strong constancy, not to be shook with eyes: I know I have the passions of a man, but if I meet with any subject that should hold my
eyes more firmly than is fit, I'le think of thee, and run away from it: let that suffice.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Three Gentlemen without to speak with me?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Yes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Let them come in.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: They are entred Sir already.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Now fellows your business? are these the Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: My Lord, I have made bold to bring these Gentlemen, my friends o'th' Sword along with me.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: I am afraid you'l fight then.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: My good Lord, I will not, your Lordship is much mistaken, fear not Lord.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Sir, I am sorry for't.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: I ask no more in honour, Gentlemen you hear my Lord is sorry.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Not that I have beaten you, but beaten one that will be beaten: one whose dull body will require a laming, as Surfeits do the diet, spring and fall; now to your Swordmen; what come they for, good Captain Stock-fish?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: It seems your Lordship has forgot my name.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: No, nor your nature neither, though they are things fitter I must confess for any thing, than my remembrance, or any honest mans: what shall these Billets do; be pil'd up in my wood-yard?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Your Lordship holds your mirth still, Heaven continue it: but for these Gentlemen, they come—

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: To swear you are a Coward, spare your book, I do believe it.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Your Lordship still draws wide, they come to vouch under their valiant hands I am no Coward.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: That would be a show indeed worth seeing: sirra be wise, and take Mony for this motion, travel with it, and where the name of Bessus has been known or a good Coward stirring, 'twill yield more than a tilting. This will prove more beneficial to you, if you be thristy, than your Captainship, and more natural: men of most valiant hands is this true?

speeches.speaker: 2 Sword.
prose: It is so, most renowned.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: 'Tis somewhat strange.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sword.
prose: Lord, it is strange, yet true; we have examined from your Lordships foot there, to this mans head, the nature of the beatings; and we do find his honour is come off clean and sufficient: this as our swords shall help us.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: You are much bound to your Bil-bow-men, I am glad you are straight again Captain; 'twere good you would think on some way to gratifie them, they have undergone a labour for you, Bessus, would have puzl'd Hercules with all his valour.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sword.
prose: Your Lordship must understand we are no men o'th' Law, that take pay for our opinions: it is sufficient we have clear'd our friend.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Yet there is something due, which I as toucht in Conscience will discharge Captain; I'le pay this Rent for you.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Spare your self my good Lord; my brave friends aim at nothing but the vertue.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: That's but a cold discharge Sir for the pains.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sword.
prose: O Lord, my good Lord.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Be not so modest, I will give you something.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: They shall dine with your Lordship, that's sufficient.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Something in hand the while, you Rogues, you Apple-squires: do you come hither with your botled valour, your windy froth, to limit out my beatings?

speeches.speaker: 1 Sword.
prose: I do beseech your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sword.
prose: O good Lord.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: S'foot what a beavy of beaten slaves are here? get me a Cudgel sirra, and a tough one.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sword.
prose: More of your foot, I do beseech your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: You shall, you shall dog, and your fellow-beagle.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sword.
prose: O' this side good my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Off with your swords, for if you hurt my foot, I'le have you slead you Rascals.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sword.
prose: Mine's off my Lord.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sword.
prose: I beseech your Lordship stay a little, my strap's tied to my Cod piece-point: now when you please.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Captain these are your valiant friends, you long for a little too?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: I am very well, I humbly thank your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: What's that in your pocket, hurts my Toe you Mungril? Thy Buttocks cannot be so hard, out with it quickly.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sword.
prose: Here 'tis Sir, a small piece of Artillery, that a Gentleman a dear friend of your Lordships sent me with, to get it mended Sir, for if you mark, the nose is somewhat loose.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: A friend of mine you Rascal? I was never wearier of doing any thing, than kicking these two Foot-balls.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
prose: Here is a good Cudgel Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: It comes too late l'me weary, pray thee do thou beat them.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sword.
prose: My Lord, this is soul play i'saith, to put a fresh man upon us, men are but men Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: That jest shall save your bones; Captain, Rally up your rotten Regiment and be gone: I had rather thrash than be bound to kick these Rascals, till they cry'd ho; Bessus you may put your hand to them now, and then you are quit. Farewel, as you like this, pray visit me again, 'twill keep me in good health.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sword.
prose: H'as a devilish hard foot, I never felt the like.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sword.
prose: Nor I, and yet I am sure I have felt a hundred.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sword.
prose: If he kick thus i'th' Dog-daies, he will be dry foundred: what cure now Captain besides Oyl of Baies?

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Why well enough I warrant you, you can go.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sword.
prose: Yes, heaven be thanked; but I feel a shrowd ach, sure h'as sprang my huckle-bone.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sword.
prose: I ha' lost a hanch.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: A little butter, friend a little butter, butter and parseley and a soveraign matter: probatum est.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sword.
prose: Captain we must request your hand now to our honours.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Yes marry shall ye, and then let all the world come, we are valiant to our selves, and there's an end.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sword.
prose: Nay then we must be valiant; O my ribs.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sword.
prose: O my small guts, a plague upon these sharptoed shooes, they are murtherers.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: It is resolv'd, I bare it whilst I could, I can no more, I must begin with murther of my friends, and so go on to that incestuous ravishing, and end my life and sins with a forbidden blow, upon my self.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: What Tragedy is near? That hand was never wont to draw a sword, but it cry'd dead to something.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Mardonius, have you bid Gobrias come?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: How do you Sir?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Well, is he coming?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Why Sir, are you thus? why do your hands proclaim a lawless War against your self?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Thou answerest me one question with an other, is Gobrias coming?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Sir he is.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: 'Tis well, I can forbear your questions then, be gone.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Sir, I have mark't.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Mark less, it troubles you and me.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: You are more variable than you were.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: It may be so.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: To day no Hermit could be humbler than you were to us all.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: And what of this?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: And now you take new rage into your eyes, as you would look us all out of the Land.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: I do confess it, will that satisfie? I prethee get thee gone.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Sir, I will speak.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Will ye?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: It is my duty. I fear you will kill your self: I am a subject, and you shall do me wrong in't: 'tis my cause, and I may speak.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Thou art not train'd in sin, it seems Mardonius: kill my self! by Heaven I will not do it yet; and when I will, I'le tell thee then: I shall be such a creature, that thou wilt give me leave without a word. There is a method in mans wickedness, it grows up by degrees: I am not come so high as killing of my self, there are a hundred thousand sins 'twixt me and it, which I must doe, and I shall come to't at last; but take my oath not now, be satisfied, and get thee hence.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: I am sorry 'tis so ill.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Be sorry then, true sorrow is alone, grieve by thy self.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: I pray you let me see your Sword put up before I go: I'le leave you then.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Why so? what folly is this in thee, is it not as apt to mischief as it was before? can I not reach it thinkst thou? these are toyes for Children to be pleas'd with, and not men, now I am safe you think: I would the book of fate were here, my Sword is not so sure but I would get it out and mangle that, that all the destinies should quite forget their sixt decrees, and hast to make us new, for other fortunes, mine could not be worse, wilt thou now leave me?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Heaven put into your bosome temperate thoughts, I'le leave you though I fear.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Go, thou art honest, why should the hasty error of my youth be so unpardonable to draw a sin helpless upon me?

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: There is the King, now it is ripe.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Draw near thou guilty man, that art the authour of the loathedst crime five ages have brought forth, and hear me speak; curses more incurable, and all the evils mans body or his Spirit can receive be with thee.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: Why Sir do you curse me thus?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Why do I curse thee? if there be a man subtil in curses, that exceeds the rest, his worst wish on thee, thou hast broke my heart.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: How Sir, have I preserv'd you from a child, from all the arrows, malice, or ambition could shoot at you, and have I this for my pay?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: 'Tis true, thou didst preserve me, and in that wert crueller than hardned murtherers of infants and their Mothers? thou didst save me only till thou hadst studied out a way how to destroy me cunningly thy self: this was a curious way of torturing.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: What do you mean?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Thou knowst the evils thou hast done to me; dost thou remember all those witching letters thou sent'st unto me to Armenia, fill'd with the praise of my beloved Sister, where thou extol'st her beauty, what had I to do with that? what could her beauty be to me? and thou didst write how well she lov'd me, dost thou remember this? so that I doted something before I saw her.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: This is true.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Is it? and when I was return'd thou knowst thou didst pursue it, till thou woundst me into such a strange and unbeliev'd affection, as good men cannot think on.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: This I grant, I think I was the cause.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Wert thou? Nay more, I think thou meant'st it.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: Sir, I hate to lie, as I love Heaven and honesty, I did, it was my meaning.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Be thine own sad judge, a further condemnation will not need, prepare thy self to dy.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: Why Sir to dy?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Why shouldst thou live? was ever yet offender so impudent, that had a thought of Mercy after confession of a crime like this? get out I cannot where thou hurl'st me in, but I can take revenge, that's all the sweetness left for me.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: Now is the time, hear me but speak.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: No, yet I will be far more mercifull than thou wert to me; thou didst steal into me and never gav'st me warning: so much time as I give thee now, had prevented thee for ever. Notwithstanding all thy sins, if thou hast hope, that there is yet a prayer to save thee, turn and speak it to thy self.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: Sir, you shall know your sins before you do 'em, if you kill me.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: I will not stay then.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: Know you kill your Father.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: How?

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: You kill your Father.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: My Father? though I know't for a lie, made out of fear to save thy stained life; the very reverence of the word comes cross me, and ties mine arm down.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: I will tell you that shall heighten you again, I am thy Father, I charge thee hear me.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: If it should be so, as 'tis most false, and that I should be found a Bastard issue, the despised fruit of lawless lust, I should no more admire all my wild passions: but ano~ther truth shall be wrung from thee: if I could come by the Spirit of pain, it should be poured on thee, till thou allow'st thy self more full of lies than he that teaches thee.

speeches.speaker: Ara.
prose: Turn thee about, I come to speak to thee thou wicked man, hear me thou tyrant.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: I will turn to thee, hear me thou Strumpet; I have blotted out the name of Mother, as thou hast thy shame.

speeches.speaker: Ara.
prose: My shame! thou hast less shame than any thing; why dost thou keep my Daughter in a prison? why dost thou call her Sister, and do this?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Cease thy strange impudence, and answer quickly if thou contemnest me, this will ask an answer, and have it.

speeches.speaker: Ara.
prose: Help me Gentle Gobrias.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Guilt d^a^ not help guilt though they grow together in doing ill, yet at the punishment they sever, and each flies the noise of other, think not of help, answer.

speeches.speaker: Ara.
prose: I will, to what?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: To such a thing, as if it be a truth think what a creature thou hast made thy self, that didst not shame to do, what I must blush only to ask thee: tell me who I am, whose son I am without all circumstance, be thou as hasty as my Sword will be if thou refusest.

speeches.speaker: Ara.
prose: Why, you are his son.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: His Son? swear, swear, thou worse than woman damn'd.

speeches.speaker: Ara.
prose: By all that's good you are.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Then art thou all that ever was known bad, now is the cause of all my strange mis-fortunes come to light: what reverence expectest thou from a child, to bring forth which thou hast offended heaven, thy husband, and the Land? adulterous witch, I know now why thou wouldst have poyson'd me, I was thy lust which thou wouldst have forgot: then wicked Mother of my sins, and me, show me the way to the inheritance I have by thee: which is a spacious world of impious acts, that I may soon possess it: plagues rot thee, as thou liv'st, and such diseases, as use to pay lust, recompence thy deed.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: You do not know why you curse thus.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Too well; you are a pair of Vipers; and behold the Serpent you have got; there is no beast but if he knew it, has a pedigree as brave as mine, for they have more descents, and I am every way as beastly got, as far without the compass of Law as they.

speeches.speaker: Ara.
prose: You spend your rage and words in vain, and rail upon a guess; hear us a little.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose:
No, I will never hear, but talk away my breath,

^d die.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: Why, but you are no Bastard.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: How's that?

speeches.speaker: Ara.
prose: Nor child of mine.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Still you go on in wonders to me.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: Pray you be more patient, I may bring comfort to ^ou.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: I will kneel, and hear with the obedience of a ^hild; good Father speak, I do acknowledge you, so you ^ring comfort.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: First know, our last King, your supposed Father ^as old and feeble when he married her, and almost all ^he Land thought she was past hope of issue from him.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Therefore she took leave to play the whore, because ^he King was old: is this the comfort?

speeches.speaker: Ara.
prose: What will you find out to give me satisfaction, ^hen you find how you have injur'd me? let fire consume ^e, if ever I were a whore.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: For-bear these starts, or I will leave you wedded to despair, as you are now: if you can find a temper, my breath shall be a pleasant western wind that cools and blasts not.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Bring it out good Father. I'le lie, and listen here ^s reverently as to an Angel: if I breath too loud, tell me; for I would be as still as night.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: Our King I say, was old, and this our Queen desir'd to bring an heir, but yet her husband she thought was past ^t, and to be dishonest I think she would not: if she would have been, the truth is, she was watcht so narrowly, and had so slender opportunities, she hardly could have been: but yet her cunning found out this way; she feign'd her self with child, and posts were sent in hast throughout the Land, and humble thanks was given in every Church, and prayers were made for her safe going and delivery: she feign'd now to grow bigger, and perceiv'd this hope of issue made her fear'd, and brought a far more large respect from every man, and saw her power increase, and was resolv'd, since she believ'd, she could not hav't indeed, at least she would be thought to have a child.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Do I not hear it well? nay I will make no noise at all; but pray you to the point, quickly as you can.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: Now when the time was full, she should be brought to bed, I had a Son born, which was you, this the Queen hearing of mov'd me to let her have you; and such reasons she shewed me, as she knew would tie my secrecie, she swore you should be King, and to be short, I did deliver you unto her, and pretended you were dead, and in mine own house kept a funeral, and had an empty cossin put in Earth, that night this Queen feign'd hastily to labour and by a pair of women of her own, which she had charm'd, she made the world believe she was delivered of you. You grew up as the Kings Son, till you were six years old; then did the King dye, and did leave to me Protection of the Realm; and contrary to his own expectation, left this Queen truely with child indeed, of the fair Princess Panthea: then she could have torn her hair and did alone to me, yet durst not speak in publick, for she knew she should be found a traytor: and her tale would have been thought madness, or any thing rather than truth. This was the only cause why she did seek to poyson you, and I to keep you safe; and this the reason, why I sought to kindle some sparks of love in you to fair Panthea, that she might get part of her right again.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: And have you made an end now? is this all? if not, I will be still till I be aged, till all my hairs be Silver.

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: This is all.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: And is it true say you too Madam?

speeches.speaker: Ara.
prose: Yes heaven knows it is most true.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Panthea then is not my Sister?

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: No.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: But can you prove this?

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: If you will give consent, else who dares go about it?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Give consent? why I will have 'em all that know it rackt, to get this from 'em, all that wait without come in, what ere you be, come in and be partakers of my joy, O you are welcome.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: The best news, nay draw no nearer, they all shall hear it, I am found no King.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Is that so good news?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Yes the happiest news that ere was heard.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Indeed 'twere well for you if you might be a little less obey'd.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: One call the Queen.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Why she is there.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: The Queen Mardonius, Panthea is the Queen and I am plain Arbaces; go some one, she is in Gobrias house, since I saw you there are a thousand things delivered to me, you little dream of.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: So it should seem my Lord, what fury's this?

speeches.speaker: Gob.
prose: Believe me 'tis no fury, all that he saies is truth.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: 'Tis very strange.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Why do you keep your hats off Gentlemen? is it to me? I swear it must not be; nay, trust me, in good faith it must not be; I cannot now command you, but I pray you for the respect you bare me, when you took me for your King, each man clap on his hat at my desire.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: We will, you are not found so mean a man, but that you may be cover'd as well as we, may you not?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: O not here, you may, but not I, for here is my Father in presence.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Where?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Why there: O the whole story would be a wilderness to lose thy self for ever: O pardon me dear Father for all the idle and unreverent words that I have spoke in idle moods to you: I am Arbaces, we all fellow-subjects, nor is the Queen Panthea now my Sister.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Why if you remember fellow-subject Arbaces; I told you once she was not your Sister: I, and she lookt nothing like you.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: I think you did, good Captain Bessus.

speeches.speaker: Bes.
prose: Here will arise another question now amongst the Sword-men, whether I be to call him to account for beating me, now he is proved no King.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Sir here's Lygones, the agent for the Armenian State.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Where is he? I know your business good Lygones.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: We must have our King again, and will.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: I knew that was your business: you shall have your King again, and have him so again as never King was had, go one of you and bid Bacurius bring Tigranes hither; and bring the Lady with him, that Panthea, the Queen Panthea sent me word this morrning, was brave Tigranes mistress.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: 'Tis Spaconia.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: I, I, Spaconia.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: She is my Daughter.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: She is so: I could now tell any thing I never heard: your King shall go so home, as never man went.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Shall he go on's head?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: He shall have chariots easier than air that I will have invented; and ne're think one shall pay any ransome, and thy self that art the messenger, shalt ride before him on a horse cut out of an intire Diamond, that shall be made to go with golden wheeles, I know not how yet.

speeches.speaker: Lyg.
prose: Why I shall be made for ever? they beli'd this King with us, and said he was unkind.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: And then thy Daughter, she shall have some strange thing, wee'l have the Kingdom sold utterly, and put into a toy which she shall wear about her carelesly some where or other. See the vertuous Queen; behold the humblest subject that you have kneel here before you.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Why kneel you to me that am your Vassal?

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Grant me one request.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Alas what can I grant you? what I can, I will.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: That you will please to marry me if I can prove it lawfull.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Is that all? more willingly than I would draw this air.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: I'le kiss this hand in earnest.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
prose: Sir, Tigranes is coming though he made it strange at first, to see the Princess any more.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: The Queen thou meanest, O my Tigranes. Pardon me, tread on my neck, I freely offer it, and if thou beest in given take revenge, for I have injur'd thee.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
prose: No, I forgive, and rejoyce more that you h^ found repentance, than I my liberty.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Mayest thou be happy in thy fair choice, for th^ art temperate. You owe no ransom to the state, know th^ I have a thousand joyes to tell you of, which yet I dare ^ utter till I pay my thanks to Heaven for 'em: Will you g^ with me and help me? pray you do.

speeches.speaker: Tigr.
prose: I will.

speeches.speaker: Arb.
prose: Take then your fair one with you; and you Qu^ of goodness and of us, O give me leave to take you arm in mine: come every one that takes delight i^ goodness, help to sing loud thanks for me, that I am prov^ no King.

speeches.speaker: Elder Love.
prose: BRother, is your last hope past to mollifie Morecrafts heart about your Morgage?

speeches.speaker: Young Love.
prose: Hopelesly past: I have presented the Usurer with a richer draught than ever Cleopatra swallowed; he hath suckt in ten thousand pound worth of my Land, more than he paid for at a grip, without Trumpets.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: I hav^ as hard a task to perform in this house.

speeches.speaker: Yo. Lo.
prose: Faith mine was to make an Usurer honest, or to lose my Land.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: And mine is to perswade a passionate woman, or to leave the La^. Make the boat stay, I fear I shall begin my unfortunate journey this night, though the darkness of the night and the ^ughness of the waters might easily disswade an unwilling ma^.

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: Sir, your Fathers old friends hold it the sounder course for your body and estate to stay at home and marry, and propagate and govern in our Country, than to Travel and die without issue.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: Savil, you shall gain the opinion of a better servant in seeking to execute, not alter my will, howsoever my in^nts succeed.

speeches.speaker: Yo. Lo.
prose: Yo^ le^s Mistres Younglove, Brother, the grave r^her of your Mistresses toes.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: Mistres Younglove.

speeches.speaker: Young.
prose: M^ster Loveless, truly we thought your sails had been boist: ^y Mistres is perswaded you are Sea-sick ere ^.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose:
Love^
^e her ill taken up resolution so dearly? ^ thou move her from me?
By th^ light that shines, there's no removing her, ^ngger a still opinion by the end. I attempted her to day when they say a woman can deny nothing.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: What critical minute was that?

speeches.speaker: Young.
prose: When her smock was over her ears: but she was no more pliant than if it hung about her heels.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: I prethee deliver my service, and say, I desire to see the dear cause of my banishment; and then for France.

speeches.speaker: Young.
prose: I'le do't: hark hither, is that your Brother?

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: Yes, have you lost your memory?

speeches.speaker: Young.
prose: As I live he's a pretty fellow.

speeches.speaker: Yo. Lo.
prose: O this is a sweet Brache.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: Why she knows not you.

speeches.speaker: Yo. Lo.
prose: No, but she offered me once to know her: to this day she loves youth of Eighteen; she heard a tale how Cupid struck her in love with a great Lord in the Tilt-yard, but he never saw her; yet she in kindness would needs wear a Willow-garland at his Wedding. She lov'd all the Players in the last Queens time once over: she was struck when they acted Lovers, and forsook some when they plaid Murthers. She has nine Spur-royals, and the servants say she hoards old gold; and she her self pronounces angerly, that the Farmers eldest son, or her Mistres Husbands Clerk shall be, that Marries her, shall make her a joynture of fourscore pounds a year; she tells tales of the serving-men.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: Enough, I know her Brother. I shall intreat you only to salute my Mistres, and take leave, we'l part at the Stairs.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Now Sir, this first part of your will is performed, what's the rest?

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: First, let me beg your notice for this Gentleman my Brother.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose:
I shall take it as a favour done to me, though the Gentleman hath received but an untimely grace from you^
yet my charitable disposition would have been ready to have done him freer courtesies as a stranger, than upon those cold commendations.

speeches.speaker: Yo. Lo.
prose: Lady, my salutations crave acquaintance and leave at once.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Sir I hope you are the master of your own occasions.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: Would I were so. Mistris, for me to praise over again that worth, which all the world, and you your self can see.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: It's a cold room this, Servant.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: Mistris.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: What think you if I have a Chimney for't, out here?

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: Mistris, another in my place, that were not tyed to believe all your actions just, would apprehend himself wrong'd: But I whose vertues are constancy and obedience.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Younglove, make a good sire above to warm me after my servants Exordium.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: I have heard and seen your affability to be such, that the servants you give wages to may speak.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: 'Tis true, 'tis true; but they speak toth' purpose.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: Mistris, your will leads my speeches from the purpose. But as a man—

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: A Simile servant? This room was built for honest meaners, that deliver themselves hastily and plainly, and are gone. Is this a time or place for Exordiums, and Similes and Metaphors? If you have ought to say, break into't: my answers shall very reasonably meet you.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: Mistris I came to see you.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: That's happily dispatcht, the next.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: To take leave of you.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: To be gone?

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: Yes.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: You need not have despair'd of that, nor have us'd so many circumstances to win me to give you leave to perform my command; is there a third?

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: Yes, I had a third had you been apt to hear it.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: I? Never apter. Fast (good servant) fast.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: 'Twas to intreat you to hear reason.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Most willingly, have you brought one can speak it?

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: Lastly, it is to kindle in that barren heart love and forgiveness.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: You would stay at home?

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: Yes Lady.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Why you may, and doubtlesly will, when you have deba^d that your commander is but your Mistris, a woman, a weak one, wildly overborn with passions: but the thing by her commanded, is to see Dovers dreadful cliffe, passing in a poor Water-house ^ the dangers of the merciless Channel 'twixt that and Callis, five long hours sail, with three poor weeks victuals.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: You wrong me.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Then to land dumb, unable to enquire for an English hoast, to remove from City to City, by most chargeable Post-horse, like one that rode in quest of his Mother tongue.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: You wrong me much.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: And all these (almost invincible labours) performed for your Mistris, to be in danger to forsake her, and to put on new allegeance to some French Lady, who is content to change language with your laughter, and after your whole year spent in Tennis and broken speech, to stand to the hazard of being laught at, at your return, and have tales made on you by the Chamber-maids.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: You wrong me much.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Louder yet.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: You know your least word is of force to make me seek out dangers, move me not with toyes: but in this banishment, I must take leave to say, you are unjust: was one kiss forc't from you in publick by me so unpardonable? Why all the hours of day and night have seen us kiss.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: 'Tis true, and so you told the company that heard me chide.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lov.
prose: Your own eyes were not dearer to than I.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: And so you told 'em.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I did, yet no sign of disgrace need to h^ stain'd your cheek: you your self knew your pure ^ simple heart to be most unspotted, and free from the ^ baseness.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: I did: But if a Maids heart doth but once th^ that she is suspected, her own face will write her guilty.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: But where lay this disgrace? The world the knew us, knew our resolutions well: And could it be hop^ that I should give away my freedom; and vent^e a perpetual bondage with one I never kist? or could ^n strict ^ doth take too much love upon me, from her that chose ^ for her Husband?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Believe me; if my Wedding-smock were on,
Were the Gloves bought and given, the Licence come,
Were the Rosemary-branches dipt, and all
The Hipochrist and Cakes eat and drunk off,
Were these two armes incompast with the hands
Of Bachelors to lead me to the Church,
Were my feet in the door, were I John, said,
If John should boast a favour done by me,
I would not wed that year: And you I hope,
When you have spent this year commodiously
In atchieving Languages, will at your return
Acknowledge me more coy of parting with mine eyes,
Than such a friend: More talk I hold not now
If you dare go.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I dare, you know: First let me kiss.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Farewel sweet Servant, your task perform'd,
On a new ground as a beginning Sucor,
I shall be apt to hear you.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Farewel cruel Mistres.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Brother you'l hazard the losing your tide to Gravesend: you have a long half mile by Land to Greenewich?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I go: but Brother, what yet unheard of course to live, doth your imagination flatter you with? Your ordinary means are devour'd.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Course? why Horse-coursing I think. Consume no time in this: I have no Estate to be mended by meditation: he that busies himself about my fortunes may properly be said to busie himself about nothing.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Yet some course you must take, which for my satisfaction resolve and open; if you will shape none, I must inform you that that man but perswades himself he means to live, that imagines not the means.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Why live upon others, as others have lived upon me.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I apprehend not that: you have fed others, and consequently dispos'd of 'em: and the same measure must you expect from your maintainers, which will be too heavy an alteration for you to bear.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Why I'le purse; if that raise me not, I'le bet at Bowling-alleyes, or man Whores; I would fain live by others: but I'le live whilst I am unhang'd, and after the thought's taken.

speeches.speaker: Elder Love.
prose: I see you are ty'd to no particular imp^oiment then?

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Faith I may choose my co^rse: they say nature brings forth none but she provides for them: I'le try her liberality.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Well, to keep your feet out of base and dangerous paths, I have resolved you shall live as Master of my House. It shall be your care Savil to see him fell and cloathed, not according to his present Estate, but to his birth and former fortunes.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: If it be refer'd to him, if I be not ^ Carnation Jearsie-stockins, blew devils breeches, ^ith the gad^ down, and my pocket i'th' sleeves, I'le n'er lo^ you i'th fa^ again.

speeches.speaker: Sa.
prose: A comelier wear I wuss it is than those dangling ^ps.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose:
To keep you readie to do him all service peace
^ly, and him to command you reasonably, I leave these fur
^er directions in writing, which at your best leasure toge
^er open and read.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: Sir, my Mistress commends her love to you in this ^ken, and these words; it is a Iewell (she sayes) which as favour from her she would request you to wear till your ^ears travel be performed: which once expired, she will ^astily expect your happy return.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose:
Return my service with such thanks, as she may ^agine the heart of a suddenly over-joyed man would wil
^ngly utter; and you I hope I shall with slender arguments ^erswade to wear this Diamond, that when my Mistris shall ^rough my long absence, and the approach of new Suitors, ^ffer to forget me; you may cast your eye down to your ^nger, and remember and speak of me: She will hear thee ^etter than those allied by birth to her; as we see many men ^uch swayed by the Grooms of their Chambers, not that ^hey have a greater part of their love or opinion on them, ^an on others, but for that they know their secrets.

speeches.speaker: Abi.
prose: O' my credit I swear, I think 'twas made for me: ^ar no other Suitors.

speeches.speaker: Elder Love.
prose:
I shall not need to teach you how to discre
^it their beginning, you know how to take exception at ^heir shirts at washing, or to make the maids swear they ^ and plasters in their beds.

speeches.speaker: Abi.
prose: I know, I know, and do not you fear the Suitors.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Farewell, be mindfull, and be happie; the night ^alls me.

speeches.speaker: Abi.
prose:
The Gods of the Winds befriend you Sir; a con
^ant and a liberal Lover thou art, more such God send us.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Let 'em not stand still, we have rid.

speeches.speaker: Abi.
prose: A suitor I know by his riding hard, I'le not be seen.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: A prettie Hall this, no Servant in't? I would look ^reshly.

speeches.speaker: Abi.
prose: You have delivered your errand to me then: there's ^o danger in a hansome young fellow: I'le shew my self.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Lady, may it please you to bestow upon a stranger ^he ordinary grace of salutation: Are you the Lady of this ^ouse?

speeches.speaker: Abi.
prose: Sir, I am worthily proud to be a Servant of hers.

speeches.speaker: Wel,
prose: Lady, I should be as proud to be a Servant of yours, ^id not my so late acquaintance make me despair.

speeches.speaker: Abi.
prose: Sir, it is not so hard to atchieve, but nature may ^ring it about.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: For these comfortable words, I remain your glad Debtor. Is your Lady at home?

speeches.speaker: Abi.
prose: She is no stragler Sir.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: May her occasions admit me to speak with her?

speeches.speaker: Abi.
prose: If you come in the way of a Suitor, No.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose:
I know your affable vertue will be moved to per
^wade her, that a Gentleman benighted and strayed, offers ^o be bound to her for a nights lodging.

speeches.speaker: Abi.
prose:
I will commend this message to her; but if you aim ^t her body, you will be deluded: other women of the house
^old of good carriage and government; upon any of which ^f you can cast your affection, they will perhaps be found as ^aithfull and not so coy.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: What a skin full of lust is this? I thought I had ^ome a wooing, and I am the courted partie. This is right Court fashion: Men, Women, and all woo, catch that catch may. If this soft hearted woman have infused any of her tenderness into her Lady, there is hope she will be plyant. But who's here?

speeches.speaker: Roger.
prose: Gad save you Sir. My Lady lets you know she desires to be acquainted with your name, before she confer with you?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Sir, my name calls me Welford.

speeches.speaker: Roger.
prose: Sir, you are a Gentleman of a good name. I'le try his wit.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: I will uphold it as good as any of my Ancestors had this two hundred years Sir.

speeches.speaker: Roger.
prose: I knew a worshipfull and a Religious Gentleman of your name in the Bishoprick of Durham. Call you him Cousen?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: I am only allyed to his vertues Sir.

speeches.speaker: Roger.
prose: It is modestly said: I should carry the badge of your Christianity with me too.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: What's that, a Cross? there's a tester.

speeches.speaker: Roger.
prose: I mean the name which your God fathers and God-mothers gave you at the Font.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: 'Tis Harry: but you cannot proceed orderly now in your Catechism: for you have told me who gave me that name. Shall I beg your name?

speeches.speaker: Roger.
prose: Roger.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: What room fill you in this house?

speeches.speaker: Roger.
prose: More rooms than one.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: The more the merrier: but may my boldness know, why your Lady hath sent you to decypher my name?

speeches.speaker: Roger.
prose: Her own words were these: To know whether you were a formerly denyed Suitor, disguised in this message: for I can assure you she delights not in Thalame: Hymen and she are at variance, I shall return with much hast.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: And much speed Sir, I hope: certainly I am arrived amongst a Nation of new found fools, on a Land where no Navigator has yet planted wit; if I had foreseen it, I would have laded my breeches with bells, knives, copper, and glasses, to trade with women for their virginities: yet I fear, I should have betrayed my self to a needless charge then: here's the walking night cap again.

speeches.speaker: Roger.
prose: Sir, my Ladies pleasure is to see you: who hath commanded me to acknowledge her sorrow, that you must take the pains to come up for so bad entertainment.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: I shall obey your Lady that sent it, and acknowledge you that brought it to be your Arts Master.

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: I am but a Batchelor of Art, Sir; and I have the mending of all under this roof, from my Lady on her down-bed, to the maid in the Pease straw.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: A Cobler, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Roger.
prose: No Sir, I inculcate Divine Service within these Walls.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: But the Inhabitants of this house do often imploy you on errands without any scruple of Conscience.

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: Yes, I do take the air many mornings on foot, three or four miles for eggs: but why move you that?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: To know whether it might become your function to bid my man to neglect his horse a little to attend on me.

speeches.speaker: Roger.
prose: Most properly Sir.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: I pray you doe so then: the whilst I will attend your Lady. You direct all this house in the true way?

speeches.speaker: Roger.
prose: I doe Sir.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: And this door I hope conducts to your Lady?

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: Your understanding is ingenious.

speeches.speaker: Sa.
prose: By your favour Sir, you shall pardon me?

speeches.speaker: Yo. Lo.
prose: I shall bear your favour Sir, cross me no more, I say they shall come in.

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: Sir, you forget who I am?

speeches.speaker: Yo. Lo.
prose: Sir, I do not; thou art my Brothers Steward, his cast off mill-money, his Kitchen Arithmetick.

speeches.speaker: Sa.
prose: Sir, I hope you will not make so little of me?

speeches.speaker: Yo. Lo.
prose: I make thee not so little as thou art: for indeed there goes no more to the making of a Steward, but a fair Imprimis, and then a reasonable Item infus'd into him, and the thing is done.

speeches.speaker: Sa.
prose: Nay then you stir my duty, and I most tell you?

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: What wouldst thou tell me, how Hopps grow, or hold some rotten discourse of Sheep, or when our Lady-day falls? Prethee farewel, and entertain my friends, be drunk and burn thy Table books: and my dear spark of velvet, thou and I.

speeches.speaker: Sa.
prose: Good Sir remember?

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: I do remember thee a foolish fellow, one that did put his trust in Almanacks, and Horse-fairs, and rose by Hony and Pot-butter. Shall they come in yet?

speeches.speaker: Sa.
prose: Nay then I must unfold your Brothers pleasure, these be the lessons Sir, he left behind him.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Prethee expound the first.

speeches.speaker: Sa.
prose: I leave to maintain my house three hundred pounds a year; and my Brother to dispose of it.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Mark that my wicked Steward, and I dispose of it?

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: Whilest he bears himself like a Gentleman, and my credit falls not in him. Mark that my good young Sir, mark that.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Nay, if it be no more I shall fulfil it, whilst my Legs will carry me I'le bear my self Gentleman-like, but when I am drunk, let them bear me that can. Forward dear Steward.

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: Next it is my will, that he be furnished (as my Brother) with Attendance, Apparel, and the obedience of my people.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Steward this is as plain as your old Minikinbreeches. Your wisdom will relent now, will it not? Be mollified or— you understand me Sir, proceed?

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: Next, that my Steward keep his place, and power, and bound my Brother's wildness with his care.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: I'le hear no more of this Apocrypha, bind it by it self Steward.

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: This is your Brothers will, and as I take it, he makes no mention of such company as you would draw unto you. Captains of Gallysoists, such as in a clear day have seen Callis, fellows that have no more of God, than their Oaths come to: they wear swords to reach fire at a Play, and get there the oyl'd end of a Pipe, for their Guerdon: then the remnant of your Regiment, are wealthy Tobacco-Marchants, that set up with one Ounce, and break for three: together with a Forlorn hope of Poets, and all these look like Carthusians, things without linnen: Are these fit company for my Masters Brother?

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: I will either convert thee (O thou Pagan Steward) or presently confound thee and thy reckonings, who's there? Call in the Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: Good Sir.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Nay, you shall know both who I am, and where I am.

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: Are you my Masters Brother?

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Are you the sage Master Steward, with a face like an old Ephemerides?

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: Then God help us all I say.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: I, and 'tis well said my old peer of France: welcome Gentlemen, welcome Gentlemen; mine own dear Lads y'are richly welcome. Know this old Harry Groat.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
prose: Sir I will take your love.

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: Sir, you will take my Purse.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
prose: And study to continue it.

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: I do believe you.

speeches.speaker: Trav.
prose: Your honorable friend and Masters Brother, hath given you to us for a worthy fellow, and so we hugg you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: Has given himself into the hands of Varlets, not to be curv'd out. Sir, are these the pieces?

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: They are the Morals of the Age, the vertues, men made of gold.

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: Of your gold you mean Sir.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: This is a man of War, and cryes go on, and wears his colours.

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: In's nose.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: In the fragrant field. This is a Traveler Sir, knows men and manners, and has plow'd up the S^ so far till both the Poles have knockt, has seen the Sun ^ Coach, and can distinguish the colour of his Horses, ^ their kinds, and had a Flanders-Mare leapt there.

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: 'Tis much.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: I have seen more Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: 'Tis even enough o' Conscience; sit down, and re^ you, you are at the end of the world already. Would ye had as good a Living Sir, as this fellow could lie you out o^ he has a notable gift in't.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: This ministers the smoak, and this the Mu^

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: And you the Cloaths, and Meat, and Money, yo^ have a goodly generation of 'em, pray let them multipl^ your Brothers house is big enough, and to say truth, h^ too much Land, hang it durt.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Why now thou art a loving stinkard. Fire of thy Annotations and thy Rent-books, thou hast a weak brain Savil, and with the next long Bill thou wilt run mad Gentlemen, you are once more welcome to three hundred pounds a year; we will be freely merry, shall we not?

speeches.speaker: Capt.
prose: Merry as mirth and wine, my lovely Loveless.

speeches.speaker: Poet.
prose: A serious look shall be a Jury to excommunicate any man from our company.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: We will not talk wisely neither?

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: What think you Gentlemen by all this Revenue in Drink?

speeches.speaker: Capt.
prose: I am all for Drink.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: I am dry till it be so.

speeches.speaker: Poet.
prose: He that will not cry Amen to this, let him live so~ber, seem wise, and dye o'th' Coram.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: It shall be so, we'l have it all in Drink, let Meat and Lodging go, they are transitory, and shew men meerly mortal: then we'l have Wenches, every one his Wench, and every week a fresh one: we'l keep no powdered flesh: all these we have by warrant, under the title of things necessary. Here upon this place I ground it, The obedience of my people, and all necessaries: your opinions Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: Capt.
prose: 'Tis plain and evident that he meant Wenches.

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: Good Sir let me expound it?

speeches.speaker: Capt.
prose: Here be as sound men, as your self Sir.

speeches.speaker: Poet.
prose: This do I hold to be the interpretation of it: In this word Necessary, is concluded all that be helps to Man; Woman was made the first, and therefore here the chiefest.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Believe me 'tis a learned one; and by these words, The obedience of my people, you Steward being one, are bound to fetch us Wenches.

speeches.speaker: Capt.
prose: He is, he is.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Steward, attend us for instructions?

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: But will you keep no house Sir?

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Nothing but drink Sir, three hundred pounds in drink.

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: O miserable house, and miserable I that live to see it! Good Sir keep some meat.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Get us good Whores, and for your part, I'le board you in an Alehouse, you shall have Cheese and Onions.

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: What shall become of me, no Chimney smoaking? Well Prodigal, your Brother will come home.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Come Lads, I'le warrant you for Wenches, three hundred pounds in drink.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: SIR, now you see your bad lodging, I must bid you good night.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Lady if there be any want, 'tis in want of you.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: A little sleep will ease that complement. Once more good night.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Once more dear Lady, and then all sweet nights.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Dear Sir be short and sweet then.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Shall the morrow prove better to me, shall I hope my sute happier by this nights rest?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Is your sute so sickly that rest will help it? Pray ^e let it rest then till I call for it. Sir as a stranger you have had all my welcome: but had I known your errand ere you came, your passage had been straiter. Sir, good night.

speeches.speaker: Welford.
prose: So fair, and cruel, dear unkind good night.
Nay Sir, you shall stay with me, I'le press your zeal so far.

speeches.speaker: Roger.
prose: O Lord Sir.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Do you love Tobacco?

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: Surely I love it, but it loves not me; yet with your reverence I'le be bold.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Pray light it Sir. How do you like it?

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: I promise you it is notable stinging geer indeed. It is wet Sir, Lord how it brings down Rheum?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Handle it again Sir, you have a warm text of it.

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: Thanks ever promised for it. I promise you it is very powerful, and by a Trope, spiritual; for certainly it moves in sundry places.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: I, it does so Sir, and me especially to ask Sir, why you wear a Night-cap.

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: Assuredly I will speak the truth unto you: you shall understand Sir, that my head is broken, and by whom; even by that visible beast the Butler.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: The Butler? certainly he had all his drink about him when he did it. Strike one of your grave Cassock? The offence Sir?

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: Reproving him at Tra-trip Sir, for swearing; you have the total surely.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: You told him when his rage was set a tilt, and so he crackt your Canons. I hope he has not hurt your gentle reading: But shall we see these Gentlewomen to night.

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: Have patience Sir until our fellow Nicholas be deceast, that is, asleep: for so the word is taken: to sleep to dye, to dye to sleep, a very figure Sir.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Cannot you cast another for the Gentlewomen?

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: Not till the man be in his bed, his grave: his grave, his bed: the very same again Sir. Our Comick Poet gives the reason sweetly; Plenus rimarum est, he is full of loopeholes, and will discover to our Patroness.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Your comment Sir has made me understand you.

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: Sir be addrest, the graces do salute you with the full bowl of plenty. Is our old enemy entomb'd?

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: He's safe?

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: And does he snore out supinely with the Poet?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: No, he out-snores the Poet.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Gentlewoman, this courtesie shall bind a stranger to you, ever your servant.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Sir, my Sisters strictness makes not us forget you are a stranger and a Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: In sooth Sir, were I chang'd into my Lady, a Gentleman so well indued with parts, should not be lost.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: I thank you Gentlewoman, and rest bound to you. See how this foul familiar chewes the Cud: From thee, and three and fifty good Love deliver me.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Will you sit down Sir, and take a spoon?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: I take it kindly, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: It is our best banquet Sir.

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: Shall we give thanks?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: I have to the Gentlewomen already Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Good Sir Roger. keep that breath to cool your part o'th' Posset, you may chance have a scalding zeal else; and you will needs be doing, pray tell your twenty to your self. Would you could like this Sir?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: I would your Sister would like me as well Lady.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Sure Sir, she would not eat you: but banish that imagination; she's only wedded to her self, lyes with her self, and loves her self; and for another Husband than herself, he may knock at the gate, but ne're come in: be wise Sir, she's a Woman, and a trouble, and has her many faults, the least of which is, she cannot love you.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: God pardon her, she'l do worse, would I were worthy his least grief, Mistris Martha.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Now I must over-hear her.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Faith would thou hadst them all with all my heart; I do not think they would make thee a day older.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: Sir, will you put in deeper, 'tis the sweeter.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Well said old sayings.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: She looks like one indeed. Gentlewoman you keep your word, your sweet self has made the bottom sweeter.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: Sir, I begin a frolick, dare you change Sir?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: My self for you, so please you. That smile has turn'd my stomach: this is right the old Embleme of the Moyle cropping of Thistles: Lord what a hunting head she carries, sure she has been ridden with a Martingale. Now love deliver me.

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: Do I dream, or do I wake? surely I know not: am I rub'd off? Is this the way of all my morning Prayers? Oh Roger, thou art but grass, and woman as a flower. Did I for this consume my quarters in Meditation, Vowes, and wooed her in Heroical Epistles? Did I expound the Owl, and undertook with labour and expence the recollection of those thousand Pieces, consum'd in Cellars, and Tabacco shops of that our honour'd Englishman Ni. Br. Have I done this, and am I done thus too? I will end with the wise man, and say; He that holds a Woman, has an Eel by the tail.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Sir 'tis so late, and our entertainment (meaning our Posset) by this is grown so cold, that 'twere an unmannerly part longer to hold you from your rest: let what the house has be at your command Sir.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Sweet rest be with you Lady; and to you what you desire too.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: It should be some such good thing like your self then.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Heaven keep me from that curse, and all my issue. Good night Antiquity.

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: Solamen Miseris socios habuisse Doloris: but I alone.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Learned Sir, will you bid my man come to me? and requesting a greater measure of your learning, good night, good Master Roger.

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: Good Sir, peace be with you.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Adue dear Domine. Half a dozen such in a Kingdom would make a man forswear confession: for who that had but half his wits about him, would commit the Counsel of a serious sin to such a cruel Night-cap? Why how now shall we have an Antick?
Whose head do you carry upon your shoulders, that you jole it so against the Post? Is't for your ease? Or have you seen the Celler? Where are my slippers Sir?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Here Sir.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Where Sir? have you got the pot Verdugo? have you seen the Horses Sir?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Yes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Have they any meat?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Faith Sir, they have a kind of wholesome Rushes, Hay I cannot call it.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: And no Provender?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Sir, so I take it.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: You are merry Sir, and why so?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose:
Faith Sir, here are no Oats to be got, unless you'l have 'em in Portedge: the people are so mainly given to
spoon-meat: yonder's a cast of Coach mares of the Gentlewomans, the strangest Cattel.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Why?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Why, they are transparent Sir, you may see through them: and such a house!

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Come Sir, the truth of your discovery.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Sir, they are in tribes like Jewes: the Kitchin and the Daytie make one tribe, and have their faction and their fornication within themselves; the Buttery and the Landry are another, and there's no love lost; the chambers are intire, and what's done there, is somewhat higher than my knowledge: but this I am sure, between these copulations, a stranger is kept vertuous, that is, fasting. But of all this the drink Sir.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: What of that Sir?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Faith Sir, I will handle it as the time and your patience will give me leave. This drink, or this cooling Julip, of which three spoonfuls kills the Calenture, a pint breeds the cold Palsie.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Sir, you bely the house.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: I would I did Sir. But as I am a true man, if 'twere but one degree colder, nothing but an Asses hoof would hold it.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: I am glad on't Sir, for if it had proved stronger, you had been tongue ^'d of these commendations. Light me the candle Sir, I'le hear no more.

speeches.speaker: Yo. Lo.
verse: Come my brave man of war, trace out thy darling,
And you my learned Council, ^ and turn boyes,
Kiss till the Cow come home, kiss close, kiss close knaves.
My Modern Poet, thou shalt kiss in couplets.
Strike up you merry varlets, and leave your peeping,
This is no pay for Fidlers.

speeches.speaker: Capt.
verse: O my dear boy, thy Hercules, thy Captain
Makes thee his Hyla^, his delight, his solace.
Love thy brave man of war, and let thy bounty
Clap him in Shamois: Let there be deducted out of our main potation
Five Marks in hatchments to adorn this thigh,
C^ampt with this rest of peace, and I will sight
Thy battels.

speeches.speaker: Yo. Lo.
verse: Thou shalt hav't boy, and fly in Feather,
Lead on a March you Michers.

speeches.speaker: Savill.
prose: O my head, O my heart, what a noyse and change where! would I had been cold i'th' mouth before this day, and ne're have liv'd to see this dissolution. He that lives within a mile of this place, had as good sleep in the perpetual noyse of an Iron Mill. There's a dead Sea of drink i'th' S^ller, in which goodly vessels lye wrackt, and in the middle of this deluge appear the tops of slagons and black jacks, like Churches drown'd i'th' marshes.

speeches.speaker: Yo. Lo.
prose: What, art thou come? My sweet Sir Amias welcome to ^. Come thou shalt kiss my Helen, and court her in a dance.

speeches.speaker: Sa^
prose: Good Sir consider?

speeches.speaker: Yo. Lo.
prose: Shall we consider Gentlemen? How say you?

speeches.speaker: Capt.
prose: Consider? that were a simple toy i'saith, consider? whose moral's that? The man that cryes consider is our foe: ^ my st^l know him.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Stay thy dead doing hand, he must not die yet: p^ethee be calm my Hector?

speeches.speaker: Capt.
prose: Pea^ant slave, thou groom compos'd of grudgings, ^ and than^ this Gentleman, thou hadst seen Pl^to else. The next consider kills thee.

speeches.speaker: Trav.
prose: Let him drink down his word again in a gallon of Sack?

speeches.speaker: Po^.
prose: Tis but a snusle, make it two gallons, and let him doe it kneeling in repentance.

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: Nay rather kill me, there's but a lay-man lost. Good Captain doe your office?

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Thou shalt drink Steward, drink and dance my Steward. Strike him a horn-pipe squeakers, take thy striver, and pace her till she stew.

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: Sure Sir, I cannot dance with your Gentlewomen, they are too light for me, pray break my head, and let me goe?

speeches.speaker: Capt.
prose: He shall dance, he shall dance.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: He shall dance, and drink, and be drunk and dance, and be drunk again, and shall see no meat in a year.

speeches.speaker: Poet.
prose: And three quarters?

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: And three quarters be it.

speeches.speaker: Capt.
prose: Who knocks there? let him in.

speeches.speaker: Savill.
prose: Some to deliver me I hope.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Gentlemen, God save you all, my business is to one Master Loveless?

speeches.speaker: Capt.
prose: This is the Gentleman you mean; view him, and take his Inventorie, he's a right one.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: He promises no less Sir.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Sir, your business?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Sir, I should let you know, yet I am loth, yet I am sworn to't, would some other tongue would speak it for me.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Out with it i' Gods name.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: All I desire Sir is, the patience and sufferance of a man, and good Sir be not mov'd more.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Then a pottle of sack will doe, here's my hand, pr^thee thy business?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose:
Good Sir excuse me, and whatsoever you hear, think must have been known unto you, and be your self ^
screet, and bear it nobly.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Prethee dispatch me?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Your Brother's dead Sir?

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Thou dost not mean dead drunk?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: No, no, dead and drown'd at sea Sir.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Art sure he's dead?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Too sure Sir.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: I but art thou very certainly sure of it?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: As sure Sir, as I tell it.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: But art thou sure he came not up again?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: He may come up, but ne're to call you Brother?

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: But art sure he had water enough to drown him?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Sure Sir, he wanted none.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: I would not have him want, I lov'd him better; here I forgive thee: and i'faith be plain, how do I bear it?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Very wisely Sir.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
