prose: Fill him some wine. Thou dost not see me mov'd, these transitorie toyes ne're trouble me, he's in a better place, my friend I know't. Some fellows would have cryed now, and have curst thee, and faln out with their meat, and kept a pudder; but all this helps not, he was too good for us, and let God keep him: there's the right use on't friend. Off with thy drink, thou hast a spice of sorrow makes thee dry: fill him another. Savill, your Master's dead, and who am I now Savill? Nay, let's all bear it well, wipe Savill wipe, tears are but thrown away: we shall have wenches now, shall we not Savill?

speeches.speaker: Savill.
prose: Yes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: And drink innumerable.

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: Yes forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: And you'll strain curtsie and be drunk a little?

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: I would be glad, Sir, to doe my weak endeavour.

speeches.speaker: Yo. Lo.
prose: You may be brought in time to love a wench too.

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: In time the sturdie Oak Sir.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Some more wine for my friend there.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I shall be drunk anon for my good news: but I have a loving Brother, that's my comfort.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose:
Here's to you Sir, this is the worst I wish you for your news: and if I had another elder Brother, and say it were his chance to feed Haddocks, I should be still the same
you see me now, a poor contented Gentleman. More wine for my friend there, he's dry again.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I shall be if I follow this beginning. Well my dear Brother, if I scape this drowning, 'tis your turn next to sink, you shall duck twice before I help you. Sir I cannot drink more; pray let me have your pardon.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: O Lord Sir, 'tis your modestie: more wine, give him a bigger glass; hug him my Captain, thou shalt be my chief mourner.

speeches.speaker: Capt.
prose: And this my pennon: Sir, a full carouse to you, and to my Lord of Land here.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I feel a buzzing in my brains, pray God they bear this out, and I'le ne're trouble them so far again. Here's to you Sir?

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: To my dear Steward, down o' your knees you infidel, you Pagan; be drunk and penitent.

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: Forgive me Sir, and I'le be any thing.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Then be a Baud, I'le have thee a brave Band.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Sir, I must take my leave of you, my business is so urgent.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Let's have a bridling cast before you go. Fill's a new stoupe.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I dare not Sir, by no means.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Have you any mind to a wench? I would fain gratifie you for the pains you took Sir.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: As little as to the t'other.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: If you find any stirring do but say so.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Sir, you are too bounteous, when I feel that itching, you shall asswage it Sir, before another: this only and Farewell Sir. Your Brother when the storm was most extream, told all about him, he left a will which lies close behind a Chimney in the matted Chamber: and so as well Sir, as you have made me able, I take my leave.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Let us imbrace him all: if you grow drie before you end your business, pray take a baite here, I have a fresh hogshead for you.

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: You shall neither will nor chuse Sir. My Master is a wonderfull fine Gentleman, has a fine state, a very fine state Sir, I am his Steward Sir, and his man.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Would you were your own sir, as I left you. Well I must cast about, or all sinks.

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: Farewell Gentleman, Gentleman, Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: What would you with me sir?

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: Farewell Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: O sleep Sir, sleep.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Well boyes, you see what's faln, let's in and drink, and give thanks for it.

speeches.speaker: Capt.
prose: Let's give thanks for it.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Drunk as I live.

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: Drunk as I live boyes.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Why, now thou art able to discharge thine office, and cast up a reckoning of some weight; I will be knighted, for my state will bear it, 'tis sixteen hundred boyes: off with your husks, I'le skin you all in Sattin.

speeches.speaker: Capt.
prose: O sweet Loveless!

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: All in Sattin? O sweet Loveless!

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: March in my noble Compeeres: and this my Countess shall be led by two: and so proceed we to the Will.

speeches.speaker: Morec.
prose: And Widow as I say be your own friend: your husband left you wealthy, I and wife, continue so sweet duck, continue so. Take heed of young smooth Varlets, younger Brothers: they are worms that will eat through your bags: they are very Lightning, that with a flash or two will melt your money, and never singe your pursestrings: they are Colts, wench Colts, heady and dangerous, till we take 'em up, and make 'em sit for Bonds: look upon me, I have had, and have yet matter of moment girle, matter of moment; you may meet with a worse back, I'le not commend it.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Nor I neither Sir?

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: Yet thus far by your favour Widow, 'tis tusse.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: And therefore not for my dyet, for I love a tender one.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: Sweet Widow leave your frumps, and be edified you know my state, I sell no Perspectives, Scarfs, Gloves, nor Hangers, nor put my trust in Shoe-ties; and where your Husband in an age was rising by burnt figs, dreg'd with meal and powdered sugar, saunders, and grains, wormeseed and rotten Raisins, and such vile Tobacco, that made the footmen mangie; I in a year have put up hundreds inclos'd, my Widow, those pleasant Meadows, by a forseit morgage: for which the poor Knight takes a lone chamber, owes for his Ale, and dare not beat his Hostess: nay more —

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Good Sir no more, what ere my Husband was, I know what I am, and if you marry me, you must bear it bravely off Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: Not with the head, sweet Widow.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: No sweet Sir, but with your shoulders: I must have you dub'd, for under that I will not stoop a feather. My husband was a fellow lov'd to toyle, fed ill, made gain his exercise, and so grew costive, which for that I was his wife, I gave way to, and spun mine own smocks course, and sir, so little: but let that pass, time, that wears all things out, wore out this husband, who in penitence of such fruitless five years marriage, left me great with his wealth, which if you'le be a worthie gossip to, be knighted Sir?

speeches.speaker: Morec.
prose: Now, Sir, from whom come you? whose man are you Sir?

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: Sir, I come from young Master Loveless.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: Be silent Sir, I have no money, not a penny for you, he's sunk, your Master's sunk, a perisht man Sir.

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: Indeed his Brother's sunk sir, God be with him, a perisht man indeed, and drown'd at Sea.

speeches.speaker: Morec.
prose: How saidst thou, good my friend, his Brother drown'd?

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: Untimely sir, at Sea.

speeches.speaker: Morec.
prose: And thy young Master left sole Heir?

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: Yes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Morec.
prose: And he wants money?

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: Yes, and sent me to you, for he is now to be knighted.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: Widow be wise, there's more Land coming, widow be very wise, and give thanks for me widow.

speeches.speaker: Widow.
prose: Be you very wise, and be knighted, and then give thanks for me Sir?

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: What sayes your worship to this mony?

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: I say he may have mony if he please.

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: A thousand Sir?

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: A thousand Sir, provided any wise Sir, his Land lye for the payment, otherwise —

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: He's here himself Sir, and can better tell you.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: My notable dear friend, and worthy Master Loveless, and now right worshipfull, all joy and welcom.

speeches.speaker: Yo. Lo.
prose: Thanks to my dear incloser Master Morecraft, prethee old Angel gold, salute my family, I'le do as much for yours; this, and your own desires, fair Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: And yours Sir, if you mean well; 'tis a hansome Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Sirrah, my Brother's dead.

speeches.speaker: More.
prose: Dead?

speeches.speaker: Yo. Lo.
prose: Dead, and by this time soust for Ember Week.

speeches.speaker: Morecraft.
prose: Dead?

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Drown'd, drown'd at sea man, by the next fresh Conger that comes we shall hear more.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: Now by my faith of my body it moves me much.

speeches.speaker: Yo. Lo.
prose: What, wilt thou be an Ass, and weep for the dead? why I thought nothing but a general inundation would have mov'd thee, prethe be quiet, he hath left his land behind him.

speeches.speaker: Morecraft.
prose: O has he so?

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Yes faith, I thank him for't, I have all boy, hast any ready mony?

speeches.speaker: Morecraft.
prose: Will you sell Sir?

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: No not out right good Gripe; marry, a morgage or such a slight securitie.

speeches.speaker: More.
prose: I have no mony, Sir, for Morgage; if you will sell, and all or none, I'le work a new Mine for you.

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose:
Good Sir look before you, he'l work you out of all else: if you sell all your Land, you have sold your Country, and then you must to Sea, to seek your Brother, and there lye p^ed in a Powdering tub, and break your teeth with Biskets and hard Beef, that must have wat^ing Sir: and where's your ^00 pounds a year in drink then? If you'l tun up the Straights you may, for you have no calling for drink t^re, but with a Canon, nor no scoring but on your Ships sides, and then if you scape with life, and take a Faggot boat and a bottle of
~squebaugh, come home poor men, like a tip^ of Thames street s^inking of Pitch and Poor-John. I cannot tell Sir, I would be loth to see it.

speeches.speaker: Capt.
prose:
Steward, you are an Ass, a meazel'd mungril, and were ^t not again the peace of my soveraign friend here, I would br^ your ^ore-casting Coxcomb, dog I would even with m^ staffe of Office there. Thy Pen and Inkhorn Noble ^, the God of gold here has sed thee well, take mony for th^
^: ha^ and believe, thou art cold of constitution, thy ^ unhealthful, sell and be wise; we are three that will adorn thee, and live according to thine own heart child; ^ all be only ours, and only ours shall be the black eyed beauties of the time. Mony makes men Eternal.

speeches.speaker: Poet.
prose:
Do what you will, 'tis the noblest course, then you may live without the charge of people, only we four will make a Family, I and an Age that will beget new An ^als, in which I'le write thy life my son of pleasure, equal wit^
Nero and Cal^gula.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: What m^n were they Captain?

speeches.speaker: Capt.
prose: Two roaring Boys of Rome, that made all split.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Come Sir, what dare you give?

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: You will not fell Sir?

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Who told you so Sir?

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: Good Sir have a care.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Peace, or I'le tack your Tongue up to your Roof. What money? speak.

speeches.speaker: More.
prose: Six thousand pound Sir.

speeches.speaker: Capt.
prose: Take it, h'as over bidden by the Sun: bind him to his bargain quickly.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Come strike me luck with earnest, and draw the writings.

speeches.speaker: More.
prose: There's a Gods peny for thee.

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: Sir lo^ my old Masters sake let my Farm be excepted, if I b come his Tenant I am undone, my Children begge^s, and in, Wise God knows what: consider me dear Si^.

speeches.speaker: More.
prose: I'le have all o^ none.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: All in, all in^ dispatch the writings.

speeches.speaker: W^d.
prose: Go, thou art a pretty forehanded fellow, would thou wert wis^.

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: Now do I sensibly begin to feel my self a Rascal; would I could teach a School, or beg, or lye well, I am utterly undone; now he that taught thee to deceive and consen, take thee to his mercy; so be it.

speeches.speaker: More.
prose: Come Widow come, never stand upon a Knight hood, 'tis a meer paper honour, and not proof enough for a Ser^ant. Come, Come, I'le make thee.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: To answer in short, 'tis this Sir. No Knight no Widow, if you make me any thing, it must be a Lady, and so I ta^e my leave.

speeches.speaker: M^e.
prose: Farewel sweet Widow, and think of it.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Sir, I do more than think of it, it makes me dream Sir.

speeches.speaker: More.
prose: She's rich and sober, if this itch were from her: ^ say I be at the charge to pay the Footmen, and the Trumpets, I and the Horsemen too, and be a Knight, and she refuse me thou; then am I horst into the subsidy, and so by consequence should prove a Coxcomb: I'le have a care of that. Six thousand pound, and then the Land is mine, there's some refreshing yet.

speeches.speaker: Abigal.
prose: IF he but follow me, as all my hopes tell me, he's man enough, up goes my rest, and I know I shall draw him.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: This is the strangest pampered piece of flesh towards fifty, that ever frailty copt withal, what a trim lennoy here she has put upon me, these women are a proud kind of Cattel, and love this whorson doing so directly, that they will not stick to make their very skins Bawdes to their flesh. Here's Dogskin and Storax sufficient to kill a Hawk: what to do with it, besides nailing it up amongst Irish heads of Teere, to shew the mightiness of her Palm, I know not: there she is. I must enter into Dialogue. Lady you have lost your Glove.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: Not Sir, if you have found it.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: It was my meaning Lady to restore it.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: 'Twill be uncivil in me to take back a favour, Fortune hath so well bestowed Sir, pray wear it for me.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: I had rather wear a Bell. But hark you Mistres, what hidden vertue is there in this Glove, that you would have me wear it? Is't good against sore eyes, or will it charm the Toothach? Or these red tops; being steept in white wine soluble, wil't kill the Itch? Or has it so conceal'd a providence to keep my hand from Bonds? If it have none of these and prove no more but a bare Glove of half a Crown a pair, 'twill be but half a courtesie, I wear two alwayes, faith let's draw cuts, one will do me no pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: The tenderness of his years keeps him as yet in ignorance, he's a well moulded fellow, and I wonder his bloud should stir no higher; but 'tis his want of company: I must grow nearer to him.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: God save you both.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: And pardon you Sir; this is somewhat rude, how came you hither?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Why through the doors, they are open.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: What are you? And what business have you here?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: More I believe than you have.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: Who would this fellow speak with? Art thou sober?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Yes, I come not here to sleep.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Prethee what art thou?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: As much (gay man) as thou art, I am a Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Art thou no more?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Yes more than thou dar'st be; a Souldier.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: Thou dost not come to quarrel?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: No, not with women; I come to speak here with a Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: Why, I am one.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: But not with one so gentle.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: This is a fine fellow.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Sir, I am not fine yet. I am but new come over, direct me with your ticket to your Taylor, and then I shall be fine Sir. Lady if there be a better of your Sex within this house, say I would see her.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: Why am not I good enough for you Sir?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Your way you'l be too good, pray end my business. This is another Sutor, O frail Woman!

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: This fellow with his bluntness hopes to do more than the long sutes of a thousand could; though he be sowre he's quick, I must not trust him. Sir, this Lady is not to speak with you, she is more serious: you smell as if you were new calkt; go and be hansome, and then you may fit with her Servingmen.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: What are you Sir?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Guess by my outside.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose:
Then I take you Sir, for some new silken thing wean'd from the Country, that shall (when you come to keep good company) be beaten into better manners. Pray
good proud Gentlewoman, help me to your Mistress.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
verse: How many lives hast thou, that thou talk'st thus rudely?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
verse: But one, one, I am neither Cat nor Woman.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
verse: And will that one life, Sir, maintain you ever in such bold sawciness?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
verse: Yes, amongst a Nation of such men as you are, and be no worse for wearing, shall I speak with this Lady?

speeches.speaker: Abig.
verse: No by my troth shall you not.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
verse: I must stay here then?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
verse: That you shall not neither.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
verse: Good fine thing tell me why?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
verse: Good angry thing I'le tell you:
This is no place for such companions,
Such lousie Gentlemen shall find their business
Better i'th' Suburbs, there your strong pitch perfume,
Mingled with lees of Ale, shall reek in fashion:
This is no Thames-street, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
verse: This Gentleman informs you truly:
Prethee be satisfied, and seek the Suburbs,
Good Captain, or what ever title else,
The Warlike Eele boats have bestowed upon thee,
Go and reform thy self, prethee be sweeter,
And know my Lady speaks with no Swabbers.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
verse: You cannot talk me out with your tradition
Of wit you pick from Plays, go to, I have found ye:
And for you, Sir, whose tender gentle blood
Runs in your Nose, and makes you snuff at all,
But three pil'd people, I do let you know,
He that begot your worships Sattin-sute,
Can make no men Sir: I will see this Lady,
And with the reverence of your silkenship,
In these old Ornaments.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
verse: You will not sure?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
verse: Sure Sir I shall?

speeches.speaker: Abig.
verse: You would be beaten out?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
verse: Indeed I would not, or if I would be beaten,
Pray who shall beat me? this good Gentleman
Looks as he were o'th' peace.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
verse: Sir you shall see that: will you get you out?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
verse: Yes, that, that shall correct your boys tongue.
Dare you fight, I will stay here still.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
verse: O their things are out, help, help for Gods sake,
Madam; Jesus they foin at one another.
Madam, why, who is within there?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Who breeds this rudeness?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
verse: This uncivil fellow;
He saies he comes from Sea, where I believe,
H'as purg'd away his manners.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Why what of him?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
verse: Why he will rudely without once God bless you,
Press to your privacies, and no denial
Must stand betwixt your person and his business;
I let go his ill Language.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Sir, have you business with me?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
verse: Madam some I have,
But not so serious to pawn my life for't:
If you keep this quarter, and maintain about you
Such Knights o'th' Sun as this is, to defie
Men of imployment to ye, you may live,
But in what fame?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Pray stay Sir, who has wrong'd you?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
verse: Wrong me he cannot, though uncivilly
He flung his wild words at me: but to you
I think he did no honour, to deny
The hast I come withal, a passage to you,
Though I seem course.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Excuse me gentle Sir, 'twas from my knowledge,
And shall have no protection. And to you Sir,
You have shew'd more heat than wit, and from your self
Have borrowed power, I never gave you here,
To do these vile unmanly things: my house
Is no blind street to swagger in; and my favours
Not doting yet on your unknown deserts
So far, that I should make you Master of my business,
My credit yet stands fairer with the people
Than to be tried with swords; and they that come
To do me service, must not think to win me
With hazard of a murther; if your love
Consist in fury, carry it to the Camp:
And there in honour of some common Mistress,
Shorten your youth, I pray be better temper'd:
And give me leave a while Sir.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
verse: You must have it.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Now Sir, your business?

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
verse: First, I thank you for schooling this young fellow,
Whom his own follies, which he's prone enough
Daily to fall into, if you but frown,
Shall level him a way to his repentance:
Next, I should rail at you, but you are a Woman,
And anger's lost upon you.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Why at me Sir?
I never did you wrong, for to my knowledge
This is the first sight of you.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
verse: You have done that,
I must confess I have the least curse in
Because the least acquaintance: But there be
(If there be honour in the minds of men)
Thousands when they shall know what I deliver,
(As all good men must share in't) will to shame
Blast your black memory.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: How is this good Sir?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
verse: 'Tis that, that if you have a soul will choak it:
Y'ave kill'd a Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: I kill'd a Gentleman!

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
verse: You and your cruelty have kill'd him Woman,
And such a man (let me be angry in't)
Whose least worth weighed above all womens vertues
That are; I spare you all to come too: guess him now?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: I am so innocent I cannot Sir.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
verse: Repent you mean, you are a perfect Woman,
And as the first was, made for mans undoing.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Sir, you have mist your way, I am not she.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
verse: Would he had mist his way too, though he had
Wandered farther than Women are ill spoken of,
So he had mist this misery, you Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: How do you do, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
verse: Well enough I hope.
While I can keep my self out from temptations.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Leap into this matter, whither would ye?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
verse: You had a Servant that your peevishness
Injoined to Travel.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Such a one I have
Still, and shall be griev'd 'twere otherwise.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
verse: Then have your asking, and be griev'd he's dead;
How you will answer for his worth, I know not,
But this I am sure, either he, or you, or both
Were stark mad, else he might have liv'd
To have given a stronger testimony to th' world
Of what he might have been. He was a man
I knew but in his evening, ten Suns after,
Forc'd by a Tyrant storm our beaten Bark
Bulg'd under us; in which sad parting blow,
He call'd upon his Saint, but not for life,
On you unhappy Woman, and whilest all
Sought to preserve their Souls, he desperately
Imbrac'd a Wave, crying to all that saw it,
If any live, go to my Fate that forc'd me
To this untimely end, and make her happy:
His name was Loveless: And I scap't the storm,
And now you have my business.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: 'Tis too much.
Would I had been that storm, he had not perisht.
If you'l rail now I will forgive you Sir?
Or if you'l call in more, if any more
Come from this ruine, I shall justly suffer
What they can say, I do confess my self
A guiltie cause in this. I would say more,
But grief is grown too great to be delivered.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
verse: I like this well: these women are strange things.
Tis somewhat of the latest now to weep,
You should have wept when he was going from you,
And chain'd him with those tears at home.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Would you had told me then so, these two arms had been his Sea.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Trust me you move me much: but say he lived, these were forgotten things again.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: I, say you so? Sure I should know that voice: this is knavery. I'le fit you for it. Were he living Sir, I would perswade you to be charitable, I, and confess we are not all so ill as your opinion holds us. O my friend, what penance shall I pull upon my fault, upon my most unworthy self for this?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Leave to love others, 'twas some jealousie
That turn'd him desperate.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: I'le be with you straight: are you wrung there?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: This works a main upon her.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: I do confess there is a Gentleman
Has born me long good will.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I do not like that.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: And vow'd a thousand services to me; to me, regardless of him: But since Fate, that no power can withstand, has taken from me my first, and best love, and to weep away my youth is a mere folly, I will shew you what I determine sir: you shall know all: Call M. Welford there: That Gentleman I mean to make the model of my Fortunes, and in his chast imbraces keep alive the memory of my lost lovely Loveless: he is somewhat like him too.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Then you can love.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Yes certainly Sir?
Though it please you to think me hard and cruel,
I hope I shall perswade you otherwise.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I have made my self a fine fool.

speeches.speaker: W^l.
prose: Would you have spoke with me Madam?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Yes M. Welford, and I ask your pardon before this Gentleman for being froward: this kiss, and henceforth more affection.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: So, 'tis better I were drown'd indeed.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: This is a sudden passion, God hold it.
This fellow out of his fear sure has
Perswaded her. I'le give him a new suit on't.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: A parting kiss, and good Sir, let me pray you
To wait me in the Gallerie.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: I am in another world, Madam where you please.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I will to Sea, and 't shall goe hard but I'le be drown'd indeed.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Now Sir you see I am no such hard creature,
But time may win me.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: You have forgot your lost Love.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Alas Sir, what would you have me do? I cannot call him back again with sorrow; I'le love this man as dearly, and besh^ow me I'le keep him far enough from Sea, and 'twas told me, now I remember me, by an old wise woman, that my first Love should be drown'd, and see 'tis come about.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I would she had told you your second should be hang'd too, and let that come about: but this is very strange.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Faith Sir, consider all, and then I know you'le be of my mind: if weeping would redeem him, I would weep still.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: But say that I were Loveless,
And scap'd the storm, how would you answer this?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Why for that Gentleman I would leave all the world.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: This young thing too?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: That young thing too,
^ any young thing else: why, I would lose my state.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Why then he lives still, I am he, your Loveless.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Alas I knew it Sir, and for that purpose prepared this Pageant: get you to your task. And leave these Players tricks, or I shall leave you, indeed I shall. Travel, or know me not.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Will you then marry?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: I will not promise, take your choice. Farewell.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: There is no other Purgatorie but a Woman.
I must doe something.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Mistress I am bold.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: You are indeed.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: You so overjoyed me Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Take heed you surfeit not, pray fast and welcom.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: By this light you love me extreamly.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: By this, and to morrows light, I care not for you.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Come, come, you cannot hide it.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Indeed I can, where you shall never find it.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: I like this mirth well Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: You shall have more on't.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: I must kiss you.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: No Sir.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Indeed I must.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: What must be, must be; I'le take my leave, ye^ have your parting blow: I pray commend me to those few friends you have, that sent you hither, and tell them when you travel next, 'twere sit you brought less bravery with you, and more wit, you'le never get a wife else.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Are you in earnest?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Yes faith. Will you eat Sir, your horses will be readie straight, you shall have a napkin laid in the butterie for ye.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Do not you love me then?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Yes, for that face.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: It is a good one Ladie.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Yes, if it were not warpt, the fire in time may mend it.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Me thinks yours is none of the best Ladie.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: No by my troth Sir; yet o'my conscience,
You would make shift with it.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Come pray no more of this?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: I will not: Fare you well. Ho, who's within there? bring out the Gentlemans horses, he's in haste; and set some cold meat on the Table.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: I have too much of that I thank you Ladie: take your Chamber when you please, there goes a black one with you Ladie.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Farewell young man.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: You have made me one, Farewell: and may the curse of a great house fall upon thee, I mean the Butler. The devil and all his works are in these women, would all of my sex were of my mind, I would make 'em a new Lent, and a long one, that flesh might be in more reverence with them.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: I am sorry M. Welford.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: So am I, that you are here.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: How does my Ladie use you?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: As I would use you, scurvilie.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: I should have been more kind Sir?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: I should have been undone then. Pray leave me, and look to your sweet meats; hark, your Ladie calls?

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: Sir, I shall borrow so much time without offence.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Y'are nothing but offence, for Gods love leave me.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: 'Tis strange my Ladie should be such a tyrant?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: To send you to me, 'Pray goe stitch, good doe, y'are more trouble to me than a Term.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: I do not know how my good will, if I said love I lied not, should any way deserve this?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: A thousand waies, a thousand waies; sweet creature let me depart in peace.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: What Creature Sir? I hope I am a woman.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: A hundred I think by your noise.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: Since you are angrie Sir, I am bold to tell you that I am a woman, and a rib.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Of a roasted horse.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: Conster me that?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: A Dog can doe it better; Farwell Countess, and commend me to your Ladie, tell her she's proud, and scurvie, and so I commit you both to your tempter.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: Sweet Mr. Welford.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Avoid old Satanus: Go daub your ruines, your face looks fouler than a storm: the Foot-man stayes for you in the Lobby Lady.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: If you were a Gentleman, I should know it by your gentle conditions? are these sit words to give a Gentlewoman?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: As fit as they were made for ye: Sirrah, my horses. Farwell old Adage, keep your nose warm, the Rheum will make it horn else—

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: The blessings of a Prodigal young heir be thy companions Welford, marry come up my Gentleman, are your gums grown so tender they cannot bite? A skittish Filly will be your fortune Welford, and fair enough for such a packsaddle. And I doubt not (if my aim hold) to see her made to amble to your hand.

speeches.speaker: Captain.
prose: Save thy brave shoulder, my young puissant Knight, and may thy back Sword bite them to the bone that love thee not, thou art an errant man, go on. The circumcis'd shall fall by thee. Let Land and labour fill the man that tills, thy sword must be thy plough, and Jove it speed. Mecha shall sweat, and Mahomet shall fall, and thy dear name fill up his monument.

speeches.speaker: Yo. L.
prose: It shall Captain, I mean to be a Worthy.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
prose: One Worthy is too little, thou shalt be all.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: Captain I shall deserve some of your love too.

speeches.speaker: Capt.
prose: Thou shalt have heart and hand too, noble Morecraft, if thou wilt lend me mony. I am a man of Garrison, be rul'd, and open to me those infernal gates, whence none of thy evil Angels pass again, and I will stile thee noble, nay Don Diego. I'le woo thy Infanta for thee, and my Knight shall feast her with high meats, and make her apt.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: Pardon me Captain, y'are beside my meaning.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: No Mr. Morecraft, 'tis the Captains meaning I should prepare her for ye.

speeches.speaker: Capt.
prose: Or provok her. Speak my modern man, I say provoke her.

speeches.speaker: Poet.
prose: Captain, I say so too, or stir her to it. So say the Criticks.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: But howsoever you expound it sir, she's very welcom, and this shall serve for witness. And Widow, since y'are come so happily, you shall deliver up the keyes, and free possession of this house, whilst I stand by to ratifie.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: I had rather give it back again believe me,
'Tis a miserie to say you had it. Take heed?

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: 'Tis past that Widow, come, sit down, some wine there, there is a scurvie banquet if we had it. All this fair house is yours Sir, Savil?

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: Yes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Are your keyes readie, I must ease your burden.

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: I am readie Sir to be undone, when you shall call me to't.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Come come, thou shalt live better.

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: I shall have less to doe, that's all, there's half a dozen of my friends i'th' fields sunning against a bank, with half a breech among 'em, I shall be with 'em shortly. The care and continuall vexation of being rich, eat up this rascall. What shall become of my poor familie, they are no sheep, and they must keep themselves.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Drink Master Morecraft, pray be merrie all:
Nay and you will not drink there's no societie,
Captain speak loud, and drink: widow, a word.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
prose: Expound her throughly Knight. Here God o' gold, here's to thy fair possessions; Be a Baron and a bold one: leave off your tickling of young heirs like Trouts, and let thy Chimnies smoke. Feed men of war, live and be honest, and be saved yet.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: I thank you worthie Captain for your counsel. You keep your Chimnies smoking there, your nostrils, and when you can, you feed a man of War, this makes you not a Baron, but a bare one: and how or when you shall be saved, let the Clark o'th' companie (you have commanded) have a just care of.

speeches.speaker: Poet.
prose: The man is much moved. Be not angrie Sir, but as the Poet sings, let your displeasure be a short furie, and goe out. You have spoke home, and bitterly, to me Sir? Captain take truce, the Miser is a tart and a wittie whorson—

speeches.speaker: Cap.
prose: Poet, you feign perdie, the wit of this man lies in his singers ends, he must tell all; his tongue fills his mouth like a neats tongue, and only serves to lick his hungrie chaps after a purchase: his brains and brimstone are the devils diet to a fat usurers head: To her Knight, to her: clap her aboard, and slow her. Where's the brave Steward?

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: Here's your poor friend, and Savil Sir?

speeches.speaker: Capt.
prose: Away, th'art rich in ornaments of nature. First in thy face, thou hast a serious face, a betting, bargaining, and saving face, a rich face, pawn it to the Usurer; a face to kindle the compassion of the most ignorant and frozen Justice.

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: 'Tis such I dare not shew it shortly sir.

speeches.speaker: Capt.
prose: Be blithe and bonny steward: Master Morecraft, Drink to this man of reckoning?

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: Here's e'ne to him.

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: The Devil guide it downward: would there were in't an acre of the great broom field he bought, to sweep your durtie Conscience, or to choak ye, 'tis all one to me, Usurer.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Consider what I told you, you are young, unapt for worldly business: Is it sit one of such tenderness, so delicate, so contrarie to things of care, should stir and break her better meditations, in the bare brokage of a brace of Angels? or a new Kirtel, though it be Satten? eat by the hope of surfeits, and lie down only in expectation of a morrow, that may undo some easie hearted fool, or reach a widows curses? Let out mony, whose use returns the principal? and get out of these troubles, a consuming heir: For such a one must follow necessarily, you shall die hated, if not old and miserable; and that possest wealth that you got with pining, live to see tumbled to anothers hands, that is no more a kin to you, than you to his co^zenage.

speeches.speaker: Widow.
prose: Sir you speak well, would God that charity had first begun here?

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: 'Tis yet time, Be merrie, me thinks you want wine there, there's more i'th' house. Captain, where rests the health?

speeches.speaker: Captain.
prose: It shall goe round boy?

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Say you can suffer this, because the end points at much profit, can you so far bow below your blood, below your too much beautie, to be a partner of this fellowes bed, and lie with his diseases? if you can, I will nor press you further: yet look upon him: there's nothing in that hide-bound Usurer, that man of mat, that all decai'd, but aches, for you to love, unless his perisht lungs, his drie cough, or his scurvie. This is truth, and so far I dare speak yet: he has yet past cure of Physick, spaw, or any diet, a primitive pox in his bones; and o' my Knowledge he has been ten times rowell'd: ye may love him; he had a bastard, his own toward issue, whipt, and then cropt for washing out the roses, in three farthings to make 'em pence.

speeches.speaker: Widow.
prose: I do not like these Morals?

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: You must not like him then?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: By your leave Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose:
By my troth sir you are welcom, welcom faith: Lord what a stranger you are grown; pray know this Gen~tlewoman, and if you please these friends here: we are merry,
you see the worst on't; your house has been kept warm Sir?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I am glad to hear it Brother, pray God you are wise too.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose:
Pray Mr
Morecraft know my elder Brother, and Captain do you complement. Savil I date swear is glad at heart to see you; Lord, we heard Sir you were drown'd at Sea, and see how luckily things come about?

speeches.speaker: More.
prose: This mony must be paid again Sir.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: No Sir, pray keep the Sale, 'twill make good Tailo^s measures; I am well I thank you.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: By my troth the Gentleman has stew'd him in his own Sawce, I shall love him for't.

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: I know not where I am, I am so glad: your worship is the welcom'st man alive; upon my knees I bid you welcome home: here has been such a hurry, such a din, such dismal Drinking, Swearing and Whoring, 'thas almost made me mad: we have all liv'd in a continual Turnbal-street; Sir, blest be Heaven, that sent you safe again, now shall I eat and go to bed again.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Brother dismiss these people.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose:
Captain be gone a while, meet me at my old Randevouse in the evening, take your small Poet with you. Mr
Morecraft you were best go prattle with your learned Counsel, I shall preserve your mony, I was couzen'd when time was, we are quit Sir.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Better and better still.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: What is this fellow, Brother?

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: The thirsty Usurer that supt my Land off.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: What does he tarry for?

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Si^ to be Landlord of your House and State: I was bold to make a little sale Sir.

speeches.speaker: More.
prose: Am I overreach'd? if there be Law I'le hamper ye.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: P^ethee be gone, and rave at home, thou art so base a fool I cannot laugh at thee: Sirrah, this comes of couzening, home and spa^e, eat Reddish till you raise your sums again. If you stir far in this, I'le have you whipt, your ca^s nail'd for intelligencing o'the Pillory, and your goods forfeit: you are a stale conzener, leave my house: no more.

speeches.speaker: More.
prose: A pox upon your house. Come Widow, I shall yet hamper this young Gamester.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Good twelve i'th' hundred keep your way, I am not for your diet, marry in your own Tribe Jew, and get a Broker.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: 'Tis well said Widow: will you jog on Sir?

speeches.speaker: More.
prose: Yes, I will go, but 'tis no matter whither:
But when I trust a wild Fool, and a Woman,
May I lend Gratis, and build Hospitals.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Nay good Sir, make all even, here's a Widow wants your good word for me, she's rich, and may renew me and my fortunes.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I am glad you look before you. Gentlewoman, here is a poor distressed younger Brother.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: You do him wrong Sir, he's a Knight.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I ask you mercy: yet 'tis no matter, his Knighthood is no inheritance I take it: whatsoever he is, he is your Servant, or would be, Lady. Faith be not merciless, but make a man; he's young and handsome, though he b^ my Brother, and his observances may deserve your Love: he shall not sail for means.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Sir you speak like a worthy Brother: and so much I do credit your fair Language, that I shall love your Bro~ther: and so love him, but I shall blush to say more.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Stop her mouth. I hope you shall not live to know that hour when this shall be repented. Now Brother I should chide, but I'le give no distaste to your fair Mistress. I will instruct her in't and she shall do't: you have been wild and ignorant, pray mend it.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Sir, every day now Spring comes on.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose:
To you good Mr
Savil and your Office, thus much I have to say: Y'a^ from my Steward become, first your own Drunk^d, then his Bawd: they say y'are excellent grown in both, and perfect: give me your keys Sir Savil?

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: Good Sir consider whom you left me to.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo
prose: I left you as a carb for, not to provoke my Brothers follies: where's the best drink, now? come, tell me Savil; where's the soundest Whores? Ye old he Goat, ye dried Ape, ye lame Stallion, must you be leading in my house your Whores, like Fairies dance their night rounds, without fear either of King or Constable, within my walls? Are all my Hangings safe; my Sheep unsold yet? I hope my Plate is currant, I ha' too much on't. What say you to 300 pounds in drink now?

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: Good Sir forgive me, and but hear me speak?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Me thinks thou shouldst be drunk still, and not speak, 'tis the more pardonable.

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: I will Sir, if you will have it so.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I thank ye: yes, e'ne pursue it Sir: do yo^ hear? get a Whore soon for your recreation: go look o^ Captain Broken-breech your fellow, and Quarrel if you dare: I shall deliver these Keys to one shall have more honesty, though not so much fine wit Sir. You may walk and gather Cresses sit to cool your Liver; there's something for you to begin a Diet, you'l have the Pox else. Speed yo^ well, Sir Savil: you may eat at my house to preserve life: but keep no Fornication in the Stables.

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: Now must I hang my self, my friends will look sor't.
Eating and sleeping, I do despise you both now:
I will run mad first, and if that get not pitty,
I'le drown my self, to a most dismal ditty.

speeches.speaker: Abigal.
prose:
ALas poor Gentlewoman, to what a misery hath Age brought thee: to what a scurvy Fortune? Thou that hast been a Companion for Noblemen, and at the worst of those times for Gentlemen: now like a broken Servingman, must beg for favour to those, that would have crawl'd like Pilgrims to my Chamber but for an Apparition of me. You that be coming on, make much of fifteen, and so till five and twenty: use your time with reverence, that your profits may arise: it will not tarry with you, Ecce signum: here was a face, but time that like a furfeit eats our youth, plague of his iron teeth, and draw 'em sor't, has been a little bolder here than welcome: and now to say the truth, I am fit for no man. Old men i'th' house of fifty, call me Granum; and when they are drunk, e'ne then, when Jon^
and my Lady are all one, not one will do me reason. My little Levite hath forsaken me, his silver sound of Cittern quite abolish this doleful hymns under my Chamber window, digested into tedious learning: well fool, you leapt a Haddock when you left him: he's a clean man, and a good edifier, and twenty nobles is his state de claro, besides his pigs in posse. To this good Homilist I have been ever stubborn, which God forgive me for, and mend my manners: and Love, if ever thou hadst care of forty, of such a piece of lape ground, hear my prayer, and fire his zeal so far forth that my faults in this renued impression of my love may shew corrected to our gentle reader.

See how negligently he passes by me: with what an Equipage Canonical, as though he had broken the heart of Bellarmine, or added something to the singing Brethren. 'Tis scorn, I know it, and deserve it, Mr
Roger.

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: Fair Gentlewoman, my name is Roger.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: Then gentle Roger?

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: Ungentle Abigal.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose:
Why Mr
Roger will you set your wit to a weak wo~mans?

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: You are weak indeed: for so the Poet sings.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: I do confess my weakness, sweet Sir Roger.

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: Good my Ladies Gentlewoman, or my good Ladies Gentlewoman (this trope is lost to you now) leave your prating, you have a season of your first mother in ye: and surely had the Devil been in love, he had been abused too: go Dalilah, you make men fools, and wear Fig breeches.

speeches.speaker: Abi.
prose: Well, well, hard hearted man; dilate upon the weak infirmities of women: these are fit texts, but once there was a time, would I had never seen those eyes, those eyes, those orient eyes.

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: I they were pearls once with you.

speeches.speaker: Abi.
prose: Saving your reverence Sir, so they are still.

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: Nay, nay, I do beseech you leave your cogging, what they are, they are, they serve me without Spectacles I thank 'em.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: O will you kill me?

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: I do not think I can,
Y'are like a Copy-hold with nine lives in't.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: You were wont to bear a Christian fear about you: For your own worships sake.

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: I was a Christian fool then: Do you remember what a dance you led me? how I grew qualm'd in love, and was a dunce? could expound but once a quarter, and then was out too: and then out of the stinking stir you put me in, I prayed for my own issue. You do remember all this?

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: O be as then you were?

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: I thank you for it, surely I will be wiser Abigal: and as the Ethnick Poet sings, I will not lose my oyl and labour too. Y'are for the worshipfull I take it Abigal.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: O take it so, and then I am for thee?

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: I like these tears well, and this humbling also, they are Symptomes of contrition. If I should fall into my sit again, would you not shake me into a quotidian Coxcombe? Would you not use me scurvily again, and give me possets with purging Confets in't? I tell thee Gentlewoman, thou hast been harder to me, than a long pedigree.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: O Curate cure me: I will love thee better, dearer, longer: I will do any thing, betray the secrets of the main house-hold to thy reformation. My Ladie shall look lovingly on thy learning, and when true time shall point thee for a Parson, I will convert thy egges to penny custards, and thy tith goose shall graze and multiply.

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: I am mollified, as well shall testifie this faithfull kiss, and have a great care Mistris Abigal how you depress the Spirit any more with your rebukes and mocks: for certainly the edge of such a follie cuts it self.

speeches.speaker: Abigal.
prose: O Sir, you have pierc'd me thorow. Here I vow a recantation to those malicious faults I ever did against you. Never more will I despise your learning, never more pin cards and cony tails upon your Cassock, never again reproach your reverend nightcap, and call it by the mangie name of murrin, never your reverend person more, and say, you look like one of Baals Priests in a hanging, never again when you say grace laugh at you, nor put you out at prayers: never cramp you more, nor when you ride, get Sope and Thistles for you. No my Roger, these faults shall be corrected and amended, as by the tenour of my tears appears.

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: Now cannot I hold if I should be hang'd, I must crie too. Come to thine own beloved, and do even what thou wilt with me sweet, sweet Abigal. I am thine own for ever: here's my hand, when Roger proves a recreant, hang him i'th' Bel-ropes.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Why how now Master Roger, no prayers down with you to night? Did you hear the bell ring? You are courting: your slock shall sat well for it.

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: I humbly ask your pardon: I'le clap up Prayers, but stay a little, and be with you again.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: How dare you, being so unworthie a fellow,
Presume to come to move me any more?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: What ails the fellow?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: The fellow comes to laugh at you, I tell you Ladie I would not for your Land, be such a Coxcomb, such a whining Ass, as you decreed me for when I was last here.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: I joy to hear you are wise, 'tis a rare Jewel
In an Elder Brother: pray be wiser yet?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Me thinks I am very wise: I do not come a wooing. Indeed I'le move no more love to your Ladiship.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: What makes you here then?

speeches.speaker: El er Lo.
prose: Only to see you and be merry Ladie: that's all my business. Faith let's be very merry. Where's little Rogers he's a good fellow: an hour or two well spent in wholsome mirth, is worth a thousand of these puling passions. 'Tis an ill world for Lovers.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: They were never fewer.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I thank God there's one less for me Ladie?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: You were never any Sir.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Till now, and now I am the prettiest fellow.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: You talk like a Tailor Sir.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Me thinks your faces are no such fine things now.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Why did you tell me you were wise? Lord what a lying age is this, where will you mend these faces?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: A Hogs face foust is worth a hundred of 'em.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Sure you had a Sow to your Mother.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: She brought such fine white Pigs as you, fit for none but Parsons Ladie?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: 'Tis well you will allow us our Clergie yet.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: That shall not save you. O that I were in love again with a wish.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: By this light you are a scurvie fellow, pray be gone.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: You know I am a clean skin'd man.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Do I know it?

speeches.speaker: Elder. Lo.
prose: Come, come, you would know it; that's as good: but not a snap, never long for't, not a snap dear Ladie.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Hark ye Sir, hark ye, get ye to the Suburbs, there's horse flesh for such hounds: will you goe Sir?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Lord how I lov'd this woman, how I worshipt this prettie calf with the white face here: as I live, you were the prettiest fool to play withall, the wittiest little varlet, it would talk: Lord how it talk't! and when I angred it, it would cry out, and scratch, and cat no meat, and it would say, goe hang.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: It will say so still, if you anger it.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: And when I askt it, if it would be married, it sent me of an errand into France, and would abuse me, and be glad it did so.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Sir this is most unmanly, pray by gon.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: And swear (even when it twitter'd to be at me) I was unhansome.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Have you no manners in you?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: And say my back was melted, when God he knows, I kept it at a charge: Four Flaunders Mares would have been easier to me, and a Fencer.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: You think all this is true now?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Faith whether it be or no, 'tis too good for you. But so much for our mirth: Now have at you in earnest.

speeches.speaker: Lo.
prose: There is enough Sir, I desire no more.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: Yes faith, wee'l have a cast at your best parts now. And then the Devil take the worst.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Pray Sir no more, I am not so much affected with your commendations, 'tis almost dinner, I know they stay for you at the Ordinary.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: E'ne a short Grace, and then I am gone; You are a woman, and the proudest that ever lov'd a Coach: the scornfullest, scurviest, and most senceless woman; the greediest to be prais'd, and never mov'd though it be gross and open; the most envious, that at the poor same of anothers face, would eat your own, and more than is your own, the paint belonging to it: of such a self opinion, that you think none can deserve your glove: and for your malice, you are so excellent, you might have been your Tempters tutor: nay, never cry.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Your own heart knows you wrong me: I cry for ye?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: You shall before I leave you.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Is all this spoke in earnest?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Yes and more as soon as I can get it out.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Well out with't.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: You are, let me see.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: One that has us'd you with too much respect.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: One that hath us'd me (since you will have it so) the basest, the most Foot-boy-like, without respect of what I was, or what you might be by me; you have us'd me, as I would use a jade, ride him off's legs, then turn him to the Commons; you have us'd me with discretion, and I thank ye. If you have many more such pretty Servants, pray build an Hospital, and when they are old, pray keep 'em for shame.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: I cannot think yet this is serious.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Will you have more on't?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: No saith, there's enough if it be true:
Too much by all my part; you are no Lover then?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: No, I had rather be a Carrier.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Why the Gods amend all.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Neither do I think there can be such a fellow found ^'th' world, to be in love with such a froward woman, if there be such, they're mad, Jove comfort 'em. Now you have all, and I as new a man, as light, and spirited, that I feel my self clean through another creature. O 'tis brave to be ones own man, I can see you now as I would see a Picture, sit all day by you and never kiss your hand: hear you sing, and never fall backward: but with as set a temper, as I would hear a Fidler, rise and thank you. I can now keep my mony in my purse, that still was gadding out for Scarfes and Wastcoats: and keep my hand from Mercers sheep skins finely. I can eat mutton now, and feast my self with my two shillings, and can see a play for eighteen pence again: I can my Ladie.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: The carriage of this fellow vexes me. Sir, pray let me speak a little private with you, I must not suffer this.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Ha, ha, ha, what would you with me?
You will not ravish me? Now, your set speech?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Thou perjur'd man.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Ha, ha, ha, this is a fine exordium.
And why I pray you perjur'd?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Did you not swear a thousand times you lov'd me best of all things?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I do confess it: make your best of that.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Why do you say you do not then?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Nay I'le swear it,
And give sufficient reason, your own usage.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Do you not love me then?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: No saith.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Did you ever think I lov'd you dearly?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Yes, but I see but rotten fruits on't.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Do not denie your hand for I must kiss it, and take my last farewell, now let me die so you be happy.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: I am too foolish: Ladie speak dear Ladie.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: No let me die.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Oh my Sister!

speeches.speaker: Abi.
prose: O my Ladie help, help.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Run for some Rosalis?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I have plaid the fine ass: bend her bodie, Lady, best, dearest, worthiest Ladie, hear your Servant, I am not as I shew'd: O wretched fool, to fling away the Jewel of thy life thus. Give her more air, see she begins to stir, sweet Mistris hear me?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Is my Servant well?

speeches.speaker: Elder La.
prose: In being yours I am so.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Then I care not.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: How do ye, reach a chair there; I confess my fault not pardonable, in pursuing thus upon such tenderness my wilfull error; but had I known it would have wrought thus with ye, thus strangely, not the world had won me to it, and let not (my best Ladie) any word spoke to my end disturb your quiet peace: for sooner shall you know a general ruine, than my faith broken. Do not doubt this Mistris, for by my life I cannot live without you. Come, come, you shall not grieve, rather be angrie, and heap infliction upon me: I will suffer. O I could curse my self, pray smile upon me. Upon my faith it was but a trick to trie you, knowing you lov'd me dearlie, and yet strangely that you would never shew it, though my means was all humilitie.

speeches.speaker: All.
prose: Ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: How now?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: I thank you fine fool for your most fine plot; this was a subtile one, a stiff device to have caught Dottrels with Good senceless Sir, could you imagine I should swound for you, and know your self to be an arrant ass? I, a discovered one. 'Tis quit I thank you Sir. Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Take heed Sir, she may chance to swound again?

speeches.speaker: All.
prose: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Abi.
prose: Step to her Sir, see how she changes colour.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I'le goe to hell first, and be better welcom.
I am fool'd, I do confess it, finely fool'd,
Ladie, fool'd Madam, and I thank you for it.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Faith 'tis not so much worth Sir:
But if I knew when you come next a burding,
I'le have a stronger noose to hold the Woodcock.

speeches.speaker: All.
prose: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I am glad to see you merry, pray laugh on.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: H'ad a hard heart that could not laugh at you S^ ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Pray Sister do not laugh, you'le anger him,
And then hee'l rail like a rude Costermonger.
That School-boys had couzened of his Apples,
As loud and senceless?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I will not rail.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Faith then let's hear him Sister?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Yes, you shall hear me.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Shall we be the better by it then?

speeches.speaker: Eld. L.
prose: No, he that makes a woman better by his words,
I'le have him Sainted: blows will not doe it.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: By this light hee'll beat us.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: You do deserve it richly,
And may live to have a Beadle doe it.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Now he rails?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Come scornfull Folly,
If this be railing, you shall hear me rail.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Pray put it in good words then.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: The worst are good enough for such a trifle,
Such a proud piece of Cobweblawn.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: You bite Sir?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I would till the bones crackt, and I had my will.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: We had best muzzel him, he grows mad.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I would 'twere lawfull in the next great sickness to have the Dogs spared, those harmless creatures, and knock i'th' head these hot continual plagues, women, that are more infectious. I hope the State will think on't.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Are you well Sir?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: He looks as though he had a grievous fit o'th' Colick.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Green-ginger will cure me.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: I'le heat a trencher for him.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Durty December doe, Thou with a face as old as Erra Pater, such a Prognosticating nose: thou thing that ten years since has lest to be a woman, outworn the expectation of a Baud; and thy dry bones can reach at nothing now, but gords or ninepins, pray goe fetch a trencher goe.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Let him alone, he's crackt.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: I'le see him hang'd first, is a beastly fellow to use a woman of my breeding thus; I marry is he: would I were a man, I'de make him eat his Knaves words?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Tie your she Otter up, good Lady folly, she stinks worse than a Bear-baiting.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Why will you be angry now?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Goe paint and purge, call in your kennel with you: you a Lady?

speeches.speaker: Abi.
prose: Sirra, look to't against the quarter Sessions, if there be good behaviour in the world, I'le have thee bound to it.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose:
You must not seek it in your Ladies house then; pray send this Ferret home, and spi^ good Abigal. And Madam, that your Ladiship may know, in what ^fe manner you have us'd my service, I do from this hour hate
thee heartily; and though your folly should whip you to repentance, and waken you at length to see my wrongs, 'tis not the endeavour of your life shall win me; not all the friends you have, intercession, nor your submissive letters, though they spoke as many tears as words; not your knees grown to th'ground in penitence, nor all your state, to kiss you, nor my pardon, nor will to give you Christian burial, if you dye thus; so farewell. When I am married and made sure, I'le come and visit you again, and vex you Ladie. By all my hopes I'le be a torment to you, worse than a tedious winter. I know you will recant and sue to me, but save that labour: I'le rather love a fever and continual thirst, rather contract my youth to drink and sacerdote upon quarrels, or take a drawn whore from an Hospital, that time, diseases, and Mercury had eaten, than to be drawn to love you.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Ha, ha, ha, pray do, but take heed though.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: From thee, false dice, jades, Cowards, and plaguy Summers, good Lord deliver me.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: But hark you Servant, hark ye: is he gon? call him again.

speeches.speaker: Abigal.
prose: Hang him Paddock.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Art thou here still? flie, flie, and call my Servant, flie o^ ne'r see me more.

speeches.speaker: Abigal.
prose: I had rather knit again than see that rascall, but I must doe it.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: I would be loth to anger him too much; what fine foolery is this in a woman, to use those men most frowardly they love most? If I should lose him thus, I were rightly served. I hope he's not so much himself, to take it to th'heart: how now? will he come back?

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: Never, he swears, whilst he can hear men say there's any woman living: he swore he would ha' me first.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Didst thou intreat him wench?

speeches.speaker: Abigal.
prose: As well as I could Madam. But this is still your way, to love being absent, and when he's with you, laugh at him and abuse him. There's another way if you could hit on't.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Thou saist true, get me paper, pen and ink, I'le write to him, I'de be loth he should sleep in's anger.
Women are most fools when they think th'are wisest.

speeches.speaker: Widow.
prose: Pray Sir cast off these fellows, as unsitting for your bare knowledge, and far more your companie: is't fit such Ragamussins as these are should bear the name of friends? and furnish out a civil house? ye're to be married now, and men that love you must expect a course far from your old carrier: if you will keep 'em, turn 'em toth' stable, and there make 'em grooms: and yet now consider it, such beggars once set o' horse back, you have heard will ride, how far you had best to look.

speeches.speaker: Captain.
prose: Hear you, you that must be Ladie, pray content your self and think upon your carriage soon at night, what dressing will best take your Knight, what wastcote, what cordial will do well i'th' morning for him, what triers have you?

speeches.speaker: Widow.
prose: What do you mean Sir?

speeches.speaker: Capt.
prose: Those that must switch him up: if he start well, fear not but cry Saint George, and bear him hard: when you perceive his wind growes hot and wanting, let him a little down, he's fleet, ne're doubt him, and stands sound.

speeches.speaker: Widow.
prose: Sir, you hear these fellows?

speeches.speaker: Young Love.
prose: Merrie companions, wench, Merry companions.

speeches.speaker: Widow.
prose: To one another let 'em be companions, but good Sir not to you: you shall be civil and slip off these base t^appings.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
prose: He shall not need, my most sweed Ladie Grocer, if he be civil, not your powdered Sugar, nor your Raisins shall perswade the Captain to live a Coxcomb with him; let him be civil and eat i'th' Arches, and see what will come on't.

speeches.speaker: Poet.
prose: Let him be civil, doe: undo him; I, that's the next way. I will not take (if he be civil once) two hundred pound a year to live with him; be civil? there's a trim perswasion.

speeches.speaker: Capt.
prose: If thou beest civil Knight, as Jove defends it, get thee another nose, that will be pull'd off by the angry boyes for thy conversion: the children thou shalt get on this Civillian cannot inherit by the law, th'are Ethnicks, and all thy sport meer Moral leacherie: when they are grown, having but little in 'em, they may prove Haberda^hers, or gross Grocers, like their dear Damm there: prethee be civil Knig^t, in time thou maist read to thy houshold, and be drunk once a year: this would shew finely.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: I wonder sweet heart you will offer this, you do not understand these Gentlemen: I will be short and pithy: I had rather call you off by the way of charge: these are Creatures, that nothing goes to the maintenance of but Corn and Water. I will keep these fellows just in the competencie of two Hens.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: If you can cast it so Sir, you have my liking? If they eat less, I should not be offended: But how these Sir, can live upon so little as Corn and Water, I am unbelieving.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Why prethee sweet heart what's your Ale? is not that Corn and Water, my sweet Widow?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: I but my sweet Knight where's the meat to this, and cloaths that they must look for?

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: In this short sentence Ale, is all included: Meat, Drink, and Cloth; These are no ravening Footmen, no fellows, that at Ordinaries dare eat their eighteen pence thrice out before they rise, and yet goe hungry to play, and crack more nuts than would suffice a dozen Squirrels; besides the din, which is damnable: I had rather rail, and be confin'd to a Boatmaker, than live amongst such rascals; these are people of such a clean discretion in their diet, of such a moderate sustenance, that they sweat if they but smell hot meat. Porredge is poison, they hate a Kitchin as they hate a Counter, and show 'em but a Feather-bed they swound. Ale is their eating and their drinking surely, which keeps their bodies clear, and soluble. Bread is a binder, and for that abolisht even in their Ale, whose lost room fills an apple, which is more airy and of subtiler nature. The rest they take is little, and that little is little easie: For like strict men of order, they do correct their bodies with a bench, or a poor stubborn table; if a chimny offer it self with some few broken rushes, they are in down: when they are sick, that's drunk, they may have fresh straw, else they do despise these worldly pamperings. For their poor apparel, 'tis worn out to the diet; new they seek none, and if a man should offer, they are angrie, scarce to be reconcil'd again with him: you shall not hear 'em ask one a cast doublet once in a year, which is modesty besitting my poor friends: you see their Wardrobe, though slender, competent: For shirts I take it, they are things worn out of their remembrance. Lousie they will be when they list, and mangie, which shows a fine variety: and then to cure 'em, a Tanners lime pit, which is little charge, two dogs, and these; these two may be cur'd for 3. pence.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: You have half perswaded me, pray use your pleasure: and my good friends since I do know your diet, I'le take an order, meat shall not offend you, you shall have Ale.

speeches.speaker: Capt.
prose: We ask no more, let it be mighty Lady: and if we perish, then our own sins on us.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Come forward Gentlemen, to Church my boys, when we have done, I'le give you cheer in bowles.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: THis senseless woman vexes me to th' heart, she will not from my memory: would she were a man for one two hours, that I might beat her. If I had been unhansome, old or jealous, 'thad been an even lay she might have scorn'd me; but to be young, and by this light I think as proper as the proudest; made as clean, as straight, and strong backt; means and manners equal with the best cloth of silver Sir i'th' kingdom: But these are things at some time of the Moon, below the cut of Canvas: sure she has some Meeching Rascal in her house, some Hind, that she hath seen bear (like another Milo) quarters of Malt upon his back, and sing with't, Thrash all day, and i'th' evening in his stockings, strike up a Hornpipe, and there stink two hours, and ne're a whit the worse man; these are they, these steel chin'd Rascals that undo us all. Would I had been a Carter, or a Coachman, I had done the deed e're this time.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Sir, there's a Gentleman without would speak with you.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Bid him come in.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: By your leave Sir.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: You are welcome, what's your will Sir?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Have you forgotten me?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I do not much remember you.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: You must Sir. I am that Gentleman you pleas'd to wrong, in your disguise, I have inquired you out.

speeches.speaker: E^der Lo.
prose: I was disguised indeed Sir if I wrong'd you, pray where and when?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: In such a Ladies house, I need not name her.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I do remember you, you seem'd to be a Sutor to that Lady?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: If you remember this, do not forget how s^urvily you us'd me: that was no place to quarrel in, pray you think of it; if you be honest you dare fight with me, without more urging, else I must provoke ye.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Sir I dare fight, but never for a woman, I will not have her in my cause, she's mortal, and so is not my anger: if you have brought a nobler subject for our Swords, I am for you; in this I would be loth to prick my Finger. And where you say I wrong'd you, 'tis so far from my profession, that amongst my fears, to do wrong is the greatest: credit me we have been both abused, (not by our selves, for that I hold a spleen, no sin of malice, and may with man enough be best forgoten,) but by that willfull, scornful piece of hatred, that much forgetful Lady: for whose sake, if we should leave our reason, and run on upon our sense, like Rams, the little world of good men would laugh at us, and despise us, fixing upon our desperate memories the never worn out names of Fools and Fencers. Sir 'tis not fear, but reason makes me tell you; in this I had rather help you Sir, than h^t you, and you shall find it, though you throw your self into as many dangers as she offers, though you redeem her lost name ev^ry day, and find her out new honours with your Sword, you shall l^t be her mirth as I have been.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: I ask you mercy Sir, you have ta'ne my edge off: yet I would fain be ev^n with this Lady.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: In which I l^ be your h^per: we are two, and they are two: two Sisters, ^ich alike, only the elder has the prouder Dow^y: In ^roth I pity this disgrace in you, yet of mine own I am sen^eles^: do but follow my Counsel, and I'le p^wn my sp^t, we'l over reach 'em yet; the means is th^

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Si^ there'^ a Gentlewoman will needs speak with you, I cannot keep her out, she's entred Sir.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose:
It is the waiting woman, pray be not seen: farre hold her in discourse a while: hark in your ear, go and di^
patch it quickly, when I come in, I'le tell you all the project.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: I care not which I have.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Away, 'tis done, she must not see you: no^ Lady Guin^ver what news with you?

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: Pray leave these frumps Sir, and receive this letter.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: From whom good vanity?

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: 'Tis from my Lady Sir: Alas good soul, she cries and takes on!

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose:
Do's she so good Soul? wou'd she not have a Cawdle? do's she send you with your fine Oratory goo^
Tully to tye me to believe again? bring out the Cat-hou^. I'le make you take a tree Whore, then with my ti^ bring down your Gibship, and then have you cast, and hung up i'th' Warren.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: I am no beast Sir, would you knew it.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Wou'd I did, for I am yet very doubtful; what will you say now?

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: Nothing not I.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Art thou a woman, and say nothing?

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: Unless you'l hear me with more moderation, I can speak wise enough.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: And loud enough? will your Lady love me?

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: It seems so by her letter, and her lamentations; but you are such another man.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Not such another as I was, Mumps; nor will not be: I'le read her fine Epistle: ha, ha, ha, is not thy Mistress mad?

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: For you she will be, 'tis a shame you should use a poor Gentlewoman so untowardly; she loves the ground you tread on; and you (hard heart) because she jested with you, mean to kill her; 'tis a fine conquest as they say.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Hast thou so much moisture in the Whitleather hide yet, that thou canst cry? I wou'd have sworn thou ha^ been touchwood five year since; nay let it rain, thy face chops for a shower like a dry Dunghil.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
