prose: I'le not indure this Ribauldry; farewel i'th' Devils name; if my Lady die, I'le be sworn before a jury, thou art the cause on't.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Do Mankin do, deliver to your Lady from me this: I mean to see her, if I have no other business: which before I'le want to come to her, I mean to go seek birds nests: yet I may come too: but if I come, from this door till I see her, will I think how to rail vildly at her; how to vex her, and make her cry so much, that the Physician if she fall sick upon't, shall find the cause to be want of Urine, and she remediless dye in her Heresie: Farewell old Adage, I hope to see the Boys make Potguns on thee.

speeches.speaker: Abig.
prose: Th'art a vile man, God bless my issue from thee.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Thou hast but one, and that's in thy left crupper, that makes thee hobble so; you must be ground i'th' breech like a Top, you'l ne're spin well else: Farewell Fytchock.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose:
Is it not strange that every womans will should track out new wayes to disturb her self? if I should call my reason to account, it cannot answer why I keep my self from mine own wish, and stop the man I love from his; and every hour repent again, yet still go on: I know 'tis like a man, that wants his natural sleep, and growing dull would gladly give the remnant of his life fo^ two hours rest; yet through his frowardness, will rather choose to watch another man, drowsie as he, than take his own repose. All this I know: yet a strange peevishness and anger, not to have the power to do things unexpected, carries me away to mine own ruine: I had rather ^ sometimes than not disgrace in publick him whom people think I love, and do't with oaths, and am in earnest the^
O what are we! Men, you must answer this, that dare obey ^uch things as we command. How now? what newes?

speeches.speaker: Abi.
prose: Faith Madam none worth hearing.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Is he not come?

speeches.speaker: Abi.
prose: No truly.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Nor has he writ?

speeches.speaker: Abigal.
prose: Neither. I pray God you have not undone your ^elf.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Why, but what saies he?

speeches.speaker: Abi.
prose: Faith he talks strangely.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: How strangely?

speeches.speaker: Abi.
prose: First at your Letter he laught extremely?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: What, in contempt?

speeches.speaker: Abi.
prose: He laught monstrous loud, as he would die, and when you wrote it I think you were in no such merry mood, ^o provoke him that way: and having done he cried Alas for her, and violently laught again.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Did he?

speeches.speaker: Abi.
prose: Yes, till I was angry.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Angry, why? why wert thou angry? he did doe but well, I did deserve it, he had been a fool, an unfit man for any one to love, had he not laught thus at me: you were angry, that show'd your folly; I shall love him more for that, than all that ere he did before: but said he nothing else?

speeches.speaker: Abi.
prose: Many uncertain things: he said though you had mockt him, because you were a woman, he could wish to do you so much favour as to see you: yet he said, he knew you rash, and was loth to offend you with the sight of one, whom now he was bound not to leave.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: What one was that?

speeches.speaker: Abi.
prose: I know not, but truly I do fear there is a making up there: for I heard the servants, as I past by some, whisper such a thing: and as I came back through the hall, there were two or three Clarks writing great conveyances in hast, which they said were for their Mistris joynture.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: 'Tis very like, and fit it should be so, for he does think, and reasonably think, that I should keep him with my idle tricks for ever ere he be married.

speeches.speaker: Abi.
prose: At last he said, it should go hard but he would see you for your satisfaction.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: All we that are call'd Women, know as well as men, it were a far more noble thing to grace where we are grace't, and give respect there where we are respected: yet we practise a wilder course, and never bend our eyes on men with pleasure, till they find the way to give us a neglect: then we, too late, perceive the loss of what we might have had, and dote to death.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Sister, yonder's your Servant, with a Gentlewoman with him.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Where?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Close at the door.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Alas I am undone, I fear he is berroth'd,
What kind of woman is she?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: A most ill favoured one, with her Masque on:
And how her face should mend the rest I know not.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: But yet her mind was of a milder stuff than mine was.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Now I see him, if my heart swell not again (away thou womans pride) so that I cannot speak a gentle word to him, let me not live.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: By your leave here.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: How now, what new trick invites you hither?
Ha' you a sine device again?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Faith this is the finest device I have now:
How dost thou sweet heart?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Why very well, so long as I may please
You my dear Lover. I nor can, nor will
Be ill when you are well, well when you are ill.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: O thy sweet temper! what would I have given, that Lady had been like thee: seest thou her? that face (my love) join'd with thy humble mind, had made a wench indeed.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Alas my love, what God hath done, I dare not think to mend. I use no paint, nor any drugs of Art, my hands and face will shew it.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Why what thing have you brought to shew us there? do you take mony for it?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: A Godlike thing, not to be bought for mony: 'tis my Mistris: in whom there is no passion, nor no scorn: what I will is for law; pray you salute her.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Salute her? by this good light, I would not kiss her for half my wealth.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Why? why pray you?
You shall see me do't afore you; look you.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Now sie upon thee, a beast would not have don't. I would not kiss thee of a month to gain a Kingdom.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Marry you shall not be troubled.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Why was there ever such a Meg as this?
Sure thou art mad.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I was mad once, when I lov'd pictures; for what are shape and colours else, but pictures? in that tawnie hide there lies an endless mass of vertues, when all your red and white ones want it.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: And this is she you are to marry, is't not?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Yes indeed is't.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: God give you joy.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Amen.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: I thank you, as unknown for your good wish.
The like to you when ever you shall wed.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: O gentle Spirit!

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: You thank me? I pray
Keep your breath nearer you, I do not like it.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: I would not willingly offend at all,
Much less a Lady of your worthie parts.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Sweet, Sweet!

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: I do not think this woman can by nature be thus,
Thus ugly; sure she's some common Strumpet,
Deform'd with exercise of sin?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: O Sir believe not this, for Heaven so comfort me as I am free from soul pollution with any man; my honour ta'ne away, I am no woman.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Arise my dearest Soul; I do not credit it. Alas, I fear her tender heart will break with this reproach; sie that you know no more civility to a weak Virgin. 'Tis no matter Sweet, let her say what she will, thou art not worse to me, and therefore not at all; be careless.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: For all things else I would, but for mine honor; Me thinks.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Alas, thine honour is not stain'd,
Is this the business that you sent for me about?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Faith Sister you are much to blame, to use a woman, whatsoe're she be, thus; I'le salute her: You are welcom hither.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: I humbly thank you.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Milde yet as the Dove, for all these injuries. Come shall we goe, I love thee not so ill to keep thee here a jesting stock.
Adue to the worlds end.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Why whither now?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Nay you shall never know, because you shall not find me.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: I pray let me speak with you.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: 'Tis very well: come.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: I pray you let me speak with you.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Yes for another mock.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: By Heaven I have no mocks: good Sir a word.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Though you deserve not so much at my hands, yet if you be in such earnest, I'le speak a word with you; but I beseech you be brief: for in good faith there's a Parson and a licence stay for us i'th' Church all this while: and you know 'tis night.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose:
Sir, give me hearing patiently, and whatsoever I have heretofore spoke jestingly, forget: for as I hope ^ mercy any where, what I shall utter now is from my he^
^
and as I mean.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Well, well, what do you mean?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Was not I once your Mistress, and you my Servant?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: O 'tis about the old matter.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Nay good Sir stay me out; I would but hear you excuse your self, why you should take this woman, and leave me.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Prethee why not, deserves she not as much as you?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: I think not, if you will look
With an indifferency upon us both.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Upon your faces, 'tis true: but if judiciously we shall cast our eyes upon your minds, you are a thousand women of her in worth: she cannot swound in jest, nor set her lover tasks, to shew her peevishness, and his affection, not cross what he saies, though it be Canonical. She's a good plain wench, that will do as I will have her, and bring me lusty Boys to throw the Sledge, and lift at Pigs of Lead: and for a Wife, she's far beyond you: what can you do in a houshold to provide for your issue, but lye i' bed and get 'em? your business is to dress you, and at idle hours to eat; when she can do a thousand profitable things: she can do pretty well in the Pastry, and knows how Pullen should be cram'd, she cuts Cambrick at a thread, weaves Bone-lace, and quilts Balls; and what are you good for?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Admit it true, that she were far beyond me in all respects, does that give you a licence to forswear your self?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Forswear my self, how?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Perhaps you have forgotten the innumerable oaths you have utter'd in disclaiming all for Wives but me: I'le not remember you: God give you joy.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Nay but conceive me, the intent of oaths is ever understood: Admit I should protest to such a friend, to see him at his Lodging to morrow: Divines would never hold me perjur'd if I were struck blind, or he hid him where my diligent search could not find him: so there were no cross act of mine own in't. Can it be imagined I mean to force you to Marriage, and to have you whether you will or no?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Alas you need not. I make already tender of my self, and then you are forsworn.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Some sin I see indeed must necessarily fall upon me, as whosoever deals with Women shall never utterly avoid it; yet I would chuse the least ill; which is to forsake you, that have done me all the abuses of a malignant Woman, contemn'd my service, and would have held me prating about Marriage, till I had been past getting of Children: then her that hath forsaken her Family, and put her tender body in my hand, upon my word—

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Which of us swore you first to?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Why to you.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Which oath is to be kept then?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I prethee do not urge my sins unto me,
Without I could amend 'em.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Why you may by wedding me.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: How will that satisfie my word to her?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: 'Tis not to be kept, and needs no satisfaction,
'Tis an error sit for repentance only.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Shall I live to wrong that tender hearted Virgin so? It may not be.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Why may it not be?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I swear I had rather marry thee than her: but yet mine honesty?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: What honesty? 'Tis more preserv'd this way:
Come, by this light, servant, thou shalt, I'le kiss thee on't.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: This kiss indeed is sweet, pray God no sin lie under it.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: There is no sin at all, try but another.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: O my heart!

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Help Sister, this Lady swounds.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: How do you?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Why very well, if you be so.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Since a quiet mind lives not in any Woman, shall do a most ungodly thing. Hear me one word more, which by all my hopes I will not alter, I did make a^ oath when you delai'd me so, that this very night I would be married. Now if you will go without delay, suddenly as late as it is, with your own Minister to your own Chap~pel, I'le wed you and to bed.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: A match dear servant.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: For if you should forsake me now, I care not she would not though for all her injuries, such is her spi^ If I be not ashamed to kiss her now I part, may I not live.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: I see you go, as slily as you think to steal away yet I will pray for you; all blessings of the world light o^ you two, that you may live to be an aged pair. All curses on me if I do not speak what I do wish indeed.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: If I can speak to purpose to her, I am a villa^

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Servant away.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Sister, will you Marry that inconstant ma^' think you he will not cast you off to morrow, to wrong a Lady thus, lookt she like dirt, 'twas basely done. May you ne're prosper with him.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Now God forbid. Alas I was unworthy, so I told him

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: That was your modesty, too good for him.
I would not see your wedding for a world.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Chuse chuse, come Younglove.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Dry up your eyes forsooth, you shall not think we are all such uncivil beasts as these. Would I knew how to give you a revenge.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: So would not I: No let me suffer truly, that I desire.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Pray walk in with me, 'tis very late, and you sha^l stay all night: your bed shall be no worse than mine; I wi^ I could but do you right.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: my humble thanks:
God grant I may but live to quit your love.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Did your Master send for me Savil?

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: Yes, he did send for your worship Sir.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Do you know the business?

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: Alas Sir, I know nothing, nor am imployed beyond my hours of eating. My dancing days are done Sir.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: What art thou now then?

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: If you consider me in little, I am with your worships reverence Sir, a Rascal: one that upon the next anger of your Brother, must raise a sconce by the high way, and sell switches; my wife is learning now Sir, to weave inkle.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: What dost thou mean to do with thy Children Savil?

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: My eldest boy is half a Rogue already, he was born bursten, and your worship knows, that is a pretty step to mens compassions. My youngest boy I purpose Sir to bind for ten years to a Goaler, to draw under him, that he may shew us mercy in his function.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Your family is quartered with discretion: yet are resolved to Cant then: where Savil shall your seene lie?

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: Beggers must be no chusers.
In every place (I take it) but the stocks.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: This is your drinking, and your whoring Savil, I told you of it, but your heart was hardened.

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: 'Tis true, you were the first that told me of it I do remember yet in tears, you told me you would have Whores, and in that passion Sir, you broke out thus; Thou miserable man, repent, and brew three Strikes more in a Hogshead. 'Tis noon e're we be drunk now, and the time can tarry for no man.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Y'are grown a bitter Gentleman. I see misery can clear your head better than Mustard, I'le be a sutor for your Keys again Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: Will you but be so gracious to me Sir? I shall be bound.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: You shall Sir
To your bunch again, or I'le miss foully.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: Save you Gentleman, save you.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Now Polecat, what young Rabets nest have you to draw?

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: Come, prethee be familiar Knight.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Away Fox, I'le send for Terriers for you.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: Thou art wide yet: I'le keep thee companie.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: I am about some business; Indentures,
If ye follow me I'le beat you: take heed,
A I live I'le cancel your Coxcomb.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: Thou art cozen'd now, I am no usurer:
What poor fellow's this?

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: I am poor indeed Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: Give him mony Knight.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Do you begin the offering.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: There poor fellow, here's an Angel for thee.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Art thou in earnest Morecraft?

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: Yes faith Knight, I'le follow thy example: thou hadst land and thousands, thou spendst, and flungst away, and yet it flows in double: I purchased, wrung, and wierdraw'd, for my wealth, lost, and was cozen'd: for which I make a vow, to trie all the waies above ground, but I'le find a constant means to riches without curses.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: I am glad of your conversion Master Morecraft:
Y'are in a fair course, pray pursue it still.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: Come, we are all gallants now, I'le keep thee company; Here honest fellow, for this Gentlemans sake, there's two Angels more for thee.

speeches.speaker: Savil.
prose: God quite you Sir, and keep you long in this mind.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: Wilt thou persevere?

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: Till I have a penny. I have brave cloathes a making, and two horses; canst thou not help me to a match Knight, I'le lay a thousand pound upon my crop-ear.

speeches.speaker: Yo. Lo.
prose: Foot, this is stranger than an Africk monster,
There will be no more talk of the Cleve wars
Whilst this lasts, come, I'le put thee into blood.

speeches.speaker: Sav.
prose: Would all his damn'd tribe were as tender hearted. I beseech you let this Gentleman join with you in the recovery of my Keyes; I like his good beginning Sir, the whilst I'le pray for both your worships.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: He shall Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: Shall we goe noble Knight? I would fain be acquainted.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: I'le be your servant Sir.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Faith my sweet Lady, I have caught you now, maugre your subtilties, and fine devices, be coy again now.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Prethee sweet-heart tell true.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: By this light, by all the pleasures I have had this night, by your lost maidenhead, you are cozened meerly. I have cast beyond your wit. That Gentleman is your retainer Welford.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: It cannot be so.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Your Sister has found it so, or I mistake, mark how she blushes when you see her next. Ha, ha, ha, I shall not travel now, ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Prethee sweet heart be quiet, thou hast angred me at heart.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I'le please you soon again.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Welford?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I Welford, hee's a young handsome fellow, well bred and landed, your Sister can instruct you in his good parts, better than I by this time.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Uds foot am I fetcht over thus?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Yes i'faith.
And over shall be fetcht again, never fear it.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: I must be patient, though it torture me:
You have got the Sun Sir.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: And the Moon too, in which I'le be the man.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: But had I known this, had I but surmiz'd it, you should have hunted three trains more, before you had come toth' course, you should have hankt o'th' bridle, Sir, i'faith.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: I knew it, and min'd with you, and so blew you up.
Now you may see the Gentlewoman: stand close.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: For Gods sake Sir, be private in this business,
You have undone me else. O God, what have I done?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: No harm I warrant thee.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: How shall I look upon my friends again?
With what face?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Why e'ne with that: 'tis a good one, thou canst not find a better: look upon all the faces thou shalt see there, and you shall find 'em smooth still, fair still, sweet still, and to your thinking honest; those have done as much as you have yet, or daie doe Mistris, and yet they keep no stir.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Good Sir goe in, and put your womans cloaths on:
If you be seen thus, I am lost for ever.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: I'le watch you for that Mistris: I am no fool, here will I tarry till the house be up and witness with me.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Good dear friend goe in.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: To bed again if you please, else I am sixt here till there be notice taken what I am, and what I have done: if you could juggle me into my woman-hood again, an I so cog me out of your company, all this would be forsworn, and I again an asinego, as your Sister left me. No, I'le have it known and publisht; then if you'le be a whore, forsake me and be asham'd: and when you can hold no longer, marry some cast Cleve Captain, and sell Bottle-ale.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: I dare not stay Sir, use me modestly, I am your wife.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Goe in, I'le make up all.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I'le be a witness of your naked truth Sir: this is the Gentlewoman, prethee look upon him, this is he that made me break my saith sweet: but thank your Sister, she hath soder'd it.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: What a dull ass was I, I could not see this wencher from a wench: twenty to one, if I had been but tender like my Sister, he had served me such a slippery trick too.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Twenty to one I had.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: I would have watcht you Sir, by your good patience, for ferreting in my ground.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: You have been with my Sister.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Yes to bring.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: An heir into the world he means.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: There is no chasing now.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: I have had my part on't: I have been chaft this three hours, that's the least, I am reasonable cool now.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Cannot you fare well, but you must cry to ^ meat?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: He that fares well, and will not bless the founders, is either surfeited, or ill taught, Lady, for mine own part, I have found so sweet a diet, I can commend it, though I cannot spare it.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: How like you this dish, Welford, I made a supper on't, and fed so heartily, I could not sleep.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: By this light, had I but scented out your t^, y e had slept with a bare pillow in your arms and kist that, or else the bed-post, for any wise ye had got this twelve-month yet: I would have vext you more than a try'd p st horse; and been longer bearing, than ever after game at Irish was. Lord, that I were unmarried again.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Lady I would not undertake ye, were you again a Haggard, for the best cast of four Ladys i'th' Kingdom: you were ever tickle-footed, and would not truss round.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Is she fast?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: She was all night lockt here boy.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Then you may lure her without fear of losing: take off her Cranes. You have a delicate Gentlewoman to your Sister: Lord what a prettie furie she was in, when she perceived I was a man: but I thank God I satisfied her scruple, without the Parson o'th' town.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: What did ye?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Madam, can you tell what we did?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: She has a shrewd guess at it I see it by her.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Well you may mock us: but my large Gentlewoman, my Mary Ambre, had I but seen into you, you should have had another bed-fellow, fitter a great deal for your itch.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: I thank you Lady, me thought it was well,
You are so curious.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: Get on your doublet, here comes my Brother.

speeches.speaker: Yo Lo.
prose: Good morrow Brother, and all good to your Lady.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: God save you and good morrow to you all.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: Good morrow. Here's a poor brother of yours.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Fie how this shames me.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: Prethee good fellow help me to a cup of beer.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: I will Sir.

speeches.speaker: Yo. Lo.
prose: Brother what makes you here? will this Lady do? Will she? is she not nettl'd still?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: No I have em'd her.
Mr. Welford, pray know this Gentleman is my Brother.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
prose: Sir I shall long to love him.

speeches.speaker: Yo Lo.
prose: I shall not be your debter Sir. But how is't with you?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: As well as may be man: I am married: your new acquaintance hath her Sister, and all's well.

speeches.speaker: Y^ Lo.
prose: I am glad on't. Now my prettie Lady Sister,
How do you find my Brother?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Almost as wild as you are.

speeches.speaker: Yo Lo.
prose: He will make the better husband: you have tried him?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Against my will Sir.

speeches.speaker: Yo. Lo.
prose: Hee'l make your will amends soon, do not doubt it.
But Sir I must intreat you to be better known
To this converted Jew here.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Here's Beer for you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: And here's for you an Angel:
Pray buy no Land, 'twill never prosper Sir.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: How's this?

speeches.speaker: Yo. Lo.
prose: Bless you, and then I'le tell: He's turn'd Gallant.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
prose: Gallant?

speeches.speaker: Yo. Lo.
prose: I Gallant, and is now called, Cutting Morecraft:
^ reason I'le inform you at more leisure.

speeches.speaker: W^l.
prose:
O ^
^t me know him presently.

speeches.speaker: ^ Lo.
prose:
Y^
^ll hug one another.
Sir I must keep you company.

speeches.speaker: ^ Lo.
prose: ^ on.

speeches.speaker: ^ Lo.
prose: Cutting Morecraft faces about, I must present ^
As ^ as you will Sir, I am for 'em.
^ you service.
^ look for't in good saith Sir.
^ sweet heart kiss him.
^, f^llow?
^ will it please you to remember me: my keys good Sir.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
prose: I'le doe it presently.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
prose: Come thou shalt kiss him for our sport sake.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: Let him come on then; and do you hear, do not instruct me in these tricks, for you may repent it.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
verse: That at my peril. Lusty Mr. Morecraft,
Here is a Lady would salute you.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: She shall not lose her longing Sir: what is she?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
verse: My wise Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: She must be then my Mistres.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Must I Sir?

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
verse: O yes, you must.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: And you must take this ring, a poor pawn
Of some fiftie pound.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
verse: Take it by any means, 'tis lawfull prize.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Sir I shall call you servant.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: I shall be proud on't: what fellow's that?

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
verse: My Ladies Coachman.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: There's something, (my friend) for you to buy whips,
And for you Sir, and you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
verse: Under a miracle this is the strangest
I ever heard of.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: What, shall we play, or drink? what shall we doe?
Who will hunt with me for a hundred pounds?

speeches.speaker: Wel.
verse: Stranger and Stranger!
Sir you shall find sport after a day or two.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
verse: Sir I have a sute unto you
Concerning your old servant Savil.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
verse: O, for his keys, I know it.

speeches.speaker: Savil.
verse: Now Sir, strike in.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Sir I must have you grant me.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
verse: 'Tis done Sir, take your keys again:
But hark you Savil, leave off the motions
Of the flesh, and be honest, or else you shall graze again:
I'le try you once more.

speeches.speaker: Savil.
verse: If ever I be taken drunk, or whoring,
Take off the biggest key i'th' bunch, and open
My head with it Sir: I humbly thank your worships.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
verse: Nay then I see we must keep holiday.
Here's the last couple in hell.

speeches.speaker: Roger.
verse: Joy be among you all.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Why how now Sir, what is the meaning of this emblem?

speeches.speaker: Roger.
verse: Marriage an't like your worship.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Are you married?

speeches.speaker: Roger.
verse: As well as the next Priest could doe it, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
verse: I think the sign's in Gemini, here's such coupling.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
verse: Sir Roger, what will you take to lie from your sweet-heart to night?

speeches.speaker: Roger.
verse: Not the best benifice in your worships gift Sir.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
verse: A whorson, how he swells.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
verse: How many times to night Sir Roger?

speeches.speaker: Roger.
verse: Sir you grow scurrilous:
What I shall do, I shall do: I shall not need your help.

speeches.speaker: Young Lo.
verse: For horse flesh Roger.

speeches.speaker: Elder Lo.
verse: Come prethee be not angry, 'tis a day
Given wholly to our mirth.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: It shall be so Sir: Sir Roger and his Bride,
We shall intreat to be at our charge.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
verse: Welford get you to the Church: by this light,
You shall not lie with her again, till y'are married.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
verse: I am gone.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: To every Bride I dedicate this day
Six healths a piece, and it shall goe hard,
But every one a jewell: Come be mad boys.

speeches.speaker: El. Lo.
verse: Th'art in a good beginning: come who leads?
Sir Roger, you shall have the Van: lead the way:
Would every dogged wench had such a day.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: WHY do you grieve thus still?

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: 'Twould melt a Marble,
And tame a Savage man, to feel my fortune.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: What fortune? I have liv'd this thirty years,
And run through all these follies you call fortunes,
Yet never fixt on any good and constant,
But what I made my self: why should I grieve then
At that I may mould any way?

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: You are wide still.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: You love a Gentlewoman, a young handsom woman,
I have lov'd a thosand, not so few.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: You are dispos'd.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: You hope to Marry her; 'tis a lawful calling
And prettily esteem'd of, but take heed then,
Take heed dear Brother of a stranger fortune
Than e're you felt yet; fortune my soe is a friend to it.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: 'Tis true I love, dearly, and truly love,
A noble, vertuous, and most beauteous Maid,
And am belov'd again.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: That's too much o' Conscience,
To love all these would run me out o' my wits.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: Prethee give ear, I am to Marry her.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Dispatch it then, and I'le go call the Piper.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: But O the wicked Custom of this Country,
The barbarous, most inhumane, damned Custom.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: 'Tis true, to marry is a Custom
l' the world; for look you Brother,
Wou'd any man stand plucking for the Ace of Harts,
With one pack of Cards all dayes on's life?

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: You do not
Or else you purpose not to understand me.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Proceed, I will give ear.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: They have a Custom
In this most beastly Country, out upon't.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Let's hear it first.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: That when a Maid is contracted
And ready for the tye o'th' Church, the Governour,
He that commands in chief, must have her Maiden-head,
Or Ransom it for mony at his pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: How might a man atchieve that place? a rare Custom!
An admirable rare Custom: and none excepted?

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: None, none.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: The ra^er still: how could I lay about me,
In this ra^e Office? are they born to it, or chosen?

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: Both equal damnable.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Me thinks both excellent,
Would I were the next heir.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: To this mad fortune
Am I now come, my Marriage is proclaim'd,
And nothing can redeem me from this mischief.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: She s very young.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: And fair I dare proclaim her,
Else mine ^yes fail.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: Fa^ as the ^nd unblasted.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: I cannot blame him then, if 'twere mine own case,
I would not go an Ace less.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: ^ye Rutilio,
Why do you make your brothers misery
Your sport and game?

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: There is no pastime like it.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: I look'd for your advice, your timely Counsel,
How to avoid this blow, not to be mockt at,
And my afflictions jeer'd.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: I tell thee Arnoldo,
An thou wert my Father, as thou art but my Brother,
My younger Brother too, I must be merry.
And where there is a wench yet can, a young wench,
A handsome wench, and sooner a good turn too,
An I were to be hang'd, thus must I handle it.
But you shall see Sir, I can change this habit
To do you any service; advise what you please,
And see with what Devotion I'le attend it?
But yet me thinks, I am taken with this Custom,
And could pretend to th' place.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: Draw off a little;
Here comes my Mistress and her Father.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: A dainty wench!
Wou'd I might farm his Custom.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: My dear Daughter,
Now to bethink your self of new advice
Will be too late, late, this timeless sorrow,
No price, not prayers, can infringe the fate

Your beauty hath ^
^ou, my best Zenocia,
Be rul'd by me, a Fa^ care directs ye,
Look on the Count, look chearfully and sweetly;
What though he have th^ power to possess ye,

^ pluck your Mai^
^onour, and then slight ye
^ unresistible to enjoy you;

^
^et Child, so much your youth and goodness,

^
^auty of your soul, and Saint-like Modesty,
Have won upon his mild mind, so much charm'd him,
That all power laid aside, what Law allows him,
Or sudden fires, kindled from those bright eyes,
He sues to be your servant, fairly, nobly
For ever to be tyed your faithful Husband:
Consider my best child.

speeches.speaker: Zeno.
verse: I have considered.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: The blessedness that this breeds too, consider
Besides your Fathers Honour, your own peace,
The banishment for ever of this Custom,
This base and barbarous use, for after once
He has sound the happiness of holy Marriage,
And what it is to grow up with one Beauty,
How he will scorn and kick at such an heritage
Left him by lust and lewd progenitors.
All Virgins too, shall bless your name, shall Saint it,
And like so many Pilgrims go to your shrine,
When time has turn'd your beauty into ashes,
Fill d with your pious memory.

speeches.speaker: Zeno.
verse: Good Father
Hide not that better Pill I loath to swallow
In such sweet words.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: The Count's a handsome Gentleman,
And having him, y'are certain of a fortune,
A high and noble fortune to attend you:
Where if you fling your Love upon this stranger
This young Arnoldo, not knowing from what place
Or honourable strain of blood he is sprung, you venture
All your own sweets, and my long cares to nothing,
Nor are you certain of his saith; why may not that
Wander as he does, every where?

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: No more Sir;
I must not hear, I dare not hear him wrong'd thus,
Vertue is never wounded, but I suffer.
'Tis an ill Office in your age, a poor one,
To judge thus weakly: and believe your self too,
A weaker, to betray your innocent Daughter,
To his intemp'rate, rude, and wild embraces,
She hates as Heaven hates falshood.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: A good wench,
She sticks close to you Sir,

speeches.speaker: Zeno.
verse: His faith uncertain?
The nobleness his vertue springs from, doubted?
D'ye doubt it is day now? or when your body's perfect,
Your stomach's well dispos'd, your pulse's temperate,
D'ye doubt you are in health? I tell you Father,
One hour of this mans goodness, this mans Nobleness
Put in the Scale, against the Counts whole being,
Forgive his lusts too, which are half his life,
He could no more endure to hold weight with him;
Arnoldo's very looks, are fair examples;
His common and indifferent actions,
Rules and strong ties of vertue: he has my first love,
To him in sacred vow I have given this body,
In him my mind inhabits.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Good wench still.

speeches.speaker: Zeno.
verse: And till he sting me off, as undeserving,
Which I confess I am, of such a blessing,
But would be loth to find it so—

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: O never;
Never my happy Mistress, never, never,
When your poor servant lives but in your favour,
One foot i'th' grave the other shall not linger.
What sacrifice of thanks, what age of service,
What danger, of more dreadful look than death,
What willing Martyrdom to crown me constant
May merit such a goodness, such a sweetness?
A love so Nobly great, no power can ruine;
Most blessed Maid go on, the Gods that gave this,
This pure unspotted love, the Child of Heaven,
In their own goodness, must preserve and save it,
And raise you a reward beyond our recompence.

speeches.speaker: Zeno.
verse: I ask but you, a pure Maid to possess,
And then they have crown'd my wishes: If I fall then
Go seek some better love, mine will debase you.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: A pretty innocent fool; well, Governour,
Though I think well of your custom, and could wish my self
For this night in your place, heartily wish it:
Yet if you play not fair play and above board too,
I have a foolish gin here, I say no more;
I'le tell you what, and if your honours guts are not inchanted.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: I should now chide you Sir, for so declining
The goodness and the grace you have ever shew'd me;
And your own vertue too, in seeking rashly
To violate that love Heaven has appointed,
To wrest your Daughters thoughts, part that affection
That both our hearts have tyed, and seek to give it

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: To a wild fellow, that would weary her;
A Cannibal, that feeds on the heads of Maids,
Then flings their bones and bodies to the Devil,
Would any man of discretion venture such a gristle,
To the rude clawes of such a Cat-a-mountain?
You had better tear her between two Oaks, a Town Bull
Is a meer Stoick to this fellow, a grave Philosopher,
And a Spanish Jennet, a most vertuous Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: Does this seem handsome Sir?

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Though I confess
Any man would desire to have her, and by any means,
At any rate too, yet that this common Hangman,
That hath whipt off the heads of a thousand maids already,
That he should glean the Harvest, sticks in my stomach:
This Rogue breaks young wenches to the Saddle,
And teaches them to stumble ever after;
That he should have her? for my Brother now
That is a handsome young fellow; and well thought on,
And will deal tenderly in the business;
Or for my self that have a reputation,
And have studied the conclusions of these causes,
And know the perfect manage, I'le tell you old Sir,
If I should call you wise Sir, I should bely you,
This thing, you study to betray your child to,
This Maiden-monger. When you have done your best,
And think you have fixt her in the point of honour,
Who do you think you have tyed her to? a Surgeon,
I must confess an excellent dissector,
One that has cut up more young tender Lamb-pies—

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: What I spake Gentlemen, was meer compulsion,
No Fathers free-will, nor did I touch your person
With any edge of spight; or strain your loves
With any base, or hir'd perswasions;
Witness these tears, how well I wisht your fortunes.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: There's some grace in thee yet, you are determined
To marry this Count, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: Marry him Rutilio?

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Marry him, and lye with him I mean.

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: You cannot mean that,
If you be a true Gentleman, you dare not,
The Brother to this man, and one that loves him;
I'le marry the Devil first.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: A better choice
And lay his horns by, a handsomer bed-fellow,
A cooler o' my conscience.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: Pray let me ask you;
And my dear Mistris, be not angry with me
For what I shall propound, I am confident,
No promise, nor no power, can force your love,
I mean in way of marriage, never stir you,
Nor to forget my faith, no state can wound you.
But for this Custom, which this wretched country
Hath wrought into a law, and must be satisfied;
Where all the pleas of honour are but laught at,
And modesty regarded as a may-game,
What shall be here considered? power we have none,
To make resistance, nor policie to cross it:
'Tis held Religion too, to pay this duty.

speeches.speaker: Zeno.
verse: I'le dye an Atheist then.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: My noblest Mistris,
Not that I wish it so, but say it were so,
Say you did render up part of your honour,
For whilst your will is clear, all cannot perish;
Say for one night you entertain'd this monster,
Should I esteem you worse, forc'd to this render?
Your mind I know is pure, and full as beauteous;
After this short eclipse, you would rise again,
And shaking off that cloud, spread all your lustre.

speeches.speaker: Zeno.
verse: Who made you witty, to undoe your self, Sir?
Or are you loaden, with the love I bring you,
And fain would fling that burthen on another?
Am I grown common in your eyes Arnoldo?
Old, or unworthy of your fellowship?
D'ye think because a woman, I must err,
And therefore rather wish that fall before-hand
Coloured with Custom, not to be resisted?
D'ye love as painters doe, only some pieces,
Some certain handsome touches of your Mistris,
And let the mind pass by you, unexamined?
Be not abus'd; with what the maiden vessel
Is seasoned first, you understand the proverb.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: I am afraid, this thing will make me vertuous.

speeches.speaker: Zeno.
verse: Should you lay by the least part of that love
Y'ave sworn is mine, your youth and faith has given me,
To entertain another, nay a fairer,
And make the case thus desp'rate, she must dy else;
D'ye think I would give way, or count this honest?
Be not deceiv'd, these eyes should never see you more,
This tongue forget to name you, and this heart
Hate you, as if you were born, my full Antipathie.
Empire and more imperious love, alone
Rule, and admit no rivals: the purest springs
When they are courted by lascivious land-floods,
Their maiden pureness, and their coolness perish.
And though they purge again to their first beauty,
The sweetness of their taste is clean departed.
I must have all or none; and am not worthy
Longer the noble name of wife, Arnoldo,
Than I can bring a whole heart pure and handsom.

speeches.speaker: Arnol.
verse: I never shall deserve you: not to thank you;
You are so heavenly good, no man can reach you:
I am sorrie I spake so rashly, 't was but to try you.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: You might have tryed a thousand women so,
And 900, fourscore and 19 should ha' followed your counsel.
Take heed o' clapping spurts to such free cattell.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: We must bethink us suddenly and constantly,
And wisely too, we expect no common danger.

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: Be most assur'd, I'le dye first.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: An't come to that once,
The Devil pick his bones, that dyes a coward,
I'le jog along with you, here comes the Stallion,
How smug he looks upon the imagination
Of what he hopes to act? pox on your kidneys;
How they begin to melt? how big he bears,
Sure he will leap before us all: what a sweet company
Of rogues and panders wait upon his lewdness?
Plague of your chops, you ha' more handsome bitts,
Than a hundred honester men, and more deserving.
How the dogg leers.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: You need not now be jealous,
I speak at distance to your wise, but when the Priest has done,
We shall grow nearer, and more familiar.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: I'le watch you for that trick, baboon, I'le
Smoke you: the rogue sweats, as if he had eaten
Grains, he broyles, if I do come to the
Basting of you.

speeches.speaker: Arno.
verse: Your Lordship
May happily speak this, to fright a stranger,
But 'tis not in your honour, to perform it;
The Custom of this place, if such there be,
At best most damnable, may urge you to it,
But if you be an honest man you hate it,
How ever I will presently prepare
To make her mine, and most undoubtedly
Believe you are abus'd, this custome feign'd too,
And what you now pretend, most fair and vertuous.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: Go and believe, a good belief does well Sir;
And you Sir, clear the place, but leave her here.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: Your Lordships pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: That anon Arnoldo,
This is but talk.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Shall we goe off?

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: By any means,
I know she has pious thoughts enough to guard her:
Besides, here's nothing due to him till the tye be done,
Nor dare he offer.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Now do I long to worry him:
Pray have a care to the main chance.

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: Pray Sir, fear not

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: Now, what say you to me?

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: Sir it becomes
The modestie, that maids are ever born with,
To use few words.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: Do you see nothing in me?
Nothing to catch your eyes, nothing of wonder
The common mould of men, come short, and want in?
Do you read no future fortune for your self here?
And what a happiness it may be to you,
To have him honour you, all women aim at?
To have him love you Lady, that man love you,
The best, and the most beauteous have run mad for?
Loo^ and be w^se, you have a favour offer'd you
^ not every day propound to women;
You are a prettie one; and though each hour
I am glutted with the sacrifice of beautie,
I may be brought, as you may handle it,
To call so good a grace and liking on you.
You understand, come kiss me, and be joyfull,
I give you leave.

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: Faith Sir, 'twill not shew handsome;
Our ^x is blushing, full of fear, unskil'd too
In these alarms.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: Learn then and be perfect.

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: I do beseech your honour pardon me,
And take some skilfull one can hold you play,
I am a fool.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: I tell thee maid I love thee,
^ that word make thee happie, so far love thee,
That though I may enjoy thee without ceremony,
I will descend so low, to marry thee,
Me thinks I see the race that shall spring from us,
Some Princes, some great Souldiers.

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: I am afraid
Your honour's couzen'd in this calculation;
For certain, I shall ne're have a child by you.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: Why?

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: Because I must not think to marry you,
I dare not Sir, the step betwixt your honour,
And my poor humble State.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: I will descend to thee,
And buo^ thee up.

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: I'le sink to th'Center first.
Why would your Lordship marry, and confine that pleasure
You ever have had freely cast upon you?
Take heed my Lord, this marrying is a mad matter,
Lighter a pair of shackles will hang on you,
And quiet^r a qua^tane ^eaver find you.
If you wed me I must enjoy you only,
Your eyes must be called home, your thoughts in cages,
To ^ng to no ears then but mine; your heart bound,
The custom, that your youth was ever nurst in,
Must be forgot, I shall forget my duty else,
And how that will appear

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: Wee'l talk of that more.

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: Besides I tell ye, I am naturally,
As all young women are, that shew like handsome,
Exceeding proud, being commended, monstrous.
Of an unquiet temper, seldom pleas'd,
Unless it be with infinite observance,
Which you were never bred to; once well angred,
As every cross in us, provokes that passion,
And like a Sea, I ^oule, toss, and chase a week after.
And then all mischief I can think upon,
Abusing of your bed the least and poorest,
I tell you what you're finde, and in these fitts,
This little beauty you are pleased to honour,
Will be so chang'd, so alter'd to an ugliness,
To such a vizard, ^ one, I dye too,
Take 't then upon my death you murder'd me.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: Away, away fool, why dost thou proclame these
To prevent that in me, thou hast chosen in another?

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: Him I have chosen, I can rule and master,
Temp r to what I please, you me a great one
Of ^ong will to ^, I ^are not venture.
B^ wife my ^d, and say you were well counsel'd,
^, and forget me,
'Twill b^ both ^ and noble for your honour,
And ^ fortunes shall conduct me,

So ^
^ions I shall render of you,
So vert^us and so ^.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: You will not marrie me?

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: I do beseech your honour, be not angry
At what I say, I cannot love ye, dare not;
But set a ransom, for the flowr you covet.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: No mony, nor no prayers, shall redeem that,
Not all the art you have.

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: Set your own price Sir.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: Goe to your wedding, never kneel to me,
When that's done, you are mine, I will enjoy you:
Your tears do nothing, I will not lose my custom
To cast upon my self an Empires fortune.

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: My mind shall not pay this custom, cruel man.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: Your body will content me: I'le look for you.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Strew all your withered flowers, your Autum^ sweets
By the hot Sun ravisht of bud and beauty
Thus round about her Bride-bed, hang those blacks there
The emblemes of her honour lost; all joy
That leads a Virgin to receive her lover,
Keep from this place, all fellow maids that bless her,
And blushing do unloose her Zone, keep from her:
No merry noise nor lusty songs be heard here,
Nor full cups crown'd with wine make the rooms giddy;
This is no masque of mirth, but murdered honour.
Sing mournfully that sad Epithalamion
I gave thee now: and prethee let thy lute weep.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: How now, what livery's this? do you call this a wedding?
This is more like a funeral.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: It is one,
And my poor Daughter going to her grave,
To his most loath'd embraces that gapes for her.
Make the Earles bed readie, is the marriage done Sir?

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Yes they are knit; but must this slubberdegullion
Have her maiden-head now?

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: There's no avoiding it?

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: And there's the scaffold where she must lose it.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: The bed Sir.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: No way to wipe his mouldy chaps?

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: That we know.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: To any honest well-deserving fellow,
And 'twere but to a merry Cobler, I could sit still now,
I love the game so well; but that this pucksist,
This universal rutter—fare ye well Sir;
And if you have any good prayers, put'em forward,
There may be yet a remedie.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: I wish it,
And all my best devotions offer to it.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: Now is this tye dispatch'd?

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: I think it be Sir.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: And my bed ready?

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: There you may quickly find Sir,
Such a loath'd preparation.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: Never grumble,
Nor fling a discontent upon my pleasure,
It must and shall be done: give me some wine,
And fill it till it leap upon my lips:
Here's to the foolish maidenhead you wot of,
The toy I must take pains for.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: I beseech your Lordship
Load not a Fathers love.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: Pledge it Charino,
Or by my life I'le make thee pledge thy last,
And be sure she be a maid, a perfect Virgin,
(I will not have my expectation dull'd)
Or your old pate goes off. I am hot and fiery,
And my bloud beats alarms through my body,
And fancie high. You of my guard retire,
And let me hear no noise about the lodging
But musick and sweet ayres, now fetch your Daughter,
And bid the coy wench put on all her beauties,
All her enticements, out-blush damask Roses,
And dim the breaking East with her bright Crystals.
I am all on fire, away.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: And I am frozen.

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: Come fearless on.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Nay an I budge from thee
Beat me with durty sticks.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: What Masque is this?
What pretty fancy to provoke me high?
The beauteous Huntress, fairer far, and sweeter;
Diana shewes an Ethiop to this beauty
Protected by two Virgin Knights.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: That's a lye,
A loud one, if you knew as much as I do,
The Guard's dispers'd.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: Fortune I hope invites us.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: I can no longer hold, she pulls my heart from me.

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: Stand, and stand fixt, move not a foot, nor speak not,
For if thou doest, upon this point thy death fits.
Thou miserable, base, and sordid lecher,
Thou scum of noble blood, repent and speedily,
Repent thy thousand thefts, from helpless Virgins,
Their innocence betrayed to thy embraces.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: The base dishonour, that thou doest to strangers,
In glorying to abuse the Laws of Marriage,
Thy Infamy thou hast flung upon thy Country,
In nourishing this black and barbarous Custom.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: My Guard.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: One word more, and thou diest.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: One syllable
That tends to any thing, but I beseech you,
And as y'are Gentlemen tender my case,
And I'le thrust my Javeling down thy throat.
Thou Dog-whelp, thou, pox upon thee, what
Should I call thee, Pompion,
Thou kiss my Lady? thou scour her Chamber-pot:
Thou have a Maiden-head? a mottly Coat,
You great blind fool, farewel and be hang'd to ye,
Lose no time Lady.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: Pray take your pleasure Sir,
And so we'l take our leaves.

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: We are determined,
Dye, before yield.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: Honour, and a fair grave.

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: Before a lustful Bed, so for our fortunes.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Du cat awhee, good Count, cry, prethee cry,
O what a wench hast thou lost? cry you great booby.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: And is she gone then, am I dishonoured thus,
Cozened and baffl'd? my Guard there, no man answer?
My Guard I say, sirrah you knew of this plot;
Where are my Guard? I'le have your life you villain,
You politick old Thief.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Heaven send her far enough,
And let me pay the ransom.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Did your honour call us?

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: Post every way, and presently recover
The two strange Gentlemen, and the fair Lady.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: This day was Married Sir?

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: The same.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: We saw 'em
Making with all main speed to th'Port.

speeches.speaker: Cod.
verse: Away villains.
Recover her, or I shall dye; deal truly,
Didst not thou know?

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: By all that's good I did not.
If your honour mean their slight, to say I grieve for that,
Will be to lye; you may handle me as you please.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: Be sure, with all the cruelty, with all the rigor,
For thou hast rob'd me villain of a treasure.
How now?

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: They're all aboard, a Bark rode ready for 'em,
And now are under Sail, and past recovery.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: Rig me a Ship with all the speed that may be,
I will not lose her: thou her most false Father,
Shalt go along; and if I miss her, hear me,
A whole day will I study to destroy thee.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: I shall be joyful of it; and so you'l find me.

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: I Hear and see too much of him, and that
Compels me Madam, though unwillingly,
To wish I had no Uncles part in him,
And much I fear, the comfort of a Son
You will not long enjoy.

speeches.speaker: Gui.
verse: 'Tis not my fault,
And therefore from his guilt my innocence
Cannot be tainted, since his Fathers death,
(Peace to his soul) a Mothers prayers and care
Were never wanting, in his education.
His Child-hood I pass o're, as being brought up
Under my wing; and growing ripe for study,
I overcame the tenderness, and joy
I had to look upon him, and provided
The choicest Masters, and of greatest name
Of Salamanca, in all liberal Arts.

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: To train his youth up.
I must witness that.

speeches.speaker: Gui.
verse: How there he prospered to the admiration
Of all that knew him, for a general Scholar,
Being one of note, before he was a man,
Is still remembred in that Academy,
From thence I sent him to the Emperours Court,
Attended like his Fathers Son, and there
Maintain'd him, in such bravery and height,
As did become a Courtier.

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: 'Twas that spoil'd him, my Nephew had been happy.
The Court's a School indeed, in which some few
Learn vertuous principles, but most forget
What ever they brought thither good and honest.
Trifling is there in practice, serious actions
Are obsolete and out of use, my Nephew
Had been a happy man, had he ne're known
What's there in grace and fashion.

speeches.speaker: Gui.
verse: I have heard yet,
That while he liv'd in Court, the Emperour
Took notice of his carriage and good parts,
The Grandees did not scorn his company,
And of the greatest Ladies he was held
A compleat Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: He indeed Daunc'd well;
A turn o'th'Toe, with a lofty trick or two,
To argue nimbleness, and a strong back,
Will go far with a Madam: 'tis most true,
That he's an excellent Scholar, and he knows it;
An exact Courtier, and he knows that too;
He has fought thrice, and come off still with honour,
Which he forgets not.

speeches.speaker: Gui.
verse: Nor have I much reason,
To grieve his fortune that way.

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: You are mistaken,
Prosperity does search a Gentlemans temper,
More than his adverse fortune: I have known
Many, and of rare parts from their success
In private Duels, rais'd up to such a pride,
And so transform'd from what they were, that all
That lov'd them truly, wish'd they had fallen in them.
I need not write examples, in your Son
'Tis too apparent; for e're Don Duarte
Made tryal of his valour, he indeed was
Admired for civil courtesie, but now
He's swoln so high, out of his own assurance,
Of what he dares do, that he seeks occasions,
Unjust occasions, grounded on blind passion,
Ever to be in quarrels, and this makes him
Shunn'd of all fair Societies.

speeches.speaker: Gui.
verse: Would it were
In my weak power to help it: I will use
With my entreaties th' Authority of a Mother,
As you may of an Uncle, and enlarge it
With your command, as being a Governour
To the great King in Lasbon.

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: Here he comes.
We are unseen, observe him.

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: Boy.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: My Lord.

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: What saith the Spanish Captain that I struck,
To my bold challenge?

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: He refus'd to read it.

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: Why didst not leave it there?

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: I did my Lord,
But to no purpose, for he seems more willing
To sit down with the wrongs, than to repair
His honour by the sword; he knows too well,
That from your Lordship nothing can be got
But more blows, and disgraces.

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: He's a wretch,
A miserable wretch, and all my fury
Is lost upon him; holds the Mask, appointed
I'th' honour of Hippolyta?

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: 'Tis broke off.

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: The reason?

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: This was one, they heard your Lordship
Was by the Ladies choice to lead the Dance,
And therefore they, too well assur'd how far
You would out shine 'em, gave it o're and said,
They would not serve for foiles to set you off.

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: They at their best are such, and ever shall be
Where I appear.

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: Do you note his modesty?

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: But was there nothing else pretended?

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: Yes,
Young Don Alonzo, the great Captains Nephew,
Stood on comparisons.

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: With whom?

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: With you,
And openly profess'd that all precedence,
His birth and state consider'd, was due to him,
Not were your Lordship to contend with one
So far above you.

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: I look down upon him
With such contempt and scorn, as on my slave,
He's a name only, and all good in him
He must derive from his great grandsires Ashes,
For had not their victorious acts bequeath'd
His titles to him, and wrote on his forehead,
This is a Lord, he had liv'd unobserv'd
By any man of mark, and died as one
Amongst the common route. Compare with me?
'Tis Gyant-like ambition, I know him,
And know my self, that man is truly noble,
And he may justly call that worth his own,
Which his deserts have purchas'd, I could wish
My hath were more obserue, my friends and kinsmen
Of lesser power, or that my provident Father
Had been like to that riotous Emperour
That chose his belly for his only heir;
For being of no family then, and poor
My vertues wheresoe'r I liv'd, should make
That kingdom my inheritance.

speeches.speaker: Gui.
verse: Strange self Love!

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: For if I studied the Countries Laws,
I should so easily sound all their depth,
And rise up such a wonder, that the pleaders,
That now are in most practice and esteem,
Should starve for want of Clients: if I travell'd,

Like wise
~lysses to see men and manners,
I would return in act, more knowing, than
Homer could fancy him; if a Physician,
So oft I would restore death-wounded men,
That where I liv'd, Galen should not be nam'd,
And he that joyn'd again the scatter'd limbs
Of torn Hippolytus should be forgotten.
I could teach Ovid courtship, how to win
A Julia, and enjoy her, though her Dower
Were all the Sun gives light to: and for arms
Were the Persian host that drank up Rivers, added
To the Turks present powers, I could direct,
Command, and Marshal them.

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: And yet you know not
To rule your self, you would not to a boy else
Like Plautus Braggart boast thus.

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: All I speak,
In act I can make good.

speeches.speaker: Gui.
verse: Why then being Master
Of such and so good parts do you destroy them,
With self opinion, or like a rich miser,
Hoard up the treasures you possess, imparting
Nor to your self nor others, the use of them?
They are to you but like inchanted viands,
On which you seem to feed, yet pine with hunger;
And those so rare perfections in my Son
Which would make others happy, render me
A wretched Mother.

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: You are too insolent.
And those too many excellencies, that feed
Your pride, turn to a Pleurisie, and kill
That which should nourish vertue; dare you think
All blessings are confer'd on you alone?
Y'are grosly cousen'd; there's no good in you,
Which others have not: are you a Scholar? so
Are many, ^nd as knowing: are you valiant?
Waste not that courage then in braules, but spend it
In the Wars, in service of your King and Country.

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: Yes, so I might be General, no man lives
That's worthy to command me.

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: Sir, in Lisbon
I am: and you shall know it; every hour
I am troubled with complaints of your behaviour
From men of all conditions, and all sexes.
And my authority, which you presume
Will bear you out, in that you are my Nephew,
No longer shall protect you, for I vow
Though all that's past I pardon, I will punish
The next fault with as much severity
As if you were a stranger, rest assur'd on't.

speeches.speaker: Gui.
verse: And by that love you should bear, or that duty
You owe a Mother, once more I command you
To cast this haughtiness off; which if you do,
All that is mine, is yours, if not, expect
My prayers, and vows, for your conversion only,
But never means nor favour.

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: I am Tutor'd
As if I were a child still, the base Peasants
That fear, and envy my great worth, have done this;
But I will find them out, I will o' boord
Get my disguise; I have too long been idle,
Nor will I curb my spirit, I was born free,
^d will pursue the course best liketh me.

speeches.speaker: Leop.
verse: Divide the spoil amongst you, this fair Captive
^nly challenge for my self.

speeches.speaker: Sail.
verse: You have won her
^nd well deserve her: twenty years I have liv'd
^ Burgess of the Sea, and have been present
^ many a desperate fight, but never saw
^ small a Bark with such incredible valour
^ long defended, and against such odds,
^nd by two men scarce arm'd too.

speeches.speaker: Leop.
verse: 'Twas a wonder.
^nd yet the courage they exprest being taken,
^nd their contempt of death wan more upon me
^han all they did, when they were free: me thinks
^ see them yet when they were brought aboard us,
^isarm'd and ready to be put in setters
^ow on the suddain, as if they had sworn
^ever to taste the bread of servitude,
^oth snatching up their swords, and from this Virgin,
Taking a farewel only with their eyes,
They leapt into the Sea.

speeches.speaker: Sail.
verse: Indeed 'twas rare.

speeches.speaker: Leop.
verse: It wrought so much on me, that but I fear'd
The great ship that pursued us, our own safety
Hindring my charitable purpose to 'em,
^ would have took 'em up, and with their lives
They should have had their liberties.

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: O too late,
For they are lost, for ever lost.

speeches.speaker: Leop.
verse: Take comfort
'Tis not impossible, but that they live yet,
For when they left the ships, they were within
A League o'th' shore, and with such strength and cunning
They swimming, did delude the rising Billows,
With one hand making way, and with the other,
Their bloudy swords advanced, threatning the Sea-gods
With war, unless they brought them safely off,
That I am almost confident they live,
And you again may see them.

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: In that hope
I brook a wretched being, till I am
Made certain of their fortunes; but they dead,
Death hath so many doors to let out life,
I will not long survive them.

speeches.speaker: Leop.
verse: Hope the best,
And let the courteous usage you have found,
Not usual in men of War perswade you
To tell me your condition.

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: You know it,
A Captive, my fate and your power have made me,
Such I am now, but what I was it skills not:
For they being dead, in whom I only live,
I dare not challenge Family, or Country,
And therefore Sir enquire not, let it suffice,
I am your servant, and a thankful servant
(If you will call that so, which is but duty)
I ever will be, and my honour safe,
Which nobly hitherto ye have preserv'd,
No slavery can appear in such a form,
Which with a masculine constancy I will not
Boldly look on and suffer.

speeches.speaker: Leop.
verse: You mistake me:
That you are made my prisoner, may prove
The birth of your good fortune. I do find
A winning language in your tongue and looks;
Nor can a suit by you mov'd be deni'd,
And therefore of a prisoner you must be
The Victors advocate.

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: To whom?

speeches.speaker: Leop.
verse: A Lady:
In whom all graces that can perfect beauty
Are friendly met. I grant that you are fair:
And had I not seen her before, perhaps
I might have sought to you.

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: This I hear gladly.

speeches.speaker: Leop.
verse: To this incomparable Lady I will give you,
(Yet being mine, you are already hers)
And to serve her is more than to be free,
At least I think so; and when you live with her,
If you will please to think on him that brought you
To such a happiness, for so her bounty
Will make you think her service, you shall ever
Make me at your devotion.

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: All I can do,
Rest you assur'd of.

speeches.speaker: Leop.
verse: At night I'le present you,
Till when I am your Guard.

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: Ever your servant.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: To what are we reserv'd?

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Troth 'tis uncertain,
Drowning we have scap'd miraculously, and
Stand fair for ought I know for hanging; mony
We have none, nor e're are like to have,
'Tis to be doubted: besides we are strangers,
Wondrous hungry strangers; and charity
Growing cold, and miracles ceasing,
Without a Conjurers help, cannot find
When we shall eat again.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: These are no wants
If put in ballance with Zenocias loss;
In that alone all miseries are spoken:
O my Rutilio, when I think on her,
And that which she may suffer, being a Captive,
Then I could curse my self, almost those powers
That send me from the fury of the Ocean.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: You have lost a wise indeed, a fair and chast one,
Two blessings, not found often in one woman;
But she may be recovered, questionless
The ship that took us was of Portugal,
And here in Lisbon, by some means or other
We may hear of her.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: In that hope I live.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: And so do I, but hope is a poor Sallad
To dine and sup with, after a two dayes fast too,
Have you no mony left?

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: Not a Denier.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Nor any thing to pawn? 'tis now in fashion,
Having a Mistress, sure you should not be
Without a neat Historical shirt.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: For shame
Talk not so poorly.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: I must talk of that
Necessity prompts us to, for beg I cannot,
Nor am I made to creep in at a window,
To filch to feed me, something must be done,
And suddenly resolve on't.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: What are these?

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: One by his habit is a Jew.

speeches.speaker: Zab.
verse: No more:
Thou art sure that's he.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Most certain.

speeches.speaker: Zab.
verse: How long is it
Since first she saw him?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Some two hours.

speeches.speaker: Zab.
verse: Be gone— let me alone to work him.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: How he eyes you!
Now he moves towards us, in the Devils name
What would he with us?

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: Innocence is bold:
Nor can I fear.

speeches.speaker: Zab.
verse: That you are poor and strangers,
I easily perceive.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: But that you'l help us,
Or any of your tribe, we dare not hope Sir.

speeches.speaker: Zab.
verse: Why think you so?

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Because you are a Jew Sir,
And courtesies come sooner from the Devil
Than any of your Nation.

speeches.speaker: Zab.
verse: We are men,
And have like you, compassion when we find
Fit subjects for our bounty, and for proof
That we dare give, and freely, not to you Sir,
Pray spare your pains, there's gold, stand not amaz'd,
'Tis current I assure you.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Take it man,
Sure thy good Angel is a Jew, and comes
In his own shape to help thee: I could wish now
Mine would appear too like a Turk.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: I thank you,
But yet must tell you, if this be the Prologue
To any bad act, you would have me practise,
I must not take it.

speeches.speaker: Zab.
verse: This is but the earnest
Of what which is to follow, and the bond
Which you must seal to for't, is your advancement,
Fortune with all that's in her power to give,
Offers her self up to you: entertain her,
And that which Princes have kneel'd for in vain
Presents it self to you.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: 'Tis above wonder.

speeches.speaker: Zab.
verse: But far beneath the truth, in my relation
Of what you shall possess, if you embace it.
There is an hour in each mans life appointed
To make his happiness if then he seize it,
And this, (in which, beyond all expectation,
You are invited to your good) is yours,
If you dare follow me, so, if not, hereafter
Expect not the like offer.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: 'Tis no vision.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: 'Tis gold I'm sure.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: We must like brothers share;
There's for you.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: By this light I'm glad I have it:
There are few Gallants, (for men may be such
And yet want gold, yea and sometimes silver)
But would receive such favours from the Devil,
Though he appear'd like a Broker, and demanded
Sixty i'th' hundred.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: Wherefore should I fear
Some plot upon my life? 'tis now to me
Not worth the keeping. I will follow him,
Farewel, wish me good fortune, we shall meet
Again I doubt not.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Or I'le ne're trust Jew more,
Nor Christian for his sake— plague o' my stars,
How long might I have walkt without a Cloak,
Before I should have met with such a fortune?
We elder Brothers, though we are proper men,
Ha' not the luck, ha' too much beard, that spoils us;
The smooth Chin carries all: what's here to do now?

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: I'le take you as I find you.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: That were base — you see I am unarm'd.

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: Out with your Bodkin
Your Pocket-dagger, your Steletto, out with it,
Or by this hand I'le kill you: such as you are
Have studied the undoing of poor Cutlers,
And made all manly weapons out of fashion:
You carry Poniards to murder men,
Yet dare not wear a sword to guard your Honour.

speeches.speaker: Rut
verse: That's true indeed: upon my life this gallant
Is brib'd to repeal banisht swords.

speeches.speaker: Dua
verse: I'le shew you
The difference now between a Spanish Rapier
And your pure Pisa.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: Let me fetch a sword,
Upon mine honour I'le return.

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: Not so Sir.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: Or lend me yours I pray you, and take this.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: To be disgrac'd as you are, no I thank you
Spight of the fashion, while I live, I am
Instructed to go arm'd: what folly 'tis
For you that are a man, to put your self
Into your enemies mercy.

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: Yield it quickly
Or I'le cut off your hand, and now disgrace you,
Thus kick and baffle you: as you like this,
You may again prefer complaints against me
To my Uncle and my Mother, and then think
To make it good with a Poniard.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: I am paid
For being of the fashion.

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: Get a sword,
Then if you dare redeem your reputation:
You know I am easily found: I'le add this to it
To put you in mind.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: You are too insolent,
And do insult too much on the advantage
Of that which your unequal weapon gave you,
More than your valour.

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: This to me, you Peasant?
Thou art not worthy of my foot poor fellow,
'Tis scorn, not pity, makes me give thee life:
Kneel down and thank me for't: how, do you stare?

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: I have a sword Sir, you shall find, a good one;
This is no stabbing guard.

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: Wert thou thrice arm'd,
Thus yet I durst attempt thee.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Then have at you,
I scorn to take blows.

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: O I am slain.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: Help! murther, murther!

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: Shift for your self you are dead else,
You have kill'd the Governous Nephew.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: Raise the streets there.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: If once you are beset you cannot scape,
Will you betray your-self?

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Undone for ever.

speeches.speaker: 1 Offi.
verse: Who makes this out-cry?

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: O my Lord is murdered;
This way he took, make after him,
Help help there.

speeches.speaker: 2 Offi.
verse: 'Tis Don Duarte.

speeches.speaker: 1 Offi.
verse: Pride has got a fall,
He was still in quarrels, scorn'd us Peace-makers,
And all our Bill-authority, now h'as paid for't.
You ha' met with your match Sir now, bring off his body
And bear it to the Governour. Some pursue
The murderer; yet if he scape, it skills not;
Were I a Prince, I would reward him for't,
He has rid the City of a turbulent beast,
There's few will pity him: but for his Mother
I truly grieve indeed, she's a good Lady.

speeches.speaker: Gui.
verse: He's not i'th' house?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: No Madam.

speeches.speaker: Gui.
verse: Haste and seek him,
