As love already makes me sensible
Of half her sufferings, ease her of her part,
And let me stand the butt of thy fell malice,
And I will swear th'art mercifull.

speeches.speaker: Doct.
verse: Your hand Lady;
What a strange heat is here? bring some warm water.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: She shall use nothing that is yours; my sorrow
Provides her of a better bath, my tears
Shall do that office.

speeches.speaker: Zeno.
verse: O my best Arnoldo!
The truest of all lovers! I would live
Were heaven so pleas'd, but to reward your sorrow
With my true service; but since that's denied me,
May you live long and happy: do not suffer
(By your affection to me I conjure you)
My sickness to infect you; though much love
Makes you too subject to it.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: In this only
Zenocia wrongs her servant; can the body
Subsist, the Soul departed? 'tis as easie
As I to live without you; I am your husband,
And long have been so, though our adverse fortune,
^ndying us from one hazard to another,
Would never grant me so much happiness,
As to pay a husbands debt; despite of fortune,
In death I'le follow you, and guard mine own;
And there enjoy what here my fate forbids me.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: So true a sorrow, and so feelingly
Exprest, I never read of.

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: I am struck
With wonder to behold it, as with pity

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: If you that are a stranger, suffer for them,
Being tied no further than humanity
Leads you to soft compassion; think great Sir,
What of necessity I must endure,
That am a Father?

speeches.speaker: Zab.
verse: Wait me there, I hold it
Unfit to have you seen; as I find cause,
You shall proceed.

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: You are welcom Lady.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: Sir, I come to do a charitable office,
How does the patient?

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: You may enquire
Of more than one; for two are sick, and deadly,
He languishes in her, her health's despair'd of,
And in hers, his.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: 'Tis a strange spectacle,
With what a patience they sit unmov'd?
Are they not dead already?

speeches.speaker: Doct.
verse: By her pulse,
She cannot last a day.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: Oh by that summons,
I know my time too!

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: Look to the man.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: Apply
Your Art, to save the Lady, preserve her,
A town is your reward.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: I'le treble it,
In ready gold, if you restore Arnoldo;
For in his death I dye too.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: Without her
I am no more.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: Are you there Madam? now
You may feast on my miseries; my coldness
In answering your affections, or hardness,
Give it what name you please, you are reveng'd of;
For now you may perceive, our thred of life
Was spun together, and the poor Arnoldo
Made only to enjoy the best Zenocia,
And not to serve the use of any other;
And in that she may equal; my Lord Clodio
Had long since else enjoyed her, nor could I
Have been so blind, as not to see your great
And many excellencies far, far beyond
Or my deservings, or my hopes; we are now
Going our latest journey, and together,
Our only comfort we desire, pray give it,
Your charity to our ashes, such we must be,
And not to curse our memories.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: I am much mov'd.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: I am wholly overcome, all love to women
Farewell for ever; ere you dye, your pardon;
And yours Sir; had she many years to live,
Perhaps I might look on her, as a Brother,
But as a lover never; and since all
Your sad misfortunes had original
From the barbarous Custom practis'd in my Country,
Heaven witness, for your sake I here release it;
So to your memory, chaste Wives and Virgins
Shall ever pay their vowes. I give her to you;
And wish, she were so now, as when my lust
Forc'd you to quit the Country.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: It is in vain
To strive with destiny, here my dotage ends,
Look up Zenocia, health in me speaks to you;
She gives him to you, that by divers ways,
So long has kept him from you: and repent not,
That you were once my servant, for which health
In recompence of what I made you suffer,
The hundred thousand Crowns, the City owes me,
Shall be your dower.

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: 'Tis a magnificent gift,
Had it been timely given.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: It is believe it, Sulpitia.

speeches.speaker: Sulp.
verse: Madam.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: Quick, undoe the charm;
Ask not a reason why; let it suffice,
It is my will.

speeches.speaker: Sulp.
verse: Which I obey and gladly.

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: Is to be married, sayest thou?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: So she sayes Sir,
And does desire your presence.

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: And tell her I'le come.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: Pray carry them to their rest; for though already,
They do appear as dead, let my life pay for't,
If they recover not.

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: What you have warranted,
Assure your self, will be expected from you;
Look to them carefully; and till the tryal,—

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: Which shall not be above four hours.

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: Let me
Intreat your companies: there is something
Of weight invites me hence.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: We'll wait upon you.

speeches.speaker: Guio.
verse: You understand what my directions are,
And what they guide you to; the faithfull promise
You have made me all.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: We do and will perform it.

speeches.speaker: Guio.
verse: The Governour will not fail to be here presently;
Retire a while, till you shall find occasion,
And bring me word, when they arrive.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: Wee shall Madam.

speeches.speaker: Guio.
verse: Only stay you to entertain.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
verse: I am ready.

speeches.speaker: Guio.
verse: I wonder at the bold, and practis'd malice,
Men ever have o' foot against our honours,
That nothing we can do, never so vertuous,
No shape put on so pious, no not think
What a good is, be that good ne're so noble,
Never so laden with admir'd example,
But still we end in lust; our aims, our actions,
Nay, even our charities, with lust are branded;
Why should this stranger else, this wretched stranger,
Whose life I sav'd at what dear price sticks here yet,
Why should he hope? he was not here an hour,
And certainly in that time, I may swear it
I gave him no loose look, I had no reason;
Unless my tears were flames, my curses courtships;
The killing of my Son, a kindness to me.
Why should he send to me, or with what safety
(Examining the ruine he had wrought me)
Though at that time, my pious pity found him,
And my word fixt; I am troubled, strongly troubled.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: The Gentlemen are come.

speeches.speaker: Guio.
verse: Then bid 'em welcom—I must retire.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: You are welcom Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: I thank you friend, I would speak with your Lady.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: I'le let her understand.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: It shall besit you.
How do I look Sir, in this handsome trim?
Me thinks I am wondrous brave.

speeches.speaker: Duar.
verse: You are very decent.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: These by themselves, without more helps of nature,
Would set a woman hard; I know 'em all,
And where their first aims light; I'le lay my head on't,
I'le take her eye, as soon as she looks on me,
And if I come to speak once, woe be to her,
I have her in a nooze, she cannot scape me;
I have their several lasts.

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: You are throughly studied,
But tell me Sir, being unacquainted with her,
As you confess you are—

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: That's not an hours work,
I'le make a Nun forget her beads in two hours.

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: She being set in years, next none of those lusters
Appearing in her eye, that warm the fancy;
Nor nothing in her face, but handsom ruines.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: I love old stories: those live believ'd, Authentique,
When 20. of your modern faces are call'd in,
For new opinion, paintings, and corruptions;
Give me an old confirm'd face; besides she sav'd me,
She sav'd my life, have I not cause to love her?
She's rich and of a constant state, a fair one,
Have I not cause to wooe her? I have tryed sufficient
All your young Phillies, I think this back has try'd 'em,
And smarted for it too: they run away with me,
Take bitt between the teeth, and play the Devils;
A staied pace now becomes my years; a sure one,
Where I may sit and crack no girths.

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: How miserable,
If my Mother should confirm, what I suspect now,
Beyond all humane cure were my condition!
Then I shall wish, this body had been so too.
Here comes the Lady Sir.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Excellent Lady,
To shew I am a creature, bound to your service,
And only yours —

speeches.speaker: Guio.
verse: Keep at that distance Sir;
For if you stir —

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: I am obedient.
She has found already, I am for her turn;
With what a greedy hawks eye she beholds me?
Mark how she musters all my parts.

speeches.speaker: Guio.
verse: A goodly Gentleman,
Of a more manly set, I never look'd on.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Mark, mark her eyes still; mark but the carriage of 'em.

speeches.speaker: Guio.
verse: How happy am I now, since my Son fell,
He fell not by a base unnoble hand?
As that still troubled me; how far more happy
Shall my revenge be, since the Sacrifice,
I offer to his grave, shall be both worthy
A Sons untimely loss, and a Mothers sorrow?

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Sir, I am made believe it; she is mine own,
I told you what a spell I carried with me,
All this time does she spend in contemplation
Of that unmatch'd delight: I shall be thankfull to ye;
And if you please to know my house, to use it;
To take it for your own.

speeches.speaker: Guio.
verse: Who waits without there?

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: How now? what means this, Lady?

speeches.speaker: Guio.
verse: Bind him fast.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Are these the bride-laces you prepare for me?
The colours that you give?

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: Fye Gentle Lady,
This is not noble dealing.

speeches.speaker: Guio.
verse: Be you satisfied,
If seems you are a stranger to this meaning,
You shall not be so long.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Do you call this wooing—Is there no end of womens persecutions?
Must I needs fool into mine own destruction?
Have I not had fair warnings, and enough too?
Still pick the Devils teeth? you are not mad Lady;
Do I come fairly, and like a Gentleman,
To offer you that honour?

speeches.speaker: Guio.
verse: You are deceiv'd Sir,

Yo^
^ome besotted, to your own destruction!
I sent not for you; what honour can ye add to me,
That brake that staff of honour, my age lean'd on?
That rob'd me of that right, made me a Mother?
Hear me thou wretched man, hear me with terrour,
And let thine own bold folly shake thy Soul,
Hear me pronounce thy death, that now hangs o're thee,
Thou desperate fool; who bad thee seek this ruine?
What mad unmanly fate, made thee discover
Thy cursed face to me again? was't not enough
To have the fair protection of my house,
When misery and justice close pursued thee?
When thine own bloudy sword, cryed out against thee,
Hatcht in the life of him? yet I forgave thee.
My hospitable word, even when I saw
The goodliest branch of all my blood lopt from me,
Did I not seal still to thee?

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: I am gone.

speeches.speaker: Guio.
verse: And when thou went'st, to Imp thy miserie,
Did I not give thee means? but hark ungratefull,
Was it not thus? to hide thy face and fly me?
To keep thy name for ever from my memory?
Thy cursed blood and kindred? did I not swear then,
If ever, (in this wretched life thou hast left me,
Short and unfortunate,) I saw thee again,
Or came but to the knowledge, where thou wandredst,
To call my vow back, and pursue with vengeance
With all the miseries a Mother suffers?

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: I was born to be hang'd, there's no avoiding it.

speeches.speaker: Guio.
verse: And dar'st thou with this impudence appear here?
VValk like the winding sheet my Son was put in,
Stand with those wounds?

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: I am happy now again;
Happy the hour I fell, to find a Mother,
So pious, good, and excellent in sorrows.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: The Governour's come in.

speeches.speaker: Guio.
verse: O let him enter.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: I have fool'd my self a fair thred of all my fortunes,
This strikes me most; not that I fear to perish,
But that this unmannerly boldness has brought me to it.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Are these fit preparations for a wedding Lady?
I came prepar'd a guest.

speeches.speaker: Guio.
verse: O give me justice;
As ever you will leave a vertuous name,
Do justice, justice, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Gove.
verse: You need not ask it,
I am bound to it.

speeches.speaker: Guio.
verse: Justice upon this man
That kill'd my Son.

speeches.speaker: Gove.
verse: Do you confess the act?

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Yes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: Rutilio?

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: 'Tis the same.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: How fell he thus?
Here will be sorrow for the good Arnoldo.

speeches.speaker: Gove.
verse: Take heed Sir what you say.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: I have weigh'd it well,
I am the man, nor is it life I start at;
Only I am unhappy I am poor,
Poor in expence of lives, there I am wretched,
That I have not two lives lent me for his sacrifice;
One for her Son, another for her sorrows.
Excellent Lady, now rejoyce again,
For though I cannot think, y'are pleas'd in blood,
Nor with that greedy thirst pursue your vengeance;
The tenderness, even in those tears denies that;
Yet let the world believe, you lov'd Duarte;
The unmatcht courtesies you have done my miseries,
Without this forfeit to the law, would charge me
To tender you this life, and proud 'twould please you.

speeches.speaker: Guio.
verse: Shall I have justice?

speeches.speaker: Gover.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: I'le ask it for ye,
I'le follow it my self, against my self.
Sir, 'Tis most sit I dye; dispatch it quickly,
The monstrous burthen of that grief she labours with
Will kill her else, then blood ^ blood lyes on me;
Had I a thousand lives, I'^ give 'em all,
Before I would draw one tear more from that vertue.

speeches.speaker: Guio.
verse: Be not too cruel Sir, and yet his bold sword—
But his life cannot restore that, he's a man too—
Of a fair promise, but alas my Son's dead;
If I have justice, must it kill hi^

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Guio.
verse: If I have not, it kills me, strong and goodly!
Why should he perish too?

speeches.speaker: Gover.
verse: It lies in your power,
You only may accuse him, or may quit him.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: Be there no other witnesses?

speeches.speaker: Guio.
verse: Not any.
And if I save him, will not the world proclaim,
I have forgot a Son, to save a murderer?
And yet he looks not like one, he looks manly.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: Pity so brave a Gentleman should perish.
She cannot be so hard, so cruel hearted.

speeches.speaker: Guio.
verse: Will you pronounce? yet stay a little Sir.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Rid your self, Lady, of this misery;
And let me go, I do but breed more tempests,
With which you are already too much shaken.

speeches.speaker: Guio.
verse: Do now, pronounce; I will not hear,

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: You shall not,
Yet turn and see good Madam.

speeches.speaker: Gove.
verse: Do not wonder.
'Tis he, restor'd again, thank the good Doctor,
Pray do not stand amaz'd, it is Duarte;
Is well, is safe again.

speeches.speaker: Guio.
verse: O my sweet Son,
I will not press my wonder now with questions—
Sir, I am sorry for that cruelty,
I urg'd against you.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Madam, it was but justice.

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: 'Tis true, the Doctor heal'd this body again,
But this man heal'd my soul, made my minde perfect,
The good sharp lessons his sword read to me, sav'd me;
For which, if you lov'd me, dear Mother,
Honour and love this man.

speeches.speaker: Guio.
verse: You sent this letter?

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: My boldness makes me blush now.

speeches.speaker: Guio.
verse: I'le wipe off that,
And with this kiss, I take you for my husband,
Your wooing's done Sir; I believe you love me,
And that's the wealth I look for now.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: You have it.

speeches.speaker: Dua.
verse: You have ended my desire to all my wishes.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Now 'tis a wedding again. And if Hippolyta
Make good, what with the hazard of her life,
She undertook, the evening will set clear
After a stormy day.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Here comes the Lady.

speeches.speaker: Clod.
verse: With fair Zenocia,
Health with life again
Restor'd unto her.

speeches.speaker: Zen.
verse: The gift of her goodness.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Let us embrace, I am of your order too,
And though I once despair'd of women, now
I find they relish much of Scorpions,
For both have stings, and both can hurt, and cure too;
But what have been your fortunes?

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: Wee'l defer
Our story, and at time more sit, relate it.
Now all that reverence vertue, and in that
Zenocias constancy, and perfect love,
Or for her sake Arnoldo, join with us
In th' honour of this Lady.

speeches.speaker: Cha^.
verse: She deserves it.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: Hippolytas life shall make that good hereafter,
Not will I alone better my self but others:
For these whose wants perhaps have made their actions
Not altogether innocent, shall from me
Be so supplied, that need shall not compel them,
To any course of life, but what the law
Shall give allowance to.

speeches.speaker: Zab.
verse: Sulpitia, Your Ladiships creatures.

speeches.speaker: R t.
verse: Be so, and no more you man-huckster.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: And worthy Leopold, you that with such fervour,
So long have sought me, and in that deserv'd me,
Shall now find full reward for all your travels,
Which you have made more dear by patient sufferance.
And though my violent dotage did transport me,
Beyond those bounds, my modesty should have kept in,
Though my desires were loose, from unchast art
Heaven knows I am free.

speeches.speaker: Leop.
verse: The thought of that's dead to me;
I gladly take your offer.

speeches.speaker: Rut.
verse: Do so Sir,
A piece of crackt gold ever will weigh down
Silver that's whole.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: You shall be all my guests,
I must not be denyed.

speeches.speaker: Arn.
verse: Come my Zenocia.
Our bark at length has found a quiet harbour;
And the unspotted progress of our loves
Ends not alone in safety, but reward,
To instruct others, by our fair example;
That though good purposes are long withstood,
The hand of Heaven still guides such as are good.

speeches.speaker: Lewis.
prose: NAY, I must walk you farther.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: I am tir'd, Sir, and ne'er shall foot it home.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: 'Tis for your health; the want of exercise takes from your Beauties, and sloth dries up your sweetness: That you are my only Daughter and my Heir, is granted; and you in thankfulness must needs acknowledge, you ever find me an indulgent Father, and open handed.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Nor can you tax me, Sir, I hope, for want of duty to deserve these favours from you.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: No, my Angellina, I love and cherish thy obedience to me, which my care to advance thee shall confirm: all that I aim at, is, to win thee from the practice of an idle foolish state, us'd by great Women, who think any labour (though in the service of themselves) a blemish to their fair fortunes.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Make me understand, Sir, what 'tis you point at.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: At the custom, how Virgins of wealthy Families waste their youth; after a long sleep, when you wake, your Woman presents your Breakfast, then you sleep again, then rise, and being trimm'd up by other hands, y'are led to Dinner, and that ended, either to Cards or to your Couch, (as if you were born without motion) after this to Supper, and then to Bed: and so your life runs round without variety or action, Daughter.

speeches.speaker: Syl.
prose: Here's a learned Lecture!

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: Frow this idleness, Diseases, both in body and in mind, grow strong upon you; where a stirring nature, with wholesome exercise, guards both from danger: I'd have thee rise with the Sun, walk, dance, or hunt, visit the Groves and Springs, and learn the vertue of Plants and Simples: Do this moderately, and thou shalt not, with eating Chalk, or Coles, Leather and Oatmeal, and such other trash, fall into the Green-sickness.

speeches.speaker: Syl.
prose: With your pardon (were you but pleas'd to minister it) I could prescribe a Remedy for my Lady's health, and her delight too, far transcending those your Lordship but now mention'd.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: What is it, Sylvia?

speeches.speaker: Syl.
prose: What is't! a noble Husband; in that word, a noble Husband, all content of Woman is wholly comprehended; He will rouse her, as you say, with the Sun; and so pipe to her, as she will dance, ne'er doubt it; and hunt with her, upon occasion, until both be weary; and then the knowledge of your Plants and Simples, as I take it, were superfluous. A loving, and, but add to it, a gamesome Bedfellow, being the sure Physician.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: Well said, Wench.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose:
And who gave you Commission to deliver your
Verdict, Minion?

speeches.speaker: Syl.
prose: I deserve a Fee, and not a frown, dear Madam: I but speak her thoughts, my Lord, and what her modesty refuses to give voice to. Shew no mercy to a Maidenhead of fourteen, but off with't: let her lose no time, Sir; Fathers that deny their Daughters lawful pleasures, when ^ for them, in some kinds edge their appetites to taste of the fruit that is forbidden.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: 'Tis well urg'd, and I approve it: No more blushing, Girl, thy Woman hath spoke truth, and so prevented what I meant to move to thee. There dwells near us a Gentleman of bloud, Monsieur Brisac, of a fair Estate, six thousand Crowns per annum, the happy Father of two hopeful Sons, of different breeding; the Elder, a meer Scholar; the younger, a quaint Courtier.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Sir, I know them by publick fame, though yet I never saw them; and that oppos'd antipathy between their various dispositions, renders them the general discourse and argument; one part inclining to the Scholar Charles, the other side preferring Eustace, as a man compleat in Courtship.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: And which way (if of these two you were to chuse a Husband) doth your affection sway you?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: To be plain Sir, (since you will teach me boldness) as they are simply themselves, to neither: let a Courtier be never so exact, let him be bless'd with all parts that yield him to a Virgin gracious; if he depend on others, and stand not on his own bottoms, though he have the means to bring his Mistris to a Masque, or by conveyance from some great ones lips, to taste such favour from the King: or grant he purchase precedency in the Court, to be sworn a servant Extraordinary to the Queen; nay, though he live in expectation of some huge preferment in reversion; if he want a present fortune, at the best those are but glorious dreams, and only yield him a happiness in posse, not in esse; nor can they fetch him Silks from the Mercer, nor discharge a Tailors Bill, not in full plenty (which still preserves a quiet Bed at home) maintain a Family.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: Aptly consider'd, and to my wish: But what's thy censure of the Scholar?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Troth (if he be nothing else) as of the Courtier, all his Songs and Sonnets, his Anagrams, Acrosticks, Epigrams, his deep and Philosophical Discourse of Nature's hidden Secrets, makes not up a perfect Husband; he can hardly borrow the Stars of the Celestial Crown to make me a Tire for my Head, nor Charles's Wain for a Coach, nor Ganymede for a Page, nor a rich Gown from Juno's Wardrobe, nor would I lie in (for I despair not once to be a Mother) under Heaven's spangled Canopy, or Banquet my Guests and Gossips with imagin'd Nectar; pure Orleans would do better: No, no, Father, though I could be well pleas'd to have my Husband a Courtier, and a Scholar, young, and valiant; these are but gawdy nothings, if there be not something to make a substance.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: And what is that?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: A full Estate, and that said, I've said all; and get me such a one with these Additions, farewel Virginity, and welcome Wedlock.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: But where is such a one to be met with, Daughter? A black Swan is more common; you may wear grey Tresses e're we find him.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: I am not so punctual in all Ceremonies, I will 'bate two or three of these good parts, before I'le dwell too long upon the choice.

speeches.speaker: Syl.
prose: Only, my Lord, remember, that he be rich and active, for without these, the others yield no relish, but these perfect. You must bear with small saults, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: Merry Wench, and it becomes you well; I'le to Brisac, and try what may be done; i'th' mean time home, and feast thy thoughts with th'pleasures of a Bride.

speeches.speaker: Syl.
prose: Thoughts are but airy food, Sir, let her taste them.

segments.head: Actus primus. | ACTUS I. SCENA II.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Unload part of the Library, and make room for th'other dozen of Carts; I'le straight be with you

speeches.speaker: Cook.
prose: Why, hath he more Books?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: More than ten Marts send over.

speeches.speaker: But.
prose: And can he tell their names?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Their names! he has 'em as perfect as his P^ Noster; but that's nothing, h'as read them over leaf by leaf three thousand times; but here's the wonder, thoug^ their weight would sink a Spanish Carrock, without other Ballast, he carrieth them all in his head, and yet he wa^ upright.

speeches.speaker: But.
prose: Surely he has a strong brain.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: If all thy pipes of Wine were fill'd with Books, made of the Barks of Trees, or Mysteries writ in old moth eaten Vellam, he would sip thy Cellar quite dry, and still be thirsty: Then for's Diet, he eats and digests more Volumes at a meal, than there would be Larks (though the Sky should fall) devoured in a month in Paris. Yet fear not Sons o'the Buttery and Kitchin, though his learn'd stomach cannot be appeas'd; he'll seldom trouble you, his knowing stomach contemns your Black-Jacks, Butler, and you Flagons; and Cook, thy Boil'd, thy Rost, thy Bak'd.

speeches.speaker: Cook.
prose: How liveth he?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Not as other men do, few Princes fare like him; he breaks his fast with Aristotle, dines with Tully, takes his watering with the Muses, sups with Livy, then walks a turn or two in Via Lactea, and (after six hours conference with the Stars) sleeps with old Erra Pater.

speeches.speaker: But.
prose: This is admirable.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: I'le tell you more hereafter. Here's my old Master, and another old ignorant Elder; I'le upon 'em.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: What, Andrew? welcome; where's my Charles? speak, Andrew, where did'st thou leave thy Master?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Contemplating the number of the Sands in the High way, and from that, purposes to make a Judgment of the remainder in the Sea: he is, Sir, in serious study, and will lose no minute, nor out of's pace to knowledge.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: This is strange.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Yet he hath sent his duty, Sir, before him in this fair Manuscript.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: What have we here? Pot-hooks and Andirons!

speeches.speaker: And.
prose:
I much pity you, it is the Syrian Character, or the Arabick. Would you have it said, so great and deep a Scholar as Mr
Charles is, should ask blessing in any Christian Language? Were it Greek I could interpret for you, but indeed I'm gone no farther.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: And in Greek you can lie with your smug Wife Lilly.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: If I keep her from your French Dialect, as I hope I shall, Sir; however she is your Land^ess, she shall put you to the charge of no more Soap than usual for th'washing of your Sheets.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Take in the Knave, and let him eat.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: And drink too, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: And drink too Sir, and see your Masters Chamber ready for him.

speeches.speaker: But.
prose:
Come, Dr
Andrew, without Disputation thou shalt Commence i'the Cellar.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: I had rather Commence on a cold Bak'd meat.

speeches.speaker: Cook.
prose: Thou shalt ha't, Boy.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose:
Good Monsieur Lewis, I esteem my self much ho~nour'd in your clear intent, to joyn our ancient Families, and make them one; and 'twill take from my age and cares, to live and see what you have purpos'd but in act, of which your visit at this present is a hopeful Omen; I each minute expecting the arrival of my Sons; I have not wrong d their Birth for want of Means and Education, to shape them to that course each was addicted; and therefore that we may proceed discreetly, since what's concluded rashly seldom

^rospers, you first shall take a strict perusal of them, and ^en from your allowance, your fair Daughter my fashion ^er affection.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose:
Monsieur Brisac, you offer fair and nobly, and I'le ^ot you in the same line of Honour; and I hope, being ^est but with one Daughter, I shall not appear imperti
^ently curious, though with my utmost vigilance and study, labour to bestow her to her worth: Let others speak her ^orm, and future Fortune from me descending to her; ^in that sit down with silence.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose:
You may, my Lord, securely, since Fame aloud ^roclaimeth her perfections, commanding all mens tongues ^ sing her praises; should I say more, you well might cen
^re me (what yet I never was) a Flatterer. What trampling's ^hat without of Horses?

speeches.speaker: But.
prose: Sir, my young Masters are newly alighted.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Sir, now observe their several dispositions.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Bid my Supsiser carry my Hackney to the Butt'ry, ^nd give him his Bever; it is a civil and sober Beast, and ^ill drink moderately; and that done, turn him into the Quadrangle.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: He cannot out of his University tone.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Lackey, take care our Coursers be well rubb'd, and ^oath'd; they have out-stripp'd the Wind in speed.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: I marry, Sir, there's metal in this young Fellow!
What a Sheep's look his elder Brother has!

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Your blessing, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Rise, Charles, thou hast it.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Sir, though it be unusual in the Court, (since 'tis ^he Courtiers garb) I bend my knee, and do expect what ^ollows.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Courtly begg'd. My blessing, take it.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Your Lordship's vow'd adorer. What thing this Brother is! yet I'le vouchsafe him the new ^alian shrug —
How clownishly the Book-worm does return it?

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: I'm glad ye are well.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Pray you be happy in the knowledge of this pair of ^ccomplish'd Monsieurs; they are Gallants that have seen ^oth Tropicks.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: I embrace their love.

speeches.speaker: Egr.
prose: Which we'll repay with servulating.

speeches.speaker: Cow.
prose: And will report your bounty in the Court.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose:
I pray you make deserving use on't first, Eustace,
^ive entertainment to your Friends; what's in my house is ^heirs.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Which we'll make use of; let's warm our brains with half a dozen Healths, and then hang cold discourse, for ^e'll speak Fire-works.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: What, at his Book already?

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Fie, fle, Charles, no hour of interruption?

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Plato differs from Socrates in this.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Come, lay them by; let them agree at leisure.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Man's life, Sir, being so short, and then the way ^hat leads unto the knowledge of our selves, so long and ^edious, each minute should be precious.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: In our care to manage worldly business, you must ^art with this Bookish contemplation, and prepare your ^elf for action; to thrive in this Age is held the blame of ^earning: You must study to know what part of my Land's ^ood for the Plough, and what for Pasture; how to buy ^nd sell to the best advantage; how to cure my Oxen when ^hey're o'er-grown with labour.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose:
I may do this from what I've read, Sir; for, what ^oncerns Tillage, who better can deliver it than Virgil in ^is Georgicks? and to cure your Herds, his Bucolicks is a Master-piece; but when he does describe the Common
^ealth of Bees, their industry, and knowledge of the herbs from which they gather Honey, with their care to place it with decorum in the Hive; then Government among themselves, their order in going forth, and coming loaden home; their obedience to their King, and his rewards to such as labour, with his punishments only inflicted on the slothful Drone; I'm ravish'd with it, and there reap my Harvest, and there receive the gain my Cattle bring me, and there find Wax and Honey.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: And grow rich in your imagination; heyday, heyday! Georgicks, Bucolicks, and Bees! art mad?

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: No, Sir, the knowledge of these guards me from it.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: But can you find among your bundle of Books (and put in all your Dictionaries that speak all Tongues) what pleasure they enjoy, that do embrace a well-shap'd wealthy Bride? Answer me that.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: 'Tis frequent, Sir, in Story, there I read of all kind of virtuous and vitious women; the antient Spartan Dames, and Roman Ladies, their Beauties and Deformities; and when I light upon a Portia or Cornelia, crown'd with still flourishing leaves of truth and goodness; with such a feeling I peruse their Fortunes, as if I then had liv'd, and freely tasted their ravishing sweetness; at the present loving the whole Sex for their goodness and example. But on the contrary, when I look on a Clytemnestra, or a Tullia; the first bath'd in her Husband bloud; the latter, without a touch of piety, driving on her Chariot o'er her Father's breathless Trunk, horrour invades my faculties; and comparing the multitudes o'th' guilty, with the few that did die Innocents, I detest and loath 'em as Ignorance or Atheism.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: You resolve then ne'er to make payment of the debt you owe me.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: What debt, good Sir?

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: A debt I paid my Father when I begat thee, and made him a Grandsire, which I expect from you.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: The Children, Sir, which I will leave to all posterity, begot and brought up by my painful Studies, shall be my living Issue.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Very well; and I shall have a general Collection of all the quiddits from Adam to this time, to be my Granchild.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: And such a one, I hope, Sir, as shall not shame the Family.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Nor will you take care of my Estate?

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose:
But in my wishes; for know, Sir, that the wings on which my Soul is mounted, have long since born her ^ high, to stoop to any Prey that soars not upwards ^ and dunghil minds, compos'd of earth, in that ^
^
~lement fix all their happiness; but purer Spirits ^ and refin'd, shake off that clog of humane frailty; give ^ leave t'enjoy my self; that place that does contain my Books (the best Compaions) is to me a glorious Court, where hourly I converse with the old Sages and Philosophers, and sometimes for variety, I confer with Kings and Emperors, and weigh their Counsels, calling their Victories (if unjustly got) unto a strict accompt, and in my phancy, deface their ill-plac'd Statues; can I then part with such constant pleasures, to embrace uncertain vanities? No, be it your care t'augment your heap of wealth; it shall be mine t' increase in knowledge—Lights there for my Study—

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Was ever man that had reason thus transported from all sense and feeling of his proper good? It vexes me, and if I found not comfort in my young Eustace, I might well conclude my name were at a period!

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: He is indeed, Sir, the surer base to build on.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Eustace.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Your ear in private.

speeches.speaker: And
prose:
I suspect my M ter has sound harsh welcome, he's gone Supperless into his Study; could I find out the cause, it
may be borrowing of his Books, or so, I shall be satisfied.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: My duty shall, Sir, take any form you please; and in your motion to have me married, you cut off all dangers the v^olent heats of youth might bear me to.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: It is well answer'd.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Nor shall you, my Lord, for your fair Daughter ever find just cause to mourn your choice of me; the name of Husband, not the authority it carries in it, shall ever teach me to forget to be, as I am now, her Servant, and your Lordship's; and but that modesty forbids, that I should sound the Trumpet of my own deserts, I could say, my choice manners have been such, as render me lov'd and remarkable to the Princes of the Blood.

speeches.speaker: Cow.
prose: Nay, to the King.

speeches.speaker: Egre.
prose: Nay to the King and Council.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: These are Court admirers, and ever echo him that bears the Bag. Though I be dull-ey'd, I see through this jugling.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Then for my hopes.

speeches.speaker: Cow.
prose: Nay certainties.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: They stand as fair as any mans. What can there fall in compass of her wishes, which she shall not be suddenly possess'd of? Loves she Titles? by the grace and favour of my Princely Friends, I am what she would have me.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: He speaks well, and I believe him.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: I could wish I did so. Pray you a word, Sir. He's a proper Gentleman, and promises nothing, but what is possible. So far I will go with you; nay, I add, he hath won much upon me; and were he but one thing that his Brother is, the bargain were soon struck up.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: What's that, my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: The Heir.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Which he is not, and I trust never shall be.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Come, that shall breed no difference; you see Charles has given o'er the world; I'le undertake, and with much ease, to buy his Birth right of him for a Dry-fat of new Books; nor shall my state alone make way for him, but my elder Brothers, who being issueless, to advance our name, I doubt not will add his. Your resolution?

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: I'le first acquaint my Daughter with the proceedings; on these terms I am yours, as she shall be, make you no scruple. Get the Writings ready, she shall be tractable; to morrow we will hold a second conference. Farewell noble Eustace; and you brave Gallants.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Full increase of honour wait ever on your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: The Gout rather, and a perpetual Meagrim.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: You see, Eustace, how I travel to possess you of a Fortune you were not born to; be you worthy of it: I'le furnish you for a Suitor: visit her, and prosper in't.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: She's mine, Sir, fear it not: in all my travels, I ne'er met a Virgin that could resist my Courtship.
If it take now, we're made for ever, and will revel it.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: In tough Welsh Parsly, which, in our vulgar Tongue, is strong Hempen Halters; my poor Master co~zen'd, and I a looker on! If we have studi'd our Majors and our Minors, Antecedents and Consequents, to be concluded Coxcombs, w'have made a fair hand on't. I am glad I have found out all their plots, and their Conspiracies; this shall t'old Monsieur Miramont, one, that though he cannot read a Proclamation, yet dotes on Learning, and loves my Master Charles for being a Scholar; I hear he's coming hither, I shall meet him; and if he be that old, rough, testy blade he always us'd to be, I'le ring him such a peal, as shall go near to shake their Belroom, peradventure beat'm, for he is fire and flax; and so have at him.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: NAY, Brother, Brother.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Pray, Sir, be not moved, I meddle with no business but mine own, and in mine own 'tis reason I should govern.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: But how to govern then, and understand, Sir, and be as wise as y'are hasty, though you be my Brother, and from one bloud sprung, I must tell ye heartily and home too.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: What, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: What I grieve to find, you are a fool, and an ol^ fool, and that's two.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: We'll part'em, if you please.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: No, they're entail'd to 'em. Seek to deprive an ho~nest noble Spirit, your eldest Son, Sir, and your very Image, (but he's so like you, that he fares the worse for't) because, he loves his Book, and dotes on that, and only studies how to know things excellent, above the reach of such course Brains as yours, such muddy Fancies, that never will know farther than when to cut your Vines, and cozen Merchants, and choak your hide-bound Tenants with mu^ty Harvests.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: You go too fast.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: I'am not come to my pace yet. Because h'has made his study all his pleasure, and is retir'd into his Contemplation, not medling with the dirt and chaff of Nature, that makes the spirit of the mind mud too; therefore must he be flung from his inheritance? must he be dispossess'd, and Monsieur Gingle-boy his younger Brother—

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: You forget your self.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Because h'has been at Court, and learn'd new Tongues, and how to speak a tedious piece of nothing; to vary his face as Sea-men do their compass, to worship Images of gold and silver, and fall before the She calves of the season; therefore must he jump into his Brother's Land?

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Have you done yet, and have you spoke enough it praise of Learning, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Never enough.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: But, Brother, do you know what Learning is?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: It is not to be a Justice of Peace as you are, and palter out your time i'th' penal Statutes. To hear the curious Tenets controverted between a Protestant Constable, and Jesuite Cobler; to pick Natural Philosophy o^ of Bawdry, when your Worship's pleas'd to correctifie a Lady; nor 'tis not the main Moral of blind Justice, (which is deep Learning) when your Worships Tenants bring a light cause, and heavy Hens before ye, both fat and feeble, a Goose or Pig; and then you'll sit like equity with both hands weighing indifferently the state o'th' question. These are your Quodlibets, but no Learning, Brother.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: You are so parlously in love with Learning, that I'd be glad to know what you understand, Brother; I'm sure you have read all Aristotle.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Faith no; but I believe I have a learned faith, S^, and that's it makes a Gentleman of my sort; though I ca^ speak no Greek, I love the sound of't, it goes so thund'ring as it conjur'd Devils: Charles speaks it loftily, and if thee wert a man, or had'st but ever heard of Homers Iliads, Hes^d and the Greek Poets, thou wouldst run mad, and hang th^ self for joy th'hadst such a Gentleman to be thy Son: O he has read such things to me!

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: And you do understand 'em, Brother?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose:
I tell thee, No, that's not material; the soun^s sufficient to confirm an honest man: Good Brother Bris^, does your young Courtier, that wears the fine Cloaths, an^ is the excellent Gentleman, (the Traveller, the Soldier, as you think too) understand any other power than his Tailor? or knows what motion is more than an Horse-race? Wh^ the Moon means, but to light him home from Taverns? o^ the comfort of the Sun is, but to wear slash'd clothes in?

^nd must this piece of ignorance be popt up, because 't can ^ss the hand, and cry, sweet Lady? Say it had been at
^ome, and seen the Reliques, drunk your Verdea Wine, ^nd rid at Naples, brought home a Box of Venice Treacle ^ith it, to cure young Wenches that have eaten Ashes: Must this thing therefore?—

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Yes Sir, this thing must; I will not trust my Land ^ one so sotted, so grown like a Disease unto his Study; ^e that will fling off all occasions and cares, to make him ^nderstand what state is, and how to govern it, must, by ^hat reason, be slung himself aside from managing. My ^ounger Boy is a fine Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: He is an Ass, a piece of Ginger-bread, gilt over to ^lease foolish Girls puppets.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: You are my elder Brother.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: So I had need, and have an elder Wit, thou'dst ^hame us all else. Go to, I say, Charles shall inherit.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose:
I say, no, unless Charles had a Soul to understand it; can he manage six thousand Crowns a year out of the Me
^aphysics? or can all his learn'd Astronomy look to my Vineyards? Can the drunken old Poets make up my Vines? (I know they can drink 'em) or your excellent Humanists ^ell 'em the Merchants for my best advantage? Can Histo
^y cut my Hay, or get my Corn in? And can Geometry ^end it in the Market? Shall I have my sheep kept with a
^acobs-staff now? I wonder you will magnifie this madman, you that are old, and should understand.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose:
Should, say'st thou? thou monstrous piece of ignorance in Office! thou that hast no more knowledge than ^hy Clerk infuses, thy dapper Clerk, larded with ends of Latin, and he no more than custom of offences. Thou un
^eprieveable Dunce! that thy formal Bandstrings, thy Ring, nor pomander cannot expiate for, dost thou tell me I should? I'le pose thy Worship in thine own Library and Almanack, which thou art daily poring on, to pick out days of iniquity to cozen fools in, and Full Moons to cut Cattle: dost thou taint me, that have run over Story, Poetry, Humanity?

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: As a cold nipping shadow does o'er cars of Corn, and leave 'em blasted, put up your anger, what I'll do, ^'ll do.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Thou shalt not do.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: I will.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Thou art an Ass then, a dull old tedious Ass; th' ^art ten times worse, and of less credit than Dunce Hollingshead the Englishman, that writes of Shows and Sheriffs.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Well, take your pleasure, here's one I must talk with.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: Good-day, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Fair to you, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: May I speak w'ye?

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: With all my heart, I was waiting on your goodness.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: Good morrow, Monsieur Miramont.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: O sweet Sir, keep your good morrow to cool your Worships pottage; a couple of the worlds fools met together to raise up dirt and dunghils.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: Are they drawn?

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: They shall be ready, Sir, within these two hours; and Charles set his hand.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: 'Tis necessary; for he being a joint purchaser, though your Estate was got by your own industry, unless he seal to the Conveyance, it can be of no validity.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: He shall be ready and do it willingly.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: He shall be hang'd first.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: I hope your Daughter likes.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: She loves him well, Sir; young Eustace is a bait to catch a Woman, a budding spritely Fellow; y'are resolv'd then, that all shall pass from Charles?

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: All, all, he's nothing; a bunch of Books shall be his Patrimony, and more than he can manage too.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose:
Will your Brother pass over his Land to your son
^ustace? you know he has no Heir.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: He will be flead first, and Horse-collars made of 's skin.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Let him alone, a wilful man; my Estate shall serve the turn, Sir. And how doe^ your Da^ce^?

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: Ready for the hou^, and like a blushing Rose that stays the pulling.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: To morrow then's the day.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: Why then to morrow I'll bring the Girl; get you the Writings ready.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: But hark you, Mo^, have you the virtuous conscience to help to ^ob an Heir, an Elder Brother, of that which Nature and the Law flings on him? You were your Father's eldest Son, I take it, and had his Land; would you had had his wit too, or his discretion, to consider no~bly, what 'tis to deal unworthily in these things; you'll say he's none of yours, he's his Son; and he will say, he is no Son to inherit above a shelf of Books: Why did he get him? why was he brought up to write and read, and know these things? why was he not like his Father, a dumb Justice? a flat dull piece of phlegm, shap'd like a man, a reverend Idol in a piece of Arras? Can you lay disobedience, want of manners, or any capital crime to his charge?

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: I do not, nor do weigh your words, they bite not me, Sir; this man must answer.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: I have don't already, and given sufficient reason to secure me: and so good morrow, Brother, to your patience.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: Good morrow, Monsieur Miramont.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose:
Good Night caps keep brains warm, or Maggots will breed in 'em. Well, Charles, thou shalt not want to buy thee Books yet, the fairest in thy Study are my gift, and the University of Lovain, for thy sake, hath tasted of my bounty; and to vex the old doting Fool thy Father, and thy Brother, they shall not share a Sol^
of mine between them; nay more, I'll give thee eight thousand Crowns a year, in some high strain to write my Epitaph.

segments.head: Actus Seundus. | ACTUS II. SCENA II.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: How do I look now, my Elder Brother? Nay, 'tis a handsome Suit.

speeches.speaker: Cow.
prose: All Courtly, Courtly.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: I'll assure ye, Gentlemen, my Tailor has travel'd, and speaks as lofty Language in his Bills too; the cover of an old Book would not shew thus. Fie, fie; what things these Academicks are! these Book-worms, how they look!

speeches.speaker: Egre.
prose: They're meer Images, no gentle motion or behaviour in 'em; they'll prattle ye of Primum Mobile, and tell a story of the state of Heaven, what Lords and Ladies go~vern in such Houses, and what wonders they do wh^n they meet together, and how they spit Snow, Fire, and Ha^, like a Jugler, and make a noise when they are drunk, which we call Thunder.

speeches.speaker: Cow.
prose: They are the sneaking'st things, and the contemptiblest; such Small-beer brains, but ask 'em any thing out of the Element of their understanding, and they stand ga~ping like a roasted Pig: do they know what a Court is, of a Council, or how the affairs of Christendom are manag'd? Do they know any thing but a tired Hackney? and they cry absurd as the Horse understood 'em. They have made a fair Youth of your Elder Brother, a pretty piece of flesh!

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: I thank 'em for't, long may he study to give me his Estate. Saw you my Mistris?

speeches.speaker: Egre.
prose: Yes, she's a sweet young Woman; but be sure you keep her from Learning.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose:
Songs she may have, and read a little unbak'd Poetry, such as the Dablers of our time contrive, that has no weight nor wheel to move the mind, nor indeed nothing but an empty sound; she shall have cloaths, but not made by Geometry; Horses and Coach, but of no immortal Race: I will not have a Scholar in my house above a gentle Reader; they corrupt the foolish Women with their subtle
Problems; I'le have my house call'd ignorance, to fright prating Ph^losophers from Entertainment.

speeches.speaker: Cow.
prose: It will do well, love those that love good fashions, good cloaths, and rich; they invite men to admire 'em, that speak the lisp of Court. Oh 'tis great Learning! to Ride well, Dance well, Sing well, or Whistle Courtly, they're rare endowments; that they have seen far Countreys, and can speak strange things, though they speak no truths, for then they make things common. When are you marri'd?

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: To morrow,! think; we must have a Masque, Boys, and of our own making.

speeches.speaker: Egre.
prose: 'Tis not half an hours work, a Cupid, and a Fiddle, and the thing's done: but let's be handsome, shall's be Gods or Nymphs?

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: What, Nymphs with Beards?

speeches.speaker: Cow.
prose: That's true, we'll be Knights then; some wandring Knights, that light here on a sudden.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Let's go, let's go, I must go visit, Gentlemen, and mark what sweet lips I must kiss to morrow.

segments.head: Actus Seundus. | ACTUS II. SCENA III.

speeches.speaker: Cook
prose: And how do's my Master?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: He's at's Book; peace, Coxcomb, that such an unlearned tongue as thine should ask for him!

speeches.speaker: Co.
prose: Do's he not study conjuring too?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Have you lost any Plate, Butler?

speeches.speaker: But.
prose: No, but I know I shall to morrow at dinner.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Then to morrow you shall be turn'd out of your place for't; we meddle with no spirit o'th' Buttery, they taste too small for us; keep me a Pie in Folio, I beseech thee, and thou shalt see how learnedly I'le translate him. Shall's have good cheer to morrow?

speeches.speaker: Co.
prose: Excellent good cheer, Andrew.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: The spight on't is, that much about that time, I shall be arguing, or deciding rather, which are the Males or Females of Red Herrings, and whether they be taken in the Red Sea only; a question found out by Copernicus, the learned Motion maker.

speeches.speaker: Co.
prose: I marry, Butler, here are rare things; a man that look'd upon him, would swear he understood no more than we do.

speeches.speaker: But.
prose: Certain, a learned Andrew.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: I've so much on't, and am so loaden with strong understanding, I fear, they'll run me mad. Here's a new Instrument, a Mathematical Glister to purge the Moon with when she is laden with cold phlegmatick humours; and here's another to remove the Stars, when they grow too thick in the Firmament.

speeches.speaker: Co.
prose: O Heavens! why do I labour out my life in a Beefpot? and only search the secrets of a Sallad, and know no farther?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: They are not reveal'd to all heads; these are far above your Element of Fire, Cook. I could tell you of Archimedes Glass, to fire your Coals with; and of the Philosophers Turf, that ne'er goes out: and, Gilbert Butler, I could tavish thee with two tare inventions.

speeches.speaker: But.
prose: What are they, Andrew?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: The one to blanch your Bread from chippings base, and in a moment, as thou wouldst an Almond; the Sect of the Epicureans invented that: The other for thy Trenchers, that's a strong, one, to cleanse you twenty dozen in a minute, and no noise heard, which is the wonder, Gilbert; and this was out of Plato's new Idea's.

speeches.speaker: But.
prose: Why, what a learned Master do'st thou serve, Andrew?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: These are but the scrapings of his understanding, Gilbert; with gods and goddesses, and such strange people he deals, and treats with in so plain a fashion, as thou do'st with thy Boy that draws thy drink, or Ralph there, with his Kitchin Boys and Scalders.

speeches.speaker: Co.
prose: But why should he not be familiar, and talk some~times, as other Christians do, of hearty matters, and com^ into the Kitchin, and there cut his Breakfast?

speeches.speaker: But.
prose:
And then retire to the Buttery, and there eat it, ^ drink a lusty Bowl to my young Master, that must be not the Heir, he'll do all these, I and be drunk too; these ^
~mortal things.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: My Master studies immortality.

speeches.speaker: Co.
prose:
Now thou talk'st of immortality, how do's thy W^
Andrew? my old Master did you no small Pleasure when he procur'd her, and stock'd you in a Farm. It he should l^ her now, as he hath a Colts tooth yet, what says your lea^
~ing and your strange Instruments to that, my Andrew? C^ any of your learned Clerks avoid it? can ye put by his Ma~thematical Engine?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Yes, or I'le break it: thou awaken'st me, and I'le peep i'th' Moon this month but I'le watch for him. ^ Master rings, I must go make him a fire, and conjure ^ his Books.

speeches.speaker: Co.
prose: Adieu, good Andrew, and send thee manly pati^ with thy learning.

segments.head: Actus Seundus. | ACTUS II. SCENA IV.

speeches.speaker: Cha.
prose:
I have forgot to eat and sleep with reading, and al^ my faculties turn into study; 'tis meat and sleep; what ^ I outward garments, when I can cloath my self with unde^
~standing? The Stars and glorious Planets have no Tailo^ yet ever new they are, and shine like Courtiers. The Seaso^s of the year find no fond Parents, yet some are arm'd in s^
ver Ice that glisters, and some in gawdy Green come ^ like Masquers. The Silk-worm spins her own suit and lodg~ing, and has no aid nor partner in her labours. W^ should we care for any thing but knowledge, or look upon the World but to contemn it?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Would you have any thing?

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Andrew, I find there is a flie grown o'er the E^ o'th' Bull, which will go near to blind the Constellation.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Put a Gold-ring in's nose, and that will cute him.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Ariadne's Crown's away too; two main Stats the held it fast are slip out.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Send it presently to Galateo, the Italian St^ wright, he'll set it right again with little labour.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Thou art a pretty Scholar.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: I hope I shall be; have I swept Books so often to know nothing?

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: I hear thou art married.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: It hath pleas'd your Father to match me to a Ma^ of his own chusing; I doubt her Constellation's loose too and wants nailing; and a sweet Farm he has given us a m^ off, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Marry thy self to understanding, Andrew; the^ Women are Errata in all Authors, they're fair to see to, and bound up in Vellam, smooth, white and clear, but th^ contents are monstrous; they treat of nothing but dull a^ and diseases. Thou hast not so much wit in thy head, as th^ is on those shelves, Andrew.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: I think I have not, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: No, if thou had'st, thou'ld'st ne'er married ^ Woman in thy bosom, they're Cataplasms made o'th' dea^ sins: I ne'er saw any yet but mine own Mother; or if I did, I did regard them but as shadows that pass by of unde^ creatures.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Shall I bring you one? I'le trust you with my own Wise; I would not have your Brother go beyond ye; they'^ the prettiest Natural Philosophers to play with.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: No, no, they're Opticks to delude mens eyes with Does my younger Brother speak any Greek yet, Andr^

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: No, but he speaks High Dutch, and that go^ daintily.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose:
Reach me the Books down I read yesterday, a^

^e a little fire, and get a manchet; make clean those In
^uments of Brass I shew'd you, and set the great Sphere by; ^en take the Fox tail, and purge the Books from dust; last, ^ke your L^lly, and get your part ready.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose:
Shall I go home, Sir? my Wife's name is Lilly,
^ere my best part lies, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Charles.
prose: I mean your Grammar, O thou Dunderhead ^ould'st thou be ever in thy Wife's Syntaxis? Let me have ^ noise, nor nothing to disturb me; I am to find a secret.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: So am I too; which if I find, I shall make some ^art for't—

speeches.speaker: ^ewis.
prose: THis is the day, my Daughter Angellina, the happy, that must make you a Fortune, a large and ^ll one, my care has wrought it, and yours must be as great ^ entertain it. Young Eustace is a Gentleman at all points, ^nd his behaviour affable and courtly, his person excellent, ^ know you find that, I read it in your eyes, you like his ^uth; young handsome people should be match'd together, ^en follows handsome Children, handsome fortunes; the ^ost part of his Father's Estate, my Wench, is ti'd in a ^inture, that makes up the harmony; and when ye are ^arried, he's of that soft temper, and so far will be chain'd ^ your observance, that you may rule and turn him as ^u please. What, are the Writings drawn on your side, ^?

speeches.speaker: Not.
prose: They are, and here I have so fetter'd him, that if ^e Elder Brother set his hand to, not all the power of Law all e'er release him.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: These Notaries are notable confident Knaves, and ^ble to do more mischief than an Army. Are all your Clauses ^re?

speeches.speaker: Not.
prose: Sure as proportion; they may turn Rivers sooner ^an these Writings.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: Why did you not put all the Lands in, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Not.
prose: 'Twas not condition'd; if it had been found, it ^d been but a fault made in the Writing; if not found, all ^e Land.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose:
These are small Devils, that care not who has mis
^ief, so they make it; they live upon the meer scent of ^sention. 'Tis well, 'tis well; are you contented, Girl? ^r your will must be known.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose:
A Husband's welcome, and as an humble Wife I'le ^ntertain him; no Sovereignty I aim at, 'tis the man's, Sir; ^r she that seeks it, kills her husbands honour: The Gen
^eman I have seen, and well observ'd him, yet find not that ^ac'd excellence you promise; a pretty Gentleman, and ^e may please too, and some few flashes I have heard come ^om him, but not to admiration as to others: He's young, ^nd may be good, yet he must make it, and I may help, and ^elp to thank him also. It is your pleasure I should make him ^ine, and 't has been still my duty to observe you.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: Why then let's go, and I shall love your modesty. ^o Horse, and bring the Coach out, Angellina; to morrow ^ou will look more womanly.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: So I look honestly, I fear no eyes, Sir.

segments.head: Actus Tertius. | ACTUS III. SCENA II.

speeches.speaker: Bris.
prose: Wait on your Master, he shall have that befits ^m.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: No Inheritance, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose:
You speak like a fool, a coxcomb; he shall have an
^l means to buy him Books, and find him cloathes and ^eat, what would he more? Trouble him with Land? 'tis ^at against his nature. I love him too, and honour those ^ in him.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Shall Master Eustace have all?

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: All, all; he knows how to use it, he's a than bred in the world, th'other i'th' Heavens. My Masters, pray be wary, and s^ceable; and Cock, see all your Sawe^s be sharp and poynant in the palate, that they may commend you; look to your Roast and ^ak'd meats handsomely, and what new Kickshaws and delicate made things—Is th' Musick come?

speeches.speaker: But.
prose: Yes, Sir, they're here at Breakfast.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose:
There will be a M^e too; ^ must see this Room clean, and, Butler, your door open to all good fellows; but have an eye to your Plate, for there be Furies; my Lilly, welcome you are for the L^e ^
^rt it, and see it ready for the Table, and see the Bride ^ made, and look the cords be not cut asunder by the Gallants too, there be such knacks abroad. Hark hither, Lilly, to morrow night at twelve a clook I'le sup w'ye: your husband shall be safe, I'le send ye meat too; before I cannot well slip from my company.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Will you so, will you so, Sir? I'le make one to eat it, I may chance make you stagger too.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: No answer, Lilly?

speeches.speaker: Lil.
prose: One word about the Linen; I'le be ready, and rest your Worships still.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: And I'le rest w'ye, you shall see what rest 't will be. Are ye so nimble? a man had need have ten pair of ears to watch you.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Wait on your Master, for I know he wants ye, and keep him in his Study, that the noise do not molest him. I will not fail my Lilly—Come in, sweet-hearts, all to their several duties.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Are you kissing ripe, Sir? Double but my Farm, and kiss her till thy heart ake. These Smock-vermine, how eagerly they leap at old mens kisses, they lick their lips at profit, not at pleasure; and if 't were not for the scurvy name of Cuckold, he should lie with her. I know she'll la~bour at length with a good Lordship. If he had a Wife now, but that's all one, I'le fit him. I must up unto my Master, he'll be mad with Study—

segments.head: Actus Tertius. | ACTUS III. SCENA III.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: What a noise is in this house? my head is broken, within a Parenthesis, in every corner, as if the Earth were shaken with some strange Collect, there are stits and motions. What Planet rules this house?
Who's there?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: 'Tis I, Sir, faithful Andrew.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Come near, and lay thine ear down; hea^'st no noise?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: The Cooks are chopping herbs and mince meat to make Pies, and breaking Marrow-bones—

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Can they set them again?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Yes, yes, in Broths and Puddings, and they grow stronger for the use of any man.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: What speaking's that? sure there's a Massacre.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Of Pigs and Geese, Sir, and Turkeys, for the spit. The Cooks are angry Sirs, and that makes up the medley.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Do they thus at every Dinner? I ne're mark'd them yet, nor know who is a Cook.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: They're sometimes sober, and then they beat as gently as a Tabor.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: What loads are these?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Meat, meat, Sir, for the Kitchen, and stinking Fowls the Tenants have sent in; they'll ne'r be sound out at a gene~ral eating; and there's fat Venison, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: What's that?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Why Deer, those that men fatten for their private pleasures, and let their Tenants starve upon the Commons.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: I've read of Deer, but yet I ne'er eat any.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose:
There's a Fishmongers Boy with Caviar, Sir,
Anchoves, and Potargo, to make ye drink.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Sure these are modern, very modern meats, for I understand 'em not.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: No more does any man from Caca merda, or a substance worse, till they be greas'd with Oyl, and rubb'd with Onions, and then flung out of doors, they are rare Sallads.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: And why is all this, prethee tell me, Andrew? are there any Princes to dine here to day? by this abundance sure there should be Princes; I've read of entertainment for the gods at half this charge; will not six Dishes serve 'em? I never had but one, and that a small one.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Your Brother's marri'd this day; he's marri'd your younger Brother Eustace.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: What of that?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: And all the Friends about are bidden hither; there's not a Dog that knows the house, but comes too.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Marri'd! to whom?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Why to a dainty Gentlewoman, young, sweet, and modest.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Are there modest women? how do they look?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: O you'll bless your self to see them. He parts with's Books, he ne'er did so before yet.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: What does my Father for 'em?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Gives all his Land, and makes your Brother heir.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Must I have nothing?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Yes, you must study still, and he'll maintain you.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: I am his eldest Brother.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: True, you were so; but he has leap'd o'er your shoulders, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: 'Tis well; he'll not inherit my understanding too?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: I think not; he'll scarce find Tenants to let it out to.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Hark! hark!

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: The Coach that brings the fair Lady.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Now you may see her.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Sure this should be modest, but I do not truly know what women make of it, Andrew; she has a face looks like a story, the story of the Heavens looks very like her.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: She has a wide face then.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: She has a Cherubin's, cover'd and vail'd with modell blushes Eustace, be happy, whiles poor Charles is patient. Get me my Books again, and come in with me—

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Welcome, sweet Daughter; welcome, noble Brother; and you are welcome, Sir, with all your Writings; Ladys, most welcome: What, my angry Brother! you must be welcome too, the Feast is flat else.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: I am not come for your welcome, I expect none; I bring no joys to bless the bed withall; nor Songs, nor Masques to glorifie the Nuptials; I bring an angry mind to see your folly, a sharp one too, to reprehend you for it.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: You'll stay and dine though.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: All your meat smells musty, your Table will shew nothing to content me.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: I'le answer you here's good meat.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: But your sauce is scurvie, it is not season'd with the sharpness of discretion.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: It seems your anger is at me, dear Uncle.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Thou art not worth my anger, th'art a Boy, a lump o'thy Father's lightness, made of nothing but antick cloathes and ^ringes; look in thy head, and 'twill appear a foot-ball full of fumes and rotten smoke. Lady, I pity you; you are a handsome and a sweet young Lady, and ought to have a handsom man yok'd t'ye, an understanding too; this is a Gimcrack, that can get nothing but new fashions on you; for say he have a thing shap'd like a child, 'twill either prove a Tumbler or a Tailor.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: These are but harsh words, Uncle.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: So I mean 'em. Sir, you play harsher play w'your elder Brother.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: I would be loth to give you.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Do not venture, I'le make your wedding cloaths ^ closer t'ye then; I but disturb you, I'le go see my Nephew

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: Pray take a piece of Rosemary.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: I'le wear it, but for the Ladys sake, and none ^ yours; may be I'le see your Table too.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Pray do, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: A mad old Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose:
Yes faith, sweet Daughter, he has been thus ^ whole age, to my knowledge; he has made Charles his He^ I know that certainly; then why should he grudge Eusta^
any thing?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: I would not have a light head, nor one laden w^ too much learning, as, they say, this Charles is, that makes his Book his Mistris; Sure there's something hid in this ^ man's anger, that declares him not a meer sot.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Come, shall we go and seal, Brother? all things are ready, and the Priest is here. When Charles has set his ha^ unto the Writings, as he shall instantly, then to the Wedding, and so to dinner.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: Come, let's seal the Book first for my Daughter Jointure.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Let's be private in't, Sir.

segments.head: Actus Tertius. | ACTUS III. SCENA IV.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Nay, y'are undone.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Hum.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Ha'ye no greater feeling?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: You were sensible of the great Book, Sir, when i^ fell on your head, and now the house is ready to fall, do you fear nothing?

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Will he have my Books too.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: No, he has a Book, a fair one too, to read on, and read wonders; I would thou hadst her in thy Study, Ne~phew, and 'twere but to new string her.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Yes, I saw her, and me thought 'twas a curi^ piece of Learning, handsomely bound, and of a dai^ Letter.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: He flung away his Book.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: I like that in him; would he had flung away his dulness too, and spoke to her.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: And must my Brother have all?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: All that your Father has.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: And that fair woman too?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: That woman also.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: He has enough then. May I not see her sometimes and call her Sister? I will do him no wrong.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: This makes me mad, I could now cry for anger these old Fools are the most stubborn and the wilfullest Coxcombs; Farewell, and fall to your Book, forget your Bro~ther: you are my Heir, and I'le provide y'a Wife: I'le look upon this marriage, though I hate it.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Where is my Son?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: There, Sir, casting a Figure what chopping children his Brother shall have.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: He does well. How do'st, Charles? still at thy Book?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: He's studying now, Sir, who shall be his Father.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Peace, you rude Knave — Come hither, Charles be merry.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: I thank you, I am busie at my Book, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: You must put your hand, my Charles, as I wo^ have you, unto a little piece of Parchment here: only you name; you write a reasonable hand.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: But I may do unreasonably to write it. What i^ it, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: To pass the Land I have, Sir, unto your youngs Brother.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Is't no more?

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose:
No, no, 'tis nothing you shall be provided for, and n^ Books you shall have still, and new Studies, and have you
means brought in without thy care, Boy, and one still to ^tend you.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: This shews your love, Father.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: I'm tender to you.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Like a stone, I take it.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Why Father, I'll go down, an't please you let ^ne, because I'd see the thing they call the Gentlewoman; ^ see no Woman but through contemplation, and there I'll ^o't before the company, and wish my Brother fortune.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Do, I prethee.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: I must not stay, for I have things above require my ^udy.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: No, thou shalt not stay; thou shalt have a brave ^inner too.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Now has he o'erthrown himself for ever; I will ^own into the Cellar, and be stark drunk for anger.

segments.head: Actus Tertius. | ACTUS III. SCENA V.

speeches.speaker: Not.
prose: Come, let him bring his Sons hand, and all's done. ^s your's ready?

speeches.speaker: Pri.
prose: Yes, I'll dispatch ye presently, immediately, for ^n truth I am a hungry.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Do, speak apace, for we believe exactly: do not ^e stay long, Mistress?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: I find no fault, better things well done, than want ^me to do them. Uncle, why are you sad?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Sweet smelling blossom, would I were thine Uncle ^o thine own content, I'd make thy Husband's state a ^housand better, a yearly thousand. Thou hast mist a man, ^ but that he is addicted to his study, and knows no other Mistress than his mind) would weigh down bundles of these ^mpty kexes.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Can he speak, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Faith yes, but not to Women; his language is ^o Heaven, and heavenly wonder; to Nature, and her dark ^nd secret causes.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: And does he speak well there?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: O admirably! but he's too bashful to behold a Woman, there's none that sees him, and he troubles none.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: He is a man.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Faith yes, and a clear sweet spirit.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Then conversation me thinks—

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: So think I; but it is his rugged Fate, and so I ^eave you.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: I like thy nobleness.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: See my mad Uncle is courting my fair Mistress.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose:
Let him alone; there's nothing that allays an an
^ry mind so soon as a sweet Beauty: he'll come to us.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose:
My Father's here, my Brother too! that's a won
^er, broke like a Spirit from his Cell.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Come hither, come nearer, Charles; 'twas your ^esire to see my noble Daughter, and the company, and ^ive your Brother joy, and then to Seal, Boy; you do, like ^ good Brother.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: Marry does he, and he shall have my love for ever ^or't. Put to your hand now.

speeches.speaker: Not.
prose: Here's the Deed, Sir, ready.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: No, you must pardon me a while, I tell ye, I am ^n contemplation, do not trouble me.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Come, leave thy Study, Charles.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: I'll leave my life first; I study now to be a man, ^'ve found it. Before what Man was, was but my Argument.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: I like this best of all, he has taken fire, his dull ^ist flies away.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Will you write, Brother?

speeches.speaker: Char.
