prose: No, Brother, no; I have no time for poor things, ^'m taking the height of that bright Constellation.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: I say you trifle time, Son.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: I will not seal, Sir; I am your Eldest, and I'll keep my Birth-right, for Heaven forbid I should become exam~ple: Had y'only shew'd me Land, I had deliver'd it, and been a proud man to have pa^ted with it; 'tis dirt, and labour. Do I speak right, Uncle?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Bravely, my Boy, and bless thy tongue.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: I'll forward: but you have open'd to me such a treasure, I find my mind free; Heaven direct my fortune.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Can he speak now? Is this a son to sacrifice?

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Such an inimitable piece of Beauty, that I have studied long, and now sound only, that I'll part sooner with my soul of Reason, and be a Plant, a Beast, a Fish, a Flie, and only make the number of things up, than yield to one foot of Land, if she be ti'd to't.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: He speaks unhappily.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: And methinks bravely. This the meer Scholar?

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: You but vex your self, Brother, and vex your study too.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Go you and study, for 'tis time, young Eustace; you want both man and manners; I've study'd both, although I made no shew on't. Go turn the Volumes over I have read, eat and digest them, that they may grow in thee; wear out the tedious night with thy dim Lamp, and sooner lose the day, than leave a doubt. Distil the sweetness from the Poets Spring, and learn to love; thou know'st not what fair is: Traverse the stories of the great Heroes, the wise and civil lives of good men walk through; thou hast seen nothing but the face of Countrys, and brought home nothing but their empty words: why shouldst thou wear a Jewel of this worth, that hast no worth within thee to preserve her?

Beauty clear and fair,
Where the Air
Rather like a perfume dwells,
Where the Violet and the Rose
The blew Veins in blush disclose,
And come to honour nothing else.


Where to live near,
And planted there,
Is to live, and still live new;
Where to gain a favour is
More than light, perpetual bliss.
Make me live by serving you.


Dear again back recall
To this light,
A stranger to himself and all;
Both the wonder and the story
Shall be yours, and eke the glory;
I am your servant and your thrall.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Speak such another Ode, and take all yet. What say ye to the Scholar now?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: I wonder; is he your Brother, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Yes, would he were buried; I fear he'll make an Ass of me a younger.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Speak not so softly, Sir, 'tis very likely.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Come, leave your sinical talk, and let's dispatch, Charles.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Dispatch, what?

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Why the Land.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: You are deceiv'd, Sir. Now I perceive what 'tis that wooes a woman, and what maintains her when she's woo'd: I'll stop here. A wilful poverty ne'er made a Beauty, nor want of means maintain'd it vertuously: though land and moneys be no happiness, yet they are counted good additions. That use I'll make; he that neglects a blessing, though he want a present knowledge how to use it, neglects himself. May be I have done you wrong, Lady, whose love and hope went hand in hand together; may be my Brother, that has long expected the happy hour, and bless'd my ignorance; pray give me leave, Sir, I shall clear all doubts; why did they shew me you? pray tell me that?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: (He'll talk thee into a pension for thy knavery.)

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: You, happy you, why did you break unto me? The Rosie su^ed morn ne'er broke so sweetly: I am a man, and have de^tes within me, affections too, though they were drown'd a while, and lay dead, till the Spring of beauty rais'd them; till I saw those eyes, I was but a lump, a chaos of confusedness dwelt in me; then from those eyes shot Love, and he distinguish'd, and into form he drew my faculties, and now I know my Land, and now I love too.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: We had best remove the Maid.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: It is too late, Sir. I have her figure here. Nay s^own not, ^ there are less worthy Souls for younger Brothers; this is no form of Silk, but Sanctity, which wild lascivious hearts can never dignifie. Remove her where you will, I walk along still, for, like the light, we make no separation; you may sooner part the Billows of the Sea, and put a barr betwixt their fellowships, than blot out my remembrance; sooner shut old Time into a Den, and stay his motion, wash off the swift hours from his downy wings, or steal Eternity to stop his glass, than shut the sweet Idea I have in me. Room for an Elder Brother, pray give place, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: H'as studied duel too; take heed, he'll beat thee. H'as frighted the old Justice into a Feaver; I hope he'll disinherit him too for an Ass; for though he be grave with years, he's a great Baby.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Do not you think me mad?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: No certain, Sir, I have heard nothing from you but things excellent.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: You look upon my cloaths, and laugh at me, my scurvy cloaths!

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: They have rich linings, Sir. I would your Brother.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: His are gold and gawdie.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: But touch 'em inwardly, they smell of Copper.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Can ye love me? I am an Heir, sweet Lady, however I appear a poor dependent; love you with honour, I shall love so ever. Is your eye ambitious? I may be a great man; is't wealth or lands you covet? my Father must die.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: That was well put in, I hope he'll take it deeply.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Old men are not immortal, as I take it; is it you look for, youth and handsomness? I do confess my Brother's a handsome Gentleman, but he shall give me leave to lead the way, Lady. Can you love for love, and make that the reward? The old man shall not love his heaps of Gold with a more doting superstition, than I'le love you. The young man his delights, the Merchant, when he ploughs the angry Sea up, and sees the mountain billows falling on him, as if all the Elements, and all their angers, were turn'd into one vow'd destruction; shall not with greater joy embrace his safety. We'll live together like two wanton Vines, ^cling our souls and loves in one another, we'll spring together, and we'll bear one fruit; one joy shall make us smile, and one grief mourn; one age go with us, and one ^ou^ of death shall shut our eyes, and one grave make us happy.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: And one hand seal the Match, I'm yours for ever.

speeches.speaker: Law.
prose: Nay, stay, stay, stay

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Nay certainly, 'tis done, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: These was a contract.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose:
Only conditional, that if he had the Land, he had my love too; this Gentleman's the Heir, and he'll maintain it. Pray be not angry, Sir, at what I say; or if you be, 'tis at your own adventure. You have the out-side of a pretty Gentleman, but by my troth your inside is but bar
^en; 'tis not a face I only am in love with, nor will I say your face is excellent, a reasonable hunting face to court the wind with; not they're not words, unless they be well plac'd too, not your sweet Dam-mes, not your hired. Verses, not telling me of Clothes, nor Coach and Horses, no not your visits each day in new Suits, nor your black Patches you wear variously, some cut like Stars, some in Half-moons, some Lozenges, (all which but shew you ^ a younger Brother.)

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Gramercy, Wench, thou hast a noble Soul too.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Nor your long travels, nor your little knowledg^ can make me doat upon you. Faith go study, and g^ some goodness, that you may shew manly; your Bro^ at my suit I'm sure will teach you; or only study ho^ get a Wife, Sir. Y'are cast far behind, 'tis good you ^ be melancholy, it shews like a Gamester that had lost ^ mony, and 'tis the fashion to wear your arm in a skarf, ^ for your have had a shrewd cut o'er the fingers.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: But are y'in earnest?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Yes, believe me, Father, you shall ne'er choose i^ me; y'are old and dim, Sir, and th' shadow of the ^ Eclips'd your judgment. Y'have had your time without control, dear Father, and you must give me leave to ta^ mine now, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: This is the last time of asking, will you set y^ hand to?

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: This is the last time of answering, I will never.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Out of my doors.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Most willingly.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: He shall, Jew, thou of the Tribe of Many a^a Coxcomb, and never trouble thee more till thy chops be cold, fool.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Must I be gone too?

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: I will never know thee.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Then this man will; what Fortune he shall ^ Father, be't good or bad, I must partake it with him.

speeches.speaker: Egre.
prose: When shall the Masque begin?

speeches.speaker: Lust.
prose: 'Tis done already; all, all is broken off, I am ^ done, Friend, my Brother's wise again, and has spoil'd ^ will not release the Land, has won the Wench too.

speeches.speaker: Egre.
prose: Could he not stay till the Masque was past? w^ ready. What a scurvy trick's this?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose:
O you may vanish, perform ^ at some Hall, whe^ the Citizens Wives may see't for Six pence a piece, and cold Supper. Come, let's go, Charles. And now, ^ noble Daughter, I'le sell the Tiles of my House, e're th^ shalt want, Wench. Rate up your Dinner, Sir, and ^ it cheap: some younger Brother will take't up in Comm^
dities. Send you joy, Nephew Eustace; if you study ^ Law, keep your great Pippin-pies, they'll go far with ye

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: I'd have your blessing.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: No, no, meet me no more. Farewel, thou ^ blast mine eyes else.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: I will not.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: Nor send not you for Gowns.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: I'll wear course Flannel first.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Come, let's go take some counsel.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: 'Tis too late.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Then stay and dine; it may be we shall vex'em.

speeches.speaker: Brisac.
prose: NE'er talk to me, you are no men but Masque^ shapes, shadows, and the signs of men, Co^ bubbles, that every breath or breaks or blows away. Y^ have no souls, no metal in your bloods, no heat to stir^ when ye have occasion: frozen dull things, that must be turn'd with Leavers. Are you the Courtiers, and ^ travell'd Gallants? the spritely Fellows that the people ^ of? Ye have no more spirit than three sleepy sopes.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: What would ye have me do, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose:
Follow your Brother, and get ye out of doors, ^ seek your Fortune. Stand still becalm'd, and let an ^ Dotard, a hair-brain'd Puppy, and a Bookish Boy, ^

^ever knew a Blade above a Pen-knife, and how to cut ^is meat in Characters, cross my design, and take thine own ^ench from thee, in mine own house too? Thou despis'd ^oor fellow!

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: The reverence that I ever bare to you, Sir, then ^o my Uncle, with whom 't had been but sawciness t' have ^een so rough—

speeches.speaker: Egre.
prose: And we not seeing him strive in his own cause, ^hat was principal, and should have led us on, thought it ill ^anners to begin a quarrel here.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: You dare do nothing. Do you make your care the ^xcuse of your Cowardise? Three Boys on Hobby-horses, ^ith three penny Halberds, would beat you all.

speeches.speaker: Cow.
prose: You must not say so.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Yes, and sing it too.

speeches.speaker: Cow.
prose: You are a man of peace, therefore we must give way.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose:
I'll make my way, and therefore quickly leave me, or I'll force you; and having first torn off your slanting ^eathers, I'll trample on 'em; and if that cannot teach you ^o quit my house I'll, kick ye out of my gates; you gawdy Glow-worms, carrying seeming fire, yet have no heat with
^n ye.

speeches.speaker: Cow.
prose: O blest travel! how much we owe thee for our power to suffer?

speeches.speaker: Egre.
prose: Some splenetive Youths now, that had never seen more than thy Country smoak, will grow in choler; it would shew fine in us.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Ies marry would it, that are prime Courtiers, and must know no angers, but give thanks for our injuries, if we purpose to hold our places.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Will you find the door? and find it suddenly? you shall lead the way, Sir, with your perfum'd retinue, and ^ecover the now lost Angellina, or build on it, I will adopt some beggar's doubtful issue, before thou shalt inherit.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: We'll to counsel, and what may be done by man's wit or valour, we'll put in Execution.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Do, or never hope I shall know thee.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: O Sir, have I found you?

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: I never hid my self; whence flows this fury, with which, as it appears, you come to fright me?

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: I smell a plot, meer conspiracy amongst ye all to defeat me of my Daughter; and if she be not suddenly deliver'd, untainted in her reputation too, the best of France shall know how I am jugled with. She is my Heir, and if she may be ravish'd thus from my care, farewel Nobility; Honour and Blood are meer neglected nothings.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Nay then, my Lord, you go too far, and tax him, whose innocency understands not what fear is. If your unconstant Daughter will not dwell on certainties, must you thenceforth conclude that I am fickle? what have I omitted, to make good my integrity and truth? nor can her lightness, nor your supposition, cast an aspersion on me.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: I am wounded in fact, nor can words cure it: do not trifle, but speedily, once more I do repeat it, restore my Daughter as I brought her hither, or you shall hear from me in such a kind, as you will blush to answer.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: All the world, I think, conspires to vex me, yet I will not torment my self: some sprightful mirth must banish the rage and melancholy which hath almost choak'd me; t' a knowing man 'tis Physick, and 'tis thought on; one merry hour I'll have in spight of Fortune, to chear my heart, and this is that appointed; this night I'll hug my Lilly in mine arms, provocatives are sent before to chear me, we old men need 'em, and though we pay dear for our stoln pleasures, so it be done securely, the charge much like a sharp sauce, gives 'em relish. Well, honest Andrew, I gave you a Farm, and it shall have a Beacon, to give warning to my other Tenants when the Foe approaches; and presently, you being bestowed else-where, I'le graff it with dexterity on your forehead; indeed I will, Lilly, I come, poor Andrew.

segments.head: Actus Quartus. | ACTUS IV. SCENA II.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Do they chaser roundly?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: As they were rubb'd with Soap, Sir, and now they swear aloud, now calm again; like a Ring of Bells, whose sound the wind still alters, and then they sit in counsel what to do, and then they jar again what shall be done; they talk of Warrants from the Parliament, Complaints to the King, and Forces from the Province; they have a thousand heads in a thousand minutes, yet ne'er a one head worth a head of Garlick.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Long may they chafe, and long may we laugh at 'em; a couple of pure Puppies yok'd together. But what sayes the young Courtier Master Eustace, and his two warlike Friends?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: They say but little, how much they think I know not; they look ruefully, as if they had newly come from a vaulting house, and had been quite shot through 'tween wind and water by a she Dunkirk, and had sprung a Leak, Sir. Certain my Master was to blame.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Why, Andrew?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: To take away the Wench o'th' sudden from him, and give him no lawful warning; he is tender, and of a young Girls constitution, Sir, ready to get the Green sickness with conceit. Had he but ta'ne his leave in availing Language, or bought an Elegy of his condolement, that the world might have ta'ne notice, he had been an Ass, 't had been some favour.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Thou say'st true, wise Andrew; but these Scholars are such things, when they can prattle.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: And very parlous things, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: And when gain the liberty to distinguish the difference 'twixt a Father and a Fool, to look below, and spie a younger Brother pruning up, and dressing up his expectations in a rare glass of beauty, too good for him; those dreaming Scholars then turn Tyrants, Andrew, and shew no mercy.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: The more's the pity, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Thou told'st me of a trick to catch my Brother, and anger him a little farther, Andrew. It shall be only anger, I assure thee, and little shame.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: And I can fit you, Sir. Hark in your ear.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Thy Wife?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: So I assure ye; this night at twelve a clock.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: 'Tis neat and handsome; there are twenty Crowns due to thy project, Andrew; I've time to visit Charles, and see what Lecture he reads to his Mistris. That done, I'le not fail to be with you.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Nor I to watch my master —

segments.head: Actus Quartus. | ACTUS IV. SCENA III.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: I'm worse than e'er I was; for now I fear, that that I love, that that I only dote on; he follows me through every room I pass, and with a strong set eye he gazes on me, as if his spark of innocence were blown into a flame of lust. Virtue defend me. His Uncle too is absent, and 'tis night; and what these opportunities may teach him — What fear and endless care 'tis to be honest! to be a Maid what misery, what mischief! Would I were rid of it, so it were fairly.

speeches.speaker: Syl.
prose: You need not fear that, will you be a child still? He follows you, but still to look upon you; or if he did desire to lie with ye, 'tis but your own desire, you love for that end; I'le lay my life, if he were now a bed w'ye, he is so modest; he would fall asleep straight.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Dare you venture that?

speeches.speaker: Syl.
prose: Let him consent, and have at ye; I fear him not, he knows not what a woman is, nor how to find the mystery men aim at. Are you afraid of your own shadow, Madam?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: He follows still, yet with a sober face; would I might know the worst, and then I were satisfied.

speeches.speaker: Syl.
prose: Ye may both, and let him but go with ye.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Why do you flie me? what have I so ill about me, or within me, to deserve it?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: I am going to bed, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: And I am come to light ye; I am a Maid, and 'tis a Maidens office.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: You may have me to bed, Sir, without a scruple, and yet I am cha^y too who comes about me. Two Innocents should not seat one another.

speeches.speaker: Syl.
prose: The Gentleman says true. Pluck up your heart, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: The glorious Sun both rising and declining we boldly look upon; even then, sweet Lady, when, like a modest Bride, he draws nights curtains, even then he blushes, that men should behold him.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: I fear he will perswade me to mistake him.

speeches.speaker: Syl.
prose: 'Tis easily done, if you will give your mind to't.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Pray ye to your bed.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Why not to yours, dear Mistris? one heart and one bed

speeches.speaker: Ang
prose: ^ue, Sir, when 'tis lawful: but yet you know—

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: I would not know, forget it; those are but sickly loves that hang on Ceremonies, nurs'd up with doubts and fears, ours high and healthful, full of belief, and fit to teach the Priest: Love shall seal first, then hands confirm the bargain.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: I shall be a Heretick if this continue. What would you do a bed? you make me blush, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: I'd see you sleep, for sure your sleeps are excellent, you that are waking such a noted wonder, must in your slumber prove an admiration. I would behold your dreams too, if 't were possible; those were rich showes.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: I am becoming Traitor.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Then like blew Neptune courting of an Island, where all the perfumes and the precious things that wait upon great Nature are laid up, I'd clip it in my arms, and chastly kiss it, dwell in your bosome like your dearest thoughts, and sigh and weep.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: I've too much woman in me.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: And those true tears falling on your pure Crystals, should turn to armelets for great Queens t'adore.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: I must be gone.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Do not, I will not hurt ye; this is to let you know, my worthiest Lady, y'have clear'd my mind, and I can speak of love too: I can not my manners, though I never knew, before these few hours, what a Beauty was, and such a one that ^i^es all hearts that feel it; yet I have read of vertuous Temperance, and study'd it among my other Secrets; and ^ would I force a separation betwixt this spirit and the case of flesh, than but conceive one rudeness against Chast ty.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Then we may walk.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose:
And talk of any thing, any fit for your ears, and my language; though I was bred up dull, I was ever civil; 'tis true, I have sound it hard to look on you, and not desire, 'twill prove a wise mans task; yet those desires I have so mingled still, and tempered with the quality of honour, that if you should yield, I should ^ate you for't. I am no Courtier of a light co ^ition, apt to take fire at every beauteous face; that only serves his will and wantonness, and lets the serious part run by as thin neglected sand. Whiteness of name, you must be mine, why should I rob my self of that that lawfully must make me happy? why should I seek to cuckold my delights, and widow all those sweets I aim at in you? We ^
^ose our selves in Venus Groves of Myrtle, where every little wind shall be a Cupid, and sing of love and ^th, each ^nd that blows, and curls the velvet leaves, shall breed delights, the wanton Springs shall call us to ^ banks, and on the perfum'd flowers we'll least our sen^, yet we'll walk by untainted of their plea~sures, and as they ^e pure Temples we'll talk in them.

To bee, and pray then, we may have a fair end of ^ loves, would I were worth of you, or of such pa
^nts ^ you thanks: but I am poor in all but in your love. Once more, good night.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: A good night t'ye, and may the dew of sleep f^ll gently on you, sweet one, and lock up those fair lights in pleasing slumbers; no dreams but chaste and clear attempt your fancy, and break betimes sweet morn, I've lost my light else.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Let it be ever night when I lose you.

speeches.speaker: Syl.
prose: This Scholar never went to a Free-School, he's so simple.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
prose: Your Brother, with two Gallants, is at door, Sir, and they're so violent, they'll take no denial.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: This is no fit time of night.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Let 'em in, Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
prose: They stay no leave; shall I raise the house on 'em?

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Not a man, nor make no murmur of 't I charge ye.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: They're here, my Uncle absent, stand close to me. How do you, Brother, with your curious story? have you not read her yet sufficiently?

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: No, Brother, no; I stay yet in the Preface: the style's too hard for you.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: I must entreat her; she's parcel of my goods.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: She's all when you have her.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Hold off your hands, unmannerly, rude Sir; nor I, nor what I have depend on you.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Do, let her alone, she gives good counsel; do not trouble your self with Ladies, they are too light: Let out your Land, and get a provident Steward.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: I cannot love ye, let that satisfie you; such vanities as you, are to be laugh'd at.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Nay, then you must go; I must claim mine own.

speeches.speaker: Both.
prose: Away, away with her.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose:
Let her alone, pray let her alone, and take your Coxcomb up: Let me talk
civilly a while with you, Brother. It may be on some terms I may part with her.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: O, is your heart come down? what are your terms, Sir? Put up, put up.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: This is the first and chiefest, let's walk a turn. Now stand off, fools, I advise ye, stand as far off as you would hope for mercy: this is the first sword yet I ever handled, and a sword's a beauteous thing to look upon; and if it hold, I shall so hunt your insolence: 'tis sharp, I'm sure, and if I put it home, 'tis ten to one I shall new pink your Sattins; I find I have spirit enough to dispose of it, and will enough to make ye all examples; let me toss it round, I have the full command on't. Fetch me a native Fencer, I defie him; I feel the fire of ten strong spirits in me. Do you watch me when my Uncle is absent? this is my grief, I shall be flesh'd on Cowards; teach me to fight, I willing am to learn. Are ye all gilded flies, nothing but shew in ye? why stand ye gaping? who now touches her? who calls her his, or who dares name her to me? but name her as his own; who dares look on her? that shall be mortal too; but think, 'tis dangerous. Art thou a fit man to inherit Land, and hast no wit nor spirit to maintain it? Stand still, thou sign of a man, and pray for thy friends, pray heartily, good prayers may restore ye.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: But do not kill 'em, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: You speak too late, Dear; it is my first fight, and I must do bravely, I must not look with partial eyes on any; I cannot spare a button of these Gentlemen; did life lie in their heel, Achilles like, I'd shoot my anger at those parts, and kill 'em. Who waits within?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: View all these, view 'em well, go round about 'em, and still view their faces; round about yet, see how death waits upon 'em, for thou shalt never view 'em more.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Pray hold, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose:
I cannot hold, you stand so fair before me; I must
not ^old; 'twill darken all my glories. Go to my Uncle, b^d him post to the King, and get my pardon instantly, I have need on't.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Are you so unnatural?

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: You shall die last, Sir, I'll take thee dead, thou ^art no man to fight with. Come, will ye come? Me-thinks I've fought whole Battels.

speeches.speaker: Cow.
prose: We have no quarrel to you that we know on, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Egre.
prose: We'll quit the house, and ask ye mercy too. Good Lady, let no murther be done here; we came but to parly.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: How my sword thirsts after them? Stand away, Sweet.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Pray, Sir, take my submission, and I disclaim for ever.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Away, ye poor things, ye despicable creatures! do you come poste to fetch a Lady from me? from a poor School-boy that ye scorn'd of late, and grow lame in your hearts when you should execute? Pray take her, take her, I am weary of her: What did you bring to carry her?

speeches.speaker: Egre.
prose: A Coach and four Horses.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: But are they good?

speeches.speaker: Egre.
prose: As good as France can shew Sir.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Are you willing to leave those, and take your safeties? Speak quickly.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Yes with all our hearts.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: 'Tis done then. Many have got one Horse, I've got four by th' bargain.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: How now, who's here?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Nay, now y'are gone without bail.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: What, drawn, my Friends? Fetch me my two-hand Sword; I will not leave a head on your shoulders, Wretches.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: In troth, Sir, I came but to do my duty.

speeches.speaker: Both.
prose: And we to renew our loves.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Bring me a Blanket. What came they for?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose:
To borrow me a while, Sir; but one that never fought yet, has so curri'd, so bastinado'd them with manly carriage, they stand like things Gorgon had turn'd to stone: they watch'd your being absent, and then thought they might do wonders here, and they have done so; for by my troth I wonder at their coldness, the nipping North or Frost never came near them; St
George upon a sign would grow more sensible. If the name of Honour were for ever to be lost, these were the most sufficient men to do it in all the world; and yet they are but young, what will they rise to? They're as full of fire as a frozen Glow-worms rattle, and shine as goodly: Nobility and patience are match'd rarely in these three Gentlemen, they have right use on't; they'll stand still for an hour and be beaten. These are the Anagrams of three great Worthies.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: They will infect my house with cowardize, if they breath longer in it; my roof covers no baffl'd Monsieurs, walk and air your selves; as I live they stay not here. White-liver'd wretches, without one word to ask a reason why. Vanish, 'tis the last warning, and with speed; for if I take ye in hand, I shall dissect you, and read upon your flegmatick dull Carcases. My Horse again there: I have other business, which you shall hear hereafter, and laugh at it. Good-night Charles, fair goodness to your dear Lady; 'tis late, 'tis late.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Pray, Sir, be careful of us.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: It is enough, my best care shall attend ye.

segments.head: Actus Quartus. | ACTUS IV. SCENA IV.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose:
Are you come, old Master? Very good, your Horse is well set up; but ere you part, I'll ride you, and spur your Reverend Justiceship such a question, as I shall make the sides of your Reputation bleed, truly I will. Now must I play at ^o peep— A Banquet— well, Potatoes and Eringoes, and, as I take it, Cantharides—Excellent, a Priapism follows, and as I'll handle it, it shall, old Lecherous Goat in Authority. Now they begin to Bill; how he slavers her! Gramercy Lilly, she spits his kisses out, and now he offers to fumble, she falls off, (that's a good Wench) and cries fair play above board. Who are they in the corner? As I live, a ^ of Fidlers; I shall have some Musick yet at my making free o th' Company of Horners; there's the comfort, and a Song too! He beckons for one— Sure 'tis no Anthem, nor no borrow'd Rhymes out of the School of vertue; I will listen—
This was never pe^'d at Geneva, the Note's too sprightly. So, so, the Musick's paid for, and now what follows? O that Monsieur Miramont would but keep his word; here were a Feast to make him fat with laughter; at the most 'tis not six minutes riding from his house, nor will he break, I hope— O are you come, Sir? the prey is in the N^t, and will break in upon occasion.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Thou shalt rule me, Andrew. O th'infinite fright that will assail this Gentleman! the Quartans, Tertians, and Quotidians that will hang like Serjeants on his Worships shoulders! the humiliation of the flesh of this man, this grave, austere man will be wondred at. How will those solemn looks appear to me; and that severe face, that speaks chains and shackles? Now I take him in the nick, e'^ I have done with him, he had better have stood between two panes of Wainscot, and made his recantation in the Market, than hear me conjure him.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: He must pass this way to th' only Bed I have; he comes, stand close.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Well done, well done, give me my night-cap. So. Quick, quick, untruss me; I will truss and ^rounce thee. Come, Wench, a kiss between each point; kiss close, it is a sweet Parenthesis.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
prose: Y'are merry, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Merry I will be anon, and thou shalt feel it, thou shalt, my Lilly.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
prose: Shall I air your Bed, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: No, no; I'll use no Warming pan but thine, Girl, that's all. Come kiss me again.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
prose: Ha'ye done yet?

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: No; but I will do, and do wonders, Lilly. Shew me the way.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
prose: You cannot miss it, Sir; you shall have a Cawdle in the morning for your Worship's breakfast.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: How, i'th' morning, Lilly? th'art such a witty thing to draw me on. Leave fooling, Lilly, I am hungry now, and th'hast another Kickshaw, I must taste it.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
prose: 'Twill make you surfeit, I am tender of you: y'have all y'are like to have.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: And can this be earnest?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: It seems so, and she honest.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Have I not thy promise, Lilly?

speeches.speaker: Lil.
prose: Yes, and I have performed enough to a man of your years, this is truth; and you shall find, Sir, you have kiss'd and tous'd me, hand I'd my leg and foot; what would you more, Sir? As for the rest, it requires youth and strength, and the labour in an old man would breed Agues, Sciatica's, and Cramps: You shall not curse me for taking from you what you cannot spare, Sir. Be good unto your self, y'have ta'ne already all you can take with ease; you are past threshing, it is a work too boisterous for you, leave such drudgery to Andrew.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: How she jeers him?

speeches.speaker: Lil.
prose: Let Andrew alone with his own tillage, he's tough, and can manure it.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Y'are a quean, a scoffing, jeering quean.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
prose: It may be so, but I'm sure I'll ne'^ be yours.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Do not provoke me, if thou do'st I'll have my Farm again, and turn thee out a begging.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
prose:
Though you have the will, and want of honesty to deny your deed, Sir; yet I hope Andrew has got so much learning from my young Master, as to keep his own; at the worst I'll tell a short tale to the Judges, for what grave
ends you sign'd your Lease, and on what terms you would revoke it.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Whore, thou dar'st not. Yield, or I'll have thee whipt: how my Bloud boils, as if 't were o're a Furnace!

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: I shall cool it.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Yet, gentle Lilly, pity and forgive me, I'll be a friend t'ye, such a loving bountiful friend —

speeches.speaker: Lil.
prose: To avoid Suits in Law, I would grant a little; but should fierce Andrew know it, what would become of me?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: A Whore, a Whore!

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Nothing but well Wench, I shall put such a strong bit in his mouth, as thou shalt ride him how thou wilt, my Lilly; nay, he shall hold the door, as I will work him, and thank thee for the Office.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Take heed, Andrew, these are shrewd temptations.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Pray you know your Cue, and second me, Sir. By your Worship's savour.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Andrew!

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: I come in time to take possession of th'Office you assign me; hold the door! alas, 'tis nothing for a simple man to stay without, when a deep understanding holds con~ference within, say with his Wife: a trifle, Sir. I know I hold my Farm by Cuckolds Tenure; you are Lord o'th' Soil, Sir. Lilly is a West, a stray, she's yours to use, Sir, I claim no interest in her.

speeches.speaker: Bri
prose: Art thou serious? speak, honest Andrew, since thou hast o'er heard us, and wink at small faults, man; I'm but a pidla^, a little will serve my turn; thou'lt find enough when I've my belly full: Wilt thou be private and silent?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: By all means, I'll only have a Ballad made of't, sung to some lewd Tune, and the name of it shall be Justice Trap; it will fell rarely with your Worships name, and Lilly's on the top.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Seek not the ruine o' my reputation, Andrew.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: 'Tis for your credit, Monsieur Brisac, printed in Capital Letters, then pasted upon all the posts in Paris.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: No mercy, Andrew?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: O, it will proclaim you from the City to the Court, and prove Sport Royal.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Thou shalt keep thy Farm.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: He does affect him ^nely.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: You trouble me. Then his intent arriving, the vizard of his hypocrisie pull'd of to the Judge criminal.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: O I am undone.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: He's put out of Commission with disgrace, and hold uncapable of bearing Office ever hereafter. This is my revenge, and this I'll put in practice.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Do but hear me.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: To bring me back from my Grammar to my Hornbook, it is unpardonable.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Do not play the Tyrant; accept of composition.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
prose: Hear him, Andrew.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: What composition?

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: I'll confirm thy Farm, and add unto it a hundred Acres more, adjoyning to it.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Umb, this mollifies; but y'are so fickle, and will again deny this, there being no witness by.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Call any witness, I'll presently assure it.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Say you so? troth there's a friend of mine, Sir, within hearing, that's familiar with all that's past, his testimony will be authentical.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Will he be s cret?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: You may tie his tongue up, as you would do your purse strings.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Mi^amont!

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Ha ha ha!

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: This is my witness. Lord how you are troubled! si^e you have an Agn^, you shake so with choler: Here's your loving Brother, Sir, and will tell no body but all he meets, that you have eat a Snake, and are grown young, gamesome, and rampant.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Caught thus?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: If he were o^ that would make jests of you, or playne ye, with making your Religious gravity ridiculous to your Neighbours, then you had some cause to be per~plex'd.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: I shall become discourse for Clowns and Tapsters.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Quick, Lilly, quick, he's now past kissing, between point and point. He swounds, fetch him some Cordial— Now put in, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose:
Who may this be? sure this is some mistake: let me see his face, wears he not a false beard? it cannot be Br^
sac that worthy Gentleman, the Pillar and the Patron of his Country; he is too prudent, and too cautelous, experience hath taught him t'avoid these fooleries, he is the punisher, and not the doer; besides he's old and cold, unfit for Wo~man: This is some counterfeit, he shall be whipt for't, some base abuser of my worthy Brother.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Open the doors; will ye imprison me? are ye my Judges?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: The man raves! this is not judicious Brisac: yet now I think on't, h'has a kind of Dog look like my Brother, a guilty hanging face.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: I'll suffer bravely, do your worst, do, do.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Why, it's manly in you.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: Nor will I ^ail nor curse, you slave, you whore, I will not meddle with you; but all the torments that e're fell on men, that sed on mischief, fall heavily on you all.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
prose: You have given him a heat, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: He will ride you the better, Lilly.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: We'll teach him to meddle with Scholars.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: He shall make good his promise t'increase thy Farm, Andrew, or I'll jeer him to death. Fear nothing. Lilly, I am thy Champion. This jeast goes to Charles, and then I'll hunt him out, and Monsieur Eustace the gallant Courtier, and laugh heartily to see 'em mourn together.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: 'Twill be rare, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: TUrn'd out of doors and baffled!

speeches.speaker: Egre.
prose: We share with you in the affront.

speeches.speaker: Cow.
prose: Yet bear it not like you with such dejection.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: My Coach and Horses made the ransom of ou^ Cowardize!

speeches.speaker: Cow.
prose: Pish, that's nothing, 'tis damnum reparabile, and soon recover'd.

speeches.speaker: Egre.
prose: It is but feeding a Suitor with false hopes, and after squeeze him with a dozen of Oaths, You are new rigg'd, and this no more remembred.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: And does the Court, that should be the Example and Oracle of the Kingdom, read to us no other Doctrine?

speeches.speaker: Egre.
prose: None that thrives so well as that, within my knowledge.

speeches.speaker: Cow.
prose: Flattery rubs out; but since great men learn to admire themselves, 'tis something crest-faln.

speeches.speaker: Egre.
prose: To be of no Religion, argues a subtle, moral understanding, and it is often cherish'd.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Piety then, and valour, nor to do and suffer wrong, are they no virtues?

speeches.speaker: Egre.
prose: Rather vices, Eustace; Fighting! what's fighting? it may be in fashion among p^ovant swords, and Buff-jerkin men: But w'us that swim in choice of Silks and Tissues; though in defence of that word Reputation, which is indeed a kind of glorious nothing, to lose a dram of blood must needs appear as coarse as to be honest.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: And all this you seriously believe?

speeches.speaker: Cow.
prose: It is a faith that we will die in, since from the bla^ Guard to the grim Sir in Office, there are few hold oth^ Tenets.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Now my eyes are open, and I behold a strong necessity that keeps me knave and coward.

speeches.speaker: Cow.
prose: Y'are the wiser.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Nor can I change my copy, if I purpose to be of your ^ociety.

speeches.speaker: Egre.
prose: By no means.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Honour is nothing with you?

speeches.speaker: Cow.
prose: A meer bubble; for what's grown common, is no ^o^e regarded.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: My sword forc'd from me too, and still detain'd, ^ou think 'tis no blemish.

speeches.speaker: Egre.
prose:
Get me a Batton, 'tis twenty times more Court
^ke, and less trouble.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: And yet you wear a sword.

speeches.speaker: Cow.
prose:
Yes, and a good one, a Milan hilt, and a Damasco
^lade for ornament, not use, the Court allows it.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Will't not fight of it self?

speeches.speaker: Cow.
prose: I ne'er tri'd this, yet I have worn as fair as any man; ^'m sure I've made my Cutler rich, and paid for several weapons, Turkish and Toledo's, two thousand Crowns, and ^et could never light upon a fighting one.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: I'le borrow this, I like it well.

speeches.speaker: Cow.
prose: 'Tis at your service, Sir, a Lath in a Velvet Scabbard will serve my turn.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose:
And now I have it, leave me; y'are infectious, the plague and leprosie of your baseness spreading on all that do ^ome near you; such as you render the Throne of Majesty, ^he Court, suspected and contemptible; you are Scarabee's that batten in her dung, and have no palats to taste her ^urious Viands; and like Owles, can only see her night de
^ormities, but with the glorious splendor of her beauties, you are struck blind as Moles, that undermine the sum
^tuous Building that allow'd you shelter: you stick like ^unning ulcers on her face, and taint the pureness of her na
^ive candor, and being bad Servants, cause your Masters goodness to be disputed of; you make the Court, that is the abstract of all Academies, to teach and practise noble un
^ertakings, (where courage sits triumphant crown'd with ^awrel, and wisdom loaded with the weight of honour) a ^chool of Vices.

speeches.speaker: Egre.
prose: What sudden rapture's this?

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: A heavenly one, that raising me from sloth and ^gnorance, (in which your conversation long hath charm'd ^ne) carries me up into the air of action, and knowledge of my self; even now I feel, but pleading only in the Court's defence (though far short of her merits and bright lustre) a ^appy alteration, and full strength to stand her Champion against all the world, that throw aspersions on her.

speeches.speaker: Cow.
prose: Sure he'll beat us, I see it in his eyes.

speeches.speaker: Egre.
prose: A second Charles; pray look not, Sir, so furiously.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Recant what you have said, ye Mungrils, and lick ^p the vomit ye have cast upon the Court, where you unworthily have had warmth and breeding, and swear that you, like Spiders, have made poison of that which was a saving Antidote.

speeches.speaker: Egre.
prose: We will swear any thing.

speeches.speaker: Cow.
prose: We honour the Court as a most sacred place.

speeches.speaker: Egre.
prose: And will make oath, if you enjoyn us to'r, nor knave, nor fool, nor coward living in it.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Except you two, you Rascals.

speeches.speaker: Cow.
prose: Yes, we are all these, and more, if you will have ^it so.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: And that until you are again reform'd and grown new men, you ne'ere presume to name the Court, or press into the Porter's Lodge but for a penance, to be disciplin'd for your roguery, and this done with true contrition.

speeches.speaker: Both.
prose: Yes, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: You again may eat scraps, and be thankful.

speeches.speaker: Cow.
prose: Here's a cold breakfast after a sharp nights walking.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Keep your oaths, and without grumbling vanish.

speeches.speaker: Both.
prose: We are gone, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: May all the poorness of my spirit go with you: the fetters of my thraldom are fil'd off, and I at liberty to right my self; and though my hope in Angellina's little, my honour (unto which compar'd she's nothing) shall, like the Sun, disperse those lowring Clouds that yet obscure and dim it; not the name of Brother shall divert me, but from him, that in the world's opinion ruin'd me, I will seek reparation, and call him unto a strict accompt. Ha! 'tis near day, and if the Muses friend, Rose-check'd Aurora, invite him to this solitary Grove, as I much hope she will, he seldome missing to pay his vows here to her, I shall hazard to hinder his devotions— The door opens, 'tis he most certain, and by's side my Sword. Blest opportunity.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: I have o'er slept my self, and lost part of the morn, but I'le recover it: Before I went to bed, I wrote some Notes within my Table-book, which I will now consider. Ha! what means this? What do I with a Sword? Learn'd Mercury needs not th'aid of Mars, and innocence is to it self a guard, yet since Arms ever protect Arts, I may justly wear and use it; for since 'twas made my prize, I know not how I'm grown in love with't, and cannot cat nor study, and much less walk without it. But I trifle, matters of more weight ask my judgment.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Now, Sir, treat of no other Theme, I'le keep you to it, and see y'expound it well.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Eustace!

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: The same, Sir, your younger Brother, who, as duty binds him, hath all this night (turn'd out of door) attended, to bid Good-morrow t'ye.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: This not in scorn, commands me to return it. Would you ought else?

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: O much, Sir, here I end not, but begin; I must speak to you in another strain than yet I ever us'd; and if the language appear in the delivery rough and harsh, you (being my Tutor) must condemn your self, from whom I learn'd it.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: When I understand (be't in what style you please) what's your demand, I shall endeavour, in the self-same phrase, to make an answer to the point.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: I come not to lay claim to your birth-right, 'tis your own, and 'tis fit you enjoy it; nor ask I from you your learning and deep knowledge; (though I am not a Scholar as you are) I know them Diamonds by your sole industry, patience and labour, forc'd from steep Rocks, and with much toil attended, and but to few that prize their value granted, and therefore without Rival freely wear them.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: These not repin'd at (as you seem t'inform me) the motion must be of a strange condition, if I refuse to yield to't; therefore, Eustace, without this tempest in your looks, propound it, and fear not a denial.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: I require then (as from an Enemy, and not a Brother) the reputation of a man, the honour, not by a fair War won when I was waking, but in my sleep of folly ravish'd from me; with these, the restitution of my Sword, with large acknowledgment of satisfaction, my Coach, my Horses; I will part with life, ere lose one hair of them; and, what concludes all, my Mistris Angellina, as she was before the musical Magick of thy tongue inchanted and seduc'd her. These perform'd, and with submission, and done publickly, at my Father's and my Uncle's intercession, (that I put in too) I perhaps may listen to terms of reconcilement; but if these, in every circumstance, are not subscrib'd to, to the last gasp I defie thee.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: These are strict conditions to a Brother.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: My rest is up, nor will I give less.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: I'm no Gamester, Eustace, yet I can ghess your resolution stands to win or lose all; I rejoyce to find ye thus tender of your honour, and that at length you understand what a wretched thing you were, how deeply wounded by your self, and made almost incurable in your own hopes, the dead flesh of pale cowardise growing over your festred ^eputation, which no Balm or gentle Unguent could ever make way to; and I am happy that I was the Surgeon that ^ apply those burning co^rosives, that render you already ^sible o'th'danger you were plung'd in, in teaching you, and ^ a fair gradation, how far, and with what curious respect and care the peace and credit of a man within, (which you ^ thought till now) should be prese^r'd before a gawdy on ^e; pray you fix here, for so far I go with you.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: This discourse is from the subject.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: I'le come to it, Brother; but if you think to build upon my ruines, you'll find a false foundation: your high offers, taught by the Masters of dependencies, that by compounding differences 'tween others, supply their own ne~cessities, with me will never carry 't: as you are my Bro~ther, I will dispense a little, but no more than honour can give way to; nor must I destroy that in my self I love in you; and therefore let not hopes or threats persuade you I will descend to any composition for which I may be censur'd.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: You shall fight then.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: With much unwillingness with you; but if there's no evasion —

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: None.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Hear yet a word; as for the Sword and other fripperies, in a fair way send for them, you shall have 'em. But rather than surrender Angellina, or hear it again mention'd, I oppose my breast unto loud thunder, cast behind me all tyes of Nature.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: She detain'd, I'm deaf to all persuasion.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Guard thy self then, Eustace; I use no other Rhetorick.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Clashing of swords so near my house! Brother oppos'd to Brother! here's no fencing at half sword, hold, hold, Charles, Eustace.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Second him, or call in more help. Come not between us, I'le not know nor spare you; D'ye fight by th'book?

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: 'Tis you that wrong me, off Sir, and suddenly, I'le conjure down the Spirit that I have rais'd in him.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Never, Charles, 'tis thine, and in thy death, be doubled in me.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose:
I'm out of breath, yet trust not too muc^
^, Boys; for if you pause not suddenly, and hear reason, ^ kill your Uncle, do; but that I'm patient, and not ^ lerick old teasty fool, like your Father, I'd dance a m^
^ with you, should make you sweat your best blou^
^ would, and it may be I will Charles, I command ^, and Eustace, I entreat thee, th'art a brave Spark, a tr^
^ough metall'd blade, and I begin to love thee heartily; give me a fighting Courtier, I'le cherish him for example; in our Age they're not born every day.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: You of late, Sir, in me lov'd learning.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: True, but take me w'ye, Charles; 'twas when young Eustace wore his heart in 's breeches, and sought his Battels in Complements and Cringes, when's understanding wav'd in a flanting Feather, and his best contemplation look'd no further than a new fashion'd doublet; I confess then, the lofty noise your Greek made, only pleas'd me; but now he's turn'd an Ol^r and a Rowland, nay, the whole dozen of Peers are bound up in him: L^t me remember, when I was of his years ^d look very li^e him; and did you see my Picture as I was then, you would swear that gallant Eustace (I mean, now he da^es light) was the true substance, and the perfect figure. Nay, nay, no anger, you shall have enough, Charles.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Sure, Sir, I shall not need addition from him.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Nor I from an^, this shall decide my interest; though I am lost to all deserving men, to all that men call good, for suffering ^ainely insufferable wrongs, and justly slighted by yielding to a minute of delay in my revenge, and from that made a stranger unto my Father's house and favour, o'erwhelm'd with all disgraces; yet I will mount up ward, and force my self a fortune, though my birth and breeding do deny it

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose:
Such not, Eustace, by violence, what will be offer'd to you on easier composition; though I was not alli'd unto your weakness, you shall find me a Brother to your bravery of spirit, and one that, not compell'd to't by your sword, (which I must never fear) will share with you in all but
^elli^a.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Nobly said, Charles, and learn from my experience, you may hear reason, and never maint your fighting; for your credit, which you think you have lost, spare, Charles, and swinge me and soundly three or four walking vehe^ Cloaks, that wear no swords to guard 'em yet deserve ^ thou art made up again.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: All this is Lip-salve.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: It shall be Hearts-ease, Eustace, ere I have done; as for thy Father's anger, now thou dar'st fight, ne'er fear it, for I've the dowcets of his gravity fast in a string, I will so pin^ and wring him, that, spight of his authority, thou sha^ make thine own conditions with him.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: I'le take leave a little to consider.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Here comes Andrew.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: But without his comical and learned face; what sad disaster, Andrew?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: You my read, Sir, a Tragedy in my face.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Art thou in earnest?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Yes, by my life, Sir; and if now you help not, and speedily, by force, or by persuasion, my good old Master (for now I pity him) is ruin'd for ever.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Ha, my Father!

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: He, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: By what means? speak.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: At the suit of Monsieur Lewis; his house is seiz'd upon, and he in person is under guard, (I saw it with these eyes, Sir) to be convey'd to Paris, and there Sentenc'd.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Nay, then there is no jesting.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Do I live, and know my Father injur'd?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: And what's worse, Sir, my Ladie Angellina—

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: What of her?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: She's carri'd away too.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: How?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose:
While you were absent, a crew of Monsieur Lewis friends and kinsmen, by force, brake in at th' back part of the house, and took her away by violence; faithful Andre^
(as this can witness for him) did his best in her defence, ^ 'twould not do.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Away, and see our Horses sadled, 'tis no time to talk, but do. Eustace, you now are offer'd a spatious field, and in a pious War to exercise your valour; here's a cause, and such a one, in which to fall is honourable, your dutie and reverence due to a fathers name commanding it; but these unnatural jars arising between Brothers (should you prosper) would shame your victory.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: I would do much, Sir, but still my reptation!

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Charles shall give you all decent satisfaction; nay, joyn hands, and heartily, why, this is done like Brothers; and as old as I am, in this cause that concerns the honour of our Family, Monsieur Lewis (if reason cannot work) shall find and feel there's hot blood in this arm, I'le lea^ you bravely.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: And if I follow not, a cowards name be branded on my forehead.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: This spirit makes you a sharer in my fortunes.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: And in mine, of which (Brisac once freed, and Angellina again in our possession) you shall know, my heart speaks in my tongue.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: I dare not doubt it, Sir.

segments.head: Actus Quintus. | ACTUS V. SCENA II.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: I'm deaf to all perswasions.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: I use none, nor doubt I, though a while my innocence suffers, but when the King shall understand how false your malice hath inform'd him, he in justice must set me right again.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose:
Sir, let not passion so far transport you, as to think it reason, this violent course repairs, but ruins it; that honour you would build up, you destroy; what you would seem to nourish, if respect of my preferment or my pattern may challenge your paternal love and care, why do you, now good fortune has provided a better Husband for me that your hopes could ever fancy, strive to rob me of him? In what is my Lord Charles defective, Sir? unless deep Lear~ning
be a blemish in him, or well proportion'd limbs be ^ulcts in nature, or, what you only aim'd at, large Reve
^ues, are, on the sudden, grown distasteful to you. Of what ^an you accuse him?

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: Of a Rape done to Honour, which thy ravenous lust ^ade thee consent to.

speeches.speaker: Syl.
prose: Her lust! you are her Father.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: And you her Bawd.

speeches.speaker: Syl.
prose: Were you ten Lords, 'tis false; the pureness of her ^haste thoughts entertains not such spotted instruments.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: As I have a Soul, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: I am not to be alter'd; to sit down with this disgrace, would argue me a Peasant, and not born Noble: all ^igour that the Law, and that increase of power by favour ^ields, shall be with all severity inflicted; you have the King's hand for't, no Bail will serve, and therefore at your perils, Officers, away with 'em.

speeches.speaker: Bri.
prose: This is madness.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: Tell me so in open Court, and there I'le answer you.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Well overtaken.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Ill if they dare resist.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: He that advances but one step forward dies.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: Shew the King's Writ.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Shew your discretion, 'twill become you better.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Y'are once more in my power, and if again I part with you, let me for ever lose thee.

speeches.speaker: Eust.
prose: Force will not do't, nor threats; accept this service from your despair'd of Eustace.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: And beware your Reverend Worship never more attempt to search my Lilly pot, you see what follows.

speeches.speaker: Lew.
prose: Is the King's power contemn'd?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: No, but the torrent o' your wilful folly stopp'd. And for you, good Sir, if you would but be sensible, what can you wish, but the satisfaction of an obstinate will, that is not endear'd to you? rather than be cross'd in what you purpos'd, you'll undo your Daughter's same, the credit of your judgment, and your old foolish Neighbour; make your Estates, and in a Suit not worth a Cardecue, a prey to Advocates, and their buckram Scribes, and after they have plum'd ye, return home like a couple of naked Fowles without a feather.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: This is a most strong truth, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: No, no, Monsieur, let us be right Frenchmen, violent to charge; but when our follies are repell'd by reason, 'tis fit that we retreat, and ne'er come on more: Observe my learned Charles, he'll get thee a Nephew on Angellina shall dispute in her belly, and suck the Nurs^ by Logick: and here's Eustace, he was an Ass, but now is grown an Amadis; nor shall he want a Wife, if all my Land, for a Joynture, can effect: Y'are a good Lord, and of a gentle nature, in your looks I see a kind consent, and it shews lovely: and do you hear, old Fool? but I'le not chide, hereafter, like me, ever doat on Learning, the meer belief is excellent, 'twill save you; and next love Valour, though you dare not fight your self, or fright a foolish Officer, young Eustace can do it to a hair. And, to conclude, let Andrew's Farm b' encreas'd, that is your penance, you know for what, and see you rut no more; you understand me. So embrace on all sides.

I'le pay those Bilmen, and make large amends,
Provided we preserve you still our Friends—

speeches.speaker: Arsenio.
verse: LEandro paid all.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: 'Tis his usual custom,
And requisite he should: he has now put off
The Funeral black, (your rich heir wears with joy,
When he pretends to weep for his dead Father)
Your gathering Sires, so long heap muck together,
That their kind Sons, to rid them of their care,
Wish them in Heaven, or if they take a taste
Of Purgatory by the way, it matters not,
Provided they remove hence; what is befaln
To his Father, in the other world, I ask not;
I am sure his prayer is heard: would I could use one
For mine, in the same method.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Fie upon thee.
This is prophane.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Good Doctor, do not school me
For a fault you are not free from: On my life
Were all Heirs in Corduba, put to their Oaths,
They would confess with me, 'tis a sound Tenet:
I am sure Leandro do's.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: He is th'owner
Of a fair Estate.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: And fairly he deserves it,
He's a Royal Fellow: yet observes a mean
In all his courses, careful too on whom
He showers his bounties: he that's liberal
To all alike, may do a good by chance,
But never out of Judgment: This invites
The prime men of the City to frequent
All places he resorts to, and are happy
In his sweet Converse.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Don Jamie the Brother
To the Grandee Don Henrique, appears much taken
With his behaviour.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: There is something more in't:
He needs his Purse, and knows how to make use on't.
Tis now in fashion for your Don, that's poor,
To vow all Leagues of friendship with a Merchant
That can supply his wants, and howsoe're
Don Jamie's noble born, his elder Brother
Don Henrique rich, and his Revenues long since
Encreas'd by marrying with a wealthy Heir
Call'd, Madam Vialante, he yet holds
A hard hand o're Jamie, allowing him
A bare annuity only.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Yet 'tis said
He hath no child, and by the Laws of Spain
If he die without issue, Don Jamie
^nherits his Estate.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Why that's the reason
Of their so many jarrs: though the young Lord
^e sick of the elder Brother, and in reason
Should flatter, and observe him, he's of a nature
Too bold and fierce, to stoop so, but bears up,
Presuming on his hopes.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: What's the young Lad
That all of'em make so much of?

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: 'Tis a sweet one,
And the best condition'd youth, I ever saw yet,
So humble, and so affable, that he wins
The love of all that know him, and so modest,
That (in despight of poverty) he would starve
Rather than ask a courtesie: He's the Son
Of a poor cast Captain, one Octavio;
And She, that once was call'd th'fair Jacinta,
Is happy in being his Mother: for his sake,
(Though in their Fortunes faln) they are esteem'd of,
And cherish'd by the best. O here they come.
I now may spare his Character, but observe him,
He'l justifie my report.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: My good Ascanio,
Repair more often to me: above Women
Thou ever shalt be welcome.

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: My Lord your favours
May quickly teach a raw untutour'd Youth
To be both rude and sawcy.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: You cannot be
Too frequent where you are so much desir'd:
And give me leave (dear friend) to be your Rival
In part of his affection; I will buy it
At any rate.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Stood I but now possess'd
Of what my future hope presages to me,
I then would make it clear thou hadst a Patron
That would not say but do: yet as I am,
Be mine, I'le not receive thee as a servant,
But as my Son, (and though I want my self)
No Page attending in the Court of Spain
Shall find a kinder master.

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: I beseech you
That my refusal of so great an offer
May make no ill construction, 'tis not pride
(That common vice is far from my condition)
That makes you a denyal to receive
A favour I should sue for: nor the fashion
Which the Country follows, in which to be a servant
In those that groan beneath the heavy weight
Of poverty, is held an argument
Of a base abject mind, I wish my years
Were sit to do you service in a nature
That might become a Gentleman (give me leave
To think my self one) My Father serv'd the King
As a Captain in the field; and though his fortune
Return'd him home a poor man, he was rich
In Reputation, and wounds fairly taken.
Nor am I by his ill success deterr'd,
I rather feel a strong desire that sways me
To follow his profession, and if Heaven
Hath mark'd me out to be a man, how proud,
In the service of my Country, should I be,
To trail a Pike under your brave command!
There, I would follow you as a guide to honour,
Though all the horrours of the War made up
To stop my passage.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Thou art a hopeful Boy,
And it was bravely spoken: For this answer,
I love thee more than ever.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Pity such seeds
Of promising courage should not grow and prosper.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: What ever his reputed Parents be,
He hath a mind that speaks him right and noble.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: You make him blush: it needs not sweet Ascanio,
We may hear praises when they are deserv'd,
Our modesty unwounded. By my life
I would add something to the building up
So fair a mind, and if till you are fit
To bear Arms in the Field, you'l spend some years
In Salamanca, I'le supply your studies
With all conveniences.

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: Your goodness (Signiors)
And charitable favours overwhelm me.
If I were of your blood, you could not be
More tender of me: what then can I pay
(A poor Boy and a stranger) but a heart
Bound to your service? with what willingness
I would receive (good Sir) your noble offer,
Heaven can bear witness for me: but alas,
Should I embrace the means to raise my fortunes,
I must destroy the lives of my poor Parents
(To whow I ow my being) they in me
Place all their comforts, and (as if I were
The light of their dim eyes) are so indulgent
They cannot brook one short dayes absence from me;
And (what will hardly win belief) though young,
I am their Steward and their Nurse: the bounties
Which others bestow on me serves to sustain 'em,
And to forsake them in their age, in me
Were more than Murther.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: This is a kind of begging
Would make a Broker charitable.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Here, (sweet heart)
I wish it were more.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: When this is spent,
Seek for supply from me.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Thy piety
For ever be remembred: nay take all,
Though 'twere my exhibition to a Royal
For one whole year.

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: High Heavens reward your goodness.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: So Sir, is this a slip of your own grafting,
You are so prodigal?

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: A slip Sir?

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Yes,
A slip; or call it by the proper name,
Your Bastard.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: You are foul-mouth'd; do not provoke me,
I shall forget your Birth if you proceed,
And use you, (as your manners do deserve) uncivilly.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: So brave! pray you give me hearing,
Who am I Sir?

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: My elder Brother: One
That might have been born a fool, and so reputed,
But that you had the luck to creep into
The world a year before me.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: Be more temperate.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: I neither can nor will, unless I learn it
By his example: let him use his harsh
Unsavoury reprehensions upon those
That are his Hinds, and not on me. The Land
Our Father left to him alone rewards him,
For being twelve months elder, let that be
Forgotten, and let his Parasites remember
One quality of worth or vertue in him
That may authorize him, to be a censurer
Of me, or my manners, and I will
Acknowledge him for a Tutor, till then, never.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: From whom have you your means Sir?

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: From the will
Of my dead Father; I am sure I spend not
Nor give't upon your purse.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: But will it hold out
Without my help?

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: I am sure it shall, I'le sink else,
For sooner I will seek aid from a Whore,
Than a courtesie from you.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: 'Tis well; you are proud of
Your new Exchequer, when you have cheated him
And worn him to the quick, I may be found
In the List of your acquaintance.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: Pray you hold
And give me leave (my Lord) to say thus much
(And in mine own defence) I am no Gull
To be wrought on by perswasion: nor no Coward
To be beaten out of my means, but know to whom
And why I give or lend, and will do nothing
But what my reason warrants; you may be
As sparing as you please, I must be bold
To make use of my own, without your licence.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: 'Pray thee let him alone, he is not worth thy anger.
All that he do's (Leandro) is for my good,
I think there's not a Gentleman of Spain,
That has a better Steward, than I have of him.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Your Steward Sir?

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Yes, and a provident one:
Why, he knows I am given to large expence,
And therefore lays up for me: could you believe else
That he, that sixteen years hath worn the yoke
Of barren wedlock, without hope of issue
(His Coffers full, his Lands and Vineyards fruitful)
Could be so sold to base and fordid thrift,
As almost to deny himself, the means
And necessaries of life? Alas, he knows
The Laws of Spain appoint me for his Heir,
That all must come to me, if I out-live him,
Which sure I must do, by the course of Nature,
And the assistance of good Mirth, and Sack,
How ever you prove Melancholy.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: If I live,
Thou dearly shalt repent this.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: When thou art dead,
I am sure I shall not.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Now they begin to burn
Like oppos'd Meteors.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Give them line, and way,
My life for Don Jamie.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Continue still
The excellent Husband, and joyn Farm to Farm,
Suffer no Lordship, that in a clear day
Falls in the prospect of your covetous eye
To be anothers; forget you are a Grandee;
Take use upon use, and cut the throats of Heirs
With cozening Mortgages: rack your poor Tenants,
Till they look like so many Skeletons
For want of Food; and when that Widows curses,
The ruines of ancient Families, tears of Orphans
Have hurried you to the Devil, ever remember
All was tak'd up for me (your thankful Brother)
That will dance merrily upon your Grave,
And perhaps give a double Pistolet
To some poor needy Frier, to say a Mass
To keep your Ghost from walking.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: That the Law
Should force me to endure this!

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Verily,
When this shall come to pass (as sure it will)
If you can find a loop-hole, though in Hell,
To look on my behaviour, you shall see me
Ransack your Iron Chests, and once again
Pluto's flame-colour'd Daughter shall be free
To domineer in Taverns, Masques, and Revels
As she was us'd before she was your Captive.
Me thinks the meer conceipt of it, should make you
Go home sick, and distemper'd; if it do's,
I'le send you a Doctor of mine own, and after
Take order for your Funeral.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: You have said, Sir,
I will not fight with words, but deeds to tame you,
Rest confident I will, and thou shalt wish
This day thou hadst been dumb.—

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: You have given him a heat,
But with your own distemper.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Not a whit,
Now he is from mine eye, I can be merry,
Forget the cause and him: all plagues go with him,
Let's talk of something else: what news is stirring?
Nothing to pass the time?

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Faith it is said
That the next Summer will determine much
Of that we long have talk'd of, touching the Wars.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: What have we to do with them? Let us discourse
Of what concerns our selves. 'Tis now in fashion
To have your Gallants set down in a Tavern,
What the Arch-Dukes purpose is the next spring, and what
Defence my Lords (the States) prepare: what course
The Emperour takes against the encroaching Turk,
And whether his Moony-standards are design'd
For Persia or Polonia: and all this
The wiser sort of State-Worms seem to know
Better than their own affairs: this is discourse
Fit for the Council it concerns; we are young,
And if that I might give the Theme, 'twere better
To talk of handsome Women.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: And that's one,
Almost as general.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Yet none agree
Who are the fairest.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: Some prefer the French,
For their conceited Dressings: some the plump
Italian Bona-Robas, some the State
That ours observe; and I have heard one swear,
(A merry friend of mine) that once in London,
He did enjoy the company of a Gamester,
(A common Gamester too) that in one night
Met him th' Italian, French, and Spanish wayes,
And ended in the Dutch; for to cool her self,
She kiss'd him drunk in the morning.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: We may spare
The travel of our tongues in forraign Nations,
When in Corduba, if you dare give credit
To my report (for I have seen her, Gallants)
There lives a Woman (of a mean birth too,
And meanly match'd) whose all-excelling Form
Disdains comparison with any She
That puts in for a fair one, and though you borrow
From every Country of the Earth the best
Of those perfections, which the Climat yields
To help to make her up, if put in Ballance,
This will weigh down the Scale.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: You talk of wonders.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: She is indeed a wonder, and so kept,
And, as the world deserv'd not to behold
What curious Nature made without a pattern,
Whose Copy she hath lost too, she's shut up,
Sequestred from the world.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: Who is the owner
Of such a Jem? I am fire'd.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: One Bartolus,
^ wrangling Advocate.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: A knave on Record.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: I am sure he cheated me of the best part
Of my Estate.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Some Business calls me hence,
And of importance) which denies me leisure
To give you his full character: In few words
Though rich) he's covetous beyond expression,
And to encrease his heap, will dare the Devil,
And all the plagues of darkness: and to these
^o ^alous, as if you would parallel

Old Argu^
to him, you must multiply
His Eyes an hundred times: of these none sleep.
He that would charm the heaviest lid, must hire
A better Mercurie, than Jove made use of:
Bless your selves from the thought of him and her,
For 'twill be labour lost: So farewel Signiors.—

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Leandro? in a dream? wake man for shame.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Trained into a fools paradise with a tale
Of an imagin'd Form.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: Jamie is noble,
And with a forg'd Tale would not wrong his Friend,
Nor am I so much fir'd with lust as Envie,
That such a churl as Bartolus should reap
So sweet a harvest, half my State to any
To help me to a share.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Tush do not hope for
^mpossibilities.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: I must enjoy her,
And my prophetique love tells me I shall,
Lend me but your assistance.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Give it o're.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: I would not have thee fool'd.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: I have strange Engines
Fashioning here: and Bartolus on the Anvil,
Disswade me not, but help me.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Take your fortune,
If you come off well, praise your wit; if not,
Expect to be the subject of our Laughter.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: You met Don Henrique?

speeches.speaker: Oct.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: What comfort bring you?
Speak cheerfully: how did my letter work
On his hard temper? I am sure I wrote it
So feelingly, and with the pen of sorrow,
That it must force Compunction.

speeches.speaker: Oct.
verse: You are cozen'd;
Can you with one hand prop a falling Tower?
Or with the other stop the raging main,
