speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: The Lady, whom my Father calls his Wife,
Abhors my sight, is sick of me, and forc'd him
To turn me out of doors.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: By my best hopes
I thank her cruelty, for it comes near
A saving Charity.

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: I am only happy
That yet I can relieve you, 'pray you share
My Father's wondrous kind, and promises
That I should be supplied: but sure the Lady
Is a malicious Woman, and I fear
Means me no good.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: I am turn'd a stone with wonder,
And know not what to think.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: From my Lady,
Your private ear, and this—

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: New Miracles?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: She says, if you dare make your self a Fortune,
She will propose the means; my Lord Don Henrique
Is now from home, and she alone expects you,
If you dare trust her, so, if not despair of
A second offer.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Though there were an Ambash
Laid for my life, I'le on and found this secret.
Retire thee, my Ascanio, with thy Mother:
But stir not forth, some great design's on foot,
Fall what can fall, if e're the Sun be set
I see you not, give me for dead

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: We will expect you,
And those bless'd Angels, that love goodness, guard you.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Is't possible he should be rich?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Most possible,
He hath been long, though he had but little gettings,
Drawing together, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Accounted a poor Sexton,
Honest poor Diego.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: I assure ye, a close Fellow,
Both close, and scraping, and that fills the Bags, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: A notable good fellow too?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Sometimes, Sir,
When he hop'd to drink a man into a Surfeit,
That he might gain by his Grave.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: So many thousands?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Heaven knows what.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: 'Tis strange,
'Tis very strange; but we see by endeavour,
And honest labour—

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Milo, by continuance
Gr^w from a silly Calf (with your worships reverence)
To carry a Bull, from a penny, to a pound, Sir,
And from a pound, to many: 'tis the progress.

speeches.speaker: Ba^.
verse: Ye say true, but he lov'd to feed well also,
And that me thinks—

speeches.speaker: L^p.
verse: From another mans Trencher, Sir,
And there he found it season'd with small charge:
There he would play the Tyrant, and would devour ye
More than the Graves he made; at home he liv'd
Like a Camelion, suckt th'Air of misery,
And g^ew fat by the Brewis of an Egg-shell,
Would smell a Cooks-shop, and go home and surfeit.
And be a month in fasting out that Fever.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: These are good Symptoms: do's he lye so sick say ye?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Oh, very sick.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: And chosen me Executor?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Only your Worship.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: No hope of his amendment?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: None, that we find.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: He hath no Kinsmen neither?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: 'Truth, very few,

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: His mind will be the quieter.
What Doctors has he?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: There's none, Sir, he believes in.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: They are but needless things, in such extremities.
Who draws the good mans Will?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Marry that do I, Sir,
And to my grief.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Grief will do little now, Sir,
Draw it to your comfort, Friend, and as I counsel ye,
An honest man, but such men live not always:
Who are about him?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Many, now he is passing,
That would pretend to his love, yes, and some Gentlemen
That would fain counsel him, and be of his Kindred;
Rich men can want no Heirs, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: They do ill,
Indeed they do, to trouble him; very ill, Sir.
But we shall take a care.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Will ye come near, Sir?
Pray ye bring him out; now ye may see in what state:
Give him fresh Air.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I am sorry, Neighbour Diego,
To find ye in so weak a state.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Ye are welcome,
But I am fleeting, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Me thinks he looks well,
His colour fresh, and strong, his eyes are chearful.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: A glimmering before death, 'tis nothing else, Sir,
Do you see how he sumbles with the Sheet? do ye note that?

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: My learned Sir, 'pray ye sit: I am bold to send for ye,
To take a care of what I leave.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Do ye hear that?

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Play the Knave finely.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: So I will, I warrant ye,
And carefully.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: 'Pray ye do not trouble him,
You see he's weak and has a wandring fancy.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: My honest Neighbours, weep not, I must leave ye,
I cannot always beat ye company,
We must drop still, there is no remedy:
'Pray ye Master Cu^ate, will ye write my Testament,
And write it largely it may be remembred,
And be witness to my Legacies, good Gentlemen;
Your Worship I do make my full Executor,
You are a man of wit and understanding:
Give me a cup of Wine to raise my Spirits,
For I speak low: I would before these Neighbours
Have ye to swear, Sir, that you will see it executed,
And what I g^ve let equally be rendred
For my souls health.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I vow it truly, Neighbours,
Let not that trouble ye, before all these,
Once more I give my Oath.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Then set me higher,
And pray ye come near me all.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: We are ready for ye.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Now spur the Ass, and get our friend time.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: First then,
After I have given my body to the worms,
(For they must be serv'd first, they are seldom cozen'^)

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Remember your Parish, Neighbour.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: You speak truly,
I do remember it, a lewd vile Parish,
And pray it may be mended: To the poor of it,
(Which is to all the Parish) I give nothing,
For nothing, unto nothing, is most natural,
Yet leave as much space, as will build an Hospital,
Their Children may pray for me.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: What do you give to it?

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Set down two thousand Duckets.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: 'Tis a good gift,
And will be long remembred.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: To your worship,
(Because you must take pains to see all finish'd)
I give two thousand more, it may be three, Sir,
A poor gratuity for your pains-taking.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: These are large sums.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Nothing to him that has 'em.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: To my old Master Vicar, I give five hundred,
(Five hundred and five hundred are too few, Sir)
But there be more to serve.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: This fellow coins sure.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Give me some more drink. Pray ye buy Books, b^ Books
You have a learned head, stuff it with Libraries,
And understand 'em, when ye have done, 'tis Justice.
Run not the Parish mad with Controversies,
Nor preach Abstinence to longing Women,
'Twill burge the bottoms of their Consciences:
I would give the Church new Organs, but I prophesie
The Church-wardens would quickly pipe'em out o'th' Parish
Two hundred Duckets more to mend the Chancel,
And to paint true Orthographie, as many,
They write Sunt with a C, which is abominable,
'Pray you set that down; to poor Maidens Marriages.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: I that's well thought of, what's your will in that po^
A meritorious thing.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: No end of this Will?

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: I give per annum two hundred Ells of Lockram,
That there be no strait dealings in their Linnens,
But the Sails cut according to their Burthens.
To all Bell-ringers, I bequeath new Ropes,
And let them use 'em at their own discretions.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: You may remember us.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: I do good Gentlemen,
And I bequeath you both good careful Surgions,
A Legacy, you have need of, more than mony,
I know you want good Diets, and good Lotions,
And in your pleasures, good take heed.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: He raves now,
But 'twill be quickly off.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: I do bequeath ye
Commodities of Pins, Brown-papers, Pack-threads,
Rost Pork, and Puddings, Ginger-bread, and Jews tru^
Of penny Pipes, and mouldy Pepper, take 'em,
Take 'em even where you please and be cozen'd with 'em,
I should bequeath ye Executions also,
But those I'le leave to th' Law.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Now he grows temperate.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: You will give no more?

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: I am loth to give more from ye,
Because I know you will have a care to execute.
Only, to pious uses, Sir, a little.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: If he be worth all these, I am made for ever.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: I give to fatal Dames, that spin mens threads out,
^nd poor distre^sed Damseis, that are militant
^s members of our own Afflictions,

^
^red Crowns to buy warm Tubs to work in,
^ give five hundred pounds to buy a Church-yard,
^ spacious Church-yard, to lay Thieves and Knaves in,
^ich men and honest men take all the room up.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Are ye not weary?

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Never of well doing.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: These are mad Legacies.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: They were got as madly;
My S^eep, and Oxen, and my moveables,
My Plate, and Jewels, and five hundred Acres;
^ have no heirs.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: This cannot be, 'tis monstrous.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Three Ships at Sea too.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: You have made me full Executor?

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Full, full, and total, would I had more to give ye,
^ut these may serve an honest mind.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Ye say true,
^ very honest mind, and make it rich too;
^ich, wondrous rich, but where shall I raise these moneys,
^bout your house? I see no such great promises;
Where shall I find these sums?

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Even where you please, Sir,
^ou are wise and provident, and know business,
^v'n raise 'em where you shall think good, I am reasonable.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Think good? will that raise thousands?
What do you make me?

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: You have sworn to see it done, that's all my comfort.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Where I please? this is pack'd sure to disgrace me.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Ye are just, and honest, and I know you will do it,
^'n where you please, for you know where the wealth is.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I am abused, betrayed, I am laugh'd at, scorn'd,
^affl'd, and boared, it seems.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: No, no, ye are fooled.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Most finely fooled, and handsomely, and neatly,
^ch cunning Masters must be fool'd sometimes, Sir,
^nd have their Worships noses wiped, 'tis healthful,
We are but quit: you fool us of our moneys
^ every Cause, in every Quiddit wipe us.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Ha, ha, ha, ha, some more drink, for my heart, Gentlemen.
^his merry Lawyer—ha, ha, ha, ha, this Scholar—
^ think this fit will cure me: this Executor—
^ shall laugh out my Lungs.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: This is derision above sufferance, villany
^otted and set against me.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Faith 'tis Knavery,
^ troth I must confess, thou art fool'd indeed, Lawyer.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Did you think, had this man been rich—

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: 'Tis well, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: He would have chosen such a Wolf, a Canker,
^ Maggot-pate, to be his whole Executor?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: A Lawyer, that entangles all mens honesties,
^nd lives like a Spider in a Cobweb lurking,
^nd catching at all Flies, that pass his pit-falls?
^uts powder to all States, to make 'em caper?
Would he trust you? Do you deserve?

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: I find, Gentlemen,
^his Cataplasm of a well cozen'd Lawyer
^aid to my stomach, lenisies my Feaver,
Methinks I could eat now, and walk a little.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I am asham'd to feel how stat I am cheated,
^ow grossly, and maliciously made a May-game,
^ damned trick; my Wife, my Wife, some Rascal:
My Credit, and my Wife, some lustful Villain,
^ome Bawd, some Rogue.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Some crafty Fool has found ye:
This 'tis, Sir, to teach ye to be too busie,
^o covet all the gains, and all the rumours,
^o have a stirring Oare in all mens actions.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: We did this, but to vex your fine officiousness.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Good yield ye, and good thank ye: I am fooled, Gentlemen;
The Lawyer is an Ass, I do confess it,
A weak dull shallow Ass: good even to your Worships:
Vicar, remember: Vicar, Rascal, remember,
Thou notable rich Rascal.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: I do remember, Sir,
'Pray ye stay a little, I have ev'n two Legacies
To make your mouth up, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Remember Varlets,
Quake and remember, Rogues;
I have brine for your Buttocks.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Oh how he frets, and sumes now like a Dunghil!

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: His gall contains fine stuff now to make poysons,
Rare damned stuff.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Let's after him, and still vex him,
And take my Friend off: by this time be has prosper'd,
He cannot lose this dear time: 'tis impossible.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Well Diego, thou hast done.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Hast done it daintily.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: And shalt be as well paid, Boy—

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Go, let's crucifie him.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: I have told ye all my story, and how desperately.

speeches.speaker: Ama.
verse: I do believe: let's walk on, time is pretious,
Not to be spent in words, here no more wooing,
The open Air's an enemy to Lovers,
Do as I tell ye.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: I'le do any thing,
I am so over-joy^'d, I'le fly to serve ye

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Take your joy moderately, as it is ministred,
And as the cause invites: that man's a fool
That at the sight o'th' Bond, dances and leaps,
Then is the true joy, when the mony comes.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: You cannot now deny me.

speeches.speaker: Ama.
verse: Nay, you know not,
Women have crotchets, and strange fits.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: You shall not.

speeches.speaker: Ama.
verse: Hold ye to that and swear it confidently,
Then I shall make a scruple to deny ye:
'Pray ye let's step in, and see a friend of mine,
The weather's sharp: we'll slay but half an hour,
We may be miss'd else: a private fine house 'tis, Sir,
And we may find many good welcomes.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: Do Lady,
Do happy Lady.

speeches.speaker: Ama.
verse: All your mind's of doing,
You must be modester.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: I will be any thing.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Open the doors, and give me room to chase in
Mine own room, and my liberty: why Maid there,
Open I say, and do not anger me,
I am subject to much fury: when, ye Dish clout?
When do ye come? asleep ye lazie Hell-hound?
Nothing intended, but your case, and eating?
No body here? why Wife, why Wife? why Jewel?
No tongue to answer me? pre'thee, good Pupil,
Dispense a little with thy careful study,
And step to th' door, and let me in; nor he neither?
Ha! not at's study? nor asleep? nor no body?
I'le make ye hear: the house of ignorance,
No sound inhabits here: I have a Key yet
That commands all: I fear I am Metamorphiz'd.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: He keeps his fury still, and may do mischief.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: He shall be hang'd first, we'll be sticklers there, boys.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: The hundred thousand Dreams now, that possess him
Of jealousie, and of revenge, and frailtie,
Of drawing Bills against us, and Petitions.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: And casting what his credit shall recover.

speeches.speaker: Mil
verse: Let him cast till his Maw come up, we care not.
You shall b still se^nt^.

speeches.speaker: Di^.
verse: We'll pay him home then;
H^ w^t a noise he keeps within!

speeches.speaker: ^ p
verse:
W^
^, or the Devil roars there.

speeches.speaker: D^
verse: ^ Law are broke loose, Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: A s
verse: H ^ghting sure.
I'^ t^ll ye that immediately—

speeches.speaker: Mil
verse: O^ doing some strange out rage on himself.

speeches.speaker: A s.
verse: Ha^g him, ^ da^s not be so valiant.

speeches.speaker: Di^.
verse: There's no body at home, and he chases like a Lyon,
And ^ withal.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: No body?
Not a Creature,
Nothing within, but he and his Law tempest,
The Ladl^s, D^shes, Kettles, how they she all!
And how the Glasses through the Rooms!

speeches.speaker: Ars
verse: My friend sure
Has got her out, and now he has made an end on't.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: See where the Sea comes? how it soums, and brustles?
Th^ great L^ v^athan o'th' Law, how it tumbles?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Made every way an Ass? abus'd on all sides?
And f^om all quarters, people come to laugh at me?
Rise like a Comet, to be wonder'd at?
A ho^d Com t, for Boys tongues, and Ballads?
I will run from my wits.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Do, do, good Lawyer,
And from thy mony too, then thou wilt be quiet.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Here she comes home: now mark the salutations;
How like an Ass my friend goes?

speeches.speaker: A^s.
verse: She has pull'd his cars down.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Now, what sweet voyage? to what Garden, Lady?
Or to what Coulins hous^?

speeches.speaker: Ama.
verse: Is this my welcome?
I cannot go to Church, but thus I am scandal'd,
U^ no devotion for my soul, but Gentlemen

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: ^o Church?

speeches.speaker: A^.
verse: Yes, and ye keep sweet youths to wait upon me,
Sweet bred up youths, to be a credit to me.
T^e's your delight again, pray take him to ye,
He never comes nea^ me more to debase me.

speeches.speaker: Bar
verse: How's this how's this good wise, how, has he wrong'd ye?

speeches.speaker: Ama
verse: I was ^m to drive him like a sheep before me,
I blu^h to think how people steer'd, and scorn'd me.
Others have handsome men, that know behaviour,
Place, and observance: this silly thing knows nothing,
Cannot tell ten; let every Rascal just^e me,
And still I push'd him on as he had been coming.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Ha^ did ye push him on? is he so stupid?

speeches.speaker: Ama
verse: When others were attentive to the Priest,
G^od devout Gentleman, then fell he fast,
^ast, sound asleep: then hist began the Bag pipes,
^ several stops on's no^e made a rate musick,
A ^e and l^ud, and those plaid many an Anthem.
^u^ out of that, he ^ell straight into dreaming.

speeches.speaker: Ars
verse: As cunning, as she is sweet, I like this carriage.

speeches.speaker: Bar
verse: What ^id he then?

speeches.speaker: Ama
verse: Why then be talked in his Sleep too,
Nay, I'le divulge your moral vertues (sheeps face)
And talk^d a loud, t^at every ^a^ was fixt to him:
D^ not I suffer (do you think) in this time?
^ of your baw^ng Law, of app^lations
O^ Declarations, and Excommunications:
Wa^ants, and ^x^utions: and such Devils
^ a^l the Gentlem^n out o'th' Church, by hurryes,

W^
^, they would never come there again.
Thus am I served and man'd.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: I pray ye forgive me,
I must confess I am not fit to wait upon ye:
Alas, I was brought up—

speeches.speaker: Ama.
verse: To be an Asse,
A Lawyers Asse, to carry Books, and Buckrams.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: But what did you at Church?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: At Church, did you ask her?
Do you hear Gentlemen, do you mark that question?
Because you are half an Heretick your self, Sir,
Would ye breed her too? this shall to the Inquisition,
A pious Gentlewoman reproved for praying?
I'le see this filed, and you shall hear further, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ars
verse: Ye have an ill heart.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: It shall be found out, Gentlemen,
There be those youths will search it.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: You are warm Signiour,
But a Faggot will warm ye better: we are witnesses.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Enough to hang him, do not doubt.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Nay certain,
I do believe h'as rather no Religion.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: That must be known too, because she goes to Church S^
O monstrum informe ingens!

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Let him go on, Sir,
His wealth will build a Nunnery, a fair one,
And this good Lady, when he is hang'd and rotten,
May there be Abbess.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: You are cozen'd, honest Gentlemen,
I do not forbid the use but the form, mark me.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Form? what do you make of form?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: They will undo me,
Swear, as I oft have done, and so betray me;
I must make fair way, and hereafter, Wife,
You are welcome home, and henceforth take your pleasure,
Go when ye shall think fit, I will not hinder ye,
My eyes are open now, and I see my errour,
My shame, as great as that, but I must hide it.
The whole conveyance now I smell, but Basta,
Another time must serve: you see us friends, now
Heartily friends, and no more chiding, Gentlemen,
I have been too foolish, I confess, no more words,
No more, sweet Wife.

speeches.speaker: Ama.
verse: You know my easie nature.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Go get ye in: you see she has been angry:
Forbear her fight a while and time will pacify;
And learn to be more bold.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: I would I could,
I will do all I am able.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Do Leandro,
We will not part, but friends of all hands.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Well said,
Now ye are reasonable, we can look on ye.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Ye have jerkt me: but for all that I forgive ye,
Forgive ye heartily, and do invite ye
To morrow to a Breakfast, I make but seldom,
But now we will be merry.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Now ye are friendly,
Your doggedness and niggardize slung from ye.
And now we will come to ye.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Give me your hands, all;
You shall be welcome heartily.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: We will be,
For we'll eat hard.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: The harder, the more welcome,
And till the morning farewell; I have business.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Farewel good bountiful Bartolus, 'tis a brave wen^,
A suddain witty thief, and worth all service:
Go we'll all go, and crucifie the Lawyer.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: I'le clap four tire of teeth into my mouth more
But I will grind his substance.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Well Leandro,
Thou hast had a strange Voyage, but I hope
Thou rid'st now in safe harbour.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Let's go drink, Friends,
And laugh aloud at all our merry may-games.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: A match, a match, 'twill whet our stomachs better.
MAdam, he's come.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: 'Tis well, how did he look,
^en he knew from whom you were sent? was he not startled?
Or confident? or fearful?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: As appear'd
^ike one that knew his fortune at the worst,
And car'd not what could follow.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: 'Tis the better,
^each me a Chair: so, bring him in, be careful
That none disturb us: I will try his temper,
And if I find him apt for my employments,
^le work him to my ends; if not, I shall
^ind other Engines.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: There's my Lady.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Leave us.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: You sent for me?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: I did, and do's the favour,
Your present state considered and my power,
Deserve no greater Ceremony?

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Ceremonie?
^se to pay that where I owe a duty,
^o^ to my Brothers wife: I cannot fawn,
^ you expect it from me, you are cozen'd,
And so farewel.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: He bears up still; I like it.
^ray you a word.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Yes, I will give you hearing
^a equal terms, and sit by you as a friend,
^et not stand as a Sutor: Now your pleasure?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: You are very bold.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: 'Tis fit: since you are proud,
^ was not made to feed that foolish humour,
^ith flattery and observance.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Yet, with your favour,
A little form joyn'd with respect to her,
That can add to your wants, or free you from 'em
Nay raise you to a fate, beyond your hopes)
^ight well become your wisdom.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: It would rather
^rite me a Fool, should I but only think
That any good to me could flow from you,
^hom for so many years I have found and prov'd
My greatest Enemy: I am still the same,
My wants have not transform'd me: I dare tell you,
^o your new cerus'd face, what I have spoken
^tely behind your back, what I think of you,
^ou are the proudest thing, and have the least
^eason to be so that I ever read of.
^n stature you are a Giantess: and your Tailor
Takes measure of you with a Jacobs Staff,
^ he can never reach you, this by the way
^or your large size: now, in a word or two,
^o treat of your Complexion were decorum:
^ou are so far from fair, I doubt your Mother
^as too familiar with the Moor that serv'd her,
^our Limbs and Features I pass briefly over,
^s things not worth description; and come roundly
To your Soul, if you have any; for 'tis doubtful.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: I laugh at this, proceed.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: This Soul I speak of,
Or rather Salt to keep this heap of flesh
^rom being a walking stench, like a large Inn,
Stands open for the entertainment of
All impious practices: but there's no Corner
An honest thought can take up: and as it were not
Sufficient in your self to comprehend
All wicked plots, you have taught the Fool, my Brother,
By your contagion, almost to put off
The nature of the man, and turn'd him Devil,
Because he should be like you, and I hope
Will march to Hell together: I have spoken,
And if the Limning you in your true Colours
Can make the Painter gracious, I stand ready
For my reward, or if my words distaste you,
I weigh it not, for though your Grooms were ready
To cut my Throat for't, be assur'd I cannot
Use other Language.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: You think you have said now,
Like a brave fellow: in this Womans War
You ever have been train'd: spoke big, but suffer'd
Like a tame Ass; and when most spur'd and gall'd
Were never Master of the Spleen or Spirit,
That could raise up the anger of a man,
And force it into action.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Yes, vile Creature,
Wer't thou a subject worthy of my Sword,
Or that thy death, this moment, could call home
My banish'd hopes, thou now wer't dead; dead, woman;
But being as thou art, it is sufficient
I scorn thee, and contemn thee.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: This shews nobly,
I must confess it: I am taken with it,
For had you kneel'd and whin'd and shew'd a base
And low dejected mind, I had despis'd you.
This bravery (in your adverse fortune) conquers
And do's command me, and upon the suddain
I feel a kind of pity, growing in me,
For your misfortunes, pity some say's the Parent,
Of future love, and I repent my part
So far in what you have suffered, that I could
(But you are cold) do something to repair
What your base Brother (such Jamie I think him)
Hath brought to ruine.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Ha?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Be not amaz'd,
Our injuries are equal in his Bastard,
You are familiar with what I groan for,
And though the name of Husband holds a tye
Beyond a Brother, I, a poor weak Woman,
Am sensible, and tender of a wrong,
And to revenge it would break through all lets,
That durst oppose me.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Is it possible?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: By this kiss: start not: thus much, as a stranger
You may take from me; but, if you were pleas'd,
I should select you as a bosom friend,
I would print 'em thus, and thus.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Keep off.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Come near,
Near into the Cabinet of my Counsels:
Simplicity and patience dwell with Fools,
And let them bear those burthens, which wise men
Boldly shake off; be mine and joyn with me,
And when that I have rais'd you to a fortune,
(Do not deny your self the happy means)
You'll look on me with more judicious eyes
And swear I am most fair.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: What would this Woman?
The purpose of these words? speak not in riddles,
And when I understand, what you would counsel,
My answer shall be suddain.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Thus then Jamie,
The objects of our fury are the same,
For young Ascanio, whom you Snake like hug'd
(Frozen with wants to death) in your warm bosom,
Lives to supplant you in your certain hopes,
A^ falls in me all comfort.

speeches.speaker: ^am.
verse: Now 'tis plain,
I apprehend you: and were he remov'd

verse: Y^, once a^ain, were the undoubted heir.
^is not to be deny'd; I was see before,

A man that knows the World.
I needs must learn
That have so good a Tu^ss: and what think you,
That none may ^e, that shall desire to trace us
^o ou^ black paths, if that Octavio
His soft^ Father, and the sad Ja^ta,

W^ murther, let us often bath in blood,

speeches.speaker: V^
verse: And that's glorious,
And will protect the fact.

speeches.speaker: ^am.
verse: Suppose this done:
(I^ undiscovered) we may get for mony.
(As that ^ou know buyes any thing in Rome)
A disp^sation.

speeches.speaker: V^
verse: And be married?
O^ that be known, t^ss up out Gold and Jewels,
And ^ to some ^ State, ^n there with scorn

speeches.speaker: V^l.
verse: Laugh at the laws of Spain.
I were a ^able.
^ shall beg^t rare children. I am rapt with

T^
^ imagination.

speeches.speaker: V^.
verse: S^all it be done?

speeches.speaker: ^m.
verse: S^all? 'tis too tedious: furnish me with means
To ^ the instruments, and to your self
Say it is ^ already: I will shew you,
^ the Sun set, how much you have wrought upon me,
^ p ovince is only to use some means,
To find my Brother to the Grove that's neighbour
To the well Port of th' City; leave the rest
^o^, own practice, I have talk'd too long,
Put now will doe: this kiss, with my Confession,
To work a fell revenge: a man's a fool,
It not instructed in a Womans School.

speeches.speaker: B^
verse: You are well enough disguiz'd, furnish the Table,
Ma^ no shew what ye are, till I discover:
Not a so^ knows ye here: be quick and diligent,
These youths I have invited to a Breakfast,
^ut what the Sawes will ^, I am of opinion
I shall take of the ^ of their Appetites,

^ case ^
^ns for eating heartily
^ have plaid their prizes with me,
And ^ have lighted dangerously,
^ qui^ I hea^ 'em coming.
Go off and wait the bringing in your service,
And do it handsomely: you know where to have it.
Welcom i' Faith.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: That's well said, honest Lawyer.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Said like a neighbour.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Welcom all: all over,
And let's be merry.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: To that end we came Sir,
An hour of freedome's worth an age of juglings.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: I am come too Sir, to specifie my Stomach
A poor reteiner to your worships bountie.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: And thou shalt have it fill'd my merry Diego,
My liberal, and my bonny bounteous Diego,
Even fill'd till it groan again.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Let it have fair play,
And if it founder then.—

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I'le tell ye neighbours,
Though I were angry yesterday with ye all,
And very angry, for methought ye bob'd me.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: No, no, by no means.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: No, when I considered
It was a jest, and carried off so quaintly,
It made me merry: very merry, Gentlemen,
I do confess I could not sleep to think on't,
The mirth so tickled me, I could not slumber.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Good mirth do's work so: honest mirth,
Now, should we have meant in earnest—

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: You say true neighbour.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: It might have bred such a distast and sowrness,
Such fond imaginations in your Brains, Sir,
For things thrust home in earnest. —

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Very certain,
But I know ye all for merry waggs, and ere long
You shall know me too in another fashion,
Though y'are pamper'd, ye shall bear part o'th'burther
Come wife; Come bid 'em welcom; Come my Jew.
And Pupil, you shall come too; ne're hang backward,
Come, come the woman's pleas'd, her anger's over,
Come, be not bashfull.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: What do's he prepare here?
Sure there's no meat i'th' house, at least not drest,
Do's he mean to mock 'em? or some new bred crotcher
Come o're his brains; I do not like his kindness:
But silence best becomes me: if he mean foul play,
Sure they are enough to right themselves, and let 'em,
I'le sit by, so they beat him not to powder,

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Bring in the meat there, ha? Sit down dear up h^
A little meat needs little Complement,
Sit down I say.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: What do you mean by this Sir?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Convey away their weapons handsomely.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: You know there's none i'th' house to answer ye,
But the poor Girle; you know there's no meat neither.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Peace and be quiet; I shall make you smoak e^e,
There's men and meat enough, set it down formally.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: I fear some lewd trick, yet I dare not speak on't.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I have no dainties for ye Gentlemen,
Not loads of meat, to make the room smell of 'em.
Only a dish to every man I have dedicated,
And if I have pleas'd his appetite.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: O, a Capon,
A Bird of grace, and be thy will, I honour it.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: For me some fortie pound of lovely Be^,
Plac'd in a mediterranean sea of Brewis.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Fall to, fall to, that we may drink and laugh ^
Wait diligently knaves.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: What rare bit's this?
An execution! bless me!

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Nay take it to ye,
^e^'s no avoiding it, 'tis somewhat tough Sir,
^t a good stomach will endure it easily,
^he ^um is but a thousand duckets Sir.

speeches.speaker: A s.
verse: A Capias from my Surgeon, and my Silk-man!

speeches.speaker: ^ar.
verse: Your carefull makers, but they have mar'd your diet.
^ not, your Swords are gone: there's no avoiding me,
^re these are Algazeirs, do you hear that passing bell?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: A strong Citation, bless me!

speeches.speaker: ^a^
verse: Out with your Beads, Curate,
^ D^vil's in your dish: bell, book, and Candle.

speeches.speaker: Lop
verse: A warrant to appear before the Judges!
^mul^ needs rise, and turn to th' wall.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Ye need not,
^our fear I hope will make ye find your Breeches.

speeches.speaker: A^.
verse: We are betrai'd.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Invited do not wrong me,
^ to, good Guests, you have diligent men about ye,
^e shall want nothing that may persecute ye,
^se will not see ye start; Have I now found ye?
Have I requited ye? You fool'd the Lawyer,
^nd thought it meritorious to abuse him,
^ thick ram-headed knave: you rid, you spur'd him,
^nd glorified your wits, the more ye wronged him;
Within this hour ye shall have all your Creditours,
^ second dish of new debts, come upon ye,
^nd new invitements to the whip, Don Diego,
^nd Excommunications for the learned Curate,
^ Masque of all your furies shall dance to ye.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: You dare not use us thus?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: You shall be bob'd, Gentlemen,
^ir and as I have a life, ye goe to prison,
^o prison, without pitie instantly,
^efore ye speak another word to prison.
^ave a better Guard without, that waits;
^o you see this man, Don Curate? 'tis a Paratour
^ at comes to tell ye a delightfull story
Of an old whore ye have, and then to teach ye
What is the penaltie; Laugh at me now Sir,
What Legacie would ye bequeath me now,
And pay it on the nail?) to fly my fury?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: O gentle Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Do'st thou hope I will be gentle,
^hou foolish unconsiderate Curate?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Let me goe Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I'le see thee hang first.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: And as I am a true Vicar,
Hark in your ear, hark softly —

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: No, no bribery.
^'le have my swindge upon thee; Sirra? Rascal?
You Lenten Chaps, you that lay sick, and mockt me,
Mockt me abominably, abused me lewdly,
^'le make thee sick at heart, before I leave thee,
And groan, and dye indeed, and be worth nothing,
Not worth a blessing, nor a Bell to knell for thee,
A sheet to cover thee, but that thou stealest,
^tealest from the Merchant, and the Ring he was buried with
^tealest from his Grave, do you smell me now?

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Have mercy on me!

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: No Psalm of mercy shall hold me from hanging thee.
How do ye like your Breakfast? 'tis but short, Gentlemen,
But sweet and healthfull; Your punishment, and yours, Sir,
For some near reasons that concern my Credit,
I will take to my self

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Doe Sir, and spare not:
I have been too good a wife, and too obedient,
But since ye dare provoke me to be foolish —

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: She has, yes, and too worthie of your usage,
Before the world I justifie her goodness,
And turn that man, that dares but taint her vertues,
To my Swords point; that lying man, that base man,
Turn him, but face to face, that I may know him.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: What have I here?

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: A Gentleman, a free man,
One that made trial of this Ladies constancie,
And found it strong as la^e; leave off your fooling,
For if you follow this course, you will be Chronicled
For a devil, whilst a Saint she is mentioned,
You know my name indeed; I am now no Lawyer.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Som comfort now I hope, or else would I were hanged up.
And yet ^ Ju^g^, he ma^es me sweat.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: What news now?

speeches.speaker: Jam
verse: I will justifie upon my life and credit
What you have heard, for truth, and will make proof of.

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: I will be ready at the appointed hour there,
And so I leave ye.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Stay I beseech your worship,
And do but hear me.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Good Sir, intend this business,
And let this bawling fool, no more words lawyer,
And no more angers, for I guess your reasons,
This Gentleman, I'le justifie in all places,
And that fair Ladies worth; let who dare cross it.
The Plot was cast by me, to make thee jealous,
But not to wrong your wife, she is fair and vertuous.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Take us to mercy too, we beseech your honour,
We shall be justified the way of all flesh else.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: No more talk, nor no more dissention lawyer,
I know your anger, 'tis a vain and flight one,
For if you doe, I'le lay your whole life open,
A life that all the world shall — I'le bring witness,
And tip before a Judge the ulcerous villanies,
You know I know ye, and I can bring witness

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Nay good Sir, noble Sir.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Be at peace then presently,
Immediatley take honest and fair truce
With your good wise, and shake hands with that Gentleman;
H'as honour'd ye too much, and doe it cheerfully.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Take us along, for Heaven sake too.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I am friends,
There is no remedie, I must put up all,
And like my neighbours rub it out byth' shoulders,
And perfect friends; Leandro now I thank ye,
And there's my hand, I have no more grudge to ye,
But I am too mean hence forward for your Companie.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: I shall not trouble ye.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: We will be friends too.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Nay Lawyer, you shall not fright us farther,
For all your devils we will bolt.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I grant ye,
The Gentleman's your Bail, and thank his coming,
Did not he know me too well, you should smart ^or't;
Goe all in peace, but when ye fool next, Gentlemen,
Come not to me to Breakfast.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: I'le be bak'd first.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: And pray ye remember, when ye are bold and merry,
The Lawyers Banquet, and the Sawce he gave ye.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Come: goe along; I have employm^nt to ye,
Employment for your lewd brains too, to cool ye,
For all, for every one.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: We are all your Servants.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: All, all for any thing, from this day forward
I'le hate all Breakfasts, and depend on dinners.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: I am glad you come off fair.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: The fair has blest me.

speeches.speaker: Oct.
verse: This is the place, but why we are appointed
By Don Jamie to stay here, is a depth
I cannot sound.

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: Believ't he is too noble
To purpose any thing but for our good.
Had I assurance of a thousand lives,
And with them perpetuitie of pleasure,
And should lose all, if he prov'd only false,
Yet I durst run the hazard.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: 'Tis our comfort.
We cannot be more wretched than we are,
And death concludes all misery.

speeches.speaker: Oc^.
verse: Undiscovered
We must attend him.

speeches.speaker: As^.
verse: Out stay is not long.
With him Don Henrique?

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Now I fear;
Be ^lent.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Why dost thou follow me?

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: To save your life,
A p^ot is laid for't, all my wrongs forgot,
I have a Brothers Love.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: But thy false self
I fear no enemy.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: You have no friend,
But what breathes in me: If you move a step
Beyond this ground you tread on, you are lost.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: 'Tis by thy practice then: I am sent hither
To meet her, that prefers my life and safetie
Before her own.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: That you should be abus'd thus
With weak credulitie! She for whose sake
You have forgot we had one noble Father,
Or that one Mother bare us, for whose love
You brake a contract to which heaven was witness,
To satisfie whose pride and wilfull humour
You have expos'd a sweet and hopefull Son
To all the miseries that want can bring him,
And such a Son, though you are most obdurate,
To give whom entertainment Savages
Would quit their Caves themselves, to keep him from
Bleak cold and hunger: This dissembling woman,
This Idol, whom you worship, all your love
And service trod under her feet, designs you
To fill a grave, or dead to lye a prey
For Wolves and Vul^ms.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: 'Tis false; I defie thee,
And stand upon my Guard.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Alas, 'tis weak:
Come on, since you will teach me to be cruel,
By having no faith in me, take your fortune,
Bring the rest forth, and bind them fast.

speeches.speaker: Oct.
verse: My Lord.

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: In what have we offended?

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: I am deaf,
And following my will, I do not stand
Accomptable to reason: See her Ring
(The first pledge of your love, and service to her)
Deliver'd as a Warrant for your death:
These ^ags of gold you gave up to her trust,
(The use of which you did deny your self)
Bestow'd on me, and with a prodigal hand,
Whom ^he pick'd forth to be the Architect
Of her most bloudy building; and to see
These Instruments, to bring Materials
To raise it up, she bad me spare no cost,
And (as a surplusage) offer'd her self
To be at my devotion.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: O accurs'd!

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: But be incredulous still, think this my plot;
^a^en excuses to your self, and swear
That she is innocent, that she doats on ye;
To have this, as a fearfull Dream, and that
^ he not at my mercy, which in this
I w^l ^h^ only. She he^ self shall give

^
^ull Sent^n^e, to remove all scruple
Who 'tis that sends you to the other world.
Appears my Violante? speak (my dearest)
Do's not the object please you?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: More than if
All treasure that's above the earth, with that,
That lyes conceal'd in both the Indian Mines,
Were laid down at my feet: O bold Jamy,
Thou only canst deserve me.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: I am forward,
And (as you easily may perceive,) I sleep not
On your commands.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: But yet they live: I look'd
To find them dead.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: That was deferr'd, that you
Might triumph in their misery, and have the power
To say they are not.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: 'Twas well thought upon:
This kiss, and all the pleasures of my Bed
This night, shall thank thee.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Monster!

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: You Sir, that
Would have me Mother Bastards, being unable
To honour me with one Child of mine own,
That underneath my roof, kept your cast-Strumpet,
And out of my Revenues would maintain
Her riotous issue: now you find what 'tis
To tempt a woman: with as little feeling
As I turn off a slave, that is unfit
To doe me service; or a horse, or dog
That have out-liv'd their use, I shake thee off,
To make thy peace with heaven.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: I do deserve this,
And never truly felt before, what sorrow
Attends on wilfull dotage.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: For you, Mistris,
That had the pleasure of his youth before me,
And triumph'd in the fruit that you had by him,
But that I think, to have the Bastard strangled
Before thy face, and thou with speed to follow
The way he leads thee, is sufficient torture,
I would cut off thy nose, put out thine eyes,
And set my foot on these bewitching lips,
That had the start of mine: but as thou art,
Goe to the grave unpitied.

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: Who would believe
Such rage could be in woman?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: For this fellow,
He is not worth my knowledge.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Let him live then,
Since you esteem him innocent.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: No Jamy,
He shall make up the mess: now strike together,
And let them fall so.

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: Unheard of crueltie!
I can endure no longer: seise on her.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Am I betrai'd?
Is this thy faith, Jamy?

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Could your desires
Challenge performance of a deed so horrid?
Or, though that you had sold your self to hell,
I should make up the bargain? Live (dear Brother)
Live long, and happy: I forgive you freely;
To have done you this service, is to me
A fair Inheritance: and how e're harsh language
(Call'd on by your rough usage) pass'd my lips,
In my heart I ever lov'd you: all my labours
Were but to shew, how much your love was cozen'd,
When it beheld it self in this false Glass,
That did abuse you; and I am so far
From envying young Ascanio his good fortune,
That if your State were mine, I would adopt him,
These are the Murtherers my noble friends,
Which (to make trial of her bloudy purpose)
^won, to come disguis'd thus.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: I am too full
Of grief, and shame to speak: but what I'le doe,
^all to the world proclaim my penitence;
^d howsoever I have liv'd, I'le die
^ much chang'd man.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Were it but possible
You could make satisfaction to this woman,
^r joyes were perfect.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: That's my only comfort,
That it is in my power: I ne're was married
To this bad woman, though I doted on her,
But daily did defer it, still expecting
When grief would kill Jacintha.

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: All is come out,
And finds a fair success: take her Don Henrique,
And once again embrace your Son.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Most gladly.

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: Your Brother hath deserv'd all.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: And shall share
The moitie of my State.

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: I have heard, advocate,
What an ill Instrument you have been to him,
From this time strengthen him with hones^ counsels,
As you'le deserve my pardon.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I'le change my Copy:
But I am punish'd, for I fear I have had
A smart blow, though unseen.

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: Curate, and Sexton,
I have heard of you too, let me hear no more,
And what's past, is forgotten; For this woman,
Though her intent were bloody, yet our Law
Calls it not death: yet that her punishment
May deter others from such bad attempts,
The dowry she brought with her, shall be emploi'd
To build a Nunnery, where she shall spend
The remnant of her life.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Since I have miss'd my ends,
I scorn what can fall on me.

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: The strict discipline
Of the Church, will teach you better thoughts. And Signiors,
You that are Batchelours, if you ever marry,
In Bartolus you may behold the issue
Of Covetousness and Jealousie; and of dotage,
And falshood in Don Henrique: keep a mean then;
For be assur'd, that weak man meets all ill,
That gives himself up to a womans will.

speeches.speaker: Merc.
prose: WHen saw you Valentine?

speeches.speaker: ~ncle.
prose: Not since the Horse-race, he's taken up with those that woo the Widow.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: How can he live by snatches from such people? he bore a worthy mind,

speeches.speaker: ~ncle.
prose: Alas, he's sunk, his means are gone, he wants, and which is worse,
Takes a delight in doing so.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: That's strange.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Runs Lamatick, if you but talk of states, he cannot be brought (now he has spent his own) to think there's inheritance, or means, but all a common riches, all men bound to be his Bailiffs.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: This is something dangerous.

speeches.speaker: ~ncle.
prose: No Gentleman that has estate to use it in keeping house, or followers, for those wayes he cries against, for Eating sins, dull Surfeits, cramming of Serving men, mustering of Beggars, maintaining Hospitals for Kites, and Cu^s, grounding their fat faiths upon old Country proverbs, God bless the Founders; these he would have ventured into to more manly uses, Wit, and carriage, and never thinks of state, or means, the ground-works: holding it monstrous, men should feed their bodies, and starve their understandings

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: That's most certain.

speeches.speaker: ~ncle.
prose: Yes, if he could stay there.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Why let him marry, and that way rise again.

speeches.speaker: ~ncle.
prose: It's most impossible, he will not look with any handsomeness upon a Woman.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Is he so strange to Women?

speeches.speaker: ~ncle.
prose: I know not what it is, a foolish glory he has goe, I know not where, to balk those benefits, and yet he wil converse and flatter 'em, make 'em, or fair, or soul, ^gged, or smooth, as his impression serves, for he affirms they are only lumps, and undigested pieces, lickt over to a form by our affections, and then they show. The Lovers let 'em pass.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: He might be one, he carries as much promise; they are wondrous merry.

speeches.speaker: ~ncle.
prose: O their hopes are high, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fount.
prose: Is Valentine come to Town?

speeches.speaker: Bella.
prose: Last night, I heard.

speeches.speaker: Fount.
prose: We miss him monstrously in our directions, for this Widow is as stately, and as crafty, and stands I war~rant you—

speeches.speaker: Hair.
prose: Let her stand sure, she falls before us else, co^ let's go seek Valentine.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: This Widow seems a Gallant.

speeches.speaker: ~ncle.
prose: A goodly Woman, and to her handsomness ^ bears her state, reserved, and great Fortune has made ^ Mistress of a full means, and well she knows to use it.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: I would Valentine had her.

speeches.speaker: ~ncle.
prose: There's no hope of that, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: O' that condition, he had his Mortgage in again.

speeches.speaker: ~ncle.
prose: I would he had.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose:
Seek means, and see what I'le do, however let ^e Money be paid in, I never sought a Gentlemans undo
^g, nor eat the bread of other mens vexations, you told ^e of another Brother.

speeches.speaker: ~ncle.
prose: Yes Sir, more miserable than he, for he has eat ^m, and drunk him up, a handsome Gentleman, and fine ^holar.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: What are these?

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: The Tenants, they'll do what they can.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: It is well prepared, be earnest, honest friends, and ^d upon him, he is deaf to his own good.

speeches.speaker: Lance.
prose: We mean to tell him part of our minds an't please ^ou.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Do, and do it home, and in what my care may ^elp, or my perswasions when we meet next.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Do but perswade him fairly; and for your money, ^ine, and these mens thanks too, and what we can be able.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Y'are most honest, you shall find me no less, and ^ I leave you, prosper your business my friends.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Pray Heaven it may, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lance.
prose:
Nay if he will be mad, I'le be mad with him, and ^ell him that I'le not spare him, his Father kept good Meat, ^ood Drink, good Fellows, good Hawks, good Hounds, ^nd bid his Neighbours welcome; kept him too, and sup
^lied his prodigality, yet kept his state still; must we turn Tenants now, after we have lived under the race of Gentry, ^nd maintained good Yeomantry, to some of the City, to ^ great shoulder of Mutton and a Custard, and have our ^ate turned into Cabbidge Gardens, must it be so?

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: You must be milder to him.

speeches.speaker: Lance.
prose: That's as he makes his game.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Intreat him lovingly, and make him feel.

speeches.speaker: Lance.
prose: I'le pinch him to the bones else.

speeches.speaker: Valen.
prose: And tell the Gentleman, I'le be with ^im presently, say I want money too, I must not fail boy.

speeches.speaker: Lance.
prose: You'l want Cloaths, I hope.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Bid the young Courtier repair to me anon, I'le read ^o him.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: He comes, de diligent, but not too rugged, start ^im, but affright him not.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Phew, are you there?

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: We come to see you Nephew, be not angry.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose:
Why do you dog me thus, with these strange peo
^le? why, all the world shall never make me rich more, ^or master of these troubles.

speeches.speaker: Tenants.
prose: We beseech you for our poor Childrens sake.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Who bid you get 'em? have you not threshing work ^nough, but Children must be bang'd out o'th' sheaf too? other men with all their delicates, and healthful diets, can ^et but wind eggs: you with a clove of Garlick, a piece of Cheese would break a Saw, and sowre Milk, can mount ^ike Stallions, and I must maintain these tumblers.

speeches.speaker: Lance.
prose: You ought to maintain us, we have maintained you, and when you slept provided for you; who bought the Silk you wear? I think our labours; reckon, you'll find it so: who found your Horses perpetual pots of Ale, maintain'd your Taverns, and who extol'd you in the Half-crown-boxes, where you might sit and muster all the Beauties? we had no hand in these; no, we are all puppies?
Your Tenants base vexations.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Very well, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lance.
prose: Had you Land, Sir, and honest men to serve your purposes, honest and faithful, and will you run away from 'em, betray your self, and your poor Tribe to misery; mortgage all us, like old Cloaks; where will you hunt next? you had a thousand Acres, fair and open: The Kings-Bench is enclosed, there's no good ^iding, the Counter is full of tho^ as and brakes, take heed Si^, and boggs, you'l quickly find what broth they're made of.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Y'are short and pithy.

speeches.speaker: Lance.
prose: They say y'are a fine Gentleman, and of excellent judgement, they report you have a wit; keep your self out o'th' Rain, and take your Cloak with you, which by interpretation is your State, Sir, or I shall think your same belied you, you have money, and may have means.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: I pret^ee leave p^ating, does my good lye within thy brain to further, or my undoing in thy pity? go, go, get you home, there whistle to your Ho^ses, and let them edifie; away, fow Hemp to hang your selves withal: what am I to you, or you to me; am I your Landlord, puppies?

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: This is un^vil.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: More unmerciful you, to vex me with these Bacon Broth and Puddings, they are the walking shapes of all my sorrows.

speeches.speaker: 3 Tenants.
prose: Your Fathers Worship would have used us better.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: My Fathers Worship was a Fool.

speeches.speaker: Lance.
prose: Hey, hey boys, old Valentine i'saith, the old boy still.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Fie Cousin.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: I mean besotted to his state, he had never left me the misery of so much means else, which till I fold, was a meer meagrim to me: If you will talk, turn out these Tenants, they are as killing to my nature Uncle, as water to a Feaver.

speeches.speaker: Lance.
prose: We will go, but it is like Rams, to come again the stronger, and you shall keep your state.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Thou lyest, I will not.

speeches.speaker: Lance.
prose: Sweet Sir, thou lyest, thou shalt, and so good morrow.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: This was my man, and of a noble breeding: now to your business Uncle.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: To your state then.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: 'Tis gone, and I am glad on't, name it no more, 'tis that I pray against, and Heaven has heard me, I tell you, Sir, I am more fearful of it, I mean, of thinking of more lands, or livings, than sickly men are travelling of Sundays, for being quell'd with Carriers; out upon't, cav^at emptor, let the fool out-sweat it, that thinks he has got a catch on't.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: This is madness to be a wilful begger.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: I am mad then, and so I mean to be, will that content you? How bravely now I live, how jo^nd, how near the first inheritance, without fears, how free from t^e troubles!

speeches.speaker: ~ne.
prose: And from means too.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Means? why all good men's my means; my wit's my Plow, the Town's my stock, Tavern's my standing house, and all the world knows there's no want; all Gentlemen that love Society, love me; all Purses that wit and pleasure opens, are my Tenants; every mans Cloaths fit me, the next fair lodging is but my next remove, and when I please to be more eminent, and take the Air, a piece is lev^ed, and a Coach prepared, and I go I care not whither, what need state here?

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: But say these means were honest, will they last, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Far longer than your jerkin, and wear fairer, should I take ought of you, 'tis true, I beg'd now, or which is worse than that, I stole a kindness, and which is worst of all, I lost my way in't; your mind's enclosed, nothing lies open nobly, your very thoughts are Hinds that work on nothing but daily sweat and trouble: were my way so full of dirt as this, 'tis true I'd shift it; are my acquaintance Grasiers? but Sir, know, no man that I am allied to, in my living, but makes it equal, whether his own use, o^ my necessity pull first, nor is this forc'd, but the mee^ quality and poisure of goodness, and do you think I venture nothing equal?

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: You pose me Cousin.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose:
What's my knowledge Uncle, is't not worth mony? what's my understanding, travel, reading, wit, all these
digested, my daily making men, some to speak, that too much ^legm had frozen up, some that spoke too much, to hold their peace, and put their tongues to pensions, some to wear then cloaths, and some to keep 'em, these are nothing Uncle; besides these wayes, to teach the way of nature, a manly love, community to all that are deservers, not examining how much, or what's done for them, 'tis wicked, and such a one like you, chews his thoughts doule, making 'em only food for his repentance.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
prose: This cloak and hat Sir, and my Masters love.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Commend's to thy Master, and take that, and leave '^m at my lodging.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
prose: I shall do it Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: I do not think of these things.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
prose: Please you Sir, I have gold here for you.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Give it me, drink that and commend me to thy Master; look you Uncle, do I beg these?

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: No sure, 'tis your worth, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: 'Tis like enough, but pray satisfie me, are not these ways as honest as persecuting the starved inheritance, with musty Corn, the very rats were fain to run away from, or selling rotten wood by the pound, like spices, which Gentlemen do after burn by th'ounces? do not I know your way of feeding beasts with grains, and windy stuff, to blow up Butchers? your racking Pastures, that have eaten up as many ^nging Shepherds, and their issues, as Andeluzia breeds? these are authentique, I tell you Sir, I would not change ways with you, unless it were to sell your state that hour, and if it were possible to spend it then too, for all your Beans in Rumnillo, now you know me.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: I would you knew your self, but since you are grown such a strange enemy to all that sits you, give me leave to make your Brothers fortune.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: How?

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: From your mortgage, which yet you may recover, I'le find the means.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Pray save your labour Sir, my Brother and my self will run one fortune, and I think what I hold a meer vexation, cannot be safe for him, I love him better, he has wit at will, the world has means, he shall live without this trick of state, we are heirs both, and all the world before us.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: My last offer, and then I am gone.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: What is't, and then I'le answer.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: What think you of a wise yet to restore you, and tell me seriously without these trifles.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: And you can find one, that can please my fancy, you shall not find me stubborn.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Speak your Woman.

speeches.speaker: Val
prose: One without eyes, that is, self commendations, for when they find they are handsom, they are unwholsome, one without ears, not giving time to flatterers, for she that hears her self commended, wavers, and points men out a way to make 'em wicked; one without substance of her self; that woman without the pleasure of her life, that's wanton; though she be young, forgetting it, though fair, making her glass the eyes of honest men, not her own admiration, all her ends obedience, all her hours new blessings, if there may be such a woman.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Yes there may be.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: And without state too

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: You are disposed to trifle, well, fare you well Sir, when you want me next, you'l seek me out a better sence.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Farewell Uncle, and as you love your estate, let not me hear on't.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: It shall not trouble you, I'le watch him still,
And when his friends fall off then bend his will.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: I know the cause of all this sadness now, your sister ^a ^ng^ost all the brave Lovers.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: She has where withall, much good may't do her, prethee speak softly, we are open to mens ears.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: Fear not, we are safe, we may see all that pass, her all, and make our selves merry with their language, a^ yet stand undiscovered, be not melancholy, you are as far as she.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Who I? I thank you, I am as haste ordain'd me, ^ thing slubber'd, my sister is a goodly portly Lady, a wo^ of a presence, she spreads sattens, as the Kings ships ^ canvas every where, she may spare me her misen, and ^ bonnets, strike her main Petticoat, and yet outsail me, ^ am a Carvel to her.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: But a tight one.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: She is excellent, well built too.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: And yet she's old.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: She never saw above one voyage Luce, and cr^ me after another, her Hull will serve again, a right go^ Merchant: she plaies, and sings too, dances and discourses comes very near Essays, a pretty Poet, begins to piddle w^ Philosophie, a subtil Chymick Wench, and can ex^ the Spirit of mens Estates, she has the light before her, and cannot miss her choice for me, 'tis reason I wait my ^e^ fortune.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: You are so bashfull.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: It is not at first word up and ride, thou art cozen, that would shew mad i' faith: besides, we lose the main pe^ of our politick government: if we become provokers, the^ we are fair, and fit for mens imbraces, when like tow^ they lie before us ages, yet not carried, hold out th^ strongest batteries, then compound too without the l^ of honour, and march off with our fair wedding, Colo^ slying. Who are these?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: I know not, nor I care not.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Prethee peace then, a well built Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: But poorly thatcht.

speeches.speaker: Lance.
prose: Has he devour'd you too?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: H'as gulp'd me down Lance.

speeches.speaker: Lance.
prose: Left you no means to study?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Not a farthing: dispatcht my poor annuity I tha^ him, here's all the hope I have left, one bare ten shillings.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: You are sit for great mens services.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: I am sit, but who'le take me thus? mens miseries are now accounted stains in their natures. I have travelled, and I have studied long, observed all Kingdoms, know all the promises of Art and manners, yet that I am not bold, t^ cannot flatter, I shall not thrive, all these are but vain Studies art thou so rich as to get me a lodging Lance?

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: I'le sell the titles of my house else, my Horse, my Hawk, nay's death I'le pawn my wife: Oh Mr. Francis, that I should see your Fathers house fall thus!

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: An honest fellow.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Your Fathers house, that fed me, that bred up al my name!

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: A gratefull fellow.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: And fall by—

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Peace, I know you are angry Lance, but I m^ not hear with whom, he is my Brother, and though you hold him slight, my most dear Brother: A Gentleman, excepting some few rubs, he were too excellent to live here else, fraughted as deep with noble and brave parts, the issues of a noble and manly Spirit, as any he alive. I must not hear you; though I am miserable, and he made me so, yet still he is my brother, still I love him, and to that tye of blood link my affections.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: A noble nature! dost thou know him Luce?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: No, Mistress.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Thou shouldest ever know such good men, what a fair body and mind are married! did he not say be wanted?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: What's that to you?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: 'Tis true, but 'tis great pity.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: How she changes! ten thousand more than he, as handsom men too.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose:
'Tis like enough, but as I live, this Gentleman ^ong ten thousand thousand! is there no knowing him? ^y should he want? fellows of no merit, slight and pus^
^ls, that walk like shadows, by leaving no print of what ^ey are, or poise, let them complain.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: Her colour changes strangely.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: This man was made, to mark his wants to waken ^; alas poor Gentleman, but will that keep him from cold ^d hunger, believe me he is well bred, and cannot be but of noble linage, mark him, mark him well.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: 'Is a handsom man.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose:
The sweetness of his sufferance sets him off, O Luce,
^t whither go I?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: You cannot hide it.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: I would he had what I can spare.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: 'Tis charitable.

speeches.speaker: Lance.
prose: Come Sir, I'le see you lodg'd, you have tied my ^ngue fast, I'le steal before you want, 'tis but a hanging.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: That's a good fellow too, an honest fellow, why, this ^ould move a stone, I must needs know; but that some ^ther time.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: Is the wind there? that makes for me.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Come, I forgot a business.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: MY sister, and a woman of so base a pity! what was the fellow?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: Why, an ordinary man, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Poor?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: Poor enough, and no man knows from whence either.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: What could she see?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: Only his misery, for else she might behold a hundred and somer.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Did she change much?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: Extreamly, when he spoke, and then her pity, like ^ Orator, I fear her love framed such a commendation, and ^llowed it so far, as made me wonder.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
Is she so hot, or such a want of lovers, that she must ^oat upon afflictions? why does she not go romage all the ^risons, and there bestow her youth, bewray her wanton
^ess, and flie her honour, common both to beggery: did she ^eak to him?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: No, he saw us not, but ever since, she hath been ^ainly troubled.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Was he young?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: Yes, young enough.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: And looked he like a Gentleman?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: Like such a Gentleman, that would pawn ten oaths or twelve pence.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: My sister, and sink basely! this must not be, does ^e use means to know him?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: Yes Madam, and has employed a Squire called shorthose.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: O that's a precious Knave: keep all this private, but ^ill be near her lodging: Luce, what you can gather by any ^eans, let me understand: I'le stop her heat, and turn her ^harity another way, to bless her self first; be still close to ^er counsels; a begger and a stranger! there's a bless'dness! ^'le none of that; I have a toy yet, sister, shall tell you this ^ soul, and make you find it, and for your pains take you the ^ast gown I wore; this makes me mad, but I shall force a ^emedy.

speeches.speaker: Fount.
prose: Sirra, we have so lookt for thee, and long'd for ^hee; this widow is the strangest thing, the stateliest, and ^ands so much upon her excellencies.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: She hath put us off, this month now, for an answer.

speeches.speaker: Hare.
prose: No man must visit her, nor look upon her, no, not say, good morrow, not good even, till that's past.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: She has found want dough you are made of, and so kneads you: are you good at nothing, but these after games? I have told you often enough what things they are, w^at precious things, these widows—

speeches.speaker: Hare.
prose: If we ^ad ^m.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Why the Devil has not craft enough to wooe 'em, there be three kinds of fools, mark this nose Gentlemen, mark it, and understa^ it.

speeches.speaker: Fount.
prose: Well, go forward.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: An Innocent, a knave fool, a fool politick: the last of which are lovers, widow lovers.

speeches.speaker: Bell.
prose: Will you allow no fortune?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: No such blind one.

speeches.speaker: Fount.
prose: We gave you reasons, why 'twas needful for us.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: As you are those fools, I did allow those reasons, but is my Scholars and companions damn'd 'em: do you know what it is to wooe a widow? answer me coolely now, and understandingly.

speeches.speaker: Hare.
prose: Why to lie with her, and to enjoy her wealth.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Why the^e you are fools still, crafty to catch your selves, pure politick fools, I lookt for such an answer; once more hear me, it is, to wed a widow, to be doubted mainly, whether the state you have be yours or no, or those old boots you ride in. Mark me, widows are long extents in Law upon news, livings upon their bodies winding-sheets, they that enjoy 'em, lie but with dead mens monuments, and beget only their own ill Epitaphs: Is not this plain now?

speeches.speaker: Bell.
prose: Plain spoken.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: And plain truth; but if you'le needs do things of danger, do but lose your selves, not any part concerns your understandings, for th^u you are Meacocks, fools, and mi~serable, march off amain, within an inch of a F^g, turn me o'th' toe like a Weather-cock, kill every day a Sergeant for a twelve month, rob the Exchequer, and burn all the Rolls, and these will make a shew.

speeches.speaker: Hare.
prose: And these are trifles.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Considered to a Widow, empty nothings, for here you venture but your persons, there the varnish of your per~sons, your discretions; why 'tis a monstrous thing to marry at all, especially as now 'tis made; me thinks a man, an understanding man, is more wise to me, and of a nobler ^ie, than all these trinkets; what do we get by wom^n, but ou^ senses, which is the rankest part about us, satisfied, and when that's done, what are we? Crest-fallen Cowards. Wh^ benefit can children be, but charges and disobedience? What's the love they render at one and twenty years? I pray die Father: when they are young, they are like bells rung backwards, nothing but noise and giddiness; and come to years once, there drops a son byth' swords in his Mistresses quarel, a great joy to his parents: A Daughter ripe too, grows high and lusty in her blood, must have a heating, runs away with a supple ham'd Servingman: his twenty Nobles spent, takes to a trade, and learns to spin mens hair off; there's another, and most are of this nature, will you marry?

speeches.speaker: Fount.
prose: For my part yes, for any doubt I feel yet.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: And this same widow?

speeches.speaker: Fount.
prose: If I may, and me thinks, however you are pleased to dispute these dangers, such a warm match, and for you, Sir, were not hurtfull.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Not half so killing as for you, for m^ she cannot with all the Art she has, make me more miserable, or much more fortunate, I have no state left, a benefit that none of you can brag of, and there's the Antidote against a Widow, nothing to lose, but that my soul inherits, which she can neither law nor claw away; to that, but little flesh, it were too much else; and that unwholsom too, it were too rich else; and to all this contempt of what she do's I can laugh at her tears, neglect her angers, hear her without a faith, so pity her as if she were a Traytour, moan her p^son, but deadly hate her pride; if you could do these, and had but this discretion, and like fortune, it were but an equal venture.

speeches.speaker: Fo^nt.
prose: This is malice.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: When she lies with your land, and not with you, grows great with joyntures, and is brought to bed with all the state you have, you'le find this certain; but is it come to pass you must marry, is there no buff will hold you?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: Grant it be so.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Then chuse the tamer evil, take a maid, a maid not worth a penny; make her yours, knead her, and mould her yours, a maid worth nothing, there's a vertuous spell in that word nothing; a maid makes conscience of half a Crown a week for pins and puppits, a maid will be content with one Coach and two Horses, not falling out because they are not matches; with one man satisfied, with one rein guided, with one saith, one content, one bed, aged she makes the wise, preserves the fame and issue; a widow is a Christmas box that sweeps all.

speeches.speaker: Fount.
prose: Yet all this cannot sink us.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: You are my friends, and all my loving friends, I spend your mony, yet I deserve it too, you are my friends still, I ^ide your horses, when I want I sell 'em; I eat your meat, help to wear her linnen, sometimes I make you drunk, and then you seal, for which I'le do you this commodity, be ruled, and let me try her, I will discover her, the truth is, I will never leave to trouble her, till I see through her, then if I find her worthy.

speeches.speaker: Hare.
prose: This was our meaning Valentine.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: 'Tis done then, I must want nothing.

speeches.speaker: Hare.
prose: Nothing but the woman.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: No jealousie; for when I marry, the Devil must be wiser than I take him; and the flesh foolisher: come let's to dinner, and when I am well whetted with wine, have at her.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: But art thou sure?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: No surer than I heard.

speeches.speaker: Hare.
prose: That it was that slouting fellows Brother?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: Yes, Shorthose told me so.

speeches.speaker: Hare.
prose: He did scarce out the truth?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: It seems he did.

speeches.speaker: Har.
prose: Prethee Luce call him hither, if he be no worse, I never repent my pity, now sirra, what was he we sent you after, the Gentleman i'th' black?

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: I'th' torn black?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Yes, the same Sir.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: What would your Worship with him?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Why, my Worship would know his name, and what he is.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: 'Is nothing, he is a man, and yet he is no man.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: You must needs play the fool.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: 'Tis my profession.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: How is he a man, and no man?

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: He's a begger, only the sign of a man, the bush pull'd down, which shows the house stands emptie.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: What's his calling?

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: They call him begger.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: What's his kindred?

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Beggers.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: His worth?

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: A learned begger, a poor Scholar.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: How does he live?
