speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Like worms, he eats old Books.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Is Valentine his Brother.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: His begging Brother.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: What may his name be?

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Orson.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Leave your fooling.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: You had as good say, leave your living.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Once more tell me his name directly.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: I'le be hang'd first, unless I heard him Christned, but I can tell what foolish people call him.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: What?

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Francisco.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Where lies this learning, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: In Pauls Church yard forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: I mean the Gentleman, fool.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: O that fool, he lies in loose sheets every whe^ that's no where.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose:
You have glean'd since you came to Londo^
it ^ Country, Shorthose, you were an arrant fool, a cu^
^ coxcombe, here every Tavern teaches you, the pint pot ^ so belaboured you with wit, your brave acquaintance ^ gives you Ale, so fortified your mazard, that now there's a^ talking to you.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: 'Is much improved, a fellow, a fine discourser.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: I hope so, I have not waited at the tail of wit ^ long to be an Ass.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: But say now, Shorthose, my Lady should re^ into the Country.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: I had as lieve she should remove to Heaven, and ^ soon I would undertake to follow her.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: Where no old Charnico is, nor no Anchoves, to Master such-a-one, to meet at the Rose, and bring my La^ such-a-ones chief Chamber-maid.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose:
No bouncing healths to this brave Lad, dear S^
~hose, nor down o'th'knees to that illustrious Lady.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: No siddles, nor no lusty noise of drawer, carry ^ pottle to my Father Shorthose.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: No plays, nor gally foists, no strange Embass^ to run and wonder at, till thou beest oyl, and then come home again, and lye byth'Legend.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Say she should go.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: If I say, I'le be hang'd, or if I thought f^ would go.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: What?

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: I would go with her.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: But Shorthose, where thy heart is?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Do not fright him.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: By this hand Mistris 'tis a noise, a loud one ^ and from her own mouth, presently to be gone too, ^ why, or to what end?

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: May not a man die first? she'l give him so ^ time.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose:
Gone o'th' sudden? thou dost but jest, she mus^
^ mock the Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: She has put them off a month, thy dare not i^ her, believe me Mistris, what I hear I tell you.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Is this true, wench? gone on so short a warn^ what trick is this? she never told me of it, it must not be sirra, attend me presently, you know I have been a caref^ friend unto you, attend me in the Hall, and next be faithf^ cry not, we shall not go.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Her Coach may crack.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Which way to live! how darest thou come to to^ to ask such an idle question?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Me thinks 'tis necessary, unless you could restor^ that Annuitie you have tipled up in Taverns.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose:
Where hast thou been, and how brought up Fran^
that thou talkest thus out of France? thou wert a pretty f^llow, and of a handsom knowledge; who has spoiled thee?

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: He that has spoil'd himself, to make him sport, and by Copie, will spoil all comes near him: buy but a Glass, ^ you be yet so wealthy, and look there who?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Well said, old Copihold.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: My heart's good Freehold Sir, and so you'l find ^ this Gentleman's your Brother, your hopeful Brother, f^ there is no hope of you, use him thereafter.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: E'ne as well as I use my self, what wouldst thou ha^e Frank?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Can you procure me a hundred pound?

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose:
Hark what he saies to you, O try your wits, ^ say you are excellent at it, for your Land has lain long ^
rid, and unsensible.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose:
And I'le forget all wrongs, you see my state, and ^
what wretchedness your will has brought me; but what it may be, by this benefit, if timely done, and like a noble Brother, both you and I may feel, and to our comforts.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: (A hundred pound!) dost thou know what thou hast said Boy?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: I said a hundred pound.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose:
Thou hast said more than any man can justifie, be
^eve it: procure a hundred pounds! I say to thee there's no ^uch sum in nature, forty shillings there may be now i'th' Mint and that's a Treasure, I have seen five pound, but let me ^ell it, and 'tis as wonderful as Calves with five Legs; here's ^ve ^illings, Frank, the harvest of five weeks, and a good ^rop too, take it, and pay thy first fruits, I'le come down ^nd eat it out.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: 'Tis patience must meet with you Sir, not love.

speeches.speaker: Lanc.
prose: Deal roundly, and leave these fiddle faddles.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Leave thy prating, thou thinkest thou art a notable wise fellow, thou and thy rotten Sparrow Hawk; two of the reverent.

speeches.speaker: Lanc.
prose: I think you are mad, or if you be not, will be, with the next moon, what would you have him do?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: How?

speeches.speaker: Lanc.
prose: To get money first, that's to live, you have shewed him how to want.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: 'Slife how do I live? why, what dull fool would ask that question? three hundred three pilds more, I and live bravely: the better half o'th' Town live most gloriously, ^nd ask them what states they have, or what Annuities, ^r when they pray for seasonable Harvests: thou hast a handsome Wit, stir into the world, Frank, stir, stir for shame, thou art a pretty Scholar: ask how to live? write, write, write any thing, the World's a fine believing World, write News.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Dragons in Sussex, Sir, or fiery Battels seen in the Air at Aspurge.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose:
There's the way Frank, and in the tail of these, ^right me the Kingdom with a sharp Prognostication, that shall scowt them, Dearth upon Dearth, like leven Taffaties, predictions of Sea-breaches, Wars, and want of Her
^ings on our Coast, with bloudy Noses.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose:
Whirl-winds, that shall take off the top of Gran
^ham Steeple, and clap it on Pauls, and after these, a Len
^oy to the City for their sins.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Probatum est, thou canst not want a pension, go switch me up a Covey of young Scholars, there's twenty nobles, and two loads of Coals, are not these ready wayes? Cosmography thou art deeply read in, draw me a Map from the Mermaid, I mean a midnight Map to scape the Watches, and such long sensless examinations, and Gentlemen shall feed thee, right good Gentlemen, I cannot stay ^ong.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: You have read learnedly, and would you have him follow these Megera's, did you begin with Ballads?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Well, I will leave you, I see my wants are grown ridiculous, yours may be so, I will not curse you neither; you may think, when these wanton fits are over, who bred me, and who ruined me, look to your self, Sir, a providence I wait on.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Thou art passionate, hast thou been brought up with Girls?

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Rest you merry, Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Not so merry as you suppose, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Pray stay a while, and let me take a view of you, I may put my Spoon into the wrong Pottage-pot else.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Why, wilt thou muster us?

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: No, you are not he, you are a thought too handsome.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Who wouldst thou speak withal, why dost thou peep so?

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: I am looking birds nests, I can find none in your bush beard, I would speak with you, black Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: With me, my friend?

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Yes sure, and the best friend, Sir, it seems you spake withal this twelve month, Gentleman, there's mo~ney for you.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: How?

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: There's none for you, Sir, be not so brief, not a penny; law how he itches at it, stand off, you stir my colour.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Take it, 'tis money.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: You are too quick too, first be sure you have it, you seem to be a Faulkoner, but a foolish one.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Take it, and say nothing.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: You are cozen'd too, 'tis take it, and spend it.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: From whom came it, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Such another word, and you shall have none on't.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: I thank you, Sir, I doubly thank you.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Well, Sir, then buy you better Cloaths, and get your Hat drest, and your Laundress to wash your Boots white.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Pray stay Sir, may you not be mistaken.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: I think I am, give me the money again, come quick, quick, quick.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: I would be loth to render, till I am sure it be so.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Hark in your ear, is not your name Francisco?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Be quiet then, it may Thunder a hundred times, before such stones fall: do you not need it?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: And 'tis thought you have it.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: I think I have.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Then hold it fast, 'tis not fly-blown, you may pay for the poundage, you forget your self, I have not seen a Gentleman so backward, a wanting Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Your mercy, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Friend, you have mercy, a whole bag full of mercy, be merry with it, and be wise.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: I would fain, if it please you, but know—

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: It does not please me, tell over your money, and be not mad, Boy.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: You have no more such bags?

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: More such there are, Sir, but few I fear for you, I have cast your water, you have wit, you need no money.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Be not amazed, Sir, 'tis good gold, good old gold, this is restorative, and in good time, it comes to do you good, keep it and use it, let honest fingers feel it, yours be too quick Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: He named me, and he gave it me, but from whom.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Let 'em send more, and then examine it, this can be but a Preface.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Being a stranger, of whom can I deserve this?

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Sir, of any man that has but eyes, and manly understanding to find mens wants, good men are bound to do so.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Now you see, Frank, there are more wayes than certainties, now you believe: What Plow brought you this Harvest, what sale of Timber, Coals, or what Annuities? These feed no Hinds, nor wait the expectation of Quarterdaies, you see it showers in to you, you are an Ass, lie plodding, and lie fooling, about this Blazing Star, and that bopeep, whining, and fasting, to find the natural reason why a Dog turns twice about before he lie down, what use of these, or what joy in Annuities, where every man's thy study, and thy Tenant, I am ashamed on thee.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Yes, I have seen this fellow, there's a wealthy Widow hard by.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Yes marry is there.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: I think he's her servant, or I am couzen'd else, I am sure on't.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: I am glad on't.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: She's a good Woman.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: I am gladder.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: And young enough believe.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: I am gladder of all, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Frank, you shall lye with me soon.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: I thank my money.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: His money shall lie with me, three in a Bed, Sir, will be too much this weather.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Meet me at the Mermaid, and thou shalt see what things—

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Trust to your self Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fount.
prose: O Valentine!

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: How now, why do you look so?

speeches.speaker: Bella.
prose: The Widow's going, man.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Why let her go, man.

speeches.speaker: Hare.
prose: She's going out o'th' Town.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: The Town's the happier, I would they were all gone.

speeches.speaker: Fount.
prose: We cannot come to speak with her.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Not to speak to her?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: She will be gone within this hour, either now Val.

speeches.speaker: Fount.
prose: Hare. Now, now, now, good Val.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: I had rather march i'th' mouth o'th' Cannon, but adiew, if she be above ground, go, away to your prayers, away I say, away, she shall be spoken withall.

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: She will go, Shorthose.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Who can help it Roger?

speeches.speaker: Raph.
prose: Help down with the hangings.

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: By and by

speeches.speaker: Raph.
prose: I am making up o'th' trunks here.

speeches.speaker: Raph.
prose: Shorthose.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Well.

speeches.speaker: Raph.
prose: Who looks to my Ladys wardrobe? Humphrey.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
prose: Here.

speeches.speaker: Raph.
prose: Down with the boxes in the gallery, and bring away he Coach cushions.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Will it not rain, no conjuring abroad, nor no devices to stop this journey?

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: Why go now, why now, why o'th' sudden now? what preparation, what horses have we ready, what provision laid in i'th'Country?

speeches.speaker: Hum.
prose: Not an egge I hope.

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: No nor one drop of good drink boyes, there's the devil.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: I heartily pray the malt be musty, and then we must come up again.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
prose: What sayes the Steward?

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: He's at's wits end, for some four hours since, out of his haste and providence, he mistook the Millars mangie mare, for his own nagge.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: And she may break his neck, and save the journy. Oh London how I love thee!

speeches.speaker: Hum.
prose: I have no boots nor none I'le buy: or if I had, refuse me if I would venture my ability, before a Cloak-Bag, men are men.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: For my part, if I be brought, as I know it will be aimed at, to carry any du^ty dairy Cream-pot, or any gentle Lady of the Laundry, Chambring, or wantonness behind my Gelding, with all her Streamers, Knapsacks, Glasses, Gugawes, as if I were a running slippery, I'le give 'em leave to out my girts, and slay me. I'le not be troubled with their Distibations, at every half miles end, I understand my self, and am resolved.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
prose: To morrow night at Olivers! who shall be there boys, who shall meet the wenches?

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: The well brew'd stand of Ale, we should have met at!

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: These griefs like to another Tale of Troy, would mollifie the hearts of barbarous people, and Tom Butcher weep, Aeneas enters, and now the town's lost.

speeches.speaker: Raph.
prose: Well whither run you, my Lady is mad.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: I would she were in Bedlam.

speeches.speaker: Raph.
prose: The carts are come, no hands to help to load 'em? the stuff lies in the hall, the plate.
Why knaves there, where be these idle fellows?

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Shall I ride with one Boot?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Why where I say?

speeches.speaker: Raph.
prose: Away, away, it must be so.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: O for a tickling storm, to last but ten days.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: BY my troth Mistris I did it for the best.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose:
It may be so, but Luce, you have a tongue, a dish of meat in your mouth, which if it were minced L^
would do a great deal better.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: I protest Mistress.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: It will be your own one time or other: Walter.

speeches.speaker: Walter
prose: Anon forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Lay my hat ready, my fan and cloak, you are so ^ of providence; and Walter, tuck up my little bow beh^ the Coach, and bid my maid make ready, my sweet se^ to your good Lady Mistress; and my dog, good let ^ Coachman carry him.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: But hear me.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: I am in love sweet Luce, and you are so skilfull, t^ I must needs undo my self; and hear me, let Oliver pac^ my Glass discreetly, and see my Curles well carried. ^ sweet Luce, you have a tongue, and open tongues have ^p^ you know what, Luce.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: Pray you be satisfied.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Yes and contented too, before I leave you: there's a Roger, which some call a Butcher, I speak of certainties, I do not sish Luce, nay do not stare, I have a tongue can take too: and a Green Chamber Luce, a back door opens to a long Gallerie; there was a night Luce, do you perceive, ^ you perecive me yet? O do you blush Luce? a Friday night I saw your Saint, Luce: for t'other box of Marmalade, ^ thine sweet Roger, this I heard and kept too.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: E'ne as you are a woman Mistress.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: This I allow as good and Physical sometime, t^ meetings, and for the cheering of the heart, but Luce, to have your own turn served, and to your friend to be a dogbolt.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: I confess it Mistress.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: As you have made my sister jealous of me, are foolishly, and childishly pursued it, I have found out y^ haunt, and traced your purposes; for which mine ho^ suffers; your best waies must be applied to bring her ^ again, and seriously and suddenly, that so I may hare a means to clear my self, and she a fair opinion of me, ^ you peevish—

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: My power and prayers Mistress.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: What's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: I have been with the Gentleman, he has it, m^ good may do him with it.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Come, are you ready? you love so to delay time, the day grows on.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: I have sent for a few trifles, when those are co^. And now I know your reason.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Know your own honour then, about your businss, ^ the Coach ready presently, I'le tell you more then.

And understand it well, you must not think your sister ^ tender eyed as not to see your follies, alas I know your heart and must imagine, and truly too; 'tis not your charitie ^ coin such sums to give away as you have done, in that y^ have no wisdom Isabel, no nor modesty, where nobler ^ are at home; I tell you, I am ashamed to find this in yo^ years, far more in your discretion, none to chuse but th^ for pity, none to seal your thoughts on, but one of no ^
ding, of no name; nothing to bring you to but this, ^ and hunger: A jolly Joynture sister, you are happy, a mony, no not ten shillings.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: You search nearly.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
I know it as I know your folly, one that knows ^ where he shall eat his next meal, take his rest, unless it ^ i'th' stocks; what kindred has he, but a more want ^
Brother, or what vertues.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: You have had rare intelligence, I see, sister.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Or say the man had vertue, is vertue in this age a ^ll inheritance? what Joynture can he make you, Plutarchs ^rals, or so much penny rent in the small Poets? this is not ^ell, 'tis weak, and I grieve to know it.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: And this you quit the town for?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Is't not time?

speeches.speaker: Isab
prose: You are better read in my affairs than I am, that's ^ll I have to answer, I'le go with you, and willingly, and ^hat you think most dangerous, I'le sit laugh at.
^or sister 'tis not folly but good discretion governs our main ^rtunes.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: I am glad to hear you say so.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: I am for you.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
prose: The Devil cannot stay her, she'l on't, eat an egg ^ow, and then we must away.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose:
I am gaul'd already, yet I will pray, may London
^ayes from henceforth be full of holes, and Coaches crack ^heir wheels, may zealous Smiths so housel all our Hack
^eys, that they may feel compunction in their feet, and tire ^t High-gate, may it rain above all Almanacks till Carriers ^il, and the Kings Fish monger ride like Bike Arion upon ^ Trout to London.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
prose: At S. Albanes, let all the Inns be drunk, not an Host ^ober to bid her worship welcom.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose:
Not a Fiddle, but all preach't down with Puri
^ans; no meat but Legs of Beef.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
prose: No beds but Wool-Packs.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose:
And those so crammed with Warrens of starved ^leas that bite like Bandogs; let Mims be angry at their S.
^el Swagger, and we pass in the heat on't and be beaten, beaten ^bominably, beaten horse and man, and all my Ladies linnen ^prinkled with suds and dish-water.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Not a wheel but out of joynt.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
prose: Why dost thou laugh?

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: There's a Gentleman, and the rarest Gentleman, ^nd makes the rarest sport.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Where, where?

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose:
Within here, h'as made the gayest sport with Tom
^he Coachman, so tewed him up with Sack that he lies ^ashing a But of Malmsie for his Mares.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: 'Tis very good.

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose:
And talks and laughs, and sings the rarest songs, and
^horthose, he has so maul'd the Red Deer pies, made such an ^lms i'th' butterie.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Better still.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
prose: My Lady in a rage with the Gentleman?

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: May he anger her into a feather.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: I pray tell me, who sent you hither? for I imagine ^t is not your condition, you look so temperately, and like a Gentleman, to ask me these milde questions.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Do you think I use to walk of errands, gentle Lady, ^r deal with women out of dreams from others?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: You have not know me sure?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Not much.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: What reason have you then to be so tender of my ^redit, you are no kinsman?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: If you take it so, the honest office that I came to do you, is not so heavy but I can return it: now I perceive you ^re too proud, not worth my visit.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Pray stay, a little proud.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Monstrous proud, I griev'd to hear a woman of your value, and your abundant parts stung by the people, but ^ow I see 'tis true, you look upon me as if I were a rude and ^aucie fellow that borrowed all my breeding from a dunghil, or such a one, as should now fall and worship you in hope of pardon: you are cozen'd Lady, I came to prove opinion a loud liar, to see a woman only great in goodness, and Mistress of a greater fame than fortune, but—

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: You are a strange Gentleman, if I were proud now. I should be monstrous angry, which I am not, and shew the effects of pride; I should despise you, but you are welcom Sir: To think well of our selves, if we deserve it, it is a lustre in us, and every good we have, strives to shew gracious, what use is it else? old age like Seer trees, is seldom seen affected, stirs sometimes at rehearsal of such acts as his daring youth endeavour'd.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: This is well, and now you speak to the purpose, you please me, but to be place proud?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: If it be our own, why are we set here with distinction else, degrees, and orders given us? In you men, 'tis held a coolness, if you lose your right, affronts and loss of honour: streets, and walls, and upper ends of tables, had they tongues could tell what blood has followed, and what feud about your ranks; are we so much below you, that till you have us, are the tops of nature, to be accounted drones without a difference? you will make us beasts indeed.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Nay worse than this too, proud of your cloaths, they swear a Merce^s Lucifer, a tumour tackt together by a Taylour, nay yet worse, proud of red and white, a varnish that butter-milk can better.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Lord, how little will vex these poor blind people! if my cloaths be sometimes gay and glorious, does it follow, my mind must be my Mercers too? or say my beauty please some weak eyes, must it please them to think, that blows me up, that every hour blows off? this is an Infants anger.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Thus they say too, what though you have a Coach lined through with velvet, and four fair Flanders mares, why should the streets be troubled continually with you, till Carmen curse you? can there be ought in this but pride of shew Lady, and pride of bum-beating, till the learned lawyers with their fat bags, are thrust against the bulks till all their causes crack? why should this Lady, and t'other Lady, and the third sweet Lady, and Madam at Mile-end, be daily visited, and your poorer neighbours, with course napses neglected, fashions conferr'd about, pouncings, and paintings, and young mens bodies read on like Anatomies.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: You are very credulous, and somewhat desperate, to deliver this Sir, to her you know not, but you shall confess me, and find I will not start; in us all meetings lie open to these lewd reports, and our thoughts at Church, our very meditations some will swear, which all should fear to judge, at least uncharitably, are mingled with your memories, cannot sleep, but this sweet Gentleman swims in our fancies, that scarlet man of war, and that smooth Senior; not dress our heads without new ambushes, how to surprize that greatness, or that glorie; our very smiles are subject to constructions; nay Sir, it's come to this we cannot pish, but 'tis a favour for some fool or other: should we examine you thus, wer't not possible to take you without Perspectives?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: It may be, but these excuse not.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Nor yours force no truth Sir, what deadly tongues you have, and to those tongues what hearts, and what inventions? O' my conscience, and 'twere not for sharp justice, you would venture to aim at your own mothers, and account it glorie to say you had done so: all you think are counsels, and cannot erre, 'tis we still that shew double, giddy, or gorg'd with passion; we that build Babels for mens conc^usions, we that scatter, as day does his warm light; our killing curses over Gods creatures, next to the devils malice: lets intreat your good words.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Well, this woman has a brave soul.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Are not we gaily blest then, and much beholding to you for your substance? you may do what you list, we what beseems us, and narrowly do that too, and precisely, our names are served in else at Ordinaries, and be^ t abroad in Taverns.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: O most brave Wench, and able to redeem an age of women.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
You are no Whoremasters? Alas, no, Gentlemen, ^t w^e an impudence to think you vicious: you are so holy, handsome Ladies fright you, you are the cool things of the time, the temp^tance, mee^ Emblems of the Law, and veils of Vertue, you are not daily mending like Dutch Watches, and plastering like old Walls; they are not Gentlemen, that with their secret sins increase our Surgeons, and ^e in Foraign Countries, for new sores; Women are all these V^ces; you are not envious, false, covetous, va^
^s, i^
^ligious, drunken, revengeful, giddieeyed like Pa^ots, ^aters of others honours.

speeches.speaker: Va^.
prose: You are angry.

speeches.speaker: Wid
prose: No by my ^oth, and yet I could say more too, for when men make me angry, I am miserable.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Sure 'tis a man, s^e could not bea^ it thus bravely else, it may he I am tedious.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Not at all, Sir, I am content at this time you should trouble me.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: You are distrustful.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Where I find no truth, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Come, come, you are full of passion.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Some I have, I were too near the nature o' God ^lse.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: You are monstrous peevish.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Because they are monstrous foolish, and know not how to use that should try me.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: I was never answered thus; were you never drunk Lady?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: No sure, not drunk, Sir; yet I love good Wine, as I love health and joy of heart, but temperately, why do you ask that question?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: For that sin that they most charge you with, is this sin's se^vant, they say you are monstrous—

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: What, Sir, what?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Most strangely.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: It has a nam^ sure?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Infinitely lustful, without all bounds, they swear you kill'd your Husband.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Let us have it all for Heavens sake, 'tis good mirth, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: They say you will have four now, and those som stuck in four quarters, like four winds to cool you: will she not cry nor cu^s^?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: On with your story.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: And that you are forcing out of dispensations with sums of money to that purpose.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Four Husbands! should not I be blest, Sir, for example? Lord, what should I do with them? turn a Maltmill, or Tithe them out like Town bulls to my Tenants, you come to make me angry, but you cannot.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: I'le make you merry then, you are a brave Woman, and in despite of envy a right one, go thy wayes, truth thou art as good a Woman, as any Lord of them all can lay his Leg over, I do not often commend your Sex.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: It seems so, your commendations are so studied for.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: I came to see you and sift you into Flowr to know your pureness, and I have found you excellent, I thank you; continue so, and shew men how to tread, and women how to follow: get an Husband, an honest man, you are a good woman, and live hedg'd in from scandal, let him be too an understanding man, and to that stedfast; 'tis pity your fair Figure should miscarry, and then your are sixt: farewel.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Pray stay a little, I love your company now you are so pleasant, and to my disposition set so even.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: I can no longer.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: As I live a l^ fellow, this manly handsome bluntness shews him honest; what is he, or from whence? bless me, four Husbands! how prettily he fooled me into Vices, to st^ my jealousie, and find my nature; a proper Gentleman: I am not well o'th' sudden, such a companion I could live and dye with, his angers are meer mirth.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: Come, come, I am ready.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Are you so?

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose:
What ails she? the Coach staies, and the p^
^ day goes on, I am as ready now as you desire, Sister ^, ^ stays now, why do you sit and pout thus?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Prethee be quiet, I am not well.

speeches.speaker: Isa
prose: For Heav'ns sake let's not ride staggering in ^ night, come, pray you take some Sweet-meats in ^ pocket, if your stomach —

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: I have a little business.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: To abuse me, you shall not find new dreams, ^ new suspicions, to horse withal.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Lord who made you a Commander! hey ^o, ^ heart.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose:
Is the wind come thither, and Coward like, do y^ lose your Colours to 'em? are you sick o'th' Vale^t^

^ Sister, come let's away, the Country will so quicken you and we shall live so sweetly: Luce, my Ladies Cloak, ^ you have put me into such a gog of going, I would not ^ for all the world; if I live here, you have so knock'd ^ love into my head, that I shall love any body, and I ^ my body, I know not how, so apt — pray let's be g^ Sister, I stand on thorns.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
I prethee Isabella, i'saith I have s^
^siness t^ concerns me, I will suspect no more, ^ me, and I'le pay the hundred pound you ^

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: I had rather go, but—

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
Come walk in with me, we'll go to Ca^, ^
dle the Horses.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: A Jubile, a Jubile, we stay, Boys.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Are they behind us?

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Close, close, speak aloud, Sir.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: I am glad my Nephew has so much disc^etio^, ^ l^ngth to find his wants: did she entertain him?

speeches.speaker: Lance.
prose: Most bravely, nobly, and gave him such a ^ come!

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: For his own sake do you think?

speeches.speaker: Lance.
prose:
Most certain, Sir, and in his own cause bes^
^ himself too, and wan such liking from her, she d^t^s ^ him, h'as the command of all the house already.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: He deals not well with his friends.

speeches.speaker: Lance.
prose: Let him deal on, and be his own friend, he ^ most need of her.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: I wonder they would put him—

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: You are in the right on't, a man that must r^ himself, I knew he would couzen 'em, and glad I am he ha^ he watched occasion, and found it i'th' nick.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: He has deceived me.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: I told you howsoever he wheel'd about, he work charge home at length: how I could laugh now, to think of these tame fools!

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: 'Twas not well done, because they trusted him, ^

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: Hark you Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: We are upon a business, pray excuse us, they h^ it home.

speeches.speaker: Lanc.
prose: Come let it work good on Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Font.
prose: 'Tis true, he is a knave, I ever thought it.

speeches.speaker: Hare.
prose: And we are fools, tame fools.

speeches.speaker: Bell.
prose: Come let's go seek him, he shall be hang'd before he colt us basely.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Art sure she loves him?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: Am I sure I live? and I have clapt on such accomendation on your revenge.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Faith, he is a pretty Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: Handsome enough, and that her eye has sound ^

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: He talks the best they say, and yet the maddest.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: H'as the right way.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: How is she?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: Bears it well, as if she cared not, but a man may ^ with half an eye through all her forced behaviour, and ^d who is her Valentine.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: Come let's go see her, I long to prosecute.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: By no means Mistress, let her take better hold ^st.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: I could burst now.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Upbraid me with your benefits, you Pilchers, you ^tten, sold, slight fellows? was't not I that undertook ^u first from empty barrels, and brought those barking ^ouths that gaped like bung-holes to utter sence? where ^t you understanding? who taught you manners and apt ^riage to rank your selves? who filled you in fit Tave^ns? ^re those born with your worships when you came hither? ^at brought you from the Universities of moment matter ^allow you, besides your small base sentences?

speeches.speaker: Bell.
prose: 'Tis well, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose:
Long Cloaks with two-hand-rapiers, boot-hos^s ^th penny poses, and twenty fools opinions, who looked ^ you but piping rites that knew you would be prizing, ^d Prentices in Paul's Church-yard, that scented your want ^
Britains Books.

speeches.speaker: Font.
prose: This cannot save you.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Taunt my integrity you Whelps?

speeches.speaker: Bell.
prose: You may talk the stock we gave you out, but see no ^ther.

speeches.speaker: Hair.
prose: You tempt our patience, we have found you out, ^d what your trust comes to, ye're well feathered, thank ^ and think now of an honest course, 'tis time; men now ^gin to look, and narrowly into your tumbling tricks, ^ey are stale.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Is not that he?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: 'Tis he.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Be still and mark him.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: How miserable will these poor wretches be when I ^sake 'em! but things have their necessities, I am so^y, what a vomit must they turn again, now to their own ^t Dunghil breeding; never hope after I cast you off, you ^n of Motley, you most undone things below pity, any ^t has a soul and six pence dares relieve you, my name ^ll bar that blessing, there's your Cloak, Sir, keep it ^se to you, it may yet preserve you a sortnight longer ^m the fool; your Hat, pray be covered, and there's ^ Sattin that your Worship sent me, will serve you at a ^es yet.

speeches.speaker: ^eunt.
prose: Nay, faith Sir, you may e'ne rub these out now.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: No such relique, nor the least rag of such a sordid ^akness shall keep me warm, these Breeches are mine ^n, purchased, and paid for, without your compassion, Christian Breeches founded in Black-Friers, and so I'le ^intain 'em.

speeches.speaker: Hare.
prose: So they seem, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Only the thirteen shillings in these Breeches, and ^e odd groat, I take it, shall be yours, Sir, a mark to ^ow a Knave by, pray preserve it, do not displease more, ^ take it presently, now help me off with my Boots.

speeches.speaker: Hare.
prose: We are no Grooms, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: For once you shall be, do it willingly, or by this ^nd I'le make you.

speeches.speaker: Bell.
prose: To our own, Sir, we may apply our hands.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: There's your Hangers, you may deserve a strong ^r, and a girdle will hold you without buckles; now I am ^rfect, and now the proudest of your worships tell me I beholding to you.

speeches.speaker: Fou^t.
prose: No such matter.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose:
And take heed how you pity me, 'tis dangerous, ^eeding dangerous, to prate of pity; which are the poorer? ^u are now puppies; I without you, or you without my ^owledge? be Rogues, and so be gone, be Rogues and re
^ not, for if you do—

speeches.speaker: Bell.
prose: Only thus much, and then we'll leave you the Air is far sharper than our an^, Su, and th^se you may reserve to rail in wa^me^.

speeches.speaker: Hare.
prose: Pray have a care, Sir, of your health.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose:
Yes Hog hounds, more than you can have or your wits; 'tis cold, and I am very sensible, extreamly ^ too, yet I will not off, till I have shamed these Rascals; I have in su^ed as ill heats as another, and every way ^ o^ could perish my body, you'll b at th^
^ I a^ colder here, not a poor penny ^ft.

speeches.speaker:
~
^.
prose: 'Thas ta^en ra^el^, and now ^ he ^ ruled.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: To him, to whim, abus^ him, and ^ him ^

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Why how now, ^ weather?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: As you see, Sir, in a ^ot ht, I ^

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: But Cou^, where ^ you (^ are no inheritance, ^ scruple may compound with ^ I take it, this is no fashion, Cousin.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Not much followed, I must confess; yet Uncle I determine to try what may be done next Term.

speeches.speaker: Lance.
prose: How came you thus, Sir, for you are strangely moved.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Rags, toys and trifles, fit only for those fools that first possessed 'em, and to those Knaves they are rendred. Freemen, Uncle, ought to appear like innocents, old Adam, a fair Fig-leas sufficient.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Take me with you, were these your friends, that clear'd you thus?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Hang friends, and even reckonings that make friends.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: I thought till now, there ^a^ been no such living, no such purchase, for all the rest is la^our as a ^ o^ ho~nourable friends; do such men as you, Sir, in him of all your understandings, travels, and those great g^tt^ of nature, aim at no more than casting off your Coat^? I am strangely cozen'd.

speeches.speaker: Lance.
prose:
Should not the Town shake at the cold you fee^ now, and all the Gently suffer interdiction, no more sens^ spoken, all things
^oth and Vandal, t^ll you be summed a~gain, Velvets and Sca^lets, anointed with gold ^e, and Cloth of silver turned into Spanish Cottens for a penance, wits blasted with your Bulls, and Taverns withered, as though the Term lay at St
Albans?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Gentlemen, you have spoken long and lev^, I be~seech you take breath a while and hear me, you imagine now, by the twirling of your strings, that I am at the last, as also that my friends are flown like Swallows after Summer.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Yes, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: And that I have no more in this poor Pannie^, to raise me up again above your rents, Uncle.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: All this I do believe.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: You have no mind to better me

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Yes, Cousin, and to that ^nd I come, and once more offer you all that my power is matter of.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: A match then, lay me down ^y pounds there.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: There it is, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: And on it write, that you are pleased to give this, as due unto my merit, without caution of ^ tedious thanks, or thrist hereafter to be ^op^ for.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: How?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Without da^ing, when you are d^k, to ^ of revilings, to which you are prone in Sack, Uncle.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: I thank you, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lance.
prose: Come, come away, let the young wanton play a while, away I say, Sir, let him go forward with his naked fashion, he will seek you too morrow; goodly weather, sultry hot, sultry, how I sweat!

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Farewel, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose:
Would I sweat too, I am monstrous ^ext, and cold too; and these are but th^ pumps to walk the
streets in; clothes I must get, this fashion will not fadge with me; besides, 'tis an ill winter wear, — What art thou? yes, they are clothes, and rich ones, some fool has left 'em: and if I should utter — what's this paper here? Let these be only worn by the most noble and deserving Gentleman Valentine, — dropt out o'th' clouds! I think they are full of gold too; well, I'le leave my wonder, and be warm again, in the next house I'le shift.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: WHY do you deal thus with him? 'tis unnobly.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Peace Cousin peace, you are too tender of him, he must be dealt thus with, he must be cured thus, the violence of his disease Francisco, must not be jelted with, 'tis grown infectious, and now strong Corrosives must cure him.

speeches.speaker: Lance.
prose: H'as had a stinger, has eaten off his clothes, the next his skin comes.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: And let it search him to the bones, 'tis better, 'twill make him feel it.

speeches.speaker: Lance.
prose: Where be his noble friends now? will his fantastical opinions cloath him, or the learned Art of having nothing feed him?

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: It must needs greedily, for all his friends have slung him off, he is naked, and where to skin himself again, if I know, or can devise how he should get himself lodging, his Spirit must be bowed, and now we have him, have him at that we hoped for.

speeches.speaker: Lance.
prose: Next time we meet him cracking of nuts, with half a cloak about him, for all means are cut off, or borrowing six-pence, to shew his bounty in the pottage Ordinary?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Which way went he?

speeches.speaker: Lance.
prose: Pox, why should you ask after him, you have been trimm'd already, let him take his fortune, som spun it out himself, Sir, there's no pitie.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Besides some good to you now, from this miserie.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: I rise upon his ruines! fie, fie, Uncle, fie honest Lance. Those Gentlemen were base people, that could so soon take fire to his destruction.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: You are a fool, you are fool, a young man.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Morrow Uncle, morrow Frank, sweet Frank, and how, and how d'ee, think now, how shew matters? morrow Bandog.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: How?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Is this man naked, forsaken of his friends?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Th'art handsom, Frank, a pretty Gentleman, i'faith thou lookest well, and yet here may be those that look as handsom.

speeches.speaker: Lance.
prose: Sure he can conjure, and has the Devil for his Tailor.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: New and rich! 'tis most impossible he should recover.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Give him this luck, and fling him into the Sea.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: 'Tis not he, imagination cannot work this miracle.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Yes, yes, 'tis he, I will assure you Uncle, the very he, the he your wisdom plaid withall, I thank you for't, neighed at his nakednesse, and made his cold and poverty your pastime; you see I live, and the best can do no more Uncle, and though I have no state, I keep the streets still, and take my pleasure in the Town, like a poor Gentleman, wear clothes to keep me warm, poor things they serve me, can make a shew too if I list, yes uncle, and ring a peal in my pockets, ding dong, uncle, these are mad foolish wayes, but who can help 'em?

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: I am amazed.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose:
I'le sell my Copyhold, for since there are such ex^
lent new nothings, why should I labour? is there no ^ haunts him, no Rat, nor no old woman?

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: You are Valentine.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: I think so, I cannot tell, I have been call'd so, a^ some say Christened, why do you wonder at me, and sw^ if you had met a Sergeant fasting, did you ever know ^ want? y'are fools, a little stoop there may be to allay ^ he would grow too rank else, a small eclipse to shadow ^ but out he must break, glowingly again, and with a gre^ lustre, look you uncle, motion and majesty.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: I am confounded.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: I am of his faith.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Walk by his careless kinsman, and turn again a^ walk, and look thus Uncle, taking some one by the ha^ he loves best, leave them to the mercy of the hog-mar^ come Frank, Fortune is now my friend, let me instead thee.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Good morrow Uncle, I must needs go with him.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Flay me, and turn me out where none inhabits, with a two hours I shall be thus again, now wonder on, and la^ at your own ignorance.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: I do believe him.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose:
So do I, and heartily upon my conscience, b^ stark naked, he would rise again, within two hours ^
broidered: sow mustard-seeds, and they cannot come ^ thick as his new sattens do, and clothes of silver, there's ^ striving.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Let him play a while then, and let's search out wh^ hand: —

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: I, there the game lies.

speeches.speaker: Foun.
prose: Come, let's speak for our selves, we have lodg'd hi^ sure enough, his nakedness dare nor peep out to cross us.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: We can have no admittance.

speeches.speaker: Hare.
prose: Let's in boldly, and use our best arts, who she dei^ to favour, we are all content.

speeches.speaker: Foun.
prose: Much good may do her with him, no civil wars.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: By no means, now do I wonder in what old tod ^ he lies whistling for means, nor clothes he hath none, ^ none will trust him, we have made that side sure, teach h^ a new wooing.

speeches.speaker: Hare.
prose: Say it is his Uncles spite.

speeches.speaker: Foun.
prose:
It is all one Gentlemen, 'thas rid us of a fair in^
~brance, and makes us look about to our own fortunes. Wa^ are these?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose:
Not see this man yet! well, I shall be wiser: but L^
didst ever know a woman melt so? she is finely hurt to h^

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: Peace, the three Suitors.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: I could so titter now and laugh, I was lost Luce, a^ must love, I know not what; O Cupid, what pretty gins th^ hast to halter Woodcocks! and we must into the Country ^ all haste, Luce.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: For Heavens sake, Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Nay, I have done, I must laugh though; but Scho^ I shall teach you.

speeches.speaker: Foun.
prose: 'Tis her sister.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: Save you Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Fair met Gentlemen, you are visiting my sister, ^ assure my self.

speeches.speaker: Hare.
prose: We would sain bless our eyes.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Behold and welcom, you would see her?

speeches.speaker: Foun.
prose: 'Tis our business.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: You shall see her, and you shall talk with her.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: She will not see 'em, nor spend a word.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: I'le make her frat a thousand, nay now I have foc^ the sab, I will so scratch her.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: She cannot endure 'em.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: She loves 'em but too dearly, come follow me, I'le b^ you toth' party Gentlemen, then make your own condit^

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: She is sick you know.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose:
I'le make her well, or kill her, and take no idle an
^er, you are fools then, nor stand off for her state, she'l scorn ^u all then, but urge her still, and though she fret, still fol
^w her, a widow must be won so.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: She speaks bravely.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: I would fain have a Brother in law, I love mens ^mpany, and if she call for dinner to avoid you, be sure you ^y; follow her into her chamber, if she retire to Pray, pray ^th her, and boldly, like honest lovers.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: This will kill her.

speeches.speaker: Foun.
prose: You have shewed us one way, do but lead the tother.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: I know you stand o'thorns, come I'le dispatch you.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: If you live after this.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: I have lost my aim.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Did you not see 'em since.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: No hang 'em, hang 'em.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Nor will you not be seen by 'em?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Let 'em alone Frank, I'le make 'em their own ^stice, and a jerker.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Such base discourteous Dog-whelps.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: I shall dog 'em, and double dog 'em, ere I have done.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose:
Will you go with me, for I would fain find out ^is piece of bountie, it was the Widows man, that I am cer
^in of.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: To what end would you go?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: To give thanks.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Hang giving thanks, hast not thou parts deserve it? it ^cludes a further will to be beholding, beggers can do no ^ore at door, if you will go, there lies your way.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: I hope you will go.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: No not in ceremony, and to a woman, with mine ^wn Father, were he living Frank; I would toth' Court ^ith Bears first, if it be that wench, I think it is, for t'other's ^iser, I would not be so lookt upon, and laught at, so made ladder for her wit, to climb upon, for 'tis the tartest tit in Christendom, I know her well Frank, and have buckled ^ith her, so lickt, and stroaked, slear'd upon, and stouted, ^d shown to Chambermaids, like a strange beast, she had ^rchased with her penny.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: You are a strange man, but do you think it was a ^oman?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: There's no doubt on't, who can be there to do it else? ^esides the manner of the circumstances.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose:
Then such courtesies, who ever does 'em sir, saving our own wisdom, must be more lookt into, and better an
^ered, than with deserving slights, or what we ought to have ^nferred upon us, men may starve else, means are not got
^en now with crying out I am a gallant fellow, a good Soul
^er, a man of learning, or fit to be employed, immediate ^essings cease like miracles, and we must grow by second ^eans, I pray go with me, even as you love me Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: I will come to thee, but Frank, I will not stay to hear our sopperies, dispatch those e're I come.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: You will not fail me.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Some two hours hence expect me.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: I thank you, and will look for you.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Who let in these puppies? you blind rascals, you ^runken Knaves several.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Yes for sooth, I'le let 'em in presently, — Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Sprecious, you blown Pudding, bawling Rogue.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: I bawl as loud as I can, would you have me fetch ^m upon my back.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Get 'em out rascal, out with 'em, out, I sweat to ^ave 'em near me.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: I should sweat more to carry 'em out.

speeches.speaker: Roger.
prose: They are Gentlemen Madam.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Shall we get 'em into th'butterie, and make'em ^runk?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Do any thing, so I be eased.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Now to her Sir, fear nothing.

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: Slip aside boy, I know she loves 'em, howsoever s^ carries it, and has invited 'em, my young Mistress told m^ so.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Away to tables then.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: I shall burst with the sport on't.

speeches.speaker: Fount.
prose: You are too curious Madam, too full of preparation, we expect it not.

speeches.speaker: Bella.
prose: Me thinks the house is handsom, every place decent, what need you be vext?

speeches.speaker: Hare.
prose: We are no strangers.

speeches.speaker: Fount.
prose: What though we come e're you expected us, do not we know your entertainments Madam are ^ee, and fall at all times?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: You are merry, Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: We come to be merry Madam, and very merry, m^n love to laugh heartily, and now and then Lady a little of our old plea.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: I am busie, and very busie too, will none deliver me.

speeches.speaker: Hare.
prose: There is a time for all, you may be busie, but when your friends come, you have as much power Madam.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: This is a tedious torment.

speeches.speaker: Foun.
prose: How hansomly this little piece of anger shews upon her! well Madam well, you know not how to grace your self.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: Nay every thing she does breeds a new sweetness.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: I must go up, I must go up, I have a business waits upon me, some wine for the Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Hare.
prose: Nay, we'l go with you, we never saw your chambers yet.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Hold there boyes.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Say I go to my prayers?

speeches.speaker: Foun.
prose: We'l pray with you, and help your meditations.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: This is boysterous, or say I go to sleep, will you go to sleep with me?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: So suddenly before meat will be dangerous, we know your dinner's ready Lady, you will not sleep.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Give me my Coach, I will take the air.

speeches.speaker: Hare.
prose: We'l wait on you, and then your meat after a quickned stomach.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Let it alone, and call my Steward to me, and bid him bring his reckonings into the Orchard, these unmannerly rude puppies —

speeches.speaker: Foun.
prose: We'l walk after you and view the pleasure of the place.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Let her not rest, for if you give her breath, sh^ scorn and slout you, seem how she will, this is the way to win her, be bold and prosper.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: Nay if we do not tire her.—

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: I'le teach you to worm me, good Lady sister, and peep into my privacies to suspect me, I'le torture you, with, that you hate, most daintily, and when I have done that, laugh at that you love most.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: What have you done, she chases and sumes outragiously, and still they persecute her.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Long may they do so, I'le teach her to declaim against my pities, why is she not gone out o'th' town, but gives occasion for men to run mad after her?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I shall be hanged.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: This in me had been high treason, three at a time, and private in her Orchard! I hope she'l cast her reckonings right now.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Well, I shall find who brought 'em.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Why do you laugh sister? I fear me 'tis your trick, 'twas neatly done of you, and well becomes your pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: What have you done with 'em?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Lockt 'em i'th' Orchard, there I'le make 'em dance and caper too, before they get their liberty, unmannerly rude puppies.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: They are somewhat saucy, but yet I'le let 'em out, and once more sound 'em, why were they not beaten out?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: I was about it, but because they came as suiters.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Why did you not answer 'em?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: They are so impudent they will receive none: More yet! how came these in?

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: At the door, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: It is that face.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: This is the Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: She sent the money to?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: The same.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: I'le leave you, they have some business.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Nay, you shall stay, Sister, they are strangers both to me; how her face alters!

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: I am sorry he comes now.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: I am glad he is here now though. Who would you speak with, Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: You Lady, or your fair Sister there, here's a Gentleman that has received a benefit.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: From whom, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: From one of you, as he supposes, Madam, your man delivered it.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: I pray go forward.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: And of so great a goodness, that he dares not, without the tender of his thanks and service, pass by the house.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Which is the Gentleman?

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: This, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: What's your name, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: They that know me call me Francisco, Lady, one not so proud to scorn so timely a benefit, nor so wretched to hide a gratitude.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: It is well bestowed then.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Your fair self, or your Sister as it seems, for what desert I dare not know, unless a handsome subject for your charities, or aptness in your noble will to do it, have showred upon my wants a timely bounty, which makes me rich in thanks, my best inheritance.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: I am sorry 'twas not mine, this is the Gentlewoman, sie, do not blush, go roundly to the matter, the man is a pretty man.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: You have three fine ones.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Then to you, dear Lady?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: I pray no more, Sir, if I may perswade you, your only aptness to do this is recompence, and more than I expected.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: But good Lady.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: And for me further to be acquainted with it besides the imputation of vain glory, were greedy thankings of my self, I did it not to be more affected to; I did it, and if it happened where I thought it sitted, I have my end; more to enquite is cutious in either of us, more than that suspicious.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: But gentle Lady, 't will be necessary.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: About the right way nothing, do not fright it, being to pious use and tender sighted, with the blown face of Complements, it blasts it; had you not come at all, but thought thanks, it had been too much, 'twas not to see your person.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: A brave dissembling Rogue, and how she carries it!

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Though I believe few handsomer; or hear you, though I affect a good tongue well; or try you, though my years desire a friend, that I relieved you.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: A plagnie cunning quean.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: For so I carried it, my end's too glorious in mine eyes, and bettered the goodness I propounded with opinion.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Fear her not, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: You cannot catch me, Sister.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Will you both teach, and tie my tongue up Lady?

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: Let it suffice you have it, it was never mine, whilest good men wanted it.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: This is a Saint sure.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: And if you be not such a one, restore it.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: To commend my self, were more officious ^ you think my thanks are, to doubt I may be worth your ^ a treason, both to mine own good and understanding, ^ know my mind clear, and though modesty tells me, ^ intreats intrudes; yet I must think something, and of fr^ season, met with your better taste, this had not been else.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: What ward for that, wench?

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: Alas, it never touched me.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Well, gentle Lady, yours is the first money I ^ took upon a forced ill manners.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: The last of me, if ever you use other.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: How may I do, and your way to be thought: grateful taker?

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: Spend it, and say nothing, your modesty may de~serve more.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: O Sister will you bar thankfulness?

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose:
Dogs dance for meat, would ye have men do work for they can speak, cry out like Wood-mongers, good deeds by the hundreds, I did it that my best friend ^ not know it, wine and vain glory does as much as I else, t^ you will force my merit, against my meaning, use it in ^ bestowing it, in shewing it came to be a benefit, and was so; and not examining a Woman did it, or to what ^ in not believing sometimes your self, when drink and s^
~ring conversation may ripen strange perswasions.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose:
Gentle Lady, I were a base receiver of a courtes^ and you a worse disposer, were my nature unfurnished ^ these fore-sights. Ladies honours were ever in my th^
^ unspotted Crimes, their good deeds holy Temples, w^ the incense burns not; to common eyes your fears are ^
~tuous, and so I shall preserve 'em.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: Keep but this way, and from this place to tell me i^ you have paid me; and so I wish you see all fortune.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Fear not, the Woman will be thanked, I do not doubt it. Are you so crafty, carry it so precisely? this is ^ wake my fears, or to abuse me, I shall look narrowly: ^ spair not Gentlemen, there is an hour to catch a Wo^ in, if you be wise, so, I must leave you too; Now will ^ laugh at my Suitors.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Sir, what courage?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: This Woman is a founder, and cites Statutes t^ all her benefits.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: I never knew yet, so few years and so cunning, ye believe me she has an itch, but how to make her confess ^ for it is a crafty Tit, and plays about you, will not be home, she would fain, but she dares not; carry your ^ but so discreetly, Sir, that want or wantonness seem not t^ search you, and you shall see her open.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: I do love her, and were I rich, would give us thousand pound to wed her wit but one hour, oh 'tis a Dra~gon, and such a spritely way of pleasure, ha Lance.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Your ha Lance broken once, you would cry, ho, ho, Lance.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Some leaden landed Rogue will have this wend now, when all's done, some such youth will carry her, and wear her, greasie out like stuff, some Dunce that knows ^ more but Markets, and admires nothing but a long cha^ at Sizes: O the fortunes!

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Comfort your self.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: They are here yet, and alone too, boldly upon ^ nay, Mistress, I still told you, how 'twould find your ^ this 'tis to venture your charity upon a boy.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Now, what's the matter? stand fast, and like your self.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: Pret hee no more Wench.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: What was his want to you?

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: 'Tis true.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: Or misery, or say he had been i'th' Cage, was th^ no mercy to look abroad but yours?

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose: I am paid for fooling.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
prose: Must every slight companion that can purchase a ^ of poverty and beggerly planet fall under your compass^

speeches.speaker: Lanc.
prose: Here's a new matter.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: Nay, you are served but too well, here he staies ^et, yet as I live.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: How her face alters on me!

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: Out of a conscience I hope.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: I am grad on't.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: How do you gentle Lady?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose:
Much ashamed Sir, (but first stand further off me, ^ are infectious) to find such vanitie, nay almost impudence, where I believ'd a worth: is this your thanks, the grati
^ude you were so mad to make me, your trim counsel Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: Lanc.
prose: What, Lady?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Take your device again, it will not serve Sir, the woman will not bite, you are finely cozened drop it no ^ore for shame.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose:
Do you think you are here Sir am ^
^ur wast ^oateers, your base wenches that scratch at such ^
^s? you are deluded: This is a Gentlewoman of a noble hous^
^orn to a better fame than you can build ne^, and eyes above your pitch.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: I do acknowledge—

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Then I beseech you Sir what could'see, (speak boldly, ^nd speak truly, shame the Devil,) in my behaviour of such easiness that you durst venture to do this?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: You amaze me, this Ring is none of mine, nor did ^ drop it.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
prose: I saw you drop it, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Isab
prose: I took it up too, still looking when your modesty should miss it, why, what a childish part was this?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: I vow.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Vow me no vowes, he that dares do this, has bred himself to boldness, to forswear too; there take your gewgaw, you are too much pampered, and I repent my part, ^s you grow older grow wiser if you can, and so farewel Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Grow wiser if you can? she has put it to you, 'tis a ^ich Ring, did you drop it?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Never, ne're saw it afore, Lance.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Thereby hangs a tail then: what slight she makes ^o catch her self! look up Sir, you cannot lose her if you would, how daintily she flies upon the Lure, and cunningly ^he makes her stops! whistle and she'l come to you.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: I would I were so happy.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Maids are Clocks, the greatest Wheel they show, goes slowest to us, and make's hang on tedious hopes; the ^esser, which are concealed, being often oyl'd with wishes, ^ee like desires, and never leave that motion, till the ^ongue strikes; she is flesh, blood and marrow, young as her purpose, and soft as pity; no Monument to worship, but a mould to make men in, a neat one, and I know how e're she appears now, which is near enough, you are stark blind if you hit not soon at night; she would venture forty pounds more but to feel a Flea in your shape bite her: drop to more Rings forsooth, this was the prettiest thing to know her heart by.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Thou putst me in much comfort.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Put your self in good comfort, if she do not point ^ou out the way, drop no more Rings, she'l drop her self ^nto you.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: I wonder my Brother comes not.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Let him alone, and feed your self on your own fortunes; come be frolick, and let's be monstrous wise and full of counsel, drop no more Rings.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: If you will needs be foolish you must be used so: who sent for you? who entertained you Gentlemen? who bid you welcom hither? you came crowding, and impudently bold; press on my patience, as if I kept a house for ^ Companions, and of all sorts: will 'have your wills, will vex me and force my liking from you I ne're ow'd ^ou?

speeches.speaker: Fount.
prose: For all this we will dine with you.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: And for all this will have a better answer from you.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: You shall never, neither have an answer nor ^inner, unless you use me with a more staid respect, and stay your time too.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Forward with the meat now.

speeches.speaker: Rog.
prose: Come Gentlemen, march fairly.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Roger, you are a weak Serving man, your white broath runs from you; sie, how I sweat un^r this Pile of Beef; an Elephant can do more! Oh for such a back now, and in these times, what might a man arrive at! Goose, grase you up, and Woodcock march behinde thee, I am almost sound^ed.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Who bid you bring the meat yet? away you knaves, I will not dine these two hours: how am I vext and chased! go carry it back and tell the Cook, he's an arrant Ras^al, to send before I called.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Face about Gentlemen, beat a mou^nfull march then, and give some supporters, or else I perish—

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: It does me much good to see her chafe thus.

speeches.speaker: Hare.
prose: We can stay Madam, and will stay and dwell here, 'tis good Air.

speeches.speaker: Fount.
prose: I know you have beds enough, and meat you never want.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: You want a little.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: We dare to pretend no. Since you are churlis^, we'l give you Physick, you must purge this anger, it burns you and decays you.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: If I had you out once, I would be at the charge of a portcullis for you.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Good morrow noble Lady.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Good morrow Sir. How sweetly now he looks, and how full manly! what slaves were these to use him so!

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: I come to look a young man I call Brother.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Such a one was here Sir, as I remember your own Brother, but gone almost an hour agoe.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Good ee'n then.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: You must not so soon Sir, here be some Gentlemen, it may be you are acquainted with 'em.

speeches.speaker: Hare.
prose: Will nothing make him miserable?

speeches.speaker: Fount.
prose: How glorious!

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: It is the very he, does it rain fortunes, or has he a familiar?

speeches.speaker: Hare.
prose: How doggedly he looks too?

speeches.speaker: Fount.
prose: I am beyond my faith, pray let's be going.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Where are these Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Here.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Yes I know 'em, and will be more familiar.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: Morrow Madam.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Nay stay and dine.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose:
You shall stay till I talk with you, and not dine neither, but fastingly my fury, you think you have undone me, think so still, and swallow that belief, till you be company for Court-hand Clarks, and starved Atturnies, till you break in at playes like Prentices for three a groat, and crack Nuts with the Scholars in peny Rooms again, and fight for Apples, till you return to what I found you, people be^rai'd into the hands of Fencers, Challengers, Tooth draw is Bills, and tedious Proclamations in Meal-markets, with throngings to see Cutpurses: stir not, but hear, and mark, I'le cut your throats else, till Water works, and rumours of New Rivers rid you again and run you into questions who built Thames, till you run mad for Lotteries, and stand there with your Tables to glean the golden Sentences, and cite 'em secrely to Servingmen for sound Essayes, till Taverns allow you but a Towel room to Tipple Wine in, that the Bell hath gone for twice, and Glasses that look li^e broken promises, tied up with wicker proteslations, ^sh Tobacco with half Pipes, nor in half a year once burn^
and Bisket that Bawds have rubb'd their gums upon like Corals to bring the mark again, tell these hour Rascals so, this most fatal hour will come again, think I sit down the looser.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Will you stay Gentlemen, a piece of Beef and a cold Capon, that's all, you know you are welcom.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
prose: That was cast to abuse us.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: Steal off, the Devil is in his anger.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Nay I am sure you will not leave me so discourteously, now I have provided for you.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: What do you here? why do ye vex a woman of her goodness, her state and worth? can you bring a fair certificate that you deserve to be her footmen? husbands, you puppies? husbands for Whores and Bawds, away you wind sucke^s; do not look big, nor prate, nor stay, nor grumble, and when you are gone, seem to laugh at my fury, and slight this Lady, I shall hear, and know this: and though I am not bound to fight for women, as far they are good I dare preserve 'em: be not too bold, for if you be, I'le swinge you monstrously without all pity, your honours now goe, avoid me mainly.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Well Sir, you have delivered me, I thank you, and with your nobleness prevented danger, their tongues might utter, we'll all go and eat Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: No, no, I dare not trust my self with women, go to your meat, eat little, take less ease, and tie your body to a daily labour, you may live honestly, and so I thank you.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Well go thy ways, thou art a noble fellow, and some means I must work to have thee know it.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: MOst certain 'tis her hands that hold him up, and her sister relieves Frank.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: I am glad to hear it: but wherefore do they not pursue this fortune to some fair end?

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: The women are too craftie, Valentine too coy, and Frank too bashfull, had any wise man hold of such a blessing, they would strike it out o'th' slint but they would form it.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: The Widow sure, why does she stir so early?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: 'Tis strange, I cannot force him to understand me, and make a benefit of what I would bring him: tell my sister I'le use my devotions at home this morning, she may if she please go to Church.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Hey ho.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: And do you wait upon her with a torch Sir.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Hey ho.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: You lazie Knave.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Here is such a tinkle tanklings that we can ne're lie quiet, and sleep our prayers out. Ralph, pray emptie my right shooe that you made your Chamber pot, and burn a little Rosemarie in't, I must wait upon my Lady. This morning Prayer has brought me into a consumption, I have nothing left but flesh and bones about me.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: You drousie slave, nothing but sleep and swilling?

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Had you been bitten with Bandog sleas, as I have been, and haunted with the night Mare.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: With an Ale-pot.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: You would have little list to morning Prayers, pray take my fellow Ralph, he has a Psalm Book, I am an ingrum man.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Get you ready quickly, and when she is ready wait upon her handsomely; no more, be gone.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: If I do snore my part out —

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Now to our purposes.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Good morrow, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Good morrow, Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Good joy and fortune.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: These are good things, and worth my thanks, thank you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Much joy I hope you'l find, we came to grat^ your new knit marriage-band.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: How?

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: He's a Gentleman, although he be my kinsm^ my fair Niece.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Niece, Sir?

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Yes Lady, now I may say so, 'tis no shame to yo^ say a Gentleman, and winking at some light fancies, w^ you most happily may affect him for, as bravely carried, a nobly bred and managed.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: What's all this? I understand you not, what Nie^ what marriage-knot?

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: I'le tell plainly, you are my Niece, and Valentine the Gentleman has made you so by marriage.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Marriage?

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
