prose: Yes Lady, and 'twas a noble and vertuous part, t^ take a falling man to your protection, and buoy him up a~gain to all his glories.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: The men are mad.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: What though he wanted these outward thing^ that flie away like shadows, was not his mind a full or and a brave one? You have wealth enough to give h^ gloss and outside, and he wit enough to give way to love a Lady.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: I ever thought he would do well.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Nay, I knew how ever he wheel'd about ^ a loose Cabine, he would charge home at length, like a brave Gentleman; Heavens blessing o' your heart Lady, we are so bound to honour you, in all your service ^ devoted to you.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Do not look so strange Widow, it must be know^ better a general joy; no stirring here yet, come, come, ^ cannot hide 'em.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Pray be not impudent, these are the finest toyes, be like I am married then?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: You are in a miserable estate in the worlds account else, I would not for your wealth it come to doubting.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: And I am great with child?

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose:
No, great they say not, but 'tis a full opinion you^ with child, and great joy among the Gentlemen, your hu^
band hath bestirred himself fairly.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Alas, we know his private hours of entrance, h^ long, and when he stayed, could name the bed too, where i^ paid down his first-fruits.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: I shall believe anon.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: And we consider for some private reasons, you work have it private, yet take your own pleasure; and so good morrow, my best Niece, my sweetest.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: No, no, pray stay.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: I know you would be with him, love him, and love him well.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: You'l find him noble, this may beget —

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: It must needs work upon her.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: These are fine bobs i'faith, married, and with ch^ too! how long has this been, I trow? they seem grave fel~lows, they should not come to slout; married, and bedded the world takes notice too! where lies this May game? I could be vext extreamly now, and rail too, but 'tis to ^ end, though I itch a little, must I be scratcht I know not bo^ who waits there?

speeches.speaker: Hum.
prose: Madam.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Make ready my Coach quickly, and wait you only and hark you Sir, be secret and speedy, inquire out w^ he lies.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
prose: I shall do it, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Married, and got with child in a dream ^ fine i'saith, sure he that did this, would do better wa^

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Hold thy Torch handsomely: how dost thou Frank? ^ter Bassel, bear up.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: You have fried me soundly, Sack do you call this ^ink?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: A shrewd dog, Frank, will bite abundantly.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Now could I fight, and fight with thee.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: With me, thou man of Memphis?

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose:
But that thou art mine own natural master, yet ^y sack says thou art no man, thou art a Pagan, and pawn
^ thy land, which a noble cause.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose:
No arms, nor arms, good Lancelot, dear Lance,
^ fighting here, we will have Lands boy, Livings, and ^tles, thou shalt be a Vice-Roy, hang fighting, hang't 'tis ^ut of fashion.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: I would fain labour you into your lands again, go ^, it is behoveful.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Fie Lance, fie.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: I must beat some body, and why not my Master, ^efore a stranger? charity and beating begins at home.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Come, thou shalt beat me.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: I will not be compel'd, and you were two Masters, scorn the motion.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Wilt thou sleep?

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: I scorn sleep.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Wilt thou go eat?

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose:
I scorn meat, I come for rompering, I come to ^ait upon my charge discreetly; for look you, if you will ^ot take your Mortgage again, here do I lie St
George, and ^ forth.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose:
And here do I St
George, bestride the Dragon, thus ^ith my Lance.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: I sting, I sting with my tail.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Do you so, do you so, Sir? I shall tail you presently.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: By no means, do not hurt him.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Take this Nelson, and now rise, thou Maiden Knight ^f Mallig^, lace on thy Helmet of inchanted Sack, and ^harge again.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: I'le play no more, you abuse me, will you go?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: I'le bid you good morrow, Brother, for sleep I ^annot, I have a thousand fancies.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Now thou art arrived, go bravely to the matter, ^nd do something of worth, Frank.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: You shall hear from us.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: This Rogue, if he had been sober, sure had beaten ^ne, is the most tettish Knave.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: 'Tis he.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Good morrow.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Why, Sir, good morrow to you too, and you be ^o lusty.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: You have made your Brother a fine man, we met ^im.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: I made him a fine Gentleman, he was a fool before, ^rought up amongst the midst of Small-Beer-Brew-houses, what would you have with me?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: I come to tell you, your latest hour is come.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Are you my sentence?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: The sentence of your state.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Let it be hang'd then, and let it be hang'd high enough, I may not see it.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: A gracious resolution.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: What would you have else with me, will you go drink, and let the world slide, Uncle? Ha, ha, ha, boyes, ^rink Sack like Whey, boyes.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Have you no feeling, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Come hither Merchant: make me a supper, thou most reverent Land catcher, a supper of forty pounds.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: What then, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Then bring thy Wife along, and thy fair Sisters, ^hy Neighbours and their Wives, and all their trinkets, ^et me have forty Trumpets, and such Wine, we'll laugh at all the miseries of Mortgage, and then in state I'le rende^ thee an answer.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: What say you to this?

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: I dare not say, nor think neither.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Will you redeem your state, speak to the point, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Not, not if it were mine heir in the Turks Gallies.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Then I must take an order?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Take a thousand, I will not keep it, nor thou shalt not have it, because thou camest i'th' nick, thou shalt not have it, go take possession, and be sure you hold it, hold fast with both hands, for there be those hounds uncoupled, will ring you such a knell, go down in glory, and march up on my land, and cry, All's mine; cry as the Devil did, and be the Devil, mark what an Echo follows, build fine March-panes, to entertain Sir Silk-worm and his Lady, and pull the Chappel down, and raise a Chamber for Mistress Silver-pin, to lay her belly in, mark what an Earthquake comes. Then foolish Merchant my Tenants are no Subjects, they obey nothing, and they are people too never Chri~stened, they know no Law nor Conscience, they'll devour thee; and thou mortal, the stopple, they'll confound thee within three days; no bit nor memory of what thou wert, no not the Wart upon thy Nose there, shall be e're heard of more; go take possession, and bring thy Children down, to rost like Rabbets, they love young Toasts and Butter, Bow-bell Suckers; as they love mischief, and hate Law, they are Cannibals; bring down thy kindred too, that be not fruitful, there be those Mandrakes that will mollifie 'em, go take possession. I'le go to my Chamber, afore Boy go.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: He's mad sure.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: He's half drunk sure: and yet I like this unwillingness to lose it, this looking back.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Yes, if he did it handsomely, but he's so harsh and strange.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Believe it 'tis his drink, Sir, and I am glad his drink has thrust it out.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Cannibals? if ever I come to view his Regiment, if fair terms may be had.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: He tells you true, Sir, they are a bunch of the most boisterous Rascals disorder ever made, let 'em be mad once, the power of the whole Country cannot cool 'em, be patient but a while.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: As long as you will, Sir, before I buy a bargain of such Runts, I'le buy a Colledge for Bears, and live among 'em.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: How dost thou now?

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Better than I was, and straighter, but my head's a Hogshead still, it rowls and tumbles.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Thou wert cruelly paid.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: I may live to requite it, put a Snaffle of Sack in my mouth and then ride me very well.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: 'Twas all but sport, I'le tell thee what I mean now, I mean to see this Wench.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Where a Devil is she? and there were two, 'twere better.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Dost thou hear the Bell ring?

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Yes, yes.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Then she comes to prayers, early each morning thither: Now if I could but meet her, for I am of another mettle now.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: What light's yon?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Ha, 'tis a light, take her by the hand and court her.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Take her below the girdle, you'l never speed else, it comes on this way still, oh that I had but such an opportunity in a Saw-pit, how it comes on, comes on! 'tis here.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: 'Tis she: fortune I kiss thy hand— Good morrow Lady.

speeches.speaker: Isa.
prose:
What voice is that, Sirra, do you steep as you go,

'tis he, I am glad ^a't. Why, Shorthose?

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Yes forsooth, I was dreamt, I was going to Church.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: She sees you as plain as I do.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Hold the torch up.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: H^r^'s nothing but a stall, and a Butchers Dog asleep in 't, where did you see the voice?

speeches.speaker: ^an.
prose: She looks still angry.

speeches.speaker: I a^.
prose: To her and meet Sir.

speeches.speaker: I^b.
prose: Here, here.

speeches.speaker: ^a^.
prose: Yes Lady, never bless your self, I am but a man, and like an honest man, now I will thank you—

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: What do you mean, who sent for you, who desired you?

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: Shall I put out the Torch forsooth?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Can I not go about my private meditations, Ha, but such companions as you must ruffle me? you had best go with me Sir?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: 'T was my purpose.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Why, what an impudence is this! you had best, being so near the Church, provide a Priest, and perswade me to marry you.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: It was my meaning, and such a husband, so loving, and so carefull, my youth, and all my fortunes shall arrive at— Hark you?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: 'Tis strange you should be thus unmannerly, turn home again si^a, you had best now force my man to lead your way.

speeches.speaker: ^an.
prose: Yes marry shall he Lady, forward my friend.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: This is a pretty Riot, it may grow to a rape.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Do you like that better? I can ravish you an hundred times, and never hurt you.

speeches.speaker: Short.
prose: I see nothing, I am asleep still, when you have done tell me, and then I'le wake Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Are you in earnest Sir, do you long to be hang'd?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Yes by my troth Lady in these fair Tresses.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Shall I call out for help?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: No by no means, that were a weak trick Lady, I'le kiss, and stop your mouth.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: You'l answer all these?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: A thousand kisses more.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: I was never abused thus, you had best give out too, that you sound me willing, and say I doted on you?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: That's known already, and no man living shall now carry you from me.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: This is fine i'faith.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: It shall be ten times finer.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Well, seeing you are so valiant, keep your way, I will to Church.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: And I will wait upon you.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: And it is most likely there's a Lriest, if you dare venture as you profess, I would wish you look about you, to do these rude tricks, for you know the recompences, and trust not to my mercy.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: But I will Lady.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: For I'le so handle you.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: That's it I look for.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: Afore thou dream.

speeches.speaker: Shor.
prose: Have you done?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Go on Sir, and follow if you dare.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: If I do not, hang me.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
prose: 'Tis all thine own boy, an 'twere a million, god a mercy Sack, when would small Beer have done this?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Whose that that knocks and bounces, what a Devil ails you, is hell broke loose, or do you keep an Iron mill?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: 'Tis a Gentlewoman Sir that must needs speak with you.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: A Gentlewoman? what Gentlewoman, what have I to do with Gentlewomen?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: She will not be answered Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Fling up the bed and let her in, I'le try how gentle she is—

This Sack has fill'd my head so full of bables, I am a^ mad; what Gentlewoman should this be? I hope she ^ brought me no butter print along with her to lay to ^ charge, if she have 'tis all one, I'le forswear it.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: O you're a noble Gallant, send off your Serve^ pray.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: She will not ravish me? by this light she loo^ sharp set as a Sparrow hawk, what wouldst thou wom^?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: O you have used me kindly, and like a Gentle^ this is to trust to you.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Trust to me, for what?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Because I said in jest once, you were a handsom ^ one I could like well, and fooling, made you believe I love you, and might be brought to marrie.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: The widow is drunk too.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
You out of this, which is a fine discretion, give ^ the matter's done, you have won and wed me, and t^ you have put, fairly put for an heir too, these are fire ^
~mours to advance my credit: i'th' name of mischief who did you mean?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: That you loved me, and that you might be broug^ to marrie me? why, what a Devil do you mean widow?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: 'Twas a fine trick too, to tell the world though you had enjoyed your first wish you wished, the wealth you aimed at, that I was poor, which is most true, I am, ha^ sold my lands, because I love not those vexations, yet i^ mine honours sake, if you must be prating, and for my cre~dits sake in the Town.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: I tell thee widow, I like thee ten times better, ^ thou hast no Lands, for now thy hopes and cares lye on thy husband, if e're thou marryest more.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Have not you married me, and for this main cause now as you report it, to be your Nurse?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: My Nurse? why, what am I grown to, give me the Glass, my Nurse.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
You n'er said truer, I must confess I did a little favour you, and with some labour might have been pers^
ded, but when I found I must be hourly troubled, with ma^
~ing broths, and dawbing your decayes with swadling, ^ with stitching up your ruines, for the world so reports.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Do not provoke me.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: And half an eye may see.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Do not provoke me, the world's a lying world, are thou snalt find it, have a good heart, and take a strong f^ to thee, and mark what follows, my Nurse, yes, you ^ rock me: Widow I'le keep you waking.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: You are disposed Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Yes marry am I Widow, and you shall feel it, ^ and they touch my freehold, I am a Tiger.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: I think so.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Come.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Whither?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Any whither.
The sit's upon me now, the sit's upon me now,
Come quickly gentle Ladie, the sit's upon me now,
The world shall know they're fools,
And so shalt thou do too,
Let the Cobler meddle with his tools,
The sit's upon me now.
Take me quickly, while I am in this vein, away with me for if I have but two hours to consider, all the widows in the world cannot recover me.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: If you will, go with me Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Yes marrie will I, but 'tis in anger yet, and I will marrie thee, do not cross me; yes, and I will lie with thee and get a whole bundle of babies, and I will kiss thee, st^ still and kiss me handsomely, but do not provoke me, ^ neither hand nor foot, for I am dangerous, I drunk s^ yesternight, do not allure me: Thou art no widow of t^s world, come in pitie, and in spite I'le marrie thee, not a w^ more, and I may be brought to love thee.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Well met again, and what good news yet?

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Faith nothing.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: No fruits of what we fowed?

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Nothing I hear of.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: No turning in this tide yet?

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: 'Tis all flood, and till that fall away, there's no expecting.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Is not this his younger Brother?

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: With a Gentlewoman the widow's sister, as I live ^e smiles, he has got good hold, why well said Frank i'faith, ^et's stay and mark.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Well, you are the prettiest youth, and so you have ^andled me, think you ha' me sure.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: As sure as wedlock.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: You had best lie with me too.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Yes indeed will I, and get such black ey'd boyes.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: God a Mercy, Frank.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: This is a merrie world, poor simple Gentlewomen that think no harm, cannot walk about their business, but they must be catcht up I know not how.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: I'le tell you, and I'le instruct ye too, have I caught ^ou, Mistress?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: Well, and it were not for pure pity, I would give ^ou the slip yet, but being as it is.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: It shall be better.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: My sister, as I live, your Brother with her! sure, I ^hink you are the Kings takers.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Now it works.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Nay, you shall know I am a man.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: I think so.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: And such proof you shall have.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: I pray speak softly.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: I'le speak it out Widow, yes and you shall confess too, I am no Nurse-child, I went for a man, a good one, if you can beat me out o'th' pit.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: I did but jest with you.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: I'le handle you in earnest, and so handle you: Nay, when my credit calls.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Are you mad?

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: I am mad, I am mad.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Good morrow, Sir, I like your preparation.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Thou hast been at it, Frank.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Yes faith, 'tis done Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Along with me then, never hang an arf^, widow

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: 'Tis to no purpose, sister.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Well said Black-brows, advance your torches Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Yes, yes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: And keep your ranks.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Lance, carrie this before him.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Carrie it in state.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: What are you, Musicians? I know your coming, and what are those behind you?

speeches.speaker: Musi.
prose: Gentlemen that sent us to give the Lady a good morrow.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: O I know them, come boy sing the song I taught you,
And sing it lustily, come forward Gentlemen, you're welcom,
Welcom, now we are all friends, go get the Priest ready,
And let him not be long, we have much business:
Come Frank, rejoyce with me, thou hast got the start boy,
But I'le so tumble after, come my friends lead,
Lead cheerfully, and let your Fiddles ring boyes,
My follies and my fancies have an end here,
Display the morgage Lance, Merchant I'le pay you,
And every thing shall be in joynt again.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: Afore, afore.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: And now confess, and know,
Wit without Money, sometimes gives the blow.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: IS he then taken?

speeches.speaker: Her.
verse: And brought back even now, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: He was not in disgrace?

speeches.speaker: Her.
verse: No man more lov'd,
Nor more deserv'd it, being the only man
That durst be honest in this Court.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Indeed
We have heard abroad, Sir, that the State hath suffered
A great change, since the Countesses death.

speeches.speaker: Her.
verse: It hath, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: My five years absence hath kept me a stranger
So much to all the occurents of my Country,
As you shall bind me for some short relation
To make me understand the present times.

speeches.speaker: Her.
verse: I must begin then with a War was made
And seven years with all cruelty continued
Upon our Flanders by the Duke of Brabant,
The cause grew thus: during our Earls minority,
Wolfort, (who now usurps) was employed thither
To treat about a match between our Fail
And the Daughter and Heir of Brabant: during which treaty
The Brabander pretends, this Daughter was
Stoln from his Court, by practice of our State,
Though we are all confirm'd, 'twas a sought quarrel
To lay an unjust g^ipe upon this Earldom,
It being here believ'd the Duke of Brabant
Had no such loss. This War upon't proclaim'd,
Our Earl, being then a Child, although his Father
Good Gerrard liv'd, yet in respect he was
Chosen by the Countesses favour, for her Husband,
And but a Gentleman, and Florez holding
His right unto this Country from his Mother,
The State thought fit in this defensive War,
Wolfort being then the only man of mark,
To make him General.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Which place we have heard
He did discharge with houour.

speeches.speaker: Her.
verse: I, so long,
And with so blest successes, that the Brabander
Was forc't (his treasures wasted, and the choice
Of his best men of Armes tyr'd, or cut off)
To leave the field, and sound a base retreat
Back to his Country: but so broken both
In mind and means, er'e to make head again,
That hitherto he sits down by his loss,
Not daring, or for honour, or revenge
Again to tempt his fortune. But this Victory
More broke our State, and made a deeper hurt
In Flanders, than the greatest overthrow
She ever receiv'd: For Wolfort, now beholding
Himself, and actions, in the flattering glass
Of self-deservings, and that cherish't by
^e strong assurance of his power, for then
^ Captains of the Army were his creatures,
^e common Souldier too at his devotion,
^de so by full indulgence to their rapines
^d secret bounties, this strength too well known
^d what it could effect, soon put in practice,
^ further'd by the Child-hood of the Earl:
^d their improvidence, that might have pierc't
^e heart of his designs, gave him occasion
^ seize the whole, and in that plight you find it.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Sir, I receive the knowledge of thus much,
^ a choice favour from you.

speeches.speaker: Her.
verse: Only I must add,
^es holds out.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Whither, Sir, I am going,
^t there last night I had a ship put in,
^d my Horse waits me.

speeches.speaker: Her.
verse: I wish you a good journey.

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: What? Hubert stealing from me? who disarm'd him?
^ was more than I commanded; take your sword,
^m best guarded with it in your hand,
^ave seen you use it nobly.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: And will turn it
^ my own bosom, ere it shall be drawn
^ worthily or rudely.

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: Would you leave me
Without a farewel, Hubert? slie a friend
^nwearied in his study to advance you?
^hat have I e're possess'd which was not yours?
^ either did not court you to command it?
^ho ever yet arriv'd to any grace,
^eward or trust from me, but his approaches
^ere by your fair reports of him prefer'd?
^d what is more I made my self your Servant,
^ making you the Master of those secrets
Which not the rack of Conscience could draw from me,
^or I, when I askt mercy, trust my prayers with;
^et after these assurances of love,
^hese tyes and bonds of friendship, to forsake me?
^orsake me as an enemy? come you must
^ve me a reason.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Sir, and so I will,
I may do't in private: and you hear it.

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: All leave the room: you have your will, sit down
^nd use the liberty of our first friendship.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Friendship? when you prov'd Traitor first, that vanish'd,
^or do I owe you any thought, but hate,
^now my flight hath forfeited my head;
^nd so I may make you first understand
^hat a strange monster you have made your self,
welcome it.

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: To me this is strange language.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: To you? why what are you?

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: Your Prince and Master,
^he Earl of Flanders.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: By a proper title!
^ais'd to it by cunning, circumvention, force,
^ood, and proscriptions.

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: And in all this wisdom,
^ad I not reason? when by Gerrards plots
^hould have first been call'd to a strict accompt
^ow, and which way I had consum'd that mass
^f money, as they term it, in the War,
Who underhand had by his Ministers
^etracted my great action, made my faith
^nd loyalty suspected, in which failing
^e sought my life by practice.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: With what fore-head
^o you speak this to me? who (as I know't)
^ust, and will say 'tis false.

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: My Guard there.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Sir, you bad me sit, and promis'd you would hear,
Which I now say you shall; not a sound more,
For I that am contemner of mine own,
Am Master of your life; then here's a Sword
Between you, and all aids, Sir, though you blind
The credulous beast, the multitude, you pass not
These gross untruths on me.

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: How? gross untruths?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I, and it is favourable language,
They had been in a mean man lyes, and foul ones.

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: You take strange Licence.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Yes, were not those rumours
Of being called unto your answer, spread
By your own followers? and weak Gerrard wrought
(But by your cunning practice) to believe
That you were dangerous; yet not to be
Punish'd by any formal course of Law,
But first to be made sure, and have your crimes
Laid open after, which your quaint train taking
You fled unto the Camp, and their crav'd humbly
Protection for your innocent life, and that,
Since you had scap'd the fury of the War,
You might not fall by treason: and for proof,
You did not for your own ends make this danger;
Some that had been before by you suborn'd,
Came forth and took their Oaths they had been hir'd
By Gerrard to your Murther. This once heard,
And easily believ'd, th' inraged Souldier
Seeing no further than the outward-man,
Snatch'd hastily his Arms, ran to the Court,
Kill'd all that made resistance, cut in pieces
Such as were Servants, or thought friends to Gerrard,
Vowing the like to him.

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: Will you yet end?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Which he foreseeing, with his Son, the Earl;
Forsook the City; and by secret wayes
As you give out, and we would gladly have it,
Escap'd their fury: though 'tis more than fear'd
They fell amongst the rest; Nor stand you there
To let us only mourn the impious means
By which you got it, but your cruelties since
So far transcend your former bloody ills,
As if compar'd, they only would appear
Essays of mischief; do not stop your ears,
More are behind yet.

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: O repeat them not,
'Tis Hell to hear them nam'd.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: You should have thought,
That Hell would be your punishment when you did them,
A Prince in nothing but your princely lusts,
And boundless rapines.

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: No more I beseech you.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Who was the Lord of house or land, that stood
Within the prospect of your covetous eye?

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: You are in this to me a greater Tyrant,
Than e're I was to any.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I end thus
The general grief: now to my private wrong;
The loss of Gerrards Daughter Jaqueline:
The hop'd for partner of my lawful Bed,
Your cruelty hath frighted from mine arms;
And her I now was wandring to recover.
Think you that I had reason now to leave you,
When you are grown so justly odious,
That ev'n my stay here with your grace and favour,
Makes my life irksome? here, surely take it,
And do me but this fruit of all your friendship,
That I may dye by you, and not your Hang-man.

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: Oh Hubert, these your words and reasons have
As well drawn drops of blood from my griev'd heart,
As these tears from mine eyes;
Despise them not.
By all that's sacred, I am serious, Hubert,
You now have made me sensible, what furies,
Whips, Hangmen, and Tormentors a bad man
Do's ever bear about him: let the good
That you this day have done, be ever number'd
The first of your best actions;
Can you think,
Where Goswin is or Gerrard, or your love,
Or any else, or all that are proscrib'd?
I will resign, what I usurp, or have
Unjustly forc'd; the dayes I have to live
Are too too few to make them satisfaction
With any penitence: yet I vow to practise
All of a man.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: O that your heart and tongue
Did not now differ!

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: By my griefs they do not.
Take the good pains to search them out; 'tis worth it,
You have made clean a Leper: trust me you have,
And made me once more fit for the society,
I hope of good men.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Sir, do not abuse
My aptness to believe.

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: Suspect not you
A faith that's built upon so true a sorrow,
Make your own safetys: ask them all the ties
Humanity can give, Hemskirk too shall
Along with you to this so wish'd discovery,
And in my name profess all that you promise;
And I will give you this help to't: I have
Of late receiv'd certain intelligence,
That some of them are in or about Bruges
To be found out: which I did then interpret,
The cause of that Towns standing out against me;
But now am glad, it may direct your purpose
Of giving them their safety, and me peace.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Be constant to your goodness, and you have it.

speeches.speaker: 1 Mer.
verse: 'Tis much that you deliver of this Goswin.

speeches.speaker: 2 Mer.
verse: But short of what I could, yet have the Country
Confirm'd it true, and by a general oath,
And not a man hazard his credit in it:
He beats himself with such a confidence
As if he were the Master of the Sea,
And not a wind upon the Sailers compass,
But from one part or other was his factor,
To bring him in the best commodities,
Merchant e're ventur'd for.
'Tis strange.
And yet
This do's in him deserve the least of wonder,
Compared with other his peculiar fashions,
Which all admire: he's young, and rich, at least
Thus far reputed so, that since he liv'd
In Bruges, there was never brought to harbour
So rich a Bottom, but his bill would pass
Unquestion'd for her lading.

speeches.speaker: 3 Mer.
verse: Yet he still
Continues a good man.

speeches.speaker: 2 Mer.
verse: So good, that but
To doubt him, would be held an injury
Or rather malice, with the best that trassique;
But this is nothing, a great stock, and fortune,
Crowning his judgement in his undertakings
May keep him upright that way: But that wealth
Should want the power to make him dote on it,
Or youth teach him to wrong it, best commends
His constant temper; for his outward habit
'Tis suitable to his present course of life:
His table furnish'd well, but not with dainties
That please the appetite only for their rareness,
Or their dear price: nor given to wine or women,
Beyond his health, or warrant of a man,
I mean a good one: and so loves his state
He will not hazard it at play; nor lend
Upon the assurance of a well pen'd Letter,
Although a challenge second the denial
From such as make th' opinion of their valour
Their means of feeding.

speeches.speaker: 1 Mer.
verse: These are wayes to thrive,
And the means not curs'd.

speeches.speaker: 2 Mer.
verse: What follows, this
Makes many venturers with him, in their wishes,
For his prosperity: for when desert
Or reason leads him to be liberal,
His noble mind and ready hand contend
Which can add most to his free courtesies,
Or in their worth, or speed to make them so.
Is there a Virgin of good fame wants dower?
He is a Father to her; or a Souldier
That in his Countreys service, from the war
Hath brought home only scars, and want? his house
Receives him, and relieves him, with that care
As if what he possess'd had been laid up
For such good uses, and he steward of it.
But I should lose my self to speak him further
And stale in my relation, the much good
You may be witness of, if your remove
From Bruges be not speedy.

speeches.speaker: 1 Mer.
verse: This report
I do assure you will not hasten it,
Nor would I wish a better man to deal with
For what I am to part with.

speeches.speaker: 3 Mer.
verse: Never doubt it,
He is your man and ours, only I wish
His too much forwardness to embrace all bargains
Sink him not in the end.

speeches.speaker: 2 Mer.
verse: Have better hopes,
For my part I am confident; here he comes.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: I take it at your own rates, your wine of Cyprus,
But for your Candy sugars, they have met
With such foul weather, and are priz'd so high
I cannot save in them.

speeches.speaker: 4. Mer.
verse: I am unwilling
To seek another Chapman: make me offer
Of something near price, that may assure me
You can deal for them.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: I both can, and will,
But not with too much loss; your bill of lading
Speaks of two hundred chests, valued by you
At thirty thousand gilders, I will have them
At twenty eight; so, in the payment of
Three thousand sterling, you fall only in
Two hundred pound.

speeches.speaker: 4 Mer.
verse: You know, they are so cheap. —

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Why look you; I'le deal farily, there's in prisor,
And at your suit, a Pirat, but unable
To make you satisfaction, and past hope
To live a week, if you should prosecute
What you can prove against him: set him free,
And you shall have your mony to a Stiver,
And present payment.

speeches.speaker: 4 Mer.
verse: This is above wonder,
A Merchant of your rank, that have at Sea
So many Bottoms in the danger of
These water-Thieves, should be a means to save 'em,
It more importing you for your own safety
To be at charge to scour the Sea of them
Than stay the sword of justice, that is ready
To fall on one so conscious of his guilt
That he dares not deny it.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: You mistake me,
If you think I would cherish in this Captain
The wrong he did to you, or any man;
I was lately with him, (having first, from others
^e testimony been assured a man
^ more desert never put from the shore)
^ead his letters of Mart from this State granted
^ the recovery of such losses, as
^ had receiv'd in Spain, 'twas that he aim'd at,
^t at three tuns of wine, bisket, or beef,
^hi^n his necessity made him take from you.
^he had pillag'd you near, or sunk your ship,
^ thrown your men o'r board, then he deserv'd
^e Laws extreamest rigour. But since want
^ what he could not live without, compel'd him
^ that he did (which yet our State calls death)
^ity his misfortune; and to work you
^ some compassion of them, I come up
^ your own price: save him, the goods are mine;
^not, seek else-where, I'le not deal for them.

speeches.speaker: 4 Mer.
verse: Well Sir, for your love, I will once be led
^ change my purpose.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: For your profit rather.

speeches.speaker: 4 Mer.
verse: I'le presently make means for his discharge,
^l when, I leave you.

speeches.speaker: 2 Mer.
verse: What do you think of this?

speeches.speaker: 1 Mer.
verse: As of a deed of noble pity: guided
^ a strong judgement.

speeches.speaker: 2 Mer.
verse: Save you Master Goswin.

speeches.speaker: Goswin.
verse: Good day to all.

speeches.speaker: 2 Mer.
verse: We bring you the refusall
^ more Commodities.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Are you the owners
^ the ship that last night put into the Harbour?

speeches.speaker: 1 Mer.
verse: Both of the ship, and lading.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: What's the fraught?

speeches.speaker: 1 Mer.
verse: Indico, Cochineel, choise Chyna stuffs.

speeches.speaker: 3 Mer.
verse: And cloath of Gold brought from Cambal.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Rich lading,
^ which I were your Chapman, but I am
^ready out of cash.

speeches.speaker: 1 Mer.
verse: I'le give you day
^ the moiety of all.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: How long?

speeches.speaker: 3 Mer.
verse: Six months.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: 'Tis a fair offer: which (if we agree
^bout the prices) I, with thanks accept of,
^nd will make present payment of the rest;
^me two hours hence I'le come aboard.

speeches.speaker: 1 Mer.
verse: The Gunner shall speak you welcom.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: I'le not fail.

speeches.speaker: 3 Mer.
verse: Good morrow.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Heaven grant my Ships a safe return, before
^he day of this great payment: as they are
^pected three months sooner: and my credit
^ands good with all the world.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Bless my good Master,
^he prayers of your poor Beads-man ever shall
^ sent up for you.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: God o'mercy Clause,
^here's something to put thee in mind hereafter
^o think of me.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: May he that gave it you
^eward you for it, with encrease, good Master.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: I thrive the better for thy prayers.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I hope so.
^his three years have I fed upon your bounties,
^nd by the fire of your blest charity warm'd me,
^nd yet, good Master, pardon me, that must,
^hough I have now receiv'd your alms, presume
^o make one sute more to you.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: What is't Clause?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Yet do not think me impudent I beseech you,
^nce hitherto your charity hath prevented
^y begging your relief, 'tis not for mony
^o^ cloaths (good Master) but your good word for me.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: That thou shalt have, Clause, for I think thee honest.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: To morrow then (dear Mr.) take the trouble
Of walking early unto Beggars Bush,
And as you see me, among others (Brethren
In my affliction) when you are demanded
Which you like best among us, point out me,
And then pass by, as if you knew me not.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: But what will that advantage thee?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: O much Sir,
'Twill give me the preheminence of the rest,
Make me a King among 'em, and protect me
From all abuse, such as are stronger, might
Offer my age; Sir, at your better leisure
I will inform you further of the good
It may do to me.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: 'Troth thou mak'st me wonder;
Have you a King and common wealth among you?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: We have, and there are States are govern'd worse.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Ambition among Beggars?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Many great ones
Would part with half their states, to have the place,
And credit to beg in the first file, Master:
But shall I be so much bound to your furtherance
In my Petition?

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: That thou shalt not miss of,
Nor any worldly care make me forget it,
I will be early there.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Heaven bless my Master.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: COme Princes of the ragged regiment,
You o' the blood, Prig my most upright Lord,
And these (what name or title, e're they bear)
Jarkman, or Patrico, Cranke, or Clapperdudgeon,
Frater, or Abram man; I speak to all
That stand in fair Election for the title
Of King of Beggars, with the command adjoyning,
Higgen, your Orator, in this Inter-regnum,
That whilom was your Dommerer, doth beseech you
All to stand fair, and put your selves in rank,
That the first Comer, may at his first view
Make a free choice, to say up the question.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Pr. 'Tis done Lord Higgen.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Thanks to Prince Prig, Prince Ferret.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Well, pray my Masters all, Ferret be chosen,
Y'are like to have a mercifull mild Prince of me.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: A very tyrant, I, an arrant tyrant,
If e're I come to reign; therefore look to't,
Except you do provide me hum enough
And Lour to bouze with: I must have my Capons
And Turkeys brought me in, with my green Geese,
And Ducklings i'th' season: fine fat chickens,
Or if you chance where an eye of tame Phesants
Or Partridges are kept, see they be mine,
Or straight I seize on all your priviledge,
Places, revenues, offices, as forfeit,
Call in your crutches, wooden legs, false bellyes,
Fore'd eyes and teeth, with your dead arms; not leave you
A durty clout to beg with o' your heads,
Or an old rag with Butter, Frankincense,
Brimston and Rozen, birdlime, blood, and cream,
To make you an old sore; not so much soap
As you may some with i'th' Falling sickness;
The very bag you bear, and the brown dish
Shall be escheated. All your daintiest Dells too
I will deflower, and take your dearest Doxyes
From your warm sides; and then some one cold night
I'le watch you what old barn you go to roost in,
And there I'le smother you all i'th' musty hay.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: This is tyrant-like indeed: But what would
Or Clause be here, if either of them should raign?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: B^s^ask an Ass, if he were made a Camel,
What he would be; or a dog, and he were a Lyon.

speeches.speaker: Ginks.
verse: I care not what you are, Sirs, I shall be
A Begger still I am sure, I find my self there.

speeches.speaker: Snap.
verse: O here a Judge comes.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: ^, a Judge, a Judge.

speeches.speaker: G^s.
verse: What all you Sirs? what means this outcry?

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Master,
A sort of poor tou's met: Gods fools, good Master,
Have had some little variance amongst our selves
Who should be honestest of us, and which lives
Uprightest in his calling: Now, 'cause we thought
We ne're should 'gree on't our selves, because
Indeed 'tis hard to say: we all dissolv'd, to put it
To him that should come next, and that's your Master-ship,
Who, I hope, will 'termine it as your mind serves you,
Right, and no otherwise we ask it: which?
Which does your worship think is he? sweet Master
Look over us all, and tell us; we are seven of us,
Like to the seven wise Masters, or the Planets.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: I should judge this the man with the grave beard,
And if he be not —

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: Bless you, good Master, bless you.

speeches.speaker: Gos
verse: I would he were: there's something too amongst you
To keep you all honest.

speeches.speaker: Snap.
verse: King of Heaven go with you.

speeches.speaker: Omn.
verse: Now good reward him,
May he never want it, to comfort still the poor, in a good hour.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: What is't? see: Snap has got it.

speeches.speaker: Snap.
verse: A good crown, marry.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: A crown of gold.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: For our new King: good luck.

speeches.speaker: Ginks.
verse: To the common treasury with it; if't be gold,
Thither it must.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Spoke like a Patriot, Ferret—
King Clause, I bid God save thee first, first, Clause,
After this golden token of a crown;
Where's oratour Higgen with his gratuling speech now
In all our names?

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Here he is pumping for it.

speeches.speaker: Gin.
verse: H'has cough'd the second time, 'tis but once more
And then it comes.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: So, out with all: expect now

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: That thou art chosen, venerable Clause,
Our King and Soveraign; Monarch o'th'Maunders,
Thus we throw up our Nab-cheats, first for joy,
And then our silches; last, we clap our fambles,
Three subject signs, we do it without envy:
For who is he here did not with thee chosen,
Now thou art chosen? ask 'em: all will say so,
Nay swear't: 'tis for the King, but let that pass.
When last in conference at the bouzing ken
This other day we sat about our dead Prince
Of famous memory: (rest go with his rags:)
And that I saw thee at the tables end,
Rise mov'd, and gravely leaning on one Crutch,
Lift the other like a Scepter at my head,
I then presag'd thou shortly wouldst be King,
And now thou art so: but what need presage
To us, that might have read it in thy beard
As well, as he that chose thee? by that beard
Thou were found out, and mark'd for Soveraignty,
O happy beard! but happier Prince, whose beard
Was so remark'd, as marked out our Prince,
Not bating us a hair. Long may it grow,
And thick, and fair, that who lives under it,
May live as safe, as under Beggars Bush,
Of which this is the thing, that but the type.

speeches.speaker: Om.
verse: Excellent, excellent orator, forward good Higgen,
Give him leave to spit: the fine, well-spoken Higgen.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: This is the beard, the bush, or bushy-beard,
Under whose gold and silver raign 'twas said
So many ages since, we all should smile
On impositions, taxes, grievances,
Knots in a State, and whips unto a Subject,
Lye lurking in this beard, but all kemb'd out:
If now, the Beard be such, what is the Prince
That owes the Beard? a Father; no, a Grand-father;
Nay the great Grand-father of you his people.
He will not force away your hens, your bacon,
When you have ventur'd hard for't, nor take from you
The fattest of your puddings: under him
Each man shall eat his own stolen eggs, and butter,
In his own shade, or sun-shine, and enjoy
His own dear Dell, Doxy, or Mort, at night
In his own straw, with his own shirt, or sheet,
That he hath filch'd that day, I, and possess
What he can purchase, back, or belly-cheats
To his own prop: he will have no purveyers
For Pigs, and poultry.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: That we must have, my learned oratour,
It is our will, and every man to keep
In his own path and circuit.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Do you hear?
You must hereafter maund on your own pads he saies.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: And what they get there, is their own, besides
To give good words.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Do you mark? to cut been whids,
That is the second Law.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: And keep a foot
The humble, and the common phrase of begging,
Lest men discover us.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Yes, and cry sometimes,
To move compassion: Sir, there is a table,
That doth command all these things, and enjoyns 'em,
Be perfect in their crutches, their feign'd plaisters,
And their torn pass-ports, with the ways to stammer,
And to be dumb, and deaf, and blind, and lame,
There, all the halting paces are set down,
I'th' learned language.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: Thither I refer them,
Those, you at leisure shall interpret to them.
We love no heaps of laws, where few will serve.

speeches.speaker: Om.
verse: O gracious Prince, 'save, 'save the good King Cla^

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: A Song to crown him.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Set a Centinel out first.

speeches.speaker: Snap.
verse: The word?

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: A Cove comes, and fumbumbis to it —
CAst our Caps and cares away: this is Beggars Holy-day,
At the Crowning of our King, thus we ever dance and ^
In the world look out and see: where's so happy a Prince as he?
Where the Nation live so free, and so merry as do we?
Be it peace, or be it war, here at liberty we are,
And enjoy our ease and rest; To the field we are not prest;
Nor are call'd into the Town, to be troubled with the Gown.
Hang all Officers we cry, and the Magistrate too, by;
When the Subsidie's encreast, we are not a penny Sest.
Nor will any go to Law, with the Beggar for a straw.
All which happiness he brags, he doth owe unto his rags.

speeches.speaker: Snap.
verse: A Cove comes: Fumbumbis.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: To your postures; arm.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Yonder's the Town: I see it.

speeches.speaker: Hemsk.
verse: There's our danger
Indeed afore us, if our shadows save not.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Bless your good Worships.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: One small piece of mony.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Amongst us all poor wretches.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: Blind, and lame.

speeches.speaker: Ginks.
verse: For his sake that gives all.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Pitifull Worships.

speeches.speaker: Snap.
verse: One little doyt.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: King, by your leave, where are you?

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: To buy a little bread.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: To feed so many.
Mouths, as will ever pray for you.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Here be seven of us.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Seven, good Master, O remember seven,
Seven blessings.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Remember, gentle Worship.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: 'Gainst seven deadly sins.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: And seven sleepers.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: If they be hard of heart, and will give nothing—
Alas, we had not a charity this three dayes.

speeches.speaker: Hab.
verse: There's amongst you all.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Heaven reward you.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Lord reward you.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: The Prince of pity bless thee.

speeches.speaker: Hab.
verse: Do I see? or is't my fancy that would have it so?
Ha? 'tis her face: come hither maid.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: What ha' you,
Bells for my squirrel? I ha' giv'n bun meat,
You do not love me, do you? catch me a butterfly,
And I'le love you again; when? can you tell?
Peace, we go a birding: I shall have a fine thing.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Her voyce too sayes the same; but for my head
I would not that her manners were so chang'd.
Hear me thou honest fellow; what's this maiden,
That lives amongst you here?

speeches.speaker: Gin.
verse: Ao, ao, ao, ao.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: How? nothing but signs?

speeches.speaker: Gin.
verse: Ao, ao, ao, ao.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: This is strange,
I would fain have it her, but not her thus.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: He is de-de-de-de-de-de-deaf, and du-du-dude— dumb Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Slid they did all speak plain ev'n now me thought.
Do'st thou know this same maid?

speeches.speaker: Snap.
verse: Why, why, why, why, which, gu, gu, gu, gu, Gods fool
See was bo-bo-bo-bo born at the barn yonder,
By-be be-be-be-Beggars Bush-bo-bo-Bush
Her name is, My-my-my-my-my-match: so was her Mo-mo-mo-Mothers too too

speeches.speaker: Hab.
verse: I understand no word he says; how long
Has she been here?

speeches.speaker: Snap.
verse: Lo-lo-long enough to be ni-ni-nigled, and sne ha' go-go go good luck,

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I must be better inform'd, than by this way.
Here was another face too, that I mark'd
Of the old mans: but they are vanish'd all
Most suddenly: I will come here again,
O, that I were so happy, as to find it,
What I yet hope: it is put on.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: What mean you Sir,
To stay there with that stammerer?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Farewell friend,—
It will be worth return, to search: Come,
Protect us our disguise now, pre'thee Hemskirk
If we be taken, how do'st thou imagine
This town will use us, that hath stood so long
Out against Wolfort?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Ev'n to hang us forth
Upon their walls a sunning, to make Crows meat,
If I were not assur'd o' the Burgomaster,
And had a pretty excuse to see a niece there,
I should scarce venture.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Come 'tis now too late
To look back at the ports: good luck, and enter.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Still blow'st thou there? and from all other parts,
Do all my agents sleep, that nothing comes?
There's a conspiracy of windes, and servants,
If not of Elements, to ha' me break;
What should I think unless the Seas, and Sands
Had swallow'd up my ships? or fire had spoil'd
My ware-houses? or death devour'd my Factors?
I must ha' had some returns.

speeches.speaker: 1 Mer.
verse: 'Save you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: 'Save you.

speeches.speaker: 1 Mer.
verse: No news yet o' your Ships?

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Not any yet Sir.

speeches.speaker: 1 Mer.
verse: 'Tis strange.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: 'Tis true Sir: what a voyce was here now?
This was one passing bell, a thousand ravens
Sung in that man now, to presage my ruins.

speeches.speaker: 2 Mer.
verse: Goswin, good day, these winds are very constant

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: They are so Sir; to hurt —

speeches.speaker: 2 Mer.
verse: Ha' you had no letters
Lately from England, nor from Denmark?

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Neither.

speeches.speaker: 2 Mer.
verse: This wind brings them; not no news over land,
Through Spain, from the Straights?

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Not any.

speeches.speaker: 2 Mer.
verse: I am sorry Sir.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: They talk me down: and as 'tis said of Vulturs
They scent a field fought, and do smell the carkasses
By many hundred miles: So do these, my wracks
At greater distances. Why, thy will Heaven
Come on, and be: yet if thou please, preserve me;
But in my own adventure, here at home,
Of my chast love, to keep me worthy of her,
It shall be put in scale 'gainst all ill fortunes:
I am not broken yet: nor should I fall,
Me thinks with less than that, that ruins all.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Captain, you are welcom; so is this your friend
Most safely welcom, though our Town stand out
Against your Master, you shall find good quarter:
The troth is, we not love him: Margaret some wine,
Let's talk a little treason, if we can
Talk treason, 'gainst the traitors; by your leave, Gentlemen,
We, here in Bruges, think he do's usurp,
And therefore I am bold with him.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Sir, your boldness
Happily becomes your mouth, but not our ears,
While we are his servants; And as we come nere,
Not to ask questions, walk forth on your walls,
Visit your courts of guard, view your munition,
Ask of your corn-provisions, nor enquire
Into the least, as spies upon your strengths,
So let's entreat, we may receive from you
Nothing in passage or discourse, but what
We may with gladness, and our honesties here,
And that shall feal our welcom.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Good: let's drink then,
Fill out, I keep mine old pearl still Captain.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: I hang fast man.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Old Jewels commend their keeper, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Here's to you with a heart, my Captains friend,
With a good heart, and if this make us speak
Bold words, anon, 'tis all under the Rose
Forgotten: drown all memory, when we drink.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: 'Tis freely spoken noble Burgomaster,
I'le do you right.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Nay Sir mine heer Van-dunck
Is a true Statesman.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Fill my Captains cup there, O that your Master Wolfert
Had been an honest man.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Sir?

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Under the Rose.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Here's to you Marget.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Welcome, welcome Captain.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Well said my pearl still.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: And how does my Niece?
Almost a Woman, I think? This friend of mine,
I drew along with me, through so much hazard,
Only to see her: she was my errand.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: I, a kind Uncle you are (fill him his glass)
That in seven years, could not find leisure—

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: No,
^ so much

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: I'le ba^e you ne'r an hour on't,
It was before the Brabander 'gan his War,
For t^ on ^l^ine, i'the water there, his Daughter
That never was lost: yet you could not find time
To see a Kinswoman: but she is worth the seeing, Sir,
Now you are come, you ask if she were a Woman?
She is a Woman, Sir, fetch her forth Marget.
And a ^ine Woman, and has Suitors.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: How?
What Suitors are they?

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Bachellors; young Burgers:
And one, a Gallant, the young Prince of Merchant;
We call him here in Bruges.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: How? a Merchant?
I thought, Vandunke, you had understood me better,
And my Niece too, so trusted to you by me,
Than t' admit of such in name of Suitors.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Such? he is such a such, as were she mine
I'd give him thirty thousand crowns with her.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: But the same things, Sir, sit not you and me.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Why, give's some wine, then; this will sit us all:
Here's to you still, my Captains friend: All out:
And still, would Welfort were an honest man,
Under the Rose, I speak it: but this Merchant
Is a brave boy: he lives so, i'the Town here,
We know not what to think on him at some times
We ^ar he will be Bankrupt; he do's stretch
I enter his credit so; embraces all,
And to't, the winds have been contrary long.
^ut then, if he should have all his returns,
We think he would be a King, and are half sure on't.
Your Master is a Traitor, for all this,
Under the Rose: Here's to you; and usurps
The Earldom from a better man.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I marry, Sir,
Where is that man?

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Nay so^t: and I could tell you
'Tis ten to one I would not: here's my hand,
I love not Welfort: sit you still, with that:
Here comes my Captain again, and his fine Niece,
And there's my Merchant; view him well: fill wine here.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: You must not only know me for your Uncle
Now, but obey me: you, go cast your self
Away, upon a Dunghil here? a Merchant?
A petty follow? one that makes his Trade
With Oaths and perjuries?

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: What is that you say, Sir?
If it be me you speak of, as your eye
Seems to direct, I wish you would speak to me, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Sir, I do say, she is no Merchandize,
Will that suffice you?

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Merchandize good Sir:
Though ^e be Kinsman to her, take no leave thence
To use me with contempt: I ever thought
Your Niece above all price

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: And do so still, Sir,
I ass^re you, her ^at^s are more than you are worth.
Y^ do not know, what a Gentleman's worth, Sir,
Not can you value him

speeches.speaker: H^.
verse: Well ^a^ Merchant.

speeches.speaker: Va^
verse: Nay,
Let him alone, and ply your matter.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: A Gentleman?
What o'the Wool pack? or the Sugar chest?
Or lists of Velvet? which is't pound, or yard,
You vent your Gentry by?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: O Hemskirk, sye.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Come, do not mind 'em, drink, he is no W^s^,
Captain, I advise you.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Alas, my pretty man,
I think't be angry, by its look: Come hither,
Turn this way, a little: if it were the blood
Of Charlemaine, as't may (for ought I know)
Be some good Botchers issue, here in Bruges

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Nay: I'me not certain of that; of this I am,
If it once buy, and sell, its Gentry is gone.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: You are angry, though ye laugh.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: No, now 'tis pity
Of your poor argument. Do not you, the Lords
Of Land (if you be any) sell the grass,
The Corn, the Straw, the Milk, the Cheese?

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: And Butter:
Remember Butter; do not leave out Butter.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse:
The Beefs and Muttons that your grounds are sto^
^
Swine, with the very mast, beside the Woods?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: No, for those fordid uses we have Tenants,
Or else our Bailiffs.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Have not we, Sir, Chap-men,
And Factors, then to answer these? your honour
Fetch'd from the Heralds ABC, and said over
With your Court faces, once an hour, shall never
Make me mistake my self. Do not your Lawyers
Sell all their practice, as your Priests their prayers?
What is not bought, and sold? The company
That you had last, what had you for't, i'faith?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: You now grow sawcy.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Sure I have been bred
Still, with my honest liberty, and must use it.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Upon your equals then.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Sir, he that will
Provoke me first, doth make himself my equal.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Do ye hear? no more.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Yes, Sir, this little, I pray you,
And't shall be aside, then after, as you please.
You appear the Uncle, Sir, to her I love
More than mine eyes; and I have heard your scorns
With so much scoffing, and so much shame,
As each strive which is greater: But, believe me,
I suck'd not in this patience with my milk.
Do not presume, because you see me young,
Or cast despights on my profession
For the civility and tameness of it.
A good man bears a contumely worse
Than he would do an injury. Proceed not
To my offence: wrong is not still successful,
Indeed it is not: I would approach your Kins-woman
With all respect, done to your self and her.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Away Companion: handling her? take that.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Nay, I do love no blows, Sir, there's exchange

speeches.speaker: H^b.
verse: Hold, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: O murther.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Help my Goswin.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Man.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Let 'em alone; my life for one.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Nay come,
If you have will.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: None to offend you, I, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: He that had, thank himself: not hand he^? ^
And clasp her, and embrace her; and (would she
Now go with me) bear her through all her Ra^e,
Her Father, Brethren, and her Uncles, arm'd,
And all their Nephews, though they stood a wo^d
Off ^es, and wall of Canon: kiss me Gertrude,
^ake not, but kiss me.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Kiss him, Girl, I bid you;
My Merchant Royal; fear no Uncles: hang 'em,
Hang up all Uncles: Are not we in Bruges?
Under the Rose here?

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: In this circle, Love,
Thou art as safe, as in a Tower of Brass;
Let such as do wrong, fear.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: I, that's good,
Let Welfort look to that.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Sir, here she stands,
Your Niece, and my beloved. One of these titles
She must apply to; if unto the last,
Not all the anger can be sent unto her,
I^ frown, or voyce, or other art, shall force her,
Had Hercules a hand in't: Come, my Joy,
Say thou art mine, aloud Love, and profess it.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Doe: and I drink to it.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Prethee say so, Love.

speeches.speaker: Cer.
verse: 'Twould take away the honour from my blushes:
Do not you play the tyrant, sweet: they speak it.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: I thank you niece.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Sir, thank her for your life,
And fetch your sword within.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: You insult too much
With your good fortune, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: A brave clear Spirit;
Hemkirk, you were to blame: a civil habit
Ost covers a good man: and you may meet
In person of a Merchant, with a soul
As resolute, and free, and all wayes worthy,
As else in any file of man-kind: pray you,
What meant you so to slight him?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: 'Tis done now,
As^ no more of it; I must suffer.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: This
Is ^ll the punishment of rashness, sorrow.
Well; I must to the woods, for nothing here
Will be got out. There, I may chance to learn
Somewhat to help my enquiries further.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Ha?
A Looking glass?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: How now, brave Burgomaster?

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: I love no Wolforts, and my name's Vandunk,

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Van drunk it's rather: come, go sleep within.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Earl Florez is right heir, and this same Wolfort
Under the Rose I speak it—

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Very hardly.

speeches.speaker: Vand.
verse: Usurps: and a rank Traitor, as ever breath'd,
And all that do uphold him. Let me goe,
No man shall hold me, that upholds him;
Do you uphold him?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Then hold me up.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Sir, I presume, you have a sword of your own,
That can so handle anothers.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Faith you may Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: And ye have made me have so much better thoughts of you
As I am bound to call you forth.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: For what Sir?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: To the repairing of mine honour, and hurt here.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Express your way.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: By sight, and speedily.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: You have your will: Require you any more?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: That you be secret: and come single.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: I will.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: As you are the Gentleman you would be thought.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Without the Conjuration: and I'le bring
Only my sword, which I will fit to yours,
He take his length within.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Your place now Sir?

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: By the Sand hills.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Sir, nearer to the woods,
If you thought so, were sitter.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: There, then.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Good.
Your time?

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: 'Twixt seven and eight.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: You'l give me Sir
Cause to report you worthy of my Niece,
If you come, like your promise.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: If I do not,
Let no man think to call me unworthy first,
I'le do't my self, and justly with to want her.—

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: COme, English beer Hostess, English beer by 'th' belly.

speeches.speaker: 2 B.
verse: Stark beer boy, stout and strong beer: so, sit down Lads,
And drink me upsey Dutch.
Frolick, and fear not.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Have ye any work for the Sow-gelder, hoa,
My horn goes too high too low, too high too low.
Have ye any Piggs, Calves, or Colts,
Have ye any Lambs in your holts
To cut for the Stone,
Here comes a cunning one.
Have ye any braches to spade,
Or e're a fair maid
That would be a Nun,
Come kiss me, 'tis done.
Hark how my merry horn doth blow,
Too high too low, too high too low.

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: O excellent! two pence a piece boyes, two pence a piece.
Give the boys some drink there. Piper, wet your whistle,
Canst tell me a way now, how to cut off my wifes Concupiscence?

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: I'le sing ye a Song for't.
TAke her, and hug her,
And turn her and tug her,
And turn her again boy, again,
Then if she mumble,
Or if her tail tumble,
Kiss her amain boy, amain.
Do thy endeavour,
To take off her feaver,
Then her disease no longer will raign.
If nothing will serve her,
Then thus to preserve her,
Swinge her amain boy amain.
Give her cold jelly
To take up her belly,
And once a day swinge her again,
If she stand all these pains,
Then knock out her brains,
Her disease no longer will reign.

speeches.speaker: 1 Bo.
verse: More excellent, more excellent, sweet Sow-gelder.

speeches.speaker: 2 Bo.
verse: Three-pence a piece, three-pence a piece.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Will you hear a Song how the Devil was g^lded?

speeches.speaker: 3 Bo.
verse: I, I, let's hear the Devil roar, Sow-gelder.

1.
He ^an at me first in the shape of a Ram,
And over and over the Sow Gelder came;

^ and I halter'd him fast by the born,
I pl^
^ut his Stones as you'd pick out a Corn.

^, quoth the Devil, and forth he stunk,
And left us a Carcase of Mutton that stunk,

2.
The next time I ^ode a good mile and a half,
Where ^
^e did live in disguise of a Calf,
I ^ and I g^ him, ere he did any evil;
He was here at his best, but a sucking Devil.
Man, yet he cry'd, and forth he did steal,
And this was seld after, for excellent Veal.

3.
Some half a year after in the form of a Pig,
I met with the Rogue, and he look'd very big;
I catch'd at his leg, laid him down on a log,
Ere a man could fa^t twice, I had made him a Hog.
Owgh, quoth the Devil, and forth gave a Jer^,
That a few was converted, and eat of the Perk.

speeches.speaker: 1 Bo.
verse: Groats apiece, Groats apiece, Groats apiece,
There sweet Sow-Gelder.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Will ye see any feats of activity,
Some Sleight of hand, Legerdemain? hey pass,
Presto, be gone there?

speeches.speaker: 2 Bo.
verse: Sit down Jugler.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: S^rah, play you your art well; draw near Piper:
Look you, my honest friends, you see my hands;
Plain dealing is no Devil: lend me some Money,
Twelve pence a piece will serve.

speeches.speaker: 1. 2. B.
verse: There, there.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: I thank you,
Thank ye heartily: when shall I pay ye?

speeches.speaker: All B.
verse: Ha, ha, ha, by th' Mass this was a fine trick.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: A merry sleight toy: but now I'll show your Worships
A trick indeed.

speeches.speaker: ^ig.
verse: Mark him well now my Masters.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Here are three balls,
These balls shall be three bullets,
One, two, and three: ascentibus, malentibus.
Presto, be gone: they are vanish'd: fair play, Gentlemen.
Now these three, like three Bullets, from your three Noses
Will I pluck presently: fear not, no harm Boys,

T^t^
^n patul^.

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: Oh, oh, oh.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: R^bans sub jermine sa^

speeches.speaker: 2 B.
verse: Ye pull too hard; ye pull too hard.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Stand fai^ then:
Silver^ramtr^m tram.

speeches.speaker: 3 B.
verse: Hold, hold, hold.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Come alost, bullets three, with a whim-wham.
Have ye their Moneys?

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Yes, yes.

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: Oh ta^e Jugler!

speeches.speaker: 2 B.
verse: Oh admirable Jugler!

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: One trick more yet;
Hey, come alost; sa, sa, slum, slum, taradumbis?
East, West, North, South, now fly like Jack with a bumbis.
Now all your money's gone; pray search your pockets.

speeches.speaker: 1 B
verse: Humh.

speeches.speaker: 2 B.
verse: He.

speeches.speaker: 3 B.
verse: The Devil a penny's here!

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: This was a rare trick.

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: But 'twould be a fat rarer to restore it.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: I'll do ye that too; look upon me earnestly,
And move not any ways your eyes from this place,
This Button here? pow, whir, whiss, shake your po^

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: By th' Mass 'tis here again, boys.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Rest ye merry;
My first trick has paid me.

speeches.speaker: All B.
verse: I, take it, take it,
And take some drink too.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Not a drop now I thank you,
Away, we are discover'd else.

Bring out your Cony-skins, fair maids to me,
And hold 'em fair that I may see;
Grey, black, and blue: for your smaller skins,
I'll give ye looking glasses, pins:
And for your whole Coney, here's ready, ready Money
Come Gentle Jone, do thou begin
With thy black, black, black, Coney-skin.
And Mary then, and Jane will follow,
With their silver hair'd skins, and their yellow
The white Cony-skin, I will not lay by,
For though it be faint, 'tis fair to the eye;
The grey, it is warm, but yet for my Money,
Give me the bonny, bonny black Cony.
Come away fair Maids, your skins will decay:
Come, and take money, maids, put your ware away.
Cony-skins, Cony-skins, have ye any Cony-skins,
I have fine bracelets, and fine silver pins.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Buy any Brand Wine, buy any Brand Wine?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Have ye any Cony-skins?

speeches.speaker: 2 Boy.
verse: My fine Canary bird, there's a Cake for the Worship

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: Come fill, fill, fill, fill suddenly: let's see Sir,
What's this?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: A penny, Sir.

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: Fill till't be six pence,
And there's my Pig.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: This is a Counter, Sir.

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: A Counter! stay ye, what are these then?
O execrable Jugler! O damn'd Jugler!
Look in your hose, hoa, this comes of looking forward.

speeches.speaker: 3 B.
verse: Devil a Dunkirk! what a Rogue's this Jugler!
This hey pass, repass, h'as repast us sweetly.

speeches.speaker: 2 B.
verse: Do ye call these tricks.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Have ye any Ends of Gold, or Silver?

speeches.speaker: 2 B.
verse: This Fellow comes to mock us; Gold or Silver ^ Copp^

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: Yes, my good Friend,
We have e'n an end of all we have.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: 'Tis well Sir,
You have the less to care for: Gold and Silver.

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: Have ye any old Cloaks to sell, have ye any old Clo^s to sell?

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: Cloaks! Look about ye Boys: mine's gone!

speeches.speaker: 2 B.
verse: A— juggle 'em?
—O they're Prestoes: mine's gone too!

speeches.speaker: 3 B.
verse: Here's mine yet.

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: Come, come let's drink then more Brand Wine.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Here Sir.

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: If e'r I catch your Sow-gelder, by this hand I'll strip ha^
Were ever Fools so ferkt? We have two Cloaks yet;
And all our Caps; the Devil take the Flincher.

speeches.speaker: All B.
verse: Yaw, yaw, yaw, yaw.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Good do'n my honest Fellows,
You are merry here I see.

speeches.speaker: 3 B.
verse: 'Tis all we have left, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: What hast thou? Aqua vitae?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Fill out then;
And give these honest Fellows round.

speeches.speaker: All B.
verse: We thank ye.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: May I speak a word in private to ye?

speeches.speaker: All B.
verse: Yes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: I have a business for you, honest Friends,
If you dare lend your help, shall get you crowns.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Ha!
Lead me a little nearer, Boy.

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: What is't Sir?
If it be any thing to purchase money,
Which is our want, commands us.

speeches.speaker: B^rs.
verse: All, all, all, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: You know the young spruce Merchant in Bruges?

speeches.speaker: 2 B
verse: Who? Master Goswin?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: That he owes me money,
And here in town there is no stirring of him.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Say ye so?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: This day, upon a sure app^ment,

He meets me a mile hence, by th^
^ side,

Under the row of Oaks; do yo^
^
^t?

speeches.speaker: All B.
verse: Yes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Give 'em more drink: sacre if you dare but venture
When I shall give the word to seize upon him
Here's twenty pound,

speeches.speaker: 3 B.
verse: Beware the Jugler.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: If he resist, down with him, have no mercy.

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: I warrant you, we'll hamper him,

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: To discharge you,
I have a Warrant here about me.

speeches.speaker: 3 B.
verse: Here's our Warrant,
This carries fire i'th' Tail.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Away with me then,
The time draws on,
I must remove so insolent a Suitor,
And if he be so rich, make him pay ransome
E^e he see Bruges Towers again. Thus, wise men
Repair the hurts they take by a disgrace,
And piece the Lions skin with the Foxes case.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I am glad I have heard this sport yet.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: There's for thy drink, come pay the house within Boys,
And lose no time.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Away with all our haste too.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: No wind blow fair yet? no return of moneys?
Letters? nor any thing to hold my hopes up?
Why then 'tis destin'd, that I fall, fall miserably!
My credit I was built on, sinking with me.
Thou boystrous North-wind, blowing my misfortunes,
And frosting all my hopes to cakes of coldness;
Yet stay thy fury; give the gentle South
Yet leave to court those sails that bring me safety,
And you auspicious fires, bright twins in heaven
Daunce on the shrowds; he blows still stubbornly,
And on his boystrous Rack rides my sad ruin;
There is no help, there can be now no comfort,
To morrow with the Sun-set, sets my credit.
Oh misery! thou curse of man, thou plague,
In the midst of all our strength thou strik'st us;
My vertuous Love is lost too: all, what I have been,
No more hereafter to be seen than shadow;
To prison now? well, yet there's this hope left me;
I may sink fairly under this days venture,
And so to morrow's cross'd, and all those curses:
Yet manly I'll invite my Fate, base fortune
Shall never say, she has cut my throat in fear.
This is the place his challenge call'd me to,
And was a happy one at this time for me,
For let me fall before my ^oe i'th' field,
And not at Bar, before my Creditors;
Has kept his word: now Sir, your swords tongue only
Loud as you dare, all other language—

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Well Sir,
You shall not be long troubled: draw.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: 'Tis done Sir,
And now have at ye.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Now.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Betray'd to Villains!
Slaves ye shall buy me bravely,
And thou base coward.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Now upon 'em bravely,
Conjure 'em soundly Boys.

speeches.speaker: Boors.
verse: Hold, hold.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Lay on still,
Down with that Gentleman to gi^e, swinge him to s^rrup.
