Retire Sir, and take Breath: follow, and take him,
Take all, 'tis lawful prize.

speeches.speaker: Boors.
verse: We yield.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Down with 'em
Into the Wood, and risle 'em, tew 'em, swinge 'em,
Knock me their brains into their Breeches.

speeches.speaker: Boors.
verse: Hold, hold.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: What these men are I know not, nor for what cause
They shou'd thus thrust themselves into my danger,
Can I imagine. But sure Heavens hand was in't!
Nor why this coward Knave should deal so basely
To eat me up with Slaves: but Heaven I thank thee,
I hope thou hast reserv'd me to an end
Fit for thy creature, and worthy of thine honour:
Would all my other dangers here had suffered,
With what a joyful heart should I go home then?
Where now, Heaven knows, like him that waits his sentence,
Or hears his passing Bell; but there's my hope still.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Blessing upon you Master.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Thank ye; leave me,
For by my troth I have nothing now to give thee.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Indeed I do not ask Sir, only it grieves me
To see ye look so sad; now goodness keep ye
From troubles in your mind.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: If I were troubled,
What could thy comfort do? prithee Clause, leave me.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Good Master be not angry; for what I say
Is out of true love to ye.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: I know thou lov'st me.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Good Mr. blame that love then, if I prove so sawcy
To ask ye why ye are sad.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Most true, I am so,
And such a sadness I have got will sink me.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Heaven shield it, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Faith, thou must lose thy Master.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I had rather lose my neck, Sir: would I knew—

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: What would the knowledg do thee good so miserable,
Thou canst not help thy self? when all my ways
Nor all the friends I have—

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: You do not know Sir,
What I can do: cures sometimes, for mens cares
Flow, where they least expect 'em.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: I know thou wouldst do,
But farewell Clause, and pray for thy poor Master.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I will not leave ye.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I dare not leave ye, Sir, I must not leave ye,
And till ye beat me dead, I will not leave ye.
By what ye hold most precious, by Heavens goodness,
As your fair youth may prosper, good Sir tell me:
My mind believes yet somethings in my power
May case you of this trouble.

speeches.speaker: Gos
verse: I will tell thee,
For a hundred thousand crowns upon my credit,
Taken up of Merchants to supply my traffiques,
The winds and weather envying of my fortune,
And no return to help me off, yet shewing
To morrow, Clause, to morrow, which must come,
In prison thou shalt find me poor and broken.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I cannot blame your grief Sir.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Now, what say'st thou?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I say you should not shrink, for he that gave ye,
Can give you more, his power can bring ye off Sir,
When friends and all forsake ye, yet he sees you.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: There's all my hope.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Hope still S^, are you ty'd
Within the compass of a day, good Master,
To pay this mass of mony?

speeches.speaker: G^s.
verse: Ev'n to morrow:
But why do I stand mocking of my misery?
Is't not enough the floods, and friends forget me?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Will no less serve?

speeches.speaker: G^s.
verse: What if it would?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Your patience,
I do not ask to mock ye: 'tis a great sum,
A sum for mighty men to start and stick a^;
But not for honest: have ye no friends left ye,
None that have felt your bounty? worth this duty?

speeches.speaker: Gos
verse: Duty? thou know'st it not.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: It is a duty,
And as a duty, from those men have felt ye,
Should be return'd again: I have gain'd by ye,
A daily alms these seven years you have showr'd on me,
Will half supply your want?

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Why do'st thou fool me?
Can'st thou work miracles?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: To save my Master,
I can work this.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Thou wilt make me angry with thee.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: For doing good?

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: What power hast thou?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Enquire not:
So I can do it, to preserve my Master;
Nay if it be three parts.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: O that I had it,
But good Clause, talk no more, I feel thy charity,
As thou has felt mine: but alas!

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Distrust not,
'Tis that that quenches ye: pull up your Spirit,
Your good, your honest, and your noble Spirit;
For if the fortunes often thousand people
Can save ye, rest assur'd; you have forgot Sir,
The good ye did, which was the power you gave me;
Ye shall now know the King of Beggars treasure:
And let the winds blow as they list, the Seas roar,
Yet, here to morrow, you shall find your harbour.
Here sail me not, for if I live I'le fit ye.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: How sain I would believe thee!

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: If I ly Master,
Believe no man hereafter.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: I will try thee,
But he knows, that knows all.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Know me to morrow,
And if I know not how to cure ye, kill me;
So pass in peace, my best, my worthiest Master.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Thus have I stoln away disguiz'd from Hemskirk
To try these people, for my heart yet tells me
Some of these Beggars, are the men I look for:
Appearing like my self, they have no reason
(Though my intent is fair, my main end honest)
But to avoid me narrowly, that face too,
That womans face, how near it is! O may it
But prove the same, and fortune how I'le bless thee!
Thus, sure they cannot know me, or suspect me,
If to my habit I but change my nature;
As I must do; this is the wood they live in,
A place fit for concealment: where, till fortune
Crown me with that I seek, I'le live amongst 'em.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Come bring 'em out, for here we sit in justice:
Give to each one a cudgel, a good cudgel:
And now attend your sentence. That you are rogues,
And mischievous base rascalls, (there's the point now)
I take it, is confess'd.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Deny it if you dare knaves.

speeches.speaker: Boors.
verse: We are Rogues Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: To amplify the matter then, rogues as ye are,
And lamb'd ye shall be e're we leave ye.

speeches.speaker: Boors.
verse: Yes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: And to the open handling of our justice,
Why did ye this upon the proper person
Of our good Master? were you drank when you did it?

speeches.speaker: Boors.
verse: Yes indeed were we.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: You shall be beaten sober.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Was it for want you undertook it?

speeches.speaker: Boors.
verse: Yes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: You shall be swing'd abundantly.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: And yet for all that,
You shall be poor rogues still.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Has not the Gentleman,
Pray mark this point Brother Prig, that noble Gentleman
Reliev'd ye often, found ye means to live by,
By imploying some at Sea, some here, some there;
According to your callings?

speeches.speaker: Boors.
verse: 'Tis most true Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Is not the man, an honest man?

speeches.speaker: Boors.
verse: Yes truly.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: A liberal Gentleman? and as ye are true rascals
Tell me but this, have ye not been drunk, and often,
At his charge?

speeches.speaker: Boors.
verse: Often, often.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: There's the point then,
They have cast themselves, Brother Prig.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: A shrewd point, Brother.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Brother, proceed you now; the cause is open,
I am some what weary.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Can you do these things?
You most abhominable stinking Rascals,
You turnip eating Rogues.

speeches.speaker: Boors.
verse: We are truly sorry.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Knock at your hard hearts Rogues, and presently
Give us a sign you feel compunction,
Every man up with's cudgel, and on his neighbour
Bestow such alms, 'till we shall say sufficient,
For there your sentence lyes without partiality;
Either of head, or hide Rogues, without sparing,
Or we shall take the pains to beat you dead else:
You shall know your doom.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: One, two, and three about it.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: That fellow in the blue, has true Compunction,
He beats his fellows bravely, oh, well struck boyes.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Up with that blue breech, now playes he the Derd
So get ye home, drink small beer, and be honest;
Call in the Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Do, bring him presently,
His cause I'le hear my self.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Prig. With all due reverence,
We do resign Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Now hussing Sir, what's your name?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: What's that to you Sir?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: It shall be ere we part.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: My name is Hemskirk,
I follow the Earl, which you shall feel.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: No threatning,
For we shall cool you Sir; why did'st thou basely
Attempt the murder of the Merchant Goswin?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: What power hast thou to ask me?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I will know it,

O^
^ey thee till thy pain discover it.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: He did me wrong, base wrong.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: That cannot save ye,
Who sent ye hither? and what further villanies
Have you in hand?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Why would'st thou know? what profit,
If I had any private way, could rise
Out of my knowledge, to do thee commodity?
Be sorry for what thou hast done, and make amends fool,
I'le talk no further to thee, nor these Rascals.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Tye him to that tree.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: I have told you whom I follow.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: The Devil you should do, by your villanies,
Now he that has the best way, wring it from him.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: I undertake it: turn him to the Sun boyes;
Give me a fine sharp rush, will ye confess yet?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Ye have rob'd me already, now you'le murder me.

speeches.speaker: H^.
verse: Murder your nose a little: does your head purge Sir?
To it again, 'twill do ye good.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Oh,
I cannot tell you any thing.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Proceed then.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: There's maggots in your nose, I'le fetch 'em out Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: O my head breaks.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: The best thing for the rheum Sir,
That falls into your worships eyes.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Hold, hold.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Speak then.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: I know not what.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: It lyes in's brain yet,
In lumps it lyes, I'le fetch it out the finest;
What pretty faces the fool makes? heigh!

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Hold,
Hold, and I'le tell ye all, look in my doublet;
And there within the lining in a paper,
You shall find all.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Go fetch that paper hither,
And let him loose for this time.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Good ev'n my honest friends.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Good ev'n good fellow.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: May a poor huntsman, with a merry heart,
A voice shall make the forest ring about him,
Get leave to live amongst ye? true as steel, boyes?
That knows all chases, and can watch all hours,
And with my quarter staff, though the Devil bid stand,
D^l such an alms, shall make him roar again?
Prick ye the fearfull hare through cross wayes, sheep-walks,
And force the crafty Reynard climb the quicksetts;
Rouse ye the lofty Stag, and with my bell-horn,
Ring him a knel, that all the woods shall mourn him,
'Till in his funeral tears, he fall before me?
The Polcat, Marterne, and the rich skin'd Lucerne
I know to chase, the Roe, the wind out stripping
^sgrin himself, in all his bloody anger
I can be at from the bay, and the wild Sounder
Single, and with my arm'd staff, turn the Boar,
Spight of his foamy tushes, and thus strike him;
Till he fall down my feast.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: A goodly fellow.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: What mak'st thee here, ha?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: We accept thy fellowship.

speeches.speaker: Hab.
verse: Hemskirk, thou art not right I fear, I fear thee.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Here is the paper: and as he said we found it.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Give me it, I shall make a shift yet, old as I am,
To find your knavery you are sent here, Sir^a,
To discover certain Gentlemen, a spy-knave,
And if ye find 'em, if not by perswasion
To bring 'em back, by poyson to dispatch 'em.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: By poyson, ha?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Here is another, Hubert;
What is that Hubert Sir?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: You may perceive there.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I may perceive a villany and a tank ^,
Was he joyn'd partner of thy knavery?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: No.
He had an honest end, would I had had so,
Which makes him scape such cut-throats.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: So it seems.
For here thou art commanded, when that Hubert
Has done his best and worthiest service, this way
To cut his throat, for here he's set down dangerou^.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: This is most impious.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I am glad we have found ye,
Is not this true?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Yes; what are you the better?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: You shall perceive Sir, ere you get your freed^
Take him aside, and friend, we take thee to us,
Into our company, thou dar'st be true unto us?

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: I, and obedient too?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: As you had bred me.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Then take our hand: thou art now a servant to
Welcom him all.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Stand off, stand off: I'le do it,
We bid ye welcom three wayes; first for your person,
Which is a promising person, next for your quality,
Which is a decent, and a gentle quality,
Last for the frequent means you have to feed us,
You can steal 'tis to be presum'd.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Yes, venison, and if you want —

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: 'Tis well you understand right,
And shall practise daily: you can drink too?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Soundly.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: And ye dare know a woman from a weathercock?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: If I handle her.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Now swear him.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: I crown thy nab, with a gag of benbo^se,
And shall thee by the Salmon into the c^ows,
To mand on the pad, and strike all the cheats;
To Mill from the Ruffmans, commision and states,
Twang d^ll's, i' the stirom^ll, and let the Q^re Cuffin:
And Herman Beck strine, and trine to the Ruffin.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Now interpret this unto him.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: I pour on thy pate a pot of good ale,
And by the Rogues o'th' a Rogue thee instal:
To beg on the way, to rob all thou meets;
To steal from the hedge, both the shirt and the sheets:
And lye with thy wench in the straw till she twang,
Let the Constable, Justice, and D^vil go hang.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: You are welcom Brother

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: Welcom, welcom, welcom, but who shall have the keeping
Of this fellow?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Sir, if you dare but trust me;
For if I have kept wild dogs and beasts for wonder,
And made 'em tame too: give into my custody
This roaring Rascal, I shall hamper him,
With all his knacks and knaveries, and I fear me
Discover yet a further villany in him;
O he smells ranck o'th' Rascal.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Take him to thee,
But if he scape —

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Let me be ev'n hang'd for him,
Come Sir, I'le tye ye to my leath.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Away Rascal.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Be not so stubborn: I shall swindge ye soundly,
^ with me.

verse: No News yet?

verse: Good Gertrude ask not,
Ev'n by the love you bear me.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I am obedient.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Go in, my fair, I will not be long from ye,
Nor long I fear me with thee. At my return
Dispose me as you please.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: The good gods guide ye.

speeches.speaker: G^s.
verse: Now for my self, which is the least I hope ^

speeches.speaker: 1 Mer.
verse: Yes, and must have fair play:
There is no living here else; one hour's failing
Fails us of all our friends, of all our credits:
For my part, I would stay, but my wants tell me,
I must wrong others in't.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: No mercy in ye!

speeches.speaker: 2 Mer.
verse: 'Tis foolish to depend on others mercy:
Keep your self right, and even cut your cloth, Sir,
According to your calling, you have liv'd here,
In Lord-like Prodigality, high, and open,
And now ye find what 'tis: the liberal spending
The Summer of your Youth, which you should gl^an i^,
And like the labouring Ant, make use and gain of,
Has brought this bitter, stormy Winter on ye,
And now you cry.

speeches.speaker: 3 Mer.
verse: Alas, before your Poverty,
We were no men, of no mark, no endeavour;
You stood alone, took up all trade, all business
Running through your hands, scarce a Sail at Sea,
But loaden with your Goods: we poor weak Pedlers:
When by your leave, and much intreaty to it,
We could have stowage for a little Cloath,
Or a few Wines, put off, and thank your Worship.
Lord, how the World's chang'd with ye? now I hope, ^
We shall have Sea-room.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Is my misery
Become my scorn too! have ye no humanity?
No part of men left? are all the Bounties in me
To you, and to the Town, turn'd my reproaches?

speeches.speaker: 4 Mer.
verse: Well, get your moneys ready: 'tis but 2 hours.
We shall protest ye else, and suddenly.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: But two days.

speeches.speaker: 1 Mer.
verse: Not an hour, ye know the hazard.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: How soon my light's put out I hard hearted Br^
Within thy Walls may never honest Merchant
Venture his fortunes more: O my poor Wench too.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Good fortune, Master.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Thou mistak'st me, Clause,
I am not worth thy Blessing.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Still a sad man!
No belief gentle Master? come bring it in then,
And now believe your Beadsman.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Is this certain?
Or dost thou work upon my troubled sense?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: 'Tis gold, Sir,
Take it and try it.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Certainly 'tis treasure;
^ there be yet this Blessing?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Cease your wonder,
You shall not sink, for ne'r a sowst Flap-dragon,
^ a pickl'd Pilcher of 'em all, Sir,
Is there, your full sum, a hundred thousand crowns:
^ good sweet Master, now be merry; pay 'em,
^ poor pelting Knaves, that know no goodness:
^ hear your heart up handsomely.

speeches.speaker: ^s.
verse: Good Clause,
^ cam'st thou by this mighty Sum? if naughtily,
^ must not it take it of thee, 'twill undo me.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Fear not, you have it by as honest means
^s though your father gave it: Sir, you know not
To what a mass, the little we get daily,
Mounts in seven years; we beg it for Heavens charity,
And to the same good we are bound to render it.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: What great security?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Away with that, Sir,
^ere not ye more than all the men in Bruges;
And all the money in my thoughts—

speeches.speaker: Ges.
verse: But good Clause,
^ may dye presently.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Then this dies with ye:
Pay when you can good Master, I'll no Parchments,
Only this charity I shall entreat you;
Leave me this Ring.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Alas, it is too poor, Clause.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: 'Tis all I ask, and this withal, that when
^ shall deliver this back, you shall grant me
Freely one poor petition.

speeches.speaker: Ges.
verse: There, I confirm it,
And may my faith forsake me when I shun it.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Away, your time draws on. Take up the money,
And follow this young Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Farewell Clause,
And may thy honest memory live for ever.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Heaven bless you, and still keep you, farewel Master.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I have lockt my Youth up close enough for gadding,
In ^n old Tree, and set watch over him.
Now for my Love, for sure this Wench must be she,
She follows me; Come hither, pretty Minche.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: No, no, you'll kiss.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: So I will.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Y'ded law?
How will ye kiss me, pray you?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Thus, soft as my loves lips.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Oh!

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: What's your Father's name?

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: He's gone to Heaven.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Is it not Gerrard, Sweet?

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: I'll stay no longer;
My Mother's an old Woman, and my Brother
Was drown'd at Sea, with catching Cockles. O Love!
O how my heart melts in me: how thou fir'st me!

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: 'Tis certain she; pray let me see your hand, Sweet?

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: No, no, you'l bite it.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Sure I should know that Gymmal!

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: 'Tis certain he: I had forgot my Ring too.
O Hubert! Hubert!

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Ha! methought she nam'd me—
Do you know me, Chick?

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: No indeed, I never saw ye;
But methinks you kiss finely.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Kiss again then;
By Heaven 'tis she.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: O what a joy he brings me!

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: You are not Minche?

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Yes, pretty Gentleman,
And I must be marry'd to morrow to a Capper.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Must ye my Sweet, and does the Capper love ye?

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Yes, yes, he'l give me pie, and look in mine eyes thus.
'Tis he: 'tis my dear Love: O blest Fortune.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: How fain she would conceal her self, yet shew it!
Will you love me, and leave that man? I'll serve.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: O I shall lose my self!

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I'll wa^ upon you,
And make you dainty Nose gays.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: And where will you stick'em?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Here in my bosom, Sweet, and make a crown of Lilies
For your fair head.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: And will you love me deed law?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: With all my Heart.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Call me to morrow then,
And we'll have brave chear, and go to Church together:
Give you good ev'n Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: But one word fair Minche.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: I must be gone a milking.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Ye shall presently.
Did you never hear of a young maid called Jacu^n?

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: I am discover'd; hark in your ear, I'll tell ye:
You must not know me, kiss and be constant ever.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Heaven curse me else 'tis she, and now I am certain
They are all here: now for my other project—

speeches.speaker: 1 Mer.
verse: Nay, if 'twould do you courtesie.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: None at all, Sir:
Take it, 'tis yours, there's your ten thousand for ye,
Give in my Bills. Your sixteen.

speeches.speaker: 3 Mer.
verse: Pray be pleas'd Sir
To make a further use.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: 3 Mer.
verse: What I have, Sir,
You may command; pray let me be your Servant.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Put your Hats on: I care not for your courtesies,
They are most untimely done, and no truth in 'em.

speeches.speaker: 2 Mer.
verse: I have a frought of Pepper.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Rot your Pepper,
Shall I trust you again? there's your seven thousand.

speeches.speaker: 4 Mer.
verse: Or if you want fine Sugar, 'tis but sending.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: No, I can send to Barbary, those people
That never yet knew faith, have nobler freedoms.
These carry to Vanlock, and take my Bills in,
To Peter Zuten these: bring back my Jewels,
Why are these pieces?

speeches.speaker: Sayler.
verse: Health to the noble Merchant,
The Susan is return'd.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Well?

speeches.speaker: Say.
verse: Well, and rich Sir,
And now put in.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Heaven thou hast heard my prayers.

speeches.speaker: Say.
verse: The brave Rebeccah too, bound from the Straits,
With the next Tide is ready to put after.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: What news o'th' fly-boat?

speeches.speaker: Say.
verse: If this Wind hold till midnight,
She will be here, and wealthy, 'scap'd fairly.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: How, prithee, Sayler?

speeches.speaker: Say.
verse: Thus Sir, she had fight
Seven hours together, with six Turkish Gallies,
And she sought bravely; but at length was boarded
And overlaid with strength: when presently
Comes boring up the wind Captain Vannoke,
That valiant Gentleman, you redeem'd from prison;
He knew the Boat, set in, and sought it bravely:
Beat all the Gallies off, sunk three, redeem'd her,
And as a service to ye sent her home Sir.
A^ honest noble Captain, and a thankfull;

T^
^ n^ws ^o drink the Merchants health, Saylor.
^ and your bounty, and I'le do it to a doyt, S^,

speeches.speaker: 1 Mer.
verse: What miracles are pour'd upon this fellow!

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: This he^e I hope, my friends, I shall scape prison,
For all your ^a^es to catch in.

speeches.speaker:
^
Mer.
verse: You may please Sir
^o ^ of your poor servants in displeasure,
Who^ all th^ have, goods, moneys, are at your service.

speeches.speaker: Gos
verse: I thank you,
W^ I have ^ of you I shall forget you:
You are ^ I hope.

speeches.speaker: Ad.
verse: We ^, in your good fortunes.

speeches.speaker: Van d.
verse: Come Sir, come take your ease, you must go home
With me, yo^ier is one weeps and howls.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: A ^ how does she?

speeches.speaker: Van d.
verse: She will be better soon I hope.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Why soon Sir?

speeches.speaker: Van d.
verse: Why when you have her in your arms, this night
M^ boy she is thy wife.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: With all my heart I take her.

speeches.speaker: Van d.
verse: We have prepar'd, all thy friends will be there,
And all my Rooms shall smoak to see the revel;
Thou hast been wrong'd, and no more shall my service
What on the knave her Uncle, I have heard all,
All ^s b^ts for my Boy, but thou shalt have her;
H^ t^ dispatch't thy business?

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Most.

speeches.speaker: Van d
verse: By the mass Boy,
Thou ^ dost new in wealth, and I joy in it,
^ the b^st Boy, that Bruges ever nourish'd.
Thou hast been sad, I'le cheer thee up with Sack,
And when thou a^ lustly I'le sling thee to thy Mistris.
She'l ^eg t^, ^.

speeches.speaker: G^s.
verse: I ^o^g to see it,
I ha^ forgot you: there's for you my friends:
You had but heavy burthens; commend my love
To my best love, all the love I have
To honest C^aus, shortly I will thank him better.

speeches.speaker: H^.
verse: By the m^s a loyal Merchant,
^old by the han^full, here will be sport soon, Prig.
It partly seems so, and here will I be in a trice.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: And I boy,
Away ap^ce, we are look'd for.

speeches.speaker: P^
verse: Oh these bak'd meats,
M^ th^nks I smell them hither.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Thy mouth waters.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I Must not.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse:
^
^in thy power to do it, and in mine
To ^wa^th to thy w^h^s.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I dare not, no^ I will not.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Gentle Hun^man,
^ough thou hast kept me hard, though in thy duty,
W^ at requir'd to ^t, th'hast used me stubbornly;

I can for^ve th^
^
You the ^a^ls servant?

speeches.speaker: H^
verse: I swear I am near as his own thoughts to him;

A^
^ thee

speeches.speaker: H^.
verse: Come, come, leave you p^ating.

speeches.speaker: H^.
verse: I^ thou da^'st but try.

speeches.speaker: H^
verse: I thank you heartily, you will be
^ man that will hang m^ sweet recompence,
^ do, but I do not say I will,

To ^
^st f^llow that would think out,
And ^.

speeches.speaker: Hem
verse: If it be not recompenc'd, and to thy own desires,
^f within these ten days I do not make thee —

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: What, a false knave!

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Prethee, prethee conceive me righty, any thing
Of profit or of place that may advance thee.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Why what a Goose cap would'st thou make me,
Do not I know that men in misery will promise
Any thing, more than their lives can reach at?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Believe me Huntsman,
There shall not one short syllable
That comes from me, pass
Without its full performance.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Say you so Sir?
Have ye e're a good place for my quality?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: A thousand Chases, Forests, Parks: I'le make ^
Chief ^anger over all the games.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: When?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Presently.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: This may provoke me: and yet to prove a ^

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: 'Tis to prove honest: 'tis to do good service,
Service for him thou art sworn to, for thy Prince,
Then for thy self that good; what fool would live here,
Poor, and in misery, subject to all dangers,
Law, and lewd people can inflict, when bravely
And to himself he may be law and credit?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Shall I believe thee?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: As that thou holdst most holy.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Ye may play tricks.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Then let me never live more.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Then you shall see Sir, I will do a service
That shall deserve indeed.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: 'Tis well said, Huntsman,
And thou shalt be well thought of.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I will do it: 'tis not your setting free, for that meer nothing
But such a service, if the Earl be noble,
He shall for ever love me.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: What is't Huntsman?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Do you know any of these people live here?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: You are a fool then: here be those, to have 'em,
I know the Earl so well, would make him caper.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Any of the old Lords that rebel'd?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Peace, all,
I know'em every one, and can betray 'em.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: But wilt thou doe this service?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: If you'l keep
Your faith, and free word to me.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Wilt thou swear me?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: No, no, I will believe ye: more than that too,
Here's the right heir.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: O honest, honest huntsman!

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Now, how to get these Gallants, there's the ma^
You will be constant, 'tis no work for me else.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Will the Sun shine again?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: The way to get 'em.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Propound it, and it shall be done.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: No sleight;
(For they are Devilish crafty, it concerns'em,)
Nor reconcilement, (for they dare not trust neither)
Must doe this trick.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: By force?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I, that must doe it.
And with the person of the Earl himself,
Authority (and mighty) must come on 'em:
Or else in vain: and thus I would have ye do it.
To morrow-night be here: a hundred men will bear 'em,
(So he be there, for he's both wise and valiant,
And with his terrour will strike dead their forces)
The hour be twelve a Clock, now for a guide
To draw ye without danger on these persons,
The woods being thick, and hard to hit, my self
With some few with me, made unto our purpose,
Beyond the wood, upon the plain, will wait ye
By the great Oak.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: I know it: keep thy faith huntsman,
And such a shower of wealth —

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I warrant ye:
M^ss nothing that I tell ye.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Farewel;
You have your liberty, now use it wisely;
And keep your hour, goe closer about the wood there,
For fear they spy you.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Well.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: And bring no noise with ye.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: All shall be done toth' purpose: farewel huntsman.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Now, what's the news in town?

speeches.speaker: Ginks.
verse: No news, but joy Sir;
Every man wooing of the noble Merchant,
Who has his hearty commendations to ye.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Yes this is news, this night he's to be married.

speeches.speaker: Ginks.
verse: Byth' mass that's true, he marrys Vandunks Daughter,
The dainty black-ey'd bell.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: I would my clapper
Hung in his baldrick, a what a peal could I Ring?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Married?

speeches.speaker: Ginks.
verse: 'Tis very true Sir, O the pyes,
The piping hot mince-pyes!

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: O the Plum-pottage!

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: For one leg of a goose now would I venture a limb boys,
^ love a fat goose, as I love allegiance,
And — upon the Boors, too well they know it,
And therefore starve their poultry.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: To be married
To Vandunks Daughter?

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: O this pertious Merchant:
What sport he will have? but hark you brother Prig,
^hall we do nothing in the foresaid wedding?
There's mony to be got, and meat I take it,
What think ye of a morise?

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: No, by no means,
That goes no further than the street, there leaves us,
Now we must think of something that must draw us
^nto the bowels of it, intoth' buttery,
^nto the Kitchin, into the Cellar, something
That that old drunken Burgo-master loves,
What think ye of a wassel?

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: I think worthily.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: And very fit it should be, thou, and Ferret,
And Ginks to sing the Song: I for the structure,
Which is the bowl.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Which must be up-sey English,
^trong, lusty London beer; let's think more of it.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: He must not marry.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: By your leave in private,
One word Sir, with ye; Gerrard: do not start me,
^ know ye, and he knows ye, that best loves ye:
Hubert speaks to ye, and you must be Gerrard.
The time invites you to it.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Make no show then,
^ am glad to see you Sir; and I am Gerrard.
How stand affairs?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Fair, if ye dare now follow,
Hemskirk I have let goe, and these my causes,
^'le tell ye privately, and how I have wrought him,
And then to prove me honest to my friends,
^ook upon these directions, you have seen his.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Then will I speak a speech, and a brave speech
^n praise of Merchants, where's the Ape?

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: — Take him,
A gowty Bear-ward stole him the other day.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: May his Bears worry him, that Ape had paid it,
What dainty tricks? — O that bursen Bear-ward:
^n his French doublet, with his blister'd bullions,
^n a long stock ty'd up; O how daintily
Would I have made him wait, and shift a trencher,
Carry a cup of wine? ten thousand stinks
Wait on thy mangy hide, thou lowzy Bear ward.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: 'Tis passing well, I both believe and joy in't,
And will be ready: keep you here the mean while,
And keep in, I must a while forsake ye,
Upon mine anger no man stir, this two hours.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Not to the wedding Sir?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Not any whither.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: The wedding must be seen sir; we want meat too.
We are horrible out of meat.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Shall it be spoken,
Fat Capons shak't their mils at's in defiance
And turkey tombs such honorable monuments,
Shall piggs, Sir, that the Parsons self would envy,
And dainty Ducks—

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Not a word more, obey me.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Why then come dolefull death, this is stat tyranny,
And by this hand —

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: What?

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: I'le goe sleep upon't.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Nay, and there be a wedding, and we wanting,
Farewel our happy days: we do obey Sir.

speeches.speaker: 1 Mer.
verse: Well met Sir, you are for this lusty wedding.

speeches.speaker: 1 Mer.
verse: I am so, so are you I take it.

speeches.speaker: 1 Mer.
verse: Yes,
And it much glads me, that to doe him service
Who is the honour of our trade, and lustre,
We meet thus happily.

speeches.speaker: 2 Mer.
verse: He's a noble fellow,
And well becomes a bride of such a beauty.

speeches.speaker: 1 Mer.
verse: She is passing fair indeed, long may their loves
Continue like their youths, in spring of sweetness,
All the young Merchants will be here
No doubt on't,
For he that comes not to attend this wedding,
The curse of a most blind one fall upon him,
A loud wi^e, and a lazie: here's Vanlock.

speeches.speaker: Vanl.
verse: Well overtaken Gentlemen: save ye.

speeches.speaker: 1 Mer.
verse: The same to you sir; save ye fair Mistris Francis,
I would this happy night might make you blush too.

speeches.speaker: Vanl.
verse: She dreams apace.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: That's but a drowsie fortune.

speeches.speaker: 3 Mer.
verse: Nay take us with ye too; we come to that end,
I am sure ye are for the wedding.

speeches.speaker: Vanl.
verse: Hand and heart man:
And what their feet can doe, I could have tript it
Before this whorson gout.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: Bless ye Masters.

speeches.speaker: Vanl.
verse: Clause? how now Clause? thou art come to see thy Master,
(And a good master he is to all poor people)
In all his joy, 'tis honestly done of thee.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: Long may he live sir, but my business now is
If you would please to doe it, and to him too.

speeches.speaker: Vanl.
verse: He's here himself.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Stand at the door my friends?
I pray walk in: welcom fair Mistris Francis,
See what the house affords, there's a young Lady
Will bid you welcom.

speeches.speaker: Vanl.
verse: We joy your happiness.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: I hope it will be so: Clause nobly welcom,
My honest, my best friend, I have been carefull
To see thy monys —

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: Sir, that brought not me,
Do you know this Ring again?

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Thou hadst it of me.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: And do you well remember yet, the boun you gave me
Upon the return of this?

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Yes, and I grant it,
Be it what it will: ask what thou canst, I'le do it;
Within my power.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Ye are not married yet?

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: ^th I shall ask you that that will disturb ye,
But I must put ye to your promise.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Do,
And if I faint and slinch in't—

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Well said Master,
And yet it grieves me too: and yet it must be.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Prethee distrust me not.

speeches.speaker: C^a.
verse: You must not marry,
That's part of the power you gave me: which to make up,
You must presently depart, and follow me.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Not marry, Clause?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Not if you keep your promise,
And gave me power to ask.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Pre'thee think better,
I will obey, by Heaven.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: I have thought the best, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Give me thy reason, do st thou fear her honesty?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Chaste as the ice, for any thing I know, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Why should'st thou light on that then? to what purpose?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: I must not now discover.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Must not marry?
Shall I break now when my poor heart is pawn'd?
When all the preparation?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Now or never.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Come, 'tis not that thou would'st: thou do'st but fright me.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Upon my soul it is, Sir, and I bind ye.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: C^ause, can'st thou be so cruel?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: You may break, Sir,
But never more in my thoughts appear honest.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Did'st ever see her?

speeches.speaker: Cla
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: She is such a thing,
O Clause, she is such a wonder, such a mirror,
For beauty, and fair vertue, Europe has not:
Why hast thou made me happy, to undo me?
But look upon her; then if thy heart relent not,
I'le quit her presently. who waits there?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: [within] Sir.

speeches.speaker: Gos
verse: Bid my fai^ love come hither, and the Company.
Prethee be good unto me; take a mans heart
And look upon her truly: take a friends heart
And feel what misery must follow this.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Take you a noble heart and keep your promise;
I forsook all I had, to make you happy.
Can that thing call'd a Woman, stop your goodness?

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Look there she is, deal with me as thou wilt now,
Did'st ever see a fa^er?

speeches.speaker: C^a
verse: She is most goodly.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Pray ye stand still.
What a^ls my love?
Did'st thou ever,
By the fait light of Heaven, behold a sweeter?
O that thou knew'st but love, or ever felt him,
Look well, look narrowly upon her beauties.

speeches.speaker: 1 Mer.
verse: Sure h'as some strange design in hand, he starts so.

speeches.speaker: 2 Mer.
verse: This Begga^ has a strong power over his pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: View all her body.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: 'Tis exact and excellent.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Is she a thing then to be lost thus lightly?
Her mind is ten times sweeter, ten times nobler,
And but to hear her speak, a Paradise,
And such a love she ^ears to me, a chaste love,
A vertuous, fair, and fruitful love: 'tis now too
I am rea^y to enjoy it; the Priest ready, Cla^se,
To say the holy words shall make us happy,
This is a cruelty beyond mans study,
All these are ready, all our joyes are ready,
And all the expectation of our friends,
'Twill be her death to do it.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Let her dye then.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Thou canst not: 'tis impossible.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: It must be.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: 'Twill kill me too, 'twill murder me: by heaven C^
I'le give thee half I have; come thou shalt save me.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Then you must go with me: I can stay no longer,
If ye be true, and noble.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: Hard heart, I'le follow:
Pray ye all go in again, and pray be merry,
I have a weighty business, (give my Cloak there,)
Concerns my life, and state, (make no enquiry,)
This present hour befaln me: with the soonest
I shall be here again: nay pray go in, Sir,
And take them with you, 'tis but a night lost, Gentlemen

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Come, come in, we will not lose our meat yet,
Nor our good mirth, he cannot stay long from her,
I am sure of that.

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: I will not stay; believe, Sir.
Gertrude, a word with you.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Why is this stop, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Gos.
verse: I have no more time left me, but to kiss thee,
And tell thee this, I am ever thine: farewel wench.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: And is that all your Ceremony? Is this a wed^
Are all my hopes and prayers turn'd to nothing?
Well, I will say no more, nor sigh, nor sorrow;
Till to thy face I prove thee false. Ah me!

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: LEad, if thou thinkst we are right: why dost thou ma^
These often stands? thou saidst thou knewst the wa^

speeches.speaker: Bo.
verse: Fear nothing, I do know it: would 'twere homewa^

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Wrought from me by a Beggar? at the time
That most should tye him? 'tis some other Love
That hath a more command on his affections,
And he that fetcht him, a disguised Agent,
Not what he personated; for his fashion
Was more familiar with him, and more powerful
Than one that ask'd an alms: I must find out
One, if not both: kind darkness be my shrowd,
And cover loves too curious search in me,
For yet, suspicion, I would not name thee.

speeches.speaker: Bo.
verse: Mistris, it grows somewhat pretty and dark.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: What then?

speeches.speaker: Bo.
verse: Nay, nothing; do not think I am afraid,
Although perhaps you are.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I am not, forward.

speeches.speaker: Bo.
verse: Sure but you are? give me your hand, fear noth^
There's one leg in the wood, do not pull me backward:
What a sweat one on's are in, you or I?
Pray God it do not prove the plague; yet sure
It has infected me; for I sweat too,
It runs out at my knees, feel, feel, I pray you.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: What ails the fellow?

speeches.speaker: Bo.
verse: Hark, hark I beseech you,
Do you hear nothing?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: Bo.
verse: List: a wild Hog,
He grunts: now 'tis a Bear: this wood is full of 'em,
And now, a Wolf, Mistress, a Wolf, a Wolf,
It is the howling of a Wolf.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: The braying of an Ass, is it not?

speeches.speaker: Bo.
verse: Oh, now one has me;
^h my left baunch, farewel.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Look to your Shanks,
^our Breech is safe enough, the Wolf's a Fern-brake.

speeches.speaker: Bo.
verse: But see, see, see, there is a Serpent in it;
^ has eyes as broad as Platters; it spits fire;
^ow it creeps towards us, help me to say my Prayers:
^ hath swallowed me almost, my breath is stopt;
^ cannot speak: do I speak Mistress? tell me.

speeches.speaker: Cer.
verse: Why, thou strange timerous Sot, canst thou perceive
^ thing i'th' Bush but a poor Glo-worm?
It may be 'tis but a Glo-worm now, but 'twill
Grow to a fire-drake presently.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Come thou from it:
^ have a precious guide of you, and a courteous,
^hat gives me leave to lead my self the way thus.

speeches.speaker: ^o.
verse: It thunders, you hear that now?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I hear one hollow.

speeches.speaker: B^.
verse: 'Tis thunder, thunder:
^ee, a Flash of Lightning:
Are you not blasted Mistress? pull your Mask off,
^ has plaid the Barber with me here: I have lost
My Beard, my Beard, pray God you be not shaven,
^Twill spoil your Marriage Mistress.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: What strange Wonders
^ear fancies in a Coward!

speeches.speaker: Bo.
verse: Now the Earth opens.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Prithee hold thy peace.

speeches.speaker: Bo.
verse: Will you on then?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Both love and jealousie have made me bold,
Where my Fate leads me, I must go.

speeches.speaker: Bo.
verse: God be with you then.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: It was the Fellow sure, he that should guide me,
^e Hunts-man that did hollow us.

speeches.speaker: Woolf.
verse: Best make a stand,
^nd listen to his next: Ha!

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Who goes there?

speeches.speaker: B^.
verse: Mistress, I am taken.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Mistress? Look forth Souldiers.

speeches.speaker: Woo^f.
verse: What are you Sirrah?

speeches.speaker: Bo.
verse: Truly all is left
Of a poor Boor, by day-light, by night no body,
You might have spar'd your Drum, and Guns, and Pikes too
^o^ I am none that will stand out Sir, I.
You may take me in with a walking Stick,
Even when you please, and hold me with a packthred.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: What woman was't you call'd to?

speeches.speaker: Bo.
verse: Woman! none Sir.

speeches.speaker: Woolf.
verse: None! did you not name Mistress?

speeches.speaker: Bo.
verse: Yes. but she's
No woman yet: she should have been this night,
But that a Beggar stole away her Bridegroom,
Whom we were going to make hue and cry after;
^ tell you true Sir, she should ha' been married to day;
A^ was the Bride and all; but in came Clause,

^he old lame Beggar, and whips up Mr
Goswin
Under his arm; away with him as a Kite,
Or an old Fox would swoop away a Gosling.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: 'Tis she, 'tis she, 'tis she: Niece?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Ha!

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: She Sir,
This was a noble entrance to your fortune,
That being on the point thus to be married,
Upon her venture here, you should surprise her.

speeches.speaker: Woolf.
verse: I begin, Hemskirk, to believe my fate,
Works to my ends.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Yes Sir, and this adds trust
Unto the fellow our guide, who assur'd me Florez
^v'd in some Merchants shape, as Gerrard did
^ the old Beggars, and that he would use
^ for the train, to call the other forth;
All which we find is done — That's he again — Holla

speeches.speaker: Woolf.
verse: Good, we sent out to meet him.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Here's the Oa^.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I am miserably lost, thus faln
Into my Uncles hands from all my hopes,
Can I not think away my self and dye.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I like your habits well: they are safe, stand close.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: But what's the action we are for now? Ha^
Robbing a Ripper of his Fish.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Or taking
A Poulterer Prisoner, without ransome, Bullyes?

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Or cutting off a Convoy of Butter?

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Or surprizing a Boors ken, for granting cheats!

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Or cackling Cheats?

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Or Mergery-praters, Rogers,
And Tibs o'th' Buttery?

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: O I could drive a Regiment
Of Geese afore me, such a night as this,
Ten Leagues with my Hat and Staff, and not a ^
Heard, nor a wing of my Troops disordered

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Tell us,
If it be milling of a lag of duds,
The fetching of a back of cloaths or so;
We are horribly out of linnen.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: No such matter.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Let me alone with the Farmers dog,
If you have a mind to the cheese-lost; 'tis but thus,
And he is a silenc'd Mastiff, during pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Would it would please you to be silent.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Mum.

speeches.speaker: Woolf.
verse: Who's there?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: A friend, the Hunts man.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: O 'tis he.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I have kept touch Sir, which is the ^ of these
Will he know a man now?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: This my Lord's the Friend,
Hath undertook the service.

speeches.speaker: H^b.
verse: If't be worth
His Lordships thanks anon, when 'tis done
Lording, I'll look for't, a rude Wood-man,
I know how to pitch my toils, drive in my game:
And I have don't, both Florez and his Father
Old Gerrard, with Lord Arnold of Benthursea,
Cozen, and Jaculin, young Florez's Sister:
I have 'em all.

speeches.speaker: Woolf.
verse: Thou speak'st too much, too happy,
To carry faith with it.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I can bring you
VVhere you shall see, and find 'em.

speeches.speaker: Woolf.
verse: VVe will double
VVhat ever Hemskirk then hath promis'd thee.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: And I'll deserve it treble: what horse ha' you?

speeches.speaker: Woolf.
verse: A hundred. That's well: ready to ta^
Upon surprise of 'em.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Divide then
Your force into five Squadrons; for there a^
So many out-lets, ways through the wood
That issue from the place where they are lodg'd
Five several ways, of all which Passages,
VVe must possess our selves, to round 'em in;
For by one starting hole they'll all escape else:
I and 4. Boors here to me will be guides,
The Squadron where you are, my self will lead
And that they may be more secure, I'll use
My wonted whoops, and hollows, as I were
A hunting for 'em; which will make them rest
Careless of any noise, and be a direction
To the other guides, how we approach 'em still.

speeches.speaker: Woolf.
verse: 'Tis order'd well, and relisheth the Souldier,
Make the division Hemskirk; you are my charge,
Fair One, I'll look to you.

speeches.speaker: Boo.
verse: Shall no body need
To look to me? I'll look unto my self

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: 'Tis but this, remember.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Say, 'tis done, Boy

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: By this time Sir I hope you want no reasons
Why I broke off your marriage, for though I
Should as a Subject study you my Prince
In things indifferent, it will not therefore
Dise^dit you, to acknowldge me your Father,
^ha^kning to my necessary counsels.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Acknowledge you my Father? Sir I do,
A^ may impiety, conspiring with
My other Sins, sink me, and suddenly
When I forget to pay you a Sons duty
In my obedience, and that help'd forth
With all the cheerfulness.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I pray you rise,
And may those powers that see and love this in you,
R^ward you for it: Taught by your example
Having receiv'd the rights due to a Father,
I tender you th' allegeance of a Subject:
Which as my Prince accept of.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Kneel to me?
May mountains first fall down beneath their valleys,
And fire no more mount upwards, when I suffer
An act in nature so preposterous;
I must o'recome in this, in all things else
The victory be yours: could you here read me,
You should perceive how all my faculties
Triumph in my blest fate, to be sound yours;
I am your son, your son Sir, and am prouder
To be so, to the Father, to such goodness
(Which heaven be pleas'd, I may inherit from you)
Than I shall ever of those specious titles
That plead for my succession in the Earldom
(Did I possess it now) left by my Mother.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I do believe it: but—

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: O my lov'd Father,
Before I knew you were so, by instinct,
Nature had taught me, to look on your wants,
Not as a stranger's: and I know not how,
What you call'd charity, I thought the payment
Of some religious debt, nature stood bound for;
And ^ of all, when your magnificent bounty
In in, low ebb of fortune, had brought in
A stood of blessings, though my threatning wants
And fear of their effects, still kept me stupid,
I soon found out, it was no common pity
That led you to it.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Think of this hereafter
When we with joy may call it to remembrance,
There will be a time, more opportune, than now
To end our story, with all circumstances,
I add this only: when we fled from Wolfort
I sent you into England, and there placed you
With a brave Flanders Merchant, call'd rich Goswin,
A man supplyed by me unto that purpose,
As bound by oath never to discover you,
Who dying, left his name and wealth unto you
As his reputed Son, and yet receiv'd so;
But now, as Florez, and a Prince, remember
The countreys, and the subjects general good
Must challenge the first part in your affection:
The ^ai^ maid, whom you chose to be your wife,
Being so fa^ beneath you, that your love
Must grant she's not your equal.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: In descent
Or borrowed glories from dead Ancestors,
But to, her beauty, chastity, and all vertues
^v^ remembred in the best of women,
A Mona^ch might receive from her, not give,
Though ^he were his Crowns purchase; in this only
Be an in sulyent Father: in all else,
Use your authority.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Sir, here be two of 'em,
The Father and the Son, the rest you shall have
As fast as I can rouze them.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Who's this? Wolfort?

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: I Criple, your seigned crutches will not help yo^,
Nor patch'd disguise that hath so long conceal'd you,
It's now no halting: I must here find Gerrard,
And in this Merchants habit, one call'd Florez
Who would be an Earl.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: And is, wert thou a subject.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Is this that Traitor Wolfort?

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: Yes, but you
Are they that are betrai'd: Hemskirk.
My Goswin
Turn'd Prince? O I am poorer by this greatness,
Than all my former jealousies or misfortunes.

speeches.speaker: Florez.
verse: Gertrude?

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: Stay Sir, you were to day too near her,
You must no more aim at those easie accesses,
Less you can do't in air, without a head,
Which shall be suddenly tri'd.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: O take my heart, first,
And since I cannot hope now to enjoy him,
Let me but fall a part of his glad ransom.

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: You know not your own value, that entreat.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: So proud a fiend as Wolfort.

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: For so lost
A thing as Florez.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: And that would be so
Rather than she should stoop again to thee;
There is no death, but's sweeter than all life,
When Wolfort is to give it: O my Gertrude,
It is not that, nor Princedom that I goe from,
It is from thee, that loss includeth all.

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: I, if my young Prince knew his loss, he w^ sayse
Which that he yet may chew on, I will tell him
This is no Gertrude, nor no Hemskirks Niece,
Nor Vandunks Daughter: this is Bertha, Bertha,
The heir of Brabant, she that caus'd the war,
Whom I did steal, during my treaty there,
In your minority, to raise my self;
I then fore-seeing 'twould beget a quarel,
That, a necessity of my employment,
The same employment, make me master of strength,
That strength, the Lord of Flanders, so of Brabant,
By marrying her: which had not been to doe Sir,
She come of years, but that the expectation
First of her Fathers death, retarded it,
And since the standing out of Bruges, where
Hemskirk had hid her, till she was near lost:
But Sir, we have recover'd her: your Merchantship
May break, for this was one of your best bottoms
I think.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Insolent Devil!

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: Who are these, Hemskirk?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: More, more, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: How they triumph in their treachery!

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Lord Arnold of Benthusin, this Lord Costin,
This Jaqueline the sister unto Florez.

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: All found? why here's brave game, this was sp^ roy^
And puts me in thought of a new kind of death for 'em.
Hunts-man, your horn: first wind me Florez fall,
Next Gerrards, then his Daughter Jaquelins,
Those rascals, they shall dye without their rights:
Hang 'em Hemskirk on these trees; I'le take
The assay of these my self.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Not here my Lord,
Let 'em be broken up upon a scaffold,
I will shew the better when their arbour's made.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Wretch, art thou not content thou hast betrai'd us,
^ mock us too?

speeches.speaker: G^.
verse: False Hubert, this is monstrous.

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: Hubert?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Who, this?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Yes this is Hubert, Wolfort,
^ he has helpt himself to a tree.

speeches.speaker: W^l.
verse: The first,
^ first of any, and most glad I have you Sir,
^ you goe before, but for a train;
^ have done this service?

speeches.speaker: H^
verse: As your Hunts-man,
^ now as Hubert; save your selves, I will,

^
Wolfs a foot, let slip; kill, kill, kill, kill.

speeches.speaker: W^l.
verse: Betray'd?

speeches.speaker: Hab.
verse: No, but well catch'd: and I the Huntsman.

speeches.speaker: Van-d.
verse: How do you Wolfort? Rascal, good knave Wolfort,
^ speak it now without the Rose, and Hemskirk,
^ogue Hemskirk, you that have no nicce, this Lady
Was stoln by you, and ta'ne by you, and now
^esign'd by me, to the right owner here:
^ake her my Prince.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Can this be possible,
W^lcom my love, my sweet, my worthy love.

speeches.speaker: Van-d.
verse: I ha' giv'n you her twice: now keep her better, and thank
^ord Hubert, that came to me in Gerrards name,
^nd got me out, with my brave Boyes, to march

^
Caesar, when he bred his Commentaries,
^o I, to ^ my Chronicle, came forth
Casar Van-dunk, & veni, vidi, vici,
Give me my Bottle, and set down the drum;
^ou had your tricks Sir, had you? we ha' tricks too,
^ou stole the Lady?

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: And we led your Squadrons,
Where they ha' scratch'd their leggs a little, with brambles,
^ not their faces.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Yes, and run their heads
^gainst trees.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: 'Tis Captain Prig, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: And Coronel Higgen.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: We have fill'd a pit with your people, some with leggs,
^ome with arms broken, and a neck or two
^ think be loose.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: The rest too, that escap'd,
Are not yet out o'the briars,

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: And your horses, Sir,
Are well set up in Bruges all by this time:
You look as you were not well Sir, and would be
^cortly let blood; do you want a scarf?

speeches.speaker: Van-d.
verse: A halter.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: 'Twas like your self, honest, and noble Hubert:
Can'st thou behold these mirrors all together,
Of thy long, false, and bloody usurpation?
Thy tyrrannous proscription, and fresh treason:
And not so see thy self, as to fall down
And sinking, force a grave, with thine own guilt,
As deep as hell, to cover thee and it?

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: No, I can stand: and praise the toyles that took me
And laughing in them dye, they were brave snares.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: 'Twere truer valour, if thou durst repent
The wrongs th' hast done, and live.

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: Who, I repent?
And say I am sorry? yes, 'tis the fool's language
And not for Wolfort.

speeches.speaker: Van-d.
verse: Wolfort, thou art a Devil,
And speakst his language, oh that I had my longing
Under this row of trees now would I hang him.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: No let him live, until he can repent,
But banish'd from our State, that is thy doom.

speeches.speaker: Van-d.
verse: Then hang his worthy Captain here, this Hemskirk
For profit of th' example.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: No let him
Enjoy his shame too: with his conscious life,
To shew how much our innocence contemns
All practice from the guiltiest, to molest us.

speeches.speaker: Van-d.
verse: A noble Prince.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Sir, you must help to join
Apair of hands, as they have done their hearts here,
And to their loves with joy.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: As to mine own,
My gracious Sister, worthiest Brother.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: I'le go afore, and have the bon-fire made,
My fire-works, & flap dragons, and good backrack,
With a peek of little fishes, to drink down
In healths to this day.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: 'Slight, here be changes,
The Bells ha' not so many, nor a dance, Prig.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Our Company's grown horrible thin by it,
What think you Ferret?

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Many I do think,
That we might all be Lords now, if we could stand for't.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Not I if they should offer it: I'le dislodge first,
Remove the Bush to another climat.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Sir, you must thank this worthy Burgomaster,
Here be friends ask to be look'd on too,
And thank'd, who though their trade, and course of life
Be not so perfect, but it may be better'd,
Have yet us'd me with courtesy, and been true
Subjects unto me, while I was their King,
A place I know not well how to resign,
Nor unto whom: But this I will entreat
Your grace, command them follow you to Bruges;
Where I will take the care on me, to find
Some manly, and more profitable course
To fit them, as a part of the Republique

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Do you hear Sirs? do so.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Thanks to your good grace.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: To your good Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: May you both live long.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Attend meat Van-dunks, the Burgomasters.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Yes, to beat hemp, and be whipt twice a week,
Or turn the wheel, for Crab the Rope maker:
Or learn to go along with him, his course;
That's a fine course now, i' the common-wealth, Prig.
What say you to it?

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: It is the backwardst course,
I know i'the world.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Then Higgen will scarce thrive by it,
You do conclude?

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: 'Faith hardly, very hardly,

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Troth I am partly of your mind, Prince Prig;
And therefore farewel Flanders, Higgen will seek
Some safer shelter, in some other Climat,
With this his tatter'd Colony: Let me see
Snap, Ferret, Prig, and Higgen, all are left
O' the true blood: what? shall we into England?

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Agreed.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Then bear up bravely with your Brute my lads,
Higgen hath prig'd the prancers in his dayes,
And sold good penny-worths; we will have a course,
The Spirit of Bottom, is grown bottomless.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: I'le mand no more, nor cant.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Yes, your sixpenny worth
In private, Brother, sixpence is a sum
I'le steal you any mans Dogg for.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: For sixpence more
You'l tell the owner where he is.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: 'Tis right,
Higgen must practise, so must Prig to eat;
And write the Letter: and gi' the word. But now
No more, as either of these.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: But as true Beggars,
As e're we were.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: We stand here, for an Epilogue;
Ladies, your bounties first, the rest will follow,
For womens savours are a leading alms,
If you be pleas'd look cheerly, throw your eyes
Out at your masks.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: And let your beauties sparkle.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: So may you ne'er want dressings, Jewels, gowns
Still I the fashion.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Nor the men you love,
Wealth nor discourse to please you.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: May you Gentlemen,
Never want good fresh suits nor liberty.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: May every Merchant here see safe his ventures.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: And every honest Citizen his debts in.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: The Lawyers again good Clyents.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: And the Clyents good Counsel.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: All the Gamesters here good fortune.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: The Drunkards too good wine.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: The eaters meat
Fit for their tastes and palats.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: The good wives kind Husbands.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: The young maids choyce of Sutors.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: The Midwives merry hearts.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: And all good cheer.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: As you are kind unto us and our Bush,
We are the Beggars and your daily Beadsmen,
And have your mony, but the Alms we ask
And live by, is your Grace, give that, and then
We'l boldly say our word is, Come again.

speeches.speaker:
1
~sher.
verse: ROund, round, perfume it round, quick, look ye
Diligently the state be right, are these the richest
Cushions? Fie, fie, who waits i'th' wardrobe?

speeches.speaker:
2
~sh.
verse: But pray tell me, do you think for certain
^hese Embassadours shall have this morning audience?

speeches.speaker:
1
~sh.
verse: They shall have it: Lord that you live at Court
^nd understand not! I tell you they must have it.

speeches.speaker:
2
~sh.
verse: Upon what necessity?

speeches.speaker:
1
~sh.
verse: Still you are out of the trick of Court, fell your place,
And sow your grounds, you are not for this tillage.
Madams, the best way is the upper lodgings,
There you may see at ease.

speeches.speaker: Ladies.
verse: We thank you, Sir.

speeches.speaker:
1
~sh.
verse: Would you have all these slighted? who should report then,
The Embassadors were handsome men? his beard
A neat one? the fire of his eyes quicker than lightning,
And when it breaks, as blasting? his legs, though litle ones,
Yet movers of a mass of understanding?
Who shall commend their Cloaths? who shall take notice
Of the most wise behaviour of their Feathers?
Ye live a raw man here.
prose: 〈1 page duplicate〉
〈1 page duplicate〉

speeches.speaker:
2
~sh.
verse: I think I do so.

speeches.speaker:
1
~sh.
verse: Why, whither would ye all press?

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
verse:
Good Master
~sher.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
verse: My wife, and some few of my honest neighbours, here.

speeches.speaker:
1
~sh.
verse: Prethee begone thou and thy honest Neighbours,
Thou lookst like an Ass, why, whither would you sith face?

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
verse: If I might have
But the honour to see you at my poor house, Sir,
A Capon bridled and sadled, I'le assure your worship,
A shoulder of Mutton and a pottle of Wine, Sir,
I know your Brother, he was as like ye,
And shot the best at Buts—

speeches.speaker:
1
~sh.
verse: A — upon thee.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
verse: Some Musick I'le assure you too,
My toy, Sir, can play o'th' Virginals.

speeches.speaker:
1
~sh.
verse: Prethee good toy,
Take away thy shoulder of Mutton, it is flie-blown,
And shoulder take thy flap along, here's no place for ye;
Nay then you had best be knock'd.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: I wou'd fain see him,
The glory of this place makes me remember,
But dye those thoughts, dye all but my desires,
Even those to death are sick too; he's not here,
Nor how my eyes may guide me —

speeches.speaker:
1
~sh.
verse: What's your business?
Who keeps the outward door there? here's fine shuffling,
You wastcoateer you must go back.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: There is not,
There cannot be, six days and never see me?
There must not be desire; Sir, do you think
That if you had a Mistris—

speeches.speaker:
1
~sh.
verse: Death, she is mad.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: And were your self an honest man? it cannot—

speeches.speaker:
1
~sh.
verse: What a Devil hast thou to do with me or my honesty?
Will you be jogging, good nimble tongue,
My fellow door-keeper.

speeches.speaker:
2
~sh.
verse: Prethee let her alone.

speeches.speaker:
1
~sh.
verse: The King is coming,
And shall we have an agent from the Suburbs
Come to crave audience too?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Before I thought ye
To have a little breeding, some tang of Gentry;
But now I take ye plainly,
Without the help of any perspective,
For that ye cannot alter.

speeches.speaker:
1
~sh.
verse: What's that?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: An Ass, Sir, you bray as like one,
And by my troth, me thinks as ye stand now,
Considering who to kick next, you appear to me
Just with that kind of gravity, and wisdom;
Your place may bea^ the name of Gentleman,
But if ever any of that butter stick to your bread —

speeches.speaker:
2
~sh.
verse: You must be modester.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Let him use me nobler,
And wear good Cloaths to do good Offices;
They hang upon a fellow of his vertue,
As though they hung on Gibbets.

speeches.speaker:
2
~sh.
verse: A perillous wench.

speeches.speaker:
1
~sh.
verse: Thrust her into a corner, I'le no more on her.

speeches.speaker:
2
~sh.
verse: You have enough, go pretty Maid, stand close,
And use that little tongue, with a little more temper.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: I thank ye, Sir.

speeches.speaker:
2
~sh.
verse: When the show's past,
I'le have ye into the Cellat, there we'll dine.
A very pretty wench, a witty Rogue,
And there we'll be as merry; can ye be merry?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: O very merry.

speeches.speaker:
2
~sh.
verse: Only our selves; this churlish fellow shall not know

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: By no means.

speeches.speaker:
2
~sh.
verse: And can you love a little?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Love exceedingly:
I have cause to love you, dear Sir.

speeches.speaker:
2
~sh.
verse: Then I'le carry ye,
And shew you all the pictures, and the hangings,
The Lodgings, Gardens, and the walks: and then, sweet,
You shall tell me where you lye.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Yes marry will I.

speeches.speaker:
2
~sh.
verse: And't shall go hard but I'le send ye a Venison Pasty.
And bring a bottle of wine along.

speeches.speaker:
1
~sh.
verse: Make room there.

speeches.speaker:
2
~sh.
verse: Room there afore, stand close, the train is coming

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Have I yet left a beauty to catch fools?
Yet, yet, I see him not. O what a misery
Is love, expected long, deluded longer!

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Conduct in the Embassadors.

speeches.speaker:
1
~sh.
verse: Make room there.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: They shall not wait long answer—

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Yet he comes not.
Why are eyes set on these, and multitudes
Follow to make these wonders? O good gods!
What would these look like if my love were here?
But I am fond, forgetful.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Now your grievance,
Speak short, and have as short dispatch.

speeches.speaker: 1 Emb.
verse: Then thus, Sir:
In all our Royal Masters names, We tell you,
Ye have done injustice, broke the bonds of concord,
And from their equal shares, from Alexander
Parted, and so possess'd, not like a Brother,
But as an open Enemy, Ye have hedged in
Whole Provinces, man'd and maintain'd these injuries;
And daily with your sword (though they still honour ye)
Make bloudy inroads, take Towns, and ruin Castles,
And still their sufferance feels the weight.

speeches.speaker: 2 Em.
verse: Think of that love great, Sir, that honor'd friendship
Your self held with our Masters, think of that strength
VVhen you were all one body, all one mind;
VVhen all your swords struck one way, when your angers,
Like so many brother Billows rose together,
And curling up your foaming Crests, defied
Even mighty Kings, and in their falls entomb'd 'em;
O think of these; and you that have been Conquerours,
That ever led your Fortunes open ey'd,
Chain'd fast by confidence; you that fame courted,
Now ye want Enemies and men to match ye,
Let not your own Swords seek your ends to shame ye.

speeches.speaker: 3 Em.
verse: Choose which you will, or Peace or War,
We come prepar'd for either.

speeches.speaker:
1
~sh.
verse: Room for the Prince there.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Was it the Prince they said? how my heart trembled!
'Tis he indeed; what a sweet noble fierceness
Dwells in his eyes! young Meleager like,
When he return'd from slaughter of the Boar,
Crown'd with the loves and honours of the people,
With all the gallant youth of Greece, he looks now,
Who could deny him love?

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Hail Royal Father.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Ye are welcome from your sport, Sir, do you see th^s Gent.
You that bring Thunders in your mouths, and Earthquakes
To shake and totter my designs? can you imagine
(You men of poor and common apprehensions)
VVhile I admit this man, my Son, this nature
That in one look carries more fire, and fierceness,
Than all your Masters in their lives; dare I admit him,
Admit him thus, even to my side, my bosom,
When he is fit to rule, when all men cry him,
And all hopes hang about his head; thus place him,
His weapon hatched in bloud, all these attending
When he shall make their fortunes, all as sudden
In any expedition he shall point 'em,
As arrows from a Tartars bow, and speeding
D^e I do this, and fear an enemy?
Fear your great Master? yours? or yours?

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: O Hercules!
Who saies you do, Sir? Is there any thing
In these mens faces, or their Masters actions,
Able to work such wonders?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Now he speaks:
O I could dwell upon that tongue for ever.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: You call 'em Kings, they never wore those Royalties,
Nor in the progress of their lives arriv'd yet
At any thought of King: Imperial dignities,
And powerful God-like actions, fit for Princes
They can no more put on, and make 'em sit right,
Than I can with this mortal hand hold Heaven:
Poor petty men, nor have I yet forgot
The chiefest honours time, and merit gave 'em:
L^simachus your Master, at the best,
His highest, and his hopeful'st Dignities
Was but grand-master of the Elephants;
Se^chus of the Treasure; and for Ptolomey,
A thing not thought on then, scarce heard of yet,
Some Master of Ammunition: and must these men—

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: What a brave confidence flows from his spirit!
O sweet young man!

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Must these hold pace with us,
And on the same file hang their memories?
Most these examine what the wills of Kings are?
^escribe to their designs, and chain their actions
To their restraints? be friends, and foes when they please?
Send out their Thunders, and their menaces,
As if the sate of mortal things were theirs?
Go home good men, and tell your Masters from us,
We do 'em too much honour to force from 'em
Their barren Countries, ruin their vast Cities,
And tell 'em out of love, we mean to leave 'em
(Since they will needs be Kings) no more to tread on,
Than they have able wits, and powers to manage,
And so we shall befriend 'em. Ha! what does she there?

speeches.speaker: Emb.
verse: This is your answer King?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: 'Tis like to prove so.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Fie, sweet, what makes you here?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Pray ye do not chide me.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: You do your self much wrong and me.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Pray you pardon me,
I feel my fault which only was committed
Through my dear love to you: I have not seen ye,
And how can I live then? I have not spoke to ye—

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: I know this week ye have not; I will redeem all.
You are so tender now; think where you are, sweet.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: What other light have I left?

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Prethee Celia,
Indeed I'le see you presently.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: I have done, Sir:
You will not miss?

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: By this, and this, I will not.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: 'Tis in your will and I must be obedient.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: No more of these assemblies.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: I am commanded.

speeches.speaker:
1
~sh.
verse: Room for the Lady there: Madam, my service—

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: My Coach an't please you Lady.

speeches.speaker:
2
~sh.
verse: Room before there.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: The honour, Madam, but to wait upon you—
My servants and my state.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Lord, how they stock now?
Before I was afraid they would have beat me;
How these flies play i'th' Sun-shine? pray ye no services,
Or if ye needs must play the Hobby-horses,
Seek out some beauty that affects 'em: farewel,
Nay pray ye spare: Gentlemen I am old enough
To go alone at these years, without crutches.

speeches.speaker:
2
~sh.
verse: Well I could curse now: but that will not help me,
I made as sure account of this wench now, immediately,
Do but consider how the Devil has crost me,
Meat for my Master she cries, well—

speeches.speaker: 3 Em.
verse: Once more, Sir,
We ask your resolutions: Peace or War yet?
