verse: See where he lyes; did ever man but he
Love any woman for her Constancie
To her dead lover, which she needs must end
Before she can allow him for her friend,
And he himself must needs the cause destroy,
For which he loves, before he can enjoy?
Poor Shepherd, Heaven grant I at once may free
Thee from thy pain, and keep my loyaltie:
Shepherd, look up.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Thy brightness doth amaze!
So Phoebus may at noon bid mortals gaze,
Thy glorious constancie appears so bright,
I dare not meet the Beams with my weak sight.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Why dost thou pine away thy self for me?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Why dost thou keep such spotless constancie?

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Thou holy Shepherd, see what for thy sake
Clorin, thy Clorin, now dare under take.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Stay there, thou constant Clorin, if there be
Yet any part of woman left in thee,
To make thee light: think yet before thou speak

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: See what a holy vow for thee I break.
I that already have my fame far spread
For being constant to my lover dead.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Think yet, dear Clorin, of your love, how true,
If you had dyed, he would have been to you.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Yet all I'le lose for thee.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Think but how blest
A constant woman is above the rest.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: And offer up my self, here on this ground,
To be dispos'd by thee.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Why dost thou wound
His heart with malice, against woman more,
That hated all the Sex, but thee before?
How much more pleasant had it been to me
To dye, than to behold this change in thee?
Yet, yet, return, let not the woman sway.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Insult not on her now, nor use delay,
Who for thy sake hath ventur'd all her fame.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Thou hast not ventur'd, but bought certain shame,
Your Sexes curse, foul falshood must and shall,
I see, once in your lives, light on you all.
I hate thee now: yet turn.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Be just to me:
Shall I at once both lose my fame and thee?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Thou hadst no fame, that which thou didst like good,
Was but thy appetite that sway'd thy blood
For that time to the best: for as a blast
That through a house comes, usually doth cast
Things out of order, yet by chance may come,
And blow some one thing to his proper room;
So did thy appetite, and not thy zeal,
Sway thee be chance to doe some one thing well.
Yet turn.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Thou dost but try me if I would
Forsake thy dear imbraces, for my old
Love's, though he were alive: but do not fear.

speeches.speaker: Th.
verse: I do contemn thee now, and dare come near,
And gaze upon thee; for me thinks that grace,
Austeritie, which sate upon that face
Is gone, and thou like others: false maid see,
This is the gain of foul inconstancie.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: 'Tis done, great Pan I give thee thanks for it,
What art could not have heal'd, is cur'd by wit.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Will ye be constant yet? will ye remove
Into the Cabin to your buried Love?

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: No let me die, but by thy side remain.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: There's none shall know that thou didst ever stain
Thy worthy strictness, but shall honour'd be,
And I will lye again under this tree,
And pine and dye for thee with more delight,
Than I have sorrow now to know the light.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Let me have thee, and I'le be where thou wilt.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Thou art of womens race, and full of guilt.
Farewel all hope of that Sex, whilst I thought
There was one good, I fear'd to find one naught:
But since their minds I all alike espie,
Henceforth I'le choose as others, by mine eye.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Blest be ye powers that give such quick redress,
And for my labours sent so good success.
I rather choose, though I a woman be,
He should speak ill of all, than die for me.

speeches.speaker: Priest.
verse: SHepherds, rise and shake off sleep,
See the blushing Morn doth peep
Through the window, whilst the Sun
To the mountain tops is run,
Gilding all the Vales below
With his rising flames, which grow
Greater by his climbing still.
Up ye lazie grooms, and fill
Bagg and Bottle for the field;
Clasp your cloaks last, lest they yield
To the bitter North-east wind.
Call the Maidens up, and find
Who lay longest, that she may
Goe without a friend all day;
Then reward your Dogs, and pray
Pan to keep you from decay:
So unfold and then away.
What not a Shepherd stirring? sure the grooms
Have found then beds too easie, or the rooms
Fill'd with such new delight, and heat, that they
Have both forgot their hungry sheep, and day;
Knock, that they may remember what a shame
Sloath and neglect layes on a Shepherds name.

speeches.speaker: Old Shep.
verse: It is to little purpose, not a swain
This night hath known his lodging here, or lain
Within these cotes: the woods, or some near town,
That is a neighbour to the bordering Down,
Hath drawn them thither, 'bout some lustie sport,
Or spiced Wassel-Boul, to which resort
All the young men and maids of many a cote,
Whilst the trim Minstrel strikes his merry note.

speeches.speaker: Priest.
verse: God pardon sin, show me the way that leads
To any of their haunts.

speeches.speaker: Old Shep.
verse: This to the meads,
And that down to the woods.

speeches.speaker: Priest.
verse: Then this for me;
Come Shepherd let me crave your companie.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Now your thoughts are almost pure,
And your wound begins to cure:
Strive to banish all that's vain,
Lest it should break out again.

speeches.speaker: Alex.
verse: Eternal thanks to thee, thou holy maid:
I find my former wandring thoughts well staid
Through thy wise precepts, and my outward pain
By thy choice herbs is almost gone again:
Thy sexes vice and vertue are reveal'd
At once, for what one hurt, another heal'd.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: May thy grief more appease,
Relapses are the worst disease.
Take heed how you in thought offend,
So mind and body both will mend.

speeches.speaker: Amo.
verse: Beest thou the wildest creature of the wood,
That bearst me thus away, drown'd in my blood,
And dying, know I cannot injur'd be,
I am a maid, let that name sight for me.

speeches.speaker: Satyr.
verse: Fairest Virgin do not fear
Me, that do thy body bear,
Not to hurt, but heal'd to be;
Men are ruder far than we.
See fair Goddess in the wood,
They have let out yet more blood.
Some savage man hath struck her breast
So soft and white, that no wild beast
Durst ha' toucht asleep, or wake:
So sweet, that Adder, Newte, or Snake,
Would have lain from arm to arm,
On her bosom to be warm
All a night, and being hot,
Gone away and stung her not.
Quickly clap herbs to her breast;
A man sure is a kind of beast.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: With spotless hand, on spotless brest
I put these herbs to give thee rest:
Which till it heal thee, will abide,
If both be pure, if not, off slide.
See it falls off from the wound,
Shepherdess thou art not sound,
Full of lust.

speeches.speaker: Satyr.
verse: Who would have thought it,
So fair a face?

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Why that hath brought it.

speeches.speaker: Amo.
verse: For ought I know or think, these words, my last:
Yet Pan so help me as my thoughts are chast.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: And so may Pan bless this my cure,
As all my thoughts are just and pure;
Some uncleanness nigh doth lurk,
That will not let my Medicines work.
Satyr search if thou canst find it.

speeches.speaker: Stayr.
verse: Here away me thinks I wind it,
Stronger yet: Oh here they be,
Here, here, in a hollow tree,
Two fond mortals have I found.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Bring them out, they are unsound.

speeches.speaker: Satyr.
verse: By the fingers thus I wring ye,
To my Goddess thus I bring ye;
Strife is vain, come gently in,
I scented them, they're full of sin.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Hold Satyr, take this Glass,
Sprinkle over all the place,
Purge the Air from lustfull breath,
To save this Shepherdess from death,
And stand you still whilst I do dress
Her wound for fear the pain encrease.

speeches.speaker: Sat.
verse: From this glass I throw a drop
Of Crystal water on the top
Of every grass, on flowers a pair:
Send a fume and keep the air
Pure and wholsom, sweet and blest,
Till this Virgins wound be drest.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Satyr, help to bring her in.

speeches.speaker: Sat.
verse: By Pan, I think she hath no sin,
She is so light: lye on these leaves.
Sleep that mortal sense deceives,
Crown thine Eyes, and ease thy pain,
Maist thou soon be well again.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Satyr, bring the Shepherd near,
Try him if his mind be clear.

speeches.speaker: Sat.
verse: Shepherd come.

speeches.speaker: Daph.
verse: My thoughts are pure.

speeches.speaker: Sat.
verse: The better trial to endure.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: In this flame his finger thrust,
Which will burn him if he lust;
But if not, away will turn,
As loth unspotted flesh to burn:
See, it gives back, let him go,
Farewel mortal, keep thee so.

speeches.speaker: Sat.
verse: Stay fair Nymph, flye not so fast,
We must try if you be chaste:
Here's a hand that quakes for fear,
Sure she will not prove so clear.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Hold her finger to the flame,
That will yield her praise or shame.

speeches.speaker: Sat.
verse: To her doom she dares not stand,
But plucks away her tender hand,
And the Taper darting sends
His hot beams at her fingers ends:
O thou art foul within, and hast
A^nd, if nothing else, unchaste.

speeches.speaker: Alex.
verse: Is not that Cloe? 'tis my Love, 'tis she!
C^, fair Clor.

speeches.speaker: Cl^.
verse: My Alexis.

speeches.speaker: Alex.
verse: He.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Let me embrace thee.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Take her hence,
Lest her sight disturb his sence.

speeches.speaker: Alex.
verse: Take not her, take my life first.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: See, his wound again is burst:
Keep her near, here in the Wood,
Till ha'stopt these Streams of Blood.
Soon again he ease shall find,
If I can but still his mind:
This Curtain thus I do display,
To keep the piercing air away.

speeches.speaker: Priest.
verse: Sure they are lost for ever; 'tis in vain
To find 'em out with trouble and much pain,
That have a ripe desire, and forward will
To flye the Company of all but ill,
What shall be counsel'd now? shall we retire?
Or constant follow still that first desire
We had to find them?

speeches.speaker: O^d.
verse: Stay a little while;
For if the Morning mist do not beguile
My sight with shadows, sure I see a Swain;
One of this jolly Troop's come back again.

speeches.speaker: Pri.
verse: Dost thou not blush young Shepherd to be known,
Thus without care, leaving thy flocks alone,
And following what desire and present blood
Shapes out before thy burning sense, for good,
Having forgot what tongue hereafter may
Tell to the World thy falling off, and say
Thou art regardless both of good and shame,
Sp^ning at Vertue, and a vertuous Name,
And like a glorious, desperate man that buys
A poyson of much price, by which he dies,
Dost thou lay out for Lust, whose only gain
Is foul disease, with present age and pain,
And then a Grave? These be the fruits that grow
In such hot Veins that only beat to know
Where they may take most ease, and grow ambitious
Through their own wanton fire, and pride delicious.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Right holy Sir, I have not known this night,
What the smooth face of Mirth was, or the sight
Of any looseness; musick, joy, and ease,
Have been to me as bitter drugs to please
A Stomach lost with weakness, not a game
That I am skill'd at throughly; nor a Dame,
Went her tongue smoother than the feet of Time,
Her beauty ever living like the Rime
Our blessed Tityrus did sing of yore,
No, were she more enticing than the store
Of fruitful Summer, when the loaden Tree
Bids the faint Traveller be bold and free,
'Twere but to me like thunder 'gainst the bay,
Whose lightning may enclose but never stay
Upon his charmed branches; such am I
Against the catching flames of Womans eye.

speeches.speaker: Priest.
verse: Then wherefore hast thou wandred?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: 'Twas a Vow
That drew me out last night, which I have now
Strictly perform'd, and homewards go to give
Fresh pasture to my Sheep, that they may live.

speeches.speaker: Pri.
verse: 'Tis good to hear ye, Shepherd, if the heart
In this well sounding Musick bear his part.
Where have you left the rest?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I have not seen,
Since yesternight we met upon this green
To fold our Flocks up, any of that train;
Yet have I walkt these Woods round, and have lain
All this same night under an aged Tree,
Yet neither wandring Shepherd did I see,
Or Shepherdess, or drew into mine ear
The sound of living thing, unless it were
The Nightingale among the thick leav'd spring
That sits alone in sorrow, and doth sing
Whole nights away in mourning, or the Owl,
Or our great enemy that still doth howl
Against the Moons cold beams.

speeches.speaker: Priest.
verse: Go and beware
Of after falling.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Father 'tis my care.

speeches.speaker: Old.
verse: Here comes another Stragler, sure I see
A Shame in this young Shepherd. Daphnis!

speeches.speaker: Daph.
verse: He.

speeches.speaker: Pri.
verse: Where hast thou left the rest, that should have been
Long before this, grazing upon the green
Their yet imprison'd flocks?

speeches.speaker: Daph.
verse: Thou holy man,
Give me a little breathing till I can
Be able to unfold what I have seen;
Such horrour that the like hath never been
Known to the ear of Shepherd: Oh my heart
Labours a double motion to impart
So heavy tidings! You all know the Bower
Where the chast Clorin lives, by whose great power
Sick men and Cattel have been often cur'd,
There lovely Amoret that was assur'd
To lusty Perigot, bleeds out her life,
Forc'd by some Iron hand and fatal knife;
And by her young Alexis.

speeches.speaker: Amar.
verse: If there be
Ever a Neighbour Brook, or hollow tree,
Receive my Body, close me up from lust
That follows at my heels; be ever just,
Thou god of Shepherds, Pan, for her dear sake
That loves the Rivers brinks, and still doth shake
In cold remembrance of thy quick pursuit:
Let me be made a reed, and ever mute,
Nod to the waters fall, whilst every blast
Sings through my slender leaves that I was chast.

speeches.speaker: Pri.
verse: This is a night of wonder, Amaryll
Be comforted, the holy gods are still
Revengers of th^se wrongs.

speeches.speaker: Amar.
verse: Thou blessed man,
Honour'd upon these plains, and lov'd of Pan,
Hear me, and save from endless infamie
My yet unblasted Flower, Virginitie:
By all the Garlands that have crown'd that head,
By the chaste office, and the Marriage bed
That still is blest by thee, by all the rights
Due to our gods; and by those Virgin lights
That burn before his Altar, let me not
Fall from my former state to gain the blot
That never shall be purg'd: I am not now
That wanton Amaryllis: here I vow
To Heaven, and thee grave Father, if I may
Scape this unhappy Night, to know the Day,
To live a Virgin, never to endure
The tongues, or Company of men impure.
I hear him come, save me.

speeches.speaker: Pri.
verse: Retire a while
Behind th s Bush, till we have known that vile
Abuser of young Maidens.

speeches.speaker: Sul.
verse: Stay thy pace,
Most loved Amaryllis, let the Chase
Grow calm and milder, flye me not so fast,
I fear the pointed Brambles have unlac'd
Thy golden Buskins; turn again and see
Thy Shepherd follow, that is strong and free,
Able to give thee all content and ease.
I am not bashful, Virgin, I can please
At first encounter, hug thee in mine arm,
And give thee many Kisses, soft and warm
As those the Sun prints on the smiling Cheek
Of Plums, or mellow Peaches; I am sleek
And smooth as Neptune, when stern Eolus
Locks up his surly Winds, and nimbly thus
Can shew my active Youth; why dost thou flye?
Remember Amaryll^, it was I
That kill'd Alexis for thy sake, and set
An everlasting hate 'twixt Amoret
And her beloved Perigot: 'twas I
That drown'd her in the W^ll, where she must lye
Till Time shall leave to be; then turn again,
Turn with thy open arms, and clip the Swain
That hath perform'd all this, turn, turn I say:
I must not be deluded.

speeches.speaker: Pri.
verse: Monster stay,
Thou that art like a Canker to the State
Thou liv'st and breath'st in, eating with debate
Through every honest bosome, forcing still
The Veins of any that may serve thy Will,
Thou that hast offer'd with a sinful hand
To seize upon this Virgin that doth stand
Yet trembling here.

speeches.speaker: Sull.
verse: Good holiness declare,
What had the danger been, if being bare
I had embrac'd her, tell me by your Art,
What coming wonders would that sight impart?

speeches.speaker: Pri.
verse: Lust, and a branded Soul.

speeches.speaker: Sull.
verse: Yet tell me more,
Hath not our Mother Nature for her store
And great encrease, said it is good and just,
And wills that every living Creature must
Beget his like?

speeches.speaker: Pri.
verse: Ye are better read than I,
I must confess, in blood and Lechery.
Now to the Bower, and bring this Beast along,
Where he may suffer Penance for his wrong.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Here will I wash it in this mornings dew,
Which she on every little grass doth strew
In silver drops against the Sun's appear:
'Tis holy water, and will make me clear.
My hands will not be cleans'd. My wronged Love,
If thy chaste spirit in the air yet move,
Look mildly down on him that yet doth stand
All full of guilt, thy blood upon his hand,
And though I struck thee undeservedly,
Let my revenge on her that injur'd thee
Make less a fault which I intended not,
And let these dew drops wash away my spot.
It will not cleanse. O to what sacred Flood
Shall I resort to wash away this blood?
Amid'st these Trees the holy Clorin dwells
In a low Cabin of cut Boughs, and heals
All Wounds; to her I will my self address,
And my rash faults repentantly confess;
Perhaps she'll find a means by Art or Prayer,
To make my hand with chaste blood stained, fair:
That done, not far hence underneath some Tree,
I'll have a little Cabin built, since she
Whom I ador'd is dead, there will I give
My self to strictness, and like Clorin live.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Shepherd, once more your blood is staid,
Take example by this Maid,
Who is heal'd ere you be pure,
So hard it is lewd lust to cure.
Take heed then how you turn your eye
On each other lustfully:
And Shepherdess take heed lest you
Move his willing eye thereto;
Let no wring, nor pinch, nor smile
Of yours his weaker sense beguile.
Is your Love yet true and chaste,
And for ever so to last?

speeches.speaker: Alex.
verse: I have forgot all vain desires,
All looser thoughts, ill tempred fires,
True Love I find a pleasant fume,
Whose moderate heat can ne'r consume.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: And I a new fire feel in me,
Whose chaste flame is not quencht to be.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Join your hands with modest touch,
And for ever keep you such.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: You is her Cabin, thus far off I'll stand,
And call her forth; for my unhallowed hand
I dare not bring so near yon sacred place.
Clorin come forth, and do a timely grace
To a poor Swain.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: What art thou that dost call?
Clorin is ready to do good to all:
Come near.

speeches.speaker: Peri.
verse: I dare not.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Satyr, see
Who it is that calls on me.

speeches.speaker: Sat.
verse: There at hand, some Swain doth stand,
Stretching out a bloudy hand.

speeches.speaker: Peri.
verse: Come Clorin, bring thy holy waters clear,
To wash my hand.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: What wonders have been here
Tonight? stretch forth thy hand young Swain,
W^ and rub it whilest I rain
Holy water.

speeches.speaker: Peri.
verse: Still you pour,
But my hand will never scower.

speeches.speaker: Cor.
verse: Satyr, bring him to the Bower,
We will try the Soveraign power
Of other waters.

speeches.speaker: Satyr.
verse: Mortal, sure
'Tis the Blood of Maiden pure
That stains thee so.

speeches.speaker: Peri.
verse: What e're thou be,
Be'st thou her spright, or some divinitie,
That in her shape thinks good to walk this grove,
Pardon poor Ferigot.

speeches.speaker: Amor.
verse: I am thy love,
Thy Amoret, for evermore thy love:
Strike once more on my naked breast, I'le prove
As constant still. O couldst thou love me yet;
How soon should I my former griefs forget!

speeches.speaker: Peri.
verse: So over-great with joy, that you live, now
I am, that no desire of knowing how
Doth seize me; hast thou still power to forgive?

speeches.speaker: Amo.
verse: Whilest thou hast power to love, or I to live;
More welcome now than hadst thou never gone
Astray from me.

speeches.speaker: Peri.
verse: And when thou lov'st alone
And not I, death, or some lingring pain
That's worse, light on me.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Now your stain
This perhaps will cleanse again;
See the blood that erst did stay,
With the water drops away.
A^ the powers again are pleas'd,
A^ with this new knot appeas'd.
^ your hands, and rise together,
^ blest that brought you hither.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Go back again what ere thou art, unless
S^eth Maiden thoughts possess thee, do not press
^is hallowed ground. Go Satyr, take his hand,
And give him present trial.

speeches.speaker: Satyr.
verse: Mortal stand,
^l by fire I have made known
Whether thou be such a one,
That mayst freely tread this place.
Hold thy hand up; never was
More untainted flesh than this.
^rest, he is full of bliss.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Then boldly speak, why dost thou seek this place?

speeches.speaker: Priest.
verse: First, honour'd Virgin, to behold thy face
Where all good dwells that is: Next for to try
The truth of late report was given to me:
Those Shepherds that have met with foul mischance,
Through much neglect, and more ill governance,
Whether the wounds they have may yet endure
The open Air, or stay a longer cure.
And lastly, what the doom may be shall light
Upon those guilty wretches, through whose spight
A^ this confusion fell: For to this place,
T^ou holy Maiden, have I brought the race
Of these offenders, who have freely told,
Both why, and by what means they gave this bold
Attempt upon their lives.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Fume all the ground,
And sprinkle holy water, for unsound
And foul infection 'gins to fill the Air:
It gathers yet more strongly; take a pair
Of Censors fill'd with Frankincense and Mirrh,
Together with cold Camphyre: quickly stir
Thee, gentle Satyr, for the place begins
To sweat and labour with the abhorred sins
Of those offenders,; let them not come nigh,
For full of itching flame and leprosie
Their very souls are, that the ground goes back,
And shrinks to feel the sullen weight of black
And so unheard of venome; hie thee fast
Thou holy man, and banish from the chast
These manlike monsters, let them never more
Be known upon these downs, but long before
The next Suns rising, put them from the sight
And memory of every honest wight.
Be quick in expedition, lest the sores
Of these weak Patients break into new gores.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: My dear, dear Amoret, how happy are
Those blessed pairs, in whom a little jar
Hath bred an everlasting love, too strong
For time, or steel, or envy to do wrong?
How do you feel your hurts? Alas poor heart,
How much I was abus'd; give me the smart
For it is justly mine.

speeches.speaker: Amo.
verse: I do believe.
It is enough dear friend, leave off to grieve,
And let us once more in despight of ill
Give hands and hearts again.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: With better will
Than e're I went to find in hottest day
Cool Crystal of the Fountain, to allay
My eager thirst: may this band never break.
Hear us O Heaven,

speeches.speaker: Amo.
verse: Be constant.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Else Pan wreak,
With bouble vengeance, my disloyalty;
Let me not dare to know the company
Of men, or any more behold those eyes.

speeches.speaker: Amo.
verse: Thus Shepherd with a kiss all envy dyes.

speeches.speaker: Priest.
verse: Bright Maid, I have perform'd your will, the Swain
In whom such heat and black rebellions ^ gn
Hath undergone your sentence, and disgrace.
Only the Maid I have reserv'd, whose face
Shews much amendment, many a tear doth fall
In sorrow of her fault, great fair recal
Your heavy doom, in hope of better daies,
Which I dare promise; once again upraise
Her heavy Spirit that near drowned lyes
In self comsuming care that never dyes,

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: I am content to pardon, call her in;
The Air grows cool again, and doth begin
To purge it self, how bright the day doth show
After this stormy Cloud? go Satyr, go,
And with this Taper boldly try her hand,
If she be pure and good, and firmly stand
To be so still, we have perform'd a work
Worthy the Gods themselves.

speeches.speaker: Satyr.
verse: Come forward Maiden, do not lurk
Nor hide your face with grief and shame,
Now or never get a name
That may raise thee, and recure
All thy life that was impure:
Hold your hand unto the flame,
If thou beest a perfect dame,
Or hast truely vow'd to mend,
This pale fire will be thy friend.
See the Taper hurts her not.
Go thy wayes, let never spot
Henceforth seize upon thy blood.
Thank the Gods and still be good.

speeches.speaker: Cor.
verse: Young Shepherdess now ye are brought again
To Virgin state, be so, and so remain
To thy last day, unless the faithful love
Of some good Shepherd force thee to remove;
Than labour to be true to him, and live
As such a one, that ever strives to give
A b^d memory to after time.
^ famous for your good, not for your crime.
^ holy man, I offer up again
^ patients full of health, and free from pain:
^p t^m f om after ills, be ever near
^ actions, teach them how to clear

^
^ous way they pass through, from suspect,
^ from wrong^ng others, or neglect
Of ^ in themselves, correct the bloud
With thirsty b^ts and labour, let the floud,
O^ the next neig^bouring spring give remedy
To g^ly thri^, and travel not the tree
That ^angs with wanton clusters, let let not wine,
Unless in sacrifice, or ^ites divine,
Be ever known of S^p^d, have a care
Thou man of holy life. Now do not spare
Their faults through much remissness, nor forget
To cherish him, w^ose many pains and swet
Hath giv'n increase, and added to the downs.
Sort all your Shepherds from the la^y clowns
That f^d it H se^s in the budded Brooms:
Teach the young Maidens strictness, that the grooms
May ever ^ to tempt their blowing youth;
Banish all complements, but single truth
From every tongue, and every Shepherds heart,
Let them still use perswading, but no Art:
Thus holy Priest, I wish to thee and these,
All the best goods and comforts that may please.

speeches.speaker: Alex.
verse: And all those blessings Heaven did ever give,
We pray upon this Bower may ever live.

speeches.speaker: Priest.
verse: Kneel every Sh^pherd, whilest with powerful hand
I bless your after labours, and the Land
You seed your flocks upon. Great Pan defend you
From misfortune, and amend you,
Keep you from those dangers still,
That are followed by your will,
Give ye means to know at length
All your riches, all your strength,
Cannot keep your foot from falling
To lewd lust, that still is calling
At your Cottage, till his power
Bring again that golden hour
Of peace and rest to every soul.
May his care of you controul
All diseases, sores or pain
That in after time may raign
Either in your flocks or you,
Give ye all affections new,
New desires, and tempers new,
That ye may be ever true.
Now rise and go, and as ye pass away
Sing to the God of Sheep, that happy lay,
That honest Dorus taught ye, Dorus, he
That was the soul and god of melodie.
prose:
The SONG.

All ye woods, and trees and bowers,
All you vertues and ye powers
That inhabit in the lakes,
In the pleasant springs or brakes,
Move your feet
To our sound,
Whilest we greet
All this ground,
With his honour and his name
That defends our flocks from blame.


He is great, and he is just,
He is ever good, and must
Thus be honour'd: Daffadillies,
Roses, Pinks, and loved Lillies,
Let us sting,
Whilest we sing,
Ever holy,
Ever holy,
Ever honour'd ever young,
Thus great Pan is ever sung.

speeches.speaker: Satyr.
verse: Thou divinest, fairest, brightest,
Thou must powerful Maid, and whitest,
Thou most vertuous and most blessed,
Eyes of stars, and golden tressed
Like Apollo, tell me sweetest
What new service now is meetest
For the Satyr? shall I stray
In the middle Air, and stay
The sayling Rack, or nimbly take
Hold by the Moon, and gently make
Sute to the pale Queen of night
For a beam to give thee light?
Shall I dive into the Sea,
And bring thee Coral, making way
Through the rising waves that fall
In snowie fleeces; dearest, shall
I catch the wanton Fawns, or Flyes,
Whose woven wings the Summer dyes
Of many colours? get thee fruit?
Or steal from Heaven old Orpheus Lute?
All these I'le venture for, and more,
To do her service all these woods adore.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: No other service, Satyr, but thy watch
About these thickets, lest harmless people catch
Mischief or sad mischance.

speeches.speaker: Satyr.
verse: Holy Virgin, I will dance
Round about these woods as quick
As the breaking light, and prick
Down the Lawns, and down the vails
Faster than the Wind-mill sails.
So I take my leave, and pray
All the comforts of the day,
Such as Phoebus heat doth send
On the earth, may still be friend
Thee, and this arbour.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: And to thee,
All thy Masters love be free.

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: H^alth to my Soveraign.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Eumenes, welcome:
Welcome to Paph^, Souldier, to our love,
And that ^a^ health ye wish us, through the Camp
May it disp^rse it s lf, and make all happy;
How does the General, the valiant Memnon,
And how his Wars, Eumenes?

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: The Gods have giv'n you (Royal Si^) a Souldier,
Better n^e s^ught a dang^, more approv'd
In way of Wa^, more master of his fortunes,
I ^p it in leading 'em, in doing valiant,
In following all his deeds to Victories,
And holding fortun^ certain there.

speeches.speaker: King
verse: O Souldier,
Thou speak'st a man indeed; a Generals General,
A soul conceiv'd a Souldier.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Ten set Battels
Against the strong usurper Diocles
(Whom long experience had begot a Leader,
Ambition rais'd too mighty) hath your Memnon
Won, and won gloriously, distrest and shook him
Even from the head of all his hopes to nothing:
In three, he beat the Thunder-bolt his Brother,
Forc'd him to wall himself up: there not safe,
Shook him with war like Engins like an Earthquake,
Till like a Snail he left his shell and crawl'd
By night and hideous darkness to destruction:
Disarm'd for ever rising more: Twelve Castles,
Some thought impregnable; Towns twice as many;
Countries that like the wind knew no command
But savage wildness, hath this General
With loss of blood and youth, through Storms and Tempests
Call'd to your fair obedience.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: O my Souldier
That thou wert now within my arms; what drums Drums within.
Are those that beat Eumenes?

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: His, my Soveraign;
Himself i'th' head of conquest drawing home,
An old man now to offer up his glories,
And endless conquest at your shrine.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Goe all,
And entertain him with all Ceremonie,
We'l keep him now a Courtier.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Sir, a strange one,
Pray God his language bear it; by my life, Sir
He knows no complement, nor curious casting
Of words into fit places e're he speak 'em,
He can say fight well fellow, and I'le thank thee:
He that must eat, must fight; bring up the rear there,
Or charge that wing of horse home.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Goe too, goe too.
Valiant and wise are twins Sir: welcom, welcom,
Welcom my fortunate and famous General,
High in thy Princes favour, as in fame,
Welcom to Peace, and Paphos.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Thank your Grace,
And would to God my dull tongue had that sweetness
To thank you as I should; but pardon me,
My sword and I speak roughly Sir: your battels
I dare well say, I have fought well; for I bring ye
That lazie end you wish for Peace, so fully,
That no more name of war is: who now thinks
Sooner or safer these might have been ended,
Begin 'em if he dare again; I'le thank him.
Souldier and Souldiers Mate these twenty five years,
At length your General, (as one whose merit
Durst look upon no less,) I have waded through
Dangers would damp these soft souls, but to hear of.
The maiden heads of thousand lives hang here Sir,
^e which time Prince, I know no Court but Marshal,
^o oylie language, but the shock of Arms,
No dalliance but with death; No lofty measures
But weary and sad marches, cold and hunger,
Larums at midnight Valours self would shake at,
Yet I ne're shrunk: Balls of consuming Wildfire,
That lickt men up like lightning, have I laught at,
And tost 'em back again like childrens trifles.
Upon the edges of my Enemies swords
I have marcht like whirle-winds, fury at this hand waiting,
Death at my right; Fortune my forlorn hope,
When I have grapled with destruction,
And tug'd with pale fac'd Ruine, Night and Mischief,
Frighted to see a new day break in bloud;
And every where I conquer'd; and for you Sir,
Mothers have wanted wombs to make me famous,
And blown ambition, dangers; Those that griev'd ye,
I have taken order for i'th' earth: those fools
That shall hereafter —

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: No more wars my Souldier:
We must now treat of peace Sir.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: How he talks,
How gloriously.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: A goodly timber'd fellow,
Valiant no doubt.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: If valour dwell in vaunting;
In what a phrase he speaks, as if his actions
Could be set off in nothing but a noise;
Sure h'as a drum in's mouth.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I wonder wenches
How he would speak to us.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Nothing but Larum,
Tell us whose throat he cut, shew us his sword,
And bless it for sure biting.

speeches.speaker: Lucippe.
verse: And 't like your Grace,
I do not think he knows us what we are,
Or to what end; for I have heard his followers
Affirm he never saw a woman that exceeded
A Sutlers wife yet, or in execution
Old bedrid Beldames without teeth or tongues,
That would not flie his furie? how he looks.

speeches.speaker: Clea.
verse: This way devoutly.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Sure his Lordship's viewing
Our Fortifications.

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: If he mount at me,
I may chance choak his Battery.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Still his eye
Keeps quarter this way: Venus grant his valour
Be not in love.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: If he be, presently
Expect a Herald and a Trumpet with ye
To bid ye render; we two Perdu's pay for't else.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: I'le leave ye to my sister, and these Ladies
To make your welcom fuller: my good souldier
We must now turn your sternness into Courtship;
When ye have done there, to your fair repose Sir: Flourish.
I know you need it Memnon; welcom Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Now he begins to march: Madam the Van's yours,
Keep your ground sure; 'tis for your spurrs.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: O Venus.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: How he stares on me.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Knight him Madam, knight him,
He will grow toth' ground else.

speeches.speaker: Eumenes.
verse: Speak Sir, 'tis the Princess.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cap.
verse: Ye shame your self, speak to her.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Rise and speak Sir.
Ye are welcome to the Court, to me, to all Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Is he not deaf?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: The Gentleman's not well.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: F^e noble General.

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Give him fresh air, his colour goes, how do ye?
The Princess will be glad Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Peace, and hear me.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Command a silence there.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: I love thee Lady.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I thank your Lordship heartily: proceed Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Lord how it stuck in's stomach like a surfeit.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: It breaks apace now from him, God be thanked,
What a fine spoken man he is.

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: A choice one, of singular variety in carriage.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Yes and I warrant you he knows his distance.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: With all my heart I love thee,

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: A hearty Gentleman,
And I were e'en an arrant beast, my Lord,
But I lov'd you again.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Good Lady kiss me.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: I marry, Mars, there thou cam'st close up to her.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Kiss you at first my Lord? 't is no fair fashion,
Our lips are like Rose buds, blown with mens breaths,
They lose both sap and savour; there's my hand Sir,

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Fie, fie, my Lord, this is too rude.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Unhand me,
Consume me if I hurt her; good sweet Lady
Let me but look upon thee.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Doe.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Yet —

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Well Sir,
Take your full view.

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Bless your eyes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Mercy,
Is this the man they talkt of for a Souldier,
So absolute an Excellent: O the Gods,
If I were given to that vanitie
Of making sport with men for ignorance,
What a most precious subject had I purchas'd?
Speak for him Gentlemen: some one that knows,
What the man ails; and can speak sense.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Sure Madam,
This fellow has been a rare Hare finder.
See how his eyes are set.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Some one goe with me,
I'le send him something for his head, poor Gentleman,
He's troubled with the staggers.

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Keep him dark,
He will run Ma^ch mad else, the sumes of Battels
Ascend into his brains.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Clap to his feet
An old D^um head, to draw the thunder downward.

speeches.speaker: Cal
verse: Look to him Gentlemen: farewel, Lord I am sorry
We cannot kiss at this time, but believe it
We'l find an hou^ for all: God keep my Children,
From being such sweet Souldiers; Softly wenches,
Lest we disturb his dream.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Why this is Monstrous.

speeches.speaker: 1 Capt.
verse: A strange forgetfulness, yet still he holds it.

speeches.speaker: 2 Capt.
verse: Though he ne're law a woman of great fashion
Before this day, yet methinks 'tis possible
He might imagine what they are, and what
Belongs unto 'em: meer report of others.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Pish, his head had other whimsies in't: my Lord,
Death I think y'are struck dumb; my good Lord General.

speeches.speaker: 1 Capt.
verse: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: That I do love ye Madam; and so love ye
An't like your grace.

speeches.speaker: 2 Capt.
verse: He has been studying this speech.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Who do ye speak to Sir?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Why where's the Lady,
The woman, the fair woman?

speeches.speaker: 1 Capt.
verse: Who?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: The Princess,
Give me the Princess.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Give ye counsel rather
To use her like a Princess: Fy my Lord,
How have you born your self, how naked!
Laid your soul open, and your ignorance
To be a sport to all. Report and honour
Drew he^ to doe you favours, and you bluntly,
Without considering what, or who she was,
Neither collecting reason, nor distinction.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Why, what did I my Masters?

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: All that shews
A man unhandsom, undigested dough.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Did not I kneel unto her?

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Dumb and sensless,
As though ye had been cut out for your fathers tomb,
Or stuck a land mark; when she spoke unto you,
Being the excellence of all our Island,
Ye star'd upon her, as ye had seen a monster.

speeches.speaker: Mon.
verse: Was I so foolish? I confess Eumenes,
I never saw before so brave an outside,
But did I kneel so long?

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Till they laught at ye,
And when you spoke, I am asham'd to tell ye
What 'twas my Lord; how far from order;
Bless me, is't possible the wild noise of war
And what she only teaches should possess ye?
Knowledge to treat with her, and full discretion
Being at stood still in ye: and in peace,
And manly conversation smooth and civil,
Where gracefulness and glory twyn together,
Thrust your self out an exile?
Do you know Sir, what state she carries?
What great obedience waits at her beck continually?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: She ne're commanded
A hundred thousand men, as I have done,
Nor ne're won battel, Say I would have kist her.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: There was a dainty offer too, a rare one.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Why, she is a woman, is she not?

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: She is so.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Why, very well; what was she made for then?
Is she not young, and handsom, bred to breed?
Do not men kiss fair women? if they doe,
If lips be not unlawfull ware; Why a Princess
Is got the same way that we get a begger
Or I am cozen'd; and the self-same way
She must be handled e're she get another,
That's rudeness is it not?

speeches.speaker: 2 Capt.
verse: To her'tis held so, & rudeness in that high degree—

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: 'Tis reason,
But I will be more punctual; pray what thought she?

speeches.speaker: Eum.
verse: Her thoughts were merciful, but she laught at ye,
Pitying the poorness of your complement,
And so she left ye. Good Sir shape your self
To understand the place, and noble persons
You live with now.

speeches.speaker: 1 Capt.
verse: Let not those great deserts
The King hath laid up of ye, and the people,
Be blasted with Ill bearing.

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: The whole name of souldier then will suffer.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: She's a sweet one,
And good sirs leave your exhortations,
They come untimely to me, I have brains
That beat above your reaches: She's a Princess,
That's all: I have killed a King, that's greater.
Come let's to dinner, if the Wine be good,
You shall perceive strange wisdom in my blood.

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: Well, would thou wert i' the wars again
Old Memnon, there thou wouldst talk toth' purpose,
And the proudest of all these Court Camelions
Would be glad to find it sense too: plauge of this
Dead peace, this Bastard breeding, lowzie, lazie idleness,
Now we must learn to pipe, and pick our livings
Out of old rotten ends: these twenty five years
I have serv'd my Country, lost my youth and bloud,
Expos'd my life to dangers more than dayes;
Yet let me tell my wants, I know their answers;
The King is bound to right me, they good people
Have but from hand to mouth. Look to your wives
Your young trim wives, your high-day wives, your march panes,
For if the souldiers find not recompence,
As yet there's none a hatching; I believe
You men of wares, the men of wars will nick ye,
For starve nor beg they must not; my small means
Are gone in fumo: here to raise a better
Unless it be with lying, or Dog flattering,
At which our Nation's excellent; observing Dog-days,
When this good Lady broyles and would be basted
By that good Lord, or such like moral learnings,
Is here impossible; Well; I will rub among'em
If any thing for honestie be gotten,
Though't be but bread and cheese I can be satisfied:
If otherwise the wind blow, stiff as I am
Yet I shall learn to shuffle: There's an old Lass
That shall be nameless yet alive, my last hope,
Has often got me my pocket full of crowns.
If all sail — Jack-Dawes, are you alive still?
Then I see the coast clear, when fools and boyes can prosper.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: Brave Lieutenant.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: Hail to the man of worship.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: You are fine sirs,
Most passing fine at all points.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: As ye see Sir,
Home-bred and handsome, we cut not out our clothes Sir
At half sword as your Taylors doe, and pink 'em
With Pikes and Partizans, we live retir'd Sir
Gentlemen like, and Jealous of our honours.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Very fine Fool, and fine Boy, Peace playes with you,
As the wind playes with Feathers, dances ye,
You grind with all gusts, gallants.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: We can bounce Sir,
When you Soldados bend i'th' hams, and frisk too.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: When twenty of your trip coats turn their tippets,
And your cold sallets without salt or vineger
Be wambling in your stomachs; hemp and hobnails
Will bear no price now, hangings and old harness
Are like to over-run us.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
verse: Whores and hot houses.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: Surgeons and Syringes ring out your sance-bells.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: Your Jubile, your Jubile.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: Proh Deum.
How our St. Georges will bestride the Dragons,
The red and ramping Dragons.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: Advanc't fool—

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: But then the sting i'th' tail boy.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: Tanto Melior.
For so much the more danger, the more honour.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: You're very pleasant with our occupation Gent.
Which very like amongst these fierie Serpents
May light upon a Blind-worm of your blood,
A Mother or a Sister.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: Mine's past saddle,
You should be sure of her else: but say Sir Huon,
Now the Drums dubbs, and the sticks turn'd bed-staves,
All the old Foxes hunted to their holes,
The Iron age return'd to Erebus,
And Honorificabilitudinit atibus
Thrust out o'th'Kingdom by the head and shoulders,
What trade do you mean to follow?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: That's a question.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: Yes and a learned question if ye mark it,
Consider and say on.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Fooling as thou dost, that's the best trade I take it.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: Take it straight then
For fear your fellows be before ye, hark ye Lieutenant
Fooling's the thing, the thing worth all your fightings,
When all's done ye must fool Sir.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Well, I must then.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: But do you know what fooling is? true fooling,
The circumstances that belong unto it?
For every idle knave that showes his teeth,
Wants and would live, can juggle, tumble, fiddle,
Make a dog face, or can abuse his fellow,
Is not a fool at first dash; you shall find Sir
Strange turnings in this trade; to fool is nothing
As fooling has been, but to fool the fair way,
The new way, as the best men fool their friends,
For all men get by fooling, meerly fooling,
Desert does nothing, valiant, wise, vertuous,
Are things that walk by without bread or breeches.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I partly credit that.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: Fine wits, fine wits Sir,
There's the young Boy, he does well in his way too,
He could not live else in his Masters absence;
He tyes a Ladyes garters so, so prettily,
Say his hand slip, but say so.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Why let it slip then.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: 'Tis ten to one the body shall come after,
And he that works deserves his wages.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: That's true.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: He riddles finely to a waiting Gentlewoman,
Expounds dreams like a Prophet, dreams himself too,
And wishes all dreams true; they cry Amen,
And there's a Memorandum: he can sing too
Bawdy enough to please old Ladies: he lies rarely,
Pawns ye a sute of clothes at all points, fully,
Can pick a pocket if ye please, or casket;
Lisps when he lists to catch a Chambermaid,
And calls his Hostess mother, these are things now,
If a man mean to live: to fight and swagger,
Beaten about the Ears with bawling sheepskins,
Cut to the soul for Summer: here an arm lost,
And there a leg; his honourable head
Seal'd up in salves and cereclothes, like a packet,
And so sent over to an Hospital, stand there, charge there,
Swear there, whore there, dead there,
And all this sport for cheese, and chines of dog-flesh,
And mony when two wednesdayes meet together,
Where to be lowzie is a Gentleman,
And he that wears a clean shirt has his shrowd on.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I'le be your scholar, come if I like fooling.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: You cannot choose but like it, fight you one day
I'le fool another, when your Surgeon's paid,
And all your leaks stopt, see whose stops are heaviest,
I'le have a shilling for a can of wine,
When you shall have two Sergeants for a Counter.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Come learn of us Lieutenant, hang your Iron up,
We'l find you cooler wars.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Come let's together,
I'le see your tricks, and as I like 'em. —

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: Why was there not such women in the camp then
Prepar'd to make me know 'em?

speeches.speaker: Eum.
verse: 'Twas no place Sir.

speeches.speaker: 1 Capt.
verse: Why should they live in Tumults? they are creatures
Soft and of sober natures.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Cou'd not your wives,
Your Mothers, or your Sisters have been sent for
To exercise upon?

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: We thank your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: 2 Capt.
verse: But do you mean?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: I do mean.

speeches.speaker: 2 Capt.
verse: What Sir?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: To see her,
And see thee hang'd too an thou anger'st me,
And thousands of your throats cut, get ye from me,
Ye keep a prating of your points of manners,
And fill my head with lowzie circumstances,
Better have Ballads in't, your courtly worships,
How to put off my hat, you, how to turn me,
And you (forsooth) to blow my nose discreetly;
Let me alone, for I will love her, see her,
Talk to her, and mine own way.

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: She's the Princess.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Why let her be the Devil, I have spoke
When Thunder durst not check me, I must love,
I know she was a thing kept for me.

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: And I know Sir,
Though she were born yours, yet your strange behaviour
And want —

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Thou liest.

speeches.speaker: Eum.
verse: I do not.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Ha!

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: I do not lye Sir,
I say you want fair language, nay 'tis certain
You cannot say good morrow.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Ye Dog whelps,
The proudest of your prating tongues—

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: Doe, kill us,
Kill us for telling truth: for my part, General,
I would not live to see men make a may-game
Of him I have made a Master, kill us quickly,
Then ye may —

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: What?

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: Doe what you list, draw your sword childishly
Upon your Servants that are bound to tell ye;
I am weary of my life.

speeches.speaker: 1 Capt.
verse: And I.

speeches.speaker: 2 Capt.
verse: And all Sir.

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: Goe to the Princess, make her sport, cry to her
I am the glorious man of war.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Pray ye leave me,
I am sorry I was angry, I'le think better,
Pray no more words.

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: Good Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Nay then.

speeches.speaker: 2 Capt.
verse: We are gone Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: How came he hither? see for Heavens sake wenches,
What face, and what postures he puts on,
I do not think he is perfect.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: If your love
Have not betray'd his little wits, he's well enough,
As well as he will be.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Mark how he muses.

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: H'as a Batalia now in's brains, he draws out, now
Have at ye Harp^s.

speeches.speaker: C^.
verse: See, see, there the fire fails.

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Look what an Alphabet of faces he runs through.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: O love, love, how amorously thou look'st
In an old rusty armo^.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: I'll away, for by my troth I fear him.

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Fear the gods, Madam,
And ^ what man can do, this fellow
^ about him and his furies,
H^s La^ums, and his Launces, Swords, and Targets,
Na^d him up in armour Cap a pe,
Yet must I ^take within two hours,

It ^
^st can go, to give him such a shake,
Should sha^e his Valour off, and make his shanks to ake.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: For shame no more.

speeches.speaker: C^l.
verse: He muses still.

speeches.speaker: C^e.
verse: The Devil
Why should this old dryed timber chopt with thunder—

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Old Wood burns quickest.

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Out, you would say Madam,
Give me a green stick that may hold me heat,
And smoak me soundly too; He turns, and sees ye.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: There's no avoiding now, have at ye.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Lady.
The more I look upon ye.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: The more you may, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Let him alone.

speeches.speaker: M^m.
verse: I would desire your patience.
The more I say I look, the more —

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: My Fortune,
'Tis very apt, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Women, let my Fortune
And me alone I wish ye, pray come this way,
And stand you still there Lady.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Leave the words Sir, and leap into the meaning.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Then again:
I tell you I do love ye.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Why?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: No questions: pray no more questions.
I do love you, infinitely: why do you smile?
Am I ridiculous?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I am monstrous fearful, no, I joy you love me.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Joy on then, and be proud on't, I do love you,
Stand still, do not trouble me you Women.
He loves you Lady at whose feet have kneel'd
Princes to b^g their ^reedome, he whose valour
Has over ^un whole Kingdoms.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: That makes me doubt, Sir,
'Twill ov ^run me too.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: He whose Sword.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Talk not so big, Sir, you will fright the Princess,

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Ha.

speeches.speaker: Lucippe.
verse: No forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I know ye have done wonders.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: I have and will do more and greater, braver;
And for your beauty miracles, name that Kingdom
And take your choice.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Sir I am not ambitious.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Ye shall be, 'tis the Child of Glory: she that I love
Whom my desire shall magnifie, time stories,
And all the Empires of the Earth.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: I would sain ask him

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Prithee be quiet, he will beat us both else.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: What will ye make me then, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Mem
verse: I will make thee
Stand still and hold thy peace; I have a heart, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Ye were a monster else.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: A loving heart,
A truly loving heart.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Alas, how came it?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: I would you had it in your hand, sweet Lady,
To see the truth it bears you.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Do you give it.

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: That was well thought upon.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: 'Twill put him to't Wench.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: And you shall see I dare accept it, Sir,
Tak't in my hand and view it: if I find it
A loving and a sweet heart, as you call it,
I am bound, I am.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: No more, I'll send it to ye,
As I have honour in me, you shall have it.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Handsomly done, Sir, and perfum'd by all means,
The Weather's warm, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: With all circumstance.

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: A Napkin wrought most curiously.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Divinely.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Put in a Goblet of pure Gold.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Yes in Jacinth
That she may see the Spirit through,

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Ye have greas'd him
For chewing love again in haste.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: If he should do it.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: If Heaven should fall we should have larks; he do it!

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: See how he thinks upon't.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: He will think these three years
Ere he prove such an Ass, I lik't his offer,
There was no other way to put him off else.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: I will do it—
Lady expect my heart.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I do, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Love it, for 'tis a heart that— and so I leave ye.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Either he is stark mad,
Or else I thinks he means it.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: He must be stark mad
Or else he will never do it, 'tis vain Glory,
And want of judgment that provokes this in him;
Sleep and Society cures all: his heart?
No, no, good Gentleman there's more belongs to't,
Hearts are at higher prices, let's go in
And there examine him a little better.
Shut all the doors behind for fear he follow,
I hope I have lost a lover, and am glad on't.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: 'Tis but to dye, Dogs do it, Ducks with dabling,
Birds sing away their Souls, & Babies sleep 'em,
Why do I talk of that is treble vantage?
For in the other World she is bound to have me;
Her Princely word is past: my great desert too
Will draw her to come after presently,
'Tis justice, and the gods must see it done too.
Besides, no Brother, Father, Kindred there
Can hinder us, all languages are alike too.
There love is everlasting, ever young,
Free from Diseases, ages, jealousies,
Bawds, Beldames, Painters, Purgers: dye? 'tis nothing,
Men drown themselves for joy to draw in juleps
When they are hot with Wine: In dreams we do it.
And many a handsom Wench that loves the sport well,
Gives up her Soul so in her Lovers bosome;
But I must be incis'd first, cut and open'd,
My heart, and handsomely, ta'n from me; stay there,
Dead once, stay, let me think again, who do I know there?
For else to wander up and down unwaited on
And unregarded in my place and project,
Is for a Sowters Soul, not an old Souldiers.
My brave old Regiments — I there it goes,
That have been kill'd before me, right. —

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: He's here, and I must trouble him.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Then those I have conquer'd
To make my train full.

speeches.speaker: C^.
verse: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: My Captains then—

speeches.speaker: C^.
verse: Sir, I beseech ye.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: For to meet her there
Being a Princess and a Kings sole Sister
With great accommodation must be cared for.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Weigh but the Souldiers poverty.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Mine own Troop first
For they shall die.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: How, what's this?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Next—

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Shall I speak louder, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: A square Battalia—

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: You do not think of us.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Their Armours gilded —

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Good noble Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: And round about such Engines
Shall make Hell shake.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Ye do not mock me.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: For, Sir,
I will be strong, as brave—

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Ye may consider,
You know we have serv'd you long enough.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: No Souldier
That ever landed on the blest Elyzium
Did or shall march, as I will.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Would ye would march, Sir,
Up to the King and get us—

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: King not Keiser
Shall equal me in that world.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: What a Devil ails he?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Next, the rare beauties of those Towns I fir'd.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: I speak of money, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Ten thousand Coaches—

speeches.speaker: Ca.
verse: O pounds, Sir, pounds I beseech your Lordship,
Let Coaches run out of your remembrance.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: In which the wanton Cupids, and the Graces
Drawn with the Western winds kindling desires,
And then our Poets—

speeches.speaker: Ca.
verse: Then our pay.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: For Chilax when the triumph comes; the Princess
Then, for I will have a Heaven made—

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Bless your Lordship!
Stand still, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: So I do, and in it—

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Death Sir,
You talk you know not what.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Such rare devices:
Make me I say a Heaven.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I say so too, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: For here shall run a Constellation.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: And there a pissing Conduit.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Ha!

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: With wine, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: A Sun there in his height, there such a Planet.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: But where's our money, where runs that?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Ha?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Money,
Money an't like your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Why all the carriage shall come behind, the stuff,
Rich hangings, treasure;
Or say we have none.

speeches.speaker: C^.
verse: I may say so truly,
For hang me if I have a Groat: I have serv'd well
And like an honest man: I see no reason—

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Thou must needs die good Chilax.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Very well, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: I will have honest, valiant souls about me,
I cannot miss thee.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Dye?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Yes die, and Pelius,
Eumenes and Polybius: I shall think
Of more within these two hours.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Dye Sir?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: I, Sir,
And ye shall dye.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: When, I beseech your Lordship?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: To morrow see ye do dye.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: A short warning,
Troth, Sir, I am ^ll prepar'd.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: I dye my self then,
Beside there's reason—

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Oh!

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: I pray thee tell me,
For thou art a great Dreamer.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I can dream, Sir,
If I eat well and sleep well.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Was it never
By Dream or Apparition open'd to thee—

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: He's mad.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: What the other world was, or Elyzium?
Didst never travel in thy sleep?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: To Taverns,
When I was drunk o're night; or to a Wench,
There's an Elyzium for ye, a young Lady
Wrapt round about ye like a Snake: is that it?
Or if that strange Elyzium that you talk of
Be where the Devil is, I have dream't of him,
And that I have had him by the horns, and rid him,
He trots the Dagger out o'th' sheath.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Elyzium,
The blessed fields man.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I know no fields blessed, but those I have gain'd by.
I have dream't I have been in Heaven too.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: There, handle that place that's Elyzium.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Brave singing, and brave dancing,
And rare things.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: All full of flowers.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: And Pot-herbs.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Bowers for lovers,
And everlasting ages of delight.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I slept not so far.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Meet me on those banks
Some two days hence.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: In Dream, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: No in death, Sir.
And there I Muster all, and pay the Souldier.
Away, no more, no more.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: God keep your Lordship:
This is fine dancing for us.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Where's the General?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: There's the old sign of Memnon, where the soul is
You may go look as I have.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: What's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Why question him and see; he talks of Devils,
Hells, Heavens, Princes, Powers, and Potentates,
You must to th' pot too.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Do you know Elyzium? a tale he talks the Wild-goose chase of

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Elyzium? I have read of such a place.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Then get ye to him,
Ye are as fine company as can be sitted.
Your Worships fairly met.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Mercy upon us,
What ails this Gentleman?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Provision—

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: How his head works?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Between two Ribbs,
If he cut short or mangle me; I'le take him
And twirle his neck about.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Now Gods defend us.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: In a pure Cup transparent, with a writing
To signifie—

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: I never knew him thus:
Sure he's bewitch'd, or poyson'd.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Who's there?

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: I Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Come hither, Siphax.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Yes, how does your Lordship?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Well, God a mercy Souldier, very well,
But prithee tell me—

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Any thing I can, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: What durst thou do to gain the rarest Beauty
The World has?

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: That the World has? 'tis worth doing.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Is it so; but what doing bears it?

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Why? any thing; all danger it appears to.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Name some of those things: do.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: I would undertake, Sir,
A Voyage round about the World.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Short, Siphax.
A Merchant does it to spice pots of Ale.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: I wou'd swim in Armour.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Short still; a poor Jade
Loaden will take a stream and stem it strongly
To leap a Mare.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: The plague, I durst.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Still shorter,
I'll cure it with an Onion.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Surfeits.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Short still:
They are often Physicks for our healths, and help us.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: I wou'd stand a breach.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Thine honour bids thee, Souldier:
'Tis shame to find a second cause.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: I durst, Sir,
Light with the sellest Monster.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: That's the poorest,
Man was ordain'd their Master; durst ye dye, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: How? dye my Lord!

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Dye Siphax; take thy Sword,
And come by that door to her; there's a price
To buy a lusty love at.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: I am content, Sir,
To prove no Purchaser.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Away thou World-worm,
Thou win a matchless Beauty?

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: 'Tis to lose't Sir,
For being dead, where's the reward I reach at?
The love I labour for?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: There it begins Fool,
Thou art meerly cozen'd; for the loves we now know
Are but the heats of half an hour, and hated
Desires stir'd up by nature to encrease her;
Licking of one another to a lust;
Course and base appetites, earths meer inheritours
And Heirs of Idleness and blood; Pure Love,
That, that the soul affects, and cannot purchase
While she is loaden with our flesh, that Love, Sir,
Which is the price of honour, dwells not here,
Your Ladies eyes are lampless to that Vertue,
That beauty smiles not on a cheek washt over,
Nor scents the sweet of Ambers; below, Siphax
Below us, in the other World Flyzium,
Where's no more dying, no despairing, mourning,
Where all desires are full, defarts down loaden,
There Siphax, there, where loves are ever living.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Why do we love in this World then?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: To preserve it,
The maker lost his work else; but mark Siphax,
What issues that love bears.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Why Children, Sir.
I never heard him talk thus; thus divinely
And sensible before.

speeches.speaker: Mem
verse: It does so, Siphax,
Things like our selves, as sensual, vain, unvented
Bubbles, and breaths of air, got with an itching
As blisters are, and bred, as much corruption
Flows from their lives, sorrow conceives and shapes 'em,
And oftentimes the death of those we love most.
The bleeders bring them to the World to curse 'em,
Crying they creep amongst us like young Cats.
Cares and continual Crosses keeping with 'em,
They make Time old to tend them, and experience
An ass, they alter so; they grow and goodly,
Ere we can turn our thoughts, like drops of water
They fall into the main, are known no more;
This is the love of this World; I must tell thee
For thou art understanding.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: What you please, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: And as a faithful man:
Nay I dare trust thee,
I love the Princess.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: There 'tis, that has fired him,
I knew he had some inspiration.
But does she know it, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Yes marry does she,
I have given my heart unto her.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: If ye love her.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Nay, understand me, my heart taken from me,
Out of my Body, man, and so brought to her.
How lik'st thou that brave offer? there's the love
I told thee of; and after death, the living;
She must in justice come Boy, ha?

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Your heart, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: I, so by all means, Siphax.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: He loves roast well
That cats the Spit.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: And since thou art come thus fitly,
I'll do it presently and thou shalt carry it,
For thou canst tell a story and describe it.
And I conjure thee, Siphax, by thy gentry,
Next by the glorious Battels we have fought in,
By all the dangers, wounds, heats, colds, distresses,
Thy love next, and obedience, nay thy life.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: But one thing, first, Sir, if she pleas'd to grant it,
Could ye not love her here and live? consider.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Ha? Yes, I think I could.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: 'Twould be far nearer,
Besides the sweets here would induce the last love
And link it in.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Thou sayest right, but our ranks here
And bloods are bars between us, she must stand off too
As I perceive she does.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Desert and Duty
Makes even all, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Then the King, though I
Have merited as much as man can, must not let her,
So many Princes covetous of her beauty;
I wou'd with all my heart, but 'tis impossible.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Why, say she many after.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: No, she dares not;
The gods dare not do ill; come.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Do you mean it?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Lend me thy knife, and help me off.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: For heaven sake,
Be not so stupid mad, dear General.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Dispatch, I say.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: As ye love that ye look for,
Heaven and the blessed life.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Hell take thee, Coxcomb,
Why dost thou keep me from it? thy knife I say.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Do but this one thing, on my knees I beg it,
Stay but two hours till I return again.
For I will to her, tell her all your merits,
Your most unvalu'd love, and last your danger;
If she relent, then live still, and live loving,
Happy, and high in savour: if she frown—

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Shall I be sure to know it?

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: As I live, Sir,
My quick return shall either bring ye fortune,
Or leave you to your own fate.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Two hours?

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Yes, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Let it be kept, away, I will expect it.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: You dainty wits? two of ye to a Cater,
To cheat him of a dinner?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Ten at Court, Sir,
Are few enough, they are as wise as we are.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Hang ye, I'le eat at any time, and any where,
I never make that part of want, preach to me
What ye can do, and when ye list.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: Your patience,
'Tis a hard day at Court, a fish day.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: So it seems, Sir,
The fins grow out of thy face.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: And to purchase
This day the company of one dear Custard,
Or a mess of Rice ap Thomas, needs a main wit;
Beef we can bear before us lined with Brewes
And tubs of Pork; vociferating Veals,
And Tongues that ne're told lye yet.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Line thy mouth with 'em.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: Thou hast need, and great need,
For these sinny fish-dayes,
The Officers understandings are so flegmatick,
They cannot apprehend us.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: That's great pity,
For you deserve it, and being apprehended
The whip to boot; Boy what do you so near me?
I dare not trust your touch Boy.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: As I am vertuous,
What, thieves amongst our selves?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Stremon.

speeches.speaker: Stre.
verse: Lieutenant.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Welcome a shore, a shore.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: What Mounsieur Musick?

speeches.speaker: Stre.
verse: My fine Fool.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Fellow Crack, why what a consort
Are we now blest withal?

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: Fooling and sidling,
Nay and we live not now boys; what new songs, Sirra?

speeches.speaker: Stre.
verse: A thousand, man, a thousand.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: Itching Airs
Alluding to the old sport.

speeches.speaker: Stre.
verse: Of all sizes.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: And how does small Tym Treble here; the heart on't?

speeches.speaker: 2 Boy.
verse: To do you service.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: O Tym the times, the times Tym.

speeches.speaker: Stre.
verse: How does the General,
And next what money's stirring?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: For the General
He's here, but such a General!
The time's chang'd, Stremon,
He was the liberal General, and the loving,
The feeder of a Souldier, and the Father,
But now become the stupid'st.

speeches.speaker: Stre.
verse: Why, what ails he?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Nay, if a Horse knew, and his head's big enough,
I'le hang for't; did'st thou ever see a Dog
Run mad o'th' tooth-ache, such another toy
Is he now, so he glotes and grins, and bites.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: Why hang him quickly,
And then he cannot hurt folks.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: One hour raving,
Another smiling, not a word the third hour,
I tell thee Stremon h'as a stirring soul,
What ever it attempts or labours at
Would wear out twenty bodies in another.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: I'le keep it out of me, for mine's but Buckram,
He would bownce that out in two hours.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Then he talks
The strangest and the maddest stuff from reason,
Or any thing ye offer; stand thou there,
I'le show thee how he is, for I'le play Memnon
The strangest General that ere thou hearest of, Stremon.

speeches.speaker: Stre.
verse: My Lord.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Go presently and find me
A black Horse with a blew tail; bid the blank Cornet
Charge through the Sea, and sink the Navy: softly,
Our souls are things not to be waken'd in us
With larums, and loud bawlings, for in Elyzium
Stilness and quietness, and ^ness, Sirra,
I will have, for it much concerns mine honour,
Such a strong reputation for my welcome
As all the world shall say: for in the forefront
So many on white Unicorns, next them
My Gentlemen, my Cavaliers and Captains,
Ten deep and trapt with Tenter-hooks to take hold
Of all occasions: for Friday cannot fish out
The end I aim at; tell me of Diocles,
And what he dares do? dare he meet me naked?
Thunder in this hand? in his left—Fool—

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: Yes, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Fool, I would have thee fly i'th' Air, fly swiftly
To that place where the Sun sets, there deliver.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: Deliver? what, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: This Sir, this ye slave, Sir,
Death ye rude Rogues, ye Scarabe's.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: Hold for Heav'ns sake, Lieutenant, sweet Lieutenant.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I have done, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: You have wrung his neck off.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: No Boy, 'tis the nature
Of this strange passion when't hits to hale people
Along by th'hair, to kick 'em, break their heads.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: Do ye call this Acting, was your part to beat me?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Yes, I must act all that he does.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: Plague act ye,
I'le act no more.

speeches.speaker: Stre.
verse: 'Tis but to shew man.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: Then man
He should have shew'd it only, and not done it,
I am sure he beat me beyond Action,
Gouts o' your heavy fist.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I'le have thee to him,
Thou hast a fine wit, fine fool, and canst play rarely.
He'l hug thee, Boy, and stroke thee.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: I'le to the stocks first,
E're I be strok't thus.

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: But how came he, Chilax?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I know not that.

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: I'le to him.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: He loves thee well,
And much delights to hear thee sing; much taken
He has been with thy battel songs.

speeches.speaker: Stre.
verse: If Musick
Can find his madness; I'le so siddle him,
That out it shall by th' shoulders.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: My fine Fidler,
He'l sirk you and ye take not heed too: 'twill be rare sport
To see his own trade triumph over him;
His Lute lac'd to his head, ^or creeping hedges;
For mony there's none stirring; try good Stremon
Now what your silver sound can do; our voices
Are but vain Echoes.

speeches.speaker: Stre.
verse: Something shall be done.
Shall make him understand all; let's toth' Tavern,
I have some few Crowns lest yet: my whistle wet once
I'le pipe him such a Paven—

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Hold thy head up,
I'le cure it with a quart of wine; come Coxcomb,
Come Boy take heed of Napkins.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: Youl'd no more acting?

speeches.speaker: Cin.
verse: No more Chicken.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: Go then.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: God save you Sir; pray how might I see the Princess?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Why very sitly, Sir, she's even now ready
To walk out this way intoth' Park; stand there,
Ye cannot miss her sight, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: I much thank ye.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Let's have a care, for I'le assure ye Wenches
I wou'd not meet him willingly again;
For though I do not fear him, yet his fashion
I wou'd not be acquainted much with.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Gentle Lady,
Ye need not fear, the walks are view'd and empty,
But me thinks, Madam, this kind heart of his—

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: He's slow a coming.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Keep me ye blest Angels,
