verse: Good noble General.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Pray Sir be mercifull.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Weep out your shames first,
^t make me fool for companie: fie Souldiers,
My Souldiers too, and play these tricks? what's he there?
^t I have seen his face too; yes, most certain
^are a son, but I hope he is not here now,
Would much resemble this man, wondrous near him,
^ of his height and making too, you seem a Leader.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Good Sir, do not shame me more: I know your anger,
A^d less than death I look not for.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: You shall be my charge Sir, it seems you want foes,
When you would make your friends your Enemies.
A running bloud ye have, but I shall cure ye.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Good Sir—

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: No more good Lord: beat forward Souldiers:
And you, march in the rear, you have lost your places.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: You shall not be thus fullen still with me Sister,
You do the most unnobly to be angry,
For as I have a soul, I never touch'd her,
I never yet knew one unchast thought in her:
I must confess, I lov'd her: as who would not?
I must confess I doated on her strangely,
I offer'd all, yet so strong was her honour,
So fortifi'd as fair, no hope could reach her,
And whilst the world beheld this, and confirm'd it,
Why would you be so jealous?

speeches.speaker: Oly.
verse: Good Sir pardon me,
I feel sufficiently my follies penance,
And am asham'd, that shame a thousand sorrows
Feed on continually, would I had never seen her,
Or with a clearer judgement look'd upon her,
She was too good for me, so heavenly good Sir,
Nothing but Heaven can love that soul sufficiently,
Where I shall see her once again.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: No more tears,
If she be within the Dukedom, we'l recover her:
Welcom Lord Burris, fair news I hope.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Most fair Sir,
Without one drop of bloud these wars are ended,
The Souldier cool'd again, indeed asham'd Sir,
And all his anger ended.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Where's Lord Archas?

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Not far off Sir: with him his valiant son,
Head of this fire, but now a prisoner,
And if by your sweet mercy not prevented,
I fear some fatal stroke.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I hear the Drums beat,
Welcom, my worthy friend.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Stand where ye are Sir,
Even as you love your country, move not forward,
Nor plead for peace till I have done a justice,
A justice on this villain; none of mine now,
A justice on this Rebel.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: O my Brother.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: This fatal firebrand—

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Forget not old man,
He is thy son, of thine own bloud.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: In these veins
No treacherie e're harbour'd yet, no mutinie,
I ne're gave life to lewd and headstrong Rebels.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: 'Tis his first fault.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Not of a thousand Sir,
Or were it so, it is a fault so mightie,
So strong against the nature of all mercy,
His Mother were she living, would not weep for him,
He dare not say he would live.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I must not Sir,
Whilst you say 'tis not fit: your Graces mercy
Not to my life appli'd, but to my fault Sir,
The worlds forgiveness next, last, on my knees Sir,
I humbly beg,
Do not take from me yet the name of Father,
Strike me a thousand blows, but let me dye yours.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: He moves my heart: I must be suddain with him,
I shall grow faint else in my execution;
Come, come Sir, you have seen death; now meet him bravely.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Hold, hold I say, a little hold, consider
Thou hast no more sons Archas to inherit thee.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Yes Sir, I have another, and a nobler:
No treason shall inherit me: young Archas
A h^m as sweet as young, my Brother breeds him,
My ^oole Brother Br^kie breeds him nobly,
Him let your favour find: give him your honour.

speeches.speaker: Pu.
verse: Thou hast no child left Archas, none to inherit thee
If thou stri^st that stroke now: behold young Archas;
Behold thy Brother here, thou bloudy Brother,
As bloo^y to this sacrifice as thou art:
Heave up thy swo^ and mine's heav'd up: strike Archas,
And I'le strike too as s^tly, as deadly:
Have mercy, and I'le have mercy: the Duke gives it.
Look upon all these, how they weep it from thee,
Choose quickly, and begin.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: On your obedience,
On your allegeance save him.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Take him to ye,
And s^ah, be an honest man, ye have reason:
I thank ye worthy Brother: welcom child,
Mine own sweet child.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Why was this boy conceal'd thus?

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Your graces pardon:
Pea^ing the vow you made against my Brother,
And that your anger would not only light
On him, but find out all his familie,
This young boy, to preserve from after danger,
Like a young wench, hither I brought; my self
In the habit of an ordinarie Captain
Disguis'd, got entertainment, and serv'd here
That I might still be ready to all fortunes:
That boy your grace took, nobly entertain'd him,
But thought a Gitle, Alinda, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Stand away,
And let me look upon him.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: My young Mistris?
This is a strange metamorphosis, Alinda?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Your graces humble servant.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Come hither Sister:
I dare yet scarce believe mine eyes: how they view one another?
Dost thou not love this boy well?

speeches.speaker: Oly.
verse: I should lye else,
Trust me, extreamly lye Sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Didst thou never wish Olympia,
It might be thus?

speeches.speaker: Oly.
verse: A thousand times.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Here take him:
Nay, do not blush: I do not jest; kiss sweetly:
Boy, ye kiss faintly boy; Heaven give ye comfort;
Teach him, he'l quickly learn: there's two hearts eas'd not

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: You do me too much honour Sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: No Archas,
But all I can, I will; can you love me? speak truly.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Yes Sir, dearly.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Come hither Viola, can you love this man?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: I'le do the best I can Sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Seal it Burris,
We'l all to Church together instantly:
And then a vie for boyes; stay, bring Boroskie.
I had almost forgot that lump of mischief.
There Archas, take the enemie to honour,
The knave to worth: do with him what thou wilt.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: T^ to my sword again; you to your prayers;
Wash off your villanies, you feel the burthen.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Forgive me e're I die, most honest Archas;
'Tis too much honour that I perish thus;
O strike my faults to kill them, that no memorie,
No black and blasted infamy hereafter—

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Come, are ye ready?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: And truly penitent, to make your way straight?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Thus I wash off my sins.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Stand up, and live then,
And live an honest man; I scorn mens ruines:
Take him again, Sir, trie him: and believe
This thing will be a perfect man.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I take him.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: And when I fail those hopes, heavens hopes fail me.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: You are old: no more wars Father:
Theodore take you the charge, be General.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: All good bless ye.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: And my good Father, you dwell in my bosom,
From you rise all my good thoughts: when I would think
And examine time for one that's fairly noble,
And the same man through all the streights of vertue,
Upon this Silver book I'le look, and read him.
Now forward merrily to Hymens rites,
To joyes, and revels, sports, and he that can
Most honour Archas, is the noblest man.

plays.play_title: Rule a Wife, and have a Wife.

speeches.speaker: Mich.
verse: ARE your Companies full, Colonel?

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: No, not yet, Sir:
Nor will not be this month yet, as I reckon;
How rises your Command?

speeches.speaker: Mich.
verse: We pick up still, and as our monies hold out,
We have men come, about that time I think
We shall be full too, many young Gallants go.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: And unexperienced,
The Wars are dainty dreams to young hot spirits,
Time and Experience will allay those Visions,
We have strange things to fill our numbers,
There's one Don Leon, a strange goodly fellow,
Recommended to me from some noble Friends,
For my Alferes, had you but seen his Person,
And what a Giants promise it protesteth.

speeches.speaker: Mich.
verse: I have heard of him, and that he hath serv'd before too.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: But no harm done, nor never meant, Don Michael,
That came to my ears yet, ask him a question,
^e blushes like a Girl, and answers little,
In the point less, he wears a Sword, a good one,
^ good Cloaths too, he is whole skin'd, has no hurt yet,
Good promising hopes, I never yet heard certainly
^ any Gentleman that saw him angry.

speeches.speaker: Mich.
verse: Preserve him, he'll conclude a peace if need be,
^a^y as strong as he will go along with us,
^at swear as valiantly as heart can wish,
Their mouths charg'd with six oaths at once, and whole ones,
^at make the drunken Dutch creep into Mole-hills.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: 'Tis true, such we must look for: but Mich. Perez,
^en heard you of Donna Margarita, the great Heiress?

speeches.speaker: Mich.
verse: I hear every hour of her, though I never saw her,
^e is the main discourse: noble Don Juan de Castro,
^ow happy were that man could catch this Wench up,
^d live at ease! she is fair, and young, and wealthy,
^nite wealthy, and as gracious too
^ all her entertainments, as men report.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: But she is proud, Sir, that I know for certain,
^nd that comes seldome without wantonness,
^e that shall marry her, must have a rare hand.

speeches.speaker: Mich.
verse: Would I were married, I would find that Wisdom,
With a light rein to rule my Wife: if ever Woman
^ the most subtile mould went beyond me,
^ould give the Boys leave to whoot me out o'th' Parish.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Sir, there be two Gentlewomen attend to speak with you.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Wait on 'em in.

speeches.speaker: Mich.
verse: Are they two handsome Women?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: They seem so, very handsom, but they are vail'd, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mich.
verse: Thou put'st sugar in my mouth, how it melts with me!
^ve a sweet young Wench.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Wait on them in I say.

speeches.speaker: Mich.
verse: Don Juan.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: How you itch, Michael! how you burnish!
Will not this Souldiers heat out of your bones yet,
Do your Eyes glow now?

speeches.speaker: Mich.
verse: There be two.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Say honest, what shame have you then?

speeches.speaker: Mich.
verse: I would fain see that,
I have been in the Indies twice, and have seen strange things,
But two honest Women; — one I read of once.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Prithee be modest.

speeches.speaker: Mich.
verse: I'll be any thing.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: You are welcome Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Mich.
verse: Both hooded, I like 'em well though,
They come not for advice in Law sure hither;
May be they would learn to raise th^ Pike,
I am for 'em: they are very modest, 'tis a fine Preluctium,

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: With me, or with this Gentleman,
Would you speak, Lady?

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: With you, Sir, as I guess, Juan de Cast,

speeches.speaker: Mich.
verse: Her Curtain opens, she is a pretty Gentlewoman

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: I am the Man, and shall be bound to Fortune,
I may do any service to your Beauties.

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: Captain, I hear you are marching down to Flanders,
To serve the Catholick King.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: I am sweet Lady.

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: I have a Kinsman, and a noble Friend,
Imploy'd in those Wars, may be, Sir, you know him,
Don Campusano Captain of Carbines,
To whom I would request your Nobleness,
To give this poor Remembrance.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: I shall do it,
I know the Gentleman, a most worthy Captain.

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: Something in private.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Step aside: I'll serve thee.

speeches.speaker: Mich.
verse: Prithee let me see thy face.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Sir, you must pardon me,
Women of our sort, that maintain fair memories,
And keep suspect off from their Chastities,
Had need wear thicker Vails.

speeches.speaker: Mich.
verse: I am no blaster of a Ladies Beauty,
Not bold intruder on her sp^cial favours,
I know how tender Reputation is,
And with what guards it ought to be preserv'd, Lady,
You may to me.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: You must excuse me, Seignior, I come
Not here to sell my self.

speeches.speaker: Mich.
verse: As I am a Gentleman, by the honour of a Souldier.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: I believe you,
I pray you be civil, I believe you would see me,
And when you have seen me I believe you will like me,
But in a strange place, to a stranger too,
As if I came on purpose to betray you,
Indeed I will not.

speeches.speaker: Mich.
verse: I shall love you dearly,
And 'tis a sin to fling away affection,
I have no Mistress, no desire to honour
Any but you, will not this Oyster open?
I know not, you have struck me with your modesty;
She will draw sure; so deep, and taken from me
All the desire I might bestow on others,
Qu^tly before they come.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Indeed I dare not:
But since I see you are so desirous, Sir,
To view a poor face that can merit nothing
But your Repentance.

speeches.speaker: Mich.
verse: It must needs be excellent.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: And with what honesty you ask it of me,
When I am gone let your man follow me,
And view what house I enter, thither come,
For there I dare be bold to appear open:
And as I like your vertuous carriage then,
I shall be able to give welcome to you;
She hath done her business, I must take my leave, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mich.
verse: I'll kiss your fair white hand and thank you, Lady.
My man shall wait, and I shall be your Servant,
Si^ah, come near, hark.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: I shall do it faithfully.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: You will command me no more services?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: To be careful of your noble health, dear Sir,
That I may ever honour you.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: I thank you,
And kiss your hands, wait on the Ladies down there.

speeches.speaker: Mi.
verse: You had the honour to see the face that came to you?

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: And 'twas a fair one; what was yours, Don Michael?

speeches.speaker: Mi.
verse: Mine was i'th'clipse, and had a Cloud drawn over it.
But I believe well, and I hope 'tis handsome,
She had a hand would stir a holy Hermite.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: You know none of 'em?

speeches.speaker: Mich
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Then I do, Captain,
But I'll say nothing till I see the proof on't,
Sit close Don Perez, or your Worship's caught.
I fear a Flye.

speeches.speaker: Mich.
verse: Were those she brought Love-Letters?

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: A Packet to a Kinsman now in Flanders,
Yours was very modest me thought.

speeches.speaker: Mich.
verse: Some young unmanag'd thing,
But I may live to see—

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: 'Tis worth experience,
Let's walk abroad and view our Companies

speeches.speaker: Sanch.
verse: What, are you for the Wars, Alonzo?

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: It may be I,
It may be no, e'n as the humour takes me.
If I find peace amongst the female Creatures,
And easie entertainment, I'll stay at home,
I am not so far obliged yet to long Marches
And mouldy Biskets, to run mad for Honour,
When you are all gone I have my choice before me.

speeches.speaker: Sanch.
verse: Of which Hospital thou wilt sweat in; wilt thou
Never leave whoring?

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: There is less danger in't than gunning, Sanchio,
Though we be shot sometimes, the shot's not mortal,
Besides, it breaks no limbs.

speeches.speaker: Sanch.
verse: But it disables 'em,
Dost thou see how thou pull'st thy legs after thee, as they
Hung by points.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: Better to pull 'em thus than walk on wooden ones,
Serve bravely for a Billet to support me.

speeches.speaker: Sanch.
verse: Fye, fye, 'tis base.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: Dost thou count it base to suffer?
Suffer abundantly? 'tis the Crown of Honour;
You think it nothing to lie twenty days
Under a Surgeons hands that has no mercy.

speeches.speaker: Sanch.
verse: As thou hast done I am sure, but I perceive now
Why you desire to stay, the orient Heness,
The Margarita, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Alonz.
verse: I would I had her.

speeches.speaker: Sanch.
verse: They say she will marry.

speeches.speaker: Alonz.
verse: I think she will.

speeches.speaker: Sanch.
verse: And marry suddenly, as report goes too,
She fears her Youth will not hold out, Alonzo.

speeches.speaker: Alonz.
verse: I would I had the sheathing on't.

speeches.speaker: Sanch.
verse: They say too
She has a greedy eye that must be fed
With more than one mans meat.

speeches.speaker: Alonz.
verse: Would she were mine,
I would cater for her well enough; but Sanchio,
There be too many great men that a lore her,
Princes, and Princes fellows, that claim priviledge.

speeches.speaker: Sanch.
verse: Yet those stand off i'th' way of marriage,
To be tyed to a mans pleasure is a second labour.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: She has bought a brave house here in town.

speeches.speaker: Sanch.
verse: I have heard so.

speeches.speaker: Alonz.
verse: If she convert it now to pious uses,
And bid poor Gentlemen welcome.

speeches.speaker: Sanch.
verse: When comes she to it?

speeches.speaker: Alonz.
verse: Within these two days, she is in the Country ye^,
And keeps the noblest House.

speeches.speaker: Sanch.
verse: Then there's some hope of her,
Wilt thou go my way?

speeches.speaker: Alonz.
verse: No, no, I must leave you,
And repair to an old Gentlewoman
That has credit with her, that can speak a good word.

speeches.speaker: Sanch.
verse: Send thee good fortune, but make thy Body sound first.

speeches.speaker: Alonz
verse: I am a Souldier,
And too sound a Body becomes me not;
Farewel, Sanchio.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: 'Tis this or that house, or I have lost my aim,
They are both fair buildings, she walked plaguy fast,
And hereabouts I lost her; stay, that's she,
'Tis very she,— she makes me a low court'sie,
Let me note the place, the street I well remember.
She is in again, certain some noble Lady.
How happy should I be if she love my master:
A wondrous goodly house, here are brave lodgings,
And I shall sleep now like an Emperour,
And eat abundantly: I thank my fortune,
I'll back with speed, and bring him happy tidings.

speeches.speaker: 1 Lady.
verse: What should it mean, that in such haste
We are sent for?

speeches.speaker: 2 Lady.
verse: Belike the Lady Margaret has some business
She would break to us in private.

speeches.speaker: 3 Lady.
verse: It should seem so.
'Tis a good Lady, and a wise young Lady.

speeches.speaker: 2 Lady.
verse: And vertuous enough too I warrant ye
For a young Woman of her years; 'tis pity
To load her tender Age with too much Vertue.

speeches.speaker: 3 Lady.
verse: 'Tis more sometimes than we can well away with.

speeches.speaker: Alt.
verse: Good morrow, Ladies.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: 'Morrow my good Madam.

speeches.speaker: 1 Lad.
verse: How does the sweet young Beauty, Lady Margaret?

speeches.speaker: 2 Lady.
verse: Has she slept well after her walk last night?

speeches.speaker: 1 Lady.
verse: Are her dreams gentle to her mind?

speeches.speaker: Alt.
verse: All's well,
She's very well, she sent for you thus suddenly
To give her counsel in a business
That much concerns her.

speeches.speaker: 2 Lady.
verse: She does well and wisely,
To ask the counsel of the ancientst, Madam,
Our years have run through many things she knows not.

speeches.speaker: Alt.
verse: She would fain marry.

speeches.speaker: 1 Lady.
verse: 'Tis a proper calling.
And well beseems her years, who would she yoke with?

speeches.speaker: A t.
verse: That's left to argue on, I pray come in
And break your fast, drink a good cup or two,
To strengthen your understandings, then she'l tell ye.
And good wine breeds good counsel,
Well yield to ye.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Have you seen any service?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Where?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Every where.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: What office bore ye?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: None, I was not worthy.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: What Captains know you?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: None, they were above me.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Were you never hurt?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Not that I well remember,
But once I stole a Hen, and then they beat me;
Pray ask me no long questions, I have an ill memory.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: This is an Asse, did you never draw your sword yet?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Not to do any harm I thank Heaven for't.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Nor ne'r ta'ne prisoner?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: No, I ran away,
For I had ne'r no mony to redeem me.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Can you endure a Drum?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: It makes my head ake.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Are you not valiant when you are drunk?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I think not, but I am loving Sir.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: What a lump is this man,
Was your Father wise?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Too wise for me I'm sure,
For he gave all he had to my younger Brother.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: That was no foolish part I'le bear you witness.
Canst thou lye with a woman?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I think I could make shift Sir,
But I am bashfull.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: In the night?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I know not,
^ness indeed may do some good upon me.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Why art thou sent to me to be my officer,
^, and commended too, when thou darst not fight?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: There be more officers of my opinion,
O^ I am cozen'd Sir, men that talk more too.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: How wilt thou scape a bullet?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Why by chance,
They aim at honourable men, alas I am none Sir.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: This fellow has some doubts in's talk that strike me,
^e cannot be all fool: welcom Alonzo.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: What have you got there, temperance into your company?
The spirit of peace? we shall have wars
By th'ounce then. O here's another pumpion,
^et him loose for luck sake, the cram'd son
Of a stav'd Usurer, Cacafogo, both their brains butter'd,
Cannot make two spoonfulls.

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: My Father's dead: I am a man of war too,
^ocyes, demesns; I have ships at sea too,
Captains.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Take heed o'th' Hollanders, your ships may leak else.

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: I scorn the Hollanders, they are my drunkards.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: Put up your gold Sir, I'le borrow it else.

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: I am satisfied, you shall not,
Come out, I know thee, meet mine anger instantly.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I never wrong'd ye.

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: Thou hast wrong'd mine honor,
Thou look'dst upon my Mistris thrice lasciviously,
^e make it good.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Do not heat your self, you will surfeit.

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: Thou wan'st my mony too, with a pair of base bones,
^ whom there was no truth, for which I beat thee,
I beat thee much, now I will hurt thee dangerously.
This shall provoke thee.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: You struck too low by a foot Sir.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: You must get a ladder when you would beat This fellow.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I cannot chuse but kick again, pray pardon me.

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: Hadst thou not ask'd my pardon, I had kill'd thee,
I leave thee as a thing despis'd, assoles manus a vostra siniare a Maistre.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: You have scap'd by miracle, there is not in all Spain,
A spirit of more fury than this fire drake.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I see he is hasty, and I would give him leave
To beat me soundly if he would take my bond.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: What shall I do with this fellow?

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: Turn him off,
He will infect the camp with cowardise,
If he goe with thee.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: About some week hence Sir,
If I can hit upon no abler officer,
You shall hear from me.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I desire no better.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: You have made me now too bountifull amends, Lady
For your strict carriage when you saw me first,
These beauties were not meant to be conceal'd,
It was a wrong to hide so sweet an object,
I cou'd now cnide ye, but it shall be thus,
No other anger ever touch your sweetness,

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: You appear to me so honest, and so civil,
Without a blush Sir, I dare bid ye welcom.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Now let me ask your name.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: 'Tis Estifanie, the heir of this poor place.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Poor do you call it?
There's nothing that I cast mine eyes upon,
But shews both rich and admirable, all the rooms
Are hung as if a Princess were to dwell here,
The Gardens, Orchards, every thing so curious:
Is all that plate your own too?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: 'Tis but little,
Only for present use, I have more and richer,
When need shall call, or friends compel me use it,
The sutes you see of all the upper chamber,
Are those that commonly adorn the house,
I think I have besides, as fair, as civil,
As any town in Spain can parallel.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Now if she be not married, I have some hopes.
Are you a maid?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: You make me blush to answer,
I ever was accounted so to this hour,
And that's the reason that I live retir'd Sir.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Then would I counsel you to marry presently,
(If I can get her, I am made for ever)
For every year you lose, you lose a beauty,
A Husband now, an honest careful Husband,
Were such a comfort: will ye walk above stairs?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: This place will fit our talk, 'tis fitter far Sir,
Above there are day-beds, and such temptations
I dare not trust Sir.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: She is excellent wise withal too.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: You nam'd a husband, I am not so strict Sir,
Nor ti'd unto a Virgins solitariness,
But if an honest, and a noble one,
Rich, and a souldier, for so I have vowed he shall be,
Were offer'd me, I think I should accept him,
But above all he must love.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: He were base else,
There's comfort ministred in the word souldier,
How sweetly should I live!

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: I am not so ignorant, but that I know well,
How to be commanded,
And how again to make my self obey'd Sir,
I waste but little, I have gather'd much,
My rial not the less worth, when 'tis spent,
If spent by my direction, to please my Husband,
I hold it as indifferent in my duty,
To be his maid i'th' kitchin, or his Cook,
As in the Hall to know my self the Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Sweet, rich, and provident, now fortune stick
To me; I am a Souldier, and a bachelour, Lady,
And such as wise as you, I cou'd love infinitely,
They that use many words, some are deceitfull,
I long to be a Husband, and a good one,
For 'tis most certain I shall make a president
For all that follow me to love their Ladies,
I am young you see, able I would have you think too,
If 't please you know, try me before you take me.
'T is true I shall not meet in equal wealth
With ye, but Jewels, Chains, such as the war
Has given me, a thousand Duckets I dare
Presume on in ready gold, now as your
Ca^e may handle it, as rich cloths too, as
Any he bears arms Lady.

speeches.speaker: Estif
verse: You are a true gentleman, and fair, I see by ye,
And such a man I had rather take.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: Pray do so, I'le have a Priest o'th' sudden.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: And as suddenly you will repent too.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: I'le be hang'd or drown'd first,
By this and this, and this kiss.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: You are a Flatterer,
But I must say there was something when I saw you
First, in that most noble face, that stirr'd my fancy.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: I'le stir it better e're you sleep sweet Lady,
I'le send for all my trunks and give up all to ye,
Into your own dispose, before I bed ye,
And then sweet wench.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: You have the art to cozen me.

speeches.speaker: Margar
verse: SIT down and give me your opinions seriously.

speeches.speaker: 1 La.
verse: You say you have a mind to marry Lady.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: 'Tis true, I have for to preserve my credit,
Yet not so much for that as for my state Ladies,
Conceive me right, there lies the main o'th' question,
Credit I can redeem, mony will imp it,
But when my monie's gone, when the law shall
Seize that, and for incontinency strip me
Of all.

speeches.speaker: 1 La.
verse: Do you find your body so malitious that way?

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: I find it as all bodies are that are young and lusty,
Lazy, and high sed, I desire my pleasure,
And pleasure I must have.

speeches.speaker: 2 Lady.
verse: 'Tis sit you should have,
Your years require it, and 'tis necessary,
As necessary as meat to a young Lady,
Sleep cannot nourish more.

speeches.speaker: 1 La.
verse: But might not all this be, and keep ye single.
You take away variety in marriage,
The abundance of the pleasure you are bar'd then,
Is't not abundance that you arm at?

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Yes why was I made a woman?

speeches.speaker: 2 Lady.
verse: And every day a new?

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Why fair and young but to use it?

speeches.speaker: 1 Lady.
verse: You are still i'th' right, why would you marry then?

speeches.speaker: Alte.
verse: Because a husband stops all doubts in this point,
And clears all passages.

speeches.speaker: 2 Lady.
verse: What Husband mean ye?

speeches.speaker: Alte.
verse: A Husband of an easy faith, a fool,
Made by her wealth, and moulded to her pleasure,
One though he see himself become a monster,
Shall hold the door, and entertain the maker.

speeches.speaker: 2 Lady.
verse: You grant there may be such a man.

speeches.speaker: 1 Lady.
verse: Yes marry, but how to bring 'em to this ta^e Perfection.

speeches.speaker: 2 Lady.
verse: They must be chosen so, things of no honour,
Nor outward honesty.

speeches.speaker: Marga.
verse: No 'tis no matter,
I care not what they are, so they be lusty.

speeches.speaker: 2 La.
verse: Me thinks now a rich Lawyer, some such fellow,
That carries credit, and a face of awe,
But lies with nothing but his clients business.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: No there's no trusting them, they are too subt^l,
The Law has moulded 'em of natural mischief.

speeches.speaker: 1 Lady.
verse: Then some grave governor,
Some man of honour, yet an easy man.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: If he have honour I am undone, I'le none such,
I'le have a lusty man, honour will cloy me.

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: 'Tis sit ye should Lady;
And to that end, with search and wit and labour,
I have found one out, a right one and a perfect,
He is made as strong as brass, is of brave years too,
And doughty of complexion.

speeches.speaker: Marga.
verse: Is he a Gentleman?

speeches.speaker: Alt.
verse: Yes and a souldier, as gentle as you would wish him,
A good fellow, wears good cloaths.

speeches.speaker: Marga.
verse: Those I'le allow him,
They are for my credit, does he understand
But little?

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: Very little.

speeches.speaker: Marga.
verse: 'Tis the better,
Have not the wars bred him up to anger?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: No, he will not quarrel with a dog that bites hin,
Let him be drunk or sober, is one silence.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: H'as no capacity what honor is?
For that's the Souldiers god.

speeches.speaker: Alt.
verse: Honour's a thing too subtil for his wisdom,
If honour lye in eating, he is right honourable.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Is he so goodly a man do you say?

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: As you shall see Lady,
But to all this is but a trunk.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: I would have him so,
I shall adde branches to him to adorn him,
God, find me out this man, and let me see him,
If he be that motion that you tell me of,
And make no more noise, I shall entertain him,
Let him be here.

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: He shall attend your Ladiship.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Why thou art not married indeed?

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: No, no, pray think so,
Alas I am a fellow of no reckoning,
Not worth a Ladies eye.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: Wou'dst thou steal a fortune,
And make none of all thy friends acquainted with it,
Nor bid us to thy wedding?

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: No indeed,
There was no wisdom in't, to bid an Artist,
An old seducer to a femal banquet,
I can cut up my pye without your instructions.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Was it the wench i'th' veil?

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: Basto 'twas she,
The prettiest Rogue that e're you look'd upon,
The lovingst thief.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: And is she rich withal too?

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: A mine, a mine, there is no end of wealth Coronel,
I am an asse, a bashfull fool, prethee Coronel,
How do thy companies fill now?

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: You are merry Sir,
You intend a safer war at home belike now.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: I do not think I shall fight much this year Coronel,
I find my self given to my ease a little,
I care not if I sell my foolish company,
They are things of hazard.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: How it angers me,
This fellow at first sight should win a Lady,
A rich young wench, and I that have consum'd
My time and art in searching out their subtleties,
Like a fool'd Alchymist blow up my hopes still?
When shall we come to thy house and be freely merry?

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: When I have manag'd her a little more,
I have an house to entertain an army.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: If thy wife be fair, thou wilt have few less Come to thee.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: But where they'l get entertainment is the point Sign o^
I beat no Drum.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: You need none but her taber,
May be I'le march after a month or two,
To get me a fresh stomach. I find Coronel.
A wantonness in wealth, methinks I agree not with,
'Tis such a trouble to be married too,
And have a thousand things of great importance,
Jewels and plates, and fooleries molest me,
To have a mans brains whimsied with his wealth:
Before I walk'd contentedly.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: My Mistris Sir is sick, because you are absent,
She mourns and will not eat.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: Alas my Jewel,
Come I'le goe with thee, Gentlemen your fair leaves,
You see I am ti'd a little to my yoke,
Pray pardon me, would ye had both such loving wives.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: I thank ye
For your old boots, never be blank Alonzo,
Because this fellow has outstript thy fortune,
Tell me ten daies hence what he is, and how
The gracious state of matrimony stands with him,
Come, let's to dinner, when Margarita comes
We'l visit both, it may be then your fortune.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Is he come?

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: Yes Madam, h'as been here this half hour,
I have question'd him of all that you can ask him,
And find him as fit as you had made the man,
He will make the goodliest shadow for iniquity.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Have ye searcht him Ladies?

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
verse: Is a man at all points, a likely man.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Call him in Altea.
A man of a good presence, pray ye come this way,
Of a lust body, is his mind so tame?

speeches.speaker: Alt.
verse: Pray ye question him, and if you find him not
Fit for your purpose, shake him off, there's no harm
Done

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Can you love a young Lady? How he blushes!

speeches.speaker: Alt.
verse: Leave twirling of your hat, and hold your head up,
And speak to'th' Lady.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Yes, I think I can,
I must be taught, I know not what it means Madam.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: You shall be taught, and can you when she pleases
Go ride abroad, and stay a week or two?
You shall have men and horses to attend ye,
And mony in your purse.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Yes I love riding,
And when I am from home I am so merry.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Be as merry as you will: can you as handsomely
When you are sent for back, come with obedience,
And doe your dutie to the Lady loves you?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Yes sure, I shall.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: And when you see her friends here,
Or noble kinsmen, can you entertain
Their servants in the Celler, and be busied,
^nd hold your peace, what e're you see or hear of?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: 'Twere fit I were hang'd else.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Let me try your kisses,
How the fool shakes, I will not eat ye Sir,
Beshrew my heart he kisses wondrous manly,
Can ye doe any thing else?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Indeed I know not;
But if your Ladiship will please to instruct me,
Sure I shall learn.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: You shall then be instructed:
If I should be this Lady that affects ye,
Nay say I marry ye?

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: Hark to the Lady.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: What mony have ye?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: None Madam, nor friends,
I wou'd doe any thing to serve your Ladiship

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: You must not look to be my Mr Sir,
Nor talk i'th' house as though you wore the breeches,
No, not command in any thing.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I will not,
Alas I am notable, I have no wit Madam.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Nor do not labour to arrive at any,
'Twill spoil your head, I take ye upon charity,
And like a Servant ye must be unto me,
As I behold your duty I shall love ye,
And as you observe me, I may chance lye with ye,
Can you mark these?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Yes indeed forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: There is one thing,
That if I take ye in I put ye from me,
Utterly from me, you must not be sawcy,
No, nor at any time familiar with me,
Scarce know me, when I call ye not.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I will not, alas I never knew my self sufficiently.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Nor must not now.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I'le be a Dog to please ye.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Indeed you must fetch and carry as I appoint ye.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I were to blame else.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Kiss me again; a strong fellow,
There is a vigor in his lips: if you see me
Kiss any other, twenty in an hour Sir,
You must not start, nor be offended.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: No, if you kiss a thousand I shall be contented,
It will the better teach me how to please ye

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: I told ye Madam,

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: 'Tis the man I wisht for; the less you speak,

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I'le never speak again Madam,
But when you charge me, then I'le speak softly too.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Get me a Priest, I'le wed him instantly,
But when you are married Sir, you must wait
Upon me, and see you observe my ^ws.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Else you shall hang me.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: I'le give ye better clothes when you deserve 'em,
Come in, and serve for witness

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
verse: We shall Madam.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: And then away toth' city presently,
I'le to my new house and new company.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: A thousand crowns are thine, and I am a made man.

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: Do not break out too soon.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I know my time wench.

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: What, have you caught him?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: And do you find him
A man of those hopes that you aim'd at?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Yes too,
And the most kind man, and the ablest also
To give a wife content, he is sound as old wine,
And to his soundness rises on the pallat,
And there's the man; find him rich too Clara.

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: Hast thou married him?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: What dost thou think I fish without a bait wench?
I bob for fools? he is mine own, I have him,
I told thee what would tickle him like a trout,
And as I cast it so I caught him daintily,
And all he has I have 'stow'd at my devotion.

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: Does thy Lady know this? she is coming now to town,
Now to live here in this house.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Let her come,
She shall be welcom, I am prepar'd for her,
She is mad sure if she be angry at my fortune,
For what I have made bold.

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: Dost thou not love him?

speeches.speaker: Estif
verse: Yes, intirely well,
As long as there he flaies and looks no farther
Into my ends, but when he doubts, I hate him,
And that wise hate will teach me how to cozen him:
How to doctrine their wives, and curb their manners,
To put a stern and strong ioyn to their natures,
And holds he is an All not worth acquaintance,
That cannot mould a D vil to obedience,
I owe him a good turn for these opinions,
And as I find his temper I may pay him,
O here he is, now you shall see a kind man.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: My Estisama, shall we to dinner lamb?
I know thou stay'st for me.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: I cannot eat else.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: I never enter but me thinks a Paradise
Appears about me.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: You are welcom to it Sir.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: I think I have the sweetest seat in Spain wench,
Me thinks the richest too, we'l eat i'th' garden
In one o'th' a^bours, there 'tis cool and pleasant,
And have our wine cold in the running fountain.
Who's that?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: A friend of mine Sir.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: Of what breeding?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: A Gentlewoman Sir.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: What business has she?
Is she a learned woman i'th' Mathematicks,
^an the tell fortunes?

speeches.speaker: Estif
verse: More than I know Sir.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: Of has she e're a letter from a kinswoman,
That must be delivered in my absence wise,
Or comes she from the Doctor to salute ye,
And learn your health? she looks not like a confessor.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: What need all this, why are you troubled Sir?
What do you suspect, she cannot cuckold ye,
She is a woman Sir, a very woman.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: Your very woman may do very well Sir
Toward the matter, for though she cannot perform it
In her own person, she may do it by Proxie,
Your rarest jugglers work still by conspiracy.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Cry ye mercy husband, you are jealous then,
And happily suspect me.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: No indeed wise.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Me thinks you should not till you have more cause
And clearer too: I am sure you have heard say husband,
A woman forced will free her self through Iron,
A happy, calm, and good wife discontented
May be taught tricks.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: No, no, I do but jest with ye.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: To morrow friend I'le see you.

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: I shall leave ye
Till then, and pray all may goe sweetly with ye.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Why where's this girle, whose at the door?

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: Who knocks there?
Is't for the King ye come, you knock so boisterously?
Look to the door.

speeches.speaker: Maid.
verse: My Lady, as I live Mistris, my Ladie's come,
She's at the door, I peept through, and I saw her,
And a stately company of Ladies with her.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: This was a week too soon, but I must meet with her,
And set a new wheel going, and a subtile one,
Must blind this mighty Mars, or I am ruin'd.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: What are they at door?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Such my Michael
As you may bless the day they enter'd there,
Such for our good.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: 'Tis well.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Nay, 'twill be better
If you will let me but dispose the business,
And be a stranger to it, and not disturb me,
What have I now to do but to advance your fortune?

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: Doe, I dare trust thee, I am asham'd I am angry,
I find thee a wise young wife.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: I'le wise your worship
Before I leave ye, pray ye walk by and say nothing,
Only salute them, and leave the rest to me Sir,
I was born to make ye a man.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: The Rogue speaks heartily,
Her good will colours in her cheeks, I am born to love her,
I must be gentler to these tender natures,
A Souldiers rude harsh words be fit not Ladies,
Nor must we talk to them as we talk to
Our Officers, I'le give her way, for 'tis for me she
Works now, I am husband, heir, and all she has.
Who are these, what flanting things, a woman
Of rare presence! excellent fair, this is too big
For a bawdy house, too open seated too.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: My Husband, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: You have gain'd a proper man.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: What e're I am, I am your servant Lady.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Sir, be rul'd now,
And I shall make ye rich, this is my cousin,
That Gentleman dotes on her, even to death, see how he observes her.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: She is a goodly woman.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: She is a mirrour,
But she is poor, she were for a Princes side else,
This house she has brought him too as to her own,
And presuming upon me, and upon my courtesie.
Conceive me short, he knows not but she is wealthy,
Or if he did know otherwise, 'twere all one,
He is so far gone.

speeches.speaker: Perez
verse: Forward, she has a rare face.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: This we must carry with discretion Husband,
And yield unto her for four daies.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: Yield our house up, our goods and wealth?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: All this is but in seeming,
To milk the lover on, do you see this writing,
2001 a year when they are married
Has she sealed to for our good; the time's unsit now,
I'le shew it you to morrow.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: All the house?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: All, all, and we'l remove too, to confirm him,
They'l into th' country suddenly again
After they are matcht, and then she'l open to him.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: The whole possession wife? look what you doe,
A part o'th' house.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: No, no, they shall have all,
And take their pleasure too, 'tis for our 'vantage.
Why, what's four daies? had you a Sister Sir,
A Niece or Mistris that required this courtesie,
And should I make a scruple to do you good?

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: If easily it would come back.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: I swear Sir,
As easily as it came on, is't not pity
To let such a Gentlewoman for a little help—
You give away no house.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: Clear but that question.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: I'le put the writings into your hand.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: Well then.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: And you shall keep them safe.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: I am satisfied; wou'd I had the wench so too.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: When she has married him,
So infinite his love is linkt unto her,
You, I, or any one that helps at this pinch
May have Heaven knows what.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: I'le remove the goods straight,
And take some poor house by, 'tis but for four days.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: I have a poor old friend; there we'l be.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: 'Tis well then.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Goe handsom off, and leave the house clear.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: Well.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: That little stuff we'l use shall follow after;
And a boy to guide ye, peace and we are made both.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Come, let's goe in, are all the rooms kept sweet wench?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: They are sweet and neat.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Why where's your Husband?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Gone Madam.
When you come to your own he must give place Lady.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Well, send you joy, you would not let me know't,
Yet I shall not forget ye.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Thank your Ladyship.

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: ARE you at ease now, is your heart at rest,
Now you have got a shadow, an umbrella
To keep the scorching worlds opinion
From your fair credit.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: I am at peace Altea,
If he continue but the same he shews,
And be a master of that ignorance
He outwardly professes, I am happy,
The pleasure I shall live in and the freedom
Without the squint eye of the law upon me,
Or prating liberty of tongues, that envy.

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: You are a made woman.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: But if he should prove now
A crafty and dissembling kind of Husband,
One read in knavery, and brought up in the art
Of villany conceal'd.

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: My life, an innocent.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: That's it I aim at,
That's it I hope too, then I am sure I rule him,
For innocents are like obedient Children
Brought up under a hard Mother-in-law, a cruel,
Who being not us'd to break-fasts and collations,
When they have course bread offer'd 'em, are thankfull,
And take it for a favour too. Are the rooms
Made ready to entertain my friends? I long to dance now
And to be wanton let me have a song, is the great couch up
The Duke of Medina sent?

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: 'Tis up and ready.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: And day-beds in all chambers?

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: In all Lady,
Your house is nothing now but various pleasures,
The Gallants begin to gaze too.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Let 'em gaze on,
I was brought up a Courtier, high and happy,
And company is my delight, and courtship,
And handsom servants at my will: where's my good husband,
Where does he wait?

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: He knows his distance Madam,
I warrant ye he is busie in the celler
Amongst his fellow servants, or asleep,
Till your command awake him.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: 'Tis well Altea.
It should be so, my ward I must preserve him.
Who sent for him, how dare he come uncall'd for,
His bonnet on too?

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: Sure he sees you not.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: How scornfully he looks!

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Are all the chambers
Dockt and adorn'd thus for my Ladies pleasure?
New hangings every hour for entertainment,
And new plate bought, new Jewels to give lustre?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: They are, and yet there must be more and richer,
It is her will.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Hum, is it so? 'tis excellent,
It is her will too, to have feasts and banquets,
Revells and masques.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: She ever lov'd 'em dearly,
And we shall have the bravest house kept now Sir,
I must not call ye master she has warn'd me,
Nor must not put my hat off to ye.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: 'Tis no fashion,
What though I be her husband, I am your fellow,
I may cut first.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: That's as you shall deserve Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: And when I lye with her.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: May be I'le light ye,
On the same point you may doe me that service.

speeches.speaker: 1 Lady.
verse: Madam, the Duke Medina with some Captains
Will come to dinner, and have sent rare wine,
And their best services.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: They shall be welcom,
See all be ready in the noblest fashion,
The house persum'd, now I shall take my pleasure,
And not my neighbour Justice maunder at me.
Go, get your best cloths on, but till I call ye,
Be sure you be not seen, dine with the Gentlewomen,
^ be have your self cleanly Sir, 'tis for my credit.

speeches.speaker: 2 Lady.
verse: Madam, the Lady Julia.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: That's a bawd,
A three pil'd bawd, bawd major to the army.

speeches.speaker: 2 Lady.
verse: Has brought her coach to wait upon your Ladiship,
And to be inform'd if you will take the air this morning.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: The neat air of her nunnery.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Tell her no, i'th' afternoon I'le call on her.

speeches.speaker: 2 Lady.
verse: I will Madam.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Why are not you gone to prepare your self,
May be you shall be sewer to the first course,
A portly presence, Altea he looks lean,
'Tis a wash knave, he will not keep his flesh well.

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: A willing, Madam, one that needs no spurring.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Faith madam, in my little understanding,
You had better entertain your honest neighbours,
Your friends about ye, that may speak well of ye,
And give a worthy mention of your bounty.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: How now, what's this?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: 'Tis only to perswade ye,
Courtiers are but tickle things to deal withal,
A kind of march pane men that will not last Madam,
An egge and pepper goes farther than their potions,
And in a well built body, a poor parship
Will play his prize above their strong potabiles.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: The fellow's mad.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: He that shall counsel Ladies,
That have both liquorish and ambitious eyes,
Is either mad, or drunk, let him speak Gospel,

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: He breaks out modestly.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Pray ye be not angry,
My indiscretion has made bold to tell ye,
What you'l find true.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Thou darest not talk.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Not much Madam,
You have a tye upon your servants tongue,
He dares not be so bold as reason bids him,
'Twere fit there were a stronger on your temper.
Ne're look so stern upon me, I am your Husband,
But what are Husbands? read the new worlds wonders,
Such Husbands as this monstrous world produces,
And you will scarce find such deformities,
They are shadows to conceal your venial vertues,
Sails to your mills, that grind with all occasions,
Balls that lye by you, to wash out your stains,
And ^lls nail'd up with horn before your stories,
To rent out last.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Do you hear him talk?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I have done Madam,
An oxe once spoke, as learned men deliver,
Shortly I shall be such, then I'le speak wonders,
Till when I tye my self to my obedience.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: First I'le unty my self, did you mark the Gentleman,
How boldly and how sawcily he talk'd,
And how unlike the lump I took him for,
The piece of ignorant dow, he stood up to me
And mated my commands, this was your providence,
Your wisdom, to elect this Gentleman,
Your excellent forecast in the man, your knowledge,
What think ye now?

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: I think him an Asse still,
This boldness some of your people have blown
Into him, this wisdom too with strong wine,
'Tis a Tyrant, and a Philosopher also, and finds
Out reasons.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I'le have my celler lookt, no school kept there,
Not no discovery. I'le turn my drunkards,
Such as are understanding in their draughts,
And dispute learnedly the whyes and wherefores,
To grass immediatly, I'le keep all fools,
Sober or drunk, still fools, that shall know nothing,
Nothing belongs to mankind, but obedience,
And such a hand I'le keep over this Husband,

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: He will fall again, my life he cryes by this time,
Keep him from drink, he has a high constitution.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Shall I wear my new sute Madam?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: No your old clothes,
And get you into the country presently,
And see my hawks well train'd, you shall have victuals,
Such as are sit for sawcy palats Sir,
And Hodgings with the hindes, it is too good too.

speeches.speaker: Alt.
verse: Good Madam be not so rough, with repentance,
You see now he's come round again.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I see not what I expect to see.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: You shall see Madam, if it shall please your Ladyship.

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: He's humbled,
Forgive good Lady,

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Well go get you handsom,
And let me hear no more.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Have ye yet no feeling?
I'le pinch ye to the bones then my proud Lady.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: See you preserve him thus upon my favour,
You know his temper, tye him to the grindstone,
The next rebellion I'le be rid of him,
I'le have no needy Rascals I tye to me,
Dispute my life: come in and see all handsom.

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: I hope to see you so too, I have wrought ill else.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Shall I never return to mine own house again?
We are lodg'd here in the miserablest dog-hole,
A Conjurers circle gives content above it,
A hawks mew is a princely palace to it,
We have a bed no bigget than a basket,
And there we lie like butter clapt together,
And sweat our selves to sawce immediately,
The sumes are infinite inhabite here too;
And to that so thick, they cut like marmalet,
So various too, they'l pose a gold sinder,
Never return to mine own paradise?
Why wise I say, why Estifania.

speeches.speaker: Estifania
verse: I am going presently.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: Make haste good Jewel,
I am like the people that live in the sweet Islands:
I dye, I dye, if I stay but one day more here,
My lungs are rotten with the damps that rise,
And I cough nothing now but stinks of all sorts,
The inhabitants we have are two starv'd rats,
For they are not able to maintain a cat here,
And those appear as fearfull as two Devils,
They have eat a map of the whole world up already,
And if we stay a night we are gone for company.
There's an old woman that's now grown to marble,
Dri'd in this brick hill, and she sits i'th' chimnie,
Which is but three tiles rais'd like a house of cards,
The true proportion of an old smok'd Sibyl,
There is a young thing too that nature meant
For a maid-servant, but 'tis now a monster,
She has a husk about her like a chesnut
With basiness, and living under the line here,
And these two make a hollow sound together,
Like frogs or winds between two doors that murmur:
Mercy deliver me. O are you come wife,
Shall we be free again?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: I am now going,
And you shall presently to your own house Sir,
The remembrance of this small vexation
Will be argument of mirth for ever:
By that time you have said your orisons,
And broke your fast, I shall be back and ready,
To usher you to your old content, your freedom.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Break my neck rather, is there any thing here to c^t
But one another, like a race of Cannibals?
A piece of butter'd wall you think is excellent,
Let's have our house again immediatly,
And pray ye take heed unto the furniture,
None be imbezil'd.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Not a pin I warrant ye.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: And let 'em instantly depart.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: They shall both,
There's reason in all courtesies, they must both,
For by this time I know she has acquainted him,
And has provided too, she sent me word Sir,
And will give over gratefully unto you.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: I'le walk i'th' Church-yard,
The dead cannot offend more than these living,
An hour hence I'le expect ye.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: I'le not fail Sir.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: And do you hear, let's have a handsom dinner,
And see all things be decent as they have been,
And let me have a strong bath to restore me,
I stink like a stal-fish shambles, or an oyl-shop.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: You shall have all, which some interpret nothing,
I'le send ye people for the trunks afore-hand,
And for the stuff.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: Let 'em be known and honest,
And do my service to your niece.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: I shall Sir,
But if I come not at my hour, come thither,
That they may give you thanks for your fair courtesy,
And pray ye be brave for my sake.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: I observe ye.

speeches.speaker: Sanc.
verse: Thou art very brave.

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: I have reason, I have mony.

speeches.speaker: Sanc.
verse: Is mony reason?

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: Yes and rime too Captain,
If ye have no mony y'are an Asse.

speeches.speaker: Sanc.
verse: I thank ye.

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: Ye have manners, ever thank him that has mony.

speeches.speaker: Sanc.
verse: Wilt thou lend me any?

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: Not a farthing Captain,
Captains are casual things.

speeches.speaker: Sanc.
verse: Why so are all men, thou shalt have my bond.

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: Nor bonds nor setters Captain,
My mony is mine, I make no doubt on't.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: What dost thou do with it?

speeches.speaker: Cac.
verse: Put it to pious uses,
^ Wine and Wenches, and undo young Coxcombs
That would undo me.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Are those Hospitals?

speeches.speaker: Cac.
verse: I first provide to fill my Hospitals
With Creatures of mine own, that I know wretched,
And then I build: those are more bound to pray for me:
Besides, I keep th'inheritance in my Name still.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: A provident Charity; are you for the Wars, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cac.
verse: I am not poor enough to be a Souldier,
Not have I faith enough to ward a Bullet;
This is no liuing for a trench, I take it.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Ye have said wisely.

speeches.speaker: Cac.
verse: Had you but my money,
You would swear it Colonel, I had rather drill at home
A hundred thousand Crowns, and with more honour,
Than exercise ten thousand Fools with nothing,
A wise Man safely feeds, Fools cut their fingers.

speeches.speaker: Mich.
verse: A right State Usurer; why dost thou not marry,
And live a reverend Justice?

speeches.speaker: Cac.
verse: Is't not nobler to command a reverend Justice, than to be one?
And for a Wife, what need I marry, Captain,
When every courteous Fool that owes me money,
Owes me his Wife too, to appease my fury?

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Wilt thou go to dinner with us?

speeches.speaker: Cac.
verse: I will go, and view the Pearl of Spain, the Orient
Fair One, the rich One too, and I will be respected,
I bear my Patent here, I will talk to her,
And when your Captain's Ships shall stand a loof,
And pick your Noses, I will pick the purse
Of her affection.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: The Duke dines there to day too, the Duke of Medina.

speeches.speaker: Cac.
verse: Let the King dine there,
He owes me money, and so far's my Creature,
And certainly I may make bold with mine own, Captain?

speeches.speaker: Sanch.
verse: Thou wilt eat monstrously.

speeches.speaker: Cac.
verse: Like a true born Spaniard,
^r as I were in England where the Beef grows,
And I will drink abundantly, and then
^al^ ye as wantonly as Ovid did,
To stir the Intellectuals of the Ladies;
^a^nt it of my Father's amorous Scrivener.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: If we should play now, you must supply me.

speeches.speaker: Cac.
verse: You must pawn a Horse troop,
And then have at ye Colonel.

speeches.speaker: Sanch.
verse: Come, let's go:
This Rascal will make rare sport; how the Ladies
^ill laugh at him?

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: If I light on him I'll make his Purse sweat too.

speeches.speaker: Cac.
verse: Will ye lead, Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Nay, pray ye come out, and let me understand ye,
And tune your pipe a little higher, Lady;
^ hold ye fast: rub, how came my Trunks open?
^nd my Goods gone, what Pick-lock Spirit?

speeches.speaker: Old Wom.
verse: Ha, what would ye have?

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: My Goods again, how came my Trunks all open?

speeches.speaker: Old Wom.
verse: Are your Trunks open?

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Yes, and Cloaths gone,
^nd Chains, and Jewels: how she smells like hung Beef,
^e Palsey, and Picklocks, fye, how she belches,
^he Spirit of Garlick.

speeches.speaker: Old Wom.
verse: Where's your Gentlewoman?
^he young fair Woman?

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: What's that to my question?
^e is my wife, and gone about my business.

speeches.speaker: Maid.
verse: Is she your Wife, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Yes Sir, is that wonder?
^ the name of Wife unknown here?

speeches.speaker: Old Wom.
verse: Is she truly, truly your Wife?

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: I think so, for I married her;
^ was no Vision sure!

speeches.speaker: Maid.
verse: She has the Keys, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: I know she has, but who has all my goods, Spirit?

speeches.speaker: Old Wom.
verse: If you be married to that Gentlewoman,
You are a wretched man, she has twenty Husbands.

speeches.speaker: Maid.
verse: She tells you true.

speeches.speaker: Old Wom.
verse: And she has cozen'd all, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: The Devil she has! I had a fair house with her,
That stands hard by, and furnisht royally.

speeches.speaker: Old Wom.
verse: You are cozen'd too, 'tis none of hers, good Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Maid.
verse: The Lady Margarita, she was her Servant,
And kept the house, but going from her, Sir,
For some lowd tricks she plaid.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Plague o' the Devil,
Am I i'th' full Meridian of my Wisedom
Cheated by a stale Quean! what kind of Lady
Is that that owes the House?

speeches.speaker: Old Wom.
verse: A young sweet Lady.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Of a how stature?

speeches.speaker: Old Wom.
verse: She is indeed but little, but she is wondrous fair.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: I f el I am coz n'd;
Now I am sensible I am undone,
This is the very Woman sure, that Cousin
She told me would entreat but for four days,
To make the house hers; I am entreated sweetly.

speeches.speaker: Maid.
verse: When she went out this morning, that I saw, Sir,
She had two Women at the door attending,
And there sh gave 'em things, and loaded 'em,
But what they were— I heard your Trunks to open,
If they be yours?

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: They were mine while they were laden,
But now they have cast their Calves, they are not worth
Owning: was she her Mistress say you?

speeches.speaker: Old Wom.
verse: Her own Mistress, her very Mistress, Sir, and all you saw
About and in that house was hers.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: No Plate, no Jewels, nor no Hangings?

speeches.speaker: Maid.
verse: Not a farthing, she is poor, Sir, a poor shifting thing.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: No money?

speeches.speaker: Old Wom.
verse: Abominable poor, as poor as we are,
Money as rare to her unless she steal it,
But for one civil Gown her Lady gave her,
She may go bare, good Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: I am mad now,
I think I am as poor as she, I am wide else,
One civil Sute I have left too, and that's all,
And if she steal that she must fley me for it;
Where does she use?

speeches.speaker: Old Wom.
verse: You may find truth as soon,
Alas, a thousand conceal'd corners, Sir, she lurks in.
And here she gets a fleece, and there another,
And lives in mists and smoaks where none can find her.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Is she a Whore too?

speeches.speaker: Old Wom.
verse: Little better, Gentleman, I dare not say she is so Sir, because
She is yours, Sir, these five years she has firkt
A pretty Living,
Until she came to serve; I fear he will knock my
Brains out for lying.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: She has serv'd me faithfully,
A Whore and Thief? two excellent moral learnings
In one she Saint, I hope to see her legend.
Have I been fear'd for my discoveries,
And courted by all Women to conceal 'em?
Have I so long studied the art of this Sex,
And read the warnings to young Gentlemen?
Have I profest to tame the Pride of Ladies,
And make 'em bear all tests, and am I trickt now?
Caught in mine own nooze? here's a royal left yet,
There's for your lodging and your meat for this Week.
A silk Worm lives at a more plentiful ordinary,
And sleeps in a sweeter Box: farewel great Grandmother,
If I do find you were an accessary,
'Tis but the cutting off too smoaky minutes,
I'll hang ye presently.

speeches.speaker: Old Wom.
verse: And I deserve it, I tell but truth.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Not I, I am an Ass, Mother.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: A goodly house.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: And richly furnisht too, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Alonz.
verse: Hung wantonly, I like that preparation,
It stirs the blood unto a hopeful Banquet,
And intimates the Mistress free and jovial,
I love a house where pleasure prepares welcome.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Now Cacasogo, how like you this mansion?
'Twere a brave Pawn.

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: I shall be master of it,
'Twas built for my bulk, the rooms are wide and spacious,
Airy and full of ease, and that I love well,
I'll tell you when I taste the Wine, my Lord,
And take the height of her Table with my Stomach,
How my affections stand to the young Lady.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: All welcome to your Grace, and to these Souldiers,
You honour my poor house with your fair presence,
Those few slight pleasures that inhabit here, Sir,
I do beseech your Grace command, they are yours,
Your servant but preserves 'em to delight ye.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I thank ye Lady, I am bold to visit ye,
Once more to bless mine eyes with your sweet Beauty,
'T has been a long night since you left the Court,
For till I saw you now, no day broke to me.

speeches.speaker: Mar
verse: Bring in the Dukes meat.

speeches.speaker: Sanch.
verse: She is most excellent.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Most admirable fair as e'r I look'd upon,
I had rather command her than my Regiment,

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: I'll have a sling, 'tis but a thousand Duckets,
Which I can cozen up again in ten days,
And some few Jewels to justifie my Knavery,
Say, I should marry her, she'll get more money
Than all my Usury, put my Knavery to it,
She appears the most infallible way of Purchase,
I cou'd wish her a size or two stronger for the encounter,
For I am like a Lion where I lay hold,
But these Lambs will endure a plaguy load,
And never bleat neither, that Sir, time has taught us,
I am so vertuous now, I cannot speak to her,
The atrant'st shamesac'd Ass, I broil away too.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Why, where's this dinner?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: 'Tis not ready, Madam,
Nor shall not be until I know the Guests too,
Nor are they fairly welcome till I bid 'em.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Is not this my Alferes? he looks another thing;
Are miracles a foot again?

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Why, Sirrah, why Sirrah, you?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I hear you, saucy Woman,
And as you are my Wife, command your absence,
And know your duty, 'tis the Crown of modesty.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Your Wife?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Yes good my Lord, I am her Husband,
And pray take notice that I claim that honour,
And will maintain it.

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: If thou beest her Husband,
I am determin'd thou shalt be my Cuckold,
I'll be thy faithful friend.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Peace, dirt and dunghil,
I will not lose my anger on a Rascal,
Provoke me more, I'll beat thy blown body
Till thou rebound'st again like a Tennis Ball.

speeches.speaker: Alonz.
verse: This is miraculous.

speeches.speaker: Sanch.
verse: Is this the Fellow
That had the patience to become a Fool,
A sturted Fool, and on a sudden break,
As if he would shew a wonder to the World,
Both in Bravery, and Fortune too?
I much admire the man, I am astonisht.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I'll be divorced immediately.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: You shall not,
You shall not have so much will to be wicked.
I am more tender of your honour, Lady,
And of your Age, you took me for a shadow;
You took me to gloss over your discredit,
To be your Fool, you had thought you had found a Coxcon^
I am innocent of any foul dishonour I mean to ye.
Only I will be known to be your Lord now,
And be a fair one too, or I will fail for't.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I do command ye from me, thou poor fellow,
Thou cozen'd Fool.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Thou conzen'd Fool? 'tis not so,
I will not be commanded: I am above ye:
You may divorce me from your favour, Lady,
But from your state you never shall, I'll hold that,
And then maintain your wantonness, I'll wink at it.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Am I braved thus in mine own house?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: 'Tis mine, Madam,
You are deceiv'd, I am Lord of it, I rule it and all that's in't.
You have nothing to do here, Madam;
But as a Servant to sweep clean the Lodgings,
And at my farther will to do me service,
And so I'll keep it.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: As you love me, give way.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: It shall be better,
I will give none, Madam,
I stand upon the ground of mine own Honour,
And will maintain it, you shall know me now
To be an understanding feeling man,
And sensible of what a Woman aims at,
A young proud Woman that has Will to sail with,
An itching Woman, that her blood provokes too,
I cast my Cloud off, and appear my self,
The master of this little piece of mischief,
And I will put a Spell about your feet, Lady,
They shall not wander but where I give way now.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Is this the Fellow that the People pointed at,
For the meer sign of man, the walking Image?
He speaks wondrous highly.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: As a Husband ought, Sir,
In his own house, and it becomes me well too,
I think your Grace would grieve if you were put to it
To have a Wise or Servant of your own,
(For Wives are reckon'd in the rank of Servants,)
Under your own roof to command ye.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Brave, a strange Conversion, thou shalt lead
In chief now.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Is there no difference betwixt her and you, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Not now, Lord, my Fortune makes me even,
And as I am an honest man, I am nobler.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Get me my Coach.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Let me see who dares get it
Till I command, I'll make him draw your Coach too,
And eat your Coach, (which will be hard diet)
That executes your Will; or take your Coach, Lady,
I give you liberty, and take your People
Which I turn off, and take your Will abroad with ye,
Take all these freely, but take me no more,
And so farewel.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Nay, Sir, you shall not carry it
So bravely off, you shall not wrong a Lady
In a high huffing strain, and think to bear it,
VVe stand not by as Bawds to your brave fury,
To see a Lady weep.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: They are tears of anger, I beseech ye note 'em, a^ worth p^,
Wrung from her rage, because her Will prevails not,
She would swound now if she could not cry,
Else they were excellent, and I should grieve too,
But falling thus, they show nor sweet nor orient.
Put up my Lord, this is oppression,
And calls the Sword of Justice to relieve me,
The law to lend her hand, the King to right me,
All which shall understand how you provoke me,
In mine own house to brave me, is this princely?
Then to my Guard, and if I spare your Grace,
And do not make this place your Monument,
Too rich a Tomb for such a rude behaviour,
I have a Cause will kill a thousand of ye, mercy forsake me.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Hold, fair Sir, I beseech ye,
The Gentleman but pleads his own right nobly.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: He that dares strike against the husbands freedom,
The Husbands Curse stick to him, a tam'd Cuckold,
His Wife be fair and young, but most dishonest,
Most impudent, and have no feeling of it,
No conscience to reclaim her from a Monster,
Let her lye by him like a flattering ruine,
And at one instant kill both Name and Honour,
Let him be lost, no eye to weep his end,
Nor find no earth that's base enough to bury him.
Now Sir, fall on, I am ready to oppose ye.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I have better thought, I pray Sir use your Wife well.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Mine own humanity will teach me that, Sir,
And now you are all welcome, all, and we'll to dinner,
This is my Wedding day.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I'll cross your joy yet.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: I have seen a miracle, hold thine own, Souldier,
Sure they dare fight in fire that conquer Women.

speeches.speaker: Sanch.
verse: H'as beaten all my loose thoughts out of me,
As if he had thresht 'em out o'th' husk.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: 'Save ye, which is the Lady of the house?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: That's she, Sir, that pretty Lady,
If you would speak with her.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Don Michael, Leon, another darer come.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Pray do not know me, I am full of business,
When I have more time I'll be merry with ye.
It is the Woman: good Madam, tell me truly,
Had you a Maid call'd Estifania?

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Yes truly, had I.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Was she a Maid do you think?

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: I dare not swear for her,
For she had but a scant Fame.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Was she your Kinswoman?

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Not that I ever knew, now I look better
I think you married her, 'give you joy, Sir,
You may reclaim her, 'twas a wild young Girl.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Give me a halter: is not this house mine, Madam?
Was not she owner of it, pray speak truly?

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: No, certainly, I am sure my money paid for it,
And I ne'r remember yet I gave it you, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: The Hangings and the Plate too?

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: All are mine, Sir,
And every thing you see about the building,
She only kept my house when I was absent,
And so ill kept it, I was weary of her.

speeches.speaker: Sanch.
verse: What a Devil ails he?

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: He's possest I'll assure you.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Where is your Maid?

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Do not you know that have her?
She is yours now, why should I look after her?
Since that first hour I came I never saw her.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: I saw her later, would the Devil had had her,
It is all true I find, a wild-fire take her.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Is thy Wife with Child, Don Michael? thy excellent wife.
Art thou a Man yet?

speeches.speaker: Alonz.
verse: When shall we come and visit thee?

speeches.speaker: Sanch.
verse: And eat some rare fruit? thou hast admirable Orchards,
