You are so jealous now, pox o' your jealousie,
How scurvily you look!

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Prithee leave fooling,
I am in no humour now to fool and prattle,
Did she ne'r play the wag with you?

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Yes many times, so often that I was asham'd to keep her,
But I forgave her, Sir, in hope she would mend still,
And had not you o'th'instant married her,
I had put her off.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: I thank ye, I am blest still,
Which way so e'r I turn I am a made man,
Miserably gull'd beyond recovery.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: You'll stay and dine?

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Certain I cannot, Captain,
Hark in thine ear, I am the arrantst Puppy,
The miserablest Ass, but I must leave ye,
I am in haste, in haste, bless you, good Madam,
And you prove as good as my Wife.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Will you come near, Sir, will your Grace but honour me,
And taste our dinner? you are nobly welcome,
All anger's past I hope, and I shall serve ye.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Thou art the stock of men, and I admire thee.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: I'll go to a Conjurer but I'll find this Pol-cat,
This pilfering Whore: a plague of Vails, I cry,
And covers for the impudence of Women,
Their sanctity in show will deceive Devils,
It is my evil Angel, let me bless me.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: 'Tis he, I am caught, I must stand to it stoutly,
And show no shake of fear, I see he is angry,
Vext at the uttermost.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: My worthy Wise,
I have been looking of your modesty
All the town over.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: My most noble Husband,
I am glad I have found ye, for in truth I am weary,
VVeary and lame with looking out your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: I have been in Bawdy Houses.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: I believe you, and very lately too.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: 'Pray you pardon me,
To seek your Ladyship, I have been in Cellars,
In private Cellars, where the thirsty Bawds
Hear your Confessions; I have been at Plays,
To look you out amongst the youthful Actors,
At Puppet Shews, you are Mistress of the motions,
At Gossippings I hearkned after you,
But amongst those Confusions of lewd Tongues
There's no distinguishing beyond a Babel.
I was amongst the Nuns because you sing well,
But they say yours are Bawdy Songs, they mourn for ye,
And last I went to Church to seek you out,
'Tis so long since you were there, they have forgot you.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: You have had a pretty progress, I'll tell mine now:
To look you out, I went to twenty Taverns.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: And are you sober?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Yes, I reel not yet, Sir,
VVhere I saw twenty drunk, most of 'em Souldiers,
There I had great hope to find you disguis'd too.
From hence to th' dicing-house, there I found
Quarrels needless, and senceless, Swords and Pots, and Candlesticks,
Tables and Stools, and all in one confusion,
And no man knew his Friend. I left this Chaos,
And to the Chirurgions went, he will'd me stay,
For says he learnedly, if he be tipled,
Twenty to one he whores, and then I hear of him,
If he be mad, he quarrels, then he comes too.
I fought ye where no safe thing would have ventur'd,
Amongst diseases, base and vile, vile Women,
For I remembred your old Roman axiom,
The more the danger, still the more the Honour.
Last, to your Confessor I came, who told me,
You were too proud to pray, and here I have found ye.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: She bears up bravely, and the Rogue is witty,
But I shall dash it instantly to nothing.
Here leave we off our wanton languages,
And now conclude we in a sharper tongue.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Why am I cozen'd?
Why am I abused?

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Thou most vile, base, abominable—

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Captain.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Thou stinking, overstew'd, poor, pocky—

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Captain.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Do you echo me?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Yes Sir, and go before ye,
And round about ye, why do you rail at me
For that that was your own sin, your own knavery?

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: And brave me too?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: You had best now draw your Sword, Captain?
Draw it upon a Woman, do brave, Captain,
Upon your Wife, Oh most renowned Captain.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: A Plague upon thee, answer me directly;
Why didst thou marry me?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: To be my Husband;
I had thought you had had infinite, but I'm cozen'd.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Why didst thou flatter me, and shew me wonders?
A house and riches, when they are but shadows,
Shadows to me?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Why did you work on me
(It was but my part to requite you, Sir)
With your strong Souldiers wit, and swore you would bring me
So much in Chains, so much in Jewels, Husband,
So much in tight rich Cloaths?

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Thou hast 'em, Rascal;
I gave 'em to thy hands, my trunks and all,
And thou hast open'd 'em, and sold my treasure.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Sir, there's your treasure, sell it to a Tinker
To mend old Kettles, is this noble Usage?
Let all the World view here the Captain's treasure,
A Man would think now, these were worthy matters;
Here's a shooing horn Chain gilt over, how it scenteth
Worse than the mouldy durty heel it served for:
And here's another of a lesser value,
So little I would shame to tye my Dog in't,
These are my joynture, blush and save a labour,
Or these else will blush for ye.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: A fire subtle ye, are ye so crafty?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Here's a goodly jewel,
Did not you win this at Goletta, Captain,
Or took it in the field from some brave Bashaw,
How it sparkles like an old Ladies eyes,
And fills each room with light like a close Lanthorn!
This would do rarely in an Abbey Window,
To cozen Pilgrims.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Ptithee leave prating.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: And here's a Chain of Whitings eyes for pearls,
A Muscle monger would have made a better.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Nay, prithee wife, my Cloaths, my Cloaths.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: I'll tell ye,
Your Cloaths are parallels to these, all counterfeit.
Put these and them on, you are a Man of Copper,
A kind of Candlestick; these you thought, my Husband,
To have cozen'd me withall, but I am quit with you.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Is there no house then, nor no grounds about it?
No plate nor hangings?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: There are none, sweet Husband,
Shadow for shadow is as equal justice.
Can you rail now? pray put up your fury, Sir,
And speak great words, you are a Souldier, thunder.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: I will speak little, I have plaid the Fool,
And so I am rewarded.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: You have spoke well, Sir,
And now I see you are so conformable
I'll heighten you again, go to your house,
They are packing to be gone, you must sup there,
I'll meet ye, and bring Cloaths, and clean Shirts after,
And all things shall be well, I'll colt you once more,
And teach you to bring Copper.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Tell me one thing,
I do beseech thee tell me, tell me truth, Wife,
However I forgive thee, art thou honest?
The Beldam swore.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: I bid her tell you so, Sir,
It was my plot, alas my credulous Husband,
The Lady told you too.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Most strange things of thee.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Still 'twas my way, and all to try your sufferance,
And the denied the House.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: She knew me not,
No, nor no title that I had.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: 'Twas well carried;
No more, I am right and straight.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: I would believe thee,
But Heaven knows how my heart is, will ye follow me?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: I'll be there straight.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: I am fooled, yet dare not find it.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Go silly Fool, thou mayst be a good Souldier
In open field, but for our private service
Thou art an Ass, I'll make thee so, or miss else.
Here comes another Trout that I must tickle,
And tickle daintily, I have lost my end else.
May I crave your leave, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: Prithee be answered, thou shalt crave no leave,
I am in my meditations, do not vex me,
A beaten thing, but this hour a most bruised thing,
That people had compassion on it, looked so,
The next Sir Palmerin, here's fine proportion,
An Ass, and then an Elephant, sweet Justice,
There's no way left to come at her now, no craving,
If money could come near, yet I would pay him;
I have a mind to make him a huge Cuckold,
And money may do much, a thousand Duckets,
'Tis but the letting blood of a rank Heir.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: 'Pray you hear me.

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: I know thou hast some wedding Ring to pawn now,
Of Silver and gilt, with a blind posie in't,
Love and a Mill horse should go round together,
Or thy Childs whistle, or thy Squirrels Chain,
I'll none of 'em, I would she did but know me,
Or would this Fellow had but use of money,
That I might come in any way.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: I am gone, Sir,
And I shall tell the beauty sent me to ye,
The Lady Margarita.

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: Stay I prithee,
VVhat is thy will? I turn me wholly to ye,
And talk now till thy tongue ake, I will hear ye.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: She would entreat you, Sir,

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: She shall command, Sir,
Let it be so, I beseech thee, my sweet Gentlewoman,
Do not forget thy self.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: She does command then
This courtesie, because she knows you are noble.

speeches.speaker: Cac.
verse: Your Mistress by the way?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: My natural mistress,
Upon these Jewels, Sir, they are fair and rich,
And view 'em right.

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: To doubt 'em is an heresie.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: A thousand Duckets, 'tis upon necessity
Of present use, her husband, Sir, is stubborn.

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: Long may he be so.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: She desires withal a better knowledge of your parts and person,
And when you please to do her so much honour.

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: Come, let's dispatch.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: In troth I have heard her say, Sir,
Of a fat man she has not seen a sweeter.
But in this business, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cac.
verse: Let's do it first
And then dispute, the Ladies use may long for't.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: All secrecy she would desire, she told me
How wise you are.

speeches.speaker: Cac.
verse: We are not wise to talk thus,
Carry her the gold, I'le look her out a Jewel,
Shall sparkle like her eyes, and thee another,
Come prethee come, I long to serve thy Lady,
Long monstrously, now valor I shall meet ye,
You that dare Dukes.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Green goose you are now in sippets.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: He shall not have his will, I shall prevent him,
I have a toy here that will turn the tide,
And suddenly, and strangely, hear Don Juan,
Do you present it to him.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: I am commanded.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: A fellow founded out of Charity,
And moulded to the height contemn his maker,
Curb the free hand that fram'd him? This must not be.

speeches.speaker: Sanc.
verse: That such an oyster shell should hold a pearl,
And of so rare a price in prison,
Was she made to be the matter of her own undoing,
To let a slovenly unweildy fellow,
Unruly and self will'd, dispose her beauties?
We suffer all Sir in this sad Eclipse,
She should shine where she might show like her self,
An absolute sweetness, to comfort those admire her,
And shed her beams upon her friends.
We are gull'd all,
And all the world will grumble at your patience,
If she be ravish't thus.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Ne'r fear it Sanchio,
We'l have her free again, and move at Court
In her clear orb: but one sweet handsomeness,
To bless this part of Spain, and have that slubber'd?

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: 'Tis every good mans cause, and we must stir in it.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I'le warrant he shall be glad to please us,
And glad to share too, we shall hear anon
A new song from him, let's attend a little.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Coronel, I am bound to you for this nobleness,
I should have been your officer, 'tis true Sir,
And a proud man I should have been to have serv'd you,
'T has pleas'd the King out of his boundless favours,
To make me your companion, this commission
Gives me a troop of horse.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: I do rejoyce at it,
And am a glad man we shall gain your company,
I am sure the King knows you are newly married,
And out of that respect gives you more time Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Within four daies I am gone, so he commands me,
And 'tis not mannerly for me to argue it,
The time grows shorter still, are your goods ready?

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: They are aboard.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Who waits there?

speeches.speaker: Servant.
verse: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Le.
verse: Do you hear ho, go carry this unto your Mistris Sir,
And let her see how much the King has honour'd me,
Bid her be lusty, she must make a Souldier.

speeches.speaker: Lorenzo,
verse: Sir,
Go take down all the hangings,
And pack up all my cloths, my plate and Jewels,
And all the furniture that's portable,
Sir when we lye in garrison, 'tis necessary
We keep a handsom port, for the Kings honour;
And do you hear, let all your Ladies wardrobe
Be safely plac'd in trunks, they must along too.

speeches.speaker: Lor.
verse: Whither must they goe Sir?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: To the wars, Lorenzo,
And you and all, I will not leave a turn-spit,
That has one dram of spleen against a Dutchman.

speeches.speaker: Lor.
verse:
Why then St
Jaques hey, you have made us all Sir,
And if we leave ye—does my Lady goe too?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: The stuff must goe to morrow towards the sea Sir,
All, all must goe.

speeches.speaker: Lor.
verse: Why Pedro, Vasco, Dego,
Come help me, come come boys, soldadoes, comrades,
We'l fley these beer-bellied rogues, come away quickly.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: H'as taken a brave way to save his honour,
And cross the Duke, now I shall love him dearly,
By the life of credit thou art a noble Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Why how now wife, what, sick at my preferment?
This is not kindly done.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: No sooner love ye,
Love ye intirely Sir, brought to consider
The goodness of your mind and mine own duty,
But lose you instantly, be divorc'd from ye?
This is a cruelty, I'le to the King
And tell him 'tis unjust to part two souls,
Two minds so nearly mixt.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: By no means sweet heart.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: If he were married but four daies as I am.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: He would hang himself the fifth, or fly his Country.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: He would make it treason for that tongue that durst
But talk of war, or any thing to vex him,
You shall not goe.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Indeed I must sweet wife,
What shall I lose the King for a few kisses?
We'l have enough.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: I'le to the Duke my cousin, he shall to th' King.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: He did me this great office,
I thank his grace for't, should I pray him now,
To undoe't again? fye 'twere a base discredit.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Would I were able Sir to bear you company,
How willing should I be then, and how merry!
I will not live alone.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Be in peace, you shall not.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: What knocking's this? oh Heaven my head, why rascals
I thinks the war's begun i'th' house already.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: The preparation is, they are taking down,
And packing up the hangings, plate and Jewels,
And all those furnitures that shall besit me
When I lye in garrison.

speeches.speaker: Coachm.
verse: Must the Coach goe too Sir?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: How will your Lady pass toth' sea else easily?
We shall find shipping for't there to transport it.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: I goe? alas!

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I'le have a main care of ye,
I know ye are sickly, he shall drive the easier,
And all accommodation shall attend ye.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Would I were able,

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Come I warrant ye,
Am not I with ye sweet? are her cloaths packt up,
And all her linnen? give your maids direction,
You know my time's but short, and I am commanded.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Let me have a nurse,
And all such necessary people with me,
And an easie bark.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: It shall not trot I warrant ye,
Curvet it may sometimes.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: I am with child Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: At four days warning? this is something speedy,
Do you conceive as our jennets do with a west winde?
My heir will be an arrant fleet one Lady,
I'le swear you were a maid when I first lay with ye.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Pray do not swear, I thought I was a maid too,
But we may both be cozen'd in that point Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: In such a strait point sure I could not err Madam.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: This is another tenderness to try him,
Fetch her up now.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: You must provide a cradle, and what a troubles that?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: The sea shall rock it,
'Tis the best nurse; 'twill roar and rock together,
A swinging storm will sing you such a lullaby.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Faith let me stay, I shall but shame ye Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: And you were a thousand shames you shall along with me,
At home I am sure you'l prove a million,
Every man carries the bundle of his sins
Upon his own back, you are mine, I'le sweat for ye.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: What Sir, preparing for your noble journey?
'Tis well, and full of care.
I saw your mind was wedded to the war,
And knew you would prove some good man for your country,
Therefore fair Cousin with your gentle pardon,
I got this place: what, mourn at his advancement?
You are to blame, he will come again sweet cousin,
Mean time like sad Penelope and sage,
Amongst your maids at home, and huswifely.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: No Sir, I dare not leave her to that solitariness,
She is young, and grief or ill news from those quarters
May daily cross her, she shall goe along Sir.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: By no means Captain.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: By all means an't please ye.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: What take a young and tender bodied Lady,
And expose her to those dangers, and those tumults,
A sickly Lady too?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: 'Twill make her well Sir,
There's no such friend to health as wholsom travel.

speeches.speaker: Sanch.
verse: Away it must not be.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: It ought not Sir,
Go hurry her? it is not humane, Captain.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I cannot blame her tears, fright her with tempests,
With thunder of the war.
I dare swear if she were able.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: She is most able.
And pray ye swear not, she must goe, there's no remedy,
Nor greatness, nor the trick you had to part us,
Which I smell too rank, too open, too evident
(And I must tell you Sir, 'tis most unnoble)
Shall hinder me: had she but ten hours life,
Nay less, but two hours, I would have her with me,
I would not leave her same to so much ruine,
To such a desolation and discredit
As her weakness and your hot will wou'd work her to.
What Masque is this now?
More tropes and figures, to abuse my sufferance,
What cousin's this?

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Michael van owle, how dost thou?
In what dark bath or tod of aged Ivy
Hast thou lyen hid?

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: Things must both ebbe and slow, Coronel,
And people must conceal, and shine again.
You are welcom hither as your friend may say, Gentleman,
A pretty house ye see handsomely seated,
Sweet and convenient walks, the waters crystal.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: He's certain mad.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: As mad as a French Tayler,
That has nothing in's head but ends of sustians.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: I see you are packing now my gentle cousin,
And my wife told me I should find it so,
'Tis true I do, you were merry when I was last here,
But 'twas your will to try my patience Madam.
I am sorry that my swift occasions
Can let you take your pleasure here no longer,
Yet I would have you think my honour'd cousin,
This house and all I have are all your servants.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: What house, what pleasure Sir, what do you mean?

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: You hold the jest so still, 'twill prove discourteous,
This house I mean, the pleasures of this place.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: And what of them?

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: They are mine Sir, and you know it,
My wises I mean, and so confer'd upon me,
The hangings Sir I must entreat, your servants,
That are so busie in their offices,
Again to minister to their right uses,
I shall take view o'th' plate anon, and furnitures
That are of under place; you are merry still cousin,
And of a pleasant constitution,
Men of great fortunes make their mirths at placitum.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Prethee good stubborn wife, tell me directly,
Good evll wife leave fooling and tell me honestly,
Is this my kinsman?

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: I can tell ye nothing.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I have many kinsmen, but so mad a one,
And so phantastick—all the house?

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: All mine,
And all within it. I will not bate ye an ace on't.
Can you not receive a noble courtesie,
And quietly and handsomely as ye ought Couz,
But you must ride o'th' top on't?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Canst thou fight?

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: I'le tell ye presently, I could have done Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: For ye must law and claw before ye get it.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Away, no quarrels.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Now I am more temperate,
I'le have it prov'd if you were never yet in Bedlam,
Never in love, for that's a lunacy,
No great state left ye that you never lookt for,
Nor cannot manage, that's a rank distemper;
That you were christen'd, and who answer'd for ye,
And then I yield.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: H'as half perswaded me I was bred i'th'moon,
I have ne'r a bush at my breech, are not we both mad,
And is not this a phantastick house we are in,
And all a dream we do? will ye walk out Sir,
And if I do not beat thee presently
Into a sound belief, as sense can give thee,
Brick me into that wall there for a chimny piece,
And say I was one o'th' Caesars, done by a seal-cutter.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I'le talk no more, come we'l away immediatly.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Why then the house is his, and all that's in it,
I'le give away my skin but I'le undoe ye,
I gave it to his wife, you must restore Sir,
And make a new provision.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: Am I mad now or am I christen'd, you my page cous^,
My mighty Mahound kinsman, what quirk now?
You shall be welcom all, I hope to see Sir
Your Grace here, and my couz, we are all Souldiers,
And must do naturally for one another.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Are ye blank at this? then I must tell ye Sir,
Ye have no command, now ye may goe at pleasure
And ride your asse troop, 'twas a trick I us'd
To try your jealousie upon entreatie,
And saving of your wife.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: All this not moves me,
Nor stirs my gall, nor alters my affections,
You have more furniture, more houses Lady,
And rich ones too, I will make bold with those,
And you have Land i'th' Indies as I take it,
Thither we'l goe, and view a while those climats,
Visit your Factors there, that may betray ye,
'Tis done, we must goe.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Now thou art a brave Gentleman,
And by this sacred light I love thee dearly.
The house is none of yours, I did but jest Sir,
Nor you are no couz of mine, I beseech ye vanish,
I tell you plain, you have no more right than he
Has, that senseless thing, your wife has once more fool'd ye:
Goe ye and consider.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Good morrow my sweet cousin, I should be glad Sir.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: By this hand she dies for't,
Or any man that speaks for her.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: These are fine toyes.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Let me request you stay but one poor month,
You shall have a Commission and I'le goe too,
Give me but will so far.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Well I will try ye,
Good morrow to your Grace, we have private business.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: If I miss thee again, I am an arrant bungler.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Thou shalt have my command, and I'le march under thee,
Nay be thy boy before thou shalt be baffled,
Thou art so brave a fellow.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: I have seen visions.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: COme hither wife, do you know this hand?

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: I do Sir,
'Tis Estifania, that was once my woman.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: She writes to me here, that one Cacasogo
An usuring Jewellers son (I know the Rascal)
Is mortally faln in love with ye.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Is a monster, deliver me from mountains.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Do you goe a birding for all sorts of people?
And this evening will come to ye and shew ye Jewels,
And offers any thing to get access to ye,
If I can make or sport or profit on him,
(For he is fit for both) she bids me use him,
And so I will, be you conformable, and follow but my will.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: I shall not fail, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Will the Duke come again do you think?

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: No sure Sir,
H'as now no policie to bring him hither.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Nor bring you to him, if my wit hold fair wife:
Let's in to dinner.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: Had I but lungs enough to bawl sufficiently,
That all the queans in Christendom might hear me,
That men might run away from contagion,
I had my wish; would it were most high treason,
Most infinite high, for any man to marry,
I mean for any man that would live hand somely,
And like a Gentleman, in his wits and credit.
What torments shall I put her to, Phalaris bull now?
Pox they love bulling too well, though they smoak for't.
Cut her a pieces? every piece will live still,
And every morsel of her will do mischief;
They have so many lives, there's no hanging of 'em,
They are too light to drown, they are cork and feathers;
To burn too cold, they live like Salamanders;
Under huge heaps of stones to bury her,
And so depress her as they did the Giants;
She will move under more than built old Babel,
I must destroy her.

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: Be cozen'd by a thing of clouts, a she moth,
That every silkmans shop breeds; to be cheated,
And of a thousand duckets by a whim wham?

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: Who's that is cheated, speak again thou vision,
But art thou cheated? minister some comfort:
Tell me directly art thou cheated bravely?
Come, prethee come, art thou so pure a coxcomb
To be undone? do not dissemble with me,
Tell me I conjure thee.

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: Then keep thy circle,
For I am a spirit wild that flies about thee,
And who e're thou art, if thou be'st humane,
I'le let thee plainly know, I am cheated damnably.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: Dost thou laugh? damnably, I say most damnably.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: By whom, good spirit speak, speak ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: I will utter, laugh till thy lungs crack, by a rascal woman,
A lewd, abominable, and plain woman.
Dost thou laugh still?

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: I must laugh, prethee pardon me,
I shall laugh terribly.

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: I shall be angry, terrible angry, I have cause.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: That's it, and 'tis no reason but thou shouldst be angry,
Angry at heart, yet I must laugh still at thee.
By a woman cheated? art' sure it was a woman?

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: I shall break thy head, my valour itches at thee.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: It is no matter, by a woman cozen'd,
A real woman?

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: A real Devil,
Plague of her Jewels and her copper chains,
How rank they smell.

speeches.speaker: Perox.
verse: Sweet cozen'd Sir let me see them,
I have been cheated too, I would have you note that,
And lewdly cheated, by a woman also,
A scurvie woman, I am undone sweet Sir,
Therefore I must have leave to haugh.

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: Pray ye take it,
You are the merriest undone man in Europe.
What need we fiddles, bawdy songs and sack,
When our own miseries can make us merry?

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: Ha, ha, ha.
I have seen these Jewels, what a notable penniworth
Have you had next our heart? you will not take Sir
Some twenty Duck^ts?

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: Thou art deceiv'd, I will take.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: To clean your bargain now.

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: I'le take s^me ten, some any thing, some half ten,
Half a Ducket

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: An excellent lapidary set these stones sure,
Do you mark their waters?

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: Quick sand choak their waters,
And hers that bought 'em too, but I shall find her.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: And so shall I, I hope, but do not hurt her,
You cannot find in all this Kingdom,
(If you had need of cozening, as you may have,
For such gross natures will desire it often,
'Tis at some time too a fine variety,)
A woman that can cozen ye so neatly,
She has taken half mine anger off with this trick.

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: If I were valiant now, I would kill this fellow,
I have mony enough lies by me at a pinch
To pay for twenty Rascals lives that vex me,
I'le to this Lady, there I shall be satisfied.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Come, we'l away unto your country house,
And there we'l learn to live contently,
This place is full of charge, and full of hurry,
No part of sweetness dwells about these cities.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Whither you will, I wait upon your pleasure;
Live in a hollow tree Sir, I'le live with ye.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I, now you strike a harmony, a true one,
When your obedience waits upon your Husband,
And your sick will aims at the care of honour,
Why now I dote upon ye, love ye dearly,
And my rough nature falls like roaring streams,
Clearly and sweetly into your embraces.
O what a Jewel is a woman excellent,
A wise, a vertuous and a noble woman!
When we meet such, we bear our stamps on both sides,
And through the world we hold our currant virtues,
Alone we are single medals, only faces,
And wear our fortunes out in useless shadows,
Command you now, and ease me of that trouble,
I'le be as humble to you as a servant,
Bid whom you please, invite your noble friends,
They shall be welcome all, visit acquaintance,
God at your pleasure, now experience
Has link't you fast unto the chain of goodness:
What noise is this, what dismal cry?

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: 'Tis loud too.
Sure there's some mischief done i'th' street, look out there.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Look out and help.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: Oh Sir the Duke Medina.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: What of the Duke Medina?

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: Oh sweet Gentleman, is almost slain.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Away away and help him, all the house help.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: How slain? why Margarita,
Why wife, sure some new device they have a foot again,
Some trick upon my credit, I shall meet it,
I had rather guide a ship Imperial
Alone, and in a storm, than rule one woman.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: How came ye hurt Sir?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I felt out with my friend the noble Coronel,
My cause was naught, for 'twas about your honour:
And he that wrongs the Innocent ne'r prospers,
And he has left me thus for charity,
Lend me a bed to ease my tortur'd body,
That e're I perish I may show my penitence,
I fear I am slain.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Help Gentlemen to carry him,
There shall be nothing in this house my Lord,
But as your own.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I thank ye noble Sir,

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: To bed with him, and wife give your attendance.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Doctors and Surgions:

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Do not disquiet me,
But let me take my leave in peace.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Afore me
'Tis ^arely counterfeited.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: True, it is so Sir,
And take you heed, this last blow do not spoil ye,
He is not hurt, only we made a scuffle,
As though we purpos'd anger; that same scratch
On's hand he took, to colour all and draw compassion,
That he might get into your house more cunningly:
I must not stay, stand now, and y'are a brave fel^ow.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I thank ye noble Coronel, and I honour ye.
Never be quiet?

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: He's most desperate ill Sir,
I do not think these ten months will recover him.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Does he hire my house to play the fool in,
Or do ^stand on Fairy ground, we are haunted,
Are all men and their wives troubled with dreams thus?

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: What all you Sir?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Nay what all you sweet wife,
To put these daily pastimes on my patience?
What dost thou see in me, that I should suffer thus,
Have not I done my part like a true Husband,
And paid some desperate debts you never look'd for?

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: You have done handsomely I must confess Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Have I not kept thee waking like a hawk?
And watcht thee with delights to satisfy thee?
The very tithes of which had won a Widow.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Alas I pity ye.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Thou wilt make me angry,
Thou never saw'st me mad yet.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: You are alwaies,
You carry a kind of bedlam still about ye.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: If thou pursuest me further I run stark mad,
If you have more hurt Dukes or Gentlemen,
To lye here on your cure, I shall be desperate,
I know the trick, and you shall feel I know it,
Are ye so hot that no hedge can contain ye?
I'le have thee let blood in all the veins about thee,
I'le have thy thoughts sound too, and have them open'd,
Thy spirits purg'd, for those are they that fire ye,
Thy maid shall be thy Mistris, thou the maid,
And all those servise labours that she reach at,
And goe through cheerfully, or else sleep empty,
That maid shall lye by me to teach you duty,
You in a pallet by to humble ye,
And grieve for what you lose.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: I have lost my self Sir,
And all that was my base self, disobedience,
My wantonness, my stubborness I have lost too,
And now by that pure faith good wives are crown'd with,
By your own nobleness.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I take ye up, and wear ye next my heart,
See you be worth it. Now what with you?

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: I come to tell my Lady,
There is a fulsome fellow would fain speak with her.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: 'Tis Cacafogo, goe and entertain him,
And draw him on with hopes.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: I shall observe ye.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I have a rare design upon that Gentleman,
And you must work too.

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: I shall Sir most willingly.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Away then both, and keep him close in some place
From the Dukes sight, and keep the Duke in too,
Make 'em believe both, I'le find time to cure 'em.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: Why how darst thou meet me again thou rebel,
And knowst how thou hast used me thrice, thou rascal?
Were there not waies enough to fly my vengeance,
No holes nor vaults to hide thee from my fury,
But thou must meet me face to face to kill thee?
I would not seek thee to destroy thee willingly,
But now thou comest to invite me,
And comest upon me,
How like a sheep-biting Rogue taken i'th' manner,
And ready for the halter dost thou look now?
Thou hast a hanging look thou scurvy thing, hast ne'r a knife
Nor ever a string to lead thee to Elysium?
Be there no pitifull 'Pothecaries in this town,
That have compassion upon wretched women,
And dare administer a dram of rats-bane,
But thou must fall to me?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: I know you have mercy.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: If I had tuns of mercy thou deserv'st none,
What new trick is now a foot, and what new houses
Have you i'th' air, what orchards in apparition,
What canst thou say for thy life?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Little or nothing,
I know you'l kill me, and I know 'tis useless
To beg for mercy, pray let me draw my book out,
And pray a little.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: Do, a very little,
For I have farther business than thy killing,
I have mony yet to borrow, speak when you are ready.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Now now Sir, now,
Come on, do you start off from me,
Do you swear great Captain, have you seen a spirit?

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: Do you wear guns?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: I am a Souldiers wife Sir,
And by that priviledge I may be arm'd,
Now what's the news, and let's discourse more friendly,
And talk of our affairs in peace.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: Let me see,
Prethee let me see thy gun, 'tis a very pretty one.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: No no Sir, you shall feel.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: Hold ye villain, what thine own Husband?

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Let mine own Husband then
Be in's own wits, there, there's a thousand duckets,
Who mu^ provide for you, and yet you'l kill me.

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: I was not hurt thee for ten thousand millions.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: When will you redeem your Jewels, I have pawn'd 'em,
You see for what, we must keep touch.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: I'le kiss thee,
And get as many more, I'le make thee famous,
Had we the house now!

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: Come along with me,
If that be vanish't there be more to hire Sir.

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: I see I am an asse when thou art near me.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Is the fool come?

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: Yes and i'th' celler fast,
And there he staies his good hour till I call him,
He will make dainty musick among the fack-butts,
I have put him just, Sir, under the Dukes chamber.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: It is the better.

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: Has given me royally,
And to my Lady a whole load of portigues.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Better and better still, go Margarita,
Now play your prize, you say you dare be honest,
I'le put ye to your best.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Secure your self Sir, give me the candle,
Pass away in silence.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Who's there, oh oh.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: My Lord.

speeches.speaker: Duke within.
verse: Have ye brought me comfort?

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: I have my Lord,
Come forth 'tis I, come gently out I'le help ye,
Come softly too, how do you?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Are there none here?
Let me look round; we cannot be too wary,
Oh let me bless this hour, are you alone sweet friend?

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Alone to comfort you.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: What's that you tumble?
I have heard a noise this half hour under me,
A fearfull noise.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: The fat thing's mad i'th' celler,
And stumbles from one hogs-head to another,
Two cups more, and he ne'r shall find the way out.
What do you fear? come, sit down by me chearfully,
My Husband's safe, how do your wounds?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I have none Lady,
My wounds I counterfeited cunningly,
And feign'd the quarrel too, to injoy you sweet,
Let's lose no time, heark the same noise again.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: What noise, why look ye pale? I hear no stirring,
This goblin in the vault will be so tipled.
You are not well I know by your flying fancy,
Your body's ill at ease, your wounds.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I have none, I am as lusty and as full of health,
High in my blood.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Weak in your blood you would say,
How wretched is my case, willing to please ye,
And find you so disable?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Believe me Lady.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: I know you will venture all you have to satisfy me,
Your life I know, but is it fit I spoil ye,
Is it my love do you think?

speeches.speaker: Cacaf. below.
verse: Here's to the Duke.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: It nam'd me certainly,
I heard it plainly sound.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: You are hurt mortally,
And fitter for your prayers Sir than pleasure,
What starts you make? I would not kiss you wantonly,
For the worlds wealth; have I secur'd my Husband,
And put all doubts aside to be deluded?

speeches.speaker: Cacaf. below.
verse: I come, I come.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Heaven bless me.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: And bless us both, for sure this is the Devil,
I plainly heard it now, he will come to fetch ye,
A very spirit, for he spoke under ground,
And spoke to you just as you would have snatcht me,
You are a wicked man, and sure this haunts ye,
Would you were out o'th' house.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I would I were,
O' that condition I had leapt a window,

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: And that's the least leap if you mean to scape Sir,
Why what a frantick man were you to come here,
What a weak man to counterfeit deep wounds,
To wound another deeper?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Are you honest then?

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Yes then and now, and ever, and excellent honest,
And exercise this pastime but to shew ye,
Great men are fools sometimes as well as wretches.
Would you were well hurt, with any hope of life,
Cut to the brains, or run clean through the body,
To get out quietly as you got in Sir,
I wish it like a friend that loves ye dearly,
For if my Husband take ye, and take ye thus a counterfeit,
One that would clip his credit out of his honour,
He must kill ye presently,
There is no mercy nor an hour of pity,
And for me to intreat in such an agony,
Would shew me little better than one guilty,
Have you any mind to a Lady now?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Would I were off fair,
If ever Lady caught me in a trap more.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: If you be well and lusty, sy fy shake not,
You say you love me, come, come bravely now,
Despise all danger, I am ready for ye.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: She mocks my misery, thou cruel Lady.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Thou cruel Lord, wouldst thou betray my honesty,
Betray it in mine own house, wrong my Husband,
Like a night thief, thou darst not name by day-light?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I am most miserable.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: You are indeed,
And like a foolish thing you have made your self so,
Could not your own discretion tell ye Sir,
When I was married I was none of yours?
Your eyes were then commanded to look off me,
And I now stand in a circle and secure,
Your spells nor power can never reach my body,
Mark me but this, and then Sir be most miserable,
'Tis sacriledge to violate a wedlock,
You rob two Temples, make your self twice guilty,
You ruine hers, and spot her noble Husbands.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Let me be gone, I'le never more attempt ye.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: You cannot goe, 'tis not in me to save ye,
Dare ye do ill, and poorly then shrink under it?
Were I the Duke Medina, I would fight now,
For you must fight and bravely, it concerns you,
You do me double wrong if you sneak off Sir,
And all the world would say I lov'd a coward,
And you must dye too, for you will be kill'd,
And leave your youth, your honour and your state,
And all those dear delights you worship't here.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: The noise again!

speeches.speaker: Cacaf. below.
verse: Some small beer if you love me.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: The Devil haunts you sure, your sins are mighty.
A drunken Devil too, to plague your villany.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Preserve me but this once.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: There's a deep well
In the next yard, if you dare venture drowning,
It is but deah.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I would not dye so wretchedly.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Out of a garret window I'le let you down then,
But say the rope be rotten, 'tis huge high too.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Have you no mercy?

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Now you are frighted throughly,
And find what 'tis to play the fool in folly,
And see with clear eyes your detested folly,
I'le be your guard.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: And I'le be your true servant,
Ever from this hour vertuously to love ye,
Chastly and modestly to look upon ye,
And here I seal it.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: I may kiss a stranger, for you must now be so.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: How do you my Lord,
Me thinks you look but poorly on this matter.
Has my wife wounded ye, you were well before,
Pray Sir be comforted, I have forgot all,
Truly forgiven too, wife you are a right one,
And now with unknown nations I dare trust ye.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: No more seign'd fights my Lord, they never prosper.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Who's this? the Devil in the vault?

speeches.speaker: Alt.
verse: 'Tis he Sir, and as lovingly drunk, as though he had studied it.

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: Give me a cup of Sack, and kiss me Lady,
Kiss my sweet face, and make thy Husband cuckold,
An Ocean of sweet Sack, shall we speak treason?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: He is Devilish drunk.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I had thought he had been a Devil.
He made as many noises and as horrible.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Oh a true lover Sir will lament loudly,
Which of the butts is your Mistris?

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: Butt in thy belly.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: There's two in thine I am sure, 'tis grown so monstrous.

speeches.speaker: Caca.
verse: Butt in thy face.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Go carry him to sleep,
A fools love should be drunk, he has paid well for't too.
When he is sober let him out to rail,
Or hang himself, there will be no loss of him.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Who's this? my Mauhound cousin?

speeches.speaker: Per.
verse: Good Sir, 'tis very good, would I had a house too,
For there is no talking in the open air,
My Tarmogant Couz, I would be bold to tell ye,
I durst be merry too, I tell you plainly,
You have a pretty seat, you have the luck on't,
A pretty Lady too, I have mist both,
My Carpenter built in a mist I thank him,
Do me the courtesie to let me see it,
See it but once more. But I shall cry for anger.
I'le hire a Chandlers shop close under ye,
And for my foolerie, sell sope and whip-cord,
Nay if you do not laugh now and laugh heartily,
You are a fool couz.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I must laugh a little,
And now I have done, couz thou shalt live with me,
My merry couz, the world shall not divorce us,
Thou art a valiant man, and thou shalt never want,
Will this content thee?

speeches.speaker: Perez.
verse: I'le cry, and then I'le be thankfull,
Indeed I will, and I'le be honest to ye.
I would live a swallow here I must confess.
Wife I forgive thee all if thou be honest,
At thy peril, I believe thee excellent.

speeches.speaker: Estif.
verse: If I prove otherwaies, let me beg first,
Hold, this is yours, some recompence for service,
Use it to nobler ends than he that gave it.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: And this is yours, your true commission, Sir,
Now you are a Captain.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: You are a noble Prince Sir,
And now a souldier, Gentleman, we all rejoyce in't.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Sir, I shall wait upon you through all fortunes.

speeches.speaker: Alon.
verse: And I.

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: And I must needs attend my Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Will you goe Sister?

speeches.speaker: Altea.
verse: Yes indeed good Brother,
I have two ties, mine own bloud,
And my Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Is she your Sister?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Yes indeed good wife,
And my best Sister,
For she prov'd so, wench,
When she deceiv'd you with a loving Husband.

speeches.speaker: Alt.
verse: I would not deal so truly for a stranger.

speeches.speaker: Marg.
verse: Well I could chide ye,
But it must be lovingly and like a Sister,
I'le bring you on your way, and feast ye nobly,
For now I have an honest heart to love ye,
And then deliver you to the blue Neptune.

speeches.speaker: Juan.
verse: Your colours you must wear, and wear 'em proudly,
Wear 'em before the bullet, and in bloud too,
And all the world shall know
We are Vertues servants.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: And all the world shall know, a noble mind Makes women beautifull, and envie blind.

plays.play_title: The Laws of Candy. A TRAGI-COMEDY.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: SIR, you're the very friend I wish'd to meet with,
I have a large discourse invites your ear
To be an Auditor.

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: And what concerns it?

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: The sadly thriving progress of the loves
Between my Lord, the Prince, and that great Lady,
Whose insolence, and never-yet-match'd Pride,
Can by no Character be well exprest,
Bet in her only name, the proud Erota.

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: Alas, Melitus, I should guess the best
Success your Prince could find from her, to be
As harsh as the event doth prove: but now
'Tis not a time to pity passionate griess,
When a whole Kingdom in a manner lyes
Upon its Death-Bed bleeding.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Who can tell
Whether or no these plagues at once
Hang over this unhappy Land for her sake
That is a Monster in it?

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: Here's the misery
Of having a Child our Prince; else I presume
The bold Venetians had not dar'd to attempt
So bloody an invasion.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Yet I wonder
Why (Master Secretary) still the Senate
So almost superstitiously adores
Gonzalo, the Venetian Lord, considering
The outrage of his Countrymen—

speeches.speaker: Gas
verse: The Senate
Is wise, and therein just, for this Gonzalo,
Upon a Massacre performed at Sea
By the Admiral of Venice, on a Merchant
Of Candy, when the cause was to be heard
Before the Senate there, in open Court
Professed, that the cruelty the Admiral
Had shewed, deserved not only fine, but death;
For Candy then, and Venice were at peace:
Since when upon a motion in the Senate,
For Conquest of our Land, 'tis known for certain,
That only this Gonzalo dar'd to oppose it,
His reason was, because it too much savour'd
Of lawless and unjust ambition.
The Wars were scarce begun, but he (in fear
Of quarrels 'gainst his life) fled from his Country,
And hither came, where (to confirm his truth)
I know, (Melitus,) he out of his own store,
Hath monied Cassilanes the General.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: What, without other pledges than Cassilanes
Bare promise of payment?

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: No, it may be
He has some pretty Lordship to retire to;
But thus he hath done; now 'tis fit, Melitus,
The Senate should be thankful, otherwise
They should annihilate one of those Laws
For which this Kingdome is throughout the World
Unfollowed and admired.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: What Laws are those, Sir?
Let me so much importune you.

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: You shall,
And they be worth your knowledge: briefly thus:
Who e'r he be that can detect apparently
Another of ingratitude, for any
Received Benefit, the Plaintiff may
Require the Offenders life; unless he please
Freely and willingly to grant remission.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: By which strict Law, the Senate is in danger,
Should they neglect Gonzalo?

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: Right, the Law
Permits a like equality to Aliens,
As to a home-bred Patriot.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Pray Sir, the other?

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: Know, Melitus,
The elder Cretans flourished many years,
In War, in Peace unparallel'd, and they
(To spur heroick Spirits on to Vertue)
Enacted that what man so ere he were,
Did noblest in the field against his enemy,
So by the general voice approv'd, and known,
Might at his home return, make his demand
For satisfaction, and reward.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: They are
Both famous Laws indeed.

speeches.speaker: Mes.
verse: Master Secretary,
The Senate is about to sit, and crave
Your presence.

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: What, so suddenly?

speeches.speaker: Mes.
verse: These Letters
Will shew the causes why.

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: Heaven, thou n^t great,
And worthy to be thanked!

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Your countenance, Sir,
Doth promise some good tidings.

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: O the best
And happiest for this land that e'r was told!
All the Venetian Forces are defeated.

speeches.speaker: Mel
verse: How, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: And what doth add some delight more,
There is amongst the Souldiers a contention
Who shall be the triumpher, and it stands
Doubtful between a Father and his Son,
Old Cassilanes, and young Antinous.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: VVhy may not both demand it?

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: The Law denies it,
But where the Souldiers do not all consent,
The Parties in contention, are refer'd
To plead before the Senate; and from them
Upon an open audience to be judg'd
The Chief, and then to make demands.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: You ravish me
VVith wonder and delight.

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: Come; as we walk,
I shall more fully inform you.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Admit no Souldier near us till the Senate
Have took their places.

speeches.speaker: Arc.
verse: You are obey'd, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Decius, fall off.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: I shall.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Give leave Arcanes:
Young man, come nearer to me: who am I?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: It were a sin against the piety
Of silial duty, if I should forget
The debt I owe my Father on my knee:
Your pleasure?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: VVhat, so low? canst thou find joints,
Yet be an Elephant? Antinous, rise;
Thou wilt belye opinion, and rebate
The ambition of thy gallantry, that they
Whose confidence thou hast bewitch'd, should see
Their little God of War, kneel to his Father,
Though in my hand I did grasp Thunder.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Sir,
For proof that I acknowledge you the Author
Of giving me my Birth, I have discharg'd
A part of my Obedience. But if now
You should (as cruel fathers do) proclaim
Your right, and Tyrant-like usurp the glory
Of my peculiar honours, not deriv'd
From successary, but purchas'd with my bloud,
Then I must stand first Champion for my self
Against all interposers.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Boldly urg'd,
And proudly, I could love thee, did not anger
Consult with just disdain, in open language
To call thee most ungrateful. Say freely,
Wilt thou resign the flatteries whereon
The reeling pillars of a popular breath
Have rais'd thy Giant-like conceit, to add
A suffrage to thy Fathers merit? speak.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Sir, hear me: were there not a Chronicle
Well pen'd by all their tongues, who can report
What they have seen you do; or had you not
Best in your own performance writ your self,
And been your own text, I would undertake
Alone, without the help of Art, or Character,
But only to recount your deeds in Arms,
And you should ever then be fam'd a President
Of living victory: But as you are
Great, and well worthy to be stiled Great,
It would betray a poverty of Spirit
In me to obstruct my fortunes, or descent,
If I should coward-like surrender up
The interest which the inheritance of your vertue
And mine own thrifty fate can claim in honour:
My Lord, of all the mass of Fame, which any
That wears a Sword, and hath but seen me fight,
Gives me, I will not share, nor yield one jot,
One tittle.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Not to me?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: You are my Father,
Yet not to you.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Ambitious Boy, how dar'st thou
To tell me, that thou wilt contend?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Had I
Been slothful, and not follow'd you in all
The streights of death, you might have justly then
Reputed me a Bastard: 'tis a cruelty
More than to murther Innocents, to take
The life of my yet infant-honour from me.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Antinous, look upon this badge of age,
Thy Father's grey-hair'd beard: full fifty years,
(And more than half of this, ere thou wert born)
I have been known a Souldier, in which time
I sound no difference 'twixt War and Peace,
For War was Peace to me, and Peace was War.
Antinous, mark me well; there hath not liv'd
These fifty years a man whom Crete prefer'd
Before thy Father; let me boldly boast,
Thy Father, both for Discipline and Action
Hath so long been the first of all his Nation;
Now, canst thou think it honest, charitable,
Nay humane, being so young, my Son, my Child,
Be got, bred, taught by me, by me thy Father,
For one days service, and that on thy first,
To rob me of a glory which I fought for
A half of hundred years?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: My case observes
Both equity and presidents; for Sir,
That very day whereon you got your Fame,
You took it from some other, who was then
Chief in repute, as you are now, and has been
Perhaps as many years deserving that
Which you gain'd in a day, as I have mine.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: But he was not my Father then, Antinous;
Thou leav'st out that.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Sir, had he been your Father,
He had been then immortal; for a Father
^eightens his reputation where his Son
^erits it, as when you give us life,
^ life is not diminish'd but renew'd
^s when you are dead, and we are still
Your living Images,

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: So be thou curs'd
I^ to^ posterity, as I in thee,
Dishonourable Boy; O shall that Sun,
Which not a year yet since beheld me mounted
Upon a fiery Steed, waving my Sword,
And teaching this young Man to manage Arms,
That was a raw, fresh Novice in the feats
Of Chivalrie, shall that same Sun be witness
Against this Brat of his Ingratitude?
Who, to eclipse the light of my renown,
Can no way hope to get a noble Name,
^t by the treading on his Father's Greatness;
Thou wilt not yield?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: My life, but not the prize
My Sword hath purchas'd.

speeches.speaker: Arc.
verse: The Senate,
My Lord, are here at hand, and all the Souldiers
Begin to throng about them.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Now, Arcanes, the—

speeches.speaker: Arc.
verse: What, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cas
verse: Trifles will affront us; that
Fine fighting Stripling.

speeches.speaker: Arc.
verse: Let him have the shame on't;
Please you withdraw on this side.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: My great heart
Was never quail'd before.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: My Lord, be confident,
Let not your Father daunt you.

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: Decius, whither
Must I withdraw?

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: On this side.— See, the Souldiers
Attend your pleasure—courage, Sir; the Senate.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Way for the Senate.
My good Lords I know not
What tax of arrogance I may incurr,
Should I presume, though courted by your Favours,
To take a place amongst you; I had rather
Give proof of my unfeign'd humility
By force, though mean, yet more becoming place,
Than run the hazard of a doubtful censure.

speeches.speaker: Pos.
verse: My Lord, your wisdom is both known and try'd;
We cannot rank you in a nobler Friendship
Than your great service to the State deserves.

speeches.speaker: Por.
verse: Will't please you, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: What's here, my Lord Porphycio?
It must not be.

speeches.speaker: Por.
verse: My Lord, you are too modest.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: It is no season to be troublesome,
Else—but I have done: your Lordships are observ'd.

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: Is the demandant ready?

speeches.speaker: Arc.
verse: He is ready.

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: Produce him then.

speeches.speaker: Arc.
verse: Before this sacred presence,
I, by a general consent, am made
The Souldiers voice, and to your gracious Wisedoms,
Present as chief in Arms, his Countries Champion,
Cassilanes.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Most reverend Lords, you hear the lesser number
Of tho^ who have been Guardians to this Country,
Approve this Champion; I, in all their names,
Who fought for Candy, here present before you
The mightiest man in Arms, Antinous.
Speak fellow Souldiers.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: Antinous, Antinous.

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: Stand by all, save the two Competitors.

speeches.speaker: Poss.
verse: My Lords, how much your Countrey owes you both,
The due reward of your desertful glories
Must to Posterity remain: but yet
Since, by our Law, one only can make claim
To the proposed honours which you both
(It seems) have truly merited, take leave
Freely to plead your rights; we shall attend ye.

speeches.speaker: Por.
verse: Wherein priority of voice is granted,
Lord Cassilanes to you; for that your rare
And long experience in the Course of War,
As well doth challenge it as the best priviledge
Of Order and Civility, for that
You are your brave Opponents worthy Father.
Say, Country-men, are you content?

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: I, I.

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: Right grave, right gracious Fathers; how unfit
It is for me, that all my life time have
Been practis'd in the School of Bloud, and Slaughter
To bandy words now in my lifes last farewel,
Your Wisedomes will consider; were there pitcht
Another, and another field, like that
Which, not yet three days since, this Arm hath scatter'd,
Defeated, and made nothing, then the man
That had a heart to think he could but follow
(For equal me he should not) through the lanes
Of danger and amazement, might in that
That only of but following me, be happy,
Reputed worthy to be made my Rival;
For 'tis not, Lords, unknown to those about me,
(My fellow Souldiers) first, with what a confidence
I led them on to sight, went on still, and
As if I could have been a second Nature,
As well in heartening them by my example,
As by my exhortation, I gave life
To quicken courage, to inflame revenge,
To heighten resolution; in a word,
To out-doe action: It boots not to discover,
How that young man, who was not fledg'd nor skill'd
In Martial play, was even as ignorant
As childish: But I list not to disparage
His non ability: The signal given
Of Battel, when our enemies came on,
(Directed more by sury, than by warrant
Of Policy and Stratagem) I met them,
I in the sore front of the Armies met them;
And as if this old weather-beaten body
Had been compos'd of cannon proof, I stood
The volleys of their shot. I, I my self
Was he that first dis-rankt their woods of Pikes:
But when we came to handy-stroaks, as often
As I lent blows, so often I gave wounds,
And every wound a death. I may be bold
To justifie a truth, this very sword
Of mine slew more than any twain besides:
And, which is not the least of all my glorie,
When he, this young man, hand to hand in fight,
Was by the General of the Venetians,
And such as were his retinue, unhors'd,
I stept between, and rescu'd him my self,
Or horses hoo^s had trampled him to dirt;
And whilst he was re-mounting, I maintain'd
The combate with the gallant General,
Till having taken breath, he throng'd before me,
Renew'd the sight, and with a fatal blow,
Stole both that honour from me, and his life
From him, whom I before my self alone,
Had more than full three quarters kill'd: a man
Well worthy only by this hand to have dy'd,
Not by a Boys weak push: I talk too much,
But 'tis a fault of age: If to bring home
Long peace, long victorie even to your Capitol;
If to secure your Kingdom, wives, and children,
Your lives and liberties; if to renown
Your honours through the world, to six your names,
Like Blazing stars admir'd, and fear'd by all
That have but heard of Candy, or a Cretan,
Be to deserve the approvement of my man hood,
Then thus much have I done: what more, examine
The annals of my life; and then consider
What I have been, and am. Lords I have said.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: With reverence to the Senate, is it lawfull,
Without your Customes breach, to say a word?

speeches.speaker: Pos.
verse: Say on my Lord Gonzalo.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: I have heard,
And with no little wonder, such high deeds
Of Chival^ie discours'd, that I confess,
I do not think the Worthies while they liv'd
All nine, deserv'd as much applause, or memorie,
As this one: But who can do ought to gain
The crown of honour from him, must be somewhat
More than a man; you tread a dangerous path,
Yet I shall hear you gladly: for believe me,
Thus much let me profess, in honours cause,
I would not to my Father, nor my King,
(My Countries Father) yield: if you transcend
What we have heard, I can but only say,
That Miracles are yet in use. I fear
I have offended.

speeches.speaker: Porp.
verse: You have spoken nobly.
Antinous use your priviledge.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Princely Fathers,
E're I begin, one suit I have to make,
'Tis just, and honourable.

speeches.speaker: Porp. Poss.
verse: Speak, and have it.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: That you would please the souldiers might all stand
Together by their General.

speeches.speaker: Poss.
verse: 'Tis granted.
All fall to yonder side: Go on, Antinous.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I shall be brief and plain: all what my Father
(This Countries Patron) hath discours'd, is true.
Fellows in Arms: speak you, is't true?

speeches.speaker: Sol.
verse: True, true.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: It follows, that the blaze of my performance
Took light from what I saw him do: and thus
A City (though the flame be much more dreadfull)
May from a little spark be set on fire;
Of all what I have done, I shall give instance
Only in three main proofs of my desert.
First I sought out (but through how many dangers
My Lords judge ye) the chief, the great Commander,
The head of that huge body, whose proud weight
Our Land shrunk under, him I found and fought with,
Fought with, and slew. Fellows in Arms, speak you,
Is't true or not?

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: True, true.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: When he was faln,
The hearts of all our adversaries
Began to quail, till young Fernando, son
To the last Duke of Venice gather'd head,
And soon renew'd the field, by whose example
The bold Venetians doubling strength and courage
Had got the better of the day; our men
Supposing that their adversaries grew
Like Hydra's head, recoyle, and 'gan to flye:
I follow'd them; and what I said, they know;
The summe on't is; I call'd them back, new rankt them;
Led on, they follow'd, shrunk not tell the end:
Fellows in Arms is't true, or no?

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: True, true.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Lastly, to finish all, there was but one,
The only great exploit; which was to take
Fernando prisoner, and that hand to hand
In single sight I did: my self without
The help of any arm, save the arm of Heaven.
Speak Souldiers, is it true, or no?

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: Antinous, Antinous.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Behold my prisoner, Fathers.

speeches.speaker: Fern.
verse: This one man
Ruin'd our Army, and hath glorifi'd
Crete in her robes of mightiness and conquest.

speeches.speaker: Pos.
verse: We need not use long circumstance of words,
Antinous thou art conquerer: the Senate,
The souldiers, and thy valour have pronounc'd it.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: Antinous, Antinous.

speeches.speaker: Porp.
verse: Make thy demand.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Please ye (my Lords) give leave
That I may part.

speeches.speaker: Pos.
verse: No Cassilane, the Court
Should therein be dishonour'd, do not imagin
We prize your presence at so slight a rate.
Demand, Antinous.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Thus (my Lords) to witness
How far I am from arrogance, or thinking
I am more valiant, though more favour'd
Than my most matchless father, my demand is,
That for a lasting memorie of his name,
His deeds, his real, nay his royal worth,
You set up in your Capitol in Brass
My Fathers Statue, there to stand for ever
A Monument and Trophy of his victories,
With this Inscription to succeeding ages,
Great Cassilanes, Patron of Candy's Peace,
Perpetual Triumpher.

speeches.speaker: Por. Pos.
verse: It is granted. What more?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: No more.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: How Boy?

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: Thou art immortal,
Both for thy Son-like pietie, and beauties
Of an unconquer'd minde.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: My Prisoner, Lords,
To your more sacred wisedoms I surrender:
Fit you his ransom; half whereof I give
For largess to the Souldiers: the other half
To the erection of this monument.

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: Ambitious villain.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: Thou art all un-imitable.
My Lords, to work a certain peace for Candy
With Venice, use Fernando like a Prince;
His ransom I'le disburse what e're it be:
Yet you may stay him with you, till conditions
Of amitie shall be concluded on:
Are ye content?

speeches.speaker: Porp.
verse: We are, and ever rest
Both friends and debters to your nobleness.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: Souldiers attend me in the Market-place,
I'le thither send your largess.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: Antinous, Antinous.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: I have a sute too, Lords.

speeches.speaker: Porp. Pos.
verse: Propose it, 'tis yours, if fit and just.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Let not my services,
My being forty years a drudge, a pack-horse
To you, and to the State, be branded now
With Ignominy ne're to be forgotten:
Rear me no Monument, unless you mean
To have me fam'd a Coward, and be stamp'd so.

speeches.speaker: Pos.
verse: We understand you not.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Proud boy, thou dost,
And Tyrant like insult'st upon my shame.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Sir, Heaven can tell, and my integrity,
What I did, was but only to inforce
The Senates gratitude. I now acknowledge it.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Observe it Fathers, how this haughty boy
Grows cunning in his envy of mine honours:
He knows no mention can of me be made,
But that it ever likewise must be told,
How I by him was master'd; and for surety
That all succeeding times may so report it,
He would have my dishonour, and his Triumphs
Ingrav'd in Brass: hence, hence proceeds the falshood
O^ his insinuating piety.
Thou art no child of mine: thee and thy bloud.
Here in the Capitol, before the Senate,
I utterly renounce: So thrift and fate
Confirm me; henceforth never see my face,
Be, as thou art, a villain to thy Father.
Lords I must crave your leaves: come, come Arcanes.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: Here's a strange high-born spirit.

speeches.speaker: Pos.
verse: 'Tis but heat
Of suddain present rage; I dare assure
Antinous of his favour.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I not doubt it,
He is both a good man, and a good Father.
I shall attend your Lordships.

speeches.speaker: Poss.
verse: Do Antinous.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: Yes: feast thy Triumphs
With applause and pleasures.

speeches.speaker: Por. Poss.
verse: Lead on.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I utterly renounce—'Twas so?
Was't not, my Decius?

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Pish, you know, my Lord,
Old men are cholerick.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: And lastly parted
With, never henceforth see my face: O me,
How have I lost a Father? Such a Father?
Such a one Decius! I am miserable,
Beyond expression.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Fie, how unbecoming
This shews upon your day of same?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: O mischief!
I must no more come near him; that I know,
And am assur'd on't.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Say you do not?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: True:
Put case I do not: what is Candy then
To lost Antinous? Malta, I resolve
To end my dayes in thee.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: How's that?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I'le trie
All humble means of being reconcil'd,
Which if deny'd, then I may justly say,
This day has prov'd my worst: Decius, my worst,

speeches.speaker: Gasp.
verse: NOw to what you have heard; as no man can
Better than I, give you her Character;
For I have been both nurs'd, and train'd up to
Her petulant humours, and been glad to bear them,
Her Brother, my late Master, did no less:
Strong apprehensions of her beauty hath
Made her believe that she is more than woman:
And as there did not want those flatterers
'Bout the worlds Conquerour, to make him think,
And did perswade him that he was a god;
So there be those base flies, that will not stick
To buzze into her ears she is an Angel,
And that the food she feeds on is Ambrosia.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: She should not touch it then, 'tis Poets fare.

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: I may take leave to say, she may as well
Determine of her self to be a goddess,
With lesser flatterie than he a god:
For she does conquer more, although not farther.
Every one looks on her, dyes in despair,
And would be glad to do it actually,
To have the next age tell how worthily,
And what good cause he had to perish so:
Here beauty is superlative, she knows it,
And knowing it, thinks no man can deserve,
But ought to perish, and to dye for her:
Many great Princes for her love have languish'd,
And given themselves a willing sacrifice,
Proud to have ended so: And now there is
A Prince so madded in his own passions,
That he forgets the Royaltie he was born to,
And deems it happiness to be her slave.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: You talk as if you meant to winde me in,
And make me of the number.

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: Sir, mistake me not, the service that I owe ye
Shall plead for me: I tell you what she is,
What she expects, and what she will effect,
Unless you be the miracle of men,
That come with a purpose to behold,
And goe away your self.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: I thank you, I will do it: But pray resolve me,
How is she stor'd with wit?

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: As with beauty,
Infinite, and more to be admired at,
Than medled with.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: And walks her tongue the same gate with her feet?

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: Much beyond: what e're her heart thinks, she utters:
And so boldly, so readily, as you would judge
It penn'd and studied.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: She comes.

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: I must leave you then,
But my best wishes shall remain with you.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: Still I must thank you.
This is the most passionate,
Most pitifull Prince,
Who in the Caldron of affections,
Looks as he had been par-boy'ld.

speeches.speaker: Ph l
verse: If I offend with too much loving you,
It is a fault that I must still commit,
To make your mercy shine the more on me.

speeches.speaker: Erot.
verse: You are the self-same creature you condemn,
Or else you durst not follow me with hope
That I can pity you, who am so far
From granting any comfort in this kind,
That you and all men else shall perish first:
I will live free and single, till I find
Something above a man to equal me;
Put all your brave Heroes into one,
Your Kings and Emperours, and let him come
In person of a man, and I should scorn him:
Must, and will scorn him.
The god of love himself hath lost his eyes,
His Bow and Torch extinguish'd, and the Poets
That made him first a god, have lost their fire
Since I appear'd, and from my eyes must steal it.
This I dare speak; and let me see the man,
Now I have spoke it, that doth, dare deny;
Nay, not believe it.

speeches.speaker: Mo.
verse: He is mad that does not.

speeches.speaker: Erot.
verse: Have not all the nations of the Earth heard of me?
Most come to see me, and seeing me, return'd
Full of my praises? teaching their Chroniclers
To make their Stories perfect? for where the name,
Merely the word of fair Erota stands,
It is a lasting History to time,
Begetting admiration in the men,
And in my own Sex envie: which glorie's lost,
When I shall stick my beautie in a cloud,
And clearly shine through it.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: This woman's in the altitudes, and he must be
A good Astrologer shall know her Zodiack.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: For any man to think
Himself an able purchaser of you,
But in the bargain there must be declar'd
Infinite bounty: otherwise I vow,
By all that's excellent and gracious in you,
I would untenant every hope lodg'd in me,
And yield my self up loves, or your own Martyr.

speeches.speaker: Erot.
verse: So you shall please us.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: O you cannot be
So heavenly, and so absolute in all things,
And yet retain such cruel tyranny.

speeches.speaker: Erot.
verse: I can, I do, I will.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: She is in her
Moods, and her Tenses: I'le Grammer with you,
And make a trial how I can decline you:
By your leave (great Lady.)

speeches.speaker: Erot.
verse: What are you?

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: A man, a good man, that's a wealthy;
A Proper man, and a proud man too; one
That understands himself, and knows, unless
It be your self, no woman on the Universe deserves him.
Nay, Lady, I must tell you too withal,
I may make doubt of that, unless you paint
With better judgement next day than on this;
For (plain I must be with you) 'tis a dull Fucus.

speeches.speaker: Erot.
verse: Knows any one here what this fellow is?

speeches.speaker: Atten.
verse: He is of Venice (Madam) a great Magnifico,
And gracious with the Senate.

speeches.speaker: Erot.
verse: Let him keep then among them; what makes he here?
Here's state enough where I am: here's a do—
You, tell him, if he have ought with us, let him
Look lower, and give it in Petition.

speeches.speaker: Mo.
verse: Mighty Magnifico, my Mistris bid me tell you,
If you have ought with her, you must look lower,
And yield it in Petition.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: Here is for thee a Ducket.

speeches.speaker: Mon.
verse: You say well Sir, take your own course.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: I will not grace you
(Lady) so much as take you by the hand;
But when I shall vouchsafe to touch your lip,
It shall be through your Court a holy-day
Proclaimed for so high favour.

speeches.speaker: Erot.
verse: This is some
Great mans Jester: Sirrah, begon, here is
No place to fool in.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: Where are the fools you talk of?
I do keep two.

speeches.speaker: Erot.
verse: No question of it: for
In your self you do maintain an hundred.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: And besides them I keep a noble train,
Statists, and men of action: my purse is large and deep,
Beyond the reach of riot to draw drie:
Fortune did vie with Nature, to bestow
(When I was born) her bountie equally:
'Tis not amiss you turn your eyes from me;
For should you stand and gaze me in the face,
You perish would, like Semele by Jove:
In Venice at this instant there do lye
No less than threescore Ladies in their graves,
And in their Beds five hundred for my love.

speeches.speaker: Mo.
verse: You lie more than they; yet it becomes him bravel;
Would I could walk and talk so? I'le endeavour it.
