speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Shew him a glass; that false face has betrai'd me:
That base heart wrought me—

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Be more sweetly angry;
I wrong'd ye fair?

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Away with your foul flatteries:
They are too gross: but that I dare be angry,
And with as great a god as Caesar is,
To shew how poorly I respect his memory,
I would not speak to ye.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Pray ye undoe this riddle,
And tell me how I have vext ye?

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Let me think first
Whether I may put on a Patience
That will with honour suffer me: know, I hate ye,
Let that begin the story: Now I'le tell ye.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: But do it milder: In a noble Lady,
Softness of spirit, and a sober nature,
That moves like summer winds, cool, and blows sweetness;
Shews blessed like her self.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: And that great blessedness
You first reap'd of me: till you taught my nature
Like a rude storm to talk aloud, and thunder,
Sleep was not gentler than my soul, and stiller;
You had the Spring of my affections:
And my fair fruits I gave you leave to taste of:
You must expect the winter of mine anger:
You flung me oft, before the Court disgrac'd me,
When in the pride I appear'd of all my beauty,
Appear'd your Mistress; took into your eyes
The common-strumpet love of hated lucre,
Courted with covetous heart, the slave of nature,
Gave all your thoughts to gold, that men of glory,
And minds adorn'd with noble love, would kick at:
Souldiers of royal mark, scorn such base purchase:
Beauty and honour are the marks they shoot at;
I spake to ye then; I courted ye, and woo'd ye:
Call'd ye dear Caesar, hung about ye tenderly:
Was proud to appear your friend.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: You have mistaken me.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: But neither Eye, nor Favour, not a Smile
Was I blessed back with; but shook off rudely,
And, as ye had been sold to sordid infamy,
You fell before the Images of treasure,
And in your soul you worship'd: I stood slighted,
Forgotten and contemn'd; my soft embraces,
And those sweet kisses you call'd Elyzium,
As letters writ in sand, no more remembred:
The name and glory of your Cleopatra
Laugh'd at, and made a story to your Captains,
Shall I endure?

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: You are deceiv'd in all this,
Upon my life you are, 'tis your much tenderness.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: No, no, I love not that way; you ar ecozen'd:
I love with as much ambition as a Conquerour,
And where I love, will triumph.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: So you shall:
My heart shall be the Chariot that shall bear ye,
All I have won shall wait upon ye: By the gods
The bravery of this womans mind, has fired me:
Dear Mistress shall I but this night? —

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: How Caesar?
Have I let slip a second vanity
That gives thee hope?

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: You shall be absolute,
And Reign alone as Queen: you shall be any thing.

speeches.speaker: Cleo
verse: Make me a maid again, and then I'le hear thee;
Examine all thy art of War, to do that;
And if thou find'st it possible, I'le love thee:
Till when, farewel, unthankfull.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Stay.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: I will not.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: I command.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Command, and goe without, Sir.
I do command thee be my slave for ever,
And vex while I laugh at thee.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Thus low, beauty.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: It is too late; when I have found thee absolute,
The man that Fame reports thee, and to me,
May be I shall think better. Farewel Conquerour.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: She mocks me too: I will enjoy her Beauty:
I will not be deni'd; I'le force my longing.
Love is best pleas'd, when roundly we compel him,
And as he is imperious, so will I be.
Stay fool, and be advis'd: that dulls the appetite,
Takes off the strength and sweetness of delight.
By Heaven she is a miracle, I must use
A handsom way to win: how now; what fear
Dwells in your faces? you look all distracted.

speeches.speaker: Sceva.
verse: If it be fear, 'tis fear of your undoing,
Not of our selves: fear of your poor declining:
Our lives and deaths are equall benefits,
And we make louder prayers to dye nobly,
Than to live high, and wantonly: whilst you are secure here,
And offer Hecatombs of lazie kisses
To the lewd god of love, and cowardize,
And most lasciciously dye in delights,
You are begirt with the fierce Alexandrians.

speeches.speaker: Dol.
verse: The spawn of Egypt flow about your Palace,
Arm'd all: and ready to assault.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Led on
By the false and base Photinus and his Ministers;
No stirring out; no peeping through a loop-hole,
But straight saluted with an armed Dart.

speeches.speaker: Sce.
verse: No parley: they are deaf to all but danger,
They swear they will fley us, and then dry our Quarters:
A ra^her of a salt lover, is such a Shooing-horn:
Can you kiss away this conspiracy, and set us free?
Or will the Giant god of love fight for ye?
Will his fierce war-like bow kill a Cock-sparrow?
Bring out the Lady, she can quel this mutiny:
And with her powerfull looks strike awe into them:
S^e can destroy, and build again the City,
Your Goddesses have mighty gifts: shew 'em her fair brests,
The impregnable Bulworks of proud Love, and let 'em
Begin their battery there: she will laugh at 'em;
They are not above a hundred thousand, Sir.
A mist, a mist, that when her Eyes break out,
Her powerfull radiant eyes, and shake their flashes,
Will flye before her heats.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Begirt with Villains?

speeches.speaker: Sce.
verse: They come to play you, and your Love a Huntsup.
You were told what this same whorson wenching, long agoe would come to:
You are taken napping now: has not a Souldier,
A time to kiss his friend, and a time to consider,
But he must lye still digging, like a Pioneer,
Making of mines, and burying of his honour there?
'Twere good you would think —

speeches.speaker: Dol.
verse: And time too, or you will find else
A harder task, than Courting a coy Beauty.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Look out and then believe.

speeches.speaker: Sce.
verse: No, no, hang danger:
Take me provoking broth, and then goe to her:
Goe to your Love, and let her feel your valour;
Charge her whole body, when the sword's in your throat (Sir,)
You may cry, Caesar, and see if that will help ye.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: I'le be my self again, and meet their furies,
Meet, and consume their mischiefs: make some shift, Sceva,
To recover the Fleet, and bring me up two Legions,
And you shall see me, how I'le break like thunder
Amongst these beds of slimy Eeles, and scatter 'em.

speeches.speaker: Sce.
verse: Now ye speak sense I'le put my life to the hazard,
Before I goe, No more of this warm Lady,
She will spoil your sword-hand.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Goe: come, let's to Counsel
How to prevent, and then to execute.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sold.
verse: Did ye see this Penitence?

speeches.speaker: 2 Sold.
verse: Yes: I saw, and heard it.

speeches.speaker: 3 Sold.
verse: And I too: look'd upon him, and observ'd it,
He's the strangest Septinius now—

speeches.speaker: 1 Sold.
verse: I heard he was altered,
And had given away his Gold to honest uses:
Cry'd monstrously.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sold.
verse: He cryes abundantly:
He is blind almost with weeping.

speeches.speaker: 3 Sold.
verse: 'Tis most wonderfull
That a hard hearted man, and an old Souldier
Should have so much kind moisture: when his Mother dy'd
He laugh'd aloud, and made the wickedst Ballads—

speeches.speaker: 1 Sold.
verse: 'Tis like enough: he never lov'd his Parents;
Nor can I blame him, for they ne'r lov'd him.
His Mother dream'd before she was deliver'd
That she was brought abed with a Buzzard, and ever after
She whistl'd him up to th'world: his brave clothes too
He has flung away, and goes like one of us now:
Walks with his hands in's pockets, poor and sorrowfull,
And gives the best instructions. —

speeches.speaker: 2 Sold.
verse: And tells stories
Of honest and good people that were honour'd,
And how they were remembred: and runs mad
If he but hear of any ungratefull person,
A bloudy, or betraying man —

speeches.speaker: 3 Sold.
verse: If it be possible
That an Arch-Villain may ever be recovered,
This penitent Rascal will put hard: 'twere worth our labour
To see him once again.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sold.
verse: He spares us that labour,
For here he comes.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: —Bless ye my honest friends,
Bless ye from base unworthy men; come not near me,
For I am yet too taking for your company.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sold.
verse: Did I not tell ye?

speeches.speaker: 2 Sold.
verse: What book's that?

speeches.speaker: 1 Sold.
verse: No doubt
Some excellent Salve for a sore heart: are you
Septinius, that base knave, that betray'd Pompey?

speeches.speaker: Sep
verse: I was, and am; unless your honest thoughts
Will look upon my penitence, and save me,
I must be ^ver Villain: O good Souldiers
You that have Roman hearts, take heed of falsehood:
Take heed of blood; take heed of soul ingratitude.
The Gods have scarce a mercy for those mischiefs,
Take heed of pride, 'twas that that brought me to it.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sol.
verse: This fellow would make a rare speech at the gallows.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sol.
verse: 'Tis very fit he were hang'd to edifie us:

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: Let all your thoughts be humble, and obedient,
Love your Commanders, honour them that seed ye:
Pray, that ye may be strong in honesty
As in the use of arms; Labour, and diligently
To keep your hearts from ease, and her base issues,
Pride, and ambitious wantonness, those spoil'd me.
Rather lose all your limbs, than the least honesty,
You are never lame indeed, till loss of credit
Benumb ye through: Scarrs, and those maims of honour
Are memorable crutches, that shall bear
When you are dead, your noble names to Eternity.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sol.
verse: I cry.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sol.
verse: And so do I.

speeches.speaker: 3 Sol.
verse: An excellent villain.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sol.
verse: A more sweet pious knave I never heard yet.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sol.
verse: He was happie he was Rascal, to come to this.
Who's this? a Priest?

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: O stay, most holy Sir!
And by the Gods of Egypt, I conjure ye,
(Isis, and great Osiris) pity me,
Pity a loaden man, and tell me truly
With what most humble Sacrifice I may
Wash off my sin, and appease the powers that hate me?
Take from my heart those thousand thousand furies,
That restless gnaw upon my life, and save me.
Orestes bloody hands fell on his Mother,
Yet, at the holy altar he was pardon'd.

speeches.speaker: Ach.
verse: Orestes out of madness did his murther,
And therefore he found grace: thou (worst of all men)
Out of cold blood, and hope of gain, base lucre,
Slew'st thine own Feeder: come not near the altar,
Nor with thy reeking hands pollute the Sacrifice,
Thou art markt for shame eternal.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: Look all on me,
And let me be a story left to time
Of blood and Infamy, how base and ugly
Ingratitude appears, with all her profits,
How monstrous my hop'd grace, at Court? good souldiers
Let neither flattery, nor the witching sound
Of high and soft preferment, touch your goodness:
To be valiant, old, and honest, O what blessedness—

speeches.speaker: 1 Sold.
verse: Dost thou want any thing?

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: Nothing but your prayers.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sol.
verse: Be thus, and let the blind Priest do his worst,
We have gods as well as they, and they will hear us.

speeches.speaker: 3 Sol.
verse: Come, cry no more: thou hast wep't out twenty
Pompeys.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: So penitent?

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: It seems so.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Yet for all this
We must employ him.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sol.
verse: These are the arm'd Souldier leaders:
Away: and let's toth' Fort, we shall be snapt else.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: How now? why thus? what cause of this dejection?

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Why dost thou weep?

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: Pray leave me, you have ruin'd me,
You have made me a famous Villain.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Does that touch thee?

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: He will be hard to win: he feels his lewdness.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: He must be won, or we shall want our right hand.
This fellow dares, and knows, and must be heartned.
Art thou so poor to blench at what thou hast done?
Is Conscience a comrade for an old Soldier?

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: It is not that: it may be some disgrace
That he takes heavily; and would be cherish'd,
Septinius ever scorn'd to shew such weakness.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: Let me alone; I am not for your purpose,
I am now a new man.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: We have new affairs for thee,
Those that would raise thy head.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: I would 'twere off,
And in your bellies for the love you bear me.
I'le be no more Knave: I have stings enough
Already in my breast.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Thou shalt be noble:
And who dares think then that thou art not honest?

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Thou shalt command in Chief, all our strong forces
And if thou serv'st an use, must not all justifie it?

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: I am Rogue enough.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Thou wilt be more, and baser:
A poor Rogue is all Rogues: open to all shames:
Nothing to shadow him: dost thou think crying
Can keep thee from the censure of the Multitude?
Or to be kneeling at the altar save thee?
'Tis poor and servile:
Wert thou thine own Sacrifice
'Twould seem so low, people would spit the fire out.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Keep thy self glorious still, though ne're so stain'd,
And that will lessen it, if not work it out.
To goe complaining thus, and thus repenting
Like a poor Girl that had betrai'd her maidend-head—

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: I'le stop mine ears.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Will shew so in a Souldier,
So simply, and so ridiculously, so tamely—

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: If people would believe thee, 'twere some honesty,
And for thy penitence would not laugh at thee
(As sure they will) and beat thee for thy poverty:
If they would allow thy foolery, there were some hope.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: My foolery?

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Nay, more than that, thy misery,
Thy monstrous misery.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: He begins to hearken:
Thy misery so great, men will not bury thee.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: That this were true!

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Why does this conquering Caesar
Labour through the worlds deep Seas of toyls and troubles,
Dangers, and desperate hopes? to repent afterwards?
Why does he slaughter thousands in a Battel,
And whip his Country with the sword? to cry for't?
Thou killd'st great Pompey; he'l kill all his kindred,
And justifie it: nay raise up Trophies to it.
When thou hear'st him repent, (he's held most holy too)
And cry for doing daily bloody murthers,
Take thou example, and go ask forgiveness,
Call up the thing thou nam'st thy conscience,
And let it work: then 'twill seem well Septinius.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: He does all this.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Yes: and is honour'd for it;
Nay call'd the honour'd Caesar, so maist thou be:
Thou wert born as near a Crown as he.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: He was poor.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: And desperate bloody tricks got him this credit.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: I am afraid you will once more—

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Help to raise thee:
Off with thy pining black, it dulls a Souldier,
And put on resolution like a man,
A noble Fate waits on thee.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: I now feel
My self returning Rascal speedily.
O that I had the power—

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Thou shalt have all:
And do all through thy power, men shall admire thee,
And the vices of Septinius shall turn vertues.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: Off: off: thou must off: off my cowardize,
Puling repentance off.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Now thou speakst nobly.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: Off my dejected looks: and welcom impudence:
My daring shall be Deity, to save me:
Give me instructions, and put action on me:
A glorious cause upon my swords point, Gentlemen,
And let my wit, and valour work: you will raise me,
And make me out-dare all my miseries?

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: All this, and all thy wishes.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: Use me then,
Womanish fear farewell: I'le never melt more,
Lead on, to some great thing, to wake my spirit:
I cut the Cedar Pompey, and I'le fell
This huge Oak Caesar too.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Now thou singst sweetly:
And Ptolomy shall crown thee for thy service.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: He's well wrought: put him on apace for cooling.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: THE tumult still encreases.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: O my fortune!
My lustfull folly rather! but 'tis well,
And worthily I am made a bondmans prey,
That after all my glorious victories,
In which I pass'd so many Seas of dangers,
When all the Elements conspir'd against me,
Would yield up the dominion of this head
To any mortal power: so blind and stupid,
To trust these base Egyptians, that proclaim'd
Their perjuries, in noble Pompeys death,
And yet that could not warn me.

speeches.speaker: Dol.
verse: Be still Caesar,
Who ever lov'd to exercise his fate,
Where danger look't most dreadful.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: If you fall,
Fall not alone: let the King and his Sister
^e buried in your ruines: on my life
They both are guilty: reason may assure you
Photinus nor Achillas durst attempt you,
Or shake one Dart, or sword, aim'd at your safety,
Without their warrant.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: For the young King I know not
How he may be misled; but for his Sister
(Unequall'd Cleopatra) 'twere a kind
Of blasphemy to doubt her: ugly treason
Durst never dwell in such a glorious building,
Nor can so clear and great a spirit, as hers is,
Admit of falsehood.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Let us seize on him then:
And leave her to her fortune.

speeches.speaker: Ptol.
verse: If he have power
Use it to your security, and let
His honesty acquit him: if he be false
It is too great an honour he should dye
By your victorious hand.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: He comes: and I
Shall do as I find cause.

speeches.speaker: Ptol.
verse: Let not great Caesar
Impute the breach of hospitality,
To you (my guest) to me; I am contemn'd,
And my rebellious subjects lift their hands
Against my head: and would they aim'd no farther,
Provided that I fell a sacrifice
To gain you safety: that this is not feign'd,
The boldness of my innocence may confirm you:
Had I been privy to their bloody plot,
I now had led them on, and given fair gloss
To their bad cause, by being present with them:
But I that yet taste of the punishment,
In being false to Pompey, will not make
A second fault to Caesar uncompel'd
With such as have not yet shook off obedience,
I yield my self to you, and will take part
In all your dangers.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: This pleads your excuse,
And I receive it.

speeches.speaker: Ach.
verse: If they have any touch
Of justice, or religion, I will use
The authority of our Gods, to call them back
From their bad purpose.

speeches.speaker: Apo.
verse: This part of the palace
Is yet defensible: we may make it good,
Till your powers rescue us.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Caesar besieg'd?
O stain to my great actions: 'twas my custom,
An Army routed, as my feet had wings
To be first in the chase: nor walls, nor Bulworks
Could guard those that escap'd the Battels fury
From this strong Arm; and I to be enclos'd?
My heart! my heart! but 'tis necessity,
To which the Gods must yield, and I obey,
'Till I redeem it by some glorious way.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: There's no retiring now, we are broke in:
The deed past hope of pardon: if we prosper
'Twill be stil'd lawfull, and we shall give laws
To those that now command us: stop not at
Or loyalty, or duty: bold ambition,
To dare and power to do, gave the first difference
Between the King, and subject, Caesars Motto,
Aut Caesar aut Nihil, each of us must claim,
And use it as our own.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: The deed is bloody
If we conclude in Ptolomies death.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: The better,
The globe of Empire must be so manur'd.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: Rome, that from Romulus first took her name,
Had her walls water'd with a Crimson showr
Drain'd from a Brothers heart: nor was she rais'd
To this prodigious height, that overlooks
Three full parts of the Earth, that pay her tribute,
But by enlarging of her marrow bounds
By the Sack of Neighbour Cities, not made hers
Till they were Cemented with the Blood of those
That did possess 'em: Caesar, Ptolomy,
(Now I am steel'd) to me are empty names
Esteem'd as Pompeys was.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Well said Septinius,
Thou now art right again.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: But what course take we
For the Princess Cleopatra?

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Let her live
A while to make us sport: she shall authorize
Our undertakings to the ignorant people,
As if what we do were by her command:
But our triumvirat Government once confirm'd,
She bears her Brother, company that's my Province;
Leave me to work her.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: I will undertake
For Ptolomy.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: Caesar shall be my task,
And as in Pompey I began a name
I'le perfect it in Caesar.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: 'Tis resolv'd then,
We'll force our passage.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: See, they do appear
As they desir'd a Parley.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: I am proud yet
I have brought 'em to capitulate.

speeches.speaker: Ptol.
verse: Now, Photinus?

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Now, Ptolomy?

speeches.speaker: Ptol.
verse: No addition?

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: We are equal,
Though Caesars name were put into the scale,
In which our worth is weigh'd.

speeches.speaker: C^s.
verse: Presumptuous Villain,
Upon what grounds hast thou presum'd to raise
Thy servile hand against the King, or me,
That have a greater name?

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: On those, by which
Thou didst presume to pass the Rubicon
Against the Laws of Rome; and at the name
Of Traitor smile; as thou didst when Marcellus,
The Consul, with the Senates full consent
Pronounc'd thee for an Enemy to thy Country,
Yet thou wentst on, and thy rebellious Cause
Was crown'd with fair success: Why should we fear then?
Think on that, Caesar.

speeches.speaker: Caes.
verse: O the gods! be brav'd thus,
And be compell'd to bear this from a Slave
That would not brook Great Pompey his Superiour?

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Thy glories now have toucht the highest point,
And must descend.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Despair, and think we stand
The Champions of Rome, to wreak her wrongs,
Upon whose liberty thou hast set thy foot.

speeches.speaker: Sept.
verse: And that the Ghosts of all those noble Romans
That by thy Sword fell in this Civil War
Expect revenge.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Dar'st thou speak, and remember
There was a Pompey?

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: There is no hope to 'scape us:
If that against the odds we have upon you
You dare come forth, and fight, receive the honour
To dye like Romans, if ye faint, resolve
To starve like Wretches; I disdain to change
Another syllable with you.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Let us dye nobly;
And rather fall upon each others Sword
Than come into these Villains hands.

speeches.speaker: Caes.
verse: That Fortune,
Which to this hour hath been a Friend to Caesar,
Though for a while she cloath her Brow with frowns,
Will smile again upon me: who will pay her,
Or sacrifice, or Vows, if she forsake
Her best of works in me? or suffer him,
Whom with a strong hand she hath led triumphant
Through the whole western world, and Rome acknowledg'd
Her Soveraign Lord, to end in gloriously
A life admir'd by all? The threatned danger
Must by a way more horrid be avoided,
And I will run the hazard; Fire the Palace,
And the rich Magazines that neighbour it,
In which the Wealth of Egypt is contain'd:
Start not, it shall be so; that while the people
Labour in quenching the ensuing flames,
Like Caesar, with this handful of my friends
Through Fire, and Swords I force a passage to
My conquering Legions. King, if thou dar'd follow
VVhere Caesar leads, or live or dye a Free man;
If not, stay here a Bond man to thy Slave,
And dead, he thought unworthy of a Grave.

speeches.speaker: Sept.
verse: I feel my resolution melts again
And that I am not Knave alone, but fool,
In all my purposes. The Devil, Photinus,
Employs me as a Property, and grown useless
Will shake me off again; he told me so
When I kill'd Pompey; nor can I hope better,
When Caesar is dispatch'd; Services done
For such as only study their own ends,
Too great to be rewarded, are return'd
With deadly hate; I learn'd this Principle
In his own School, yet still he fools me, well;
And yet he trusts me: Since I in my nature
Was fashion'd to be false, wherefore should I
That kill'd my General, and a Roman, one
To whom I ow'd all nourishments of life,
Be true to an Egyptian? To save Caesar,
And turn Photinus's plots on his own head,
As it is in my power, redeem my credit,
And live to lye and swear again in fashion,
Oh, 'twere a master-piece? ha! — me Caesar,
How's he got off!

speeches.speaker: Caes.
verse: The fire has took,
And shews the City like a second Troy,
The Navy too is scorch'd, the people greedy
To save their Wealth and Houses, whilst their Souldiers
Make spoil of all; only Achillas's Troops
Make good their Guard, break through them, we are safe;
I'll lead you like a Thunder-bolt.

speeches.speaker: Sept.
verse: Stay, Caesar.

speeches.speaker: Caes.
verse: Who's this? the Dog, Septimius?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Cut his throat.

speeches.speaker: Dol.
verse: You bark'd but now, fawn you so soon?

speeches.speaker: Sept.
verse: O hear me,
What I'll deliver is for Caesars safety,
For all your good.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Good from a mouth like thine,
That never belch'd but blasphemy, and treason on Fes^ days

speeches.speaker: Sept.
verse: I am an altered man, altered indeed,
And will give you cause to say I am a Roman.

speeches.speaker: Dol.
verse: Rogue, I grant thee.

speeches.speaker: Sept.
verse: Trust me, I'll make the passage smooth, and easie
For your escape.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I'll trust the Devil sooner,
And make a safer Bargain.

speeches.speaker: Sept.
verse: I am trusted
With all Photinus's secrets.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: There's no doubt then
Thou wilt be false.

speeches.speaker: Sept.
verse: Still to be true to you.

speeches.speaker: Dol.
verse: And very likely.

speeches.speaker: Caes.
verse: Be brief, the means?

speeches.speaker: Sept.
verse: Thus, Caesar,
To me alone, but bound by terrible oaths
Not to discover it, he hath reveal'd
A dismal Vault, whose dreadful mouth does open
A mile beyond the City: in this Cave
Lye but two hours conceal'd.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: If you believe him,
He'll bury us alive.

speeches.speaker: Dol.
verse: I'll flye in the Air first,

speeches.speaker: Sept.
verse: Then in the dead of night I'll bring you back
Into a private room, where you shall find
Photinus, and Achillas, and the rest
Of their Commanders close at Council.

speeches.speaker: Caes.
verse: Good, what follows?

speeches.speaker: Sept.
verse: Fall me fairly on their throats,
Their heads cut off and shorn, the multitude
Will easily disperse.

speeches.speaker: Caes.
verse: O Devil! away with him;
Not true to Friend nor Enemy? Caesar scorns
To find his safety, or revenge his wrongs
So base a way; or owe the means of life
To such a leprous Traytor. I have towr'd
For Victory like a Faulcon in the Clouds,
Nor dig'd for't like a Mole; our Swords and Cause
Make way for us, and that it may appear
We took a noble Course, and hate base Treason,
Some Souldiers that would merit Caesar's favour,
Hang him on yonder Turret, and then follow
The lane this Sword makes for you.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sold.
verse: Here's a Belt,
Though I dye for it I'll use it.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sold.
verse: 'Tis too good
To truss a Cur in.

speeches.speaker: Sept.
verse: Save me, here's Gold.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sold.
verse: If Rome
Were offered for thy ransom, it could not help thee.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sold.
verse: Hang not an arse.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sold.
verse: Goad him on with thy Sword;
Thou dost deserve a worser end, and may
All such conclude so, that their friends betray.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: We are lost.

speeches.speaker: Eros.
verse: Undone.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Confusion, Fire, and Swords,
And fury in the Souldiers face more horrid
Circle us round.

speeches.speaker: Eros.
verse: The Kings Command they laugh at,
And jeer at Caesars threats.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: My Brother seiz'd on
By the Roman, as thought guilty of the tumult,
And forc'd to bear him company, as mark'd out
For his protection or revenge.

speeches.speaker: Eros.
verse: They have broke
Into my Cabinet; my Trunks are ransack'd.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: I have lost my jewels too: but that's the least:
The barbarous Rascals, against all humanity,
Or sense of pity, have kill'd my little Dog,
And broke my Monkeys Chain.

speeches.speaker: Eros.
verse: They rifled me:
But that I could endure, would they proceed no further.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: O my Sister!

speeches.speaker: Eros.
verse: My Queen, my Mistress!

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Can you stand unmov'd
VVhen the Earth-quake of Rebellion shakes the City,
And the Court trembles?

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Yes, Arsino,
And with a Masculine Constancy deride
Fortunes worst malice, as a Servant to
My Vertues, not a Mistress; then we forsake
The strong Fort of our selves, when we once yield,
Or shrink at her assaults; I am still my self,
And though disrob'd of Soveraignty, and ravish'd
Of ceremonious duty, that attends it,
Nay, grant they had slav'd my Body, my free mind
Like to the Palm-tree walling fruitful Nile,
Shall grow up straighter and enlarge it self
'Spight of the envious weight that loads it with:
Think of thy Birth (Arsino) common burdens
Fit common Shoulders; teach the multitude
By suffering nobly what they fear to touch at;
The greatness of thy mind does soar a pitch,
Their dim eyes (darkened by their narrow souls)
Cannot arrive at.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: I am new created,
And owe this second being to you (best Sister)
For now I feel you have infus'd into me
Part of your fortitude.

speeches.speaker: Eros.
verse: I still am fearful;
I dare not tell a lie; you that were born
Daughters and Sisters unto Kings, may nourish
Great thoughts, which I, that am your humble handmaid
Must not presume to rival.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Yet (my Eros)
Though thou hast profited nothing by observing
The whole cou se of my life, learn in my death,
Though not to equal, yet to imitate
Thy fearless Mistress.

speeches.speaker: Eros.
verse: O, a man in Arms!
His Weapon drawn too?

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Though upon the point
Death sate, I'll meet it, and outdare the danger.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Keep the Watch strong, and guard the passage sure
That leads unto the Sea.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: What Sea of rudeness
Breaks in upon us? or what Subjects Breath
Dare raise a storm, when we command a calm?

Are Duty and Obedience sled ^
^aven?
And in their room ambition an^ p^i^e
Sent into Egypt? That Face speaks thee, Photinus,
A thing thy Mother brought into the World;
My Brother's and my Slave: but thy behaviour,
Oppos'd to that, an insolent intruder
Upon that Soveraignty thou shouldst bow to.
If in the Gulph of base ingratitude,
All loyalty to Ptolomy the King
Be swallowed up, remember who I am,
Whose Daughter and whose Sister; or suppose
That is forgot too; let the name of Caesar
Which Nations quake at, stop the desperate madness
From running headlong on to thy Confusion.
Throw from thee quickly those rebellious Arms,
And let me read submission in thine Eyes;
Thy wrongs to us we will not only pardon,
But be a ready advocate to plead fo^ thee
To Caesar, and my Brother.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Plead my Pardon?
To you I bow, but scorn as much to stoop thus
To Ptolomy or Caesar, Nay, the gods,
As to put off the figure of a man,
And change my ^ssence with a sensual Beast;
All my designs, my counsels, and dark ends
Were aim'd to purchase you.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: How durst thou, being
The scorn of baseness, nourish such a thought?

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: They that have power are royal; and those base
That live at the devotion of another.
VVhat birth gave Ptolomy, or fortune Caesar,
By Engines fashion'd in this Protean Anvil
I have made mine; and only stoop at you,
Whom I would still preserve free to command me;
For Cesar's frowns, they are below my thoughts,
And but in these fair Eyes I still have read
The story of a supream Monarchy,
To which all hearts with mine gladly pay tribute,
Photinus's Name had long since been as great
As Ptolomies e'r was, or Caesars is,
This made me as a weaker tye to unloose
The knot of Loyalty, that chain'd my freedom,
And slight the fear that Caesars threats might cause,
That I and they might see no Sun appear
But Cleopatra in the Egyptian Sphear.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: O Giant-like Ambition! marryed to
Cymmerian darkness! inconsiderate Fool,
(Though flatter'd with self-love) could'st thou believe,
Were all Crowns on the Earth made into one,
And that (by Kings) set on thy head; all Scepters,
Within thy grasp, and laid down at my feet,
I would vouchsafe a kiss to a no man?
A guelded Eunuch?

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Fairest, that makes for me,
And shews it is no sensual appetite,
But true love to the greatness of thy Spirit,
That when that you are mine shall yield me pleasures,
Hymen, though blessing a new married Pair
Shall blush to think on, and our certain issue,
The glorious splendor of dread Majesty,
Whose beams shall dazel Rome, and aw the world,
My wants in that kind others shall supply,
And I give way to it.

speeches.speaker: C eo.
verse:
Bas^ tha^
^y Birth;

Can there be ge^
^nd hear this, and no thunder
Rain thee into the Earth?

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: They are asleep,
And cannot hear thee;
Or with open Eyes,
Did Jove look on us, I would laugh and swear
That his artillery is cloy'd by me:
Or if that they have power to hurt, his Bolts
Are in my hand.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Most impious!

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: They are dreams,
Religious Fools shake at: yet to assure thee,
If Nemesis, that scourges pride and scorn,
Be any thing but a name, she lives in me;
For by my self (an oath to me more dreadful
Than Stix is to your gods) weak Ptolomy dead,
And Caesar (both being in my toil) remov'd,
The poorest Rascals that are in my Camp
Shall in my presence qu^nc^ their lustful heat
In thee, and young Arsino, while I laugh
To hear you howl in vain:
I deride those gods,
That you think can protect you.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: To prevent thee,
In that I am the Mistress of my Fate;
So hope I of my sister to confirm it.
I spit at thee, and scorn thee.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: I will tame
That haughty courage, and make thee stoop too.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Never,
I was born to command, and will dye so.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: The King dead? this is a fair entrance to
Our future happiness.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Oh my dear Brother!

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Weep not, Arsino, common women do so,
Nor lose a tear for him, it cannot help him;
But study to dye nobly.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Caesar fled!
'Tis deadly aconite to my cold heart,
It choaks my vital Spirits: where was your care?
Did the Guards sleep?

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: He rowz'd them with his Sword;
We talk of Mars, but I am sure his Courage
Admits of no comparison but it self,
And (as inspir'd by him) his following friends
With such a confidence as young Eagles prey
Under the large wing of their fiercer Dam,
Brake through our Troops and scatter'd them, he went on
But still pursu'd by us, when on the sudden,
He turn'd his head, and from his Eyes slew terrour;
Which strook in us no less fear and amazement,
Than if we had encounter'd with the lightning
Hurl'd from Jove's cloudy Brow.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: 'Twas like my Caesar

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: We faln back, he made on, and as out fear
Had parted from us with his dreadful looks,
Again we follow'd, but got near the Sea;
On which his Navy anchor'd; in one hand
Holding a Scroll he had above the waves,
And in the other grasping fast his Sword,
As it had been a Trident forg'd by Vulcan
To calm the raging Ocean, he made away
As if he had been Neptune, his friends like
So many Tritons follow'd, their bold shouts
Yielding a chearful musick; we showr'd darts
Upon them, but in vain, they reach'd their ships
And in their safety we are sunk; for Caesar
Prepares for War.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: How fell the King?

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Unable
To follow Caesar, he was trod to death
By the Pursuers, and with him the Priest
Of Isis, good Achoreus.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: May the Earth
Lye gently on their ashes.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: I feel now,
That there are powers above us; and that 'tis not
Within the searching policies of man
To alter their decrees.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: I laugh at thee;
Where are thy threats now, Fool, thy scoffs and scorns
Against the gods? I see calamity
Is the best Mistress of Religion,
And can convert an Atheist.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: O they come,
Mountains fall on me! O for him to dye
That plac'd his Heaven on Earth, is an assurance
Of his descent to Hell; where shall I hide me?
The greatest daring to a man dishonest,
Is but a Bastard Courage, ever fainting.

speeches.speaker: Caes.
verse: Look on your Caesar; banish fear, my fairest,
You now are safe.

speeches.speaker: Sce.
verse: By Venus, not a kiss
Till our work be done; the Traitors once dispatch'd
To it, and we'll cry aim.

speeches.speaker: Caes.
verse: I will be speedy.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Farewel again, Arsino; how now, Eros?
Ever faint-hearted?

speeches.speaker: Eros.
verse: But that I am assur'd,
Your Excellency can command the General,
I fear the Souldiers, for they look as if
They would be nibling too.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: He is all honour,
Nor do I now repent me of my favours,
Nor can I think that Nature e'r made a Woman
That in her prime deserv'd him.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: He's come back,
Pursue no further; curb the Souldiers fury.

speeches.speaker: Caes.
verse: See (beauteous Mistris) their accursed heads
That did conspire against us.

speeches.speaker: Sce.
verse: Furies plague 'em,
They had too fair an end to dye like Souldiers,
Pompey fell by the Sword, the Cross or Halter
Should have dispatch'd them.

speeches.speaker: Caes.
verse: All is but death, good Sceva,
Be therefore satisfied: and now my dearest,
Look upon Caesar, as he still appear'd
A Conquerour, and this unfortunate King
Entomb'd with honour, we'll to Rome, where Caesar
Will shew he can give Kingdoms; for the Senate,
(Thy Brother dead) shall willingly decree
The Crown of Egypt (that was his) to thee.

plays.play_title: THE Little French Lawyer. A COMEDY.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: DIsswade me not.

speeches.speaker: Clere.
verse: It will breed a brawl.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: I care not, I wear a Sword.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: And wear discretion with it,
Or cast it off, let that direct your arm,
'Tis madness else, not valour, and more base
Than to receive a wrong.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Why would you have me
Sit down with a disgrace, and thank the doer?
We are not Stoicks, and that passive courage
Is only now commendable in Lackies,
Peasants, and Tradesmen, not in men of rank
And qualitie, as I am.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Do not cherish
That daring vice, for which the whole age suffers.
The blood of our bold youth, that heretofore
Was spent in honourable action,
Or to defend, or to enlarge the Kingdom,
For the honour of our Country, and our Prince,
Pours it self out with prodigal expence
Upon our Mothers lap, the Earth that bred us
For every trifle; and these private Duells,
Which had their first original from the Frcenh
(And for which, to this day, we are justly censured)
Are banisht from all civil Governments:
Scarce three in Venice, in as many years;
In Forence, they are rarer, and in all
The fair Dominions of the Spanish King,
They are never heard of: Nay, those neighbour Countries,
Which gladly imitate our other follies,
And come at a dear rate to buy them of us,
Begin now to detest them.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Will you end yet —

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: And I have heard that some of our late Kings,
For the lie, wearing of a Mistris favour,
A cheat at Cards or Dice, and such like causes,
Have lost as many gallant Gentlemen,
As might have met the great Turk in the field
With confidence of a glorious Victorie,
And shall we then —

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: No more, for shame no more,
Are you become a Patron too? 'tis a new one,
No more on't, burn't, give it to some Orator,
To help him to enlarge his exercise,
With such a one it might do well, and profit
The Curat of the Parish, but for Cleremont,
The bold, and undertaking Cleremont,
To talk thus to his friend, his friend that knows him,
Dinant that knows his Cleremont, is absurd,
And meer Apocrypha.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Why, what know you of me?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Why if thou hast forgot thy self, I'le tell thee,
And not look back, to speak of what thou wert
At fifteen, for at those years I have heard
Thou wast flesh'd, and enter'd bravely.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Well Sir, well.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: But yesterday, thou wast the common second,
Of all that only knew thee, thou hadst bills
Set up on every post, to give thee notice
Where any difference was, and who were parties;
And as to save the charges of the Law
Poor men seek arbitrators, thou wert chosen
By such as knew thee not, to compound quarrels:
But thou wert so delighted with the sport,
That if there were no just cause, thou wouldst make one,
Or be engag'd thy self: This goodly calling
Thou hast followed five and twenty years, and studied
The Criticismes of contentions, and art thou
In so few hours transform'd? certain this night
Thou hast had strange dreams, or rather visions.

speeches.speaker: Clere.
verse: Yes, Sir,
I have seen fools, and fighters, chain'd together,
And the Fighters had the upper hand, and whipt first,
The poor Sots laughing at 'em: What I have been
It skils not, what I will be is resolv'd on.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Why then you'l fight no more?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Such is my purpose.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: On no occasion?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: There you stagger me.
Some kind of wrongs there are which flesh and blood
Cannot endure.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Thou wouldst not willingly
Live a protested coward, or be call'd one?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Words are but words.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Nor wouldst thou take a blow?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Not from my friend, though drunk, and from an enemy
I think much less.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: There's some hope of thee left then,
Wouldst thou hear me behind my back disgrac'd?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Do you think I am a rogue? they that should do it
Had better been born dumb.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Or in thy presence
See me o'recharg'd with odds?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I'd fall my self first.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Would'st thou endure thy Mistris be taken from thee,
And thou sit quiet?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: There you touch my honour,
No French-man can endure that.

speeches.speaker: Dic.
verse: Pl — upon thee,

Why dost thou talk of Peace then? that da^s^
^llet
Nothing, or in thy self, or in thy friend
That is unmanly?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: That I grant, I cannot:
But I'le not quarrel with this Gentleman
For wearing slammel Breeches, or this Gamester
For playing a thousand pounds, that owes me nothing;
For this mans taking up a common Wench
In raggs, and lowsie, then maintaining her
Caroach'd in cloth of Tissue, nor five hundred
Of such like toyes, that at no part concern me;
Marry, where my honour, o^ my friend is questioned,
I have a Sword, and I think I may use it
To the cutting of a Rascals throat, or so,
Like a good Christian.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Thou art of a fine Religion,
And rather than we'l make a Schism in friendship
I will be of it: But to be serious,
Thou art acquainted with my tedious love suit
To fair Lamira?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Too well Sir, and remember
Your presents, courtship, that's too good a name,
Your slave-like services, your morning musique;
Your walking three hours in the rain at midnight,
To see her at her window, sometimes laugh'd at,
Sometimes admitted, and vouchsaf'd to kiss
Her glove, her skirt, nay, I have heard, her slippers,
How then you triumph'd?
Here was love forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: These follies I deny not,
Such a contemptible thing my dotage made me,
But my reward for this —

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: As you deserv'd,
For he that makes a goddess of a Puppet,
Merits no other recompence.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: This day friend,
For thou art so —

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I am no flatterer.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: This proud, ingratefull she, is married to
Lame Champernel.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I know him, he has been
As tall a Sea-man, and has thriv'd as well by't,
The loss of a legg and an arm deducted, as any
That ever put from Marseilles: you are tame,
Pl—on't, it mads me; if it were my case,
I should kill all the family.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Yet but now
You did preach patience.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I then came from confession,
And 'twas enjoyn'd me three hours for a penance,
To be a peaceable man, and to talk like one,
But now, all else being pardon'd, I begin
On a new Tally, Foot do any thing,
I'le second you.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: I would not willingly
Make red, my yet white conscience, yet I purpose
In the open street, as they come from the Temple,
(For this way they must pass,) to speak my wrongs,
And do it boldly.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Were thy tongue a Cannon,
I would stand by thee, boy, they come, upon 'em.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Observe a little first.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: This is fine fidling.

COme away, bring on the Bride
And place her by her Lovers side:
Yo^ fair troop of Maids attend her,
Pure and holy thoughts befriend her.
Blush, and wish, you Virgins all,
Many such fair nights may fall.

Chorus.
Hymen, fill the house with joy,
All thy sacred fires employ:
Bless the Bed with holy love,
Now fair orb of Beauty move.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Stand by, for I'le be heard.

speeches.speaker: Verta.
verse: This is strange rudeness.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: 'Tis courtship, ballanced with injuries,
You all look pale with guilt, but I will dy
Your cheeks with blushes, if in your scar'd veins
There yet remain so much of honest blood
To make the colour; first to ye my Lord,
The Father of this Bride, whom you have sent
Alive into her grave.

speeches.speaker: Champ.
verse: How? to her grave?

speeches.speaker: Dina.
verse: Be patient Sir, I'le speak of you anon
You that allow'd me liberal access,
To make my way with service, and approv'd of
My birth, my person, years, and no base fortune:
You that are rich, and but in this held wise too,
That as a Father should have look'd upon
Your Daughter in a husband, and aim'd more
At what her youth, and heat of blood requir'd
In lawfull pleasures, than the parting from
Your Crowns to pay her dowr: you that already
Have one foot in the grave, yet study profit,
As if you were assur'd to live here ever;
What poor end had you, in this choice? in what
Deserve I your contempt? my house, and honours
At all parts equal yours, my lame as fair,
And not to praise my self, the City ranks me
In the first file of her most hopefull Gentry:
But Champernel is rich, and needs a nurse,
And not your gold: and add to that, ^e's old too,
His whole estate in likelihood to descend
Upon your Family; Here was providence,
I grant, but in a Nobleman base thrift:
No Merchants nay, no Pirats, sell for Bondmen
Their Country-men, but you, a Gentleman,
To save a little gold, have sold your Daughter
To worse than slaverie.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: This was spoke home indeed.

speeches.speaker: Beau.
verse: Sir, I shall take some other time to tell you,
That this harsh language was delivered to
An old man, but my Father.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: At your pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Proceed in your design, let me alone,
To answer him, or any man.

speeches.speaker: Verd.
verse: You presume
Too much upon your name, but may be couzen'd.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: But for you, most unmindfull of my service,
For now I may upbraid you, and with honour,
Since all is lost, and yet I am a gainer,
In being deliver'd from a torment in you,
For such you must have been, you to whom nature
Gave with a liberal hand most excellent form,
Your education, language, and discourse,
And judgement to distinguish, when you shall
With feeling sorrow understand how wretched
And miserable you have made your self,
And but your self have nothing to accuse,
Can you with hope from any beg compassion?
But you will say, you serv'd your Fathers pleasure,
Forgetting that unjust commands of Parents
Are not to be obey'd, or that you are rich,
And that to wealth all pleasure else are servants,
Yet but consider, how this wealth was purchas'd,
'Twill trouble the possession.

speeches.speaker: Champ.
verse: You Sir know
I got it, and with honour.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: But from whom?
Remember that, and how: you'l come indeed
To houses bravely furnish'd, but demanding
Where it was bought, this Souldier will not lie,
But answer truly, this rich cloth of Arras
I made my prize in such a Ship, this Plate
Was my share in another; these fair Jewels,
Coming a shore, I got in such a Village,
The Maid, or Matron kill'd, from whom they were ravish'd,
The Wines you drink are guilty too, for this,
This Candie Wine, three Merchants were undone,
These Suckets break as many more: in brief,
All you shall wear, or touch, or see, is purchas'd
By lawless force, and you but revel in
The tears, and grones of such as were the owners.

speeches.speaker: Champ.
verse: 'Tis false, most basely false.

speeches.speaker: Verta.
verse: Let losers talk.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Lastly, those joyes, those best of joyes, which Hymen
Freely bestows on such, that come to tye
The sacred knot he blesses, won unto it
By equal love, and mutual affection,
Not blindly led with the desire of riches,
Most miserable you shall never taste of.
^his Marriage night you'l meet a Widows bed,
Or failing of those pleasures all Brides look for,
Sin in your wish it were so.

speeches.speaker: Champ.
verse: Thou art a Villain,
A base, malitious slanderer.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Strike him.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: No, he is not worth a blow.

speeches.speaker: Champ.
verse: O that I had thee
In some close vault, that only would yield room
To me to use my Sword, to thee no hope
To run away, I would make thee on thy knees,
Bite out the tongue that wrong'd me.

speeches.speaker: Verta.
verse: Pray you have patience.

speeches.speaker: Lamira.
verse: This day I am to be your Soveraign,
Let me command you.

speeches.speaker: Champ.
verse: I am lost with rage,
And know not what I am my self, nor you:
Away, dare such as you, that love the smoke
Of peace more than the fire of glorious War,
And like unprofitable drones, feed on
Your grand^ires labours, that, as I am now,
Were gathering Bees, and fill'd their Hive, this Country
With brave triumphant spoils, censure our actions?
You object my prizes to me, had you seen
The horrour of a Sea-sight, with what danger
I made them mine; the fire I fearless fought in,
And quench'd it in mine enemies blood, which straight
Like oyle pour'd out on't, made it burn anew;
My Deck blown up, with noise enough to mock
The lowdest thunder, and the desperate fools
That Boorded me, sent, to desie the tempests
That were against me, to the angrie Sea,
Frighted with men thrown o're; no victory,
But in despight of the four Elements,
The Fire, the Air, the Sea, and sands hid in it
To be atchiev'd, you would confess poor men,
(Though hopeless, such an honourable way
To get or wealth, or honour) in your selves
He that through all these dreadfull passages
Pursued and overtook them, unaffrighted,
Deserves reward, and not to have it stil'd
By the base name of theft.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: This is the Courtship,
That you must look for, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: 'Twill do well,
When nothing can be done, to spend the night with:
Your tongue is sound good Lord, and I could wish
For this young Ladyes sake this leg, this arm,
And there is something else, I will not name,
(Though 'tis the only thing that must content her)
Had the same vigour.

speeches.speaker: Champ.
verse: You shall buy these scoffs
With your best blood: help me once noble anger,
(Nay stir not, I alone must right my self)
And with one leg transport me, to correct
These scandalous praters: O that noble wounds
Should hinder just revenge? D'ye jear me too?
I got these, not as you do, your diseases
In Brothels, or with riotous abuse
Of wine in Taverns; I have one leg shot,
One arm disabled, and am honour'd more,
By losing them, as I did, in the face
Of a brave enemy, than if they were
As when I put to Sea; you are French-men only,
In that you have been laied, and cur'd, goe to:
You mock my leg, but every bone about you,
Makes you good Almanack-makers, to foretell
What weather we shall have.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Put up your Sword,

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Or turn it to a Crutch, there't may by usefull,
And live on the relation to your Wife
Of what a brave man you were once.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: And tell her,
What a fine vertue 'tis in a young Lady
To give an old man pap.

speeches.speaker: Cer.
verse: Or hire a Surgeon
To teach her to roul up your broken limbs.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: To make a Pultess, and endure the scent
Of oils, and nasty Plasters.

speeches.speaker: Verta.
verse: Fie Sir, fie,
You that have stood all dangers of all kinds, to
Yield to a Rivalls scoffe?

speeches.speaker: Lamira.
verse: Shed tears upon
Your Wedding day? this is unmanly Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Champ.
verse: They are tears of anger: O that I should live
To play the woman thus! All powerfull heaven,
Restore me, but one hour, that strength again,
That I had once, to chastise in these men
Their folies, and ill manners, and that done,
When you please, I'le yield up the fort of life,
And do it gladly.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: We ha' the better of him,
We ha' made him cry.

speeches.speaker: Verdo.
verse: You shall have satisfaction.
And I will do it nobly, or disclaim me.

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: I say no more, you have a Brother, Sister,
This is your wedding day, we are in the street,
And howsoever they forget their honour,
'Tis fit I lose not mine, by their example.

speeches.speaker: Vert.
verse: If there be Laws in Paris, look to answer
This insolent affront.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: You that live by them,
Study 'em for heavens sake; for my part I know not
Nor care not what they are. Is their ought else
That you would say?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Nothing, I have my ends.
Lamira weeps, I have said too much I fear;
So dearly once I lov'd her, that I cannot
Endure to see her tears.

speeches.speaker: Champ.
verse: See you perform it,
And do it like my Nephew.

speeches.speaker: Verdo.
verse: If I fail in't
Ne'r know me more, Cousin Beaupre.

speeches.speaker: Champ.
verse: Repent not
What thou hast done, my life, thou shalt not find
I am decrepit; in my love and service,
I will be young, and constant, and believe me,
For thou shalt find it true, in s^orn of all
The scandals th^se rude men have thrown upon me
I'le meet thy pleasures with a young mans ardour,
And in all circumstances of a Husband,
Perform my part.

speeches.speaker: Lamira.
verse: Good Sir, I am your s^rv^nt,
And 'tis too late now, i^ I did repent,
(Which as I am a virgin yet, I do not)
To undoe the ^not, that by the Church is tyed.
Only I would beseech ye, as you have
A good opinion of me, and my vertues,
For so you have pleas'd to stile my innocent weakness,
That what hath pass'd be w^en Dinant and me,
Or what now in your hearing he hath spoken,
Beget not doubts, or fears.

speeches.speaker: Champ.
verse: I apprehend you,
You think I will be jealous; as I live
Thou art mistaken sweet; and to confirm it
Discourse with whom thou wilt, ride where thou wilt,
Feast whom thou wilt, as often as thou wilt,
For I will have no other guards upon thee
Than thine own thoughts.

speeches.speaker: Lamira.
verse: I'le use this liberty
With moderation Sir.

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: I am resolv'd.
Steal off, I'le follow you.

speeches.speaker: Champ.
verse: Come Sir, you droop;
Till you find cause, which I shall never give,
Dislike not of your Son in Law.

speeches.speaker: Verta
verse: Sir, you teach me
The language I should use; I am most happy
In being so near you.

speeches.speaker: Lamira.
verse: O my fears! good nurse
Follow my Brother unobserv'd, and learn
Which way he takes.

speeches.speaker: Nurs.
verse: I will be carefull Madam.

speeches.speaker: Champ.
verse: Between us complements are superfluous,
On Gentlemen, th' affront we have met here
We'l think upon hereafter, 'twere unfit
To cherish any thought to breed unrest,
Or to our selves, or to our Nuptial feast.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: We shall have sport, ne'r fear't.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: What sport I prethee?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Why we must fight, I know it, and I long ^or't,
It was apparent in the fiery eye
Of young Verdo^e, Beaupre look'd pale and shook too,
Familiar signs of anger. They are both brave fellows
Tri'd and approv'd, and I am proud to encounter
With men, from whom no honour can be lost;
They will play up to a man, and set him off.
When e're I go to the field, heaven keep me from
The meeting of an unflesh'd youth or, Coward,
The first, to get a name, comes on too hot,
The Coward is so swift in giving ground,
There is no overtaking him without
A hunting Nag, well breath'd too.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: All this while,
You ne'r think on the danger.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Why 'tis no more
Than meeting of a dozen friends at Supper,
And drinking hard; mischief comes there unlook'd for,
I am sure as suddain, and strikes home as often,
For this we are prepar'd.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Lamira Loves
Her Brother Beaupre dearly.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: What of that?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: And should he call me to account for what
But now I spake, nor can I with mine honour
Recant my words, that little hope is left me,
E're to enjoy what (next to Heaven) I long for,
Is taken from me.

speeches.speaker: C^er.
verse: Why what can you hope for,
She being now married?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Oh my Cleremont,
To you all secrets of my heart lye open,
And I rest most secure that whatsoe're
I lo^k up there, is as a private thought,
And will no farther wrong me. I am a French-man,
And for the greater part we are born Courtiers,
She is a woman, and however yet
No heat of service had the power to melt
Her frozen Chastity, time and opportunitie
May work her to my ends, I confess ill ones,
And yet I must pursue 'em: now her marriage,
In probabilitie, will no way hurt,
But rather help me.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Sits the wind there? pray you tell me
How far off dwells your love from lust?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Too near,
But prethee chide me not.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Not I, goe on boy,
I have faults my self, and will not reprehend
A crime I am not free from: for her Marriage,
I do esteem it (and most batchellors are
Of my opinion) as a fair protection,
To play the wanton without loss of honour.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Would she make use of't so, I were most happy.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: No more of this, Judge now,
Whether I have the gift of prophecie.

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: Monsieur Dinant,
I am glad to find you, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: I am at your service.

speeches.speaker: Verd.
verse: Good Monsieur Cleremont, I have long wish'd
To be known better to you.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: My desires
Embrace your wishes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: Sir, I have ever
Esteem'd you truly noble, and profess
I should have been most proud, to have had the honour
To call you Brother, but my Fathers pleasure
Denied that happiness. I know no man lives,
That can command his passions, and therefore
Dare not condemn the late intemperate language
You were pleas'd to use to my Father and my Sister,
He's old and she a woman, I most sorrie
My honour does compel me to entreat you,
To do me the favour, with your sword to meet me
A mile without the Citie.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: You much honour me
In the demand, I'le gladly wait upon you.

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: O Sir you teach me what to say: the time?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: With the next Sun, if you think fit.

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: The place?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Near to the vineyard eastward from the Citie.

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: I like it well, this Gentleman if you please
Will keep me company.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: That is agreed on;
And in my friends behalf I will attend him.

speeches.speaker: Verd.
verse: You shall not miss my service.

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: Good day Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: At your Commandment.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Proud to be your servants.
I think there is no Nation under Heaven
That cut their enemies throats with complement,
And such fine tricks as we do: If you have
Any few Prayers to say, this night you may
Call 'em to mind and use 'em, for my self,
As I have little to lose, my care is less,
So till to morrow morning I bequeath you
To your devotions; and those paid, but use
That noble courage I have seen, and wo
Shall sight, as in a Castle.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Thou art all honour,
Thy resolution would steel a Coward,
And I most fortunate in such a Friend;
All tenderness and nice respect of woman
Be now far from me, reputation take
A full possession of my heart, and prove
Honour the first place holds, the second Love.

speeches.speaker: Lami.
verse: Sleeps my Lord still, Charlote?

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Not to be wak'd.
By your Ladiships cheerfull looks I well perceive
That this night the good Lord hath been
At an unusual service, and no wonder
If he rest after it.

speeches.speaker: Lamira.
verse: You are very bold.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Your Creature Madam, and when you are pleas'd
Sadness to me's a stranger, your good pardon
If I speak like a fool, I could have wisht
To have ta'ne your place to night, had bold Dinant
Your first and most obsequious servant tasted
Those delicates, which by his lethargie
As it appears, have cloy'd my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Lamira.
verse: No more.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: I am silenc'd, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Lamira.
verse: Saw you my nurse this morning?

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: No, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Lamira.
verse: I am full of fears.
Who's that?

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: She you enquir'd for.

speeches.speaker: Lamira.
verse: Bring her in, and leave me.
Now nurse what news?

speeches.speaker: Nurse.
verse: O Ladie dreadfull ones.
They are to fight this morning, there's no remedie.
I saw my Lord your Brother, and Verdone
Take horse as I came by.

speeches.speaker: Lamira.
verse: Where's Cleremont?

speeches.speaker: Nurse.
verse: I met him too, and mounted.

speeches.speaker: Lamira.
verse: Where's Dinant?

speeches.speaker: Nurse.
verse: There's all the hope, I have staid him with a trick,
If I have done well so.

speeches.speaker: Lamira.
verse: What trick?

speeches.speaker: Nurse.
verse: I told him,
Your Ladiship laid your command upon him,
To attend you presently, and to confirm it,
Gave him the ring he oft hath seen you wear,
That you bestowed on me: he waits without
Disguis'd, and if you have that power in him,
As I presume you have, it is in you
To stay or alter him.

speeches.speaker: Lamira.
verse: Have you learnt the place,
Where they are to encounter?

speeches.speaker: Nurse.
verse: Yes 'tis where
The Duke of Burgundie met Lewis th' eleventh.

speeches.speaker: Lamir.
verse: Enough, I will reward thee liberally,
Goe bring him in: full dear I loved Dinant,
While it was lawfull, but those fires are quench'd,
I being now anothers, truth forgive me
And let dissimulation be no crime,
Though most unwillingly I put it on
To guard a Brothers safetie.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Now your pleasure,
Though ill you have deserv'd it, you perceive
I am still your fool, and cannot but obey
What ever you command.

speeches.speaker: Lamira.
verse: You speak, as if
You did repent it, and 'tis not worth my thanks then,
But there has been a time, in which you would
Receive this as a favour.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Hope was left then
Of recompence.

speeches.speaker: Lamira.
verse: Why I am still Lamira,
And you Dinant, and 'tis yet in my power,
I dare not say I'le put it into act,
To reward your love and service.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: There's some comfort.

speeches.speaker: Lami.
verse: But think not that so low I prize my fame,
To give it up to any man that refuses
To buy it, or with danger of performance
Of what I shall enjoin him.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Name that danger
Be it of what horrid shape soever Ladie
Which I will shrink at; only at this instant
Be speedie in't.

speeches.speaker: Lamira.
verse: I'le put you to the trial:
You shall not light to day, do you start at that?
Not with my Brother, I have heard your difference,
Mine is no Helens beauty to be purchas'd
With blood, and so defended, if you look for
Favours from me, deserve them with obedience,
There's no way else to gain 'em.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: You command
What with mine honour I cannot obey
Which lies at pawn against it, and a friend
Equally dear as that, or life, engag'd,
Not for himself, but me.

speeches.speaker: Lamira.
verse: Why, foolish man,
Dare you solicite me to serve your lust,
In which not only I abuse my Lord,
My Father, and my family, but write whore,
Though not upon my forehead, in my conscience,
To be read hourly, and yet name your honour?
Yours suffers but in circumstance; mine in substance.
If you obey me, you part with some credit,
From whom? the giddy multitude; but mankind
Will censure me, and justly.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: I will lose,
What most I do desire, rather than hazard
So dear a friend, or write my self a coward,
'Tis better be no man.

speeches.speaker: Lamira.
verse: This will not do;
Why, I desire not, you should be a coward,
Nor do I weigh my Brothers life with yours,
Meet him, fight with him, do, and kill him fairly,
Let me not suffer for you, I am careless.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Suffer for me?

speeches.speaker: Lamira.
verse: For you, my kindness to you
Already brands me with a strumpets name.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: O that I knew the wretch!

speeches.speaker: Lamira.
verse: I will not name him,
Nor give you any Character to know him;
But if you dare, and instantly ride forth
At the west port of the City, and defend there
My reputation, against all you meet,
For two hours only, I'le not swear Dinant,
To satisfie, (though sure I think I shall)
What ever you desire, if you denie this,
Be desperate, for willingly, by this light,
I'le never see thee more.

speeches.speaker: Din
verse: Two hours, do you say?

speeches.speaker: Lamira.
verse: Only two hours.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: I were no Gentleman,
Should I make scruple of it; this favour arms me,
And boldly I'll perform it.

speeches.speaker: Lamira.
verse: I am glad on't.
This will prevent their meeting yet, and keep
My Brother safe, which was the mark I shot at.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I Am first i'th' field, that honour's gain'd of our side,
Pray Heaven I may get off as honourablie,
The hour is past, I wonder Dinant comes not,
This is the place, I cannot see him yet;
It is his quarel too that brought me hither,
And I ne'r knew him yet, but to his honour
A firm and worthy Friend, yet I see nothing,
Nor Horse nor man, 'twould vex me to be left here,
To th' mercy of two swords, and two approv'd ones.
I never knew him last.

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: You are well met Cleremont.

speeches.speaker: Verdo.
verse: You are a fair Gentleman, and love your friend Sir.
What are you ready? the time has overta'ne us.

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: And this you know the place.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: No Dinant yet?

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: We come not now to argue, but to do;
We wait you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: There's no time past yet Gentlemen,
We have day enough: is't possible he comes not?
You see I am ^ea^ here, and do but stay
Till my Friend come, walk but a turn or two,
'Twill not be long.

speeches.speaker: Verd
verse: We came to fight.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Ye shall ^ Gentlemen,
And fight enough, but a short turn or two,
I think I see him, set up your watch, we'l fight by it.

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: That is not he; we will not be deluded.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Am I bob'd thus? pray tak^ a pipe of tobacco,
Or sing but some new air; by that time, Gentlemen—

speeches.speaker: Verd.
verse: Come d^aw your Sword, you know the custome here Sir,
First come, first serv'd.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Though it be held a custom,
And practised so, I do not hold it honest;
What honour can you both win on me single?

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: Yield up your Sword then.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Yield my Sword? that's Hebrew;
I'le be first cut a pecies; hold but a while,
I'le take the next that comes.
You are an old Gentleman?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Yes indeed am I, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: And wear no Sword?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: I need none, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I would you did, and had one;
I want now such a foolish courtesie.
You see these Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: You want a second.
In good Faith Sir, I was never handsom at it,
I would you had my Son, but he's in Italy,
A proper Gentleman; you may do well gallants
If your quarrel be not capital, to have more mercy,
The Gentleman may do his Country—

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Now I beseech you, Sir,
If you dare not fight, do not stay to beg my pardon.
There lies your way.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Good morrow Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Verd.
verse: You see your fortune,
You had better yield your Sword.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Pray ye stay a little.
Upon mine honestie, you shall be fought with;
Well, Dinant, well, these wear swords and seem brave fellows.
As you are Gentlemen, one of you supply me.
I want a S^cond now to meet these gallants,
You know what honour is.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Sir you must pardon us,
We goe about the same work, you are ready for;
And must fight presently, else we were your servants.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: God speed you, and good day.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Am I thus Colted?

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: Come either yield —

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: As you are honest Gentlemen,
Stay but the next, and then I'le take my fortune,
And if I fight not like a man — Fy Dinant,
Cold now and treacherous.

speeches.speaker: La Writ.
verse: I understand your causes.
Yours about corn, yours about pins and glasses,
Will you make me mad, have I not all the parcells?
And his Petition too, about Bell-sounding?
Send in your witnesses, what will you have me do?
Will you have me break my heart? my brains are melted;
And tell your Master, as I am a Gentleman,
His Cause shall be the first, commend me to your Mistris,
And tell her, if there be an extraordinary feather,
And tall enough for her—I shall dispatch you too,
I know your cause, for transporting of Farthingales
Trouble me no more, I say again to you,
No more vexation: bid my wife send me some puddings;
I have a Cause to run through, requires puddings,
Puddings enough. Farewel.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: God speed you, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: Would he would take this fellow.

speeches.speaker: Verd.
verse: A rare Youth.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: If you be not hastie, Sir.

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: Yes, I am hastie,
Exceeding hastie, Sir, I am going to the Parliament,
You understand this bag, if you have any business
Depending there, be short, and let me hear it,
And pay your Fees.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: 'Faith, Sir, I have a business,
But it depends upon no Parliament.

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: I have no skill in't then.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I must desire you,
'Tis a Sword matter, Sir.

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: I am no Cutler,
I am an Advocate, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: How the thing looks?

speeches.speaker: Verd.
verse: When he brings him to sight.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Be not so hastie,
You wear a good Sword.

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: I know not that,
I never drew it yet, or whether it be a Sword —

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I must entreat you try, Sir, and bear a part
Against these Gentlemen, I want a second;
Ye seem a man, and 'tis a noble office.

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: I am a Lawyer, Sir, I am no fighter.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: You that breed quarels, Sir, know best to satisfie.

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: This is some sport yet.

speeches.speaker: Verd.
verse: If this fellow should fight.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: And for any thing I know, I am an arrant coward,
Do not trust me, I think I am a coward.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Try, try, you are mistaken: walk on Gentlemen,
The man shall follow presently.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Are ye mad Gentleman?
My business is within this half hour.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: That's all one,
We'll dispatch within this quarter, there in that bottom,
'Tis most convenient Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: Well, we'll wait, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Verd.
verse: Why this will be a comick fight, you'l follow.

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: As I am a true-man, I cannot fight.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Away, away,
I know you can: I like your modesty,
I know you will fight and so fight, with such metal,
And with such judgement meet your enemies fury;
I see it in your eye, Sir.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: I'le be hang'd then;

And I charge you in the Kings name, name more f^g^
^

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I charge you in the Kings name, play the man,
Which if you do not quickly, I begin with you,
I'le make you dance, do you see your fiddlestick?
Sweet Avocate thou shalt fight.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Stand farther Gentleman,
Or I'le give you such a dust o'th' chapps —

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Spoke bravely,
And like thy self, a noble Advocate:
Come to thy tools.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: I do not say I'le fight;

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I say thou shalt, and bravely.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: If I do fight;
I say, if I do, but do not depend upon't,
And yet I have a foolish itch upon me,
What shall become of my Writings?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Let 'em ly by,
They will not run away, man.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: I may be kill'd too,
And where are all my causes then? my business?
I will not fight, I cannot fight, my Causes—

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Thou shalt fight, if thou hadst a thousand causes,
Thou art a man to fight for any cause,
And carry it with honour.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Hum, say you so? if I should
Be such a coxcombe to prove valiant now —

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I know thou art most valiant.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Do you think so?
I am undone for ever, if it prove so,
I tell you that, my honest friend, forever;
For I shall ne're leave quarrelling.
How long must we fight? for I cannot stay,
Nor will not stay, I have business.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: We'l do't in a minute, in a moment.

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: Here will I hang my bag then, it may save my belly,
I never lov'd cold Iron there.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: You do wisely.

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: Help me to pluck my Sword out then, quickly, quickly,
'Thas not seen Sun these ten years.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: How it grumbles?
This Sword is vengeance angry.

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: Now I'le put my hat up,
And say my prayers as I goe; away boy,
If I be kill'd, remember the little Lawyer.

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: They are both come on, that may be a stubborn rascal,
Take you that ground,
I'le stay here, fight bravely.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: To't chearfully my boyes, you'l let's have far play,
None of your foyning tricks.

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: Come forward Monsieur;
What hast thou there? a pudding in thy belly?
I shall see what it holds.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Put your spoon home then:
Nay, since I must fight, have at you without wit, Sir:
God a mercy bagg.

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: Nothing but bumbast in ye?
The Rogue winks and fights.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Now your fine fencing, Sir:
Stand off, thou diest on point else,
I have it, I have it: yet further off:
I have his Sword.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Then keep it, be sure you keep it

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: I'le put it in my mouth else.
Stand further off yet, and stand quietly,
And look another way, or I'le be with you,
Is this all? I'le undertake within these two daies
To furnish any Cutler in this Kingdom.

speeches.speaker: Beau.
verse: Pox, what fortune's this? disarm'd by a pupp^e?
A snail? a Dog?

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: No more o' these words Gentleman,
Sweet Gentleman, no more, do not provoke me,
Go walk i'th' horse-fair; whistle Gentleman,
What must I do now?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Help me, I am almost breathless.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: With all my heart, there's a cold pye for you, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Thou strik'st me, fool.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Thou fool, stand further off then,
Deliver, deliver.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Hold fast.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: I never fail in't,
There's twelve pence, go buy you two leaden Daggers,
Have I done well?

speeches.speaker: C^er.
verse: Most like a Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Beau.
verse: And we two basely lost.

speeches.speaker: Verd.
verse: 'Tis but a fortune,
We shall yet find an hour.
