speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I shall be glad on't.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Where's my cloak, and my trinkets?
Or will you fight any longer, for a crash or two?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I am your noble friend, Sir.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: It may be so.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: What honour shall I do you,
For this great courtesie?

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: All I desire of ye,
Is to take the quarrel to your self, and let me hear no more on't,
I have no liking to't, 'tis a foolish matter,
And help me to put up my Sword.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Most willingly.
But I am bound to gratifie you, and I must not leave you.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: I tell you, I will not be gratified,
Nor I will hear no more on't: take the Swords too,
And do not anger me but leave me quietly.
For the matter of honour, 'tis at your own disposure,
And so, and so.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: This is a most rare Lawyer:
I am sure most valiant. Well Dinant, as you satisfie me,
I say no more: I am loaden like an Armorer.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: To be dispatcht upon a sleeveless errand?
To leave my friend engag'd, mine honour tainted?
These are trim things. I am set here like a Perdue,
To watch a fellow, that has wrong'd my Mistris,
A scurvy fellow that must pass this way,
But what this scurvy fellow is, or whence,
Or whether his name be William or John,
Or Anthony or Dick, or any thing, I know not;
A scurvy rascally fellow I must aim at,
And there's the office of an Asse flung on me.
S^re Cleremont has fought, but how come off,
And what the world shall think of me hereafter:
Well, woman, woman, I must look your rascals,
And lose my reputation: ye have a fine power over us.
These two long hours I have trotted here, and curiously
Survey'd all goers by, yet find no rascal,
Nor any face to quarel with:
What's that?
This is a rascally voice, sure it comes this way.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: He strook so hard, the Bason broke,
And Tarquin heard the sound.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: What Mister thing is this? let me survey it.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: And then he strook his neck in two.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: This may be a rascal, but 'tis a mad rascal,
What an Alphabet of faces he puts on?
Hey how it fences? if this should be the rogue,
At 'tis the likeliest rogue I see this day —

speeches.speaker: La-wr.
verse: Was euer man for Ladies sake? down, down.
And what are you good Sir? down, down, down, down.

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: What's that to you good Sir? down, down.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: A pox on you good Sir, down, down, down,
You with your Buckram bag, what make you here?
And from whence come you? I could fight with my shadow now.

speeches.speaker: La-wr.
verse: Thou fierce man that like Sir Lancelot dost appear,
I need not tell thee what I am, nor eke what I make here.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: This is a precious knave, stay, stay, good Tristram,
And let me ask thy mightiness a question,
Did ye never abuse a Lady?

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: Not; to abuse a Lady, is very hard, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Say you so, Sir?
Didst thou never abuse her honour?

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: Not; to abuse her honour, is impossible.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Certain this is the rascal: What's thy name?

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: My name is Cock o' two, use me respectively,
I will be Cock of three else.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: What's all this?
You say, you did abuse a Lady.

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: You ly.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: And that you wrong'd her honour.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: That's two lyes,
Speak suddenly, for I am full of business.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: What art thou, or what canst thou be, thou pea-goose,
That dar'st give me the ly thus? thou mak'st me wonder.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: And wonder on, till time make all things plain.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: You must not part so, Sir, art thou a Gentleman?

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: Ask those upon whose ruins I am mounted.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: This is some Cavellero Knight o'th' Sun.

speeches.speaker: La-wr.
verse: I tell thee I am as good a Gentleman as the Duke:
I have atchieved — goe follow thy business.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: But for this Lady, Sir —

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: Why, hang this Lady, Sir,
And the Lady Mother too, Sir, what have I to do with Ladies?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: 'Tis the little Lawyers voice: has he got my way?
It should be hereabouts.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Ye dry bisket rogue,
I will so swinge you for this blasphemie—
Have I found you out?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: That should be Dinants tongue too.

speeches.speaker: La-wr.
verse: And I defy thee do thy worst: O ho quoth Lancelot tho.
And that thou shalt know, I am a true Gentleman,
And speak according to the phrase triumphant;
Thy Lady is a scurvy Lady, and a shitten Lady,
And though I never heard of her, a debo^ed Lady,
And thou, a squire of low degree; will that content thee?
Dost thow way-lay me with Ladies? A pretty sword, Sir,
A very pretty sword, I have a great mind to't.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: You shall not lose your longing, rogue.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Hold, hold.
Hold Dinant, as thou art a Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: As much as you will, my hand is in now.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I am your friend, Sir: Dinant you draw your sword
Upon the Gentleman preserv'd your honour:
This was my second, and did back me nobly,
For shame forbear.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: I ask your mercy, Sir, and am your servant now.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: May we not fight then?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I am sure you shall not now.

speeches.speaker: La-wr.
verse: I am sorry for't, I am sure I'le stay no longer then,
Not a jot longer: are there any more on ye afore?
I will sing still, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: I look now you should chide me, and 'tis fit,
And with much bitterness express your anger,
I have deserv'd: yet when you know —.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I thank ye,
Do you think that the wrong you have off'red me,
The most unmanly wrong, unfriendly wrong—

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: I do confess —

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: That boyish sleight —

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Not so, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: That poor and base renouncing of your honour,
Can be allaied with words?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: I give you way still.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Coloured with smooth excuses? Was it a friends part,
A Gentlemans, a mans that wears a Sword,
And stands upon the point of reputation,
To hide his head then, when his honour call'd him?
Call'd him aloud, and led him to his fortune?
To halt and slip the coller? by my life,
I would have given my life I had never known thee,
Thou hast eaten Canker-like into my judgement
With this disgrace, thy whole life cannot heal again.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: This I can suffer too, I find it honest.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Can you pretend an excuse now may absolve you,
Or any thing like honest, to bring you off?
^ngage me like an Asse?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Will you but hear me?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Expose me like a Jade to tug, and hale through,
^augh'd at, and almost hooted? your disgraces
Invite mans Swords and angers to dispatch me.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: If you will be patient.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: And be abus'd still: But that I have call'd thee friend,
And to that name allow a Sanctuary,
You should hear further from me, I would not talk thus:
But hence forth stand upon your own bottom, Sir,
And b^a^ your own abuses, I scorn my sword
Should travel in so poor and empty quarrels.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Ha'you done yet? take your whole swing of anger,
I'le beat all with content.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Why were you absent?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: You know I am no Coward, you have seen that,
And therefore, out of ^ea^ forsook you not:
You know I am not false, of a treacherous nature,
Apt to betray my friend, I have fought for you too;
You know no business, that concern'd my state,
My kindred, or my life.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Where was the fault then?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: The honour of that Lady I adore,
Her credit, and her name: ye know she sent for me,
And with what haste.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: What was he that traduc'd?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: The man i'th' Moon, I think, hither I was sent,
But to what end —

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: This is a pretty slim slam.

speeches.speaker: O. La.
verse: I am glad I have met you Sir, I have been seeking,
And seeking every where.

speeches.speaker: C^.
verse: And now you have found him,
^clare what business, our Embassadour.

speeches.speaker: O Lady.
verse: What's that to ye good man s^outer? O Sir, my Lady.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: ^ thee no more of thy Lady, I have too much on't.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Let me have a little, speak to me.

speeches.speaker: O^ Lady.
verse: To you Sir?
'Tis more than time: All occasions set aside Sir,
Or whatsoever may be thought a business —

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: What then?

speeches.speaker: Ol^ Lady.
verse: Repair to me within this hour.

speeches.speaker: Cl^r.
verse: Where?

speeches.speaker: O. Lady.
verse: What's that to you? come you, Sir, when y'are sent for.

speeches.speaker: Cl^.
verse: God a m^y Mumpsinnes,
You may goe Dina^t, and follow this old Fairie,
Till you have lost your self, your friends, your credit,
And Hunt away your youth in rare adventures,
I can but gri^v^ I have known you.

speeches.speaker: Old Lady.
verse: Will ye goe Sir?
I come not often to you with these blessings,
You my believe that thing there, and repent it,
That do^ged thing.

speeches.speaker: C^.
verse: Peace tou^hwood.
I will not goe:
^ your Lady seek some fool to ^awn on her,
^ vp ^'d pupp^, to make sport with,

I ^av^
^ her mi^th too long, thus I shake from me

Th^
^ put on; thus her enchantments
^ like wind, no more her beauty—

speeches.speaker: Old Lady.
verse: Take heed Sir what you say.

speeches.speaker: C^.
verse: ^oe forward, Dinant.

speeches.speaker: D^
verse: The charms shot from her eyes —

speeches.speaker: Old Lady.
verse: Be wise.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Be Valiant.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: That tongue that tells fair tales to ^
Shall never rack me more.

speeches.speaker: Old Lady.
verse: Stay there.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Goe forward.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: I will now hear her, see her as a woman,
Survey her, and the power man has allow'd, Sir,
As I would do the course of common things,
Unmov'd, unstruck.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Hold there, and I forgive thee.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: She is not fair, and that that makes her proud,
Is not her own, our eyes bestow it on her,
To touch and kiss her is no blessedness,
A Sun-burnt Ethiops lip's as soft as her's.
Goe bid her stick some other triumph up,
And take into her favour some dull fool,
That has no pretious time to lose, no friends,
No honour, nor no life, like a bold Merchant,
A bold and banquerupt man, I have ventur'd all these,
And split my bottom: return this answer to her,
I am awake again and see her mischiefs,
And am not now, on every idle errand,
And new coyn'd anger, to be hurried,
And then despis'd again, I have forgot her.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: If this be true —

speeches.speaker: O. Lady.
verse: I am sorry, I have troubled you,
More sorrie, that my Lady has adventur'd
So great a favour in so weak a mind:
This hour you have refus'd that when you come to know it,
Will run you mad, and make you curse that fellow,
She is not fair, nor handsom, so I leave you.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Stay Lady, stay, but is there such a business?

speeches.speaker: O. Lady.
verse: You would break your neck 'twere yours.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: My back, you would say.

speeches.speaker: O. La.
verse: But play the friends part still, Sir, and undoe him,
'Tis a fair office.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: I have spoke too liberally.

speeches.speaker: O. Lady.
verse: I shall deliver what you say.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: You shall be hang'd first,
You would fain be prating now; take the man with ye^.

speeches.speaker: O. Lady.
verse: Not I, I have no power.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: You may goe Dinant.

speeches.speaker: O. Lady.
verse: 'Tis in's own will, I had no further charge, S^,
Than to tell him what I did, which if I had thought
It should have been receiv'd so —

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: 'Faith you may,
You do not know how far it may concern you.
If I perceiv'd any trick in't.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: 'Twill end there.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: 'Tis my fault then, there is an hour in fortune,
That must be still observ'd: you think I'le chide you,
When things must be, nay see, an he will hold his head up?
Would such a Lady send, with such a charge too?
Say she has plaid the fool, play the fool with her again,
The great fool, the greater still the better.
He shall goe with you woman.

speeches.speaker: Old Lady.
verse: As it please him,
I know the way alone else.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Where is your Lady?

speeches.speaker: O. Lady.
verse: I shall direct you quickly.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Well, I'le goe,
But what her wrongs will give me leave to say.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: We'll leave that to your selves: I shall hear from you.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: As soon as I come off —

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Come on then bravely;
Farewel till then, and play the man.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: You are merry;
All I expect is scorn: I'le lead you Lady.

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: WE'l venture on him.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Out of my doors I charge thee, see me no more.

speeches.speaker: Lami.
verse: Your Nephew?

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: I disclaim him,
He has no part in me, nor in my blood,
My Brother that kept fortune bound, and lest
Conquest hereditary to his Issue
Could not beget a coward.

speeches.speaker: Verd.
verse: I fought, Sir,
Like a good fellow, and a Souldier too,
But men are men, and cannot make their fates:
Ascribe you to my Father what you please,
I am born to suffer.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: All disgraces wretch.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Good Sir be patient.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Was there no tree,
(For to fall by a noble enemies sword,
A Coward is unworthy) nor no River,
To force thy life out backward or to drown it,
But that thou must survive thy imfamie?
And kill me with the sight of one I hate,
And gladly would forget?

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: Sir, his misfortune
Deserves not this reproof.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: In your opinion,
'Tis fit you two should be of one belief,
You are indeed fine gallants, and fight bravely
I'th' City with your tongues, but in the field
Have neither spirit to dare nor power to do,
Your swords are all lead there.

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: I know no duty,
(How ever you may wreak your spleen on him,)
That bindes me to endure tnis.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: From Dinant
You'l suffer more; that ever cursed I,
Should give my honour up, to the defence
Of such a thing as he is, or my Lady
That is all Innocent, for whom a dove would
Assume the courage of a daring Eagle,
Repose her confidence in one that can
No better guard her. In contempt of you
I love Dinant, mine enemy, nay admire him,
His valour claims it from me, and with justice,
He that could fight thus, in a cause not honest,
His sword edg'd with defence of right and honour,
Would pierce as deep as lightning, with that speed too,
And kill as deadly.

speeches.speaker: Verd.
verse: You are as far from justice
In him you praise, as equitie in the censure
You load me with.

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: Dinant? he durst not meet us.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: How? durst not, Brother?

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: Durst not, I repeat it.

speeches.speaker: Verd.
verse: Nor was it Cleremont's valour that disarm'd us,
I had the better of him; for Dinant,
If that might make my peace with you, I dare
Write him a Coward upon every post,
And with the hazard or my life defend it.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: If 'twere laid at the stake you'd lose it, Nephew.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Came he not, say you?

speeches.speaker: Verd.
verse: No, but in his room,
There was a Devil, hir'd from some Magician
I'th' shape of an Atturney.

speeches.speaker: Beau.
verse: 'Twas he did it.

speeches.speaker: Verd.
verse: And his the honour.

speeches.speaker: Beau.
verse: I could wish Dinant —
But what talk I of one that stept aside,
And durst not come?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: I am such a friend to truth,
I cannot hear this: why do you detract
Thus poorly (I should say to others basely)
From one of such approv'd worth?

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Ha! how's this?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: From one so excellent in all that's noble,
Whose only weakness is excess of courage?
That knows no enemies, that he cannot master,
But his affections, and in them, the worst
His love to me.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: To you?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Yes, Sir, to me,
I dare (for what is that which Innocence dares not)
To you profess it; and he shun'd not the Combat
For fear or doubt of these: blush and repent,
That you in thought e're did that wrong to valour.

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: Why, this is rare.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: 'Fore heaven, exceeding rare;
Why modest Lady, you that sing such Encomiums
Of your first Suiter —

speeches.speaker: Verd.
verse: How can ye convince us
In your reports?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: With what you cannot answer,
'Twas my command that staid him.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Your command?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Mine, Sir, and had my will rank'd with my power,
And his obedience, I could have sent him
With more ease, weaponless to you, and bound,
Than have kept him back, so well he loves his honour
Beyond his life.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Better, and better still.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: I wrought with him in private to divert him
From your assur'd destruction, had he met you.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: In private?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Yes, and us'd all Arts, all Charms
Of one that knew her self the absolute Mistris
Of all his faculties.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Gave all rewards too
His service could deserve; did not he take
The measure of my sheets?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Do not look yellow,
I have cause to speak; frowns cannot fright me,
By all my hopes, as I am spotless to you,
If I rest once assur'd you do but doubt me,
Or curb me of that freedom you once gave me —

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: What then?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: I'le not alone abuse your bed, that's nothing,
But to your more vexation, 'tis resolv'd on,
I'le run away, and then try if Dinant
Have courage to defend me.

speeches.speaker: Champ.
verse: Impudent!

speeches.speaker: Verd.
verse: And on the sudden —

speeches.speaker: Beau.
verse: How are ye transform'd
From what you were?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: I was an innocent Virgin,
And I can truly swear, a Wise as pure
As ever lay by Husband, and will dy so,
Let me live unsuspected, I am no servant,
Nor will be us'd like one: If you desire
To keep me constant as I would be, let
Trust and belief in you beget and nurse it;
Unnecessary jealousies make more whores
Than all baits else laid to entrap our frailties.

speeches.speaker: Beau.
verse: There's no contesting with her, from a child
Once mov'd, she hardly was to be appeas'd,
Yet I dare swear her honest.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: So I think too,
On better judgement: I am no Italian
To lock her up: nor would I be a Dutchman,
To have my Wife, my soveraign, to command me:
I'le try the gentler way, but if that fail,
Believe it, Sir, there's nothing but extreams
Which she must feel from me.

speeches.speaker: Beau.
verse: That, as you please, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: You have won the breeches, Madam, look up sweetly,
My Lord limps toward you.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: You will learn more manners

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: This is a fee, for counsel that's unask'd for.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Come, I mistook thee sweet, prethee forgive me,
I never will be jealous: e're I cherish
Such a mechanick humour, I'le be nothing;
I'le say, Dinant is all that thou wouldst have him,
Will that suffice?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: 'Tis well, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Use thy freedom
Uncheck'd, and unobserv'd, if thou wilt have it,
These shall forget their honour, I my wrongs.
We'll all dote on him, hell be my reward
If I dissemble.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: And that hell take me
If I affect him, he's a lustfull villain,
(But yet no coward) and sollicites me
To my dishonour, that's indeed a quarrel,
And truly mine, which I will so revenge,
As it shall fright such as dare only think
To be adulterers.

speeches.speaker: Cham
verse: Use thine own waies,
I give up all to thee.

speeches.speaker: Beau.
verse: O women, women!
When you are pleas'd you are the least of evils.

speeches.speaker: Verd.
verse: I'le time to't, but provokt, the worst of Devils.

speeches.speaker: Samp.
verse: I know Monsieur La writ.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cly.
verse: Would he knew himself, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Samp.
verse: He was a pretty Lawyer, a kind of pretty Lawyer,
Of a kind of unable thing.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cly.
verse: A fine Lawyer, Sir,
And would have s^k'd you up a business,
And out of this Court into that.

speeches.speaker: Samp.
verse: Ye are too forward
Not so fine my friends, something he could have done,
But short short.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cy.
verse: I know your worships favour,
You are Nephew to the Judge, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Samp.
verse: It may be so,
And something may be done, without trotting i'th' dirt, friends;
It may be I can take him in his Chamber,
And have an hours talk, it may be so,
And tell him that in's ear; there are such courtesies;
I will not say, I can.

speeches.speaker: 3 Cly.
verse: We know you can, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: Peradventure I, peradventure no: but where's La-writ?
Where's your sufficient Lawyer?

speeches.speaker: 1 Cly.
verse: He's blown up, Sir.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cly.
verse: Run mad and quarrels with the Dog he meets;
He is no Lawyer of this world now.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: Your reason?
Is he defunct? is he dead?

speeches.speaker: 2 Cly.
verse: No he's not dead yet, Sir;
But I would be loth to take a lease on's life for two hours:
Alas, he is possest Sir, with the spirit of fighting
And quarrels with all people: but how he came to it—

speeches.speaker: Samp.
verse: If he fight well and like a Gentleman,
The man may fight, for 'tis a lawfull calling.
Look you my friends, I am a civil Gentleman,
And my Lord my Uncle loves me.

speeches.speaker: 3 Cly.
verse: We all know it, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: I think he does, Sir, I have business too, much business,
Turn you some forty or fifty Causes in a week;
Yet when I get an hour of vacancie,
I can fight too my friends, a little does well,
I would be loth to learn to fight.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cly.
verse: But and't please you Sir,
His fighting has neglected all our business,
We are undone, our causes cast away, Sir,
His not appearance.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: There he fought too long,
A little and fight well, he fought too long indeed f^s;
But ne'r the less things must be as they may,
And there be wayes —

speeches.speaker: 1 Cly.
verse: We know, Sir, if you please —

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: Something I'le do: goe rally up your Causes.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cly.
verse: Now you may behold Sir,
And be a witness, whether we lie or no.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: I'le meet you at the Ordinary, sweet Gent^emen,
And if there be a wench or two —

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: We'll have 'em.

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: No handling any Duells before I come,
We'll have no going else, I hate a coward.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: There shall be nothing done.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Make all the quarrels
You can devise before I come, and let's all fight,
There is no sport else.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: We'll see what may be done, Sir.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cly.
verse: Ha? Monsieur La writ.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Baffled in way of business,
My causes cast away, Judgement against us?
Why there it goes.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cly.
verse: What shall we do the whilst Sir?

speeches.speaker: La-wr.
verse: Breed new dissentions, goe hang your selves
'Tis all one to me; I have a new trade of living.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cli.
verse: Do you hear what he saies Sir?

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: The Gentleman speaks finely.

speeches.speaker: La-wr.
verse: Will any of you fight? Fighting's my occupation
If you find your selves aggriev'd.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: A compleat Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Avant thou buckram budget of petitions,
Thou spittle of lame causes; I lament for thee,
And till revenge be taken —

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: 'Tis most excellent.

speeches.speaker: La-wr.
verse: There, every man chuse his paper, and his place.
I'le answer ye all, I will neglect no mans business
But he shall have satisfaction like a Gentleman,
The Judge may do and not do, he's but a Monsieur.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: You have nothing of mine in your bag, Sir.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: I know not Sir,
But you may put any thing in, any fighting thing.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: It is sufficient, you may hear hereafter.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: I rest your servant Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: No more words Gentlemen
But follow me, no more words as you love me,
The Gentleman's a noble Gentleman.
I shall do what I can, and then —

speeches.speaker: Cli.
verse: We thank you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: Not a word to disturb him, he's a Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Not cause go o' my side? the judge cast all?
And because I was honourably employed in action,
And not appear'd, pronounce? 'tis very well,
'Tis well faith, 'tis well, Judge.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Who have we here?
My little furious Lawyer?

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: I say 'tis well,
But mark the end.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: How he is metamorphos'd?
Nothing of Lawyer left, not a bit of buckram,
No solliciting face now,
This is no simple conversion.
Your servant Sir, and Friend.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: You come in time, Sir,

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: The happier man, to be at your command then.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: You may wonder to see me thus; but that's all one,
Time shall declare; 'tis true I was a Lawyer,
But I have mew'd that coat, I hate a Lawyer,
I talk'd much in the Court, now I hate talking,
I did you the office of a man.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I must confess it.

speeches.speaker: La-w.
verse: And budg'd not, no I budg'd not.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: No, you did not.

speeches.speaker: La w.
verse: There's it then, one good turn requires another.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Most willing Sir, I am ready at your service.

speeches.speaker: La-w.
verse: There, read, and understand, and then deliver it.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: This is a Challenge, Sir,

speeches.speaker: La-w.
verse: 'Tis very like, Sir,
I seldom now write Sonnets.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: O admirantis,
To Monsieur Vertaign, the President.

speeches.speaker: La w.
verse: I chuse no Fool, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Why, he's no Sword-man, Sir.

speeches.speaker: La w.
verse: Let him learn, let him learn,
Time, that trains Chickens up, will teach him quickly.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: VVhy, he's a Judge, an Old Man.

speeches.speaker: La-w.
verse: Never too Old
To be a Gentleman; and he that is a Judge
Can judge best what belongs to wounded honour.
There are my griefs, he has cast away my causes,
In which he has bowed my reputation.
And therefore Judge, or no Judge.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: 'Pray be rul'd Sir,
This is the maddest thing—

speeches.speaker: La w.
verse: You will not carry it.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I do not tell you so, but if you may be perswaded.

speeches.speaker: La w.
verse: You know how you us'd me when I would not fight,
Do you remember, Gentleman?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: The Devil's in him.

speeches.speaker: La w.
verse: I see it in your Eyes, that you dare do it,
You have a carrying face, and you shall carry it.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: The least is Banishment.

speeches.speaker: La-w.
verse: Be banish'd then;
'Tis a friends part, we'll meet in Africa,
Or any part of the Earth.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Say he will not fight.

speeches.speaker: La w.
verse: I know then what to say, take you no care, Sir,

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Well, I will carry it, and deliver it,
And to morrow morning meet you in the Louver,
Ti^l when, my service.

speeches.speaker: La-w.
verse: A Judge, or no Judge, no Judge.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: This is the prettiest Rogue that e'r I read of,
None to provoke to th'field, but the old President;
What face shall I put on? if I come in earnest,
I am sure to wear a pair of Bracelets;
This may make some sport yet, I will deliver it,
Here comes the President.

speeches.speaker: Vert.
verse: I shall find time, Gentlemen,
To do your causes good, is not that Cleremont?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: 'Tis he my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Vert.
verse: Why does he smile upon me?
Am I become ridiculous? has your fortune, Sir,
Upon my Son, made you contemn his Father?
The glory of a Gentleman is fair bearing.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Mistake me not my Lord, you shall not find that,
I come with no blown Spirit to abuse you,
I know your place and honour due unto it,
The reverence to your silver Age and Vertue.

speeches.speaker: Vert.
verse: Your face is merry still.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: So is my business,
And I beseech your honour mistake me not,
I have brought you from a wild or rather Mad-man
As mad a piece of— you were wont to love mirth
In your young days, I have known your Honour woo it,
This may be made no little one, 'tis a Challenge, Sir,
Nay, start not, I beseech you, it means you no harm,
Nor any Man of Honour, or Understanding,
'Tis to steal from your serious hours a little laughter;
I am bold to bring it to your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Vert.
verse: 'Tis to me indeed;
Do they take me for a Sword-man at these years?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: 'Tis only worth your Honours Mirth, that's all Sir
'T had been in me else a sawcy rudness.

speeches.speaker: Vert.
verse: From one La writ, a very punctual Challenge.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: But if your Lordship mark it, no great matter.

speeches.speaker: Vert.
verse: I have known such a wrangling Advocate,
Such a little figent thing; Oh I remember him,
A notable talking Knave, now out upon him,
Has challeng'd me downright, defied me mortally
I do remember too, I cast his Causes.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Why, there's the quarrel, Sir, the mortal quarrel.

speeches.speaker: Vert.
verse: Why, what a Knave is this? as y'are a Gentleman,
Is there no further purpose but meer mirth?
What a bold Man of War! he invites me roundly.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: If there should be, I were no Gentleman,
Nor worthy of the honour of my Kindred.
And though I am sure your Lordship hates my Person,
Which Time may bring again into your favour,
Yet for the manners—

speeches.speaker: Vert.
verse: I am satisfied,
You see, Sir, I have out-liv'd those days of fighting,
And therefore cannot do him the honour to beat him my self;
But I have a Kinsman much of his ability,
His Wit and Courage, for this call him Fool,
One that will spit as senseless fire as this Fellow.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: And such a man to undertake, my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Vert.
verse: Nay he's too forward; these two pitch Barrels together.
Upon my soul, no harm.

speeches.speaker: Vert.
verse: It makes me smile,
Why, what a stinking smother will they utter?
Yes, he shall undertake, Sir, as my Champion,
Since you propound it mirth, I'll venture on it,
And shall defend my cause, but as y'are honest
Sport not with bloud.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Think not so basely, good Sir.

speeches.speaker: Vert.
verse: A Squire shall wait upon you f^om my Kinsman,
To morrow morning make you sport at full,
You want no Subject; but no wounds.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: That's my care.

speeches.speaker: Vert.
verse: And so good day.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Many unto your honour.
This is a noble Fellow, of a sweet Spirit,
Now must I think how to contrive this matter,
For together they shall go.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: O Cleremont,
I am glad I have found thee.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I can tell thee rare things.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: O, I can tell thee rarer,
Dost thou love me?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Love thee?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Dost thou love me dearly?
Dar'st thou for my sake?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Any thing that's honest.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Though it be dangerous?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Pox o' dangerous.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Nay wondrous dangerous.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Wilt thou break my heart?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Along with me then.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I must part to morrow.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: You shall, you shall, be faithful for this night,
And thou hast made thy friend.

speeches.speaker: C^er.
verse: Away, and talk not.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: O Nurse, welcome, where's Dinant?

speeches.speaker: Nurse.
verse: He's at my back.
'Tis the most liberal Gentleman, this Gold
He gave me for my pains, nor can I blame you,
If you yield up the fort.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: How? yield it up?

speeches.speaker: Nurse.
verse: I know not, he that loves, and gives so largely,
And a young Lord to boot, or I am cozen'd,

May ente^
^very where.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Thou'lt make me angry.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: Why, if you are, I hope here's one will please you,
Look on him with my Eyes, good luck go with you:
Were I young for your sake —

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: I thank thee, Nurse.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: I would be tractable, and as I am—

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Leave the room,
So old, and so immodest I and be careful,
Since whispers will 'wake sleeping jealousies,
That none disturb my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Will you dispatch?
Till you come to the matter be not rapt thus,
Walk in, walk in, I am your scout for once,
You owe me the like service.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: And will pay it.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: As you respect our lives, speak not so loud.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Why, do it in dumb shew then, I am silenc'd.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Be not so hasty, Sir, the golden Apples
Had a fell Dragon for their Guard, your pleasures
Are to be attempted with Herculean danger,
Or never to be gotten.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Speak the means.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Thus briefly, my Lord sleeps now, and alas,
Each Night, he only sleeps.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Go, keep her stirring.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Now if he 'wake, as sometimes he does,
He only stretches out his hand and feels,
Whether I am a bed, which being assur'd of,
He sleeps again; but should he miss me, Valour
Could not defend our lives.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: What's to be done then?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Servants have servile faiths, nor have I any
That I dare trust; on noble Cleremont
We safely may rely.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: What man can do,
Command and boldly.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Thus then in my place,
You must lye with my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: With an old man?
Two Beards together, that's preposterous.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: There is no other way, and though 'tis dangerous,
He having servants within call, and arm'd too,
Slaves fed to act all that his jealousie
And rage commands them, yet a true friend should not
Check at the hazard of a life.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I thank you,
I love my friend, but know no reason why
To hate my self; to be a kind of pander,
You see I am willing,
But to betray mine own throat you must pardon.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Then I am lost, and all my hopes defeated,
Were I to hazard ten times more for you,
You should find, Cleremont—

speeches.speaker: Cler
verse: You shall not outdo me,
Fall what may fall, I'll do't.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: But for his Beard—

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: To cover that you shall have my night Linnen,
And you dispos'd of, my Dinant and I
Will have some private conference.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Private doing,
Or I'll not venture.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: That's as we agree.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: What can this Woman do, preserving her honour?
I have given her all the liberty that may be,
I will not be far off though, nor I will not be jealous,
Nor trust too much, I think she is vertuous,
Yet when I hold her best, she's but a Woman,
As full of frailty as of faith, a poor sleight Woman,
And her best thoughts, but weak fornifications,
There may be a Mine wrought: Well, let 'em work that,
I shall meet with it, till the signs be monstrous,
And stick upon my head, I will not believe it,
She may be, and she may not, now to my observation.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Why do you make me stay so? if you love me—

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: You are too hot and violent.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Why do you shift thus
From one Chamber to another?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: A little delay, Sir,
Like fire, a little sprinkled o'r with water
Makes the desires burn clear, and ten times hotter.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Why do you speak so loud? I pray'e go in,
Sweet Mistriss, I am mad, time steals away,
And when we would enjoy—

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Now fie, fie, Servant,
Like sensual Beasts shall we enjoy our pleasures?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: 'Pray do not kiss me then.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Why, that I will, and you shall find anon, servant.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Softly, for heavens sake, you know my friend's engag'd,
A little now, now; will ye go in again?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Ha, ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Why do you laugh so loud, Precious?
Will you betray me; ha' my friends throat cut!

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Come, come, I'll kiss thee again.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Will you so? you are liberal,
If you do cozen me—

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: What's this?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Wine, Wine, a draught or two.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: What does this Woman here?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: She shall not hinder you.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: This might have been spar'd,
'Tis but delay and time lost; pray send her softly off.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Sit down, and mix your spirits with Wine,
I will make you another Hercules.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: I dare not drink;
Fie, what delays you make? I dare not,
I shall be drunk presently, and do strange things then.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Not drink a cup with your Mistriss! O the pleasure

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Lady, why this?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: We must have mirth to our Wine, Man.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Pl— o' the Musick.

speeches.speaker: Champ.
verse: God-a-mercy Wench,
If thou dost cuckold me I shall forgive thee.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: The house will all rise now, this will disturb all.
Did you do this?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Peace, and sit quiet, fool,
You love me, come, sit down and drink.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: What a Devil ail you?
How cold I sweat! a hogs pox stop your pipes,
The thing will 'wake; now, now, methinks I find
His Sword just gliding through my throat. What's that?
A vengeance choak your pipes. Are you there, Lady?
Stop, stop those Rascals; do you bring me hither
To be cut into minced meat? why Dinant?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: I cannot do withal;
I have spoke, and spoke; I am betray'd and lost too.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Do you hear me? do you understand me?
'Plague dam your Whistles.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: 'Twas but an over-sight, they have done, lye down.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Would you had done too,
You know not
In what a misery and fear I lye.
You have a Lady in your arms.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: I would have —

speeches.speaker: Champ.
verse: I'll watch you Goodman Wou'd have.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Remove for Heavens sake,
And fall to that you come for.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Lie you down,
'Tis but an hours endurance now.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I dare not, softly sweet Lady— heart?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: 'Tis nothing but your fear, he sleeps still soundly,
Lie gently down.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: 'Pray make an end.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Come, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: These Chambers are too near.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: I shall be nearer;
Well, go thy wayes, I'le trust thee through the world,
Deal how thou wilt: that that I never feel,
I'le never fear. Yet by the honour of a Souldier,
I hold thee truly noble: How these things will look,
And how their blood will curdle! Play on Children,
You shall have pap anon. O thou grand Fool,
That thou knew'st but thy fortune—

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Peace, good Madam,
Stop her mouth, Dinant, it sleeps yet, 'pray be wary,
Dispatch, I cannot endure this misery,
I can hear nothing more; I'll say my prayers,
And down again—
A thousand Alarms fall upon my quarters,
Heaven send me off; when I lye keeping Conrses.
Pl— o' your fumbling, Dinant; how I shake!
'Tis still again: would I were in the Indies.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Why do you use me thus? thus poorly? basely?
Work me into a hope, and then destroy me?
Why did you send for me? this new way train me?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Mad-man, and fool, and false man, now I'll shew thee.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: 'Pray put your light out.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Nay I'll hold it thus,
That all chaste Eyes may see thy lust, and scorn it.
Tell me but this when you first doted on me,
And made suit to enjoy me as your Wife,
Did you not hold me honest?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Yes, most vertuous.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: And did not that appear the only lustre
That made me worth your love and admiration?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: I must confess—

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Why would you deal so basely?
So like a thief, a Villain?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Peace, good Madam.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: I'll speak aloud too; thus maliciously,
Thus breaking all the Rules of honesty,
Of honour and of truth, for which I lov'd you,
For which call'd you servant, and admir'd you;
To steal that Jewel purchas'd by another,
^ously set in Wedlock, even that Jewel,
Because it had no flaw, you held unvaluable:
Can he that has lov'd good, dote on the Devil?
For he that seeks a Whore, seeks but his Agent;
Or am I of so wild and low a blood?
^o nurs'd in infamies?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: I do not think so,
And I repent.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: That will not serve your turn, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: It was your treaty drew me on.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: But it was your villany
^e you pursue it; I drew you but to try
^ow much a man, and nobly thou durst stand,
^ow well you had deserv'd the name of vertuous;
^et you like a wild torrent, mix'd with all
^asely and base affections came floating on,
^lling your poyson'd billows—

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Will you betray me?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: To all the miseries a vext Woman may.

speeches.speaker: Dan.
verse: Let me but out,
^ve me but room to ^oss my Sword about me,
^d I will tell you y'are a treacherous woman,
^ that I had but words!

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: They will not serve you.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: But two-edg'd words to cut thee; a Lady traytor?
Perish by a proud Puppet? I did you too much honour,
To tender you my love, too much respected you
To think you worthy of my worst embraces
Go take your Groom, and let him dally with you,
Your greasie Groom; I scorn to imp your lame stock,
You are not fair, no^ handsome, I lyed lou^ly,
This tongue abus'd you when it spoke you beauteous.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: 'Tis very well, 'tis brave.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Put out your light.
Your lascivious eyes are f^mes enough
For Fools to find you out; a Lady Plotte^!
Must I begin your sacrifice of mischief?
I and my friend, the first-fruits of that bloud,
You and your honou able Husband aim at?
Crooked and wretched you are both.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: To you, Sir,
Yet to the Eye of Justice straight as Truth.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Is this a womans love? a womans in ^y?
Do you profess this seriously? do you laugh at me?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Din
verse: Pl— light upon your scorns upon your flatteries,
Upon your tempting faces, all def^tions;
A b^d ^ upon your cheeks,
And ^las^, ^a^l, ^ those ^s of Pride that paint you;
^th^n you ^s to fright m^n from these dangers:
Raise up you^ t^op^, Clerem^.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: VVhat a vengeance ^ you?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: VVhat dismal nois^ is there no honour in you?
Cleremont, we are betrayed, betrayed, sold by a woman;

D^
^ forth ^

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse:
^
^ing;
Are we made stales to one another?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Yes, we are undone, lost.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: You shall pay for't grey beard.
Up, up, you sleep your last else.

speeches.speaker: 1 Serv.
verse: No, not yet, Sir,
La^y, look up, would you have wrong'd this Beauty?
VVake so ^ a Virgin with rough t^rms?
You wear a Sword, we must entreat you leave it.

speeches.speaker: 2 Serv.
verse: Fye Sir, so sweet a lady?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Was this my bed fellow, pray give me leave to look,
I am not m^ yet, I may be by and by.
Did this lye ^e?
Did I fear this? is this a Cause to shake at?
Away with m^r shame, I am a Rascal.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: I am ^az'd too.

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: VVe'll recover you.

speeches.speaker: Verd.
verse: You walk like Robin good-fellow all the house over,
And every man afraid of you.

speeches.speaker: Di^.
verse: 'Tis well, Lady;
Th^ honour of this deed will be your own,
The world shall know your bounty.

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: VVhat shall we do with 'em?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: G^ld me,
For 'tis not fit I should be a man again,
I am an Ass, a Dog.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Take your revenges,
You know my Husbands wrongs and your own losses.

speeches.speaker: Anab.
verse: A brave man, an admirable brave man;
VVell, well, I would not be so tryed again;
A very handsome proper Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: VVill you let me lye by her but one hour more,
And then hang me?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: We wait your malice, put your swords home bravely,
You have reason to seek bloud.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Not as you are noble.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Hands off, and give them liberty, only disarm 'em.

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: We have done that already.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: You are welcome, Gentl^men,
I am glad my house has any pleasure for you,
I keep a couple of Ladies here, they say fair,
And you are young and handsome, Gentlemen;
Have you any more mind to Wenches?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: To be abus'd too? Lady, you might have help'd this.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: Sit now 'tis past, but 't may be I may stand
Your friend hereafter, in a greater matter.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Never whilst you live.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: You cannot tell— now, Sir, a parting hand.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Down and Roses:
Well I may live to see you again. A dull Rogue,
No revelation in thee.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Were you well frighted?
Were your fitts from the heart, of all colds and colours?
That's all your punishment.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: It might have been all yours,
Had not a block-head undertaken it.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Your swords you mnst leave to these Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Verd.
verse: And now, when you dare fight,
We are on even lee again.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: 'Tis well:
To be a Mistris, is to be a monster,
And so I leave your house, and you for ever.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Leave your wild lusts, and then you are a master.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: You may depart too.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I had rather stay here.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Faith we shall fright you worse.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Not in that manner,
There's five hundred Crowns, fright me but so again.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Come Cleremont, this is the hour of fool.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Wiser the next shall be or we'll to School.

speeches.speaker: Champ.
verse: How coolly these hot gallants are departed?
Faith Cousin, 'twas unconscionably done,
To lye so still, and so long.

speeches.speaker: Anab.
verse: 'Twas your pleasure,
If 'twere a fault, I may hereafter mend.

speeches.speaker: Champ.
verse: O my best Wife,
Take now what course thou wilt, and lead what life.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: The more trust you commit, the more care still,
Goodness and vertue shall attend my will.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Let's laugh this night out now, and count our gains.
We have our honours home, and they their pains.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: IT holds, they will go thither.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: To their Summer-house?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Thither i'th' evening, and which is the most infliction,
Only to insult upon our miseries.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Are you provided?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Yes, yes.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Throughly?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Throughly.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Bas^a, enough, I have your mind, I will not fail you.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: At such an hour.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Have I a memory?
A Cause, and Will to do? thou art so sullen—

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: And shall be, till I have a fair reparation.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I have more reason, for I scaped a fortune,
Which if I come so near again: I say nothing,
But if I sweat not in another fashion—
O, a delicate Wench.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: 'Tis certain a most handsome one.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: And me thought the thing was angry with it self too
It lay so long conceal'd, but I must part with you,
I have a scene of mirth, to drive this from my heart,
And my hour is come.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Miss not your time.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I dare not.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: I presume, Sir, you now need no instruction,
But fairly know, what belongs to a Gentleman;
You bear your Uncles cause.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: Do not disturb me,
I understand my cause, and the right carriage.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Be not too bloody.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: As I find my enemy; if his sword bite,
If it bite, Sir, you must pardon me.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: No doubt he is valiant,
He durst not undertake else,

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: He's most welcome,
As he is most valiant, he were no man for me else.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: But say he should relent.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: He dies relenting,
I cannot help it, he must dies relenting,
If he pray, praying, ipso facto, praying,
Your honourable way admits no prayer,
And if he fight, he falls, there's his quietus.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Y'are nobly punctual, let's retire and meet 'em,
But still, I say, have mercy

speeches.speaker: Samp.
verse: I say, honour.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Will not you go sweet-heart?

speeches.speaker: Champ.
verse: Go? I'le fly with thee.
I stay behind?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: My Father will be there too,
And all our best friends.

speeches.speaker: Beau.
verse: And if we be not merry,
We have hard luck, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Verd.
verse: Faith let's have a kind of play.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: What shall it be?

speeches.speaker: Verd.
verse: The story of Dinant.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: With the merry conceits of Cleremont,
His Fits and Feavers.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: But I'le lie still no more.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: That, as you make the Play, 'twill be rare sport,
And how 'twill vex my gallants, when they hear it?
Have you given order for the Coach?

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Yes, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: My easie Nag, and padd.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: 'Tis making ready.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Where are your Horses?

speeches.speaker: Beau.
verse: Ready at an hour, Sir: we'll not be last.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Fie, what a night shall we have!
A roaring, merry night.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: We'll flie at all, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: I'le flie at thee too, finely, and so ruffle thee,
I'le try your Art upon a Country pallet.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Brag not too much, for fear I should expect it,
Then if you fail—

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Thou saiest too true, we all talk.
But let's in, and prepare, and after dinner
Begin our mirthful pilgrimage.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: He that's sad,
A crab-face'd Mistris cleave to him for this year.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Since it cannot be the Judge—

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: 'Tis a great deal better.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: You are sure, he is his kinsman? a Gentleman?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: As arrant a Gentleman, and a brave fellow,
And so near to his blood—

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: It shall suffice,
I'le set him further off, I'le give a remove
Shall quit his kindred, I'le lopp him.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Will ye kill him?

speeches.speaker: La-w.
verse: And there were no more Cousins in the world I ki^ him,
I do mean, Sir, to kill all my Lords kindred.
For every cause a Cousin.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: How if he have no more Cousins?

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: The next a kin then to his Lordships favour;
The man he smiles upon.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Why this is vengeance, horrid, and dire.

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: I love a dire revenge:
Give me the man that will all others kill,
And last himself,

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: You stole that resolution.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: I had it in a Play, but that's all one,
I wou'd see it done.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Come, you must be more merciful.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: To no Lords Cousins in the world, I hate 'em;
A Lords Cousin to me is a kind of Cockatrice,
If I see him first, he dies.
A strange Antipathy.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: What think you of their Nieces?

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: If I like 'em,
They may live, and multiply, 'tis a cold morning.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: 'Tis sharp indeed; you have broke your fast?

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: No verily.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Your valour would have ask'd a good foundation.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Hang him, I'le kill him fasting.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Here they come,
Bear your self in your language, smooth and gently,
When your swords argue.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: 'Pray Sir, spare your precepts.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: I have brought you, Sir—

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: 'Tis very well, no words,
You are welcome, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: I thank you, Sir, few words.

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: I'le kill you for your Uncles sake.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: I love you,
I'le cut your throat for your own sake.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: I esteem of you.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Let's render 'em honest, and fair, Gentlemen,
Search my friend, I'le search yours.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: That's quickly done.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: You come with no Spells, nor Witchcrafts?

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: I come fairly to kill him honestly.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Hang Spells, and Witchcrafts,
I come to kill my Lords Nephew like a Gentleman,
^d so I kiss his hand.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: This Doublet is too stiff.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Off with't, I hate it,
And all such fortifications, feel my skin,
^ that be stiff, flea that off too.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: 'Tis no soft one.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Off with't, I say:
The fight with him like a flea'd Cat.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: You are well, you are well.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: You must uncase too.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: Yes, Sir.
^ tell me this, why should I mix mine honour
With a fellow, that has ne're a lace in's shirt?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: That's a main point, my friend has two.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: That's true, Sir.

speeches.speaker: La w.
verse: Base and degenerate Cousin, dost not thou know
^ old, and tatter'd colours, to the enemy,
^ of more honour, and shews more ominous?
^his shirt, five times, victorious I have fought under,
^ad cut through squadrons of your curious cut-works,
^ I will do through thine, shake, and be satisfied.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: This is unanswerable.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: But may I fight with a foul shirt?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Most certain, so it be a fighting shirt,
^et it be ne're so foul, or lowsie, Caesar wore such a one.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: Saint Denis then: I accept your shirt.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Not so forward, first you must talk,
^is a main point, of the French method,
Talk civilly, and make your cause Authentick.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: No weapon must be near you, nor no anger.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: When you have done, then stir your resolutions,
^ to your Weapons bravely.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: 'Tis too cold;
This for a Summer fight.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Not for a world you should transgress the rules.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: 'Tis pievish weather,
I had rather fight without.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: An 'twere in a River.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Where both stood up to th' chins.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Then let's talk quickly,
Pl— o' this circumstance.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Are the Horses come yet?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Yes certain: give your swords to us, now civilly.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: We'll stand a while off; take ^ things, and leave'em,
You know when, and let the children play:
This is a dainty time of year for puppies,
Would the old Lord were here.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: He would dye with laughter.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I am sorry I have no time to see this game out,
Away, away.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Here's like to be a hot fight,
Call when y'are fit.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Why look you Sir, you seem to be a Gentleman,
And you come in honour of your Uncle, boh, boh, 'tis very cold;
Your Uncle has offer'd me some few affronts,
Past flesh and blood to bear: boh, boh, wondrous cold.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: My Lord, mine Uncle, is an honourable man,
And what he offers, boh, boh, cold indeed,
Having made choice of me, an unworthy kinsman,
Yet take me with you: boh, boh, pestilence cold,
Not altogether.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Boh, boh, I say altogether.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: You say you know not what then? boh, boh, Sir.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Sir me with your sword in your hand;
You have a scurvy Uncle, you have a most scurvy cause,
And you are— boh, boh.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: Boh, boh, what?

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: A shitten scurvy Cousin.

speeches.speaker: Samp.
verse: Our Swords; our Swords;
Thou art a Dog, and like a Dog, our Swords.

speeches.speaker: La-w.
verse: Our weapons Gentlemen ha? where's your second?

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: Where's yours?

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: So ho; our weapons.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: Wa, ha, ho, our weapons;
Our Doublets and our weapons, I am dead.

speeches.speaker: La-w.
verse: First, second, third, a pl— be wi'you Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: Are these the rules of honour? I am starv'd.

speeches.speaker: La w.
verse: They are gone, and we are here; what shall we do?

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: O for a couple of Faggots.

speeches.speaker: La-w.
verse: Hang a couple of Faggots.
Dar'st thou take a killing cold with me?

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: I have it already.

speeches.speaker: La w.
verse: Rogues, Thieves, boh, boh, run away with our Doublets?
To fight at Bu^l^ts now, 'twere such a May-game.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: There were no honour in't, pl— on't, 'tis scurvy.

speeches.speaker: La w.
verse: Or to revenge my wrongs at fifty-cuffes.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: My Lord, mine Uncles cause, depend on Boxes?

speeches.speaker: La w.
verse: Let's go in quest, if we ever recover 'em.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: I, come, our Colds together, and our Doublets.

speeches.speaker: La w.
verse: Give me thy hand; thou art a valiant Gentleman,
I say if ever we recover 'em—

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: Let's get into a house and warm our hearts.

speeches.speaker: La w.
verse: There's ne're a house within this mile, beat me,
Kick me and beat me as I go, and I'le beat thee too,
To keep us warm; if ever we recover 'em—
Kick hard, I am frozen: so, so, now I feel it.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: I am dull yet.

speeches.speaker: La-w.
verse: I'le warm thee, I'le warm thee— Gentlemen?
Rogues, Thieves, Thieves: run now I'le follow thee.

speeches.speaker: Verta.
verse: Use legs, and have legs.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: You that have legs say so,
I put my one to too much stress.

speeches.speaker: Verdo.
verse: Your Horse, Sir,
Will meet you within half a mile.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: I like
The walk so well, I should not miss my Coach,
Though it were further. Annabel thou art sad:
What ails my Niece?

speeches.speaker: Beau.
verse: She's still musing, Sister,
How quietly her late bed-fellow lay by her.

speeches.speaker: Nurse.
verse: Old as I am, he would have startled me,
Nor can you blame her.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Had I ta'ne her place,
I know not, but I fear, I should ha'shreek'd,
Though he had never offer'd—

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: Out upon thee,
Thou wouldst have taught him.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: I think, with your pardon,
That you wish now you had.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: I am glad I yield you
Such ample scope of mirth.

speeches.speaker: Verta.
verse: Nay, be not angry,
There's no ill meant: ha? Musick, and choice Musick?

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: 'Tis near us in the Grove; what courteous bounty
Bestows it on us? my dancing days are done;
Yet I would thank the giver, did I know him.

speeches.speaker: Verdo.
verse: 'Tis questionless, some one of your own Village,
That hearing of your purpos'd journey thither,
Prepares it for your entertainment, and
The honour of my Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: I think rather,
Some of your Lordships Clients.

speeches.speaker: Beaup.
verse: What say you Cousin,
If they should prove your Suitors?

speeches.speaker: Verd.
verse: That's most likely.

speeches.speaker: Nurse.
verse: I say if you are noble, be't who will,
Go presently and thank 'em: I can jump yet,
Or tread a measure.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Like a Millers Mare.

speeches.speaker: Nurs.
verse: I warrant you well enough to serve the Country,
I'le make one, and lead the way.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Do you note,
How zealous the old Crone is?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: And you titter
As eagerly as she: come sweet, we'll follow,
No ill can be intended.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: I ne're fear'd yet.
THis way, this way come and hear,
You that hold these p easures dear,
Fill your ears with our sweet sound,
Whilst we melt the frozen ground:
This way come, make haste oh fair,
Let your clear eyes gild the Air;
Come and bless us with your fight,
This way, this way, seek delight.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: They are ours, but draw them on a little further
From the foot path into the neighbouring thicket,
And we may do't, as safe as in a Castle.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: They follow still; the President Vertaigne
Comes on a pace, and Champernel limps after;
The Women, as if they had wings, and walk't
Upon the Air, fly to us.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: They are welcome,
We'll make 'em sport; make a stand here, all know
How we are to proceed.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: We are instructed.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: One strain or two more.
Excellent, they are come.

speeches.speaker: Nurse.
verse: We cannot miss, in such a business, yet
Mine ear ne'r fail'd me.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Would we were at it once,
I do not walk, but Dance.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: You shall have dancing.
Begin, and when I give the word—

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: No more:
We are instructed.

speeches.speaker: Beaupre.
verse: But win us fairly—

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: O Sir, we do not come to try your valour,
But to possess you, yet we use you kindly
In that, like English Thieves, we kill you not,
But are contented with the spoil.

speeches.speaker: Verta.
verse: Oh Heaven!
How hath mine age deserv'd this?

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Hell confound it,
This comes of walking; had I kept my legs,
Or my good Horse, my Armour on,
My Staff in my rest, and this good Sword too, fr^nd,
How I would break and scatter these.

speeches.speaker: All Gent.
verse: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Do you scorn me Rogues?

speeches.speaker: Nurs.
verse: Nay, Gentlemen, kind Gentlemen,
Or honest keepers of these woods, but hear me,
Be not so rough; if you are taken with
My beauty, as it hath been worth the seeking,
Some one or two of you try me in private,
You shall not find me squeamish.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Do not kill me,
And do your worst, I'le suffer.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Peace vile creatures,

speeches.speaker: Vert.
verse: Do you know me, or my place, that you presume not
To touch my person?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: If you are well, rest so,
Provoke not angry Wasps.

speeches.speaker: Verta.
verse: You are Wasps indeed,
Never created to yield Wax or Honey,
But for your Countries torment; yet if you are men,
(As you seem such in shape) if true born French-men,
However want compels you to these courses,
Rest satisfied with what you can take from us,
(These Ladies honours, and our liberties safe)
We freely give it.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: You give but our own.

speeches.speaker: Verta.
verse: Look on these grey hairs, as you would be old,
Their tears, as you would have yours to find mercy
When Justice shall o'retake you.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Look on me,
Look on me Rascals, and learn of me too,
That have been in some part of your profession,
Before that most of you ere suck'd, I know it,
I have rode hard, and late too.

speeches.speaker: Verta.
verse: Take heed, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Then use me like a Brother of the Trade,
For I have been at Sea, as you on land are,
Restore my Matrimony undefil'd,
Wrong not my Neece, and for our gold or silver,
If I pursue you, hang me.

speeches.speaker: Nurs.
verse: 'Tis well offer'd,
And as I said, sweet Gentlemen, with sowre faces,
If you are high, and want some sport, or so,
(As living without action here, you may do)
Forbear their tender grissels, they are meat
Will wash away, there is no substance in it,
We that are expert in the game, and tough too,
Will hold you play.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: This Hen longs to be troden.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Lackey, my Horse.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: This way, I heard the cries
Of distress'd Women.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Stand upon your guard.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Who's here? my witty, scornful Lady-plot
In the hands of Ruffians?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: And my fine cold virgin,
That was insensible of man, and woman?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Justice too,
Without a sword to guard it self?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: And valour with its hands bound?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: And the great Souldier dull?
Why this is strange.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Dinant as thou art noble —

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: As thou art valiant Cleremont —

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: As ever I appear'd lovely —

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: As you ever hope
For what I would give gladly —

speeches.speaker: C^er.
verse: Pretty conjurations.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: All injuries a little laid behind you.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: Shew your selves men, and help us.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Though your many
And gross abuses of me should more move me
To triumph in your miseries than relieve you,—
Yet that hereafter you may know that I
The scorn'd and despis'd Dinant, know what does
Belong to honour, thus —

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I will say little,
Speak thou for me.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: 'Tis bravely fought.

speeches.speaker: Verta.
verse: Brave tempers,
To do thus for their enemies.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: They are lost yet.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: You that would rescue others, shall now feel
What they were born to.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Hurry them away.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: That I could follow them.

speeches.speaker: Verta.
verse: I only can lament my fortune, and desire of heaven
A little life for my revenge.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: The Provost
Shall fire the woods, but I will find 'em out,
No cave, no rock, nor hell shall keep them from
My searching vengeance.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: O cold! O fearfull cold! plague of all seconds.

speeches.speaker: Samp.
verse: O for a pint of burnt wine, or a sip
Of aqua-fortis.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: The rogues have met with these two
Upon my life and rob'd 'em.

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: As you are honourable Gentlemen,
Impart unto a couple of cold combatants.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: My Lord, mine uncle as I live.

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: Pox take him.
How that word has warm'd my mouth?

speeches.speaker: Verta.
verse: Why how now Cousin?
Why, why? and where man, have you been? at a Poulters
That you are cas'd thus like a rabbet? I could laugh now,
And I shall laugh, for all I have lost my Children,
Laugh monstrously.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: What are they?

speeches.speaker: Verta.
verse: Give me leave Sir,
Laugh more and more, never leave laughing.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Why Sir?

speeches.speaker: Verta.
verse: Why 'tis such a thing I smell it Sir, I smell it,
Such a ridiculous thing, —

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Do you laugh at me my Lord?
I am very cold, but that should not be laught at.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: What art thou?

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: What art thou?

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: If he had his doublet. —
And his sword by his side, as a Gentleman ought to have.

speeches.speaker: Verta.
verse: Peace Monsieur Sampson.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Come hither little Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: Base is the ^ave commanded: come to me.

speeches.speaker: Verta.
verse: This is the little advocate.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: What advocate?

speeches.speaker: Verta.
verse: The little advocate that sent me a challenge,
I told you that my Nephew undertook it,
And what 'twas like to prove: now you see the issue.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Is this the little Lawyer?

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: You have a sword Sir,
And I have none, you have a doublet too
That keeps you warm, and makes you merry.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: If your Lordship knew
The nature, and the nobleness of the Gentleman,
Though he shew slight here, and at what gusts of danger
His manhood has arrived,
But that
Mens fates are foolish,
And often headlong overrun their fortunes.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: That little Lawyer would so prick his ears up,
And bite your honour by the nose.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Say you so Sir?

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: So niggle about your grave shins Lord Vertagine too

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: No more sweet Gentleman, no more of ^.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: I will have more, I must have more.

speeches.speaker: Verta.
verse: Out with it.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: Nay he is as brave a fellow —

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Have I caught you?

speeches.speaker: Verta.
verse: Do not kill him, do not kill him.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: No, no, no, I will not. Do you peep ag^
Down down proud heart.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: O valour,
Look up brave friend, I have no means to rescue thee,
My Kingdom for a sword.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: I'le sword you presently,
I'le claw your skin coat too.

speeches.speaker: Verta.
verse: Away good Sampson,
You goe to grass else instantly.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: But do not murder my brave friend.

speeches.speaker: Verta.
verse: Not one word.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: If you do sirra—

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: Must I goe off dishonour'd?
Adversity tries valour, so I leave thee.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Are you a Lawyer Sir?

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: I was, I was Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Nay never look, your Lawyers pate is broken,
And your litigious blood about your ears sirra,
Why do you fight and snarle?

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: I was possest.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: I'le dispossess you.

speeches.speaker: Verta.
verse: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Et tu Brute?

speeches.speaker: Verta.
verse: Beat him no more.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Alas Sir I must beat him,
Beat him into his business again, he will be lost else.

speeches.speaker: Verta.
verse: Then take your way.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Ly still, and doe not struggle.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: I am patient,
I never saw my blood before, it jades me,
I have no more heart now than a goose.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Why sirra, why do you leave your trade, your trade of living,
And send your challenges like thunderbolts,
To men of honour'd place?

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: I understand Sir,
I never understood before your beating.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Does this work on you?

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Do you thank me for't?

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: As well as a beaten man can.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: And do you promise me,
To fall close to your trade again? leave brawling?

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: If you will give me leave and life.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: And ask this noble man forgiveness?

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Heartily.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Rise then, and get you gon^, and let me hear of you
As of an advocate new vampt; no more words,
Get you off quickly, and make no murmurs,
I shall pursue you else.

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: I have done sweet Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Verta.
verse: But we forget our selves, our friends and Children.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: We'l raise the country first, then take our fortunes.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Shall I entreat for what I may command?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Think on my birth.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Here I am only Noble,
A King, and thou in my dominions, fool,
A subject and a slave.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Be not a Tyrant,
A ravisher of honour, gentle Sir,
And I will think ye such, and on my knees,
As to my Soveraign, pay a Subjects duty,
With prayers and tears.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: I like this humble carriage,
I will walk by, but kneel you still and weep too,
It shews well, while I meditate on the prey,
Before I seize it.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Is there no mercie, Heaven?

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Not kiss you?
I will kiss and kiss again.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: Savage villain!
My Innocence be my strength, I do defie thee,
Thus scorn and spit at thee; will you come on Sir?
You are hot, there is a cooler.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: A virago?

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: No, loathsome Goat, more, more, I am that Goddess,
That here with whips of steel in hell hereafter
Scourge rape and theft.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: I'le try your deity.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: My chastity, and this knife held by a Virgin,
Against thy lust, thy sword and thee a Beast,
Call on for the encounter.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Now what think you?
Are you a Goddess?

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: In me their power suffers,
That should protect the Innocent.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: I am all s^e,
And thou shalt quench it, and serve my pleasures.
Come partner in the spoil and the reward,
Let us enjoy our purchase.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: O Dinant!
O Heaven! O Husband!

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: O my Cleremont!

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Two are our slaves they call on, bring 'em forth
As they are chain'd together, let them see
And suffer in the object.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: While we sit
And without pity hear 'em.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: By my life,
I suffer more for thee than for my self.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Be a man Cleremont, and look upon 'em
As such that not alone abus'd our service,
Feel us with hopes most bitter in digestion,
But when love fa^'d, to draw on further mischief,
The baits they laid for us, were our own honours,
Which thus hath made us slaves too, worse than slaves.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: He dies.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Pray hold, give him a little respite.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: I see you now beyond expression wretched,
The wit you brag'd of fool'd, that boasted honour,
As you believ'd compass'd with walls of brass,
To guard it sure, subject to be o'r^thrown
With the least blast of lust.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: A most sad truth.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: That confidence which was not to be shaken
In a perpetual s^v^, and those favours,
Which with so strong and Ceremonious duty
Your love^ and a Gentleman long sought for,
Sought, sued, and kneel'd in vain for, must you yield up
To a licentious villain, that will hardly
Allow you thanks for't.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Something I must say too,
And to you pretty one, though crying one;
To be hang'd now, when these worshipful benchers please,
Though I know not their faces that condemn me,
A little startles me, but a man is nothing,
A Maidenhead is the thing, the thing all aim at;
