Do not you wish now, and wish from your heart too,
When scarce sweet with my fears, I long lay by you
Those fears you and your good Aunt put upon me,
To make you sport, you had given a little hint,
A touch or so, to tell me I was mortal,
And by a mortal woman?

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: Pray you no more.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: If I had loos'd that virgin Zone, observe me,
I would have hired the best of all our Poets
To have sung so much, and so well in the honour
Of that nights joy, that Ovids afternoon,
Nor his Corinna should again be mention'd.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: I do repent, and wish I had.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: That's comfort,
But now —

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Another that will have it offer'd,
Compel it to be offer'd, shall enjoy it.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: A rogue, a ruffian.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: As you love your throat,—

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Away with them.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: O Cleremont!

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: O Dinant!

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: I can but add your sorrows to my sorrows,
Your fears to my fears.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: To your wishes mine,
This slave may prove unable to perform,
Till I perform the task that I was born for.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: Amen, amen.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Drag the slaves hence, for you
A while I'le lock you up here, study all ways
You can to please me, or the deed being done,
You are but dead.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: This strong Vault shall contain you,
There think how many for your maidenhead
Have pin'd away, and be prepar'd to lose it
With penitence.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: No humane help can save you.

speeches.speaker: Ladyes.
verse: Help, help?

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: You cry in vain, rocks cannot hear you.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: O Cousin how I shake all this long night!
What frights and noises we have heard, still they encrease,
The villains put on shapes to torture us,
And to their Devils form such preparations
As if they were a hatching new dishonours,
And fatal ruine, part dull mans invention.
Goe not too far, and pray good Cousin Anabel,
Hark a new noise.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: They are exquisite in mischief,
I will goe on, this room gives no protection,
More than the next, what's that? how sad and hollow,
The sound comes to us.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Groaning? or singing is it?

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: The wind I think, murmuring amongst old rooms.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Now it grows lowder, sure some sad presage
Of our foul loss — look now they peep.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: Pox peep 'em.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: O give them gentle language.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: Give 'em rats-bane.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Now they are above.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: I would they were i'th' Center.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Thou art so foolish desperate.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: Since we must lose.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Call 'em brave fellows, Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: Call 'em rogues,
Rogue as they are, rude rogues, uncivil villains.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Look an thou woo't beware, dost thou feel the danger?

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: Till the danger feel me, thus will I talk still,
And worse when that comes too; they cannot eat me.
This is a punishment, upon our own prides
Most justly laid; we must abuse brave Gentlemen,
Make 'em tame fools, and hobby-horses, laugh and jear at
Such men too, and so handsom and so Noble,
That howsoe're we seem'd to carry it —
Wou'd 'twere to do again.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: I do confess cousin,
I was too harsh, too foolish.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: Do you feel it?
Do you find it now? take heed o'th' punishment,
We might have had two gallant Gentlemen,
Proper, young, O how it tortures me!
Two Devils now, two rascals, two and twenty—

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: O think not so.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: Nay an we 'scape so modestly —

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: May we be worthy any eyes, or knowledge,
When we are used thus?

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: Why not? why do you cry?
Are we not women still? what were we made for?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: But thus, thus basely —

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: 'Tis against our vills,
And if there come a thousand so,—

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Out on thee.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: You are a fool, what we cannot resist,
Why should we grieve and blush for? there be women,
And they that bear the name of excellent women
Would give their whole estates to meet this fortune.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Hark, a new noise.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: Let 'em goe on, I fear not,
If wrangling, fighting and scratching cannot preserve me,
Why so be it Cousin; if I be ordain'd
To breed a race of rogues.—

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: They come.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: Be firm,
They are welcom.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: What mask of death is this? O my dear Brother.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: My Couz too; why now y'are glorious villains.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: O shall we lose our honours?

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: Let 'em goe,
When death prepares the way, they are but Pageants.
Why must these dye?

speeches.speaker: Beau.
verse: Lament your own misfortunes,
We perish happily before your ruins.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: Has mischief ne'r a tongue?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Yes foolish woman,
Our Captains will is death.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: You dare not do it.
Tell thy base boisterous Captain what I say,
Thy lawless Captain that he dares not;
Do you laugh you rogue? you pamper'd rogue?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Good Sir,
Good Cousin gently, as y'are a Gentleman,—

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: A Gentleman? a slave, a dog, the devils harbinger.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Sir as you had a Mother.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: He a Mother?
^me not the name of Mother, a she Bear
A bloody old wolf bitch, a woman Mother?
Looks that rude lump, as if he had a Mother?
^at him? hang him, do thy worst, thou dar'st not,
T^ou dar'st not wrong their lives, thy Captain dares not,
They are persons of more price.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: What e're we suffer
Let not your angers wrong you.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: You cannot suffer,
The men that do this deed, must live i'th' moon
Free from the gripe of Justice.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Is it not better?

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: Is it not better? let 'em goe on like rascals
And put false faces on; they dare not do it;
Flatter such scabbs of nature?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Woman, woman
The next work is with you.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: Unbind those Gentlemen,
And put their fatal fortunes on our necks

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: As you have mercy do.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: As you are monsters.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Fright us no more with shipwrack of our honours
Nor if there be a guilt by us committed
Let it endanger those.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: I say they dare not,
There be a thousand gallouses, ye rogues,
Tortures, ye bloody rogues, wheels.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Away.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Stay.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: Stay.
Stay and I'le flatter too: good sweet fac'd Gentlemen,
You excellent in honesty; O Kinsmen!
O Noble kinsmen!

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Away with 'em.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: Stay yet.
The Devil and his lovely dam walk with you,
Come fortify your self, if they do dy,
Which all their ruggedness cannot rack into me,
They cannot find an hour more Innocent,
Nor more friends to revenge 'em.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Now stand constant,
For now our tryal's come.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: This beautie's mine,
Your minute moves not yet.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: She sinks if Christian,
If any spark of noble heat.—

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Rise Lady
And fearless rise, there's no dishonour meant you,
Do you know my tongue?

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: I have heard it.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Mark it better,
I am one that loves you, fairly, nobly loves you,
Look on my face?

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: O Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: No more words, softly
Hark, but hark wisely how, understand well,
Suspect not, fear not.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: You have brought me comfort.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: If you think me worthy of your husband,
I am no rogue nor Begger, if you dare do thus —

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: You are Monsieur Cleremont.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I am the same,
If you dare venture, speak, if not I leave you,
And leave you to the mercy of these villains
That will not wooe ye much.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: Save my reputation,
And free me from these slaves.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: By this kiss I'le do it,
And from the least dishonour they dare aim at you,
I have a Priest too, shall be ready.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: You are forward.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Is this my constant cousin? how she whispers,
Kisses and huggs the thief!

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: You'l offer nothing.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Till all be tyed,
Not as I am a Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: Can you relieve my Aunt too?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Not yet Mistris,
But fear nothing, all shall be well, away quickly
It must be done i'th' moment or —

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: I am with ye.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I'le know now who sleeps by me, keep your standing.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Well, go thy way, and thine own shame dwell with thee.
Is this the constancy she shew'd, the bravery?
The dear love and the life she ow'd her kinsmen?
O brave tongue, valiant glorious woman?
Is this the noble anger you arriv'd at?
Are these the thieves you scorn'd, the rogues you rail'd at?
The scal^ and scums of nature? O fair modesty,
Excellent vertue, whither art thou fled?
What hand O Heaven is over us, when strong virgins
Yield to their f^ars, and to their fears their fortunes?
Never belief come ^ear me more, farewel wench,
A long farewel from all that ever knew thee:
My turn is n^xt,
I am resolv'd, it comes
But in a nobler shape, ha?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Blesse ye Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Indeed Sir, I had need of many blessings,
For all the hours I have had since I came here,
Have been so many curses. How got you liberty?
For I presume you come to comfort me.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: To comfort you, and love you, 'tis most true,
My bondage was as yours, as full of bitterness
And every hour my death.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Heaven was your comfort.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Till the last evening, sitting full of sadness,
Wa^l^ng, sweet Mistris, your unhappy fortunes,
(Mine own I had the least care of) round about me
The Captain and the company stood gaping,
When I began the story of my love
To you fai^ Saint, and with so full a sorrow,
Follow'd each point, that even from those rude eyes,
T^a^ n^ver knew w^at ^ or mercy,
^ Mistris,
And let no ^ unholy hearts ou^ to you
The soft plum'd god will see again, thus taken,
As men transform'd with the strange tale I told,
They stood a^z'd, then bid me rise and live,
Take liberty and means to see your p^on,
And wisht me prosperous in your love, wi^h you so,
Be wise and loving Lady, shew but you so.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: O Sir, are these fit hours to talk of love in?
Shall we make fools of our afflictions?
Can any thing sound sweetly in mine ears,
Where all the noise of bloody horrour i^?
My Brother, and my Cousin, they are dead Sir,
Dead, basely dead, is this an age to fool in?
And I my s^f, I know not what I shall be,
Yet I must thank you, and if happily
You had ask'd me yesterday, when these were living,
And my fears less, I might have hearkned to you.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Peace to your grief, I bind you to your word.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: How? do you conjure?

speeches.speaker: D^n.
verse: Not to raise dreadfull apparitions, Madam,
But such as you would gladly see.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: My Brother, and nephew living?

speeches.speaker: Beau.
verse: And both owe their lives
To the favour of these Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Verd.
verse: Who deserve
Our service, and for us, your gracious thanks.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Which I give freely, and become a suitor,
To be hereafter more familiar
With such g^eat worth and vertue.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Ever think us
Your servants, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Why if thou wilt needs know
How we are f^d, I will discover it,
And with laconick brevity: these Gentlemen
This night incountring with those outlaws that
Yesterday made us prisoners, and as we were
Attempted by 'em they with greater courage,
(I am sure with better fortune) not alone,
Guarded themselves, but forc'd the bloody thieves,
Being got between them, and this hellish Cave,
For safety of their lives, to fly up higher
Into the woods, all left to their possession,
This sav'd your Brother, and your nephew from
The gibbet, this redeem'd me from my Chains,
And gave my friend his liberty, this preserv'd
Your honour ready to be lost.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: But that
I know this for a ly, and that the thieves
And gentlemen, are the same men, by my practice
Suborn'd to this, he does deliver it
With such a constant brow, that I am doubtfull,
I should believe him too.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: If we did well,
We are rewarded.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Thanks but takes away
From what was freely purpos'd.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Now by this hand,
You have so cunningly discharg'd your parts,
That while we live, rest confident you shall
Command Dinant and Cleremont; nor Beaupre,
Nor Verdone scents it: for the Ladies, they
Were easie to be gull'd.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: 'Twas but a jest,
And yet the jest may chance to break our necks
Should it be known.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Fear nothing.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Cleremont,
Say, what success?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: As thou wouldst wish, 'tis done Lad,
The grove will witness with me, that this night
I lay not like a block: but how speed you?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: I yet am in suspence, devise some means
To get these off, and speedily.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: I have it,
Come, we are dull, I think that the good fellows,
Our predecessors in this place, were not
So foolish, and improvident husbands, but
'Twill yield us meat and wine.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Let's ransack it,
'Tis ours now by the Law.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: How say you sweet one,
Have you an appetit?

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: To walk again
I'th' Woods, if you think fit, rather than eat.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: A little respite prethee; nay blush not,
You ask but what's your own, and warrantable:
Monsieur, Beaupre, Verdone,
What think you of the motion?

speeches.speaker: Verd.
verse: Lead the way.

speeches.speaker: Beau.
verse: We follow willingly.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: When you shall think fit,
We will expect you.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Now be mistris of
Your promise Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: 'Twas to give you hearing.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: But that word hearing, did include a grant,
And you must make it good.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Must?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Must and shall,
I will be fool'd no more, you had your tricks;
Made properties of me, and of my friend;
Presum'd upon your power, and whip'd me with
The rod of mine own dotage: do not flatter
Your self with hope, that any humane help
Can free you, and for aid by miracle
A base unthankfull woman is unworthy.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: You will not force me?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Rather than enjoy you
With your consent, because I will torment you;
I'le make you feel the effects of abus'd love,
And glory in your torture.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Brother, Nephew,
Help, help, for Heavens sake.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Tear your throat, cry louder,
Though every leaf, these trees bear, were an Echo,
And summon'd in your best friends to redeem you,
It should be fruitless: 'tis not that I love you,
Or value those delights you prize so high,
That I'le enjoy you, a French crown will buy
More sport, and a companion, to whom,
You in your best trim are an Ethiop.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Forbear me then.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Not so, I'le do't in spite,
And break that stubborn disobedient will,
That hath so long held out, that boasted honour
I will make equal with a common Whores;
The spring of Chastity, that fed your pride,
And grew into a River of vain glory,
I will defile with mudd, the mudd of lust,
And make it loathsome even to goats.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: O Heaven!
No pity Sir?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: You taught me to be cruel,
And dare you think of mercy? I'le tell thee fool,
Those that surpriz'd thee, were my instruments,
I can plot too, good Madam, you shall find it:
And in the stead of licking of my fingers,
Kneeling and whining like a boy new breech'd,
To get a toy forsooth, not worth an apple,
Thus make my way, and with Authority
Command what I would have.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: I am lost for ever:
Good Sir, I do confess my fault, my gross fault,
And yield my self up, miserable guilty;
Thus kneeling I confess, you cannot study
Sufficient punishments to load me with;
I am in your power, and I confess again,
You cannot be too cruel: if there be,
Besides the loss of my long guarded honour,
Any thing else to make the ballance even,
Pray put it in, all hopes, all helpes have left me;
I am girt round with sorrow; hell's about me,
And ravishment the least that I can look for,
Do what you please.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Indeed I will do nothing,
Nor touch nor hurt you Lady, nor had ever
Such a lewd purpose.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Can there be such goodness,
And in a man so injur'd?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Be confirm'd in't.
I seal it thus: I must confess you vex'd me,
In fooling me so often, and those fears
You threw upon me call'd for a requital,
Which now I have return'd, all unchast love
Dinant thus throws away; live to man-kind,
As you have done to me, and I will honour
Your vertue, and no more think of your beauty.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: All I possess, comes short of satisfaction.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: No complements: the terrours of this night
Imagine but a fearfull dream, and so
With ease forget it: for Dinant, that labour'd
To blast your honour, is a Champion for it,
And will protect and guard it.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: 'Tis as safe then,
As if a compleat Army undertook it.

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: Do not perswade me gentle Monsieur Sampson,
I am a mortal man again, a Lawyer,
My martiall part I have put off.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: Sweet Monsieur,
Let ^t our honours teach us.

speeches.speaker: La writ.
verse: Monsieur Sampson,
My honourable friend, my valiant friend,
Be but so beaten, forward my brave Clients,
I am yours, and you are mine again, be but so thrasht,
Receive that Castigation with a cudgel.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: Which calls upon us for a Reparation.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: I have, it cost me half a crown, I bear it
All over me, I bear it Monsieur Sampson;
The oyls, and the old woman that repairs to me,
To 'noint my beaten body.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: It concerns you,
You have been swing'd.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Let it concern thee too;
Goe and be beaten, speak scurvy words, as I did,
Speak to that Lion Lord, waken his anger,
And have a hundred Bastinado's, doe;
Three broken pates, thy teeth knockt out, do Sampson,
Thy valiant arms and leggs beaten to Poultesses,
Do silly Sampson, do.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cly.
verse: You wrong the Gentleman,
To put him out of his right mind thus:
You wrong us, and our Causes.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Down with him Gentlemen,
Turn him, and beat him, if he break our peace,
Then when thou hast been Lam'd, thy small guts perisht,
Then talk to me, before I scorn thy counsel,
Feel what I feel, and let my Lord repair thee.

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: And can the brave La-writ—

speeches.speaker: 2 Cly.
verse: Tempt him no further,
Be warn'd and say no more.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: If thou doest, Sampson,
Thou seest my Mirmidons, I'le let 'em loose,
That in a moment —

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: I say nothing, Sir, but I could wish—

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: They shall destroy thee wishing;
There's ne'r a man of these, but have lost ten causes,
Dearer then ten mens lives; tempt, and thou diest:
Goe home, and smile upon my Lord, thine Uncle,
Take Mony of the men thou mean'st to Cousin,
Drink Wine, and eat good meat, and live discreetly,
Talk little, 'tis an antidote against a bea^ing;
Keep thy hand from thy sword, and from thy Laundress placket,
And thou wilt live long.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cly.
verse: Give ear, and be instructed.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: I find I am wiser than a Justice of Peace now,
Give me the wisdom that's beaten into a man
That sticks still by him: art thou a new man?

speeches.speaker: Sam.
verse: Yes, yes,
Thy learned precepts have inchanted me.

speeches.speaker: La-writ.
verse: Goe my son Sampson, I have now begot thee,
I'le send thee causes; speak to thy Lord, and live,
And lay my share by, goe and live in peace,
Put on new suits, and shew sit for thy place;
That man neglects his living, is an Asse:
Farewel; come chearily boyes, about our business,
Now welcom tongue again, hang Swords.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cly.
verse: Sweet Advocate.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: I know not wench, they may call 'em what they will,
Outlawes, or thieves, but I am sure, to me
One was an honest man, he us'd me well,
What I did, 'tis no matter, he complain'd not.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: I must confess, there was one bold with me too,
Some coy thing would say rude, but 'tis no matter,
I was to pay a Waiting womans ransom,
And I have don't, and I would pay't again,
Were I ta'n to morrow.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: Alas, there was no hurt,
If't be a sin for such as live at hard meat,
And keep a long Lent, in the woods as they do,
To taste a little flesh.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: God help the Courtiers,
That lye at rack and manger.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: I shall love
A thief the better for this while I live,
They are men of a charitable vocation,
And give where there is need, and with discretion,
And put a good speed penny in my purse,
That has been empty twenty years.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Peace Nurse,
Farewel, and cry not rost meat, me thinks Cleremont
And my Lady Anabel are in one night,
Familiarly acquainted.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: I observe it,
If she have got a penny too.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: No more,
My Lord Monsieur Vertaigne, the provost too,
Haste and acquaint my Lady.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Wonderous strange.

speeches.speaker: Vert.
verse: 'Tis true Sir, on my credit.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: O mine honour.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: I have been provost-Marshal twenty years,
And have trussed up a thousand of these rascals,
But so near Paris yet I never met with
One of that Brotherhood.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: We to our cost have,
But will you search the wood?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: It is beset,
They cannot scape us, nothing makes me wonder,
So much as having you within their power
They let you goe, it was a Courtesy,
That French thieves use not often, I much pity
The Gentle Ladies, yet I know not how,
I rather hope than fear.
Are these the prisoners?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: We were such.

speeches.speaker: Verd.
verse: Kill me not, excess of joy.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: I see thou livest, but hast thou had no soul play?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: No on my soul, my usage hath been noble,
Far from all violence,

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: How were you freed?
But kiss me first, we'l talk of that at leasure,
I am glad I have thee; Niece how you keep off,
As you knew me not?

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: Sir, I am where
I owe most duty.

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: 'Tis indeed most true Sir,
The man that should have been your bedfellow
Your Lordships bedfellow, that could not smell out
A Virgin of sixteen, that was your fool,
To make you merry, this poor simple fellow
Has met the maid again, and now she knows
He is a man.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: How! is she dishonoured?

speeches.speaker: Cler.
verse: Not unless marriage be dishonourable,
Heaven is a witness of our happy contract,
And the next Priest we meet shall warrant it
To all the world: I lay with her in jeast,
'Tis turn'd to earnest now.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Is this true, Niece?

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: Her blushing silence grants it; nay Sir storm not,
He is my friend, and I can make this good,
His birth and fortunes equal hers, your Lordship
Might have sought out a worse, we are all friends too,
All differences end thus. Now Sir, unless
You would raise new dissentions, make perfect
What is so well begun.

speeches.speaker: Vert.
verse: That were not manly.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Let me perswade you.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Well God give you joy,
She shall not come a Begger to you Sir.
For you Monsieur Dinant 'ere long I'le shew you
Another Niece, to this not much inferiour,
As you shall like proceed.

speeches.speaker: Din.
verse: I thank you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cham.
verse: Back then to Paris: well that travel ends
That makes of deadly enemies perfect friends.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
verse: I Never saw the like, she's no more stirr'd,
No more another Woman, no more alter'd
With any hopes or promises laid to her
(Let 'em be ne're so weighty, ne're so winning)
Than I am with the motion of mine own legs.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Chilax,
You are a stranger yet in these designs,
At least in Rome; tell me, and tell me truth,
Did you ere know in all your course of practice,
In all the wayes of Women you have run through
(For I presume you have been brought up Chilax,
As we to fetch and carry.)

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: True I have so.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Did you I say again in all this progress,
Ever discover such a piece of beauty,
Ever so rare a Creature, and no doubt
One that must know her worth too, and affect it,
I and be flatter'd, else 'tis none: and honest?
Honest against the tide of all temptations,
Honest to one man, to her Husband only,
And yet not eighteen, not of age to know
Why she is honest?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I confess it freely,
I never saw her fellow, nor e're shall,
For all our Grecian Dames, all I have tri'd,
(And sure I have tri'd a hundred, if I say two
I speak within my compass) all these beauties,
And all the constancy of all these faces,
Maids, Widows, Wives, of what degree or calling,
So they be Greeks, and fat, for there's my cunning,
I would undertake and not sweat for't, Proculus,
Were they to try again, say twice as many,
Under a thousand pound, to lay 'em bedrid;
But this Wench staggers me.

speeches.speaker: Lyc.
verse: Do you see these Jewels?
You would think these pretty baits; now I'le assure ye
Here's half the wealth of Asia.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
verse: These are nothing
To the full honours I propounded to her;
I bid her think, and be, and presently
What ever her ambition, what the Counsel
Of others would add to her, what her dreams
Could more enlarge, what any President
Of any Woman rising up to glory,
And standing certain there, and in the highest,
Could give her more, nay to be Empress.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: And cold at all these offers?

speeches.speaker: Bal.
verse: Cold as Crystal,
Never to be thaw'd again.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I tri'd her further,
And so far, that I think she is no Woman,
At least as Women go now.

speeches.speaker: Lyc.
verse: Why what did you?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I offered that, that had she been but Mistris
Of as much spleen as Doves have, I had reach'd her;
A safe revenge of all that ever hates her,
The crying down for ever of all beauties
That may be thought come near her.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: That was pretty.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I never knew that way fail, yet I'le tell ye
I offer'd her a gift beyond all yours,
That, that had made a Saint start, well consider'd,
The Law to be her creature, she to make it,
Her mouth to give it, every creature living
From her aspect, to draw their good or evil
Fix'd in 'em spight of Fortune; a new Nature
She should be called, and Mother of all ages,
Time should be hers, and what she did, lame vertue
Should bless to all posterities: her Air
Should give us life, her earth and water feed us.
And last, to none but to the Emperour,
(And then but when she pleas'd to have it so)
She should be held for mortal.

speeches.speaker: Lyc.
verse: And she heard you?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Yes, as a Sick man hears a noise, or he
That stands condemn'd his judgment, let me perish,
But if there can be vertue, if that name
Be any thing but name and empty title,
If it be so as fools have been pleas'd to feign it,
A power that can preserve us after ashes,
And make the names of men out-reckon ages,
This Woman has a God of vertue in her.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
verse: I would the Emperor were that God.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: She has in her
All the contempt of glory and vain seeming
Of all the Stoicks, all the truth of Christians,
And all their Constancy: Modesty was made
When she was first intended: when she blushes
It is the holiest thing to look upon;
The purest temple of her sect, that ever
Made Nature a blest Founder.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Is there no way
To take this Phenix?

speeches.speaker: Lyc.
verse: None but in her ashes.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: If she were fat, or any way inclining
To ease or pleasure, or affected glory,
Proud to be seen and worship'd, 'twere a venture;
But on my soul she is chaster than cold Camphire.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
verse: I think so too; for all the waies of Woman,
Like a full sail she bears against: I askt her
After my many offers walking with her,
And her as many down-denyals, how
If the Emperour grown mad with love should force her:
She pointed to a Lucrece, that hung by,
And with an angry look, that from her eyes
Shot Vestal fire against me, she departed.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: This is the first wench I was ever pos'd in,
Yet I have brought young loving things together
This two and thirty years.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I find by this wench
The calling of a Bawd to be a strange,
A wise, and subtile calling; and for none
But staid, discreet, and understanding people:
And as the Tutor to great Alexander,
Would say, a young man should not dare to read
His moral books, till after five and twenty;
So must that he or she, that will be bawdy,
(I mean discreetly bawdy, and be trusted)
If they will rise, and gain experience,
Well steept in years, and discipline, begin it,
I take it 'tis no Boys play.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
verse: Well, what's thought of?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: The Emperour must know it.

speeches.speaker: Lyc.
verse: If the woman should chance to fail too.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: As 'tis ten to one.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Why what remains, but new nets for the purchase?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Let's go consider then: and if all fail,
This is the first quick Eele, that sav'd her tail.

speeches.speaker: Ardel.
verse: You still insist upon that Idol, Honour,
Can it renew your y^uth, can it add wealth,
That takes off wrinkles: can it draw mens eyes,
To gaze upon you in your age? can honour,
That truly is a Saint to none but Souldiers,
And look'd into, bears no reward but danger,
Leave you the most respected person living?
Or can the common kisses of a Husband,
(Which to a sprightly Lady is a labour)
Make ye almost Immortal? ye are cozen'd,
The honour of a woman is her praises;
The way to get these, to be seen, and sought too,
And not to bury such a happy sweetness
Under a smoaky roof.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: I'le hear no more.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: That white, and red, and all that blessed beauty,
Kept from the eyes, that make it so, is nothing;
Then you are rarely fair, when men proclaim it;
The Phenix, were she never seen, were doubted;
That most unvalued Horn the Unicorn
Bears to oppose the Huntsman, were it nothing
But tale, and meer tradition, would help no man;
But when the vertue's known, the honour's doubled:
Vertue is either lame, or not at all,
And love a Sacriledge, and not a Saint,
When it bars up the way to mens Petitions.

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: Nay ye shall love your Husband too; we come not
To make a Monster of ye.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Are ye women?

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: You'll find us so, and women you shall thank too,
If you have grace to make your use.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Fye on ye.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: Alas poor bashful Lady, by my soul,
Had ye no other vertue, but your blushes,
And I a man, I should run mad for those:
How daintily they set her off, how sweetly!

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: Come Goddess, come, you move too near the earth,
It must not be, a better Orb stayes for you:
Here: be a Maid, and take 'em.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Pray leave me.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: That were a sin sweet Lady, and a way
To make us guilty of your melancholy:
You must not be alone; in conversation
Doubts are resolv'd, and what sticks near the conscience
Made easie, and allowable.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Ye are Devils,

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: That you may one day bless for your damnation.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: I charge ye in the name of Chastity,
Tempt me no more; how ugly ye seem to me?
There is no wonder men defame our Sex,
And lay the vices of all ages on us,
When such as you shall bear the names of women;
If ye had eyes to see your selves, or sence
Above the base rewards ye play the bawds for:
If ever in your lives ye heard of goodness,
(Though many Regions off, as men hear Thunder)
^f ever ye had Mothers, and they souls:
If ever Fathers, and not such as you are;
If ever any thing were constant in you,
Besides your sins, or coming, but your courses;
If ever any of your Ancestors
Dyed worth a noble deed, that would be cherish'd;
Soul-frighted with this black infection,
You would run from one another, to repentance,
And from your guilty eyes drop out those sins,
That made ye blind, and beasts.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: Ye speak well, Lady;
A sign of fruitful education,
If your religious zeal had wisdom with it.

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: This Lady was ordain'd to bless the Empire,
And we may all give thanks for't.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: I believe ye.

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: If any thing redeem the Emperour
From his wild flying courses, this is she;
She can instruct him if ye mark; she is wise too.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: Exceeding wise, which is a wonder in her,
And so religious, that I well believe,
Though she would sin she cannot.

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: And besides,
She has the Empires cause in hand, not loves;
There lies the main consideration,
For which she is chiefly born.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: She finds that point
Stronger than we can tell her, and believe it
I look by her means for a reformation,
And such a one, and such a rare way carried
That all the world shall wonder at.

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: 'Tis true;
I never thought the Emperor had wisdom,
Pity, or fair affection to his Country,
Till he profest this love: gods give 'em Children,
Such as her vertues merit, and his zeal.
I look to see a Numa from this Lady,
Or greater than Octavius.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: Do you mark too,
Which is a Noble vertue, how she blushes,
And what a flowing modesty runs through her,
When we but name the Emperour?

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: But mark it,
Yes, and admire it too, for she considers,
Though she be fair as Heaven, and vertuous
As holy truth, yet to the Emperour
She is a kind of nothing but her service,
Which she is bound to offer, and she'll do it,
And when her Countries cause commands affection,
She knows obedience is the key of vertues,
Then flye the blushes out like Cupid's arrows,
And though the tye of Marriage to her Lord
Would fain cry, stay Lucina, yet the cause
And general wisdom of the Princes love,
Makes here find surer ends and happier,
And if the first were chaste, this is twice doubled.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: Her tartness unto us too.

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: That's a wise one.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: I rarely like, it shews a rising wisdom,
That chides all common fools as dare enquire
What Princes would have private

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: What a Lady
Shall we be blest to serve?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Go get ye from me:
Ye are your purses Agents, not the Princes
Is this the vertuous Lo^e ye train'd me out to?
Am I a woman fit to imp your v^ces?
But that I had a Mother, and a woman
Whosoever living fame turns all it touches,
Into the good it self is, I should now
Even doubt my self, I have been s^arch't so near
The very soul of honour: why should you two.
That happily have been as chaste as I am,
Fairer, I think, by much, for yet your faces,
Like ancient well built piles, shew worthy ruins,
After that Angel age, turn mortal Devils?
For shame, for woman-hood, for what ye have been,
For rotten Cedars have born goodly branches,
If ye have hope of any Heaven, but Court,
Which like a Dream, you'l find hereafter vani^h,
Or at the best but subject to repentance,
Study no more to be ill spoken of;
Let women live themselves, if they must fall,
Their own destruction find 'em, not your F^vours.

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: Madam, ye are so excellent in all,
And I must tell it you with admiration,
So true a joy ye have, so sweet a fear,
And when ye come to anger, tis so noble,
That for mine own part, I could still offend,
To hear you angry; women that want t^
And your way guided (else I count ^)
Are either Fools, or Cowards

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse:
She were a Mistris for no p^
^
Could she not frown a ravish'd kiss ^

And such an anger as this Lady lea^
^
Stuck with such pleasing ^angers. ^
Which of ye all could hold from?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: I perceive ye,
Your own dark sins dwell with ye, and t' at pr^
You sell the chastity of modest wives at
Runs to diseases with your bones: I scor^,
And all the nets ye've pitcht to catch my v^
Like Spiders Webs, I sweep away before me
Go tell the Emperour, ye have met a woman,
That neither his own person, which is God like,
The world he rules, nor what that world can purchase,
Nor all the glories subject to a Caesar,
The honours that he offers for my body,
The hopes, gifts, everlasting flatteries,
Nor any thing that's his, and apt to tempt me,
No not to be the Mother of the Empire,
And Queen of all the holy fires he worships,
Can make a Whore of.

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: You mistake us Lady.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Yet tell him this has thus much weaken'd me,
That I have heard his Knaves, and you his Matrons,
Fit Nurses for his sins, which gods forgive me;
But ever to be leaning to his folly,
Or to be brought to love his lust, assure him,
And from her mouth, whose life shall make it certain,
I never can: I have a noble Husband,
Pray tell him that too, yet a noble name,
A Noble Family, and last a Conscience:
Thus much for your answer: For your selves,
Ye have liv'd the shame of women, dye the better.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: What's now to do?

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: Ev'n as she said, to dye,
For there's no living here, and women thus,
I am sure for us two.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: Nothing stick upon her?

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: We have lost a mass of mony; well Dame Vertue,
Yet ye may halt if good luck serve.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: Worms take her,
She has almost spoil'd our trade.

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: So godly;
This is ill breeding, Phorba.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: If the women
Should have a longing now to see this Monster,
And she convert 'em all.

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: That may be, Phorba,
But if it be, I'll have the young men gelded;
Come, let's go think, she must not scape us thus;
Th^re is a certain season, if we hit,
That women may be rid without a Bit.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: I cannot blame the Nations, noble friend,
That they fall off so fast from this wild man,
When (under our Allegiance be it spoken,
And the most happy tye of our affections)
The worlds weight groans beneath him; Where lives vertue,
Honour, discretion, wisdom? who are call'd
And chosen to the steering of the Empire
But Bawds, and singing Girls? O my Aecius
The glory of a Souldier, and the truth
Of men made up for goodness sake, like shells
Grow to the ragged walls for want of action;
Only your happy self, and I that love you,
Which is a larger means to me than favour.

speeches.speaker: A^ci.
verse: No more, my worthy friend, though these be truths,
And though these truths would ask a Reformation,
At least a little squating: yet remember,
We are but Subj cts, Maximus; obedience
To what is done, and grief for what is ill done,
Is all we can call ours: The hearts of Princes
Are like the Templ^s of the gods; pure incense,
Until unhallowed hands defile those offerings,
Burns ever there; we mu^t not put 'em out,
Because the Priests that touch those sweets, are wicked;
We dare not, dearest Friend, nay mo^ we cannot,
While we consider who we are, and how,
To what laws bound, much more to what Law-giver;
Whilest Majesty is made to be obeyed,
And not to b inquired into, whilst gods and angels
Make but a rule as we do, though a stricter;
Like desperate and unseason'd Fools let flye
Our killing angers, and forsake our honours.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: My noble Friend, from whose instructions
I never yet took surfeit, weigh but thus much,
Nor think I speak it with ambition,
For by the gods, I do not; why Aecius,
Why are we thus, or how become thus wretched?

speeches.speaker: Aecius.
verse: You'll fall again into your fit.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: I will not;
Or are we now no more the Sons of Romans,
No more the followers of their happy fortunes,
But conquer'd Gauls, or Quivers for the Parthians?
Why, is this Emperour, this man we honour,
This God that ought to be?

speeches.speaker: Aecius.
verse: You are too curious.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Good, give me leave, why is this Author of us?

speeches.speaker: Aecius.
verse: I dare not hear ye speak thus.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: I'll be modest,
Thus led away, thus vainly led away,
And we Beholders? misconceive me not,
I sow no danger in my words; But wherefore,
And to what end, are we the Sons of Fathers
Famous and fast to Rome? why are their Vertues
Stampt in the dangers of a thousand Battels?
For goodness sake, their honours, time outdaring?
I think for our example.

speeches.speaker: Aecius.
verse: Ye speak nobly.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Why are we seeds of these then, to shake hands
With Bawds and base informers, kiss discredit,
And court her like a Mistriss? 'pray, your leave yet;
You'll say the Emperour is young, and apt
To take impression rather from his pleasures
Than any constant worthiness, it may be,
But why do these, the people call his pleasures,
Exceed the moderation of a man?
Nay to say justly, friend, why are they vices,
And such as shake our worths with forreign Nations?

speeches.speaker: Aecius.
verse: You search the sore too deep, and I must tell ye.
In any other man this had been boldness,
And forewarded; 'pray depress your spirit,
For though I constantly believe you honest,
Ye were no friend for me else, and what now
Ye freely spake, but good you owe to th'Empire,
Yet take heed, worthy Maximus, all ears
Hear not with that distinction mine do, few
You'll find admonishers, but urgers of your actions,
And to the heaviest (friend;) and pray consider
We are but shadows, motions others give us,
And thougn our pities may become the times,
Justly our powers cannot; make me worthy
To be your friend ever in fair Allegiance,
But not in force; For durst mine own soul urge me,
(And by that Soul I speak my just affections)
To turn my hand from Truth, which is obedience,
And give the helm my Vertue holds, to Anger;
Though I had both the Blessings of the Bruti,
And both their instigations, though my Cause
Carried a face of Justice beyond theirs,
And as I am a servant to my fortunes,
That daring soul, that first taught disobedience,
Should feel the first example: say the Prince,
As I may well believe, seems vicious,
Who justly knows 'tis not to try our honours?
Or say he be an ill Prince, are we therefore
Fit sires to purge him? No, my dearest friend,
The Elephant is never won with anger,
Nor must that man that would reclaim a Lion,
Take him by th' teeth.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: I pray mistake me not.

speeches.speaker: Aecius.
verse: Our honest actions, and the light that breaks
Like morning from our service, chaste and blushing,
Is that that pulls a Prince back; then he sees,
And not till then truly repents his errours,
When Subjects Crystal Souls are glasses to him.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: My ever honour'd friend, I'll take your counsel.
The Emperour appears, I'll leave ye to him.
And as we both affect him, may he flourish.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Is that the best news?

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: Yet the best we know, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Bid Maximus come to me, and be gone then;
Mine own head be my helper, these are fools:
How now Aecius, are the Souldiers quiet?

speeches.speaker: Aecius.
verse: Better I hope, Sir, than they were.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: They are pleas'd, I hear,
To censure me extreamly for my pleasures,
Shortly they'll fight against me.

speeches.speaker: Aecius.
verse: Gods defend, Sir.
And for their censures they are such shrew'd Judgers;
A donative of ten Sestertias
I'll undertake shall make 'em ring your praises
More than they sang your pleasures.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: I believe thee;
Art thou in love, Aecius, yet?

speeches.speaker: Aecius.
verse: O no Sir;
I am too course for Ladies; my embraces,
That only am acquainted with Alarms,
Would break their tender Bodies.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Never fear it,
They are stronger than ye think, they'll hold the Hammer.
My Empress swears thou art a lusty Souldier,
A good one I believe thee.

speeches.speaker: Aecius.
verse: All that goodness
Is but your Graces Creature.

speeches.speaker: Emp
verse: Tell me truly,

Fo^
^ou dar'st tell me.

speeches.speaker: Aec^u^.
verse: Any thing concerns ye,
Tha^'s fit for me to speak and you to pardon.

speeches.speaker: Emp
verse: What say the Souldiers of me, and the same words,

Min^
^m not, good Aecius, but deliver
The very forms and tongues they talk withal.

speeches.speaker: Aecius.
verse: I'll tell your Grace, but with this caution
You be not stir'd, for should the gods live with us,
Even those we certainly believe are righteous,
Give 'em but drink, they would censure them too.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Forward.

speeches.speaker: Aecius.
verse: Then to begin, they say you sleep too much,
By which they judge your Majesty too sensual,
Apt to decline your strength to ease and pleasures,
And when you do not sleep, you drink too much,
From which they fear suspicions first, then ruines;
And when ye neither drink nor sleep, ye wench much,
Which they affirm first breaks your understanding,
Then takes the edge of Honour, makes us seem,
That are the ribs, and rampires of the Empire,
Fencers, and beaten Fools, and so regarded;
But I believe 'em not; for were these truths,
Your vertue can correct them.

speeches.speaker: Emp
verse: They speak plainly.

speeches.speaker: A^c.
verse: They say moreover (since your Grace will have it,
For they will talk their freedoms, though the Sword
Were in their throat) that of late time, like Nero,
And with the same forgetfulness of glory,
You have got a vein of fidling, so they term it.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Some drunken dreams, Aecius.

speeches.speaker: Aecius.
verse: So I hope, Sir:
And that you rather study cruelty,
And to be fear'd for blood, than lov'd for bounty,
Which makes the Nations, as they say, despise ye,
Telling your years and actions by their deaths,
Whose truth and strength of duty made you Caesar:
They say besides you nourish strange devourers,
^ed with the fat o'th' Empire, they call Bawds,
Lazie and lustful Creatures that abuse ye,
A ^eople as they term 'em, made of paper,
In which the secret sins of each man's monies
Are seal'd and sent a working.

speeches.speaker: ^mp.
verse: What sin's next?
For I perceive they have no mind to spare me.

speeches.speaker: Aecius.
verse: Nor hurt you o' my soul, Sir; but such People
(Nor can the power of man restrain it)
When they are full of meat and ease, must prattle.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Forward.

speeches.speaker: Aecius.
verse: I have spoken too much, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: I'll have all.

speeches.speaker: Aecius.
verse: It fits not
Your ears should hear their Vanities; no profit
Can justly rise to you from their behaviour,
Unless ye were guilty of those crimes.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: It may be
I am so, therefore forward.

speeches.speaker: Aecius.
verse: I have ever
Learn'd to obey, nor shall my life resist it.

speeches.speaker: Emp
verse: No more Apologies.

speeches.speaker: Aecius.
verse: They grieve besides, Sir,
To see the Nations, whom our ancient Vertue
With many a weary march and hunger conquer'd,
With loss of many a daring life subdu'd,
Fall from their fair obedience, and even murmur
To see the warlike Eagles mew their honours
In obscure Towns, that wont to prey on Princes,
They cry for Enemies, and tell the Captains
The fruits of Italy are luscious, give us Egypt,
Or sandy Africk to display our valours,
There where our Swords may make us meat, and danger
Digest our well got Vyands; here our weapons
And bodies that were made for shining brass,
Are both unedg'd and old with ease and women.
And then they cry again, where are the Germans,

Lin'd with hot Spain, o^
Gallia, bring 'em on,
And let the Son of War, steel'd Mithridates,
Lead up his winged Parthians like a storm,
Hiding the face of Heaven with showrs of Arrows?
Yet we dare fight like Romans; then as Souldiers
Tir'd with a weary march, they tell their wounds
Even weeping ripe they were no more nor deeper,
And glory in those scars that make them lovely,
And sitting where a Camp was, like sad Pilgrims
They reckon up the times, and living labours
Of Julius or Germanicus, and wonder
That Rome, whose Turrets once were topt with Honours,
Can now forget the Custom of her Conquests;
And then they blame your Grace, and say Who leads us,
Shall we stand here like Statues? were our Fathers
The Sons of lazie Moors, our Princes Persians,
Nothing but silks and softness? Curses on 'em
That first taught Nero wantonness and blood,
Tiberius doubts, Caligula all vices;
For from the spring of these, succeeding Princes—
Thus they talk, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Well,
W^y do you hear these things?

speeches.speaker: Aecius.
verse: Why do you do 'em?
I take the gods to witness, with more sorrow,
And more vexation do I hear these tainters
Than were my life dropt from me through an hour glass.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Belike then you believe 'em, or at least
Are glad they should be so; take heed, you were better
Build your own Tomb, and run into it living,
Than dare a Princes anger.

speeches.speaker: Aecius.
verse: I am old, Sir,
And ten years more addition, is but nothing;
Now if my life be pleasing to ye, take it,
Upon my knees, if ever any service,

(As let ^
^ag some have been worthy notice)
If ev^ an^ wo^th, o^ trust ye gave me
Deserv d a word ^pect, if all my actions,
The ha^ of my youth, colds, burnings, wants,
For you, and ^or the Empire, be not vices;
By that stil^ ye hav^ stampt upon me, Souldier,
Let me not fa^l into the hands of Wretches.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: I understand you not.

speeches.speaker: Aecius.
verse: Let not this body
That has look'd bravely in his blood for Caesar,
And cov^tous of wounds, and for your safety,

After th^
^eape of Swords, Spears, Slings, and Arrows,
'Gainst which my beaten body was mine armour,
The Seas and thirsty Desarts now be purchase
For Slav^s, and base Informers; I see anger,
And death look through your Eyes; I am markt for slaughter,
And know the telling of this truth has made me
A man clean lost to thi^ World; I embrace it;
Only my last P^tition, sacred Caesar,
Is, I may dye a Roman.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Rise, my friend still,
And worthy of my love, reclaim the Souldier,
I'll study to do so upon my self too,
Go, keep your Command, and prosper.

speeches.speaker: Aecius.
verse: Lif^ to Caesar—

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Lord Maximus attends your Grace.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Go tell him
I'll meet him in the Gallery:
The honesty of this Aecius,
Who is indeed the Bull-wark of the Empire,
Has div'd so deep into me, that of all
The sins I covet, but this Womans beauty,
With much repentance now I could be quit of;
But she is suc^ a pleasure, being good,
That though I were a god, she'd fire my blood.

speeches.speaker: Emp
verse: NAy ye shall set my hand out, 'tis not just
I should neglect my fortune now 'tis prosperous.

speeches.speaker: La^
verse: If I have any thing to set your Grace,
But Cloaths or good conditions, let me perish.
You have all my money, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: And mine.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: And mine too.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Unless your Grace will credit us.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: No bare board.

speeches.speaker: L^.
verse: Then at my Garden-House.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: The Orchard too.

speeches.speaker: Lic.
verse: And't please your Grace.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Have at 'em.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: They are lost.

speeches.speaker: Lic.
verse: Why, farewel Fig-trees.

speeches.speaker: Emp
verse: Who sets more?

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: At my horse, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: The dapl'd Spaniard?

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: He.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: He's mine.

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: He is so.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Your short horse is soon curried.

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: So it seems, Sir,
So may your Mare be too, if luck serve.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Ha?

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: Nothing my Lord, but grieving at my fortune.

speeches.speaker: Emp
verse: Come Maximus, you were not wont to flinch thus.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: I have lost all.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: There's a Ring yet.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: This was not made to lose, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Some love token;
Set it I say.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: I do beseech your Grace,
Rather name any house I have.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: How strange
And curious you are grown of toys! redeem't
If so I win it, when you please, to morrow,
Or next day, as you will, I care not,
But only for my lucks sake, 'tis not Rings
Can make m^ richer.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Will you throw, Sir? there 'tis.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Why, then have at it fairly, mine.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Your Grace
Is only ever fortunate; to morrow,
And't be your pleasure, Sir, I'll pay the price on't.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: To morrow you shall have it without price, Sir,
But this day 'tis my Victory; good Maximus,
Now I bethink my self, go to Aecius,
And bid him muster all the Cohorts presently;
They mutiny for pay I hear, and be you
Assistant to him; when you know their numbers,
Ye shall have monies for 'em, and above,
Something to stop their tongues withal.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: I will Sir,
And gods preserve you in this mind still.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Shortly I'll see 'em march my self.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Gods ever keep ye —

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: To what end do you think this Ring shall serve now?
For ye are Fellows only know by rote,
As Birds record their lessons.

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: For the Lady.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: But how for her?

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: That I confess I know not.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Then pray for him that does: fetch me an Eunuch
That never saw her yet, and you two see
The C^t made like a Paradise.

speeches.speaker: Lic.
verse: We will, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Full of fair shews and Musicks; all your arts
(As I shall give instructions) screw to th' highest,
For my main piece is now a doing; and for fear
You should not take, I'll have another Engine,
Such as if vertue be not only in her,
She shall not chuse but lean to, let the Women
Put on a graver shew of welcome.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Well Sir.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: They are a thought too eager.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Here's the Eunuch.

speeches.speaker: Eun.
verse: Long life to Caesar.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: I must use you, Lycias:
Come, let's walk in, and then I'll shew ye all,
If women may be frail, this wench shall fall.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
verse: Sirrah, what ails my Lady that of late
She never cares for Company?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I know not,
Unless it be that Company causes Cuckolds.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
verse: That were a childish fear.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: What were those Ladies,
Came to her lately
From the Court?

speeches.speaker: Claud.
verse: The same wench,
Some grave instructors on my life, they look
For all the world like old hatcht hilts.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: 'Tis true, Wench,
For here and there, and yet they painted well too,
One might discover where the Gold was worn,
Their iron ages.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
verse: If my judgement fail not,
They have been sheathed like rotten Ships.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: It may be.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
verse: For if you mark their rudders, they hang wealth.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: They have past the line belike; wouldst live Clau^s
Till thou wert such as they are?

speeches.speaker: Claud.
verse: Chimney pieces:
Now heaven have mercy upon me, and young men,
I had rather make a drollery till thirty,
While I am able to endure a tempest,
And hear my fights out bravely, till my tackle
Whilstl'd i'th' Wind, and held against all weathers,
While I were able to bear with my tyres,
And so discharge 'em, I would willingly
Live, Marcellina, not till barnacles
Bred in my sides.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Thou art i'th' right, Wench;
For who would live whom pleasures had forsaken,
To stand at mark, and cry a Bow short, Seigneur?
Were there not men came hither too?

speeches.speaker: Claud.
verse: Brave fellows:
I fear me Bawds of five i'th' Pound.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: How know you?

speeches.speaker: Claud.
verse: They gave me great lights to it.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Take heed, Claudia.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: Let them take heed, the spring comes on.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: To me now
They seem'd as noble Visitants.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
verse: To me now
Nothing less, Marcellina, for I markt 'em,
And by this honest light, for yet 'tis morning,
Saving the reverence of their gilded doublets,
And Millan skins.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Thou art a strange Wench, Claudia.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
verse: Ye are deceiv'd, they shew'd to me directly
Court Crabs that creep a side-way for their living,
I know 'em by the Breeches that they beg'd last.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Peace, my Lady comes; what may that be?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: A Sumner
That cites her to appear.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: No more of that wench.

speeches.speaker: Eun.
verse: Madam, what answer to your Lord?

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Pray tell him, I am subject to his will.

speeches.speaker: Eun.
verse: Why weep you Madam?
Excellent Lady, there are none will hurt you.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: I do beseech you tell me Sir.

speeches.speaker: Eun.
verse: What, Lady?

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Serve ye the Emperor?

speeches.speaker: Eun.
verse: I do.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: In what place?

speeches.speaker: Eun.
verse: In's chamber Madam.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Do ye serve his will too?

speeches.speaker: Eun.
verse: In fair and just commands.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Are ye a Roman?

speeches.speaker: Eun.
verse: Yes noble Lady, and a Mantuan.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: What office bore your parents?

speeches.speaker: Eun.
verse: One was Pretor.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Take heed then how you stain his reputation.

speeches.speaker: Eun.
verse: Why worthy Lady?

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: If ye know, I charge ye,
Ought in this Message, but what honesty,
The trust and fair obedience of a servant
May well deliver, yet take heed, and help me.

speeches.speaker: Eun.
verse: Madam, I am no Broker.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
verse: I'le be hang'd then.

speeches.speaker: Eun.
verse: Nor base procurer of mens lusts; Your husband,
Pray'd me to do this office, I have done it,
It rests in you to come, or no.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: I will Sir.

speeches.speaker: Eun.
verse: If ye mistrust me, do not.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Ye appear so worthy,
And to all my sense so honest,
And this is such a certain sign ye have brought me,
That I believe.

speeches.speaker: Eun.
verse: Why should I cozen you?
Or were I brib'd to do this villany,
Can mony prosper, or the fool that takes it,
When such a vertue falls?

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Ye speak well Sir;
Would all the rest that serve the Emperour,
Had but your way.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
verse: And so they have ad unguem.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Pray tell my Lord, I have receiv'd his Token,
And will not fail to meet him; yet good Sir, thus much
Before you goe, I do beseech ye too,
As little notice as ye can, deliver
Of my appearance there.

speeches.speaker: Eun.
verse: It shall be Madam,
And so I wish you happiness.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: I thank you —

segments.head: Actus Secundus. | SCENA II. Tumult & noise within.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Temper your self Aecius.

speeches.speaker: Pon.
verse: Hold my Lord,
I am a Roman, and a Souldier.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Pray Sir.

speeches.speaker: Aeci.
verse: Thou art a lying Villain, and a Traytor;
Give me my self, or by the Gods my friend
You'l make me dangerous; how dar'st thou pluck
The Souldiers to sedition, and I living,
And sow Rebellion in 'em, and even then
When I am drawing out to action?

speeches.speaker: Pon.
verse: Hear me.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Are ye a man?

speeches.speaker: Aeci.
verse: I am a true hearted, Maximus,
And if the Villain live, we are dishonour'd.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: But hear him what he can say.

speeches.speaker: Aeci.
verse: That's the way,
To pardon him; I am so easie natur'd,
That if he speak but humbly I forgive him.

speeches.speaker: Pon.
verse: I do beseech ye noble General.

speeches.speaker: Aeci.
verse: Has found the way already give me room,
One stroak, and if he scape me then h'as mercy.

speeches.speaker: Pon.
verse: I do not call ye noble, that I fear ye,
I never car'd for death; if ye will kill me,
Consider first for what, not what you can do.
'Tis true, I know ye for my General,
And by that great Prerogative may kill.
But do it justly then.

speeches.speaker: Aeci.
verse: He argues with me,
A made up Rebel.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Pray consider,
What certain grounds ye have for th^.

speeches.speaker: Aeci.
verse: What grounds?
Did I not take him preaching to the Souldier
How lazily they liv'd, and what dishonours
It was to serve a Prince so full of woman?
Those were his very words, friend.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: These, Aecius,
Though they were rashly spoke, which was an errour
(A great one Pontius) yet from him that hungers
Fo^ wars, and brave imployment, might be pardon'd.
The heart, and harbou 'd thoughts of ill, make Traytors,
Not spleeny speeches.

speeches.speaker: A^ci.
verse: Why should you protect him?
Goe to, it shews not honest.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Taint me not,
For that shews worse A^cius: All your friendship
And that p entended love ye lay upon me,
Hold back my honesty, is like a favour
You do you slave to day, to morrow hang him,
Was I your bosome piece for this?

speeches.speaker: Aeci.
verse: Forgive me,
The nature of my zeal, and for my Country,
Makes me sometimes forget my self; for know,
Though I most strive to be without my passions,
I am no God: For you Sir, whose infection
Has spread it self like poyson through the army,
And cast a killing fog on fair allegiance,
First thank this noble Gentleman, ye had dy'd else;
Next from your place, and honour of a Souldier,
I here seclude you.

speeches.speaker: Pon.
verse: May I speak yet?

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Hear him.

speeches.speaker: Aeci.
verse: And while Aecius holds a reputation,
At least command, ye bear no arms for Rome Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pon.
verse: Against her I shall never: the condemn'd man
Has yet that priviledge to speak, my Lord;
Law were not equall else.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Pray hear Aecius,
For happily the fault he has committed,
Though I believe it mighty, yet considered,
If mercy may be thought upon, will prove
Rather a hastie sin, than heynous.

speeches.speaker: Aeci.
verse: Speak.

speeches.speaker: Pon.
verse: 'Tis true my Lord, ye took me tir'd with peace,
My words almost as ragged as my fortunes.
'Tis true I told the Souldier, whom we serv'd,
And then bewail'd, we had an Emperour
Led from us by the flourishes of Fencers;
I blam'd him too for women.

speeches.speaker: Aec.
verse: To the rest Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pon.
verse: And like enough I blest him then as Souldiers
Will do sometimes: 'Tis true I told 'em too,
We lay at home, to show our Country
We durst goe naked, durst want meat, and mony,
And when the slave drinks wine, we durst be thirstie:
I told 'em this too, that the Trees and Roots
Were our best pay-masters; the Charity
Of longing women, that had bought our bodies,
Our beds, fires, Taylers, Nurses. Nay I told 'em,
(For you shall hear the greatest sin, I said Sir)
By that time there be wars again, our bodies
Laden with sca^s, and aches, and ill lodgings,
H^ats, and perpetual wants, were fitter prayers
And certain graves, than cope the foe on crutches:
'Tis likely too, I counsell'd 'em to turn
Their warlike pikes to plough-shares, their sure Targets
And Swords hatcht with the bloud of many Nations,
To Spades, and prunning Knives, for those get mony,
Th^i^ warlike Eagles, into Daws, or Starlings,
To ^ve an Ave Caesar as he passes,
And be rewarded with a thousand drachma's,

For th^
^ but years and be^ts.

speeches.speaker: A^c^
verse: W^at thin^ you,
Were these words to be spoken by a Captain,
One that should g^ve example?

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: 'Twas too much.

speeches.speaker: Pon
verse: My Lord, I did not wooe 'em from the Empire,

No^
^ 'em turn their daring steel 'gainst Caesar,
The Gods for ever hate me, if that motion
Were part of me: Give me but imployment, Sir;
And way to live, and where you hold me vicious,
Bred up in mutiny, my Sword shall tell ye,
And if you please, that place I held, maintain it,
'Gainst the most daring foes of Rome. I am honest,
A lover of my Country, one that holds
His life no longer his, than kept for Caesar.
Weigh not (I thus low on my knee beseech you)
What my rude tongue discovered, 'twas my want,
No other pair of Pontius: you have seen me,
And you my Lord, do something for my Country,
And both beheld the wounds I gave and took,
Not like a backward Traytor.

speeches.speaker: Aeci.
verse: All this language
Makes but against you Pontius, you are cast,
And by mine honour, and my love to Caesar,
By me shall never be restor'd; In my Camp
I will not have a tongue, though to himself
Dare talk but near sedition; as I govern,
All shall obey, and when they want, their duty
And ready service shall redress their needs,
Not prating what they would be.

speeches.speaker: Pon.
verse: Thus! leave ye,
Yet shall my prayers still, although my fortunes
Must follow you no more, be still about ye,
Gods give ye where ye fight the Victory,
Ye cannot cast my wishes.

speeches.speaker: Aeci.
verse: Come my Lord,
Now to the Field again.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Alas poor Pontius.

speeches.speaker: Lici.
verse: How how?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: She's come.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
verse: Then I'le to'th Emperour.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Do; Is the Musick placed well?

speeches.speaker: Lici.
verse: Excellent.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Licinius, you and Proclus receive her
In the great Chamber, at her entrance,
Let me alone; and do you hear Licinius,
Pray let the Ladies ply her further off,
And with much more discretion: one word more.

speeches.speaker: Lici.
verse: Well.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Are the Jewels, and those ropes of Pearl,
Laid in the way she passes?

speeches.speaker: Lici
verse: Take no care man —

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: What is she come?

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: She is Sir; but 'twere best,
Your Grace were seen last to her.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: So I mean;
Keep the Court emptie Proculus.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: 'Tis done Sir.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Be not too sudden to her.

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: Good your Grace,
Retire, and man your self; let us alone,
We are no children this way: do you hear Sir?
'Tis necessary that her waiting women
Be cut off in the Lobby, by some Ladies,
They'd break the business else.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: 'Tis true, they shall.

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: Remember your place Proculus.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: I warrant ye.—

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: She enters: who are waiters there? the Emperour
Calls for his Horse to air himself.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: I am glad,
I come so happily to take him absent,
This takes away a little fear; I know him,
Now I begin to fear again: O honour,
If ever thou hadst temple in weak woman,
And sacrifice of modesty burnt to thee,
Hold me fast now, and help me.

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: Noble Madam,
Ye are welcom to the Court, most nobly welcom,
Ye are a stranger Lady.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: I desire so.

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: A wondrous stranger here,
Nothing so strange:
And therefore need a guide I think.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: I do Sir,
And that a good one too.

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: My service Lady,
Shall be your guide in this place; But pray ye tell me,
Are ye resolv'd a Courtier?

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: No I hope Sir.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: You are, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: Yes, my fair one.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: So it seems,
You are so ready to bestow your self,
Pray what might cost those Breeches?

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: Would you wear 'em?
Madam ye have a witty woman.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Two Sir,
Or else ye underbuy us.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Leave your talking:
But is my Lord here, I beseech ye, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: He is sweet Lady, and must take this kindly,
Exceeding kindly of ye, wondrous kindly
Ye come so far to visit him: I'le guide ye.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Whither?

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: Why to your Lord.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Is it so hard Sir,
To find him in this place without a Guide?
For I would willingly not trouble you.

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: It will be so for you that are a stranger;
Nor can it be a trouble to do service
To such a worthy beauty, and besides—

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I see he will goe with us.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: Let him amble.

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: It fits not that a Lady of your reckoning
Should pass without attendants.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: I have two Sir.

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: I mean without a man; You'l see the Emperour?

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Alas I am not fit Sir.

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: You are well enough,
He'l take it wondrous kindly: Hark.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Ye flatter,
Good Sir, no more of that.

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: Well, I but tell ye.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Will ye goe forward, since I must be man'd,
Pray take your place.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
verse: Cannot ye man us too Sir?

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: Give me but time.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: And you'l try all things.

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: No:
I'le make no such promise.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
verse: If ye do Sir,
Take heed ye stand to't.

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: Wondrous merry Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: The wenches are dispos'd, pray keep your way Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lici.
verse: She is coming up the stairs; Now the Musick;
And as that stirs her, let's set on: perfumes there.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Discover all the Jewels.

speeches.speaker: Lici.
verse: Peace.

NOw the lusty Spring is seen,
Golden yellow, gaudy Blew,
Daintily invite the view.
Every where, on every Green,
Roses blushing as they blow,
And inticing men to pull,
Lillies whiter than the snow,
Woodbines of sweet hony full.
All Loves Emblems and all cry,
Ladys, if not pluckt we dye.

Yet the lusty Spring hath staid,
Blushing red and purest white,
Daintily to love invite,
Every Woman, every Maid,
Cherries kissing as they grow;
And inviting men to taste,
Apples even ripe below,
Winding gently to the waste:
All loves emblems and all cry,
Ladies, if not pluckt we dye.

HEar ye Ladies that despise
What the mighty Love has done,
Fear examples, and be wise,
Fair Calisto was a Nun,

Laeda sailing on the stream,
To deceive the hopes of man,
Love accounting but a dream,
Doted on a silver Swan,

Danae in a Brazen Tower,
Where no love was, lov'd a Showr.

Hear ye Ladys that are coy,
What the mighty Love can do,
Fear the fierceness of the Boy,
The chaste Moon he makes to wooe:

Vesta kindling holy fires,
Circled round about with spies,
Never dreaming loose desires,
Doting at the Altar dies.

Ilion in a short hour higher
He can build, and once more fire.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Pray Heaven my Lord be here, for now I fear it.
Well Ring, if thou bee'st counterfeit, or stoln,
As by this preparation I suspect it,
Thou hast betrai'd thy Mistris: pray Sir forward,
I would fain see my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: But tell me Madam,
How do ye like the Song?

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: I like the air well,
But for the words, they are lascivious,
And over light for Ladies,

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: All ours love 'em.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: 'Tis like enough, for yours are loving Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Lici.
verse: Madam, ye are welcom to the Court. Who waits?
Attendants for this Lady.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Ye mistake Sir;
I bring no triumph with me.

speeches.speaker: Lici.
verse: But much honour.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Why this was nobly done; and like a neighbour,
So freely of your self to be a visitant,
The Emperour shall give ye thanks for this.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: O no Sir;
There's nothing to deserve 'em.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Yes, your presence.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Good Gentlemen be patient, and believe
I come to see my husband, on command too,
I were no Courtier else.

speeches.speaker: Lici.
verse: That's all one Lady,
Now ye are here, y'are welcom, and the Emperour
Who loves ye, but too well.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: No more of that Sir.
I came not to be Catechiz'd.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Ah Sirrah;
And have we got you here? saith Noble Lady,
We'l keep you one month Courtier.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Gods defend Sir,
I never lik'd a trade worse.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Hark ye.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: No Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Ye are grown the strangest Lady.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: By Heaven,
'Tis true I tell ye, and you'l find it.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: I?
I'le rather find my grave, and so inform him.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Is it not pity Gentlemen, this Lady,
(Nay I'le deal roughly with ye, yet not hurt ye)
Shold live alone, and give such heavenly beauty
Only to walls, and hangings?

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Good Sir, patience:
I am no wonder, neither come to that end,
Ye do my Lord an injury to stay me,
Who though ye are the Princes, yet dare tell ye
He keeps no wife for your wayes.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
verse: Well, well Lady;
However you are pleas'd to think of us,
Ye are welcom, and ye shall be welcome.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Shew it
In that I come for then, in leading me
Where my lov'd Lord is, not in flattery:—
Nay ye may draw the Curtain, I have seen 'em,
But none worth half my honesty.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
verse: Are these Sir,
Laid here to take?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Yes, for your Lady, Gentlewomen.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: We had been doing else.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
verse: Meaner Jewels
Would fit your worths.

speeches.speaker: Claud.
verse: And meaner clothes your bodies.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: The Gods shall kill me first.

speeches.speaker: Lici.
verse: There's better dying;
I'th' Emperours arms goe to, but be not angry—
These are but talks sweet Lady.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: Where is this stranger? rushes, Ladys, rushes,
Rushes as green as Summer for this stranger.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Here's Ladies come to see you.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: You are gone then?
I take it 'tis your Q^

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Or rather manners,
You are better fitted Madam, we but tire ye,
Therefore we'l leave you for an hour, and bring
Your much lov'd Lord unto you —

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Then I'le thank ye,
I am betrai'd for certain; well Lucina,
If thou do'st fall from vertue, may the Earth
That after death should shoot up gardens of thee,
Spreading thy living goodness into branches,
Fry from thee, and the hot Sun find thy vices.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: You are a welcom woman.

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: Bless me Heaven,
How did you find the way to Court?

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: I know not,
Would I had never trod it.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: Prethee tell me,
Good noble Lady, and good sweet heart love us,
For we love thee extreamly; is not this place
A Paradise to live in?

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: To those people
That know no other Paradise but pleasure,
That little I enjoy contents me better.

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: What, heard ye any Musick yet?

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Too much.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: You must not be thus froward; what, this gown
Is one o'th' prettiest by my troth Ardelia,
I ever saw yet; 'twas not to frown in Lady,
Ye put this gown on when ye came.

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: How do ye?
Alas poor wretch how cold it is!

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Content ye;
I am as well as may be, and as temperate,
If ye will let me be so: where's my Lord?
For there's the business that I came for, Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
