speeches.speaker: 1 Guard.
verse: Dye he accurs'd
That thinks of rest or sleep, before he sets
His soot on Persian-Earth.

speeches.speaker: Nig.
verse: We know our glory;
The dignity of Rome, and what's above
All can be urg'd, the quiet of your mind
Depends upon our haste.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: Remove to night;
Five days shall bring me to you.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: Happiness
To Caesar, and glorious victory.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: The cheerfulness of my Souldiers gives assurance
Of good success abroad; if first I make
My peace at home here. There is something chides me,
And sharply tells me, that my breach of faith
To Delphia and Drusilla, is the ground
Of my misfortunes; And I must remember,
While I was lov'd, and in great Delphia's Grace,
She was as my good Angel, and bound Fortune
To prosper my designs; I must appease her;
Let others pay their Knees, their Vows, their Prayers
To weak imagin'd Powers; She is my All,
And thus I do invoke her. Knowing Delphia,
Thou more than Woman, and though thou vouchsafest
To grace the Earth with thy celestial Steps,
And taste this grosser air, thy heavenly Spirit
Hath free access to all the secret Counsels
Which a full Senate of the gods determine
When they consider man: The brass-leav'd Book
Of Fate lies open to thee, where thou read'st,
And fashionest the destinies of men
At thy wish'd pleasures; Look upon thy creature,
And as thou twice hast pleased to appear
To reprehend my falshood, now vouchsafe
To see my low submission.

speeches.speaker: Del.
verse: What's thy Will?
False, and unthankful, (and in that deserving
All humane sorrows) darst thou hope from me
Relief or Comfort?

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: Penitence does appease
Th' incensed Powers, and Sacrifice takes off
Their heavy angers; thus I tender both;
The Master of great Rome, and in that, Lord
Of all the Sun gives heat and being to,
Thus sues for mercy; Be but as thou wert,
The Pilot to the Bark of my good fortunes,
And once more steer my actions to the Port
Of glorious Honour, and if I fall off
Hereafter from my faith to this sweet Virgin,
Joyn with those Powers that punish perjury,
To make me an example to deter
Others from being false.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: Upon my soul,
You may believe him; nor did he e'r purpose
To me but nobly; he made tryal how
I could endure unkindness; I see Truth
Triumphant in his sorrow. Dearest Aunt,
Both credit him, and help him; and on assurance
That what I plead for, you cannot deny,
I raise him thus, and with this willing kiss
I seal his pardon.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: O that I e'r lookt
Beyond this abstract of all womans goodness.

speeches.speaker: Del.
verse: I am thine again; thus I confirm our league;
I know thy wishes, and how much thou suffer'st
In honour for thy friends; thou shalt repair all;
For to thy Fleet I'll give a fore-right wind
To pass the Persian Gulf; remove all lets
That may molest thy Souldiers in their March
That pass by land, and destiny is false,
If thou prove not victorious; Yet remember,
When thou art rais'd up to the highest point
Of humane happiness, such as move beyond it
Must of necessity descend. Think on't,
And use those Blessings that the gods pour on you
With moderation.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: As their Oracle
I hear you, and obey you, and will follow
Your grave directions.

speeches.speaker: Del.
verse: You will not repent it.

speeches.speaker: Nig.
verse: How do you like your entrance to the War?
When the whole Body of the Army moves,
Shews it not gloriously?

speeches.speaker: Get.
verse: 'Tis a fine May-game;
But eating and drinking I think are forbad in't,
(I mean, with leisure) we walk on, and feed
Like hungry Boys that haste to School; or as
We carried Fish to the City, dare stay no where,
For fear our ware should stink.

speeches.speaker: 1 Guard.
verse: That's the necessity
Of our speedy March.

speeches.speaker: Get.
verse: Sir, I do love my ease,
And though I hate all Seats of Judicature,
I mean in the City, for conveniency,
I still will be a Justice in the War,
And ride upon my foot-cloth. I hope a Captain
(And a gown'd-Captain too) may be dispenc'd with.
I tell you, and do not mock me, when I was poor,
I could endure like others, cold and hunger;
But since I grew rich, let but my finger ake,
Or feel but the least pain in my great Toe,
Unless I have a Doctor, mine own Doctor,
That may assure me, I am gone.

speeches.speaker: Nig.
verse: Come, fear not;
You shall want nothing.

speeches.speaker: 1 Guard.
verse: We will make you fight,
As you were mad.

speeches.speaker: Get.
verse: Not too much of fighting, friend;
It is thy trade, that art a common Souldier;
We Officers, by our place, may share the spoil,
And never sweat for't.

speeches.speaker: 2 Guard.
verse: You shall kill for practice
But your dozen or two a day.

speeches.speaker: Get.
verse: Thou talkst as if
Thou wert lousing thy self; but yet I will make danger,
If I prove one of the Worthies, so; However,
I'll have the fear of the gods before my eyes,
And do no hurt I warrant you.

speeches.speaker: Nig.
verse: Come, march on,
And humour him for our mirth.

speeches.speaker: 1 Guard.
verse: 'Tis a fine peak-Goose.

speeches.speaker: Nig.
verse: But one that fools to the Emperour, and in that,
A wise man, and a Souldier.

speeches.speaker: 1 Guard.
verse: True morality.

speeches.speaker: Cos.
verse: Now by the Persian gods, most truly welcome,
Encompass'd thus with tributary Kings,
I entertain you. Lend your helping hands
To seat her by me; and thus rais'd, bow all
To do her honour; O my best Cassana,
Sister, and Partner of my Life and Empire,
We'll teach thee to forget with present pleasures
Thy late Captivity; and this proud Roman,
That us'd thee as a Slave, and did disdain
A Princely Ransome, shall, if she repine,
Be forc'd by various Tortures, to adore
What she of late contemn'd.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: All greatness ever
Attend Cosroe; though Persia be styl'd
The Nurse of Pomp and Pride, we'll leave to Rome
Her native Cruelty. For know, Aurelia,
A Roman Princess, and a Caesars Sister
Though late, like thee captiv'd, I can forget
Thy barbarous usage; and though thou to me
(When I was in thy power) didst shew thy self,
A most insulting Tyranness, I to thee
May prove a gentle Mistriss.

speeches.speaker: Aur.
verse: O my Stars,
A Mistriss? can I live and owe that name
To flesh and blood? I was born to command,
Train'd up in Soveraignty; and I, in death
Can quit the name of Slave; she that scorns life,
May mock Captivity.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Rome will be Rome
When we are nothing; and her power's the same
Which you once quak'd at.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Dioclesian lives;
Hear it and tremble; Lives (thou King of Persia)
The Master of his Fortune, and his Honour;
And though by devilish arts we were surpriz'd,
And made the prey of Magick and of Theft,
And not won nobly, we shall be redeem'd,
And by a Roman War; and every wrong
We suffer here, with interest, be return'd
On the insulting doer.

speeches.speaker: 1 Per.
verse: Sure these Romans
Are more than men.

speeches.speaker: 2 Per.
verse: Their great hearts will not yield,
They cannot bend to any adverse Fate,
Such is their Confidence.

speeches.speaker: Cos.
verse: They then shall break.
Why, you rebellious Wretches, dare you still
Contend when the last breath, or nod of mine
Marks you out for the fire? or to be made
The prey of Wolves or Vulturs? the vain name
Of Roman Legions, I slight thus, and scorn;
And for that boasted bug bear, Dioclesian,
(Which you presume on) would he were the master
But of the spirit, to meet me in the field,
He soon should find that our immortal Squadrons,
That with full numbers ever are supply'd,
(Could it be possible they should decay)
Dare front his boldest Troops, and scatter him,
As an high towring Falcon on her stretches,
Severs the fearful fowl. And by the Sun,
The Moon, the Winds, the nourishers of life,
And by this Sword, the instrument of death,
Since that you fly not humbly to our mercy
But yet dare hope your liberty by force;
If Dioclesian dare not attempt
To free you with his Sword, all slavery
That cruelty can find out to make you wretched,
Falls heavy on you.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: If the Sun keep his course,
And the Earth can bear his Souldiers march, I fear not.

speeches.speaker: Aur.
verse: Or liberty, or revenge.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: On that I build too.

speeches.speaker: Aur.
verse: A Roman Trumpet!

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: 'Tis; comes it not like
A pardon to a man condemn'd?

speeches.speaker: Cos.
verse: Admit him.
The purpose of thy coming?

speeches.speaker: Nig.
verse: My great Master,
The Lord of Rome, (in that all Power is spoken)
Hoping that thou wilt prove a noble Enemy,
And (in thy bold resistance) worth his conquest,
Defies thee, Cosroe.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: There is fire in this.

speeches.speaker: Nig.
verse: And to encourage thy laborious powers
To tug for Empire, dares thee to the field,
With this assurance, if thy Sword can win him,
Or force his Legions with thy barbed horse,
But to forsake their ground, that not alone
Wing'd Victory shall take stand on thy Tent,
But all the Provinces, and Kingdoms held
By the Roman Garrisons in this Eastern World,
Shall be deliver'd up, and he himself
Acknowledge thee his Sovereign. In return
Of this large offer, he asks only this,
That till the doubtful Die of War determine
Who has most power, and should command the other,
Thou wouldst entreat thy Prisoners like their Births,
And not their present Fortune; and to bring 'em,
Guarded, into thy Tent, with thy best strengths,
Thy ablest men of War, and thou thy self
Sworn to make good the place. And if he fail
(Maugre all opposition can be made)
In his own person to compel his way,
And fetch them safely off, the day is thine,
And he, like these, thy Prisoner.

speeches.speaker: Cos.
verse: Though I receive this
But as a Roman Brave, I do embrace it,
And love the sender. Tell him, I will bring
My Prisoners to the field, and without odds,
Against his single force, alone defend 'em;
Or else with equal numbers. Courage, noble Princes,
And let Posterity record, that we
This memorable day restor'd to Persia,
That Empire of the World, great Philip's Son,
Ravish'd from us, and Greece gave up to Rome.
This our strong comfort, that we cannot fall
Ingloriously, since we contend for all.

speeches.speaker: Get.
verse: I'll swear the Peace against 'em, I am hurt,
Run for a Surgeon, or I faint.

speeches.speaker: 1 Guard.
verse: Bear up, man,
'Tis but a scratch.

speeches.speaker: Get.
verse: Scoring a man o'r the Coxcomb
Is but a scratch with you! —o' your occupation,
Your scurvy scuffling trade; I was told before
My face was had enough; but now I look
Like bloody Bone, and raw head, to fright Children;
I am for no use else.

speeches.speaker: 2 Guard.
verse: Thou shalt fright men.

speeches.speaker: 1 Guard.
verse: You look so terrible now; but see your face
In the Pummel of my Sword.

speeches.speaker: Get.
verse: I dye, I am gone.
Oh my sweet physiognomy.

speeches.speaker: 2 Guard.
verse: They come,
Now fight, or dye indeed.

speeches.speaker: Get.
verse: I will 'scape this way;
I cannot hold my Sword; what would you have
Of a maim'd man?

speeches.speaker: 1 Guard.
verse: Nay, then I have a goad
To prick you forward, Oxe.

speeches.speaker: 2 Guard.
verse: Fight like a Man,
Or dye like a Dog.

speeches.speaker: Get.
verse: Shall I, like Caesar, fall
Among my friends? no mercy? Et tu Brute?
You shall not have the honour of my death,
I'll fall by the Enemy first.

speeches.speaker: 1 Guard.
verse: O brave, brave Geta,
He plays the Devil now.

speeches.speaker: Nig.
verse: Make up for honour,
The Persians shrink. The passage is laid open,
Great Dioclesian, like a second Mars,
His strong arm govern'd by the fierce Bellona,
Performs more than a man; his shield struck full
Of Persian Darts, which now are his defence
Against the Enemies Swords, still leads the way.
Of all the Persian Forces, one strong Squadron,
In which Cosroe in his own person fights,
Stands firm, and yet unrouted; Break thorow that,
The day, and all is ours.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: Victory, Victory.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: I am rewarded in the Act; your freedome
To me's ten thousand Triumphs; You Sir, share,
In all my glories. And unkind Aurelia,
From being a Captive, still command the Victor.
Nephew, remember by whose gift you are free;
You I afford my pity; baser minds
Insult on the afflicted, you shall know,
Vertue and Courage are admir'd and lov'd
In Enemies; but more of that hereafter.
Thanks to your valour; to your Swords I owe
This Wreath triumphant. Nor be thou forgot
My first poor Bondman, Geta, I am glad
Thou art turn'd a fighter.

speeches.speaker: Get.
verse: 'Twas against my will;
But now I am content with't.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: But imagine
What honours can be done to you beyond these,
Transcending all example; 'tis in you
To will, in us to serve it.

speeches.speaker: Nig.
verse: We will have
His Statue of pure gold set in the Capitol,
And he that bows not to it as a god,
Makes forfeit of his head.

speeches.speaker: Max
verse: I burst with envy;
And ^ these honours, which conferr'd on me,
Would make me pace on air, seem not to move him.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: Suppose this done, or were it possible
I could rise higher still, I am a man,
And all these glories, Empires heap'd upon me,
Confirm'd by constant friends, and faithful Guards,
Cannot defend me from a shaking Feaver,
Or bribe the uncorrupted Dart of Death
To spare me one short minute. Thus adorn'd
In these triumphant Robes, my body yields not
A greater shadow, than it did when I
Liv'd both poor and obscure; a Swords sharp point
Enters my flesh as far; dreams break my sleep
As when I was a private man; my passions
Are stronger tyrants on me; nor is Greatness
A saving Antidote to keep me from
A Traytors poyson. Shall I praise my fortune,
Or raise the building of my happiness
On her uncertain favour? or presume
She is mine own, and sure, that yet was never
Constant to any? Should my reason fail me
(As flattery oft corrupts it) here's an example,
To speak how far her smiles are to be trusted;
The rising Sun, this morning, saw this man
The Persian Monarch, and those Subjects proud
That had the honour but to kiss his feet;
And yet e're his diurnal progress ends,
He is the scorn of Fortune: but you'll say,
That she forsook him for his want of courage,
But never leaves the bold. Now by my hopes
Of peace and quiet here, I never met
A braver Enemy; and to make it good,
Cosroe, Cassana, and the rest, be free,
And ransomless return.

speeches.speaker: Cos.
verse: To see this vertue
Is more to me than Empire; and to be
O'rcome by you, a glorious victory.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: What o' Devil means he next?

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: I know that glory
Is like Alcides's Shirt, if it stay on us
Till pride hath mixt it with our blood; nor can we
Part with it at pleasure: when we would uncase,
It brings along with it both flesh and sinews,
And leaves us living Monsters.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Would it were come
To my turn to put it on: I'd run the hazard.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: No, I will not be pluck'd out by the ears
Out of this glorious Castle; uncompell'd
I will surrender rather; Let it suffice
I have toucht the height of humane happiness,
And here I fix nil ultra. Hitherto
I have liv'd a servant to ambitious thoughts,
And fading glories; what remains of life,
I dedicate to Vertue; and to keep
My faith untainted, farewel Pride and Pomp,
And circumstance of glorious Majestie,
Farewel for ever. Nephew, I have noted,
That you have long with sore eyes look'd upon
My flourishing Fortune; you shall have possession
Of my felicity; I deliver up
My Empire, and this gem I priz'd above it,
And all things else that made me worth your envy,
Freely unto you. Gentle Sir, your suffrage,
To strengthen this; the Souldiers love I doubt not;
His valour, Gentlemen, will deserve your favours,
Which let my prayers further. All is yours;
But I have been too liberal, and giv'n that
I must beg back again.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: What am I faln from!

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: Nay, start not; it is only the poor Grange,
The Patrimony which my father left me,
I would be Tenant to.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Sir, I am yours;
I will attend you there.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: No, keep the Court;
Seek you in Rome for honour: I will labour
To find content elswhere. Disswade me not,
By—, I am resolv'd. And now Drusilla,
Being as poor as when I vow'd to make thee
My wife, if thy love since hath felt no change,
I am ready to perform it.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: I still lov'd
Your Person, not your fortunes: in a cottage,
Being yours, I am an Empress.

speeches.speaker: Del.
verse: And I'le make
The change most happy.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: Do me then the honour,
To see my vow perform'd. You but attend
My Glories to the urn; where be it ashes,
Welcom my mean estate: and as a due,
Wish rest to me, I honour unto you.

speeches.speaker: Cho.
verse: The War with glory ended; and Cosroe
(Acknowledging his fealtie to Charinus)
Dismiss'd in peace, returns to Persia:
The rest, arriving safely unto Rome,
Are entertain'd with triumphs: Maximinian,
By the grace and intercession of his ~ncle;
Saluted Caesar: but good Dioclesian,
Weary of Pomp and State, retires himself
With a small Train, to a most private Grange
In Lombardie; where the glad Countrey strives
With Rural Sports to give him entertainment:
With which delighted, he with ease forgets
All specious trifles, and securely tastes
The certain pleasures of a private life.
But oh Ambition, that eats into
With venom'd teeth, true thankfulness, and honour,
And to support her greatness, fashions fears,
Doubts, and preventions to decline all dangers,
Which in the place of safetie, prove her ruine:
All which be pleas'd to see in Maximinian,
To whom, his confer'd Soveraginsy was like
A large sail fill'd full with a fore-right wind,
That drowns a smaller Bark: and he once faln
Into ingratitude, makes no stop in mischief,
But violently runs on. Allow Maximinian all,
Honour, and Empire, absolute command;
Yet being ill, long great he cannot stand.

speeches.speaker: Aur.
verse: Why droops my Lord, my Love, my life, my Caesar?
How ill this dulness doth comport with greatness!
Does not (with open arms) your fortune court you?
Rome know you for her Master, I my self
Confess you for my husband? love, and serve you?
If you contemn not these, and think them curses,
I know no blessings that ambitious flesh
Could wish to feel beyond 'em.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Best Aurelia,
The parent and the nurse to all my Glories,
'Tis not that thus embracing you, I think
There is a Heaven beyond it, that begets
These sad retirements; but the fear to lose
What it is hell to part with: better to have liv'd
Poor and obscure, and never scal'd the top
Of hilly Empire, than to die with fear
To be thrown headlong down, almost as soon
As we have reach'd it.

speeches.speaker: Aur.
verse: These are Pannick terrours
You fashion to your self: Is not my Brother
(Your equal and copartner in the Empire)
Vow'd and confirm'd your friend? the Souldier constant?
Hath not your Uncle Dioclesian taken
His last farewel o'th' world? What then can shake ye?

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: The thought I may be shaken: and assurance
That what we do possess is not our own,
But has depending on anothers favour:
For nothing's more uncertain (my Aurelia)
Than power that stands not on his proper Basis,
But borrows his foundation. I'le make plain
My cause of doubts and fears; for what should I
Conceal from you, that are to be familiar
With my most private thoughts? Is not the Empire
My Uncles gift? and may he not resume it
Upon the least distaste? Does not Charinus
Cross me in my designs? And what is Majestie
When 'tis divided? Does not the insolent Souldier
Call my command his donative? And what can take
More from our honour? No (my wise Aurelia,)
If I to you am more than all the world;
As sure you are to me; as we desire
To be secure, we must be absolute,
And know no equal: when your Brother borrows
The little splendor that he has from us,
And we are serv'd for fear, not at entreaty,
We may live safe; but till then, we but walk
With heavie burthens on a sea of glass,
And our own weight will sink us.

speeches.speaker: Aur.
verse: Your Mother brought you
Into the world an Emperour: you perswade
But what I would have counsell'd: Nearness of blood,
Respect of pietie, and thankfulness,
And all the holy dreams of vertuous fools
Must vanish into nothing, when Ambition
(The maker of great minds, and nurse of honour)
Puts in for Empire. On then, and forget
Your simple Uncle; think he was the Master
(In being once an Emperour) of a Jewel,
Whose worth and use he knew not: For Charinus,
No more my Brother, if he be a stop
To what you purpose; he to Me's a stranger,
And so to be remov'd.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Thou more than woman,
Thou masculine Greatness, to whose soaring spirit
To touch the stars seems but an easie flight;
O how I glory in thee! those great women
Antiquitie is proud of, thou but nam'd,
Shall be no more remembred: but persevere,
And thou shalt shine among those lesser lights,
To all posteritie like another Phebe,
And so ador'd as she is.

speeches.speaker: Aur.
verse: Here's Charinus,
His brow furrow'd with anger.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Let him storm,
And you shall hear me thunder.

speeches.speaker: Cha.
verse: He dispose of
My Provinces at his pleasure? and confer
Those honours (that are only mine to give)
Upon his creatures?

speeches.speaker: Nig.
verse: Mighty Sir, ascribe it
To his assurance of your love and favour,
And not to pride or malice.

speeches.speaker: Cha.
verse: No, good Niger,
Courtesie shall not fool me; he shall know
I lent a hand to raise him, and defend him,
While he continues good: but the same strength
If pride make him usurp upon my Right,
Shall strike him to the Center. You are well met, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: As you make the Encounter: Sir, I hear,
That you repine, and hold your self much griev'd,
In that, without your good leave, I bestow'd
The Gallian Proconsulship upon
A follower of mine.

speeches.speaker: Cha.
verse: 'Tis true: and wonder
You durst attempt it.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Durst, Charinus?

speeches.speaker: Cha.
verse: Durst:
Again, I speak it: Think you me so tame,
So leaden and unactive, to sit down
With such dishonour? But, recal your grant,
And speedily; or by the Roman —
Thou tripst thine own heels up, and hast no part
In Rome, or in the Empire.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Thou hast none,
But by permission: Alas, poor Charinus,
Thou shadow of an Emperour, I scorn thee,
Thee, and thy foolish threats: the gods appoint him
The absolute disposer of the Earth,
That has the sharpest sword. I am sure, Charinus,
Thou wear'st one without edge. When cruel Aper
Had kill'd Numerianus, thy Brother,
(An act that would have made a trembling coward
More daring than Alcides) thy base fear
Made thee wink at it: then rose up my Uncle
(For the honour of the Empire, and of Rome)
Against the Traitor, and among his Guards
Punish'd the treason: This bold daring act
Got him the Souldiers suffrages to be Caesar.
And howsoever his too gentle nature
Allow'd thee the name only, as his gift,
I challenge the succession.

speeches.speaker: Cha.
verse: Thou are cozen'd.
When the receiver of a courtesie
Cannot sustain the weight it carries with it,
'Tis but a Trial, not a present Act.
Thou hast in a few dayes of thy short Reign,
In over-weening pride, riot and lusts,
Sham'd noble Dioclesian, and his gift:
Nor doubt I, when it shall arrive unto
His certain knowledge, how the Empire groans
Under thy Tyranny, but he will forsake
His private life, and once again resume
His laid-by Majestie: or at least, make choice
Of such an Atlas as may bear this burthen,
Too heavie for thy shoulders. To effect this,
Lend your assistance, Gentlemen, and then doubt not
But that this mushroom (sprung up in a night)
Shall as soon wither. And for you, Aurelia,
If you esteem your honour more than tribute
Paid to your loathsome appetite, as a Furie
Flie from his loose embraces: so farewel;
E're long you shall hear more.

speeches.speaker: Aur.
verse: Are you struck dumb,
That you make no reply?

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Sweet, I will do,
And after talk: I will prevent their plots,
And turn them on their own accursed heads.
My Uncle? good: I must not know the names
Of Pietie or Pitie. Steel my heart,
Desire of Empire, and instruct me, that
The Prince that over others would bear sway,
Checks at no Let that stops him in his way.

speeches.speaker: 1 Shep.
verse: Do you think this great man will continue here?

speeches.speaker: 2 Shep.
verse: Continue here? what else? he has bought the great Farm;
A great man, with a great Inheritance,
And all the ground about it, all the woods too;
And stock'd it like an Emperour. Now, all our sports again.
And all our merry Gambols, our may-Ladies,
Our evening-daunces on the Green, our Songs,
Our Holiday good cheer, our Bag-pipes now Boyes,
Shall make the wanton Lasses skip again,
Our Sheep-sheerings, and all our knacks.

speeches.speaker: 3 Shep.
verse: But hark ye,
We must not call him Emperour.

speeches.speaker: 1 Countr.
verse: That's all one;
He is the King of good fellows, that's no treason;
And so I'le call him still, though I be hang'd for't.
I grant ye, he has given his honour to another man,
He cannot give his humour: he is a brave fellow,
And will love us, and we'l love him. Come hither Ladon,
What new Songs, and what geers?

speeches.speaker: 3 Shep.
verse: Enough: I'le tell ye
He comes abroad anon to view his grounds,
And with the help of Thirsis, and old Egon,
(If his whorson co^ld be gon) and Amaryllis,
And some few more o'th' wenches, we will meet him,
And strike him such new springs, and such free welcoms,
Shall make him scorn an Empire, forget Majestie,
And make him bless the hour he liv'd here happy.

speeches.speaker: 2 Countr.
verse: And we will second ye, we honest Carters,
We lads o'th' lash, with some blunt entertainment,
Our Teams to two pence, will give him some content,
Or we'll bawl fearfully.

speeches.speaker: 3 Shep.
verse: He cannot expect now
His Courtly entertainments, and his rare Musicks,
And Ladies to delight him with their voyces;
Honest and cheerful toyes from honest meanings,
And the best hearts they have. We must be neat all:
On goes my russet jerkin with blue buttons.

speeches.speaker: 1 Shep.
verse: And my green slops I was married in; my bonnet
With my carnation point with Silver tags, boyes:
You know where I won it.

speeches.speaker: 1 Countr.
verse: Thou wilt ne're be old, Alexis.

speeches.speaker: 1 Shep.
verse: And I shall find some toyes that have been favors,
And nose-gayes, and such knacks: for there be wenches.

speeches.speaker: 3 Shep.
verse: My mantle goes on too I plaid young Paris in,
And the new garters Amaryllis sent me.

speeches.speaker: 1 Count.
verse: Yes, yes: we'l all be handsom, and wash our faces.
Neighbour, I see a remnant of March dust
That's hatch'd into your chaps: I pray ye be carefull,
And mundifie your muzzel.

speeches.speaker: 2 Countr.
verse: I'le to th' Barbers,
It shall cost me I know what. Who's this?

speeches.speaker: 3 Shep.
verse: Give room, neighbours,
A great man in our State: gods bless your worship.

speeches.speaker: 2 Countr.
verse: Encrease your Mastership.

speeches.speaker: Get.
verse: Thanks, my good people:
Stand off, and know your duties: as I take it
You are the labouring people of this village,
And you that keep the sheep. Stand farther off yet,
And mingle not with my authoritie,
I am too mighty for your companie.

speeches.speaker: 3 Shep.
verse: We know it Sir; and we desire your worship
To reckon us amongst your humble servants,
And that our Country Sports, Sir,—

speeches.speaker: Get.
verse: For your Sports, Sir,
They may be seen, when I shall think convenient,
When out of my discretion, I shall view 'em,
And hold 'em fit for licence. Ye look upon me,
And look upon me seriously, as ye knew me:
'Tis true, I have been a Rascal, as you are,
A fellow of no mention, nor no mark,
Just such another piece of durt, so fashion'd:
But Time, that purifies all things of merit,
Has set another stamp. Come nearer now,
And be not fearfull; I take off my austeritie:
And know me for the great and mighty Steward
Under this man of honour: know ye for my vassals,
And at my pleasure I can dispeople ye,
Can blow you and your cattel out o'th' Country:
But fear me, and have favour. Come, go along with me,
And I will hear your Songs, and perhaps like 'em.

speeches.speaker: 3 Shep.
verse: I hope you will, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Geta.
verse: 'Tis not a thing impossible,
Perhaps I'le sing my self, the more to grace ye,
And if I like your women.

speeches.speaker: 3 Shep.
verse: We'l have the best, Sir,
Handsom young Girls.

speeches.speaker: Geta.
verse: The handsomer, the better.
'May bring your wives too, 'twill be all one charge to ye;
For I must know your families.

speeches.speaker: Del.
verse: 'Tis well said,
'Tis well said, honest friends; I know ye are hatching
Some pleasurable sports for your great Landlord:
Fill him with joy, and win him a friend to ye,
And make this little Grange seem a large Empire,
Let out with home contents: I'le work his favour,
Which daily shall be on ye.

speeches.speaker: 3 Shep.
verse: Then we'l sing daily,
And make him the best Sports.

speeches.speaker: Del.
verse: Instruct 'em Geta,
And be a merry man again.

speeches.speaker: Geta.
verse: Will ye lend me a devil,
That we may dance a while?

speeches.speaker: Del.
verse: I'le lend thee two.
And Bag-pipes that shall blow alone.

speeches.speaker: Get.
verse: I thank ye:
But I'le know your devils of a cooler complexion first.
Come, follow, follow; I'le go sit and see ye.

speeches.speaker: Del.
verse: Do; and be ready an hour hence, and bring 'em;
For in the Grove you'l find him.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: Come Drusilla,
The partner of my best contents: I hope now
You dare believe me:

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: Yes, and dare say to ye,
I think ye now most happie.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: You say true, Sweet,
For by my—, I find now by experience,
Content was never Courtier.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: I pray ye walk on, Sir;
The cool shades of the Grove invite ye.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: O my Dearest!
When man has cast off his ambitious greatness,
And sunk into the sweetness of himself;
Built his foundation upon honest thoughts,
Not great, but good desires his daily servants;
How quiely he sleeps! how joyfully
He wakes again, and looks on his possessions,
And from his willing labours feeds with pleasure?
Here hang no Comets in the shapes of Crowns,
To shake our sweet contents: nor here, Drusilla,
Cares, like Eclipses, darken our endeavours:
We love here without rivals, kiss with innocence;
Our thoughts as gentle as our lips; our children
The double heirs both of our forms and faiths.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: I am glad ye make this right use of this sweetness,
This sweet retiredness.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: 'Tis sweet indeed, love,
And every circumstance about it, shews it.
How liberal is the spring in every place here?
The artificial Court shews but a shadow,
A painted imitation of this glory.
Smell to this flower, here nature has her excellence:
Let all the perfumes of the Empire pass this,
The carefull'st Ladies cheek shew such a colour,
They are gilded and adulterate vanities.
And here in Povertie dwells noble nature.
What pains we take to cool our wines, to allay us,
And bury quick the fuming god to quench us,
Methinks this Crystal Well. — Ha! what strange Musick?
'Tis underneath, sure: how it stirs and joys me?
How all the birds set on? the fields redouble
Their ^doriferous sweets? Hark how the echo's—

speeches.speaker: Drus.
verse: See, Sir, those flowers
From out the Well, spring to your entertainment.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: Bless me.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: Be not afraid, 'tis some good Angel
That's come to welcome ye.

speeches.speaker: Del.
verse: Go near and hear, Son.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: O Mother, thank ye, thank ye, this was your will.

speeches.speaker: Del.
verse: You shall not want delights to bless your presence.
Now ye are honest, all the Stars shall honour ye.
Stay, here are Country-shepherds; here is some sport too,
And you must grace it, Sir; 'twas meant to welcom ye;
A King shall never feel your joy. Sit down Son.
Hold, hold, my Messenger appears: leave off, friends,
Leave off a while, and breathe.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: What news? ye are pale, Mother.

speeches.speaker: Del.
verse: No, I am careful of thy safety, Son,
Be not affrighted, but sit still; I am with thee.
And now dance out your dance. Do you know that person?
Be not amaz'd, but let him shew his dreadfullest.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: How confident he sits amongst his pleasures,
And what a chearful colour shews in's face,
And yet he sees me too, the Souldiers with me.

speeches.speaker: Aur.
verse: Be speedie in your work, (you will be stopt else)
And then you are an Emperour.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: I will about it.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: My Royal Cousin, how I joy to see ye,
You, and your Royal Emperess!

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: You are too kinde, Sir.
I come not to eat with ye, and to surfeit
In these poor Clownish pleasures; but to tell ye
I look upon ye like my Winding-sheet,
The Coffin of my Greatness, nay, my Grave:
For whilst you are alive—

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: Alive, my Cousin?

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: I say, Alive. I am no Emperour;
I am nothing but mine own disquiet.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: Stay, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: I cannot stay. The Souldiers doat upon ye.
I would fain spare ye; but mine own securitie
Compels me to forget you are my Uncle,
Compels me to forget you made me Caesar:
For whilst you are remembred, I am buried.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: Did not I make ye Emperour, dear Dousin,
The free gift from my special grace?

speeches.speaker: Del.
verse: Fear nothing.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: Did not I chuse this povertie, to raise you?
That Royal woman gave into your arms too?
Bless'd ye with her bright beautie? gave the Souldiers,
The Souldier that hung to me, fix'd him on ye?
Gave ye the worlds command?

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: This cannot help ye.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: Yet this shall ease me. Can ye be so base, Cousin,
So far from Nobleness, so far from nature,
As to forget all this? to tread this Tie out?
Raise to your self so foul a monument
That every common foot shall kick asunder?
Must my blood glue ye to your peace?

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: It must, Uncle;
I stand too loose else, and my foot too feeble:
You gone once, and their love retir'd, I am rooted.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: And cannot this remov'd poor State obscure me?
I do not seek for yours, nor enquire ambitiously
After your growing fortunes. Take heed, my kinsman,
Ungratefulness and blood mingled together,
Will, like two furious Tides—

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: I must sail thorow 'em:
Let 'em be Tides of death, Sir, I must stem up.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: Hear but this last, and wisely yet consider:
Place round about my Grange a Garison,
That if I offer to exceed my limits,
Or ever in my common talk name Emperour,
Ever converse with any greedy Souldier,
Or look for adoration, nay, for courtesie
Above the days salute. — Think who has fed ye,
Think, Cousin, who I am. Do ye slight my misery?
Nay, then I charge thee; nay, I meet thy crueltie.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: This cannot serve; prepare: now fall on, souldiers,
And all the treasure that I have.

speeches.speaker: Sould.
verse: The Earth shakes;
We totter up and down; we cannot stand, Sir;
Me thinks the mountains tremble too.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sould.
verse: The flashes
How thick and hot they come? we shall be burn'd all.

speeches.speaker: Del.
verse: Fall on, Souldiers:
You that fell innocent blood, fall on full bravely.

speeches.speaker: Sould.
verse: We cannot stir.

speeches.speaker: Del.
verse: You have your libertie,
So have you, Lady. One of you come do it.
Do you stand amaz'd? Look o're thy head, Maximinian,
Look to thy terrour, what over-hangs thee:
Nay, it will nail thee dead; look how it threatens thee:
The Bolt for vengeance on ungrateful wretches;
The Bolt of innocent blood: read those hot characters,
And spell the will of heaven. Nay, lovely Lady,
You must take part too, as spur to ambition,
Are ye humble? Now speak; my part's ended.
Does all your glory shake?

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Hear us, great Uncle,
Good and great Sir, be pitiful unto us:
Below your feet we lay our lives: be merciful:
Begin you, heaven will follow.

speeches.speaker: Aur.
verse: Oh, it shakes still.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: And dreadfully it threatens. We acknowledge
Our base and foul intentions. Stand between us;
For faults confess'd, they say, are half forgiven.
We are sorry for our sins. Take from us, Sir,
That glorious weight that made us swell, that poison'd us;
That mass of Majestie I laboured under,
(Too heavie and too mighty for my manage)
That my poor innocent days may turn again,
And my mind pure, may purge me of these curses;
By your old love, the blood that runs between us.

speeches.speaker: Aur.
verse: By that love once ye bare to me, by that Sir,
That blessed maid enjoys—

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: Rise up, dear Cousin,
And be your words your judges: I forgive ye:
Great as ye are, enjoy that greatness ever,
Whilst I mine own content make mine own Empire.
Once more I give ye all; learn to deserve it,
And live to love your Good more than your Greatness.
Now shew your loves to entertain this Emperour
My honest neighbours. Geta, see all handsom.
Your Grace must pardon us, our house is little;
But such an ample welcom as a poor man
And his true love can make you and your Empress.
Madam, we have no dainties.

speeches.speaker: Aur.
verse: 'Tis enough, Sir;
We shall enjoy the riches of your goodness.

speeches.speaker: Sould.
verse: Long live the good and gracious Dioclesian.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: I thank ye, Souldiers, I forgive your rashness.
And Royal Sir, long may they love and honour ye.
What Drums are those?

speeches.speaker: Del.
verse: Meet 'em, my honest Son,
They are thy friends, Charinus and the old Souldiers
That come to rescue thee from thy hot Cousin.
But all is well, and turn all into welcoms:
Two Emperours you must entertain now.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: O dear Mother,
I have will enough, but I want room and glory.

speeches.speaker: Del.
verse: That shall be my care. Sound your pipes now merrily,
And all your handsom sports. Sing 'em full welcoms.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: And let 'em know, our true love breeds more stories
And perfect joys, than Kings do, and their glories.

plays.play_title: The Queen of Corinth, A TRAGI-COMEDY.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: THe General is returned then?

speeches.speaker: Nean.
verse: With much honour.

speeches.speaker: Sos.
verse: And peace concluded with the Prince of Argos?

speeches.speaker: Nean.
verse: To the Queens wishes: the conditions sign'd
So far beyond her hopes, to the advantage
Of Corinth, and the good of all her Subjects;
That though Leonidas our brave General
Ever came home a fair and great example,
He never yet return'd, or with less loss
Or more deserved honour.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: Have you not heard
The motives to this general good?

speeches.speaker: Nean.
verse: The main one
Was admiration first in young Agenor,
(For by that name we know the Prince of Argos)
Of our Leonidas wisdom and his valour,
Which though an enemy, first in him bred wonder;
That liking, Love succeeded that, which was
Followed by a desire to be a friend
Upon what terms soever to such goodness;
They had an enterview; and that their friendship.
Might with our peace be ratified, 'twas concluded,
Agenor yielding up all such strong places
As he held in our territories, should receive
(With a sufficient Dower, paid by the Queen)
The fair Merione for his wife.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: But how
Approves the Queen of this? since we well know
Nor was her Highness ignorant, that her Son
The Prince Theanor made love to this Lady,
And in the noblest way.

speeches.speaker: Nean.
verse: Which she allowed of,
And I have heard from some familiar with
Her nearest secrets, she so deeply priz'd her
Being ^om an Infant train'd up in her service,
(Or to speak better, rather her own Creature)
She once did say, That if the Prince should steal
A Marriage without her leave, or knowledge,
With this Merione, with a little suit
She should grant both their pardons: whereas now
To shew her self forsooth a Spartan Lady,
And that 'tis in her power, now it concerns
The common good, not alone to subdue
Her own affections, but command her Sons;
She has not only forc'd him with rough threats
To leave his Mistriss, but compell'd him when
Ag^n^nor made his entrance into Corinth
To wait upon his Rival.

speeches.speaker: Sos.
verse: Can it be
The Prince should sit down with this wrong?

speeches.speaker: Nean.
verse: I know not,
I am sure I should not.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: Trust me nor I,
A Mother is a name, but put in ballance
With a young Wench 'tis nothing; where did you leave him?

speeches.speaker: Nean.
verse: Near Vesta's Temple, for there he dismiss'd me,
And full of troubled thoughts, calling for Crates:
He went with him, but whither, or to what purpose
I am a stranger.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: They are come back Neanthes.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I like the place well.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Well Sir? it is built
As if the Architect had been a Prophet,
And fashion'd it alone for this nights action;
The Vaults so hollow, and the Walls so strong,
As Di^n there might suffer violence,
And with loud shrikes in vain call J^ve to help her;
Or should he hear, his Thunder could not find
An entrance to it.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I give up my self
Wholly to thy direction, worthiest Crates;
And yet the desperate cure that we must practice
Is in it self so foul, and full of danger,
That I stand doubtful whether 'twere more manly
To dye not seeking help, or that help being
So deadly, to pursue it.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: To those reasons
I have already urg'd, I will add these.
For but consider Sir—

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: It is of weight
What e'r it be, that with such vehement action,
Of Eye, Hand, Foot, nay all his bodies motion,
Crates incites the Prince to.

speeches.speaker: Nean.
verse: Then observe,
With what variety of passions he
Receives his reasons; now he's pale, and shakes
For fear or anger; now his natural red
Comes back again, and with a pleasing smile
He seems to entertain it; 'tis resolv'd on
Be it what 'twill: to his ends may it prosper
Though the State sink for't.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Now you are a Prince
Fit to rule others, and in shaking off
The Bonds in which your Mother fetters you
Discharge your debt to nature, she's your guide,
Follow her boldly, Sir.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I am confirm'd,
Fall what may fall.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Yet still disguise your malice
In your humility.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I am instructed.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Though in you heart there rage a thousand tempests,
All calmness in your looks.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I shall remember.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: And at no hand, though these are us'd as agents
Acquaint them with your purpose till the instant
That we employ them; 'tis not fit they have
Time to consider, when 'tis done, reward
Or fear will keep them silent: yet you may
Grace them as you pass by, 'twill make them surer,
And greedier to deserve you.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I'll move only
As you would have me: Good-day Gentleman;
Nay, spare this ceremonious form of duty
To him that brings love to you, equal love,
And is in nothing happier, than in knowing
It is return'd by you; we are as one.

speeches.speaker: Sos.
verse: I am o'r-joy'd, I know not
How to reply: but —

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: Hang all buts; my Lord,
For this your bounteous favour—

speeches.speaker: Nean.
verse: Let me speak,
If to feed Vultures here, after the halter
Has done his part, or if there be a Hell
To take a swinge or two there, may deserve this.

speeches.speaker: Sos.
verse: We are ready.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: Try us any way.

speeches.speaker: Nean.
verse: Put us to it.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: What jewels I have in you?

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Have these souls,
That for a good look, and a few kind words
Part with their Essence?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Since you will compell me
To put that to the tryal, which I doubt not,
Crates, may be, suddainly will instruct you
How, and in what to shew your loves; obey him
As you would bind me to you:

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: 'Tis well-grounded;
Leave me to rear the building.

speeches.speaker: Nean.
verse: We will do.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: I know it.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: Any thing you'll put us to.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Sister, I reap the harvest of my labours
In your preferment, be you worthy of it,
And with an open bosom entertain
A greater fortune than my love durst hope for;
Be wise, and welcome it: play not the coy
And foolish wanton, with the offered bounties
Of him that is a Prince. I was woo'd for you,
And won Merione: then if you dare
Believe the object that took me was worthy,
Or trust my judgement, in me think you were
Courted, sued to, and conquer'd.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Noble Brother,
I have, and still esteem you as a Father,
And will as far obey you; my heart speaks it:
And yet without your anger, give me leave
To say, That in the choice of that on which
All my lifes joyes or sorrows have dependance,
It had been fit e'r you had made a full
And absolute grant of me to any other,
I should have us'd mine own eyes, or at least
Made you to understand, whether it were
Within my power to make a second gift
Of my poor self.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: I know what 'tis you point at,
The Prince Theanor's love; let not that cheat you;
His vows were but meer Courtship; all his service
But practice how to entrap a credulous Lady:
Or grant it serious, yet you must remember
He's not to love, but where the Queen his Mother
Must give allowance, which to you is barr'd up
And therefore study to forget that ever
You cherisht such a hope.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I would I could.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: But brave Agenor, who is come in person
To celebrate this Marriage, for your love
Forgives the forfeit of ten thousand lives,
That must have fall'n under the sword of War
Had not this peace been made; which general good
Both Countreys owe to his affection to you:
O happy Sister, ask this noble Lady
Your bosome friend (since I fail in my credit)
What palme Agenor's name, above all Princes
That Greece is proud of, carries, and with lustre.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Indeed Fame gives him out for excellent;
And friend, I doubt not but when you shall see him
He'll so appear to you. Art sure 'tis he?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: As I live Madam —

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Virtue enable me to contain my joy.
'Tis my Euphanes.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: And he's in health?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Most certainly Madam.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I'll see him instantly.
So prethee tell him.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I yield my self too weak
In argument to oppose you: you may lead me
Whither you please.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: 'Tis answer'd like my Sister;
And if in him you find not ample cause
To pray for me, and daily on your knees,
Conclude I have no judgement.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: May it prove so:
Friend, shall we have your company?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Two hours hence
I will not fail you.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: At your pleasure Madam.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Could I in one word speak a thousand welcomes
(And hearty ones) you have 'em: Fie, my hand,
We stand at no such distance, by my life
The parting kiss you took before your travel
Is yet a Virgin on my lips, preserv'd
With as much care as I would do my fame
To entertain your wish'd return.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Best Lady,
That I do honour you, and with as much reason
As ever man did virtue; that I love you,
Yet look upon you with that reverence
As Holy men behold the Sun, the Stars,
The Temples, and their gods, they all can witness;
And that you have deserv'd this duty from me;
The life, and means of life, for which I owe you,
Commands me to profess it, since my fortune
Affords no other payment.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I had thought,
That for the trifling courtesies, as I call them,
(Though you give them another name) you had
Made ample satisfaction in th' acceptance,
And therefore did presume you had brought home
Some other Language.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: No one I have learn'd
Yields words sufficient to express your goodness;
Nor can I ever choose another theme
And not be thought unthankful.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Pray you no more
As you respect me.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: That charm is too powerful
For me to disobey it: 'Tis your pleasure,
And not my boldness Madam.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Good Euphanes,
Believe I am not one of those weak Ladies,
That (barren of all inward worth) are proud
Of what they cannot truly call their own,
Their birth or fortune, which are things without them:
Nor in this will I imitate the world,
Whose greater part of men think when they give
They purchase bondmen, not make worthy friends:
By all that's good I swear, I never thought
My great estate was an addition to me,
Or that your wants took from you.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: There are few
So truly understanding o^ themselves
Or what they do possess.

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: Good Euphanes,
Where benefits
Are ill conferr'd, as to unworthy men,
That turn them to bad uses, the bestower
For wanting judgement how, and on whom to place them,
Is partly guilty: but when we do favours
To such as make them grounds on which they build
Their noble actions, there we improve our fortunes
To the most fair advantage. If I speak
Too much, though I confess I speak well,
Prethee remember 'tis a womans weakness,
And then thou wilt forgive it.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: You speak nothing
But what would well become the wisest man:
And that by you deliver'd is so pleasing
That I could hear you ever.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Fly not from
Your word, for I arrest it: and will now
Express my self a little more, and prove
That whereas you profess your self my debtor,
That I am yours.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Your Ladyship then must use
Some Sophistry I ne'r heard of.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: By plain reasons,
For look you, had you never sunk beneath
Your wants, or if those wants had found supply
From Crates, your unkind and covetous brother,
Or any other man, I then had miss'd
A subject upon which I worthily
Might exercise my bounty: whereas now
By having happy opportunity
To furnish you before, and in your travels,
With all conveniencies that you thought useful,
That Gold which would have rusted in my Coffers
Being thus imploy'd, has rendred me a partner
In all your glorious actions. And whereas
Had you not been, I should have dy'd a thing
Scarce known, or soon forgotten: there's no Trophy
In which Euphanes for his worth is mentioned,
But there you have been careful to remember,
That all the good you did came from Beliza.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: That was but thankfulness.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: 'Twas such an honour,
And such a large return for the poor trash
I ventur'd with you, that if I should part
With all that I possess, and my self too
In satisfaction for it, 'twere still short
Of your deservings.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: You o'r-prize them Madam.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: The Queen her self hath given me gracious thanks
In your behalf, for she hath heard Euphanes
How gallantly you have maintain'd her honour
In all the Courts of Greece: and rest assur'd
(Though yet unknown) when I present you to her,
Which I will do this evening, you shall find
That she intends good to you.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Worthiest Lady,
Since all you labour for is the advancement
Of him that will live ever your poor servant,
He must not contradict it.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Here's your Brother,
'Tis strange to see him here.

speeches.speaker: Cra,
verse: You are welcome home, Sir,
(Your pardon Madam) I had thought my house,
Considering who I am, might have been worthy
Of your first visit.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: 'Twas not open to me
When last I saw you; and to me 'tis wonder
That absence which still renders m^n forgotten
Should make my presence wish'd for.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: That's not it,
Your too kind Brother understanding that
You stand in no need of him, is bold to offer
His entertainment.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: He had never wanted,
Or yours, or your assistance, had he practis'd
The way he might have took, to have commanded,
Whatever I call mine,

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: I studied many,
But could find none.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: You would not find your self, Sir,
Or in your self, what was due to me from you:
The priviledge my birth bestow'd upon me
Might challenge some regard.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: You had all the Land, Sir,
What else did you expect? and I am certain
You kept such strong Guards to preserve it yours
I could force nothing from you.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Did you ever
Demand help from me?

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: My wants have, and often,
With open mouths, but you nor heard, nor saw them;
May be you look'd should petition to you
As you went to your Horse; flatter your servants,
To play the Brokers for my furtherance,
Sooth your worst humors, act the Parasite
On all occasions, write my name with theirs
That are but one degree remov'd from slaves,
Be drunk when you would have me, then wench with you,
Or play the Pander; enter into Quarrels
Although unjustly grounded, and defend them
Because they were yours; these are the tyrannies
Most younger Brothers groan beneath; yet bear them
From the insulting Heir, selling their freedoms
At a less rate than what the State allows
The sallary of base and common Strumpets:
For my part, e'r on such low terms I feed
Upon a Brothers trencher, let me dye
The Beggars death, and starve.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: 'Tis bravely spoken,
Did what you do rank with it.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Why, what does he
You would not wish were yours?

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: I'll tell you Lady,
Since you rise up his Advocate, and boldly,
(For now I find, and plainly in whose favor
My Love and Service to you was neglected)
For all your wealth, nay, add to that your beauty,
And put your virtues in, if you have any,
I would not yet be pointed at, as he is.
For the fine Courtier, the womans man,
That tells my Lady stories, dissolves Riddles,
Ushers her to her Coach, lies at her feet
At solemn Masks, applauding what she laughs at;
Reads her asleep anights, and takes his oath
Upon her Pantoffles, that all excellence
In other Madams do but zany hers:
These you are perfect in, and yet these take not
Or from your birth and freedom.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Should another
Say this, my deeds, not looks should shew —

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Contemn it:
His envie fains this, and he's but reporter,
Without a second, of his own dry fancies.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Yes Madam, the whole City speaks it with me,
And though in my distaste, 'tis certain you
Are brought into the scene, and with him censur'd;
For you are given out for the provident Lady,
That not to be unfurnish'd for her pleasures
(As without them to what vain use is greatness)
Have made choice of an able man, a young man
Of an Herculean back to do you service,
And one you may command too, that is active,
And does what you would have him.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: You are foul-mouth'd.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: That can speak well, write Verses too, and good ones,
Sharp and conceited, whose wit you may lie with
When his performance fails him; one you have
Maintain'd abroad to learn new ways to please you,
And by the gods you well reward him for it,
No night (in which while you lye sick and panting)
He watches by you, but is worth a talent:
No conference in your Coach, which is not paid with
A Scarlet Suit; this the poor people mutter,
Though I believe, for I am bound to do so,
A Lady of your youth, that feeds high too,
And a most exact Lady, may do all this
Out of a virtuous love, the last bought vizard
That Leachery purchas'd.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Not a word beyond this,
The reverence I owe to that one womb
In which we both were embrions, makes me suffer
What's past; but if continu'd—

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Stay your hand,
The Queen shall right my honor.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Let him do it,
It is but marrying him; and for your anger
Know that I slight it: when your goddess here
Is weary of your sacrifice, as she will be,
You know my house, and there amongst my servants
Perhaps you'll find a livery.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Be not mov'd,
I know the rancor of his disposition,
And turn it on himself by laughing at it;
And in that let me teach you.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: I learn gladly.

speeches.speaker: Nean.
verse: You are met unto my wishes, if you ever
Desir'd true mirth so far as to adventure
To dye with the extremity of laughter,
I come before the object that will do it;
Or let me live your fool.

speeches.speaker: Sos.
verse: Who is't Neanthes?

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: Lamprias the Usurers Son.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: Lamprias? the youth
Of six and fifty?

speeches.speaker: Sos.
verse: That was sent to travel
By rich Beliza, till he came to age,
And was fit for a Wife?

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: The very same,
This gallant with his Guardian, and his Tutor,
(And of the three, who is most fool I know not)
Are newly come to Corinth, I'll not stale them
By giving up their characters, but leave you
To make your own discoveries: here they are, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Tutor.
verse: That leg a little higher; very well.
Now put your Face into the Travellers posture;
Exceeding good.

speeches.speaker: ~ncle.
verse: Do you mark how they admire him?

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: They will be all my Scholars; when they know
And understand him truly.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: Phoebus guard me
From this new Python.

speeches.speaker: Sos.
verse: How they have trimm'd him up
Like an old Reveller?

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: Curl'd him and perfum'd him,
But that was done with judgement, for he looks
Like one that purg'd perpetually; trust me,
That Witches face of his is painted too,
And every ditch upon it buries more
Then would set off ten Bawds, and all their tenants.

speeches.speaker: Sos.
verse: See how it moves towards us.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: There's a salutation:
'Troth Gentlemen, you have bestowed much travel
In training up your Pupil.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: Sir, great buildings
Require great labours, which yet we repent not,
S^ for the Countreys good we have brought home
An absolute man.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: As any of his years,
Corinth can shew you.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: He's exceeding meagre.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: His contemplation—

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: Besides, 'tis sit
Learners should be kept hungry.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: You all contemplate;
For three such wretched pictures of lean famine
I never saw together.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: We have fat minds, Sir,
And travell'd to save charges. Do you think
'Twas fit a young and hopeful Gentleman
Should be brought up a glutton? he's my Ward,
Nor was there ever where I bore the bag
Any superfluous waste.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: Pray you can it speak?

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: He knows all Languages, but will use none,
They are all too big for his mouth, or else too little
T'express his great conceits: and yet of late
With some impulsion he hath set down
In a strange method by the way of question,
And briefly to all business whatsoever
That may concern a Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: Good Sir, let's hear him.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: Come on, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: They have taught him like an Ape,
To do his tricks by signs: now he begins.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: When shall we be drunk together?

speeches.speaker: Tut,
verse: That's the first.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: Where shall we whore to night?

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: That ever follows.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: 'Odds me, he now looks angry.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: Shall we quarrel?

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: With me at no hand, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: Then lets protest.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: Is this all?

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: These are, Sir, the four new Virtues
That are in fashion: many a mile we measur'd
Before we could arrive to this knowledge.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: You might nave spar'd that labour, for at home here
There's little else in practice: Ha? the Queen?
Good friends, for half an hour remove your motion,
To morrow willingly when we have more leasure
We'll look on him again.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: Did I not rarely?

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: Excellent well.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: He shall have six Plumbs for it.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: How much my Court is honour'd Princely Brother?
In your vouchsafing it your long'd-for presence
Were tedious to repeat, since 'tis already
(And heartily) acknowledg'd; may the gods
That look into Kings actions, smile upon
The league we have concluded; and their justice
Find me out to revenge it, if I break
One Article.

speeches.speaker: Age.
verse: Great miracle of Queens,
How happy I esteem my self in being
Thought worthy to be numbred in the rank
Of you confederates, my love and best service
Shall teach the world hereafter: but this gift
With which you have confirm'd it, is so far
Beyond my hopes and means e'r to return,
That of necessity I must dye oblig'd
To your unanswer'd bounty.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: The sweet Lady
In blushes gives your Highness thanks.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: Believe it
On the Queens word, she is a worthy one,
And I am so acquainted with her goodness,
That but for this peace that hath chang'd my purpose,
And to her more advancement, I should gladly
Have call'd her Daughter.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Though I am depriv'd of
A blessing, 'tis not in the Fates to equal,
To shew my self a Subject as a Son,
Here I give up my claim, and willingly
With mine own hand deliver you what once
I lov'd above my self; and from this hour
(For my affection yields now to my duty)
Vow never to sollicite her.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: 'Tis well cover'd;
Neanthes, and the rest,

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: Nay, for this night
You must (for 'tis our Countrey fashion, Sir)
Leave her to her Devotions, in the morning
We'll bring you to the Temple.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: How in this
Your Highness honours me?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Sweet rest to all.

speeches.speaker: Age.
verse: This kiss, and I obey you

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Please it your Highness,
This is the Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: You are welcome home, Sir,
(Now as I live, one of a promising presence)
I have heard of you before, and you shall find
I'll know you better: find out something that
May do you good, and rest assur'd to have it.
Were you at Sparta lately?

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Three daies since
Madam, I came from thence.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: 'Tis very late,
Good night my Lord, do you Sir follow me,
I must talk further with you.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: All rest with you.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: She must pass through this Cloyster, suddainly
And boldly seize upon her.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: Where's the Prince?

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: He does expect us at the place I shew'd you.
I hear ones footing, peace, 'tis she;

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Now leave me,
I know the way, though Vesta witness with me
I never trode it with such fear: help, help.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Stop her mouth close, out with the Light, I'll guide you.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: TO whom now shall I cry? What pow'r thus kneel to?
And beg my ravisht honor back upon me
Deaf, deaf, you gods of goodness, deaf to me,
Deaf Heaven to all my cries; deaf hope, deaf justice,
I am abus'd, and you, that see all, saw it;
Saw it, and smil'd upon the villain did it:
Saw it, and gave him strength: why have I pray'd to ye,
When all the worlds eyes have been sunk in slumbers?
Why have I then powr'd out my tears? kneel'd to ye?
And from the Altar of a pure heart sent ye
Thoughts like your selves, white, innocent, vows purer
And of a sweeter flame than all the earths odours?
Why have I sung your praises, s^rew'd your Temples,
And crown'd your Holy Priests with Virgin Roses?
Is it we hold ye powerful, to destroy us?
Believe, and honor ye, to see us ruin'd?
These tears of anger thus I sprinkle toward ye,
You that dare sleep secure whilst Virgins suffer,
These stick like Comets, blaze eternally,
Till, with the wonder, they have wak'd your justice,
And forc't ye fear our curses, as we yours.
My shame still follows me, and still proclaims me;
He turns away in scorn, I am contemned too,
A more unmanly violence than the other;
Bitten, and slung away? What e'r you are
Sir, you that have abus'd me, and now most basely
And sacrilegiously robb'd this fair Temple,
I sling all these behind me, but look upon me,
But one kind loving look, be what ye will,
So from this hour you will be mine, my Husband;
And you his hand in mischief, I speak to you too,
Counsel him nobly now; you know the mischief,
The most unrighteous act he has done, perswade him,
Perswade him like a friend, knock at his Conscience
Till fair Repentance follow: yet be worthy of me,
And shew your self, if ever good thought guided ye;
You have had your soul will, make it yet fair with marriage;
Open your self and take me, wed me now:
More fruits of villany? your Dagger? come
Ye are merciful, I thank you for your medicine:
Is that too worthy too?
Devil, thou with him,
Thou penny Bawd to his Lust, will not that stir thee?
Do you work by tokens now? Be sure I live not,
For your own safeties knaves. I will sit patiently:
But as ye are true villains, the Devils own servants,
And those he loves and trusts, make it as bloody
An Act, of such true horror, Heaven would shake at,
'Twill shew the braver: goodness hold my hope fast,
And in thy mercies look upon my ruines,
And then I am right: my eyes grow dead and heavy:
Wrong me no more as ye are men.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: She is fast.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Away with her.

speeches.speaker: Age.
verse: Now Gentlemen, the time's come now t'enjoy
That fruitful happiness my heart has long'd for:
This day be happy call'd, and when old Time
Brings it about each year, crown'd with that sweetness
It gives me now, see every man observe it,
And laying all aside bears shew of business,
Give this to joy and triumph: How fits my cloaths?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent,
verse: Handsome, and wondrous well, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Do they shew richly?
For to those curious eyes even beauty envies,
I must not now appear poor, or low fashion'd;
Methinks I am younger than I was, far younger;
And such a promise in my bloud I feel now,
That if there may be a perpetual youth
Bestowed on man, I am that soul shall win it:
Does my hair stand well, Lord how ill-favourdly
You have drest me to day? how baldly? why this Cloak?

speeches.speaker: 2 Gen,
verse: Why 'tis the richest, Sir,

speeches.speaker: Age.
verse: And here ye have put me on
A pair of Breeches look like a pair of Bagpipes.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Believe Sir, they shew bravely.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Why these Stockins?

speeches.speaker: 2 Gen.
verse: Your Leg appears—

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Pe^h, I would have had 'em Peach-colour,
All young, and new about me: and this Scarf here
A goodly thing: you have trickt me like a Puppet.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: I'll undertake to rig forth a whole Navy,
And with less labor than one man in love.
They are never pleas'd.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gen.
verse: Methinks he looks well.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Well:
As man can look, as handsome: now do I wonder
He found not fault his Nose was put on ugly,
Or his Eyes lookt too gray, and rail at us,
They are the way wards things, these Lovers.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: All will be right
When once it comes to th' push.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: I would they were at it
For our own quiet sake.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Come, wait upon me,
And bear your selves like mine, my friends, and nobly.

speeches.speaker: Erat.
verse: This is her Brothers door.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: There lay her down then.
Lay her along: she is fast still.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: As forgetfulness.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Be not you stirr'd now, but away to your Mother,
Give all attendance, let no stain appear
Of fear, or doubt in your face: carry your self confidently.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: But whither runs your drift now?

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: When she wakes,
Either what's done will shew a meer dream to her,
And carry no more credit: or say she find it,
Say she remember all the circumstances,
Twenty to one the shapes in which they were acted,
The horrors, and the still affrights we shew'd her,
Rising in wilder figures to her memory
Will run her mad, and no man guess the reason:
If all these fail, and that she rise up perfect,
And so collect her self, believe this, Sir,
Not knowing who it was that did this to her,
Nor having any power to ghess; the thing done too
Being the utter undoing of her honor
If it be known, and to the worlds eye publish'd,
Especially at this time when Fortune courts her,
She must and will conceal it; nay, forget it,
The woman is no Lucrece; get you gone Sir,
And as you would have more of this sport, fear not.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I am confirm'd, farewel.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Farewel, away Sir:
Disperse your selves, and as you love his favour,
And that that crowns it, Gold, no tongues amongst ye.
You know your charge, this way goes no suspicion.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: You are stirring early, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: It was my duty
To wait upon your Grace.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: How fares your Sister,
My beauteous Mistriss, what is she ready yet?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: No doubt she'll lose no time Sir, young Maids in her way
Tread upon thorns, and think an hour an age
Till the Priest has done his part, that theirs may follow:
I saw her not since yesterday i' th' evening:
But Sir, I am sure she is not slack; believe me,
Your grace will find a loving soul.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: A sweet one,
And so much joy I carry in the thought of it,
So great a happiness to know she is mine;
Believe me noble Brother, that to express it
Methinks a Tongue's a poor thing: can do nothing,
Imagination less: who's that that lies there?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Where Sir?

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Before the door, it looks like a woman:

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: This way I came abroad, but then there was nothing,
One of the Maids o'rwatch'd belike:

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: It may be.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: But methinks this is no fit place to sleep in.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: 'Tis sure a woman Sir, she has jewels on too:
She fears no foul play sure.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Bring a Torch hither,
Yet t'is not perfect day: I should know those Garments.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: How sound she sleeps?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: I am sorry to see this.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Do you know her?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: And you now I am sure Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: My Mistriss, how comes this?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: The Queen and her train?

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: You know my pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: And will be most careful.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: Be not long absent, the suit you preferr'd
Is granted.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: This fellow mounts apace, and will
Towre o'r us like a Falcon.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: Good morrow to ye all, why stand ye wondring?
Enter the house Sir, and bring out your Mistriss,
You must observe our Ceremonies: what's the matter?
What's that ye stand at? How Merione?
Asleep i'th' street? belike some sudden Palsie
As she stept out last night upon devotion,
To take her farewel of her Virgin state,
The air being sharp and piercing, struck her suddenly:
See if she breath.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: A little.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: Wake her then,
'Tis sure a fit.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: She wakes her self,
Give room to her.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: See how the spirits struggle to recover,
And strongly reinforce their strength; for certain
This was no natural sleep.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I am of your mind, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: No Son, it cannot be.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Pray Heaven no trick in't;
Good Soul she little merits such a mischief.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: She is broad awake now, and her sence cleers up,
'Twas sure a fit; stand off.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: The Queen, my Love here,
And all my noble friends? Why where am I?
How am I tranc'd, and moap'd? i'th'street? Heaven bless.
Shame to my Sex; oth' ground too? O I remember —

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: How wild she looks?

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Oh my cold heart, how she trembles?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Oh I remember, I remember.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: What's that?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: My shame, my shame, my shame: Oh I remember
My never-dying shame.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Here has been villanie.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: I fear so too.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: You are no Furies are ye?
No horrid shapes sent to affright me?

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: No sweet,
We are your friends: look up, I am Agenor,
O my Merione, that loves you dearly:
And come to marry ye.

speeches.speaker: Leo
verse: Sister, what ail ye?
Speak out your griefs, and boldly —

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Something sticks here
Will choak ye else.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I hope it will.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: Be free Lady,
You have your loving friends about ye.

speeches.speaker: Ah.
verse: Dear Merione,
By the unspotted love I ever bore ye,
By thine own goodness—

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Oh 'tis gone, 'tis gone Sir,
I am now I know not what: pray ye look not on me,
No name is left me, nothing to inherit
But that detested, base, and branded —

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Speak it,
And how; diseases of most danger
Their causes once discover'd are easily cur'd:
My fair Merione.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I thank your love Sir;
When I was fair Merione, unspotted,
Pure, and unblasted in the bud you honour'd,
White as the heart of truth, then Prince Agenor,
Even then I was not worthy of your favour;
Wretch that I am, less worthy now of pitty:
Let no good thing come near me, virtue flie me;
You that have honest noble names despise me,
For I am nothing now but a main pestilence
Able to poison all. Send those unto me
That have forgot their names, ruin'd their fortunes,
Despis'd their honours; those that have been Virgins
Ravish'd and wrong'd,, and yet dare live to tell it.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Now it appears too plain.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Send those sad people
That hate the light, and curse society;
Whose thoughts are Graves, and from whose eyes continually
Their melting souls drop out, send those to me;
And when their sorrows are most excellent,
So full that one grief more cannot be added,
My Story like a torrent shall devour 'em.
Hark, it must out; but pray stand close together,
And let not all the world hear.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Speak it boldly.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: And Royal Lady, think but charitably,
Your Grace has known my breeding.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: Prethee speak it.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Is there no stranger here? send off your servants,
And yet it must be known: I shake.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Sweet Mistriss.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I am abus'd, basely abus'd; do you ghess yet?
Come close, I'll tell ye plainer; I am whor'd,
Ravish'd, and robb'd of Honour.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Oh the Devil.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: What hellish Slave was this?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: A wretch, a wretch,
A damned wretch: do you know the Villain, Lady?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Not by ghess?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Oh no.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: It must be known,

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: Where was the place?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I know not neither.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: O Heaven,
Is this the happy time? my hope to this come?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Neither the man nor circumstances?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: His tongue,
Did you not hear his tongue, no voice?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: None, none Sir:
All I know of him was his violence.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: How came ye hither, Sweet?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I know not neither.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: A cunning piece of villany.

speeches.speaker: M^r.
verse: All I remember
Is only this: Going to Vestas Temple
To give the goddess my last Virgin prayers,
Near to that place I was suddainly surpriz'd,
By five or six disguis'd, and from thence violently
To my dishonour hal'd: that Act perform'd,
Brought back, but how, or whether, till I wak'd here.—

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: This is so monstrous, the gods cannot suffer it;
I have not read in all the villanies
Committed by the most obdurate Rascals,
An act so tru y impious.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Would I knew him.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: He must be known, the Devil cannot hide him.

speeches.speaker: Qu.
verse: If all the Art I have, or power can do it,
He shall be found, and such a way of justice
Inflicted on him: A Lady wrong'd in my Court,
And this way rob'd, and ruin'd?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Be contented Madam,
If he be above ground I will have him.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Fair virtuous Maid, take comfort yet and flourish,
In my love flourish: the stain was forc'd upon ye
None of your wills, nor yours; rise, and rise mine still,
And rise the same white, sweet, fair soul, I lov'd ye,
Take me the same.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I kneel and thank ye, Sir,
And I must say ye are truly honourable:
And dare confess my Will, yet still a Virgin;
But so unfit and weak a Cabinet
To keep your love and virtue in am I now,
That have been forc'd and broken, lost my lustre,
I mean this body, so corrupt a Volume
For you to study goodness in, and honor,
