The gods defend, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: See me, and understand me: This is he
Left to fill up your triumph; he that basely
Whistled his honour off to th'wind; that coldly
Shrunk in his politick head, when Rome like reapers
Sweat blood, and spirit, for a glorious harvest,
And bound it up, and brought it off: that fool,
That having gold and copper offer'd him,
Refus'd the wealth, and took the wast: that soldier
That being courted by loud fame and fortune,
Labour in one hand, that propounds us gods,
And in the other, glory that creates us,
Yet durst doubt, and be damned.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: It was an errour.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: A foul one, and a black one.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Yet the blackest
May be washt white again.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Never.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Your leave, Sir,
And I beseech ye note me; for I love ye,
And bring all comfort: Are we gods,
Allied to no infirmities? are our natures
More than mens natures? when we slip a little
Out of the way of virtue, are we lost?
Is there no medicine called Sweet mercy?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: None, Petillius;
There is no mercy in mankind can reach me,
Nor is it fit it should; I have sinn'd beyond it.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Forgiveness meets with all faults.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: 'Tis all faults,
All sins I can commit, to be forgiven:
'Tis loss of whole man in me, my discretion
To be so stupid, to arrive at pardon.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: O but the General —

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: He's a brave Gentleman,
A valiant, and a loving; and I dare say
He would, as far as honor durst direct him,
Make even with my fault, but 'tis not honest,
Nor in his power: examples that may nourish
Neglect and disobedience in whole bodies.
And totter the estates and faiths of armies,
Must not be plaid withall; nor out of pitty
Make a General forget his duty:
Nor dare I hope more from him than is worthy.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: What would ye do?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Dye.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: So would sullen children,
Women that want their wills, slaves, disobedient,
That fear the law, die. Fie, great Captain; you
A man to rule men, to have thousand lives
Under your Regiment, and let your passion
Betray your reason? I bring you all forgiveness,
The noblest kind commends, your place, your honour.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Prethee no more; 'tis foolish: didst not thou?
By—thou didst, I over-heard thee, there,
There where thou standst now, deliver me for rascal,
Poor, dead, cold coward, miserable, wretched,
If I out-liv'd this ruine?

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: I?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: And thou dist it nobly,
Like a true man, a souldier: and I thank thee,
I thank thee, good Petillius; thus I thank thee,

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Since ye are so justly made up, let me tell ye,
'Tis fit ye dye indeed.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: O how thou lov'st me!

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: For say he had forgiven ye; say the peoples whispers
Were tame again, the time run out for wonder,
What must your own Command think, from whose Swords
Ye have taken off the edges, from whose valours
The due and recompence of Arms; nay, made it doubtful
Whither they knew obedience? must not these kill ye?
Say they are won to pardon ye, by meer miracle
Brought to forgive ye; what old valiant Souldier,
What man that loves to fight, and fight for Rome,
Will ever follow you more? dare ye know these ventures?
If so, I bring ye comfort; dare ye take it?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: No, no, Petillius, no.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: If your mind serve ye.
Ye may live still; but how? yet pardon me,
You may outwear all too, but when? and certain
There is a mercy for each fault, if tamely
A man will take't upon conditions.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: No, by no means: I am only thinking now, Sir,
(For I am resolved to go) of a most base death,
Fitting the baseness of my fault. I'll hang.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Ye shall not; y'are a Gentleman I honor,
I would else flatter ye, and force ye live,
Which is far baser. Hanging? 'tis a dogs death,
An end for slaves.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: The fitter for my baseness.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Besides, the man that's hang'd, preaches his end,
And fits a sign for all the world to gape at.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: That's true: I'll take a fitter poison.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: No,
'Tis equal ill; the death of rats and women,
Lovers, and lazie boys, that fear correction,
Die like a man.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Why my sword then.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: I, If your Sword be sharp, Sir,
There's nothing under heaven that's like your Sword;
Your Sword's a death indeed.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: It shall be sharp, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Why Mithridates was an arrant asse
To dye by poison, if all Bosphorus
Could lend him Swords: your Sword must do the deed:
'Tis shame to dye choak'd, fame to dye and bleed.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Thou hast confirmed me: and, my good Petillius,
Tell me no more I may live.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: 'Twas my Commission;
But now I see ye in a nobler way,
A way to make all even.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Fare-well, Captain:
Be a good man, and fight well: be obedient:
Command thy self, and then thy men. Why shakest thou?

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: I do not Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: I would thou hadst, Petillius:
I would find something to forsake the world with
Worthy the man that dies: a kind of earth-quake
Through all stern valors but mine own.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: I feel now
A kind of trembling in me.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Keep it still,
As thou lov'st virtue, keep it.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: And brave Captain,
The graet and honoured Penyus.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: That again:
O how it heightens me! again, Petillius.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Most excellent Commander.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Those were mine,
Mine, only mine.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: They are still.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Then to keep 'em
For ever falling more, have at ye, heavens,
Ye everlasting powers, I am yours: The work's done,
That neither fire nor age, nor melting envy
Shall ever conquer. Carry my last words
To the great General: kiss his hands and say,
My soul I give to heaven, my fault to justice
Which I have done upon my self: my virtue,
If ever there was any in Poor Penyus,
Made more, and happier, light on him. I faint.
And where there is a foe, I wish him fortune.
I dye: lye lightly on my ashes, gentle earth.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: And on my sin. Farewell, great Penyus,
The souldier is in fury. Now I am glad
'Tis done before he comes. This way, for me,
The way of toile; for thee, the way of honor.

speeches.speaker: Sould.
verse: Kill him, kill him, kill him.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: What will ye do?

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: Good soldiers, honest soldiers.

speeches.speaker: Sould.
verse: Kill him, kill him, kill him.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: Kill us first; we command too.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: Valiant Soldiers,
Consider but whose life ye seek. O Drusus,
Bid him be gone, he dies else. Shall Rome say
(Ye most approved Souldiers) her dear children
Devoured the fathers of the fights? shall rage
And stubborn fury guide those swords to slaughter,
To slaughter of their own, to civil ruine?

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: O let 'em in: all's done, all's ended, Regulus,
Penyus has found his last eclipse. Come, Souldiers,
Come, and behold your miseries: come bravely,
Full of your mutinous and bloody angers,
And here bestow your darts. O only Romane,
O father of the Wars.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: Why stand ye stupid?
Where be your killing furies? whose sword now
Shall first be sheath'd in Penyus? do ye weep?
Howl out, ye wretches, ye have cause: howl ever.
Who shall now lead ye fortunate? whose valor
Preserve ye to the glory of your Countrey?
Who shall march out before ye, coy'd and courted
By all the Mistrisses of War, care, counsel,
Quick-ey'd experience, and victory twin'd to him?
Who shall beget ye deeds beyond inheritance
To speak your names, and keep your honors living,
When children faill, and time that takes all with him,
Build houses for ye to oblivion?

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: O ye poor desperate fools: no more now, souldiers?
Go home, and hang your arms up; let rust rot 'em;
And humble your stern valors to soft prayers;
For ye have sunk the frame of all your virtues;
The sun that warm'd your bloods is set for ever:
I'll kiss thy honor'd cheek. Farewell, great Penyus,
Thou thunder-bolt, farewell. Take up the body;
To morrow morning to the Camp convey it.
There to receive due Ceremonies. That eye
That blinds himself with weeping, gets most glory.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Bring up the Catapults and shake the wall,
We will not be out out-brav'd thus.

speeches.speaker: Nen.
verse: Shake the earth,
Ye cannot shake our souls. Bring up your Rams,
And with their armed heads, make the Fort totter;
Ye do but rock us into death.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: See, Sir,
See the Icenian Queen in all her glory
From the strong battlements proudly appearing,
As if she meant to give us lashes.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Yeild, Queen.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: I am unacquainted with that language, Roman.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Yield honour'd Lady, and expect our mercy,
We love thy nobleness.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: I thank ye, ye say well;
But mercy and love are sins in Rome and hell.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Ye cannot scape our strength; ye must yield, Lady,
Ye must adore and fear the power of Rome.

speeches.speaker: ^ond.
verse: If Rome be earthly, why should any knee
With bending adoration worship her?
She's vitious; and your partial selves confess,
Aspires the height of all impiety:
Therefore 'tis fitter I should reverence
The thatched houses where the Britains dwell
In careless mirth, where the blest houshold gods
See nought but chast and simple purity.
'Tis not high power that makes a place divine,
Nor that the men from gods derive their line
But sacred thoughts in holy bosoms stor'd,
Make people noble, and the place ador'd.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Beat the wall deeper.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Beat it to the center,
We will not sink one thought.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: I'll make ye.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: 2. Dau.
verse: O mother, these are fearful hours: speak gently.
To these fierce men, they will afford ye pitty.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Pitty? thou fearful girl; 'tis for those wretches
That misery makes tame. Wouldst thou live less?
Wast not thou born a Princess? Can my blood,
And thy brave fathers spirit, suffer in thee
So base a separation from thy self,
As mercy from these Tyrants? Thou lov'st lust sure,
And long'st to prostitute thy youth and beauty
To common slaves for bread. Say they had mercy;
The divel a relenting conscience:
The lives of Kings rest in their Diadems,
Which to their bodies lively souls do give,
And ceasing to be Kings, they cease to live.
Show such another fear, and —
I'll fling thee to their fury.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: He is dead then?

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: I think so certainly; yet all my means, Sir,
Even to the hazzard of my life—

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: No more:
We must not seem to mourn here.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: There's a breach made,
Is it your will we charge, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Once more mercy,
Mercy to all that yield

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: I scorn to answer:
Speak to him girl; and hear thy Sister.

speeches.speaker: 1. Dau.
verse: General,
Hear me, and mark me well, and look upon me
Directly in my face, my womans face.
Whose only beauty is the hate it bears ye;
See with thy narrowest eyes, thy sharpest wishes,
Into my soul, and see what there inhabits;
See if one fear, one shadow of a terror,
One paleness dare appear but from my anger,
To lay hold on your mercies. No, ye fools,
Poor fortunes fools, we were not born for triumphs,
To follow your gay sports, and fill your slaves
With hoots and acclamations.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Brave behaviour.

speeches.speaker: 1. Dau.
verse: The children of as great as Rome, as noble,
Our names before her, and our deeds her envy;
Must we guild ore your Conquest, make your State,
That is not fairly strong, but fortune?
No, no, ye Romans, we have ways to scape ye,
To make ye poor again, indeed our prisoners,
And stick our triumphs full.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: 's death, I shall love her.

speeches.speaker: 1. Dau.
verse: To torture ye with suffering, like our slaves;
To make ye curse our patience, wish the world
Were lost again, to win us only, and esteem
The end of all ambitions.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Do ye wonder?
We'll make our monuments in spite of fortune,
In spight of all your Eagles wings: we'll work
A pitch above ye; and from our height we'll stoop
As fearless of your bloody soars; and fortunate,
As if we prey'd on heartless doves.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Strange stiffness.
Decius, go charge the breach.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Charge it home, Roman,
We shall deceive thee else. Where's Nennius?

speeches.speaker: Nen.
verse: They have made a mighty breach.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Stick in thy body,
And make it good but half an hour.

speeches.speaker: Nen.
verse: I'll do it.

speeches.speaker: 1. Dau.
verse: And then be sure to dye.

speeches.speaker: Nen.
verse: It shall go hard else.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Fare well with all my heart; we shall meet yonder,
Where few of these must come.

speeches.speaker: Nen.
verse: Gods take thee, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Bring up the swords, and poison.

speeches.speaker: 2. Dau.
verse: O my fortune!

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: How, how, ye whore?

speeches.speaker: 2. Dau.
verse: Good mother, nothing to offend ye.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Here, wench:
Behold us, Romans.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Mercy yet.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: No talking:
Puff, there goes all your pitty. Come, short prayers,
And let's dispach the business: you begin,
Shrink not; I'll see ye do't.

speeches.speaker: 2. Dau.
verse: O gentle mother,
O Romans, O my heart; I dare not.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Woman, woman,
Unnatural woman.

speeches.speaker: 2. Dau.
verse: O perswade her, Romans:
Alass, I am young, and would live. Noble mother,
Can ye kill that ye gave life? are my years
Fit for destruction?

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Yield, and be a Queen still,
A mother and a friend.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Ye talk: come, hold it,
And put it home.

speeches.speaker: 1. Dau.
verse: Fie, sister, fie,
What would you live to be?

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: A whore still.

speeches.speaker: 2 Dau.
verse: Mercy.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Hear her, thou wretched woman.

speeches.speaker: 2 Dau.
verse: Mercy, mother:
O whither will you send me? I was once
Your darling, your delight.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: O gods,
Fear in my family? do it, and nobly.

speeches.speaker: 2 Dau.
verse: O do not frown then.

speeches.speaker: 1 Daugh.
verse: Do it, worthy Sister:
'Tis nothing, 'tis a pleasure; we'll go with ye,

speeches.speaker: 2 Daugh.
verse: Oh if I knew but whither.

speeches.speaker: 1 Daugh.
verse: To the blessed,
Where we shall meet our Father.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Woman.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Talk not.

speeches.speaker: 1 Daugh.
verse: Where nothing but true joy is.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: That's a good wench, mine own sweet girl; put it close to thee.

speeches.speaker: 2 Daugh.
verse: Oh comfort me still for heavens sake.

speeches.speaker: 1 Daugh.
verse: Where eternal
Our youths are, and our beauties; where no Wars come,
Nor lustful slaves to ravish us.

speeches.speaker: 2 Daugh.
verse: That steels me:
Along farewel to this world.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Good: I'll help thee.

speeches.speaker: 1 Daugh.
verse: The next is mine.
Shew me a Roman Lady in all our stories,
Dare do this for her honor: they are cowards,
Eat coals like compell'd Cats: your great Saint Lucrece
Dy'd not for honor; Tarquin topt her well,
And mad she could not hold him, bled.

speeches.speaker: Petil.
verse: By—
am in love: I would give an hundred pound now
But to lie with this womans behaviour. Oh the devil.

speeches.speaker: 1 Daugh.
verse: Ye shall see me example. All your Rome,
If I were proud and lov'd ambition;
If I were lustful, all your ways of pleasure;
If I were greedy, all the wealth ye conquer—

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Make haste.

speeches.speaker: 1 Daugh.
verse: I will_Could not intice to live
But two short hours this frailty: would ye learn
How to die bravely Romans, to fling off
This case of flesh, lose all your cares for ever?
Live as we have done, well, and fear the gods,
Hunt Honor, and not Nations with your swords,
Keep your minds humble, your devotions high;
So shall ye learn the noblest part, to die.

speeches.speaker: Bend.
verse: I come, wench; to ye all Fates hangmen; you
That ease the aged destinies, and cut
The threds of Kingdoms, as they draw 'em: here,
Here's the draught would ask no less than Caesar
To pledge it for the glories sake.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Great Lady.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Make up your own conditions.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: So we will.

speeches.speaker: Swet,
verse: Stay.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Stay,

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Be any thing.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: A Saint, Swetonius,
When thou shalt fear, and die like a slave. Ye fools,
Ye should have ti'd up death first, when ye conquer'd,
Ye sweat for us in vain else: see him here,
He's ours still, and our friend; laughs at your pities;
And we command him with as easie reins
As do our enemies. I feel the poison.
Poor vanquish'd Romans, with what matchless tortures
Could I now rack ye? But I pittie ye,
Desiring to die quiet: nay, so much
I hate to prosecute my victory,
That I will give ye counsel e'r I die.
If you will keep your Laws and Empire whole,
Place in your Romans flesh, a Britain soul.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Desperate and strange,

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: 'Tis won, Sir, and the Britains
All put to th' sword.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Give her fair Funeral;
She was truly noble, and a Queen.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: —Take it,
A Love-mange grown upon me? what, a spirit?

speeches.speaker: Jun,
verse: I am glad of this, I have found ye.

speeches.speaker: Petil.
verse: In my belly,
Oh how it tumbles?

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Ye good gods, I thank ye.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Thus we afflicted Britains climb for safeties,
And to avoid our dangers, seek destructions;
Thus we awake to sorrows. O thou Woman,
Thou agent for adversities, what curses
This day belong to thy improvidence?
To Britanie by thy means, what sad millions
Of Widows weeping eyes? The strong mans valour
Thou hast betraid to fury; the childs fortune
To fear and want of friends, whose pieties
Might wipe his mournings off, and build his sorrows
A house of rest by his blest Ancestors:
The Virgins thou hast rob'd of all their wishes,
Blasted their blowing hopes, turned their songs,
Their mirthful marriage-son^ to funerals,
The Land thou hast left a wilderness of wretches.
The boy begins to stir: thy safety made,
Would my soul were in Heaven.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: O noble Uncle,
Look out: I dream'd we were betrai'd.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: No harm, boy;
'Tis but thy emptiness that breeds these fancies:
Thou shalt have meat anon,

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: A little, Uncle,
And I shall hold out bravely. What are those?
Look, Uncle, look, those multitudes that march there?
They come upon us stealing by.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: I see 'em;
And prethee be not fearful.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: Now ye hate me,
Would I were dead.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Thou know'st I love thee dearly.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: Did I e'r shrink yet, Uncle? were I a man now;
I should be angry with ye.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: My sweet chicken,
See, they have reach'd us, and as it seems they bear
Some soldiers body, by their solemn gestures,
And sad solemnities; it well appears too
To be of eminence. Most worthy Soldiers,
Let me intreat your knowledge to inform me
What noble Body that is which you bear
With such a sad and ceremonious grief,
As if ye meant to wooe the World and Nature
To be in love with death? Most honorable
Excellent Romans, by your antient valours,
As ye love Fame, resolve me.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: 'Tis the Body
Of the great Captain Penyus, by himself
Made cold and spiritless.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: O stay, ye Romans,
By the Religion which you owe those gods
That lead ye on to Victories, by those glories
Which made even pride a virtue in ye—

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: Stay:
What's thy Will, Caratach

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Set down the body,
The body of the noblest of all Romans,
As ye expect an offering at your Graves
From your friends sorrows, set it down awhile.
That with your griefs an enemy may mingle;
A noble enemy that loves a Soldier;
And lend a tear to virtue; even your foes,
Your wild foes, as you call'd us, are yet stor'd
With fair affections, our hearts fresh, our spirits,
Though sometime stubborn, yet when virtue dies,
Soft and relenting as a Virgins prayers,
Oh set it down.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: Set down the body, soidiers.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Thou hallowed relique, thou rich Diamond
Cut with thine own dust; thou for whose wide fame
The world appears too narrow, mans all thoughts,
Had they all tongues, too silent; thus I bow
To thy most honour'd ashes: though an enemy,
Yet friend to all thy worths: sleep peaceably;
Happiness crown thy soul, and in thy earth
Some Lawrel fix his seat, there grow, and flourish,
And make thy grave an everlasting triumph.
Farewell all glorious Wars, now thou art gone,
And honest Arms adieu: all noble battels
Maintain'd in thirst of honour, not of bloud,
Farewell for ever.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: Was this Roman, Uncle,
So good a man?

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Thou never knew'st thy Father.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: He dy'd before I was born.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: This worthy Roman
Was such another piece of endless honor,
Such a brave soul dwelt in him: their proportions
And faces were not much unlik, boy; excellent nature,
See how it works into his eyes; mine own boy.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: The multitudes of these men, and their fortunes,
Could never make me fear yet: one mans goodness—

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: O now thou pleasest me: weep still, my child,
As if thou saw'st me dead; with such a flux
Or flood of sorrow: still thou pleasest me.
And worthy soldiers, pray receive these pledges,
These hatchments of our griefs, and grace us so much
To place 'em on his Hearse. Now if ye please,
Bear off the noble burden; raise his pile
High as Olympus, make heaven to wonder
To see a star upon earth out-shining theirs.
And ever loved, ever living be
Thy honoured and most sacred memory.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: Thou hast done honestly, good Caratach,
And when thou diest, a thousand virtuous Romans
Shall sing thy soul to heaven. Now march on, soldiers.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Now dry thine eyes, my boy.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: Are they all gone?
I could have wept this hour yet.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Come, take cheer,
And raise thy spirit, child: if but this day
Thou canst bear out thy faintness, the night coming
I'll fashion our escape.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: Pray fear not me;
Indeed I am very hearty.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Be so still;
His mischiefs lessen, that controuls his ill.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: What do I ail, i'th' name of heaven I did but see her,
And see her die: she stinks by this time strongly,
Abominably stinks: she was a woman,
A thing I never car'd for: but to die so,
So confidently, bravely, strongly; Oh the devil,
I have the bots, by—she scorn'd us strangely,
All we could do, or durst do; threatned us
With such a noble anger, and so governed
With such a fiery spirit—; the plain bots;
A—upon the bots, the love-bots: hang me,
Hang me even out o'th' way, directly hang me.
Oh penny pipers, and most painful penners
Of bountiful new Ballads, what a subject,
What a sweet subject for your silver founds,
Is crept upon ye?

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Here he is; have at him.
She set the sword unto her Breast.
great pity it was to see,
That three drops of her Life-warm bloud,
run trickling down her knee.
Art thou there, bonny boy? and i'faith how dost thou?

speeches.speaker: Petil.
verse: Well, gramercie, how dost thou? h'as found me,
Sented me out: the shame the devil ow'd me.
H'as kept his day with. And what news, Junius?

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: It was an old tale ten thousand times told,
Of a young Lady was turn'd into mold,
Her life it was lovely, her death it was bold.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: A cruel rogue, now h'as drawn, pursue it on me,
He hunts me like a devil. No more singing;
Thou hast got a cold: come, let's go drink some Sack, boy.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Ha, ha, ha, ha, ha, ha,

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Why dost thou laugh?
What Mares nest hast thou found?

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Ha, ha, ha.
I cannot laugh alone: Decius, Demetrius,
Curius, oh my sides, Ha, ha, ha,
The strangest jest.

speeches.speaker: Petil.
verse: Prethee no more.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: The admirablest fooling.

speeches.speaker: Pet,
verse: Thou art the prettiest fellow.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Sirs.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Why Junius;
Prethee away, sweet Junius.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Let me sing then.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Whoa, here's a stir now: sing a song o' six pence,
By—(if) prethee;—on't: Junius.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: I must either sing; or laugh.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: And what's your reason?

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: What's that to you?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: And I must whistle.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Do so.
Oh, I hear 'em coming.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: I have a little business.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Thou shalt not go, believe it: what a Gentleman
Of thy sweet conversation?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Captain Junius,
Sweet Captain, let me go with all celerity;
Things are not always one: and do not question,
Nor jeer, nor gybe: none of your doleful Ditties,
Nor your sweet conversation, you will find then
I may be anger'd.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: By no means, Petillius;
Anger a man that never knew passion?
'Tis most impossible: a noble Captain,
A wise and and generous Gentleman?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Tom Puppie.
Leave this way to abuse me: I have found ye,
But for your mothers sake I will fo^give ye.
Your subtil understanding may discover
(As you think) some trim toy to make you merry;
Some straw to tickle ye; but do not trust to't;
Y' are a young man, and may do well: be sober:
Carry your self discreetly.

speeches.speaker: Jun,
verse: Yes forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: How does the brave Petillius?

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Monstrous merry:
We two were talking what a kind of thing
I was when I was in love; what a strange monster
For little Boys and Girls to wonder at;
How like a fool I lookt.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: So they do all,
Like great dull slavering fools.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Petillius saw too.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: No more of this, 'tis scurvie, peace.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: How nastily,
Indeed, how beastly all I did became me?
How I forgot to blow my nose? there he stands,
An honest and a wise man; if himself
(I dare avouch it boldly, for I know it)
Should find himself in love—

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: I am angry.

speeches.speaker: Jun,
verse: Surely his wise self would hang his beastly self,
His understanding-self so mawl his ass-self—

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: He's bound to do it; for he knows the follies,
The poverties, and baseness that belongs to't,
Ha's read upon the reformations long.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: He has so.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: 'Tis true, and he must do't:
Nor is it fit indeed any such coward—

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: You'll leave prating.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Should dare come near the Regiments, especially
Those curious puppies (for believe there are such)
That only love behaviours: those are dog-whelps,
Dwindle away, because a Woman dies well;
Commit with passions only: fornicate
With the free spirit merely: you, Petillius,
For you have long observ'd the World.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Dost thou hear?
I'll beat thee damnably within these three hours:
Go pray; may be I'll kill thee. Farewel Jack-daws.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: What a strange thing he's grown?

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: I am glad he is so;
And stranger he shall be before I leave him.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Is 't possible her mere death—

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: I observ'd him,
And found him taken, infinitely taken
With her bravery, I have follow'd him,
And seen him kiss his sword since, court his scabbard,
Call dying, dainty deer; her brave mind, Mistriss;
Casting a thousand ways, to give those forms,
That he might lie with 'em, and get old Armors:
He had got me o' th' hip once: it shall go hard, friends,
But he shall find his own coin.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: How now Macer?
Is Judas yet come in?

speeches.speaker: Mac.
verse: Yes, and has lost
Most of his men too. Here he is.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: What news?

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: I have lodg'd him; rouze him he that dares.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Where, Judas?

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: On a steep rock i' th' woods, the boy too with him,
And there he swears he will keep his Christmas Gentlemen,
But he will come away with full conditions,
Bravely, and like a Britain: he paid part of us.
Yet I think we fought bravely: for mine own part,
I was four several times at half sword with him,
Twice stood his partizan: but the plain truth is,
He's a meer devil, and no man; i' th' end he swing'd us,
And swing'd us soundly too, he fights by Witchcraft:
Yet for all that I see him lodg'd.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Take more men,
And scout him round. Macer, march you along.
What victuals has he?

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: Not a piece of Bisket,
Not so much as will stop a tooth; nor Water,
More than they make themselves: they lie
Just like a brace of Bear-whelps, close, and crafty,
Sucking their fingers for their food.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Cut off then
All hope of that way: take sufficient forces.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: But use no foul play, on your lives: that man
That does him mischief by deceit, I'll kill him.

speeches.speaker: Macer.
verse: He shall have fair play, he deserves it.

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: Hark ye.
What should I do there then? you are brave Captains,
Most valiant men; go up your selves; use virtue,
See what will come on't: pray the Gentleman
To come down, and be taken. Ye all know him,
I think ye have felt him too: there ye shall find him,
His sword by his side, plums of a pound weight by him
Will make your chops ake: you'll find it a more labour
To win him living, than climbing of a Crows-nest.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Away, and compass him; we shall come up
I am sure within these two hours. Watch him close.

speeches.speaker: Macer.
verse: He shall flee thorow the air, if he escape us.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: What's this loud lamentation?

speeches.speaker: Mac.
verse: The dead body
Of the great Penyus is new come to the Camp, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Dead!

speeches.speaker: Macer.
verse: By himself, they say.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: I fear'd that fortune.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Peace guide him up to heaven.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Away good Macer.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: If thou be'st guilty,
Some sullen plague thou hat'st most light upon thee.
The Regiment return on Junius,
He well deserves it.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: So.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Draw out three Companies,
Yours Decius, Junius, and thou Petillius,
And make up instantly to Caratach,
He's in the Wood before ye; we shall follow
After due ceremony done to the dead,
The noble dead: Come: let's go burn the Body.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: The Regiment given from me; disgrac'd openly;
In love too with a trifle to abuse me?
A merry world, a fine world: serv'd seven years
To be an ass o'both sides, sweet Petillius,
You have brought your hogs to a fine market: you are wise, Sir,
Your honourable brain-pan full of crotchets,
And understanding Gentleman; your projects
Cast with assurance ever: wouldst not thou now
Be bang'd about the pate, Petillius
Answer to that sweet soldier; surely, surely,
I think ye would; pull'd by the nose, kick'd; hang thee,
Thou art the arrant'st Rascal: trust thy wisdom
With any thing of weight; the wind with feathers.
Out ye blind puppie; you command? you govern?
Dig for a groat a day, or serve a Swine-herd;
Too noble for thy nature too. I must up;
But what I shall do there, let time discover.

speeches.speaker: Mac.
verse: Hang it o' th' side o' th' rock, as though the Britains
Stole hither to relieve him; who first ventures
To fetch it off, is ours. I cannot see him.

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: He lies close in a hole above, I know it,
Gnawing upon his anger: ha? no, 'tis not he,

speeches.speaker: Macer.
verse: 'Tis but the shaking of the boughs,

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: —Shake 'em,
I am sure they shake me soundly. There.

speeches.speaker: Macer.
verse: 'Tis nothing.

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: Make no noise if he stir, a deadly tempest
Of huge stones fall upon us: 'tis done: away close.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Sleep still, sleep sweetly child, 'tis all thou feedst on.

No gentle Britain
^ear; no valiant charity
To bring thee food? poor knave, thou art sick extreme sick,
Almost grown wild for meat; and yet thy goodness
Will not confess, nor shew it. All the woods
Are double lin'd with soldiers; no way left us
To make a noble scape: I'll sit down by thee,
And when thou wak'st, either get meat to save thee,
O^ lose my life i'th' purchase, Good gods comfort thee.

speeches.speaker: Guide.
verse: Ye are not far off now, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Draw the Companies
The closest way thorow the woods; we'll keep on this way.

speeches.speaker: Guide.
verse: I will Sir: half a furlong more you'll come
Within the sight o' th' Rock; keep on the left side,
You'll be discover'd else: I'll lodge your Companies
In the wild Vines beyond ye.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Do ye mark him?

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Yes, and am sorry for him.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Junius,
Pray let me speak two words with you.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Walk afore,
I'll overtake ye straight.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: I will.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Now, Captain.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: You have oft told me, you have lov'd me, Junius.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Most sure I told you truth then.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: And that love
Should not deny me any honest thing.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: It shall not.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Dare ye swear it?
I have forgot all passages between us
That have been ill, forgiven too, forgot you.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: What would this man have? By — I do, Sir,
So it be fit to grant ye.

speeches.speaker: Petell.
verse: 'Tis most honest.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Why, then I'll do it.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Kill me.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Pray kill me.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Kill ye?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: I, kill me quickly, suddenly,
Now kill me.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: On what reason? ye amaze me.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: If ye do love me, kill me, ask me not why:
I would be killed, and by you.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Mercy on me,
What ails this man? Petillius.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Pray ye dispatch me,
Ye are not safe whilst I live: I am dangerous,
Troubled extreamly, even to mischief, Junius,
An enemy to all good men: fear not, 'tis justice;
I shall kill you else.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Tell me but the cause,
And I will do it.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: I am disgrac'd, my service
Slighted, and unrewarded by the General,
My hopes left wild and naked; besides these,
I am grown ridiculous, an ass, a folly
I dare not trust my self with: prethee kill me.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: All these may be redeem'd as easily
As you would heal your finger.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Nay—

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Stay, I'll do it,
You shall not need your anger: But first, Petillius,
You shall unarm your self; I dare not trust
A man so bent to mischief.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: There's my sword;
And do it handsomely.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Yes, I will kill ye,
Believe that certain: but first I'll lay before ye
The most extreme fool ye have plaid in this,
The honor purpos'd for ye, the great honor
The General intended ye,

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: And then I'll kill ye,
Because ye shall die miserable. Know Sir,
The Regiment was given me, but till time
Call'd ye to do some worthy deed, might stop
The peoples ill thoughts of ye, for Lord Penyus,
I mean his death. How soon this time's come to ye,
And hasted by Swetonius? Go, says he,
Junius and Decius, and go thou Petillius;
Distinctly, thou Petillius, and draw up,
To take stout Caratach; there's the deed purpos'd,
A deed to take off all faults, of all natures:
And thou Petillius; Mark it, there's the honor,
And that done, all made even.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Stay.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: No, I'll kill ye.
He knew thee absolute, and full in soldier,
Daring beyond all dangers, found thee out
According to the boldness of thy spirit,
A Subject, such a Subject.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Harke ye Junius,
I will live now.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: By no means. Wooed thy worth,
Held thee by the chin up, as thou sunk'st, and shew'd thee
How Honor held her arms out: Come, make ready,
Since ye will die an ass.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Thou wilt not kill me?

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: By—but I will, Sir: I'll have no man dangerous
Live to destroy me afterward. Besides, you have gotten
Honor enough, let young men rise now. Nay,
I do perceive too by the General, (which is
One main cause ye shall die) how e'r he carry it,
Such a strong doting on ye, that I fear,
You shall command in chief: how are we paid then?
Come, if you will pray, dispatch it.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Is there no way?

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Not any way to live.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: I will do any thing,
Redeem my self at any price: good Junius,
Let me but die upon the Rock, but offer
My life up like a Soldier.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: You will seek then
To out-doe every man.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Believe it Junius,
You shall goe stroke by stroke with me.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: You'l leave off too,
As you are noble, and a soldier,
For ever these mad fancies.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Dare ye trust me?
By all that's good and honest.

speeches.speaker: Jun,
verse: There's your sword then,
And now come on a new man: Virtue guide thee. Exeunt.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Courage my Boy, I have found meat: look Hengo,
Look where some blessed Britain, to preserve thee,
Has hung a little food and drink: cheer up Boy,
Do not forsake me now.

speeches.speaker: Hengo.
verse: Oh Uncle. Uncle,
I feel I cannot stay long: yet I'll fetch it,
To keep your noble life: Uncle, I am heart-whole,
And would live.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Thou shalt, long I hope.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: But my head, Uncle:
Methinks the Rock goes round.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
verse: Mark 'em well, Judas.

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: Peace, as you love your life.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Do not you hear
The noise of Bels?

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Of Bels Boy? 'tis thy fancie,
Alas, thy bodies full of wind.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Methinks, Sir,
They ring a strange sad knell, a preparation
To some near funeral of State: nay, weep not,
Mine own sweet Uncle, you will kill me sooner.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Oh my poor chicken.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Fie, faint-hearted Uncle:
Come, tie me in your Belt, and let me down.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: I'll go my self Boy.

speeches.speaker: Hengo.
verse: No, as ye love me, Uncle;
I will not eat it, if I do not fetch it;
The danger only I desire: pray tie me.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: I will, and all my care hang o'r thee: come child,
My valiant child,

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Let me down apace, Uncle,
And ye shall see how like a Daw I'll whip it
From all their policies: for 'tis most certain
A Roman train: and ye must hold me sure too,
You'll spoil all else. When I have brought it Uncle,
We'll be as merry—

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Go i' th' name of heaven, Boy.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Quick, quick, Uncle, I have it. Oh.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: What ail'st thou?

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: O my best Uncle, I am slain.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: I see ye, and heaven direct my hand: destruction
Caratach kills Judas with a stone from the rock.
Go with thy coward soul. How dost thou Boy?
Oh villain, pocky villain.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Oh Uncle, Uncle,
Oh how it pricks me: am I preserv'd for this?
Extremely pricks me.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Coward, rascal Coward,
Dogs eat thy flesh.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Oh I bleed hard: I faint too, out upon't,
How sick I am? the lean Rogue, Uncle.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Look Boy,
I have laid him sure enough.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Have ye knockt his brains out?

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: I warrant thee for stirring more: cheer up, child.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Hold my sides hard, stop, stop, oh wretched fortune,
Must we part thus? Still I grow sicker, Uncle.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Heaven look upon this noble child.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: I once hop'd
I should have liv'd to have met these bloody Romans
At my swords point, to have reveng'd my Father,
To have beaten 'em: oh hold me hard. But Uncle—

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Thou shalt live still I hope Boy. Shall I draw it?

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Ye draw away my soul then, I would live
A little longer; spare me heavens, but only
To thank you for your tender love. Good Uncle,
Good noble Uncle weep not.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Oh my chicken,
My dear Boy, what shall I lose?

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Why, a child,
That must have died however: had this scap'd me,
Feaver or famine—I was born to die. Sir.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: But thus unblown, my boy?

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: I go the straighter
My journey to the gods: Sure I shall know ye
When ye come, Uncle.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Yes, Boy

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: And I hope
We shall enjoy together that great blessedness
You told me of.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Most certain, child.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: I grow cold,
Mine eyes are going.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Lift 'em up.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Pray for me;
And noble Uncle, when my bones are ashes,
Think of your little Nephew. Mercy.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Mercy.
You blessed Angels take him.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Kiss me: so.
Farewel, farewel.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Farewel the hopes of Britain,
Thou Royal graft, Farewel for ever. Time and Death,
Ye have done your worst. Fortune now see, now proudly
Pluck off thy vail, and view thy triumph: Look
Look what thou hast brought this Land to. Oh fair flower,
How lovely yet thy ruines show, how sweetly
Even death embraces thee! The peace of heaven,
The fellowship of all great souls be with thee.
Hah? dare ye Romans? ye shall win me bravely.
Thou art mine.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Not yet, Sir,

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Breath ye, ye poor Romans,
And come up all, with all your antient valors,
Like a rough wind I'll shake your souls, and send 'em—

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Yield thee bold Caratach; by all—
As I am Soldier, as I envie thee,
I'll use thee like thy self, the valiant Britain.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Brave soldier yield; thou stock of Arms and Honor,
Thou filler of the World with Fame and Glory.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Most worthy man, we'll wooe thee, be thy prisoners.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Excellent Britain, do me but that Honor,
That more to me than Conquests, that true happiness,
To be my friend.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Oh Romans, see what here is:
Had this Boy liv'd—

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: For Fames sake, for thy Swords sake,
As thou desirest to build thy virtues greater:
By all that's excellent in man, and honest—

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: I do believe: Ye have had me a brave foe;
Make me a noble friend, and from your Goodness,
Give this Boy honourable earth to lie in.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: He shall have fitting Funeral.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: I yield then.
Not to your blows, but your brave courtesies.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Thus we conduct then to the arms of Peace
The wonder of the World.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Thus I embrace thee,
And let it be no flattery that I tell thee,
Thou art the only Soldier.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: How to thank ye,
I must hereafter find upon your usage.
I am for Rome.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Ye must.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Then Rome shall know
The man that makes her spring of glory grow.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Petillius, you have shown much worth this day,
redeem'd much error,
Ye have my love again; preserve it, Junius,
With you I make him equal in the Regiment.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: The elder and the nobler: I'll give place, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Ye shew a friends soul.
March on, and through the Camp in every tongue.
The Virtues of great Caratach be sung.

plays.play_title: The Knight of the Burning Pestle.

speeches.speaker: Merch.
verse: Sirrah, I'll make you know you are my Prentice,
And whom my charitable love redeem'd
Even from the fall of fortune; gave thee heat
And growth, to be what now thou art, new cast thee,
Adding the trust of all I have at home,
In forreign Staples, or upon the Sea
To thy direction, ti'de the good opinions
Both of self and friends to thy endeavors,
So fair were thy beginnings: but with these
As I remember you had never charge,
To love your Masters Daughter, and even then,
When I had found a wealthy Husband for her,
I take it, Sir, you had not: but however,
I'll break the neck of that Commission,
And make you know you are but a Merchants Factor.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Sir,
I do liberally confess I am yours,
Bound both by love and duty to your service;
In which my labor hath been all my profit;
I have not lost in bargain, nor delighted
To wear your honest gains upon my back,
Nor have I given a pension to my bloud,
Or lavishly in play consum'd your stock.
These, and the miseries that do attend them,
I dare with innocence, proclaim are strangers
To all my temperate actions: for your Daughter,
If there be any love to my deservings,
Born by her virtuous self, I cannot stop it:
Nor am I able to refrain her wishes.
She's private to her self, and best of knowledge,
Whom she'll make so happy as to sigh for·
Besides, I cannot think you mean to match her,
Unto a fellow of so lame a presence,
One that hath little left of Nature in him.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: 'Tis very well, Sir, I can tell your wisdom
How all this shall be cur'd.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Your care becomes you.

speeches.speaker: Merc.
verse: And thus it shall be, Sir, I here discharge you,
My house, and service, take your liberty,
And when I want a Son I'll send for you.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: These be the fair rewards of them that love,
Oh you that live in freedom never prove
The travel of a mind led by desire.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: Why how now friend, struck with my Fathers thunder?

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Struck, and struck dead, unless the remedy
Be full of speed and virtue; I am now,
What I expected long, no more your father's.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: But mine.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: But yours, and only yours I am,
That's all I have to keep me from the statute:
You dare be constant still?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: O fear me not.
In this I dare be better than a woman.
Nor shall his anger, nor his offers move me,
Were they both equal to a Princes power.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: You know my Rival?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: Yes, and love him dearly,
Even as I love an ague, or foul weather,
I prethee Jasper fear him not.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Oh no,
I do not mean to do him so much kindness,
But to our own desires you know the plot
We both agreed on.

speeches.speaker: Lu^e.
verse: Yes, and will perform
My part exactly.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: I desire no more,
Farewel, and keep my heart, 'tis yours.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: I take it,
He must do miracles,
Makes me forsake it.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: Fie upon 'em little infidels,
What a matter's here now?
Well, I'll be hang'd for a half-penny,
If there be not some abomination knavery in this Play,
Well, let 'em look to't,
Ralph must come,
And if there be any tricks a brewing —

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: Let 'em brew and bake too Husband, a gods name,
Ralph will find all out I warrant you,
And they were older than they are.
I pray my pretty youth, is Ralph ready?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: He will be presently.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: Now I pray you make my commendations unto him,
And withal, carry him this stick of Licoras,
Tell him his Mistriss sent it him,
And bid him Mistriss sent it him,
'Twill open his pipes the better, say.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Come, Sir, she's yours, upon my faith she's yours,
You have my hand, for other idle letts
Between your hopes and her, thus, with a wind,
They are scattered, and no more: my wanton Prentice,
That like a bladder blew himself with love,
I have lett out, and sent him to discover
New masters yet unknown.

speeches.speaker: Humph.
verse: I thank you Sir,
Indeed I thank you, Sir, and e'r I stir,
It shall be known however you do deem,
I am of gentle blood and gentle seem.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Oh Sir, I know it certain.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: Sir, my friend,
Although as Writers say, all things have end,
And that we call a Pudding, hath his two,
Oh let it not seem strange I pray to you,
If in this bloudy simile, I put
My love, more endless, than frail things or gut.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: Husband,
I prethee sweet lamb tell me one thing,
But tell me truly:
Stay youths I beseech you,
Till I question my Husband.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: What is it Mouse?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: Sirrah,
Didst thou ever see a prettier child?
How it behaves it self, I warrant ye:
And speaks and looks, and pearts up the head?
I pray you brother with your favour,
Were you never none of Mr. Moncasters Scholars?

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: Chickin,
I prethee heartily contain thy self,
The childer are pretty childer,
But when Ralph comes, Lamb.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: I when Ralph comes, Conie,
Well my youth you may proceed

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Well Sir, you know my love, and rest, I hope
Assur'd of my consent; get but my daughters,
And wed her when you please: you must be bold,
And clap in close unto her, come, I know
You have language good enough to win a wench.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: A whoresone tyrant,
Hath been an old stringer in his days,
I warrant him.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: I take your gentle offer, and withal
Yield love again for love reciprocal.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: What Luce, within there?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: Call'd you Sir?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I did
Give entertainment to this Gentleman,
And see you be not froward to her, Sir:
My presence will but be an eye-soar to you.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: Fair Mistriss Luce, how do you, are you well?
Give me your hand, and then I pray you tell,
How doth your little Sister, and your Brother?
And whether you love me or any other.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: Sir, these are quickly answer'd.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: So they are,
Where Women are not cruel: but how far
Is it now distant from the place we are in,
Unto that blessed place your Fathers Warren.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: What makes you think of that, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: Even that face,
For stealing Rabbets whilome in that place,
God Cupid, or the Keeper, I know not whether,
Unto my cost and charges brought you thither,
And there began.

speeches.speaker: Luec.
verse: Your game, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: Let no game,
Or any thing that tendeth to the same,
Be evermore remembred, thou fair killer
For whom I sate me down and brake my Tiller.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: There's a kind Gentleman, I warrant you, when will you do as much for me George?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: Beshrew me Sir, I am sorry for your losses,
But as the proverb says, I cannot cry,
I would you had not seen me.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: So would I.
Unless you had more maw to do me good.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: Why, cannot this strange passion be withstood,
Send for a Constable and raise the Town.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: Oh no, my valiant love will batter down
Millions of Constables, and put to flight,
Even that great Watch of Midsummer day at night.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: Beshrew me, Sir, 'twere good I yielded then,
Weak Women cannot hope, where valiant men
Have no resistance.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: Yield then, I am full
Of pity, though I say it, and can pull
Out of my pocket thus a pair of Gloves.
Look Lucy, look, the dogs tooth, nor the Doves
Are not so white as these; and sweet they be,
And whipt about with silk, as you may see:
If you desire the price, sute from your eye,
I beam to this place, and you shall espie
F. S. which is to say my sweetest Honey,
They cost me three and two pence, or no money.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: Well Sir, I take them kindly, and I thank you;
What would you more?

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: Nothing.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: Why then farewel.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: Nor so, nor so, for Lady I must tell,
Before we part, for what we met together,
God grant me time, and patience, and fair weather.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: Speak and declare your mind in terms so brief.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: I shall; then first and foremost for relief
I call to you, if that you can afford it,
I care not at what price, for on my word, it
Shall be repaid again, although it cost me
More than I'll speak of now, for love hath tost me
In furious blanket like a Tennis-ball,
And now I rise aloft, and now I fall.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: Alas good Gentleman, alas the day.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: I thank you heartily, and as I say,
Thus do I still continue without rest,
I' th' morning like a man, at night a beast,
Roaring and bellowing mine own disquiet,
That much I fear, forsaking of my diet,
Will bring me presently to that quandary,
I shall bid all adieu.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: Now by S. Mary
That were great pity.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: So it were beshrew me,
Then ease me lusty Luce, and pity shew me.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: Why Sir, you know my will is nothing worth
Without my Fathers grant, get his consent,
And then you may with assurance try me.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: The Worshipful your Sire will not deny me,
For I have ask'd him, and he hath reply'd,
Sweet Master Humphrey, Luce shall be thy Bride.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: Sweet Master Humphrey then I am content.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: And so am I in truth.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: Yet take me with you,
There is another clause must be annext,
And this it is I swore, and will perform it,
No man shall ever joy me as his wife,
But he that stole me hence: if you dare venture,
I am yours; you need not fear, my father loves you:
If not, farewel for ever.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: Stay Nymph, stay,
I have a double Gelding coloured bay,
Sprung by his Father from Barbarian kind,
Another for my self, though somewhat blind,
Yet true as trusty tree.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: I am satisfied,
And so I give my hand, our course must lie
Through Waltham Forrest, where I have a friend
Will entertain us, so farewell Sir Humphrey.
And think upon your business.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: Though I die,
I am resolv'd to venture lise and lim,
For one so young, so fair, so kind, so trim,

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: By my faith and troth George, and as I am virtuous, It is e'n the kindest young man that ever trode on shooe-leather: well, go thy waies, if thou hast her not, 'tis not thy fault 'isaith.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: I prethee Mouse be patient, a shall have her, or I'll make some of 'em smoak for't.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Thats my good lamb George, fie, this stinking Tobacco kills men, would there were none in England: now I pray Gentlemen, what good does this stinking Tobacco? do you nothing; I warrant you make chimneys a your faces: Oh Husband, Husband, now, now there's Ralph, there's Ralph.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Peace fool, let Ralph alone, hark you Ralph; do not strain your self too much at the first, peace, begin Ralph.

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
prose: Then Palmerin and Trineus snatching their Lances from their Dwarfs, and clasping their Helmets, gallopt amain after the Giant, and Palmerin having gotten a sight of him, came posting amain, saying, Stay traiterous thief, for thou maist not so carry away her, that is worth the greatest Lord in the World, and with these words gave him a blow on the Shoulder, that he struck him besides his Elephant; and Trineus coming to the Knight that had Agricola behind him, set him soon besides his horse, with his neck broken in the fall, so that the Princess getting out of the throng, between joy and grief said; All happy Knight, the mirror of all such as follow Arms, now may I be well assured of the love thou bearest me, I wonder why the Kings do not raise an Army of fourteen or fifteen hundred thousand men, as big as the Army that the Prince of Portigo brought against Ro^icler, and destroy these Giants, they do much hurt to wandring Damsels, that go in quest of their Knights.

speeches.speaker: Wife,
prose: Faith Husband, and Ralph says true, for they say the King of Portugal cannot sit at his meat, but the Giants and the Ettins will come and snatch it from him.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Hold thy tongue; on Ralph.

speeches.speaker: Ralph,
prose: And certainly those Knights are much to be commended, who neglecting their possessions, wander with a Squire and a Dwarfe through the Desarts, to relieve poor Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I by my faith are they Ralph, let 'em say what they will, they are indeed: our Knights neglect their possessions well enough, but they do not the rest.

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
prose: There are no such courteous, and fair well-spoken Knights in this age, they will call one the Son of a whore, that Palmerin of England, would have called fair Sir; and one that Rosicler would have called Right beautiful Damsel, they will call Damn'd bitch.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I'll be sworn will they Ralph, they have called me so an hundred times about a scurvy pipe of Tobacco.

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
prose: But what brave spirit could be content to sit in his shop with a slapet of Wood, and a blew Apron before him selling Methridatam and Dragons water to visited houses, that might pursue seats of Arms, and through his noble atchievements, procure such a famous History to be written of, in his Heroick prowesse.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Well said Ralph, some more of those words Ralph.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: They go finely by my troth.

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
prose: Why should I not then pursue this course, both for the credit of my self and our company, for amongst all the worthy Books of Atchievements, I do not call to mind, that I yet read of a Grocer Errant, I will be the said Knight: Have you heard of any that hath wandred unfurnished of his Squire and Dwarfe? my elder Prentice Tom shall be my trusty Squire, and little George my Dwarfe, hence my blew Apron, yet in remembrance of my former Trade, upon my shield shall be pourtraid a Burning Pestle, and I will be call'd the Knight of the burning Pestle.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Nay, I dare swear thou wilt not forget thy old Trade, thou wert ever meek. Ralph, Tim, Tim. Anon.

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
prose: My beloved Squire, and George my Dwarfe, I charge you that from henceforth you never call me by any other name, but the Right courteous and valiant Knight of the Burning Pestle, and that you never call any Female by the name of a Woman or Wench, but fair Lady, if she have her desires; if not, distressed Damsel; that you call all Forrests and Heaths, Desarts, and all Horses Palfries.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: This is very fine: faith do the Gentlemen like Ralph, think you Husband?

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: I, I warrant thee, the Players would give all the shooes in their shop for him.

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
prose: My beloved Squire Tim, stand out, admit this were a Desart, and over it a Knight Errant pricking, and I should bid you enquire of his intents, what would you say?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Sir, my Master sent me to know whither you are riding?

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
prose: No, thus; fair Sir, the Right courteous, and valiant Knight of the Burning Pestle, commanded me to enquire upon what adventure you are bound, whether to relieve some distressed Damsel, or otherwise.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Whorson blockhead cannot remember.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I'faith, and Ralph told him on't before: all the Gentlemen heard him, did he not Gentlemen, did not Ralph tell him on't?

speeches.speaker: George.
prose: Right courteous and valiant Knight of the Burning Pestle, here is a distressed Damsel, to have a halfepenny worth of Pepper.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: That's a good boy, see, the little boy can hit it, by my troth it's a fine child.

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
prose: Relieve her with all courteous language, now shut up shop, no more my Prentice, but my trusty Squire and Dwarfe, I must bespeak my Shield, and arming Pestle.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Go thy ways Ralph, as I am a true man, thou art the best on 'em all.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Ralph, Ralph.

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
prose: What say you Mistriss?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I prethee come again quickly, sweet Ralph.

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
prose: By and by.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Mer.
prose: Give thee my blessing? no, I'll never give thee my blessing, I'll see thee hang'd first; it shall ne'r be said I gave thee my blessing: thou art thy Fathers own Son, of the bloud of the Merry-thoughts; I may curse the time that e'r I knew thy Father, he hath spent all his own, and mine too, and when I tell him of it, he laughs and dances, and sings and cries; A merry heart lives long-a. And thou art a wast-thrift, and art run away from thy Master, that lov'd thee well, and art come to me, and I have laid up a little for my younger Son Michael, and thou thinkst to bezle that, but thou shalt never be able to do it, Come hither Michael, come Michael, down on thy knees, thou shalt have my blessing.

speeches.speaker: Mich.
prose: I pray you Mother pray to God to bless me.

speeches.speaker: Mist Mer.
prose: God bless thee: but Jasper shall never have my blessing, he shall be hang'd first, shall he not Michael? how saist thou?

speeches.speaker: Mich.
prose: Yes forsooth Mother and grace of God.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Mer.
prose: That's a good boy.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I'faith it's a fine spoken child:

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
prose: Mother, though you forget a Parents love,
I must preserve the duty of a child:
I ran not from my Master, nor return
To have your stock maintain my idleness.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Ungracious child I warrant him, harke how he chops Logick with his Mother: thou hadst best tell her she lies, do, tell her she lies.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: If he were my son, I would hang him up by the heels, and flea him, and salt him, whorson halter-sack.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
prose: My coming only is to beg your love,
Which I ever though I never gain it,
And howsoever you esteem of me,
There is no drop of bloud hid in these veins,
But I remember well belongs to you,
That brought me forth; and would be glad for you
To rip them all again, and let it out.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Mer.
prose: I'faith I had sorrow enough for thee: (God knows) but I'll hamper thee well enough: get thee in thou vagabond, get thee in, and learn of thy brother Michael.

speeches.speaker: Old Mer. within.
prose: Nose, Nose, jolly red Nose, and who gave thee this jolly red Nose?

speeches.speaker: Mist. Mer.
prose: Hark my Husband he's singing and hoiting,
And I'm fain to car^ and care, and all little enough.
Husband, Charles, Charles Merry-thought.

speeches.speaker: Old Mer.
prose: Nutmegs and Gingers, Cinamon and Cloves,
And they gave me this jolly red Nose.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Mer.
prose: If you would consider your estate, you would have little list to sing, I-wisse.

speeches.speaker: Old Mer.
prose: It should never be consider'd, while it were an estate, if I thought it would spoil my singing.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Mer.
prose: But how wilt thou do Charles, thou art an old man, and thou canst not work, and thou hast not forty shillings left, and thou eatest good meat, and drinkest good drink, and laughest?

speeches.speaker: Old Mer.
prose: And will doe.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Mer.
prose: But how wilt thou come by it Charles?

speeches.speaker: Old Mer.
prose: How? why how have I done hitherto these forty years? I never came into my Dining-room, but at eleven and six a clock, I found excellent meat and drink a' th' Table: my Cloaths were never worn out, but next morning a Tailor brought me a new suit; and without question it will be so ever! use makes perfectness, If all should fail, it is but a little straining my self extraordinary, and laugh my self to death.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: It's a foolish old man this: is not he George?

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Yes Cunny.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Give me a penny i' th' purse while I live George.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: I by Lady Cunnie, hold thee there.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Mer.
prose: Well Charles, you promis'd to provide for Jasper, and I have laid up for Michael: I pray you pay Jasper his portion, he's come home, and he shall not consume Michaels stock: he saies his Master turn'd him away, but I promise you truly, I think he ran away.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: No indeed Mistriss Merry-thought, though he be a notable gallows, yet I'll assure you his Master did turn him away, even in this place, 'twas i'faith within this half hour, about his Daughter, my Husband was by.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Hang him rogue, he serv'd him well enough: love his Masters Daughter! by my troth Cunnie, if there were a thousand boys, thou wouldst spoil them all, with taking their parts; let his Mother alone with him.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I George, but yet truth is truth.

speeches.speaker: Old. Mer.
prose: Where is Jasper? he's welcome however, call him in, he shall have his portion, is he merry?

speeches.speaker: Mist. Mer.
prose: I foul chive him, he is too merry. Jasper. Michael.

speeches.speaker: Old Mer.
prose: Welcome Jasper, though thou run'st away, welcome, God bless thee, 'tis thy mothers mind thou shouldst receive thy portion: thou hast been abroad, and I hope hast learnt experience enough to govern it: thou art of sufficient years, hold thy hand: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, there is ten shillings for thee, thrust thy self into the world with that, and take some setled course, if fortune cross thee, thou hast a retiring place; come home to me, I have twenty shillings left, be a good Husband, that is, wear ordinary Cloaths, eat the best meat, and drink the best drink; be merry, and give to the poor, and and believe me, thou hast no end of thy goods.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
prose: Long may you live free from all thought of ill,
And long have cause to be thus merry still.
But Father?

speeches.speaker: Old Mer.
prose: No more words Jasper, get thee gone, thou hast my blessing, thy Fathers spirit upon thee. Farewel Jasper; but yet, or e'r you part (oh cruel) kiss me, kiss me sweeting, mine own dear jewel: So, now begone; no words.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Mer.
prose: So Michael, now get thee gone too.

speeches.speaker: Mich.
prose: Yes forsooth Mother, but I'll have my Father's blessing first.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Mer.
prose: No Michael, 'tis no matter for his blessing; thou hast my blessing, begone; I'll fetch my money and jewels, and follow thee: I'll stay no longer with him I warrant thee; truly Charles I'll begon too.

speeches.speaker: Old Mer.
prose: What you will not?

speeches.speaker: Old Mer.
prose: What you will not?

speeches.speaker: Mist. Mer.
prose: Yes indeed will I.

speeches.speaker: Old Mer.
prose: Hay ho, farewel Nan, I'll never trust wench more again, if I can.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Mer.
prose: You shall not think (when all your own is gone) to spend that I have been scraping up for Michael.

speeches.speaker: Old Mer.
prose: Farewel good wife, I expect it not; all I have to do in this world, is to be merry: which I shall, if the ground be not taken from me: and if it be,
When Earth and Seas from me are rest,
The Skies aloft for me are left.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I'll be sworn he's a merry old Gentleman for all that: Hark, hark Husband, hark, Fiddles, Fiddles; now surely they go finely. They say 'tis present death for these Fidlers to tune their Rebecks before the great Turks grace, is 't not George? But look, look, here's a youth dances: now good youth do a turn o' th' toe; Sweet: heart, I'faith I'll have Ralph come, and do some of his Gambols; he'll ride the Wild Mare Gentlemen, 'twould do your hearts good to see him: I thank you kind youth, pray bid Ralph come.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Peace Connie. Sirrah, you scurvy boy, bid the Players send Ralph, or by gods—and they do not, I'll tear some of their Periwigs beside their heads: this is all Riff-Raff.

speeches.speaker: Merch.
verse: And how faith? how goes it now Son Humphrey?

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: Right worshipful and my beloved friend
And Father dear, this matter's at an end.

speeches.speaker: Merch.
verse: 'Tis well, it should be so, I'm glad the Girl
Is found so tractable.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: Nay, she must whirl
From hence, and you must wink: for so I say,
The story tells to morrow before day.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: George, dost thou think in thy conscience now 'twill be a match? tell me but what thou think'st sweet Rogue, thou seest the poor Gentleman (dear heart) how it labours and throbs I warrant you, to be at rest: I'll go move the Father for't.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: No, no, I prethee sit still Honey-suckle, thou'lt spoil all; if he deny him, I'll bring half a dozen good fellows my self, and in the shutting of an evening knock't up, and there's an end.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I'll buss thee for that I'faith boy; well George, well you have been a wag in your days I warrant you: but God forgive you, and I do with all my heart.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: How was it Son? you told me that to morrow
Before day break, you must convey her hence.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: I must, I must, and thus it is agreed,
Your Daughter rides upon a brown-bay Steed,
I on a Sorrel, which I bought of Brian,
The honest Host of the red roaring Lion
In Waltham situate: then if you may,
Consent in seemly sort, lest by delay,
The fatal Sisters come, and do the office,
And then you'll sing another Song.

speeches.speaker: Merch.
verse: Alas.
Why should you be thus full of grief to me,
That do as willing as your self agree
To any thing so it be good and fair?
Then steal her when you will, if such a pleasure
Content you both, I'll sleep and never see it,
To make your joys more full: but tell me why
You may not here perform your marriage?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Gods blessing o'thy soul, old man, i' faith thou art loth to part true hearts: I see a has her, George, and I'm as glad on't; well, go thy ways Humphrey for fair a spoken man, I believe thou hast not thy fellow within the walls of London, and I should say the Suburbs too, I should not lie: why dost not thou rejoyce with me George?

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: If I could but see Ralph again, I were as merry as mine Host i' faith.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: The cause you seem to ask, I thus declare;
Help me oh Muses nine, your Daughter sware
A foolish oath, the more it was the pity:
Yet none but my self within this City
Shall dare to say so, but a bold defiance
Shall meet him, were he of the noble Science.
And yet she sware, and yet why did she swear?
Truly I cannot tell, unless it were
For her own ease: for sure sometimes an oath,
Being sworn thereafter, is like cordial broth.
And this it was, she swore never to marry,
But such a one whose mighty arm could carry
(As meaning me, for I am such a one)
Her bodily away through stick and stone,
Till both of us arrive at her request,
Some ten miles off in the wide Waltham Forrest.

speeches.speaker: Merch.
verse: If this be all, you shall not need to fear
Any denial in your love, proceed,
I'll neither follow, nor repent the deed.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: Good night, twenty good nights, and twenty more,
And twenty more good nights, that makes threescore.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Mer.
prose: Come Michael, art thou not weary Boy?

speeches.speaker: Mich.
prose: No forsooth Mother not I.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Mer.
prose: Where be we now child?

speeches.speaker: Mich.
prose: Indeed forsooth Mother I cannot tell, unless we be at Mile-end, is not all the world Mile-end, Mother?

speeches.speaker: Mist. Mer.
prose: No Michael, not all the world boy; but I can assure thee Michael, Mile-end is a goodly matter, there has been a pitcht field my child, between the naughty Spaniels, and the Englishmen, and the Spaniels ran away Michael, and the Englishmen followed: my neighbor Coxstone was there boy, and kill'd them all with a birding-piece.

speeches.speaker: Mich.
prose: Mother forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Mer.
prose: What says my white boy?

speeches.speaker: Mich.
prose: Shall not my Father go with us too?

speeches.speaker: Mist. Mer.
prose: No Michael, let thy Father go snick up, he shall never come between a pair of sheets with me again, while he lives: let him stay at home and sing for his supper boy; come child sit down, and I'll shew my boy-fine knacks indeed, look here Michael, here's a Ring, and here's a Bruch, and here's a Bracelet, and here's two Rings more, and here's Money, and Gold by th' eye my boy.

speeches.speaker: Mich.
prose: Shall I have all this Mother?

speeches.speaker: Mist. Mer.
prose: I Michael thou shalt have all Michael.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: How lik'st thou this wench?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I cannot tell, I would have Ralph, George; I'll see no more else indeed: law, and I pray you let the youths understand so much by word of mouth, for I will tell you truly, I'm afraid o'my boy: come, come George, let's be merry and wise, the child's a fatherless child, and say they should put him into a strait pair of Gaskins, 'twere worse than knot-grass, he would never grow after it.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Here's Ralph, here's Ralph

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: How do you Ralph? you are welcome Ralph, as I may say, it' a good boy, hold up thy head, and be not afraid, we are thy friends. Ralph, the Gentlemen will praise thee Ralph, if thou plai'st thy part with audacity, begin Ralph a Gods name.

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
prose: My trusty Squire unlace my Helme, give me my hat, where are we, or what desart might this be?

speeches.speaker: Dw.
prose: Mirror of Knigthood, this is, as I take it, the perilous Waltham Down; in whose bottom stands the inchanted Valley.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Mer.
prose: Oh Michael, we are betraid, we are betraid, here be Giants, flie boy, flie boy flie.

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
verse: Lace on my Helme again: what noise is this?
A gentle Lady flying the embrace
Of some uncourteous Knight, I will relieve her.
Go Squire, and say, the Knight that wears this Pestle
In honor of all Ladies swears revenge
Upon that recreant Coward that pursues her,
Goe comfort her, and that same gentle Squire
That bears her company.

speeches.speaker: Squ.
verse: I go brave Knight.

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
verse: My trusty Dwarf and friend, reach me my shield,
And hold it while I swear, first by my Knighthood,
Then by the soul of Amadis de Gaule,
My famous Ancestor, then by my Sword,
The beauteous Brionella girt about me,
By this bright burning Pestle of mine honor,
The living Trophie, and by all respect
Due to distressed Damsels, here I vow
Never to end the quest of this fair Lady,
And that forsaken Squire, till by my valour
I gain their liberty.

speeches.speaker: Dw.
verse: Heaven bless the Knight
That thus relieves poor errant Gentlewomen.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I marry Ralph, this has some favour in't, I would see the proudest of them all offer to carry his Books after him. But George, I will not have him go away so soon, I shall be sick if he go away, that I shall; call Ralph again George, call Ralph again, I prethee sweetheart let him come fight before me, and let's ha some Drums, and Trumpets, and let him kill all that comes near him, and thou lov'st me George.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Peace a little bird, he shall kill them all, and they were twenty more on 'em then there are,

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Now fortune, if thou be'st not only ill,
Shew me thy better face, and bring about
Thy desperate wheel, that I may climb at length
And stand, this is our place of meeting,
If love have any constancy. Oh age!
Where only wealthy men are counted happy:
How shall I please thee? how deserve thy smiles?
When I am only rich in misery?
My fathers blessing, and this little coin
Is my inheritance, a strong revenue,
From earth thou art, and to earth I give thee,
There grow and multiply, whilst fresher air
Breeds me a fresher fortune: how, illusion!
What hath the Devil coyn'd himself before me?
