'Tis mettle good, it rings well, I am waking,
And taking too I hope, now Gods dear blessing
Upon his heart that left it here, 'tis mine,
These pearls, I take it, were not left for Swine.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I do not like that this unthrifty youth should embesil away the money, the poor Gentlewoman his mother will have a heavy heart for it, God knows.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: And reason good, sweet heart.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: But let him go, I'll tell Ralph a tale in's ear, shall fetch him again with a wanion, I warrant him, if he be above ground; and besides George, here be a number of sufficient Gentlemen can witness, and my self, and your self, and the Musicians, if we be call'd in question, but here comes Ralph, George, thou shalt hear him speak, as he were an Emperal.

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
verse: Comes not Sir Squire again?

speeches.speaker: Dwarf.
verse: Right courteous Knight,
Your Squire doth come, and with him comes the Lady.
For and the Squire of Damsels as I take it.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: Madam, if any service or devoir
Of a poor errant Knight may right your wrongs,
Command it, I am prest to give you succor,
For to that holy end I bear my Armour.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Mer.
verse: Alas, Sir, I am a poor Gentlewoman, and I
have lost my money in this Forrest.
Desart, you would say, Lady, and not lost
Whilst I have Sword and Launce, dry up your tears
Which ill befits the beauty of that face:
And tell the story, if I may request it,
Of your disastrous fortune.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Mer.
prose: Out alas, I left a thousand pound a thousand pound, e'n all the money I had laid up for this youth, upon the sight of your Mastership, you lookt so grim, and as I may say it, saving your presence, more like a Giant than a mortal man.

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
verse: I am as you are, Lady, so are they
All mortal, but why weeps this gentle Squire?

speeches.speaker: Mist. Mer.
prose: Has he not cause to weep do you think, when he has lost his inheritance?

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
verse: Young hope of valour, weep not, I am here
That will confound thy foe, and pay it dear
Upon his coward head, that dare denie,
Distressed Squires, and Ladies equity.
I have but one horse, on which shall ride
This Lady fair behind me, and before
This courteous Squire, fortune will give us more
Upon our next adventure; fairly speed
Beside us Squire aed Dwarfe to do us need.

speeches.speaker: Cit,
prose: Did not I tell you Nell what your man would do? by the faith of my body wench, for clean action and good delivery, they may all cast their caps at him.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: And so they may i'faith, for I dare speak it boldly, the twelve Companies of London cannot match him, timber for timber: well George, and he be not inveigled by some of these paltery Players, I ha much marvel: but George we ha done our parts, if the Boy have any grace to be thankful.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Yes, I warrant you duckling.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: Good Mistriss Luce, how ever I in fault am,
For your lame horse; you're welcome unto Waltham.
But which way now to go, or what to say
I know not truly till it be broad day.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: O fear not master Humphrey, I am guide
For this place good enough.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: Then up and ride,
Or if it please you, walk for your repose,
Or sit, or if you will, go pluck a Rose:
Either of which shall be indifferent,
To your good friend and Humphrey, whose consent
Is so intangled ever to your will,
As the poor harmless horse is to the ill.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: Faith and you say the word, we'll e'n sit down,
And take a nap.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: 'Tis better in the Town,
Where we may nap together: for believe me,
To sleep without a snatch would mickle grieve me.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: You're merry master Humphrey.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: So I am,
And have been every merry from my Dam.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: Your Nurse had the less labour.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: Faith it may be,
Unless it were by chance I did beray me.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Luce, dear friend Luce,

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: Here Jasper.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: You are mine.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: If it be so, my friend, you use me fine:
What do you think I am?

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: An arrant Noddy.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: A word of obloquie: now by gods body,
i'll tell thy Master, for I know thee well.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Nay, and you be so forward for to tell,
Take that, and that, and tell him, Sir, I gave it:
And say I paid you well.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: O Sir I have it,
And do confess the payment, pray be quiet.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Go, get you to your night-cap and the diet,
To cure your beaten bones.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: Alas, poor Humphrey,
Get thee some wholsome broth with Sage and Cumfrie:
A little oil of Roses and a Feather
To noint thy back withal.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: When I came hither,
Would I had gone to Paris with John Dorry.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: Farewel my pretty Nump, I am very sorry
I cannot bear thee company.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: Farewel,
The Devils Dam was ne'r so bang'd in Hell.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: This young Jasper will prove me another Things, a my conscience and he may be suffered; George, dost not see George how a swaggers, and flies at the very heads a fokes as he were a Dragon; well if I do not do his lesson for wronging the poor Gentleman, I am no true Woman, his friends that brought him up might have been better occupied, I wis, then have taught him these fegaries: he's e'n in the high-way to the Gallows, God bless him.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: You're too bitter, Connie, the young man may do well enough for all this.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Come hither master Humphrey, has he hurt you? now beshrew his fingers for't, here Sweet-heart, here's some Green Ginger for thee, now beshrew my heart, but a has Pepper-nel in's head, as big as a Pullets egg: alas, sweet Lamb, how thy Temples beat; take the peace on him sweet heart, take the peace on him.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: No, no, you talk like a foolish woman, I'll ha Ralph fight with him, and swinge him up well-favour'dly: sirrah boy come hither, let Ralph come in and fight with Jasper,

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I and beat him well,, he's an unhappy boy.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Sir, you must pardon us, the plot of our Play lies contrary, and 'twill hazard the spoiling of our Play.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Plot me no plots, I'll ha Ralph come out, I'll make your house too hot for you else.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Why Sir, he shall, but if any thing fall out of order, the Gentlemen must pardon us.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Go your ways good-man boy, I'll hold him a penny he shall have his belly full of fighting now, ho here comes Ralph, no more.

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
verse: What Knight is that, Squire, ask him if he keep
The passage bound by love of Lady fair,
Or else but prickant.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: Sir, I am no Knight,
But a poor Gentleman, that this same night,
Had stoln from me on yonder Green,
My lovely Wife, and suffered to be seen
Yet extant on my shoulderr such a greeting,
That whilst I live, I shall think of that meeting.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: I Ralph, he beat him unmercifully, Ralph, and thou spar'st him Ralph, I would thou wert hang'd,

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: No more, wife, no more.

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
verse: Where is the Caitiff wretch hath done this deed,
Lady, your pardon, that I may proceed
Upon the quest of this injurious Knight.
And thou fair Squire repute me not the worse,
In leaving the great venture of the purse,
And the rich Casket till some better leisure.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: Here comes the Broker hath purloin'd my treasure.

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
verse: Go, Squire, and tell him I am here,
And Errant Knight at Arms, to crave delivery
Of that fair Lady to her own Knights arms.
If he deny, bid him take choice of ground,
And so defie him.

speeches.speaker: Squire.
verse: From the Knight that bears
The Golden Pestle; I defie thee Knight.
Unless thou make fair restitution
Of that bright Lady.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Tell the Knight that sent thee
He is an ass, and I will keep the wench,
And knock his Head-piece.

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
verse: Thou art but dead,
If thou recall not thy uncourteous terms:

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: Break's pate Ralph, break's pate Ralph, soundly.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Come Knight, I am ready for you, now your Pestle.
Shall try what temper, Sir, your Mortar's of:
With that he stood upright in his stirrops,
And gave the Knight of the Calve-skin such a knock,
That he forsook his horse, and down he fell,
And then he leaped upon him, and plucking off his Helmet.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: Nay, and my noble Knight be down so soon,
Though I can scarcely go, I needs must run-

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Run Ralph, run Ralph, run for thy life boy, Jasper comes, Jasper comes.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
prose: Come Luce, we must have other Arms for you, Humphrey and Golden Pestle both adieu.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Sure the Devil, God bless us, is in this Springald, why George, didst ever see such a fire-drake, I am afraid my boy's miscarried; if he be, though he were Master Merry-thoughts Son a thousand times, if there be any Law in England, I'll make some of them smart for't.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: No, no, I have found out the matter sweet-heart, Jasper is enchanted as sure as we are here, he is enchanted, he could no more have stood in Ralph's hands, than I can stand in my Lord Mayor's: I'll have a Ring to discover all enchantments, and Ralph shall beat him yet: be no more vext, for it shall be so.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Oh Husband, here's Ralph again, stay Ralph, let me speak with thee, how dost thou Ralph? art thou not shrewdly hurt? the foul great Lungies laid unmercifully on thee, there's some Sugar-candy for thee, proceed, thou shalt have another bout with him.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: If Ralph had him at the Fencing-School, if he did not make a puppy of him, and drive him up and down the School, he should ne'r come in my shop more.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Mer.
prose: Truly master Knight of the Burning Pestle, I am weary.

speeches.speaker: Mich.
prose: Indeed-law Mother, and I am very hungry.

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
verse: Take comfort gentle Dame, and your fair Squire.
For in this Desart there must needs be plac'd
Many strong Castles, held by courteous Knights,
And till I bring you safe to one of those
I swear by this my Order ne'r to leave you.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Well said Ralph, George, Ralph was ever comfortable, was he not?

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Yes Duck.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I shall ne'r forget him: when we had lost our child, you know it was straid almost alone, to Puddle-wharfe, and the Cryers were abroad for it, and there it had drown'd it self but for a Sculler, Ralph was the most comfortablest to me: peace Mistriss, saies he, let it go, I'll get you another as good, did he not George? did he not say so?

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Yes indeed did he Mouse.

speeches.speaker: Dwarfe.
prose: I would we had a mess of Pottage, and a pot of Drink, Squire, and were going to bed.

speeches.speaker: Squire.
prose: Why we are at Waltham Towns end, and that's the Bell Inne.

speeches.speaker: Dwarfe.
verse: Take courage valiant Knight, Damsel, and Squire,
I have discovered, not a stones cast off,
An antient Castle held by the old Knight
Of the most holy Order of the Bell,
Who gives to all Knights Errant entertain:
There plenty is of food, and all prepar'd,
By the white hands of his own Lady dear.
He hath three Squires that welcome all his Guests:
The first, High Chamberlain, who will see
Our beds prepar'd, and bring us snowy sheets,
Where never footman stretch'd his butter'd Hams.
The second height Tapstro, who will see
Our pots full filled, and no froth therein;
The third, a gentle Squire Ostlero height,
Who will our Palfries slick with wisps of straw,
And in the Maunger put them Oats enough,
And never grease their teeth with Candle-snuffe.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: That same Dwarfe's a pretty boy, but the Squire's a grout-nold.

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
prose: Knock at the Gates my Squire, with stately Lance.

speeches.speaker: Tap.
prose: Who's there, you're welcome Gentlemen, will you see a room?

speeches.speaker: Dwarfe.
prose: Right courteous and valiant Knight of the Burning Pestle, This is the Squire Tapstro.

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
verse: Fair Squire Tapstro, I a wandring Knight,
Height of the Burning Pestle in the quest
Of this fair Ladies Casket, and wrought purse,
Losing my self in this vast wilderness,
And to this Castle well by fortune brought,
Where hearing of the goodly entertain
Your Knight of holy Order of the Bell,
Gives to all Damsels, and all Errant Knights,
I thought to knock, and now am bold to enter.

speeches.speaker: Tapst.
prose: An't please you see a chamber, you are very welcome.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: George, I would have something done, and I cannot tell what it is.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: What is it Nell?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Why George, shall Ralph beat no body again? prethee sweet-heart let him.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: So he shall Nell, and if I joyn with him, we'll knock them all.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: O George, here's master Humphrey again now, that lost Mistriss Luce, and Mistriss Luce's Father, master Humphrey will do some bodies arrant I warrant him.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: Father, it's true in arms I ne'r shall clasp her,
For she is stoln away by your man Jasper.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: I thought he would tell him.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Unhappy that I am to lose my child:
Now I begin to think on Jasper's words,
Who oft hath urg'd to me thy foolishness,
Why didst thou let her go, thou lov'st her not,
That wouldst bring home thy life, and not bring her.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: Father forgive me, I shall tell you true,
Look on my shoulders they are black and blue,
Whilst too and fro fair Luce and I were winding,
He came and basted me with a hedge binding.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Get men and horses straight, we will be there
Within this hour; you know the place again?

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: I know the place where he my loins did swaddle,
I'll get six horses, and to each a saddle.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Mean time I'll go talk with Jaspers Father.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: George, What wilt thou lay with me now, that Master Humphrey has not Mistriss Luce yet, speak George what wilt thou lay with me?

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: No Nell, I warrant thee, Jasper is at Puckeridge with her by this.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Nay George, you must consider Mistriss Lucies feet are tender, and besides, 'tis dark, and I promise you truly, I do not see how he should get out of Waltham Forrest with her yet.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Nay Cunny, what wilt thou lay with me that Ralph has her not yet.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I will not lay against Ralph, Honny, because I have not spoken with him: but look George, peace, here comes the merry old Gentleman again.

speeches.speaker: Old Mer.
prose: When it was grown to dark midnight,
And all were fast asleep,
In came Margarets grimly Ghost,
And stood at William's feet.

I have money, and meat, and drink before hand, till to morrow at noon, why should I be sad? methinks I have halfe a dozen jovial spirits within me, I am three merry men, and three merry men: To what end should any man be sad in this world? give me a man that when he goes to hanging cries troul the black boul to me: and a Woman that will sing a catch in her Travel. I have seen a man come by my door, with a serious face, in a black cloak, without a Hatband, carrying his head as if he lookt for pins in the street. I have lookt out of my window halfe a year after, and have spied that mans head upon London Bridge: 'tis vile, never trust a Tailor that does not sing at his work, his mind is of nothing but filching.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Mark this George, 'tis worth noting: Godfrey my Tailor, you know never sings, and he had fourteen yards to make this Gown; and I'll be sworn, Mistriss Penistone the Drapers Wife had one made with twelve.

speeches.speaker: Old Mer.
verse: 'Tis mirth that fills the veins with blood,
More than Wine, or Sleep, or Food,
Let each man keep his heart at ease
No man dies of that disease,
He that would his body keep
From diseases, must not weep,
But whoever laughs and sings,
Never his body brings
Into Feavers, Gouts, or Rhumes,
Or lingringly his Lungs consumes:
Or meets with aches in the bone,
Or Catarrhs, or griping Stone:
But contented lives for aye,
The more he laughs, the more he may.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Look George, how sayst thou by this George? is't not a fine old man? Now Gods blessing a thy sweet lips. When wilt thou be so merry George? Faith thou art the frowningst little thing, when thou art angry, in a Countrey.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Peace Conny, Thou shalt see him took down too I warrant thee: here's Luce's Father come now.

speeches.speaker: Old Mer.
prose: As you came from Walsingam, from the Holy Land, there met you not with my true love by the way as you came.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Oh Master Merry-thought! my Daughters gone,
This mirth becomes you not, my Daughter's gone.

speeches.speaker: Old Mer.
verse: Why an if she be, what care I?
Or let her come, or go, or tarry.

speeches.speaker: Merch.
verse: Mock not my misery, it is your Son,
Whom I have made my own, when all forsook him,
Has stoln my only joy, my child away.

speeches.speaker: Old Mer.
verse: He set her on a milk white Steed, and himself upon a gray,
He never turn'd his face again, but he bore her quite away.

speeches.speaker: Merch.
verse: Unworthy of the kindness I have shewn
To thee, and thine: too late, I well perceive
Thou art consenting to my Daughters loss.

speeches.speaker: Old Mer.
prose: Your Daughter, what a-stirs here wi' y'r daughter? Let her go, think no more on her, but sing loud. If both my sons were on the gallows, I would sing down, down, down: they fall down, and arise they never shall.

speeches.speaker: Merch.
verse: Oh might I behold her once again.
And she once more embrace her aged sire.

speeches.speaker: Old Mer.
verse: She cares not for her Daddy, nor she cares not for her Mammy.
For she is, she is, she is my Lord of Low-gaves Lassie.
prose: Fie, how scurvily this goes: and she once more embrace her aged sire? you'll make a dog on her, will ye; she cares much for her aged sire, warrant you.

speeches.speaker: Merch.
verse: For this thy scorn I will pursue
That son of thine to death.

speeches.speaker: Old Mer.
verse: Do, and when you ha kill'd him,
Give him flowers i'now Palmer, give him flowers i'now,
Give him red and white, and blue, green, and yellow.

speeches.speaker: Merch.
verse: I'll fetch my Daughter.

speeches.speaker: Old Mer.
prose: I'll hear no more o' your Daughter, it spoils my mirth.

speeches.speaker: Merch.
verse: I say I'll fetch my Daughter.

speeches.speaker: Old Mer.
verse: Was never man for Ladies sake, down, down,
Tormented as I Sir Guy? de derry down,
For Lucies sake, that Lady bright, down, down,
As over men beheld with eye? de derry down.

speeches.speaker: Merch.
verse: I'll be reveng'd by heaven.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: How dost thou like this George?

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Why this is well Cunnie: but if Ralph were hot once: thou shouldst see more.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: The Fidlers go again Husband.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: I Nell, but this is scurvy Musick: I gave the whoreson gallows money, and I think he has not got me the Waits of Southwark, if I hear him not anan, I'll twinge him by the ears.
Your Musicians play Baloo.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: No good George, let's ha Lachrymae.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Why this is it Cunny.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: It's all the better George: now sweet Lamb, what story is that painted upon the cloth? the confutation of Saint Paul?

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: No Lamb, that's Ralph and Lucrece.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Ralph and Lucrece? which Ralph? our Ralph?

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: No Mouse, that was a Tartarian.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: A Tartarian? well, I wo'd the Fidlers had done, that we might see our Ralph again.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Come my dear, though we have lost our way,
We have not lost our selves: are you not weary
With this nights wandring, broken from your rest?
And frighted with the terror that attends
The darkness of this wild unpeopled place?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: No my best friend, I cannot either fear,
Or entertain a weary thought, whilst you
(The end of all my full desires) stand by me:
Let them that lose their hopes, and live to languish
Amongst the number of forsaken Lovers,
Tell the long weary steps, and number time,
Start at a shadow, and shrink up their bloud,
Whilst I (possest with all content and quiet)
Thus take my pretty love, and thus embrace him.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: You have caught me Luce, so fast, that whilst I live
I shall become your faithful prisoner:
And wear these chains for ever. Come, sit down,
And rest your body, too too delicate
For these disturbances; so, will you sleep?
Come, do not be more able than you are,
I know you are not skilful in these Watches,
For Women are no soldiers; be not nice,
But take it, sleep I say.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: I cannot sleep.
Indeed I cannot friend.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Why then we'll sing,
And try how that will work upon our sences.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: I'll sing, or say, or any thing but sleep.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Come little Mermaid, rob me of my heart
With that inchanting voice.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: You mock me Jasper

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Tell me (dearest) what is Love?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: 'Tis a lightning from above,
'Tis an Arrow, 'tis a Fire,
'Tis a Boy they call desire.
'Tis a smile
Doth beguile

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: The poor hearts of men that prove,
Tell me more, are Women true?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: Some Love change, and so do you.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Are they fair, and never kind?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: Yes, when men turn with the wind.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Are they froward?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: Ever toward
Those that love, to love anew.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Dissemble it no more, I see the God
Of heavy sleep, lay on his heavy Mace,
Upon your eye-lids.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: I am very heavy.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Sleep, sleep, and quiet rest crown thy sweet thoughts:
Keep from her fair blood distempers, startings,
Horrors and fearful shapes: let all her dreams
Be joys, and chaste delights, embraces, wishes,
And such new pleasures as the ravish'd soul
Gives to the sences. So my charms have took.
Keep her you powers divine, whilst I contemplate
Upon the wealth and beauty of her mind.
She is only fair, and constant: only kind,
And only to thee Jasper. Oh my joyes!
Whither will you transport me? let not fulness
Of my poor buried hopes come up together,
And over-charge my spirits; I am weak,
Some say (how ever ill) the Sea and Women
Are govern'd by the Moon, both ebb and flow,
Both full of changes: yet to them that know,
And truly judge, these but opinions are,
And heresies to bring on pleasing War
Between our tempers, that without these were
Both void of after-love, and present fear.
Which are the best of Cupid. O thou child!
Bred from despair, I dare not entertain thee,
Having a love without the faults of Women,
And greater in her perfect goods th^n men:
Which to make good, and please my self the stronger,
Though certainly I am certain of her love,
I'll try her, that the world and memory
May sing to after-times her constancy.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: Luce awake. Luce why do you fright me friend,
With those distempered looks? what makes your sword
Drawn in your hand? who hath offended you?
I prethee Jasper sleep, thou art wild with watching,

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Come make your way to Heaven, and bid the world
(With all the villanies that stick upon it)
Farewell; you're for another life.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: Oh Jasper.
How have my tender years committed evil,
(Especially against the man I love)
Thus to be cropt untimely?

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Foolish girl,
Canst thou imagine I could love his daughter
That flung me from my fortune into nothing?
Discharged me his service, shut the doors
Upon my poverty, and scorn'd my prayers,
Sending me, like a boat without a malt,
To sink or swim? Come, by this hand you dye,
I must have life and blood to satisfie
Your fathers wrongs.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Away George, away, raise the Watch at Ludgate, and bring a Mitrimus from the Justice for this desperate Villain. Now I charge you Gentlemen, see the Kings peace kept. O my heart what a varlet's this, to offer Man-slaughter upon the harmless Gentlewoman?

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: I warrant thee (sweet heart) we'll have him hampered.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: Oh Jasper! be not cruel,
If thou wilt kill me, smile, and do it quickly.
And let not many deaths appear before me.
I am a woman made of fear and love
A weak, weak woman, kill not with thy eyes,
They shoot me through and through. Strike I am ready.
And dying still I love thee.

speeches.speaker: Merch.
verse: Where abouts?

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: No more of this, now to my self again.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: There, there he stands with Sword like martial Knight.
Drawn in his hand, therefore beware the fight
You that are wise: for were I good Sir Bevis,
I would not stay his coming, by your leaves.

speeches.speaker: Merc.
verse: Sirrah, restore my daughter.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Sirrah, no.

speeches.speaker: Merch.
verse: Upon him then.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: So, down with him, down with him, down with him: cut him i'the leg boyes, cut him i'th'leg.

speeches.speaker: Merc.
prose: Come your ways Minion, I'll provide a Cage for you, you're grown so tame. Horse her away.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: Truly I'm glad your forces have the day.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: They are gone, and I am hurt, my Love is lost,
Never to get again. Oh me unhappy!
Bleed, bleed, and dye, I cannot: Oh my folly!
Thou hast betray'd me, Hope where art thou sled?
Tell me if thou be'st any where remaining.
Shall I but see my love again? Oh no!
She will not dain to look upon her Butcher,
Nor is fit she should; yet I must venter.
Oh chance, or fortune, or what ere thou art
That men adore for powerful, hear my cry,
And let me loving live; or loosing dye.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: Is a gone George?

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: I conny.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Marry and let him go (sweet heart) by the faith a my body a has put me into such a fright, that I tremble (as they say) as 'twere an Aspine leaf: look a my little finger George, how it shakes: now in truth every member of my body is the worse for't.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Come, hug in mine arms sweet Mouse, he shall not fright thee any more: alass mine own dear heart how it quirers.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: O Rafe, how dost thou Rafe? how hast thou slept to night? has the Knight us'd thee well?

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: Peace Nell, let Rafe alone.

speeches.speaker: Tapst.
verse: Master, the reckoning is not paid.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: Right courteous Knight, who for the orders sake
Which thou hast tane, hang'st out the holy Bell,
As I this flaming Pestle bear about,
We render thanks to your puissant self,
Your beauteous Lady, and your gentle Squires,
For thus refreshing of our wearied limbs,
Stifned with hard atchievements in wild Desart.

speeches.speaker: Tapst.
verse: Sir, there is twelve shillings to pay.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: Thou merry Squire Tapstero, thanks to thee,
For comforting our souls with double Jug,
And if adventurous Fortune prick thee forth,
Thou jovial Squire, to follow seats of Arms,
Take heed thou tender every Ladies cause,
Every true Knight, and every Damsel fair
But spill the blood of treacherous Sarazens,
And false inchanters, that with Magick spels,
Have done to death full many a noble Knight.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Thou valiant Knight of the burning Pestle, give ear to me, there is twelve shillings to pay, and as I am a true Knight, I will not bate a penny.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: George, I prethee tell me, must Rafe pay twelve shillings now?

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: No, Nel, no, nothing but the old Knight is merry with Rafe.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: O is't nothing else? Rafe will be as merry as he.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: Sir Knight, this mirth of yours becomes you well,
But to requite this liberal courtesie,
If any of your Squires will follow Arms,
He shall receive from my Heroick hand
A Knighthood, by the virtue of this Pestle.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Fair Knight, I thank you for your noble offer,
Therefore gentle Knight,
Twelve shillings you must pay, or I must cap you.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Look George, did not I tell thee as much, the Knight of the Bell is in earnest, Rafe shall not be beholding to him, give him his money George, and let him go snick up.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Cap Rafe? no, hold your hand sir Knight of the Bell, there's your Money, have you any thing to say to Rafe now? cap Rafe?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I would you should know it, Rafe has friends that will not suffer him to be capt for ten times so much, and ten times to the end of that, now take thy course Rafe.

speeches.speaker: M. mer.
prose: Come Michael, thou and I will go home to thy father, he hath enough left to keep us a day or two, and we'll set fellows abroad to cry our Purse and Casket: Shall we Michael?

speeches.speaker: Mich.
prose: I, I pray mother, in truth my feot are full of chilblains with travelling.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Faith and those chilblaines are a foul trouble, Mistris Merry-thought when your youth comes home, let him rub all the soles of his feet, and his heels, and his ankles, with a Mouseskin; or if none of your can catch a Mouse, when he goes to bed, let him rowl his feet in the warm embers, and I warrant you he shall be well, and you may make him put his fingers between his toes, and smell to them, it's very soveraign for his head, if he be cos^ive.

speeches.speaker: Mist. mer.
prose: Master Knight of the burning Pestle, my son Michael, and I bid you farewell, I thank your Worship hartily for your kindness.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: Fare-well fair Lady, and your tender Squire.
If pricking through these Desarts, I do hear
Of any traiterous Knight who through his guile,
Hath light upon your Casket and your Purse,
I will despoil him of them and restore them.

speeches.speaker: Mist. mer.
verse: I thank your Worship.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: Dwarf bear my shield, Squire elevate my lance,
And now farewell you Knight of holy Bell,

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: I, I Rafe, all is paid.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: But yet before I go, speak worthy Knight,
If oft you do of sad adventures know,
Where errant Knights may through his prowess win
Eternal fame, and free some gentle souls,
From endless bounds of steel and lingring pain.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Sirrah go to Nick the Barber, and bid him prepare himself, as I told you before quickly.

speeches.speaker: Tap.
verse: I am gone Sir.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Sir Knight, this wilderness affordeth none
But the great venture, where full many a Knight
Hath tried his prowess, and come off with shame,
And where I would not have you loose your life,
Against no man, but furious fiend of Hell.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: Speak on Sir Knight, tell what he is, and where:
For here I vow upon my blazing badge,
Never to blaze a day in quietness;
But bread and water will I only eat,
And the green herb and rock shall be my couch
Till I have queld that man, or beast, or fiend,
That works such damage to all Errant Knights.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Not far from hence, near a craggy cliff
At the North end of this distressed Town,
There doth stand a lowly house
Ruggedly builded, and in it a Cave
In which an ugly Giant now doth won,
Ycleped Barbaroso: in his hand
He shakes a naked Lance of purest steel,
With sleeves turn'd up, and him before he wears,
A motly garment to preserve his clothes
From blood of those Knights which he massacres,
And Ladies Gentle: without his door doth hang
A copper bason, on a prickant Spear;
At which, no sooner gentle Knights can knock,
But the shrill sound, fierce Barbaroso hears,
And rushing forth, brings in the Errant Knight,
And sets him down in an inchanted chair:
Then with an Engine, which he hath prepar'd
With forty teeth, he claws his courtly crown,
Next makes him wink, and underneath his chin,
He plants a brazen piece of mighty board,
And knocks his bullets round about his cheeks,
Whilst with his fingers, and an instrument
With which he snaps his hair off, he doth fill
The wretches ears with a most hideous noyse.
Thus every Knight Adventurer he doth trim,
And now no creature dares encounter him.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: In Gods name, I will fight with him, kind sir,
Go but before me to this dismal Cave
Where this huge Giant Barbaroso dwells,
And by that virtue that brave Rosicleere,
That damn'd brood of ugly Giants slew,
And Palmerin Frannarco overthrew:
I doubt not but to curb this Traytor foul,
And to the Devil send his guilty Soul.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Brave sprighted Knight, thus far I will perform
This your request, I'll bring you within sight
Of this most loathsome place, inhabited
By a more lothsome man: but dare not stay,
For his main force swoops all he sees away.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: Saint George set on before, march Squire and Page.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: George, dost think Rafe will confound the Giant?

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: I hold my cap to a farthing he does: why Nell, I saw him wrestle with the great Dutchman, and hurle him.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Faith and that Dutchman was a goodly man, if all things were answerable to his bigness: and yet they say there was a Scottishman higher than he, and that they two and a Knight met, and saw one another for nothing: but of all the sights that ever were in London, since I was married, methinks the little child that was so fair grown about the members, was the prettiest, that and the Hermaphrodite.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Nay, by your leave Nil, Ninivie was better.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Ninivie, O that was the story of Jone and the wall, was it not George?

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Yes lamb.

speeches.speaker: Wife
prose: Look George, here comes Mistris Merry-thoughauh ain, and I would have Rafe come and fight with the Gyant, I tell you true I long to see't.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Good Mistriss Merri-thought be aone, I pray you for my sake, I pray you forbear a little, you shall have audience presently, I have a little business.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Mistris Merri-thought,, if it please you to refrain your passion a little, till Rafe have dispatcht the Giant out of the way, we shall think our selves much bound to thank you: I thank you good Mistris Merri-thought.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Boy, come hither, send away Rafe and this whoreson Giant quickly.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: In good faith sir we cannot, you'l utterly spoil our Play, and make it to be hist, and it cost money, you will not suffer us to go on with our plots, I pray Gentlemen rule him.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Let him come now and dispatch this, and I'll trouble you no more.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Will you give me your hand of that?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Give him thy hand George, do, and I'll kiss him, I warrant thee the youth means plainly.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: I'll send him to you presently.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I thank you little youth, feth the child hath a sweet breath George, but I think it be troubled with the Worms, Carduus Benedictus and Mares milk were the only thing in the world for't. O Rafe's here George; God send thee good luck Rafe.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Puissant Knight yonder his Mansion is,
Lo, where the Spear and Copper Bason are,
Behold the string on which hangs many a tooth,
Drawn from the gentle jaw of wandring Knights,
I dare not stay to sound, he will appear.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: O faint not heart, Susan my Lady dear:
The Coblers Maid in Milkstreet, for whose sake,
I take these Arms, O let the thought of thee,
Carry thy Knight through all adventurous deeds,
And in the honor of thy beauteous self,
May I destroy this monster Barbaroso,
Knock Squire upon the Bason till it break
With the shrill strokes, or till the Giant spake.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: O George, the Giant, the Giant, now Rafe for thy life.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: What fond unknowing wight is this, that dares,
So rudely knock at Barbarossa's Cell,
Where no man comes, but leaves his fleece behind?

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: I, traiterous Caitiffe, who am sent by fate
To punish all the sad enormities
Thou hast committed against Ladies gentle,
And Errant Knights, Traytor to God and men:
Prepare thy self, this is the dismal hour
Appointed for thee to give strict account
Of all thy beastly treacherous villanies.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Fool-hardy Knight, full soon thou shalt aby
This fond reproach, thy body will I bang,
And loe upon that string thy teeth shall hang:
Prepare thy self, for dead soon shalt thou be.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: Saint George for me

speeches.speaker: Barba.
verse: Gargantua for me.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: To him Rafe, to him, hold up the Giant, set out thy leg before Rafe.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Falsifie a blow Rafe, falsifie a blow, the Giant lies open on the left side.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Bear't off, bear't off still; there boy, O Rafe's almost down, Rafe's almost down.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: Susan inspire me, now have up again.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Up, up, up, up, up, so Rafe, down with him, down with him Rafe.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: Fetch him over the hip boy.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: There boy, kill, kill, kill, kill, kill, Rafe.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: No Rafe, get all out of him first.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: Presumptuous man, see to what desperate end
Thy treachery hath brought thee, the just Gods,
Who never prosper those that do despise them,
For all the villanies which thou hast done
To Knights and Ladies, now have paid thee home,
By my stiff arm, a Knight adventurous.
But say, vile wretch, before I send thy soul
To sad Avernus, whither it must go,
What captives holdst thou in thy sable cave?

speeches.speaker: Barba.
verse: Go in and free them all, thou hast the day.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: Go Squire and Dwarf, search in this dreadful cave,
And free the wretched prisoners from their bonds.

speeches.speaker: Barb.
verse: I crave for mercy as thou art a Knight,
And scornst to spill the blood of those that beg.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: Thou shewest no mercy, nor shalt thou have any,
Prepare thy self, for thou shalt surely dye.

speeches.speaker: Squire.
verse: Behold brave Knight here is one prisoner,
Whom this wild man hath used as you see.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: This is the wise word I hear the Squire speak.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: Speak what thou art, and how thou hast been us'd,
That I may give him condign punishment

speeches.speaker: 1. Kni.
verse: I am a Knight that took my journey post
Northward from London, and in courteous wise,
This Gyant train'd me to his den,
Under pretence of killing of the itch,
And all my body with a powder strew'd,
That smarts and stings, and cut away my beard,
And my curl'd locks wherein were Ribands ty'de,
And with a water washt my tender eyes,
Whilst up and down about me still he skipt,
Whose virtue is, that till my eyes be wip't
With a dry cloth, for this my soul disgrace,
I shall not dare to look a dog i'th'face.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: Alass poor Knight, relieve him Rafe, relieve poor Knights whilst you live.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: My trusty Squire convey him to the Town,
Where he may find relief, adieu fair Knight.

speeches.speaker: Dwar.
verse: Puissant Knight of the burning Pestle height,
See here another wretch, whom this soul beast
Hath scorcht and scor'd in this inhumane wise.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: Speak me thy name, and eke thy place of birth,
And what hath been thy usage in this Cave.

speeches.speaker: 2. Knight.
verse: I am a Knight, Sir Pock-hole is my name,
And by my birth I am a Londoner,
Free by my Copy, but my Ancestors
Were Frenchmen all, and riding hard this way.
Upon a trotting horse my bones did ake,
And I faint Knight to ease my weary limbes,
Light at this Cave, when straight this furious fiend,
With sharpest instrument of purest steel,
Did cut the gristle of my Nose away,
And in the place this velvet plaster stands,
Relieve me gentle Knight out of his hands.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Good Rafe relieve Sir Pockhole, and send him away, for in truth his breath stinks.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: Convey him straight after the other Knight:
Sir Pockhole fare you well.

speeches.speaker: 3. Knight.
verse: Kind Sir goodnight

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: Deliver us.

speeches.speaker: Woman.
verse: Deliver us.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Harke George, what a woful cry there is, I think some woman lyes in there.

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: Deliver us

speeches.speaker: Woman.
verse: Deliver us.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: What gastly noise is this? speak Barbaroso
Or by this blazing steel thy head goes off.

speeches.speaker: Barb.
verse: Prisoners of mine, whom I in diet keep,
Send lower down into the Cave,
And in a Tub that's heated smoaking hot,
There may they find them and deliver them.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: Run Squire and Dwarf, deliver them with speed.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: But will not Rafe kill this Giant, surely I am afraid if he let him go he will do as much hurt, as ever he did.

speeches.speaker: Citizen.
verse: Not so Mouse neither, if he could convert him.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I George, if he could convert him; but a Gyant is not so soon converted as one of us ordinary people. There's a pretty tale of a Witch, that had the Divels mark about lier, God bless us, that had a Gyant to her son, that was call'd Lob-lie-by-the-fire, didst never hear it George.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: Peace Nell, here comes the prisoners.

speeches.speaker: Dwar.
verse: Here be these pined wretches, manfull Knight,
That for this six weeks have not seen a wight.

speeches.speaker: Raph.
verse: Deliver what you are, and how you came
To this sad Cave, and what your usage was?

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: I am an errant Knight that followed Arms,
With spear and shield, and in my tnder years
I strucken was with Cupids fiery shaft,
And fell in love with this my Lady dear,
And stole her from her friends in Turne-ball street,
And bore her up and down from Town to Town,
Where we did eat and drink and Musick here;
Till at the length at this unhappy Town
We did arrive, and coming to this Cave,
This beast us caught, and put us in a Tub,
Where we this two months sweat, and should have done.
Another Month if you had not relieved us.

speeches.speaker: Wom.
verse: This bread and water hath our dyet been,
Together with a rib cut from a neck
Of burned Mutton, hard hath been our fare,
Release us from this ugly Gyants snare.

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: This hath been half the food we have receiv'd,
But only twice a day for novelty,
He gave a spoonful of his hearty broth
To each of us, through this same tender quill.

speeches.speaker: Raph.
verse: From this infernall Monster you shall go,
That useth Knights and gentle Ladies so.
Convey them hence.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: Cunny, I can tell thee the Gentleman like Rafe.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I George, I see it well enough. Gentlemen I thank you all heartily for gracing my man Ralph, and I promise you, you shall see him oftner.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Mercy great Knight, I do recant my ill,
And henceforth never gentle blood will spill.

speeches.speaker: Raph.
verse: I give thee mercy, but yet thou shalt swear
Upon my burning Pestle to perform
Thy promise utter'd.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I swear and kiss.

speeches.speaker: Raph.
verse: Depart then and amend.
Come Squire and Dwarf, the Sun grows towards his set,
And we have many more adventures yet.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Now Raph is in this humor, I know he would ha beaten all the boys in the house, if they had been set on him.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I George, but it is well as it is: I warrant you the gentlemen do consider what it is to overthrow a Gyant: but look George, here comes Mistriss Merri-thought, and her son Michael, now you are welcome Mistriss Merri-thought, now Raph has done you may go on.

speeches.speaker: Mist. mer·
verse: Micke My Boy?

speeches.speaker: Mich.
verse: I forsooth Mother.

speeches.speaker: Mist. mer.
prose:
Be merry Micke, we are at home now: where I warrant you, you shall find the house flung out of the
windows: Hark: hey dogs, hey, this is the old world y'faith with my Husband: I'll get in among them, I'll play them such lesson, that they shall have little list to come scraping hither again. Why Master Merry-thought, Husband, Charles Merry-thought.

speeches.speaker: Old Mer. within.
verse: One, two, three, and four,
We shall be merry within this hour.
prose: If you will sing, and dance, and laugh, and hollow, and laugh again: and then cry there boys there: why then,

speeches.speaker: Mist. Mer.
prose: Why Charles do you not know your own natural wife? I say open the door, and turn me out those mangy companions; 'tis more than time that they were fellow like with you: you are a Gentleman Charles, and an old man, and father of two children; and I my self, (though I say it) by my mothers side, Niece to a Worshipful Gentleman, and a Conductor, he has been three times in his Majesties service at Chester, and is now the fourth time, God bless him, and his charge upon his journey.

speeches.speaker: Old Mer.
verse: Go from my window, love go:
Go from my window my dear,
The wind and the rain will drive you back again,
You cannot be lodged here.
Hey-ho, my heart is heavy.
prose: Hark you Mistriss Merri-thought, you that walk upon Adventures, and forsake your Husband, because he sings with never a penny in his purse; what shall I think my self the worse? Faith no, I'll be merry.
You come not here, here's none but Lads of mettle, lives of a hundred years, and upwards, care never drunk their bloods, nor want made them warble.

speeches.speaker: Mist. Mer.
prose: Why M. Merrithought, what am I that you should laugh me to scorn thus abruptly? am I not your fellow-feeler, (as we may say) in all our miseries? your comforter in health and sickness? have I not brought you Children? are they not like you Charles? look upon thine own Image, hard-hearted man; and yet for all this—

speeches.speaker: Old Mer. within.
prose: Begon, begon my juggy, my puggy, begon my love my dear.
The weather is warm, 'twill do thee no harm, thou canst not be lodged here.
Be merry boys, some light musick, and more wine.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: He's not in earnest, I hope George, is he?

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: What if he be, sweet heart?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Marry if he be George, I'll make bold to tell him he's an ingrant old man, to use his bed-fellow so scurvily.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: What how does he use her Honey?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Marry come up sir sauce-box, I think you'll take his part, will you not? Lord how hot are you grown: you are a fine man an you had a fine Dog, it becomes you sweetly.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Nay, prethee Nell chide not: for as I am an honest man, and a true Christian Grocer, I do not like his doings.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I cry you mercy then George, you know we are all frail, and full of infirmities. Dee hear Master Merri-thought, may I crave a word with you?

speeches.speaker: Old Mer within.
verse: Strike up lively lads.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I had not thought in truth, Master Merri-thought, that a man of your age and discretion (as I may say) being a Gentleman, and therefore known by your gentle conditions, could have used so little respect to the weakness of his wife: for your wife is your own flesh, the staff of your age, your yoke-fellow, with whose help you draw through the myre of this transitory world: Nay, she's your own rib. And again—

speeches.speaker: Old Mer.
verse: I come not hither for thee to teach,
I have no pulpit for thee to preach,
I would thou hadst kist me under the breech,
As thou art a Lady gay.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: Marry with a vengeance,
prose: I am heartily sorry for the poor Gentlewoman: but if I
were thy wife, i'faith gray-beard, i'faith—

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: I prethee sweet Hony-suckle, be content.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Give me such words that am a Gentlewoman born, hang him hoary Rascal. Get me some drink George, I am almost molten with fretting: now beshrew his Knaves heart for it.

speeches.speaker: Old mer.
prose: Play me a light Lavalto: come, be frollick, fill the good fellows wine.

speeches.speaker: Mist. mer.
prose: Why Master Merri-thought, are you disposed to make me wait here: you'll open I hope, i'll fetch them that shall open else.

speeches.speaker: Old mer.
prose: Good woman, if you will sing, I'll give you something, if not —

verse: You are no love for me Marget, I am no love for you.
Come aloft Boys, aloft.

speeches.speaker: Mist. mer.
prose: Now a Churles fart in your teeth Sir: Come Mick, we'll not trouble him, a shall not ding us i'th'teeth with his bread and his broth, that he shall not: come boy, I'll provide for thee, I warrant thee: wee'll go to Master Venterwels the Merchant, I'll get his letter to mine Host of the Bell in Waltham, there I'll place thee with the Tapster, will not that do well for thee Mick? and let me alone for that old Cuckoldly Knave your father, I'll use him in his kind, I warrant ye.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Come George, where's the beer?

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Here Love.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: This old fornicating fellow will not out of my mind yet; Gentlemen, I'll begin to you all, I desire more of your acquaintance, with all my heart. Fill the Gentlemen some beer George.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Look George, the little boy's come again, methinks he looks something like the Prince of Orange in his long stocking, if he had a little harness about his neck. George, I will have him dance Fading; Fading, is a fine Jig I'll assure you Gentlemen: begin brother, now a capers sweet heart, now a turn a th'toe, and then tumble: cannot you tumble youth?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: No indeed forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Nor eat fire?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Neither.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Why then I thank you heartily, there's two pence to buy you points withall.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Able to carry me? and art thou perfect
In all thy business?
prose: There boy, deliver this: but do it well. Hast thou
provided me four lusty fellows?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Sir you need not fear,
I have my lesson here, and cannot miss it:
The men are ready for you, and what else
Pertains to this imployment.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: There my boy,
Take it, but buy no land.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Faith sir 'twere rare
To see so young a purchaser: I flie,
And on my wings carry your destiny.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Go, and be happy: Now my latest hope
Forsake me not, but fling thy Anchor out,
And let it hold: stand, fix thou rolling stone,
Till I enjoy my dearest: hear me all
You powers that rule in men celestial.

speeches.speaker: Wife,
prose: Go thy ways, thou art as crooked a sprig as ever grew, in London, I warrant him he'll come to some naughty end or other: for his looks say no less: Besides, his father (you know George) is none of the best, you heard him take me up like a Gill flirt: and sing bawdy Songs upon me: but i'faith if I live George—

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Let me alone sweet-heart, I have a trick in my head shall lodge him in the Arches for one year, and make him sing Peccavi, 'ere I leave him, and yet he shall never know who hurt him neither.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Do my good Geerge, do.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: What shall we have Rafe do now boy?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: You shall have what you will sir.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Why so sir, go and fetch me him then, and let the Sophy of Persia come and christen him a child.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Believe me Sir, that will not do so well, 'tis stale, it has been had before at the Red Bull.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: George, let Rafe travell over great hills, and let him be weary, and come to the King of Cracovia's house, covered with velvet, and there let the Kings daughter stand in her window all in beaten gold, combing her golden locks with a comb of Ivory, and let her spye Rafe, and fall in love with him, and come down to him, and carry him into her fathers house, and then let Rafe talk with her.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Well said Nel, it shall be so: boy let's ha't done quickly.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Sir, if you will imagine all this to be done already, you shall hear them talk together: but we cannot present a house covered with black Velvet, and a Lady in beaten gold.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Sir Boy, lets ha't as you can then.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Besides, it will shew ill-favoredly to have a Grocers Prentice to court a Kings daughter.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Will it so Sir? you are well read in Histories: I pray you what was Sir Dagonet? was not he Prentice to a Grocer in London? read the Play of the Four Prentices of London, where they toss their Pikes so: I pray you fetch him in Sir, fetch him in.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: It shall be done, it is not our fault Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Now we shall see fine doings I warrant thee George.
O here they come; how prettily the King of Cracovia's daughter is drest.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: I Nell, it is the fashion of that Countrey, I warrant thee.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Welcome sir Knight unto my fathers Court.
King of Moldavia, unto me Pompiona
His daughter dear: but sure you do not like
Your entertainment, that will stay with us
No longer but a night.

speeches.speaker: Raph.
verse: Damsell right fair,
I'm on many sad adventures bound,
That call me forth into the Wilderness:
Besides, my horses back in something gal'd,
Which will enforce me ride a sober pace.
But many thanks (fair Lady) be to you,
For using errant Knight with courtesie.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: But say (brave Knight) what is your name and birth?

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: My name is Rafe, I am an Englishman,
As true as steel, a hearty Englishman,
And Prentice to a Grocer in the Strand,
By deed indent, of which I have one part:
But fortune calling me to follow Arms,
On me this holy Order I did take,
Of burning Pestle, which in all mens eyes,
I bear, confounding Ladies enemies.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Oft have I heard of your brave Countrymen,
And fertile soil, and store of wholosome food;
My father oft will tell me of a drink
In England found, and Nipitato call'd.
Which driveth all the sorrow from your hearts.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: Lady 'tis true, you need not lay your lips
To better Nipitato than there is.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: And of a wild-fowl he will often speak,
Which poudred beef and mustard called is:
For there have been great Wars 'twixt us and you,
But truely Rafe, it was not long of me.
Tell me then Rafe could you contented be,
To wear a Ladies favor in your shield?

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: I am a Knight of Religious Order,
And will not wear a favor of a Ladies
That trusts in Antichrist, and false traditions.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: Well said Rafe, convert her if thou canst.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: Besides, I have a Lady of my own
In merry England; for whose virtuous sake
I took these Arms, and Susan is her name,
A Coblers maid in Milkstreet, whom I vow
Nere to forsake, whilst life and Pestle last.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Happy that Cobling Dame, who ere she be
That for her own (dear Rafe) hath gotten thee.
Unhappy I, that nere shall see the day
To see thee more, that bear'st my heart away.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: Lady farewell, I must needs take my leave.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Hard-hearted Rafe, that Ladies dost deceive.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Hark thee Rafe, there's money for thee; give something in the King of Cracovia's house, be not beholding to him.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: Lady before I go, I must remember
Your fathers Officers, who truth to tell,
Have been about me very diligent:
Hold up thy snowy hand thou princely maid,
There's twelvepence for your fathers Chamberlain.
And another shilling for his Cook,
For by my troth the Goose was rosted well.
And twelve pence for your fathers Horse-keeper,
For nointing my horse back, and for his butter
There is another shilling to the maid
That washt my boot-hose, there's an English groat,
And twopence to the boy that wip't my boots.
And last, fair Lady, there is for your self
Three pence to buy you pins at Bumbo Fair.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Full many thanks, and I will keep them safe
Till all the heads be off, for thy sake Rafe.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: Advance my Squire and Dwarf, I cannot stay.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Thou kil'st my heart in parting thus away.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I commend Rafe, yet that he will not stoop to a Cracovian, there's properer women in London than any are there I-wis. But here comes Master Humphrey, and his love again, now George.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: I Cunny, peace.

speeches.speaker: Merc.
verse: Go get you up, I will not be intreated.
And Gossip mine I'll keep you sure hereafter
From gadding out again, with boys and unthrifts,
Come they are womens tears, I know your fashion.
Go sirrah, lock her in, and keep the key.
Safe as your life. Now my son Humphrey,
You may both rest assured of my love
In this, and reap your own desire.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: I see this love you speak of, through your daughter.
Although the hole be little, and hereafter
Will yield the like in all I may or can,
Fitting a Christian, and a Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Merc·
verse: I Do believe you (my good son) and thank you.
For 'twere an impudence to think you flattered.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: It were indeed, but shall I tell you why,
I have been beaten twice about the lye.

speeches.speaker: Merc.
verse: Well son, no more of complement, my daughter
Is yours again; appoint the time and take her.
Wee'll have no stealing for it, I my self
And some few of our friends will see you married.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: I would you would i'faith, for be it known
I ever was afraid to lye alone.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Some three days hence then.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: Three days, let me see,
'Tis somewhat of the most, yet I agree,
Because I mean against the pointed day,
To visit all my friends in new array.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Sir, there's a Gentlewoman without would speak with your Worship.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: What is she?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Sir I askt her not.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Bid her come in.

speeches.speaker: Mist. mer.
verse: Peace be to your Worship, I come as a poor
Suitor to you Sir, in the behalf of this child.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Are you not wise to Merri-thought?

speeches.speaker: Mist. mer.
prose: Yes truly, would I had nere seen his eyes, he has undone me and himself, and his children, and there he lives at home and sings, and hoyts, and revels among his drunken companions, but I warrant you, where to get a penny to put bread in his mouth, he knows not: And therefore if it like your Worship, I would intreat your Letter, to the honest Host of the Bell in Waltham, that I may place my child under the protection of his Tapster, in some setled course of life.

speeches.speaker: Mer
verse: I'm glad the heavens have heard my prayers: thy Husband
When I was ripe in sorrows laught at me,
Thy son, like an unthankful wretch, I having
Redeem'd him from his fall, and made him mine,
To shew his love again, first stole my daughter:
Then wrong'd this Gentleman, and last of all,
Gave me that grief, had almost brought me down
Unto my grave, had not a stronger hand
Reliev'd my sorrows, go, and weep as I did,
And be unpittied, for here I profess
An everlasting hate to all thy name.

speeches.speaker: Mist. mer.
prose: Will you so Sir, how say you by that? come Micke, let him keep his wind to cool his Pottage, we'll go to thy Nurses, Micke, she knits silk stockings boy, and we'll knit too boy, and be beholding to none of them all.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Sir, I take it you are the Master of this house.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: How then boy?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Then to your self Sir, comes this Letter.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: From whom my pretty boy?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: From him that was your servant, but no more
Shall that name ever be, for he is dead,
Grief of your purchas'd anger broke his heart,
^ saw him dye, and from his hand receiv'd
This paper with a charge to bring it hither,
Read it, and satisfie your self in all.

speeches.speaker: Merch.
verse: Gods hand is great in this, I do forgive him,
Yet am I glad he's quiet, where I hope
He will not bite again: boy bring the body,
And let him have his will, if that be all.
prose:
LETTER.
SIR that I have wronged your love, I must confess, in which I have purchast to my self, besides mine own undoing, the ill opinion of my friends, let not your anger, good Sir, outlive me, but suffer me to rest in peace with your forgiveness; let my body (if a dying man may so much prevail with you) be brought to your daughter, that she may know my hot flames are now buried, and withall, receive a testimony of the zeal I bore her vertue: farewell for ever, and be ever happy.
Jasper.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: 'Tis here without Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: So Sir, if you please
You may conduct it in, I do not fear it.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: I'll be your Usher boy, for though I say it,
He ow'd me something once, and well did pay it.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: If there be any punishment inflicted
Upon the miserable, more than yet I feell,
Let it together seize me, and at once
Press down my soul, I cannot bear the pain
Of these delaying tortures: thou that art
The end of all, and the sweet rest of all;
Come, come oh death bring me to thy peace,
And blot out all the memory I nourish
Both of father and my cruel friend.
O wretch'd maid still living to be wretched,
To be a say to fortune in her changes.
And grow to number times and woes together,
How happy had I been, if being born
My grave had been my cradle?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: By your leave
Young Mistris, here's a boy hath brought a Coffin,
What a would say I know not: but your father
Charg'd me to give you notice, here they come.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: For me I hope 'tis come, and 'tis most welcome

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Fair Mistriss, let me not add greater grief
To that great store you have already; Jasper
That whilst he liv'd was yours, now dead,
And here inclos'd, commanded me to bring
His body hither, and to crave a tear
From those fair eyes, though he deserve not pitty,
To deck his Funeral; for so he bid me
Tell her for whom he di'd.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: He shall have many:
Good friends depart a little, whilst I take
My leave of this dead man, that once I lov'd:
Hold, yet a little, life, and then I give thee
To thy first heavenly being; O my friend!
Hast thou deceiv'd me thus, and got before me?
I shall not long be after, but believe me,
Thou wert too cruel Jasper 'gainst thy self,
In punishing the fault I could have pardoned,
With so untimely death; thou didst not wrong me,
But ever wer't most kind, most true, most loving
And I the most unkind, most false, most cruell.
Didst thou but ask a tear? I'll give thee all,
Even all my eyes can pour down, all my sigh's
And all my self, before thou goest from me
There are but sparing Rites: But if thy soul
Be yet about this place, and can behold
And see what I prepare to deck thee with,
It shall go up, born on the wings of peace,
And satisfied: first will I sing thy Dirge,
Then kiss thy pale lips, and then dye my self,
And fill one Coffin and one grave together.
Thou fable cloth, sad cover of my joys,
I lift thee up, and thus I meet with death.
prose:
SONG.

Come you whose loves are dead,
And whilst I sing
Weep and wring
Every hand and every head,
Bind with Cipress and sad Ewe,
Ribbands black, and Candles blue,
For him that was of men most true.


Come with heavy mourning,
And on his grave
Let him have
Sacrifice of sighs and groaning,
Let him have fair flowers enow,

White and purple, green and yellow,
For him that was of men most true.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: And thus you meet the living.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: Save me Heaven.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Nay, do not flye me fair, I am no spirit,
Look better on me, do you know me yet?

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: O thou dear shadow of my friend.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Dear substance,
I swear I am no shadow feel my hand,
It is the same it was, I am your Jasper,
Your Jasper that's yet living, and yet loving,
Pardon my rash attempt, my foolish proof
I put in practice of your constancy:
For sooner should my sword have drunk my blood,
And set my soul at liberty, than drawn
The least drop from that body, for which boldness
Doom me to any thing: if death, I take it
And willingly.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: This death I'll give you for it,
So, now I am satisfied: you are no spirit,
But my own truest, truest, truest friend,
Why do you come thus to me?

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: First, to see you,
Then to convey you hence.

speeches.speaker: Luce.
verse: It cannot be,
For I am lockt up here, and watcht at all hours,
That 'tis impossible for me to scape.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Nothing more possible, within this Coffin
Do you convey your self, let me alone,
I have the wits of twenty men about me,
Only I crave the shelter of your Closet
A little and then fear me not; creep in
That they may presently convey you hence:
Fear nothing dearest love, I'll be your second,
Lye close, so, all goes well yet; boy.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: At hand Sir.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Convey away the Coffin, and be wary.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: 'Tis done already.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Now must I go conjure.

speeches.speaker: Merch.
verse: Boy, boy.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Your servant Sir.

speeches.speaker: Merch.
prose: Do me this kindness boy, hold here's a crown: before thou bury the body of this fellow, carry it to his old merry father, and salute him from me, and bid him sing, he hath cause.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: I will Sir.

speeches.speaker: Merch.
verse: I have fitted him a bargain, now, will vex him.
prose: And then bring me word what tune he is in, and have another crown: but do it truly.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: God bless your Worships health Sir.

speeches.speaker: Merch.
verse: Farewell boy.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Ah old Merry-thought, art thou there again? let's hear some of thy Songs.

speeches.speaker: Old Mer.
verse: Who can sing a merrier note
Th^ be that cannot change a great?
I would not be a Servingman to carry the cloke-bag still.
Nor would I be a Fawlconer the greedy Hawkes to fill.
But I would be in a good house, and have a good Master ^o:
But I would eat and drink of the best, and no work would I do.
prose: Not a Dinner left, and yet my heart leaps; I do wonder yet, as old as I am, that any man will follow a Trade, or serve, that may sing and laugh, and walk the streets: my wife and both my sons are I know not where, I have nothing left, nor know I how to come by meat to supper, yet am I merry still; for I know I shall find it upon the Table at six a Clock; therefore hang Thought
This is that keeps life and soul together, mirth: this is the Philosophers stone that they write so much on, that keeps a man ever young.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Sir, they say they know all your Money is gone, and they will trust you for no more drink.

speeches.speaker: Old mer.
verse: For Jillian of Berry, she dwells on a hill,
And she hath good Beer and Ale to sell,
And of good fellows she thinks no ill,
And thither will we go now, now, now, and thither
Will we go now.
And when you have made a little stay,
You need not know what is to pay,
But kiss your Hostess and go your way. And thither, &c.
prose: Will they not? let 'em chuse: the best is I have mirth at home, and need not send abroad for that; let them keep their drink to themselves.

speeches.speaker: 2. Boy.
verse: Sir, I can get no bread for supper.

speeches.speaker: Old mer.
verse: Ho, ho, no body at home, meat, nor drink, nor money ha we none, fill the pot Eedy, never more need I.
prose: Hang bread and supper, let's preferve our mirth, and we shall never feel hunger, I'll warrant you, let's have a Catch, boy follow me, come sing this Catch.

speeches.speaker: Old mer.
prose: So boyes enough, follow me, let's change our place and we shall laugh afresh.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Let him go George, a shall not have any countenance from us, not a good word from any i'th' Company, if I may strike stroke in't.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: No more, a shannot love; but Nell, I will have Rafe, do a very notable matter now, to the eternal honour and glory of all Grocers: sirrah, you there, boy, can none of you hear?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Sir, your pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Let Rafe come out on May day in the morning, and speak upon a Conduit with all his Scarfs about him, and his Feathers, and his Rings, and his Knacks.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Why sir, you do not think of our plot, what will become of that then?

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Why sir, I care not what become on't, I'll have him come out, or I'll fetch him out my self, I'll have something done in honor of the City: besides he hath been long enough upon Adventures, bring him out quickly, for I come amongst you—

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Well sir, he shall come out, but if our Play miscarry, Sir you are like to pay for't.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Bring him away then.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: This will be brave i'faith: George shall not he dance the Morrice too for the credit of the Strand.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: No sweet-heart it will be too much for the boy. O there he is Nell, he's reasonable well in reparel, but he has not Rings enough.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: London, to thee I do present the merry Month of May,
Let each true Subject be content to hear me what I say:
For from the top of Conduit head, as plainly may appear,
I will both tell my name to you, and wherefore I came here.
My name is Rafe, by due descent, though not ignoble I,
Yet far inferiour to the flock of gracious Grocery.
And by the Common-counsel of my fellows in the Strand,
With gilded Staff, and crossed Skarfe, the May-lord here I stand.
Rejoyce O English hearts, rejoyce, rejoyce O Lovers dear;
Rejoyce O City, Town, and Countrey, rejoyce eke every Shire;
For now the flagrant flowers do spring and sprout in seemly sort,
The little Birds do sit and sing, the Lambs do make fine sport,
And now the Burchin Tree doth bud that makes the Schoolboy cry,
The Morrice rings while Hobby horse doth foot it featuously:
The Lords and Ladies now abroad for their disport and play,
Do kiss sometimes upon the Grass, and sometimes in the Hay.
Now butter with a leaf of Sage is good to purge the blood,
Fly Venus and Phlebotomy for they are neither good.
Now little fish on tender stone, begin to cast their bellies,
And sluggish snails, that erst were mute, do creep out of their shellies,
The rumbling Rivers now do warm for little boys to paddle,
The Sturdy Steed, now goes to grass, and up they hang his saddle.
The heavy Hart, the blowing Buck, the Rascall and the Pricket,
Are now among the Yeomans Pease, and leave the fearful thicket.
And be like them, O you, I say, of this same noble Town,
And lift aloft your velvet heads, and slipping of your gown:
With bels on legs, and napkins clean unto your shoulders ti'de,
With Scarfs and Garters as you please, and Hey for our Town cry'd:
March out and shew your willing minds, by twenty, and by twenty,
To Hogsdon or to Newington, where Ale and Cakes are plenty.
And let it nere be said for shame, that we the youths of London,
Lay thruming of our caps at home, and left our custom undone.
~p then I say, both young and old, both man and maid a Maying
With Drums and Guns that bounce aloud, and merry Taber playing.
Which to prolong, God save our King, and send his Countrey peace,
And root out Treason from the Land, and so my friends I cease.

speeches.speaker: Merch.
prose: I will have no great store of company at the wedding, a couple of neighbors and their wives, and we will have a Capon in stewed broth, with marrow, and a good piece of beef, stuck with Rose-mary.

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Forbear thy pains fond man, It is too late.

speeches.speaker: Merch.
verse: Heaven bless me: Jasper?

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: I, I am his Ghost
Whom thou hast injur'd for his constant love:
Fond worldly wretch, who dost not understand
In death that true hearts cannot parted be.
First know thy daughter is quite born away,
On wings on Angels: through the liquid Ayre
Too far out of thy reach, and never more
Shalt thou behold her face: But she and I
Will in another world enjoy our loves,
Where neither fathers anger, poverty,
Nor any cross that troubles earthly men
Shall make us sever our united hearts,
And never shalt thou sit, or be alone
In any place, but I will visit thee
With gastly looks, and put into thy mind
The great offences which thou didst to me.
When thou art at thy Table with thy friends,
Merry in heart, and sild with swelling wine,
I'll come in midst of all thy pride and mirth,
Invisible to all men but thy self,
And whisper such a sad tale in thine ear,
Shall make thee let the Cup fall from thy hand,
And stand as mute and pale as Death it self.

speeches.speaker: Merch.
verse: Forgive me Jasper; Oh! what might I do?
Tell me to satisfie thy troubled Ghost?

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: There is no means, too late thou thinkst on this.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: But tell me what were best for me to do?

speeches.speaker: Jasp.
verse: Repent thy deed, and satisfie my father,
And beat fond Humphrey out of thy doors.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Look George, his very Ghost would have folks beaten.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: Father, my bride is gone, fair Mistris Luce,
My soul's the font of vengeance, mischiefs sluce.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Hence fool out of my sight, with thy fond passion,
Thou hast undone me.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: Hold my father dear,
For Luce thy daughters sake, that had no peer.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Jasper, I hope thy Ghost be well appeased,
To see thy will perform'd, now I'll go
To satisfie thy father for thy wrongs.
prose: Thy father fool? there's some blows more, begon.

speeches.speaker: Hum.
verse: What shall I do? I have been beaten twice.
And Mistris Luce is gone? help me device:
Since my true-love is gone, I never more,
Whilst I do live, upon the Skie will pore;
But in the dark will wear out my shoo-soles
In passion, in Saint Faiths Church under Pauls.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: George call Rafe hither, if you love me call Rafe hither, I have the bravest thing for him to do George,; prethee. call him quickly

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: Rafe, why Rafe boy.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
verse: Here Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: Come hither Rafe, come to thy Mistris Boy.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Rafe I would have thee call all the youths together in battle-ray, with Drums, and Guns, and flags, and march to Mile-end in pompous fashion, and there exhort your Souldiers to be merry and wise, and to keep their beards from burning Rafe, and then skirmish, and let your flags fly, and cry, kill, kill, kill: my husband shall lend you his Jerkin Rafe, and there's a Scarfe for the rest, the house shall furnish you, and we'll pay for't: do it bravely Rafe, and think before whom you perform, and what person you represent.

speeches.speaker: Rafe.
prose: I warrant you Mistress, if I do it not, for the honor of the City, and the credit of my Master, let me never hope for freedome.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: 'Tis well spoken i'faith; go thy waies, thou art a spark indeed.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Ralph, double your files bravely Ralph.

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
prose: I warrant you Sir,

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Let him look narrowly to his service, I shall take him else; I was there my self a Pike-man once, in the hottest of the day, wench, had my feather shot shaer away, the fringe of my pike burnt off with powder, my pate broken with a scouring-stick, and yet I thank God I am here.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Hark George, the Drums.

speeches.speaker: Cit,
prose: Ran, tan; tan, tan, ran tan: Oh wench an thou hadst but seen little Ned of Aldgate, drum Ned, how he made it roar again, and laid on like a tyrant: and then struck softly till the Ward came up, and then thundred again, and together we go: sa, sa, sa, bounce quoth the Guns: courage my hearts, quoth the Captains: Saint George, quoth the pike-men; and withal here they lay, and there they lay: And yet for all this I am here wench.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Be thankful for it George, for indeed 'tis wonderful.

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
prose: March fair my hearts; Lieutenant beat the rear up: Ancient let your Colours flie; but have a great care of the Butchers hooks at White-Chappel, they have been the death of many a fair Ancient. Open your files, that I may take a view both of your persons and munition: Serjeant call a Muster.

speeches.speaker: Serg.
prose: A stand, William Hamerton Pewterer.

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: Here Captain.

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
prose: A Corslet and a Spanish Pike; 'tis well, can you shake it with a terror?

speeches.speaker: Ham.
prose: I hope so Captain.

speeches.speaker: Ralph.
