All my desire is, you would come alone;
That you might have the hope of the enterprise,
That you might hear 'em first, and then proceed, Sir,

speeches.speaker: Ju.
verse: I come, I come.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: 'Tis very well.

speeches.speaker: Ju.
verse: Keep all my doors fast, 'tis something late.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: So, so, and please your worship I direct you.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: My Master staies, I doubt his lime-twigs catch not,
If they doe, all's provided; but I all
This while forget my own state, fair Maria
Is certainly alive, I met her in
Another habit, with her Nurse, 'twas she:
There is some trick in't, but when this is over,
I'll find it out, this project for the Usurer
May have good effect; however, 'twill be sport
To mortifie him a little;
He's come without him:
Have you fail'd, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: Prosper'd? my little Ingineer; away,
He is i'th' next room, be not you seen, sirrah.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: The pitfall's ready, never Justice
Was catcht in such a nooze: e'er he get out.
He shall run through a scouring purgatory,
Shall purge him to the quick, 'tis night already.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: Come softly, yet Sir, softly, are you not weary?

speeches.speaker: Ju.
verse: Th'ast brought me into a melancholy place,
I see no creature.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: This is, Sir, their Den
Where they suppose themselves secure, I am faint,
With making haste; but I must be thus troubled,
And therefore never go without a Cordial;
Without this I should dye;
How it refreshes me
Already? will't please your worship? I might have had
The manners to ha' let you drink before me;
Now am I lusty.

speeches.speaker: Ju.
verse: 'Twas a good taste.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: Taste? how d'ye find the virtue, nay Sir, spare it not:
My wife has the Receipt, does it not stir
Your Worships body? when you come to examine,
'Twill make you speak like thunder.

speeches.speaker: Ju.
verse: Hoy he.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: It works already.

speeches.speaker: Ju.
verse: Is there never a chair, I was wearier than I thought,
But who shall we have to take 'em. Mr. Constable?

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: Let me alone, when I but give the watch-word
We will have men enough to surprize an Army.

speeches.speaker: Ju.
verse: I begin to be sleepy; what, hast a chair?

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: They do not dream of us, 'tis early rising;
Care, care, and early rising, Common-wealths men
Are ever subject to the nods; sit down, Sir,
A short nap is not much amiss; so, so, he's fast;
Fast as a fish i'th' net, he has winking powder
Shall work upon him to our wish, remove him,
Nay, we may cut him into collops now
And he ne'r seel; have you prepar'd the vault, sirrah?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Yes, yes, Sir, every thing in's place.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: When you have plac'd him, you and I boy
Must about another project hard by, his potion
Will bind him sure enough till we return,
This villany weighs mainly, But we'll purge ye.

speeches.speaker: Sex.
verse: Now for mine ears, mine ears be constant to me;
They ring a wager, and I must deal justly, ha boys.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: Dost hear 'em, hark, these be the Ringers?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Are you sure the same?

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: Or my directions fail;
The coast is clear:
How the bells go? how daintily they tumble?
And methinks they seem to say; Fine fools I'll fit you.

speeches.speaker: Sex.
verse: Excellent agen, good boys—oh that was nought.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: Who's that?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Be you conceal'd by any means yet, hark,
They stop, I hope they'll to't agen, close Sir.

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: A palpable knock.

speeches.speaker: Ring.
verse: 'Twas none.

speeches.speaker: To.
verse: Be judg'd by the Sexton then,
If I have ears.

speeches.speaker: Sex.
verse: A knock, a knock, a gross one.

speeches.speaker: To.
verse: Carman, your gallon of wine, you ring most impiously,
Art thou o'th' worshipful company of the Knights o'th West,
And handle a bell with no more dexterity?
You think you are in Thames-street
Justling the Carts: oh a clean hand's a Jewel.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Good speed to your good exercise.

speeches.speaker: To.
verse: Y' are welcome

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: I come, Sir, from a Gentleman, and neighbor hard by,
One that loves your Musick well.

speeches.speaker: To.
verse: He may have more on't,
Handle a bell, as you were haling timber?
Gross, gross, and base, absurd.

speeches.speaker: Ring.
verse: I'll mend it next peal.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: To intreat a knowledge of you, whether it be
By the Ear you ring thus cunningly, or by the Eye;
For to be plain, he has laid ten pounds upon't.

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: But which way has he laid?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: That your Ear guides you,
And not your Eye.

speeches.speaker: To.
verse: Has won, has won, the Ear's our only instrument:

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: But how shall we be sure on't.

speeches.speaker: To.
verse: Put all the lights out, to what end serve our eyes then?

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: A plain Case,

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: You say true, 'tis a fine cunning thing to ring by th' Ear sure
And can you ring i'th' dark so?

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: All night long, boy.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: 'Tis wonderful, let this be certain Gentlemen,
And half his wager he allows among ye;
Is't possible you should ring so?

speeches.speaker: To.
verse: Possible, thou art a child, I'll ring when I am dead drun^
Out with the lights, no twinkling of a candle,
I know my rope too, as I know my nose,
And can bang it soundly i'th' dark, I warrant you..

speeches.speaker: Wi.
verse: Come, let's confirm him straight, and win the wager.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Let me hear to strengthen me;
And when y'ave rung, I'll bring the money to you.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: So, so, follow 'em;
They shall have a cool reward, one hath gold of mine,
Good store in's pocket,
But this will be reveng'd in a short warning.
They are at it lustily; hey, how wantonly
They ring away their cloaths, how it delights me;

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Here, here, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: Hast Wildbrain's?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: His whole cafe, Sir; I felt it out, and by the guards
This should be the Coachmans, another suit too.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: Away boy, quickly now to the Usurer,
His hour to wake approaches.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: That once finished,
You'll give me leave to play, Sir: here they come.

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: I am monstrous weary.

speeches.speaker: To.
verse: Fie, how I sweat? Reach me my cloak to cover me,
I run to oyl like a Porpise: 'twas a brave peal.

speeches.speaker: Sex.
verse: Let me light the candle first, then I'll wait on you.

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: A very brave peal.

speeches.speaker: To.
verse: Carman, you came in close now.

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: Sure 'tis past midnight.

speeches.speaker: Ring.
verse: No stirring in the streets I hear.

speeches.speaker: To.
verse: Walk further, was that a pillar? 'tis harder than ^ nos^
Where's the boy promis'd us five pounds?

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: Room, I sweat still; come, come, my cloak,
I shall take cold.

speeches.speaker: Sex.
verse: Where lies it?

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: Here, here, and all our cloaths.

speeches.speaker: Sex.
verse: Where, where?

speeches.speaker: Ring.
verse: I'th' corner.

speeches.speaker: To.
verse: Is thy candle blind too, give me the bottle,
I can drink like a Fish now, like an Elephant.

speeches.speaker: Sex.
verse: Here are the corners, but here are no cloaths;
Yes, here is a cuff.

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: A cuff? give me the candle,
Cuffes wonot cover me—I smell the knavery.

speeches.speaker: Tob.
verse: Is't come to a cuff? my whole suit turned to a button?

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: Now am I as cold again as though 'twere Christmas;
Cold with my fear, I'll never ring by the ear more.

speeches.speaker: To.
verse: My new cloaths vanish'd?

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: All my cloaths Toby.

speeches.speaker: Ring.
verse: Here's none.

speeches.speaker: Tob.
verse: Not one of my dragons wings left to adorn me,
Have I muted all my feathers?

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: Cheated by the ear; a plot to put out the candle;
I could be mad; my chain, my rings, the gold, the gold.

speeches.speaker: Tob.
verse: The cold, the cold I cry, and I cry truly,
Not one sleeve, nor a cape of a cloak to warm me.

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: What miserable fools were we?

speeches.speaker: Tob.
verse: We had e'en best, gentlemen,
Every man chuse his rope again, and fasten it,
And take a short turn to a better fortune,
To be bawds to our miseries, and put our own lights out?

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: Prethee Sexton lets have a fire at thy house.
A good fire, we'll pay thee some way for't, I am stone cold.

speeches.speaker: Sex.
verse: Alas I pity you, come quickly Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: Sure I ha been in a dream, I had no Mistriss,
Nor gold, nor cloaths, but am a ringing rascal.

speeches.speaker: Tob.
verse: Fellows in affliction, let's take hands all,
Now are we fit for tumblers.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: So, so, presently his sleep will leave him.
And wonder seize upon him,
B^d 'em within be ready.

speeches.speaker: Ju.
verse: What sound's this?
What horrid dinne? what dismal place is this?
I never saw before, and now behold it;
But by the halflight of a Lamp, that burns here:
My spirits shake, tremble through my body;
Help, help,
Mercy protect me, my soul quakes,
What dreadful apparitions! how I shudder!

speeches.speaker: 1. 2. Fu.
verse: Algripe.

speeches.speaker: Ju.
verse: What are you?
We are hellhounds, hellhounds, that have commission
From the Prince of darkness,
To fctch thy black soul to him.

speeches.speaker: Ju.
verse: Am I not alive still?
Thou art, but we have brought thee instruments
Will quickly rid thy miserable life, Stabb,
Poyson.
Hang thy self, this choice is offer'd,
Thou canst not hope for heaven; thy base soul is
Lost to all hope of mercy.
Quickly, quickly,
The torments, cool.
And all thy friends expect thee.
Come with us to that pit of endless horror,
Or we will force thee.

speeches.speaker: Ju.
verse: Oh, oh, oh.
Groans are too late, sooner the ravisher,
Whose soul is hurl'd into eternal frost,
Stung with the force of twenty thousand winters,
To punish the distempers of his blood,
Shall hope to get from thence, than thou avoid
The certainty of meeting hell^ where he is,
Shall murderers be there for ever dying,
Their souls shot through with Adders, torn on Engines,
Dying as many deaths for killing one,
Could any imagination number them,
As there be moments in eternity:
And shall that Justice spare thee, that hast slain,
Murdered by thy extortion so many?

speeches.speaker: Ju.
verse: Oh, oh.
Do execution quickly, or we'll carry thee alive to hell

speeches.speaker: Ju.
verse: Gently, gentle devils, do not force me
To kill my self, nor do not you do't for me;
Oh let me live, I'll make amends for all.
Tell us of thy repentance? perjur'd villain,
Pinch off his flesh, he must be whipt, salted and whipt.

speeches.speaker: Ju.
verse: Oh misery of miseries!

speeches.speaker: Recorders 1. 2.
verse: Tear his accursed limbs, to hell with him, ha!
A mischief on that innocent face, away.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Malicious furies hence, choak not the seeds
Of holy penitence.

speeches.speaker: Ju.
verse: This must be an Angel,
How at his presence the fiends crawl away?
Here is some light of mercy.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Be thou wise,
And entertain it, wretched, wretched man;
What poor defence hath all thy wealth been to thee?
What says thy conscience now?

speeches.speaker: Ju.
verse: Be my good Angel, here I promise thee,
To become honest, and renounce all villany;
Enjoyn me any pennance, I'll build Churches;
A whole City of Hospitals.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Take heed,
There is no dallying, nor are these impos'd.

speeches.speaker: Ju.
verse: Name any thing within my power, sweet Angel;
And if I do not faithfully perform it,
Then whip me every day, burn me each minute,
Whole years together let me freeze to Isicles.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: I'th' number of thy foul oppressions;
Thou hast undone a faithful Gentleman,
By taking forfeit of his Land.

speeches.speaker: Ju.
verse: Young Lurcher,
I do confess.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: He lives most miserable,
And in despair may hang or drown himself;
Prevent his ruine, or his blood will be
More sin in thy account: hast thou forgotten
He had a sister?

speeches.speaker: Ju.
verse: I do well remember it.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Couldst thou for Mammon break thy solemn vow,
Made once to that unhappy maid, that weeps
A thousand tears a day for thy unkindness,
Was not thy faith contracted, and thy heart?
And couldst thou marry another?

speeches.speaker: Ju.
verse: But she is dead,
And I will make true satisfaction.

speeches.speaker: Boy
verse: What do I instance these that hast been false
To all the world.

speeches.speaker: Ju.
verse: I know it, and will henceforth
Practice repentance, do not frown sweet Angel;
I will restore all Mortgages, forswear
Abominable Usury, live chaste;
For I have been wanton in my shroud, my age;
And if that poor innocent maid, I so abus'd,
Be living, I will marry her, and spend
My days to come religiously.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: I was commanded but a Messenger
To tell thee this, and rescue thee from those,
Whose malice would have dragg'd thee quick to hell,
If thou abuse this mercy and repent not,
Double damnation will expect thee for it;
But if thy life be virtuous hereafter,
A blessedness shall reward thy good example,
Thy fright hath much distracted thy weak sences,
Drink of this viol, and renew thy spirits
I ha done my office, think on't and be happy.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: So, so, he gapes already, now he's fast;
Thou hast acted rarely, but this is not all;
First, help to convey him out o' th' vault.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: You will dispense with me now, as you promis'd, Sir,

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: We will make shift without thee, th'ast done well,
By our device this bondage may scape hell.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Didst think Maria, this poor outside, and
Dissembling of thy voice could hide thee from
A mothers searching eye, though too much fear,
Lest thou wert not the same, might blind a Lover
That thought thee dead too, oh my dear Maria,
I hardly kept my joyes in from betraying thee:
Welcome again to life, we shall find out
The mystery of thy absence; conceal
Thy person still, for Algripe must not know thee:
And exercise this pretty Dialect;
If there be any course in Law to free thee,
Thou shalt not be so miserable; be silent
Good Nurse.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: Yo^ should not need to fear me, Madam,
I do not love the usuring Jew so well;
Beside, 'twas my trick to disguise her so.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Be not dejected Mall.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
verse: Your care may comfort me;
But I despair of happiness:

speeches.speaker: Hartlove,
verse: I dare not see him.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: We'll withdraw.

speeches.speaker: L^.
verse: I shall but grieve to see his passions too,
Since there's no possibility to relieve him.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: The world's a Labyrinth, where unguided men
Walk up and down to sind their weariness;
No sooner have we measured with much toil
One crooked path with hope to gain our freedom,
But it betrays us to a new affliction;
What a strange mockery will man become
Shortly to all the creatures?
Oh Maria^!
If thou be'st dead, why does thy shadow fright me?
Sure 'tis because I live; were I but certain
To meet thee in one grave, and that our dust
Might have the priviledge to mix in silence,
How quickly should my soul shake off this burthen!
Thus far my wishes have success, I'll lose
No time: Sir, are not you call'd Mr. Hartlove?
Pardon my rudeness.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: What does that concern
Thee Boy, 'tis a name cannot advantage thee;
And I am weary on't.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Had you conce^l'd,
Or I forgot it, Sir, so large were my
Directions, that you could not speak this language,
But I should know you by your sorrow.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: Thou
Wert well inform'd, it seems; well, what's your business?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: I come to bring you comfort.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: Is Maria
Alive agen? that's somewhat, and yet not
Enough to make my expectation rise, to
Past half a blessing; since we cannot meet
To make it up a full one; th'art mistaken.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: When you have heard me, you'll think otherwise:
In vain I should report Maria living:
The comfort that I bring you, must depend
Upon her death.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: Th'art a dissembling boy,
Some one has sent thee to mock me; though my anger
Stoop not to punish thy green years unripe
For malice; did I know what person sent thee
To tempt my sorrow thus, I should reveng it.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Indeed I have no thought so uncharitable,
Nor am I sent to grieve you, let me suffer
More punishment than ever boy deserv'd,
If you do find me false; I serve a Mistriss
Would rather dye than play with your misfortunes;
Then good Sir hear me out.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: Who is your Mistriss?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Before I name her, give me some encouragement,
That you receive her message: she is one
That is full acquainted with your misery,
And can bring such a portion of her sorrow
In every circumstance so like your own,
You'll love and pity her, and wish your griefs
Might marry one anothers.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: Thou art wild?
Canst thou bring comfort from so sad a creature?
Her miserable story can at best,
But swell my Volume, large enough already.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: She was late belov'd, as you were, promis'd faith,
And marriage; and was worthy of a better
Than he, that stole Maria's heart.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: How's that?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Just as Maria dealt with your affection,
Did he that married her deal with my Mistriss,
When careless both of Honor and Religion,
They cruelly gave away their hearts to strangers.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: Part of this truth I know, but prethee boy
Proceed to that thou cam'st for; thou didst Promise
Something, thy language cannot hitherto
Encourage me to hope for.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: That I come to:
My Mistriss thus unkindly dealt withal,
You may imagine, wanted no affliction;
And had e'r this, wept her self dry as Marble,
Had not your fortune come to her relief,
And twinn to her own sorrow brought her comfort.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: Could the condition of my fate so equal,
Lessen her sufferings?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: I know not how
Companions in grief sometimes diminish
And make the pressure easie by degrees:
She threw her troubles off, remembring yours,
And from her pity of your wrongs, there grew
Affection to your person thus increas'd,
And with it, confidence, that those whom Nature
Had made so even in their weight of sorrow,
Could not but love as equally one another,
Were things but well prepar'd, this gave her boldness
To employ me thus far.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: A strange message, boy.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: If you incline to meet my Mistriss love,
It may beget your comforts; besides that,
'Tis some revenge, that you above their scorn
And pride can laugh at them, whose perjury
Hath made you happy, and undone themselves.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: Have you done boy?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Only this little more;
When you but see, and know my Mistriss well,
You will forgive my tediousness, she's fair,
Fair as Maria was.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: I'll hear no more,
^o foolish boy, and tell thy fonder Mistriss
^e has no second Faith to give away;
^d mine was given to Maria, though her death
Allow me freedom, see the Picture of her.
^ would give ten thousand Empires for the substance;
Yet for Maria's sake, whose divine Figure
That rude frame carries, I will love this counterfeit
Above all the world, and had thy Mistriss had all
The grace and blossom of her sex; now she
^s gone, that was, walking, a Spring of beauty,
I would not look upon her.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Sir, your pardon,

^
^ave but done a message, as becomes
A servant, nor did she on whose commands
^ gladly waited, bid me urge her love
To your disquiet, she would chide my diligence
^f I should make you angry.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: Pretty boy.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Indeed I fear I have offended you:
Pray if I have, enjoyn me any pennance for it:
^ have perform'd one duty, and could as wi^lingly
To purge my faul^, and shew I suffer with you,
^ l^ad your cause to another.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: And I'll take thee
At thy word boy, thou hast a moving language,
That pretty innocent, Copy of Maria
^ all I love, I know not how to speak,
Winn her to think well of me, and I wi^l
Reward thee to thy wishes.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: I undertake
Nothing for gain, but since you have resolv'd,
To love no other, I'll be faithful to you,
And my prophetick thoughts bid me already
^y I shall prosper.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: Thou wert sent to bless me.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Pray give us opportunity.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: Be happy.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: He's gone.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: With your fair leave Mistriss.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
verse: Have you business with her pray you?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: I have a message from a Gentleman,
Please you vouchsafe your ear more private.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: You shall have my absence Neece.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
verse: Was the sentleman afear'd to declare his matters openly, here was no bodies was not very honest, if her like ^ her errands the petter, was wist to keep her preaths ^ cool her porridges, can tell her, that now for aule her ^ivate hearings and tawgings.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: You may, if please you, find another language.
And with less pains be understood.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
verse: What is her meaning?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Come, pray speak your own English.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
verse: Have boyes lost her itts and memories? bless us aule.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: I must be plain then, come, I know you are
^is, this thin vail cannot obscure you:
I'll tell the world you live, I have not lost ye,
S^ce first with grief and shame to be surpriz'd,
A violent trance, took away shew of life;
I could discover by what accident
You were convey'd away at midnight, in
Your coffin, could declare the place, and minute,
When you reviv'd, what you have done since as perfectly—

speeches.speaker: Ma.
verse: Alas, I am betraid to new misfortunes.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: You are not, for my knowledge, I'll be dumb
For ever, rather than be such a traitor;
^deed I pity you, and bring no thoughts,
^ f^ll of peace, call home your modest blood,
^le hath too long usurp'd upon your face;
Think upon love agen, and the possession
Of full blown joyes, now ready to salute you.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
verse: These words undo me more than my own griefs.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: I see how fear would play the tyrant with you,
But I'll remove suspition; have you in
Your heart, an entertainment for his love
To whom your Virgin faith made the first promise?

speeches.speaker: Ma.
verse: If thou mean'st Hartlove, thou dost wound me still,
I have no life without his memory,
Nor with it any hope to keep it long:
Thou seest I walk in darkness like a thief,
That fears to see the world in his own shape,
My very shadow frights me, 'tis a death
To live thus, and not look day in the face,
Away, I know thee not.

speeches.speaker: Boy
verse: You shall hereafter know, and thank me Lady,
I'll bring you a discharge at my next visit,
Of all your fears, be content, fair Maria,
'Tis worth your wonder.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
verse: Impossible.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Be wise and silent,
Dress your self, you shall be what you wish.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
verse: Do this, and be
My better Angel.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: All your care's on me.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: I Must applaud thy diligence.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: It had been nothing
To have left him in t^e Porch; I call'd his servants,
With wonders they acknowledg'd him, I pretended
It was some spice, sure of the falling sickness,
And that, 'twas charity to bring him home;
They rubb'd and chaf'd him, ply'd him with Strong water,
Still he was senseless, clamors could not wake him;
I wish'd 'em then get him to bed, they did so,
And almost smother'd him with ruggs and pillows;
And 'cause they should have no cause to suspect me,
I watch'd them till he wak'd.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: 'Twas excellent.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: When his time came to yawn, and stretch himself,
I bid 'em not be hasty to discover
How he was brought home; his eyes fully open
With trembling he began to call his servants,
And told 'em he had seen strange visions,
That should convert him from his heathen courses;
They wondred, and were silent, there he preach'd
How sweet the air of a contented conscience
Smelt in his nose now, ask'd 'em all forgiveness
For their hard pasture since they liv'd with him;
Bid 'em believe, and fetch out the cold Sur-loin:
Pierce the strong beer, and let the neighbors joy in't:
The conceal'd Muskadine should now lie open
To every mouth; that he would give to th' poor,
And mend their wages; that his doors should be
Open to every miserable sutor.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: What said his servants then?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: They durst not speak,
But blest themselves, and the strange means that had
Made him a Christian in this over-joy,
I took my leave, and bad 'em say their prayers,
And humor him, lest he turn'd Jew agen.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: Enough, enough. Who's this?
'Tis one of my ringers; stand close, my Ladies Coachman.

speeches.speaker: To.
verse: Buy a mat for a bed, buy a mat;
Would I were at rack and manger among my horses;
We have divided the Sextons
Houshold-stuff among us, one has the rugg, and he's
Turn'd Irish, and another has a blanket, and he must beg in't
The sheets serve another for a frock, and with the bed-cord,
He may pass for a Porter, nothing but the mat would fall
To my share, which with the help of a tune and a hassock
Out o'th' Church, may disguise me till I get home;
A pox o' bell-ringing by the ear, if any man take me
At it agen, let him pull mine to the Pillory: I could wish
I had lost mine, ears, so I had my cloaths again:
The weather wo'not allow this fashion,
I do look for an Ague besides.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: How the raskal shakes?

speeches.speaker: To.
verse: Here are company:
Buy a Mat for a Bed, buy a Mat,
A hassock for your feet, or a Piss clean and sweet;
Buy a Mat for a Bed, buy a Mat:
Ringing I renounce thee, I'll never come to church more.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: You with a Mat.

speeches.speaker: Tob.
verse: I am call'd.
If any one should offer to buy my Mat, what a case were I in?
Oh that I were in my Oat-tub with a horse-loaf,
Something to hearten me:
I dare not hear 'em;
Buy a mat for a bed, buy a mat.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: He's deaf.

speeches.speaker: Tob.
verse: I am glad, I am: buy a mat for a bed.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: How the raskal sweats? What a pickle he's in?
Every street he goes through will be a new torment.

speeches.speaker: Tob.
verse: If ever I meet at midnight more a jangling:
I am cold, and yet I drop; buy a mat for a bed, buy a mat.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: He has punishment enough.
Who's this, my tother youth? he is turn'd Bear.

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: I am halfe afraid of my self: this poor shift
I got o'th' Sexton to convey me handsomly
To some harbor, the wench will hardly know me;
They'll take me for some Watchman o'th' parish;
I ha ne'r a penny left me, that's one comfort;
And ringing has begot a monstrous stomach,
And that's another mischief: I were best go home,
For every thing will scorn me in this habit.
Besides, I am so full of these young bell-ringers;
If I get in adoors, not the power o'th' countrey,
Nor all my Aunts curses shall disembogue me.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: Bid her come hither presently,—hum, 'tis he.

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: I am betraid to one that will eternally laugh at me,
Three of these rogues will jeer a horse to death.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: 'Tis Mr. Wildbrain sure, and yet me thinks
His fashion's strangely alt'red, sirrah Watchman,
You rugamuffin, turn you louzie Bears skin:
You with the Bed-rid Bill.

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: H'as found me out;
There's no avoiding him, I had rather now
Be arraign'd at Newga^e for a robbery,
Than answer to his Articles: your Will Sir,
I am in haste.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: Nay, then I will make bold wi'ye;
A Watchman, and asham'd to shew his countenance,
His face of authority? I have seen that physiognomy;
Were you never in prison for pilfering?

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: How the rogue worries me.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: Why may not this
Be the villain robb'd my house last night,
And walks disguis'd in this malignant rugg,
Arm'd with a tun of Iron? I will have you
Before a Magistrate.

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: What will become of me?

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: What art thou? speak.

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: I am the wandring Jew, and please your worship.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: By your leave Rabbi, I will shew you then
A Synagogue, iclip't Bridewel, where you,
Under correction, may rest your self:
You have brought a bill to guard you, there be dog-whpis
To firk such rugg'd currs, whips without bells
Indeed.

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: Bells.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: How he sweats?

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: I must be known, as good at first; now jeer on,
But do not anger me too impudently,
The Rabbi will be mov'd then.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: How? Jack Wildbrain,
What time o'th' Moon man, ha? what strange bells
Hast in thy brains?

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: No more bells,
No more bells, they ring backwards.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: Why, where's the wench, the blessing that befel thee
The unexpected happiness? where's that Jack?
Where are thy golden days?

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: It was his trick, as sure as I am louzie,
But how to be reveng'd—

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: Fie, fie, Jack,
Marry a Watchmans widow in thy young daies,
With a revenue of old Iron and a Rugg?
Is this the Paragon, the dainty piece,
The delicate divine rogue?

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: 'Tis enough, I am undone,
Mark'd for a misery, and so leave prating;
Give me my Bill.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: You need not ask your Taylors,
Unless you had better Linings; it may be,
To avoid suspition, you are going thus
Disguis'd to your fair Mistriss.

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: Mock no further,
Or as I live, I'll lay my Bill o' thy pate,
I'll take a Watchmans fury into my fingers,
To ha no judgement to distinguish persons,
And knock thee down.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: Come, I ha done, and now
Will speak some comfort to thee, I will lead thee
Now to my Mistriss hitherto conceal'd;
She shall take pity on thee too, she loves
A handsome man; thy misery invites me
To do thee good, I'll not be jealous, Jack;
Her beauty shall commend it self; but do not,
When I have brought you into grace, supplant me.

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: Art thou in earnest? by this cold Iron—

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: No oaths, I am not costive; here she comes.
Sweet-heart, I have brought a Gentleman,
A friend of mine to be acquainted with you,
He's other than he seems; why d'ye stare thus?

speeches.speaker: Mist.
verse: Oh Sir, forgive me, I have done ye wrong.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: What's the matter? didst ever see her afore Jack

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: Prethee do what thou wot wi'me, if thou hast
A mind, hang me up quickly.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: Never despair, I'll give thee my share rather,
Take her, I hope she loves thee at first sight,
She has petticoats will patch thee up a suit;
I resign all, only I'll keep these trifles.
I took some pains for 'em, I take it Jack;
What think you pink of beauty, come let me
Counsel you both to marry, she has a trade,
If you have audacity to hook in Gamesters:
Let's ha a wedding, you will be wondrous rich;
For she is impudent, and thou art miserable;
'Twill be a rare match.

speeches.speaker: Mist.
verse: As you are a man, forgive me, I'll redeem all.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: You wo'not to this geer of marriage then?

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: No, no, I thank you Tom, I can watch for
A groat a night, and be every gentlemans fellow.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: Rise and be good, keep home and tend your busine^

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: Thou hast don't to purpose, give me thy hand To^
Shall we be friends? thou seest what state I am in,
I'll undertake this pennance to my Aunt,
J^t as I am, and openly I'll goe;
Where, if I be received again for currant,
And fortu^e smile once more.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: Nay, nay, I'm satisfied, so farew^l honest louzie Jack.

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: I cannot help it, some men meet with strange destinies.
^f things go right thou mayst be hang'd, and I
May live to see't, and purchase thy apparel:
So farewel Tom. commend me to thy Polcat.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Now that I have my counsel ready, and my cause ripe;
The Judges all inform'd of the abuses;
Now that he should be gone.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: No man knows whether,
And yet they talk he went forth with a Constable
Th^t told him of strange business that would bring him
Money and Lands, and Heaven knows what; but they
Have search'd, and cannot find out such an Officer:
And as a secret, Madam, they told your man
Nicholas, whom you sent thither as a spie,
They had a shrewd suspition 'twas the devil
I'th' likeness of a Constable, that has tempted him:
By this time to strange things; there have been men
As rich as he, have met convenient rivers,
And so forth; many trees have born strange fruits:
D'ye think he has not hang'd himself?

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: If he be hang'd, who has his goods?

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: They are forfeited, they say.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: He has hang'd himself for certain then,
Only to cosin me of my Girls portion.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: Very likely.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Or did not the Constable carry him to some prison?

speeches.speaker: Nu.
verse: They thought on that too, and search'd every where.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: He may be close for treason, perhaps executed,

speeches.speaker: Nu.
verse: Nay, they did look among the quarters too,
And must^red all the bridge-house for his night-cap.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Madam, here is the gentleman agen.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: What Gentleman?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: He that lov'd my young Mistriss.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Alas, 'tis Hartlove, 'twill but feed his melancholy.
To let him see Maria, since we dare not
Yet tell the world she lives; and certainly,
Did not the violence of his passion blind him,
^ would see past her borrowed tongue and habit.

speeches.speaker: Nu.
verse: Please you entertain him awhile, Madam,
^ cast about for something with your daughter.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Do what thou wot, pray Mr. Har^love enter.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: Madam, I come to ask your gentle pardon.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Pardon, for what? you ne'^ offended me.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: Y^, if ye be the mother of Maria.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: I was her mother, but that word is cancell'd,
And buried with her in that very minute
Her soul fled from her; we lost both our names
Of mother and of daughter.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: Alas, Madam,
If your relation did consist but in
Those naked terms, I had a title nearer,
^ce love unl^es more than the tie of blood;
No matter for the empty voice of mother;
Your nature still is left, which in her absence
^ love Maria, and not see her ashes
A^d memory polluted.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: You amaze me, by whom?

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: By me, I am the vile profaner.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Why do you speak thus indiscr^etly, Sir?
You ever honour'd her.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: I did live,
But since she died, I ha been a villain to her.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: I do beseech you say not so; all this
Is but to make me know how much I sinn'd
In forcing her to marry.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: Do not mock me,
I charge you by the Virgin you have wept for;
For I have done an impious act against her,
A deed able to fright her from her sleep,
And through her marble, ought to be reveng'd;
A wickedness, that if I should be silent,
You as a witness must accuse me for't.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Was I a witness?

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: Yes, you knew I lov'd
Maria once; or grant, you did but think so,
By what I ha profest, or she has told you,
Was't not a fault unpardonable in me,
When I should drop my tears upon her grave,
Yes, and proof sufficient.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: To what?

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: That I, forgetful of my fame and vows
To fair Maria, e'r the worm could pierce
Her tender shroud, had chang'd her for another;
Did you not blush to see me turn a rebel?
So soon to court a shadow, a strange thing,
Without a name? Did you not curse my levity,
Or think upon her death with the less sorrow
That she had scap'd a punishment more killing,
Oh how I shame to think on't.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Sir, in my
Opinion, 'twas an argument of love
To your Maria, for whose sake you could
Affect one that but carried her small likeness.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: No more, you are too charitable, but
I know my guilt, and will from henceforth never
Change words with that strange maid, whose innocent face
Like your Maria's won so late upon me:
My passions are corrected, and I can
Look on her now, and woman-kind, without
Love in a thought; 'tis thus, I came to tell you,
If after this acknowledgement, you'll be
So kind to shew me in what silent grave
You have dispos'd your daughter, I will ask
Forgiveness of all her dust, and never leave,
Till with a loud confession of my shame,
I wake her ghost, and that pronounce my pardon:
Will you deny this favour? then farewel,
I'll never see you more: ha!

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Be not deluded, Sir, upon my life
This is the soul whom you but thought Maria
In my daughters habit; what did you mean Nurse?
I knew she would but cozen you, is she not like now?
One dew unto another is not nearer.

speeches.speaker: Nu.
verse: She thinks she is a gentlewoman;
And that imagination has so taken her,
See scorns to speak, how handsomly she carries it,
As if she were a well bred thing, her body?
And I warrant you, what looks?

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Pray be not foolish.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: I disturb no body, speak but half a word
And I am satisfied, but what needs that?
I'll swear 'tis she.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: But do not, I beseech you,
For trust me, Sir, you know not what I know.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: Peace then,
And let me pray, she holds up her hands with me.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: This will betray all.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: Love ever honor'd,
And ever young, thou Soveraign of all hearts,
Of all our sorrows, the sweet ease.
Does she still cosin me?

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: You will see anon,
'Twas her desire, expect the issue, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: My soul's so big, I cannot pray; 'tis she,
I will go nearer.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: Here's Mr. Algripe, and other strangers, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Here good Lady,
Upon my knees I ask thy worships pardon;
Here's the whole summ I had with thy fair Daughter;
Would she were living, I might have her peace too,
And yield her up again to her old liberty:
I had a wife before, and could not marry;
My pennance shall be on that man that honor'd her,
To conferr some Land.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: This is incredible.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: 'Tis truth

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: Do you know me, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Ha. the Gentleman I deceiv'd.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: My name is Lurcher.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: 'Shat have thy Mortgage.

speeches.speaker: Lu.
verse: I ha that already, no matter for the Deed
If you release it.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I'll do't before thy witness;
But where's thy Sister? if she live I am happy, though
I conceal our contract, which was
Stolen from me with the Evidence of this Land.

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: Your daughter smiles.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: I hope she lives, but where, I cannot tell, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Even here, and please you, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Nay, 'tis she;
To work thy fair way, I preserved you brother,
That would have lost me willingly, and serv'd ye
Thus like a boy; I served you faithfully,
And cast your plots to preserve your credit;
Your soul ones I diverted to fair uses;
So far as you would hearken to my counsel;
That all the world may know how much you owe me.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Welcome entirely, welcome my dear Alathe,
And when I lose thee agen, blessing forsake me:
Nay, let me kiss thee in these cloaths.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: And I too,
And bless the time I had so wise a sister, wer't thou the little thief?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: I stole the contract, I must confess,
And kept it to my self, it most concern'd me.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: Cotracted? this destroys his after marriage.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
verse: Dare you give this hand
To this young Gentleman? my heart goes with it.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Maria alive! how my heart's exalted, 'tis my duty;
Take her Frank Hartlove, take her; and all joyes
With her; besides some Lands to advance her Joynture:

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: What I have is your own, and blessings crown ye.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: Give me room,
And fresh air to consider, Gentlemen,
My hopes are too high.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
verse: Be more temperate,
Or I'll be Welsh again.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: A day of wonder.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: Lady, your love, I ha kept my word; there was
A time, when my much suffering made me hate you,
And to that end I did my best to cross you:
And fearing you were dead, I stole your Coffin,
That you might never more usurp my Office:
Many more knacks I did, which at the Weddings
Shall be told of as harmless tales.

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: Hollow your throats a pieces, I am at home;
If you can roar me out again —

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: What thing is this?

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: A continent of Fleas: room for the Pageant;
Make room afore there; your kinsman Madam.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: My kinsman? let me wonder!

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: Do, and I'll wonder too to see this company
At peace one with another; 'tis not worth
Your admiration, I was never dead yet;
Y're merry Aunt, I see, and all your company:
If ye be not, I'll fool up, and provoke ye:
I will do any thing to get your love again:
I'll forswear Midnight, Taverns and Temptations;
Give good example to your Grooms, the Maids
Shall go to bed, and take their rest this year;
None shall appear with blisters in their bellies.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: And when you will fool again, you may go ring.

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: Madam, have mercy.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Your submission, Sir,
I gladly take; we will
Enquire the reason of this habit afterwards;
Now you are soundly sham'd, well, we restore you
Where's Toby?
Where's the Coachman?

speeches.speaker: Nur.
verse: He's a bed, Madam.
And has an ague, he says.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: I'll be his Physitian.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: We must a foot then.

speeches.speaker: Lur.
verse: E'er the Priest ha done
Toby shall wait upon you with his Coach,
And make your Flanders Mares dance back agen we'ye,
I warrant you Madam you are mortified,
Your sute shall be granted too.

speeches.speaker: Wild.
verse: Make, make room afore thee.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Home forward with glad hearts, home child.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
verse: I wait you.

speeches.speaker: Ha.
verse: On joyfully, the cure of all our grief,
Is owing to this pretty little Thief.

plays.play_title: THE WOMANS PRIZE, OR THE TAMER TAM'D. A Comedy.

speeches.speaker: M^.
verse: GOd give 'em joy.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Amen.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Amen, say I too:
The pudding's now i'th' proof, alas poor wench.
Through what a mine of patience must thou work,
^ thou know'st good hour more?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: 'Tis too true: Certain,
Methinks her father has dealt harshly with her,
Exceeding harshly, and not like a Father,
To match her to this Dragon; I protest
I pity the poor Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Methinks now,
He's not so terrible as people think him.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: This old thief flatters, out of meer devotion,
To please the Father for his second daughter.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: But shall he have her?

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Yes, when I have Rome.
And yet the father's for him.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: I'll assure ye,
I hold ^im a good man.

speeches.speaker: Sop^.
verse: Yes sure a wealthy,
But whether a good womans man, is doubtful.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Would 'twere no worse.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: What though his other wife,
Out of her most abundant soberness,
Out of her daily hue and cries upon him,
(For sure she was a rebel) turn'd his temper,
And forc'd him blow as high as she? dos't follow
He must retain that long since buried Tempest,
To this soft Maid?

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: I fear it.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: So do I too:
And so far, that if God had made me woman,
And his wife that must be—

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: What would you do, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: I would learn to eat coals with an angry Cat,
And spit sire at him: I would (to prevent him)
Do all the ramping, roaring tricks, a whore
Being drunk, and tumbling ripe, would tremble at:
There is no safety else, nor moral wisdom.
To be a wife, and his.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: So I should think too.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: For yet the bare remembrance of his first wife
(I tell ye on my knowledge, and a truth too)
Will make him start in's sleep, and very often
Cry out for Cudgels, Colestaves, any thing;
Hiding his breeches out of fear, her Ghost
Should walk, and wear 'em yet. Since his first marriage,
He is no more the still Petruchio,
Than I am Babylon.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: He's a good fellow,
And on my word I love him: but to think
A fit match for this tender soul—.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: His very frown, if she but say her prayers
Louder than men talk treason, makes him tinder;
The motion of a Dial, when he's testy,
Is the same trouble to him as a Water-work;
She must do nothing of her self; not eat,
Drink, say Sir, how do ye? make her ready, unready,
Unless he bid her.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: He will bury her,
Ten pound to twenty shillings, within these three weeks

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: I'll be your half.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: He loves her most extreamly,
And so long 'twill be Honey-moon. Now Jaques.
You are a busie man I am sure.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: Yes certain,
This old sport must have eggs,

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: Not yet this ten daies.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: Sweet Gentlemen with Muskadel.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: That's right, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: This fellow broods his Master: speed ye Jaques.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: We shall be for you presently.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: Your worships
Shall have it rich and neat: and o' my conscience
As welcome as our Lady-day: Oh my old Sir,
When shall we see your worship run at Ring?
That hour, a standing were worth money.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: So Sir.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: Upon my little honesty, your Mistriss,
If I have any speculation, must think
This single thrumming of a Fiddle,
Without a Bow, but even poor sport.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Y'are merry.

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: Would I were wise too: so God bless your worship.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: The fellow tells you true.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: When is the day man?
Come, come, you'll steal a marriage.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Nay, believe me:
But when her Father pleases, I am ready,
And all my friends shall know it.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Why no^ now?
One charge had serv'd for both.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: There's reason in't.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Call'd Rowland—

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Will ye walk?
They'll think we are lost: Come Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: You have wip'd him now.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: So will he never the wench, I hope.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: I wish it.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Now Livia, if you'll go away to night,
If your affections be not made of words.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: I love you, and vou know how dearly Rowland,
Is there none near us? my affections ever
Have been your servants; with what superstition
I have ever Sainted you—

speeches.speaker: Row:
verse: Why then take this way.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: 'Twill be a childish, and a less prosperous course;
Than ^ that knows not care: why should we do
Our honest and our hearty love such wrong,
To over-run our fortunes?

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Then you flatter.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Alas, you know I cannot.

speeches.speaker: Rom.
verse: What hope's left else
But flying to enjoy ye?

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: None so far,
For let it be admitted, we have time,
And all things now in other expectation,
My father's bent against us; what but ruine,
Can such a by-way bring us? if your fears
Would let you look with my eyes, I would shew you,
And certain, how our staying here would win us
A course, though somewhat longer, yet far surer.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: And then Moroso h'as ye.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: No such matter
For hold this certain, begging, stealing, whoring,
Selling, (which is a sin unpardonable)
Of counterfeit Cods, or musty English Croacus;
Switches, or Stones for th' tooth-ache sooner finds me,
Than that drawn Fox Moroso.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: But his money,
If wealth may win you—

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: If a Hog may be
High Priest among the Jews? his money Rowland?
Oh Love forgive me, what faith hast thou?
Why, can his money kiss me?

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Behind,
Laid out upon a Petticoat: or graspe me
While I cry, Oh good thank you? o'my troth
Thou mak'st me merry with thy fear: or lie with me,
As you may do? alas, what fools you men are?
His mouldy money? half a dozen Riders,
That cannot sit, but stampt fast to their Saddles?
No Rowland, no man shall make use of me;
My beauty was born free, and free I'll give it
To him that loves, not buys me. You yet doubt me,

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: I cannot say I doubt ye.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Goe thy ways,
Thou art the prettiest puling piece of passion:
Y'faith I will not fail thee.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: I had rather—

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Prethee believe me, if I do not carry it,
For both our goods—

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: But—

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: What but?

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: I would tell you.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: I know all you can tell me; all's but this,
^ would have me, and lie with me; is't not so?

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Why you shall; will that content you? Goe.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: I am very loth to goe.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Now o' my conscience
Thou art an honest fellow: here's my Sister;
Go, prethee go; this kiss, and credit me,
E'r I am three nights older, I am for thee:
You shall hear what I do.
Farewel.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Farewel.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Alas poor fool, how it looks?
It would ev'n hang it self, should I but cross it.
For pure love to the matter I must hatch it.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: Nay, never look for merry hour, Maria,
If now you make it not; let not your blushes,
Your modesty, and tenderness of spirit,
Make you continual Anvile to his anger:
Believe me, since his first wife set him going,
Nothing can bind his rage: Take your own council,
You shall not say that I perswaded you.
But if you suffer him—

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Stay, shall I do it?

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: Have you a stomach to't?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I never shew'd it.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: 'Twill shew the rarer and the stronger in you.
^ do not say I urg'd you.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I am perfect,
Like Curtius, to redeem my Countrey, I have
L^ap'd into this gulph of marriage, and I'll do it.
Farewel all poorer thoughts, but spight and anger,
Till I have wrought a miracle. Now cosin,
^ am no more the gentle, tame Maria;
^stake me not; I have a new soul in me
^ade of a North wind, nothing but tempest;
^ad like a tempest shall it make all ruin,
Till I have run my Will out.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: This is brave now,
If you continue it; but your own Will lead you.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Adieu all tenderness, I dare continue;
Maids that are made of fears, and modest blushes,
V^w me, and love example.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: Here is your Sister.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Here is the brave old mans love.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: That loves the young man.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I and hold thee there wench: what a grief of heart is't?
When Paphos Revels should rowze up old night,
To sweat against a Cork; to lie and tell
The clock o'th lungs, to rise sport starv'd?

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Dear Sister,
Where have you been, you talk thus?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Why at Church, wench;
Where I am ti'd to talke thus: I am a wife now.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: It seems so, and a modest.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: You are an ass;
When thou art married once, thy modesty
Will never buy thee pins.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: 'Bless me.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: From what?

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: From such a tame fool as our cosin Livia?

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: You are not mad.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Yes wench, and so must you be,
^ none of our acquaintance: mark me Livia;
^ indeed fit for our sex: 'Tis bed time.
^ardon me yellow Hymen, that I mean
Thine offerings to protract, or to keep fasting
^ valiant Bridegroom.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Whither will this woman?

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: You may perceive her end.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Or rather fear it.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Dare you be partner in't?

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Leave it Maria,
I fear I have mark'd too much, for goodness leave it;
Divest you with obedient hands, to bed.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: To bed? no Livia, there are Comets hang
Prodigious over that yet; there's a fellow
Must yet before I know that heat (ne'r start wench)
Be made a man, for yet he is a monster;
Here must his head be Livia.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Never hope it.
'Tis as easie with a Sive to scoop the Ocean, as
To tame Petruchio.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Stay: Lucina hear me,
Never unlock the treasure of my womb
For humane fruit, to make it capable;
Nor never with thy secret hand make brief
A mothers labor to me; if I do
Give way unto my married Husband's Will,
Or be a Wife in any thing but hopes,
Till I have made him easie as a child,
And tame as fear, he shall not win a smile,
Or a pleas'd look, from this austerity,
Though it would pull another Joynture from him,
And make him ev'ry day another man;
And when I kiss him, till I have my Will,
May I be barren of delights, and know
Only what pleasures are in dreams, and guesses.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: A strange Exordium.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: All the several wrongs
Done by Imperious Husbands to their Wives
These thousand years and upwards, strengthen thee:
Thou hast a brave cause.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: And I'll do it bravely,
Or may I knit my life out ever after.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: In what part of the world got she this spirit?
Yet pray Maria, look before you truly,
Besides the obedience of a wife;
Which you will find a heavy imputation,
Which yet I cannot think your own, it shews
So distant from your sweetness.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: 'Tis I swear.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Weigh but the person, and the hopes you have,
To work this desperate cure.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: A weaker subject
Would shame the end I aim at, disobedience.
You talk too tamely: By the faith I have
In mine own noble Will, that childish woman
That lives a prisoner to her Husbands pleasure,
Has lost her making, and becomes a beast,
Created for his use, not fellowship.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: His first wife said as much.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: She was a fool,
And took a scurvy course; let her be nam'd
'Mongst those that wish for things, but dare not do 'em:
I have a new dance for him.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Are you of this faith?

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: Yes truly, and will die in't.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Why then let's all wear breeches.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Now thou com'st near the nature of a woman;
Hang these tame hearted Eyasses, that no sooner
See the Lure out, and hear their Husbands hollow,
But cry like Kites upon 'em: The free Haggard
(Which is that woman, that hath wing, and knows it,
Spirit and plume) will make an hundred checks,
To shew her freedom, sail in ev'ry air,
And look out ev'ry pleasure; not regarding
Lure, nor quarry, till her pitch command
What she desires, making her foundred keeper
Be glad to fling out trains, and golden ones,
To take her down again.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: You are learned, Sister;
Yet I say still take heed.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: A witty saying;
I'll tell thee Livia, had this fellow tired
As many wives as horses under him,
With spurring of their patience; had he got
A Patent, with an Office to reclaim us,
Confirm'd by Parliament; had he all the malice
And subtilty of Devils, or of us,
Or any thing that's worse than both.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Hey, hey boys, this is excellent.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Or could he
Cast his wives new again, like Bels, to make 'em
Sound to his Will; or had the fearful name
Of the first breaker of wild women: yet,
Yet would I undertake this man, thus single,
And, spight of all the freedom he has reach'd to,
Turn him and bend him as I list, and mold him
Into a babe again; that aged women,
Wonting both teeth and spleen, may Master him.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: Thou wilt be chronicl'd.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: That's all I aim at.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: I must confess, I do with all my heart
Hate an imperious Husband, and in time
Might be so wrought upon.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: To make him cuckold?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: If he deserve it.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Then I'll leave ye Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: Thou hast not so much noble anger in thee.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Go sleep, go sleep, what we intend to do,
Lies not for such starv'd souls, as thou hast Livia.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Good night: the Bridegroom will be with you presently.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: That's more than you know,

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: If ye work upon him,
As you have promised, ye may give example,
Which no doubt will be followed.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: So.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: Good night: we'll trouble you no further.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: If you intend no good, pray do no harm.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: None, but pray for you.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: Cheer wench.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Now Byancha,
Those wits we have, let's wind 'em to the height.
My rest is up wench, and I pull for that
Will make me ever famous. They that lay
Foundations, are half-builders, all men say.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: My Master forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Oh how does thy Master? prethee commend me to him.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: How's this? my Master stays forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Why let him stay, who hinders him forsooth?

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: The Revel's ended now,
To visit you.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I am not sick.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: I mean to see his chamber forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Am I his Groom? where lay he last night forsooth?

speeches.speaker: Jap.
verse: In the low matted Parlour.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: There lies his way by the long Gallery.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: I mean your chamber: y'are very merry Mistriss.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: 'Tis a good sign I am sound hearted Jaques:
But if you'll know where I lie, follow me;
And what thou seest, deliver to thy Master.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: Do gentle Jaques.

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: Ha, is the wind in that door?
By'r Lady we shall have foul weather then:
I do not like the shuffling of these women,
They are mad beasts, when they knock their heads together:
I have observ'd them all this day; their whispers,
One in anothers ear, their signs and pinches,
And breaking often into violent laughters:
As if the end they purpos'd were their own.
Call you this weddings? Sure this is a knavery,
A very trick, and dainty knavery,
Marvellous finely carried, that's the comfort:
What would these women do in ways of honor?
That are such Masters this way? Well, my Sir
Has been as good at finding out these toys,
As any living; if he lose it now,
At his own peril be it. I must follow.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: You that are married, Gentlemen; have at ye
For a round wager now.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Of this nights Stage?

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: I am your first man, a pair of Gloves of twenty shilling^

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Done: who takes me up next? I am for all bet^

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Well lusty Lawrence, were but my night now,
Old as I am, I would make you clap on Spurs,
But I would reach you, and bring you to your trot too:
I would Gallants.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Well said good Will; but where's the staff boy, ha
Old father Time, your hour-glass is empty.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: A good tough train would break thee all to pieces;
Thou hast not breath enough to say thy prayers.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: See how these boys despise us. Will you to bed son
This pride will have a fall.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Upon your daughter;
But I shall rise again, if there be truth
In Eggs, and butter'd Parsnips.

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: Will you to bed son, and leave talking?
To morrow morning we shall have you look,
For all your great words, like St. George at Kingston,
Running a foot-back from the furious Dragon,
That with her angry tail belabours him
For being lazie.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: His courage quench'd, and so far quench'd —

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: 'Tis well Sir.
What then?

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Fly, fly, quoth then the fearfuldwarfe;
Here is no place for living man.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
prose: Well my masters, if I do sink under my busine^ as I find 'tis very possible, I am not the first that has m^ carried; So that's my comfort, what may be done wit^ out impeach or waste, I can and will do.
How now, is my fair Bride a bed?

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
prose: No truly, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
prose: Not a bed yet? body o' me: we'll up and ^ her: here's a coil with a Maiden-head, 'tis not intail'd, it?

speeches.speaker: Petru.
prose: If it be, I'll try all the Law i'th' Land, but I'll it off: let's up, let's up, come.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
prose: That you cannot neither.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
prose: Why?

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
prose: Unless you'll drop through the Chimney like a D^ or force a breach i'th' windows: you may untile the ho^ 'tis possible.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
prose: What dost thou m^an?

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
prose: A moral, Sir, the Ballad will express it:
The wind and the rain, has turn'd you back again,
And you cannot be lodged there. The truth is, all the d^
Are baracadoed; not a Cathole, but holds a murd'rer i^
She's victuall'd for this month.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
prose: Art not thou drunk?

speeches.speaker: Soph.
prose: He's drunk, he's drunk; come, come, let's up.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
prose: Yes, yes, I am drunk: ye may go up, ye may ^tlemen, but take heed to your heads: I say no more.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
prose: I'll try that.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
prose: How dost thou say? the door fast lock'd fellow

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
prose:
Yes truly Sir, 'tis lock'd, and guarded too; two as desperate tongues planted behind it, as e'er yet ^ter'd: they stand upon their honors, and will not give
without strange composition, I'll assure you; marching a ^ay with their Pieces cockt, and Bullets in their mouths, will not satisfie them.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
prose: How's this? how's this? they are—
Is there another with her?

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
prose: Yes marry is there, and an Enginier.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Who's that for Heavens sake?

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
prose: Colonel Byancha, she commands the works: Spi^la's but a Ditcher to her, there's a half-moon: I am but a poor man, but if you'll give me leave, I'll venture a years wages, draw all your force before it, and mount your ablest Piece of battery, you shall not enter it these three nights yet.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
prose: I should laugh at that good Jaques.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
prose: Beat back again, she's fortified for ever.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
prose: Am I drunk now, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Soph.
prose: He that dares most, go up now, and be cool'd.
I have scap'd a pretty scowring.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
prose: What are they mad? have we another Bedlam?
They do not talke I hope?

speeches.speaker: Soph.
prose: Oh terribly, extreamly fearful, the noise at London-bridge is nothing near her.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
prose: How got she tongue?

speeches.speaker: Soph.
prose: As you got tail, she was born to't.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
prose: Lock'd out a doors, and on my wedding night?
Nay, and I suffer this, I may goe graze:
Come Gentlemen, I'll batter; are these virtues?

speeches.speaker: Soph.
prose:
Do, and be beaten off with shame, as I was: I went up, came to th'door, knock'd, no body answer'd; knock'd lo^der, yet heard nothing: would have broke in by force; when suddainly a Water-work flew from the window with such violence, that had I not duck'd quickly like a Fryer,
^ra quis nescit? The chamber's nothing but a meer Ostend, in every window Pewter Cannons mounted, you'll quickly ^d with what they are charg'd, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
prose: Why then tantara for us.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
prose: And all the lower Works lin'd sure with small shot, long tongues with Fire-locks, that at twelve score blank hit to the heart: now and ye dare go up.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: The window opens, beat a parley first;
I am so much amaz'd, my very hair stands.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: Why how now Daughter: what intrench'd?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: A little guarded for my safety, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: For your safety Sweet-heart? why who offends you?
I come not to use violence.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I think you cannot, Sir, I am better fortified.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: I know your end,
You would fain reprieve your Maiden-head
A night, or two.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Yes, or ten, or twenty, or say an hundred;
Or indeed, till I list lie with you.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: That's a shrewd saying from this present hour,
I never will believe a silent woman.
When they break out they are bonfires.

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: Till you list, lie with him? why who are you Madam?

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: That trim Gentlemans wife, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Cry you mercy, do you command too?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Yes marry does she, and in chief.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: I do command, and you shall go without:
(I mean your wife, for this night)

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: And for the next too wench, and so as'tfol wols

speeches.speaker: Petr^.
verse: Thou wilt not, wilt 'a?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Yes indeed dear father,
A^d till he seal to what I shall set down,
^ any thing I know for ever.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Indeed these are Bug-words.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: You hear Sir, she can talk, God be thanked.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: I would I heard it not, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: I find that all the pity bestow'd upon this woman,
Makes but an Anagram of an ill wife,
For she was never virtuous.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: You'll let me in I hope, for all this jesting.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Hope still, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: You will come down I am sure.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I am sure I will not.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: I'll fetch you then.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: The power of the whole County cannot, Sir,
Unless we please to yield, which yet I think
We shall not; charge when you please, you shall
Hear quickly from us.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Bless me from a chicken of thy hatching,
Is this wiving?

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Prethee Maria tell me what's the reason,
And doe it freely, you deal thus strangely with me?
You were not forc'd to marry, your consent
Went equally with mine, if not before it:
I hope you do not doubt I want that mettle
A man should have to keep a woman waking;
I would be sorry to be such a Saint yet:
My person, as it is not excellent,
So 'tis not old, nor lame, nor weak with Physick,
But well enough to please an honest woman,
That keeps her house, and loves her Husband.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: 'Tis so.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: My means and my conditions are no shamers
Of him that owes 'em, all the world knows that,
And my friends no reliers on my fortunes.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: All this I believe, and none of all these parcels
I dare accept against; nay more, so far
I am from making these the ends I aim at,
These idle outward things, these womens fears,
That were I yet unmarried, free to choose
Through all the Tribes of man, I'll take Petruchio
In's shirt, with one ten Groats to pay the Priest,
Before the best man living, or the ablest
That e'er leap'd out of Lancashire, and they are right ones.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: Why do you play the fool then, and stand prating
Out of the window like a broken Miller!

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: If you will have me credit you Maria,
Come down, and let your love confirm it.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Stay there, Sir, that bargain's yet to make.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: Play sure wench, the Pack s in thine own hand.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Let me die lowsie, if these two wenches
Be not brewing knavery to stock a Kingdom.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Why this is a Riddle:
I love you, and I love you not.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: It is so:
And till your own experience do untie it,
This distance I must keep,

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: If you talk more,
I am angry, very angry.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I am glad on't, and I will talk.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Prethee peace,
Let me not think thou art mad. I tell thee woman,
If thou goest forward, I am still Petruchio.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: And I am worse, a woman that can fear
Neither Petruchio Furius, nor his fame,
Nor any thing that tends to our allegeance;
There's a short method for you, now you know me.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: If you can carry't so, 'tis very well.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: No, you shall carry it, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Peace gentle Low-bel.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: Use no more words, but come down instantly,
I charge thee by the duty of a child.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Prethee come Maria, I forgive all.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Stay there; That duty, that you charge me by
(If you consider truly what you say)
Is now another man's, you gave't away
I' th' Church, if you remember, to my Husband:
So all you can exact now, is no more
But only a due reverence to your person,
Which thus I pay: Your blessing, and I am gone
To bed for this night.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: This is monstrous:
That blessing that St. Dunstan gave the Devil,
If I were neer thee, I would give thee —
Pull thee down by th' nose.

speeches.speaker: By.
verse: Saints should not rave, Sir;
A little Rubarb now were excellent.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Then by that duty you owe to me Maria,
Open the door, and be obedient: I am quiet yet.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I do confess that duty, make your best on't.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Why give me leave, I will.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: Sir, there's no learning
An old stiff Jade to trot, you know the moral.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Yet as I take it, Sir, I owe no more
Than you owe back again.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: You will not Article?
All I owe, presently, let me but up, I'll pay.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Y'are too hot, and such prove Jades at length;
You do confess a duty, or respect to me from you again:
That's very near, or full the same with mine?

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Then by that duty, or respect, or what
You please to have it, go to bed and leave me,
And trouble me no longer with your fooling;
For know, I am not for you.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Well, what remedy?

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: A sine smart Cudgel. Oh that I were near thee.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: If you had teeth now, what a case were we in?

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: These are the most authentique Rebels, next
Tyrone, I ever read of.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: A week hence, or a fortnight, as you bear you,
And as I find my Will observ'd, I may,
With intercession of some friends, be brought
May be to kiss you; and so quarterly
To pay a little Rent by composition,
You understand me?

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Thou Boy thou.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Well there are more Maids than Maudlin, that's my comfort.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Yes, and more men than Michael.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: I must not to bed with this stomach, and no moat Lady.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Feed where you will, so it be sound and wholsome,
Else live at Livery, for I'll none with you.

speeches.speaker: By.
verse: You had best back one of the Dairy Maids, they'll carry.
But take heed to your girths, you'll get a bruise else.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Now if thou wouldst come down and tender me:
All the delights due to a marriage-bed,
Study such kisses as would melt a man,
And turn thy self into a thousand Figures,
To add new flames unto me, I would stand
Thus heavy, thus regardless, thus despising
Thee, and thy best allurings: all the beauty
That's laid upon your bodies, mark me well,
For without doubt your mind's are miserable,
You have no Masques for them: all this rare beauty,
Lay but the Painter and the Silk-worm by,
The Doctor with his Dyets, and the Tailor,
And you appear like flea'd Cats, not so handsome.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: And we appear like her that sent us hither,
That only excellent and beauteous nature;
Truly our selves for men to wonder at,
But too divine to handle; we are Gold,
In our own natures pure; but when we suffer
The husbands stamp upon us, then allays,
And base ones of you men are mingled with us,
And make us blush like Copper.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Then, and never
Till then are women to be spoken of,
For till that time you have no souls I take it:
Good night: come Gentlemen; I'll fast for this night,
But by this hand, well; I shall come up yet?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: There will I watch thee like a wither'd Jury,
Thou shalt neither have meat, Fire, nor Candle,
Nor any thing that's easie: do you rebel so soon?
Yet take mercy.

speeches.speaker: By.
verse: Put up your Pipes: to bed Sir, I'll assure you
A months siege will not shake us.

speeches.speaker: Moro.
verse: Well said Colonel.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: To bed, to bed Petruchio: good night Gentlemen.
You'll make my Father sick with sitting up:
Here you shall find us any time these ten days,
Unless we may march off with our contentment.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: I'll hang first.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: And I'll quarter if I do not,
I'll make you know, and fear a wife Petruchio,
There my cause lies.
You have been famous for a woman-tamer,
And bear the fear'd-name of a brave Wife-breaker:
A woman now shall take those honors off,
And tame you; nay, never look so bigg, she shall believe me,
And I am she: what think ye; good night to all,
Ye shall find Centinels.

speeches.speaker: By.
verse: If ye dare sally.

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: The devil's in 'em, ev'n the very devil, the down-right devil.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
prose: I'll devil 'em: by these ten bones I will: I'll bring it to the old Proverb, no sport no pie:—taken dow^ i'th' top of all my speed? this is fine dancing: Gentlemen stick to me. You see our Freehold's touch'd, and by thi^ light, we will beleagure 'em, and either starve 'em out, or make 'em recreant.

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: I'll see all passages stopt, but those about 'em:
If the good women of the Town dare succor 'em,
We shall have wars indeed.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: I'll stand perdue upon 'em.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: My Regiment shall lie before.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: I think so. 'tis grown too old to stand.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Let's in, and each provide his tackle,
We'll fire 'em out, or make 'em take their pardons:
Hear what I say on their bare knees—
Am I Petruchio, fear'd, and spoken of,
And on my wedding night am I thus jaded?

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Now Pedro?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Very busie Master Rowland.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: What haste man?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I beseech you pardon me,
I am not mine own man.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Thou art not mad?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: No; but believe me, as hasty—

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: The cause good Pedro?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: There be a thousand Sir; you are not married?

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Not yet.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Keep your self quiet then.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Why?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
