verse: He might have look'd more calmly for all that,
I begin to fear; but do not yet seem troubled.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: With what news travels his haste? I must secure
My self betimes, not be a King in jest,
And wear my Crown a Tenant to their breath.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Demetrius, Sir, your brother,
With other Traitors that oppose your claims,
Are fled to the Castle of Nestorius,
And fortifie.

speeches.speaker: Mes.
verse: I said not so my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: I'll have it thought so, hence.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Plant forces to batter
The walls, and in their ruin bring us work
They live not.

speeches.speaker: Eub.
verse: Good Sir hear me.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Let it work,
Were Demetrius dead, we easily might uncrown
This swoln Impostor, and my Son be fair
To piece with young Sophia, who I hear
Repents her late affront.

speeches.speaker: Eub.
verse: Their lives may do
You service, let not blood stain your beginnings
The people not yet warm in their allegeance,
May think it worth their tumult to revenge it
With hazard of your self.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Who dares but think it?
Yet offer first our mercy, if they yield,
Demetrius must not live, my Lord your counsel,
What if he were in heaven?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: You have my consent,
You sha'not stay long after him.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Sophia is
Not my Sister,
To prevent all that may indanger us, we'll marry her;
That done, no matter though we stand discover'd,
For in her Title then we are King of Epire,
Without dispute,

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Hum; in my judgement, Sir,
That wonot do so well.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: What's your opinion?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: He countermines my plot: are you so cunning

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: What's that you mutter; Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: I mutter, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Best say I am no King, but some impostor
Rais'd up to gull the state.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Very fine to have said within
Few hours you'd been no King, nor like to be,
Was not in the compass of High Treason
I take it.

speeches.speaker: Eub.
verse: Restrein your anger, the Kings mov'd, speak not.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: I will speak louder; do I not know him?
That self-same hand that rais'd him to the throne
Shall pluck him from it, is this my reward?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Our guard, to prison with him,

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Me to prison?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Off with his head.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: My head?

speeches.speaker: Eub.
verse: Vouchsafe to hear me, great Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: How dares he be so insolent?
I ha' wrought my self into a fine condition,
Do'e know me Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Very well my Lord;
How are we bound to heaven for multiplying
These blessings on the Kingdom.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: We allow it.

speeches.speaker: Eub.
verse: Counsel did never blast a Princes ear.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Convey him to the sanctuary of Rebels,
N^storius house, where our proud brother has
Enscons'd himself, they'll entertain him lovingly,
He will be a good addition to the Traitors,
Obey me, or you dye for't, what are Kings
When subjects dare affront 'em?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: I shall vex
Thy soul for this.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Away with him: when Kings
Frown, let offenders tremble, this flows not
From any cruelty in my nature, but
The fate of an Usurper: he that will
Be confirm'd great without just title to't,
Must lose compassion, know what's good, not do't.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: Madam, the Princess Sophia.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: I attend her Highness.
How much your grace honors your humble servant

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: I hope my brother's well.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: I hope so too, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: Do you but hope? he came to be your guest.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: We are all his, whilst he is pleas'd to honor
This poor roof with his royal presence, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: I came to ask your pardon Polidora.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: You never, Madam, trespass'd upon me,
Wrong not your goodness.

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: I can be but penitent,
Unless you point me out some other way
To satisfie.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Dear Madam, do not mock me.

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: There's no injury like that to love,
I find it now in my own sufferings:
But though I would have rob'd thee of Arcadius
Heaven knew a way to reconcile your hearts,
And punish me in those joys you have found:
I read the story of my loss of honor,
Yet can rejoyce, and heartily, that you
Have met your own agen.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Whom do you mean?

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: My brother.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: He is found to himself and honor,
He is my King, and though I must acknowledge
He was the glory of my thoughts, and I
Lov'd him, as you did, Madam, with desire
To be made his, reason, and duty since,
Form'd me to other knowledge, and I now
Look on him without any wish of more
Than to be call'd his subject.

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: Has he made
Himself less capable by being King?

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Of what?

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: Of your affection.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: With your pardon, Madam.
Love in that sense you mean, lost Polidora
When he forsook Arcadius, I disclaim
All ties between us, more than what a name
Of King must challenge from my obedience.

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: This does confirm my jealousie, my heart,
For my sake, Madam, has he lost his value?

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Let me beseech your grace, I may have leave
To answer in some other cause, or person:
This argument but opens a sad wound
To make it bleed afresh; we may change this
Discourse: I would elect some subject, whose
Praises may more delight your ear than this
Can mine; let's talk of young Lisimachus.

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: Ha! my presaging fears.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: How does your grace?

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: Well, you were talking of Lisimachus,
Pray give me your opinion of him.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Mine?
It will be much short of his worth: I think him
A gentleman so perfect in all goodness,
That if there be one in the world deserves
The best of women, heaven created him,
To make her happy.

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: You have, in a little, Madam,
Exprest a volume of mankind, a miracle;
But all have not the same degree of faith,
He is but young.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: What Mistriss would desire
Her servant old? he has both Spring to please
Her eye, and Summer to return a harvest.

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: He is black.

speeches.speaker: Pil.
verse: He sets a beauty off more rich,
And she that's fair will love him; faint complexions
Betray effeminate minds, and love of change:
Two beauties in a bed, compound few men;
He's not so fair to counterfeit a woman,
Nor yet so black, but blushes may betray
His modesty.

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: His proportion exceeds not.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: That praises him, and a well compacted frame
Speaks temper, and sweet flow of elements:
Vast buildings are more oft for shew than use:
I would not have my eyes put to the travel
Of many acres, e'r I could examine
A man from head to foot; he has no great,
But he may boast, an elegant composition.

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: I'll hear no more, you have so far out-done
My injuries to you, that I call back
My penitence, and must tell Polidora,
This revenge ill becomes her. Am I thought
So lost in soul to hear, and forgive this?
In what shade do I live? or shall I think
I have not, at the lowest, enough merit,
Setting aside my birth, to poize with yours:
Forgive my modest thoughts, if I rise up
In my own defence, and tell this unjust Lady
So great a winter hath not frozen yet
My cheek, but there's something nature planted,
That carries as much bloom, and spring upon't,
As yours. What flame is in your eye, but may
Find competition here? (forgive agen
My Virgin honor, what is in your lip
To tice the enamour'd soul, to dwell with more
Ambition, than the yet unwither'd blush
That speaks the innocence of mine?
Oh brother?

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: I'll talk with you anon, my Polidora,
Allow thy patience till my breath recover,
Which now comes laden with the richest news
Thy ear was ever blest with.

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: Both your looks,
And voice express some welcome accident.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Guess what in wish could make me fortunate
And heaven hath dropt that on Demetrius.

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: What means this extasie?

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: 'Twere sin to busie
Thy thoughts upon't, I'll tell thee that I could
Retein some part; 'tis too wide a joy
To be exprest so soon, and yet it falls
In a few syllables, thou wot scarce believe me,
I am no King.

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: How's that!

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Good Heaven forbid.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Forbid? Heaven has reliev'd me with a mercy
I knew not how to ask, I have, they say,
An elder brother living, crown'd already,
I only keep my name Demetrius,
Without desire of more addition,
Than to return thy servant.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: You amaze me,
Can you rejoyce to be deposed:

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: It but
Translates me to a fairer and better Kingdom
In Polidora.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Me?

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Did you not say,
Were I no King, you could be drawn to love
Me agen, that was consented to in Heaven:
A Kingdom first betraid my ambitious soul
To forget thee, that, and the flattering glories,
How willingly Demetrius does resign,
The Angels know: thus naked without Titles
^ throw me on thy charity, and shall
Boast greater Empire to be thine agen, than
To wear the triumphs of the world upon me.

speeches.speaker: Mac.
verse: Be not so careless of your self, the people
Gather in multitudes to your protection
Offering their lives and fortunes, if they may
But see you Sir, and hear you speak to 'em,
Accept their duties, and in time prevent
^our ruin.

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: Be not desperate, 'tis counsel.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: You trouble me with noise, speak Polidora

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: For your own sake preserve your self,
My fears distract my reason.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Lord Lisimachus,
With something that concerns your safety, is
^led hither, and desires a present hearing.

speeches.speaker: Mac.
verse: His soul is honest, be not, Sir, a mad man,
^nd for a Lady, give up all our freedoms.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: I'll say any thing here, Lisimachus.

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: Dear brother hear him.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: Sir, I come to yield
My self your prisoner, if my father have
^ais'd an Impostor to supplant your Title
Which I suspect, and inwardly do bleed for,
^ shall not only, by the tender of
My self, declare my innocence, but either,
^y my unworthy life, secure your person,
Or by what death you shall impose, reward
The unexpected Treason.

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: Brave young man,
Did you not hear him Brother?

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: I am not minded.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Be witness Madam, I resign my heart
^ never was anothers, you declare
^oo great a satisfaction, I hope
This will destroy your jealousie,
Remember now your danger.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: I despise it,
What fate dares injure me?

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: Yet hear me Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: Forgive me Polidora, you are happy,
My hopes are remov'd farther, I had thought
Lisimachus had meant you for his Mistriss,
'Tis misery to feed, and not know where
To place my jealousie.

speeches.speaker: Mac.
verse: Now 'tis too late,
You may be deafe, until the Cannon make,
You find your sense, we are shut up now by
A troop of Horse, thank your self.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: They will
Admit conditions.

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: And allow us quarter.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: We are all lost.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Be comforted.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: News my Lord Cassander sent by the new King.
To bear us company.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Not as prisoner?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: It does appear no otherwise, the soldiers
Declare how much they love him, by their noise
Of scorn, and joy to see him so rewarded.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: It cannot be.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: You'll find it presently,
He curses the new King, talks treason 'gainst him
As nimble as he were in's shirt, he's here.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Oh let me beg untill my knees take root
I'th'earth, Sir, can you pardon me?

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: For what?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: For Treason, desperate, most malicious Treason:
I have undone you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: It does appear
You had a Will.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: I'll make you all the recompence I can,
But e'r you kill me, hear me, know the man,
Whom I to serve my unjust ends, advanc'd
To your throne, is an impostor, a mere counterfeit,
Eubulus' Son.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: It is not then our brother?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: An insolent usurper, proud, and bloudy;
Seleucus, is no leprosie upon me?
There is not punishment enough in nature
To quit my horrid act, I have not in
My stock of blood, to satisfie with weeping,
Nor could my soul, though melted to a flood
Within me, gush out tears to wash my stain off.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: How? an Impostor, what will become on's now?
We are at his mercy:

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Sir, the peoples hearts
Will come to their own dwelling, when they see
I dare accuse my self, and suffer for it,
Have courage then young King, thy fate cannot
Be long compell'd.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Rise, our misfortune
Carries this good, although it lose our hopes,
It makes you friend with virtue, we'll expect
What providence will do.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: You are too merciful.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: Our duties shall beg heaven still to preserve you.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Our enemy desires some parley, Sir,

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: 'Tis not amiss to hear their proposition.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: I'll wait upon you.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Thou art my Angel, and canst best instruct me,
Boldly present our selves, you'll with Cassander.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: And in death be blest
To find our charity,

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: Lisimachus.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: Madam.

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: They will not miss your presence, the small time
Is spent in asking of a question.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: I wait your pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: Sir, I have a suit to you.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: To me? it must be granted.

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: If you have
Cancell'd your kind opinion of me,
Deny me not to know, who hath succeeded
Sophia in your heart, I beg the name
Of your new Mistriss.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: You shall know her, Madam,
If but these tumults cease, and fate allow us
To see the Court agen, I hope you'll bring
No mutiny against her, but this is
No time to talk of Love, let me attend you.

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: I must expect, till you are pleas'd to satisfie
My poor request, conduct me at your pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: They are too slow, dispatch new messengers,
To intreat 'em fairly hither, I am extasi'd,
Were you witness for me too? is it possible
I am what this affirms, true Leonatus,
And were you not my Father, was I given
In trust to you an Infant?

speeches.speaker: Eub.
verse: 'Tis a truth,
Our soul's bound to acknowledge, you supply'd
The absence and opinion of my Son.
Who died, but to make you my greater care
I know not of Demetrius, but suppos'd
Him dead indeed, as Epire thought you were,
Your Fathers character doth want no testimony,
Which but compar'd with what concerns Demetrius
Will prove it self King Theodosius act,
Your Royal Father.

speeches.speaker: Bish.
verse: I am subscrib'd to both his Legacies
By oath oblig'd to secresie, until
Thus fairly summon'd to reveal the trust.

speeches.speaker: Eub.
verse: Cassander had no thought you would prove thus,
To whose policie I gave this aim, although
He wrought you up to serve but as his Engine
To batter young Demetrius, for it was
Your Fathers prudent jealousie, that made him
Give out your early deaths, as if his soul
Prophecy'd his own first, and fear'd to leave
Either of you, to the unsafe protection,
Of one, whose study would be to supplant
Your right, and make himself the King of Epire.

speeches.speaker: Bish.
verse: Your Sister, fair Sophia, in your Fathers
Life, was design'd to marry with Lisimachus
That guarded her; although she us'd some Art
To quit her pupillage, and being absolute,
Declar'd love to Demetrius, which enforc'd
Macarius to discover first your brother.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: No more, lest you destroy agen Leonatus
With wonder of his fate, are they not come yet?
Something it was, I felt within my envy
Of young Demetrius's fortune, there were seeds
Scattered upon my heart, that made it swell
With thought of Empire, Princes I see cannot
Be totally eclips'd, but wherefore stays
Demetrius and Sophia, at whose names
A gentle spirit walk'd upon my blood

speeches.speaker: Eub.
verse: They are here,

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Then thus I flie into their bosoms,
Nature has rectifi'd in me, Demetrius,
The wandrings of ambition, our dear Sister
You are amaz'd, I did expect it, read
Assurance there, the day is big with wonder,

speeches.speaker: Mac.
verse: What means all this?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Lisimachus, be dear to us,
Cassander, you are welcome too.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Not I,
I do not look for't, all this sha'not bribe
My conscience to your faction, and make
Me false agen, Seleucus is no son
Of Theodosius, my dear Countrey-men
Correct your erring duties, and to that,
Your lawful King, prostrate your selves, Demetrius
Doth challenge all your knees.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: All Love and Duty,
Flow from me to my Royal King, and Brother
I am confirm'd.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: You are two credulous,
What can betray your faith so much?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Sophia, you appear sad, as if your Will
Gave no consent to this days happiness.

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: No joy exceeds Sophia's for your self.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: With your pardon, Sir, I apprehend
A cause that makes her troubled, she desires
To know, what other Mistriss, since her late
Unkindness, I have chosen to direct
My faith and service.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Another Mistriss?

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: Yes, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: And does our Sister love Lisimachus?

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: Here's something would confess.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: He must not dare
To affront Sophia.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: How my shame confounds me,
I beg your justice, without pity on
My age.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Your pennance shall be, to be faithful
To our state hereafter,

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
verse: May you live long and happy,
Leonatus, King of Epire.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: But where's your other Mistriss?

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: Even here, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Our Sister? is this another Mistriss, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Sis.
verse: It holds
To prove my thoughts were so when she began
Her sorrow for neglecting me, that sweetness
Deserv'd, I should esteem her another Mistriss,
Then when she cruelly forsook Lisimachus,
Your pardon Madam, and receive a heart
Proud with my first devotions to serve you.

speeches.speaker: Sop.
verse: In this I am crown'd agen, now mine for ever.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: You have deceiv'd her happily,
Joy to you both.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: We are ripe for the same wishes,
Polidora's part of me.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: He all my blessing.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Heaven pour full joys upon you.

speeches.speaker: Mac.
verse: We are all blest,
There wants but one to fill your arms.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: My Mistriss,
And Wife shall be my Countrey, to which I
Was in my birth contracted, your love since
Hath plaid the Priest to perfect what was ceremony
Though Kingdoms by just Titles prove our own,
The subjects hearts do best secure a Crown.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: LEt us make use of this stolen privacy,
And not loose time in protestation, Mistriss,
For 'twere in me a kind of breach of faith,
To say again I love you.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Sweet, speak softly
For though the venture of your love to me,
Meets with a willing, and a full return:
Should it arrive unto my Fathers knowledge;
This were our last discourse.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: How shall he know it?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: His watching cares are such, for my advancement,
That every where his eye is fix'd upon me:
This night that does afford us some small freedom,
At the request and much intreaty of
The Mistriss of the House, was hardly given me:
For I am never suffer'd to stir out,
But he hath spies upon me: yet I know not
You have so won upon me, that could I think
You would love faithfully (though to entertain
Another thought of you, would be my death)
I should adventure on his utmost anger.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Why do you think I can be false?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: No faith,
You'ave an honest face, but if you should —

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Let all the stor'd vengeance of heaven's justice—

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: No more, I do believe you, the dance ended,
Which this free womans ghests have vow d to have
E'r they depart, I will make home, and store me
With all the Jewels, Chains, and Gold are trusted
Unto my custody, and at the next corner,
To my Fathers house, before one at the farthest,
Be ready to receive me.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: I desire
No bond beyond your promise, let's go in,
To talk thus much, before the door, may breed Suspition.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Here are company too.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Away,
Those powers that prosper true and honest loves
Will bless our undertakings.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: 'Tis my wish, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Nay, Sir, excuse me, I have drawn you to
Too much expence already in my travel:
And you have been too forward in your love;
To make my wants your own, allow me manners
Which you must grant I want, should I increase,
The bond in which your courtesies have ti'd me:
By still consuming you, give me leave
To take mine own ways now, and I shall often,
With willingness, come to visit you, and then thank you.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: By this hand I could be angry, what do you think me?
Must we that have so long time been as one
Seen Cities, Countreys, Kingdoms, and their wonders;
Been bedfellows, and in our various journey
Mixt all our observations, part (as if
We were two Carriers at two several ways,
And as the fore-horse guides, cry God be with you)
Without or compliment, or ceremony?
In Travellers, that know transalpine garbs,
Though our designs are nee'r so serious, friend,
^t were a capital crime, it must not be:
Nay, what is more, you shall not; you e'r long,
^hall see my house, and find what I call mine
Is wholly at your service.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: 'Tis this tires me,
Sir, I were easily woo'd, if nothing else
But my Will lay in the choice: but 'tis not so,
My friends and kindred that have part of me,
And such on whom my chiefest hopes depend,
Justly expect the tender of my love
After my travel: then mine own honesty
Tells me 'tis poor, having indifferent means
To keep me in my quality and rank,
At my return, to tire anothers bounty,
And let mine own grow lusty, pardon me.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I will not, cannot, to conclude, I dare not:
Can any thing conferr'd upon my friend
Be burthensome to me? for this excuse
Had I no reason else, you should not leave me,
By a travellers faith you should not, I have said,
And then you know my humor, there's no contending.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Is there no way to 'scape this Inundation?
I shall be drown'd with folly if I go:
And after nine days, men may take me up,
With my gall broken.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Are you yet resolv'd?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Wou'd you would spare me.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: By this light I cannot
By all that may be sworn by.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Patience help me,
And heaven grant his folly be not catching:
If it be, the Town's undone, I now would give
A reasonable sum of gold to any Sheriff,
That would but lay an execution on me,
And free me from his company; while he was abroad,
His want of wit and language kept him dumb?
But Balaam's Asse will speak now, without spurring.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Speak, have I won you?—

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: You are not to be resisted.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Be ready I intreat you, the dance done,
Besides a liberal reward I have,
A bottle of Sherry in my power shall beget
New crotchets in your heads.

speeches.speaker: Musi.
verse: Tush, fear not us, we'll do our parts.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: Go in.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I know this fellow.
Belong you to the house?

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: I serve the Mistriss.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Pretty, and short, pray you Sir then inform her,
Two Gentlemen are covetous to be honor'd,
With her fair presence.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: She shall know so much,
This is a merry night with us, and forbid not
Welcome to any that looks like a man:
I'll guide you the way.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Nay, follow, I have a trick in't.

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
verse: Come, where's this Masque? fairest, for our chear,
Our thanks and service, may you long survive,
To joy in many of these nights.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I thank you.

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
verse: We must have Musick too, or else you give us,
But half a welcome.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Pray you Sir, excuse me.

speeches.speaker: Silv.
verse: By no means, Lady.

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
verse: We'll crown our liberal feast,
With some delightful strain sitting your love:
And this good company.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Since you enforce it,
I will not plead the excuse of want of skill
Or be, or nice, or curious, every year
I celebrate my marriage night; and will
Till I see my absent Husband.

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
verse: 'Tis fit freedom,

speeches.speaker: Silv.
verse: Richardo thou art dull—

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: I shall be lighter,
When I have had a heat.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Now Sir, the news?

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: Mistriss, there are two Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Where?

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: Complimenting who should first enter.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: What are they?

speeches.speaker: Serv.
prose: Heaven knows, but for their strangeness, have you never seen a Cat wash her face?

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: Just such a stir they keep, if you make but haste,
You may see 'em yet before they enter.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Let 'em be what they we'll, I'll keep them fair
Entertain, and gentle welcome.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: It shall be so.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Then let it be your pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Lets stand aside, and you shall see us have
Fine sport anon.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: A fair society, do you know these Gentlewomen?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: What are they?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: The second is a neighbors Daughter, her name is Viola. There is my kinsmans wife, Portia her name, and a Friend too.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Let her—what's she that leads the dance?

speeches.speaker: 1 Serv.
verse: A Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I see that.

speeches.speaker: 1 Serv.
verse: Indeed?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: What?

speeches.speaker: 1 Serv.
verse: A Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Udsfoot, good Sir, what's she that leads the dance?

speeches.speaker: 2 Serv.
verse: My Mistriss.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: What else?

speeches.speaker: 2 Serv.
verse: My Mistriss, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Your Mistriss? a pox on you,
'Tis my wife.
prose: What a fry of fools are here? I see 'tis treason to understand in this house: if nature were not better to them, than they can be to themselves, they would scant hit their mouths my Mistriss? is there any one with so much wit in's head, that can tell me at the first sight, what Gentlewoman that is that leads the dance?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Hum.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: How dost thou like her?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Well, a pretty Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Prethee be quiet.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I would I could
Let never any hereafter that's a man,
That has affections in him, and free passions,
Receive the least tye from such a fool as this is,
That holds so sweet a wife, 'tis lamentable to consider truly
What right he robs himself of, and what wrong
He doth the youth of such a Gentlewoman?
That knows her beauty, is no longer hers,
Than men will please to make it so, and use it
Neither of which lies freely in a Husband,
Oh what have I done, what have I done, Coxcomb?
If I had never seen, or never tasted
The goodness of this kix, I had been a made man,
But now to make a Cuckold is a sin
Against all forgiveness, worse than a murther;
I have a Wolf by the ears, and am bitten both ways.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: How now friend, what are you thinking of?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Nothing concerning you, I must be gone.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Pardon me, I'll have no going, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Then good Sir, give me leave to go to bed,
I am very weary, and ill-temper'd.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: You shall presently, the dance is done.

speeches.speaker: 1 Serv.
verse: Mistriss, these are the Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: My Husband's welcome home, dear Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: She's fair still, oh that I were a knave, or durst be one,
For thy sake coxcomb; he that invented honesty, undid me.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I thought you had not known me, y'are merry 'tis well
And how ist with these worthy Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: ~b. & Sil.
verse: We are glad to see you here again.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Oh Gent, what ha' you lost? but get you into travels, thought,
There you may learn, I cannot say what hidden virtues.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Hidden from you I am sure,
My blood boils like a furnace,
She's a fair one.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Pray entertain this Gent. with all the courtes^e,
Fitting my most especial friend.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: What this poor house may yield,
To make you welcome, dear Sir, command
Without more compliment.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I thank you:
She's wise, and speaks well too, oh what a blessing
Is gone by me, ne'er to be recovered?
prose: Well, 'twas an old shame the Devil laid up for me, and now has hit me home; if there be any ways to be dishonest, and save my self yet,— No, it must not be, why should I be a fool too—Yet those eyes would tempt another Adam, how they call to me, and tell me—S'foot, they shall not tell me any thing, Sir, will you walk in?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: How is't, Signior?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Crazie a little.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: What all you, Sir?
What's in my power, pray make use of, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: 'Tis that must do me good, she does not mock me sure?
And 't please you nothing, my disease is only weariness.

speeches.speaker: ~b.
prose: Come Gentlemen, we, ll not keep you from your beds too long.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: I ha' some business, and 'tis late, and you far from your lodging.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Well.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Come my dear Mercury, I'll bring you to your chamber, and then I am for you Maria, thou art a new wife to me now, and thou shalt find it e'r I sleep.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: This fool and his fair Wife have made me frantick
From two such Physicks for the soul, deliver me.
prose: And I, an old ass to my self, mine own rod whips me,—good Sir, no more of this, 'tis tedious, you are the best guide in your own house—go Sir—

speeches.speaker: ~b.
verse: Well you must have this wench then.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse: I hope so, I am much o'th' bow-hand else.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: Wou'd I were hang'd, 'tis a good loving little fool, that dares venture her self upon a coast she never knew yet, but these women, when they are once thirteen, god speed the plough.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Faith they'll venture further for their lading, than a Merchant, and through as many storms, but they'll be fraughted, they are mad like Carrecks, only strength and storage.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse: Come, come, you talk, you talk.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: We do so, but tell me Richardo, wot thou marry her? her?

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse: Marry her? why, what should I do with her?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: Pox, I thought we should have all shares in her, like lawful prize.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
prose: No by my faith, Sir, you shall pardon me, I lanch'd her at my own charge, without partners, and so I'll keep her.

speeches.speaker: ~b.
verse: What's the hour?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Twelve.

speeches.speaker: ~b.
verse: What shall we do the while? 'tis yet scarce eleven.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: There's no standing here, is not this the place?

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: And to go back unto her fathers house, may breed ^spition,
Let's slip into a Tavern, for an hour, 'tis very cold.

speeches.speaker: ~b.
prose:
Content, there is one hard by, a quart of burnt ^ack will recover us, I am as cold as Christmas, this steal
^ng flesh in the frosty weather, may be sweet i'th' eating, ^ut sure the Woodmen have no great catch on't; Shall's ^o?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: Thou art the strangest lover of a Tavern, What ^hall we do there now? lose the hour and our selves ^oo.

speeches.speaker: ~b.
prose: Lose a pudding; What do'st thou talk of the ^our; Will one quart muzle us? have we not ears to ^ear, and tongues to ask the Drawers, but we must stand ^ere like bawds to watch the minutes?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Prethee content thy self, we shall scout here, as ^hough we went a haying, and have some mangey prentice, ^hat cannot sleep for scratching, over-hear us; Come, Will ^ou go Sirs? when your love fury is a little frozen, you'll ^ome to us.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse: Will you drink but one quart then?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: No more I'faith.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Content.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse:
Why then, have with you, but lets be very watch
^.

speeches.speaker: ~b.
verse: The night is terrible, and I enclos'd
^ith that my vertue and my self hate most,
^arkness; yet must I fear that which I wish,
^me company, and every step I take
^nds louder in my fearful ears to night
^han ever did, the shrill and sacred bell
^hat rang me to my prayers; the house will rise
^hen I unlock the dore, were it by day
^ am bold enough, but then a thousand eyes
^arne me from going, might not heaven have made
^ time for envious prying folk to sleep,
^hilst lovers met, and yet the Sun have shone?
^et I was bold enough, to steal this key
^t of my fathers Chamber, and dare yet
^e^ture upon mine enemy, the night,
^rm'd only with my love, to meet my friend.
^las how valiant, and how fraid at once
^ove makes a Virgin? I will throw this key
^ack through a window, I had wealth enough
^ Jewels with me, if I hold his love
^ steal e'm for; farewell my place of birth,
^ never make account to look on thee again;
^nd if there be, as I have heard men say,
^hese houshold gods, I do beseech them look
^o this my charge, bless it from theeves and fire,
^nd keep, till happily my love I win,
^e from thy door, and hold my Father in.
prose: As watchful as the Belman, come, I'll lead, because ^ hate good manners, they are too tedious.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse: No more for Gods sake, how is the night boy?

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: Faith Sir, 'tis very late.

speeches.speaker: ~b.
prose: Faith, Sir, you lie, is this your jack i'th' clock-house? ^ill you strike, Sir? gi's some more sack, you varlet.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse:
Nay, if you love me, good
~berto goe,
^m monstrous hot with Wine.

speeches.speaker: ~b.
prose: Quench it again with love, Gentlemen, I will drink ^e health more, and then if my legs say me not shamefully ^y, I will go with you, give me a singular quart.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: Of what Wine Sir?

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
prose: Of Sack, you that speak confusion at the bar, of Sack, I say, and every one his quart, what a Devil lets be merry.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: You shall, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: We will, Sir, and a dryed tongue.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: And an Olive, boy, and a whole bunch of fidlers, my head swims plaguely, 'uds pretious I shall be clawd.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
prose: Pray go, I can drink no more, think on your promise, 'tis midnight Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: ~b.
prose: O that it were dum midnight now, not a word more, every man on's knees, and betake himself to his saint, here's to your wench, seignior, all this, and then away.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: I cannot drink it.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: 'Tis a toy, a toy, away wo't.

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
prose: Now dare I speak any thing, to any body living, come, Where's the fault? off with it.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
prose: I have broke my wind, Call you this Sack? — I wonder who made it? he was a sure workman, for 'tis plaguy strong work, Is it gone round?

speeches.speaker: ~b.
prose: 'Tis at the last, out of my way, good boy, Is the Moon up yet?

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: Yes, Sir.

speeches.speaker: ~b.
verse: Where is she boy?

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: There, Sir.

speeches.speaker: ~b.
verse: We shall have rain and thunder, boy.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: When Sir?

speeches.speaker: ~b.
verse: I cannot tell, but sure we shall, boy.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: The Gentleman is Wine-wise.

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
verse: Drawer?

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: Here, Sir.

speeches.speaker: ~b.
verse: Can you procure?

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: What Sir?

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
verse: A Whore, or two or three, as need shall serve, boy?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I, a good Whore were worth money, boy.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: I protest Sir, we are all together unprovided.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
prose: The mor's the pitty, boy, Can you not 'vize us where my Child?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: Why where were you brought up, boy? no inckling of a Whore? no aym my boy?

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
prose: It cannot sink in my head now, that thou shouldst marry, Why shouldst thou marry, tell me?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: I marry? I'll be hang'd first: some more wine boy.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Is she not a Whore translated? and she be, lets repair to her.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
prose: I cannot tell, she may be an offender; but signior Silvio, I shall scratch your head, indeed I shall.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Judge me, I do but jest with thee, what an she were inverted with her heeles upward, like a traitor's Coat? what care I.

speeches.speaker: ~b.
prose: I, hang her, Shall we fall out for her?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: I am a little angry, but these wenches, Did you not talke of wenches?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Boy, lend me your Candle.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
prose: Why Sir?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: To set fire to your rotten feeling, you'll keep no Whores, Rogue, no good members.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
prose: Whores, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Silv.
prose: I, Whores Sir, Do you think we come to lye with your hogsheads?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: I must beat the watch, I have long'd for't any time this three weeks.

speeches.speaker: Silv.
prose: Wee'll beat the Town too, and thou wilt, we are proof boy; Shall she kill any body?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: No, but wee'll hurt 'em dangerously.

speeches.speaker: ~ber. Silv.
prose: Now must I kill one, I cannot avoid it, boy, easily afore there with your candle; Where's your Mistriss?

speeches.speaker: Draw.
prose: A bed, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: With whom?

speeches.speaker: Draw.
prose: With my Master.

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
prose: You lye Boy, shee's better brought up than to lye with her husband, Has he not cast his head yet? next year he will be a velvet-headed Cuckold.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
prose: You are a merry Gentleman, there Sir, take hold.

speeches.speaker: Viola.
verse: This is the place, I have out-told the Clock,
For haste, he is not here. Richardo? no;
Now every power that loves and is belov'd:
Keep me from shame to night, for all you know
Each thought of mine is innocent, and pure,
As flesh and blood can hold: I cannot back;
I threw the Kywi thin, and ere I raise
My Father up, to see his daughters shame,
I'll set me down, and tell the Northern Wind,
That it is gentler than the curling West;
If it will blow me dead, but he will come;
I'saith 'tis cold; if he deceive me thus,
A woman will not easily trust a Man. Hark, What's that?

speeches.speaker: Sil. within.
prose: Th'art over long at thy pot, tom, tom, thou art over long at the pot tom.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Bless me! Whose that?

speeches.speaker: Pedro within.
verse: Whoo!

speeches.speaker: ~ber within.
verse: There Boyes.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Darkness be thou my cover, I must fly,
To thee I haste for help—

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: They have a light,
Wind, if thou lov'st a Virgin, blow it out,
And I will never shut a window more,
To keep thee from me.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: Boy?

speeches.speaker: Draw.
prose: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: Why Boy?

speeches.speaker: Draw.
prose: What say you, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: Why Boy? Art thou drunk Boy?

speeches.speaker: Draw.
prose: What would you, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: Why very good, Where are we?

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
prose: I, that's the point.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
prose: Why Sir, you will be at your Lodging presently.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: I'll go to no lodging Boy.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
prose: Whither will you go then, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: I'll go no farther.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
prose: For Gods sake, Sir, do not stay here all night.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: No more I will not, Boy, lay me down, and rowle me to a Whore.

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
prose: And me.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: There spoke an—

speeches.speaker: Silvio.
prose: Then set your foot to my foot, and up tailes all.

speeches.speaker: Viola.
prose: That is Richardo, what a noise they make?
'Tis ill done on 'em: here, Sirs, Richardo?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: What's that Boy?

speeches.speaker: Draw.
prose: 'Tis a Wench, Sir, pray Gentlemen come away.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
prose: O my dear love! How doest thou?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: Faith sweet heart? even as thou seest.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: Where's thy Wench?

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
prose: Where's this bed worme?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
prose: Speak softly for the love of heaven.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
prose: Mistriss, get you gone, and do not entice the Gentlemen, now you see they'r drunk, or I'll call the Watch, and lay you fast enough.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Alas, What are you? or, What do you mean?
Sweet love, Where's the place?

speeches.speaker: Ric.
prose: Marry sweet love, e'en here, lye down, I'll feese thee.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Good God! What mean you?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: I'll have the Wench.

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
prose: If you can get her.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: No, I'll lye with the Wench to night, and she shall be yours to morrow.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: Let go the Wench.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Let you go the Wench.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
prose: O Gentlemen, as you had mothers!

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
prose: They had no mothers; they are the Sons of bitches.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
prose: Let that be maintain'd.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Marry then.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
prose: Oh bless me heaven!

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
prose: How many is there on's?

speeches.speaker: Ric.
prose: About five.

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
prose: Why then lets fight three to three.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Content,

speeches.speaker: Draw.
prose: The Watch? the watch? the watch? Where are you?

speeches.speaker: Ric.
prose: Where are these Cowards?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: There's the Wore.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
prose: I never saw a drunken man before,
But these I think are so.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Oh!

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: I mist you narrowly there.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
prose: My state is such, I know not how to think,
A prayer fit for me, only I could move,
That never Maiden more might be in love.

speeches.speaker: Watch.
prose: Where are they, Boy?

speeches.speaker: Draw.
prose: Make no such haste, Sir, they are no runners.

speeches.speaker: ~b.
prose: I am hurt, but that's all one, I shall light upon some of ye.
Pedro, thou art a tall Gentleman, let me kiss thee.

speeches.speaker: Watch.
prose: My friend.

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
prose: Your friend? you lie.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
prose: Stand further off, the watch, you are full of fleas.

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose: Gentlemen, either be quiet, or we must make you quiet.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: Nay, good Mr. Constable, be not so Rigorou s.

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
prose: Mr. Constable, lend me thy hand of Justice.

speeches.speaker: Const.
prose: That I will Sir.

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
prose: Fy Mr. Constable, What golls you have? is Justice so blind
Y' cannot see to wash your hands? I cry you Mercy, Sir;
Your gloves are on.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
prose: Now you are up, Sir, Will you go to bed?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: I'll truckle here, Boy, give me another pillow.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
prose: Will you stand up, and let me lay it on then?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
prose: There hold him two of ye, now they are up, be going Mr. Constable.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: And this way, and that way, tom.

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
prose: And here away, and there away, tom.

speeches.speaker: Silv.
prose: This is the right way, the others the wrong.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: Th' others the wrong.

speeches.speaker: All.
prose: Thou art over-long at the pot, tom, tom.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: Lead valiantly, sweet Constable, whoop! ha Boyes.

speeches.speaker: Const.
prose: This Wine hunts in their heads.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: Give me the bill, for I'll be the Sergeant.

speeches.speaker: Const.
prose: Look to him, Sirs.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: Keep your Ranks, you Rascalls,, keep your Ranks.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: I Cannot sleep for thinking of this Asses Wife, I'll be gon presently, there's no staying here, with this Devil about me? hoe, this is the house of sleep hoe? again there, 'sfoot, the darkness, and this love together, will make me lunatick; ho?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Who calls there?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Pray take the pains to rise and light a candle.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Presently,

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Was ever man but I in such a stocks? well, this shall be a warning to me, and a fair one too, how I betray my self to such a Dunce, by way of benefit.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Did you call?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Yes, pray do me the kindness, Sir, to let me out, and not enquire why, for I must needs be gone.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Not to night, I hope, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Good Sir to night, I would not have troubled you else, pray let it be so.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Alas, Sir, my Master will be offended.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: That I have business? no I warrant ye.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Good Sir take your rest.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Pray my good friend let me appoint my own rest.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Yes, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Then shew me the way out, I'll consider you.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Good Lord, Sir,

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: If I had not an excellent temper'd patience, now should I break this fellows head, and make him understand 'twere necessary; the onely plague of this house is the unhandsome love of servants, that ne'er do their duty in the right place, but when they muster before dinner, and sweep the Table with a wodden dagger, and then they are troublesome too, to all mens shoulders, the Woodcocks flesht agen, now I shall have a new stir.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Why how now friend? What do you up so late? are you well? Do you want any thing? pray speak.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Onely the cause I rise for.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: What knaves are these? What do you want? why Sirrah?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Nothing i'th' World, but the keyes to let me out of dores; I must be gon, be not against it, for you cannot stay me.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Be gon at this time? that were a merry jest.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: If there be any mirth in't, make you use on't, but I must go.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Why for loves sake?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: 'Twill benefit your understanding nothing to know the cause, pray go to bed, I'll trouble your Man only.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Nay, Sir, you have rais'd more, that has reason to curse you, and you knew all, my Wifes up, and coming down too.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Alas, it will be a trouble, pray go up to her, and let me disturbe no more, 'tis unmannerly.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Shee's here already; sweet heart: How say you by this Gentleman? he would away at midnight.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: That I am sure he will not.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Indeed I must.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Good Sir let not your homely entertainment press you to leave your bed at midnight; if you want, what my house or our town may afford you, make it your own fault if you call not for it; pray go to bed again; let me compel you, I am sure you have no power to deny a Woman; the ayr is piercing, and to a body beaten with long travel, 'twill prove an ill Physitian.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: If she speak longer I shall be a knave, as rank as ever sweat for't; Sir, if you will send your Wife up presently, I will either stay with you, d'ye mark me, or deliver you, so just a cause, that you your self, shall thrust me out of dores, both suddenly, and willingly.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I would fain hear that 'faith, pray thee go up sweet heart, I have half perswaded him, besides, he hath some private business with me.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Good night, Sir, and what content you would have,
I wish with you.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Could any man that had a back ask more! O me!
O me!

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Now deal directly with me: Why should you go?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: If you be wise do not enquire the cause, 'twill trouble you.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Why? prithee why?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: 'Faith I would not have you know it, let me go, 'twill be far better for you.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Who's that, that knocks there? i'st not at the street door?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Yes, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Who's there, cannot you speak?

speeches.speaker: Within Vio.
prose: A poor distressed Maid, for gods sake let me in.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Let her in and me out together, 'tis but one labor, 'tis pity she should stand i'th' street, it seems she knows you.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: There she shall stand for me, you are ignorant; this is a common custome of the Rogues that lie about the loose parts of the City.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: As how?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: To knock at doors in dead time of night, and use some feigned voice to raise compassion, and when the doors are open, in they rush, and cut the throats of all, and take the booty, we cannot be too careful.

speeches.speaker: Within Vi.
prose: As ever you had pity let me in, I am undone else.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Who are you?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: My name is Viola, a Gentlewoman, that ill chance hath distressed; you know my Father.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Alas of god we'll let her in, 'tis one of the Gentlewomen were here i'th' evening, I know her by her name, (poor soul) shee's cold I warrant her, let her have my warme Bed, and I'll take her fortune; come, pray come.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: It is not Viola, that's certain, she went home to her Fathers, I am sure.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Will not you be so good to let me in?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I'll be so good to have you whipt away if you stay a little longer: Shee's gone I warrant her, now let me know your cause, for I will hear it, and not repent the knowing.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Since you are so importunate, I'll tell you, I love your Wife extreamly.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Very well.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: And so well that I dare not stay.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Why?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: For wronging you, I know I am flesh and blood, and you have done me friendships infinite and often, that must require me honest, and a true Man, and I will be so, o^ I'll break my heart.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Why, you may stay for all this, methinks.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: No, though I wood be good, I am no saint, nor is it safe to try me, I deal plainly.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Come, I dare try you, do the best you can.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: You shall not, when I am right agen, I'll come and see you, till when, I'll use all Countryes, and all means, but I will lose this folly, 'tis a Divel.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Is there no way to stay you?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: No, unless you will have me such a villain to you, as all men shall spit at me.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Do's she know you love her?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: No, I hope not, that were recompence fit for a Rogue to render her.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: If ever any had a faithful friend, I am that Man, and I may glory in't, this is he, that ipse, he that passes all Christendome for goodness, he shall not over goe me in his friendship, 'twere recreant and base, and I'll be hang'd first, I am resolv'd, go thy wayes, a Wife will never part us: I have consider'd, and I find her nothing to such a friend as thou art; I'll speak a bold world, take your time and woe her, you have overcome me clearly, and do what's fitting with her, you conceive me, I am glad at heart you love her: by this light, ne're stare upon me, for I will not flye from it, if you had spoken sooner, sure you had been serv'd; Sir, you are not every Man, now to your taske, I give you free leave, and the sin is mine if there be any in it.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: He will be hang'd before he makes this good, he cannot be so innocent a Coxcombe, he can tell ten sure, if I had never known you as I have done, I might be one, as others perhaps sooner, but now 'tis impossible, there's too much good between us.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Well, thou art e'en the best man— I can say no more, I am, so over-joy'd, you must stay this night, and in the morning go as early as you please, I have a toy for you.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: I thought this pill would make you sick.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: But where you mean to be I must have notice,
And it must be hard by too, do you mark me?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Why, What's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: There is a thing in hand.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Why? What thing?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: A sound one, if it take right, and you be not peevish. We two will be— you would little think it; as famous for our friendship—

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: How?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: If Heaven please, as ever Damon was, and Pytheas; or Pylades, and Orestes, or any two that ever were: do you conceive me yet?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: No, by my troth, Sir; he will not help me up sure.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: You shall anon, and for our names, I think they shall live after us, and be remember'd while there is a story; or I'll lose my aime.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: What a vengeance ailes he? How do you?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Yes faith, we two will be such friends, as the world shall ring of.

speeches.speaker: M^r.
prose: And why is all this?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: You shall enjoy my wife.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Away, away.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: The wonder must begin, so I have cast it, 'twill be scurvy else, you shall not stir a foot in't, pray be quiet till I have made it perfect.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: What shall a Man do with this wretched fellow? there is no mercy to be used towards him, he is not capable of any pitty, he will in spight of course be a Cuckold, And who can help it? must it begin so needs Sir? — think agen.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Yes marry must it, and I my self will woe this woman for you, Do you perceive it now? ha?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Yes, now I have a little sight ith' matter; O that thy head should be so monstrous, that all thy Servants hats may hang upon't! but do you meane to do this?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Yes certain, I will woe her, and for you, strive not against it, 'tis the overthrow of the best plot that ever was then.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Nay, I'll assure you, Sir, I'll do no harm, you have too much about you of your own.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Have you thought of a place yet?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: A place?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I a place where you will bide, prethee no more of this modesty, 'tis foolish, and we were not determin'd to be absolute friends indeed, 'twere tolerable.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: I have thought, and you shall hear from me.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Why, this will gain me everlasting glory; I have the better of him, that's my comfort, good night.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Good night, well go thy wayes, thou art the tydiest wittall this day I think above ground, and yet thy end for all this must be mottly.

speeches.speaker: Tink.
prose: 'Tis better cold; a plague upon these Rogues, how wary they are grown? not a door open now, but double barr'd; not a Window, but up with a case of wood like a spice box, and their locks unpickable, the very Smiths that were half ventures, drink penitent, single Ale, this is the Iron age, the Ballad sings of; well, I shall meet with some of our loose Linnen yet, good fellows must not starve; here's he shall shew God a mighties dog bolts, if this hold.

speeches.speaker: Dorothy.
prose: Faith thou art but too merciful, that's thy fault, thou art as sweet a Thief, that sin excepted, as ever suffer'd, that's a proud word, and I'll maintain it.

speeches.speaker: Tinck.
prose: Come, prethee let's shogg off, and browze an hour or two, there's Ale will make a Cat speak, at the harrow, we shall get nothing now, without we batter, 'tis grown too near morning, the Rogues sleep sober, and are watchful.

speeches.speaker: Dorit.
prose: We want a Boy extreamly for this function, kept under for a year, with milk, and knot-grass; in my time I have seen a boy do wonders Bobbin the red Tinker had a Boy, Rest his Soul, he suffer'd this time 4 years, for two Spoons, and a Pewter Candlestick, that sweet Man had a Boy, as I am Curstend Whore, would have run through a Cat hole, he would have boulted such a piece of Linen in an evening —

speeches.speaker: Tinck.
prose: Well, we will have a Boy, prethee lets go, I am vengeance cold I tell thee.

speeches.speaker: Dorothy.
prose: I'll be hang'd before I stir without some purchase, by these ten bones, I'll turn she-ape, and untile a house, but I'll have it, it may be I have a humor to be hang'd, I cannot tell.

speeches.speaker: Tinck.
prose: Peace, you flead Whore, thou hast a mouth like a Bloodhound, here comes a night-shade.

speeches.speaker: Dorit.
prose: A Gentlewoman Whore, by this darkness I'll case her to the skin.

speeches.speaker: Tinck.
prose: Peace, I say.

speeches.speaker: Viola,
verse: What fear have I endur'd this dismal night?
And what disgrace, if I were seen and known?
In which this darkness onely is my friend,
That onely has undone me; a thousand curses
Light on my easie, foolish, childish love,
That durst so lightly lay a confidence
Upon a Man, so many being false;
My weariness, and weeping, makes me sleepy, I must lie down.

speeches.speaker: Tinck.
prose: What's this? a Prayer, or a Homily, or a Ballad of good councel? she has a Gown, I am sure.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: Knock out her brains, and then shee'll nee'r bite.

speeches.speaker: Tinck.
prose: Yes, I will knock her, but not yet, you? woman?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
prose: For Gods sake what are you?

speeches.speaker: Tinck.
prose: One of the groomes of your wardrobe, come, uncase, uncase; byr Lady a good Kersey.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Pray do not hurt me, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: Let's have no pitty, for if you do, here's that shall cut your whistle.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
prose: Alas, what would you have? I am as miserable as you can make me any way.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: That shall be try'd.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Here, take my Gown, if that will do you pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Tink.
prose: Yes marry will it, look in the Pockets Doll, there may be birds.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: They are flown, a pox go with them, I'll have this Hat, and this Ruffe too, I like it, now will I flourish like a Lady, brave, I faith boy.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Y'are so gentle people to my seeming,
That by my truth I could live with you.

speeches.speaker: Tin.
prose: Could you so? a pretty young round wench, well bloudded, I am for her, Theeves.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: But by this I am not, coole your Codpiece, Rogue, or I'll clap a spell upon't, shall take your edge off with a very vengeance.

speeches.speaker: Tin.
prose: Peace, horse-flesh, peace, I'll cast off my Amazon, she has walk'd too long, and is indeed notorious, shee'll fight and scould, and drink like one of the worthies.

speeches.speaker: Dort.
prose: Uds, pretious you young contagious Whore, must you be ticing? and, Is your flesh so wranck, Sir, that two may live upon't? I am glad to hear your Cortalls grown so lusty; he was dry founder'd t'other day, wehee my pamper'd Jade of Asia.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Good Woman do not hurt me, I am sorry that I have given any cause of anger.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose:
Either bind her quickly, and come away, or by this
steel I'll tell thee, though I truss for company; now could I eate her broyl'd, or any way, without Vinegar, I must have her Nose.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: By any thing you love best, good Sir, good Woman.

speeches.speaker: Tin.
prose: Why her Nose, Dorothy?

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: If I have it not, and presently warm, I lose that I go withal.

speeches.speaker: Tin.
prose: Wood the Devil had that thou goest withall, and thee together, for sure he got thy whelps if thou hast any, shees thy deere dad, Whore! put up your cutpurse; an I take my switch up, 'twill be a black time with you else, sheth your bung Whore.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: Will you bind her? we shall stand here prating, and be hang'd both.

speeches.speaker: Tin.
prose: Come, I must bind you, not a word, no crying.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Do what you will, indeed I will not cry.

speeches.speaker: Tin.
prose: Hurt her not, if thou dost, by Ale and Beer, I'll clout thy old bald brain pan, with a piece of Brass, you Bitch incarnate.

speeches.speaker: Viola.
verse: O Heaven, to what am I reserv'd, that knew not
Through all my childish hours and actions,
More sin, than poor imagination,
And too much loving of a faithless Man?
For which I'm paid, and so, that not the day
That now is rising to protect the harmless,
And give the innocent a sanctuary
From theeves and spoilers, can deliver me
From shame, at lea^t suspition—

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Sirrah, lead down the horses easily, I'll walke a foot till I be down the hill, 'tis very early, I shall reach home betimes. How now, whose there?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Night, that was ever friend to Lovers, yet
Has rais'd some weary Soul, that hates his bed,
To come and see me blush, and then laugh at me.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: H'ad a rude heart that did this.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Gentle Sir,
If you have that which honest men call pitty,
And be as far from evil as you shew;
Help a poor Maid, that this night by bad fortune
Has been thus us'd by Robbers,

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: A pox upon his heart that would not help thee, this Thief was half a Lawyer by his bands, How long have you been tyed here?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
prose: Alas, this hour, and with cold and fear am almost perisht.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Where were the watch the while? good sober Gent. ^hey were like careful members of the City, drawing in diligent Ale, and singing catches, while Mr. Constable contriv'd the Tosts: these fellows would be more severely punisht than wandring Gipsies, that every statute whips; for ^f they had every one two eyes a piece more, three pots would put them out.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
prose: I cannot tell, I found no Christian to give me succor.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose:
When they take a Thief, I'll take Ostend agen; the ^horsons drink Opium in their Ale, and then they sleep like ^ops; as for their bills, they only serve to reach down Ba
^on to make Rashers on; now let me know whom I have ^one this courtesie too, that I may thank my early rising for it?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
prose: Sir, All I am, you see.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: You have a name I'm sure, and a kindred, a Father, ^riend, or something that must own you; shee's a handsome ^oung Wench; What Rogues were these to Rob ^er?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Sir, you see all I dare reveale,
And as you are a Gentleman press me no further;
For there begins a grief, whose bitterness
Will break a stronger heart than I have in me,
^nd 'twill but make you heavy with the hearing,
For your own goodness sake desire it not.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: If you would not have me enquire that, How do you live then?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: How I have liv'd, is still one question,
Which must not be resolv'd —
How I desire to live, is in your liking,
So worthy an opinion I have of you.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Is in my liking? How I pray thee? tell me, i'faith I'll do you any good lies in my power; she has an eye would raise a bedrid man; come, leave your fear, and tell me, that's a good Wench.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
prose: Sir, I would serve—

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Who would'st thou serve? do not weep and tell me,

speeches.speaker: Viol.
prose: Faith, Sir, even some good woman, and such a wife if you be married, I do imagine yours.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Alas! thou art young and tender, let me see thy hand, this was ne'er made to wash, or wind up water, beat cloaths, or rub a floor, by this light, for one use that shall be nameless, 'tis the best wanton hand that e're I lookt on.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Dare you accept me, Sir, my heart is honest,
Among your vertuous charitable deeds,
This will not be the least.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Thou canst in a Chamber?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: In a Chamber, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I mean wait there upon a Gentlewoman,
How quick she is, I like that mainly too;
I'll have her, though I keep her with main strength like a besieged Town, for I know I shall have the Enemy afore me within a week.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Sir, I can sow too, and make pretty laces,
Dress a head handsome, teach young Gentlewomen,
For in all these I have a little knowledge.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: 'Tis well, no doubt I shall encrease that knowledge; I like her better still, how she provokes me; pritty young Maid, you shall serve a good Gentlewoman, though I say't, that will not be unwilling you should please me, nor I forgetful if you do.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
prose: I am the happier.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: My man shall make some shift to carry you behind him, Can you ride well?

speeches.speaker: Viola.
prose: But I'll hold fast for catching of a fall.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: That's the next way to pull another on you, I'll work her as I go, I know shee's wax, now, now, at this time could I beget a Worthy on this Wench,

speeches.speaker: Viol.
prose: Sir, for this Gentleness, may Heaven requite you tenfold.

speeches.speaker: Val
prose: 'Tis a good Wench, however others use thee, be sure I'll be a loving Master to thee, come.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I hope I am wild enough, for being known, I have writ a Letter here, and in it have abus'd my self most bitterly, yet all my fear is not enough, for that must do it, that must lay it on, I'll win her out i'th' flint, 'twill be more famous, now for my language.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Now, Sir, Who would you speak with?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Where be thy Mastres Man? I would speak with her,
I have a Letter.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Cannot I deliver it?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: No, by my trot, and fait, can'st thou not Man.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Well, Sir, I'll call her to you, pray shake your ears without a little.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Cran a Cree do it quickly; this rebbel tonge sticks in my teeth worse than a tough Hen, sure it was ne'er known at Babel, for they sould no Apples, and this was made for certain at the first planting of Orchards, 'tis so crabbed.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: What's he wood speak with me?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: A kill kenny ring, there he stands Madam.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: What would you have with me, friend?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: He has a Letter for other Women, Wilt thou read it.

speeches.speaker: Ma^.
prose: From whence?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: De Crosse creest from my Master.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Who is your Master?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I pray do you look.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Do you know this fellow?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: No Maddam, not I; more than an Irish Footman, stand further friend, I do not like your roperunners, What stallion Rogues are these, to weare such dowsetts, the very Cotton may commit adultery.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: I cannot find whose hand this should be, I'll read, To the beauteous wi^e of Don Antonio, sure this is some blind scribe — well now, What follows?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Pray God it take, I have given her that, will stir her conscience, how it works with her; hope, if it be thy will, let the flesh have it.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: This is the most abhor'd, intollerable knavery, that ever slave entertain'd, sure there is more than thine own head in this villany, it goes like practic'd mischiefe; disabled in his body? O good God, as I live he lies fearfully, and basely, ha? I should know that Jewel, 'tis my husband, come hither shat, Are you an Irish Man?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Sweete Woman a Cree I am an Irish man?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Now I know it perfectly; is this your trick, Sir? I'll trick you for it; How long have you serv'd this Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Ant
prose: Please thee a little day, O my Mac dermond put me to my Mastree, 'tis don I know.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: By my faith he speaks as well as if he had been lousy for the language a year or two; well, Sir, you had been better have kept your own shape as I will use you, What have I done that should deserve this tryal? I never made him Cuckold, to my knowledge, Sirrah come hither.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Now will she send some Jewel, or some Letter, I know her mind as well; I shall be famous.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Take this Irish bawde here.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: How?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: And kick him till his breeches and breech be of one colour, a bright blew both.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I may be well swing'd thus, for I dare not reveale my self, I hope she does not mean it, O hone, O hone, O St. Patricke, O a Cree, O sweet Woman.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: No, turn him, and kick him o' t'other side, that's well.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: O good waiting Man, I beseech thee good waiting man, a pox fyre your Legs.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: You Rogue, you enemy to all, but little breeches,
How dar'st thou come to me with such a Letter?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Prethee pitty the poor Irishman, all this makes for me, if I win her yet, I am still more glorious.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Now could I weep at what I have done, but I'll harden my heart agen, go shut him up, 'till my husband comes home, yet thus much ere ye go, sirrah thach'd head, Would'st not thou be whipt, and think it Justice? well Aquavitae Barrel, I will bounce you.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I pray do, I beseech you be not angry.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: O you hobby headed Rascal, I'll have you flead, and trossers made of thy skin to tumble in, go a way with him, let him see no fun, till my husband come home, Sir, I shall meet with you for your knavery, I fear it not.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Wilt thou not let me go? I do not like this.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Away with him.

speeches.speaker: Servingman.
prose: Come, I'll lead you in by your Jack a lent hair, go quietly, or I'll make your crupper crack.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: And do you hear me, Sirrah? and when you have done, make my Coach ready.

speeches.speaker: Serving.
prose: Yes forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Lock him up safe enough, I'll to this Gentleman,
I know the reason of all this business, for I do suspect it,
If he have this plot, I'll ring him such a peal, shall make his eares deaf for a month at least.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse: Am I not mad? Can this weak temper'd head,
That will be mad with drink, endure the wrong
That I have done a Virgin, and my Love?
Be mad, for so thou ought'st, or I will beate
The walls and trees, down with thee, and will let
Either thy memory out, or madness in;
But sure I never lov'd fair Viola,
I never lov'd my Father, nor my Mother,
Or any thing but drink; had I had love;
Nay, had I known so much charity,
As would have sav'd an Infant from the fire,
I had been naked, raving in the street;
With halfe a face, gashing my self with knives,
Two houres ere this time.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Good morrow Sir.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Good morrow Gentlemen, shall we go drink agen?
I have my wits.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: So have I, but they are unsetled ones, would I had some porrige.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: The Tavern boy was here this morning with me
And told me, that there was a Gentlewoman,
Which he took for a Whore, that hung on me:
For whom we quarrel'd, and I know not what.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I faith nor I.

speeches.speaker: ~be.
verse: I have a glimmering of some such thing.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Was it you, Silvio,
That made me drink so much? 'twas you or Pedro.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I know not who.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: We are all apt enough.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: But I will lay the fault on none but me,
That I would be so entreated, come Silvio,
Shall we go drink agen, come Gentlemen,
Why do you stay, let's never leave off now,
Whil'st we have Wine, and Throats, I'll practise it,
Till I have made it my best quality;
For what is best for me to do but that?
For Heaven sake come and drink; when I am nam'd,
Men shall make answer, VVhich Richardo mean you?
The excellent drinker? I will have it so,
VVill you go drink?

speeches.speaker: Silv.
verse: VVe drunk too much too lately.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: VVhy there is then the less behind to drink,
Let's end it all, dispatch that, wee'l send abroad,
And purchase all the VVine the world can yield,
And then drink it off, then take the fruits o'th' earth,
Distil the Juice from them, and drink that off;
Wee'l catch the rain before it fall to ground,
And drink off that that never more may grow;
Wee'l set our mouths to Springs, and drink them off,
And all this while wee'l never think of those
That love us best, more than we did last night.
We will not give unto the poor a drop
Of all this drink, but when we see them weep,
Wee'l run to them, and drink their tears off too,
Wee'l never leave whilst there is heat or moisture,
In this large globe, but suck it cold and dry,
Till we have made it Elemental earth;
Merely by drinking.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Is't flattery to tell you, you are mad?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: If it be false,
There's no such way to bind me to a Man;
He that will have me, lay my goods and lands,
My life down for him, need no more, but say,
Richardo thou art mad, and then all these
Are at his service, then he pleases me,
And makes me think that I had vertue in me,
That I had love, and tenderness of heart,
That though I have committed such a fault,
As never creature did, yet running mad,
As honest men should do for such a crime,
I have exprest some worth, though it be late:
But I alas have none of these in me,
But keep my wits still like a frozen Man,
That had no fire within him.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Nay, good Richardo leave this wild talk, and send a letter to her, I'll deliver it.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: 'Tis to no purpose; perhaps she's lost last night,
Or she got home agen, she's now so strictly
Look'd to, the wind can scarce come to her, or admit
She were her self; if she would hear from me,
From me unworthy, that have us'd her thus,
She were so foolish, that she were no more
To be belov'd.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Sir, we have found this night-gown she took with her.

speeches.speaker: Ricb.
prose: Where? where? speak quickly.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Searching in the Suburbs, we found a Tinker and his Whore that had it in a Tap-house, whom we apprehended, and they confest they stole it from her.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: And murthered her?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: What aile you man?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: Why all this doth not make me mad.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: It does, you would not offer this else, good Pedro look to his sword.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
