verse: My Aminta?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: She Sir,
That walks here up and down an empty shadow,
One, that for some few hours
But wanders here, carrying her own sad Coffin,
Seeking some Desart place to lodge her griefs in.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Sweet sorrow welcome, welcome noble grief;
How got you this fair liberty to see me?
For sorrows in your shape are strangers to me.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: I come to counsel ye.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Ye are still more welcome;
For good friends in afflictions give good Councels.
Pray then proceed.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Pray eat first, ye shew faint;
Here's Wine to refresh ye too.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: I thank ye dear.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Drink again.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Here's to our loves.
How, turn and weep!
Pray pledge it: this happiness we have yet left,
Our hearts are free. Not pledge it? Why?
And though beneath the Axe this health were holy,
Why do ye weep thus?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: I come to woo ye.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: To woo me Sweet? I am woo'd and won already,
You know I am yours. This pretty way becomes ye.
But you would deceive my sorrows; that's your intent.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: I would I could, I should not weep, but smile.
Do ye like your Meat and Wine?

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Like it?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Do you like your liberty?

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: All these I well may like.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Then pray like her that sent 'em.
Do ye like wealth, and most unequal'd beauty?

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Peace, indeed you'l make me angry.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Would I were dead that ask it,
Then ye might freely like, and I forgive ye.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: What like, and who? add not more misery
To a man that's fruitful in afflictions.
Who is't you would have me like?
Who sent these comforts?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: I must tell.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Be bold.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: But be you temperate.
If you be bold I die. The young fair Virgin;
(Sorrow hath made me old.) O hearken,
And wisely hark, the Governess daughter:
That Star that strikes this Island full of wonder,
That blooming sweetness.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: What of her?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: She sent it: and with it,
It must be out, she dotes on ye,
And must enjoy ye: else no joy must find ye.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: And have you the patience to deliver this?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: A sister may say much, and modestly.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: A sister?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Yes, that name undid ye;
Undid us both: had ye nam'd Wife, she had fear'd ye;
And fear'd the sin she follow'd; She had shun'd, yea
Her Virgin modesty had not touch'd at ye.
But thinking you were free, hath kindled a fire,
I fear will hardly be extinguisht.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Indeed I played the ^ool.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: O my best Sir, take heed,
Take heed of lies. Truth, though it trouble some minds,
Some wicked minds, that are both dark and dangerous:
Yet it preserves it self, comes off pure, innocent,
And like the Sun, though never so eclips'd,
Must break in glory. O Sir, lie no more.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Ye have read me a fair Lecture,
And put a spell upon my tongue for fayning.
But how will you counsel now?

speeches.speaker: Amin
verse: Ye must study to forget me.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Be patient.
Be wise and patient, it concens ye highly.
Can ye lay by our loves? But why should I doubt it?
Ye are a man, and man may shift affections,
'Tis held no sin. To come to the point,
Ye must lose me; many and mighty reasons.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Hear me Aminta,
Have you a man that loves you too, that feeds ye,
That sends ye liberty? Has this great Governess
A noble son too, young, and apt to catch ye?
Am I, because I am in bonds, and miserable,
My health decay'd, my youth and strength half blasted,
My fortune like my waining self, for this despis'd?
Am I for this forsaken? a new love chosen,
And my affections, like my fortunes, wanderers?
Take heed of lying, you that chid me for it;
And shew'd how deep a sin it was, and dangerous.
Take heed, your self, you swore you lov'd me dearly;
No few, nor little oathes you swore Aminta,
Those seal'd with no small faith, I then assur'd my self.
O seek no new wayes to cozen truth,

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: I do not.
By love it self I love thee,
And ever must, nor can all deaths dissolve it.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Why do you urge me thus then?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: For your safety,
To preserve your life.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: My life, I do confess, is hers,
She gives it,
And let her take it back, I yield it.
My loves intirely thine, none shall touch at it;
None, my Aminta, none.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Ye have made me happy,
And now I know ye are mine. Fortune, I scorn thee.
Goe to your rest, and I'll sit by ye;
Whilst I have time I'll be your mate, and comfort ye,
For only I am trusted: you shall want nothing,
Not a liberty that I can steal ye.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: May we not celebrate our loves Aminta?
And where our wishes cannot meet.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: You are wanton,
But with cold kisses I'll allay that fever;
Look for no more, and that in private too.
Believe me, I shall blush else.
But, let's consider, we are both lost else.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Let's in, and prevent fate.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: You do well to ayr us, Ladies, we shall be m^sty else
What are your wise wills now?

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: You are very crank still.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: As crank as a holy Fryer, fed with hail-stones.
But do ye bring us out to bait, like Bulls?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Or are you weary of the charge ye are at?
Turn us abroad again, let's jog Ladies;
We are gross, and course, unsit for your sweet pleasures.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Knock off our shooes, and turn's to grass.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: You are determined
Still to be stubborn then: it well becomes ye.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: An humour Lady that contents a prisoner.
A sullen sit sometimes serves for a second course.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Ye may as well be kind,
And gain our favours; gain meat and drink,
And lodging to rest your bones.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: My bones have bore me thus long,
And had their share of pains and recreations;
If they fail now, they are no fair companions.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: Are ye thus harsh to all our Sex?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: We cannot be merry without a Fidler,
Pray strike up your Tabors, Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: The fools despise us.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: We know ye are very hungry now.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Yes 'tis very wholsom, Ladies;
For we that have gross bodies, must be careful
Have ye no piercing air to stir our stomachs?
We are beholding to ye for our Ordinary.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Why slaves, 'tis in our power to hang ye.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Very likely.
'Tis in our powers then to be hang'd, and scorn ye.
Hanging's as sweet to us, as dreaming to you.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: Come, be more courteous.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Do, and then ye shall be pleas'd, and have all necessaries.

speeches.speaker: Tib..
verse: Give me some Ratsbane then.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: And why Ratsbane, Mounsieur?

speeches.speaker: Tib
verse: We live like vermine here, and eat up your cheese,
Your mouldy cheese, that none but Rats would bite at;
Therefore 'tis just that Ratsbane should reward us.
We are unprofitable, and our Ploughs are broken;
There is no hope of Harvest this year, Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Ye shall have all content

speeches.speaker: M^st.
verse: I, and we'll serve your uses.
I had rather serve hogs, there's more delight in't;
Your greedy appetites are never satisfied;
Just like hungry Camels, sleeping or waking
You chew the cud still.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: By this hand we'll starve ye.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: 'Tis a noble courtesie.
I had as lief ye should famish me, as founder me:
To be jaded to death, is only fit for a hackney.
Here be certain Tarts of Tarr about me,
And parcels of potargo in my Jerkin,
As long as these last.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Which will not last ever.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Then we'll eat one another like good fellows.
A shoulder of his for a haunch of mine.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: 'Tis excellent.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: 'Twill be as we'll dress it Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: Why sure ye are not men?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Ye had best come search us,
A Seaman is seldom without a salt Eele.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: I am bad enough,
And in my nature a notorious wencher;
And yet ye make me blush at your immodesty.
Tell me good Master, didst ever see such things?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: I could like 'em, though they were lewdly given,
If they could say no;

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Well, ye may hang, or starve us;
But your commanding impudence shall never fear us.
Had ye by blushing signs, soft cunings, crept into us,
And shew'd us your necessities: we had met your purposes,
Supply'd your wants. We are no Saints Ladies;
I love a good wench, as I love my life,
And with my life I will maintain my love:
But such a sordid impudence I'll spit at.
Let's to our dens again. Come noble Master.
You know our minds Lad^es:
This is the faith in which we'll die.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: I do admire 'em

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: They are noble f^lows,
And they shall not want, ^o^ this.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: But see, Clarinda comes.
Farewel, I'll to my charge.

speeches.speaker: Cl^
verse: ^ out those prisoners now,
And ^, a^d hear their business.
^ Madam.
^ hath prevail'd upon her brother.

^
^ongue, and can describe the happiness
^ ready to fling on him.

^ su^e he m^
^ glad for certain, wonder,
^nd bl^ss the hou^ that brought him to this Island.
^long to hear t^e ^ll joy that he labours with.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Bless thy Divine Beauty.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: Mirror of sweetness.

speeches.speaker: La-m.
verse: Ever-springing brightness.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Nay, S^and up Gentlemen, and leave your flatteries.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: She calls us Gentl^men, sure we shall have some meat now.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: I am a mortal creature,
Worship Heaven, and give these at^ributes
To their Divinities. Methinks ye ^ook but thin.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Oh we are starv'd, immortal beauty.

speeches.speaker: La-m.
verse: We are all poor starv'd knaves.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: Neither liberty nor meat, Lady

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: We were handsome men, and Gentlemen, and sweet men,
And were once gracious in the eyes of beauties,
But now we look like Rogues;
Like poor starv'd rogues.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: What would ye do if ye were to die now?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: Alas, we were prepar'd. If you will hang us,
Let's have a good meal or two to die with,
To put's in heart.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Or if you'll drown us,
Let's be drunk first, that we may die merrily,
And bless the founders.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Ye shall not die so hastily.
What dare ye do to deserve my favour?

speeches.speaker: La-m.
verse: Put us to any service,

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: Any bondage,
Let's but live.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: We'll get a world of children,
For we know ye are hainously unprovided that way;
And ye shall beat us when we offend ye;
Beat us abundantly, and take our meat from us.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: These are weak abject things, that shew ye poor ones.
What's the great service ye so oft have threatned,
If ye might see me, and win my favour?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: That business of discovery.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Oh, Ill tell ye Lady.

speeches.speaker: La-m.
verse: And so will I.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: And I,
Pray let me speak first.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Good, no confusion.
We are before a Lady that knows manners;
And by the next meat I shall eat, 'tis certain,
This little Gentlewoman that was taken with us.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Your Captains Sister, she you mean.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I, I, she's the business that we would open to ye.
You are cousened in her.

speeches.speaker: Lam,
verse: How, what is't you would open?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: She is no Sister.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Good Sirs how quick you are.
She is no Sister, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: She is his.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Peace I say.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: What is she?

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Faith, sweet Lady,
She is, as a man would say, his.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: What?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: His Mistriss.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Or, as some new Translators read, his.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Oh me!

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: And why he should delude you thus,
Unless he meant some villany? these ten weeks
He has had her at Sea, for his own proper appetite.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: His Cabin-mate I'll assure ye.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: No Sister, say ye?

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: No more than I am brother to your beauty.
I know not why he should juggle thus.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Do not lie to me.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: If ye find me lie, Lady, hang me empty.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: How am I fool'd!
Away with 'em Juletta, and feed 'em
But hark ye, with such food as they have given me.
New misery!

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: Nor meat nor thanks for all this.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Make 'em more wretched.
Oh I could burst! curse and kill now,
Kill any thing I meet, Juletta, follow me,
And call the rest along.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: We follow, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: I must be gone now, else she may suspect me;
How shall I answer her?

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Tell her directly.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: That were too suddain, too improvident;
Fires of this nature must be put out cunningly,
They'll waste all come near 'em else.
Farewel once more.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Farewel,
And keep my love entire.
Nay, kiss me once again, me thinks we should not part.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Oh be wise, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Nay, one kiss more.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Indeed you're wanton;
We may be taken too.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Out thou base woman.
I'll shoot 'em both.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: Nay stay, brave Lady, hold;
A suddain death cuts off a Nobler vengeance.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Am I made Bawd to your lascivious meetings?
Are ye grown so wise in sin?
Shut up that villany: and sirrah,
Now expect my utmost anger.
Let him there starve.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: I mock at your mischiefs.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Tie that false witch unto that Tree,
There let that savage beasts
Gnaw off her sweetness, and Snakes
Embrace her beauties; tie her, and watch
That none relieve her.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: We could wish ye better fortune, Lady,
But dare not help ye.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Be your own friends, I thank ye.
Now only my last audit, and my greatest,
Oh Heaven, be kind unto me,
And if it be thy Will, preserve.

speeches.speaker: Ray.
verse: Who is this?
Sure 'tis a woman, I have trode this place,
And found much footing; now I know 'tis peopl'd.
Ha, let me see! 'tis her face.
Oh Heaven! turn this way Maid.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Oh Raymond, oh Brother.

speeches.speaker: Raym.
verse: Her tongue too: 'tis my Sister; what rude hand!
Nay kiss me first, Oh joy!

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Fly, fly dear brother,
You are lost else.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: A man, a man, a new man.

speeches.speaker: Raym.
verse: What are these?

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: An enemy, an enemy.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Dispatch him,
Take him off, shoot him straight.

speeches.speaker: Raym.
verse: I dare not use my sword, Ladies,
Against such comely foes.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Oh brother, brother!

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Away with 'em, and in dark prisons bind 'em.
One word reply'd, ye die both.
Now brave ^other, follow thy noble anger,
And ^l help thee.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: I Am deaf to all your intreaties: she that moves me
For pity or compassion to these Pirats,
Digs up her Fathers, or her Brothers Tomb,
And spurns about their ashes.
Couldst thou remember what a Father thou hadst once,
'Twould steel thy heart against all foolish pity.
By his memory'and the remembrance of his dear embraces,
I am taught, that in a Noble cause revenge is Noble;
And they shall fall the sacrifices to appease
His wandring Ghost, and my incensed fury.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: The new come prisoner too!

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: He too yet that we may learn
Whether they are the same, or near ally'd
To those that forc'd me to this cruel course,
Better their poor allowance, and permit 'em
To meet together and confer,
Within the distance of your ear; perhaps
They may discover something that may kill
Despair in me, and be a means to save 'em
From certain ruine.

speeches.speaker: Ceo.
verse: That shall be my charge.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Yet to prevent
All hope of rescue: for this new-come Captain
Hath both a Ship and Men not far from us,
Though ignorant to find the only Port,
That can yield entrance to our happy Island,
Guard the place strongly, and e'r the next Sun
Ends his diurnal progress, I will be
Happy in my revenge, or set 'em free.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: So serve it plentifully,
And lose not time to enquire the cause;
There is a main design that hangs upon this bounty.
See the Table furnisht with Wine too,
That discovers secrets which tortures cannot open:
Open the doors too of the several prisons,
And give all free entrance into this room.
Undiscover'd I can here mark all.
Here's Captain careless, and the tough Ship-master,
The slaves are nos'd like Vultures
How wild they look.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Ha, the mistery of this,
^ome good Hobgoblin rise and reveal.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: I'm amazed at it: nor can I sound the intent.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Is not this bread,
^ubstantial bread, not painted?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: But take heed,
You may be poisoned.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: I am sure I am famish'd;
And famine, as the wise man says,
Gripes the guts as much as any Mineral.
This may be Treacle sent to preserve me
After a long Fast: or be it Vipers spittle,
^'ll run the hazard.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: We are past all fear, I'll take part with ye.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Do: and now i'faith, how d'ye feel your self?
find great ease in't. What's here;
Vine, and it be thy Will;
^trong lusty Wine. Well, fools may talk
Of Mythridate, Cordials, and Elixirs.
But from my youth this was my only Physick.
Here's a colour, what Ladies cheek,
Though cerus'd over, comes near it?
^t sparkles too: hangs out Diamonds.
Oh my sweet-heart, how I will hug thee,
Again, and again! They are poor drunkards,
And not worth thy favors,
That number thy moist kisses in these Crystals.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: But Mounsieur,
^ere are Suckets, and sweet dishes.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Tush, boys meat,
^ am past it; here's strong food fit for men:
Nectar, old lad. Mistriss of merry hearts,
Once more I am bold with you.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Take heed (man)
Too much will breed distemper.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Hast thou liv'd at Sea
The most part of thy life, where to be sober
While we have Wine aboard, is capital Treason;
And dost thou preach sobriety?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Prethee forbear,
We may offend in it; we know not for whom
^t was provided.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: I am sure for me: therefore footra,
When I am full, let 'em hang me, I care not.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: This has been his temper ever.
^e, provoking dishes; candid Eringoes,
^nd Potatoes.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: I'll not touch 'em, I will drink;
But not a bit on a march, I'll be an Eunuch rather.

speeches.speaker: Mast
verse: Who are these?

speeches.speaker: Tib,
verse: Marry, who you will;
^ keep my Text here.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Raymond!

speeches.speaker: Ray.
verse: Albert!

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Away, I'll be drunk alone;
Keep off Rogues, or I'll belch ye into air;
^ot a drop here.

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Dear brother, put not in your eyes such anger;
Those looks poison'd with fury, shot at him,
^ef^ect on me. Oh brother, look milder, or
The Crystal of his temperance
Will turn 'em on your self.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Sir, I have sought ye long
To find your pardon: you have plough'd the Ocean
To wreak your vengeance on me, for the rape
Of this fair Virgin. Now our fortune guides us
To meet on such hard terms, that we need rather
^ mutual pitty of our present state,
Than to expostulate of breaches past,
Which cannot be made up. And though it be
Far from your power, to force me to confess,
That I have done ye wrong, or such submission
Failing to make my peace, to vent your anger;
You being your self slav'd, as I to others:
Yet for you Sisters sake, her blessed sake,
In part of recompence of what she has suffer'd
For my rash folly; the contagion
Of my black actions, catching hold upon
Her purer innocence, I crave your mercy;
And wish however several motives kept us
From being friends, while we had hope to live,
Let death which we expect, and cannot fly from,
End all contention.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Drink upon't, 'tis a good motion;
Ratifie it in Wine, and 'tis authentical.

speeches.speaker: Ray.
verse: When I consider
The ground of our long difference, and look on
Our not to be avoided miseries,
It doth beget in me I know not how
A soft Religious tenderness; which tells me,
Though we have many faults to answer for
Upon our own account, our Fathers crimes
Are in us punish'd. Oh Albert, the course
They took to leave us rich, was not honest,
Nor can that friendship last, which virtue joyns not.
When first they forc'd the industrious Portugals,
From their Plantations in the Happy Islands.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: This is that I watch for.

speeches.speaker: Ray.
verse: And did omit no tyranny, which men,
Inured to spoil, and mischief could inflict,
On the griex'd sufferers; when by lawless rapine
They reap'd the harvest, which their Labourer; sow'd;
And not content to force 'em from their dwelling,
But laid for 'em at Sea, to ravish from 'em
The last remainder of their wealth: then, then,
After a long pursuit, each doubting other,
As guilty of the Portugals escape,
They did begin to quarrel, like in men;
(Forgive me piety, that I call 'em so)
No longer love, or correspondence holds,
Than it is cimented with prey or profit:
Then did they turn these swords they oft had bloodi'd
With innocent gore, upon their wretched selves,
And paid the forfeit of their cruelty
Shewn to Sebastian, and his Colonie,
By being fatal enemies to each other.
Thence grew Amintas rape, and my desire
To be reveng'd. And now observe the issue:
As they for spoil ever forgot compassion
To women, (who should be exempted
From the extremities of a lawful War)
We now, young able men, are fall'n into
The hands of Women; that, against the soft
Tenderness familiar to their Sex,
Will shew no mercy.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: None, unless you shew us
Our long lost Husbands.
We are those Portugals you talk'd of.

speeches.speaker: Ray.
verse: Stay,
I met upon the Sea in a tall Ship
Two Portugals, famish'd almost to death.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Our Ship by this Wine.
And those the rogues that stole her,
Lest us to famish in the barren Islands.

speeches.speaker: Ray.
verse: Some such tale they told me,
And something of a Woman, which I find,
To be my Sister.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: Where are these men?

speeches.speaker: Ray.
verse: I left 'em,
Supposing they had deluded me with forg'd tales,
In the Island, where they said
They had liv'd many years the wretched owners
Of a huge mass of treasure.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: The same men: and that the fatal muck
We quarrell'd for.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: They were Portugals you say.

speeches.speaker: Ray.
verse: So they profess'd.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: They may prove such men as may save your lives,
And so much I am taken with fair hope,
That I will hazard life to be resolv'd on't:
How came you hither?

speeches.speaker: Ray.
verse: My ship lies by the Rivers mouth,
That can convey ye to these wretched men,
Which you desire to see.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: Back to your prisons,
And pray for the success: if they be those
Which I desire to find, you are safe;
If not, prepare to die to morrow:
For the world cannot redeem ye.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: However, we are arm'd
For either fortune.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: What must become of me now
That I am not dismiss'd?

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: Oh Sir, I purpose
To have your company.

speeches.speaker: Ti.
verse: Take heed wicked woman,
I am apt to mischief now.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: You cannot be so unkind,
To her that gives you liberty.

speeches.speaker: Ti.
verse: No, I shall be too kind, that's the devil on't;
I have had store of good wine: and when I am drunk,
Joan is a Lady to me, and I shall
Lay about me like a Lord: I feel strange motions:
Avoid me temptation.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: Come Sir, I'll help ye in.

speeches.speaker: Nicu.
verse: What may that be
That moves upon the Lake?

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
verse: Still it draws nearer,
And now I plainly can discern it.
'Tis the French Ship.

speeches.speaker: Nicu.
verse: In it a woman,
Who seems to invite us to her,

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
verse: Still she calls with signs of Love to hasten to her;
So lovely hope doth still appear:
I feel nor age, nor weakness.

speeches.speaker: Nicu.
verse: Though it bring death,
To us 'tis comfort: and deserves a meeting.
Or else fortune tyr'd with what we have suffer'd,
And in it overcome, as it may be,
Now sets a period to our misery.

speeches.speaker: Ray.
verse: What dreadful sounds are these?

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: Infernal Musick,
Fit for a bloody Feast.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: It seems prepar'd
To kill our courages e'r they divorce
Our souls and bodies.

speeches.speaker: Ray.
verse: But they that fearless fall,
Deprive them of their triumph.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: See the furies,
^n their full trym of cruelty,

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: 'Tis the last
Duty that I can pay to my dead Lord,
Set out the Altar, I my self will be
The Priest, and boldly do those horrid Rites
You shake to think on, lead these Captains nearer,
For they shall have the honor to fall first
To my Sebastian's ashes: and now wretches,
As I am taught already, that you are,
And lately by your free confession,
French Pirats, and the sons of those I hate,
Even equal with the devil; hear with horror,
What 'tis invites me to this cruel course,
And what you are to suffer, no Amazons we,
But women of Portugal that must have from you
Sebastian and Nicusa; we are they
That groan'd beneath your fathers wrongs:
We are those wretched women,
Their injuries pursu'd, and overtook;
And from the sad remembrance of our losses
We are taught to be cruel; when we were forc'd
From that sweet air we breathed in, by their rapine,
And sought a place of being; as the Seas
And Winds conspir'd with their ill purposes,
To load us with afflictions in a storm
That fell upon us; the two ships that brought us,
To seek new fortunes in an unknown world
Were severed: the one bore all the able men,
Our Treasure and our Jewels: in the other,
We Women were embarqu'd: and fell upon,
After long tossing in the troubled main,
This pleasant Island: but in few months,
The men that did conduct us hither, died,
We long before had given our Husbands lost:
Remembring what we had suff'red by the French
We took a solemn Oath, never to admit
The curs'd society of men: necessity
Taught us those Arts, not usual to our Sex,
And the fertile Earth yielding abundance to us,
We did resolve, thus shap'd like Amazons
To end our lives; but when you arriv'd here,
And brought as presents to us, our own Jewels;
Those which were boorn in the other Ship,
How can ye hope to scape our vengeance?

speeches.speaker: Amint.
verse: It boots not then to swear our innocence?

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Or that we never forc'd it from the owners?

speeches.speaker: Ray.
verse: Or that there are a remnant of that wrack,
And not far off?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: All you affirm, I know,
Is but to win time; therefore prepare your throats,
The world shall not redeem ye: and that your cries
May find no entrance to our ears,
To move pity in any: bid loud Musick sound
Their fatal knells; if ye have prayers use 'em quickly,
To any power will own ye; but ha!
Who are these? what spectacles of misfortune?
Why are their looks
So full of Joy and Wonder?

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: Oh! lay by
These instruments of death, and welcome
To your arms, what you durst never hope to imbrace:
This is Sebastian, this Nicusa, Madam:
Preserv'd by miracle: look up dear Sir,
And know your own Rossella: be not lost
In wonder and amazement; or if nature
Can by instinct, instruct you what it is,
To be blessed with the name of Father,
Freely enjoy it in this fair Virgin.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Though my miseries,
And many years of wants I have endur'd,
May well deprive me of the memory
Of all joys past; yet looking on this building,
This ruin'd building of a heavenly form
In my Rosilla; I must remember, I am Sebastian.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Oh my joyes!

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: And here,
I see a perfect model of thy self,
As thou wert when thy choice first made thee mine:
These cheeks and fronts, though wrinkled now with time
Which Art cannot restore: had equal pureness,
Of natural white and red, and as much ravishing:
Which by fair order and succession,
I see descend on her: and may thy virtues
Wind into her form, and make her a perfect dower:
No part of thy sweet goodness wanting to her.
I will not now Rosilla, ask thy fortunes,
Nor trouble thee with hearing mine;
Those shall hereafter serve to make glad hours
In their relation: All past wrongs forgot;
I'm glad to see you Gentlemen; but most,
That is in my power to save your lives;
You sav'd ours, when we were near starv'd a^ Sea,
And I despair not, for if she be mine,
Rosilla can deny Sebastian nothing.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: She does give up her self,
Her power and joys, and all, to you,
To be dischar^d of 'em as too burthensom;
Welcome in any shape.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Sir, in your looks,
I read your sute of my Clarinda: she is yours:
And Lady, if it be in me to confirm
Your hopes in this brave Gentleman,
Presume I am your servant.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: We thank you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Oh happy hour!

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: O my dear Aminta;
Now all our fears are ended.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Here I fix: she's mettle,
Steel to the back: and will cut my leaden dagger,
If not us'd with discretion.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: You are still no changling.

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
verse: Nay,
All look chearfully, for none shall be
Deny'd their lawful wishes; when a while
We have here refresh'd our selves; we'll return
To our several homes; and well that voyage ends,
That makes of deadly enemies, faithful friends.

plays.play_title: Wit at several weapons. A COMEDY.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: SIR, I'm no boy, I'm deep in one and twenty,
The second years approaching,

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: A fine time
For a youth to live by his wits then I should think,
If e'er he mean to make account of any.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Wits, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: I Wits Sir, if it be so strange to thee,
I'm sorry I spent that time to get a Fool,
I might have imploy'd my pains a great deal better;
Thou knowst all that I have, I ha' got by my wits,
And yet to see how urgent thou art too;
It grieves me thou art so degenerate
To trouble me for means, I never offer'd it
My Parents from a School-boy, past nineteen once.
See what these times are grown to, before twenty
I rush'd into the world, which is indeed
Much like the Art of swiming, he that will attain to't
Must fall plump, and duck himself at first,
And that will make him hardy and advent'rous,
And not stand putting in one foot, and shiver,
And then draw t'other after, like a quake-buttock;
Well he may make a padler i'th' world,
From hand to mouth, ^ut never a brave Swimmer,
Born up by th' chi^, as I bore up myself,
With my strong industry that never fail'd me;
For he that lies born up with Patrimonies,
Looks like a long great Ass that swims with bladders,
Come but one prick of adverse fortune to him
He sinks, because he never try'd to swim
When Wit plaies with the billows that choak'd him.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Why is it not a fashion for a Father, Sir,
Out of his yearly thousands to allow
His only Son, a competent brace of hundreds;
Or such a toy?

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Yes, if he mean to spoil him,
Or mar his wits he may, but never I,
This is my humor, Sir, which you'll find constant;
I love Wit so well, because I liv'd by't,
That I'll give no man power out of my means to hurt it,
And that's a kind of gratitude to my raiser,
Which great ones ost forget; I admire much
This Ages dulness, when I scarce writ man,
The first degree that e'er I took in thriving,
I lay intelligencer close for wenching,
Could give this Lord or Knight a true Certificate
Of all the Maiden-heads extant,, how many lay
'Mongst Chamber-maids, how many 'mongst Exchange
Though never many there I must confess
They have a trick to utter Ware so fast;
I knew which Lady had a mind to fall,
Which Gentlewoman new divorc'd, which Tradesman breaking,
The price of every sinner to a hair,
And where to raise each price; which were the Tearmers,
That would give Velvet Petticoats, Tissue Gowns,
Which Pieces, Angels, Suppers, and Half Crowns;
I knew how to match, and make my market.
Could give intelligence where the Pox lay leidger,
And then to see the Letchers shift a point,
'Twas sport and profit too; how they would shun
Their ador'd Mistriss chambers, and run fearfully,
Like Rats from burning houses, so brought I
My Clyents the game still safe together,
And noble gamesters lov'd me, and I felt it.
Give me a man that lives by his wits, say I,
And's never left a Groat, there's the true Gallant.
When I grew somewhat pursie, I grew then
In mens opinions too, and confidences,
They put things call'd Executorships upon me,
The charge of Orphans, little sensless creatures,
Whom in their Childhoods I bound forth to Felt-makers,
To make 'em lose, and work away their Gentry,
Disguise their tender natures with hard custom,
So wrought 'em out in time there rise ungently,
Nor do I fear to discourse this unto thee,
I'm arm'd at all points against treachery,
I hold my humor firm, if I can see thee thrive by
Thy wits while I live, I shall have the more courage
To trust thee with my Lands when I dye; if not,
The next best wit I can hear of, carries 'em:
For since in my time and knowledge, so many rich children
Of the City, conclude in beggery, I'de rather
Make a wise stranger my Executor, then a foolish
^on my Heir, and to have my Lands call'd after my
Wit, than after my name; and that's my nature.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: 'Tis a strange harsh one, must I still shift then?
^ come brave Cheats, once to my trade agen.
And I'll ply't harder now than e'er I did for't,
You'll part with nothing then, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Not a jot, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: If I should ask you blessing e'r I goe, Sir,
^ think you would not give't me.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Let me but hear thou liv'st by thy wits once
Thou shalt have any thing, thou'rt none of mine else,
Then why should I take care for thee?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: 'Thank your bounty.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: So wealth love me, and long life, I beseech it,
As I do love the man that lives by his wits,
He comes so near my nature; I'm grown old now,
And even arriv'd at my last cheat I fear me,
^t 'twill make shift to bury me, by day-light too,
And discharge all my Legacies, 'tis so wealthy,
And never trouble any Interest money:
^'ve yet a Neece to wed, over whose steps
^ have plac'd a trusty watchful Guardianess,
For fear some poor Earl steal her, 't has been threat'ned,
To redeem mortgag'd Land, but he shall miss on't;
To prevent which, I have sought out a match for her,
^op of Fop-Hall, he writes himself, I take it,
The antient'st Fop in England, with whom I've privately
Compounded for the third part of her portion.
And she seems pleas'd, so two parts rest with me,
He's come; Sir Gregory, welcome, what's he Sir?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Young Cuningham, a N^rfolk Gentleman,
One that has liv'd upon the Feps, my kindred,
Ever since my remembrance; he's a wit indeed,
And we all strive to have him, nay, 'tis certain
Some of our name has gone to I aw for him;
Now 'tis my turn to keep him, and indeed
He's plaguy chargeable, as all your wits are,
But I will give him over when I list,
I ha' us'd wits so before.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: I hope when y'are married Sir, you'll shake him off.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Why what do you take me to be, old Father-i'Law that shall be, do you think I'll have any of the Wits hang upon me, after I am married once? none of my kindred ever had before me; but where's this Neece? is't a fashion in London, to marry a woman and never see her?

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Excuse the niceness, Sir, that care's your friend's,
Perhaps had she been seen, you had never seen her;
There's many a spent thing call'd, and't like your honor,
That lies in wait for her, at first snap she's a Countess,
Drawn with six Mares through Fleetstreet, and a Coachman,
Sitting bare-headed to their Flanders buttocks,
This whets him on.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Pray let's clap up the business, Sir,
I long to see her, are you sure you have her,
Is she not there already, Hark? Hark, oh hark.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: How now, what's that Sir?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Every Caroach goes by,
Goes ev'n to th' heart of me-

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: I'll have that doubt eas'd, Sir,
Instantly eas'd, Sir Gregory, and now I think on't
A toy comes i' my mind, seeing your friend there,
We'll have a little sport, give you but way to't,
And put a trick upon her, I love Wit pretiously,
You shall not be seen yet, we'll stale your friend first,
If 't please but him to stand for the Anti-mask.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: Puh, he shall stand for any thing, why his supper

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Then come you forth more unexpectedly
The Mask it self, a thousand a year joynture,
The cloud (your friend) will be then drawn away,
And only you the beauty of the Play.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: For Red and Black, I'll put down all your Fallers,
Let but your Neece bring White, and we have three colours.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: I'm given to understand you are a Wit, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cuning.
verse: I'm one that Fortune shews small favour to, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: To tell you truth, I'm taken with a Wit.
prose: Why there you conclude it, whether you will or no, Sir;

speeches.speaker: Cun.
prose: Fowlers catch Woodcocks so, let not them know so much,

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: A pestilence mazard, a Duke Humphrey spark

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: W'are that Arrow.

speeches.speaker: Old K.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Puh.

speeches.speaker: Neece.

speeches.speaker: Cun.

speeches.speaker: Neece.

speeches.speaker: Old K.

speeches.speaker: Neece?

speeches.speaker: Old K.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.

speeches.speaker: Neece.

speeches.speaker: Old K.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.

speeches.speaker: Neece.

You may have good for an Angel, the least cost
You can bestow upon a woman, Sir
Trebles ten Counsellors Fees in Lady-ware,
Y'are over head and ears, e'r you be aware,
Faith keep a batchelor still, and go to Bowls, Sir,
Follow your Mistriss there, and prick and save, Sir;
For other Mistresses will make you a slave, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.

speeches.speaker: Old K.

speeches.speaker: Neece.

speeches.speaker: Old K.

speeches.speaker: Cun.

speeches.speaker: Neece.

Alass, you cannot go beyond me Uncle,
You carry a Jest well, I must confess,
For a man of your years, but—

speeches.speaker: Old K.

speeches.speaker: Cun.

speeches.speaker: Guar.

To an old Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cun.

speeches.speaker: Neece.

speeches.speaker: Cun.

speeches.speaker: Guard.

speeches.speaker: Cun.

speeches.speaker: Guard.

speeches.speaker: Neece.

speeches.speaker: Cun.

speeches.speaker: Old K.

Hang from the Gentleman, art thou not asham'd

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Are you angry, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Old K.

Your honest wise acquaintance; vex me not
After my care and pains to find a match for thee,
Lest I confine thy life to some out-chamber,
Where thou shalt waste the sweetness of thy youth,
Like a consuming Light in her own socket,
And not allow'd a male creature about thee;
A very Monky, thy necessity

speeches.speaker: Neece.

speeches.speaker: Old K.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Pray let me look upon the Gentleman

Beshrew my blood, a tollerable man,

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: Hum, hum, hum.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Say he be black, he's of a very good pitch,
Well ankled, two good confident calves, they look
As if they would not shrink at the ninth child;
The redness i'th face, why that's in fashion,
Most of your high bloods have it, sign of greatness marry;
'Tis to be taken down too with May-butter,
I'll send to my Lady Spend-tail for her Medicine.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: Lum te dum, dum, dum, de dum.

speeches.speaker: Neece.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: Lum te dum, te dum, te dum.

speeches.speaker: Neece.

The error of my Sex.

speeches.speaker: Old K.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: I'll do't by course, do you think I'm an ass, Knight?

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Formally finisht, how goes this Suit forward?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I'm taking measure of the Widows mind, Sir,

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Who would have dreamt

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: Trust him not Widow, he's a younger brother,

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: He brings more content to a woman with that nothing,

verse: Come, come, no language now shall be in fashion,
But your Love-phrase, the bell to procreation.

verse: This last illiterate share, there's no conscience in't.

End, and shuff^le the Almanack together, vacations and

My Father, put on Priscian he has Latine frag

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
prose: Sir, lets reward um I pray you, and be gone. If any quarrel should arise amongst us, I am able to answer neither of them, his Iron and Steel tongue is as hard as the t'others Latine one.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Stay, stay Sir I will talk a little with him first,
Let me alone with both, I will try whether they
Live by their wits or no; for such a man I love,
And what? you both beg together then;

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Conjunctis manibus, profecto, Domine.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
prose: With equal fortunes, equal distribution, there's not the breadth of a swords point uneven in our division.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
prose: What two qualities are here cast away upon two poor fellows, if a man had um that could maintain um? what a double man were that, if these two fellows might be bought and sodden, and boil'd to a jelly, and eaten fasting every morning, I do not think but a man should find strange things in his stomach.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
prose: Come Sir, joyn your charity with mine, and we'll make up a couple of pence bewixt us.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
prose: If a man could have a pennyworth for his penny,
I would bestow more money with 'em.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Save you Gentlemen, how now? what are you encount'red here? what fellows are these?

speeches.speaker: Old K.
prose: Faith Sir, here's Mars and Mercury, a pair of poor Planets it seems, that Jupiter has turn'd out to live by their wits, and we are e'en about a little spark of charity to kindle um a new fire.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Stay, pray you stay Sir, you may abuse your charity, nay, make that goodness in you no better than a vice; so many deceivers walk in these shadows now a days; that certainly your bounties were better spilt than reserv'd to so lewd and vicious uses; which is he that professes the Soldier?

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
prose: He that professes his own profession, Sir, and the dangerous life he hath led in it, this pair of half score years.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: In what services have you been, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
prose: The first that flesht me a Soldier, Sir, was that great battel at Alcazar in Barbary, where the noble English Stukely fell, and where that royal Portugal Sebastian ended his untimely days.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Are you sure Sebastian died there?

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
prose:
Faith Sir, there was some other rumour hop't amongst us, that he, wounded, escap'd, and toucht on his Native shore agen, where finding his Countrey at home more distrest by the invasion of the Spaniard, than his loss abroad, forsook it, still supporting a miserable and unfortunate
fortunate life, which (where he ended) is yet uncertain.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: By my faith Sir, he speaks the nearest fame of truth in this.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
prose: Since Sir, I serv'd in France, the Low Countreys, Lastly, at that memorable skirmish at Newport, where the forward and bold Scot there spent his life so freely, that from every single heart that there fell, came home from his resolution, a double honor to his Countrey.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: This should be no counterfeit, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
prose: I do not think he is, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: But Sir, me thinks you do not shew the marks of a Soldier, could you so freely scape, that you brought home no scarrs to be your chronicle?

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
prose: Sir, I have wounds, and many, but in those parts where nature and humanity bids me shame to publish.

speeches.speaker: Witty,
prose: A good Soldier cannot want those badges.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Now am not I of your mind in that, for I hold him the best soldier that scapes best, alwaies at a Cock-fencing I give him the best that has the fewest knocks.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Nay, I'll have a bout with your Scholar too,
To ask you why you should be poor (yet richly learn'd)
Were no question, at least, you can easily
Answer it; but whether you have learning enough,
To deserve to be poor or no (since poverty is
Commonly the meed of Learning) is yet to be tryed;
You have the Languages, I mean the chief,
As the Hebrew, Syriack, Greek, Latine, &c.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Aliquantulum, non totaliter, Domine,

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: The Latine I have sufficiently tried him in,
And I promise you Sir, he is very well grounded.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: I will prove him in some of the rest.
Toia miois fatherois iste Cock-scomboy?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Kay yonkeron nigitton oy fouleroi Asinisoy.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Cheateron ton biton?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Tous pollous strikerous, Angelo to peeso.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Certainly Sir, a very excellent Scholar in the Greek.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: I do note a wondrous readiness in him.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: I do wonder how the Trojans could hold out ten years siege (as 'tis reported against the Greeks, if Achilles spoke but this tongue? I do not think but he might have shaken down the Walls in a seven-night, and ne'er troubled the wooden horse.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: I will try him so far as I can in the Syriack.
Kircom bragmen, shag a dou ma dell mathou.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Hashagath rabgabosh shobos onoriadka.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Colpack Rubasca, gnawerthem shigshag.
Napshamothem Ribsie bongomosh lashemech nagothi.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Gentlemen I have done, any man that can go farther,
I confess my self at a Nonplus.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Faith not I, Sir, I was at my farthest in my natural language, I was never double-tongu'd, I thank my hard fortune.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Well Gentlemen, 'tis pity, (walk farther off a little my friends) I say, 'tis pity such fellows so endow'd, so qualified with the gifts of Nature and Arts, yet should have such a scarcity of fortune's benefits, we must blame our Iron-hearted age for it.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: 'Tis pity indeed, and our pity shall speak a little, for 'em;
Come Sir, here's my groat.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: A Groat Sir? oh sie, give nothing rather, 'twere better you rail'd on 'em for begging, and so quit your self, I am a poor Gentleman, that have but little but my wits to live on.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Troth and I love you the better, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Yet I'll begin a better example than so, here fellows, there's between you, take Purse and all, and I would it were here heavier for your sakes, there's a pair of Angels to guide you to your lodgings, a poor Gentleman's good Will.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Gratias, maximas gratias, benignissime Domine.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
prose: This is an ill example for us, Sir, I would this bountiful Gentleman had not come this way to day.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
prose: Pox, we must not shame our selves now, Sir, I'll give as much as that Gentleman, though I never be Soldier or Scholar while I live; here friends, there's a piece, that if he were divided, would make a pair of Angels for me too, in the love I bear to the Sword and the Tongues.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
prose: My largess shall be equal too, and much good do you, this bounty is a little abatement of my wit, though I feel that.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
prose: May soldiers ever defend such charities.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
prose: And Scholars pray for their increase.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
prose: Fare you well, Sir, these fellows may pray for you, you have made the Scholars Commons exceed to day, and a word with you, Sir, you said you liv'd by your wits, if you use this bounty, you'll begger your wits, believe it.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Oh Sir, I hope to encrease 'em by it, this seed never wants his harvest, fare you well, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
prose: I think a man were as good meet with a reasonable Thief, as an unreasonable Begger sometimes, I could find in my heart to beg half mine back agen, can you change my piece my friends?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Tempora mutantur, & nos mutamur in illis.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: My Gold is turn'd into Latine.
Look you good fellows, here's one round
Shilling more that lay conceal'd.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
prose: Sir, away, we shall be drawn farther into damage else.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
prose: A pox of the Fool, he live by his wits? if his wits leave him any money, but what he begs or steals very shortly, I'll be hang'd for him.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
prose: This breakfast parcel was well fetcht off i'faith.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Tush, a by-blow for mirth, we must have better purchase, we want a fourth for another project that I have ripen'd.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
prose: My wife she shares, and can deserve it.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: She can change her shape, and be masculine.

speeches.speaker: Ruin,
prose: 'Tis one of the free'st conditions, she fears not the crack of a Pistol, she dares say Stand to a Grazier.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
prose: Probatum fuit, profecto Domine.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Good, then you Sir Bacchus, Apollo shall be dispatcht with her share, and some contents to meet us to morrow (at a certain place and time appointed) i^ the Masculine Gender, my Father has a Nephew, and ^ an own Cosin coming up from the University, whom he loves most indulgently, easie Master Credulous Oldcraft (for you know what your meer Academique is) your Carrier never misses his hour, he must not be rob'd (because he has but little to lose) but he must joyn with ^ in a devise that I have, that shall rob my Father of a hundred pieces, and thank me to be rid on't, for there's the ambition of my wit, to live upon his profest wit, that has turn'd me out to live by my wits.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
prose: Cum hirundinis alis tibi regratulor.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: A male habit, a bag of an hunder'd weight, though it be Counters (for my Alchimy shall turn 'em into Gold of my Fathers) the hour, the place, the action shall be a^ large set down, and Father, you shall know, that I put my portion to use, that you have given me to live by;
And to confirm your self in me renate,
I hope you'll find my wits legitimate.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: NAy Lady.
Lady. Put me not in mind on't, prethee,
You cannot do a greater wrong to Women,
For in our wants, 'tis the most chief affliction
To have that name remembred; 'tis a Title
That misery mocks us by, and the worlds malice,
Scorn and contempt has not wherewith to work
On humble Callings; they are safe, and lye
Level with pitty still, and pale distress
Is no great stranger to 'em; but when fortune
Looks with a stormy face on our conditions,
We find affliction work, and envy pastime,
And our worst enemy than that, most abuses us,
Is that we are call'd by, Lady, Oh my spirit,
Will nothing make thee humble? I am well methinks,
And can live quiet with my fate sometimes,
Until I look into the world agen,
Then I begin to rave at my Stars bitterness,
To see how many muckhils plac'd above me;
Peasants and Droyls, Caroches full of Dunghils,
Whose very birth stinks in a generous nostril,
Glistring by night like Glow-worms through the High streets
H^rried by Torch-light in the Foot-mans hands
That shew like running Fire-drakes through the City,
And I put to my shifts and wits to live,
Nay sometimes danger too; on Foot, on Horseback,
And earn my supper manfully e'r I get it,
Many a meal I have purchas'd at that rate,
Fed with a wound upon me, stampt at midnight.
Hah, what are you?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Now you may tell your self, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Oh Mr. Priscian, what's the project,
For you ne'r come without one.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: First, your Husband,
Sir Ruinous Gentry greets you with best wishes,
And here has sent you your full share by me
In five Cheats and two Robberies.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: And what comes it too?

speeches.speaker: Prisc.
verse: Near upon thirteen pound.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: A goodly share,
'Twill put a Lady scarce in Philip and Cheyney,
With three small Bugle Laces, like a Chamber-maid,
Here's precious listing.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: 'Las you must consider, Lady,
'Tis but young Term, Attornies ha small doings yet,
Then Highway Lawyers, they must needs ha little,
We'ave had no great good luck to speak troth, Beauty,
Since your stout Ladyship parted from's at Highgate,
But there's a fair hope now for a pr^sent hunder'd,
Here's mans Apparel, your Horse stands at door.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: And what's the virtuous plot now?

speeches.speaker: Prisc.
verse: Marry Lady,
You, like a brave young Gallant must be robb'd.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: I robb'd?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Nay then—

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Well, well, go on, let's hear Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Here's a seal'd bag of a Hunder'd, which indeed
Are Counters all, only some sixteen Groats
Of white money i'th' mouth on't.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: So, what Saddle have I?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Monsieur Laroon's the Frenchmans.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: That agen,
You know so well it is not for my stride,
How oft have I complain'd on't?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: You may have Jocke's then, the little Scotch one,
You must dispatch.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: I'll soon be ready, Sir,
Before you ha shifted Saddles, many Women
Have their wealth flow to 'em, I was made I see
To help my fortune, not my fortune me.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: My ways are Goblin-led, and the night-Elf
Still draws me from my home, yet I follow,
Sure, 'tis not altogether fabulous,
Such Haggs do get dominion of our tongues
So soon as we speak, the Inchantment binds;
I have dissembled such a trouble on me,
As my best wits can hardly clear agen;
Piping through this old reed, the Guardianess,
With purpose that my harmony shall reach
And please the Ladies ear, she stops below,
And ecchoes back my Love unto my Lips,
Perswaded by most violent arguments
Of self-love in her self; I am so self-fool,
To doat upon her hunder'd wrinkl'd face;
I could beggar her to accept the gifts
She would throw upon me; 'twere charity,
But for pities sake I will be a niggard
And undo her, refusing to take from her;
I'm haunted agen, if it take not now
I'll break the Spell.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Sweet Cuningam, welcome;
What? a whole day absent? Birds that build Nests
Have care to keep 'em.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: That's granted,
But not continually to sit upon 'em;
Less in the youngling season, else they desire
To fly abroad, and recreate their labours,
Then they return with fresher appetite
To work agen.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Well, well, you have built a Nest
That will stand all storms, you need not mistrust
A weather-wrack, and one day it may be
The youngling season too, then I hope
You'll ne'er fly out of sight.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: There will be pains,
I see to shake this Burr off, and sweetest,
Prethee how fares thy charge? has my good friend
Sir Gregory, the countenance of a Lover?

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: No by my troth, not in my mind, methinks
(Setting his Worship aside) he looks like a fool.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Nay i'faith, ne'r divide his Worship from him for that
Small matter; Fool and Worship are no such
Strangers now adaies, but my meaning is,
Has he thy Ladies countenance of Love?
Looks she like a welcome on him? plainly,
Have they as good hope of one another,
As Cupid bless us, we have?

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Troth I know not,
I can perceive no forwardness in my charge,
But I protest I wish the Knight better
For your sake, Bird.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Why thanks sweet Bird, and with my heart I wish,
That he had as strong and likely hope of her
As thou hast of me.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Well, he's like to speed
Ne'er the worse for that good wish, and I'll tell you
Bird (for secrets are not to be kept betwixt us two)
My charge thinks well of you.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Of me? for what?

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: For my sake' I mean so, I have heard her
A hundred times, since her Uncle gave her
The first bob about you, that she'd doe somewhat
For my sake, if things went well together,
We have spoke of doors and bolts, and things and things,
Go too, I'll tell you all, but you'll find
Some advancement, for my sake, I do believe.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Faith be not sparing, tell me.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: By my Lady
You shall pardon me for that, 'twere a shame
If men should hear all that women speak behind
Their backs sometimes.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: You must give me leave yet,
At least to give her thanks.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Nor that neither,
She must not take notice of my blabbing,
It is sufficient you shall give me thanks,
For 'tis for my sake if she be bountiful,
She loves me, and loves you too for my sake.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: How shall I, knowing this, but be ingrate,
Not to repay her with my dearest duty.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: I, but you must not know it, if you tell
All that I open to you; you'll shame us both;
A far off you may kiss your hand, blush or so,
But I'll allow no nearer conference.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Whoop! you'll be jealous I perceive now.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Jealous? why there's no true love without it, Bird,
I must be jealous of thee, but for her,
(Were it within my duty to my Master)
I durst trust her with the strongest temper,
And I dare swear her now as pure a Virgin
As e'er was welcom'd to a marriag^ bed;
If thoughts may be untainted, hers are so.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: And where's the cause of your fear then?

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Well, well;
When things are past, and the wedding Torches
Lighted at Matches, to kindle better fire,
Then I'll tell you more.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Come, come, I see farther,
That if we were married, you'd be jealous.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: I protest I should a little, but not of her
It is the married woman (if you mark it)
And not the Maid that longs, the appetite
Follows the first taste, when we have relisht
We wish cloying, the taste once pleas'd before,
Then our desire is whetted on to more,
But I reveal too much to you, i'faith Bird.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Not a whit i'faith, Bird, betwixt you and I,
I am beholding for bettering of my knowledg.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Nay, you shall know more of me, if you'll, be rul'd
But make not things common.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Ud' so, your Lady?

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: I, 'tis no matter, she'll like well of this,
Our familiarity is her content.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
prose: This present from Sir Gregery?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: From my Master, the Worshipful, right Sir Gregery Fop.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
prose: A Ruffe? and what might be his high conceit
In sending of a Ruff?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: I think he had two conceits in it forsooth, too high too Low, Ruff high, because as the Ruff does embrace your neck all day, so does he desire to throw his Knightly Arms.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
prose: But then I leave him off a-nights.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Why then he is ruffe low, a ruffian, a bold adventurous errand to do any rough service for his Lady.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
prose: A witty and unhappy conceit. does he mean
As he seems to say unto that reverence?
He does wooe her sure.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: To tell you you truth, Lady, his conceit was far better than I have blaz'd it yet.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
prose: Do you think so, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Nay, I know it forsooth, for it was two days, e'r he compass'd it, to find a sitting present for your Ladyship, he was sending once a very fine Puppy to you.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
prose: And that he would have brought himself.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: So he would indeed, but then he alter'd his device, and sent this Ruffe; requesting with all, that whensoever it is foul, you (with your own hands) would bestow the starching of it.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
prose: Else she wooes him, now his eyes s^oots this way;
And what was the reason for that, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: There lies his main conceit, Lady, for says he, in so doing she cannot chuse but in the starching, to clap it often between her hands, and so she gives a great liking and applause to my Present, whereas, if I should send a Puppy, she ever calls it to her with hist, hiss, hiss, which is a fearful disgrace, he drew the device from a Play, at the Bull tother day.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
prose: I marry Sir, this was a rich conceit indeed.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: And far fetch'd, therefore good for you, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
prose: How now? which way look you, Bird?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
prose: At the Fool Bird, shall I not look at the Fool?

speeches.speaker: Guard.
prose: At the Fool and I here? what need that? pray look this way.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: I'll fit him aptly, either I'll awake
His wits (if he have any,) or force him
To appear (as yet I cannot think him)
Without any. Sirrah, tell me one thing true
That I shall aske you now, Was this device
Your Masters own? I doubt his wit in it;
He's not so ingenuous.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: His own I assure you, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
prose: Nay, you must not lye.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Not with a Lady, I'd rather lye with you, than lie with my Master, by your leave in such a case as this.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
prose: Yet agen your eye?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
prose: The fool makes mirth i'faith,
I would hear some.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
prose: Come, you shall hear none but me.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Come hither, friend, nay, come nearer me; did
Thy Master send thee to me? he may be wise,
But did not shew it much in that; men sometimes
May wrong themselves unawares, when they least think on't,
Was Vulcan ever so unwise to send Mars
To be his spokesman, when he went a wooing?
Send thee? hey-ho, a pretty rowling eye.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: I can turn vp the white and the black too, and need be forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Neec.
prose: Why, here's an amorus nose.
You see the worst of my nose, forsooth

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: A cheek, how I could put it now in dalliance,
A pair of Lips, oh that we were uney'd,
I could suck Sugar from 'em, what a beard's here?
When will the Knight thy Master have such a
Stamp of man-hood on his face? nay, do not blush.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: 'Tis nothing but my flesh and blood that rises so.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: 'Death, she courts the fool.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Away, away, 'tis sport, do not mind it.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Give me thy hand, come, be familiar;
Here's a promising palm; what a soft
Handful of pleasure's here, here's Down compar'd
With Flocks and quilted Straw, thy Knights fingers
Are lean mattrice rubbers to these Feathers,
I prethee let me lean my cheek upon't.
What a soft pillow's here?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Hum, umh, hu, hum.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Why there's a courage in that lively passion,
Measure thee all o'r, there's not a limb
But has his full proportion, it is my voice,
There's no compare betwixt the Knight and thee,
The goodlier man behalf, at once now
I see thee all over.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose:
If you had seen me swim t'other day on my back, you would have sed you had seen, there was two Chambermaids that saw me, and my legs by chance were tangled in the flags, and when they saw how I was hang'd,
they cryed out, Oh help the man for fear he be drown'd.

speeches.speaker: Neec.
prose: They could do no less in pity, come thine arm, we'll walk together.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
prose: Blindness of Love and Women, why she dotes upon the fool.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: What's that to you, mind her not.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Away you Burr.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: How's that?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Hang of Fleshook, fasten thine itchy claspe
On some dry Toad-stool that will kindle with thee,
And burn together.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Oh abominable,
Why do you not love me?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: No, never did;
I took thee down a little way to
Enforce a Vomit from my offended stomach,
Now thou'rt up agen, I loath thee filthily.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Oh villain.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Why dost thou not see a sight.
Would make a man abiure the sight of Women.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Ha, ha, ha,, he's vext; ha, ha, ha,

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Why dost thou laugh?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Because thou laugh'st, nothing else i'faith.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: She has but mockt my folly, else she finds not
The bosome of my purpose, some other way,
Must make me know; I'll try her, and may chance quit
The fine dexterity of her Lady-wit.

speeches.speaker: Neec.
verse: Yes introth, I laught to think of thy Master,
Now, what he would think if he knew this?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: By my troth I laugh at him too, faith sirrah, he's but a fool to say the truth, though I say't, that should not say't.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Yes, thou shouldst say truth, and I believe thee;
Well, for this time we'll part, you perceive something,
Our tongues betray our hearts, there's our weakness,
But pray be silent.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: As Mouse in Cheese, or Goose in Hay i'faith.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Look, we are cut off, there's my hand where my Lips would be.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: I'll wink, and think 'em thy Lips, farewel.

speeches.speaker: Neece,
verse: Now Guardianess, I need not ask where you have been.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Oh Lady, never was woman so abus'd.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Dost thou hear Lady, sweet-heart, I had forgot to tell thee, if you will, I will come back in the evening.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
prose: By no means, come not till I send for you.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: If there be any need, you may think of things when I am gone, I may be convey'd into your chamber, I'll lye under the bed while midnight, or so, or you shall put me up in one of your little boxes, I can creep in at a small hole.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
prose: These are things I dare not venture, I charge you on my love, never come till I send for you.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Verbum insapienti, 'tis enough to the wise, nor I think it is not fit the Knight should know any thing yet.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
prose: By no means, pray you go now, we are suspected.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: For the things that are past, let us use our secrets.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Now I'll make a firm trial of your love,
As you love me, not a word more at this time,
Not a syllable, 'tis the seal of love, take heed.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Hum, hum, hum, hum—.
He humhs loath to depart.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: So, this pleasant trouble's gone, now Guardianess,
What? your eyes easing your heart, the cause woman?

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: The cause is false man, Madam, oh Lady,
I have been gull'd in a shining Carbuncle,
A very Glo-worm, that I thought had fire in't,
And 'tis as cold as Ice.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: And justly serv'd,
Wouldst thou once think that such an early spring
Would dote upon thine Autumn?

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Oh, had you heard him but protest.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: I would not have believ'd him,
Thou might'st have perceiv'd how I mock'd thy folly.
In wanton imitation with the Fool,
Go weep the sin of thy credulity,
Not of thy loss, for it was never thine,
And it is gain to miss it; wert thou so dull?
Nay, yet thou'rt stupid and uncapable,
Why, thou wert but the bait to fish with, not
The prey, the stale to catch another Bird with.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Indeed he call'd me Bird.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Yet thou perceiv'st not,
It is your Neece he loves, wouldst thou be made
A stalking Jade? 'tis she examine it,
I'll hurry all awry, and tread my path
Over unbeaten grounds, go level to the mark,
Not by circular bouts, rare things are pleasing,
And rare's but seldom in the simple sence,
But has her Emphasis with eminence.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: My Neece? she the rival of my abuse?
My flesh and blood wrong me? I'll Aunt her for't;
Oh opportunity, thou blessest me
Now Gentlewoman are you parted so soon?
Where's your friend I pray? your Cuningam?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: What say you Aunt?

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Come, come, your Cuningame?
I am not blind with age yet, nor deaf.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Dumb I am sure you are not, what all you Aunt?
Are you not well?

speeches.speaker: Guard.
prose: No, nor sick, nor mad, nor in my wits, nor sleeping, nor waking, nor nothing, nor any thing; I know not what I am, nor what I am not,

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Mercy cover us, what do you mean, Aunt?

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: I mean to be reveng'd.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: On whom?

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: On thee Baggage.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Revenge should follow injury,
Which never reacht so far as thought in me
Towards you Aunt,

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Your cunning, minion.
Nor your Cuningame; can either blind me,
The gentle Beggar loves you.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Beseech you,
Let me stay your error, I begin to hear,
And shake off my amazement; if you think
That ever any passage treating love
Hath been betwixt us yet commenc'd, any
Silent eye-glance that might but sparkle fire,
So much as Brother and Sister might meet with,
The Lip-salute, so much as strangers might
Take a farewel with, the commixed hands,
Nay, but the least thought of the least of these;
In troth you wrong your bosom, by that truth
(Which I think yet you durst be bail for in me,
If it were offer'd ye) I am as free
As all this protestation.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: May I believe this?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: If ever you'll believe truth: why, I thought he had spoke love to you, and if his heart prompted his tongue, sure I did hear so much.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Oh falsest man, Ixion's plague fell on me,
Never by woman (such a masculine cloud)
So airy and so subtle was embrac'd.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: By no cause in me, by my life dear Aunt.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: I believe you, then help in my revenge,
And you shall do't, or lose my love for ever,
I'll have him quitted at his equal weapon,
Thou art young, follow him, bait his desires
With all the Engines of a womans wit,
Stretch modesty even to the highest pitch;
He cannot freeze at such a flaming beauty;
And when thou hast him by th' amorous gills,
Think on my vengeance, choak up his desires,
Then let his banquetings be Tantalisme,
Let thy disdain spurn the dissembler out;
Oh I should climb my Stars, and sit above,
To see him burn to ashes in his love.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: This will be a strange taste, Aunt, and an
Unwilling labour, yet in your injunction
I am a servant to't.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Thou'lt undertak't?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Yes, let the success commend it self hereafter.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Effect it Girl, my substance is thy store,
Nothing but want of Will makes woman poor.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Why Pompey, thou art not stark mad, art thou?
Wilt thou not tell me how my Lady does?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Your Lady.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Did she receive the thing that I sent her kindly, or no:

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: The thing that you sent her, Knight, by the thing that you sent, was for the things sake that was sent to carry the thing that you sent, very kindly receiv'd; first, there is your Indenture, now go seek you a servant: secondly, you are a Knight: thirdly and lastly, I am mine own man: and fourthly, fare you well.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Why Pompey? prethee let me speak with thee,
I'll lay my life some hare has crost him.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Knight, if you be a Knight, so keep you; as for the Lady, who shall say that she is not a fair Lady, a sweet Lady, an honest and a virtuous Lady, I will say he is a base fellow, a blab of his tongue, and I will make him eat these fingers ends.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Why, here's no body says so Pompey.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Whatsoever things have past between the Lady and the other party, whom I will not name at this time, I say she is virtuous and honest, and I will maintain it, as long as I can maintain my self with bread and water.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Why I know no body thinks otherwise.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Any man that does but think it in my hearing, I will make him think on't while he has a thought in his bosom; shall we say that kindnesses from Ladies are common? or that favours and protestations are things of no moment betwixt parties and parties? I say still, whatsoever has been betwixt the Lady and the party, which I will not name, that she is honest, and shall be honest, whatsoever she does by day or by night, by light or by darkness, with cut and long tail.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Why I say she is honest.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Is she honest? in what sense do you say she is honest, Knight?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: If I could not find in my heart to throw my dagger at thy head, hilts and all, I'm an ass, and no Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Throw your Dagger at me! do not Knight, I give you fair warning, 'tis but cast away if you do, for you shall have no other words of me, the Lady is an honest Lady, whatsoever reports may go of sports and toys, and thoughts, and words, and deeds, betwixt her and the party which I will not name; this I give you to understand, That another man may have as good an eye, as amorous a nose, as fair a stampt beard, and be as proper a man as a Knight, (I name no parties) a Servingman may be as good as a Sir, a Pompey as a Gregory, a Doodle as a Fop; so Servingman Pompey Doodle, may be respected as well with Ladies (though I name no parties) as Sir Gregory Fop; so farewell:

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: If the fellow be not out of his wits, then will I never have any more wit while I live; either the sight of the Lady has gaster'd him, or else he's drunk, or else he walks in his sleep, or else's a fool, or a knave, or both, one of the three, I'm sure 'tis; yet now I think on't, she has not us'd me so kindly as her Uncle promis'd me she should, but that's all one, he says I shall have her, and I dare take his word for the best worse I have, and that's a weightier thing than a Lady, I'm sure on't.

speeches.speaker: Lady Ruin.
verse: Nay, I am your own, 'tis in your pleasure
How you'll deal with me; yet I would intreat,
You will not make that which is bad enough,
Worse than it need be, by a second ill,
When it can render you no second profit;
If it be coin you seek, you have your prey,
All my store I vow, (and it weighs a hundred)
My life, or any hurt you give my body,
Can inrich you no more.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: You may pursue.

speeches.speaker: L. Ruin.
verse: As I am a Gentleman; I never will,
Only we'll bind you to quiet behaviour
Till you call out for Bail, and on th' other
Side of the hedge leave you; but keep the peace
Till we be out of hearing, for by that
We shall be out of danger, if we come back,
We come with a mischief.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: You need not fear me.

speeches.speaker: Prise.
verse: Come, we'll bestow you then.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
prose: Why law you Sir, is not this a swifter Reven^ than, Sic probas, ergo's & igitur's can bring in? why is not this one of your Syllogismes in Barbara? Omne utile est bonestum.

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: Well Sir, a little more of this acquaintance,
