Will make me know you fully, I protest.
You have (at first sight) made me conscious
Of such a deed my dreams ne'er prompted, yet
I could almost have wish'd rather ye'ad rob'd me
Of my Cloak, (for my Purse 'tis a Scholars)
Than to have made me a robber.
I had rather have answered three difficult questions,
Than this one, as easie, as yet it seems.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Tush, you shall never come to farther answer for't;
Can you confess your penurious Uncle,
In his full face of love, to be so strict
A Nigard to your Commons, that you are fain
To size your belly out with Shoulder Fees?
With Rumps and Kidneys, and Cues of single Beer,
And yet make Daymy to feed more daintily,
At this easier rate? sie Master Credulous,
I blush for you.

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: This is a truth undeniable.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Why go to then, I hope I know your Uncle,
How does he use his Son, nearer than you?

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: Faith, like his Jade, upon the bare Commons,
Turn'd out to pick his living as he can get it;
He would have been glad to have shar'd in such
A purchase, and thank'd his good fortune too.
But mum no more—is all safe, Bullies?

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
verse: Secure, the Gentleman thinks him most happy in his loss,
With his safe life and limbs, and redoubles
His first vow, as he is a Gentleman,
Never to pursue us.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Well away then,
Disperse you with Master Credulous, who still
Shall bear the purchase, Priscian and I,
Will take some other course: You know our meeting
At the Three Cups in St Gile's, with this proviso,
(For 'tis a Law with us) that nothing be open'd
Till all be present, the looser saies a hundred,
And it can weigh no less.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
verse: Come, Sir, we'll be your guide.

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: My honesty, which till now was never forfeited,
All shall be close till our meeting.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Tush, I believ't,
And then all shall out; where's the thief that's robb'd?

speeches.speaker: L. Rui.
verse: Here Master Oldcraft, all follows now.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: 'Twas neatly done, wench, now to turn that bag
Of counterfeits to current pieces, & actum est.

speeches.speaker: L. Rui.
verse: You are the Chymist, we'll blow the fire still,
If you can mingle the ingredients.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: I will not miss a cause, a quantity, a dram,
You know the place.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: I have told her that, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Good, turn Ruinous to be a Constable, I'm sure
We want not beards of all sorts, from the
Worshipful Magistrate to the under Watchman;
Because we must have no danger of life,
But a cleanly cheat, attach Credulous,
The cause is plain, the theft found about him;
Then fall I in his own Cosins shape
By mere accident, where finding him distrest,
I with some difficulty must fetch him off,
With promise that his Uncle shall shut up all
With double restitution: Master Constable, Ruinous
His mouth shall be stopt; you, Mistriss rob-thief,
Shall have your share of what we can gull my Father of;
Is't plain enough?

speeches.speaker: L. Rui.
verse: As plain a cozenage as can be, faith.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Father, I come again, and again when this is
Past too, Father, one will beget another;
I'd be loath to leave your posterity barren,
You were best come to composition Father,
Two hundred pieces yearly allow me yet,
It will be the cheaper (Father) than my wit,
For I will cheat none but you, dear Father.

speeches.speaker: Old. K.
verse: WHy now you take the course Sir Gregory Fop:
I could enforce her, and I list but love
That's gently won, is a man's own for ever,
Have you prepar'd good Musick?

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: As fine a noise, Uncle, as heart can wish.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Why that's done like a Suitor,
They must be woo'd a hundred several ways,
Before you obtain the right way in a woman,
'Tis an odd creature, full of creeks and windings.
The Serpent has not more; for sh'as all his,
And then her own beside came in by her mother.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: A fearful portion for a man to venture on.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: But the way found once by the wits of men,
There is no creature lies so tame agen.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: I promise you, not a house-Rabbit, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: No sucker on 'em all.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: What a thing's that?
They're pretty fools I warrant, when they'r tame
As a man can lay his lips too.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: How were you bred, Sir?
Did you never make a fool of a Tenants daughter?

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: Never i'faith, they ha' made some fools for me,
And brought 'em many a time under their aprons.

speeches.speaker: Old R.
verse: They could not shew you the way plainlier, I think,
To make a fool again.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: There's fools enough, Sir,
'Less they were wiser.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: This is wondrous rare,
Come you to London with a Maiden-head, Knight?
A Gentleman of your rank ride with a Cloak-bag?
Never an Hostess by the way to leave it with?
Nor Tapsters Sister? nor head-Ostlers Wife?
What no body?

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: Well mock'd old Wit-monger,
I keep it for your Neece.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Do not say so for shame, she'll laugh at thee,
A wife ne'er looks for't, 'tis a batchelors penny,
He may giv't to a begger-wench, i'th' progress time,
And ne'er be call'd to account for't.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: Would I had known so much,
I could ha' stopt a beggers mouth by th' way.
That rail'd upon me, 'cause I'd give her nothing—
What, are they come?

speeches.speaker: Pag.
verse: And plac'd directly, Sir,
Under her window.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: What may I call you, Gentleman?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: A poor servant to the Viol, I'm the Voice, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: In good time Master Voice.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Indeed good time does get the mastery.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: What Countreyman, Master Voice?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Sir, born at Ely, we all set up in Ela
But our house commonly breaks in Rutland-shire.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: A shrewd place by my faith, it may well break your voice,
It breaks many a mans back; come, set to your business.
FAin would I wake you, Sweet, but fear
I should invite you to worse chear;
In your dreams you cannot fare
Meaner than Musick; no compare;
None of your slumbers are compil'd
~nder the pleasure makes a Child;
Your day-delights, so well compact,
That what you think, turns all to act:
I'd wish my life no better play,
Your dream by night, your thought by day.
Wake gently, wake,
Part softly from your dreams;
The morning flies
To your fair eyes,
To take her special beams:

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: I hear her up, here Master Voice,
Pay you the Instruments, save what you can.
To keep you when you're crackt.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Who should this be?
That I'm so much beholding to, for sweetness?
Pray Heaven it happens right.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: Good morrow, Mistriss.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: An ill day and a thousand come upon thee,

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: 'Light, that's six hundred more than any Almanack has.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Comes it from thee? it is the mangiest Musick
That ever woman heard.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: Nay, say not so, Lady,
There's not an itch about 'em.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: I could curse
My attentive powers, for giving entrance to't;
There is no boldness like the impudence
That's lockt in a fools bloud, how durst you do this?
In conscience I abus'd you as sufficiently
As woman could a man; insatiate Coxcomb,
The mocks and spiteful language I have given thee,
Would o' my life ha? serv'd ten reasonable men,
And rise contented too, and left enough for their friends.
Thou glutton at abuses, never satisfied?
I am perswaded thou devour'st more flouts
Than all thy body's worth, and still a hungred!
A mischief of that maw, prethee seek elsewhere,
Introth I am weary of abusing thee;
Get thee a fresh Mistriss, thou'st make work enough;
I do not think there's scorn enough in Town
To serve thy turn, take the Court-Ladies in,
And all their Women to 'em, that exceed 'em.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: Is this in earnest, Lady?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Oh unsatiable!
Dost thou count all this but an earnest yet?
I'd thought I'd paid thee all the whole sum, trust me;
Thou'lt begger my derision utterly
If thou stay'st longer, I shall want a laugh:
If I knew where to borrow a contempt
Would hold thee tack, stay and be hang'd, thou shouldst then:
But thou'st no conscience now to extort hate from me,
When one has spent all she can make upon thee;
Must I begin to pay thee hire again?
After I have rid thee twice? faith 'tis unreasonable.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: Say you so? I'll know that presently.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Now he runs
To fetch my Uncle to this musty bargain,
But I have better ware always at hand.
And lay by this still, when he comes to cheapen.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I met the Musick now, yet cannot learn
What entertainment he receiv'd from her

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: There's some body set already, I must to't, I see,
Well, well, Sir Gregory?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Hah, Sir Gregory?

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Where e'er you come, you may well boast your conquest.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: She's lost y'saith, enough, has fortune then
Remembred her great boy? she seldom fails 'em.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: H' was the unlikeliest man at first, methought,
To have my love, we never met but wrangled,

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: A pox upon that wrangling, say I still,
I never knew it sail yet, where e'er't came;
It never comes but like a storm of hail,
'Tis sure to bring fine weather at the tail on't,
There's not one match 'mongst twenty made without it,
It fights i' th' tongue, but sure to agree i' th' haunches.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: That man that should ha' told me when time was.
I should ha' had him, had been laught at piteously,
But see how things will change?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Here's a heart feels it—Oh the deceitful promises of love!
What trust should a man put i' th' lip of woman?
She kist me with that strength, as if sh'ad meant
To ha' set the fair print of her soul upon me.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: I would ha' sworn 'twould ne'er ha been a match once.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I'll hear no more, I'm mad to hear so much,
Why should I aim my thoughts at better fortunes
Than younger brothers have? that's a Maid with nothing.
Or some old Soap-boilers Widow, without Teeth,
There waits my fortune for me; seek no farther.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: You tell me things, Sir Gregory, that cannot be.
She will not, nor she dares not.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: Would I were whipt then.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: I'll make as little shew of love, Sir Gregory.
As ever Woman did, you shall not know
You have my heart a good while.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Heard you that?

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Man will insult so soon, 'tis his condition,
'Tis good to keep him off as long as we can,
I've much ado, I swear; and love i' th' end
Will have his course, let Maids do what they can,
They are but frail things till they end in man.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: What say you to this, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: This is somewhat handsome.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: And by that little wrangling that I fain'd,
Now I shall try how constant his love is,
Although't went sore against my heart to chide him.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: Alas poor Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Old K,
verse: Now y'are sure of truth,
You hear her own thoughts speak.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: They speak indeed.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Go, you're a brainless Coax; a Toy, a Fop,
I'll go no farther than your name, Sir Gr.
I'll right my self there; were you from this place,
You should perceive I'm heartily angry with you,
Offer to sow strife 'twixt my Neece and I?
Good morrow Neece, good morrow.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Many fair one to you, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Go, you're a Coxcomb. How dost Neece this morning?
An idle shallo^ fool: sleep'st thou well, Girl?
Fortune may very well provide thee Lordships,
For honesty has left thee little manners.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: How am I ^ang' do' both sides?

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Abuse kindnesse? Will't take the air to day Neece?

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: When you please, Sir,
There stands the Heir behind you I must take,
(Which I'd as liaeve take, as take him I swear.)

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: La' you; do you hear't continued to your teeth now?
A pox of all such Gregories; what a hand
Have I with you?

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: No more y'seck, I ha' done, Sir:
Lady, your Scarf's fal'n down.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: 'Tis but your luck, Sir,
And does presage the Mistriss must fall shortly,
You may wear it, and you please.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: There's a trick for you,
You're parlously belov'd, you should complain.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: Yes, when I complain, Sir,
Then do your worst, there I'll deceive you, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: You are a Dolt, and so I leave you, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: Ah sirrah, Mistriss were you caught, i'faith?
We overheard you all; I must not know
I have your heart, take heed o' that, I pray,
I knew some Scarf would come.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: He's quite gone, sure:
Ah you base Coxcomb, couldst thou come again?
And so abus'd as thou wast?

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: 'Twould ha' kill'd
A sensible man, he would ha' gone to his chamber,
And broke his heart by this time.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: Thank you heartily.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Or sixt a naked Rapier in a Wall,
Like him that earn'd his Knighthood, e'r he had it,
And then refus'd upon't, ran up to th' hilts.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: Yes, let him run for me, I was never brought up to 't,
I never profest running i' my life.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: What art thou made on? thou tough villanous vermin.
Will nothing destroy thee?

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: Yes, yes, assure your self
Unkind words may do much.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Why, dost thou want 'em?
I've e'en consum'd my spleen to help thee to 'em:
Tell me what sort of words they be would speed thee?
I'll see what I can do yet.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: I'm much beholding to you,
You're willing to bestow huge pains upon me.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: I should account nothing too much to rid thee.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: I wonder you'd not offer to destroy me,
All the while your Uncle was here.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Why there thou betray'st thy house; we of the Old-Crafts.
Were born to more wit than so.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I wear your favor here.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Would it might rot thy arme off: if thou knewst
With what contempt thou hast it, what hearts bitterness,
How many cunning curses came along with it,
Thoud'st quake to handle it.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: A pox, tak't again then;
Who'd be thus plagu'd of all hands?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: No, wear't still,
But long I hope thou shalt not, 'tis but cast
Upon thee, purposely to serve another
That has more right to't, as in some Countries they convey
Their treasure upon Asses to their friends;
If mine be but so wise, and apprehensive,
As my opinion gives him to my heart,
It stayes not long on thy desertless arme;
I'll make thee e'er I ha' done, not dare to wear
Anything of mine, although I give't thee freely;
Kiss it you may, and make what shew you can,
But sure you carry't to a worthier Man,
And so good morrow to you.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Hu hum, ha hum;
I han't the spirit now to dash my brains out,
Nor the audacity to kill my self,
But I could cry my heart out, that's as good,
For so't be out, no matter which way it comes,
If I can dye with a sillip, or depart
At hot-cockles, What's that to any man?
If there be so much death that serves my turn there.
Every one knows the state of his own body,
No Carrion kills a Kite, but then agen
There's Cheese will choak a Daw; time I were dead I'faith,
If I knew which way without hurt or danger.
I am a Maiden-Knight, and cannot look
Upon a naked weapon with any modesty,
Else 'twould go hard with me, and to complain
To Sir Persidious the old Knight agen,
Were to be more abus'd; perhaps he would beat me well,
But ne'er believe me.
And few Men dye o' beating, that were lost too:
Oh, here's my friend, I'll make my moan to him.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I cannot tear her memory from my heart,
That treads mine down, was ever man so fool'd
That profest wit?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: O Cuningame?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Sir Gregory?
The choice, the Victor, the Towns happy Man?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: 'Snigs, What do'st mean? come I to thee for comfort, and do'st abuse me too?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Abuse you? How Sir?
With justifying your fortune, and your joyes?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Pray hold your hand, Sir, I've been bob'd enough,
You come with a new way now; strike me merrily,
But when a man's sore beaten o' both sides already,
Then the least tap in jest goes to the guts on him;
Wilt ha the truth? I'm made the rankest ass
That e'er was born to Lordships.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: What? No Sir?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I had not thought my body could a yielded
All those foul scurvie names that she has call'd me,
I wonder whence she fetcht 'em?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Is this credible?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: She pin'd this Scarf upon me before her Unckle,
But his back turn'd, she cur'st me so for wearing on't,
The very brawn of mine arme has ak'd ever since,
Yet in a manner forc't me to wear't still,
But hop't I should not long; if good luck serve
I should meet one that has more wit and worth
Should take it from me, 'twas but lent to me,
And sent to him for a token.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I conceit it, I know the Man
That lies in wait for't, part with't by all means,
In any case, you are way-laid about it.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: How Sir? way-laid?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Pox of a Scarf, say I,
I prize my friends life 'bove a million on 'em,
You shall be rul'd, Sir, I know more than you.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: If you know more than I, let me be rid on't,
'Lass, 'tis not for my wearing, so she told me.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: No, no, give me't, the knave shall miss his purpose,
And you shall live.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I would, as long as I could, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: No more replyes, you shall, I'll prevent this,
Pompey shall ma^ch without it.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: What, is't he?
My Man that was?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Call him your deadly Enemy;
You give him too fair a name, you deal too nobly,
He bears a bloody mind, a cruel foe, Sir,
I care not if he heard me.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: But, Do you hear, Sir?
Can't found with reason she should affect him?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Do you talk of reason? I never thought to have heard
Such a word come from you; reason in love?
Would you give that, no Doctor could e'er give?
Has not a Deputy married his Cook-maid?
An Aldermans Widow, one that was her turn-broach?
Nay, Has not a great Lady brought her Stable
Into her Chamber: lay with her Horse-keeper?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Did ever love play such Jades tricks, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Oh thousands, thousands: Beware a sturdy Clown e're while you live, Sir;
'Tis like a huswifery in most Shires about us;
You shall ha' Farmers Widows wed thin Gentlemen,
Much like your self, but put 'em to no stress;
What work can they do, with small trap-stick legs?
They keep Clowns to stop gaps, and drive in pegs,
A drudgery fit for Hindes, e'en back agen, Sir,
Your're safest at returning.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Think you so, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: But, How came this Clown to be call'd Pompey first?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Push, one good-man Caesar, a Pump-maker kersen'd him;
Pompey he writes himself, but his right name's Pumpey,
And stunk too when I had him, now he's crank.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I'm glad I know so much to quell his pride, Sir,
Walk you still that way, I'll make use of this,
To resolve all my doubts, and place this favor
On some new Mistriss, only for a try,
And if it meet my thoughts, I'll swear 'tis I.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Is Pompey grown so malepert? so srampel?
The onely cutter about Ladies honors?
And his blade soonest out?

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Now, What's the news, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Sir Gre.
verse: I dare not say but good; oh excellent good, Sir.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: I hope now you're resolv'd she loves you, Knight?

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: Cuds me, What else Sir? that's not to do now.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: You would not think how desperately you anger'd me,
When you bely'd her goodness; oh you vext me,
Even to a Palsey.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: What a thing was that Sir?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: 'Tis, that 'tis; as I have hope of sweetness, the Scarfe's gone;
Worthy wise friend, I doat upon thy cunning,
We two shall be well matcht, our Issue-male, sure
Will be born Counsellors; is't possible?
Thou shalt have another token out of hand for't;
Nay, since the way's found, pitty thou shouldst want, y'faith,
O my best joy, and dearest.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Well said, Neece,
So violent 'fore your Uncle? What will you do
In secret then?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Marry call me slave, and rascal.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Your Scarfe—the Scarfe I gave you—

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Mass that's true Neece,
I ne'er thought upon that; the Scarfe she gave you—Sir?
What dumb? No answer from you? the Scarfe?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I was way-laid about it, my life threatned;
Life's life, Scarfe's but a Scarfe, and so I parted from't.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Unfortunate woman! my first favor too?

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Will you be still an ass? no reconcilement
'Twixt you and wit? Are you so far fallen out,
You'l never come together? I tell you true,
I'm very Iowsily asham'd on you,
That's the worst shame that can be;
Thus bayting on him: now his heart's hook't in,
I'll make him, e'er I ha' done, take her with nothing,
I love a man that lives by his wits alife;
Nay leave, sweet Neece, 'tis but a Scarfe, let it go.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: The going of it never grieves me, Sir.
It is the manner, the manner—

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: O dissembling Marmaset! If I durst speak,
Or could be believ'd when I speak,
What a tale could I tell, to make hair stand upright now?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Nay, Sir, at your request you shall perceive,
Uncle,
With what renewing love I forgive this?
Here's a fair Diamond, Sir, I'll try how long
You can keep that?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Not very long, you know't too,
Like a cunning witch as you are.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Y'are best let him ha' that too.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: So I were, I think, there were no living else,
I thank you, as you have handled the matter.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Why this is musical now, and Tuesday next
Shall tune your Instruments, that's the day set.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: A match, good Uncle.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Sir, you hear me too?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Oh very well, I'm for you.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: What e'er you hear, you know my mind.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: I, a— on't, too well, if I do not wonder how we two shall come together, I'm a Bear whelp? he talks of Tuesday next, as familiarly, as if we lov'd one another, but 'tis as unlikely to me, as 'twas seven year before I saw her; I shall try his cunning, it may be he has a way was never yet thought on, and it had need to be such a one, for all that I can think on will never do't; I look to have this Diamond taken from me very speedily, therefore I'll take it off o' my finger, for if it be seen, I shall be way-laid for that too.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: OH torture! torture! thou carriest a sting i'thy tail,
Thou never brought'st good news i'thy life yet,
And that's an ill quality, leave it when thou wilt.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Why you receive a blessing the wrong way, Sir,
Call you not this good newes? to save at once Sir
Your credit and your kinsmans life together;
Would it not vex your peace, and gaule your worth?
T'have one of your name hang'd?

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Peace, no such words, boy.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Be thankful for the blessing of prevention then.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Le' me see, there was none hang'd out of our ho^se since Brute,
I ha' search't both Stow, and Hollinshead.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: O Sir.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: I'll see what Polychronicon sayes anon too.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: 'Twas a miraculous fortune that I heard on't

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: I would thou'dst never heard on't,

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: That's true too,
So it had ne'er been done; to see the luck on't,
He was ev'n brought to Justice Aurums threshold,
There had slew'n forth a Mittimus straight for Newgate;
And note the fortune too, Sessions a Thursday,
Jury cull'd out a Friday, Judgment a Saturday,
Dungeon a Sunday, Tyburne a Munday,
Miseries quotidian ague, when't begins once,
Every day pulls him, till he pull his last.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: No more, I say, 'tis an ill theam: where left you him?

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: He's i'th' Constables hands below i'th' Hall, Sir,
Poor Gentleman, and his accuser with him.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: What's he?

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: A Judges Son 'tis thought, so much the worse too,
He'l hang his enemy, an't shall cost him nothing,
That's a great priviledge.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Within there?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Sir?

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Call up the folks i'th' Hall. I had such hope on him,
For a Scholar too, a thing thou ne'er wast sit for
Therefore erected all my joyes in him;
Got a Welch Benefice in reversion for him,
Dean of Cardigan, has his grace already,
He can marry and bury, yet ne'er a hair on's face;
Like a French Vicar, and, Does he bring such fruits to Town with him?
A Thief at his first lighting? Oh good den to you.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Nay, sweet Sir, you'r so vext now, you'l grie^e him,
And hurt your self.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Away, I'll hear no counsel;
Come you but once in seven year to your Uncle,
And at that time must you be brought home too?
And by a Constable?

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Oh speak low, Sir,
Remember your own credit, you profess
You love a Man o'wit, begin at home, Sir,
Express it i'your self.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Nay, Master Constable,
Shew your self a wise man, 'gainst your nature too.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
verse: Sir, no Dish-porridgment, we have brought home
As good men as ye.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Out, a North-Brittain Constable, that tongue
Will publish all, it speaks so broad already;
Are you the Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: The unfortunate one, Sir,
That fell into the power of merciless Thieves,
Whereof this fellow, whom I'd call your kinsman,
As little as I could (for the fair reverence
I owe to fame and years) was the prime villain.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: A wicked prime.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Nay, not so loud, sweet father.

speeches.speaker: Lad.
verse: The rest are fled, but I shall meet with 'em,
Hang one of 'em I will certain, I ha' swore it,
And 'twas my luck to light upon this first.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: A Cambridge man for this? these your degrees, Sir?
Nine years at University for this fellowship?

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Take your voice lower, dear Sir.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: What's your loss, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: That which offends me to repeat, the Money's whole, Sir,
'Tis i'th' Constables hands there, a seal'd hundred,
But I will not receive it.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: No? Not the Money, Sir,
Having confest 'tis all?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: 'Tis all the Money, Sir,
But 'tis not all I lost, for when they bound me,
They took a Diamond hung at my shirt string,
Which fear of life made me forget to hide;
It being the sparkling witness of a Contract,
'Twixt a great Lawyers daughter and my self.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: I told you what he was; What does the Diamond
Concern my Cozen, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: No more did the Money,
But he shall answer all now.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: There's your conscience,
It shewes from whence you sprung.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Sprung? I had leapt a Thief,
Had I leapt some of your alliance.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Slave!

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: You prevent me still.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: 'Slid, Son, Are you mad?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Come, come, I'll take a legal course.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Will you undo us all? What's your demand, Sir?
Now we're in's danger too.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: A hundred Mark, Sir,
I will not bate a doit.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: A hundred Rascals.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Sir, find 'em out in your own blood, and take 'em.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Go take your course, follow the Law, and spare not.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Does fury make you drunk? know you what you say?

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: A hundred dogs dungs, do your worst.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: You do I'm sure; Whose loud now?

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: What his own asking?

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Not in such a case?

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: You shall have but threescore pound; spite a your teeth,
I'll see you hang'd first.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: And what's seven pound more man?
That all this coyle's about? stay, I say, he shall ha't.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: It is your own, you may do what you please with it;
Pardon my zeal, I would ha' sav'd you money;
Give him all his own asking?

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: What's that to you, Sir?
Be sparing of your own, teach me to pinch
In such a case as this? go, go, live by your wits, go.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: I practise all I can.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Follow you me, Sir,
And, Master Constable, come from the knave,
And be a witness of a full recompence.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Pray stop the Constables mouth, what ere you do Sir.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Yet agen? as if I meant not to do that my self,
Without your counsel? As for you, precious kinsman,
Your first years ^ruits in Wales shall go to rack for this,
You lie not in my house, I'll pack you out,
And pay for your lodging rather.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Oh sie Cozen,
The^e are ill courses, you a Scholar too?

speeches.speaker: Cr^
verse: ^ was drawn into't most unfortunately,
By ^ bo^t company.

speeches.speaker: W^
verse: '^ the spoil of all our youth in England.
^ they Gentlemen?
Faith so like some on 'em,
They were ev'n the worse agen.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Hum.

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: Great Tobacco whiffers,
They would go near to rob with a pipe in their mouths.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: What, no?

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: Faith leave it Cozen, because my Rascals use it,

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: So they do meat and drink, must worthy Gentlemen.
Refrain their food for that? an honest man
May eat of the same Pig some Parson dines with,
A Lawyer and a fool feed of one Woodcock,
Yet one ne'er the simpler, t'other ne'er the wiser;
'Tis not meat, drink, or smoak, dish, cup, or pipe,
Co-operates to the making of a Knave,
'Tis the condition makes a slave, a slave,
There's London Philosophy for you; I tell you Cozen,
You cannot be too cautelous, nice, or dainty,
In your society here, especially
When you come raw from the University,
Before the World has hard'ned you a little,
For as a butter'd loaf is a Scholars breakfast there,
So a poach't Scholar is a cheaters dinner here,
I ha' known seven of 'em supt up at a Meale.

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: Why a poacht Scholar?

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: 'Cause he powres himself forth,
And all his secrets, at the first acquaintance,
Never so crafty to be eaten i'th' shell,
But is outstript of all he has at first,
And goes down glib, he's swallowed with sharp wit,
Stead of Wine Vinegar.

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: I shall think, Cozen,
O' your poach't Scholar, while I live.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: Master Credulous,
Your Uncle wills you to forbear the House,
You must with me, I'm charg'd to see you plac'd
In some new lodging about Theeving Lane,
What the conceit's, I know not, but commands you
To be seen here no more, till you hear further.

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: Here's a strange welcome, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: This is the World, Cozen;
When a Man's fame's once poyson'd, fare thee well Lad.
This is the happiest cheat I e'er claim'd share in,
It has a two-fold fortune, gets me coyne,
And puts him out of grace, that stood between me,
My fathers Cambridge Jewel, much suspected
To be his Heir, now there's a bar in's hopes.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
verse: It chinks, make haste.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: The Goat at Smithfield Pens.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Zo, zo, zufficient. Master Cunningame?
I never have ill luck when I meet a wit.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: A Wit's better to meet, than to follow then,
For I ha' none so good I can commend yet,
But commonly men unfortunate to themselves,
Are luckiest to their friends, and so may I be.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: I run o'er so much worth, going but in haste from you,
All my deliberate friendship cannot equal.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: 'Tis but to shew, that you can place sometimes,
Your modesty a top of all your virtues.
This Gentleman may pleasure me yet agen;
I am so haunted with this broad-brim'd hat,
Of the last progress block, with the young hat-band,
Made for a sucking Devil of two years old,
I know not where to turn my self.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: More torture?

speeches.speaker: Mi^
verse: 'Tis rumor'd that you love me.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: A my troth Gentlewoman,
Rumor's as false a knave as ever pist then,
Pray tell him so from me; I cannot fain
With a sweet Gentlewoman, I must deal down right.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I heard, though you dissembled with my Aunt, Sir,
And that makes me more confident.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: There's no falshood,
But payes us our own some way, I confess
I Fain'd with her, 'twas for a weightier purpose,
But not with thee, I swear.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Nor I with you then,
Although my Aunt enjoyn'd me to dissemble,
To right her splene, I love you faithfully.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Light, this is worse than 'twas.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I find such worth in you,
I cannot, nay I dare not dally with you,
For fear the flame consume me.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Here's fresh trouble,
This drives me to my conscience, for 'tis soul
To injure one that deals directly with me.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I crave but such a truth from your love, Sir,
As mine brings you, and that's proportionable.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: A good Geometrician, 'shrew my heart;
Why are you out o'your wits, pretty plump Gentlewoman,
You talk so desperately? 'tis a great happiness,
Love has made one on's wiser than another,
We should be both cast away else;
Yet I love gratitude, I must requite you,
I shall be sick else, but to give you me,
A thing you must not take, if you mean to live,
For a' my troth I hardly can my self;
No wise Physitian will prescribe me for you.
Alass, your state is weak, you had need of Cordials,
Some rich Electuary, made of a Son an Heir,
An elder brother, in a Cullisse, whole,
'Tmust be some wealthy Gregory, boyl'd to a Jelly,
That must restore you to the state of new Gowns,
French Russs, and mutable head-tires,

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: But, Where is he, Sir?
One that's so rich will ne'er wed me with nothing.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Then see thy Conscience, and thy wit together,
Would'st thou have me then, that has nothing neither?
What say you to Fop Gregory the first, yonder?
Will you acknowledge your time amply recompenc'd?
Full satisfaction upon loves record?
Without any more suit, if I combine you?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Yes, by this honest kiss.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: You're a wise Clyent,
To pay your see before-hand, but all do so,
You know the worst already, that's the best too.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I know he's a fool,

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: You'r shrewdly hurt then;
This is your comfort, your great wisest Women
Pick their first Husband still out of that house,
And some will have 'em to chuse, if they bury twenty.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I'm of their minds, that like him for a Husband,
To run youths race with, 'tis very pleasant,
But when I'm old, I'd alwayes wish for a wiser.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: You may have me by that time:
For this first business,
Rest upon my performance.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: With all thankfulness.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I have a project you must aid me in too.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: You bind me to all lawful action, Sir,

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Pray wear this Scarf about you;

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I conjecture now—

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: There's a Court Principle for't, one office must help another;
As for example, for your cast o' Manchits out o'th' Pantry,
I'll allow you a Goose out o'th' Kitchin.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: 'Tis very sociably done, Sir, farewel performance,
I shall be bold to call you so.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Do, sweet confidence,
If I can match my two broad brim'd hats;
'Tis he, I know the Maggot by his head;
Now shall I learn newes of him, my precious chief.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I have been seeking for you i'th' bowling-Green,
Enquir'd at Net^letons, and Anthonies Ordinary,
T'ha's vext me to the heart, look, I've a Diamond here,
And it cannot find a Master.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: No? That's hard y'faith.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: It does belong to some body, a—on him,
I would he had it, do's but trouble me,
And she that sent it, is so waspish too,
There's no returning to her till't be gone.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Oh, ho, ah sirrah, are you come?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: What's that friend?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Do you note that corner sparkle?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Which? which? which Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: At the West end o'th' Coller.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Oh I see't now.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: 'Tis an apparent mark; this is the stone, Sir,
That so much blood is threatned to be sned for.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I pray.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: A tun at least.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: They must not find't i'me then, they must
Goe where 'tis to be had.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: 'Tis well it came to my hands first, Sir Gregory,
I know where this must go.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Am I discharg'd on't?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: My life for yours now.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: What now?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: 'Tis discretion, Sir,
I'll stand upon my Guard all the while I ha't.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: 'Troth thou tak'st too much danger on thee still,
To preserve me alive.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: 'Tis a friends duty, Sir,
Nay, by a toy that I have late thought upon,
I'll unndertake to get your Mistriss for you.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Thou wilt not? Wilt?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Contract her by a trick, Sir,
When she least thinks on't.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: There's the right way to't,
For if she think on't once, shee'l never do't.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: She does abuse you still then?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: A —damnably,
Every time worse than other; yet her Uncle
Thinks the day holds a Tuesday; say it did, Sir,
She's so familiarly us'd to call me Rascal,
She'll quite forget to wed me by my own name,
And then that Marriage cannot hold in Law, you know.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Will you leave all to me?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Who should I leave it to?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: 'Tis our luck to love Neeces; I love a Neece too.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I would you did y'faith.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: But mine's a kind wretch.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I marry Sir, I would mine were so too.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: No rascal comes in her mouth.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Troth, and mine has little else in hers.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Mine sends me tokens,
All the World knows not on.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Mine gives me tokens too, very sine tokens,
But I dare^ not wear 'em.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Mine's kind in secret.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: And there mine's a hell-cat.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: We have a day set too.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: 'Slid, so have we man,
But there's no sign of ever coming together.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I'll tell thee who 'tis, the old womans Neece.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Is't she?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I would your luck had been no worse for mildness;
But mum, no more words on't to your Lady.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Foh!

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: No blabbing, as you love me.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: None of our blood
Were ever bablers

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Prethee convey this Letter to her,
But at any hand let not your Mistriss see't.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Yet agen Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: There's a Jewel in't,
The very art would make her doat upon't.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Say you so?
And she shall see't for that trick only.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Remember but your Mistriss, and all's well.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg
verse: Nay, if I do not, hang me.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I believe you;
This is the onely way to return a token,
I know he will do't now, 'cause he's charg'd to'th' contrary.
He's the nearest kin to a Woman, of a thing
Made without substance, that a man can find agen,
Some Petticoat begot him, I'll be whipt else,
Engendring with an old pair of paund hose,
Lying in some hot chamber o'er the Kitchin:
Very steame bred him,
He never came where Rem in Re e'er grew;
The generation of a hundred such
Cannot make a man stand in a white sheet,
For 'tis no act in Law, nor can a Constable
Pick out a bawdy business for Bridewell in't;
A lamentable case, he's got with a Mans Urine, like a Mandrake.
How now? hah? What prodigious bravery's this?
A most preposterous Gallant, the Doublet sits
As if it mock't the breeches.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Save you, Sir,

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: H'as put his tongue in the fine suit of words too.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: How does the party?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Takes me for a Scrivener. Which of the parties?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Hum, simplicity betide thee—
I would fain hear of the party; I would be loath to go
Farther with her; honor is not a thing to be dallied withall,
No more is reputation, no nor fame, I take it, I must not
Have her wrong'd when I'm abroad; my party is not
To be compell'd with any party in an oblique way;
'Tis very dangerous to deal with Women;
May prove a Lady too, but shall be nameless,
I'l bite my tongue out, e'er it prove a Traitor.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Upon my life I know her.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Not by me,
Know what you can, talk a whole day with me,
Y'are ne'er the wiser, she comes not from these lips.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: The old Knights Neece.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: 'Slid he has got her, pox of his heart that told him,
Can nothing be kept secret? let me entreat you
To use her name as little as you can, though.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: 'Twill be small pleasure, Sir, to use her name.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: I had intelligence in my solemn walks,
'Twixt Paddington and Pan^ridge, of a Scarfe,
Sent for a token, and a Jewel follow'd,
But I acknowledge not the receipt of any,
How e'er 'tis carried, believe me, Sir,
Upon my reputation I receiv'd none.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: What, neither Scarfe nor Jewel?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: 'Twould be seen
Some where about me, you may well think that,
I have an arme for a Scarfe, as others have,
An Ear, to hang a Jewel too, and that's more
Then some men have, my betters a great deal,
I must have restitution, where e'er it lights.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: And reason good.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: For all these tokens, Sir,
Pass i' my name.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: It cannot otherwise be.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Sent to a worthy friend.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I, that's to thee.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: I'm wrong'd under that title.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I dare sware thou art,
'Tis nothing but Sir Gregories circumvention,
His envious spite, when thou'rt at Paddington,
He meets the gifts at Pan^ridge.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Ah false Knight?
False both to honor, and the Law of Arms?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: What wilt thou say if I be reveng'd for thee?
Thou sit as Witness?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: I should laugh in state then.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I'll fob him, here's my hand.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: I shall be as glad as any Man alive, to see him well fob'd, Sir; but now you talk of fobbing, I wonder the Lady sends not for me according to promise? I ha' kept out o' Town these two dayes, a purpose to be sent for; I am almost starv'd with walking.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Walking gets men a stomach.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: 'Tis most true, Sir, I may speak it by experience, for I ha' got a stomach six times, and lost it agen, as often as a traveller from Chelsy shall lose the sight of Pauls, and get it agen.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Go to her, Man.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Not for a Million, enfringe my oath? there's a toy call'd a Vow, has past between us, a poor trifle, Sir; Pray do me the part and office of a Gentleman, if you chance to meet a Footman by the way, in Orange tawny ribbands, running before an empty Coach, with a Buzard i'th' Poop on't, direct him and his horses toward the new River by Islington, there they shall have me looking upon the Pipes, and whistling.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: A very good note; this love makes us all Monkeyes,
Yet I'll go forward with my surer proof.
prose: But to my work: 'Scarfe first? and now a Diamond? these should be sure signs of her affections truth;

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Is't possible?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Nay, here's his Letter too, there's a fine Jewel in't,
Therefore I brought it to you.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: You tedious Mongril! Is't not enough
To grace thee, to receive this from thy hand,
A thing which makes me almost sick to do,
But you must talk too?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I ha' done.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Fall back,
Yet backer, backer yet, you unmannerly puppy,
Do you not see I'm going about to read it?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Nay, these are golden dayes, now I stay by't,
She was wont not to endure me in her sight at all,
The World mends, I see that.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: What an ambiguous Superscription's here?

speeches.speaker: To the best of Neeces.
verse: Why that title may be mine,
And more than her's:
Sure I much wrong the neatness of his art;
'Tis certain sent to me, and to requite
My cunning in the carriage of my Tokens,
Us'd the same Fop for his.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: She nodded now to me, 'twill come in time.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: What's here? an entire Rubye, cut into a heart,
And this the word, Istud Amoris opus?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Yes, yes, I have heard him say, that love is the best stone-cutter.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Why thou sawcy issue of some travelling. Sowgelder.
What makes love in thy mouth? Is it a thing
That ever will concern thee? I do wonder
How thou dar'st think on't? hast thou ever hope
To come i' the same roome where lovers are;
And scape unbrain'd with one of their velvet slippers?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Love tricks break out I see, and you talk of slippers once,
'Tis not far off to bed time.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Is it possible thou canst laugh yet?
I would ha' undertook to ha' kill'd a spider
With less venome far, than I have spit at thee.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: You must conceive,
A Knight's another manner a piece of flesh.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Back, Owles-face.

speeches.speaker: Within.
verse: O. K. Do, do.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: 'Tis my Unckles voice, that.
Why keep you so far off, Sir Gregory?
Are you afraid, Sir, to come near your Mistriss?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Is the proud heart come down? I lookt for this still.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: He comes not this way yet: Away, you dog-whelp,
Would you offer to come near me, though I said so?
I'll make you understand my mind in time;
You run in greedily, like a hound to his breakfast,
That chops in head and all to beguile his fellows;
I'm to be eaten, Sir, with Grace and leisure,
Behaviour and discourse, things that ne'er trouble you;
After I have pelted you sufficiently,
I tro you will learn more manners.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I'm wondring still when we two shall come together?
Tuesday's at hand, but I'm as far off, as I was at first, I swear.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Now Cuningame, I'll be reveng'd at large:
Lady, what was but all this while suspition,
Is truth, full blown now, my Neece wears your Scarfe.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Hah?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Do but follow me, I'll place you instantly
Where you shall see her courted by Cuningame.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: I go with greediness; we long for things
That break our hearts sometimes, there's pleasures misery,

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Where are those gad-flies going? to some Junket now;
That some old bumble-bee toles the young one forth
To sweet meats after kind, let 'em look to't,
The thing you wot on be not mist or gone,
I bring a Maiden-head, and I look for one.
Which is only a Papper so drest.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Yes, yes.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Too manifest now, the Scarfe and all.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: It cannot be, you're such a fearful soul.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: I'll give her cause of fear e'er I part from her.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Will you say so? Is't not your Aunts desire too?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: What a dissembling croane's that? she'l sorswear't now.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I see my project takes, yonder's the grace on't.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Who would put confidence in wit again,
I'm plagu'd for my ambition, to desire
A wi^e Man for a husband, and I see
Fate will not have us go beyond our stint,
We are allow'd but one dish, and that's Woodcock,
It keeps up wit to make us friends and servants of,
And thinks any thing's good enough to make us husbands;
Oh that Whores hat o' thine, o' the riding block,
A shade for lecherous kisses.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Make you doubt on't?
Is not my love of force?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Yes, me it forces
To tear that sorcerous strumpet from th' imbraces.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Lady?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Oh thou hast wrong'd the exquisit'st love—

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: What mean you, Lady?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Mine, you'l answer for't.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Alas, What seek you?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Sir, mine own with loss.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: You shall.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: I never made so hard a bargain.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Sweet Lady?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Unjust man, let my wrath reach her,
As you owe virtue duty;

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: falls on purpose.
Your cause trips you,
Now Minion, you shall feel what loves rage is,
Before you taste the pleasure; smile you false, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: How can I chuse? to see what pains you take,
Upon a thing will never thank you for't.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: See what things you women be, Lady,
When cloaths are taken for the best part of you?
This was to show you, when you think I love you not,
How y'are deceiv'd still, there the Moral lies,
'Twas a trap set to catch you, and the only bait
To take a Lady nibling, is fine clothes;
Now I dare boldly thank you for your love,
I'm pretty well resolv'd in't by this fit,
For a jealous ague alwayes ushers it.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Now blessings still maintain this wit of thine,
And I have an excellent fortune coming in thee,
Bring nothing else I charge thee.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Not a groat I warrant ye.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Thou shalt be worthily welcome, take my faith for't,
Next opportunity shall make us.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: The old Gentlewoman has fool'd her revenge sweetly.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: 'Lass, 'tis her part, she knows her place so well yonder;
Alwayes when Women jumpe upon threescore,
Love shoves e'm from the chamber to the door.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Thou art a precious she-wit.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: FRiend, met in the harvest of our designs,
Not a thought but's busie.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: I knew it Man,
And that made me provide these needful Reapers,
Hooks, Rakers, Gleaners; we'll sing it home
With a melodious Horne-pipe; this is the Bond,
That as we further in your great affair,
You'l suffer us to glean, pick up for crums,
And if we snatch a handful from the~ sheaf,
You will not look a churle on's.

speeches.speaker: Cu^.
verse: Friend, we'll share
The sheaves of gold, only the Love Aker
Shall be peculiar.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Much good do you, Sir,
Away, you know your way, and your stay; get you
The Musick ready, while we prepare the dancers.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
verse: We are a consort of our selves.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: And can strike up lustily.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: You must bring Sir Fop.

speeches.speaker: Cun,
verse: That's perfect enough.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
verse: Bring all the Fops you can, the more, the better fare
So the proverb runs backwards.

speeches.speaker: L. Ruin.
verse: I'll bring the Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Do so first, and then the Fops will follow;
I must to my Father, he must make one.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: While I dispatch a business with the Knight,
And I go with you. Well sed, I thank you,
This small Banquet will furnish our few Guests
With taste and state enough; one reach my Gown.
The action craves it rather than the weather.

speeches.speaker: 1 Serv.
verse: There's one stayes to speak with you, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: What is he?

speeches.speaker: 1 Serv.
verse: Faith I know not what, Sir, a Fool, I think,
That some Brokers shop has made half a Gentleman;
Has the name of a Worthy too.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Pompey? Is't not?

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
verse: That's he, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Alas, poor fellow, prethee enter him, he will need too.
He shall serve for a Witness. Oh Gramercy:
^f my friend Sir Gregory comes, you know him,
Entertain him kindly. Oh Master Pompey, How is't man?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: 'Snails, I'm almost starv'd with Love, and cold, and one thing or other;
Has not my Lady sent for me yet?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Not that I hear, sure some unfriendly Messenger ^s imploy'd betwixt you,

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: I was ne'er so cold in my life, in my Conscience I ^ave been seven mile in length, along the New River; I ^ave seen a hundred stickle bags; I do not think but there's ^udgeons too; 'twill ne'er he a true water.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Why think you so?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: I warrant you, I told a thousand Millers thumbs in it,
I'll make a little bold with your Sweet-meats.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: And welcome Pompey.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: 'Tis a strange thing, I have no taste in any thing.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Oh, that's Love, that distasts any thing but it self.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: 'Tis worse than Cheese in that point, may not a Man break his word with a Lady? I could find in my heart and my hose too.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: By no means, Sir, that breaks all the Laws of Love.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Well, I'll ne'er pass my word without my deed to
A Lady, while I live agen, I would fain recover my taste.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Well, I have news to tell you.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Good news, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Happy news, I help you away with a Rival your
Master bestow'd.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Where, for this Plumbs sake —

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Nay, listen me.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: I warrant you, Sir, I have two ears to one mouth,
I hear more than I eat, I'de ne'er row by Queen Hive
While I liv'd else.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I have a Wife for him, and thou shalt witness the Contract.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: The old one I hope, 'tis not the Lady?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Choak him first, 'tis one which thou shalt see,
See him, see him deceiv'd, see the deceit, only
The injunction is, you shall smile with modesty.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: I'll simper I'faith, as cold as I am yet, the old one
I hope.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: Sir, here's Sir Gregory.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: U'd so, shelter, shelter, if you be seen,
All's ravell'd out again; stand there private,
And you'll find the very opportunity
To call you forth, and place you at the Table.
You are welcome, Sir, this Banquet will serve,
When it is crown'd with such a dainty as you
Expect, and must have.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: 'Tush, these sweet-meats are but sauce to that,
Well, if there be any honesty, or true word in a dream,
She's mine own, nay, and chang'd extreamly,
Not the same Woman.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Who, not the Lady?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: No, not to me, the edge of her tongue iS taken off,
Gives me very good words, turn'd up-side-down to me,
And we live as quietly as two Tortoises, if she hold on,
As she began in my dream.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Nay, if Love send forth such Predictions,
You are bound to believe 'em, there's the watch-word
Of her coming; to your practis'd part now,
If you hit it, Aequus Cupido nobis.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I will warrant you, Sir, I will give armes to
Your Gentry, look you forward to your business,
I am an eye behind you, place her in that Chair,
And let me alone to grope her out.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Silence, Lady, your sweet presence illustrates
This homely roof, and, as course entertainment;
But where affections are both Host and Guest,
They cannot meet unkindly; please you sit,
Your something long stay made me unmannerly,
To place before you, you know this friend here,
He's my Guest, and more especially,
That this our meeting might not be too single,
Without a witness to't.

speeches.speaker: Mirab.
verse: I came not unresolv'd, Sir,
And when our hands are clasp'd in that firm faith
Which I expect from you; same shall be bold
'To speak the loudest on't: oh you grasp me
Somewhat too hard friend.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: That's Loves eager will,
I'll touch it gentlier.

speeches.speaker: Mirab.
verse: That's too low in you,
Less it be doubly recompenc'd in me.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: ^Puh, I must stop my mouth, I shall be choakt else.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Come, we'll not play and trifle with delayes,
We met to joyn these hands, and willingly
I cannot leave it till confirmation.

speeches.speaker: Mirab.
prose: One word first, how does your friend, kind Sir Gregory?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Why do you mention him? you love him not?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I shall love you the less if you say so, Sir,
In troth I love him, but 'tis you deceive him,
This flattering hand of yours does rob him now,
Now you steal his right from him, and I know
I shall have hate for't, his hate extreamly.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Why I thought you had not come so weakly arm'd,
Upon my life the Knight will love you for't,
Exceedingly love you, for ever love you.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I, you'll perswade me so.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Why he's my friend,
And wishes me a fortune equal with him,
I know, and dare speak it for him.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Oh, this hand betrayes him, you might remember him in some courtesie yet at least.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
prose: I thank your help in't, here's to his health Where e'er he be.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: I'll pledge it, were it against my health.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Oh, oh, my heart hops after twelve mile a day, upon a good return, now could I walk three hundred mile a foot, and laugh forwards and backwards.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: You'll take the Knights health, Sir,

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Yes, yes forsooth, oh my sides! such a Banquet once a week, would make me grow fat in a fortnight.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Well, now to close our meeting, with the close
Of mutual hands and hearts, thus I begin,
Here in Heavens eye, and all loves sacred powers,
(Which in my Prayers stand propitious)
I knit this holy hand fast, and with this hand
The heart that owes this hand, ever binding
By force of this initiating Contract
Both heart and hand in love, faith, loyalty,
Estate, or what to them belongs, in all the dues,
Rights and honors of a faithful husband,
And this firm vow, henceforth till death, to stand
Irrevocable, seal'd both with heart and hand.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Which thus I second, but oh, Sir Gregory.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Agen? this interposition's ill, believe me.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Here, in Heavens eye, and all Loves sacred powers,
I knit this holy hand fast, and with this hand
The heart that owes this hand, ever binding
Both heart and hand in love, honor, loyalty,
Estate, or what to them belongs in all the dues,
Rights, and duties of a true faithful Wife;
And this firm Vow, henceforth till death, to stand,
Irrevocable, seal'd both with heart and hand.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: A full agreement on both parts.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I, here's witness of that.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Nay, I have over-reacht you Lady, and that's much,
For any Knight in England to over-reach a Lady.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I rejoyce in my deceit, I am a Lady
Now, I thank you, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Good morrow Lady Fop.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: 'Snails, I'm gull'd, made a worshipful ass, this is not my Lady.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: But it is Sir, and true as your dream told you,
That your Lady was become another Woman.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: I'll have another Lady, Sir, if there were no more Ladies in London, blind-man buff is an unlawful Game.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Come, down on your knees first, and thank your
Stars.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: A fire of my stars, I may thank you, I think.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: So you may pray for me, and honor me,
That have preserv'd you from a lasting torment,
For a perpetual comfort; Did you call me friend?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: I pray pardon me for that, I did miscall you, I confess.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: And should I, receiving such a thankful name,
Abuse it in the act? Should I see my friend
Baffed, disgrac'd, without any reverence
To your title, to be call'd slave, rascal?
Nay curst to your face, fool'd, scorn'd, beaten down
With a womans peevish hate, yet I should stand
And suffer you to be lost, cast away?
I would have seen you buried quick first,
Your spurs of Knighthood to have wanted rowels,
And to be kickt from your heels; slave, rascall?
Hear this Tongue?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: My dearest Love, sweet Knight, my Lord, my Husband.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: So, this is not slave, and rascall then.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: What shall your eye command, but shall be done,
In all the duties of a loyal Wife?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Good, good, are not curses fitter for you? wer't not better
Your head were broke with the handle of a fan,
Or your nose bor'd with a silver bodkin?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Why, I will be a servant in your Lady.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: 'Pox, but you shall not, she's too good for you,
This contract shall be a nullity, I'll break't off,
And see you better bestow'd.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: 'Slid, but you shall not, Sir, she's mine own, and I am hers, and we are one anothers lawfully, and let me see him that will take her away by the Civil Law: if you be my friend, keep you so, if you have done me a good turn, do not hit me i'th' teeth with't, that's not the part of a friend.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: If you be content —.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I'll not change her for both the Exchanges, New or the Old.
Come, kiss me boldly.
prose: Content? I was never in better content on it my life.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Give you joy, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Oh Sir, I thank you as much as though I did, you are belov'd of Ladies, you see we are glad of underwomen.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Ladies? let not Ladies be disgrac'd, you are as it were a Married Man, and have a family, and for the parties sake that was unnam'd before, being Pese-cod time, I am appeas'd, yet I would wish you make a Ruler of your Tongue.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Nay, no dissention here, I must bar that,
And this (friend) I entreat you, and be advis'd,
Let this private contract be yet conceal'd,
And still support a seeming face of love
Unto the Lady; mark how it availes you,
And quits all her scorns, her Unckle is now hot
In pursuit of the match, and will enforce her,
Bend her proud stomach, that she shall proffer
Her self to you, which when you have flouted,
And laught your fill at, you shall scorn her off,
With all your disgraces trebled upon her,
For there the pride of all her heart will bow,
When you shall foot her from you, not she you.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Good I'faith; I'll continue it, I'd fain laugh a^ the old fellow too, for he has abus'd me as scurvily as hi^ Neece, my Knight-hoods upon the spur, we'll go to Bed, and then to Church as fast as we can.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: I do wonder I do not hear of the Lady yet.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: The good minute may come sooner than you are aware of,
I do not think but 'twill e'r night yet, as near as 'tis.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Well, I will go walk by the New River, in that meditation, I am o'er shooes, I'm sure upon the drie bank, this gullery of my Master will keep me company this two hours too, if love were not an enemy to laughter, I should drive away the time well enough; you know my walk, Sir, if she sends, I shall be found angling, for I will try what I can catch for luck sake, I will fish fair for't,
Oh Knight, that thou shouldst be gull'd so; ha, ha, it does me good at heart,
But oh Lady, thou tak'st down my merry part.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Friend.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Here friend.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Alls afoot, and will goe smooth away,
The woman has conquer'd the women, they are gone,
Which I have already complain'd to my Father,
Suggesting that Sir Gregory is fall'n off
From his charge, for neglects and ill usage,
And that he is most violently bent
On Gentries wise (whom I have call'd a widow)
And that without most sudden prevention
He will be married to her.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: All this is wrong,
prose: This wings his pursuit, and will be before me; I am lost for ever.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: No, stay, you shall not go
But with my Father, on my wit let it lie,
You shall appear a friendly assistant,
To help in all affairs, and in execution
Help your self only.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Would my belief
Were strong in this assurance.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: You shall credit it,
And my wit shall be your slave, if it deceive you.
My Father —

speeches.speaker: Old K.
prose: Oh Sir? you are well met, where's the Knight your friend?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Sir, I think your Son has told you.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Shall I stand to tell't agen? I tell you he loves,
But not my Kinswoman, her base usage,
And your slack performance which he accuses most
Indeed, has turn'd the Knights heart upside down.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: I'll curb her for't, can he be but recover'd,
He shall have her, and she shall be dutiful,
And love him as a Wife too.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: With that condition, Sir,
I dare recall him where he enter'd the Church,
So much interest of love I assure in him.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Sir, it shall be no loss to you if you do.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: I, but these are words still, will not the deeds
Be wanting at the recovery, if it should be agen;

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Why here fool, I am provided, five hunder'd in earnest,
Of the thousands in her Dower, but were they married once,
^'d cut him short enough, that's my agreement.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: I, now I perceive some purpose in you, Father..

speeches.speaker: Old K.
prose: But wherefore is she then stol'n out of doors to him?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: To him? oh sie upon your error, she has another object, believe it, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: I never could perceive it.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I did Sir, and to her shame I should speak it,
To my own sorrow I saw it, dalliance,
Nay, dotage with a very Clown, a Fool.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Wit and wantons? nothing else? nothing else?
She love a fool? she'll sooner make a Fool
Of a wise man.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I, my friend complains so,
Sir Gregory says flatly, she makes a fool of him,
And these hold circumstances are approv'd:
Favours have been sent by him, yet he ignorant
Whither to carry 'em; they have been understood,
And taken from him, certain, Sir, there is
An unsuspected fellow lies conceal'd,
What, or where e'er he is, these slight neglects
Could not be of a Knight else.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
prose: Well Sir, you have promis'd (if we recover him Unmarried) to salve all these old bruises?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I'll do my best, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: I shall thank you, costly Sir, and kindly too.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Will you talk away the time here, Sir, and come behind all your purposes?

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Away good Sir.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Then stay a little, good Sir, for my advice,
Why, Father are you broke? your wit beggar'd,
Or are you at your wits end? or out of
Love with wit? no trick of wit to surprize
Those designs, but with open Hue and Cry,
For all the world to talk on, this is strange,
You were not wont to slubber a project so.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Can you help at a pinch now? shew your self?
My Son, go too, I leave this to your wit,
Because I'll make a proof on't.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: 'Tis thus then,
I have had late intelligence, they are now
Bucksom as Bacchus Froes, revelling, dancing,
Telling the Musicks numbers with their feet,
Awaiting the meeting of permonish'd friends,
That's questionless, little dreading you,
Now Sir, with a dexterous trick indeed, suddain
And sufficient were well, to enter on um
As something like the abstract of a Masque;
What though few persons? if best for our purpose
That commends the project.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: This takes up time.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Not at all, I can presently furnish
With loose disguises that shall fit that Scene.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Why what wants then?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Nothing but charge of Musick,
That must be paid, you know.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: That shall be my charges, I'll pay the Musick.
What e'er it cost.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: And that shall be all your charge,
Now on, I like it, there will be wit in't Father.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I will neither distrust his wit nor friendship,
Yet if his Master brain should be o'er-thrown
My resolution now shall seize mine own.

speeches.speaker: L. Rui.
verse: Nay, let's have Musick, let that sweet breath at least
Give us her airy welcome, 'twill be the best
I fear this ruin'd receptacle will yield,
But that most freely.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: My welcome follows me,
Else I am ill, come hither, you assure me
Still Mr. Cunningame will be here, and that it was
His kind entreaty that wish'd me meet him.

speeches.speaker: L. Ruin.
verse: Else let me be that shame unto my Sex,
That all belief may flie um.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Continue still
The Knights name unto my Guardianess,
She expects no other.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
verse: He will, he will, assure you
Lady, Sir Gregory will be here, and suddainly
This Musick fore-ran him, is't not so consorts?

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
verse: Yes Lady, he stays on some device to bring along
Such a labour he was busie in, some witty device.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: 'Till belong e'r he comes then, for wits a great
Labour to him.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Well, well, you'll agree better one day.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Scarce two I think.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Such a mock-beggar suit of cloaths as led me
Into the fools pair-of-Dice, with Dewze Ace,
He that would make me Mistriss Cun, Cun, Cunnie,
He's quite out of my mind, but I shall ne'er
Forget him, while I have a hole in my head;
Such a one I think would please you better,
Though he did abuse you.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
verse: Fye, speak well of him now,
Your Neece has quitted him.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: I hope she has,
Else she loses me for ever; but for Sir Gregory.
Would he were come, I shall ill answer this
Unto your Uncle else.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: You know 'tis his pleasure
I should keep him company.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: I, and should be your own
If you did well too: Lord, I do wonder
At the niceness of you Ladies now a days,
They must have Husbands with so much wit forsooth.
Worship and wealth were both wont to be
In better request I'm sure, I cannot tell,
But they get ne'er the wiser children that I see.

speeches.speaker: La. Ruin.
verse: La, la, la, la, Sol, this Musick breaths in vain;
Methinks 'tis dull to let it move alone,
Let's have a female motion, 'tis in private,
And we'll grace't our selves, however it deserves.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: What say you Guardianess?

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: 'Las I'm weary with the walk,
My jaunting days are done.

speeches.speaker: L. Ru.
verse: Come, come, we'll fetch her in by course, or else
She shall pay the Musick.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Nay, I'll have a little for my money then.

speeches.speaker: L. Ru.
verse: Hark? upon my life the Knight; 'tis your friend,
This was the warning-piece of his approach.

speeches.speaker: L. Ru.
verse: Ha? no words but mum? well then,
We shall need no counsel-keeping

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Cunningam?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Yes, fear nothing.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Fear? why do you tell me of it?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Your Uncles here.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Aye me.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Peace.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: We have caught 'em.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Thank my wit Father.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Which is the Knight think you?

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: I know not, he will be found when he speaks,
No Masque can disguise his tongue.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Are you charg'd?

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Are you awake?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: I'm answer'd in a question.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Next change we meet, we lose our hands no more.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Are you prepar'd to tye 'em?

speeches.speaker: Cun,
verse: Yes,
You must go with me.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Whither Sir? not from my charge believe me.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: She goes along.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Will you venture and my Uncle here?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: His stay's prepar'd for.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: 'Tis the Knight sure, I'll follow.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: How now, the Musick tir'd before us?

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
verse: Yes Sir, we must be paid now.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Oh that's my charge, Father.

speeches.speaker: Old. K.
verse: But stay, where are our wanton Ladies gone?
Son, where are they?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Only chang'd the room in a change, that's all sure.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: I'll make 'em all sure else, and then return to you.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
verse: You must pay for your Musick first, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Must? are there musty Fidlers? are Beggars choosers now?
Ha? why Witty-pate, Son, where am I?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: You were dancing e'en now, in good measure, Sir,
Is your health miscarried since? what all you, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Death, I may be gull'd to my face, where's my Neece?
What are you?

speeches.speaker: L. Ru.
verse: None of your Neece, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: How now? have you loud instruments too? I'll hear
No more, I thank you; what have I done tro
To bring these fears about me? Son, where am I?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Not where you should be, Sir, you shall be paying
For your Musick, and you are in a maze.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Oh, is't so, put up, put up, I pray you,
Here's a crown for you.

speeches.speaker: L. Ruin.
verse: Pish, a crown?

speeches.speaker: Ruin. Pris.
verse: Ha, ha, ha, a crown?

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Which way do you laugh? I have seen a crown
Has made a Consort laugh heartily.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Father,
To tell you truth, these are no ordinary
Musicians, they expect a bounty
Above their punctual desert.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
