verse: A— on your Punks, and their deserts too.
Am I not cheated all this while think you?
Is not your pate in this?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: If you be cheated,
You are not to be indicted for your own goods,
Here you trifle time to market your bounty
And make it base, when it must needs be free
For ought I can perceive.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Will you know the lowest price, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: That I will Sir, with all my heart.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Unless I was discover'd, and they now fled
Home agen for fear, I am absolutely beguil'd,
That's the best can be hop'd for.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Faith 'tis somewhat too dear yet, Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
verse: There's not a Denier to be bated, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Now Sir, how dear is it?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Bate but the t'other ten pound?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Not a Bawbee, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: How? bate ten pound? what's the whole sum then?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Faith Sir, a hundred pound, with much adoe,
I got fifty bated, and faith Father, to say truth,
'Tis reasonable for men of their fashion.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: La, la, la, down, a hunder'd pound? la, la, la,
You are a Consort of Thieves, are you not?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: No Musicians, Sir, I told you before.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Fiddle faddle, is it not a robbery? a plain robbery.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: No, no, no, by no means Father, you have receiv'd
For your money, nay and that you cannot give back,
'Tis somewhat dear I confess, but who can help it?
If they had been agreed with before-hand,
'Twas ill forgotten.

speeches.speaker: Old C.
verse: And how many snares have you in this? I see my force,
Case up your instruments, I yield, here, as robb'd and
Taken from me, I deliver it.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: No Sir, you have perform'd your promise now,
Which was, to pay the charge of Musick, that's all.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: I have heard no Musick, I have receiv'd none, Sir,
There's none to be found in me, nor about me.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Why Sir, here's witness against you, you have danc'd,
And he that dances, acknowledges a receipt of Musick.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
prose: I denie that, Sir, look you, I can dance without Musick, do you see, Sir? and I can sing without it too; you are a Consort of Thieves, do you hear what I do?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Pray you take heed, Sir, if you do move the Musick agen, it may cost you as much more.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
prose: Hold, hold, I'll depart quietly, I need not bid you farewel, I think now, so long as that hundred pound lasts with you.
Ha, ha, am I snapt i'faith?

speeches.speaker: Guar.
prose: Oh, Sir, Persidious,

speeches.speaker: Old K.
prose: I, I, some howling another while, Musick's too damnable dear.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
prose: Oh Sir, my heart-strings are broke, if I can but live to tell you the tale, I care not, your Neece my charge is—

speeches.speaker: Old K.
prose: What, is she sick?

speeches.speaker: Guard.
prose: No, no Sir, she's lustily well married.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
prose: To whom?

speeches.speaker: Guard.
prose: Oh, to that cunning dissembler, Cuningam.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
prose: I'll hang the Priest, first, what was he?

speeches.speaker: Guard.
prose: Your kinsman, Sir, that has the Welch Benefice.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
prose: I sav'd him from the Gallows to that end, good: is there any more?

speeches.speaker: Guard.
prose: And Sir Gregory is married too.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
prose: To my Neece too, I hope, and then I may hang her.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
prose: No Sir, to my Neece, thank Cupid; and that's all that's likely to recover me, she's Lady Fop now, and I am One of her Aunts, I thank my promotion.

speeches.speaker: Gred.
verse: I have perform'd your best, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: What have you perform'd, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Faith Sir I must excuse my Cosin in this act,
If you can excuse your self for making him
A Priest, there's the most difficult answer.
I put this practise on him, as from your desire,
A truth, a truth; Father.

speeches.speaker: Cred,
prose: I protest, Sir, he tells you truth, he mov'd me to't in your namh.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
prose: I protest, Sir, he told you a lye in my name, and were you so easie, Mr. Credulous, to believe him?

speeches.speaker: Cred.
prose: If a man should not believe his Cosin; Sir, whom should he believe?

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Good'en to you, good Mr. Cosin Cuningam,
And your fair Bride, my Cosin Cuningam too,
And how do you Sir Gregory, with your fair Lady?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: A little better than you would have had me, I thank you Sir, the days of Puppy, and Slave, and Rascal, are pretty well blown over now, I know Crabs from Verjuyce, I have tryed both, and thou'dst give me thy Neece for nothing, I'd not have her.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
prose: I think so Sir Gregory, for my sake you would not.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
prose: I wou'd thou hadst scap'd her too, and then she had died of the Green sickness: know this, that I did marry in spight, and I will kiss my Lady in spight, and love her in spight, and beget children of her in spight, and when I dye, they shall have my Lands in spight; this was my resolution, and now 'tis out.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: How spightful are you now, Sir Gregory?
Why look you, I can love my dearest Husband,
With all the honors, duties, sweet embraces,
That can be thrown upon a loving man,

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
prose: —This is afore your Uncles face, but behind his back, in private, you'll shew him another tale—

speeches.speaker: Cun.
prose: You see, Sir, now the irrecoverable state of all these things before you: come out of your muse, they have been but Wit-weapons, you were wont to love the Play.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
prose: Let me alone in my muse a little, Sir, I will wa to you anon.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
prose: U'd so, your friend Pompey, how will you answer him?

speeches.speaker: Nee.
prose: Very well, if you'^ but second it, and help me.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: I do hear strange stories, are Ladies things obnoxious?

speeches.speaker: Nee.
prose: Oh, the dissembling falsest wretch is come.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
prose: How now Lady?

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Let me come to him, and instead of love
Let me have revenge.

speeches.speaker: Witty,
prose: Pray you now, will you first examine, whether he be guilty or no.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: He cannot be excus'd,
How many Messengers (thou perjur'd man)
Hast thou return'd with Vows and Oaths, that thou
Wouldst follow, and never till this unhappy hour
Could I set eye of thee, since thy false eye
Drew my heart to it? oh I could tear thee now,
Instead of soft embraces, pray give me leave —

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Faith this was ill done of you Sir, if you promis'd otherwise.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: By this hand, never any Messenger came at me, since the first time I came into her company; that a man should be wrong'd thus?

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Did not I send thee Scarfs and Diamonds?
And thou return'dst me Letters, one with a false heart in't.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Oh fie, to receive favours, return falshoods, and hold a Lady in hand —

speeches.speaker: Claw.
prose: Will you believe me, Sir? if ever I receiv'd Diamonds, or Scarf, or sent any Letter to her, would this sword might ne'er go through me.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Some bad Messengers have gone between you then.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Take him from my sight if I shall see to morrow.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Pray you forbear the place, this discontent may impair her health much.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: 'Foot, if a man had been in any fault, 'twould ne'er a griev'd him, Sir, if you'll believe.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Nay, nay, protest no more, I do believe you,
But you see how the Lady is wrong'd by't;
She has cast away her self, it is to be fear'd,
Against her Uncles Will, nay, any consent,
But out of a mere negl^ and spigh^ to her self,
Married suddainly without any advice.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose:
Why, who can help it? if she be cast aw^
^ thank her self, she might have gone ^rther an^
^ worse; I could do no more than I ^ for 'twas ^ own pleasure to command me, that I should not come, till I was sent for, I had been with her every minute of a^ hour else.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Truly I believe you.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Night and day she might have commanded me, and that she knew well enough; I said as much to her between her and I; yet I protest, she's as honest a Lady for my part, that I'd say, if she would see me hang'd: if she be cast away I cannot help it, she might have stay'd to have spoke with a man.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Well, 'twas a hard miss on both parts.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: So 'twas, I was within one of her, for all this cross luck, I was sure I was between the Knight and home.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
prose: Not gone yet? oh my heart! none regard my health?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Good Sir, forbear her sight awhile, you hear how ill she brooks it.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose:
Foolish woman, to overthrow her fortunes so; I shall think the worse of a Ladies wit, while I live for't— I could almost cry for anger, if she should miscarry now, 'twould touch my conscience a little, and who knows
what love and conceit may do? what would people say, as I go along? there goes he that the Lady died for love on, I am sure to hear on't i'th' streets, I shall weep before hand; foolish woman, I do grieve more for thee now, than I did love thee before; well, go thy ways, wouldst thou spare thy Husbands head, and break thine own heart? if thou hadst any wit, I would some other had been the cause of thy undoing, I shall be twitted i'th' teeth with it, I'm sure of that, foolish Lady.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
prose: So, so, this trouble's well shook off, Uncle, how d'ye there's a Dowrie due, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: We have agreed it sweetest,
And find your Uncle fully recover'd, kind to both of us.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: To all the rest I hope;

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Never to thee, nor thee, easie cosin Credulous,
Was your wit so raw?

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: Faith yours Sir, so long season'd
Has been faulty too, and very much to blame,
Speaking it with reverence, Uncle.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
prose: Yes faith, Sir, you have paid as dear for your time, as any man here.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: I Sir, and I'll reckon it to him. Imprimis, The first preface cheat of a pair of pieces to the Beggars, you remember that I was the example to your bounty there, I spake Greek and Syriack, Sir, you understand me now. Next, the Robbery put upon your indulgent Cosin, which indeed was no Robbery, no Constable, no Justice, no Thief, but all Cheaters; there was a hunder'd Mark, mark you that: Lastly, this memorable 100 pounds worth of Musick, this was both cheats and wit too, and for the assistance of this Gentleman to my Cosin (for which I am to have a Fee) that was a little practice of my wit too, Father; will you come to composition yet, Father?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
prose: Yes faith Sir, do, two hundr'd a year will be easier than so much weekly, I do not think he's barren if he should be put to't agen.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Why this was the day I look'd for, thou shalt have't,
And the next cheat makes it up three hundr'd;
Live thou upon thy ten pound Vicarage,
Thou get'st not a penny more, here's thy full
Hire now.

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: I thank you, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Why there was the sum of all my Wit, Father,
To shuve him out of your favour, which I fear'd
Would have disinherited me.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Most certain it had,
Had not thy wit recover'd it; is there any here
That had a hand with thee?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Yes, all these, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Nephew, part a hundr'd pound amongst 'em,
I'll repay it; wealth, love me as I love wit;
When I die,
I'll build an Alms-house for decay'd wits.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
prose: I'll entertain one in my life time; Scholar, you shall be my Chaplain, I have the gift of twenty Benefices, simple as I am here.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Thanks my great Patron.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
prose: Sir your Gentry and your name shall both be rais'd as high as my fortunes can reach 'em, for your friend^ sake.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Something will be in my present power, the future more,
You shall snare with me.

speeches.speaker: Ruin and Wife.
verse: Thanks worthy Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Sir, I would beg one thing of you?

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: You can beg nothing of me.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Oh Sir, if she begs, there's your power over her.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: She has begg'd me for a fool already, but 'tis no matter.
I have begg'd her for a Lady, that she might have been,
That's one for another.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Nay, but if she beg—

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: Let her beg agen then.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
prose: That your man Pompey's Coat may come over his ears back agen, I would not he should be lost for my sake.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: Well, 'tis granted, for mine own sake.

speeches.speaker: Mirab.
verse: I'll intreat it Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: Why then 'tis granted for your sake.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Come, come, down with all weapons now, 'tis Musick time,
So it be purchas'd at an easie rate;
Some have receiv'd the knocks, some giv'n the hits,
And all concludes in love, there's happy wits.

plays.play_title: The Fair Maid of the Inn. A TRAGI-COMEDY.

speeches.speaker: Cesario.
verse: INterpret not Clarissa, my true zeal
In giving you counsel, to transcend the bounds
That should confine a brother; 'tis your honor,
And peace of mind (which honor last will leave you)
I labor to preserve, and though you yet are
Pure and untainted, and resolve to be so:
Having a Fathers eye, and Mothers care
In all your ways to keep you fair, and upright.
In which respects my best advices must
Appear superfluous; yet since love, dear Sister
Will sometimes tender things unnecessary,
Misconstrue not my purpose.

speeches.speaker: Claris.
verse: Sir, I dare not:
But still receive it as a large addition,
To the much that I already stand ingag'd for,
Yet pardon me, though I profess upon
A true examination of my self,
Even to my private thoughts I cannot find
(Having such strong supporters to uphold me)
On what slight ground the least doubt can be rais'd
To render me suspected, I can fall,
Or from my Fame or Virtue.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Far be it from me,
To nourish such a thought; and yet excuse me,
As you would do a Lapidary, whose whole fortunes
Depend upon the safety of one Jewel,
^f he think no case precious enough
To keep it in full l^stre, nor no locks,
^ough lending strength to Iron doors sufficient
^o guard it, and secure him; you to me are
A Gemm of more esteem, and priz'd higher
^han ^ers do their Muck, or great men Title
^ any s^w (which heaven avert) in you,
^ reputation like a Diamond
Cut newly from the rock, women with envie,
And men with covetous desires look up at)
By prying ei^s discovered in a moment
Would r^nder what the braveries of Florence
For want o^ counterpoize, forbear to cheapen,
Of ^e or no value,

speeches.speaker: Cl^is.
verse: I see brother
The mark you shoot at, and much thank your love;
^ut for my Virgin Jewel which is brought
In comparison with your Diamond, rest assur'd
^t shall not fall in such a workmans hands
Whose ignorance or malice shall have power
To cast one cloud upon it, but still keep
Her native splendor.

speeches.speaker: Cesa.
verse: 'Tis well, I commend you;
And study your advancement with that care
As I would do a Sisters, whom I love
With more than common order.

speeches.speaker: Claris.
verse: That from me,
I hope's return'd to you.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: I do confess it,
Yet let me tell you, (but still with that love,
I wish to increase between us) that you are
Observ'd against the gravity long maintain'd
^n Italy (where to see a maid unmasqu'd
Is held a blemish) to be over-frequent
In giving or receiving visits.

speeches.speaker: Clari.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Whereas the custom is here to wooe by Picture,
And never see the substance: you are fair,
And beauty draws temptations on; You know it,
I wou^d not live to see a willing grant
^m ^ou, to one unworthy of your birth,
^e^ture or fortune; yet there have been Ladies
Of rank, proportion, and of means beyond you,
That have prov'd this no miracle.

speeches.speaker: C^aris.
verse: One unworthy?
Why, pray you gentle brother, who are they
That I vouchsafe these bounties to? I hope
In your strict Criticisme of me, and my manners,
That you will not deny they are your equals.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Angry?

speeches.speaker: Claris.
verse: I have reason, but in cold blood tell me,
Had we not one Father?

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Yes, and Mother too.

speeches.speaker: Claris.
verse: And he a Soldier.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: True;

speeches.speaker: Claris.
verse: If I then borrow
A little of the boldness of his temper.
Imparting it to such as may deserve it;
(However indulgent to your selves, you brothers
Allow no part of freedom to your Sisters)
I hope 'twill not pass for a crime in me,
To grant access and speech to noble suitors;
And you escape for innocent, that descend
To a thing so far beneath you. Are you touch'd?
Why did you think that you had Giges Ring,
Or the Herb that gives invisibility?
Or that Biancha's name had ne'er been mention'd;
The fair Maid of the grand Osteria, brother,

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: No more.

speeches.speaker: Claris.
verse: A little, brother. Your night walks,
And offer'd presents; which coy she, contemn'd,
Your combats in disguises with your Rivals,
Brave Muletiers. Scullions perfum'd with grease,
And such as want meat for Cats must be remembred;
And all this pother for a common trull,
A tempting sign, and curiously set forth,
To draw in riotous guests, a thing expos'd
To every Russians rude assault; and subject
For a poor salary, to a rich mans lust,
Though made up of diseases.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Will you end yet?

speeches.speaker: Claris.
verse: And this a Mistriss for Albertus Son,
One that I should call Sister?

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Part not with
Your modesty in this violent heat; the truth is,
(For you shall be my Confessor) I love her,
But virtuously; report that gives her out
Only for fair, and adds not she is chaste,
Detracts much from her: for indeed she is,
Though of a low condition; compos'd
Of all those graces, dames of highest birth,
Though rich in natures bounties, should be proud of;
But leave her, and to you my nearest care,
My dearest best Clarissa. Do not think
(For then you wrong me) I wish you should live
A barren Virgin life; I rather aim at
A noble Husband, that may make you mother
Of many children, one that when I know him
Worth your embraces, I may serve, and sue too:
And therefore scorn not to acquaint me with
That man, that happy man; you please to favour.

speeches.speaker: Claris.
verse: I ever purpos'd it, for I will like
With your allowance:

speeches.speaker: Cesa.
verse: As a pawn of this;
Receive this Ring, but e'r you part with it
On any terms, be certain of your choice,
And make it known to me.

speeches.speaker: Claris.
verse: You have my hand sor't;

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Which were it not my Sisters, I should kiss:
With too much heat.

speeches.speaker: Claris.
verse: My Father and his guests, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: Oh my old friend, my tri'd friend, my Bapties:
These days of rest and feasting, sute not with
Our tougher natures, those were golden ones,
Which were enjoy'd at Sea; that's our true Mother:
The Land's to us a step-dame; there we sought
Honor, and wealth through dangers: yet those dangers
Delighted more than their rewards, though great ones,
And worth the undertakers: here we study
The Kitchin Arts, to sharpen appetite,
Dull'd with abundance; and dispute with Heaven;
If that the least puff of the rough North-wind,
Blast our times burthen, rendring to our Palats
The charming juice less pleasing; whereas there
If we had Bisket, powder'd flesh, fresh water,
We thought them Persian delicates, and for Musick
If a strong gale but made the main yard crack,
We danc'd to the loud Minstrel.

speeches.speaker: Bapt.
verse: And fear'd less,
(So far we were in love with noble action)
A tempest than a calm.

speeches.speaker: Alber,
verse: 'Tis true Baptista;
There, there, from mutual aids lent to each other,
And virtuous emulation to exceed
In manly daring, the true School of friendship,
We learnt those principles, which confirm'd us friends
Never to be forgot.

speeches.speaker: Baptist.
verse: Never I hope.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: We were married there, for bells the roaring Canon,
A loud proclaim'd it lawful, and a prize
Then newly ta'en, and equally divided,
Serv'd as a dowry to you, then stil'd my wife;
And did enable me to be a Husband,
Fit to encounter so much wealth, though got
With bloud and horror.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: If so got, 'tis fit Sir
Now you possess it, that you should enjoy it
In peace, and quiet; I, your Son, and Daughter
That reap the harvest of your winters labour,
Though debtors for it yet have often trembled,
When, in way of discourse, you have related
How you came by it.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: Trembled? how the softness
Of your sex may excuse you, I'll not argue,
But to the world, howe'er I hold thee noble
I should proclaim this boy some cowards bastard,
And not the Image of Albertus youth,
If when some wish'd occasion calls him forth,
To a brave trial, one weak artery
Of his, should show a fever, though grim death
Put on a thousand dreadful shapes to fright him;
The Elements, the Sea, and all the Winds
We number on our compass, then conspiring
To make the Scaene more ghastly; I must have thee
Sirrah, I must, ^f once you grapple with
An enemies ship, to board her, though you see
The desperate Gunner ready to give fire,
And blow the deck u^, or like Caesar's Soldier
Thy hands like his cut off, hang by the teeth,
And die undaunted.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: I even die to hear you:
My son, my lov'd Cesario run such hazards?
Bless'd Saints forbid it: you have done enough
Already for one family, that rude way;
I'll keep him safe at home, and train him up
A compleat Courtier: may I live to see him,
By sweet discourse, and gracious demeanor,
Winn, and bring home a fair Wife and a rich;
'Tis all I rest ambitious of.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: A Wife!
As if there were a course to purchase one
Prevailing more than honourable action?
Or any Intercessors move so far,
To take a Mistriss of a noble spirit,
As the true fame of glorious victories,
Atchiev'd by sweat and bloud! Oh the brave dames
Of warlike Genoua! they had eyes to see
The inward man, and only from his worth,
Courage, and conquests: the blind Archer knew
To head his shafts, or light his quenched Torch,
They were proof against them else.
No Carpet Knight
That spent his youth in Groves, or pleasant Bowers;
Or stretching on a Couch his lazy limbs,
Sung to his Lute such soft and melting Notes,
As Ovid, nor Anacreon ever knew,
Could work on them, nor once bewitch'd their sense;
Though he came so perfund as he had robb'd
Sabea, or Arabia, of their wealth;
And stor'd it in one sute:
^ still remember,
And still remember it with joy, Baptista,
When from the rescue of the Genoua Fleet,
Almost surpriz'd by the Venetian Gallies,
Thou didst return, and wert receiv'd in triumph.
How lovely in thy honor'd wounds and scars
Thou didst appear what worlds of amorous glances
The beauties of the City (where they stood,
Fix'd like so many of the fairest stars)
Shot from their windows at thee? how it fir'd
Their blouds to see the enemies captive stream
Born through the streets? nor could chaste Juliana
The Duke's fair Neece, though guarded with her greatness
Resist this gallant charge, but laying by
Desparity of fortune from the object,
Yielded her self thy prisoner.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Pray you chuse some other theme.

speeches.speaker: Mari.
verse: Can there be one more pleasing?

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: That triumph drew on me a greater torture,
And 'tis in the remembrance little less
Than ever Captive suffer'd.

speeches.speaker: Mari.
verse: How? to gain the savour of so great a Lady?

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Yes, since it prov'd fatal, t'have been happy, Madam,
Adds to calamity, and the heavy loss
Of her I durst not hope for, once enjoy'd,
Turns what you think a blessing to a curse,
Which grief would have forgotten.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: I am sorry I touch'd upon it.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: I burn rather, Sir,
With a desire to hear the story of
Your loves, and shall receive it as a favour,
Which you may grant.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: You must not be deny'd,
Yet with all brevity I must report it;
'Tis true, fair Juliana (Genoua's pride)
Enamour'd of my actions, lik'd my person;
Nor could I but with joy meet her affection;
Since it was lawful, for my first wife dead;
We were closely married, and for some few months
Tasted the fruits of't; but malicious fate,
Envying our too much happiness, wrought upon
A faithless servant, privy to our plot,
And Cabinet-Counselor to Juliana,
Who either for hope, or reward, or fear,
Discover'd us to the incensed Duke:
Whose rage made her close prisoner, and pronounc'd
On me perpetual banishment: some three years
I wander'd on the Seas, since entertain'd
By the great Duke of Florence; but what sate
Attended her? or Prospero my friend,
That staid at Genoua, to expect the issue,
Is yet uncertain.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: From the Duke:

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: He's welcome, to end my forc'd relation.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: Signior Baptista;
The Great Dukes Will commands your present care,

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: It points indeed at both of you;

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: I wait it.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: In Mariana, to your rest.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Nay leave us, we must be private,

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: Stay not long Cesario:

speeches.speaker: Mentivo.
verse: So these old men vanish'd, 'tis allow'd
That we may speak, and howsoe'r they take
Delight in the discourse of former dangers,
It cannot hinder us to treat a little
Of present pleasures.

speeches.speaker: Cesario,
verse: Which if well injoy'd,
Will not alone continue, but increase
In us their friendship.

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: How shall we spend the night?
To snore it out like drunken Dutchmen, would
Sort ill with us Italians. We are made
Of other metall, fiery, quick, and active;
Shall we take our fortune? and while our cold fathers
(In whom long since their youthful heats were dead,)
Talk much of Mars, serve under Venus Ensigns,
And seek a Mistriss,

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: That's a game dear friend,
That does admit no rival in chase of it.
And either to be undertook alone,
Or not to be attempted.

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: I'll not press you;
What other sports to entertain the time with
The following morning?

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Any that may become us.

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: Is the Neopolitan horse the Viceroy sent you,
In a fit plight to run?

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: So my Groom tells me.
I can boast little of my horsemanship;
Yet upon his assurance, I dare wager
A thousand Crowns, 'gainst any horse in Florence,
For an eight mile course,

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: I would not win of you,
In respect you are impatient of loss:
Else I durst match him with my Barbary
For twice the sum.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: You do well to excuse it, being certain to be beaten

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: Tush. You know the contrary.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: To end the controversie
Put it to trial, by my life I'll meet you.
With the next rising Sun.

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: A match. But here
Appears a Cynthia, that scorns to borrow
A beam of light from the great eye of Heaven,
She being her self all brightness; how I envy
Those amorous smiles, those kisses, but sure chaste ones
Which she vouchsafes her brother?

speeches.speaker: Claris.
verse: You are wanton:
Pray you think me not Biancha, leave I pray you;
My Mother will not sleep before she see you,
And since you know her tenderness, nay fondness;
In every circumstance that concerns your safety,
You are not equal to her.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: I must leave you, but will not fail to meet you

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: Soft sleeps to you.

speeches.speaker: Mariana:
verse: Cesario.

speeches.speaker: Claris.
verse: You are call'd again.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Some Sons
Complain of too much rigor in their Mothers;
I of too much indulgence; you will follow.—

speeches.speaker: Claris
verse: You are her first care, therefore lead the way.

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: She staies: blest opportunity, she staies:
As she invited conference, she was ever
Noble, and free: but thus to tempt my frailty,
Argues a yielding in her; or contempt
Of all that I dare offer; stand I now
Consulting? No, I'll put it home.

speeches.speaker: Claris.
verse: Who waits there? more Lights.

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: You need them not, they are as useless,
As at noon-day; can there be darkness, where
Nature then wisely liberal, vouchsaf'd
To lend two Suns.

speeches.speaker: Claris.
verse: Hyperboles:

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: No, truths:
Truths beauteous Virgin, so my love-sick heart
Assures me, and my understanding tells me
I must approach them wisely, should I rashly
Press near their scorching beams, they would consume me
And on the contrary, should your disdain
Keep me at too much distance, and I want
Their comfortable heat, the frost of death
Would seize on all my faculties.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Pray you pause, Sir.
This vehemency of discourse must else needs tire you.
These gay words take not me, 'tis simple faith
Honest integrity, and lawful flames
I am delighted with:

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: Such I bring with me, and therefore Lady,

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: But that you took me off
E're I came to a period; I had added
A long experience must be requir'd
Both of his faith and trust, with whom a Virgin
Trafficks for, what's dearest in this life,
Her liberty, and honor; I confess
I oft have view'd you with an eye of favour,
And with your generous parts the many tenders
Of doing me all fair offices, have won
A good opinion from me.

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: Oh speak ever, I never heard such Musick;

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: A plain tune, Sir:
But 'tis a hearty one; when I perceive
By evident proofs, your aims are truly noble,
And that you bring the Engines of fair Love,
Not of foul Lust, to shake and undermine
My Maiden-fortress: I may then make good
What now I dare not promise.

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: You already
In taking notice of my poor deservings,
Have been magnificent, and 'twill appear
A frontless impudence to ask beyond this
Yet qualifie, though not excuse my error,
Though now I am ambitious to desire
A confirmation of it.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: So it wrong not my modesty to grant it,

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: 'Tis far from me,
I only am a suitor, you would grace me
With some toy, but made rich in that you wore it,
To warrant to the world that I usurp not
When I presume to stile my self your servant,
A ribond from your shooe:

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: You are too humble,
I'll think upon't; and something of more value
Shall witness how I prize you, it grows late,
I'll bring you to the door,

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: You still more bind me.—

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: You find by this assur'd intelligence
The preparation of the Turks against us.
We have met him oft and beat him; now to fear him
Would argue want of courage, and I hold it.
A safer policie for us and our signiories
To charge him in his passage o'er the Sea,
Than to expect him here.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: May it please your Highness
Since you vouchsafe to think me worthy of
This great imployment, if I may deliver
My judgement freely, 'tis not flattery
Though I say my opinion waits on you,
Nor would I give my suffrage and consent
To what you have propos'd, but that I know it
Worth the great speaker, though that the denial
Call'd on your heavy anger. For my self
I do profess thus much, if a blunt Soldier,
May borrow so much from the oyl'd tongu'd Courtier,
(That ecchoes whatsoe'er the Prince allows of)
All that my long experience hath taught me
That have spent three parts of my life at Sea,
(Let it not taste of arrogance that I say it)
Could not have added reasons of more weight
To fortifie your affections' than such
As your grace out of observation meerly
Already have propounded.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: With the honor to give the daring enemy an affront
In being the first opposer it will teach
Your Soldiers boldness: and strike fear in them
That durst attempt you.

speeches.speaker: 1 Magi.
verse: Victuals and Ammunition,
And Money too, the sinews of the War, are stor'd up in the Magazine.

speeches.speaker: 2 Magi.
verse: And the Gallies new rig'd and train'd up,
And at two dayes warning fit for the service.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: We commend your care,
Nor will we e'er be wanting in Our counsels,
As we doubt not your action; you Baptista
Shall stay with us; that Merchant is not wise,
That ventures his whole fortunes in one bottom.

speeches.speaker: Albert^.
verse: Be our Admiral, spare your thanks,
'Tis Merit in you that invites this honor,
Preserve it such; ere long you shall hear more,
Things rashly undertaken end as ill,
But great acts thrive when reason guides the will.
No question 'twas not well done in Caesario,
To cross the horse of young Mentivole
^n the midst of this course.
That was not all, the switching him dull'd him.
Would that both the jades
Had broke their necks, when they first started; 'Slight,
We stand here prating, give them leave to whisper,
And when they have cut one anothers throats
Make in to part 'em.
There is no such hazard,
Their Fathers friendship, and their love forbid it;
^ee where they come!
With fury in their looks.

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: You have the wager, with what foul play got
^ll not dispute:

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Foul play?

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: I cannot speak it
^n a fairer language, and if some respects
^amiliar to my self chain'd not my tongue,
^ should say no more. I should, but I'll sit down,
With this disgrace; how e'er press me no farther.
^or if once more provok'd, you'll understand
^ dare no more suffer an Injury,
Than I dare do one.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Why Sir are you injur'd
^n that I take my right which I would force,
Should you detain it?

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: Put it to judgment.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: No; my will in this shall carry it.

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: Your will? nay, farewell softness then.
This I foresaw.
Hold, hold.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: I am hurt.
Shift for your self, 'tis death.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: As you respect me, bear him off with care,
^f he miscarry since he did the wrong,
^'ll stand the shock of't.
Gently, he will faint else—

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: And speedily, I beseech you; my rage over,
That pour'd upon my reason clouds of error,
^ see my folly, and at what dear loss
^ have exchang'd a real innocence,
To gain a meer fantastical report,
Transported only by vain popular wind,
To be a daring, nay, fool-hardy Man.
But could I satisfie my self within here,
How should I bear my fathers frown? They meet me,
My guilt conjures him hither.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Sirrah:

speeches.speaker: Mentiv.
verse: Sir:

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: I have met the trophies of your russian sword:
Was there no other Anvile to make triall
How far thou durst be wicked, but the bosome
Of him, which under the adulterate name
Of friendship, thou hast murder'd.

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: Murder'd Sir?
My dreams abhor so base a fact; true valour
Imploy'd to keep my reputation fair
From the austerest Judge, can never merit
To be branded with that title; you begot me
A man, no coward; and but call your youth
To memory, when injur'd, you could never
Boast of the Asses fortitude, slave-like patience:
And you might justly doubt I were your son,
If I should entertain it; if Caesario
Recover, as I hope his wound's not mortal,
A second tryal of what I dare doe
In a just cause, shall give strong witness for me
I am the true heir to Baptista's courage,
As to his other fortunes.

speeches.speaker: Baptist.
verse: Boy, to neither:
But on this strict condition, which intreaties
From Saints, nay Angels, shall not make me alter.
A friendship so began, and so continu'd
Between me and Alberto my best friend,
Your brawls shall not dissolve; it is my will,
And as I am thy Father, I command thee,
That instantly, on any termes, how poor
So e'er, it skills not, thou desire his pardon,
And bring assurance to me, he has sign'd it,
Or by my Fathers soul I'll never know thee:
But as a stranger to my blood; perform it,
And suddenly, without reply, I have said it.

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: And in it given a heavier sentence on me
Than the most cruel death; you are my father
And your will to be serv'd, and not disputed
By me, that am your Son: But I'll obey,
And though my heart-strings crack for't, make it known,
When you command, my faculties are your own.

speeches.speaker: Phys.
verse: HAve patience, Noble Sir; your son Caesario
Will recover without question.

speeches.speaker: Surgeon.
verse: A slight wound.
Though it pierc't his body, it hath miss'd the vitals.

speeches.speaker: Phys.
prose: My life for't, he shall take the air again within these ten dayes.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: O but from a friend,
To receive this bloody measure from a friend!
If that a man should meet a violent death,
In a place where he had taken sanctuary,
Would it not grieve him? such all Florence held
Their friendship, and 'tis that which multiplies
The injury.

speeches.speaker: Physi.
verse: Have patience worthy Signior.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: I do protest, as I am Man and Soldier,
If I had buried him in a wave at Sea,
(Lost in some honorable action)
I would not, to the saltness of his grave,
Have added the least tear; but these quarrels
Bred out of game and wine, I had as live
He should have died of a Surfet.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: Oh what comfort? How is it with our Son Sir?

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: His Work-masters
Bear me in hand here, as my Lawyer does,
When I have a crackt Title, or bad Sute in Law,
All shall go well.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: I pray you Gentlemen, what think you of his wound.

speeches.speaker: Physi.
verse: 'Tis but a scratch, nothing to danger.

speeches.speaker: Claris.
verse: But he receiv'd it from a friend,
And the unkindness ta'en at that, may kill him.

speeches.speaker: Mari.
verse: Let me see him:

speeches.speaker: Physi.
verse: By no means, he slumbers.

speeches.speaker: Mari.
verse: Then I cannot believe you,
When you tell me there's hope of him.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: Yet many Ladies
Do give more saith to their Physitian
Than to their Confessor.

speeches.speaker: Claris.
verse: O my poor lost brother,
And friend more dear than Brother.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: More loud instruments
To disturb his slumbers! goe, goe, take Caroch:
And as you love me, you and the Girle retire
To our Summer house, i'th' Country; I'll be with you
Within these two days.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: I am yours in all things,
Though with much sorrow to leave him.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: I pray you Gentlemen,
With best observance tend your Patient;
The loss of my heir-male, lies now a bleeding.
And think what payment his recovery
Shall show'r upon you,
Of all men breathing;
Wherefore do you arrive here? Are you mad?
My injury begins to bleed afresh
At sight of you; why this affront of yours
I receive more malitious than the other.
Your hurt was only danger to my son:
But your sight to me is death; Why come you hither?
Do you come to view the wounds, which you have made?
And glory in them?

speeches.speaker: Menti.
verse: Rather worthy Sir, to pour Oyl into them.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: I am a Soldier Sir,
Least part of a Courtier, and understand
By your smooth Oyl,
Your present flattery.

speeches.speaker: Menti.
verse: Sir, for my Fathers sake acknowledge me
To be born a Gentleman, no slave; I ever
Held flatterers of that breed; do not misconstrue
In your distaste of me, the true intent
Of my coming hither, for I do protest
I do not come to tell you I am sorry
For your sons hurt.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: Not sorry?

speeches.speaker: Menti.
verse: No not sorry; I have to the lowest ebbo, lost all my fury:
But I must not lose my honesty; 'twas he
Gave heat unto the injury, which return'd
(Like a Petar, ill lighted, into 'th' bosome
Of him, gave fire to't) yet I hope his hurt,
Is not so dangerous, but he may recover;
When if it please him, call me to account,
For the loss of so much blood, I shall be ready
To do him noble reason.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: You are arm'd me thinks with wondrous confidence.

speeches.speaker: Menti.
verse: O with the best Sir;
For I bring penitence, and satisfaction.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: Satisfaction? Why I heard you say but now,
You were not sorry for his wounds.

speeches.speaker: Menti.
verse: Nor am I: the satisfaction which I bring Sir, is to you;
You are a Gentleman ne'er injur'd me;
One ever lov'd my Father, the right way,
And most approv'd of noble amity.
Yet I have run my sword quite through your heart,
And slightly hurt your son, for't may be scar'd,
A grief ta'en at these years for your sons loss,
May hazard yours: And therefore I am sent
By him that has most interest in your sorrow;
Who having chid me almost to the ruin
Of a disheritance, for violating
So continued and so sacred a friendship
Of 50 Winters standing: such a friendship,
That ever did continue like the spring;
Ne'er saw the fall o'th' leaf; by him I am sent
To say the wrong I have done Sir, is to you:
And that I have quite lost him for a Father,
Until I find your pardon; nay there follows
A weightier deprivation; his Estate
I could with a less number of sighs part with.
Fortune might attend my youth, and my deservings
In any Climate: but a Fathers blessing,
To settle and confirm that fortune, no where;
But only here. Your pardon, give me that;
And when you have done, kill me; for 'tis that
Takes from me the effect of excommunication;
A Fathers heavy curse.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: Nay, may that curse
Light on himself, for sending thee in this minute:
When I am grown as deaf to all compassion,
As the cruellest Sea-fight, or most horrid tempest.
That I had drown'd i'th' Sea a thousand duckets,
Thou hadst not made this visit: rash young man,
Thou tak'st me in an ill Planet, and hast cause
To curse thy Father; for I do protest,
If I had met thee in any part o'th' World,
But under my own roofe, I would have kill'd thee.
Look you!
Here's a triumph sent for the death of your young Master.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: Shall we kill him?

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: No, I'll not be so unhospitable; but Sir,
By my life, I vow to take assurance from you,
That right hand never more shall strike my son.

speeches.speaker: Menti.
verse: That will be easily protested.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: Not easily, when it must be exacted, and a bloody seal to't.
Bind him, and cut off's right hand presently:
Fair words shall never satisfie foul deeds.
Chop's hand off.

speeches.speaker: Menti.
verse: You cannot be so unrighteous, to your own honor.

speeches.speaker: Phy.
verse: O Sir, collect your self;
And recall your bloody purpose.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: My intents of this nature, do ever come to action.

speeches.speaker: Chirur.
verse: Then I must fetch another stickler.—

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: Yet I do grieve at heart;
And I do curse thy Father heartily,
That's the cause of my dishonor; sending thee
In such an hour, when I am apt for mischief:
Apt, as a Dutch-man after a Sea-fight,
When his enemy kneels afore him; come dispatch.

speeches.speaker: Phys.
verse: Intreat him, Noble Sir;

speeches.speaker: Menti.
verse: You shall excuse me;
Whatsoever he dares do, that I dare suffer.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Oh Sir, for honors sake stay your foul purpose,
For if you do proceed thus cruelly,
There is no question in the wound you give him,
I shall bleed to death for't.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: Thou art not of my temper,
What I purpose, cannot be alter'd.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: Sir; the Duke
With all speed expects you. You must instantly
Ship all your followers, and to sea.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: My blessing stay with thee upon this condition,
Take away his use of fighting; as thou hop'st
To be accounted for my son, perform't —

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: You hear what I am injoyn'd to.

speeches.speaker: Menti.
verse: Pray thee take it,
Only this ring, this best esteem'd Jewel:
I will not give't to'th' hangman chops it off;
It is too dear a relique. I'll remove it nearer my heart.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Ha, that Rings my Sisters.
The Ring I injoyn'd her never part withal
Without my knowledge; come, Sir, we are friends:
Pardon my fathers heat, and melancholy;
Two violent Fevers which he caught at Sea,
And cannot yet shake off: only one promise
I must injoyn you to, and seriously.
Hereafter you shall never draw a Sword
To the prejudice of my life.

speeches.speaker: Menti.
verse: By my best hopes I shall not.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: I pray deliver me your sword
On that condition.

speeches.speaker: Menti.
verse: I shall Sir, may it hereafter
Ever fight on your part.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Noble Sir, I thank you;
But for performance of your vow, I intreat
Some gage from you.

speeches.speaker: Menti.
verse: Any Sir.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Deliver me that ring.

speeches.speaker: Menti.
verse: Ha, this Ring? indeed this Jewel binds me,
If you knew the vertue of it, never more
To draw my sword against you.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Therefore I will have it.

speeches.speaker: Menti.
verse: You may not.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Come: you must.
I that by violence could take your hand,
Can inforce this from you; this is a token Sir,
That we may prove friends hereafter.

speeches.speaker: Phys.
verse: Why did you ceise his Sword Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: To perform what my Father bade me,
I have for the present ta'en away his
Use of fighting.

speeches.speaker: Phys.
verse: Better so,
Than take that which your Father meant.

speeches.speaker: Menti.
verse: Was ever the like usage? O that Ring!
Dearer than life, Whither is honor fled?

speeches.speaker: Cesario.
verse: Thou art unmanly in each part,
To seize my sword first, and then split my heart.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Thy Master that lodges here in my Osteria,
Is a rare man of art, they say he's a Witch.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: A Witch? Nay, he's one step of the Ladder to preferment higher, he is a Conjurer?

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Is that his higher title?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Yes, I assure you, for a Conjurer is the Devils Master, and commands him; whereas a Witch is the Devils Prentice, and obeys him.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Bound Prentice to the Devil!

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Bound and inroll'd I assure you, he cannot start; and therefore I would never wish any Gentleman to turn Witch.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Why Man?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Oh he loses his Gentility by it, the Devil in this case cannot help him, he must go to the Herald for new Armes believe it.

speeches.speaker: H^st.
verse: As I am true Inkeeper, yet a Gentleman born,
I'll ne'er turn Witch for that trick;
And thou hast been a great Traveller?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: No indeed, not I Sir;

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Come, you are modest.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: No, I am not modest, for I told you a lye, that you might the better understand I have been a Traveller,

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: So Sir, they say your Master is a great Physitian too.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: He was no fool told you that, I assure you.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: And you have been in England? but they say, Ladies in England take a great deal of Physick.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Both wayes on my reputation.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: So 'tis to be understood:
But they say, Ladies there take Physick for fashion.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Yes Sir, and many times dye to keep fashion.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: How? dye to keep fashion!

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Yes, I have known a Lady sick of the small Pocks, onely to keep her face from Pitholes, take cold, strike them in again, kick up the heels, and vanish.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: There was kicking up the heels with a witness.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: No Sir; I confess a good face has many times been the motive to the kicking up of the heels with a witnss: but this was not.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Here comes my wife and daughter.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: You have a prety commodity of this night-worm?

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Why Man?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: She is a pretty lure to draw custom to your ordinary.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Do'st think I keep her to that purpose?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: When a Dove-house is empty, there is cuminseed used to purloine from the rest of the neighbors; In England you have several Adamants, to draw in spurs and rapiers; one keeps silk-worms in a Gallery: A Milliner has choice of Monkies, and Paraketoes; another shewes bawdy East-Indian Pictures, worse than ever were Aretines: a Goldsmith keeps his Wife wedged into his shop like a Mermaid, nothing of her to be seen (thats Woman) but her upper part?

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Nothing but her upper part?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Nothing but her upper bodies, and he lives at the more hearts ease.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: What's the reason?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Because her nether part can give no temptation; by your leave, Sir, I'll tend my Master, and instantly be with you for a cup of Cherally this hot weather.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: A nimble pated Rascal, come hither Daughter,
When was Cesario here?

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Sir, not this fortnight.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: I do not like his visits, commonly
He comes by Owl-light, both the time and manner
Is suspitious; I do not like it.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Sir, the Gentleman
Is every way so noble, that you need not
Question his intent of coming, though you did;
Pray Sir preserve that good opinion of me,
That though the custome of the place I was born in,
Makes me familiar to every guest,
I shall in all things keep my self a stranger
To the vices they bring with them.

speeches.speaker: Hostis.
verse: Right my daughter:
She has the right strain of her Mother.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Of her Mother?
And I would speak, I know from whence she took it;
When I was as young, I was as honest.

speeches.speaker: Hostess.
verse: Leave your prating.
prose: And study to be drunk; and abuse your guests over and over.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Peace Wife. My honorable guest.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: My indear'd Landlord?
And the rest o'th' complements o'th' house.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Breakfast is ready Sir;
It waites only the tide of your stomach.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: And mine gapes for't like a stale Oyster.
Ere you go to bed, fail not of that I pray.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: We will instantly be with you;
Now we are all fellows.
Nine a Clock, and no Clyents come
Yet, sure thou do'st not set up bills enough.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: I have set up bills in abundance.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: What Bills?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Marry for curing of all diseases,
Recovery of stoln goods,
And a thousand such impossibilities.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: The place is unlucky.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: No certain, 'tis scarcity of mony; do not you hear the Lawyers complain of it? Men have as much Malice as ever they had to wrangle, but they have no Mony: Whither should this Mony be travell'd?

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: To the Devil I think.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: 'Tis with his Cofferer I am certain, that's the Usurer.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Our cheating does not prosper so well as it was wont to do.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: No sure, why in England we coo'd cozen 'em as familiarly, as if we had travell'd with a Brief, or a Lottery.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: I'th' Low-countries we did pretty well.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: So so: as long as we kept the Mop-headed butter-boxes sober; marry when they were drunk, then they grew buzards: You should have them reel their heads together, and deliberate; your Dutchman indeed, when he is foxt, is like a Fox; for when he's sunk in drink, quite earth to a Mans thinking, 'tis full Exchange time with him, then he's subtlest; but your Switzer, 'twas nothing to cheat him.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Nothing?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: No, nor conscience to be made of it; for since nature afore-hand cozen'd him of his wit, 'twas the less sin for us to cozen him of his Mony.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: But these Italians are more nimble-pated; we must have some new trick for them; I protest but that our Hostess's daughter is a sweet Lass, and draws great resort to'th' house, we were as good draw teeth a horseback.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: I told 'em in the Market-place you could conjure, and no body would believe me: but ere long I will make 'em believe you can conjure with such a figuary.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: What language shall's conjure in? high Dutch I think, that's full i'th' mouth.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: No, no, Spanish, that roars best; and will appear more dreadful.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Prethee tell me thy conceit thou hast to gull them.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: No, no, I will not stael it; but my dear Jewstrump, for thou art but my instrument, I am the plotter, and when we have cozen'd 'em most titely, thou shalt steal away the Inn-keepers daughter, I'll provide my self of another moveable: and we will most purely retire our selves to Geneva.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Thou art the compass I sail by.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Was ever expectation of so Noble
A requital answered with such contumely!
A wild Numidian that had suck'd a Tigress,
Would not have been so barbarous; Did he threat
To cut thy hand off?

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: Yes Sir, and his slaves were ready to perform't.

speeches.speaker: Bapt.
verse: What hind'red it?

speeches.speaker: Meut.
verse: Only his sons intreaty.

speeches.speaker: Bapt.
verse: Noble youth,
I wish thou wert not of his blood; thy pitty
Gives me a hope thou art not.

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: You mistake Sir,
The injury that followed from the son,
Was worse than the fathers; he did first disarme
And took from me a Jewel, which I prize
Above my hand or life.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Take thy sword from thee?
He stole it like a Thief rather, he could not
I'th' Field deprive thee of it.

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: He took it from me,
And sent me forth so thin, and so unmade up,
As if I had been a Foot-boy.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: O my fury!
I must now ask thee forgiveness, that my rashness,
Bred out of too much friendship, did expose thee
To so eminent a danger; which I vow
I will revenge on the whole Family:
All the calamities of my whole life,
My banishment from Genoa, my wifes loss
Compar'd to this indignity, is nothing;
Their Family shall repair't; it shall be to them
Like a plague, when the Dog-star reigns most hot:
An Italian's revenge may pause, but's ne'er forgot.

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: I would I had conceal'd this from my Father,
For my interest in Clarissa; my care now
Must be to untangle this division,
That our most equal flames may be united;
And from these various and perturbed streames,
Rise, like a sweet Morn, after terrible dreams.—

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Brother, I am happy in your recovery,

speeches.speaker: Caes.
verse: And I Sister, am ever best pleased in your happiness:
But I miss a toy should be on your finger.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: My Ring; this morning when I wash't
I put it off, 'tis in my Window.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: Where's your Looking-glass?

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Here, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: 'Tis a fair one.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: 'Tis pure Chrystal.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: Can a Diamond cut in Crystal? let me see,
I'll grave my name in't.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Oh, you'll spoyl my glass.
Would you not have your brother in your eye?

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: I had thought he had been Planted in your heart,
Look you, the Diamond cuts quaintly, you are cozen'd,
Your Chrystal is too britle.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: 'Tis the Ring
I gave unto Mentivole, sure the same.
You put me to amazement Sir, and horror;
How came you by that Ring?

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: Does the blood rise?

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Pray Sir resolve me, O for pitty do;
And take from me a trembling at the heart,
That else will kill me: for I too much fear
Nothing but Death could ravish it from his hand
That wore it.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Was it given to Mentivola on that condition?

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Tell me of his health first.
And then I'll tell you any thing.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: By my life he's well,
In better health than I am.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Then it was Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Then shall I ever hate thee, Oh thou false one;
Hast thou a Faith to give unto a friend,
And break it to a brother? Did I not,
By all the tyes of blood importune thee
Never to part with it without my knowledge?
Thou might'st have given it to a Muliter,
And made a contract with him in a stable,
At as cheap a price of my vengeance: never more
Shall a Womans trust beguile me; You are all
Like Relicks: you may well be look't upon,
But come a Man to'th' handling of you once,
You fall in pieces.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Dear Sir, I have no way
Look't either beneath reason, or my self,
In my election; there's parity in our blood,
And in our fortunes, antient amity
Betwixt our parents: to which wants nothing,
But the Fruit of blest Marriage between us,
To add to their posterities: nor does now
Any impeachment rise, except the sad
And unexpected quarrel, which divided
So noble, and so excellent a friendship,
Which as I ne'er had Magick to foresee,
So I could not prevent.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Well, you must give me leave
To have a hand in your disposing, I shall,
In the absence of my Father, be your Guardian;
His Suit must pass through my office.
He has too much of my blood already; he has,
And he get's no more of't—
Wherefore weep you Mother?

speeches.speaker: Marian.
verse: 'Tis occasion'd by a sorrow,
Wherein you have a Child's part, and the mainest,
Your Father's dead.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Dead?

speeches.speaker: Marian.
verse: There's one can relate the rest.

speeches.speaker: Sailor.
verse: I can Sir, your Father's drown'd,
Most unfortunately drown'd.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: How? In a tempest?

speeches.speaker: Sailor.
verse: No Sir, in a calm,
Calm as this evening; the Gunner being drunk,
Forgot to fasten the Ordnance to their ports,
When came a sudden gust, which tumbled them
All to the Starboord side, o'erturn'd the Ship,
And sunk her in a moment, some six men
That were upon the deck were sav'd: the rest
Perish'd with your Father.

speeches.speaker: Claris.
verse: O my dearest Father—

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: I pray thee leave us.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: I have a sorrow of another nature, equal to the former.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: And most commonly they come together.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: The Family of the Baptisti
Are grown to faction, and upon distast
Of the injury late offer'd in my house,
Have vow'd a most severe, and fell revenge
'Gainst all our family, but especially
'Gainst you my dear Caesario.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Let them threat, I am prepar'd to oppose them.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: And is your loss then
Of so easie an estimation? What comfort
Have I but in your life, and your late danger
Presents afore me what I am to suffer,
Should you miscarry; therefore I'll advise you
When the Funeral is over, you would travel,
Both to prevent their fury, and wear out th' injury.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: No Mother, I will not travel,
So in my absence he may marry my Sister,
I will not travel certain.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: O my Cesario,
Whom I respect and love 'bove my own life,
Indeed with a kind of dotage, he shall never
Go forth o' doors, but the contrary faction
Will indanger's life, and then am I most wretched.
I am thinking of a strange prevention,
Which I shall witness with a bleeding eye,
Fondness sometimes is worse than cruelty.—

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: HAunted, my house is haunted with goblins. I shall be frighted out of my wits, and set up a sign only to invite Carriers and Foot-posts; scar-crows to keep off the Cavalry, and Gentry of the best rank. I will nail up my doors, and wall up my Girle (wife) like an Anchoress; or she will be ravisht before our faces, by rascalls and cacafugo's (wife) cacafugo's.

speeches.speaker: Hostess.
prose: These are your In-comes, remember your own proverb, the savor of every gain smelt sweet; thank no body but your self for this trouble.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: No gauling (dear Spouse) no gauling, every days new vexation abates me two inches in the waste, terrible pennance for an Host, Girle, girle, girle, Which of all this gally-maufry of Mans flesh appears tolerable to thy choice, speak shortly, and speak truely: I must and will know, must and will; Hear ye that?

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Sir, be not jealous of my care and duty;
I am so far from entertaining thoughts
Of liberty, that much more excellent objects
Than any of such course contents as these are,
Could not betray mine eye to force my heart;
Conceive a wish of any dearer happiness
Than your direction warrant's. I am yours Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hostess.
prose: What thinks the Man now? Is not this strange at 13.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Very good words, there's a tang in e'm, and a sweet one, 'tis musick (wife) and now I come t'ee. Let us a little examine the several conditions of our Paragraphistical suitors. The first, a travelling Tailor, who by the mystery of his Needle and Thimble, hath survey'd the fashions of the French, and English; this Signior Ginger-bread, stitcht up in the shreds of a gudy outside, sows Linings with his cross-leg'd complement, like an Ape doing tricks over a staffe, cringes, and crouches, and kisses his forefinger.

speeches.speaker: Hostess.
prose: Out upon him.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: A second, a lavolteteere, a saltatory, a dancer with a Kit at his Bum, one that, by teaching great Madonnas to foot it, has miraculously purchast a ribanded Wastcote, and four clean pair of socks; a fellow that skips as he walkes, and instead of sensible discourse, vents the curious conceit of some new tune stolen from a Mask, or a bawdy dittie, elevated for the Pole Artick of a Ladies chamber, in that file stands another of your inamoratoes.

speeches.speaker: Hostess.
prose: Hang him and his Fiddle together, he never fidles any child of ours.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: The third, a Mongrel, got by a Switzer on an Italian; this puppy, being left well estated, comes to Florence, that the world may take notice, how impossible it is for experience to alter the course of nature; a fool (wife) and indeed, a Clown turn'd Gallant, seldom or never proves other than a gallant fool, this toy prates to little purpose other than What's a Clock? Shall's go drink? De'e forsooth? and thank ye heartily; I fear no art in him to catch thee, and yet we must be tormented with this buzard amongst the rest.

speeches.speaker: Hostess.
prose: 'Tis your own folly, forbid him the House.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: The fourth, a Mule-driver, a stubborn and a harsh knave: the fifth a School-Master, a very amorous Pedant, run almost mad with study of Sonnets, and Complements out of old Play-ends, the last an Advocates Clerk, that speaks pure Fustian in Law-terms: excellent Courtiers all, and all as neate as a Magnifio's post new painted, at his entrance to an office; thou shalt have none of 'em. Laugh at 'em, do. I say thou shalt have none of 'em.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: Still your command to me shall stand a Law.

speeches.speaker: H^st.
prose: Now they throng like so many horse-coursers at a ^air, in clusters about the Man of Art, for Love-powders, i^gredients, potions, counsels, postures, complements, philt^rs: the Devil and the—How now? Tumults? Batteries, Noise? ha, get from my sight.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Murther me, do, pound me to Mummy, do; see what will come on't.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Dog, leave thy snarling, or I'll cut thy tongue out,
Thou un ickt Bear, dar'st thou yet stand my fury,
My generous rage? yet! by the sulpherous damps
That feed the hungry and incessant darkness,
Which curles around the grim Alastors back,
Mutter again, and with one powerful word,
Ill call an Host up from the Stygian Lakes,
Shall wast thee to the Acherontick fens;
Where choak't with Mists as black as thy impostures,
Thou shalt live still a dying.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Conjure me to the Devil and you can, I live in Hell upon earth already, and you had any mercy, you would not practice upon a kind heart thus.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: You have drawn blood from him Signior, Is his offence unpardonable?

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: A lump of ignorance, pray speak not for him,
A drowsie grossness, in all Christian Kingdoms,
The mention of my art, my name, my practise,
Merit and Glory hath begot at once
Delight and wonder; I'll not be entreated;
Spare intercession for him,— O thou scorn
Of learning, shame of duty; must thy sloth
Draw my just same in question? I discharge thee
From my service; see me no more henceforth.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Discharge me! Is that my years wages?
I'll not be so answer'd.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Not Camel? Sirrah I am liberal to thee;
Thou hast thy life, be gone.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Vengeance, sweet vengeance.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: D^'e mumble?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: I'll be reveng'd, monstrously, suddenly, and insatiably; my bulk begins to swell.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Homotolenton, Pragmatophoros, Heliostycorax.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Call up your Spirits, I defie 'em; well, I'll have Law for my broken pate, twelve ounces of pure blood; Troy-weight. In despight of thee my Master, and thy Master the grand Devil himself, vindicta, vindicta.—

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Signior, you are exceeding mov'd.

speeches.speaker: H^stess.
verse: Mercy upon us, What terrible words thou talk'st?

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: A slave, a curr—but be not you afrighted
Young Virgin, 'twere an injury to sweetness:
Should any rough found draw from your cheeks,
The pretious tincture which makes nature proud
Of her own workmanship.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Wise, Mark, mark that Wife.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Shake then your anger off Sir;

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: You command it
Fair one, mine Host and Hostess, with your leaves
I have a motion joyntly to you all.

speeches.speaker: Hostess.
verse: An honest one I hope.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Well put in Wife.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: A very necessary one, the Mess
And half of suitors, that attend to usher
Their Loves sir-reverence to your daughter, wait
With one consent, which can best please her eye;
In offering at a Dance, I have provided
Musick. And, 'twill be something I dare promise
Worthy your laughter, Shall they have admittance?

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: By any means, for I am perswaded the manner will be so
Ridiculous, that it will confirm the assurance of their
Miserable fooleries, but no longer trouble with 'em here,
Than they are in these May-games.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: So I am resolv'd.

speeches.speaker: Hostess.
verse: Nor any wise word of senceless love.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Not any; I have charm'd them, Did you see
How they prepar'd themselves? how they stroak up
Their foretops, how they justle for the Looking-lass,
To set their faces by it;
You would look for some most impossible antick.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: So, so, so, so, here flutter the nest of Hornets, the hotch-potch of rascallity; now, now, now, now, the dunghill of corruption hath yawn'd forth the burthen of abhomination. I am vext, vext to the soul, will rid my house of this unchristen'd fry, and never open my doors again.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Some other time, I'll give no answer now,
But have preserred your suits, here shew your cunning.
First, every one in order do his honor
To the fair mark you shoot at; courtly, courtly,
Convey your several loves in lively measure:
Come, let us take our seates, some sprightly Musick.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Dance all and part, 'tis a very necessary farewell.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Well done my lusty bloods, precisely well done,
One lusty rouse of Wine, and take leave on all sides.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Thanks for your Revels Gentlemen; accept
This Gold, and drink as freely as you danc'd.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: My noble Lord Cesario, clear the rooms Sirs.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Away. Attend your answers.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
prose: With your favor Rolando, I would change a word or two with your fair daughter.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: At your Lordships pleasure, come Wife, no muttering, have a care Girle, my love, service, and duty to you good Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: My often visits (sweet Bianca) cannot
But constantly inform thy judgment, wherein
Thy happiness consists, for to steal minutes
From great imployments, to converse with beauty,
Lodg'd in so mean a fortune, to lay by
Consideration of the unequal distance
Between my blood and thine, to shun occasions
Of courtship with the Ladies of the time:
Noble, and fair, only for love to thee,
Must of necessity invite a tenderness;
As low as nature could have stampt a Bondwomans.
To entertain quick motions of rare gratitude
For my uncommon favors.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: 'Deed my Lord, as far as my simplicity can lead me,
I freely thank your curtesies.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: To thank them, is to reward them pretty one.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Then teach me
How I may give them back again; in truth
I never yet receiv'd a pair of Gloves:
A trifling Ring from any that expected
An equall satisfaction, but as willingly
I parted with the guift unto the owner, as he bestow'd it.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: But I pour before thee
Such plenties, as it lies not in the ability
Of thy whole kindred, to return proportionable
One for a thousand.

speeches.speaker: Bi^n.
verse: You my Lord conclude
For my instruction, to ingage a debt
Beyond a possibility of paiment,
I ever thought a sin; and therefore justly
Without conceit of scorn, or curious rudeness,
I must refuse your bounty.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Canst thou love?

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Love! Is there such a word in any Language
That carries honest sence?

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Never dwelt ignorance
In so sweet-shap't a building: love, Bianca,
Is that firm knot which ties two hearts in one:
Shall ours be tied so?

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Use a plainer word,
My Lord. In stead of tyes, say marries hearts,
Then I may understand.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Their hearts are married
Whose enterchange of pleasures, and embraces,
Soft kisses, and the privacies of sweets,
Keeps constant league together, when temptation
Of great mens oathes and gifts, shall urge contempt,
Rather than batter resolution, novelty
Of sights, or taste of new delights in wantonness,
Breeds surfeit more than appetite in any
Reserv'd to noble vowes; my excellent Maid,
Live thou but true to me, and my contents,
Mine only, that no partner may partake
The treasure of those sweets thy youth yet glories in,
And I will raise thy lowness to abundance
Of all varieties, and more triumph
In such a Mistris, than great Princes doating
On truth-betraying Wives.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Thus to yield up then
The cottage of my virtue, to be swallow'd
By some hard-neighbouring Landlord, such as you are,
Is in effect to love, a Lord so vicious!
O where shall innocence find some poor dwelling,
Free from temptations tyranny.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Nay prethee.

speeches.speaker: Byan.
verse: Gay clothes, high feeding, easie beds of lust,
Change of unseemly sights; with base discourse,
Draw curses on your Pallaces; for my part,
This I will be confirm'd in, I will eate
The bread of labour, know no other rest
Than what is earn'd from honest pains, ere once more
Lend ear to your vile toyles; Sir, would you were
As noble in desires, as I could be in knowing virtue.
Pray do not afflict a poor soul thus.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: I swear — to me? —

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: The Duke my Lord commands your speedy presence
For answering agrievances lately urg'd
Against you by your Mother?

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: By my Mother.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: The Court is near on sitting.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: I wait on it Sir, —

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: What waste of blood, what tumults, what divisions,
What outrages, what uprores in a State,
Factions, though issuing from mean springs at first,
Have (not restrain'd) stowed to, the sad example

At Rome, between the
~rsins and Columni's:
Nay, here at home, in Florence, 'twixt the Neers
And the Bianchi, can too mainly witness.
I sit not at the Helm (my Lords) of Sovereignty
Deputed Pilot for the Common-wealth,
To sleep while others steere (as their wild fancies
Shall counsel) by the compass of disorders.
Baptista, This short Preface is directed
Chiefly to you, the petty brawls and quarrels
Late urg'd betwixt th' Alberti and your family;
Must, yes, and shall, like tender unknit joynts,
Fasten again together of themselves:
Or like an ^gry Chyrurgion, we will use
The ro^ghness of our justice, to cut off
^ be stubborn ^ancour of the limbes offending.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Most gracious Florence.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Our comman^ was signified,
^hat neither of the followers of each party
Sho^l^ appe^r here with weapons.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: 'Tis obey'd Sir, on my side.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: We must leave the general cause
Of State employments, to give ^ar to brawls
Of some particular grudges, pollitick government
For tutor'd Princes, but no more henceforth.
Our frown shall check presumption, not our clemency.

speeches.speaker: Mari.
verse: All blessings due to unpartial Princes,
Crown Florence with eternity of happiness.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: If double Prayers can double blessings (great Sir)
Mine joyn for your prosperity with my Mothers.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Rise both; now briefly (Lady) without circumstance
Deliver those agrievances, which lately
Your importunity possest our Counsel,
Were fit for audience, wherein you petition'd,
You might be heard without an Advocate,
Which boon you find is granted.

speeches.speaker: Mari.
verse: Though divided.
I stand between the Laws of truth and modesty,
Yet let my griefs have vent: Yet the clearness
Of strange necessity requires obedience
To nature and your Mercy, in my weeds
Of mourning, emblems of too dear misfortunes,
Badges of griefs, and Widdowhood, the burthe^
Of my charg'd soul, must be laid down before you;
Wherein, if strict opinion cancel shame,
My frailty is my plea;
Stand forth young Man,
And hear a story that will strike all reason
Into amazement.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: I attend.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Alberto (peace dwell upon his ashes) still the husband
Of my remembrance and unchanging vowes,
Has, by his death, left to his heir possession
Of fair revenew, which this young man claimes
As his inheritance. I urg'd him gently,
Friendly, and privately, to grant a partage
Of this estate to her who ownes it all,
This his supposed Sister.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: How supposed?

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Pray Madam recollect your self.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: The relish
Of a strange truth begins to work like Physick
Already: I have bitterness to mingle
With these preparatives, so deadly loathsome;
It will quite choak digestion; shortly hear it
Cesario, for I dare not rob unjustly
The poor soul of his name; this, this Cesario
Neither for Father had Alberto, me
For Mother, nor Clarissa for his Sister.

speeches.speaker: Claris.
verse: Mother, O Mother.

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: I am in a Dream sure.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: No interruptions. Lady on.

speeches.speaker: Mari.
verse: Mistake not,
Great Duke of Tuscany, or the beginning
Or process of this novelty; my husband
The now deceas'd Alberto, from his youth
In-ur'd to an impatiency, and roughness
Of disposition, when not many months
After our Marriage were worn out, repin'd
At the unfritful barrenness of youth,
Which, as he pleas'd to terme it, cut our hopes off
From blessing of some issue; to prevent it
I grew ambitious of no fairer honor
Than to preserve his love, and as occasions
Still call'd him from me, studied in his absence
How I might frame his welcome home with comfort.
At last I fain'd my self with Child; the Message
Of freedome, or relief, to one half starv'd
In prison, is not utter'd with such greediness
Of expectation, and delight, as this was
To my much affected Lord; his care, his goodness;
(Pardon me that I use the word) exceeded
All former fears, the hour of my deliverance
As I pretended, drawing near, I fashion'd
My birth-rights at a Country Garden-house,
Where then my Faulk'ners Wife was brought a bed
Of this Cesario; him I own'd for mine;
Presented him unto a joyful Father.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Can ^ou prove this true?

speeches.speaker: Mari.
verse: Proof, I have most evident;
But oh the curse of my impatiency; shortly,
