Young Maids were as cold as Cowcumbers
And much of that complexion:
Bawds were abolisht: and, to which misery
It must come again,
There were no Cuckolds,
Well, we had need pray to keep these
Divels from us,
The times grow mischievous.
There he goes, Lord!
This is a sacriledge I have not heard of:
Would I were gelt, that I might not
Feel what follows.

speeches.speaker: Age.
verse: And I too. You shall see within these
Few years, a fine confusion i'the Countrey: mark it:
Nay, and we grow for to depose the Powers,
And set up Chastity again, well, I have done.
A fine new goddess certainly, whose blessings
Are hunger and hard beds.

speeches.speaker: Nis.
verse: This comes of fulness, a sin too frequent with us
I believe now we shall find shorter commons.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: Would I were married, somewhat has some savour;
The race of Gentry will quite run out now,
'Tis only left to Husbands, if younger Sisters
Take not the greater charity, 'tis lawful.

speeches.speaker: Age.
verse: Well, let come what will come,
I am but one, and as the plague salls,
I'll shape my self: If Women will be honest, I'll be found.
If the god be not too unmerciful,
I'll take a little still, where I can get it,
And thank him, and say nothing.

speeches.speaker: Nis.
verse: This ill wind yet may blow the City good,
And let them, (if they can) get their own children,
prose: They have hung long enough in doubt, but howsoever, the old way was the surer, then they had 'em.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: Farewel my Lords, I'll e'en take up what Rent I can before the day, I fear the year will fall out ill.

speeches.speaker: Age.
verse: We'll with you Sir: And love so favour us,
As we are still thy servants. Come my Lords;
Let's to the Duke, and tell him to what folly
His doting now has brought him.

speeches.speaker: Priest.
verse: Come my children, let your feet,
In an even measure meet:
And your chearful voices rise.
For to present this Sacrifice;
Lo great Cupid, in whose name,
I his Priest begin the same.
Young men take your Loves and kiss,
Thus our Cupid honour'd is
Kiss again, and in your kissing,
Let no promises be missing:
Nor let any Maiden here,
Dare to turn away her ear,
Unto the whisper of her Love,
But give Bracelet, Ring or Glove,
As a token to her sweeting,
Of an after secret meeting:
Now boy sing to stick our hearts
Fuller of great Cupids darts.

LOvers rejoyce, your pains shall be rewarded,
The god of Love himself grieves at your crying:
No more shall frozen honor be regarded,
Nor the coy faces of a Maids denying.
No more shall Virgins sigh, and say we dare not,
For men are false, and what they do they care not,
All shall be well again, then do not grieve,
Men shall be true, and Women shall believe.

Lovers rejoyce, what you shall say henceforth,
When you have caught your Sweet-hearts in your arms,
It shall be accounted Oracle, and Worth:
No more faint-hearted Girls shall dream of harms.
And cry they are too young, the god hath said,
Fifteen shall make a Mother of a Maid:
Then wise men, pull your Roses yet unblown,
Love hates the too ripe fruit that falls alone.

speeches.speaker: Nilo.
verse: No more of this: here break your Rights for ever,
The Duke commands it so; Priest do not stare,
I must deface your Temple, though unwilling,
And your god Cupid here must make a Scare-crow
For any thing I know, or at the best,
Adorn a Chimney-piece.

speeches.speaker: Priest.
verse: Oh Sacriledge unheard of?

speeches.speaker: Nilo,
verse: This will not help it, take down the Image
And away with 'em.
Priest, change your coat you had best, all service now
Is given to men: Prayers above their hearing
Will prove but bablings: learn to lye and thrive,
'Twill prove your best profession: for the gods,
He that lives by 'em now, must be a beggar.
There's better holiness on earth they say,
Pray God it ask not greater sacrifice. Go home,
And if our god be not deaf as well as blind,
He will some smoak for it.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Sir—

speeches.speaker: Nilo.
verse: Gentlemen, there is no talking,
This must be done and speedily;
I have commission that I must not break.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: We are gone, to wonder what shall follow.

speeches.speaker: Nilo.
verse: On to the next Temple.

speeches.speaker: Cupid.
verse: Am I then scorn'd? is my all-doing Will
And Power, that knows no limit, nor admits none,
Now look'd into by less than gods? and weak'ned
Am I, whose Bow struck terror through the earth,
No less than Thunder, and in this, exceeding
Even gods themselves, whose knees before my Altars
Now shook off; and contemn'd by such, whose lives
Are but my recreation! anger rise
My sufferance and my self are made the subject
Of sins against us. Go thou out displeasure,
Displeasure of a great god, flying thy self
Through all this Kingdom: sow what ever evils
Proud flesh is taking off, amongst these Rebels:
And on the first heart that despise my Greatness,
Lay a strange misery, that all may know
Cupid's revenge is mighty; with his Arrow
Hotter than plagues or mine own anger, will I
Now nobly right my self: nor shall the prayers
Nor smoaks on my Altars hold my hand,
Till I have left this a most wretched Land,

speeches.speaker: Hidas.
verse: Cleophila, what was he that went hence?

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: What means your Grace now?

speeches.speaker: Hidas.
verse: I mean that handsome man.
That something more than man I met at door.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Here was no handsome man.

speeches.speaker: Hidas.
verse: Come, he's some one
You would preserve in private, but you want
Cunning to do it, and my eyes are sharper
Than yours, and can with one neglecting glance,
See all the graces of a man. Who was't?

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: That went hence now?

speeches.speaker: Hidas.
verse: That went hence now, I, he

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Faith here was no such one as your Grace thinks.
Zoylous your Brothers Dwarf went out but now.

speeches.speaker: Hidas.
verse: I think 'twas he: how bravely he past by:
Is he not grown a goodly Gentleman?

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: A goodly Gentleman, Madam?
He is the most deformed fellow i'the Land.

speeches.speaker: Hidas.
verse: Oh blasphemy: he may perhaps to thee
Appear deform'd, for he is indeed
Unlike a man: his shape and colours are
Beyond the Art of Painting; he is like
Nothing that we have seen, yet doth resemble
Apollo, as I oft have fancied him,
When rising from his bed, he stirs himself
And shakes day from his hair.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: He resembles Apollo's Recorder.

speeches.speaker: Hidas.
verse: Cleophila, go send a Page for him,
And thou shalt see thy error, and repent.
Alas, what do I feel, my bloud rebells,
And I am one of those I us'd to scorn,
My Maiden-thoughts are fled against my self?
I harbor Traitors in my Virginity,
That from my Childhood kept me company,
Is heavier than I can endure to bear:
Forgive me Cupid, for thou art a god,
And I a wretched creature; I have sinn'd,
But be thou merciful, and grant that yet
I may enjoy what thou wilt have me, Love.
Zoylous is here Madam.

speeches.speaker: Hida.
verse: He's there indeed.
Now be thine own Judge; see thou worse than mad,
Is he deformed? look upon those eyes,
That let all pleasure out into the world,
Unhappy that they cannot see themselves;
Look on his hair, that like so many beams,
Streaking the East, shoot light o'er half the world,
Look on him altogether, who is made
As if two Natures had contention
About their skill, and one had brought forth him.

speeches.speaker: Zoy.
verse: Ha, ha, ha: Madam, though Nature
Hath not given me so much
As others in my outward shew;
I bear a heart as loyal unto you
In this unsightly body (which you please
To make your mirth) as many others do
That are far more befriended in their births;
Yet I could wish my self much more deformed
Than yet I am, so I might make your Grace
More merry than you are, ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Hidas.
verse: Beshrew me then if I be merry;
But I'm content whilst thou art with me:
Thou that art my Saint:
By hope of whose mild favour I do live
To tell thee so: I pray thee scorn me not;
Alas what can it add unto thy worth
To triumph over me, that am a Maid,
Without deceit? whose heart doth guide her tongue,
Drown'd in my passions; yet I will take leave
To call it reason that I dote on thee.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: The Princess is besides her Grace I think.
To talk thus with a fellow that will hardly
Serve i'th' dark when one is drunk.

speeches.speaker: Hida.
verse: What answer wilt thou give me?

speeches.speaker: Zoy.
verse: If it please your Grace to jest on, I can abide it.

speeches.speaker: Hida.
verse: If it be jest, not to esteem my life,
Compar'd with thee: If it be jest in me,
To hang a thousand kisses in an hour
Upon those Lips, and take 'em off again:
If it be jest for me to marry thee,
And take obedience on me whilst I live:
Then all I say is jest:
For every part of this, I swear by those
That see my thoughts, I am resolv'd to do,
And I beseech thee, by thine own white hand,
(Which pardon me, that I am bold to kiss
With so unworthy Lips) that thou wilt swear
To marry me, as I do here to thee,
Before the face of heaven.

speeches.speaker: Zoy.
verse: Marry you? ha, ha, ha,

speeches.speaker: Hida.
verse: Kill me or grant, wilt thou not speak at all?

speeches.speaker: Zoy.
verse: Why I will do your Will for ever.

speeches.speaker: Hida.
verse: I ask no more: but let me kiss that mouth
That is so merciful; that is my will:
Next go with me before the King in haste,
That is my Will; where I will make our Peers
Know, that thou art their better.

speeches.speaker: Zoy.
verse: Ha, ha, ha, that is fine, ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Madam, what means your Grace?
Consider for the love of Heaven to what
You run madly; will you take this Viper
Into your bed?

speeches.speaker: Hida.
verse: Away, hold off thy hands:
Strike her sweet Zoylus, for it is my Will,
Which thou hast sworn to doe.

speeches.speaker: Zoy.
verse: Away for shame.
Know you no manners: ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Thou know'st none I fear,
This is just Cupid's Anger, Venus look down mildly on us:
prose: And command thy Son to spare this Lady once, and let me be in love withal: and none in love with me.

speeches.speaker: Timan.
verse: Is your Lordship for the Wars this Summer?

speeches.speaker: Ismen.
verse: Timantus, wilt thou go with me?

speeches.speaker: Timan.
verse: If I had a Company, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Ismen.
verse: Of Fidlers: Thou a company?
No, no, keep thy Company at home, and cause cuckolds:
The Wars will hurt thy face, there's no Semsters,
Shoomakers, nor Taylors, nor Almond-milk i'th' morning,
Nor poach'd Egs to keep your worship soluble,
No man to warm your Shirt, and blow your Roses:
Nor none to reverence your round lace Breeches:
If thou wilt needs goe, and goe thus,
Get a Case for thy Captainship, a shower will spoil thee else.
Thus much for thee.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Your Lordship's wondrous witty, very pleasant believe't.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: No news yet of my Son?

speeches.speaker: Tela.
verse: Sir, there be divers out in search:
No doubt they'll bring the truth where he is,
Or the occasion that led him hence.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: They have good eyes then.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: The gods goe with them:
Who be those that wait there?

speeches.speaker: Tele.
verse: The Lord Ismenus, your General, for his dispatch.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Oh Nephew: we have no use to imploy your
Virtue in our War: now the Province is well setled.
Hear you ought of the Marquis?

speeches.speaker: Ismen.
verse: No Sir?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: 'Tis strange he should be gone thus:
These five days he was not seen,

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: I'll hold my hold, I could bolt him in an hour:

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Where's my Daughter?

speeches.speaker: Dori.
verse: About the purging of the Temples, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: She's chaste and virtuous; fetch her to me,
And tell her I am pleas'd to grant her now
Her last request, without repenting me.
Be it what it will: she is wise, Dorialus
And will not press me farther than a Father.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: I pray the best may follow; yet if your Grace
Had taken the opinions of your people,
At least of such, whose wisdoms ever wake
About your safety, I may say it, Sir,
Under your noble pardon: that this change
Either had been more honor to the gods,
Or I think not at all. Sir, the Princess.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Oh my Daughter, my health!
And did I say my soul, I ly'd not;
Thou art so near me, speak, and have whatever
Thy wise Will leads thee too: had I a Heaven,
It were too poor a place for such a goodness.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: What's here?

speeches.speaker: Agen.
verse: An Apes skin stuft I think, 'tis so plump.

speeches.speaker: Hida.
verse: Sir, you have past your word,
Still be a Prince, and hold you to it.
Wonder not I press you, my life lies in your word:
If you break that, you have broke my heart, I must ask
That's my shame, and your Will must not deny me:
Now for Heaven be not forsworn.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: By the gods I will not,
I cannot, were there no other power,
Than my love call'd to a witness of it.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: They have much reason to trust,
You have forsworn one of 'em out o'th' countrey already.

speeches.speaker: Hida.
verse: Then this is my request: This Gent.
Be not ashamed, Sir:
You are worth a Kingdom.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: In what?

speeches.speaker: Hida.
verse: In the way of marriage.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Hida.
verse: In the way of marriage, it must be so,
Your oath is ti'd to Heaven: as my love to him.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I know thou dost but try my age,
Come ask again.

speeches.speaker: Hida.
verse: If I should ask all my life-time, this is all still.
Sir, I am serious, I must have this worthy man without enquiring why; and suddenly, and freely:
Doe not look for reason or obedience in my words: my
Love admits no wisdom:
Only haste, and hope hangs on my fury,
Speak Sir, speak, but not as a Father,
I am deaf and dull to counsel: inflamed blood
Hears nothing but my Will;
For Gods sake speak.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: Here's a brave alteration.

speeches.speaker: Nis.
verse: This comes of Chastity.

speeches.speaker: Hida.
verse: Will not you speak Sir?

speeches.speaker: Agen.
prose: The god begins his vengeance; what a sweet youth he has sent us here, with a pudding in's belly?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Oh let me never speak,
Or with my words let me speak out my life;
prose: Thou power abus'd: great Love, whose vengeance now we feel and fear, have mercy on this Land.

speeches.speaker: Nis.
verse: How does your Grace?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Sick, very sick I hope.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: Gods comfort you.

speeches.speaker: Hida.
verse: Will not you speak? is this your Royal word?
Do not pull perjurie upon your soul.
Sir, you are old, and near your punishment; remember.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Away base woman.

speeches.speaker: Hidas.
verse: Then be no more my Father, but a plague,
I am bound to pray against: be any sin
May force me to despair, and hang my self,
Be thy name never more remembred King
But in example of a broken faith,
And curst even to forgetfulness:
May thy Land bring forth such Monsters as thy Daughter is?
I am weary of my rage. I pray forgive me,
And let me have him, will you Noble Sir?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Mercy, mercy heaven:
Thou heir of all dishonor, shamest thou not to draw
This little moisture lest for life, thus rudely from me?
Carry that slave to death.

speeches.speaker: Zoy.
verse: For heavens sake Sir, it is no fault of mine,
That she will love me.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: To death with him, I say.

speeches.speaker: Hida.
verse: Then make haste Tyrant, or I'll be for him:
This is the way to Hell.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Hold fast, I charge you away with him.

speeches.speaker: Hida.
verse: Alas old man, Death hath more doors than one,
And I will meet him.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Dorialus, Pray see her in her chamber,
And lay a guard about her:
The greatest curse the gods lay on our frailties,
Is Will and Disobedience in our Issues,
Which we beget as well as them to plague us,
With our fond loves; Beasts you are only blest
That have that happy dulness to forget
What you have made, your young ones grieve not you
They wander where they list, and have their ways
Without dishonor to you; and their ends,
Fall on 'em without sorrow of their Parents,
Or after ill remembrance: Oh this Woman
Would I had made my self a Sepulcher,
When I made her: Nephew, where is the Prince?
Pray God he have not more part of her baseness
Than of her bloud about him.
Gentlemen: where is he?

speeches.speaker: Isin.
verse: I know not Sir.
H'as his ways by himself, is too wise for my company.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I do not like this hiding of himself,
From such society as his person
Some of it ye needs must know.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
verse: Let him have this swinge, 'twill make him.
There's some good matter now in hand:
How the slave jeers and grins; the Duke is pleas'd,
There's a new pair of Scarlet Hose now, and as much
Garters and Stockings come by nature.
prose: I am sure not I: nor have known twice this ten days, which if I were as proud as some of 'em, I should take scurvily, but he is a young man.
Money to spare, as will fetch the old from pawn, a Hat and a Cloak to goe out to morrow:

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Be sure of this.

speeches.speaker: Tima.
verse: I durst not speak else, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cupid.
verse: LEucippus thou art shot through with a shaft
That will not rankle long, yet sharp enough
To sow a world of helpless misery—
In this unhappy Kingdom, dost thou think
Because thou art a Prince, to make a part
Against my power, but it is all the fault
Of thy old Father, who believes ^his age
Is cold enough to quench my burning Darts,
But he shall know e'r long, that my smart loose,
Can thaw Ice, and inflame the wither'd heart
Of Nestor, thou thy self art lightly struck,
But his mad love, shall publish that the rage
Of Cupid, has the power to conquer Age.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Why, what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: Have you got the spoil
You thirsted for? Oh tyrannie of men!

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: I pray thee leave,

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: Your envy is, Heaven knows,
Beyond the reach of all our feeble sex:
What pain alas, could it have been to you,
If I had kept mine honor? you might still
Have been a Prince, and still this Countreys Heir,
That innocent Guard which I till now had kept,
For my defence, my virtue, did it seem
So dangerous in a State, that your self came to suppress it?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Drie thine eyes again, I'll kiss thy tears away,
This is but folly, 'tis past all help.

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: Now you have won the treasure,
'Tis my request that you would leave me thus:
And never see these empty Walls again,
I know you will do so, and well you may:
For there is nothing in 'em that's worth
A glance, I loath my self, and am become
Another Woman; One methinks with whom
I want acquaintance.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: If I do offend thee, I can be gone,
prose: And though I love thy sight, so highly do I prize thine own content, that I will leave thee.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Nay, you may stay now;
You should have gone before: I know not now
Why I should fear you: All I should have kept
Is stol'n: Nor is it in the power of man
To rob me farther: if you can invent,
Spare not; No naked man fears robbing less
Than I doe: now you may for ever stay

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Why, I could do thee farther wrong.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: You have a deeper reach in evill than I:
'Tis past my thoughts.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: And past my will to act: but trust me I could do it.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Good Sir do, that I may know there is a wrong beyond what you have done me.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: I could tell all the world what thou hast done.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Yes you may tell the world
And do you think I am so vain to hope
You will not? you can tell the world but this,
That I am a widow, full of tears in shew,
My Husband dead: And one that lov'd me so,
Hardly a week, forgot my modestie,
And caught with youth and greatness,
Gave my self to live in sin with you;
This you may tell: And this I do deserve.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Why dost thou think me so base to tell!
These limbs of mine shall part
From one another on a wrack,
Ere I disclose; But thou dost utter words
That much afflict me: you did seem as ready
Sweet Bacha, as my self.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: They lay the fault on us:
But be it so; for Prince Leucippus sake
I will bear any thing.
prose: You are right a man: when they have 'witcht us into miserie, poor innocent souls,

speeches.speaker: Leucip.
verse: Come weep no more,
I wrought thee to it, it was my fault:
Nay, see if thou wilt leave? Here, take this pearl,
Kiss me sweet Bacha, and receive this purse.

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
prose: What should I do with these? they will not deck my mind.

speeches.speaker: Leucip.
verse: Why keep 'em to remember me.
I must be gone, I have been absent long:
I know the Duke my Father is in rage,
But I will see thee suddenly again.
Farewell my Bacha.

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: Gods keep you,
Do you here Sir: pray give me a point to wear.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Alas good Bacha, take on, I pray thee where thou wilt.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Coming from you. This Point is of as high Esteem with me, as all pearl and gold: nothing but good be ever with or near you.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Fare thee well mine own good Bacha;
I will make all haste.

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: Just as you are a Dosen I steem you:
No more, does he think I would prostitute
My self for love? it was the love of these pearls
And gold that won me, I confess
I lust more after him than any other,
And would at any rate if I had store,
Purchase his fellowship: but being poor,
I'll both enjoy his bodie and his purse,
And he a Prince, nere think my self the worse.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Nay, you must back and shew us what it is,
That 'witches you out of your Honor thus.

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: Who's that?

speeches.speaker: Tima.
verse: Look there Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leon,
verse: Lady, never flye you are betray'd.

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: Leave me my tears a while,
And to my Just rage give a little place:
What saucy man are you, that without leave,
Enter upon a Widows mournfull house?
You hinder a dead man from many tears.
Who did deserve more than the world can shed,
Though they should weep themselves to Images.
If not for love of me, yet of your self
Away, for you can bring no comforts to me.
But you may carry hence, you know not what.
Nay sorrow is infectious.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Thou thy self
Art grown infectious: wouldst thou know my name?
I am the Duke, father to this young-man
Whom thou corrupt'st?

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: Has he than told him all?

speeches.speaker: Leue.
verse: You do her wrong Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: O he has not told. Sir I beseech you pardon
My wild tongue, directed by a weak distemper'd head
Madded with ^rief: Alas I did not know
You were my Sovereign; but now you may
Command my poor unworthy life,
Which w^ll be none I hop^ ere long.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: All thy dissembling will never hide thy shame:
And wer't not more respecting Woman-hood in
General, than any thing in thee, thou shouldst
Be made such an example, that posteritie,
When they would speak most bitterly, should say,
Thou art as imp^dent as Bacha was.

speeches.speaker: Bacha
verse: Sir, though you be my King, whom I will
Serve in all just causes: yet when wrongfully
You seek to take my Honor, I will rise
Thus, and defie you; for it is a Jewell
Dearer than you can give, which whilst I keep,
(Though in this lowly house) I shall esteem
My self above the Princes of the earth
That are without it. If the Prince your son,
Whom you accuse me with know how to speak
Dishonor of me, if he do not do it,
The plagues of hell light on him, may he never
Govern this Kingdome: here I chalenge him
Before the face of heaven, my Liege, and these,
To speak the worst he can: if he will lye,
To lose a womans fame, I'll say he is
Like you (I think I cannot call him worse.)
He's dead, that with his life would have defended
My reputation and I forct to play
(That which I am) the foolish woman,
And use my liberal tongue.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Is't possible! we men are children in our
Carriages, compar'd with women: 'wake thy self
For shame, and leave not her whose honor thou
Shou'dst keep safe as thine own, alone to free her self:
But I am prest I know not how, with guilt,
And feel my conscience (never us'd to lye)
Loth to allow my tongue to add a lye
To that too much I did: but it is lawfull
To defend her, that only for my Love lov'd evill.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Tell me, why did you Leucip: stay here so long?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: If I can urge ought from me but a truth, hell Take me.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: What's the matter, why speak you not?

speeches.speaker: Tima.
verse: Alas good Sir, forbear
To urge the Prince, you see his shamefastness.

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: What does he say Sir? if thou be a Prince
Shew it, and tell the truth.

speeches.speaker: Ismen.
verse: If you have lain with her tell your Father
No doubt but he has done as ill before now:
The Gentlewoman will be proud on't.

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: For God's sake speak.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Have you done prating yet?

speeches.speaker: Ismen.
verse: Who prates?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Thou know'st I do not speak to thee Ismenus:
But what said you Tima; concerning my shamefastness?

speeches.speaker: Tima.
verse: Nothing I hope that might displease your Highness.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: If any of thy great, Great-grandmothers
This thousand years, had been as chast as she,
It would have made thee honester, I stay'd
To here what you wou'd say: she is by heaven
Of the most strict and blameless chastitie
That ever woman was: (good gods forgive me)
Had Tarquin, met with her, she had been kil'd
With a Slave by her ere she had agreed:
^ lye with her! wou'd I might perish then.
Our Mothers, whom we all must reverence,
Could nere exceed her for her chastitie,
Upon my soul: for by this light she's
A most obstinate modest creature.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: What did you with her then so long Leucippus?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: I'll tell you Sir: You see she's beautifull.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I see it well.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Mov'd by her face,
I came with lustful thoughts,
Which was a fault in me:
But telling truth, something more pardonable,
(And for the world I will not lye to you:)
Proud of my self, I thought a Princes name
Had power to blow 'em down flat of their backs;
But here I found a Rock not to be shook:
For as I hope for good Sir, all the battery
That I could lay to her, or of my person,
My greatness, or gold, could nothing move her.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: 'Tis very strange, being so young and fair.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: She's almost thirty Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: How do you know her age so just?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: She told it me her self
Once when she went about to shew by reason
I should leave wooing her.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: She stains the ripest Virgins of her age.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: If I had sin'd with her, I would be loth
To publish her disgrace: but by my life
I would have told it you, because I think
You would have pardon'd me the rather:
And I will tell you father: By this light Sir,
(But that I never will bestow my self
But to your liking) if she now would have me,
I now would marry her.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: How's that Leucippus!

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Sir, will you pardon me one fault, which yet
I have not done, but had a will to do, and I will tell it?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Be't what it will I pardon thee.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: I offered marriage to her.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Did she refuse it?

speeches.speaker: Leucip.
verse: With that earnestnss, and almost scorn
To think of any other after her lost Mate, that she
Made me think my self unworthy of her.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: You have stay'd too long Leucippus

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Yes Sir, forgive me Heaven, what multitude
Of oaths have I bestow'd on lies, and yet they were
Officious lyes, there was no malice in 'em.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: She is the fairest creature that ever I beheld;
And then so chaste, 'tis wonderfull: the more I look
On her, the more I am amaz'd.
I have long thought of a wife, and one I would have
Had, but that I was afraid to meet a woman
That might abuse my age: but here she is
Whom I may trust to; of a chastitie
Impregnable, and approved so by my son:
The meaness of her birth will still preserve her
In due obedience; and her beauty is
Of force enough to pull me back to youth.
My son once sent away, whose rivall-ship
I have just cause to fear, if power, of gold,
Or wit, can win her to me, she is mine.
Nephew Ismenus, I have new intelligence,
Your Province is unquiet still.

speeches.speaker: Ismen.
verse: I am glad on't.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: And so dangerously, that I must send the
Prince in person with you.

speeches.speaker: Ismen.
verse: I am glad of that too: Sir, will you dispatch
Us we shall wither here for ever.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: You shall be dispatcht within this hour:
Leucippus. never wonder, nor ask, it must be thus.
Lady I ask your pardon, whose virtue I have
Slubberd with my tongue, and you shall ever be
Chast in my memory hereafter;
But we old men often doat: to make amends for
My great fault, receive that Ring:
I'm sorry for your grief, may it soon leave you:
Come my Lords lets begon.

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: Heaven bless your Grace.
One that had but so much modestie left, as to blush,
Or shrink a little at his first encounter,
Had been undone; where I come off with honor,
And gain too: they that never wou'd be tract
In any course, by the most subtle sense
Must bear it through with frontless impudence.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: Gentlemen this is a strange peece of Justice,
To put the wretched Dwarf to death because
She doated on him; Is she not a woman, and
Subject to those mad figaries her whole Sex
Is infected with? Had she lov'd you, or you, or I,
Or all on's (as indeed the more the merryer still
With them) must we therefore have our heads par'd
With a Hatchet? So she may love all the Nobility
Out o'th Dukedome in a month, and let the raskals in.

speeches.speaker: Nis.
verse: You will not, or you do not see the need
That makes this just to the world?

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: I cannot tell, I would be loth to feel it:
But the best is, she loves not proper men, we three
Were in wise cases else: but make me know this need.

speeches.speaker: Eis.
prose: Why yes: He being taken away, this base incontinence dyes presently, and she must see her shame and sorrow for it.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: Pray God she do: but was the Sprat beheaded, Or did they swing him about like a chickin, and so break his neck?

speeches.speaker: Agen.
prose: Yes, he was beheaded, and a solemn Justice made of it.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: That might have been deducted.

speeches.speaker: Agenor.
prose: Why how would you have had him dyed?

speeches.speaker: Dori.
prose: Faith I would have had him rosted like a warden in a brown paper, and no more talk on't: or a feather stuck in's head, like a Quail: or a hanged him in a Dog-coller: what should he be beheaded? we shall have it grow so base shortly, Gentlemen will be out of love with it.

speeches.speaker: Nis.
prose: I wonder from whence this of the Dwarf's first sprung?

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: From an old leacherous pair of breeches that lay upon a wench to keep her warm: for certainly they are no mans work: and I am sure a Monkey would get one of the guard to this fellow, he was no bigger than a small Portmanteu, and much about that making if'tad legs.

speeches.speaker: Age.
prose: But Gentlemen, what say you to the Prince?

speeches.speaker: Nis.
prose: I, concerning his being sent I know not whither.

speeches.speaker: Dorialus.
prose: Why then he will come home I know not when: you shall pardon me, I'll talk no more of this subject, but say, gods be with him where ere he is, and send him well home again: For why, he is gone, or when he will return, let them know that directed him: Only this, there's mad Morisco's in the state; but what they are, I'll tell you when I know. Come, let's go, hear all, and say nothing.

speeches.speaker: Agen.
prose: Content.

speeches.speaker: Tela.
prose: Timantus, is the Duke ready yet?

speeches.speaker: Tima.
prose: Almost.

speeches.speaker: Tela.
prose: What ails him?

speeches.speaker: Tima.
prose: Faith I know not, I think he has dreamt he's but eighteen: has been worss since he sent you forth for the frizling iron.

speeches.speaker: Tel.
prose:
That cannot be, he lay in Gloves all night, and this morning I brought him a new Periwig, with a lock
at it, and knockt up a swing in's chamber.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: O but since, his Taylor came, and they have fallen out about the fashion on's cloaths: and yonders a fellow come, has board a hole in's ear; and he has bespoke a Vaulting-horse, you shall see him come forth presently: he looks like Winter, stuck here and there with fresh flowers.

speeches.speaker: Tela.
prose: Will he not Tilt think you?

speeches.speaker: Tima.
prose: I think he will.

speeches.speaker: Tela.
prose: What does he mean to doe?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: I know not: but by this light I think he is in love; he wou'd ha' bin shav'd but for me.

speeches.speaker: Tela.
prose: In love with whom?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: I could guess, but you shall pardon me: he will take me along with him some-whither,

speeches.speaker: Tela.
prose: I over-heard him ask your opinion of some bodies beauty.

speeches.speaker: Tima.
prose: Yes, there it goes, that makes him so youthfull, and has layd by his Crutch, and halts now with a leading staff.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Timantus.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: This Feather is not large enough.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Yes faith, 'tis such an one as the rest of the young Gallants wear.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Telamon, does it doe well?

speeches.speaker: Tela:
prose: Sir, it becomes you, or you become it, tho rareliest—

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: A way, dost think so?

speeches.speaker: Tela.
prose: Think Sir, I know it. Sir, the Princess, is past all hope of life since the Dwarf was put to death.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Let her be so, I have other matters in hand: but this same Taylor angers me, he has made my doublet so wide: and see, the knave has put no points at my arme.

speeches.speaker: Tima.
prose: Those will be put to quickly Sir, upon any occasion.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Telamon, have you bid this Dancer come a mornings?

speeches.speaker: Tela.
prose: Yes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Temantus, let me see the glass again: look you how careless you are grown, is this tooth well put in?

speeches.speaker: Tima.
prose: Which Sir?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: This Sir.

speeches.speaker: Tima.
prose: It shall be.

speeches.speaker: Telam.
prose: Me thinks that tooth should put him in mind on's years: and Timantus, stands as if (seeing the Duke, in such a youthfull habit) he were looking in's mouth how old he were.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: So, so.

speeches.speaker: Tela.
prose: Will you have your Gown sir?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: My Gown? why, am I sick? bring me my Sword.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Let a couple of the great horses be brought out for us

speeches.speaker: Tima.
prose: He'll kill himself. Why, will you ride Sir:

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Ride? Dost thou think I cannot ride?

speeches.speaker: Timan.
prose: O yes Sir, I know it: but as I conceive your journey, you wou'd have it private; and then you were better take a Coach.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: These Coaches make me sick: yet 'tis no matter, let it be so.

speeches.speaker: Tel.
prose: Sir, here's your sword.

speeches.speaker: Leon,
prose: O well sed: let me see it, I could me thinks Why Telamon, bring me another: what, thinkst thou I will wear a sword in vain?

speeches.speaker: Tela.
verse: He has not strength enough to draw it,
A yoak of Fleas ty'd to a hair would have drawn it.
'Tis out sir now, the Scabbard is broke.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: O put it up again, and on with it; me thinks I am not drest till I feel my sword on.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Telamon, if any of my counsell aske for me,
Say I am gone to take the air.

speeches.speaker: Tima.
prose: He has not been drest this twenty years then, If this vain hold but a week, he will learn to play o'th base violl and sing to't: He's poetical alreadie;
For I have spide a Sonnet on's making lye by's beds side, I'll be so unmannerly to read it.
He's dead, he's dead, and I am following.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Ask Cupid mercie Madam.

speeches.speaker: Hida.
verse: O my heart.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Help!

speeches.speaker: Hero.
verse: Stir her:

speeches.speaker: Hida.
verse: O, O!

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: She's going, wretched woman that we are:
Look to her, and I'll pray the while.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
verse: Why Madam?

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Cupid, pardon what is past,
And forgive our sins at last,
Then we will be coy no more,
But thy Deity Adore,
Troths at fifteen we will plight,
And will tread a Dance at night.
In the fields, or by the Fire,
With the youths that have desire.
(How does she yet?

speeches.speaker: Hero.
verse: O ill:

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Given Ear-rings we will wear,
Bracelets of our Lovers hair,
Which they on our Arms shall twist,
With their Names carv'd on our wrist:
All the money that we owe,
We in Tokens will bestow:
And learn to write, that when 'tis sent,
Onely our Loves know what it meant:
O then pardon what is past,
And forgive our Sins at last.
(What, Mends she?

speeches.speaker: Hero.
verse: Nothing, you do it not wantonly, you shou'd sing.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
verse: Leave, leave, 'tis now too late.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Why?
Shee is dead:

speeches.speaker: Hero.
verse: Her last is breathed.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: What shall we doe.

speeches.speaker: Hero.
verse: Go run,
And tell the Duke; And whilst I'll close her eyes.
Thus I shut thy faded light,
And put it in eternall night.
Where is she can boldly say
Though she be as fresh as May:
She shall not by this Corps be laid,
Ere to morrows light doe fade.
Let us all now living be,
Warn'd by thy strict Chastitie;
And marry all fast as we can,
Till then we keep a piece of man,
Wrongfully from them that owe it
Soon may every Maid bestow it.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Who is it?

speeches.speaker: Maid.
verse: Forsooth there's gallant Coach at the dore,
And the brave old man in't, that you said was the Duke.

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: Cupid, grant he may be taken.

speeches.speaker: Maid.
prose: He is coming up, and looks the swaggeringst, and has such glorious cloaths.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Let all the house see me sad, and see all handsome.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Nay widow flie not back, we come not now to chide, stand up and bid me welcome.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: To a poor widows house that knows no en^ of her ill fortune: your Highness is most welcome.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Come kiss me then, this is but manners widow: Nere fling your head aside, I have more cause of grief than you: my Daughters dead: but what? 'Tis nothing. Is the rough French horse brought to the dore?
They say he is a high goer, I shall soon try his mettle.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: He will be Sir, and the gray Barbary, they are fiery both.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: They are the better: Before the gods I am lightsome, very lightsome: How doest thou like me widow?

speeches.speaker: Bach.
prose: As a person in whom all graces are.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Come, come, ye flatter: I'll clap your cheek for that, and you shall not be angry.
Hast no Musick: Now could I cut three times with ease, and do a cross point, should shame all your gallants.

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: I do believe you, and your self too:
Lord what a fine old Zany my Love has made him?
'Is mine, I am sure: Heaven make me thankful for him.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Tell me how old thou art, my pretty sweet heart?

speeches.speaker: Timantus.
prose: Your Grace will not buy her, she may trip Sir?

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
prose: My sorrow showes me elder then I am by many years?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Thou art so witty I must kiss agen.

speeches.speaker: Tima.
prose: Indeed her Age lyes not in her mouth: nere look it there Sir, she has a better Register, if it be not burnt.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: I will kiss thee, I am a fire Timantus.

speeches.speaker: Tima.
prose: Can you chuse Sir, having such heavenly fire before you?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Widow, guess why I come, I prethee do,

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
prose: I cannot Sir, unless you be pleas'd to make a mirth out of my rudeness: and that I hope your pity will not let ye, the subject is so Barren: Bite King, Bite, I'll let you play a while.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Now as I am an honest man, I'll tell thee truely, how many foot did I Jump yesterday Timantus?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Fourteen of your own, and some three fingers.

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
prose: This fellow lyes as lightly, as if hee were in cut Taffata.
Alas good Almanack get thee to Bed, and tell what weather we shall have to morrow.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Widow I am come in short to be a Suiter.

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
prose: For whom?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Why by my troth, I come to wooe thee wench:
And win thee for my self: Nay, look upon me:
I have about me that will do it.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Now Heaven defend me, your Whore shall never: I thank the Gods, I have a little left me to keep me warm, and honest: if your grace take not that, I seek no more.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: I am so far from taking any thing, I'll add unto thee.

speeches.speaker: Bach.
verse: Such Additions may be for your ease Sir,
prose: Not my honestie: I am well in being single, good Sir seek another, I am no meat for money.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Shall I fight for thee?
This sword shall cut his throat, that dars lay claim
But to a Finger of thee, but to a look, I would
See such a fellow.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: It would be but a cold sight to you:
This is the father of S. George a foot-back,
Can such dry mumming talk.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Before the gods, your grace lookes like Aeneas.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: He looks like his old father upon his back,
Crying to get A boord.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: How shall I win thy love, I pray thee tell me? I'll marry thee if thou desirest that: That is an honest Course, I am in good earnest, and presently within this hour, am mad for thee: prethee deny me not, For as I live I'll pine thee, but I'll have thee

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: Now he's in the Toyl, I'll hold him fast.

speeches.speaker: Tima.
prose: You do not know what 'tis to be a Queen, Go too you Maid, else what the old man falls short of, there's others can eech out, when you please to call on 'em.

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: I understand you not, Love I adore thee, Sir, on my knees I give you hearty thanks, for so much Honoring your humble Hand-mayd above her birth:
Far more her weak deservings, I dare not trust the Envious tongues of all that must repine at my unworthy rising.
Beside, you have many fair ones in your Kingdome
Porn to such worth: O turn your self about
And make a Noble choice.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: If I do, let me famish: I will have thee,
Or break up house, and boord here.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Sir, you may command an unwilling woman to obey ye: but heaven knows—

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: No more: these half a dozen kisses, and this Jewell, and every thing I have, and away with me, and clap it up; and have a boy by morning. Timantus let one be sent post for my son again: and for Ismenus, they are scarce twenty miles on their way yet, by that time we'll be married.

speeches.speaker: Tima.
verse: There shall Sir.

speeches.speaker: Nisus.
prose: Is not this a fine marriage?

speeches.speaker: Agenor.
prose: Yes, yes, let it alone.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: I, I, the King may marry whom's list, let's talk of other matters.

speeches.speaker: Nis.
prose: Is the Prince coming home certainly?

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: Yes, yes, he was sent post for yesterday, lets make haste we'll see how his new Mother-in-law will entertain him.

speeches.speaker: Nis.
prose: Why well I warrant you: did you not mark how humbly she carried her self to us on her marriage day, acknowledging her own unworthiness, and that she would be our servant.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: But mark what's done.

speeches.speaker: Nis.
prose: Regard not shew.

speeches.speaker: Age.
prose: O God! I knew her when I have been off'red her to be brought to my bed for five pounds: whether it could have been perform'd or no, I know not.

speeches.speaker: Nis.
prose: Her Daughters a pretty Lady.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: Yes: and having had but mean bringing up, it talks the pretilest and innocentliest, the Queen will be so angry to hear her betray her breeding by her language: but I am perswaded sh^'^ well dispos'd.

speeches.speaker: Agenor.
prose: I think better than her Mother.

speeches.speaker: Nis.
prose: Come, we stay too long.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose: How now man, strook dead with a tale?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: No, but with a truth.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose: Stand off your self: can you endure blows, and shrink at words?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Thou knowst I have told thee all.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose: But that all's nothing to make you thus: your Sisters dead.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: That's much, but not the most.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose: Why, for the other let her marry and hang, 'tis no purpos'd fault of yours: and if your Father will needs ^ave your cast Whore, you shall shew the duty of a child better in being contented, and bidding much good doe his good old heart with her, than in repining thus at it; let her go: what, there are more wenches man, we'll have another.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: O thou art vain, thou knowst I doe not love her:
What shall I doe? I would my tongue had led me
To any other thing, but blasphemy,
So I had mist commending of this woman,
Whom I must reverence now: she is my Mother,
My sin Ismenus has wrought all this ill:
And I beseech thee, to be warn'd by me,
And doe not lye, if any man should aske thee
But How thou dost, or What a clock 'tis now.
Be sure thou doe not lye, make no excuse
For him that is most near thee: never let
The most officious falsehood scape thy tongue,
For they above (that are intirely truth)
Will make that seed, which thou hast sown
Of lyes, ^ield miseries a thousand fold
Upon thine head, as they have done on mine.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Sir, your Highness is welcome home, the Duke and Queen will presently come forth to you.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: I'll wait on them.

speeches.speaker: Tima.
prose: Worthy Ismenus, I pray you, have you sped in your wars?

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose: This Rogue mocks me. Well Timantus, Pray how have you sped here at whom at shovelboord?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Faith reasonable. How many Towns have you taken in this Summer?

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose: How many Stags have you been at the death of this grass?

speeches.speaker: Tima.
prose: A number: 'Pray how is the Province settled?

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose: Prethee how does the dun Nag?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: I think you mock me my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose: Mock thee? Yes by my troth doe I: why what wouldst thou have me doe with thee; Art good for any thing else?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: My good Ismenus, hold me by the wrist:
And if thou see'st me fainting, wring me hard,
For I shall swoon again else—

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Welcome my son; rise, I did send for thee
Back from the province, by thy Mothers counsell,
Thy good Mother here, who loves thee well:
She would not let me venture all my joy
Amongst my enemies: I thank thee for her,
And none but thee. I took her on thy word.

speeches.speaker: Leucip.
verse: Pinch harder.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: And she shall bid thee welcome: I have now
Some near affairs, but I will drink a Health
To thee anon: Come Telamon, I am grown
Lustier, I thank thee for't, since I marryed;
I can stand now alone, why Telamon,
And never stagger.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Welcome most noble Sir, whose fame is come
Hither before you: out alas you scorn me,
And teach me what to doe.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: No, you are my Mother.

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: Far unworthy of that name God knows:
But trust me, here before these Lords,
I am no more but Nurse unto the Duke;
Nor will I breed a faction in the State,
It is too much for me that I am rais'd
Unto his bed, and will remain the servant
Of you that did it.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Madam I will serve you
As shall become me. O dissembling woman!
Whom I must reverence though. Take from thy
Quiver ^ure-aim'd Apollo, one of thy swift darts,
Headed with thy consuming golden beams,
And let it melt this body into mist,
That none may find it.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Shall I beg my Lords
This Room in private for the Prince and me?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: What will she say now?

speeches.speaker: Bach.
verse: I must still enjoy him:
Yet there is still left in me a spark of woman,
That wishes he should move it, bu^ he stands,
As if he grew there with his eyes on earth,
Sir, you and I when we were last together
Kept not this distance as we were afraid
Of blasting by our selves.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Madam 'tis true, Heaven pardon it.

speeches.speaker: Bach.
verse: Amen Sir.
You may think that I have done you wrong in this strange marriage.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: 'Tis past now.

speeches.speaker: Bach.
verse: But it was no fault of mine:
The world had call'd me mad, had I refus'd
The King: nor layd I any train to catch him,
It was your own Oaths did it.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: 'Tis a truth: that takes my sleep away, but
Would to Heaven, if it had so been pleas'd, you had
Refus'd him, though I had gratifi'd that courtesie
With having you my self: But since 'tis thus,
I doe beseech you that you will be honest
From henceforth; and not abuse his credulous Age,
Which you may easily doe. As for my self
What I can say, you know alas too well
Is ty'd within me, here it will sit like lead,
But shall offend no other, it will pluck me
Back from my ent'rance into any mirth,
As if a servant came, and whisper'd with me
Of some friends death, but I will bear my self,
To you, with all the due obedience
A son owes to a Mother: more than this,
Is not in me, but I must leave the rest to the
Just gods: who in their blessed time,
When they have given me punishment enough,
For my rash Sin, will mercifully find
As unexpected means to ease my grief
As they did now to bring it.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Grown so godly? this must not be.
And I will be to you, no other than a natural Mother ought;
And for my honesty, so you will swear
Never to urge me, I shall keep it safe from any other.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Bless me I should urge you?

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: Nay but swear then that I may be at peace,
For I doe feel a weakness in my self,
That can denie you nothing, if you tempt me,
I shall embrace Sin as it were a friend, and run to meet it.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: If you knew how far
It were from me, you would not urge an Oath.
But for your satisfaction, when I tempt you

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Swear not: I cannot move him, this sad talk
Of things past help, does not become us well.
Shall I send one for my Musicians, and we'll dance?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Dance Madam?

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Yes, Alaualta.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: I cannot dance Madam.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Then lets be merry.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: I am as my Fortunes bid me.
Do not you see me sowr?

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Yes.
And why think you I smile?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: I am so far from any joy my self,
I cannot fancie a cause of mirth.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: I'll tell you, we are alone:

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Alone?

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: 'Tis true: what then?

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: What then? you make my smiling now
Break into laughter: what think you is to be done then?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: We shou'd pray to Heaven for mercy.

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: Pray? that were a way indeed
To pass the time: but I will make you blush,
To see a bashfull woman teach a man
What we should doe alone try again
If you can find it out.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: I dare not think I understand you.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: I must teach you then; Come, kiss me.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Kiss you?

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Yes, be not asham'd:
You did it not your self, I will forgive you.

speeches.speaker: Leue.
verse: Keep you displeas'd gods, the due respect
I ought to bear unto this wicked woman,
As she is now my Mother, Haste within me,
Lest I add sins to sins, till no repentance will cure me.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Leave these melancholly moods,
That I may swear thee welcome on thy Lipps
A thousand times.

speeches.speaker: Leue.
verse: Pray leave this wicked talk,
You doe not know to what my Fathers wrong
May urge me.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: I'm careless, and doe weigh
The world, my life, and all my after hopes
Nothing without thy Love, mistake me not:
Thy Love, as I have had it, free and open
As wedlock is, within it self, what say you?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Nothing.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Pitty me, behold a Duchess
Kneels for thy mercie, and I swear to you
Though I should lye with you, it is no Lust,
For it desires no change, I could with you
Content my self; what answer will you give?

speeches.speaker: Leue.
verse: They that can answer must be less amaz'd,
Than I am now: you see my tears deliver
My meaning to you.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Shall I be contem'd? thou art a beast, worse than a savage beast,
To let a Lady kneel, to beg that thing
Which a right man would offer.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: 'Tis your will Heaven: but let me hear me like
My self, how ever she does.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Were you made an Eunuch, since you went hence?
Yet they have more desire than I can find in you:
How sond was I to beg thy love? I'll force thee to my will.
Dost thou not know that I can make the King
Dote as my list? yield quickly, or by Heaven
I'll have thee kept in prison for my purpose,
Where I will make thee serve my turn, and have thee fed
With such meats as best shall sit my ends
And not thy health, why dost not speak to me?
And when thou dost displease me, and art grown
Less able to perform; then I will have thee
Kill'd and forgotten: Are you striken dumb?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: All you have nam'd but making of me sin
With you, you may command, but never that;
Say what you will, I'll hear you as becomes me,
If you speak, I will not follow your counsell,
Neither will I tell the world to your disgrace,
But give you the just honor
That is due from me to my Father's wife.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Lord how full of wise formality you'r grown
Of late: but you were telling me
You could have wisht that I had marry'd you,
If you will swear so yet, I'll make away the King.

speeches.speaker: Leue.
verse: You are a strumpet.

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: Nay, I care not
For all your Railings: They will Batter walls
And take in Towns, as soon as trouble me:
Tell him, I care not, I shall undoe you only, which is no matter.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: I appeal to you still, and for ever, that are
And cannot be other, Madam, I see 'tis in your power
To work your will on him: And I desire you
To lay what trains you will for my wish'd death,
But suffer him to find his quiet grave
In peace, Alas he never did you wrong,
And farther I beseech you pardon me,
For the ill word I gave you, for how ever
You may deserve, it became not me
To call you so, but passion urges me
I know not whither: my heart break now, & ease me ever

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: Pray yo^ g^t you hence
With your goodly humor, I am weary of you extreamely:

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Trust me, so am I of my self too:
Madam, I'll take my leave; gods set all right.

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: Amen, Sir, get you gon;
Am I deny'd? it does not trouble me
That I have mov'd, but that I am refus'd:
I have lost my patience: I will make him know
Lust is not Love, for Lust will find a mate
While there are men, and so will I: and more.
Than one, or twenty: yonder is Timantus,
A fellow void of any worth, to raise himself,
And therefore like to catch at any evil
That will but pluck him up: him will I make
Mine own: Timantus, Timantus. Madam?

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Thou know'st well
Thou wert by chance, a means of this my raising:
Brought the Duke to me, and though 'twere but chance
I must reward thee.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: I shall bend my service unto your Highness.

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: But do it then entirely, and in everything,
And tell me, couldst thou now think that thing
Thou wouldst not do for me?

speeches.speaker: Timant.
verse: No by my soul Madam.

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: Then thou art right.
Go to my Lodging, and I'll follow thee.
With my instruction I do see already,
This Prince that did but now contemn me, dead:
Yet will I never speak an evil word
Unto his Father of him, till I have won
A belief, I love him, but I'll make
His virtues his undoing, and my praises
Shall be so many swords against his breast,

Which once perform'd, I'll make
~rania
My Daughter, the Kings heir, and plant my issue
In this large Throne: nor shall it be withstood,
They that begin in Lust, must end in Blood.

speeches.speaker: Doria.
verse: We live to know a fine time, Gentl.

speeches.speaker: Nis.
verse: And a fine Duke, that through his doting age
Suffers him to be a child again
Under his Wives tuition.

speeches.speaker: Agen.
verse: All the Land holds in that tenor too: in womans service? sure we shall learn to spinn.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: No, that's too honest: we shall have other
Liberal Sciences taught us too soon;
Lying, and flattering, those are the studies now:
And Murther shortly I know, will be humanity, Gent.
If we live here we must be knaves, believe it.

speeches.speaker: Nisus.
verse: I cannot tell my Lord Dorialus, though my
Own nature hate it, if all determine to be knaves,
I'll try what I can do upon my self: that's certain,
I will not have my throat cut for my goodness,
The virtue will not quit the pain.

speeches.speaker: Age.
verse: But pray you tell me,
Why is the Prince now ripe and full experient,
Not made a dore in the State?

speeches.speaker: Nis.
verse: Because he is honest.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Goodness attend your Honors.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: You must not be amongst us then.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: The Dutchess, whose humble servant I am proud to be, would speak with you.

speeches.speaker: Age.
prose: Sir, we are pleas'd to wait: when is it?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: An hour hence my good Lords, and so I leave my service.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: This is one of her Ferrets that she bolts business out withall: this fellow, if he were well ript, has all the linings of a knave within him: how slye he looks?

speeches.speaker: Nis.
prose: Have we nothing about our cloaths that he may catch at?

speeches.speaker: Agenor.
prose: O my conscience, there's no treason in my dublet, it there be, my elbows will discover it, they are out.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: Faith, and all the harm that I can find in mine is, that they are not pay'd for; let him make what he can of that, so he discharge that. Come, let's go.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: And you shall find Sir what blessing heaven gave you in such a son.

speeches.speaker: Le.
prose: Pray gods, I may, Let's walk & change our subject.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: O Sir, can anything come sweeter to you, or strike a deeper joy into your heart than your son's virtue?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: I allow his virtues: but 'tis not handsome thus to feed my self with such moderate praises of mine own.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: The subject of our comendations is it self grown so infinite in goodness, that all the glory we can lay upon it, though we should open volumes of his praises, is a mere modesty in his expression, and shews him lame still, like an ill wrought peece wanting proportion.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
prose: Yet still he is a man, and subject still to more inordinate vices, than our love can give him blessing.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Else he were a god. yet so near as he is, he comes to heaven, that we may see so far as flesh can point us things only worthy them, and only these in all his actions.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: This is too much my Queen.

speeches.speaker: Bach.
prose: Had the gods, lov'd me; that my unworthy womb had bred this brave man.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Still you run wrong.

speeches.speaker: Bach.
prose: I would have liv'd upon the comfort of him, fed on his growing hopes.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
prose: This touches me.

speeches.speaker: Bach.
prose: I know no friends, nor Being, but his virtues.

speeches.speaker: Le.
prose: You have laid out words enough upon a subject.

speeches.speaker: Bach.
prose: But words cannot express him Sir: why what a shape Heaven has conceiv'd him in, oh Nature made him up!

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: I wonder Dutchess.

speeches.speaker: Bach.
prose: So you must: for less than admiration loses this god-like man.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Have you done with him?

speeches.speaker: Bach.
prose: Done with? O good gods, what frailties thus pass by us without reverence?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: I see no such perfection.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: O dear Sir: you are a father, and those joys
To you, speak in your heart, not in your tongue.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: This leaves a tast behind it worse than physick.

speeches.speaker: Baca.
verse: Then for all his wisdome, valour,
Good fortune, and all those friends of honor,
They are in him as free and natural, as passions
In a Woman.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: You make me blush at all these years
To see how blindly you have flung your praises
Upon a Boy, a very child, and worthless,
Whilst I live, of these Honors.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: I would not have my love Sir, make my tongue
Shew me so much a woman: as to praise
Or dispraise, where my will is, without reason,
Or generall allowance of the people.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Allowance of the people, what allow they!

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: All, I have sed for truth, and they must do it,
And do at upon him: love him, and admire him.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: How's that?

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: For in this youth and noble forwardness
All things are bound together that are kingly,
A fitness to bear rule:

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: No more.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: And Sovereignty not made to know command.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I have sed, no more.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: I have done Sir, though unwilling, and pardon me.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I do, not a word more.

speeches.speaker: Baca.
verse: I have gi'n thee poyson
Of more infection than the Dragons tooth,
Or the gross Air o'er heated.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Timantus when saw you the Prince?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: I left him now Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Tell me truely, out of your free opinion without courting. How you like him.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: How I like him?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Yes: for you in conversation may see more Than a Father.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: It works.

speeches.speaker: Timantus.
verse: Your Grace has chosen out an ill observer.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Yes, I mean of his ill: you talk rightly.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: But you take me wrong; All I know by him
I dare deliver boldly: He is the store-house
And head of virtue; your great self excepted,
That feeds the Kingdome.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: These are flatteries: speak me his vices, there you do a service worth a Fathers thanks.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Sir, I cannot. If there be any, sure they are the times which I could wish less dangerous.
But pardon me, I am too bold.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: You are not, forward and open what these dangers are.

speeches.speaker: Timan.
prose: Nay, good Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
prose: Nay, fall not off again, I will have all.

speeches.speaker: Timan.
verse: Alas Sir, what am I, you should believe
My eyes or ears, so subtle to observe
Faults in a State: all my main business
Is service to your Grace, and necessaries
For my poor life.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Do not displease me Sirrah,
But that you know tell me, and presently.

speeches.speaker: Timan.
verse: Since your Grace will have it
I'll speak it freely: Alwayes my obedience
And love preserv'd unto the Prince.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Prethee to the matter.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: For Sir, if you consider
How like a Sun in all his great employments,
How full of heat.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Make me understand what I desire.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: And then at his return.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Do not anger me.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Then thus Sir: All mislike ye,
As they would do the gods, if they did dwell with 'em.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: What?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Talke and prate, as their ignorant rages
Leads 'em without Alleageance or Religion.
For Heavens sake have a care of your own person:
I cannot tell, their wickedness may lead
Farther than I dare think yet.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: O base people.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Yet the Prince, for whom this is pretended may
Persuade 'em, and no doubt will: virtue is ever watchfull,
But be you still secur'd and comforted.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Heaven how have I offended, that this rod
So heavy and unnaturall, should fall upon me
When I am old and helpless.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Brave Gentl. that such a madding love should follow thee, to rob thee of a Father:
All the Court is full of dangerous whispers.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I'll cut him shorter first, then let him rule.
prose: I perceive it, and 'spight of all their strengths will make my safety: I'll cut him shorter.

speeches.speaker: Bach.
prose: What a foul Age is this, when Virtue is made a sword to smite the virtuous? Alas, alas:

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I'll teach him to fly lower.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: By no means Sir, rather, make more your love,
And hold your favor to him: for 'tis now
Impossible to yoke him, if his thoughts,
As I must ne'er believe, run with their rages,
He never was so innocent, but what reason
His Grace has to withdraw his love from me,
And other good men that are near your person,
I cannot yet find out: I know my duty
Has ever been attending.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: 'Tis too plain: He means to play the villain,
I'll prevent him, not a word more of this, be private.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Madam 'tis done.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: He cannot escape me. Have you spoken with the noble men?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Yes Madam they are here: I wait a farther service.

speeches.speaker: Bac,
verse: Till yet be the Prince, you need no more instructions.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: No, I have it.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: That fool that willingly provoks a woman,
Has made himself another evill Angell,
And a new Hell, to which all other torments
Are but mere pastime: Now my noble Lords,
You must excuse me, that unmannerly
We have broke your private business.

speeches.speaker: Agen.
verse: Your good Grace may command us, and that.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Faith my Lord Agenor: 'Tis so good a cause
I am confident, you cannot loose by it.

speeches.speaker: Dorialus.
verse: Which way does she fish now?
The devill is but a fool to a right woman.

speeches.speaker: Nisus.
prose: Madam, we must needs win in doing service to such a gracious Lady.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: I thank you, and will let you know the business:
So I may have your helps, never be doubtfull,
For 'tis so just a cause, and will to you
Upon the knowledge seem so honorable,
That I assure my self your willing hearts
Will strait be for me in it.

speeches.speaker: Age.
verse: If she should prove good now, what wer't like?

speeches.speaker: Dorial.
verse: Thunder in Ianuarie, or a good woman,
That's stranger than all Affrick.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: It shall not need your wonder, this it is:
The Duke you know is old, and rather subject
To ease and prayers now, than all those troubles,
Cares, and continuall watchings, that attend
A^ Kingdomes safety, therefore to prevent
The fall of such a flourishing Estate
As this has been, and to put off
The murmure of the people that encrease
Against my government, which the gods knows
I onely feel the trouble of: I present
The Prince unto your loves, a Gent.
In whom all Excellencies are knit together,
All peeces of a true man, let your prayers
Win from the Duke half his Vexation,
That he may undertake it, whose discretion
I must confess, though it be from the Father,
Yet now is stronger, and more apt to govern.
'Tis not my own desire, but all the Lands,
I know the weakeness of it.

speeches.speaker: Nisus.
verse: Madam, this noble care and love has won us
For ever to your lives, we'll to the King,
And since your Grace has put it in our mouths,
We'll win him with the cunning'st words we can.

speeches.speaker: Dorial.
verse: I was never cousen'd in a woman before:
For commonly they are like Apples: If once they bruise
prose: They will grow rotten thorow, and serve for nothing but to asswage swellings.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Good Lords delay no time, since 'tis your good
Pleasures to think my counsell good, and by no means
Let the Prince know it, whose affections
Will stir mainly against it: besides his Father
May hold him dangerous, if it be not carried
So that his forward will appear not in it,
Go, and be happy.

speeches.speaker: Dorial.
verse: Well, I would not be Chronicl'd as thou
Wilt be for a good woman, for all the world.

speeches.speaker: Nisus.
verse: Madam, we kiss your hand, and so inspire.
Nothing but happiness can crown our prayers.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: ANd thus she has us'd me, is't not a good mother?

speeches.speaker: Ismenus.
verse: Why kill'd you her not?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: The gods forbid it.

speeches.speaker: Ismenus.
verse: S'light, if all the women i'th' world were barren, shee had dy'd.

speeches.speaker: Leuc.
verse: But 'tis not reason directs thee thus.

speeches.speaker: Ismen.
verse: Then have I none at all, for all I have in me
Directs me: Your Father's in a pretty rage.

speeches.speaker: Leucippus.
verse: Why?

speeches.speaker: Ismenus.
prose: Nay, 'tis well, if he know himself, but some of the Nobility have deliver'd a petition to him: what's in't, I know not, but it has put him to his trumps: he has taken a months time to answer it, and chafes like himself.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: He's here Ismenus..

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Set me down Tellamon. Leucippus.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bach.
prose: Nay good Sir, be at peace, I dare swear he knows not of it.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: You are foolish: peace.

speeches.speaker: Bach.
prose: All will go ill, deny it boldly Sir, trust me he cannot prove it by you.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: What?

speeches.speaker: Bach.
verse: You'll make all worse too with your facing it.

speeches.speaker: Leuc.
verse: What is the matter?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Know'st thou that petition?
Look on it well: wouldst thou be joyn'd with me
(Unnaturall child to be weary of me)
E'r Fate esteem me sit for other worlds.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: May be he knows not of it.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Oh strange carriages!
Sir, as I have hope that there is any thing
To reward doing well, my usages
Which have been (but 'tis no matter what)
Have put me so far from the thought of Greatness,
That I should welcome it like a disease
That grew upon me, and I could not cure.
They are my enemies that gave you this,
And yet they call me friend, and are themselves
I fear abus'd. I am weary of my life,
For Gods sake take it from me: it creates
More mischief in the State than it is worth,
The usage I have had, I know would make
Wisdom her self run frantick through the streets,
And Patience quarrel with her shadow.
Sir, this sword—

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Alas! help for the love of Heaven,
Make way through me first, for he is your Father.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: What, would he kill me?

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: No Sir, no.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Thou always makes mak'st the best on't, but I sear—

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Why do you use me thus? who is't can think
That I would kill my Father, that can yet
Forbear to kill you? Here Sir, is my sword;
I dare not touch it, lest she say again
I would have kill'd you: let me not have mercy
When I most need it, if I would not change
Place with my meanest servant. Let these faults
Be mended Madam: if you saw how ill
They did become you, you would part with them.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: I told the Duke as much before.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: What? what did you tell him?

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: That it was only an ambition,
Nurst in you by your youth, provok'd you thus,
Which age would take away.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: It was his doing then? come hither Love.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: No indeed, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: How am I made, that I can bear all this?
If any one had us'd a friend of mine ne'r this,
My hand had carried death about it.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Lead me hence Tellamon: come my dear
Bacha, I shall find time for this.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: Madam, you know I dare not speak before
The King; but you know well, if not, I'll tell you,
You are the most wicked'st, and most murderous
Strumpet, that ever was call'd Woman.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: My Lord, what can I do for him? he shall command me.

speeches.speaker: Leon,
verse: I know thou art too kind; away I say.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
verse: Sir, I am sure we dream, this cannot be.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Oh that we did, my wickedness has brought
All this to pass, else I should bear my self.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose: Look, doe you see who's there? your virtuous Mothers issue: kill her, yet take some little pidling revenge.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Away, the whole Court calls her virtuous; for they say, she is unlike her Mother, and if so, she can have no vice.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: I'll trust none of 'em that come of such a breed.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: But I have found
A kind of love in her to me: alas,
Think of her death! I dare be sworn for her,
She is as free from any hate to me
As her bad Mother's full. She was brought up
I'th' Countrey, as her tongue will let you know.
If you but talk with her, with a poor Uncle,
Such as her Mother had.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: She's come again.

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
prose: I would ^ene speak to the good Marquess my brother, if I but thought he could abaid me.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Sister, how do you?

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
verse: Very well I thank you.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: How does your good Mother?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Fie, fie, Ismenus for shame, mock such an innocent soul as this.

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
verse: Feth a she be no good, god may her so.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: I know you wish it with your heart dear Sister, but she is good I hope.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: Are you so simple, to make so much of this?
Do you not know,
That all her wicked Mother labours for, is but to raise
Her to your right, and leave her this Dukedom?

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
verse: I, but ne'r Sir be afred,
For though she take th' ungain'st weas she can,
I'll ne'er ha't fro' you.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: I should hate my self Ismenus;
If I should think of her simplicity,
Ought but extreamly well.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: Nay, as you will

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
verse: And though she be my Mother,
If she take any caurse to do you wrong,
If I can see't, youst quickly hear on't Sir:
And so I'll take my leave.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Farewel good Sister, I thank you.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: You believe all this.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: A good faith doth well, but methinks
It were no hard matter now, for her Mother to send her
Yonder's one you may trust if you will too.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: So I wi^l, if he can shew me as apparent signs
Of truth as she did; Does he weep Ismenus?

speeches.speaker: Ism.
prose: Yes, I think so: some good's happen'd I warrant: Do you hear, you? What honest man has scap'd misery, that thou art crying thus?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Noble Ismenus, where's the Prince?

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: Why there? hast wept thine eyes out?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Sir, I beseech you hear me.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Well, speak on.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: Why, will you hear him?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Yes Ismenus, why?

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: I would hear blasphemy as willingly.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: You are too blame.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: No Sir: he is not to blame:
If I were as I was.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: Nor as thou art, ysaith awhit too blame,

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: What's your business?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Faith Sir, I am ashamed to speak before you,
My conscience tells me I have injur'd you,
And by the earnest instigation
Of others, have not done you to the King
Always the best and friendliest ostices;
Which pardon me, or I will never speak.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
