verse: Never pardon him and silence a knave.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: I pardon thee.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Your Mother sure is naught.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Why shouldst thou think so?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Oh noble, Sir, your honest eyes perceive not
The dangers you are led to; shame upon her,
And what fell miseries the gods can think on
Shower down upon her wicked head, she has plotted
I know too well your death: would my poor life
Or thousand such as mine is, might be offer'd
Like sacrifices up for your preserving,
What free oblations would she have to glut her,
But she is merciless, and bent to ruin;
If heaven and good men step not to your rescue,
And timely, very timely: Oh this Dukedom!
I weep, I weep for the poor Orphans i'th' Countrey
Left with but Friends or Parents.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Now Ismenus, what think you of this fellow?
This was a lying knave, a flatterer,
Does not this Love still shew him so.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: This Love? this Halter: if he prove not yet
The cunning'st rankest rogue that ever Canted,
I'll never see man again: I know him to bring,
And can interpret every new face he makes;
Look how he wrings like a good stool for a tear:
Take heed, Children and Fools
First feel the smart, Then weep.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Away, away, such an unkind distrust,
Is worse than a dissembling, if it be one,
And sooner leads to mischief, I believe it,
And him an honest man: he could not carry
Under an evil cause, so true a sorrow.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: Take heed, this is your Mothers scorpion,
That carries stings even in his tears,
Whose soul is a rank poison through: Touch
Not at him, if you do, you are gone, if you had twenty
Lives: I knew him for a Roguish boy, when
He would poison Dogs, and keep tame Toads,
He lay with his Mother, and infected her, and now
She begs i'th' Hospital, with a patch of Velvet,
Where her Nose stood: like the Queen of Spades.
And all her teeth in her purse, the Devil and this
Fellow are so near, 'Tis not yet known which is the eviler Angel.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Nay, then I see 'tis spite: Come hither friend.
prose: Hast thou not heard the cause yet that incens'd my Mother to my death, for I protest I feel none in my self?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Her Will Sir, and Ambition, as I think,
Are the provokers of it, as in Women,
Those two are ever powerful to destruction,
Beside a hate of your still growing virtues,
She being only wicked.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Heavens defend me as I am innocent,
And ever have been from all immoderate thoughts and
Actions, that carry such rewards along with 'em.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Sir, all I know, my duty must reveal,
My Countrey and my Love command it from me,
For whom I'll lay my life down: this night coming,
A Counsel is appointed by the Duke,
To sit about your apprehension:
If you dare trust my faith: which by all good things
Shall ever watch about you: goe along,
And to a place I'll guide you: where no word
Shall scape without your hearing, nor no plot.
prose: Without discovering to you, which once known, you have your answers and prevention.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
prose: You are not so mad to goe; shift off this fellow, you shall be rul'd once by a wise man: Ratsbane get you gone, or—

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Peace, peace for shame, thy love is too suspitious, 'tis a way offer'd to preserve my life, and I will take it: be my Guide Timantus, and do not mind this angry man, thou know'st him: I may live to requite thee.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Sir, this service is done for virtues sake, not for reward, however he may hold me.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
prose: The great pox on you: but thou hast that curse so much, 'twill grow a blessing in thee shortly. Sir, for wisdoms sake court not your death, I am your friend and subject, and I shall lose in both: if I lov'd you not, I would laugh at you, and see you run your neck into the noose, and cry a Woodcock.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: So much of man, and so much fearful; ^ie, prethee have peace within thee: I shall live yet many a golden day to hold thee here dearest and nearest to me: Go on Timantus, I charge you by your love ^o ^re, ^o more.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: Goe, and let your own rod whip you:
I pity you. And dog, if he miscarry thou shalt pay for't,
I'll study for thy punishment, and it shall last
Longer and sharper than a tedious Winter,
Till thou blas^hem'st, and then thou diest and damn'st.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I wonder the Dutchess comes not.

speeches.speaker: Tel.
verse: She has heard, Sir, your Will to speak with her:
But there is something leaden at her heart;
(Pray God it be not mortal) that even keeps her
From conversation with her self.

speeches.speaker: B.
verse: Oh whither will you my cross affections pull me?
Fortune, Fate, and you whose powers direct our actions,
And dwell within us: you that are Angels
Guiding to virtue, wherefore have you given
So strong a hand to evil? wherefore suffer'd
A Temple of your own, you Deities
Where your fair selves dwelt only, and your goodness
Thus to be soyl'd with sin?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Heaven bless us all.
From whence comes this distemper? speak my fair one.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: And have you none, Love and Obedience,
You ever faithful Servants to imploy
In this strange story of impiety,
But me a Mother; Must I be your strumpet?
To lay black Treason upon, and in him,
In whom all sweetness was: in whom my love
Was prov'd to have a Being, in whom Justice,
And all the gods for our imaginations
Can work into a man, were more than virtues,
Ambition down to hell, where thou wert foster'd,
Thou hast poison'd the best soul, the purest, whitest,
And meerest innocent'st it self that ever
Mens greedy hopes gave life to.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: This is still stranger: lay this treason
Open to my correction.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Oh what a combat duty and affection
Breeds in my blood!

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: If thou conceal'st him, may,
Beside my death, the curses of the Countrey,
Troubles of conscience, and a wretched end,
Bring thee unto a poor forgotten grave.

speeches.speaker: Bach.
verse: My Being. for another tongue to tell it,
Cease, a Mother! some good man that dares
Speak for his King and Countrey: I am full
Of too much womans pity: yet oh Heaven,
Since it concerns the safety of my Sovereign,
Let it not be a cruelty in me,
Nor draw a Mothers name in question,
Amongst unborn people, to give up that man
To Law and Justice, that unrighteously
Has sought his Fathers death: be deaf: be deaf Sir,
Your Son is the offender: Now have you all,
Would I might never speak again.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: My Son! Heaven help me.
No more! I thought it, and since
His life is grown so dangerous: Let them that
Gave him, take him: he shall dye,
And with him all my fears.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Oh use your mercy: you have a brave subject
To bestow it on. I'll forgive him, Sir; and for his
Wrong to me, I'll be before ye.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Durst his villany extend to thee?

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Nothing but heats of youth, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Upon my life he sought my bed.

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: I must confess he loved me
Somewhat beyond a Son: and still pursu'd it
With such a Lust, I will not say Ambition:
That clean forgetting all obedience,
And only following his first heat unto me,
He hotly sought your death, and me in Marriage.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Oh Villain!

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: But I forget all: and am half asham'd
To press a man so far.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Where is the Duke? for Gods sake bring me to him:

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Here I am: each corner of the Dukedom
Sends new affrights forth: what wouldst thou? speak.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: I cannot Sir, my fear ties up my tongue:

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Why, what's the matter? Take thy courage
To thee, and boldly speak, where are the Guard?
In the gods name, out with it:

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Treason, treason.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: In whom?

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: Double the Guard.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: There is a fellow, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Leave shaking man.

speeches.speaker: Timan.
verse: 'Tis not for fear, but wonder.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Well.

speeches.speaker: Timan.
verse: There is a fellow, Sir, close i'th' Lobby:
You o'the Guard, look to the door there.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: But let me know the business.

speeches.speaker: Tima.
verse: Oh that the hearts of men should be so hard'ned
Against so good a Duke, for Gods sake, Sir,
Seek means to save your self; This wretched slave
Has his sword in his hand, I know his heart:
Oh it hath almost kill'd me with the thought of it.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Where is he?

speeches.speaker: Timan.
verse: I'th' Lobby Sir, close in a corner:
Look to your selves for Heavens sake,
Me thinks he is here already.
Fellows of the Guard be valiant.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Goe Sirs, and apprehend him; Treason shall
Never dare me in mine own Gates.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: 'Tis done.

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: And thou shalt find it to thy best content.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Are these the comforts of my age?
They're happy that end their daies contented
With a little, and live aloof from dangers, to a King
Every content doth a new peril bring.
Oh let me live no longer, shame of Nature,
Bastard to Honor: Traytor, Murderer,
Devil in a humane shape. Away with him,
He shall not breathe, his hot affection here.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Sir, hear me.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Am I or he your Duke? away with him
To a close prison: your Highness now shall know,
Such branches must be cropt before they grow.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Whatever fortune comes, I bid it welcome,
My innocency is my Armor: gods preserve you.

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: Fare thee well, I shall never see so brave a Gent.
Would I could weep out his offences.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Or I could weep out mine eyes.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Come Gentlemen, we'll determine presently
About his death: we cannot be too forward in our
Safety: I am very sick, lead me unto my bed.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: Sir. ah, goe fetch my Fox from the Cutlers:
prose: There's money for the scowring: Tell him I stop a groat s^nce the last great Muster: he had in stone Pitch for the bruise: he took with the recoyling of his Gun.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Yes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: And do you hear? when you come, Take down my Buckler, and sweep the Cobwebs ost: and grind the pick out, and fetch a Nail or two: and ta^k on bracers: your Mistriss made a pot-lid ont't,
I thank her, at her Mans Wedding, and burnt off the Handle.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: I will Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
prose: Who's within here, hoe Neighbor, not stir^ng yet?

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
prose: Oh, good morrow, good morrow: what news, what news?

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
prose: It holds, he dies this morning.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
prose: Then happy man be his fortune, I am resolv'd.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
prose: And so am I, and forty more good fellows,
That will not give their heads for the wa^hing, I ^a^e it.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
prose: 'S^ot man, who would not hang in such good company, and such a cause? A Fire, a Wife and Children; 'Tis such a jest that men should look b^hind 'em to the world: and let their honors, their honors neighbor slip.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
prose: I'll give thee a pint of Bastard and a Roll for that bare word.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
verse: I'sack, take down my Bill, 'tis ten to one I use it. Take a good heart man, all the low ward is ours, with a wet finger.
An lay my ^ut-sing'red Gautlet ready for me,
That, that I us'd to work in, when the Gentl^ were
Up against us, and beaten out of Town, and almost out o'
Debt too: for a plague on 'em they never paid we^l since:
And take heed sirrah, your Mistriss hears not of this
Business, she's near her time: yet if she do,
I care not, she may long for Rebellion,
For she has a devilish spirit.
prose: They say, that we Tailors, are things that ^ay one another, and our Geese hatch us: I'll make some of'em feel they are Geese o'th' game then.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
prose: Come, let's call up the new ^remonger, he's as tough as steel, and has a sine wit in these resurrections; Are you stirring neighbor?

speeches.speaker: 3. Within.
verse: Oh, Good morrow neighbors,
I'll come to you presently.
Goe to, this is his Mothers doing; she's a P^lecat.
As any is in the world.

prose: Then say, I have hit it, and a vengeance on her, let her be what she will.
Amen say I, she has brought things to a fine pass with her wisdom: do you mark it?

One thing I am sure she has, the good old Duke, she gives him pap again they say, and dandles him, and hangs a corral and bells about his neck, and makes him believe his teeth will come agen; which if they did, and I he, I would worry her as never Curr was worried: I would neighbor, till my teeth met I know where, but that's counsel.
Good morrow neighbors: hear you the sad news?
Yes, would we knew as well how to prevent it.
I cannot tell, methinks 'twere no great matter, if men were men: but—
You do not twit me with my calling neighbo^?
No surely: for I know your spirit to be tall; pray be not vext.
Pray forward with your counsel:
I am what I am, and they that prove me shall find me to their cost: do you mark me neighbor, to their cost I say.
Nay, look how soon you are angry?
They shall neighbors: yes, I say they shall.
I do believe they shall.
I know they shall.

verse: Whether you do or no I care not two pence,
I am no beast, I know mine own strength neighbors;
God bless the King, your companies is fair.

prose: Nay neighbor, now ye erre, now I must tell you so, and ye are twenty Neighbors.
You had best goe peach, doe, peach.
Peach; I scorn the motion.
Doe, and see what follows: I'll spend an hundred pound, and be two I care not: but I'll undoe thee.
Peach, Oh disgrace! Peach in thy face, and doe the worst thou canst: I am a true-man, and a free-man: peach!
Nay, look, you will spoil all.
Peach!
Whilst you two brawl together, the Prince will lose his life.
Come, give me your hand, I love you well, are you for the action?
Yes: but Peach provokes me, 'tis a cold fruit, I feel it cold in my stomach still.
No more, I'll give you Cake to disgest it.

Shut up my sho^, and be ready at a call boys, and one of you run over my old tuck with a few ashes, 'tis grown odious with tosting Cheese: and burn a little Juniper in my Murrin, the Maid made it her Chamber-pot: an hour hence I'll come again; and as you hear from me, send me a clean shirt.
The Chandler by thy Wharf, and it be thy Will.
Gossip, good morrow.
Oh good morrow Gossip: good morrow all, I see ye of one mind you cleave so close together: come 'tis time, I have prepared an hundred if they stand.
'Tis well done: shall we sever, and about it?
First, let's to the Tavern, and a pint a piece will make us Dragons.
I will have no mercy, come what will of it.
If my tuck hold, I'll spit the Guard like Larks with sage between 'em.
I have a foolish Bill to reckon with 'em, will make some of their hearts ake, and I'll lay it on: now shall I fight, 'twill do you good to see me.
Come, I'll do something for the Town to talk of when I am rotten: pray God there be enough to kill, that's all.

speeches.speaker: Age.
prose: How black the day begins!

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: Can you blame it, and look upon such a deed as shall be done this morning?

speeches.speaker: Nis.
prose: Does the Prince suffer to day?

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: Within this hour they say.

speeches.speaker: Agen.
prose: Well, they that are most wicked are most safe: 'twill be a strange justice, and a lamentable, gods keep us from the too soon feeling of it.

speeches.speaker: Doria.
prose: I care not if my throat were next: for to live still, and live here, were but to grow sat for the Shambles.

speeches.speaker: Nis.
prose: Yet we must do it, and thank 'em too, that our lives may be accepted.

speeches.speaker: Age.
prose: Faith I'll go starve my my self, or grow diseas'd to shame the hangman; for I am sure he shall be my Herald, and quarter me.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: I, a plague on him, he's too excellent at Arms.

speeches.speaker: Nisus.
prose: Will you go see this sad fight, my Lord Agenor?

speeches.speaker: Age.
prose: I'll make a mourner.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: If I could do him any good, I would goe,
The bare sight else will but afflict my spirit,
My prayers shall be as near him as your eyes:
As you find him setled, remember my love and service to his Grace.

speeches.speaker: Nis.
verse: We will weep for you, Sir: farewel.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: Farewell to all our happiness, a long farewel.
Thou angry power, whether of Heaven or Hell,
Thou laist this sharp correction on our Kingdom
For our offences, infinite and mighty!
Oh hear me, and at length be pleas'd, be pleas'd
With pity to draw back thy vengeance,
Too heavy for our weakness; and accept,
(Since it is your discretion, heavenly Wisdoms,
To have it so) this sacrifice for all,
That now is flying to your happiness,
Only for you most fit: let all our sins suffer in him.
Gods, what's the matter? I hope 'tis joy;
How now my Lords?

speeches.speaker: Nis.
verse: I'll tell you with that little breath I have;
More joy than you dare think, The Prince is safe from danger.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: How!

speeches.speaker: Age.
verse: 'Tis true, and thus it was; his hour was come
To lose his life, he ready for the stroke,
Nobly, and full of Saint-like patience,
Went with his Guard: which when the people saw,
Compassion first went out, mingled with tears,
That bred desires, and whispers to each other,
To do some worthy kindness for the Prince,
And e'r they understood well how to do,
Fury stept in, and taught them what to do,
Thrusting on every hand to rescue him,
As a white innocent: then flew the roar
Through all the streets, of Save him, save him, save him:
And as they cry'd, they did; for catching up
Such sudden weapons as their madness shew them.
In short, they beat the Guard, and took him from 'em,
And now march with him like a royal Army.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: Heaven, heaven I thank thee,
What a slave was I to have my hand so far from
This brave rescue, 't 'ad been a thing to brag on
When I was old. Shall we run for a wager to the
Next Temple, and give thanks?

speeches.speaker: Nis.
verse: As fast as wishes.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Good friends goe home again, there's not a man shall goe with me.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
verse: Will you not take revenge? I'll call them on.

speeches.speaker: Leuc.
verse: All that love me, depart:
I thank you, and will serve you for your loves:
But I will thank you more to suffer me
To govern 'em once: more, I do beg ye,
For my sake to your houses.

speeches.speaker: All within.
verse: Gods preserve you.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: And what house will you goe to?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Ismenus, I will take the wariest courses that I can think of to defend my self, but not offend.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose: You may kill your Mother, and never offend your Father, an honest man.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Thou know'st I can scape now, that's all I look for:
I'll leave.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose: Timantus, a pox take him, would I had him here. I would kill him at his own weapon single, sithes we have built enough on him: plague on't, I'm out of all patience: discharge such an Army as this, that would have followed you without paying, Oh gods!

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: To what end should I keep 'em? I am free.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose: Yes, free o'th' Traitors, for you are proclaim'd one.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Should I therefore make my self one?

speeches.speaker: Isme.
verse: This is one of your moral Philosophy, is it?
Heaven bless me from subtilties to undoe my self with:
But I know, if reason her self were here,
She would not part with her own safety.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Well, pardon Ismenus, for I know
My courses are most just; nor will I stain 'em
With one bad action; for thy self thou know'st,
That though I may command thee, I shall be
A ready servant to thee if thou needst: and so I'll take my leave.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
verse: Of whom?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Of thee.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
verse: Heart, you shall take no leave of me.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Shall I not?

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose: No, by the gods shall you not: nay, if you have no more wit but to goe absolutely alone, I'll be in a little.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Nay, prethee good Ismenus part with me.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose: I wonnot i'faith, never move it any more; for by this good light I wonnot.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: This is an ill time to be thus unruly:

speeches.speaker: Ismenus,
prose: You must leave me.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose: Yes, if you can beat me away: else the gods refuse me if I will leave you till I see more reason; you sha'nt undoe your self.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: But why wilt not leave me?

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose: Why I'll tell you: Because when you are gone, then—life, if I have not forgot my reason— hell take me: you put me out of patience so: Oh! marry when you are gone, then will your Mother (a pox confound her) she never comes in my head, but she spoils my memory too: there are a hundred reasons.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: But shew me one.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose: Shew you; what a stir here is; why I will shew you: Do you think; well, well, I know what I know, I pray come, come. 'Tis in vain: but I am sure. Devils take 'em; what do I meddle with 'em? You know your self. Soul I think I am: is there any man i'th' world? as if you knew not this already better than I. Pish, pish, I'll give no reason.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: But I will tell thee one, why thou shouldst stay:
I have not one friend in the Court but thou,
On whom I may be bold to trust to send me
Any intelligence: and if thou lov'st me
Thou wilt do this, thou needst not fear to stay,
For there are new-come Proclamations out,
Where all are pardon'd but my self.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose:
'Tis true, and in the same Proclamation, your fine Sister
~rania, whom you us'd so kindly, is proclaim'd Heir apparent to the Crown.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: What though, thou mayst stay at home without danger?

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose: Danger, hang danger, what tell you me of danger?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Why if thou wilt not do't, I think thou dar'st not.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose: I dare not: if you speak it in earnest, you are a Boy.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Well Sir, if you dare, let me see you do't.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose: Why so you shall, I will stay.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Why God-a-mercy-

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose: You know I love you but too well.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Now take these few directions: farewel, send to me by the wariest ways thou canst: I have a soul tells me we shall meet often. The gods protect thee.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose: Pox o' my self for an ass, I'm crying now, God be with you, if I never see you again: why then pray get you gone, for grief and anger wonnot let me know what I say, I'll to the Court as fast as I can, and see the new Heir apparant.

speeches.speaker: ~ran.
verse: WHat hast thou sound him?

speeches.speaker: Wo.
verse: Madam, he is coming in.

speeches.speaker: ~ran.
verse: Gods bless my brother, wheresoe'er he is:
And I beseech you keep me fro the bed
Of any naughty Tyrant, whom my Mother
Would ha me have to wrong him.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
verse: What would her new Grace have with me?

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
verse: Leave us a while. My Lord Ismenus.
I pray for the love of Heaven and God,
That you would tell me one thing, which I know
You can do weell.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
verse: Where's her sain Grace?

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
prose: You know me well inough, but that you mock, I an she my sen.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose: God bless him that shall be thy husband, if tho wear'st the breeches thus soon, thou'lt be as impudent a thy Mother.

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
prose: But will you tell me this one thing?

speeches.speaker: Ism.
prose: What is't? if it be no great matter whether I do or no, perhaps I will.

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
prose: Yes faith, 'tis matter.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
prose: And what is't?

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
prose: I pray you let me know whaire the Prince my Brother is.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
prose: I'saith you shan be hang'd first, is your Mother so foolish to think your good Grace can sift it out of me?

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
prose: If you have any mercy le^t i' you to a poor wench, tell me.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
prose: Why wouldst thou not have thy brains beat out for this, to follow thy Mothers steps so young?

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
prose: But believe me, she knows none of this.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
prose: Believe you? why do you think I never had wits? or that I am run out of them? how should it belong to you to know, if I could tell?

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
verse: Why I will tell you, and if I speak false
Let the devil ha me: yonder's a bad man,
Come from a Tyrant to my Mother, and what name
They ha' for him, good faith I cannot tell.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
verse: An Ambassador.

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
verse: That's it: but he would carry me away,
And have me marry his Master; and I'll day
E'r I will ha' him.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: But what's this to knowing where the Prince is?

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
verse: Yes: for you know all my Mother does:
Agen the Prince is but to ma me great.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: Pray, I know that too well, what ten?

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
verse: Why I could goe to the good Marquis my
Brother, and put my self into his hands, that so
He may preserve himself.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
prose: Oh that thou hadst no seed of thy Mother in thee, and couldst mean this now.

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
prose: Why feth I do, wou'd I might ne'er stir more if I do not.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
prose: I shall prove a ridiculous fool, I'll be damn'd else: hang me if I do not half believe thee.

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
verse: By my troth you may.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: By my troth I doe: I know I'm an Ass for't,
But I cannot help it.

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
verse: And won you tell me then?

speeches.speaker: Ism.
prose: Yes faith will I, or any thing else i'th' world: for I think thou art as good a creature as ever was born.

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
verse: But ail goe i' this ladst apparel:
But you mun help me to Silver.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
prose: Help thee? why the pox take him that will not help thee to any thing i'th' world, I'll help thee to Money, and I'll do't presently too, and yet soul, If you should play the scurvy Harlotry little pocky baggage now and cosin me, what then?

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
verse: Why, an I do, wou'd I might ne'r se^day agen.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: Nay, by this light, I do not think thou wilt:
I'll presently provide thee Money and a Letter.

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
verse: I, but I'll ne'er deliver it.
When I have found my Brother, I will beg
To serve him; but he shall never know who I am:
For he must hate me then for my bad mother:
I'll say I am a Countrey Lad that want a service,
And have straid on him by chance, lest he discover me;
I know I must not live long, but that taime
I ha' to spend, shall be in serving him.
And though my Mother seek to take his life away,
In a^ day my brother shall be taught
That I was ever good, though she were naught.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
verse: Run away, the Devil be her guide.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Faith she's gone: there's a Letter I found it in her pocket, would I were with her, she's a handsome Lady, a plague upon my bashfulness, I had bobb'd her long ago else.

speeches.speaker: Bach.
verse: What a base whore is this, that after all
My ways for her advancement, should so poorly
Make virtue her undoer, and choose this time,
The King being deadly sick, and I intending
A present marriage with some forreign Prince,
To strengthen and secure my self. She writes here
Like a wise Gentlewoman, She will not stay:
And the example of her dear brother, makes her
Fear her self, to whom she means to flie.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Why, who can help it?

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Now Poverty and Lechery, which is thy end, rot thee, where e'er thou goest with all thy goodness.

speeches.speaker: Timan.
prose: Berlady they'll bruze her: and she were of brass I am sure they'll break stone Walls: I have had experience of them both, and they have made me desperate: but there's a messenger, Madam, come from the Prince with a Letter to Ismenus, who by him returns an answer.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: This comes as pat as wishes: thou shalt presently away Timantus.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Whither Madam?

speeches.speaker: Ba
prose: To the Prince, and take the Messenger for guide.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: What shall I do there? I have done too much mischief to be believ'd again; or indeed, to scape with my head on my back, if I be once known.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Thou art a weak shallow fool: get thee a disguise, and withal, when thou com'st before him, have a Letter fain'd to deliver him: and then, as thou hast ever hope of goodness by me, or after me, strike one home stroke that shall not need another: dar'st thou speak, dar'st thou? if thou sali'^t off, go be a Rogue again, and lie and pander to procure thy meat? dar'st thou? speak to me?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: Sure I shall never walk when I am dead: I have no spirit, Madam, I'll be drunk but I'll do it, that's all my refuge.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Away, no more, then I'll raise an Army whilst the King yet lives, if all the means and power I have can do it, I cannot tell.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
prose: Are you inventing still? we'll ease your studies.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Why how now saucy Lords?

speeches.speaker: Ism.
prose: Nay I'll shake ye; yes devil, I will shake ye.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Do ^ you know me Lords?

speeches.speaker: Nis.
prose:
Y^
^ sin we know ye, would we did not.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
prose: Doe you hear whore, a plague a God upon thee, the Duke is dead.

speeches.speaker: Bach.
prose: Dead!

speeches.speaker: Ism.
prose: I, wild-fire and brimstone take thee: good man be is dead, and past those miseries which thou, salt infection-like; like a disease slungst upon his head. Dost thou hea^, and 'twere not more respect in Womanhood in general than thee, because I had a Mother, who I will not say she was good, she liv'd so near thy time, I would have thee in vengeance of this man, whose peace is made in heaven by this time, tied to a post; and d^ied i' th' fun, and after carried about, and shewn at Fairs for money, with a long story of the devil thy father, that taught thee to be whorish, envious, bloudy.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
prose: You steering harlot, I'll have a horse to leap thee, and thy base issue shall carry Sumpters. Come Lords, bring her along, we'll to the Prince all, where her hell hood shall wait his censure; and if he spare the she-Goat, may he lie with thee again: and beside, maist thou lay upon him some nasty foul disease, that hate still follows, and his end a dry ditch. Lead you corrupted whore, or I'll draw a goad shall make you skip: away to the Prince.

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: I la, ha, ha, I hope yet I shall come too late to find him.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Alas poor boy, why dost thou follow me?
What canst thou hope for? I am poor as thou art.

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
verse: In good feth I shall be weel and rich enough
If you will love me, and not put me from you.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Why dost thou choose out me Boy to undo thee?
Alas, for pitty take another Master,
That may be able to deserve thy love
In breeding thee hereafter: me thou knowest not,
More than my misery: and therefore canst not
Look for rewards at my hands: would I were able
My pretty knave, to doe thee any kindness: truly
Good Boy, I would upon my faith, thy harmless
Innocence moves me at heart: wilt thou goe
Save thy self; why dost thou weep?
Alas, I do not chide thee.

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
prose: I cannot tell if I go from you; Sir, I shall ne'er dawn day more: Pray if you can, I will be true to you: Let me wait on you: if I were a man, I would fight for you: Sure you have some ill-willers, I would slay em.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Such harmless souls are ever Prophets: well, I take thy wish, thou shalt be with me still: But prethee eat, my good boy: Thou wilt die my child if thou fast one day more. This four daies thou hast tasted nothing: Goe into the Cave and eat: thou shalt find something for thee, to bring thy bloud again, and thy fair colour.

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
verse: I cannot eat, God thank you.
But I'll eat to morrow.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Thou't be dead by that time.

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
verse: I should be well then, for you will not love me.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Indeed I will. This is the prettiest passion that e'er
I felt yet: why dost thou look so earnestly upon me?

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
verse: You have fai^ eyes Master.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Sure the boy dotes: why dost thou sigh my child?

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
prose: To think that such a fine man should live, and no gay Lady love him.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Thou wilt love me?

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
prose: Yes sure till I die, and when I am in heaven, I'll e'en wish for you.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: And I'll come to thee boy.
prose:
This is a Love I never yet heard tell of: come, thou art sleepy child; goe in, and I'll sit with thee: heaven what po^
tends this?

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
prose: You are sad, but I am not sleepy, would I could do ought to make you merry: shall I sing?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: If thou wilt good Boy.
prose: Alas my boy, that thou shouldst comfort me, and art far worse than I!

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
verse: Law Master, there's one, look to your self;

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: What art thou that in this dismal place,
Which nothing could find out but misery,
Thus boldly stepst? Comfort was never here,
Here is no food, nor beds, nor any house
Built by a better Architect than beasts;
And e'r you get dwelling from one of them,
You must fight for it: if you conquer him,
He is your meat: if not, you must be his.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
prose: I come to you (for if I not mistake, you are the Prince) from that most Noble Lord Ismenus with a Letter.

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
verse: Alas, I fear I shall be discover'd now.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Now I feel my self the poorest of all mortal things.
Where is he that receives such courtesies
But he has means to shew his gratefulness
Some way or other? I have none at all:
I know not how to speak so much as well
Of thee, but to these trees.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: His Letters speak him, Sir—

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
prose: Gods keep me but from knowing him till I die: aye me, sure I cannot live a day, Oh thou soul Traitor: How do you Master?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: How dost thou my child? alas, look on his, it may make thee repentant, to behold those innocent drops that thou hast drawn from thence.

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
verse: 'Tis nothing Sir, and you be well.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Oh pardon me, know you me now, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: How couldst thou find me out?

speeches.speaker: Tima.
prose: We intercepted a Letter from Ismenus, and the bearer directed me.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Stand up Timantus boldly,
The world conceives that thou art guilty
Of divers treasons to the State and me:
But oh far be it from the innocence
Of a just man, to give a Traitor death
Without a tryal: here the Countrey is not
To purge thee or condemn thee; therefore
A nobler trial than thou dost deserve,
Rather than none at all, here I accuse thee
Before the face of Heaven, to be a Traitor
Both to the Duke my Father and to me, and the
Whole Land: speak, is it so or no?

speeches.speaker: Tima.
verse: 'Tis true Sir, pardon me.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Take heed Timantus how thou dost cast away thy self, I must proceed to execution hastily if thou confess it: speak: once againe, is it so or no?

speeches.speaker: Tima.
verse: I am not guilty, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Gods and thy sword acquit thee, here it is.

speeches.speaker: Tima.
prose: I will not use any violence against your Highness.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: At thy peril then, for this must be thy trial: and from henceforth look to thy self.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: I do beseech you, Sir, let me not fight.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Up, up again Timantus,
There is no way but this, believe me.
Now if—Fie, fie Timantus, is there no
Usage can recover thee from baseness,? wert thou
Longer to converse with men, I would have chid
Thee for this: be all thy faults forgiven.

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Oh spare me Sir, I am not sit for death.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: I think than art not, yet trust me, fitter than for life: Yet tell me e'r thy breath be gone, know'st of any other plots against me?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Of none.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: I would have ta'en your Page, and married her.
prose: What course wouldst thou have taken, when thou hadst kill'd me?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: What Page?

speeches.speaker: Tim.
verse: Your boy there.—Dies.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Is he fall'n mad in death, what does he mean?
Some good god help me at the worst: how dost thou?
Let not thy misery vex me, thou shalt have
What thy poor heart can wish: I am a Prince,
And I will keep thee in the gayest cloaths,
And the finest things, that ever pretty boy had given him.

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
verse: I know you well enough,
Feth I am dying, and now you know all too.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: But stir up thy self; look what a Jewel here is,
See how it glisters: what a pretty shew
Will this make in thy little ear? ha, speak,
Eat but a bit, and take it.

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
verse: Do you not know me?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: I prethee mind thy health: why that's well said my good boy, smile still.

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
verse: I shall smile till death an I see you,

I am
~rania, your Sister-in-law.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
verse:
I am
~rania.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Dulness did seize me, now I know thee well;
Alas, why cam'st thou hither?

speeches.speaker: ~ra.
prose: Feth for love, I would not let you know till I was dying; for you could not love me, my Mother was so naught.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: I will love thee, or any thing: what? wilt
Thou leave me as soon as I know thee?
Speak one word to me: alas she's past it,
She will ne'er speak more
What noise is that? it is no matter who
Comes on me now. What worse than mad are you
That seek out sorrows? if you love delights
Begone from hence.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose: Sir, for you we come, as Soldiers to revenge the wrongs you have suffer'd under this naughty creature: what shall be done with her? say, I am ready.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Leave her to Heaven, brave Cosin, they shall tell her how she has sinn'd against 'em, my hand shall never be stain'd with such base bloud: live wicked Mother: that reverend Title be your pardon, for I will use no extremity against you, but leave you to Heaven.

speeches.speaker: Bacha.
verse: Hell take you all, or if there be a place
Of torment that exceeds that, get you thither:
And till the devils have you, may your lives
Be one continued plague, and such a one,
That knows no friends nor ending.
May all ages that shall succeed, curse you as I do:
And if it be possible, I ask it heaven,
That your base issues may be ever Monsters,
That must for shame of nature and succession,
Be drown'd like dogs.
Would I had breath to please you.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Would you had love within you, and such grief
As might become a Mother: look you there,

Know you that face? that was
~rania:
These are the fruits of those unhappy Mothers,
That labour with such horrid births as you do:
If you can weep, there's cause; poor innocent,
Your wickedness has kill'd her: I'll weep for you.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
verse: Monstrous woman,
Mars would weep at this, and yet she cannot.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Here lies your Minion too, slain by ^,
I will not say you are the cause: yet certain,
I know you were too blame, the gods forgive you,

speeches.speaker: Isme.
verse: See, she stands as if she were inventing
Some new destruction for the world.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Ismenus, thou art welcome yet to my sad company.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
verse: I come to make you somewhat sadder, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: You cannot, I am at the height already.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
verse: Your Fathers dead.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: I thought so, Heaven be with him: Oh woman, woman, weep now or never, thou hast made more sorrows than we have eyes to utter,

speeches.speaker: Bac.
prose: Now let Heaven fall, I am at the worst of evils, a a thing so miserably wretched, that every thing, the last of humane comforts hath left me: I will not be so base and cold, to live and wait the mercies of these men I hate, no, 'tis just I die, since fortune hath left me, my step discent attends me: hand, strike thou home, I have soul enough to guide; and let all know, as I stood a Queen, the same I'll fall, and one with me.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Ho.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
verse: How do you, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Nearer my health, than I think any here, my tongue begins to faulter: what is man? or who would be one, when he sees a poor weak woman can in an instant make him none.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: She is dead already.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose: Let her be damn'd already as she is: post all for Surgeons.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Let not a man stirr, for I am but dead:
I have some few words which I would have you hear,
And am afraid I shall want breath to speak 'em:
First to you my Lords, you know Ismenus is
Undoubtedly Heir of Lycia, I do beseech you all,
When I am dead, to shew your duties to him.

speeches.speaker: Lords.
verse: We vow to do't.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: I thank you.
Next to you Cosin Ismenus, that shall be the Duke,
I pray you let the broken Image of Cupid
Be re-edified, I know all this is done by him.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
verse: It shall be so.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
prose: Last, I beseech you that my Mother-in-law may have a burial according to—Dies.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
verse: To what, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: There is a full point.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
prose: I will interpret for him; she shall have burial according to her own deserts, with dogs.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: I would your Majesty would haste for setling of the people.

speeches.speaker: Isme.
verse: I am ready.

speeches.speaker: Age.
verse: Goe, and let the Trumpets sound
Some mournful thing, whilst we convey the body
Of this unhappy Prince unto the Court,
And of that virtuous Virgin to a Grave:
But drag her to a ditch, where let her lie,
Accurst, whilst one man has a memory.
The time now of my Revenge draws near.
Nor shall it lessen as I am a god,
With all the cries and prayers that have been;
And those that be to come, though they be infinite,
In need and number.

ROses their sharp spines being gone,
Not royal in their smells alone,
But in their hew,
Maiden-Pinks, of odour faint,
Daizies smell-less, yet most quaint
And sweet Time true.

Primrose first born, child of Ver,
Merry Spring time's Harbinger,
With her bels dimm.
Oxlips in their Cradles growing,
Marigolds on death-beds blowing,
Larks-heels trim.

All dear natures children sweet,
Lie fore Bride and Bridegrooms feet,

Blessing their sence.
Not an Angel of the Air,
Bird melodious, or Bird fair,
Is absent hence.

The Crow, the slanderous Cuckooe,
The boading Raven, nor Clough
Nor chatt'ring Pie,
May on our Bridehouse pearch or sing,
Or with them any discord bring
But from it fly.

speeches.speaker: 1 Qu.
verse: For pities sake, and true gentilit^es,
Hear and respect me.

speeches.speaker: 2 Qu.
verse: For your Mothers sake.
And as you wish your womb may thrive with fair ones,
Hear and respect me,

speeches.speaker: 3 Qu.
verse: Now for the love of him whom Jove hath mark'd
The honor of your Bed, and for the sake
Of clear Virginity, be Advocate
For us, and our distresses: This good deed
Shall raze you out o'th' Book of Trespasses
All you are set down there.

speeches.speaker: Thes.
verse: Sad Lady rise.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: Stand up.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: No knees to me.
What Woman I may steed that is distrest,
Does bind me to her.

speeches.speaker: Thes.
verse: What's your request? Deliver you for all?

speeches.speaker: 1 Qu.
verse: We are three Queens, whose Sovereigns fell before
The wrath of cruel Creon; who endur'd
The Beaks of Ravens, Talle^ of the Kites,
And pecks of Crows in the foul field of Thebe.
He will not suffer us to burn their bones,
To urne their ashes, nor to take th' offence
Of mortal loathsomness from the blest eye
Of holy Phaebus, but insects the winds
With stench of our slain Lords. Oh pity Duke,
Thou purger of the earth, draw thy fear'd Sword
That does good turns to th' world; give us the Bones
Of our dead Kings, that we may Chap^el them;
And of thy boundless goodness take some note
That for our crowned heads we have no roof;
Save this which is the Lions and the Bears,
And vault to every thing.

speeches.speaker: Thes.
verse: Pray you kneel not,
I was transported with your Speech, and suffer'd
Your knees to wrong themselves; I have heard the fortunes
Of your dead Lords, which gives me such lamenting
As wakes my vengeance, and revenge for 'em:
King Capaneus, was your Lord: the day
That he should marry you, at such a season,
As now it is with me, I met your Groom;
By Mars's Altar you were that time fair;
Not Juno's Mantle fairer than your Tresses,
Nor in more bounty spread her. Your wheaten wreath
Was then not thrash'd, nor blasted; Fortune at you
Dimpled her Cheek with smiles: Hercules our kinsman
(Then weaker than your eyes) laid by his Club,
He tumbled down upon his N^nu^n hide
And swore his sinews thaw'd: Oh grief, and time,
Fearful consumers, you will all devour.

speeches.speaker: 1 Qu.
verse: Oh I hope some God,
Some God hath put his mercy in your manhood
Whereto he'll infuse power, and press you forth
Our undertaker.

speeches.speaker: Thes.
verse: Oh no knees, none Widow,
Unto the Helmeted-Belona use them,
And pray for me your Soldier.
Troubl'd I am.

speeches.speaker: 2 Qu.
verse: Honoured Hippolita
Most dreaded Amazonian, that hast slain
The Sith-tusk'd-Bore; that with thy Arm as strong
As it is white, was't near to make the male
To thy Sex captive; but that this thy Lord
Born to uphold Creation, in that honor
First nature stil'd it in, shrunk thee into
The bound thou wast o'er-flowing; at once subduing
Thy ^orce, and thy affection: Soldieress
That equally canst poize sternness with pity,
Whom now I know hast much much more power on him
Than ever he had on thee, who ow'st his strength,
And his Love too, who is a Servant for
The Tenor of the Speech. Dear Glass of Ladies.
Bid him that we whom flaming war doth scorch,
Under the shadow of his Sword, may cool us:
Require him he advance it o'er our heads;
Speak't in a womans key: like such a woman
As any of us three; weep e'r you fail; lend us a knee;
But touch the ground for us no longer time
Than a Doves motion, when the head s pluckt off:
Tell him if he i'th' blood-^iz'd field, lay swoln
Shewing the Sun his Teeth, grinning at the Moon
What you would do.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: Poor Lady say no more:
I had as leif trace this good action with you
As that whereto I'm going, and never yet
Went I so willing, way. My Lord is taken
Heart deep with your distress: Let him consider;
I'll speak anon.

speeches.speaker: 3 Qu.
verse: Oh my petition was,
Set down in Ice, which by hot grief uncandied
Melts into drops, so sorrow wanting form
Is prest with deeper matter.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: Pray stand up,
Your grief is written in your cheek.

speeches.speaker: 3 Qu.
verse: Oh woe,
You cannot read it there; there through my tears,
Like wrinkl'd pebbles in a Glass stream
You may behold 'em (Lady, Lady, alack)
He that will all the treasure know o'th' earth
Must know the Center too; he that will fish
For my least minnow, let him lead his line
To catch one at my heart. O^ pardon me;
Extremity that sharpens sundry wits
Makes me a fool.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: Pray you say nothing, pray you,
Who cannot feel, nor see the rain being in't,
Knows neither wet, nor dry; if that you were
The ground-piece of some Painter, I would buy you
T'instruct me 'gainst a capital grief indeed
Such heart-pierc'd demonstration; but alas
Being a natural Sister of our Sex
Your sorrow beats so ardently upon me:
That it shall make a counter-reflect 'gainst
My Brothers heart, and warm it to some pity
Though it were made of stone: pray have good comfort:

speeches.speaker: Thes.
verse: Forward to th' Temple, leave not out a jot
O'th' sacred ceremony.

speeches.speaker: 1 Qu.
verse: Oh this celebration
Will long last, and be more costly than
Your Suppliants war: Remember that your Fame
Knowls in the ear o'th' world: what you do quickly,
Is not done rashly; your first thought is more,
Than others laboured meditance: your premeditating
More than their actions: But oh Jove, your actions,
Soon as they move, as Asprays do the fish,
Subdue before they touch: think, dear Duke think
What beds our slain Kings have.

speeches.speaker: 2 Qu.
verse: What griefs our beds
That our dear Lords have none.

speeches.speaker: 3. Qu.
verse: None fit for th' dead:
Those that with Cords, Knives, Drams precipitance,
Weary of this worlds light, have to themselves
Been deaths most horrid Agents, humane grace
Affords them dust and shadow.

speeches.speaker: 1 Qu.
verse: But our Lords
Lie blist'ring 'fore the visitating Sun,
And were good Kings, when living.

speeches.speaker: Thes.
verse: It is true, and I will give you comfort,
To give your dead Lords graves:
The which to do must make some work with Creon.

speeches.speaker: 1 Qu.
verse: And that work presents it self to th' doing:
Now 'twill take form, the heats are gone to morrow,
Then bootless toil must recompence it self,
With its own sweat; Now he's secure,
Not dretms, we stand before your puissance
Wrinching our holy begging in our eyes
To make petition clear.

speeches.speaker: 2 Qu.
verse: Now you may take him,
Drunk with his victory.

speeches.speaker: 3 Qu.
verse: And his Army full
Of Bread, and sloth.

speeches.speaker: Thes.
verse: Artesis that best knowest
How to draw out, fit to this enterprize,
The prim'st for this proceeding, and the number
To carry such a business, forth and levy
Our worthiest Instruments, whilst we dispatch
This grand act of our life, this daring deed
Of Fate in wedlock.

speeches.speaker: 1 Qu.
verse: Dowagers, take hands
Let us be Widows to our woes, delay
Commends us to a famishing hope.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: Farewell.

speeches.speaker: 2 Qu.
verse: We come unseasonably: But when could grief
Cull forth as unpanged judgement can, fit'st time
For best solicitation.

speeches.speaker: Thes.
verse: Why good Ladies,
This is a service, whereto I am going,
Greater than any was; it more imports me
Than all the actions that I have foregone,
Or futurely can cope.

speeches.speaker: 1 Qu.
verse: The more proclaiming
Our suit shall be neglected, when her Arms,
Able to lock Jove from a Synod, shall
By warranting Moon-light corslet thee, oh when
Her twining Cherries shall their sweetness fall
Upon thy tastful Lips, what wilt thou think
Of rotten Kings, or blubber'd Queens, what care
For what thou feel'st not? what thou feel'st being able
To make Mars spurn his Dr^m. Oh if thou couch
But one night with her, every hour in't will
Take hostage of thee for a hundred, and
Thou shalt remember nothing more, than what
That Banquet bids thee too.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: Though much unlike
You should be so transported, as much sorry
I should be such a Suitor; yet I think
Did I not by th' abstaining of my joy
Which breeds a deeper longing, cure their surfeit
That craves a present med'cine, I should pluck
All Ladies scandal on me. Therefore Sir
As I shall here make trial of my Prayers,
Either presuming them to have some force,
Or sentencing for ay their vigor dumb,
Prorogue this business, we are going about, and hang
Your Shield afore your heart, about that neck
Which is my Fee, and which I freely lend
To do these poor Queens service.

speeches.speaker: All Queens.
verse: Oh help now
Our Cause cries for your knee.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: If you grant not
My Sister her petition in that force,
With that Celerity, and nature which
She makes it in: from henceforth I'll not dare
To ask you anything, nor be so hardy
Ever to take a Husband.

speeches.speaker: Thes.
verse: Pray stand up.
I am intreating of my self to do
That which you kneel to have me; Pyrithous
Lead on the Bride; get you and pray the gods
For success, and return omit not any thing
In the pretended Celebration; Queens
Follow your Soldier (as before) hence you
And at the banks of Anly meet us with
The forces you can raise, where we shall find
The moiety of a number, for a business,
More bigger look't; since that our Theme is haste
I stamp this kiss uppon thy currant Lip,
Sweet keep it as my token; set you forward
For I will see you gone.
Farewel my beauteous Sister; Pyrithous
Keep the Feast full, bate not an hour on't.

speeches.speaker: Pyri.
verse: Sir,
I'll ollow you at heels; The Feasts solemnity
Shall want till your return.

speeches.speaker: Thes.
verse: Cosin I charge you
Budge not from Atheus; we shall be returning
E'r ^ou can end this Feast; of which I pray you
Ma e no abatement; once more farewel all.

speeches.speaker: 1 Qu.
verse: Thus dost thou still make good the tongue o'th' world.

speeches.speaker: 1 Qu.
verse: And earnst a Deity equal with Mars.

speeches.speaker: 3 Qu.
verse: If not above him, for
Thou being but mortal, makest affections bend
To godlike honors; they themselves some say
Groan under such a Mast'ry.

speeches.speaker: Thes.
verse: As we are men
Thus should we doe, being sensually subdu'd
We loose our humane Title; good cheer Ladies.
Now turn we towards our Comforts.

speeches.speaker: Arcite.
verse: Dear Palamon, dearer in Love than Blood
And our prime Cosin, yet unhard'ned in
The Crimes of nature; Let us leave the City
Thebs, and the temptings in't, before we further
Sully our gloss of youth,
And here to keep in abstinence we shame
As in Incontinence; for not to swim
I'th' aid o'th' current, were almost to sink,
At least to frustrate striving, and to follow
The common stream, 't would bring us to an Eddy
Where we should turn or drown; if labour through,
Our gain but life, and weakness.

speeches.speaker: Pal.
verse: Your advice
Is cry'd up with example; what strange ruins
Since first we went to School, may we perceive
Walking in Thebs? Skars, and bare weeds
The gain o'th' Martialist, who did propound
To his bold ends, honor, and golden Ingots,
Which though he won, he had not, and now flurted
By peace, for whom he fought, who then shall offer
To Mars's so scorn'd Altar? I doe bleed
When such I meet, and wish great Juno would
Resume her antient fit of jealousie
To get the Soldier work, that peace might purge
For her repletion, and retain anew
Her charitable heart now hard, and harsher
Than strife, or war could be.

speeches.speaker: Arcite.
verse: Are you not out?
Meet you no ruin, but the Soldier in
The crancks and turns of Thebs? you did begin
As if you met decaies of many kinds:
Perceive you none, that do arouse your pity
But th' unconsider'd Soldier?

speeches.speaker: Pal.
verse: Yes, I pity
Decaies where-e'er I find them, but such most
That sweating in an honourable toil
Are paid with Ice to cool 'em.

speeches.speaker: Arcite.
verse: 'Tis not this
I did begin to speak of, this is virtue
Of no respect in Thebs, I spake of Thebs
How dangerous if we will keep our honors,
It is for our residing, where every evil
Hath a good colour; where ev'ry seeming good's
A certain evil, where not to be ev'n jump
As they are, here were to be strangers, and
Such things to be meer Monsters.

speeches.speaker: Pal.
verse: 'Tis in our power,
(Unless we fear that Apes can Tutor's) to
Be Masters of our manners: what need I
Affect anothers gate, which is not catching
Where there is faith, or to be fond upon
Anothers way of speech, when by mine own
I may be reasonably conceiv'd; sav'd too,
Speaking it truly; why am I bound
By any generous bond to follow him
Follows his Taylor, haply so long, until
The follow'd, make pursuit? or let me know,
Why mine own Barber is unblest, with him
My poor Chinn too, for 'tis not Cizard just
To such a Favorites glass: What Cannon is there
That does command my Rapier from my hip
To dangle't in my hand, or to goe tip toe
Before the street be soul? either I am
The fore-horse in the Team, or I am none
That draw i'th' sequent trace: these poor slight sores,
Need not a Plantain; That which tips my bosome
Almost to th' heart's,

speeches.speaker: Arcite.
verse: Our Uncle Creon.

speeches.speaker: Pal.
verse: He,
A most unbounded Tyrant, whose successes
Makes Heaven unfear'd, and villany assured
Beyond its power: there's nothing, almost puts
Faith in a Feavor, and deifies alone
Voluble chance, who only attributes
The faculties of other Instruments
To his own Nerves and act; Commands men service,
And what they win in't, boot and glory on;
That fears not to harm; good dares not; Let
The bloud of mine that's sibbe to him, be suckt
From me with Leeches, let them break and fall
Off me with that corruption.

speeches.speaker: Arc.
verse: Clear spirited Cosin
Let's leave his Court, that we may nothing share,
Of his loud infamy: for our milk,
Will relish of the pasture, and we must
Be vile, or disobedient, not his kinsmen
In blood, unless in quality.

speeches.speaker: Pal.
verse: Nothing truer:
I think the ecchoes of his shames have deaf't
The ears of heav'nly Justice: widdows cries
Descend again into their throats, and have not
Due audience of the gods; Valerius

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: The King calls for you; yet be leaden-footed
Till his great rage be off him. Phebus when
He broke his whipstock, and exclaim'd against
The Horses of the Sun, but whisper'd to
The loudness of his fury.

speeches.speaker: Pal.
verse: Small winds shake him,
But what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Theseus (who where he threats appals,) hath sent
Deadly defiance to him, and pronounces
Ruin to Thebs, who is at hand to seal
The promise of his wrath.

speeches.speaker: Arc.
verse: Let him approach:
But that we fear the gods in him, he brings not
A jot of terror to us; yet what man
Thirds his own worth (the case is each of ours)
When that his actions dregg'd, with mind assur'd
'Tis bad he goes about.

speeches.speaker: Pal.
verse: Leave that unreason'd.
Our services stand now for Thebs, not Creon,
Yet to be neutral to him, were dishonor;
Rebellious to oppose: therefore we must
With him stand to the mercy of our Fate,
Who hath bounded our last minute.

speeches.speaker: Arc.
verse: So we must;
Ist sed this wars a foot? or it shall be
On fail of some condition.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: 'Tis in motion
The intelligence of state came in the instant
With the defier.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Let's to the King, who, were he
A quarter carrier of that honor, which
His enemy came in, the bloud we venture
Should be as for our health, which were not spent,
Rather laid out for purchase: but alas
Our hands advanc'd before our hearts, what will
The fall o' th' stroke do damage?

speeches.speaker: Arci.
verse: Let th' event,
That never-erring Arbitrator, tell us
When we know all our selves, and let us follow
The becking of our chance.

speeches.speaker: Pir.
verse: No further.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: Sir farewel; repeat my wishes
To our great Lord, of whose success I dare not
Make any timerous question; yet I wish him
Excess, and overflow of power, and't might be
To dure ill-dealing fortune; speed to him,
Store never hurts good Governors.

speeches.speaker: Pir.
verse: Though I know
His Ocean needs not my poor drops, yet they
Must yield their tribute there: My precious Maid,
Those best affections that the heavens infuse
In their best temper'd pieces, keep enthron'd
In your dear heart.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: Thanks Sir; remember me
To our all-Royal Brother, for whose speed
The great Bellona I'll solicite; and
Since in our terrene State, petitions are not
Without gifts understood: I'll offer to her
What I shall be advis'd she likes; our hearts
Are in his Army, in his Tent.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: In's bosom:
We have been Soldiers, and we cannot weep
When our Friends do'n their helms, or put to Sea,
Or tell of Babes broach'd on the Launce, or Women
That have sod their Infants in (and after eat them)
The brine, they wept at killing 'em; Then if
You stay to see of us such Spinsters, we
Should hold you here for ever,

speeches.speaker: Pir.
verse: Peace be to you
As I pursue this war, which shall be then
Beyond further requiring.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: How his longing
Follows his friend; since his depart, his sports
Though craving seriousness, and skill, past slightly
His careless execution, where nor gain
Made him regard, or loss consider, but
Playing o'er business in his hand, another
Directing in his head, his mind, nurse equal
To these so diff'ring Twins; have you observ'd him.
Since our great Lord departed?

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: With much labour:
And I did love him sor't, they two have Cabin'd
In many as dangerous, as poor a corner,
Peril and want contending, they have skift
Torrents, whose roaring tyranny and power
I'th' least of these was dreadful, and they have
Fought out together, where Death's-self was lodg'd,
Yet Fate hath brought them off, their knot of love
Ti'd, weav'd, intangl'd, with so true, so long,
And with a finger of so deep a cunning
May be out-worn, never undone. I think
Theseus cannot be umpire to himself
Cleaving his conscience into twain, and doing
Each side like Justice, which he loves best.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: Doubtless
There is a best, and reason has no manners
To say it is not you I was acquainted
Once with a time, when I enjoy'd a Play-fellow;
You were at wars, when she the grave enrich'd,
Who made too proud the Bed, took leave o'th' Moon
(Which then lookt pale at parting) when our count
Was each eleven.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: 'Twas Flavia.
Two Hearses ready with Palamon, and Arcite:
The three Queens. Theseus, and his Lords ready.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: Yes,
You talk of Pirithous and Theseus love;
Theirs has more ground, is more maturely season'd,
More buckled with strong judgement, and their needs
The one of th' other may be said to water
Their intertangled roots of love, but I
And she (I sigh and spoke of) were things innocent,
Lov'd for we did, and like the Elements
That know not what, nor why, yet do effect
Rare issues by their operance; our souls
Did so to one another; what she lik'd,
Was then of me approv'd, what not condemn'd
No more arraignment; the flower that I would pluck
And put between my breasts, oh (then but beginning
To swell about the blossom) she would long
Till she had such another, and commit it
To the like innocent Cradle, where Phenix-like
They di'd in perfume: on my head no toy
But was her pattern, her affections (pretty
Though happily, her careless were, I followed
For my most serious decking, had mine ear
Stol'n some new air, or at adventure humm'd on
From musical Coynage, why, it was a Note
Whereon her spirits would sojourn (rather dwell on)
And sing it in her slumbers; This rehearsal
(Which fury innocent wots well) comes in
Like old importments-bastard, has this end;
That the true love 'tween Maid, and Maid, may be
More than in sex individual.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: Y'are out of breath
And this high speeded-pace, is but to say
That you shall never (like the Maid Flavina)
Love any that's call'd Man

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: I 'm sure I shall not.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: Now alack weak Sister,
I must no more believe thee in this point
(Though in't I know thou dost believe thy self)
Then I will trust a sickly appetite,
That loaths even as it longs, but sure my Sister
If I were ripe for your perswasion, you
Have said enough to shake me from the Arm
Of the all noble Theseus, for whose fortunes,
I will now in, and kneel with great assurance,
That we, more than his Pirathous, possess
The high Throne in his heart.

speeches.speaker: Ewil.
verse: I am not against your saith,
Yet I continue mine.

speeches.speaker: 1 Qu.
verse: To thee no Star be dark.

speeches.speaker: 2. Qu.
verse: Both Heaven and Earth
Friend thee for ever.

speeches.speaker: 3 Qu.
verse: All the good that may
Be wish'd upon thy head, I cry Amen to't.

speeches.speaker: Thes.
verse: Th'impartial gods, who from the mounted heavens
View us their mortal Herd, behold who erre,
And in their time chastise: goe and find out
The bones of your dead Lords, and honor them
With treble ceremony, rather than a gap
Should be in their dear rights, we would supply't.
But those we will depute, which shall invest
You in your dignities, and even each thing
Our haste does leave imperfect; So adieu
And heavens good eyes look on you, what are those?

speeches.speaker: Herald.
verse: Men of great quality, as may be judg'd
By their appointment; some of Thebs have told's
They are Sisters children, Nephews to the King.

speeches.speaker: Thes.
verse: By th' Helme of Mars, I saw them in the War,
Like to a pair of Lions, smear'd with prey,
Make lanes in troops agast. I fixt my note
Constantly on them; for they were a mark
Worth a god's view: what prisoner was't that told me
When I enquir'd their names?

speeches.speaker: Herald.
verse: We leave, they'r called
Arcite and Palamon,

speeches.speaker: Thes.
verse: 'Tis right, those, those
They are not dead?

speeches.speaker: Her.
verse: Nor in a state of life, had they been taken
When their last hurts were given, 'twas possible
They might have been recover'd; Yet they breathe
And have the name of men.

speeches.speaker: Thes.
verse: Then like men use 'em
The very lees of such (millions of rates)
Exceed the Wine of others, all our Surgeons
Convent in their behoof, our richest balmes
Rather than niggard waste, their lives concern us,
Much more than Thebs is worth, rather than have 'em
Freed of this plight, and in their morning state
(Sound and at liberty) I would 'em dead,
But forty thousand sold, we had rather have 'em
Prisoners to us, than death, bear 'em speedily
From our kind air, to them unkind, and minister
What man to man may do for our sake more,
Since I have known frights, fury, friends, beheasts,
Loves, provocations, zeal, a Mistriss taske,
Desire of liberty, a feavor, madness,
Hath set a mark which nature could not reach too
Without some imposition, sickness in Will
Or wrestling strength in reason, for our Love
And great Apollos mercy, all our best,
Their best skills tender. Lead into the City,
Where having bound things scatter'd, we willl post.
To Athens for our Army.

~rns and Odours, bring away,
Vapors, sighs, darken the day;
Our dole more deadly looks, than dying
Balmes, and Gumms, and heavy cheers,

Sacred viols fill'd with tears,
And clamors, through the wild air flying:

Come all sad and solemn Shows,
That are quick-ey'd pleasures foes;
We convent nought else but woes.
We convent, &c.

speeches.speaker: 3 Qu.
verse: This funeral path, brings to your houshold graver
Joy seize on you again: peace, sleep with him.

speeches.speaker: 2 Qu.
verse: And this to yours.

speeches.speaker: 1 Qu.
verse: Yours this way: Heavens lend
A thousand differing ways to one sure end.

speeches.speaker: 3 Qu.
verse: This world's a City full of straying streets,
And Death's the Market-place, where each one meets.

speeches.speaker: Jail.
verse: I May depart with little, while I live, something I
May cast to you, not much: Alas the Prison I
Keep, though it be for great ones, yet they seldom
Come; before one Salmon, you shall take a number
Of Minnows: I am given out to be better lin'd
Than it can appear, to me report is a true
Speaker: I would I were really, that I am
Deliver'd to be: Marry, what I have (be it what
It will) I will assure upon my daughter at
The day of my death.

speeches.speaker: Wooer.
verse: Sir, I demand no more than your own offer,
And I will estate your Daughter, in what I
Have promised,

speeches.speaker: Jail.
verse: Well, we will talk more of this, when the solemnity
Is past; But have you a full promise of her?
When that shall be seen, I tender my consent.

speeches.speaker: Wooer.
verse: I have Sir; here she comes.

speeches.speaker: Jail.
verse: Your friend and I have chanced to name
You here, upon the old business: but no more of that.
Now, so soon as the Court-hurry is over, we will
Have an end of it: I' th' mean time look tenderly
To the two prisoners. I can tell you they are Princes.

speeches.speaker: Daugh.
verse: These strewings are for their Chamber; 'tis pity they
Are in prison, and 'twere pity they should be out: I
Do think they have patience to make any adversity
Asham'd; the prison it self is proud of 'em; and
They have all the world in their Chamber.

speeches.speaker: Jail.
verse: They are fam'd to be a pair of absolute men.

speeches.speaker: Daugh.
verse: By my troth, I think Fame but stammers 'em, they
Stand a grief above the reach of report.

speeches.speaker: Jail.
verse: I heard them reported in the battel, to be the only doers.

speeches.speaker: Daugh.
verse: Nay, most likely, for they are noble sufferers; I
Marvel how they would have look'd, had they been
Victors, that with such a constant Nobility, enforce
A freedom out of bondage, making misery their
Mirth, and affliction a toy to jest at.

speeches.speaker: Jail.
verse: Doe they so?

speeches.speaker: Daugh.
verse: It seems to me, they have no more sence of their
Captivity, than I of ruling Athens: they eat
Well, look merrily, discourse of many things,
But nothing of their own restraint, and disasters:
Yet sometime a divided sigh, martyr'd as 'twere
I' th' deliverance, will break from one of them,
When the other presently gives it so sweet a rebuke,
That I could wish my self a sigh to be so chid,
Or at least a sigher to be comforted.

speeches.speaker: Wooer.
verse: I never saw 'em.

speeches.speaker: Jail.
verse: The Duke himself came privately in the night.
And so did they, what the reason of it is, I
Know not: Look, yonder they are; that's
Arcite looks out.

speeches.speaker: Daugh.
verse: No Sir, no, that's Palamon: Arcite is the
Lower of the twain; you may perceive a part
Of him.

speeches.speaker: Jail.
verse: Go to, leave your pointing; they would not
Make us their object; out of their sight.

speeches.speaker: Daugh.
verse: It is a holliday to look on them: Lord, the
Diff'rence of men.

speeches.speaker: Pal.
verse: How do you, Noble Cosin?

speeches.speaker: Arcite.
verse: How do you, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Pal.
verse: Why, strong enough to laugh at misery,
And bear the chance of war yet, we are prisoners
I fear for ever Cosin.

speeches.speaker: Arcite.
verse: I believe it,
And to that destiny have patiently
Laid up my hour to come.

speeches.speaker: Pal.
verse: Oh Cosin Arcite,
Where is Thebs now? where is our noble Countrey?
Where are our friends, and kindreds? never more
Must we behold those comforts, never see
The ha^dy youths strive for the Games of honor
(Hung with the painted favours of their Ladies)
Like tail Ships under Sail: then start amongst'em
And as an Eastwind leave 'em all behind us,
Like lazy Clouds, whilst Palamon and Arcite.
Even in the wagging of a wanton leg
Out-stript the peoples praises, won the Garlands,
E'r they have time to wish 'em ours. Oh never
Shall we two exercise, like twins of honor,
Our Arms again, and feel our fiery horses,
Like proud Seas under us, our goo^ Swords, now
(Better the red-ey'd god of War nev'r were)
Bravish'd our sides, like age, must run to rust,
And deck the Temples of those gods that hate us,
These hands shall never draw 'em out like light'ning
To blast whole Armies more.

speeches.speaker: Arcite.
verse: No Palamon,
Those hopes are prisoners with us, here we are
And here the graces of our youths must wither
Like a too-timely Spring; here age must find us,
And which is heaviest (Palamon) unmarried,
The sweet embraces of a loving wife
Loaden with kisses, arm'd with thousand Cupid's
Shall never claspe our necks, no issue know us,
No figures of our selves shall we ev'r see,
To glad our age, and like young Eagles teach 'em
Boldly to gaze against bright arms, and say
Remember what your Fathers were, and conquer.
The fair-ey'd Maids, shall weep our banishments,
And in their Songs, curse ever-blinded fortune
Till she for shame see what a wrong she has done
To youth and nature; This is all our world;
We shall know nothing here, but one another,
Hear nothing, but the clock that tels our woes.
The Vine shall grow, but we shall never see it:
Summer shall come, and with her all delights;
But dead-cold winter must inhabit here still.

speeches.speaker: Pal.
verse: 'Tis too true Arcite. To our Theban hounds,
That shook the aged Forrest with their ecchoes,
No more now must we hollo, no more shake
Our pointed Javelins, whilst the angry Swine
Flies like a Parthian quiver from our rages,
Struck with our well-steel'd Darts: All valiant uses,
(The food and nourishment of noble minds,)
In us two here shall perish; we shall die
(Which is the curse of honor) lastly,
Children of grief, and Ignorance,

speeches.speaker: Arc.
verse: Yet Cosin,
Even from the bottom of these miseries
From all that fortune can inflict upon us,
I see two comforts rising, two meer blessings,
If the gods please to hold here a brave patience,
And the enjoying of our griefs together.
Whilst Palamon is with me, let me perish
If I think this our prison.

speeches.speaker: Pala.
verse: Certainly,
'Tis a main goodness, Cosin, that our fortunes
Were twin'd together; 'tis most true, two souls
Put in two noble bodies, let 'em suffer
The gaul of hazard, so they grow together,
Will never sink, they must not, say they could,
A willing man dies sleeping, and all's done.

speeches.speaker: Arc.
verse: Shall we make worthy uses of this place
That all men hate so much?

speeches.speaker: Pal.
verse: How gentle Cosin?

speeches.speaker: Arc.
verse: Let's think this prison, Holy Sanctuary,
To keep us from corruption of worse men,
We are young, and yet desire the wayes of honour,
That liberty and common conversation,
The poison of pure spirits, might, like women,
Wooe us to wander from. What worthy blessing
Can be but our imaginations
May make it ours? And here being thus together,
We are an endless mine to one another;
We are one anothers Wife, ever begetting
New births of love; we are Father, Friends, Acquaintance,
We are, in one another, Families,
I am your Heir, and you are mine: This place
Is our Inheritance: no hard oppressor
Dare take this from us; here with a little patience
We shall live long, and loving: No surfeits seek us:
The hand of War hurts none here, nor the Seas
Swallow their youth: were we at liberty,
A Wife might part us lawfully, or business,
Quarrels consume us: Envy of ill men
Crave our acquaintance, I might sicken Cosin,
Where you should never know it, and so perish
Without your noble hand to close mine eyes,
Or prayers to the gods; a thousand chances
Were we from hence, would sever us.

speeches.speaker: Pal.
verse: You have made me
(I thank you Cosin Arcite) almost wanton
With my Captivity: what a misery
It is to live abroad? and every where:
'Tis like a Beast me thinks: I find the Court here,
I'm sure a more content, and all those pleasures
That wooe the Wills of men to vanity,
I see through now; and am sufficient
To tell the world, 'tis but a gaudy shadow,
That old Time, as he passes by, takes with him,
What had we been old in the Court of Creon,
Where sin is Justice, Lust, and Ignorance,
The virtues of the great ones: Cosin Ar^ite
Had not the loving gods found this place for us
We had di'd as they doe, ill old men unwept,
And had their Epitaphs, the peoples Curses.
Shall I say more?

speeches.speaker: Arc.
verse: I would hear you still.

speeches.speaker: Pal.
verse: Ye shall.
Is there record of any two that lov'd
Better than we two Arcite?

speeches.speaker: Arc.
verse: Sure there cannot.

speeches.speaker: Pal.
verse: I doe not think it possible our friendship
Should ever leave us.

speeches.speaker: Arc.
verse: Till our deaths it cannot.
And after death our spirits shall be led
To those that love eternally. Speak on Sir.
This Garden has a world of pleasures in't.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: What Flower is this?

speeches.speaker: Wom.
verse: 'Tis call'd Narcissus, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: That was a fair Boy certain, but a fool,
To love himself, were there not Maids enough?

speeches.speaker: Arc.
verse: Pray forward.

speeches.speaker: Pal.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: Or were they all hard-hearted?

speeches.speaker: Wom.
verse: They could not be to one so fair.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: Thou wouldst not.

speeches.speaker: Wom.
verse: I think I should not, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: That's a good wench:
But take heed to your kindness though.

speeches.speaker: Wom.
verse: Why Madam?

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: Men are mad things.

speeches.speaker: Arcite.
verse: Will ye go forward, Cosin?

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: Canst not thou work such Flowers in Silk wench?

speeches.speaker: Wom.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: I'll have a Gown full of 'em, and of these,
This is a pretty colour, wil't not do
Rarely upon a skirt wench?

speeches.speaker: Wom.
verse: Dainty Madam.

speeches.speaker: Arc.
verse: Cosin, Cosin, how do you, Sir? Why Palamon?

speeches.speaker: Pal.
verse: Never till now, I was in prison Arcite.

speeches.speaker: Arc.
verse: Why, what's the matter man?

speeches.speaker: Pal.
verse: Behold, and wonder.
By heaven she is a Goddess.

speeches.speaker: Arcite.
verse: Ha.

speeches.speaker: Pal.
verse: Do reverence.
She is a Goddess Arcite.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: Of all Flowers,
Methinks a Rose is best.

speeches.speaker: Wom.
verse: Why gentle Madam?

speeches.speaker: Emil.
verse: It is the very Emblem of a Maid.
For when the West wind courts her gently
How modestly she blows, and paints the Sun;
With her chaste blushes? When the North comes near her,
Rude and impatient, then like Chastity
She locks her beauties in her bud again,
And leaves him to base briers,

speeches.speaker: Wom.
verse: Yet good Madam,
Sometimes her modesty will blow so far
She falls for't: a Maid
If she have any honor, would be loth
To take example by her.

speeches.speaker: Emil.
