Turn inward, make me all one piece, though earth.
My tears shall over-whelm you else too.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: What moves my Lord to this strange sadness?
If any late discerned want in me,
Give cause to your repentance, care and duty
Shall find a painful way to recompence.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Are you yet frozen veins, feel you a breath,
Whose temperate heat would make the North Star reel,
Her Icy pillars thaw'd, and do you not melt?
Draw nearer, yet nearer,
That from thy barren kiss thou maist confess
I have not heat enough to make a blush.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: Speak nearer to my understanding, like a Husband.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: How should he speak the language of a Husband.
Who wants the tongue and organs of his voice?

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: It is a phrase will part with the same ease
From you, with that you now deliver.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Bind not his ears up with so dull a charm
Who hath no other sense left open, why should thy words
Find more restraint than thy free speaking actions,
Thy close embraces, and thy midnight sighs
The silent Orators to slow desire?

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: Strive not to win content from ignorance
Which must be lost in knowledge: heaven can witness
My farthest hope of good, reacht at your pleasure,
Which seeing alone, may in your look be read:
Add not a doubtful comment to a text
That in it self is direct and easie.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Oh thou hast drunk the juyce of hemlock too,
Or did upbraided nature make this pair
To shew she had not quite forgot her first
Justly prais'd Workmanship, the first chast couple
Before the want of joy, taught guilty sight
A way through shame and sorrow to delight:
Say, may we mix, as in their innocence
When Turtles kist, to confirm happiness,,
Not to beget it.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: I know no bar.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Should I believe thee, yet thy pulse beats, woman,
And says the name of Wife did promise thee
The blest reward of duty to thy mother,
Who gave so often witness of her joy,
When she did boast thy likeness to her Husband.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: 'Tis true, that to bring forth a second to your, self.
Was only worthy of my Virgin loss;
And should I prize you less, unpattern'd Sir?
Then being exemplify'd, is't not more honor
To be possessor of unequall'd virtue,
Than what is paralell'd, give me belief,
The name of mother, knows no way of good,
More than the end in me: who weds for Lust
Is oft a widow: when I married you,
I lost the name of Maid to gain a Title
Above the wish of change, which that part can
Only maintain, is still the same in man,
His virtue and his calm society,
Which no gray hairs can threaten to dissolve
Nor wrinkles bury.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Confine thy self to silence, lest thou take
That part of reason from me, is only left
To give perswasion to me, I'm a man:
Or say thou hast never seen the Rivers haste
With gladsome speed, to meet th' amorous sea.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
prose: We are but to praise the coolness of their streams.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Nor view'd the Kids, taught by their lustful fires,
Pursue each other through the wanton lawns,
And lik'd the sport.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: As it made way unto their envied rest
With weary knots, binding their harmless eyes.

speeches.speaker: Thier
verse: Nor do you know the reason why the Dove,
One of the pair, your hands wont hourly feed,
So often clipt and kist her happy mate.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: Unless it were to welcome his wish'd sight,
Whose absence only gave her mourning voice.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: And you could, Dove-like to a single object,
Bind your loose spirits to one, nay, such a one
Whom only eyes and ears must flatter good,
Your surer sence made useless, my self, nay
As in my all of good, already known.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: Let proof plead for me; let me be mew'd up.
Where never eye may reach me, but your own;
And when I shall repent, but in my looks, if sigh.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Or shed a tear that's warm.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: But in your sadness.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Or when you hear the birds call for their mates.
Ask if it be St. Valentine, their coupling day.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: If any thing may make a thought suspected
Of knowing any happiness but you,
Divorce me, by the Title of Most Falshood.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Posterity henceforth, lose the name of blessing
And leave the earth inhabited to people heaven.
prose: Oh, who would know a wife, that might have such a friend?

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: All happiness to Thierry and Ordella.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: 'Tis a desire but borrowed from me, my happiness.
Shall be the period of all good mens wishes,
Which friends, nay dying Fathers shall bequeath,
And in my one give all: is there a duty
Belongs to any power of mine, or love
To any virtue I have right to? here, place it here,
Ordella's name shall only bear command,
Rule, Title. Sovereignty.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: What passion sways my Son?

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Oh Mother, she has doubled every good
The travel of your bloud made possible
To my glad being.

speeches.speaker: Prot.
verse: He should have done
Little to her, he is so light hearted.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Brother, friends, if honor unto shame
If wealth to want inlarge the present sense,
My joyes are unbounded, instead of question
Let it be envy, not bring a present
To the high offering of our mirth, Banquets, and Masques;
Keep waking our delights, mocking nights malice,
Whose dark brow would fright pleasure from us,
Our Court be but one stange of Revels, and each ye
The Scene where our content moves.

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: There shall want
Nothing to express our shares in your delight, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Till now I ne'er repented the estate
Of Widower.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Musick, why art thou so slow voic'd? it staies thy presence
My Ordella, this chamber is a sphere
Too narrow for thy all-moving virtue.
Make way, free way I say;
Who must alone, her Sexes want supply,
Had need to have a room both large and high.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: This passion's above utterance.

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: Nay, credulity.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Why Son what mean you, are you a man?

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: No Mother I am no man, were I a man?
How could I be thus happy?

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: How can a wife be author of this joy then?

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: That being no man, I am married to no woman;
The best of men in full ability,
Can only hope to satisfie a wife,
And for that hope ridiculous, I in my want
And such defective poverty, that to her bed
From my first Cradle brought no strength but thought
Have met a temperance beyond hers that rockt me,
Necessity being her bar; where this
Is so much sensless of my depriv'd sire;
She knows it not a loss by her desire.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: It is beyond my admiration.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Beyond your sexes faith,
The unripe Virgins of our age, to hear't
Will dream themselves to women, and convert
Th' example to a miracle.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Alas, 'tis your defect moves my amazement,
But what Ill can be separate from ambition?
Cruel Theodoret.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: What, of my brother?

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: That to his name your barrenness adds rule;
Who loving the effect, would not be strange
In favouring the cause; look on the profit,
And gain will quickly point the mischief out.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: The name of Father, to what I possess
Is shame and care.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Were we begot to single happiness
I grant you; but from such a wife, such virtue
To get an heir, what hermet would not find
Deserving argument to break his vow
Even in his age of chastity?

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: You teach a deaf man language.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: The cause found out, the malady may cease,
Have you heard of one Forts?

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: A learned Astronomer, great Magician,
Who lives hard by retir'd.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Repair to him, with the just hour and place
Of your nativity; fools are amaz'd at sate,
Griefs but conceal'd are never desperate.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: You have timely waken'd me, nor shall I sleep
Without the satisfaction of his Art.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Wisdom prepares you to't, Lecure, met happily.

speeches.speaker: Lecure.
verse: The ground answers your purpose, the convenience
Being secure and easie, falling just
Behind the state set for Theodoret.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: 'Tis well, your trust invites you to a second charge,
You know Leforte's Cell.

speeches.speaker: Lecure.
verse: Who constellated your fair birth.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Enough, I see thou know'st him, where's Bawdber?

speeches.speaker: Lec.
verse: I left him careful of the project cast,
To raise Protaldie's credit.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: A sore that must be plaister'd, in whose wound
Others shall find their graves, think themselves sound,
Your ear, and quickest apprehension.

speeches.speaker: Bawdb.
verse: This man of war will advance.

speeches.speaker: Lecu.
verse: His hour's upon the stroke.

speeches.speaker: Bawdb.
verse: Wind him back, as you favour my ears,
I have no noise in my head, my brains have hitherto
Been imploy'd in silent busineses.

speeches.speaker: Lecu.
verse: The Gentleman is within your reach Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bawdb.
verse: Devitry, I take it.
prose: Give ground, whilst I drill my wits to the encounter,

speeches.speaker: Devi.
verse: All's that left of him.

speeches.speaker: Bawdb.
verse: Is there another parcel of you, if it be at pawn
I will gladly redeem it, to make you wholly mine.

speeches.speaker: Vitry.
verse: You seek too hard a pennyworth.

speeches.speaker: Bawdb.
verse: You too ill to keep such distance; your parts have been long known
To me, howsoever you please to forget acquaintance.

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: I must confess I have been subject to lewd company.

speeches.speaker: Bawdb.
verse: Thanks for your good remembrance,
You have been a soldier Devitry, and born Arms.

speeches.speaker: Vit.
prose: A couple of unprofitable ones, that have only serv'd to get me a stomach to my dinner.

speeches.speaker: Bawdb.
verse: Much good may it do you, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Vitry.
prose: You shall have heard me say I had din'd first, I have built on an unwholsome ground, rais'd up a house, before I knew a Tenant, matcht to meet weariness, sought to find want and hunger.

speeches.speaker: Bawdb.
prose: It is time you put up your sword, and run away for meat, Sir, nay, if I had not withdrawn e'r now, I might have kept thee; fast with you: but since the way to thrive is never late, what is the nearest course to profit think you?

speeches.speaker: Vitry.
prose: It may be your worship will say bawdry.

speeches.speaker: Bawdb.
prose: True sense, bawdry.

speeches.speaker: Vitry.
prose: Why, is their five kinds of them, I never knew but one.

speeches.speaker: Bawdb.
prose: I'll shew you a new way of prostitution, fall back, further yet, further, there is fifty crowns, do but as much to Protaldye the Queens favorite, they are doubled.

speeches.speaker: Vitry.
prose: But thus much.

speeches.speaker: Bawdb.
prose: Give him but an affront as he comes to the presence, and in his drawing make way, like a true bawd to his valour, the son's thy own; if you take a scratch in the arm or so, every drop of bloud weighs down a ducket.

speeches.speaker: Vitry.
prose: After that rate, I and my friends would begger the kingdom. Sir, you have made me blush to see my want, whose cure is such a cheap and easie purchase, this is Male-bawdry belike.

speeches.speaker: Bawdb.
prose: See, you shall not be long earning your wages, your work's before your eyes.

speeches.speaker: Vitry.
prose: Leave it to my handling, I'll fall upon't instantly.

speeches.speaker: Bawdb.
verse: What opinion will the managing of this affair
Bring to my wisdom? my invention tickles
With apprehension on't:

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: These are the joyes of marriage, Lady,
Whose sights are able to dissolve Virginity.
Speak freely, do you not envy the Brides felicity?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: How should I, being partner of't?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: What you enjoy is but the Banquets view,
The taste stands from your pallat; if he impart
By day so much of his content, think what night gave?

speeches.speaker: Vitry.
verse: Will you have a relish of wit, Lady?

speeches.speaker: Bawdb.
verse: This is the man.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: If it be not dear, Sir,

speeches.speaker: Vitry.
prose: If you affect cheapness, how can you prize this sullied ware so much? mine is fresh, my own, not retail'd.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: You are saucy, sirrah.

speeches.speaker: Vitry.
prose: The fitter to be in the dish with such dry Stock-fish as you are, how, strike?

speeches.speaker: Bawdb.
prose: Remember the condition as you look for payment.

speeches.speaker: Vitry.
prose: That box was left out of the bargain.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
prose: Help, help, help.

speeches.speaker: Bawdb.
verse: Plague of the Scriveners running hand,
What a blow is this to my reputation?

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: What villain dares this outrage?

speeches.speaker: Devitry.
prose: Hear me, Sir, this creature hir'd me with fifty crowns in hand, to let Protaldye have the better of me at single Rapier on a made quarrel; he mistaking the weapon, laies me over the chops with his club fist, for which I was bold to teach him the Art of memory.

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
verse: Ha, ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Your General, Mother, will display himself.
'Spight of our Peace I see.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Forbear these civil jars, fie Protaldy,
So open in your projects, avoid our presence, sirrah.

speeches.speaker: Devi.
verse: Willingly; if you have any more wages to earn,
You see I can take pains.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: There's somewhat for thy labour,
More than was promis'd, ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Bawdb.
verse: Where could I wish my self now? in the Isle of Dogs.
So I might scape scratching, for I see by her Cats eyes
I shall be claw'd fearfully.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: We'll hear no more on't,
Musick drown all sadness;
Command the Revellers in, at what a rate I do purchase
My Mothers absence, to give my spleen full liberty.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Speak not a thoughts delay, it names thy ruin.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: I had thought my life had born more value with you.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Thy loss carries mine with't, let that secure thee.
The vault is ready, and the door conveys to't
Falls just behind his chair, the blow once given,
Thou art unseen.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: I cannot feel more than I fear, I'm sure.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Be gone, and let them laugh their own destruction.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: You will add unto her rage.

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: 'Foot, I shall burst, unless I vent my self, ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Me Sir, you never could
Have found a time to invite more willingness
In my dispose to pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Memb.
verse: Would you would please to make some other choise.

speeches.speaker: Revel.
verse: 'Tis a disgrace would dwell upon me, Lady,
Should you refuse.

speeches.speaker: Memb.
verse: Your reason conquers; my Grandmothers looks
Have turn'd all air to earth in me, they sit
Upon my heart like night-charms, black and heavy.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: You are too much libertine.

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: The fortune of the fool perswades my laughter
More than his cowardize; was ever Rat
Ta'en by the tail thus? ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Forbear I say.

speeches.speaker: Prot.
verse: No eye looks this way, I will wink and strike,
Lest I betray my self.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Ha, did you not see one near me?

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: How near you, why do you look so pale, brother?
Treason, treason.

speeches.speaker: Memb.
verse: Oh my presage! Father.

speeches.speaker: Ordella.
verse: Brother,

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Prince, Noble Prince.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Make the gates sure, search into every angle
And corner of the Court, oh my shame! Mother,
Your Son is slain, Theodoret, noble Theodoret,
Here in my arms, too weak a Sanctuary
'Gainst treachery and murder, say, is the Traitor taken?

speeches.speaker: 1 Guard.
verse: No man hath past the chamber on my life Sir.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Set present fire unto the place, that all unseen
May perish in this mischief, who moves slow to't.
Shall add unto the flame.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: What mean you? give me your private hearing.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Perswasion is a partner in the crime,
I will renounce my claim unto a mother,
If you make offer on't.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: E'er a Torch can take flame, I will produce
The author of the fact.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Withdraw but for your Lights.

speeches.speaker: Memb.
verse: Oh my too true suspition.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Speak, where's the Engine to this horrid act?

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Here you do behold her; upon whom make good
Your causeless rage; the deed was done by my incitement,
Not yet repented.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Whether did nature start, when you conceiv'd?
A birth so unlike woman? say, what part
Did not consent to make a son of him,
Reserv'd it self within you to his ruine.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Ha, ha, a son of mine! doe not dissever
Thy fathers dust, shaking his quiet urn,
To which my breath would send so foul an issue.
My Son, thy Brother?

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Was not Theodoret my brother, or is thy tongue
Confederate with thy heart, to speak and do
Only things monstrous?

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Hear me and thou shalt make thine own belief,
Thy, still with sorrow mention'd, father liv'd
Three careful years, in hope of wished heirs,
When I conceiv'd, being from his jealous fear
Injoyn'd to quiet home, one fatal day
Transported with my pleasure to the chase,
I forc'd command, and in pursuit of game
Fell from my horse, lost both my child and hopes.
Despair which only in his love saw life
Worthy of being, from a Gard'ners Arms
Snatcht this unlucky brat, and call'd it mine,
When the next year repaid my loss with thee:
But in thy wrongs preserv'd my misery,
Which that I might diminish, though not end,
My sighs, and wet eies from thy Fathers Will,
Bequeath this largest part of his Dominions
Of France unto thee, and only left
Austracia unto that changling, whose life affords
Too much of ill 'gainst me to prove my words,
And call him stranger.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Come, doe not weep, I must, nay do believe you.
And in my fathers satisfaction count it
Merit, not wrong, or loss:

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: You doe but flatter, there's anger yet flames
In your eyes.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: See, I will quench it, and confess that you
Have suffer'd double travel for me.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: You will not fire the house then?

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Rather reward the author who gave cause
Of knowing such a secret, my oath and duty
Shall be assurance on't.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Protaldye, rise good faithful servant, heaven knows.
How hardly he was drawn to this attempt.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Protaldye? he had a Gard'ners face I'll swear:
Tell by thy hand, Sir, we doe owe unto you for this service.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Why lookest thou so dejected?

speeches.speaker: Prot.
verse: I want a little shift, Lady, nothing else.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: The fires are ready, please it your grace withdraw,
Whilst we perform your pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Reserve them for the body; since he had the fate
To live and die a Prince, he shall not lose
The Title in his Funeral.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: His fate to live a Prince,
Thou old impiety, made up by lust and mischief,
Take up the body.

speeches.speaker: Lecu.
verse: Dost think Leforte's sure enough?

speeches.speaker: Serv.
prose: As bonds can make him, I have turn'd his eyes to the East; and left him gaping after the Morning star, his head is a meer Astrolobe, his eyes stand for the Poles, the gag in his mouth being the Coachman, his five teeth have the nearest resemblance to Charles Wain.

speeches.speaker: Lecure.
prose: Thou hast cast a figure which shall raise thee, direct my hair a little: and in my likeness to him, read a fortune suiting thy largest hopes.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: You are so far'bove likeness, you are the same,
If you love mirth, perswade him from himself.
'Tis but an Astronomer out of the way,
And lying, will bear the better place for't

speeches.speaker: Lecure.
verse: I have profitable use in hand, haste to the Queen
And tell her how you left me chang'd.
Who would not serve this virtuous active Queen?
She that loves mischief'bove the man that does it,
And him above her pleasure, yet knows no heaven else.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: How well this loans suits the Art I seek,
Discovering secret, and succeeding Fate,
Knowledge that puts all lower happiness on,
With a remiss and careless hand,
Fair peace unto your meditations, father.

speeches.speaker: Lecure.
verse: The same to you, you bring, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Drawn by your much fam'd skill. I come to know
Whether the man who owes his character,
Shall e'er have issue.

speeches.speaker: Lecure.
verse: A resolution falling with most ease,
Of any doubt you could have nam'd, he is a Prince
Whose fortune you enquire.

speeches.speaker: Thie.
verse: He is nobly born.

speeches.speaker: Lecure.
verse: He had a Dukedom lately fall'n unto him,
By one, call'd Brother, who has left a Daughter.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: The question is, of Heirs, not Lands.

speeches.speaker: Lecure.
verse: Heirs, yes, he shall have Heirs.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Begotten of his body, why look'st thou p^le?
Thou canst not suffer in his want.

speeches.speaker: Lecure.
verse: Nor thou, I neither can nor will
Give farther knowledge to thee.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Thou must, I am the man my self,
Thy Sovereign, who must owe unto thy wisdom
In the concealing of my barren shame.

speeches.speaker: Lecure.
verse: Your Grace doth wrong your Stars; if this be yours,
You may have children.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Speak it again.

speeches.speaker: Lecure.
verse: You may have fruitful issue.

speeches.speaker: Thie.
verse: By whom? when? how?

speeches.speaker: Lecure.
verse: It was the fatal means first struck my bloud
With the cold hand of wonder, when I read it
Printed upon your birth.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Can there be any way unsmooth, has end
So fair and good?

speeches.speaker: Lecure.
verse: We that behold the sad aspects of Heaven,
Leading sence blinded, men feel grief enough
To know, though not to speak their miseries.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Sorrow must lose a name, where mine finds life;
If not in thee, at least ease pain with speed,
Which must know no cure else.

speeches.speaker: Lecure.
verse: Then thus,
The first of Females which your eye shall meet
Before the Sun next rise, coming from out
The Temple of Diana, being slain, you live
Father of many sons.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Call'st thou this sadness, can I beget a Son?
Deserving less than to give recompence
Unto so poor a loss? what e'er thou art,
Rest peaceable blest creature, born to be
Mother of Princes, whose grave shall be more fruitful
Than others marriage beds: methinks his Art
Should give her form and happy figure to me,
I long to see my happiness, he is gone,
As I remember, he nam'd my brothers Daughter,
Were it my Mother, 'twere a gainful death
Could give Ordella's virtue living breath.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: YOur Grace is early stirring.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: How can he sleep,
Whose happiness is laid up in an hour.
He knows comes stealing towards, him Oh Martel!
Is't possible the longing Bride, whose wishes
Out-runs her fears, can on that day she is married
Consume in slumbers; or his Arms rust in ease,
That hears the charge, and sees the honor'd purchase
Ready to gil'd his valour? Mine is more,
A power above these passions; this day France,
France that in want of issue withers with us;
And like an aged River, runs his head
Into forgotten ways, again I ransome,
And his fair course turn right: this day, Thierry,
The Son of France, whose manly powers like prisoners
Have been tied up, and fetter'd; by one death
Give life to thousand ages; this day beauty
The envy of the world, Pleasure the glory,
Content above the world, desire beyond it
Are made mine own, and useful.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Happy Woman
That dies to do these things.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: But ten times happier
That lives to do the greater; oh Martel,
The gods have heard me now, and those that scorn'd me,
Mothers of many children, and blest fathers
That see their issues like the Stars un-number'd,,
Their comfort more than them, shall in my praises
Now teach their Infants songs; and tell their ages
From such a Son of mine, or such a Queen,
That chaste Ordella brings me: blessed marriage
The chain that links two Holy Loves together
And in the marriage, more than blest Ordella,
That comes so near the Sacrament it self,
The Priests doubt, whether purer.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Sir, y'are lost.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: I prethee let me be so.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: The day ^ears,
And those that have been offering early prayers,
Are now retiring homeward.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Stand and mark then.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Is it the first must suffer.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: The first Woman.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: What hand shall do it, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: This hand Martell,
For who less dare presume to give the gods
An incense of this offering?

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Would I were she,
For such away to die, and such a blessing
Can never crown my parting.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: What are those?

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Men, men, Sir, men.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: The plagues of men light on 'em,
They cross my hopes like Hares, who's that?

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: A Priest, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Would he were gelt.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: May not these rascals serve, Sir,
Well hang'd and quarter'd?

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Nov

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Here comes a woman.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Stand and behold her then.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: I think a fair one.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Move not whilst I prepare her: may her peace
Like his whose innocence the gods are pleas'd with,
And offering at their Altars, gives his soul
Far purer than those fires; pull heaven upon her
You holy powers, no humane spot dwell in her,
No love of any thing, but you and goodness,
Tie her to earth; fear be a stranger to her,
And all weak blouds affections, but thy hope
Let her bequeath to Women: hear me heaven,
Give her a spirit masculine, and noble,
Fit for your selves to ask, and me to offer.
Oh let her meet my blow, doat on her death;
And as a wanton Vine bows to the pruner,
That by his cutting off, more may increase,
So let her fall to raise me fruit; hail woman.
The happiest, and the best (if the dull Will
Do not abuse thy fortune) France e'er found yet.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: Sh'is more than dull, Sir, less, and worse than Woman,
That may inherit such an infinite
As you propound, a greatness so near goodness;
And brings a Will to rob her.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Tell me this then,
Was there e'er woman yet, or may be found,
That for fair Fame, unspotted memory,
For virtues sake, and only for it self sake
Has, or dare make a story?

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: Many dead Sir,
Living I thing as many.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Say, the kingdom
May from a womans Will receive a blessing,
The King and kingdom, not a private safety.
A general blessing, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: A general curse
Light on her heart, denies it.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Full of honor;
And such examples as the former ages
Were but dim shadows of, and empty figures.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: You strangely stir me, Sir, and were my weakness
In any other flesh but modest womans,
You should not ask more questions, may I do it?

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: You may, and which is more, you must.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: I joy in't,
Above a moderate gladness, Sir, you promise
It shall be honest.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: As ever time discover'd.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: Let it be what it may then, what it dare,
I have a mind will hazard it.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: But hark ye,
What may that woman merit, makes this blessing!

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: Only her duty, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: 'Tis terrible.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: 'Tis so much the more noble.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: 'Tis full of fearful shadows.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: So is sleep, Sir.
Or any thing that's meerly ours, and mortal,
We were begotten gods else; but those fears
Feeling but once the fires of nobler thoughts.
Flie, like the shapes of clouds we form, to nothing.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Suppose it death.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: I do.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: And endless parting
With all we can call ours, with all our sweetness,
With youth, strength, pleasure, people, time, nay reason:
For in the silent grave, no conversation,
No joyful tread of friends, no voice of Lovers,
No careful Fathers counsel, nothing's h^d;
Nor nothing is, but all oblivion,
Dust and an endless darkness; and dare you woman
Desire this place?

speeches.speaker: Ordeel.
verse: 'Tis of all sleeps the sweetest,
Children begin it to us, strong men seek it,
And Kings from heighth of all their painted glories
Fall like spent exhalations, to this centre:
And those are fools that fear it, or imagine
A few unhandsome pleasures, or lifes profits
Can recompence this place; and mad that staies it,
Till age blow out their lights, or rotten humors.
Bring them dispers'd to th' earth.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Then you can suffer?

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: As willingly as say it.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Martell, a wonder,
Here's a woman that dares die, yet tell me,
Are you a Wife?

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: I am Sir.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: And have children?
She sighs and weeps.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: Oh none Sir.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Dare you venture
For a poor barren praise you ne'er shall hear,
To part with these sweet hopes?

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: With all but Heaven,
And yet die full of children; he that reads me
When I am ashes, is my Son in wishes,
And those chaste dames that keep my memory,
Singing my yearly requiems, are my Daughters.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Then there is nothing wanting but my knowledg.
And what I must doe, Lady?

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: You are the King, Sir,
And what you do I'll suffer, and that blessing
That you desire, the gods showr on the Kingdom.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Thus much before I strike then, for I must kill you,
The gods have will'd it so they're made the blessing
Must make France young again, and me a man,
Keep up your strength still nobly.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: Fear me not.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: And meet death like a measure.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: I am stedfast.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Thou shalt be sainted woman, and thy Tomb
Cut out in Chrystal, pure and good as thou art;
And on it shall be graven every age,
Succeeding Peers of France that rise by thy fall,
Tell thou liest there like old and fruitful nature.
Darest thou behold thy happiness?

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: I dare Sir.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Ha?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Oh Sir, you must not doe it.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: No, I dare not.
There is an Angel keeps that Paradice,
A fiery Angel friend; oh virtue, virtue,
Ever and endless virtue.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: Strike, Sir, strike;
And if in my poor death fair France may merit,
Give me a thousand blows, be killing me
A thousand days.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: First let the earth be barren,
And man no more remembred, rise Ordella,
The nearest to thy maker, and the purest
That ever dull flesh shewed us,— oh my heart-strings

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: I see you full of wonder, therefore noblest,
And truest amongst Women, I will tell you
The end of this strange accident.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: Amazement
Has so much wove upon my heart, that truly
I feel my self unfit to hear, oh Sir,
My Lord has slighted me.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Oh no sweet Lady.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: Robb'd me of such a glory by his pity,
And most unprovident respect.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Dear Lady,
It was not meant to you.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: Else where the day is,
And hours distinguish time, time runs to ages,
And ages end the world, I had been spoken.

speeches.speaker: De^.
verse: I'll tell you what it was, if but your patience
Will give me hearing.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: If I have transgrest,
Forgive me, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Your noble Lord was counsel'd,
Grieving the barrenness between you both,
And all the Kingdom with him, to seek out
A man that knew the secrets of the gods,
He went, found such an one, and had this answer,
That if he wou'd have issue, on this morning,
For this hour was prefixt him, he should kill
The first he met, being Female, from the Temple;
And then he should have children, the mistake
Is now too perfect, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Ordel,
verse: Still 'tis I, Sir,
For may this work be done by common women?
Durst any but my self that knew the blessing,
And felt the benefit, assume this thing
In any other, 't'ad been lost, and nothing,
A curse and not a blessing; I was figur'd;
And shall a little fondness barr my purchase?

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Where should he then seek children?

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: Where they are
In wombs ordain'd for issues, in those beauties
That bless a marriage-bed, and makes it proceed
With kisses that conceive, and fruitful pleasures;
Mine like a grave, buries those loyal hopes,
And to a grave it covets.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: You are too good,
Too excellent, too honest; rob not us
And those that shall hereafter seek example,
Of such inestimable worthies in woman,
Your Lord of such obedience, all of honor
In coveting a cruelty is not yours,
A Will short of your Wisdom; make not error
A Tomb-stone of your virtues, whose fair life
Deserves a constellation: your Lord dare not;
He cannot, ought not, must not run this hazard,
He makes a separation, nature shakes at,
The gods deny, and everlasting justice
Shrinks back, and sheaths her sword at.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: All's but talk, Sir,
I find to what I am reserv'd, and needful,
And though my Lord's compassion makes me poor,
And leaves me in my best use, yet a strength
Above mine own, or his dull fondness finds me;
The gods have given it to me.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Self-destruction!
Now all good Angels bless thee, oh sweet Lady,
You are abus'd, this is a way to shame you,
And with you all that knows you, all that loves you,
To ruin all you build, would you be famous?
Is that your end?

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: I would be what I should be.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Live and confirm the gods then, live and be loaden
With more than Olive-bear, or fruitful Autumn;
This way you kill your merit, kill your cause,
And him you would raise life to, where, or how
Got you these bloudy thoughts? what Devil durst
Look on that Angel face, and tempt? doe you know
What is't to die thus how you strike the Stars,
And all good things above, do you feel
What follows a self-bloud, whether you venture,
And to what punishment? excellent Lady,
Be not thus cozen'd, do not fool your self,
The Priest was never his own sacrifice,
But he that thought his hell here.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: I am counsell'd,

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: And I am glad on't, lie, I know you dare not.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: I never have done yet.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Pray take my comfort,
Was this a soul to lose? two more such women
Would save their sex; see, she repents and prayes,
Oh hear her, hear her, if there be a faith
Able to reach your mercies, she hath sent it.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: Now good Martel confirm me.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: I will Lady,
And every hour advise you, for I doubt
Whether this plot be heavens, or hells; your mother,
And I will find it, if it be in mankind
To search the center of it: in the mean time
I'll give you out for dead, and by your self,
And shew the instrument, so shall I find
A joy that will betray her.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: Do what's fittest;
And I will follow you.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Then ever live
Both able to engross all love, and give.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: I'm in labour
To be deliver'd of that burthenous project
I have so long gone with; ha, here's the Midwife,
Or life, or death.

speeches.speaker: Lecu.
verse: If in the supposition
Of her death in whose life you die, you ask me,
I think you are safe.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Is she dead?

speeches.speaker: Lecu.
verse: I have us'd
All means to make her so, I saw him waiting
At the Temple door, and us'd such Art within,
That only she of all her Sex was first
Giv'n up unto his fury.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Which if love
Or fear made him forbear to execute
The vengeance he determin'd, his fond pity
Shall draw it on himself, for were there left
Not any man but he, to serve my pleasures,
Or from me to receive commands, which are
The joyes for which I love life, he should be
Remov'd, and I alone left to be Queen
O'er any part of goodness that's left in me.

speeches.speaker: Lecu.
verse: If you are so resolv'd, I have provided
A means to ship him hence: look upon this,
But touch it sparingly, for this once us'd.
Say but to dry a tear, will keep the eye-lid
From closing, until death perform that office.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Give't me, I may have use of it, and on you
I'll make the first experiment: if one sigh
Or heavy look beget the least suspition,
Childish compassion can thaw the Ice
Of your so long congeal'd and flinty hardness.
Slight, go on constant, or I shall.

speeches.speaker: Prot.
verse: Best Lady,
We have no faculties which are not yours.

speeches.speaker: Lecu.
verse: Nor will be any thing without you.

speeches.speaker: Baun.
verse: Be so, and we will stand or fall together, for
Since we have gone so far, that death must stay
The journey, which we wish should never end;
And innocent, or guilty, we must die,
When we do so, let's know the reason why.

speeches.speaker: Lecu.
verse: The King.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: We'll be alone.

speeches.speaker: Prot.
verse: I would I had
A Convoy too, to bring me safe off.
For rage although it be allai'd with sorrow,
Appears so dreadful in him, that I stake
To look upon 't.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Coward I will meet it,
And know from whence 't has birth: Son, kingly Thierry.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Is cheating grown so common among men?
And thrives so well here, that the gods endeavour
To practise it above?

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Your Mother.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Ha!. or are they only careful to revenge,
Not to reward? or when, for your offences
We study satisfaction, must the cure
Be worse than the disease?

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Will you not hear me?

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: To lose th' ability to perform those duties
For which I entertain'd the name of Husband,
Ask'd more than common sorrow; but t'impose
For the redress of that defect, a torture
In marking her to death, for whom alone
I felt that weakness as a want, requires
More than the making the head bald: or falling
Thus flat upon the earth, or cursing that way,
Or praying this, oh such a Scene of grief,
And so set down, (the world the stage to act on)
May challenge a Tragedian better practis'd
Than I am to express it; for my cause
Of passion is so strong, and my performance
So weak, that though the part be good, I fear
Th'ill acting of it, will defraud it of
The poor reward it may deserve, mens pity.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: I have given you way thus long, a King, and what
Is more, my Son, and yet a slave to that
Which only triumphs over cowards sorrow,
For shame look up.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Is't you, look down on me:
And if that you are capable to receive it,
Let that return to you, that have brought forth
One mark'd out only for it: what are these?
Come they upon your privilege to tread on
The Tomb of my afflictions?

speeches.speaker: Prot.
verse: No, not we Sir.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: How dare you then omit the ceremony
Due to the funeral of all my hopes.
Or come unto the marriage of my sorrows,
But in such colours as may sort with them.

speeches.speaker: Prot.
verse: Alas; we will wear any thing.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: This is madness
Take but my counsel.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Yours? dare you again
Though arm'd with th' authority of a mother,
Attempt the danger that will fall on you
If such another syllable awake it?
Goe, and with yours be safe, I have such cause
Of grief, nay more, to love it, that I will not
Have such as these be sharers in it.

speeches.speaker: Lecu.
verse: Madam.

speeches.speaker: Prot.
verse: Another time were better.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Do not stirr,
For I must be resolv'd, and will, be statues.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: I, thou art welcome, and upon my soul
Thou art an honest man, do you see, he has tears
To lend to him whom prodigal expence
Of sorrow, has made bankrupt of such treasure,
Nay, thou dost well.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: I would it might excuse.
The ill I bring along.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Thou mak'st me smile
I the heighth of my calamities, as if
There could be the addition of an Atome,
To the gyant-body of my miseries
But try, for I will hear thee, all sit down, 'tis death
To any that shall dare to interrupt him
In look, gesture, or word.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: And such attention
As is due to the last, and the best story
That ever was deliver'd, will become you,
The griev'd Ordella, (for all other titles
But take away from that) having from me
Prompted by your last parting groan, enquir'd,
What drew it from you, and the cause soon learn'd:
For she whom barbarism could deny nothing,
With such prevailing earnestness desir'd it,
'Twas not in me, though it had been my death,
To hide it from her, she I say, in whom
All was, that Athens, Rome, or warlike Sparta,
Have registred for good in their best Women:
But nothing of their ill; knowing her self
Mark'd out, (I know not by what power, but sure
A cruel one) to dye, to give you children;
Having first with a setled countenance
Look'd up to Heaven, and then upon her self,
(It being the next best object) and then smil'd,
As if her joy in death to do you service,
Would break forth, in despight of the much sorrow
She shew'd she had to leave you: and then taking
Me by the hand, this hand which I must ever
Love better than I have done, since she touch'd it,
Go said she, to my Lord, (and to goe to him
Is such a happiness I must not hope for)
And tell him that he too much priz'd a trifle
Made only worthy in his love, and her
Thankful acceptance, for her sake to rob
The Orphan Kingdom of such guardians, as
Must of necessity descend from from him;
And therefore in some part of recompence
Of his much love, and to shew to the world
That 'twas not her fault only, but her fate,
That did deny to let her be the mother
Of such most certain blessings: yet for proof,
She did not envy her, that happy her,
That is appointed to them, her guick end
Should make way for her, which no sooner spoke,
But in a moment this too ready engine
Made such a battery in the choisest Castle
That ever nature made to defend life,
That strait it shook, and sunk.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Stay, dares any
Presume to shed a tear before me? or
Ascribe that worth unto themselves to merit:
To do so for her? I have done, now on.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Fall'n thus, once more she smil'd, as if that death
For her had studied a new way to sever
The soul and body, without sense of pain;
And then tell him (quoth she) what you have seen,
And with what willingness 'twas done: for which
My last request unto him is, that he
Would instantly make choice of one (most happy
In being so chosen) to supply my place,
By whom if heaven bless him with a daughter,
In my remembrance let it bear my name
Which said she dy'd.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: I hear this, and yet live;
Heart! art thou thunder proof, will nothing break thee?
She's dead, and what her entertainment may be
In th'other world without me is uncertain,
And dare I stay here unresolv'd?

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Oh Sir!

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Dear son.

speeches.speaker: Prot.
verse: Great King.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Unhand me, am I fall'n
So low, that I have lost the power to be
Disposer of my own life?

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Be but pleas'd
To borrow so much time of sorrow, as
To call to mind her last request, for whom
(I must confess a loss beyond expression)
You turn your hand upon your self, 'twas hers
And dying hers, that you should live and happy
In seeing little models of your self,
By matching with another, and will you
Leave any thing that she desir'd ungranted?
And suffer such a life that was laid down
For your sake only to be fruitless?

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Oh thou dost throw charms upon me, against which
I cannot stop my ears, bear witness heaven
That not desire of life, nor love of pleasure
Nor any future comforts, but to give
Peace to her blessed spirit in satisfying
Her last demand, makes me defer our meeting,
Which in my choice, and suddain choice shall be
To all apparent,

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: How? doe I remove one mischief
To draw upon my head a greater?

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Go, thou only good man, to whom for her self
Goodness is dear, and prepare to interr it
In her that was; oh my heart! my Ordella,
A monument worthy to be the casket
Of such a jewel.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Your command that makes way
Unto my absence is a welcome one,
For but your self there's nothing here Martel,
Can take delight to look on; yet some comfort
Goes back with me to her, who though she want it
Deserves all blessings.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: So soon to forget
The loss of such a wife, believe it will
Be censur'd in the world.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Pray you no more,
There is no argment you can use to cross it,
But does increase in me such a suspition
I would not cherish — who's that?

speeches.speaker: Memb.
verse: One, no guard
Can put back from access, whose tongue no threats
Nor praises can silence, a bold suitor, and
For that which if you are your self, a King,
You were made so to grant it, Justice, Justice.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: With what assurance dare you hope for that
Which is deny'd to me? or how can I
Stand bound to be just, unto such as are
Beneath me, that find none from those that are
Above me?

speeches.speaker: Memb.
verse: There is justice, 'twere unfit
That any thing but vengeance should fall on him,
That by his giving way to more than murther,
(For my dear fathers death was parricide)
Makes it his own.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: I charge you hear her not.

speeches.speaker: Memb.
verse: Hell cannot stop just prayers from ent'ring heaven,
I must and will be heard Sir; but remember
That he that by her plot fell, was your brother,
And the place where, your Palace, against all
Th'inviolable rites of hospitality,
Your word, a Kings word, given up for his safety,
His innocence, his protection, and the gods
Bound to revenge the impious breach of such
So great and sacred bonds; and can you wonder,
(That in not punishing such a horrid murther
You did it) that heavens favour is gone from you?
Which never will return, until his bloud
Be wash'd away in hers.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Drag hence the wretch.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Forbear, with what variety
Of torments do I meet? oh thou hast open'd
A Book, in which writ down in bloudy Letters,
My conscience finds that I am worthy of
More than I undergoe, but I'll begin
For my Ordella's sake, and for thine own
To make less heavens great anger: thou hast lost
A father, I to thee am so; the hope
Of a good Husband, in me have one; nor
Be fearful I am still no man, already
That weakness is gone from me.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: That it might
Have ever grown inseparably upon thee,
What will you do? Is such a thing as this
Worthy the lov'd Ordella's place, the daughter
Of a poor Gardener?

speeches.speaker: Memb.
verse: Your Son.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: The power
To take away that lowness is in me.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Stay yet, for rather than thou shalt add
Incest unto thy other sins, I will
With hazard of my own life, utter all,
Theodoret was thy Brother.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: You deny'd it.
Upon your oath, nor will I now believe you,
Your Protean turnings cannot change my purpose.

speeches.speaker: Memb.
verse: And for me, be assur'd the means to be
Reveng'd on thee, vile hag, admits no thought,
But what tends to it.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Is it come to that?
Then have at the last refuge: art thou grown
Insensible in all, that thou goest on
Without the least compunction? there, take that
To witness, that thou hadst a mother, which
Foresaw thy cause of grief, and sad repentance,
That so soon after blest Ordella's death
Without a tear thou canst imbrace another,
Forgetful man.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Mine eyes when she is nam'd
Cannot forget their tribute, and your gift
Is not unuseful now

speeches.speaker: Lecu.
verse: He's past all cure, that only touch is death.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: This night I'll keep it,
To morrow I will send it you, and full of my affliction.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Is the poison mortal?

speeches.speaker: Lecu.
verse: Above the help of Physick.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: To my wish,
Now for our own security, you Protaldye
Shall this night post towards Austracia,
With Letters to Theodorets bastard son,
In which we will make known what for his rising
We have done to Thierry: no denial,
Nor no excuse in such acts must be thought of,
Which all dislike, and all again commend
When they are brought unto a happy end.

speeches.speaker: Devi.
prose: NO War, no Money, no Master; banish'd the Court, not trusted in the City, whipt out of the Countrey, in what a triangle runs our misery? let me hear which of you has the best voice to beg in, for other hopes or fortunes I see you have not; be not nice, nature provided you with tones for the purpose, the peoples charity was your heritage, and I would see which of you deserves his birth-right.

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
prose: We understand you not Captain.

speeches.speaker: Devit.
prose: You see this cardicue, the last, and the only quintessence of 50 Crowns, distill'd in the limbeck of your gardage, of which happy piece thou shalt be treasurer: now he that can soonest perswade him to part with't, enjoyes it, possesses it, and with it, me and my future countenance.
If they want Art to perswade it, I'll keep it my self.

speeches.speaker: Devit.
prose: So you be not a partial judge in your own cause, you shall.

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
prose: A match.

I'll begin to you, brave Sir; be proud to make him happy by your liberality, whose tongue vouchsafes now to petition, was never heard before less than to command. I am a Soldier by profession, a Gentleman by birth, and an Officer by place, whose poverty blushes to be the cause, that so high a virtue should descend to the pity of your charity.
In any case keep your high stile, it is not charity to shame any man, much less a virtue of your eminence, wherefore preserve your worth, and I'll preserve my money.

You perswade? you are shallow, give way to merit: ah by the bread of a good man, thou hast a bonny countenance and a blith, promising mickle good to a sicker womb, that has trode a long and a fore ground to meet with friends, that will owe much to thy reverence, when they shall hear of thy courtesie to their wandring countreyman.
You that will use your friends so hardly to bring them in debt, Sir, will deserve worse of a stranger, wherefore pead on, pead on, I say.

It is the Welch must do't I see, comrade man of urship, St. Tavy be her Patron, the gods of the mountains keep her cow and her cupboard; may she never want the green of the Leek, and the fat of the Onion, if she part with her bounties to him, that is a great deal away from her cozines, and has two big suits in law to recover her heritage.

Pardon me Sir, I will have nothing to do with your suits, it comes within the statute of maintenance: home to your cozines, and some garlick and hempseed, the one will stop your hunger; the other end your suits, gammawash comrade, gammawash.
'Foot he'll hoord all for himself.

speeches.speaker: Vitry.
prose: Yes, let him; now comes my turn, I'll see if he can answer me: save you Sir, they say, you have that I want, Money.
And that you are like to want, for ought I perceive yet.

speeches.speaker: Vitry.
prose: Stand, deliver.
'Foot what mean you, you will not rob the Exchequer?

speeches.speaker: Vit.
prose: Do you prate?
Hold, hold, here Captain.
Why I could have done this before you?
And I.
And I.

speeches.speaker: Vit.
prose: You have done this, brave man be proud to make him happy, by the bread of God man, thou hast a bonny countenance, comrade man of urship, St. Tavy be her patron, out upon you, you uncurried colts, walking cans that have no souls in you, but a little Rosin to keep your ribs sweet, and hold in liquor.

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
prose: Why, what would you have us to do Captain?

speeches.speaker: Devit.
prose: Beg, beg, and keep Constables waking, wear out stocks and whipcord, maunder for butter-milk, dye of the Jaundice, yet have the cure about you, Lice, large Lice, begot of your own dust, and the heat of the Brick-kills, may you starve, and fear of the gallows, which is a gentle consumption to't, only preferr it, or may you fall upon your fear, and be hanged for selling those purses to keep you from famine, whose monies my valour empties, and be cast without other evidence; here is my Fort, my Castle of defence, who comes by shall pay me toll, the first purse is your mitimus slaves.
The purse, 'foot we'll share in the money Captain, if any come within a furlong of our fingers.
Did you doubt but we could steal as well as your self, did not I speak Welsh?
We are thieves from our cradles, and will dye so.

speeches.speaker: Vit.
prose: Then you will not beg again.

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
prose: Yes, as you did, stand, and deliver.
Hark, here comes handsel, 'tis a Trade quickly set up and as soon cast down.

speeches.speaker: Vitry.
prose: Have goodness in your minds varlets, and to't like men; he that has more money than we, cannot be our friend, and I hope there is no law for spoiling the enemy.
You need not instruct us farther, your example pleads enough.

speeches.speaker: Devitry.
prose: Disperse your selves, and as their company is, fall on.
Come, there are a band of 'em, I'll charge single.

speeches.speaker: Prot.
prose: 'Tis wonderful dark, I have lost my man, and dare not call for him, lest I should have more followers than I would pay wages to; what throws am I in, in this travel? these be honourable adventures; had I that honest bloud in my veins again Queen, that your feats and these frights have drain'd from me, honor should pull hard, e'r it drew me into these brakes.

speeches.speaker: Devitry.
prose: Who goes there?

speeches.speaker: Prot.
prose: Hey ho, here's a pang of preferment.

speeches.speaker: Devi.
prose: 'Heart, who goes there?

speeches.speaker: Prot.
prose: He that has no heart to your acquaintance, what shall I do with my Jewels and my Letter, my codpiece that's too loose; good, my boots, who is't that spoke to me? here's a friend.

speeches.speaker: Devit.
prose: We shall find that presently, stand, as you love your safety, stand.

speeches.speaker: Prot.
prose: That unlucky word of standing, has brought me to all this, hold, or I shall never stand you.

speeches.speaker: Devit.
prose: I should know that voice, deliver.

speeches.speaker: Prot.
prose: All that I have is at your service Gentlemen, and much good may it do you.

speeches.speaker: Devit.
prose: Zones down with him, do you prate?

speeches.speaker: Prot.
prose: Keep your first word as you are Gentlemen, and let me stand, alas, what do you mean?
To tye you to us Sir, bind you in the knot of friendship.

speeches.speaker: Prot.
prose: Alas Sir, all the physick in Europe cannot bind me.

speeches.speaker: Devit.
prose: You should have jewels about you, stones, precious stones.
Captain away, there's company within hearing, if you stay longer, we are surpriz'd.

speeches.speaker: Devit.
prose: Let the Devil come, I'll pillage this Fregat a little better yet.
'Foot we are lost, they are upon us.

speeches.speaker: Devit.
prose:
Ha, upon us, make the least noise, 'tis thy part
^ng gaspe.
Which way shall we make Sir?

speeches.speaker: Devit.
prose: Every man his own; do you hear, only bind me, bind me before you goe, and when the company's past, make to this place again, this karvel should have better lading in him, you are slow, why do you not tye harder?
You are sure enough I warrant you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Devit.
prose: Darkness befriend you, away.

speeches.speaker: Prot.
prose: What tyrants have I met with, they leave me alone in the dark, yet would not have me cry. I shall grow won drous melancholly if I stay long here without company; I was wont to get a nap with saying my prayers, I'll see if they will work upon me now; but then, if I should talk in my sleep, and they hear me, they would make a Recorder of my windpipe, slit my throat: heaven be prais'd, I hear some noise, it may be new purchase, and then I shall have fellows.

speeches.speaker: Devit.
prose: They are gone past hearing, now to taske Devitry, help, help, as you are men help; some charitable hand, relieve a poor distressed miserable wretch, thieves, wicked thieves have robb'd me; bound me.

speeches.speaker: Prot.
prose: 'Foot, would they had gagg'd you top, your noise will betray us, and fetch them again.

speeches.speaker: Devit.
prose: What blessed tongue spake to me, where, where where are you Sir?

speeches.speaker: Prot.
prose: A plague of your bawling throat, we are well enough if you have the grace to be thankful for't, do but snore to me, and 'tis as much as I desire, to pass away time with, till morning, then talk as loud as you please Sir, I am bound not to stir, therefore lie still and snore I say.

speeches.speaker: Devit.
prose: Then you have met with thieves too I see.

speeches.speaker: Prot.
prose: And desire to meet with no more of them.

speeches.speaker: Devit.
prose: Alas, what can we suffer more? they are far enough by this time; have they not all, all that we have Sir?

speeches.speaker: Prot.
prose: No by my faith have they not Sir; I gave them one trick to boot for their learning, my Boots Sir, my Boots, I have ^'d my stock, and my jewels in them, and therefore desire to hear no more of them.

speeches.speaker: Devit.
prose: Now blessing on your wit, Sir, what a dull slave was I? dreamt not of your conveyance, help to unbind me Sir, and I'll undoe you, my life for yours, no worse thief than my self meets you again this night.

speeches.speaker: Prot.
prose: Reach me thy hands,

speeches.speaker: Devit.
prose: Here Sir, here, I could beat my brains out, that could not think of boots, boots Sir, wide top^ boots, I shall love them the better whilst I live; but are you fare your Jewels are here Sir?

speeches.speaker: Prot.
prose: Sure sayst thou? ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Devit.
prose: So ho, illo ho.
Here Captain. here.

speeches.speaker: Prot.
prose: 'Foot what do you mean Sir?

speeches.speaker: Devit.
prose: A trick to boot, say you; here you dull slaves, purchase, purchase the soul of the Rock, Diamonds, spark~ling Diamonds.

speeches.speaker: Prot.
prose: I'm betraid, lost, past recovery, lost, as you are men

speeches.speaker: Devit.
prose: Nay rook, since you will be prating, we'll s^are your carrion with you, have you any other conveyance now Sir?
'Foot hereare Letters, Epistles, familiar Epistles, we'll see what treasure is in them, they are seal'd sure.

speeches.speaker: Prot.
prose: Gentlemen, as you are Gentlemen spare my Letters, and take all willingly, all: I'll give you a release, a general release, and meet you here to morrow with as much more.

speeches.speaker: Devit.
prose: Nay, since you have your tricks, and your conveyances, we will not leave a wrinkle of you unseare^t.

speeches.speaker: Prot.
prose: Hark, there comes company, you will be betraid, as you love your safeties, beat out my brains, I shall betray you else.

speeches.speaker: Devit.
prose: Treason, unheard of Treason, monstrous, monstrous villanies.

speeches.speaker: Prot.
prose: I confess my self a Traitor, shew your selves good subjects, and hang me up for't.
If it be treason, the discovery will get our pardon, Captain.

speeches.speaker: Devit.
prose: Would we were all lost, hang'd, quarter'd, to save this one, one innocent Prince; Thierry's poison'd, by his mother poison'd, the Mistriss to this stallion, who by that poison ne'er shall sleep again.
'Foot let us mince him by piece-meals, till he eat himself up.
Let us dig out his heart with needles, and half broil him, like a Mussel.

speeches.speaker: Prot.
prose: Such another and I prevent you, my bloud's setled already.

speeches.speaker: Devit.
prose: Here's that shall remove it, road, viper, drag him unto Martel, unnatural paricide, cruel, bloudy woman.

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
prose: On you dogfish, leech, caterpillar.

speeches.speaker: Devit.
prose: A longer sight of him will make my rage turn pity, and with his suddain end, prevent revenge and torture, wicked, wicked Brunhalt.
Not sleep at all, no means.
No Art can do it.

speeches.speaker: Bawdb.
verse: I will assure you, he can sleep no more
Than a hooded Hawks, a centinel to him,
Or one of the City Constables are tops.
How came he so?

speeches.speaker: Bawdb.
verse: They are too wise that dare know,
Something's amiss, heaven help all.
What cure has he?

speeches.speaker: Bawdb.
verse: Armies of those we call
Physitians, some with glisters,
Some with Lettice-caps, some posset-drinks, some Pills,
Twenty consulting here about a drench,
The bringing in of Leonor the bastard
Son to your murther'd brother, her Physitian
By this time is attacht to that damn'd devil.

speeches.speaker: Mess.
verse: 'Tis like he will be so, for e'er we came
Fearing an equal justice for his mischiefs,
He drencht himself.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: He did like one of mine then.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Must I still see these miseries, no night
To hide me from their horrors, that Protaldy
See justice fall upon.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Now I could sleep too.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: I'll give you yet more Poppy, bring the Lady
And heaven in her embraces; gives him quiet,
Madam, unveil your self.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: I do forgive you,
And though you sought my bloud, yet I'll pray for you.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: Art thou alive?

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Now could you sleep?

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: For ever.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Go carry her without wink of sleep, or quiet,
Where her strong knave Protaldye's broke o'th' wheel,
And let his cries and roars be musick to her,
I mean to waken her.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Do her no wrong.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Nor right, as you love justice.

speeches.speaker: Brun.
verse: I will think,
And if there be new curses in old nature,
I have a soul dare send them.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Keep her waking.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: What's that appears so sweetly? there's that face.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Be moderate, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: That Angels face.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Goe nearer.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Martel. I cannot last long, see the soul,
I see it perfectly of my Ordella,
The heavenly figure of her sweetness there,
Forgive me gods, it comes, Divinest substance,
Kneel, kneel, kneel every one, Saint of thy Sex,
If it be for my cruelty thou comest,
Do ye see her hoe?

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Yes Sir, and you shall know her.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Down, down again, to be reveng'd for bloud,
Sweet Spirit I am ready, she smiles on me,
O blessed sign of Peace.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Goe nearer Lady.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: I came to make you happy.

speeches.speaker: Thier,
verse: Hear you that, Sir?
She comes to crown my soul away, get sacrifice
Whilst I with holy Honors.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: She's alive, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: In everlasting life, I know it friend,
Oh happy, happy soul.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: Alas, I live Sir,
A mortal woman still.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Can spirits weep too?

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: She's no spirit Sir, pray kiss her, Lady,
Be very gentle to him.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Stay, she is warm,
And by my life the same lips tell me brightness,
Are you the same Ordella still?

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: The same, Sir.
Whom heavens and my good Angel staid from ruin.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Kiss me again.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: The same still, still your servant.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: 'Tis she, I know her now Martel; sit down sweet.
Oh blest and happiest woman, a dead slumber
Begins to creep upon me, oh my jewel!

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: Oh sleep my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: My joyes are too much for me.

speeches.speaker: Mess.
verse: Brunhalt impatient of her constraint to see
Protaldye tortur'd, has choak'd her self.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: No more, her sins go with her.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Love, I must die, I faint, close up my glasses.

speeches.speaker: 1 Doct.
verse: The Queen faints too, and deadly.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: One dying kiss.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: My last Sir, and my dearest, and now
Close my eyes too.

speeches.speaker: Thier.
verse: Thou perfect woman.
Martel, the Kingdom's yours, take Memberge to you,
And keep my line alive; nay, weep not, Lady,
Take me, I go.

speeches.speaker: Ordel.
verse: Take me too, farewel honour

speeches.speaker: 2 Doct.
verse: They are gone for ever.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: The peace of happy souls go after them,
Bear them to their last beds, whilst I study
A Tomb to speak their loves; whilst old time lasteh
I am your King in sorrows.

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
verse: We your subjects.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Devitry, for your service, be near us,
Whip out these instruments of this mad mother
From Court, and all good people; and because
She was born Noble, let that Title find her
A private grave, but neither tongue nor honor:
And now lead on, they that shall read this story,
Shall find that Virtue lives in Good, not Glory.
TIs now the sweetest time for sleep, the night is scarce spent, Arrigo, what's a clock?

speeches.speaker: Arri.
verse: Past four.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Is it so much, and yet the morn not up?
See yonder where the shamefac'd Maiden comes
Into our sight how gently doth she slide,
Hiding her chaste cheeks, like a modest Bride,
With a red veil of blushes; as if she,
Even such all modest virtuous Women be.
Why thinks your Lordship I am up so soon?

speeches.speaker: Lucio.
verse: About some weighty State plot.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: And what thinks your knighthood of it?

speeches.speaker: Arr.
verse: I do think to cure some strange corruptions in the Common-wealth.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Y'are well conceited of your selves to think
I chuse you out to bear me company
In such affairs and business of state:
For am not I a pattern for all Princes,
That break my soft sleep for my subjects good?
Am I not careful? very provident?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Your Grace is careful.

speeches.speaker: Arri.
verse: Very provident.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Nay, knew you how my serious working plots,
Concern the whole Estates of all my subjects,
I, and their lives; then Lucio thou wouldst swear,
I were a loving Prince.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I think your Grace intends to walk the publick streets disguis'd, to see the streets disorders.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: It is not so

speeches.speaker: Arri.
prose: You secretly will cross some other states, that do conspire against you.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Weightier far:
You are my friends, and you shall have the cause;
I break my sleeps thus soon to see a wench.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Y'are wond'rous careful for your subjects good.

speeches.speaker: Arri.
verse: You are a very loving Prince indeed.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: This care I take for them, when their dull eyes,
Are clos'd with heavy slumbers.

speeches.speaker: Arri.
verse: Then you rise to see your wenches?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: What Milan beauty hath the power, to charme her Sovereign eyes, and break his sleeps:

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Sister to Count Valore, she's a Maid
Would make a Prince forget his throne, and sta^e,
And lowly kneel to her: the general fate
Of all mortality, is hers to give;
As she disposeth, so we die and live.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: My Lord, the day grows clear, the Court will rise.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose:
We stay too long, is the
~mbrances head as we commanded, sent to the sad Gondarino, our General?

speeches.speaker: Arr.
verse: 'Tis sent.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: But stay, where shines that light?

speeches.speaker: Arri.
verse: 'Tis in the chamber of Lazarello.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Lazarillo? what is he?

speeches.speaker: Ar^i.
prose: A Courtier my Lord, and one that I wonder your Grace knows not: for he hath followed your Court, and your last predecessors, from place to place, any time this seven years, as faithfully as your Spits and your Drippingpans have done, and almost as greasily.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Oh we know him, as we have heard, he keeps a Kalender of all the dishes of meat, that have been in the Court, ever since our great Grandfathers time; and when he can thrust in at no Table, he makes his meat of that.

speeches.speaker: Lucio.
prose: The very same my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: A Courtier call'st thou him?
B^lieve me Lucio, there be many such
About our Court, respected, as they think,
Even by our self; with thee I will be plain:
Than ^or love of it, though we seldom hate it:
And yet we know all these, and when we please,
Can touch the wheel, and turn their names about.
prose: We Princes do use, to preferre many for nothing, and to take particular and free knowledg, almost in the nature of acquaintance of many; whom we do use only for our pleasures, and to give largely to numbers; more out of policy ^o be thought liberal, and by that means to make the people strive to deserve our Love; than to reward any particular desert of theirs, to whom we give: and do suffer our s^lves to hear flatterers, more for recreation

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I wonder they that know their states so well, should ^ancy such base slaves.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Thou wond'rest Lucio,
Dost not thou think, if thou wert Duke of Milan,
Thou should'st be flattered?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: I know my Lord, I would not.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Arrigo it grows late, for see, fair Thetis hath undone the barrs
To Phebus team; and his unrival'd light,
Hath chac'd the mornings modest blush away:
Now must we to our love, bright Paphian Queen;
Thou Cytberean goddess, that delights
In stirring glances, and art still thy self,
More toying than thy team of Sparrows be;
Thou laughing Errecina, oh inspire
Her heart with love, or lessen my desire.
prose: Why so, I thought till I was Duke, I thought I should have left me no more flatterers, than there are now Plain-dealers; and yet for all this my resolution, I am most palpably flattered: the poor man may loath covetousness and flattery, but fortune will alter the mind when the wind turns: there may be well a little conflict, but it will drive the billows before it.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: Go run, search, pry in every nook and angle of the Kitchins, Larders, and Pasteries, know what meat's boil'd, bak'd, rost, stew'd, fri'd, or sous'd, at this dinner to be serv'd directly, or indirectly. to every several Table in the Court, be gone.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: I run, but not so fast as your mouth will do upon the stroke of Eleven.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: Oh thou goddess of Plenty
Fill me this day with some rare delicates
And I will every year most constantly,
As this day celebrate a sumptuous Feast,
If thou wilt send me victuals in thine honor?
And to it shall be bidden for thy sake,
Even all the valiant stomachs in the Court:
All short-cloak'd Knights, and all cross-garter'd Gentlemen,
All pump and pantosle, foot-cloth riders;
With all the swarming generation
Of long stocks, short pain'd hose, and huge stuff'd doublets:
All these shall eat, and which is more than yet
Hath e'er been seen, they shall be satisfied
I wonder my Ambassador returns not?
prose: What an excellent thing did God bestow upon man, when he gave him a good stomach? what unbounded graces there are pour'd upon them that have the continual command of the very best of these blessings? 'tis an excellent thing to be a Prince; he is serv'd with such admirable variety of Fare; such innumerable choice of Delicates; his Tables are full fraught with most nourishing food, and his Cubbards heavy laden with rich Wines; his Court is still filled with most pleasant variety: In the Summer, his Palace is full of Green Geese; and in Winter it swarmeth with Woodcocks,

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Here I am Master.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
verse: And welcome:
Never did that sweet Virgin in her smock,
Fair-cheek'd Andromeda, when to the rock
Her Ivorie limbs were chain'd, and straight before
A huge Sea-monster, tumbling to the shore,
To have devour'd her, with more longing sight
Expect the coming of some hardy Knight,
That might have quell'd his pride, and set her free,
Than I with longing sight have look'd for thee.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Your Perseus is come Master, that will destroy him,
The very comfort of whose presence shuts
The monster hunger from your yelping guts

speeches.speaker: Laza.
prose: Brief boy, brief, discourse the service of each several Table compendiously.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Here's a Bill of all Sir.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
verse: I, this is it on which my hopes relye,
Within this paper all my joyes are clos'd:
Boy, open it, and read it with reverence.
prose: Give it me, a Bill of all the several services this day appointed for every Table in the Court,

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: For the Captain of the Guards Table, three chines of Beef, and two joals of Sturgeon.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
verse: A portly service, but gross, gross, proceed to the
Dukes own Table, dear boy, to the Dukes own Table,

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse:
For the Dukes own Table, the head of an
~mbrana.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
prose: Is't possible? can Heaven be so propitious to the Duke?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Yes, I'll assure you Sir, 'tis possible, Heaven is so propitious to him.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
verse: Why then he is the richest Prince alive:
He were the wealthiest Monarch in all Europe,
Had he no other Territories, Dominions, Provinces, Seats,,

Not Palaces, but only that
~mbrana's head.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: 'Tis very fresh and sweet, Sir, the fish was taken but this night, and the head, as a rare novelty, appointed by special commandement for the Dukes own Table, this dinner.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
verse: If poor unworthy I may come to eat
Of this most sacred dish, I here do vow
(If that blind Huswife, Fortune will bestow
But means on me) to keep a sumptuous house,
prose: A board groaning under the heavy burden of the beasts that cheweth the cudd, and the Fowl that cutteth the Air: I shall not like the Table of a countrey Justice, besprinkled over with all manner of cheap Sallads, sliced Beef, Giblets, and Petitoes, to fill up room, nor should there stand any great, cumbersom, un-cut-up pies, at the nether end fill'd with moss and stones, partly to make a shew with and partly to keep the lower Mess from eating, nor shall my meat come in sheaking, like the City service, one dish a quarter of an hour after another, and gone, as if they had appointed to meet there, and had mistook the hour, nor should it, like the new Court service, come in in haste, as if it fain would be gone again, all courses at once, like a hunting breakfast, but I would have my several courses, and my dishes well fill'd, my first course should be brought in after the antient manner, by a score of old bleer-ey'd Serving-men, in long blew coats, (marry they shall buy Silk, Facing, and Buttons themselves) but that's by the way.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Master the time calls on, will you be walking?

speeches.speaker: Laza.
verse: Follow boy, follow, my guts were half an hour since in the privy Kitchin.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
verse: Faith brother, I must needs go yonder.

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: And faith Sister what will you do yonder?

speeches.speaker: Oria.
verse: I know the Lady Honoria will be glad to see me.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Glad to see you? faith the Lady Honoria cares for you as she doth for all other young Ladies, she's glad to see you, and will shew you the Privy Garden, and tell you how many Gowns the Duchess had; Marry if you have ever an old Uncle, that would be a Lord, or ever a kinsman that hath done a murther, or committed a robbery, and will give good store of Money to procure his pardon, then the Lady Honoria will be glad to see you.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
verse: I, but they say one shall see fine fights at the Court.

speeches.speaker: Count.
