prose: I'll tell you what you shall see, you shall see many faces of mans making, for you shall find very few as God left them: and you shall see many legs too; amongst the rest you shall behold one pair, the feet of which, were in times past, sockless, but are now through the change of time (that alters all things) very strangely become the legs of a Knight and a Courtier; another pair you shall see, that were heir apparent legs to a Glover, these legs hope shortly to be honourable; when they pass by they will bow, and the mouth to these legs, will seem to offer you some Courtship; it will not swear, but it it will lye, hear it not.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
verse: Why, and are not these fine sights?

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: Sister, in seriousness you yet are young
And fair, a fair young Maid, and apt.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
verse: Apt?

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: Exceeding apt to be drawn to.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
verse: To what?

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: To that you should not be, 'tis no dispraise,
She is not bad that hath desire to ill,
But she that hath no power to rule that Will:
For there you shall be wooed in other kinds
Than yet your years have known, the chiefest men
Will seem to throw themselves
As vassals at your voice, kiss your hand,
Prepare your Banquets, Masques, Shews, all inticements
That Wit and Lust together can devise,
To draw a Lady from the state of Grace
To an old Lady widdows Gallery;
And they will praise your virtues, beware that,
The only way to turn a Woman whore,
Is to commend her chastity: you'll goe?

speeches.speaker: Oria.
verse: I would go, if it were but only to shew you, that
I could be there, and be mov'd with none of these tricks.

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: Your servants are ready!

speeches.speaker: Oria.
verse: An hour since.

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: Well, if you come off clear from this hot service,
Your praise shall be the greater. Farewel Sister.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
verse: Farewel Brother.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Once more, if you stay in the presence till candle-light, keep on the foreside o'th' Curtain; and do you hear, take heed of the old Bawd, in the cloth of Tissue sleeves, and the knit Mittines. Farewel Sister.

Now am I idle, I would I had been a Scholar, that I might a studied now: the punishment of meaner men is, they have too much to do; our only misery is, that without company we know not what to do; I must take some of the common courses of our Nobility; which is thus: if I can find no company that likes me, pluck off my Hatband, throw an old Cloak over my face, and as if I would not be known, walk hastily through the streets, till I be discovered; then there goes Count such a one, says one; there goes Count such a one, says another: Look how fast he goes, says a third; there's some great matters in hand questionless, says a fourth; when all my business is to hav^ them say so: this hath been used; or if I can find any com~pany, I'll after dinner to the Stage, to see a Play; where, when I first enter, you shall have a m^rmure in the house, every one that does not know cries, What Nobleman is that? all the Gallants on the Stage rise, vail to me, kiss their hand, offer me their places: then I pick out some one, whom I please to grace among the rest, take his seat, use it, throw my cloak over my face, and laugh at him: the poor Gentleman imagines himself most highly grac'd, thinks all the Auditors esteem him one of my bosom friends; and in right special regard with me. But here comes a Gentleman, that I hope will make me better sport, than either street and stage fooleries.

This man loves to eat good meat, always provided, he do not pay for it himself, he goes by the name of the Hungry Courtier, marry, because I think that name will not sufficiently distinguish him, for no doubt he hath more fellows there, his name is Lazarello, he is none of these ordinary eaters, that will devour three breakfasts, and as many dinners, without any prejudi^e to their Beavers, Drinkings, or Suppers; but he hath a more courtly kind of hunger, and doth hunt more after novelty, than plenty, I'll over-hear him.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
verse: Oh thou most itching kindly appetite,
Which every creature in his stomach feels;
Oh leave, leave yet at last thus to torment me.
Three several Sallads have I sacrific'd,
Bedew'd with precious oil and vinegar
Already to appease thy greedy wrath. Boy.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
verse: Will the Count speak with me?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: One of his Gentlemen is gone to inform him of your coming, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
prose: There is no way left for me to compass the Fish-head, but by being presently made known to the Duke.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: That will be hard Sir.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
verse: When I have tasted of this sacred dish,
Then shall my bones rest in my Fathers tomb
In peace; then shall I dye most willingly,
And as a dish be serv'd to satisfie,
Deaths hunger, and I will be buried thus:
My Bier shall be a charger born by four,
The Cossin where I lye, a powd'ring-tub,
Bestrew'd with Lettice, and cool Sallad herbs,
My Winding-sheet of Tansies, the black Guard
Shall be my solemn Mourners, and instead
Of ceremonies, wholsom burial Prayers:
A printed dirge in rhyme, shall bury me.
Instead of tears, let them pour Capon sauce upon my h^arse,
And salt instead of dust, Manchets for stones, for other glorious shields
Give me a Voider; and above my Hearse
For a Trutch sword, my naked knife stuck up.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Master, the Count's here.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
verse: Where? my Lord I do beseech you.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Y'are very welcome Sir, I pray you stand up, you shall dine with me.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
verse: I do beseech your Lordship by the love
I still have born to your honourable house.

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: Sir, what need all this? you shall dine with me, I pray rise.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
prose: Perhaps your Lordship takes me for one of these same fellows, that do as it were respect victuals.

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: Oh Sir by no means.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
prose: Your Lordship has often promised, that whensoever I should affect greatness, your own hand should help to raise me.

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: And so much still assure your self of.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
prose: And though I must confess, I have ever shun'd popularity, by the example of others, yet I do now feel my self a little ambitious, your Lordship is great, and though young, yet a Privy Counsellor.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: I pray you Sir leap into the matter, what would
You have me do for you?

speeches.speaker: Laza.
prose: I would intreat your Lordship to make me known to the Duke.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: When Sir?

speeches.speaker: Laza.
prose: Suddainly my Lord, I would have you present me unto him this morning.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: It shall be done, but for what virtues, would you have him take notice of you?

speeches.speaker: Laza.
prose: Your Lordship shall know that presently.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: 'Tis pity of this fellow, he is of good wit, and sufficient understanding, when he is not troubled with this greedy worm.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
prose: 'Faith, you may intreat him to take notice of me for any thing; for being an excellent Farrier, for playing well at Span-counter, or sticking knives in walls, for being impudent, or for nothing; why may not I be a Favorite on the suddain? I see nothing against it.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Not so Sir, I know you have not the face to be a
Favourite on the suddain.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: Why then you shall present me as a Gentleman well qualified, or one extraordinary seen in divers strange mysteries.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: In what Sir? as how?

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: Marry as thus.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Yonder's my old Spirit, that hath haunted me daily, ever since I was a privy Counsellor, I must be rid of him, I pray you stay there, I am a little busie, I will speak with you presently.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
prose: You shall bring me in, and after a little other talk taking me by the hand, you shall utter these words to the Duke: May it please your grace, to take note of a Gentleman, well read, deeply learned, and throughly grounded in the hidden knowledge of all Sallads and Pot-herbs whatsoever.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: 'Twill be rare if you will walk before, Sir, I will overtake you instantly.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
prose: Your Lordships ever.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: This fellow is a kind of an informer, one that lives in Alehouses and Taverns, and because he perceives some worthy men in this Land, with much labour and great expence, to have discovered things dangerously hanging over the State; he thinks to discover as much out of the talk of drunkards in Tap-houses: he brings me informations, pick'd out of broken words, in mens common talk, which, with his malicious mis-application, he hopes will seem dangerous, he doth besides, bring me the names of all the young Gentlemen in the City, that use Ordinaries, or Taverns, talking (to my thinking) only as the freedom of their youth teach them, without any further ends; for dangerous and seditious spirits; he is besides, an arrant whoremaster, as any is in Milan, of a Lay-man; I will not meddle with the Clergy: he is parcel Lawyer, and in my conscience much of their religion, I must put upon him some piece of service; come hither Sir, what have you to do with me?

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: Little my Lord, I only come to know how your Lordship would employ me.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Observed you that Gentleman, that parted from me but now?

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: I saw him now my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: I was sending for you, I have talked with this man, and I do find him dangerous.

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: Is your Lordship in good earnest?

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Hark you Sir, there may perhaps be some within ear-shots.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: Sirrah, will you venture your life, the Duke hath sent the Fish-head to my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Sir if he have not, kill me, do what you will with me.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: How uncertain is the state of all mortal things? I have these crosses from my Cradle, from my very Cradle, insomuch that I do begin to grow desperate: Fortune I do despise thee, do thy worst; yet when I do better gather my self together, I do find it is rather the part of a wise man, to prevent the storms of Fortune by stirring, than to suffer them by standing still, to pour themselves upon his naked body, I will about it.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Who's within there?

Let this Gentleman out at the back door, forget not my instructions, if you find any thing dangerous; trouble not your self to find out me, but carry your informations to the Lord Lucio, he is a man grave, and well experienced in these businesses.

speeches.speaker: Int.
prose: Your Lordships Servant.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Your Lordships servant.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: Will it please your Lordship to walk?

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Sir I was coming, I will overtake you.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: I will attend you over against the Lord Gonderinoes house.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: You shall not attend there long.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: Thither must I to see my Loves face, the chaste
Virgin head
Of a dear Fish, yet pure and undeflowred,
Not known of man no rough bred countrey hand,
Hath once toucht thee, no Pandars withered paw,
Nor an un-napkin'd Lawyers greasie fist,
Hath once slubbered thee: no Ladies supple hand,
Wash'd o'er with Urine, hath yet seiz'd on thee
With her two nimble talents: no Court hand,
Whom his own natural filth, or change of air,
Hath bedeck'd with scabs, hath marr'd thy whiter grace:
Oh let it be thought lawful then for me,
To crop the flower of thy Virginity.

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: This day I am for fools, I am all theirs,
Though like to our young wanton cocker'd heirs,
Who do affect those men above the rest,
In whose base company they still are best:
I do not with much labour strive to be
The wisest ever in the company:
But for a fool, our wisdom oft amends,
As enemies do teach us more than friends.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: MY Lord:

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: Ha!

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: Here's one hath brought you a present,

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: From whom? from a woman? if it be from a woman, bid him carrie it back, and tell her she's a whore; what is it?

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: A Fish head my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: What Fish head?

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: I did not aske that my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: Whence comes it?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: From the Court.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: O 'tis a Cods-head.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
prose: No my Lord, 'tis some strange head, it comes from the Duke.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Let it be carried to my Mercer, I doe owe him money for silks, stop his mouth with that.
Was there ever any man that hated his wife after death but I? and for her sake all women, women that were created only for the preservation of little dogs.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
prose: My Lord the Count's sister being overtaken in the streets, with a great hail-storm, is light at your gate, and desires Rome till the storm be overpast.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Is she a woman?

speeches.speaker: Serv.
prose: I my Lord I think so.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: I have none for her then: bid her get her gone, tell her she is not welcome.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
prose: My Lord, she is now comming up.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: She shall not come up, tell her any thing; tell her I have but one great room in my house, and I am now in it at the close stool.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
prose: She's here my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: O impudence of women: I can keep dogs out of my house, or I can defend my house against theeves, but I cannot keep out women.
Now Madam, what hath your Ladyship to say to me?

speeches.speaker: Oria.
prose: My Lord, I was bold to crave the help of your house against the storm.

speeches.speaker: Gond,
prose: Your Ladyships boldness in coming will be impudence in staying; for you are most unwelcome.

speeches.speaker: Oriana.
prose: Oh my Lord!

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Doe you laugh? by the hate I bear to you, 'tis true.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
prose: Y'are merry my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Let me laugh to death if I be, or can be whilst thou art here, or livest; or any of thy sex.

speeches.speaker: Oriana.
prose: I commend your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Gond,
prose: Doe you commend me? why doe you commend ^e? I give you no such cause: thou art a silthy impudent whore; a woman, a very woman.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
prose: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Begot when thy father was drunk.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
prose: Your Lordship hath a good wit.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: How? what have I a good wit?

speeches.speaker: Orian.
prose:
Come my Lord, I have heard before of your Lord
^hip merry vain in jesting against our Sex, which I being ^esirous to hear, made me rather choose your Lordships ^ouse, than any other, but I know I am welcome.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Let me not live if you be: me thinks it doth not ^ecome you, to come to my house being a stranger to you, I have no woman in my house, to entertain you, nor to shew you your chamber; why should you come to me? I have no Galleries, nor banqueting houses, nor bawdy pictures to shew your Ladyship.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
prose: Believe me this your Lordships plainess makes me think my self more welcome, than if you had sworn by all the pretty Court oaths that are, I had been welcomer than your soul to your body.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Now she's in, talking treason will get her out, I durst sooner undertake to talk an Intelligencer out of the room, and speak more than he durst hear, than talk a woman out of my company.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
prose: My Lord the Duke being in the streets, and the storm continuing, is entred your gate, and now coming up.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: The Duke! now I know your Errand Madam; you have plots and private meetings in hand: why doe you choose my house? are you asham'd to goe to't in the old coupling place, though it be less suspicious here; for no Christian will suspect a woman to be in my house? yet you may do it cleanlyer there, for there is a care had of those businesses; and wheresoever you remove, your great maintainer and you shall have your lodgings directly opposite, it is but putting on your night-gown, and your shippers; Madam, you understand me?

speeches.speaker: Orian.
prose: Before I would not understand him, but now he speaks riddles to me indeed.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: 'Twas a strange hail-storm.

speeches.speaker: Lucio.
prose: 'Twas exceeding strange.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Good morrow to your grace.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Good morrow Gonderino.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Justice great Prince.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Why should you beg for justice, I never did you wrong; What's the offendor?

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: A woman.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: I know your ancient quarrell against that Sex; but what hainous crime hath she committed?

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: She hath gone abroad.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: What? it cannot be.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: She hath done it.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: How? I never heard of any woman that did so before.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: If she have not laid by that modesty
That should attend a Virgin, and, quite void
Of shame, hath left the house where she was born,
As they should never doe; let me endure
The pains that she should suffer.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Hath she so? Which is the woman?

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: This, this.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: How! Arrigo: Lucio:

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: I then it is a plot, no Prince alive
Shall force me make my house a Brothell house;
Not for the sins, but for the womans sake,
I will not have her in my doors so long:
Will they make my house as bawdy as their own are?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Is it not Oriana?

speeches.speaker: Lucio.
verse: 'Tis.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Sister to Count Valero?

speeches.speaker: Arri.
verse: The very same.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: She that I love?

speeches.speaker: Lucio.
verse: She that you love.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I do suspect

speeches.speaker: Lucio.
verse: So doe I.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: This fellow to be but a counterfeit,
One that doth seem to loath all woman-kind,
To hate himself, because he hath some part
Of woman in him; seems not to endure
To see, or to be seen of any woman,
Only, because he knows it is their nature
To wish to tast that which is most forbidden:
And with this shew he may the better compass
(And with far less suspition) his base ends.

speeches.speaker: Lucio.
verse: Upon my life 'tis so.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: And I doe know,
Before his slain wife gave him that offence,
He was the greatest servant to that Sex
That ever was: what doth this Lady here
With him alone? why should he rail at her to me?

speeches.speaker: Lucio.
verse: Because your grace might not suspect.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: 'Twas so: I doe love her strangely:
I would fain know the truth: counsell me.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: It falls out better than we could expect Sir, that we should find the Duke and my Lord Gondarino together; both which you desire to be acquainted with.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: 'Twas very happy: Boy, goe down into the kitchen, and see if you can spy that same; I am now in some hope: I have me thinks a kind of fever upon me.

A certain gloominess within me, doubting as it were, betwixt two passions: there is no young maid upon her wedding night, when her husband sets first foot in the bed, blushes, and looks pale again, oftner than I doe now. There is no Poet acquainted with more shakings and quakings, towards the latter end of this new play, when he's in that case, that he stands peeping betwixt Curtains, so fearfully that a Bottle of Ale cannot be opened, but he thinks some body hisses, than I am at this instant.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Are they in consultation? If they be, either my young Duke hath gotten some Bastard, and is persuading my Knight yonder to father the child, and marry the wench, or else some Cock-pit is to be built.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: My Lord! what Nobleman's that?

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: His name is Lucio, 'tis he that was made a Lord at the request of some of his friends for his wives sake: he affects to be a great States-man, and thinks it consists in night-caps and jewells, and tooth-picks?

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: And what's that other?

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: A Knight Sir, that pleaseth the Duke to favour, and to raise to some extraordinary fortunes, he can make as good men as himself, every day in the week, and doth—

speeches.speaker: Laz:
prose: For what was he raised?

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Truely Sir, I am not able to say directly, for what; But for wearing of red breeches as I take it; he's a brave man, he will spend three Knighthoods at a Supper without Trumpets.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
prose: My Lord I'll talk with him, for I have a friend, that would gladly receive the humor.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: If he have the itch of Knighthood upon him, let him repair to that Physitian, he'll cure him: but I will give you a note; is your friend fat or lean?

speeches.speaker: Laz,
prose: Something fat.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: 'Twill be the worse for him.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
prose: I hope that's not material.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Very much, for there is an impost set upon Knighthoods, & your friend shall pay a Noble in the pound.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I doe not like examinations,
We shall find out the truth more easily,
Some other way less noted, and that course,
Should not be us'd, till we be sure to prove
Some thing directly, for when they perceive
Themselves suspected, they will then provide
More warily to answer.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Doth she know your Grace doth love her?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: She hath never heard it.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Then thus my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: What's he that walks alone so sadly with his hands behind him?

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: The Lord of the house, he that you desire to be acquainted with, he doth hate women for the same cause that I love them.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: What's that?

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: For that which Apes want: you perceive me Sir?

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: And is he sad? Can he be sad that hath so rich a gem under his roof, as that which I doe follow.
What young Lady's that?

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Which? Have I mine eye-sight perfect, 'tis my sister: did I say the Duke had a Bastard? What should she make here with him and his Councell? She hath no papers in her hand to petition to them, she hath never a husband in prison, whose release she might sue for: That's a fine trick for a wench; to get her husband clapt up, that she may more freely, and with less suspition, visit the private studies of men in authority. Now I doe discover their consultation, you fellow is a Pander without all salvation: But let me not condemn her too rashly without weighing the matter, she's a young Lady, she went forth early this morning with a waiting woman, and a Page, or so: This is no garden house, in my conscience she went forth with no dishonest intent: for she did not pretend going to any Sermon in the further end of the City: Neither went she to see any odd old Gentlewoman, that mourns for the death of her husband, or the loss of her friend, and must have young Ladys come to comfort her: those are the damnable Bawds: 'Twas no set meeting certainly; for there was no wafer-woman with her these three days on my knowledge: I'll talk with her; Good morrow my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Y'are welcome Sir: here's her brother come now to doe a kind office for his sister; is it not strange?

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: I am glad to meet you here sister.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
prose: I thank you good brother: and if you doubt of the cause of my coming I can satisfie you.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: No faith, I dare trust thee, I doe suspect thou art honest; for it is so rare a thing to be honest amongst you, that some one man in an age, may perhaps suspect some two women to be honest, but never believe it verily.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
prose: Let your return be suddain.

speeches.speaker: Arri.
prose: Unsuspected by them.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: It shall; so shall I best perceive their Love, if there be any; Farewell.

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: Let me entreat your grace to stay a little,
To know a gentleman, to whom your self
Is much beholding; he hath made the sport
For your whole Court these eight years, on my knowledge.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: His name?

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Lazarello.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: I heard of him this morning, which is he?

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Lazarello, pluck up thy spirits, thy Fortune is now raising, the Duke calls for thee, and thou shalt be acquainted with him.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: He's going away, and I must of necessity stay here upon business.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: 'Tis all one, thou shalt know him first.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: Stay a little, if he should offer to take me away with him, and by that means I should loose that I seek for; but if he should I will not goe with him.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Lazarello, the Duke stayes, wilt thou lose this opportunity?

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: How must I speak to him?

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: Look how many Muses there doth dwell
Upon the sweet banks of the learned Well;
And just so many stroaks the clock hath struck,
And so forth; And you must now and then enter into a description.
prose: 'Twas well thought of: you must not talk to him as you doe to an ordinary man, honest plain sence, but you must wind about him: for example, if he should aske you what a clock, it is, you must not say; If it please your grace 'tis nine; but thus; thrice three a clock, so please my Sovereign: or thus;

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: I hope I shall doe it.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Come: May it please your grace to take note of a Gentleman, wel seen, deeply read, and throughly grounded in the hidden knowledge of all sallets and potherbs whatsoever.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: I shall desire to know him more inwardly.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: I kiss the Oxe-hide of your graces foot.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Very well: will your grace question him a little?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: How old are you?

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: Full eight and twenty several Almanacks
Have been compiled, all for several years
Since first I drew this breath, four prentiships
Have I most truely served in this world:
And eight and twenty times hath Phoebus Car
Run out his yearly course since—

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: I understand you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
prose: How like an ignorant Poet he talks.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: You are eight and twenty years old? what time of the day doe you hold it to be?

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: About the time that mortals whet their knives
On thresholds, on their shooe sols, and on stairs,
New bread is grating, and the testy Cook
Hath much to doe now, now the Tables all.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: 'Tis almost dinner time?

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: Your grace doth apprehend me very rightly.

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: Your grace shall find him in your further conference
Grave, wise, courtly, and scholar like, understandingly read
In the necessities of the life of man.
He knows that man is mortal by his birth;
He knows that man must dye, and therefore live;
He knows that must live, and therefore eat,
prose: And if it shall please your grace, to accompany your self with him, I doubt not, but that he will, at the least, make good my commendations.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Attend us Lazarello, we doe want
Men of such Action, as we have received you
Reported from your honorable friend.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
prose: Good my Lord stand betwixt me and my overthrow, you know I 'm ti'd here, and may not depart, my gracious Lord, so waightie are the businesses of mine own, which at this time do call upon me, that I will rather chuse to die, than to neglect them.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Nay you shall perceive, besides the virtues that I have alreadie inform'd you of, he hath a stomach which will stoop to no Prince alive.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Sir at your best leisure, I shall thirst to see you.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
verse: And I shall hunger for it.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Till then farewell all.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: Count. Long life attend your Grace.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: I doe not tast this sport, Arrigo Lucio.

speeches.speaker: Arrigo.
verse: Luci. We doe attend.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: His grace is gone, and hath left his
The twyns of Adders, and of Scorpions
About my naked brest, will seem to me
More tickling than those claspes, which men adore;
The lustfull, dull, ill spirited embraces
Of women; The much praysed Amazones,
Knowing their own infirmities so well,
Made of themselves a people, and what men
They take amongst them, they condemne to die,
Perceiving that their folly made them fit
To live no longer that would willingly
Come in the worthless presence of a woman.
I will attend, and see what my young Lord will doe with his sister.
prose: Hellen with me, I 'm no pander for him, neither can I be won with the hope of gain, or the itching desire of tasting my Lords lecherie to him, to keep her at (my house) or bring her in disguise, to his bed Chamber.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: My Lord; The fish head is gone again.

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: Wither?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: I know whither my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Keep it from Lazarillo: Sister shall I confer with you in private, to know the cause of the Dukes coming hither, I know he makes you acquainted with his business of State.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
prose: I'll satisfie you brother, for I see you are jealous of me.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Now there shall be some course taken for her conveiance.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
prose: Lazarillo, thou art happy, thy carriage hath begot love, and that love hath brought forth fruits; thou art here in the company of a man honorable, that will help thee to tast of the bounties of the Sea, and when thou hast so done thou shalt retire thy self unto the court, and there tast of the delicates of the earth, and be great in the eyes of thy Sovereign: now no more shalt thou need to scramble for thy meat, nor remove thy stomach with the Court; But thy credit shall command thy hearts desire, and all novelties shall be sent as p^esents unto thee.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Good Sister, when you see your own time, wil you return home.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
prose: Yes brother, and not before.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
prose: I will grow popu^ar in this State, and overthrow the fortunes of a number, that live by extortion.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Laz^rello, bestirr thy self nimbly and sodainly, and hear me with patience to ^ear.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
prose: Let me not fall from my self; Speak I 'm bound.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: So art thou to revenge, when thou shalt hear the fish head is gone, and we know not whither.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
verse: I will not curse, nor swear, nor rage, nor rail,
Nor with contemptuous tongue, accuse my Fate;
Though I might justly doe it, nor will I
Wish my self uncreated for this evil:
Shall I entreat your Lordship to be seen
A little longer in the company
Of a man cross'd by Fortune?

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: I hate to leave my friend in his extremities.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
verse: 'Tis noble in you, then I take your hand,
And doe protest, I doe not follow this
For any malice or for private ends,
But with a love, as gentle and as chast,
As that a brother to his sister bears:
And if I see this fish head yet unknown;
The last words that my dying father spake,
Before his eye strings brake, shall not of me
So often be remembred, as our meeting:
Fortune attend me, as my ends are just,
Full of pure love, and free from servile lust.

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: Farwell my Lord, I was entreated to invite your
Lordship to a Lady's upsiting.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: O my ears, why Madam, will not you follow your brother? you are waited for by great men, heel bring you to him.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
prose: I'm very well my Lord, you doe mistake me, if you think I affect greater company than your self.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: What madness possesseth thee, that thou canst imagine me a sit man to entertain Lady's; I tell thee, I doe use to tear their hair, to kick them, and twindge their noses, if they be not carefull in avoiding me.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
prose: Your Lordship may discant upon your own behavior as please you, but I protest, so sweet and courtly it appeares in my eye, that I mean not to leave you yet.

speeches.speaker: Crnd.
prose: I shall grow rough,

speeches.speaker: Oria.
prose: A rough carriage is best in a man,
I'll dine with you my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Why I will starve thee, thou shalt have nothing.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
prose: I have heard of your Lordships nothing, I'll put that to the venture.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Well thou shalt have meat, I'll send it to thee.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
verse: I'll keep no state my Lord, neither doe I mourn,
I'll dine with you.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: Is such a think as this allowed to live?
What power hath let the loose upon the earth
To plague us for our Sins? Out of my doors.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
verse: I would your Lordship did but see how well
This fury doth become you, it doth shew
So neer the life, as it were natural.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: O thou damn'd woman, I will flie the vengeance
That hangs above thee, follow if thou dar'st.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
verse: I must not leave this fellow, I will torment him to madness,
To teach his passions against kind to move,
The more he hates, the more I'll seem to love.
Exeunt Oriana and Maid.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: Sir, what may be done by art shall be done,
I wear nor this black cloak for nothing.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Perform this, help me to this great heir by learning, and you shall want no black cloaks; taffaties, silkgrograns, sattins and velvets are mine, they shall be yours; perform what you have promis'd, and you shall make me a lover of Sciences, I will study the learned languages, and keep my shop-book in Latine.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
prose: Trouble me not now, I will not fail you within this hour at your shop.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Let Art have her course.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
prose: 'Tis well spoken, Madona.

speeches.speaker: Mad.
prose: Hast thou brought me any customers.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: No.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: What the devil do'st thou in black?

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose: As all solemn professors of setled courses, doe, cover my knavery with it: will you marry a citizen; Reasonably rich, and unreasonably foolish, silks in his shop, mony in his purse, and no wit in his head?

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: Out upon him, I could have otherwise than so, there was a Knight swore he would have had me, if I would have lent him but forty shillings to have redeem'd his cloak, to goe to Church in.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Then your wastcote wayter shall have him, call her in?

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: Francessina?

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: Anon?

speeches.speaker: Ma.
verse: Get you to the Church, and shrive your self,
For you shall be richly marryed anon.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: And get you after her, I will work upon my citizen whilst he is warm, I must not suffer him to consult with his neighbours, the openest fools are hardly cousened, if they once grow jealous.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: SAve me ye better powers, let me not fall
Between the lose embracements of a woman:
Heaven, if my Sins be ripe grown to a head,
And must attend your vengeance: I beg not to divert my fate,
Or to reprive a while thy punishment
Only I crave, and hear me equall heavens,
Let not your furious rod, that must afflict me
Be that imperfect peece of nature,
That art makes up, woman, unsatiate woman.
Had we not knowing fouls, at first infus'd
To teach a difference, 'twixt extremes and goods?
Were we not made our selves, free, unconfin'd
Commanders of our own affections?
And can it be, that this most perfect creature,
This image of his maker, well squar'd man,
Should leave the handfast, that he had of grace,
To fall into a womans easie armes.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
prose: Now Venus, be my speed, inspire me with all the severall subtil temptations, that thou hast already given, or hast in store heareafter to bestow upon our Sex: grant that I may apply that Physick that is most apt to work upon him: whether he will soonest be mov'd with wantonness, singing, dancing; or being passionate, with scorn; or with sad and serious looks, cunningly mingled with fighs, with smiling, lisping, kissing the hand, and making short curt'sies, Or with whatsoever other nimble power, he may be caught, doe thou infuse into me, and when I have him, I will sacrifice him up to thee.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: It comes again; New apparitions,
And tempting spirits: Stand and reveal thy self,
Tell why thou followest me? I fear thee
As I fear the place thou cam'st from: Hell.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
verse: My Lord, I 'm a woman, and such a one—

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: That I hate truely, thou hadst better bin a devill,

speeches.speaker: Orian.
verse: Why my unpatient Lord?

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: Devils were once good, there they excell'd you woman.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
verse: Can ye be so uneasie, can ye freeze, and
Such a summers heat so ready
To dissolve? nay gentle Lord, turn not away in scorn,
Nor hold me less fair than I am: look on these cheeks,
They have yet enough of nature, true complexion,
If to be red and white, a forehead high,
An easie melting lip, a speaking eye,
And such a tongue, whose language takes the ear
Of strict religion, and men most austere:
If these may hope to please, look here.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: This woman with entreaty wo'd show all,
Lady there lies your way, I pray ye farewell.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
verse: Y'are yet too harsh, too dissonant,
There's no true musick in your words, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: What shall I give thee to be gone?
prose: Here's ta, and tha wants lodging, take my house, 'tis big enough, 'tis thine own, 'twill hold five leacherous Lords, and their lackies without discovery: there's stoves and bathing tubs.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
verse: Dear Lord: y'are too wild.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Shalt have a Doctor too, thou shat, 'bout six and twentie, 'tis a pleasing age; Or I can help thee to a handsome Vsher: or if thou lack'st a page, I'll give thee one, preethee keep house, and leave me.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
verse: I doe confess I 'm too easie, too much woman,
Not coy enough to take affection,
Yet I can frown and nip a passion,
Even in the bud: I can say
Men please their present heats; Then please to leave us.
I can hold off, and, by my Chymick power,
Draw Sonnets from the melting lovers brain;
Ayme's and Elegies: yet to you my Lord
My Love, my better self, I put these off,
Doing that office, not befits our sex,
Entreat a man to love;
Are ye not yet relenting? ha'ye blood and Spirit
In those veins? ye are no image, though ye be as hard
As marble: sure ye have no liver, if ye had,
'Twould send a lively and desiring heat
To every member; Is not this miserable?
A thing so truely form'd, shapt out by Symetry,
Has all the organs that belong to man,
And working too, yet to shew all these
Like dead motions moving upon wyers?
Then good my Lord, leave off what you have been,
And freely be what you were first intended for, a man.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: Thou art a precious peece of slie damnation,
I will be deaf, I will lock up my ears,
Tempt me not, I will not love; If I doe.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
verse: Then I'll hate you.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: Let me be 'nointed with hony, and turn'd into the Sun,
To be stung to death with horse-flies,
Hear'st thou, thou breeder, here I'll sit,
And, in despight of thee, I will say nothing.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
verse: Let me with your fair patience, sit beside you.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: Madam, Lady, tempter, tongue, woman, ayr.
Look to me, I shall kick; I say again,
Look to me I shall kick.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
prose: I cannot think your better knowledg can use a woman so uncivilly.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: I cannot think, I shall become a coxcombe,
To ha'my hair curl'd, by an idle finger,
My cheeks turn Tabers, and be plaid upon,
Mine eyes lookt babies in, and my nose blowd to my hand,
I say again I shall kick, sure I shall.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
verse: 'Tis but your outside that you shew, I know your mind
Never was guilty of so great a weakness,
Or could the tougues of all men joyn'd together.
Possess me with a thought of your dislike
My weakness were above a womans, to fall off
From my affection, for one crack of thunder,
O wo'd you could love, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: I wo'd thou wouldst sit still, and say nothing: what mad-man let thee lose to do more mischief than a dousen whirlwinds, keep thy hands in thy muff, and warm the idle worms in thy fingers ends: will ye be doing still? will no entreating serve ye? no lawfull warning? I must remove and leave your Ladyship; Nay never hope to stay me, for I will run, from that Smooth, Smiling, Witching, Cousening, Tempting, Damning face of thine, as far as I can find any land, where I will put my self into a daily course of Curses for thee, and all thy Familie.

speeches.speaker: Oria,
verse: Nay good my Lord sit still, I'll promise peace
And fold mine Armes up, let but mine eye discourse;
Or let my voyce, set to some pleasing cord, found out
The sullen strains of my neglected love.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: Sing till thou crack thy treble-string in peeces,
And when thou hast done, put up thy pipes and walk,
Doe any thing, sit still and tempt me not.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
prose: I had rather sing at doors for bread, than sing to this fellow, but for hate: if this should be told in the Court, that I begin to woe Lords, what a troop of the untrust nobilitie should I have at my lodging to morrow morning?

verse: Come sleep, and with the sweet deceiving,
Look me in delight a while,
Let some pleasing Dreams beguile
All my fancies; That from thence,
I may feel an influence,
All my powers of care bereaving.
Though but a shadow, but a sliding,
Let me know some little Ioy,
We that suffer long anoy
Are contented with a thought
Through an idle fancie wrought
O let my joyes, have some abiding.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Have you done your wassayl? 'tis a handsome drowsie dittie I'll assure ye, now I had as leave hear a Cat cry, when her tail is cut off, as hear these lamentations, these lowsie love-layes, these bewailements: you think you have caught me Lady, you think I melt now, like a dish of May butter, and run, all into brine, and passion? yes, yes, I 'm taken, look how I cross my arms, look pale, and dwyndle, and wo'd cry, but for spoyling my face; we must part, nay we'll avoyd all Ceremony, no kissing Lady, I desire to know your Ladiship no more; death of my soul the Duke!

speeches.speaker: Oria.
verse: God keep your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Gond,
verse: From thee and all thy sex.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
verse: I'll be the Clark, and crie, Amen,
Your Lordships ever assured enemie Oriana.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: ALL the days good, attend your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: We thank you Gondarino, is it possible?
Can belief lay hold on such a miracle,
To see thee, one that hath cloyst'red up all passion,
prose: Turn'd wilfull votary, and forsworn converse with women, in company and fair discourse, with the best beauty of Millain?

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: 'Tis true, and if your Grace that hath the sway
Of the whole State, will suffer this lude sex,
These women: to pursue us to our homes,
Not to be prayd, not to be rail'd away,
But they will woe, and dance, and sing,
And, in a manner, looser than they are
By nature (which should seem impossible)
To throw their armes, on our unwilling necks.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: No more, I can see through your vislore, dissemble it no more.
Doe not I know thou hast us'd all Art,
To work upon the poor simplicitie
Of this yong Maid, that yet hath known none ill?
Thinkest that damnation will fright those that wo^e
From oaths, and lies? But yet I think her chast,
And will from thee, before thou shalt apply
Stronger temptations, bear her hence with me.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: My Lord, I speak not this to gain new grace,
But howsoever you esteeme my words,
My love and dutie will not suffer me
To see you favour such a prostitute,
And I stand by dumb; Without Rack, Torture,
Or Strappado, I unrip my self:
prose: I doe confess I was in company with that pleasing peece of frailtie, that we call woman; I doe confess after along and tedious seige, I yielded.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Forward.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Faith my Lord to come quickly to the point, the woman you saw with me is a whore; An arrant whore.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Was she not Count Valores, Sister?

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: Yes, that Count Valores Sister is naught.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Thou dar'st not say so.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Not if it be distasting to your Lordship, but give me freedome, and I dare maintain, she ha's imbrac'd this body, and grown to it as close, as the hot youthfull vine to the elme.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose: Twice have I seen her with thee, twice my thoughts were prompted by mine eye, to hold thy strictness false and imposterous: Is this your mewing up, your strict retirement, your bitterness and gaul against that sex? Have I not heard thee say, thou wouldst sooner meet the Basilisks, dead doing eye, than meet a woman for an object? Look it be true you tell me, or by our countries Saint your head goes off: if thou prove a whore, no womans face shall ever move me more.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: So, so, 'tis as 't should be, are women grown so mankind? Must they be wooing, I have a plot shall blow her up, she flyes, she mounts; I'll teach her Ladyship to dare my fury, I will be known, and fear'd, and more truely nated of women than an Eunuch.
She's here again, good gaul be patient, for I must dissemble.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
prose: Now my cold, frosty Lord, my woman-Hater, you that have sworn an everlasting hate to all our sex: by my troth good Lord, and as I'm yet a maid, my thought 'twas excellent sport to hear your honor swear out an Alphabet, chafe nobly like a Generall, kick like a resty Jade, and make ill faces: Did your good Honor think I was in love? where did I first begin to take that heat? From those two radiant eyes, that piercing sight? oh they were lovely, if the balls stood right; and there's a leg made out of a dainty staff, Where, the Gods be thanked, there is calf enough.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: Pardon him Lady, that is now a convert.
Your beauty, like a Saint hath wrought this wonder.

speeches.speaker: Oriana.
prose: Alass, ha's it been prick'd at the heart? is the stomach come down? will it rail no more at women, and tall 'em Divells, she Cats, and Goblins?

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: He that shall marry thee, had better spend the poor remainder of his days in a dung-barge, for two pence a week, and find him self.

Down again Spleen, I prethee down again, shall I find favour Lady? shall at length my true unfeigned penitence get pardon for my harsh unseasoned follies? I'm no more an Atheist, no I doe acknowledge, that dread powerfull Deity, and his all quic'kning heats burn in my breast: oh be not as I was, hard unrelenting; but as I'm, be partner of my fires.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
prose: Sure we have store of Larks, the Skies will not hold up long, I should have look'd as soon for Frost in the dog days, or another Inundation, as hop'd this strange conversion above miracle: let me look upon your Lordship; is your name Gondarino? are you Millains Generall, that great Bug-bear bloody-bones, at whose name all women, from the Lady to the Landress, shake like a cold fit?

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Good patience help me, this Fever will inrage my blood again: Madam I'm that man; I'm even he that once did owe unreconcil'd hate to you, and all that bear the name of woman: I'm the man that wrong'd your Honor to the Duke: I'm the man that said you were unchast, and prostitute, yet I'm he that dare deny all this.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
prose: Your big Nobility is very merry.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: Lady 'tis true that I have wrong'd you thus,
And my contrition is as true as that,
Yet have I found a means to make all good again,
I doe beseech your beautie, not for my self,
My merits are yet in conception,
But for your honors safety and my zeal
Retire a while, while I unsay my self unto the Duke,
And cast out that ill Spirit I have possest him with,
I have a house conveniently private.

speeches.speaker: Ori.
prose: Lord, thou hast wrong'd my innocence, but thy confession hath gain'd thee faith.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: By the true honest service, that I owe these eyes strangely,
My meaning is as spotless as my faith.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
verse: The Duke doubt mine honor? a may judge
'Twill not be long, before I'll be enlarg'd again.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: A day or two.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
verse: Mine own servants shall attend me.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: Your Ladyships command is good.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
verse: Look you be true.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Else let me lose the hopes my soul aspires to: I will be a scourge to all females in my life, and after my death, the name of Gondarino, shall be terrible to the mighty women of the earth; They shall shake at my name, and at the sound of it, their knees shall knock together; And they shall run into Nunneries, for they and I are beyond all hope irreconcilable: for if I could endure an ear with a hole in't, or a pleated lock, or a bare headed Coachman, that sits like a sign where great Ladys are to be sold within; agreement betwixt us, were not to be dispaired of; if I could be but brought to endure to see women, I would have them come all once a week, and kiss me, as Witches doe the devill, in token of homage: I must not live here; I will to the Court, and there pursue my plot; when it hath took, women shall stand in awe, but of my look.

speeches.speaker: 1. Intel.
prose: THere take your standing, be close and vigilant, here will I set my self, and let him look to his language, a shall know the Duke has more ears in Court than two.

speeches.speaker: 2. Int.
prose: I'll quote him to a tittle, let him speak wisely, and plainly, and as hidden as a can, or I shall crush him, a shall not scape charracters, though a speak Babel, I shall crush him: we have a Fortune by this service hanging over us, that within this year or two, I hope we shall be called to be examiners, wear politick gowns garded with copper lace, making great faces full of fear and office, our labors may deserve this.

speeches.speaker: 1. Int.
prose: I hope it shall: why has not many men been raised from this worming trade, first to gain good access to great men, then to have commissions out for search, and lastly, to be worthily nam'd at a great Arraignment: yes, and why not we? They that endeavor well deserve their Fee.
Close, close, a comes: mark well, and all goes well.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: Farewell my hopes, my Anchor now is broken,
Farewell my quondam joys, of which no token
Is now remaining, such is the sad mischance,
Where Lady Fortune leads the slipp'ry dance.
Yet at the length, let me this favour have,
Give me my wishes, or a wished grave.

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: The gods defend so brave and valiant maw,
Should slip into the never satiate jaw
Of black Despair; no, thou shalt live and know
Thy full desires, hunger thy ancient foe,
Shall be subdued; those guts that daily tumble
Through ayr and appetite, shall cease to rumble:
And thou shalt now at length obtain thy dish,
That noble part, the sweet head of a fish.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: Then am I greater than the Duke.

speeches.speaker: 2. Int.
verse: There, there's a notable peece of treason, greater than the Duke, mark that.

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: But how, or where, or when this shall be compas'd, is yet out of my reach.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: I am so truely miserable, that might
I be now knockt oth' head, with all my heart
I would forgive a dog-killer.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Yet doe I see through this confusedness some little comfort.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: The plot my Lord, as er'e you came of a woman, discover.

speeches.speaker: 1. Int.
prose: Plots, dangerous plots, I will deserve by this most liberally.

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: 'Tis from my head again.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: With their knives drawn, which were a dismall sight,
And after twenty leisurely were told,
I to be let loose only in my shirt,
To trie the valour, how much of the spoyl,
I would recover from the enemies mouths:
Upon country people in progress time, and
Wilt thou lose this opinion, for the cold head of a Fish?
I say, let it goe: I'll help thee to as good a dish of meat.
prose: O that it would stand me, that I might fight, or have some venture for it, that I might be turn'd loose, to try my fortune amongst the whole frie in a Colledge, or an Inn of Court; or scramble with the prisoners in the dungeon; nay were it set down in the outward court, And all the Guard about it in a ring,

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: God let me not live, if I doe not wonder,
Men should talk so propanely:
But it is not in the power of loose words,
Of any vain or misbeleeving man,
To make me dare to wrong thy purity.
Shew me but any Lady in the Court,
That hath so full an eye, so sweet a breath,
So soft and white a flesh: this doth not lie
In almond gloves, nor ever hath bin washt
In artificiall baths: no traveller
That hath brought doctor home with him, hath dar'd
With all his waters, powders, Fucusses,
To make thy lovely corps sophisticate.

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: I have it, 'tis now infus'd, be comforted.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: Can there be that little hope yet left in nature? shall I once more erect up Trophies? Shall I enjoy the sight of my dear Saint, and bless my pallate with the best of creatures, ah good my Lord, by whom I breathe again, shall I receive this Being?

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Sir I have found by certain calculation, and setled revolution of the stars, the Fish is sent by the Lord Gondarino to his Mercer, now 'tis a growing hope to know where 'tis.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: O'tis far above the good of women, the Pathick cannot yield more pleasing titilation.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: But how to compass it search, cast about, and bang your brains, Lazarello, thou art too dull and heavy to deserve a blessing.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: My Lord, I will not be idle; now Lazarello, think, think, think,

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: Yonder's my informer
And his fellow with table books, they nod at me
Upon my life, they have poor Lazarello, that beats
His brains about no such waighty matter, in for
Treason before this—

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: My Lord, what doe you think, if I should shave my self,
Put on midwives apparell, come in with a hand-kercher,
And beg a piece for a great bellied woman, or a sick child?

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Good, very good.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: Or corrupt the waiting prentise to betray the reversion.

speeches.speaker: 1. Inte.
prose: There's another point in's plot, corrupted with money; to betray: sure 'tis some Fort a means: mark, have a care.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: And 'twere the bare vinegar 'tis eaten with, it would in some sort satisfie nature: but might I once attain the dish it self, though I cut out my means through sword and fire, through poison, through any thing that may make good my hopes.

speeches.speaker: 2. Int.
prose: Thanks to the gods, and our officiousness, the plots discover'd, fire, steel, and poison, burn the Palace, kill the Duke and poison his privie Councell.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: To the mercers, let me see: how, if before we can attain the means, to make up our acquaintance, the fish be eaten?

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: If it be eaten, here he stands, that is the most dejected, most unfortunate, miserable, accursed, forsaken slave this Province yields: I will not sure outlive it, no I will dye bravely, and like a Roman; and after death, amidst the Elizian shades, I'll meet my love again.

speeches.speaker: 1. In.
prose: I will dye bravely, like a Roman: have a care, mark that, when he hath done all, he will kill himself.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Will nothing ease your appetite but this?

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: No could the Sea throw up his vastness,
And offer free his best inhabitants: 'twere not so much as a bare temptation to me.

speeches.speaker: Count,
verse: If you could be drawn to affect Beef, Venison, or Fowl, 'twould be far the better.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
verse: I doe beseech your Lordships patience,
I doe confess that in this heat of blood,
I have contemn'd all dull and grosser meats,
But I protest I doe honor a Chine of Beef,
I doe reverence a loyn of Veal,
But good my Lord, give me leave a little to adore this:
But my good Lord, would your Lordship, under color of taking up some silks, goe to the Mercers, I would in all humilitie attend your honor, where we may be invited, if Fortune stand propitious.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Sir you shall work me as you please.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
prose: Let it be suddenly, I doe beseech your Lordship, 'tis now upon the point of dinner time.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: I am all yours.

speeches.speaker: 1. In.
verse: Come let us confer,
prose: Imprimis he saith, like a blasphemous villain, he 's greater than the Duke, this peppers him, and there were nothing else.

speeches.speaker: 2. In.
prose: Then he was naming plots; did you not hear?

speeches.speaker: 1. In.
prose: Yes but he fell from that unto discovery, to corrupt by money, and so attain.

speeches.speaker: 2. In.
prose: I, I, he meant some Fort, or Cyttadell the Duke hath, his very face betraid his meaning, O he is very subtile and a dangerous knave, but if he deal a Gods name, we shall worm him

speeches.speaker: 1. In.
prose: But now comes the Stroak, the fatall blow, Fire, Sword and Poyson, O Canibal, thou bloody Canibal.

speeches.speaker: 2. In.
prose: What had become of this poor state, had we not been?

speeches.speaker: 1. In.
prose: Faith it had lyen buried in his own ashes; had not a greater hand been in't.

speeches.speaker: 2. In.
prose: But note the rascalls resolution, after th'acts done, because he wo'd avoid all fear of torture, and cousen the Law, he wo'd kill himself; was there ever the like danger brought to light in this age? sure we shall merit much, we shall be able to keep two men a peece, and a two hand-sword between us, we will live in favour of the State, betray our ten or twelve treasons a week, and the people shall fear us: come, to the Lord Lucio, the Sun shall not goe down till he be hang'd.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: LOok to my shop, and if there come ever a Scholar in black, let him speak with me; we that are shopkeepers in good trade, are so pester'd, that we can scarce pick out an hour for our mornings meditation: and howsoever we are all accounted dull, and common jesting stocks for your gallants; There are some of us doe not deserve it: for, for my own part, I doe begin to be given to my book, I love a scholar with my heart, for questionless there are merveilous things to be done by Art: why Sir, some of them will tell you what is become of horses, and silver spoons, and will make wenches dance naked to their beds: I am yet unmarried, and because some of our neighbours are said to be Cuckolds, I will never be married without the consent of some of these scholars, that know what will come of it.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Are you busie Sir?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Never to you Sir, nor to any of your coat.
Sir is there any thing to be done by Art, concerning the great heir we talk'd on?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Will she, nill she: she shall come running into my house at the farther corner, in Sa. Marks street, betwixt three and four.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Betwixt three and four? she's brave in cloaths, is she not?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose:
O rich! rich! where should I get cloaths to dress her in? Help me invention: Sir, that her running through the
street may be less noted, my Art more shown, and your fear to speak with her less, she shall come in a white wastcoat, And—

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: What shall she?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: And perhaps torn stockings, she hath lest her old wont else.

speeches.speaker: Pren.
prose: Sir my Lord Gond. hath sent you a rare fish head.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: It comes right, all things sute right with me since I began to love scholars, you shall have it home with you against she come: carrie it to this Gentleman's house.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: The fair white house at the farther corner at S. Marks street, make haste, I must leave you too Sir, I have two hours to study; buy a new Accedence, and ply your book, and you shall want nothing that all the scholars in the Town can doe for you.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Heaven prosper both our studies, what a dull slave was I before I fell in love with this learning? not worthy to tread upon the earth, & what fresh hopes it hath put in to me? I doe hope within this twelve-month to be able by Art to serve the Court with silks, and not undoe my self; to trust Knights, and yet get in my money again; to keep my wife brave, and yet she keep no body else so.
Your Lordship is most honourably welcome in regard of your Nobility; but most especialy in regard of your scholarship: did your Lordship come openly?

speeches.speaker: Count,
prose: Sir this cloak keeps me private, besides no man will suspect me to be in the company of this Gentleman, with whom, I will desire you to be acquainted, he may prove a good customer to you.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
prose: For plain silks and velvets.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Are you scholasticall?

speeches.speaker: Laza.
prose: Something addicted to the Muses.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: I hope they will not dispute.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: You have no skill in the black Art.

speeches.speaker: Pren.
prose: Sir yonder's a Gentleman enquires hastily for Count Valore,

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: For me? what is he?

speeches.speaker: Pren.
prose: One of your followers my Lord I think.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Let him come in.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Shall I talk with you in private Sir?

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Count, come to the Court your business calls you thither, I will goe, farewell Sir, I will see your silks some other time: Farewell Lazarillo.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Will not your Lordship take a peice of Beef with me?

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Sir I have greater business than eating; I will leave this Gentleman with you.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
prose: No, no, no, no: now doe I feel that strain'd strugling within me, that I think I could prophesie.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: The Gentleman is meditating.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
prose: Hunger, valour, love, ambition are alike pleasing, and let our Philosophers say what they will, are one kind of heat, only hunger is the safest: ambition is apt to fall; love and valour are not free from dangers; only hunger, begotten of some old limber Courtier, in pan'de hose, and nurs'd by an Attourneys wife; now so thriven, that he need not fear to be of the great Turks guard: is so free from all quarrels and dangers, so full of hopes, joyes, and ticklings, that my life is not so dear to me as his acquaintance.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Sir the Fish head is gone.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
verse: Then be thou henceforth dumb, with thy ill-boding voice.
Farewell Millain, farewell Noble Duke,
Farewell my fellow Courtiers all, with whom,
I have of yore made many a scrambling meal
In corners, behind Arasses, on stairs;
And in the action oftentimes have spoil'd,
Our Doublets and our Hose with liquid stuff:
Farewell you lusty Archers of the Guard,
To whom I now doe give the bucklers up,
And never more with any of your coat
Will eat for wagers, now you happy be,
When this shall light upon you, think on me:
You sewers, carvers, ushers of the court
Sirnamed gentle for your fair demean,
Here I doe take of you my last farewell,
May you stand stifly in your proper places, and execute your offices aright.
Farewell you Maidens, with your mother eke,
Farewell you courtly Chaplains that be there
All good attend you, may you never more
Marry your Patrons Ladys wayting-woman,
But may you raised be by this my fall
May Lazarillo suffer for you all.

speeches.speaker: Merc.
prose: Sir I was hearkning to you.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: I will hear nothing, I will break my knife, the Ensign of my former happy state, knock out my teeth, have them hung at a Barbers, and enter into Religion.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Why Sir, I think I know whither it is gone.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
prose: See the rashness of man in his nature, whither? I do unsay all that I have said, go on, go on: Boy, I humble my self and follow thee; Farewell Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Not so Sir, you shall take a piece of Beef with me.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: I cannot stay.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: By my say but you shall Sir, in regard of your love to learning, and your kill in the black Art.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: I do hate learning, and I have no skill in black Art; I would I had.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Why your desire is sufficient to me, you shall stay.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: The most horrible and detested curses that can be imagined, light upon all the professors of that Art; may they be drunk, and when they goe to conjure, and reel in the Circle, may the spirits by them rais'd, tear 'em in pieces, and hang their quarters on old broken walls and Steeple tops.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: This speech of yours, shews you to have some skill in the Science, wherefore in civilitie, I may not suffer you to depart empty.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: My stomach is up, I cannot endure it, I will fight in this quarrell as soon as for my Prince.
Room, make way:
Hunger commands, my valour must obey.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: IS the Duke private?

speeches.speaker: Arr.
prose: He is alone, but I think your Lordship may enter.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Who's with the Duke?

speeches.speaker: Arr.
prose:
The Count is new gone in, but the Duke will come
forth, before you can be weary of waiting.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: I will attend him here.

speeches.speaker: Arr.
prose: I must wait without the door.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Doth he hope to clear his Sister? she will come no more to my house, to laugh at me: I have sent her to a habitation, where when she shall be seen, it will set a gloss upon her name; yet upon my soul I have bestow'd her amongst the purest hearted creatures of her sex, and the freest from dissimulation; for their deeds are all alike, only they dare speak, what the rest think: the women of this age, if there be any degrees of comparison amongst their sex, are worse than those of former times; for I have read of women, of that truth, spirit, and constancy; that were they now living, I should endure to see them: but I fear the writers of the time belied them, for how familiar a thing is it with the Poets of our age, to extoll their whores, which they call Mistresses, with heavenly praises? but I thank their furies, and their craz'd brains, beyond belief: nay, how many that would fain seem serious, have dedicated grave Works to Ladies, toothless, hollow-ey'd, their hair shedding, purple fac'd, their nails apparently coming off; and the bridges of their noses broken down, and have call'd them the choice handy works of nature, the patterns of perfection, and the wonderment of Women. Our Women begin to swarm like Bees in the Summer: as I came hither, there was no pair of stairs, no entry, no lobby, but was pestred with them: methinks there might be some course taken to destroy them.

speeches.speaker: Arri.
prose: I do accept your money, walk here, and when the Duke comes out, you shall have sit opportunity to deliver your petition to him.

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
prose: I thank you heartily, I pray you who's he that walks there?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: A Lord, and a Soldier, one in good favour with the Duke; if you could get him to deliver your Petition —

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
prose: What do you say, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: If you could get him to deliver your petition for you, or to second you, 'twere sure.

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
prose: I hope I shall live to requite your kindness.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: You have already.

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
prose: May it please your Lordship—

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: No, no.

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
prose: To consider the estate—

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: No.

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
prose: Of a poor oppressed countrey Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: No, it doth not please my Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
prose: First and formost, I have had great injury, then I have been brought up to the Town three times.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: A pox on him, that brought thee to the Town.

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
prose: I thank your good Lordship heartily; though I cannot hear well, I know it grieves you; and here we have been delaid, and sent down again, and fetch'd up again, and sent down again, to my great charge: and now at last they have fetch'd me up, and five of my daughters —

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Enough to damn five worlds.

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
prose: Handsome young women, though I say it, they are all without, if it please your Lordship I'll call them in.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: Five Women! how many of my sences should I have left me then? call in five Devils first.
No, I will rather walk with thee alone,
And hear thy tedious tale of injury,
And give thee answers; whisper in thine ear,
And make thee understand through thy French hood:
And all this with tame patience.

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
prose: I see your Lordship does believe, that they are without, and I perceive you are much mov'd at our injury: here's a paper will tell you more.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Away.

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
prose: It may be you had rather hear me tell it viva voce, as they say.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Oh no, no, no, no, I have heard it before.

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
prose: Then you have heard of enough injury, for a poor Gentlewoman to receive.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Never, never, but that it troubles my conscience, to wish any good to these woman; I could afford them to be valiant, and able, that it might be no disgrace for a Soldier to beat them.

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
prose: I hope your Lordship will deliver my petition to his grace, and you may tell him withal—

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: What? I will deliver any thing against my self, to be rid on thee.

speeches.speaker: Gent^ew.
prose: That yesterday about three a clock in the after noon, I met my adversary.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Give me thy paper, he can abide no long tales.

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
prose: 'Tis very short my Lord, and I demanding of him—

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: I'll tell him that shall serve thy turn.

speeches.speaker: Gentlew,
prose: How?

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: I'll tell him that shall serve thy turn, begone: man never doth remember how great his offences are, till he do meet with one of you, that plagues him for them: why should Women, above all other creatures that were created for the benefit of man, have the use of speech? or why should any deed of theirs, done by their fleshly appetites, be disgraceful to their owners? nay, why should not an act done by any beast I keep, against my consent, disparage me as much as that of theirs?

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
prose: Here's some few Angels for your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Again? yet more torments?

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
prose: Indeed you shall have them.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Keep off.

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
prose: A small gratuity for your kindness.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Hold away.

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
prose: Why then I thank your Lordship, I'll gather them up again, and I'll be sworn, it is the first money that was refus'd since I came to the Court.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: What can she devise to say more?

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
prose: Truly I would have willingly parted with them to your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: I believe it, I believe it.

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
prose: But since it is thus—

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: More yet.

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
prose: I will attend without, and expect an answer.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Do, begone, and thou shalt expect, and have any thing, thou shalt have thy answer from him; and he were best to give thee a good one at first, for thy deaf importunity, will conquer him too, in the end.

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
prose: God bless your Lordship, and all thar favour a poor distressed countrey Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: All the diseases of man light upon them that doe, and upon me when I do. A week of such days, would either make me stark mad or tame me: yonder other woman that I have sure enough, shall answer for thy sins: dare they incense me still, I will make them fear as much to be ignorant of me and my moods, as men are to be ignorant of the law they live under. Who's there? My bloud grew cold, I began to fear my Suiters return; 'tis the Duke.

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: I know her chaste, though she be young and free,
And is not of that forc'd behaviour
That many others are, and that this Lord,
Out of the boundless malice to the sex,
Hath thrown this scandal on her.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Fortune befriended me against my Will, with this good old countrey gentlewoman; I beseech your grace, to view favourably the petition of a wronged Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: What Gondarino, are you become a petitioner for your enemies?

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose:
My Lord, they are no enemies of mine, I confess, the better to recover my deeds, which sometimes were loose
enough, I pretended it, as it is wisdom, to keep close our incontinence, but since you have discover'd me, I will no more put on that vizard, but will as freely open all my thoughts to you, as to my Confessor.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: What say you to this?

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: He that confesses he did once dissemble,
I'll never trust his words: can you imagine
A Maid, whose beauty could not suffer her
To live thus long untempted, by the noblest,
Richest, and cunningst Masters in that Art
And yet hath ever held a fair repute;
Could in one morning, and by him be brought,
To forget all her virtue, and turn whore?

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: I would I had some other talk in hand,
Than to accuse a Sister to her Brother:
Nor do I mean it for a publick scandal,
Unless by urging me you make it so.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I will read this at better leisure:

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: Where is the Lady?

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: At his house.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: No, she is departed thence,

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: Whither?

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: Urge it not thus, or let me be excus'd,
If what I speak betray her chastity,
And both increase my sorrow, and your own?

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: Fear me not so, if she deserve the fame
Which she hath gotten, I would have it publisht,
Brand her my self, and whip her through the City:
I wish those of my bloud that doe offend,
Should be more strictly punish, than my foes.
Let it be prov'd.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Gondarino, thou shalt prove it, or suffer worse than she should do.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: Then pardon me, if I betray the faults
Of one, I love more dearly than my self,
Since opening hers, I shall betray mine own:
But I will bring you where she now intends
Not to be virtuous, pride and wantonness,
That are true friends indeed, though not in shew,
Have entr'd on her heart, there she doth bathe,
And sleek her hair, and practise cunning looks
To entertain me with; and hath her thoughts
As full of lust, as ever you did think
Them full of modesty.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Gondarino, lead on, we'll follow thee.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: HEre hope I to meet my Citizen, and hopes he to meet his Scholar; I am sure I am grave enough, to his eyes, and knave enough to deceive him: I am believ'd to conjure, raise storms, and devils, by whose power I can do wonders; let him believe so still, belief hurts no man; I have an honest black cloak, for my knavery, and a general pardon for his foolery, from this present day, till the day of his breaking. Is't not a misery, and the greatest of our age, to see a handsome, young, fair enough, and well mounted wench, humble her self, in an old stammel petticoat, standing possest of no more fringe, than the street can allow her: her upper parts so poor and wanting, that ye may see her bones through her bodies: shooes she would have, if our Captain were come over, and is content the while to devote her self to antient slippers. These premisses well considered, Gentlemen, will move, they make me melt I promise ye, they stirr me much: and wer't not for my smooth, soft, silken Citizen, I would quit this transitory Trade, get me an everlasting Robe, sear up my conscience, and turn Serjeant.
