But here he comes, is mine as good as prize: Sir Pandarus be my speed, ye are most fitly met Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: And you as well encount'red, what of this heir? hath your Books been propitious?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Sir, 'tis done, she's come, she's in my house, make your self apt for Courtship, stroke up your stockings, loose not an inch of your legs goodness; I am sure ye wear socks.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: There your Books sail ye Sir, in truth I wear no socks.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
prose: I would you had, Sir, it were the sweeter grace for your legs; get on your Gloves, are they perfum'd.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: A pretty wash I'll assure you.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
prose: 'Twill serve: your offers must be full of bounty, Velvets to furnish a Gown, Silks for Peticoats, and Foreparts Shag for lining; forget not some pretty Jewel to fasten, after some little compliment? if she deny this courtesie, double your bounties, be not wanting in abundance, fulness of gifts, link'd with a pleasing tongue, will win an Anchorite. Sir, ye are my friend, and friend to all that professes good Letters; I must not use this office else, it fits not for a Scholar, and a Gentleman: those stockins are of Naples, they are silk.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Ye are again beside your Text, Sir, they're of the best of Wooll, and the clipped Jersey.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Sure they are very dear.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Nine shillings, by my love to learning.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Pardon my judgement, we Scholars use no other objects, but our Books.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: There is one thing entomb'd in that grave breast, that makes me equally admire it with your Scholarship.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
prose: Sir, but that in modesty I am bound not to affect mine own commendation, I would enquire it of you.

speeches.speaker: Merc.
prose: Sure you are very honest; and yet ye have a kind of modest fear to shew it: do not deny it, that face of yours is a worthy, learned modest face.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
prose: Sir, I can blush.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Virtue and grace are always pair'd together: but I will leave to stirr your bloud Sir, and now to our business.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
prose: Forget not my instructions.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: I apprehend ye Sir, I will gather my self together with my best phrases, and so I shall discourse in some sort takingly.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
prose: This was well worded Sir, and like a Scholar.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: The Muses favour me as my intents are virtuous; Sir, ye shall be my Tutor, 'tis never too late Sir, to love Learning.
When I can once speak true Latine—

speeches.speaker: Pand.
prose: What do you intend Sir?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Marry I will then begger all your bawdy Writers, and undertake, at the peril of my own invention, all Pageants, Poesies, for Chimneys, Speeches for the Dukes enterrainment, whensoever and whatsoever; nay I will build, at mine own charge, an Hospital, to which shall retire all diseased opinions, all broken Poets, all Prose-men that are fall'n from small sence, to meer Letters; and it shall be lawful for a Lawyer, if he be a civil man, though he have undone others and himself by the language, to retire to this poor life, and learn to be honest.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
prose: Sir, ye are very good, and very charitable: ye are a true pattern for the City Sir.

speeches.speaker: Merc.
prose: Sir, I doe know sufficiently, their Shop-books cannot save them, there is a farther end—

speeches.speaker: Pand.
prose: Oh Sir, much may be done by manuscript.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: I do confess it Sir, provided still they be Canonical, and I have some worthy hands set to 'em for probation: but we forget our selves.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
prose: Sir, enter when you please, and all good language tip your tongue.

speeches.speaker: Merc.
prose: All that love Learning pray for my good success.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: WHereabouts are we?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Sir, by all tokens this is the house, bawdy I am sure, because of the broken windows, the Fish head is within; if ye dareventure, here you may surprize it.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: The misery of man may fitly be compar'd to a Didapper, who when she is under water, past our sight, and indeed can seem no more to us, rises again; shakes but her self, and is the same she was, so is it still with transitory man, this day: oh but an hour since, and I was mighty, mighty in knowledge, mighty in my hopes, mighty in blessed means, and was so truly happy, that I durst have said, live Lazarello., and be satisfied: but now—

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Sir, ye are yet afloat, and may recover, be not your own wreck, here lies the harbor, goe in and ride at ease.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: Boy, I am receiv'd to be a Gentleman, a Courtier, and a man of action, modest, and wise, and be it spoken with thy reverence, Child, abounding virtuous; and wouldst thou have a man of these choise habits, covet the cover of a bawdy-house? yet if I goe not in, I am but—

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: But what Sir?

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: Dust boy, but dust, and my soul unsatisfied, shall haunt the keepers of my blessed Saint, and I will appear.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: An ass to all men; Sir, these are no means to stay your appetite, you must resolve to enter.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: Were not the house subject to Martial Law—

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: If that be all, Sir, ye may enter, for ye can know nothing here that the Court is ignorant of, only the more eyes shall look upon you, for there they wink one at anothers faults.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: If I doe not.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Then ye must beat fairly back, again fall to your physical mess of porridge, and the twice sack'd carkass of a Capon: Fortune may favour you so much, to send the bread to it: but it's a meet venture, and money may be put out upon it.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: I will go in and live; pretend some love to the Gentlewoman, screw my self in affection, and so be satisfied.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: This Fly is caught, is mash'd already, I will suck him, and lay him by.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Muffle your self in your cloak by any means, 'tis a receiv'd thing among gallants, to walk to their leachery, as though they had the rheum, 'twas well you brought not your horse.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: Why Boy?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Faith Sir. 'tis the fashion of our Gentry, to have their horses wait at door like men, while the beasts their Masters, are within at rack and manger, 'twould have discover'd much.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: Be'st thou in Hell, rap't by Proserpina,
To be a rival in black Pluto's love;
Or mov'st thou in the heavens, a form Divine:
Lashing the lazie Sphear,
Or if thou be'st return'd to thy first Being,
Thy mother Sea, then will I seek thee forth.
Earth, Air, nor Fire,
Nor the black shades below shall bar my sight
So daring is my powerful appetite.
prose: I will lay by these habits, forms, and grave respects of what I am, and be my self; only my appetite, my fire, my soul, my being, my dear appetite shall go along with me, arm'd with whose strength, I fearless will attempt the greatest danger dare oppose my fury: I am resolv'd where ever that thou art, most sacred dish, hid from unhallow'd eyes, to find thee out.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Sir, you may save this long voyage, and take a shorter cut: you have forgot your self, the fish head's here, your own imaginations have made you mad.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: Term it a jealous sury, good my boy.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Faith Sir term it what you will, you must use other terms before you can get it.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: The looks of my sweet love are fair,
Fresh and feeding as the air.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Sir, you forget your self.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: Was never seen so rare a head,
Of any Fish alive or dead.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Good Sir remember: this is the house, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: Cursed be he that dare not venture.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Pity your self, Sir, and leave this fury

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: For such a prize, and so I enter.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Dun's i'th' mire, get out again how he can:
My honest gallant, I'll shew you one trick more
Than e'er the fool your father dream'd of yet.
Madona Julia?

speeches.speaker: Julia.
prose: What news my sweet rogue, my dear sins-broker, what good news?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: There is a kind of ignorant thing,
Much like a Courtier, now gone in.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: Is he gallant?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: He shines not very gloriously, nor does he wear one skin perfum'd to keep the other sweet; his coat is not in Or, nor does the world run yet on wheels with him; he's rich enough, and has a small thing follows him, like to a boat tyed to a tall ships tail: give him entertainment, be light, and flashing like a Meteor, hug him about the neck, give him a kiss, and lisping cry, good Sir; and he's thine own, as fast as he were tied to thine arms by Indenture.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: I dare doe more than this, if he be o'th' true Court cut; I'll take him out a lesson worth the Learning: but we are but their Apes; what's he worth?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Be he rich, or poor; if he will take thee with him, thou maist use thy trade from Constables, and Marshals: who hath been here since I went out?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: There is a Gentlewoman sent hither by a Lord, she's a piece of dainty stuff my rogue, smooth and soft, as new Sattin; she was never gumm'd yet boy, nor fretted.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Where lies she?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: She lies above, towards the street, not to be spoke with, but by my Lord that sent her, or some from him, we have in charge from his servants.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Peace, he comes out again upon discovery; up with all your Canvas, hale him in; and when thou hast done, clap him aboard bravely, my valiant Pinnace.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: Begone, I shall doe reason with him.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: Are you the special beauty of this house?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: Sir, you have given it a more special regard by your good language, than these black brows can merit,

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: Lady, you are fair

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: Fair Sir: I thank ye? all the poor means I have left to be thought grateful, is but a kiss, and ye shall have it Sir.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: Ye have a very moving lip.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: Prove it again Sir, it may be your sense was set too high, and so over-wrought it self.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: 'Tis still the same; how far may ye hold the time to be spent Lady?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: Four a clock, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: I have not eat to day.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: You will have the better stomach to your supper; in the mean time I'll feed you with delight.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: 'Tis not so good upon an empty stomach: if it might be without the trouble of your house, I would eat?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: Sir, we can have a Capon ready,

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: The day?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: 'Tis Friday, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: I do eat little flesh upon these days.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: Come sweet, ye shall not think on meat; I'll drown it with a better appetite.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: I feel it work more strangely, I must eat.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: 'Tis now too late to send; I say ye shall not think on meat: if ye do, by this kiss I'll be angry.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: I could be far more sprightful, had I eaten, and more lasting.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: What will you have Sir? name but the Fish, my Maid shall bring it, if it may be got,

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: Methinks your house should not be so unfurnish'd, as not to have some pretty modicum.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: It is now: but cou'd ye stay till supper?

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: Sure I have offended highly, and much, and my afflictions makes it manifest, I will retire henceforth, and keep my chamber, live privately, and dye forgotten.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose:
Sir, I must crave your pardon, I had forgot my self; I have a dish of meat within, and it is fish; I think this Dukedom holds not a daintier: 'tis an
~mbranoes head.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: This kiss is yours, and this.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: Hoe within there? cover the board, and set the Fish head on it.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: Now am I so truly happy, so much above all fate and fortune, that I should despise that man, durst say, remember Lazarello, thou art mortal.

speeches.speaker: 2 Int.
prose: This is the villain, lay hold on him.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: Gentlemen, why am I thus intreated? what is the nature of my crime?

speeches.speaker: 2 Int.
prose: Sir, though you have carried it a great while privately, and (as you think) well; yet we have seen you Sir, and we do know thee Lazarello, for a Traitor.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: The gods defend our Duke,

speeches.speaker: 2 Int.
prose: Amen, Sir, Sir, this cannot save that stiff neck from the halter.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: Gentlemen, I am glad you have discover'd him, he should not have eaten under my roof for twenty pounds; and surely I did not like him, when he call'd for Fish,

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: My friends, will ye let me have that little favour—

speeches.speaker: 1 Int.
prose: Sir, ye shall have Law, and nothing else.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: To let me stay the eating of a bit or two, for I protest I am yet fasting.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: I'll have no Traitor come within my house.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: Then lead along, I am prepar'd for all:
Since I have lost my hopes, welcome my fall.
prose: Now could I wish my self I had been a Traitor, I have strength enough for to endure it, had I but patience: Man thou art but grass, thou art a bubble, and thou must perish.

speeches.speaker: 2 Int.
verse: Away Sir.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: As thou hast hope of man, stay but this dish this two hours, I doubt not but I shall be discharged: by this light I will marry thee.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: You shall marry me first then.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: I do contract my self unto thee now, before these Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: I'll preserve it till you be hang'd or quitted.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: Thanks, thanks.

speeches.speaker: 2 Int.
prose: Away, away, you shall thank her at the gallows.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: Adieu, adieu.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: If he live I'll have him, if he be hang'd, there's no loss in it.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
prose: Hast thou provided one to bear my Letter to my brother?

speeches.speaker: Wait.
prose: I have enquir'd, but they of the house will suffer no Letter nor message to be carried from you, but such as the Lord Gondarino shall be acquainted with: truly Madam I suspect the house to be no better than it should be.

speeches.speaker: Ori.
prose: What dost thou doubt?

speeches.speaker: Wait.
prose: Faith I am loth to tell it, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Ori.
prose: Out with it, 'tis not true modesty to fear to speak that thou dost think.

speeches.speaker: Wait.
prose: I think it to be one of these Bawdy houses.

speeches.speaker: Ori.
prose: 'Tis no matter wench, we are warm in it, keep thou thy mind pure, and upon my word, that name will do thee no hurt: I cannot force my self yet to fear any thing; when I do get out, I'll another encounter with my Woman-Hater. Here will I sit. I may get sight of some of my friends, it must needs be a comfort to them to see me here.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Are we all sufficiently disguis'd? for this house where she attends me, is not to be visited in our own shapes.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: We are not our selves.

speeches.speaker: Arr.
prose: I know the house to be sinful enough, yet I have been heretofore, and durst now, but for discovering of you, appear here in my own likeness.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Where's Lucio?

speeches.speaker: Arri.
prose: My Lord, he said the affairs of the Common-wealth would not suffer him to attend always.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Some great ones questionless that he will handle.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Come, let us enter.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: See how Fortune strives to revenge my quarrel upon these women, she's in the window, were it not to undoe her, I should not look upon her.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Lead us Gondarino.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Stay; since you force me to display my shame,
Look there, and you my Lord, know you that face?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Is't she?

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: It is.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: 'Tis she, whose greatest virtue ever was
Dissimulation; she that still hath strove
More to sin cunningly, than to avoid it:
She that hath ever sought to be accounted
Most virtuous, when she did deserve most scandal:
'Tis she that itches now, and in the height
Of her intemperate thoughts, with greedy eyes
Expects my coming to allay her Lust:
Leave her; forget she's thy sister.

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: Stay, stay.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I am as full of this, as thou canst be,
The memory of this will easily
Hereafter stay my loose and wandring thought
From any Woman.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: This will not down with me, I dare not trust this fellow.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Leave her here, that only shall be her punishment, never to be fetcht from hence; but let her use her trade to get her living.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Stay good my Lord, I do believe all this, as great men as I, have had known whores to their Sisters, and have laught at it: I would fain hear how she talks, since she grew thus light: will your grace make him shew himself to her, as if he were now come to satisfie her longing! whilst we, unseen of her, over-hear her wantonness, let's make our best of it now, we shall have good mirth.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Do it Gondarino.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: I must; fortune assist me but this once.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Here we shall stand unseen, and near enough.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Madam, Oriana.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
prose: Who's that? oh! my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Shall I come up?

speeches.speaker: Oria.
prose: Oh you are merry, shall I come down?

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: It is better there.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
prose: What is the confession of the lye you made to the Duke, which I scarce believe, yet you had impudence enough to do? did it not gain you so much faith with me, as that I was willing to be at your Lordships bestowing, till you had recover'd my credit, and confest your self a lyar, as you pretended to do? I confess I began to fear you, and desir'd to be out of your house, but your own followers forc'd me hither.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: 'Tis well suspected, dissemble still, for there are some may hear us.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
prose: More tricks yet, my Lord? what house this is I know not, I only know my self: it were a great conquest, if you could fasten a scandal upon me: 'saith my Lord, give me leave to write to my brother?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Come down.

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: Come down.

speeches.speaker: Arr.
verse: If it please your Grace, there's a back door.

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: Come meet us there then.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: It seems you are acquainted with the house.

speeches.speaker: Arr.
verse: I have been in it.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: She saw you and dissembled.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Sir, we shall know that better,

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: Bring me unto her, if I prove her not
To be a strumpet, let me be contemn'd
Of all her sex.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: NOw whilst the young Duke follows his delights,
We that do mean to practise in the State,
Must pick our times, and set our faces in,
And nod our heads as it may prove most fit
For the main good of the dear Common-wealth:
Who's within there?

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: My Lord?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Little know they that do not deal in State,
How many things there are to be observ'd,
Which seem but little; yet by one of us
(Whose brains do wind about the Common-wealth)
Neglected, cracks our credits utterly.
prose: Secretary, fetch the Gown I use to read Petitions in, and the Standish I answer French Letters with: and call in the Gentleman that attends:
Sir, but that I do presume upon your secresie, I would not have appear'd to you thus ignorantly attir'd without a tooth-pick in a ribbond, or a Ring in my bandstring.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
prose: Your Lordship send for me?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I did: Sir, your long practice in the State, under a great man, hath led you to much experience.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
prose: My Lord.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Suffer not your modesty to excuse it: in short, and in private, I desire your direction, I take my study already to be furnisht after a grave and wise method.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
prose: What will this Lord do?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: My Book-strings are sutable, and of a reaching colour.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
prose: How's this?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: My Standish of Wood, strange and sweet, and my sore-flap hangs in the right place, and as near Machiavel's, as can be gathered by tradition.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
prose: Are there such men as will say nothing abroad, and play the fools in their Lodgings? this Lord must be followed: and hath your Lordship some new made words to scatter in your speeches in publick, to gain note, that the hearers may carry them away, and dispute of them at dinner?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I have Sir: and besides, my several Gowns and Caps agreeable to my several occasions.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
prose: 'Tis well, and you have learn'd to write a bad hand, that the Readers may take pains for it.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Yes Sir, and I give out I have the palsie.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
prose: Good, 'twere better though, if you had it: your Lordship hath a Secretary, that can write fair, when you purpose to be understood.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: 'Faith Sir I have one, there he stands, he hath been my Secretary these seven years, but he hath forgotten to write.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
prose: If he can make a writing face, it is not amiss, so he keep his own counsel: your Lordship hath no hope of the Gout?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Uh, little Sir, since the pain in my right foot left me.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
prose: 'Twill be some scandal to your wisdom, though I see your Lordship knows enough in publick business.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I am not imploy'd (though to my desert) in occasions forreign, nor frequented for matters domestical.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
prose: Not frequented? what course takes your Lordship?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: The readiest way, my door stands wind, my Sectetary knows I am not denied to any.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
prose: In this (give me leave) your Lordship is out of the way: make a back door to let out Intelligencers; seem to be ever busie, and put your door under keepers, and you shall have a troop of Clients sweating to come at you.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I have a back door already, I will henceforth be busie, Secretary, run and keep the door.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
prose: This will fetch 'um?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I hope so.

speeches.speaker: Secr.
prose: My Lord, there are some require access to you, about weighty affairs of State.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Already?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
prose: I told you so.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: How weighty is the business?

speeches.speaker: Secr.
prose: Treason my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Sir, my debts to you for this are great.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
prose: I will leave your Lordship now.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Sir, my death must be suddain, if I requite you not: at the back door good Sir.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
prose: I will be your Lordships Intelligencer for once.

speeches.speaker: Secr.
prose: My Lord.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Let 'em in, and say I am at my study.

speeches.speaker: 1 Int.
prose: Where is your Lord?

speeches.speaker: Secr.
prose: At his study, but he will have you brought in.

speeches.speaker: Laza.
prose: Why Gentlemen, what will you charge me withal?

speeches.speaker: 2 Int.
prose: Treason, horrible treason, I Hope to have the leading of thee to prison, and prick thee on i'th' arse with a Halbert: to have him hang'd that salutes thee, and call all those in question that spit not upon thee.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose:
My thred is spun, yet might I but call for this dish
of meat at the gallows, instead of a Psalm, it were to be endur'd: the Curtain opens, now my end draws on.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Gentlemen, I am not empty of weighty occasions at this time; I pray you your business.

speeches.speaker: 1 Int.
prose: My Lord, I think we have discover'd one of the most bloudy Traitors, that ever the world held.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Signior Lazarillo, I am glad ye are one of this discovery, give me your hand.

speeches.speaker: 2 Int.
prose: My Lord, that is the Traitor.

speeches.speaker: Luc,
prose: Keep him off, I would not for my whole estate have touchd him.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: My Lord.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Peace Sir, I know the devil is at your tongue's end, to furnish you with speeches: what are the particulars you charge him with?

speeches.speaker: Both Int.
prose: We conferr'd our Notes, and have extracted that, which we will justifie upon our oaths.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: That he would be greater than the Duke, that he had cast plots for this, and meant to corrupt some to betray him, that he would burn the City, kill the Duke, and poison the Privy Council; and lastly kill himself. Though thou deserv'st justly to be hang'd, with silence yet I allow thee to speak, be short.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: My Lord, so may my greatest wish succeed,
So may I live, and compass what I seek,
As I had never treason in my thoughts,
Nor ever did conspire the overthrow
Of any creatures but of brutish beasts,
Fowls, Fishes, and such other humane food,
As is provided for the good of man.
If stealing Custards, Tarts, and Florentines
By some late Statute be created Treason;
How many fellow-Courtiers can I bring,
Whose long attendance and experience,
Hath made them deeper in the plot than I?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Peace, such hath ever been the clemency of my gracious Master the Duke, in all his proceedings, that I had thought, and thought I had thought rightly; that malice would long e'r this have hid her self in her Den, ahd have turn'd her own sting against her own heart: but I well perceive, that so froward is the disposition of a deprav'd nature, that it doth not only seek revenge, where it hath receiv'd injury, but many times thirst after their destruction, where it hath met with benefits.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: But my good Lord —

speeches.speaker: 2 Int.
prose: Let's gagg him.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Peace again, but many times thirst after destruction, where it hath met with benefits; there I left: Such, and no better are the business that we have now in hand.

speeches.speaker: 1 Int.
prose: He's excellently spoken.

speeches.speaker: 1 Int.
prose: He'll wind a Traitor I warrant him,

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: But surely methinks, setting aside the touch of conscience, and all inward convulsions.

speeches.speaker: 2 Int.
prose: He'll be hang'd, I know by that word.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: Your Lordship may consider—

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Hold thy peace: thou canst not answer this speech: no Traitor can answer it: but because you cannot answer this speech, I take it you have confess'd the Treason.

speeches.speaker: 1 Int.
prose: The Count Valore was the first that discover'd him, and can witness it; but he left the matter to your Lordship's grave consideration.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I thank his Lordship, carry him away speedily to the Duke.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: Now Lazarillo thou art tumbl'd down
The hill of fortune, with a violent arm;
All plagues that can be, Famine, and the Sword
Will light upon thee, black despair will boil
In thy despairing breast, no comfort by,
Thy friends far off, thy enemies are nigh.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Away with him, I'll follow you, look you pinion him, and take his money from him, lest he swallow a shilling, and kill himself.

speeches.speaker: 2 Int.
prose: Get thou on before.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: NOw Gondarino, what can you put on now
That may deceive us?
Have ye more strange illusions, yet more mists,
Through which, the weak eye may be led to error:
What can ye say that may do satisfaction
Both for her wrong'd honor, and your ill?

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: All I can say, or may, is said already:
She is unchaste, or else I have no knowledge,
I do not breathe, nor have the use of sense.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: In mine own hearing confess
They brought her to that house we found her in,
Almost by force: and with a great distrust
Of some ensuing hazard?
prose: Dare ye be yet so wilful, ignorant of your own nakedness? did not your servants

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: He that hath begun so worthily,
It fits not with his resolution
What says your Lordship to them?
prose: To leave off thus, my Lord, I know these are but idle proofs.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Count, I dare yet pronounce again, thy Sister is not honest.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: You are your self my Lord, I like your setledness.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Count, thou art young, and unexperienc'd in the dark, hidden ways of Women: Thou dar'st affirm with confidence, a Lady of fifteen may be a Maid.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Sir, if it were not so, I have a Sister would set near my heart.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Let her sit near her shame, it better fits her: call back the bloud that made our stream in nearness, and turn the Current to a better use; 'tis too much mudded, I do grieve to know it.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Dar'st thou make up again, dar'st thou turn face, knowing we know thee, hast thou not been discover'd openly? did not our ears hear her deny thy courtings? did we not see her blush with modest anger, to be so overtaken by a trick; can ye deny this Lord?

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: Had not your Grace, and her kind brother
Been within level of her eye,
You should have had a hotter volley from her,
More full of bloud and fire, ready to leap the window where she stood.
So truly sensual is her appetite.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Sir, Sir, these are but words and tricks, give me the proof.

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: What need a better proof than your Lordship?
I am sure ye have lain with her my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: I have confest it Sir.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I dare not give thee credit without witness.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose:
Does your grace think we carry seconds with us, to search us, and see fair play: your Grace hath been ill tutor'd in the business; but if you hope to try her truly, and satisfy your self what frailty is, give her the Test: do not remember Count she is your Sister; nor let my Lord the Duke believe she is fair; but put her to it without hope or pity, then ye shall see that golden form flie off, that all eyes wonder at for pure and fixt, and under't base blushing Copper; metall not worth the
meanest honor: you shall behold her then my Lord transparent, look through her heart, and view the spirits how they leap, and tell me then I did belie the Lady.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: It shall be done: come Gondarino bear us company,
We do believe thee: she shall die, and thou shalt see it.
How now my friends, who have you guarded hither?

speeches.speaker: 2 Int.
prose: So please your Grace we have discover'd a villain and a Traitor: the Lord Lucio hath examin'd him, and sent him to your Grace for Judgement.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: My Lord, I dare absolve him from all sin o^ Treason: I know his most ambition is but a dish of meat; which he hath hunted with so true a scent, that he deserveth the Collar not the Halter.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Why do they bring him thus bound up? the poor man had more need have some warm meat, to comfort his cold stomach.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Your Grace shall have the cause hereafter, when you shall laugh more freely:
But these are call'd Informers: men that live by Treason, as Rat-catchers do by poison.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Would there were no heavier prodigies hung over us, than this poor fellow, I durst redeem all perils ready to pour themselves upon this State, with a cold Custard.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Your Grace might do it without danger to your person.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: My Lord, if ever I intended treason against your Person, or the State, unless it were by wishing from your Table some dish of meat, which I must needs confess, was not a subjects part: or coveting by stealth, sups from those noble bottles, that no mouth, keeping allegiance true, should dare to taste: I must confess, with more than covetous eye, I have beheld those dear conceal'd dishes, that have been brought in by cunning equipage, to wait upon your Graces pallat: I do confesse, out of this present heat, I have had Stratagems and Ambuscado's; but God be thank'd they have never took.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Count, this business is your own; when you have done, repair to us.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: I will attend your Grace: Lazarello, you are at liberty, be your own man again; and if you can be master of your wishes, I wish it may be so.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: I humbly thank your Lordship: I must be unmannerly, I have some present business, once more I heartily thank your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Now even a word or two to you, and so farewell; you think you have deserv'd much of this State by this discovery: y'are a slavish people, grown subject to the common course of all men. How much unhappy were that noble spirit, could work by such baser gains? what misery would not a knowing man put on with willingness, e'r he see himself grown fat and full fed, by fall of those you rise by? I do discharge ye my attendance; our healthful State needs no such Leeches to suck out her bloud.

speeches.speaker: 1 Int.
prose: I do beseech your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: 2 Int.
prose: Good my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Count.
verse: I will be willing to accept your labours:
Till then I will keep back my promis'd favours:
Here comes another remnant of folly:
prose: Go learn to be more honest, what I see you work your means from honest industry,
I must dispatch him too. Now Lord Lucio, what business brings you hither?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Faith Sir, I am discovering what will become of that notable piece of treason, intended by that Varlet Lazarillo; I have sent him to the Duke for judgement.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Sir, you have perform'd the part of a most careful Statesman, and let me say it to your face, Sir, of a Father to this State: I would wish you to retire, and insconce your self in study: for such is your daily labour, and our fear, that our loss of an hour may breed our overthrow.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Sir, I will be commanded by your judgement, and though I find it a trouble scant to be waded through, by these weak years: yet for the dear care of the Common-wealth, I will bruise my brains, and confine my self to much vexation.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Go, and maist thou knock down Treason like an Ox.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Amen.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Have I spoke thus much in the honor of Learning? learn'd the names of the seven liberal Sciences, before my marriage; and since, have in haste written Epistles congratulatory, to the Nine Muses, and is she prov'd a Whore and a Begger?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: 'Tis true, you are not now to be taught, that no man can be learn'd of a suddain; let not your first project discourage you, what you have lost in this, you may get again in Alchumie.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Fear not Husband, I hope to make as good a wife, as the best of your neighbors, have, and as honest.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: I will goe home; good Sir, do not publish this, as long as it runs amongst our selves; 'tis good honest mirth: you'll come home to supper; I mean to have all her friends, and mine, as ill as it goes.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Do wisely Sir, and bid your own friends, your whole wealth will scarce feast all hers, neither is it for your credit, to walk the streets with a woman so noted; get you home and provide her cloaths: let her come an hour hence with an Hand-basket, and shift her self, she'll serve to sit at the upper end of the Table, and drink to your customers.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Art is just, and will make me amends.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: No doubt Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: The chief note of a Scholar you say, is to govern his passions; wherefore I do take all patiently; in sign of which, my dear Wife, I do kiss thee, make haste home after me, I shall be in my study.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
prose: Go, avaunt, my new City Dame, send me what you promis'd me for consideration; and may'st thou prove, a Lady.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
prose: Thou shalt have it, his Silks shall flie for it.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: How sweet is a Calm after a Tempest, what is there now that can stand betwixt me and felicity? I have gone through all my crosses constantly; have confounded my enemies, and know where to have my longing satisfied: I have my way before me, there's the door, and I may freely walk into my delights: knock boy.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: Who's there?

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: Madona, my Love, not guilty, not guilty, open the door.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: Art thou come sweet-heart?

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: Yes, to my soft embraces, and the rest of my overflowing blisses; come, let us in and swim in our delights: a short Grace as we go, and so to meat.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: Nay my dear Love, you must bear with me in this; we'll to the Church first.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: Shall I be sure of it then?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: By my love you shall.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: And as a holy Lover that hath spent
The tedious night with many a sigh and tears;
Whilst he pursu'd his wench: and hath observ'd
The smiles, and frowns, not daring to displease
When at last, hath with his service won
Her yielding heart; that she begins to dote
Upon him, and can hold no longer out,
But hangs about his neck, and wooes him more
Than ever he desir'd her love before:
Then begins to flatter his desert,
And growing wanton, needs will cast her off;
Try her, pick quarrels, to breed fresh delight,
And to increase his pleasing appetite.
prose: I am content, for I do now wish to hold off longer, to whet my appetite, and do desire to meet with more troubles, so I might conquer them:

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Come Mouse will you walk?

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: How I contemn my fellows in the Court,
With whom I did but yesterday converse?
And in a lower, and an humbler key
Did walk and meditate on grosser meats?
There are they still poor rogues, shaking their chops,
And sneaking after Cheeses, and do run
Headlong in chace, of every Jack of Beer
That crosseth them, in hope of some repast,
That it will bring them to, whilst I am here,
The happiest wight that ever set his tooth
To a dear novelty: approach my love,
Come, let's go to knit the True Loves knot,
That never can be broken.
prose: I pray thee let me be deliver'd of the joy I am so big with, I do feel that high heat within me, that I begin to doubt whether I be mortal:

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: That is to marry a whore.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: When that is done, then will we taste the gift,
Which Fates have sent my Fortunes up to lift.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: When that is done, you'll begin to repent upon a full stomach; but I see, 'tis but a form in destiny, not to be alter'd.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
prose: Sir, what may be the current of your business, that thus you single out your time and place?

speeches.speaker: Arri.
prose: Madam, the business now impos'd upon me, concerns you nearly, I wish some worser man might finish it.

speeches.speaker: Ori.
verse: Why are ye chang'd so? are ye not well Sir?

speeches.speaker: Arr.
verse: Yes Madam, I am well, wo'd you were so.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
verse: Why Sir, I feel my self in perfect health.

speeches.speaker: Arri.
verse: And yet ye cannot live long, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
verse: Why good Arrigo?

speeches.speaker: Arr.
verse: Why? ye must dye.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
verse: I know I must, but yet my fate calls not upon me.

speeches.speaker: Arr.
verse: It does; this hand the Duke commands shall give you death.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
verse: Heaven, and the powers Divine, guard well the innocent.

speeches.speaker: Arr.
verse: Lady, your Prayers may do your soul some good.
That sure your body cannot merit by'em:
You must prepare to die.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
verse: What's my offence? what have these years committed,
That may be dangerous to the Duke, or State?
Have I conspir'd by poison, have I giv'n up,
My honor to some loose unsetl'd bloud
That may give action to my plots?
Dear Sir, let me not dye ignorant of my faults?

speeches.speaker: Arr.
verse: Ye shall not.
Then Lady, you must know, you 're held unhonest;
The Duke, your Brother, and your friends in Court,
With too much grief condemn ye: though to me,
The fault deserves not to be paid with death.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
verse: Who's my accuser?

speeches.speaker: Arri.
verse: Lord Gondarino.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
verse: Arrigo, take these words, and bear them to the Duke,
It is the last petition I shall ask thee:
Tell him the child this present hour brought forth
To see the world has not a soul more pure, more white,
prose: More Virgin than I have; Tell him Lord Gondarino's Plot, I suffer for, and willingly: tell him it had been a greater honor, to have sav'd than kill'd: but I have done: strike, I am arm'd for heaven. Why, stay you? is there any hope?

speeches.speaker: Arri.
verse: I would not strike.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
verse: Have you the power to save?

speeches.speaker: Arri.
verse: With hazard of my life, if it should be known.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
verse: You will not venture that?

speeches.speaker: Arri.
prose: I will Lady: there is that means yet to escape your death, if you can wisely apprehend.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
verse: Ye dare not be so kind?

speeches.speaker: Arri.
verse: I dare, and will, if you dare but deserve't.

speeches.speaker: Ori.
verse: If I should slight my life, I were too blame.

speeches.speaker: Arri.
verse: Then Madam, this is the means, or else you die:
I love you.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
verse: I shall believe it, if you save my life.

speeches.speaker: Arri.
verse: And you must lie with me.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
verse: I dare not buy my life so.

speeches.speaker: Arri.
verse: Come, ye must resolve, say yea or no.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
verse: Then no; nay, look not ruggedly upon me, I am made up too strong to fear such looks:
prose: Come, do your Butchers part: before I would wish life, with the dear loss of honour, I dare find means to free my self.

speeches.speaker: Arr.
verse: Speak, will ye yield?

speeches.speaker: Orian.
prose: Villain, I will not; Murtherer, do thy worst, thy base unnoble thoughts dare prompt thee to; I am above thee slave.

speeches.speaker: Arri.
prose: Wilt thou not be drawn to yield by fair perswasions?

speeches.speaker: Orian.
verse: No, nor by —

speeches.speaker: Arri.
prose: Peace, know your doom then; your Ladyship must remember, you are not now at home, where you dare feast all that come about you: but you are fallen under my mercy, which shall be but small; if thou refuse to yield: hear what I have sworn unto my self; I will enjoy thee, though it be between the parting of thy soul and body; yield yet and live.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
verse: I'll guard the one, let Heaven guard the other,

speeches.speaker: Arri.
verse: Are you so resolute then?
Hold, hold I say.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
verse: What I? yet more terror to my tragedy?

speeches.speaker: Arri.
prose: Lady, the Scene of bloud is done; ye are now as free from scandal, as from death.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Thou Woman which wert born to teach men virtue,
Fair, sweet, and modest Maid, forgive my thoughts,
My trespass was my love.
Seize Gondarino, let him wait our dooms.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: I do begin a little to love this woman; I could endure her already twelve miles off.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Sister, I am glad you have brought your honor off so fairly, without loss: you have done a work above your sex, the Duke admires it: give him fair encounter.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Best of all comforts, may I take this hand, and call it mine?

speeches.speaker: Ori.
prose: I am your Graces handmaid.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Would ye had sed my self: might it not be so Lady?

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Sister, say I, I know you can afford it.

speeches.speaker: Ori.
prose: My Lord, I am your subject, you may command me, provided still, your thoughts be fair and good.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Here I am yours, and when I cease to be so,
Let heaven forget me: thus I make it good.

speeches.speaker: Ori.
prose: My Lord, I am no more mine own.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: So, this bargain was well driven.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Duke, thou hast sold away thy self to all perdition; thou art this present hour becomming Cuckold: methinks I see thy gaul grate through thy veins, and jealousie seize thee with her talons: I know that womans nose must be cut off, she cannot scape it.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Sir, we have punishment for you.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
prose: I do beseech your Lordship, for the wrongs this man hath done me, let me pronounce his punishment.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Lady, I give't to you, he is your own.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: I do beseech your Grace, let me be banisht with all the speed that may be.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: Stay still, you shall attend her sentence.

speeches.speaker: Orian.
prose: Lord Gondarino, you have wrong'd me highly; yet since it sprung from no peculiar hate to me, but from a general dislike unto all women, you shall thus suffer for it; Arrigo, call in some Ladies to assist us; will your Grace make your State?

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: My Lord, I do beseech your Grace for any punishment saving this woman, let me be sent upon discovery of some Island; I do desire but a small Gondela, with ten Holland Cheeses, and I'll undertake it.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
prose: Sir, ye must be content, will ye sit down? nay, do it willingly: Arrigo, tie his Arms close to the chair, I dare not trust his patience.

speeches.speaker: Cond.
prose: Mayst thou be quickly old and painted; mayst thou dote upon some sturdy Yeoman of the Wood-yard, and he be honest; mayst thou be barr'd the lawful lechery of thy Coach, for want of instruments; and last, be thy womb unopen'd.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: This fellow hath a pretty gaul.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: My Lord, I hope to see him purg'd e'r he part,

speeches.speaker: Oria.
prose: Your Ladyships are welcome:
I must desire your helps, though you are no Physitians, to do a strange cure upon this Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Ladies.
prose: In what we can assist you Madam, ye may command us.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Now do I sit like a Conjurer within my circle, and these the Devils that are rais'd about me, I will pray that they may have no power upon me.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
prose: Ladies, fall off in couples, then with a soft still march, with low demeanors, charge this Gentleman, I'll be your Leader.

speeches.speaker: Gond,
prose: Let me be quarter'd Duke quickly, I can endure it: these women long for Mans flesh, let them have it.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Count, have you ever seen so strange a passion? what would this fellow do; if he should find himself in bed with a young Lady?

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: 'Faith my Lord, if he could get a knife, sure he wou'd cut her throat, or else he wou'd do as Hercules did by Lycas, swing out her soul: h'as the true hate of a woman in him.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
prose: Low with your Cursies Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Come not too near me, I have a breath will poison ye, my lungs are rotten, and my stomach is raw: I am given much to belching: hold off, as you love sweet airs; Ladies, by your first nights pleasure, I conjure you, as you wou'd have your Husbands proper men, strong backs, and little legs, as you would have 'em hate your Waiting-women.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
prose: Sir, we must court ye, till we have obtain'd some little favour from those gracious eyes, 'tis but a kiss a piece.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: I pronounce perdition to ye all; ye are a parcel of that damned crew that fell down with Lucifer, and here ye staid on earth to plague poor men; vanish, avaunt, I am fortified against your charms; heaven grant me breath and patience.

speeches.speaker: 1 Lady.
prose: Shall we not kiss then?

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: No fear my lips with hot irons first, or stitch them up like a Ferrets: oh that this brunt were over!

speeches.speaker: 2 Lady.
prose: Come, come, little rogue, thou art too maidenly by my troth, I think I must box thee till thou be'st bolder; the more bold, the more welcome: I prethee kiss me, be not afraid.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: If there be any here, that yet have so much of the fool left in them, as to love their mothers, let them on her, and loath them too.

speeches.speaker: 2. Lady.
prose: What a slovenly little villain art thou, why dost thou not stroke up thy hair? I think thou ne'er comb'st it: I must have it lie in better order; so, so, so, let me see thy hands, are they wash'd?

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: I would thy were loose for thy sake.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: She tortures him admirably.

speeches.speaker: Count.
prose: The best that ever was.

speeches.speaker: 2 Lady.
prose: Alas, how cold they are, poor golls, why dost thee not get thee a Muff?

speeches.speaker: Arri.
prose: Madam, here's an old Countrey Gentlewoman at the door, that came nodding up for justice, she was with the Lord Gondarino to day, and would now again come to the speech of him, she says.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
prose: Let her in, for sports sake, let her in.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Mercy, oh Duke, I do appeal to thee: plant Canons there, and discharge them against my breast rather: nay, first let this she-fury sit still where she does, and with her nimble fingers stroke my hair, play with my fingers ends, or any thing, until my panting heart have broke my breast.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: You must abide her censure.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: I see her come, unbutton me, for she will speak.

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
prose: Where is he Sir?

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Save me, I hear her.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: There he is in state to give you audience

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
prose: How does your Lordship?

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Sick of the spleen.

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
prose: How?

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: Sick.

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
prose: Will you chew a Nutmeg, you shall not refuse it, it is very comfortable.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
verse: Nay, now thou art come, I know it
Is the Devils Jubile, Hell is broke loose:
My Lord, if ever I have done you service,
Or have deserv'd a favour of your Grace,
Let me be turn'd upon some present action,
Where I may sooner die, than languish thus;
Your Grace hath her petition, grant it her, and ease me now at last.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: No Sir, you must endure,

speeches.speaker: Gentlew.
verse: For my petition, I hope your
Lordship hath remembred me.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
prose: 'Faith I begin to pity him, Arrigo, take her off, bear her away, say her petition is granted.

speeches.speaker: Centlew.
prose: Whither do you draw me Sir? I know it is not my Lords pleasure I should be thus used, before my business be dispatched?

speeches.speaker: Arr.
prose: You shall know more of that without.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
prose: Unbind him Ladies, but before he go, this he shall promise; for the love I bear to our own sex, I would have them still hated by thee, and injoyn thee as a punishment, never hereafter willingly to come in the presence, or sight of any woman, nor never to seek wrongfully, the publick disgrace of any.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: 'Tis that I would have sworn, and do: when I meditate with them, for their good, or their bad; may Time call back this day again, and when I come in their companies, may I catch the pox, by their breath, and have no other pleasure for it.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Ye are most merciful.

speeches.speaker: Oria.
prose: My Lord, I shew'd my sex the better.

speeches.speaker: Gond.
prose: All is over-blown Sister: y'are like to have a fair night of it, and a Prince in your Arms: let's goe my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Thus through the doubtful streams of joy and grief,
True Love doth wade, and finds at last relief.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: SHamount, welcome; we have mist thee long,
Though absent but two days: I hope your sports
Answer your time and wishes.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Very nobly Sir;
We found game, worthy your delight my Lord,
It was so royal.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I've enough to hear on't.
Prethee bestow't upon me in discourse.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: What is this Gentleman, Coz? you are a Courtier,
Therefore know all their insides.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: No farther than the Tassaty goes, good Coz.
For the most part, which is indeed the best part
Of the most general inside; marry thus far
I can with boldness speak this one mans character,
And upon honor, pass it for a true one;
He has that strength of manly merit in him,
That it exceeds his Sovereigns power of gracing;
He's faithfully true to valour, that he hates
The man from Caesar's time, or farther off,
That ever took disgrace unreveng'd:
And if he chance to read his abject story,
He tears his memory out; and holds it virtuous,
Not to let shame have so much life amongst us;
There is not such a curious piece of courage
Amongst mans fellowship, or one so jealous
Of honors loss, or repuations glory:
There's so much perfect of his growing story.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: 'Twould make one dote on virtue as you tell it.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: I have told it to much loss, believe it Coz.

speeches.speaker: 3 Gent.
verse: How the Duke graces him? what is he brother?

speeches.speaker: 4 Gent.
verse: Do you not yet know him? a vain-glorious coxcomb,
As proud as he that fell for't:
Set but aside his valour; no virtue;
Which is indeed, not fit for any Courtier;
And we his fellows are as good as he,
Perhaps as capable of favour too,
For one thing or another, if 'twere look'd into:
Give me a man, were I a Sovereign now
Has a good stroke of Tennis, and a stiff one,
Can play at AEquinoctium with the Line,
As even, as the thirteenth of September,
When day and night lie in a scale together:
Or may I thrive, as I deserve at Billiards;
No otherwise at Chesse, or at Primero:
These are the parts requir'd, why not advanc'd?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Trust me, it was no less than excellent pleasure,
And I'm right glad 'twas thine. How fares our kinsman?
Who can resolve us best?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: I can my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: There, if I had a pity without bounds,
It might be all bestowed—A man so lost
In the wild ways of passion, that he's sensible
Of nought, but what torments him?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: True my Lord,
He runs through all the Passions of mankind,
And shifts 'em strangely too: one while in love,
And that so violent, that for want of business,
He'll court the very Prentice of a Laundress,
Though she have kib'd heels: and in's melancholly agen,
He will not brook an Empress though thrice fairer
Than ever Maud was; or higher spirited
Than Cleopatra, or your English Countess:
Then on a suddain he's so merry again,
Out laughs a Waiting-woman before her first Child:
And turning of a hand, so angry—
Has almost beat the Northern fellow blind;
That is for that use only; if that mood hold my Lord,
Had need of a fresh man; I'll undertake,
He shall bruise three a month.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I pity him dearly:
And let it be your charge, with his kind brother
To see his moods observ'd; let every passion
Be fed ev'n to a surfet, which in time
May breed a loathing: let him have enough
Of every object, that his sence is wrapt with;
And being once glutted, then the taste of folly
Will come into his rellish.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: I shall see
Your charge my Lord, most faithfuly effected:
And how does noble Shamount?

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Never ill man
Until I hear of baseness, then I sicken:
I am the healthfull'st man i'th' kingdom else.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Be arm'd then for a fit,
Here comes a fellow
Will make you sick at heart, if baseness do't.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: Let me be gone: what is he?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Let me tell you first,
It can be but a qualm: pray stay it out Sir,
Come, y'ave born more than this.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: Born? never any thing
That was injurious.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Ha, I am far from that.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: He looks as like a man as I have seen one:
What would you speak of him? speak well I prethee,
Even for humanities cause.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: You'd have it truth though?

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: What else Sir? I have no reason to wrong heav'n
To favour nature; let her bear her own shame
If she be faulty.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Monstrous faulty there Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: I'm ill at ease already.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Pray bear up Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: I prethee let me take him down with speed then;
Like a wild object that I would not look upon.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Then thus: he's one that will endure as much
As can be laid upon him.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: That may be noble:
I'm kept too long from his acquaintance.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Oh Sir,
Take heed of rash repentance, y'are too forward
To find out virtue where it never setl'd:
Take the particulars first, of what he endures;
Videlicet, Bastinadoes by the great.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: How!

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Thumps by the dozen, and your kicks by wholesale.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: No more of him.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: The twinges by the nostril he snuffs up,
And holds it the best remedy for sneezing.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Away.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: H'as been thrice switch'd from 7 a clock till 9.
Yet with a Cart-Horse stomach, fell to breakfast;
Forgetful of his smart.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Nay, the disgrace on't;
There's no smart but that: base things are felt
More by their shames than hurts, Sir. I know you not.
But that you live an injury to nature:
I'm heartily angry with you.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Pray give your blow or kick and begone then:
For I ne'er saw you before; and indeed,
Have nothing to say to you, for I know you not.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Why wouldst thou take a blow?

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: I would not Sir,
Unless 'twere offer'd me; and if from an enemy?
I'd be loth to deny it from a stranger.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: What, a blow?
Endure a blow? and shall he live that gives it?

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Many a fair year—why not Sir?

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Let me wonder!
As full a man to see to, and as perfect—
I prethee live not long—

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Let me intreat it:
Thou dost not know what wrong thou dost mankind,
To walk so long here; not to dye betimes.
Let me advise thee, while thou hast to live here,
Ev'n for man's honour sake, take not a blow more.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: You should advise them not to strike me then Sir,
For I'll take none I assure you, 'less they are given.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: How fain would I preserve mans form from shame
And cannot get it done? however Sir,
I charge thee live not long.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: This is worse than beating.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Of what profession art thou, tell me Sir,
Besides a Tailor? for I'll know the truth.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: A Tailor? I'm as good a Gentleman—
Can shew my Arms and all,

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: How black and blew they are?
Is that your manifestation? upon pain
Of pounding thee to dust, assume not wrongfully
The name of Gentleman, because I'm one,
That must not let thee live.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: I have done, I have done Sir.
If there be any harm, beshrew the Herald,
I'm sure I ha' not been so long a Gentleman,
To make this anger: I have nothing no where,
But what I dearly pay for.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Groom begone;
I never was so heart-sick yet of man.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Here comes a cordial, Sir, from th'other sex,
Able to make a dying face look chearful.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: The blessedness of Ladies —

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Y'are well met Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: The sight of you has put an evil from me,
Whose breath was able to make virtue sicken,

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: I'm glad I came so fortunately. What was't Sir?

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: A thing that takes a blow, lives, and eats after it,
In very good health; you ha' not seen the like, Madam,
A Monster worth your sixpence, lovely worth,
Speak low Sir; by all likely-hoods 'tis her Husband, ^,
That now bestow'd a visitation on me. Farewel Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Husband? is't possible that he has a wise?
Would any creature have him? 'tis some forc'd match,
If he were not kick'd to th'Church o' th'wedding day,
I'll never come at Court. Can be no otherwise:
Perhaps he was rich, speak mistriss Lapet, was't not so?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: Nay, that's without all question.

speeches.speaker: Sh.
verse: O ho, he would not want kickers enow then;
If you are wise, I much suspect your honesty;
For wisdom never fastens constantly,
But upon merit: if you incline to fool,
You are alike unfit for his society;
Nay, if it were not boldness in the man
That honors you, to advise you, troth his company
Should not be frequent with you.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: 'Tis good counsel Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Oh, I am so careful where I reverence,
So just to goodness, and her precious purity,
I'm as equally jealous, and as fearful,
That any undeserved stain might fall
Upon her sanctified whiteness, as of the sin
That comes by wilfulness.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: Sir, I love your thoughts,
And honor you for your counsel and your care.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: We are your servants.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: He's but a Gentleman o'th' chamber; he might have kist me:
Faith, where shall one find less courtesie, than at Court?
Say I have an undeserver to my Husband:
That's ne'er the worse for him: well strange lip'd men,
'Tis but a kiss lost, there'll more come agen.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Look, who comes here Sir, his love-fit's upon him:
I know it, by that sett smile, and those congies.
How courteous he's to nothing? which indeed,
Is the next kin to woman; only shadow
The elder Sister of the twain, because 'tis seen too.
See how it kisses the fore-finger still;
Which is the last edition, and being come
So near the thumb, every Cobler has got it.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: What a ridiculous piece, humanity
Here makes it self?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Nay good give leave a little, Sir,
Y'are so precise a manhood—

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: It afflicts me
When I behold unseemliness in an Image
So near the Godhead, 'tis an injury
To glorious Eternity.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Pray use patience, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: I do confess it freely, precious Lady,
And loves suit is so, the longer it hangs
The worse it is; better cut off, sweet Madam;
Oh, that same drawing in your neather Lip there,
Fore shews no goodness, Lady; make you question on't?
Shame on me, but I love you.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Who is't Sir,
You are at all this pains for? may I know her?

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: For thee thou fairest, yet the falsest woman,
That ever broke man's heart-strings.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: How? how's this Sir?

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: What the old trick of Ladies? man's apparel,
Will't ne'er be left amongst you? steal from Court in't?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: I see the Fit grows stronger.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Pray le^'^ talk a little.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: I can endure no more.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Good, let's alone a little:
You are so exa^ a work: love light things somewhat, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Th'a^e ^ but shames.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: What ^ yo^'d say to me, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse:
Can you ^
^orgetful to enquire it Lady?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Yes truely, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: The more I admire your slintiness:
What cause have I given you, ^ Madam,
To play this strange part with ^

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Cause enough,
Do but look back Sir, into your memory,
Your love to other women, oh lewd man:
'Tas almost kill'd my heart, you see I'm chang'd with it,
I ha' lost the fashion of my Sex with grief on t,
When I have seen you courting of a Dowdie;
Compar'd with me, and kissing your fore-finger
To one o'th' Black-Guards Mistresses: would not this
Crack a poor Ladies heart, that believ'd love,
And waited for the comfort? but 'twas said, Sir,
A Lady of my hair cannot want pittying:
The Countrey's coming up, farewel to you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Whither intend you, Sir?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: A long journey, Sir:
The truth is, I'm with child, and goe to travel.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: With child? I never got it.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: I heard you were busie
At the same time, Sir, and was loth to trouble you.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Why, are not you a whore then, excellent Madam?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Oh by no means, 'twas done Sir in the state
Of my belief in you, and that quits me;
It lies upon your falshood.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Does it so?
You shall not carry her though Sir, she's my contract.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: I prethee, thou four Elements ill brued,
Torment none but thy self; away I say
Thou beast of passion, as the drunkard is
The beast of Wine; dishonor to thy making,
Thou man in fragments.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Hear me, precious Madam.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Kn^l for thy wits to Heaven.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Lady, I'll father it,
Who e'er begot it: 'tis the course of greatness.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: How virtue groans at this?

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: I'll raise the Court, but I'll stay your flight.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: How wretched is that piece?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: He's the Dukes kinsman, Si^.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: That cannot take a passion away, Sir,
Nor cut a Fit, but one poor hour shorter,
He must endure as much as the poorest begger,
That cannot change his money; there's th' equality
In our impartial Essence:
What's the news now?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Your worthy brother, Sir, 'has left his charge,
And come to see you.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Oh the noblest welcome
That ever came from man, meet thy deservings:
Methinks I've all joyes treasure in mine arms now,

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: You are so fortunate in prevention, brother,
You always leave the answerer barren, Sir,
You comprehend in few words so much worth—

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: 'Tis all too little for thee: come th'art welcome
So I include all: take especial knowledge pray,
Of this dear Gentleman, my absolute friend,
That loves a Soldier far above a Mistriss,
Thou excellently faithful to 'em both.
But love to manhood, owns the purer troth.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: THere should be in this Gallery—oh th'are here,
Pray sit down, believe me Sir, I'm weary.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: It well becomes a Lady to complain a little
Of what she never feels: your walk was short, Madam,
You can be but afraid of weariness;
Which well employs the softness of your Sex,
As for the thing it self, you never came to't.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: You're wond'rously well read in Ladies, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: Shall I think such a creature as you Madam,
Was ever born to feel pain, but in Travel?
There's your full portion,
Besides a little tooth-ach in the breeding,
Which a kind Husband too, takes from you, Madam.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: But where do Ladies, Sir, find such kind Husbands?
Perhaps you have heard
The Rheumatick story of some loving Chandler now,
Or some such melting fellow that you talk
So prodigal of mens kindness: I confess Sir,
Many of those wives are happy, their ambition
Does reach no higher, than to Love and Ignorance,
Which makes an excellent Husband, and a fond one:
Now Sir, your great ones aim at height, and cunning,
And so are oft deceiv'd, yet they must venture it;
For 'tis a Ladies contumely, Sir,
To have a Lord an Ignorant; then the worlds voice
Will deem her for a wanton, e'r she taste on't:
But to deceive a wise man, to whose circumspection,
The world resigns it self, with all his envy;
'Tis less dishonor to us, than to fall,
Because his believ'd wisdom keeps out all.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: Would I were the man, Lady, that should venture
His wisdom to your goodness.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: You might fail
In the return, as many men have done, Sir:
I dare not justifie what is to come of me,
Because I know it not, though I hope virtuously;
Marry what's past, or present, I durst put
Into a good mans hand, which if he take
Upon my word for good, it shall not cozen him.

speeches.speaker: Sol.
verse: No, nor hereafter?

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: It may hap so too, Sir:
A womans goodness, when she is a wife,
Lies much upon a mans desert, believe it Sir,
If there be fault in her, I'll pawn my life on't,
'Tis first in him, if she were ever good,
That makes one; knowing not a Husband yet,
Or what he may be: I promise no more virtues,
Than I may well perform, for that were cozenage.

speeches.speaker: Sol.
verse: Happy were he that had you with all fears,
That's my opinion, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: What say you now, Sir?
Dare you give confidence to your own eyes?

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Not yet I dare not.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: No?

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Scarce yet, or yet:
Although I see 'tis he. Why can a thing,
That's but my self divided, be so false?

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: Nay, do but mark how the chair plays hie part too:
How amoroesly 'tis bent.

speeches.speaker: Shvm.
verse: Hell take thy bad thoughts,
For they are strange ones. Never take delight
To make a torment worse. Look on 'em heaven,
For that's a brother: send me a fair enemy,
And take him; for a fouler Fiend there breathes not:
I will not sin to think there's ill in her,
But what's of his producing.
Yet goodness, whose inclosure is but flesh,
Holds out oft times but sorrily. But as black Sir,
As ever kindred was: I hate mine own bloud,
Because is is so near thine. Live without honesty,
And mayst thou dye with an unmoist'ned eye,
And no tear follow thee.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Y'are wond'rous merry Sir; I would your Brother heard you.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: Oh my Sister,
I would not out o'th' way, let fall my words Lady,
For the precisest humor.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Yea, so close.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: Th'are merry, that's the worst you can report on 'em:
Th'are neither dangerous, nor immodest.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: So Sir,
Shall I believe you, think you?

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: Who's this, Lady?

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Oh the Dukes Cosin, he came late from travel, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: Respect belongs to him.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: For as I said, Lady,
Th'are merry, that's the worst you can report of 'em:
Th'are neither dangerous, nor immodest.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: How's this?

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: And there I think I left.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: Abuses me.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Now to proceed, Lady; perhaps I swore I lov'd you,
If you believe me not, y'are much the wiser.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: He speaks still in my person, and derides me.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: For I can cog with you.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: You can all do so:
We make no question of mens promptness that way.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: And smile, and wave a chair with comely grace too,
Play with our Tastle gently, and do fine things,
That catch a Lady sooner than a virtue.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: I never us'd to let man live so long
That wrong'd me.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Talk of Battalions, wooe you in a skirmish;
Divine my mind to you Lady; and being sharp set,
Can court you at Half pike: or name your weapon,
We cannot fail you Lady.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: Now he dies:
Were all succeeding hopes stor'd up wichin him.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Oh fie, i'th' Court, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: I most dearly thank you; Sir.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: 'Tis rage ill spent upon a passionate mad man.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: That shall not priviledge him for ever, Sir:
A mad man call you him? I have sound too much reason
Sound in his injury to me, to believe him so.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: If ever truth from mans lips may be held
In reputation with you, give this confidence;
And this his Love-fit, which we observe still,
By's flattering and his fineness: at some other time,
He'll go as slovenly as heart can wish.
The love and pity that his Highness shews to him,
Makes every man the more respectful of him:
Has never a passion, but is well provided for,
As this of Love, he is full fed in all
His swinge, as I may tearm it: have but patience,
And ye shall witness somewhat.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: Still he mocks me:
Look you, in action, in behaviour, Sir;
Hold still the chair, with a grand mischief to you,
Or I'll let so much strength upon your heart, Sir—

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: I feel some power has restrain'd me Lady:
If it be sent from Love, say, I obey it,
And ever keep a voice to welcome it.
THou Deity, swift winged Love,
Sometimes below, sometimes above,
Little in shape, but great in power,
Thou that mak'st a heart thy Tower,
And thy loop-holes Ladies eyes,
From whence thou strik'st the fond and wise.
Did all the Shafts in thy fair Quiver
Stick fast in my ambitious Liver;
Yet thy power would I adore.
And call upon thee to shoot more,
Shoot more, shoot more.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: I prethee hold though, sweet Celestial boy;
I'm not requited yet with love enough,
For the first Arrow that I have within me;
And if thou be an equal Archer Cupid,
Shoot this Lady, and twenty more for me.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Me Sir?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: 'Tis nothing but device, fear it not Lady;
You may be as good a Maid after that shaft, Madam,
As e'er your mother was at twelve and a half:
'Tis like the boy that draws it, 'tas no sting yet.

speeches.speaker: Cup.
verse: 'Tis like the miserable Maid that draws it—
That sees no comfort yet, seeing him so passionate,

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Strike me the Duchess of Valois in love with me,
With all the speed thou canst, and two of her Women.

speeches.speaker: Cu.
verse: You shall have more.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Tell 'em I tarry for 'em.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Who would be angry with that walking trouble now?
That hurts none but it self?

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: I am better quieted.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: I'll have all women-kind struck in time for me
After thirteen once:
I see this Cupid will not let me want,
And let him spend his forty shafts an hour,
They shall be all found from the Dukes Exchequer;
He's come already.
OH turn thy bow,
Thy power we feel and know,
Fair Cupid turn away thy Bow:
They be those golden Arrows,
Bring Ladies all their sorrows,
And till there be more truth in men,
Never shoot at Maid agen.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: What a felicity of whores are here?
And all my Concubines struck bleeding new:
A man can in his life time, make but one woman,
But he may make his fifty Queans a month.

speeches.speaker: Cu.
verse: Have you remembred a Priest, honest brothers?

speeches.speaker: 1 Bro.
verse: Yes Sister, and this is the young Gentleman,
Make you no question of our faithfulness.

speeches.speaker: 2 Bro.
verse: His growing shame, Sister, provokes our care:

speeches.speaker: Priest.
verse: He must be taken in this fit of Love, Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: 1 Bro.
verse: What else Sir, he shall do't.

speeches.speaker: 2 Bro.
verse: Enough.

speeches.speaker: 1 Bro.
verse: Be chearful wench.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Now by the stroke of pleasure, a deep oath,
Nimbly hopt Ladies all; what height they bear too?
A story higher than your common statures;
A little man must go up stairs to kiss 'em:
What a great space there is
Betwixt Loves Dining Chamber, and his Garret?
I'll try the utmost height — the Garret stoops methinks;
The rooms are made all bending, I see that,
And not so high as a man takes 'em for.

speeches.speaker: Cu.
verse: Now if you'll follow me Sir, I've that power,
To make them follow you.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Are they all shot?

speeches.speaker: Cu.
verse: All, all Sir, every mothers daughter of 'em.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Then there's no fear of following; if they be once shot
They'll follow a man to th' devil—As for you, Sir—

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: Me Sir?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Nay sweet Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: A noise, a threatening, did you not hear it Sir?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Without regard, Sir, so would I hear you
