The satisfaction than the promise.

speeches.speaker: 1 Law.
verse: Is not this a satisfaction to engage
My self for this assurance, if he

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: No Sir, my ruin never shall import
Anothers loss, if not by accident,
And that my purpose is not guilty of:
You're engag'd in nothing but your care.
Attend the Procurator to the Court,
Observe how things incline, and bring me word.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: I dare not, Sir, if I be taken there,
Mine ears will be in danger.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Why? hast thou
Committed something that deserves thine ears?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: No, but I fear the noise; my hearing will be
Perished by the noise; 'tis as good 't want
A member, as to loose the use—
A member as to lose the use—

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: The ornament is excepted.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Well my Lord
I'll put 'em to the hazard.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cred.
verse: Your desires be prosperous to you.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cred.
verse: Our best Prayers wait
Upon your fortune.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: For your selves, not him.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Thou canst not blame 'em: I am in their debts.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: But had your large expence (a part whereof
You owe 'em) for unprofitable Silks
And Laces, been bestowed among the poor,
That would have prayed the right way for you:
Not upon you.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: For unprofitable Silks
And Laces? now believe me honest boy
Th'ast hit upon a reprehension that belongs
Unto me.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: By — my Lord,
I had not so unmannerly a thought,
To reprehend you.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Why I love thee sor't.
Mine own acknowledgement confirms thy words:
For once I do remember, comming from
The Mercers, where my Purse had spent it self
On those unprofitable toys thou speak'st of,
A man half naked with his poverty
Did meet me, and requested my relief:
I wanted whence to give it, yet his eyes
Spoke for him, those I could have satisfied
With some unfruitful sorrow, (if my tears
Would not have added rather to his grief,
Than eas'd it) but the true compassion that
I should have given I had not: this began
To make me think how many such mens wants
The vain superfluous cost I wore upon
My outside, would have clothed, and left my self
A habit as becomming: to increase
This new consideration there came one
Clad in a garment plain and thrifty, yet
As decent as these fair dear follies; made
As if it were of purpose to despise
The vanity of shew: his purse had still
The power to do a charitable deed,
And did it.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Yet your inclination, Sir,
Deserv'd no less to be commended, than his action.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Prethee do not flatter me;
He that intends well, yet deprives himself
Of means, to put his good thoughts into deed,
Deceives his purpose of the due reward
That goodness merits: oh antiquity
Thy great examples of Nobility
Are out of imitation, or at least
So lamely follow'd, that thou art as much
Before this age in virtue, as in time,

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Sir, it must needs be lamely followed, when
The chiefest men love to follow it
Are for the most part cripples.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Who are they?

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Soldiers, my Lord, soldiers.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: 'Tis true Duboys: but if the law disables me no more
For Noble actions, than good purposes,
I'll practice how to exercise the worth
Commended to us by our ancestors;
The poor neglected soldier shall command
Me from a Ladies Courtship, and the form
I'll study shall no more be taught me by
The Taylor, but the Scholar; that expence
Which hitherto has been to entertain
Th' intemperate pride and pleasure of the taste
Shall fill my Table more to satisfie,
And less to surfeit.
What an honest work it would be; when we find
A Virgin in her poverty, and youth
Inclining to be tempted, to imploy
As much perswasion, and as much expence
To keep her upright, as men use to do upon her falling.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: 'Tis charity that many Maids will be unthankful for,
And some will rather take it for a wrong,
To buy 'em out of their inheritance,
The thing that they were born to.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Longueville, thou bringst a chearful promise in thy face.
There stands no pale report upon thy cheek,
To give me fear or knowledge of my loss, 'tis red and lively.
How proceeds my suit?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: That's with leave, Sir, a labour that to those of Hercules,
May add another; or (at least) be call'd
An imitation of his burning shirt:
For 'twas a pain of that merciful
Perplexity, to shoulder through the throng
Of people, that attended your success:
My sweaty linnen sixt upon my skin,
Still as they pull'd me, took that with it; 'twas
A fear I should have left my flesh among 'em:
Yet I was patient, for (methought) the to^l
Might be an emblem of the difficult
And weary passage to get out of Law.
And to make up the dear similitude,
When I was forth seeking my handkerchief
To wipe my sweat off, I did find a cause
To make me sweat more, for my Purse was lost
Among their fingers.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: There 'twas rather sound.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: By them.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: I mean so.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Well, I will restore
Thy damage to thee: how proceeds my suit?

speeches.speaker: Lang.
verse: Like one at Brokers; I think forfeited.
Your promising Counsel at the first
Put strongly forward with a labour d speed,
And such a violence of pleading, that
His Fee in Sugar-candy scarce will make
His throat a satisfaction for the hurt
He did it, and he carried the whole cause
Before him, with so clear a passage, that
The people in the savour of your side
Cried Montague, Montague: in the spight of him
That cryed out silence, and began to laugh
Your adversaries advocate to scorn:
Who like a cunning Footman set me forth
With such a temperate easie kind of course
To put him into exercise of strength,
And follow'd his advantages so close,
That when your hot mouth'd pleader thought h' had won,
Before he reacht it, he was out of breath,
And then the other stript him.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: So all is lost.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: But how I know not; for, (methought) I stood
Confounded with the clamour of the Court,
Like one embark'd upon a storm at Sea,
Where the tempestuous noise of Thunder mixt
With roaring of the billows, and the thick,
Imperfect language of the Sea men, takes
His understanding and his safety both
Together from him.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Thou dost bring ill news

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Of what I was unwilling to have been
The first reporter.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Didst observe no more?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: At least no better

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Then th'art not inform'd
So well as I am; I can tell thee that
Will please thee, for when all else left my cause,
My very adversaries took my part.

speeches.speaker: Long
verse: — Whosoever told you that, abused you.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Credit me, he took my part
When all forsook me.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Took it from you.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Yes I mean so, and I think he had just cause
To take it. when the verdict gave it him.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: His Spirit would ha' sunk him, e'r he could
Have carried an ill fortune of this weight so lightly.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Nothing is a misery, unless our weakness apprehend it so;
We cannot be more faithful to our selves
In any thing that's manly, than to make
Ill fortune as contemptible to us
As it makes us to others.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Here come they
Whose very countenances will tell you how
Contemptible it is to others.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Sir?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: The Sir of Knighthood may be given him, e'r
They hear you now?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Good Sir but a word.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: How soon the loss of wealth makes any man
Grow out of knowledge.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Let me see, I pray, Sir,
Never stood you upon the Pillory?

speeches.speaker: 1 Law.
verse: The Pillory?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Oh now I know you did not.
Y'ave ears, I thought ye had lost 'em; pray observe,
Here's one that once was gracious in your eyes.

speeches.speaker: 1 Law.
verse: Oh my Lord, have an eye upon him.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: But ha' you ne'er a Counsel to redeem
His Land yet from the judgement?

speeches.speaker: 2 Law.
prose: None but this, a Writ of error to remove the cause.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: No more of error, we have been in that too much already.

speeches.speaker: 2 Law.
prose: If you will reverse the judgement, you must trust to that delay.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Delay? indeed he's like to trust to that,
With you has any dealing-

speeches.speaker: 2 Law.
verse: E'r the Law proceeds to an Habere facias possessionem.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: That's a language Sir, I understand not.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Th'art a very strange unthankful fellow to have taken Fees of such a liberal measure, and then give a man hard words for's money.

speeches.speaker: 1 Law.
verse: If men will hazard their salvations,
What should I say; I've other business.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Y'are i'th' right;
That's it you should say, now prosperity has left me.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cred.
verse: Have an eye upon him; if
We lose him now, he's gone for ever; stay
And dog him: I'll go fetch the Officers.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Dog him you Bloud-hound: by this point thou shalt more safely dog an angry Lion, than attempt him.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: What's the matter:

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Do but stir to fetch a Serjeant; and besides your loss
Of labour, I'll have you beaten, till
Those easement in your faces be false lights.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Falser than those you sell by.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Who gave you Commission to abuse my friends thus?

speeches.speaker: Lon.
verse: Sir, are those your friends that would betray you?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: 'Tis to save themselves rather than betray me.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cred.
verse: Your Lordship makes a just construction of it.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cred.
verse: All our desire is but to get our own.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Your wives desires and yours do differ then.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: So far as my ability will go
You shall have satisfaction Longeville.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: And leave your self neglected; every man
Is first a debtor to his own demands, being honest.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: As I take it, Sir, I did
Not entertain you for my Counselor.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Counsel's the office of a servant,
When the master falls upon a danger; as
Defence is; never threaten with your eyes,
They are no cockatrices; do you hear?
Talk with the Girdler, or the Mill'ner,
He can inform you of a kind of men
That first undid the profit of those trades
By bringing up the form of carrying
Their Morglays in their hands: with some of those
A man may make himself a priviledge
To ask a question at the prison gates
Without your good permission.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cred.
verse: By your leave.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Stay Sir, what one example since the time
That first you put your hat off to me, have
You noted in me to encourage you
To this presumption? by the justice now
Of thine own rule, I should begin with thee,
I should turn thee away ungratified
For all thy former kindness, forget
Thou ever didst me any service: 'tis not fear
Of being arrested, makes me thus incline
To satisfy you; for you see by him,
I lost not all defences with my state;
The curses of a man to whom I am
Beholding, terrify me more, than all
The violence he can pursue me with.
Duboys, I did prepare me for the worst;
These two small Cabinets do comprehend
The sum of all the wealth that it hath pleased
Adversity to leave me, one as rich
As th'other, both in Jewels; take thou this,
And as the Order put within it, shall
Direct thee, distribute it half between
Those Creditors, and th' other half among
My servants: for (Sir) they are my Creditors
As well as you are, they have trusted me
With their advancement: if the value sail,
To please you all, my first increase of means
Shall offer you a fuller payment; be content
To leave me something, and imagine that
You put a new beginner into credit.

speeches.speaker: Cred.
prose: So prosper our own blessings, as we wish you to your merit.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Are you silences of discontent, or of sorrow?

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Sir, we would not leave you.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Do but suffer us to follow you, and what our present means, or industries hereafter can provide, shall serve you.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Oh desire me not to live
To such a baseness, as to be maintained
By those that serve me; pray begone, I will
Defend your honesties to any man
That shall report, you have forsaken me;
I pray begone.
Why, dost thou weep my boy,
Because I do not bid thee go to?

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: No, I weep (my Lord) because I would not go;
I fear you will command me.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: No my child,
I will not; that would discommend th' intent
Of all my other actions: thou art yet
Unable to advise thy self a course,
Should I put thee to seek it; after that
I must excuse, or at the least forgive
Any charitable deed that can be done against my self.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: Every day (my Lord) I tarry with you, I'll account
A day of blessing to me; for I shall
Have so much less time left me of my life
When I am from you: and if misery
Befall you (which I hope so good a man
Was never born to) I will take my part,
And make my willingness increase my strength
To bear it. In the Winter I will spare
Mine own cloths from my self to cover you;
And in the Summer, carry some of yours
To ease you: I'll doe any thing I can.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Why, thou art able to make misery
Ashamed of hurting, when thy weakness can
Both bear it, and despise it: Come my boy
I will provide some better way for thee
Than this thou speakst of: 'tis the comfort that
I'll fortune has undone me into the fashion:
For now in this age most men do begin,
To keep but one boy, that kept many men.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Where is she? call her.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: I attend you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Your friend sweet Madam.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: What friend, good my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Your Montague, Madam, he will shortly want
Those Courtly graces that you love him for;
The means wherewith he purchased this, and this;
And all his own provisions to the least
Proportion of his feeding, or his clothes,
Came out of that inheritance of land
Which he unjustly lived on: but the law
Has given me right in't, and possession; now
Thou shalt perceive his bravery vanish, as
This Jewell does from thee now, and these Pearls
To him that owes 'em.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Ye are the owner Sir of every thing that does belong to me.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: No, not of him, sweet Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: O good Heaven!

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: But in a while your mind will change, and be
As ready to disclaim him; when his wants
And miseries have perish'd his good face,
And taken off the sweetness that has made
Him pleasing in a womans understanding.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: O Heaven, how gratious had Creation been
To women, who are born without defence,
If to our hearts there had been doors through which
Our husbands might have lookt into our thoughts,
And made themselves undoubtfull.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Made 'em mad.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: With honest women.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Thou dost still pretend
A title to that virtue: prethee let
Thy honesty speak freelie to me now.
Thou know'st that Montague, of whose Land
I'm the master, did affect thee first,
And should have had thee, if the strength of friends
Had not prevail'd above thine own consent.
I have undone him; tell me how thou dost
Consider his ill fortune and my good.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: I'll tell you justly his undoing is
An argument for pity and for tears
In all their dispositions that have known
The honor and the goodness of his life:
Yet that addition of prosperity,
Which you have got by't, no indifferent man
Will malice or repine at, if the Law
Be not abused in't; howsoever since
You have the upper fortune of him, 'twill
Be some dishonor to you to bear your self
With any pride or glory over him.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: This may be truely spoken, but in thee
It is not honest.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Yes, so honest, that I care not if the chast Penelope
Were now alive to hear me.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Who comes there?

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: My brother.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Save ye.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Now Sir, you have heard of prosperous Montague,

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: No Sir, I have heard of Montague,
But of your prosperity.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Is he distracted.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: He does bear his loss with such a noble strength
Of patience that,
Had fortune eyes to see him, she would weep
For having hurt him, and pretending that
Shee did it but for triall of his worth:
Hereafter ever love him.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: I perceive you love him, and because (I must confess)
He does d^rve that though for some respects,
I have not ^n him that acknowledgement,
Yet in mine honor I did still conclude to use him nobly.

speeches.speaker: Am.
prose: Sir, that will become your reputation and make me grow proud of your alliance.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: I did reserve the doing of this friendship till I had
His fortunes at my mercy, that the world
May tell him 'tis a willing courtesie.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: This change will make me happy.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: 'Tis a change; thou shalt behold it: then observe me when
That Montague, had possession of my Land,
I was his rivall, and at last obtain'd
This Lady who, by promise of her own
Affection to him, should ha' bin his wife;
I had her, and withheld her like a pawn,
Till now my Land is rend'red to me again,
And since it is so, you shall see I have
The conscience not to keep her—give him her—
For by the faithfull temper of my sword, she shall not tarry with me.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Give me way—
Thou most unworthy man —give me way;
Or by the wrong he does the Innocent,
I'll end thy misery and his wickedness, together.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Stay and let me justifie
My husband in that, I have wrong'd his bed.
Never—all shames that can afflict me fall
Upon me if I ever wrong'd you;

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Didst thou not confess it;

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: 'Twas to save your blood from shedding, that has
Turn'd my brothers edge;
He that beholds our thoughts as plainely as
Our faces, knowes it, I did never hurt
My honesty but by accusing it.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Womens consents are sooner credited
Than their denials: and I'll never trust
Her body that prefers any defence
Before the safety of her honor—here
Show forth that stranger — give me not a word
Thou seest a danger readie to be tempted.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Cast that upon me rather than my shame,
And as I am now dying I will vow—
That I am honest.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Put her out of dores; but that I fear my land
May go again to Montague, I would kill thee, I am loth,
To make a beggar of him that way; or else—
Go now you have the liberty of flesh,
And you may put it to a double use,
One for your pleasure, th'other to maintain
Your well beloved, he will want.
In such a charitable exercise
The virtue will excuse you for the vice.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: What means your Lordship?

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: For the love of Heaven.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Thou hast advantage of me, cast away this buckler.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: So he is Sir, for he lives
With one that is undone — avoyd us boy.

speeches.speaker: ~er.
verse: I'll first avoid my safety,
prose: Your Rapier shall be button'd with my head, before it touch my Master.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Montague?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: You know my sister?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Yes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: For a whore?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: You lye, and shall lie lower if you dare abuse her honor.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: I am honest.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Honest!

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Upon my faith I am.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: What did then parsuade thee to condemn thy self?

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Your safety.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: I had rather be expos'd
To danger, than dishonor; th'ast betray'd
The reputation of my familie
More basely by the falseness of that word,
Than if thou hadst delivered me asleep
Into the hands of base enemies.
Relief will never make thee sensible
Of thy disgraces; let thy wants compell thee to it.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: O I am a miserable woman.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Why Madam? are you utterly without means to relieve you?

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: I have nothing Sir, unless by changing of these cloaths for worse, and then at last the worst for nakedness.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Stand off boy, nakedness would be a change
To please us Madam, to delight us both.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: What nakedness Sir?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Why the nakedness of body Madam, we were Lovers once.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Never dishonest Lovers.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Honestie has no allowance now to give our selves.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Nor you allowance against honestie.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: I'll send my Boy hence, opportunitie
Shall be our servant, come and meet me first
With kisses like a stranger at the door,
And then invite me nearer to receive
A more familiar inward wellcome; where,
Instead of tapers made of Virgins wax
Th'increasing flames of our desires shall light
Us to a banquet: and before the taste
Be dull with satisfaction, I'll prepare
A nourishment compos'd of every thing
That bears a naturall friendship to the blood,
And that shall set another edge upon 't,
Or else between the courses of the feast
We'll dallie out an exercise of time,
That ever as one appetite expires another may succeed it.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: O my Lord, how has your nature lost her worthiness?
When our affections had their liberty,
Our kisses met as temperatelie as
The hands of sisters, or of brothers, that
Our bloods were then as moving; then you were
So noble, that I durst have trusted your
Embraces in an opportunity
Silent enough to serve a ravisher,
And yet come from you—undishonor'd—how
You think me altered, that you promise your
Attempt success I know not; but were all
The sweet temptations that deceive us set
On this side, and one that side all the waiters,
These neither should parsuade me, nor these force.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Then misery may waste your body.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Yes, but lust shall never.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: I have found you still as uncorupted as I left you first
Continue so; and I will serve you with
As much devotion as my word, my hand
Or purse can show you; and to justifie
That promise, here is half the wealth I have,
Take it, you owe me nothing, till you fall
From virtue, which the better to protect
I have bethought me of a present means:
Give me the Letter; this commends my Boy
Into the service of a Lady, whose
Free goodness you have bin acquainted with, Lamira.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Sir I know her.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Then believe her entertainment will be noble to you?
My boy shall bring you thither: and relate
Your manner of misfortune if your own
Report needs any witness: so I kiss your hand good Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Sir, I know not how to promise, but I cannot be unthankfull.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: All that you can implore in thankfulness
Be yours, to make you the more prosperous.
Farwell my boy,—I am not yet oppress'd.
Having the power to helpe one that's distress'd.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: WHat shall we do now: swords are out of use,
And words are out of credit.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: We must serve.

speeches.speaker: Leng.
verse: The means to get a service will first spend
Our purses; and except we can allow
Our selves an entertainment, service will
Neglect us; now 'tis grown into a doubt
Whether the Mr. or the servants gives the countenance.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Then fall in with Mistresses.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: They keep more servants now (indeed) than men,
But yet the age is grown so populous
Of those attendants, that the women are
Grown full too.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: What shall we propound our selves?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: I'll think on't.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Do; Old occupations have too many setters up to prosper, some uncommon trade would thrive now.

speeches.speaker: Long,
verse: Wee'll e'en make up some half a dozen proper men.
And should not we get more
Than all your female sinners?

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: If the house be seated as it should be privately.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: I, but that would make a multitude of witches.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Witches? how prethee?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Thus the bands would all turn witches to revenge
Themselves upon us, and the women that
Come to us, for disguises must wear beards,
And that's they say, a token of a witch.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: What shall we then do;

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: We must study on't
With more consideration; stay Duboyes
Are not the Lord of Orleans and the Lord
Of Amiens enemies?

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Yes, what of that.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Methinks the factions of two such great men.
Should give a promise of advancement now
To us that want it.

speeches.speaker: Dub,
prose: Let the plot be thine, and in the enterprize I'll second thee.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: I have it we will first set down our selves
The Method of a quarrell; and make choyce
Of some frequented Tavern; or such a place
Of common notice, to perform it in
By way of undertaking to maintain
The severall honors of those enemies.
Thou for the Lord of Orleans; I for Amiens.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: I like the project, and I think 'twill take
The better, since their difference first did rise
From his occasion whom we followed once.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: We cannot hope less after the report,
Than entertainment or gratuity,
Yet those are ends, I do not aim at most;
Great spirits that are needy, and will thrive,
Must labour whiles such troubles are alive.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: Slander is sharper than the sword. I have fed this three dayes upon leaf Tobacco, for want of other Victuals.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: You have liv'd the honester Captain; but be not so dejected, but hold up thy head, and meat will sooner fall i'thy mouth.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: I care not so much for meat, so I had but good liquor, for which my guts croak like so many Frogs for rain.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: It seems, you are troubled with the wind-Collick, Captain, swallow a bullet: 'tis present remedy I'll assure you.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: A bullet? I'll tell you Sir, my panch is nothing but a pile of bullets; when I was in any service I stood between my Generall and the shot, like a mud-wall; I am all lead, from the crown of the head to the soal of the foot, not a sound bone about me.

speeches.speaker: Lau.
prose: It seems you have bin in terrible hot service Captain.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: It has ever bin the fate of the low Country wars to spoil many a man, I ha' not bin the first nor shall not be the last: but I'll tell you Sir, (hunger has brought it in to mind) I served once at the Siege of Braste, 'tis memorable to this day, where we were in great distress for victuals, whole troops fainted more for want of food then for blood, and died, yet we were resolved to stand it out; I my self was but then Gentleman of a Company, and had as much need as any man, and indeed I had perished had not a miraculous providence preserved me.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: As how good Captain?

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: Marry Sir, e'en as I was fainting and falling down for want of sustenance, the enemy made a shot at me, and struck me full ith' paunch with a penny loaf.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Instead of a bullet!

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: In stead of a bullet.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: That was miraculous indeed; and that loaf sustained you.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: Nourished me or I had famished with the rest.

speeches.speaker: Lav,
prose: You have done worthy acts being a soldier, and now you shall give me leave to requite your tale, and to acquaint you with the most notorious deeds that I have done being a Courtier. I protest Captain I will lie no more than you have done.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: I can indure no lies.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: I know you cannot Captain, therefore I'll only tell you of strange things: I did once a deed of charity for it self; I assisted a poor widow in a sute, and obtained it, yet I protest I took not a penny for my labor.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: 'Tis no such strange thing.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: By Mars Captain, but it is, and a very strange thing too in a Courtier, it may take the upper hand of your penny loaf for a miracle. I could ha' told you how many Ladyes have languished for my love, and how I was once sollicited by the mother, the daughter, and grand-mother; out of the least of which I might have digg'd my self a fortune; they were all great Ladyes, for two of them were so big I could hardly embrace them: but I was sluggish in my rising courses, and therefore let them pass; what means I had is spent upon such as had the wit to cheat me; That wealth being gone, I have only bought experience with it, with a strong hope to cheat others; but see here comes the much declined Montague, who had all the Manor houses, which were the body of his estate, overthrowen by a great wind.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: How by a great wind? was he not overthrown by law?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Yes, marry was he: but there was terrible puffing and blowing before he was overthrown, if you observ'd, and believe it Captain, there's no wind so dangerous to a building as a lawyers breath.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: What's he with him?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: An eminent Citizen. Mounsier Mallicorne, let's stand a side and listen their design.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Sir, profit is the Crown of labor, it is the life, the soul of the industrious Merchant, in it he makes his paradise, and for it neglects Wife, Children, Friends, Parents, nay all the world, and delivers up himself to the violence of storms, and to be tos'd into unknown ayrs; as there is no faculty so perillous, so there's none so worthy profitable.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Sir, I am very well possest of it, and what of my poore fortunes remaines, I would gladly hazard upon the Sea: it cannot deal worse with me than the Land, though it sink or throw it in the hands of Pirats. I have yet five hundred pounds left, and your honest and worthy acquaintance may make me a young Merchant; th'one moity of what I have I would gladly adventure.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: How adventure? you shall hazard nothing: you shall only joyn with me in certain commodities that are safe arrived unto the Key; you shall neither be in doubt of danger nor dammage; But so much money disburst, so much receive; Sir, I would have you conceive I pursue it not for any good your money will do me, but meerly out of mine own freeness and courtesie to pleasure you.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: I can believe no less, and you express a noble nature, seeking to build up a man so ruin'd as my self.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose:
Captain here is subject for us to work upon if we have wit; you hear that there is money yet left, and it is going to be layd out in Rattels, Bels, Hobby-Horses, brown paper, or some such like sale commodities; now it would do better in our purses, upon our backs in good Gold-lace, and Scarlat, and then we might pursue our projects, and our devices towards my Lady Annabella; go to, there's a conceit newly landed; heark I stand in good reputation with him, and there^ore may
the better cheat him: Captain, take a few instructions from me.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: What monies I have is at your disposing, and upon twelve I will meet you at the Pallace with it.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: I will there expect you, and so I take my leave.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: You apprehend me?

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: Why do ye think I am a dunce?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Not a dunce Captain, but you might give me leave to misdoubt that pregnancy in a Soldier, which is proper and hereditary to a Courtier; but prosecute it, I will both second, and give credit to it. Good Mounsier Montague, I would your whole revenues lay within the circuit of mine armes, that I might as easily bestow, or restore it unto you as my curtesie.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: My zealous wishes Sir, do accompany his for your good fortunes.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Believe it Sir, our affection towards you is a strong band of friendship.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: To which I shall most willingly seal. But believe me Gentlemen in a broken estate, the bond of friendship oft is forfeited, but that it is your free and ingenuous nature to renew it.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Sir, I will amply extend my self to your use, and am very zealously afflicted as not one of your least friends for your crooked fate; But let it not seise you with any dejection, you have as I hear a sufficient competency left, which well disposed may erect you as high in the worlds account as ever.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: I cannot live to hope it, much less injoy it, nor is it any part of my endeavor; my study is to render every man his own, and to contain my self within the limits of a Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: I have the grant of an Office given me by some noble favorites of mine in Court, there stands but a small matter between me and it, if your ability be such to lay down the present summ, out of the love I bear you, before any other man, it shall be confirmed yours.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: I have heard you often speak of such a thing; If it be assur'd to you I will gladly deal in it: that portion I have, I would not hazard upon one course, for I see the most certain is incertain.

speeches.speaker: La-p,
prose: Having money Sir, you could not light upon men that could give better direction; there is at this time a friend of mine upon the Seas; to be plain with you, he is a pyrate, that hath wrote to me to work his fredom, and by this Gentlemans means, whose acquaintance is not small at Court; we have the word of a worthy man for it, only there is some money to be suddainly disburst, and if your happiness be such to make it up you shall receive treble gain by it, and good assurance for it.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Gentlemen, out of the weakness of my estate you seem (to have some knowledge of my brest) that wou'd if it were possible advance my declined fortunes, to satisfie all men of whom I have had credit, and I know no way better than these which you propose; I have some money ready under my command, some part of it is already promis'd, but the remainder is yours to such uses as are propounded.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Appoint some certain place of meeting, for these affaires require expedition.

speeches.speaker: Mount.
prose: I will make it my present business: at twelve, I am to meet Mallicorne, the Marchant at the Pallace, you know him Sir, about some negotiation of the same nature, there I will be ready to tender you that money, upon such conditions as we shall conclude of.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: The care of it be yours, so much as the affair concerns you.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Your caution is effectuall, and till then I take my leave.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Good Mr Montague.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Nay Gentlemen what mean you? pray be quiet, have some respect unto the house.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: A treacherous slave.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: Thou dost revile thy self base Longavile.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: I say thou art a villain and a corrupt one, that hast some seven years sed on thy masters trencher, yet never bredst good blood towards him: for if thou hadst, thou'dst have a sounder heart.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: So Sir, you can use your tongue something nimbler than your sword.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Wou'd you cou'd use your tongue well of your Master, friend you might have better imployment for your sword.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: I say again, and I will speak it loud and often, that Orleans, is a noble Gentleman with whom Amiens is too light to poyse the scale.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: He is the weaker for taking of a prayse out of thy mouth.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: This hand shall seal his merit at thy heart.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Part them my masters, part them.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Part them Sir, why do you not part them, you stand by with your sword in your hand, and cry part 'em.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Why you must know my friend my cloaths are better than yours, and in a good suit, I do never use to part any body.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: And it is discretion.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: I marry is it Captain.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Dubois though this place priviledge thee, know where next we meet, the blood which at thy heart flows drops at thy feet.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: I would not spend it better than in this quarrell, and on such a hazard.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: What uprore's this, must my name here be question'd in Tavern brawls, and by affected Ruffins?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Not we indeed Sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: Fear cannot make me shrink out of your fury, though you were greater than your name doth make you, I am one, and the opposer; if your swoln rage have ought in malice to inforce express it.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: I seek thee not, nor shalt thou ever gain
That credit, which a blow from me wou'd give thee,
By my—I more detest that fellow
Which took my part than thee, that he durst offer
To take my honor in his feeble armes,
And spend it in a drinking room; which way went he?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: That way Sir, I wou'd you wou'd after; for I do fear we shall have some more scuffling.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: I'll follow him, and if my speed o'er take him,
I shall ill thank him, for his forwardness.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: I am glad he's gone, for I doe not love to see a sword drawn in the hand of a man that lookes so furious, there's no jesting with edge tooles, how say you Captain?

speeches.speaker: Cap.
prose: I say 'tis better jesting than to be in earnest with them.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: How now? what's the difference? they say there have bin swords drawn, and in my quarrell: let me know that man, whose love is so sincere to spend his blood for my sake, I will bounteously requite him.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: We were all of your side, but there he stands begun it.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: What's thy name?

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Duboyes?

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: Give me thy hand, hast received no hurt?

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Not any, nor were this body stuck full of wounds, I should not count them hurts, being taken in so honorable a cause as the defence of my most worthy Lord.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: The dedication of thy love to me requires my ample bounty, thou art mine, for I do find thee made unto my purposes: Mounsieur Laverdine, pardon my neglect I not observed you, and how runs rumour?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Why, it runs my Lord like a foot-man without a cloak, to show that what's once rumour'd it cannot be hid.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: And what say the rable, am not I the subject of their talk?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Troth my Lord the common mouth speaks foul words.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: Of me, for turning away my wife, do they not?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Faith the men do a little murmure at it and say, 'tis an ill president in so great a man; marry the women; they rayl out right.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: Out upon them rampallions. I'll keep my self safe enough out of their fingers, but what say my pritty jolly composed gallants that censure every thing more desperate than it is dangerous; what say they?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Marry they are laying wagers, what death you shall die; one offers to lay five hundred pounds; And yet he had but a groat about him, & that was in two two-pences too to, any man that wou'd make it up a shilling; that you were kil'd with a Pistoll charg'd with white Powder; another offerd to pawn his soul for five shillings, and yet no body wou'd take him, that you were stab'd to death, and shou'd die with more wounds than Cesar.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: And who shou'd be the Butchers that shou'd do it? Montague and his associates?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: So 'tis conjectured.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: And believe it, sweet Prince, it is to be feared, and therefore prevented.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: By turning his purpose on himself, were not that the way?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: The most direct path for your safety. For where doth danger sit more furious than in a desperate man?

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: And being you have declined his means, you have increast his malice.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Besides the generall report that steems in every mans breath, and stains you all over with infamy, that Time the devourer of all things cannot eat out.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: I, for that former familiarity, which he had with your Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Men speak it as boldly as words of compliment; good morrow, good even, or save you Sir, are not more usuall; if the word cuckold had been written upon your forehead in great Capitall Letters, it could not have been dilated with more confidence.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: He shall not sleep another night, I will have his blood, though it be required at my hands again.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Your Lordship may, and without hazarding your own person; here's a Gentleman in whose looks I see a resolution to perform it.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Let his Lordship give me but his honorable word for my life, I'll kill him as he walks.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Or pistoll him as he sits at meat.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: Or at game.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Or as he is drinking.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Any way.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: Wou't thou? call what is mine thine own, thy reputation shall not be brought in question for it, much less thy life; it shall be nam'd a deed of valour in thee, not murder: Farewell.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose:
I need no more 'encouragement, it is ^
^k I will persuade my self that I was born to.

speeches.speaker: Laver.
prose: And you may persuade your self too that you shall be sav'd by it, being that it is for his honorable Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: But you must yield me means, how, when and where.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: That shall be our tasks;
Nay more, we will be agents with thee:
This hour we are to meet him, on the receipt of certain moneys,
Which indeed we purpose honestly to cheat him of,
And that's the main cause I wou'd have him slain,
Who works with safety makes a double gain.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: Stay Sir, I have took some pains to overtake you.
—Your name is Longaville.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: I have the word of many honest men for't, I crave your Lordships pardon, your sudden apprehension on my steps made me to frame an answer unwitting and unworthy your respect.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: Doe you know me?

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Yes, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: I know not you; nor am I well pleased to make this time, as the affair now stands, the induction of your acquaintance; you are a fighting fellow.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: How my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: I think I too much grace you; rather you are a fellow dares not fight, but spit and pufte and make a noyse, whilst your trembling hand draws out your Sword, to lay it upon andirons, stools or tables, rather than on a man,

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Your honor may best speak this; yet — with little safety, if I thought it serious.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: Come, you are a verie braggart, and you have given me cause to tell you so: what weakness have you ever seen in me to prompt your self, that I could need your help; or what other reason could induce you to it? you never yet had a meals meat from my Table, nor as I remember from my Wardrop any cast Suit.

speeches.speaker: Lon.
prose: 'Tis true, I never durst yet have such a servile spirit, to be the minion of a full swoln Lord; but alwaies did detest such slavery: a meals meat, or a cast Suit? I wou'd first eat the stones, and from such rags the dunghils doe afford, pick me a garment.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: I have mistook the man, his resolute spirit
Proclaimes him generous, he has a noble heart
As free to utter good deeds as to act them;
For had he not been right, and of one piece,
He would have crumpled, curled, and struck himself
Out of the shape of man into a shaddow.
But prethee tell me, if no such fawning hope
Did lead thee on to hazard life for my sake;
What was it that incited thee?
Tell me; speak it without the imputation of a Sycophant.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Your own desert, and with it was joyn'd the unfained friendship that I judged you ever held unto my former Lord.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: The noble Montague?

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Yes, the noble and much injured Montague.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: To such a man as thou art, my heart shall be
A Casket: I will lock thee up there,
And esteem thee as a faithfull friend,
The richest Jewell that a man enjoyes;
And in thy thou didst follow once my friend,
And in thy heart still dost not with his fortunes casting him off,
Thou shalt go hand in hand with me, and share
As well in my ability as love; 'tis not my end
To gain men for my use, but a true friend.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: There's no such thriving way to live in grace,
As to have no sence of it; his back nor belly
Shall not want warming that can practise me mischief;
I walk now with a full purse, grow high and wanton,
Prune and briske my self in the bright shine
Of his good Lordships favours; and for what virtue?
For fashioning my self a murderer.
O noble Montague, to whom I owe my heart,
With all my best thoughts, though my tongue have promis'd
To exceed the malice of thy destiny,
Never in time of all my service knew I
Such a sin tempt thy bounty; those that did feed
Upon thy charge had merit or else need.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Duboys, most prosperously met.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: How now? will he come this way?

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: This way, immediately; therefore thy assistance, dear Duboys.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: What have you cheated him of the money you spoke of?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Fough, as easily as a silly Countrey wench of her maydenhead; we had it in a twinkling.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: 'Tis well Captain, let me help you, you must be our leader in this action.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: Tut, fear not, I'll warrant you if my Sword hold, we'll make no sweating sickness of it.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Why that's well said, but let's retire a little, that we may come on the more bravely; this way, this way.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cre.
prose: Officers look to him, and be sure you take good security before he part from you.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Why but my friends, you take a strange course with me; the sums I owe you are rather forgetfulness, they are so slight, than want of will or honesty to pay you.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cred.
prose: I Sir, it may be so; but we must be paid, and we will be paid before you scape: we have wife and children, and a charge, and you are going down the wind, as a man may say; and therefore it behooves us to look to't in time.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cred.
prose: Your cloak here wou'd satisfie me, mine's not above a three pound matter, besides the arrest.

speeches.speaker: 3 Cred.
prose: 'Faith and mine is much about that matter too; your Girdle and Hangers, and your Beaver, shall be sufficient bail sor't.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cred.
prose: If you have ever a plain black sute at home, this Silken one, with your Silke-stockings, Garters, and Roses shall pacifie me too; for I take no delight, if I have a sufficient pawn, to cast any Gentleman in prison; therefore 'tis but an untrussing matter: and you are free, we are no unreasonable creatures you see; for mine own part, I protest I am loth to put you to any trouble for security.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Is there no more of you? he wou'd next demand my skin,

speeches.speaker: 1 Cred.
prose: No Sir, here's no more of us, nor do any of us demand your skin, we know not what to do with it: but it may be if you ow'd your Glover any money, he knew what use to make of it.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Ye dregs of baseness, vultures amongst men,
That tyre upon the hearts of generous spirits.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cred.
prose: You do us wrong Sir, we tyre no generous spirits, we tyre nothing but our hackneys.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: But here comes one made of another piece;
A man well meriting that free born name
Of Citizen; welcome my deliverer, I am falen
Into the hands of blood-hounds, that for a sum
Lesser than their honesties, which is nothing,
Wou'd tear me out of my skin.

speeches.speaker: Mol.
prose: Why Sir, what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: 1 Cre.
prose: Why Sir the matter is, that we must have our money, which if we cannot have, we'll satisfie our selves with his carcass, and be payd that wayes: you had as good Sir, not have been so peremptory. Officer, hold fast.

speeches.speaker: 1 Offi.
prose: The strenuous fist of vengeance now is clutcht; therefore fear nothing.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: What may be the debt in gross?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Some forty Crowns, nay rather not so much, 'tis quickly cast.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: 'Tis strange to me, that your estate shou'd have so low an ebb, to stick at such sleight sums: why my friends, you are too strict in your accounts, and call too sudden on this Gentleman, he has hopes left yet to pay you all.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cred.
prose: Hopes? I marry; bid him pay his friends with hopes, and pay us with currant Coyn: I knew a gallant once that fed his creditors still with hopes, and bid 'em they shou'd fear nothing, for he had 'em tyed in a string; and trust me so he had indeed, for at last he and all his hopes hopt in a halter.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Good Sir, with what speed you may, free me out of the company of these slaves, that have nothing but their names to show 'em men.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: What wou'd you wish me do Sir? I protest I ha' not the present sum (small as it is) to lay down for you; and for giving my word, my friends no later than yester-night made me take bread and eat it, that I shou'd not do it for any man breathing i'th' world; therefore I pray hold me excused.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: You do not speak this seriously?

speeches.speaker: Mal,
prose: As ever I said my prayers, I protest to you.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: What may I think of this?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Troth Sir thought is free for any man; we abuse our betters in it, I have done it my self.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Trust me, this speech of yours doth much amaze me; pray leave this language, and out of that same sum you lately did receive of me, lay down as much as may discharge me.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: You are a merry man Sir, and I am glad you take your crosses so temperately; fare you well Sir, and yet I have something more to say to ye, a word in your ear I pray; to be plain with you I did lay this plot to arrest you to enjoy this money I have of yours, with the more safety. I am a fool to tell you this now; but in good faith I could not keep it in. And the money wou'd a done me little good else. An honest Citizen cannot wholly enjoy his own wife for you, they grow old before they have true use of them, which is a lamentable thing, and truely much hardens the hearts of us Citizens against you: I can say no more, but am heartily sorry for your heaviness, and so I take my leave.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cred.
prose: Officers take hold on him again, for Mounsier Mallycorne will do nothing for him I perceive.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Nay come my masters, leave dancing of the old measures, and let's assault him bravely.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: By no means; for it goes against my stomach to kill a roan in an unjust quarrell.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: It must needs be a clog to a mans conscience all his life time.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: It must indeed Captain: besides doe ye not see he has gotten a guard of friends about him, as if he had some knowledge of our purpose?

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Had he a guard of Devils, as I think them little better, my Sword should doe the message that it came for.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: If you will be so desperate, the blood lie upon your own neck, for we'll not meddle in't.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: I am your friend and servant.
Struggle with me and take my Sword;
Noble Sir, make your way, you have slain an Officer.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Some one of them has certainly
Requited me; for I doe lose much blood.

speeches.speaker: 1 Offic.
prose: Udsprecious, we have lost a brother, pursue the Gentleman,

speeches.speaker: 2 Offic.
prose: I'll not meddle with him: you see what comes on't; besides I know he will be hang'd ere he be taken.

speeches.speaker: 1 Offic.
prose: I tell thee yeoman he must be taken ere he be hanged; he is hurt in the guts, run afore therefore and know how his wife will rate his Sawsages a pound.

speeches.speaker: 3 Offic.
prose: Stay brother, I may live, for surely I find I'm but hurt in the leg, a dangerous kick on the shin-bone.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: YOU see Lady
What harmless sports ous Countrey life affords;
And though you meet not here with City dainties,
Or Courtly entertainment, what you have
Is free and hearty.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: Madam, I find here
What is a stranger to the Court, content,
And receive curtesies done for themselves,
Without an expectation of return,
Which binds me to your service.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Oh your love;
My homely house built more for use than shew
Observes the Golden mean equally distant
From glittering pomp, and sordid avarice;
For Maskes, we will observe the works of nature,
And in the place of visitation, read:
Our Physick shall be wholsome walks, our viands,
Nourishing, not provoking: for I find
Pleasures are tortures that leave stings behind.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: You have a great estate.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: A competency
Sufficient to maintain me and my rank,
Nor am I, I thank Heaven, so Courtly bred
As to imploy the utmost of my Rents
In paying Tailors for phantastick Robes;
Or rather than be second in the fashion,
Eat out my Officers and my Revenues
With grating usury; my back shall not
Be the base on which your soothing Citizen
Erects his Summer-houses; nor on th' other side
Will I be so penuriously wife,
As to make money (that's my slave) my Idoll,
Which yet to wrong, merits as much reproof,
As to abuse our servant.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: Yet with your pardon
I think you want the Crown of all contentment.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: In what good Madam?

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: In a worthy husband.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: — It is strange the galley-slave should praise
His Oar, or stroaks; or you, that have made shipwrack
Of all delight upon this Rock, cal'd marriage,
Should sing Encomions ou't.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: Madam, though one fall
From his horse and break his neck, will you
Conclude from that it is unfit to ride?
Or must it follow, because Orleans
My Lord's pleased to make his passionate triall
Of my suspected patience, that my brother,
(Were he not so, I might say, worthy Amiens)
Will imitate his ills, that cannot fancy
What's truely Noble in him?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: I must grant
There's as much worth in him as can be lookt for
From a young Lord, but not enough to make
Me change my golden liberty and consent
To be a servant to it, as wives are
To the Imperious humors of their Lords:
Me thinks I'm well, I rise and goe to bed
When I think fit, eat what my appetite
Desires without controle, my servants study
Is my contentment, and to make me merry
Their farthest ayms; my sleeps are enquired after,
My rising up saluted with respect:
Command and liberty now wait upon
My Virgin state; what would I more; change all,
And for a husband? no; these freedoms die,
In which they live with my Virginity;
'Tis in their choice that's rich to be a wife,
But not being yoakt to chuse the single life.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: Madam.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: How like you the Countrey?

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: I like the ayr of it well Madam, and the rather because, as on Irish Timber your Spider will not make his web, so for ought I see yet your Cheater, Pander, and Informer being in their dispositions too soggy for this piercing climate, shun it, and chose rather to walk in mists in the City.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
prose: Who did you serve first boy?

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: A rich Merchants widow, and was by her preferred to a young Court-Lady.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
prose: And what difference found you in their service?

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: Very much: for look how much my old City Madam gave to her young visitants, so much my Lady received from her hoary Court-servants.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
prose: And what made you to leave her?

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: My father (Madam) had a desire to have me a tall-man, took me from thence.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
prose: Well, I perceive you inherit the wag, from your father.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: Doves beget Doves; and Eagles, Eagles, Madam: A Citizen here, tho left never so rich, seldome at the best proves a Gentleman: the son of an Advocate, tho dub'd like his father, will shew a relish of his descent, and the fathers thriving practice, as I have heard: she that of a Chambermayd is metamorphosed into a Madam, will yet remember how oft her daughter by her mother ventured to lie upon the rushes before she could get in that which makes many Ladyes.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
prose: But what think you of your late Master?

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: Oh Madam—

speeches.speaker: Lam.
prose: Why doe you sigh? you are sorry that you lest him,
He made a wanton of you.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: Not for that:
Or if he did, for that my youth must love him.
Oh pardon me, if I say liberty
Is bondage, if compar'd with his kind service;
And but to have power now to speak his worth
To its desert; I should be well content
To be an old man when his praise were ended:
And yet, if at this instant you were pleased,
I should begin, the livery of age
Would take his lodging upon this head
Ere I should bring it to a period.
^n brief he is a man (for Heaven forbid
That I should ever live to say he was)
Of such a shape as would make one beloved,
That never had good thought; and to his body
He hath a mind of such a constant temper
In which virtues throng to have a room:
Yet 'gainst this noble Gentleman, this Montague,
For in that name I comprehend all goodness,
Wrong, and the wrested law, false witnesses,
And envy sent from hell, have rose in Armes,
And though not pierc'd, batter'd his honor'd shield.
What shall I say? I hope you will forgive me,
That if you were but pleas'd to love,
I know no Juno worthy such a Jove.

speeches.speaker: Lam,
verse: 'Tis well yet that I have the second place
In your affection: From whence?

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: From the Lord Amiens, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: 'Tis wellcome, though it bear his usual language:
I thought so much, his love-suit speaks his health.
What's he that brought it?

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: A Gentleman of good rank, it seems.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Where is he?

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Receiving entertainment in your house
Sorting with his degree.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: 'Tis well.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: He waits your Ladyships pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: He shall not wait long:
I'll leave you for a while; nay stay you boy,
Attend the Lady.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Would I might live once
To wait on my poor Master.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: That's a good boy:
This thankfulness looks lovely on thy forehead,
And in it, as a book, me thinks I read
Instructions for my self, that am his debtor,
And wou'd do much that I might be so happy
To repair that which to our grief is ruin'd.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: It were a work a King might glory in,
If he saw with my eyes: If you please Madam,
For sure to me you seem unapt to walk,
To sit, although the churlish Birds deny
To give us musick in this grove, where they
Are prodigall to others: I'll strain my voyce
For a sad Song, the place is safe and private.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: 'Twas my desire; begin good Viramour.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: What's he Viramour?

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: A goodly personage.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Am I yet safe? or is my slight a dream;
My wounds and hunger tell me that I wake:
Whither have my fears born me? no matter where,
Who hath no place to goe to, cannot err:
What shall I do? cunning calamity!
That others gross wits uses to refine,
When I most need it duls the edg of mine.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: Is not this Montagues voyce?

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: My Masters? sie.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: What sound was that, 'pish,
Fear makes the wretch think every leaf oth' Jury:
What course to live, 'beg? better men have done it,
But in another kind: steal? Alexander
Though stil'd a Conqueror, was a proud thief,
Though he rob'd with an Army; sie how idle
These meditations are: though thou art worse
Than sorrows tongue can speak thee, thou art still,
Or shouldst be, honest Montague.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: 'Tis too true.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: 'Tis he: what villains hands did this? oh that my flesh
Were Balm; in faith Sir, I would pluck it off
As readily as this; pray you accept
My will to do you service: I have heard
The Mouse once sav'd the Lyon in his need,
As the poor S^arab spild the Eagles seed.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: How do you?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: As a forsaken man.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: Do not say so, take comfort,
For your misfortunes have been kind in this,
To cast you on a hospitable sh^
Where dwels a Lady—

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: She to whom, good Master,
You prefer'd me.

speeches.speaker: L, Orl.
verse: In whose house, whatsoere
Your dangers are, I'll undertake your safety.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: I fear that I am pursued, and doubt that I,
In my defence have kild an Officer.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Is that all? there's no law under the Sun
But will I hope confess, one drop of blood
Shed from this arme is recompence enough
Though you had cut the throats of all the Catchpoles
In France, nay in the world.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: I would be loth
To be a burthen, or feed like a drone
On the industrious labor of a Bee,
And baser far I hold it to owe for
The bread I eat, what's not in me to pay;
Then since my full fortunes are declin'd,
To their low ebb I'll fashion my high mind.
It was no shame to Hecuba, to serve
When Troy was fir'd: if't be in your power
To be a means to make her entertainment,
And far from that I was; but to supply
My want with habit fit for him that serves,
I shall owe much to you.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: Leave that care to me.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
prose: Good Sir, lean on my shoulder; help good Madam: oh that I were a horse for half an hour, that I might carry you home on my back: I hope you will love me still?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Thou dost deserve it boy, that I should live
To be thus troublesome.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: Good Sir, 'tis none.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Trouble? most willingly I would be chang'd
Like Apuleius, weare his Asses ears,
Provided I might still this burthen bear.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: 'Tis a kind boy.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: I find true proof of it.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: You'll carry it.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: As I live although my packet were like Bellerophon's, what have you seen in me or my behavior since your favors so plentifully showr'd upon my wants, that may beget distrust of my preformance?

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Nay, be not angry, if I entertained
But the least scruple of your love, or courage,
I would make choyce of one which my estate
Should do me right in this, nor can you blame me
If in a matter of such consequence
I am so importunate.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Good my Lord let me prevent your farther conjurations
To rayse my spirit, I know this is a challenge
To be delivered unto Orleane hand,
And that my undertaking ends not there,
But I must be your second, and in that
Not alone search your enemy, measure weapons,
But stand in all your hazards, as our blouds
Ran in the self-same veins, in which if I
Better not your opinion, as a limb
That's putrifi'd and useless, cut me off,
And underneath the Gallows bury it.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: At full you understand me, and in this
Bind me, and what's mine to you and yours,
I will not so much wrong you as to add
One syllable more, let it suffice I leave
My honor to your guard: and in that prove,
You hold the first place in my heart and love.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: The first place in a Lords affection? very good; and how long doth that last? perhaps the changing of some three shirts in the Tennis-Court; well, it were very necessary that an order were taken (if it were possible,) that younger brothers might have more wit, or more money: for now, however the fool hath long been put upon him that inherits, his revenue hath bought him a spunge, and wip't off the imputation, and for the understanding of the younger, let him get as much Rhetorick as he can, to grace his language.
They will see, he shall have gloss little enough to set out his Bark; stand Dubois, look about, 's all safe?

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Approach not near me but with reverence
Lawrel and adorations, I have done more than deserves, a hundred thanks.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: How now, what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: With this hand, only aided by this brain,
Without an Orpheus Harp redeem'd from Hells
Three headed Porter, our Euridice.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Nay, prethee speak sence, this is like the stale bragart in a Play.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Then in plain Prose thus, and with as little action as thou canst desire, the three headed Porter, were three unexorable Catch-poles, out of whose jaws without the help of Orpheus Harp, bait or bribe; for those two strings make the Musick, that molifies those flinty furies, I rescued our Euridice, I mean my old Master Montague.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: And is this all? a poor rescue; I thought thou hadst revers'd the judgement for his overthrow in his sute, or wrought upon his adversary Orleance, taken the shape of a Ghost, frighted his mind into distraction, and for the appeasing of his conscience, forc'd him to make restitution of Montague's Lands, or such like rescue; S'light I would have hired Acrocheture for two Cardekues, to have done so much with his whip.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: You wood Sir, and yet 'tis more than three on their foot-cloaths, durst do for a sworn Brother, in a Coach.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Besides, what proof's of it? for ought I know, this may be a trick, I had rather have him a prisoner, where I might visit him, and do him service, than not at all, or I know not where.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Well Sir, the end will shew it, what's that, a challenge?

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Yes, where's Orleance? though we fight in jest, he must meet with Amiens in earnest, — fall off, we are discovered; my horse garson; ha!

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Were it not in a house, and in his presence,
To whom I owe all duty —

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: What would it do? prate as it does? but be as far from striking, as he that owes it Orleance.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: How?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: I think thou art his Porter,
Set here to answer creditors, that his Lordship
Is not within, or takes the diet: I am sent,
And will grow here until I have an answer,
Not to demand a debt of money, but
To call him to a strict account for wrong
Done to the honors of a Gentleman,
Which nothing but his heart-bloud shall wash off.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Shall I hear this?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: And more, that if I may not
Have access to him, I will fix this here
To his disgrace and thine.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: And thy life with it.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Then have the copies of it p^sted on posts,
Like Pamphlet Titles, that sue to be so^d;
Have his disgrace talk for Tobacco-shops,
His picture baffled.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: All respect away, wer't in a Church—

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: This is the ^ook I pray with.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: ^or ^ your lives.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: ^ are you ^ I hope your Lordship can read (thought ^ not his ^ Scholar-ship) doth it not please you ^ muster up the rest of your attendance, which ^ Cook, a Pander, Coach-man, and a Footm^n, in t^e day, a great ^ Lords train, pretending I ^ unworthy to bring you a ^hallenge, instead of answering it have me ^

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: If he does, tho^ deserv'st it.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: I dare you all to touch me, I'll not stand still,
What answer?

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: That thou hast done to Ami^as
The office of a faithful friend, whi^h
Would cherish in thee, were he not my ^oe,
How ever since on honourable terms
He calls me forth, say I will meet with him,
And by Dubois e'r Sun-set make him know
The time and place, my swords length, and what ever
Scruple of circumstance he can expect.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: This answer comes unlookt for, fare you well,
Finding your temper thus, wou'd I had said less.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Now comes thy love to the test.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: My Lord, 'twill hold,
And in all dangers prove it self true Gold.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: I will acquaint my Lady with your coming.
Please you repose your selves here.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: There's a Tester, nay, now I am a wooer, I must be bountiful.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: If you would have two three-pences for it Sir, To give some of your kindred as you ^ide, I'll s^e ^ I can get them; we use not (tho servants) to take ^

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Then thou art unfit to be in office, either in Court or City.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: Indeed, corruption is a Tree, whose branches are of an unmeasurable length, they spread every where, and the dew, that drops from thence, hath infected some chairs and stools of authority.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Ah Captain! lay not all the fault upon Officers, you know you can shark, tho you be out of action, witness Montague.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Hang him, he's safe enough; you had a hand in it too, and have gained by him; but I wonder you Citizens, that keep so many books, and take such strict accounts for every farthing due to you from others, reserve not so much as a memorandum for the courtesies you receive.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Would you have a Citizen book those? thankfulness is a thing, we are not sworn to in our Indentures: you may as well urge conscience.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Talk no more of such vanities, Mountague is it recoverably sunk, I would we had twenty more to send after him; the Snake that would be a Dragon, and have wings, must eat; and what implies that, but this, that in this Cannibal age, he that would have the sute of wealth, must not care—whom he feeds on? and as I have heard, no flesh battens better, then that of a profest friend; and he that would mount to honor, must not make dainty to use the head of his mother, back of his Father, or neck of his Brother, for ladders to his preferment; for, but observe, and you shall find for the most part, cunning villany sit at a Feast as principal guest, and innocent honesty wait as a contemn'd servant with a trencher.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: The Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Do ye smell nothing?

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Not I Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: The carrion of knaves is very strong in my nostrils

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: we came to admire, and find Fame was a niggard,
Which we thought prodigal in our report
Before we saw you.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: ^ush Sir, this Courtship's old.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: I'll sight for thee, sweet wench,
This is my tongue, and woes for me.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Good man of War,
Hands off; if you take me, it must be by siege,
Not by an onset; and for your valour, I
Think that I have derseved few enemies,
And therefore need it not.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Thou need'st nothing, sweet Lady, but an obsequious husband, and where wilt thou find him, if not in the City? We are true Muscovites to our Wives, and are never better pleased, than when they use us as slaves, bridle and Saddle us; Have me, thou shalt command all my wealth as thine own, thou shalt sit like a Queen in my Ware-house; And my Factors at the return with my ships, shall pay thee tribute of all the rarities of the earth, thou shalt wear gold, feed on delicates, the first Peascods, Strawberries, Grapes, Cherries shall—

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Be mine? I apprehend what you would say,
Those dainties which the City pays so dear for,
The Countrey yields for nothing, and as early;
And, credit me, your far-fet viands please not
My appetite better than those that are near hand.
Then for your promis'd service and subjection
To all my humors, when I am your wife,
Which is as it seems, is frequent in the City,
I cannot find what pleasure they receive
In using their fond Husbands like their Maids;
But of this, more hereafter: I accept
Your proffer kindly, and yours; my house stands open
To entertain you, take your pleasure in it,
And ease after your journey.

speeches.speaker: La. Orl.
verse: Do you note the boldness of the fellows?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Alas Madam, a Virgin must in this be like a Lawyer,
And as he takes all Fees; she must hear all suitors; the
One for gain, the other for her mirth; stay with the
Gentlemen, we'll to the Orchards.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: — What art thou?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: An honest man, though poor;
And look they like to monsters, are they so rare?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: Rose from the dead.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Do you hear Monsieur Serviture, didst thou never hear of one Montague, a prodigal gull, that lives about Paris?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: So Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: One that after the loss of his main estate in a Law-sute, bought an Office in the Court.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: And should have Letters of Mart, to have the Spanish treasure as it came from the Indies; were not thou and he twins? put off thy Hat, let me see thy Fore-head.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Though you take priviledge to use your tongue,
I pray you hold your fingers,
'Twas your base cozenages made me as I am:
And were you somewhere else, I would take off
This proud film from your eyes, that will not let you,
Know I am Montague.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
prose: I will observe this better.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: And art thou he? I will do thee grace; give me thy hand: I am glad thou hast taken so good a course; serve God, and please thy Mistriss; if I prove to be thy Master, as I am very likely, I will do for thee.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Faith the fellow's well made for a Serving-man, and will no doubt, carry a chine of Beef with a good grace.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: Prethee be careful of me in my chamber, I will remember thee at my departure.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: All this I can endure under this roof,
And so much owe I her, whose now I am,
That no wrong shall incense me to molest,
Her quiet house, while you continue here,
I will not be ashamed to do you service
More than to her, because such is her pleasure.
But you that have broke thrice, and fourteen times
Compounded for two shillings in the pound,
Know I dare kick you in your shop; do you hear?
If ever I see Paris, though an Army
Of musty Murrions, rusty brown Bills and Clubs,
Stand for your guard — I have heard of your tricks,
And you that smell of Amber at my charge,
And triumph in your cheat; well, I may live
To meet thee, be it among a troop of such
That are upon the fair face of the Court
Like running Ulcers, and before thy whore
Trampel upon thee.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: This a language for a Livery? take heed, I am a Captain.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: A Coxcomb are you not? that thou and I,
To give proof, which of us dares most, were now
In midst of a rough Sea, upon a piece
Of a split Ship, where only one might ride,
I would — but foolish anger makes me talk
Like a Player.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Indeed you act a part
Doth ill become you my servant; is this your duty?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: I crave your pardon, and will hereafter be more circumspect.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Oh the power of a Womans tongue: it hath done more than we three with our swords durst undertake; put a mad man to silence.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Why sirrah, these are none of your comrades
To drink with in the Cellar; one of them
For ought you know, may live to be your Master.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: There's some comfort yet.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Here's choice of three, a wealthy Merchant.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Hem, she's taken, she hath spy'd my good Calf,
And many Ladies chuse their Husbands by that.
