speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: A Courtier that's in grace, a valiant Captain,
And are these mates for you, away, be gone.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: I humbly pray you will be pleased to pardon,
And to give satisfaction to you Madam,
(Although I break my heart) I will confess
That I have wrong'd them too, and make submission.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: No I'll spare that; go bid the Cook haste supper.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: Oh brave Lady, thou art worthy to have servants, to be commandress of a Family, that knowest how to use and govern it.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: You shall have many Mistresses that will so mistake, as to take their Horse-keepers, and Footmen instead of their Husbands, thou art none of those.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: But she that can make distinction of men, and knows when she hath gallants, and fellows of rank and quality in her house —.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Gallants indeed, if it be the Gallants fashion
To triumph in the miseries of a man,
Of which they are the cause: one that transcends
(In spight of all that fortune hath, or can be done)
A million of such things as you, my doors
Stand open to receive all such as wear
The shape of Gentlemen, and my gentler nature
(I might say weaker) weighs not the expence
Of entertainment; think you I'll forget yet
What's due unto my self? do not I know,
That you have dealt with poor Montague, but like
Needy Commanders, cheating Citizens,
And perjur'd Courtiers? I am much mov'd, else use not
To say so much, if you will bear your selves
As fits such, you would make me think you are,
You may stay; if not, the way lies before you.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: What think you of this Captain?

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: That this is a bawdy-house, with Pinacles and Turrets, in which this disguised Montague goes to Rut gratis, and that this is a landed pandress, and makes her house a brothel for charity.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Come, that's no miracle; but from whence derive you the supposition?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Observe but the circumstance; you all know that in the height of Mountagues prosperity, he did affect, and had his love return'd by this Lady Orleans; since her divorcement, and his decay of estate, it is known they have met, not so much as his boy but is wanting; and that this can be any thing else than a meer plot for their night-work, is above my imagination to conceive.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Nay, it carries probability, let us observe it better, but yet with such caution, as our prying be not discovered: here's all things to be had without cost, and therefore good staying here.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: Nay, that's true, I would we might wooe her twenty years, like Penelopes sutors; come Laverdine.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: I follow instantly, yonder he is.
The thought of this boy hath much cool'd my affection to his Lady, and by all conjectures, this is a disguised whore; I will try if I can search this Mine, Page —

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: Your pleasure, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Thou art a pretty boy.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: And you a brave man; now I am out of your debt.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Nay, prethee stay.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: I am in haste, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: By the faith of a Courtier.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: Take heed what you say, you have taken a strange oath.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: I have not seen a youth that hath pleased me better; I would thou couldst lie me, so far as to leave thy Lady and wait on me, I would maintain thee in the bravest cloaths.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: Though you took them up on trust, or bought 'em at the Brokers.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Or any way: then thy imployments should be so neat and cleanly, thou shouldst not touch a pair of pantables in a month, and thy lodging —

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: Should be in a brothel.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: No, but in mine arms.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: That my be the circle of a Bawdy-house, or worse.

speeches.speaker: Lev.
prose: I mean thou should'st lye with me.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: Lie with you? I had rather lye with my Ladies Monkey; 'twas never a good world, since our French Lords learned of the Neapolitans, to make their Pages their Bed-fellows, doth more heart to the Suburb Ladies, than twenty dead vacations; 'Tis supper time, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: I thought so, I know by that 'tis a woman, for because, peradventure she hath made trial of the Monkey, she prefers him before me, as one unknown; well, these are standing creatures, and have strange desires; and men must use strange means to quenceh strange fires.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: NOw Montague, who discerns thy spirit now?
Thy breeding, or thy bloud? here's a poor cloud
Eclipseth all thy splendor; who can read
In thy pale face, dead eye, or lenten shute,
The liberty thy ever-giving hand
Hath bought for others, manacling it self
In gyves of parchment indissoluble?
The greatest hearted man supplyed with means,
Nobility of birth and gentlest parts,
I, thought the right hand of his Sovereign,
If virtue quit her seat in his high soul,
Glitters but like a Palace set on fire,
Whose glory whilst it shines, but ruins him,
And his bright show each hour to ashes tending
Shall at the last be rak'd up like a sparkle,
Unless mens lives and fortunes feed the slame.
Not for my own wants, though blame I my Stars,
But suffering others to cast love on me,
When I can neither take, nor thankful be.
My Ladies woman, fair and virtuous
Young as the present month, sollicites me
For love and marriage now being nothing worth —

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: Oh! Master, I have sought you a long hour,
Good faith, I never joy'd out of your sight;
For Heavens sake, Sir, be merry, or else bear
The buffets of your fortunes with more scorn;
Do but begin to rail, teach me the way,
And I'll sit down, and help your anger forth:
I have known you wear a suit; full worth a Lordship,
Give to a man whose need ne'er frighted you
From calling of him friend, five hundred Crowns
E'er sleep had left your sences to consider
Your own important present uses; yet
Since I have seen you with a tencher wait,
Void of all scorn, therefore I'll wait on you.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Would Heaven thou wert less honest.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: Would to Heaven you were less worthy: I am ev'n w'e Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mon.
verse: Is not thy Master strangely fall'n, when thou
Servest for no wages, but for charity?
Thou dost surcharge me with thy plenteous love:
The goodness of thy virtue shown to me,
More opens still my disability
To quit thy pains: credit me loving boy,
A free and honest nature may be opprest,
Tir'd with courtesies from a liberal spirit,
When they exceed his means of gratitude.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: But 'tis a due in him that to that end
Extends his love or duty,

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Little world
Of virtue, why dost love and follow me?

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: I will follow you through all Countreys,
I'll run (fast as I can) by your horse side,
I'll hold your stirrop when you do alight,
And without grudging, wait till you return:
I'll quit offer'd means, and expose my self
To cold and hunger, still to be with you;
Fearless I'll travel through a wilderness,
And when you are weary, I will lay me down
That in my bosom you may rest your head,
Where whilst you sleep, I'll watch, that no wild beast
Shall hurt or trouble you: and thus we'll breed a story
To make every hearer weep,
When they discourse our fortunes and our loves,

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Oh what a scoff might men of women make,
If they did know this boy? but my desire
Is, that thou wouldest not (as thou usest still:
When like a servant, I'mong servants sit)
Wait on my Trencher, fill my cups with Wine:
Why should'st thou do this boy? prethee consider,
I am not what I was.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: Curst be the day when I forget that Montague was
Thy Lord, or not remember him my Master still.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Rather curse me, with whom thy youth hath spent,
So many hours, and yet untaught to live
By any worldly quality.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: Indeed you never taught me how to handle Cards
To cheat and cozen men with oaths and lies:
Those are the worldly qualities to live:
Some of our scarlet Gallants teach their boys
These worldly qualities.
Since stumbling fortune then leaves virtue thus
Let me leave fortune, e'r be vicious.

speeches.speaker: Mon.
verse: Oh lad, thy love will kill me.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: In truth, I think in conscience I shall dye for you:
Good Master weep not, do you want aught, Sir?
Will you have any money, here's some Silver;
And here's a little Gold, 'twill serve to play,
And put more troublesome thoughts out of your mind:
I pray Sir take it, I'll get more with singing.
And then I'll bring it you, my Lady ga't me,
And—it was not covetousness,
But I forgot to tell you sooner on't.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Alas boy, thou art not bound to tell it me,
And less to give it, buy thee Scarfs and Garters,
And when I have money, I will give thee a sword:
Nature made thee a beauteous Cabinet
To lock up all all the goodness of the earth.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: I have lost my voice with the very sight of this Gentlewoman? good Sir steal away, you were wont to be a curious avoider of womens company.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Why boy, thou dar'st trust me any where, dar'st thou not?

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: I had rather trust you by a roaring Lion, than a ravening woman.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Why boy?

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: Why truly she devours more mans flesh—

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: I, but she roars not boy.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: No Sir, why she is never silent but when her mouth is full.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
prose: Monsieur Montague.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: My sweet fellow, since you please to call me so,

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: Ah my conscience, she wou'd be pleas'd well enough to call you bed-fellow: oh Master, do not hold her by the hand so: a woman is a Lime-bush, that catcheth all she toucheth.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
prose: I do most dangerously suspect this boy to be a wench; art thou not one? come hither, let me feel thee.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: With all my heart.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
prose: Why dost thou pull off thy Glove?

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: Why, to feel whether you be a boy, or no.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
prose: Fie boy, go too. I'll not look your head, nor comb your locks any more, if you talk thus.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: Why, I'll sing to you no more then.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
prose: Fie upon't, how sad you are? a young Gentleman that was the very Sun of France.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: But I am in the eclipse now.

speeches.speaker: Chal.
verse: That sleeps at Anchor when the Ocean's calm;
But when she rages, and the wind blows high,
He cuts his way with skill and Majesty.
prose: Suffer himself to be over-run with a Lethargy of melancholy and discontent! rouze up thy spirit, man, and shake it off: A Noble Soul is like a Ship at Sea,
I would turn a Fool, or Poet, or any thing, or marry, to make you merry; prethee let's walk: good Veramour, leave thy Master and me, I have earnest business with him.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: What have you to do with him? come Sir will you go?
And I'll sing to you again:
prose: Pray do you leave my Master, and me: we were very merry before you came, he does not covet womens company.
I'faith his mind is stronger than to credit Womens vows, and too pure to be capable of their loves.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
prose: The boy is jealous, sweet lad leave us: my Lady call'd for you I swear: that's a good child, there's a piece of Gold for thee, go buy a Feather.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: There's two pieces for you, do you go and buy one, or what you will, or nothing, so you go. Nay then I see you would have me go. Sir; why, i'faith I will, now I perceive you love her better than you do me; but Heaven bless you whatever you do, or intend, I know you are a very honest man.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Still will I wooe thee, whilst thy ears reply
I cannot, or I will not marry thee?
Why hast thou drawn the bloud out of my cheeks,
And given a quicker motion to my heart?
Oh thou hast bred a Feaver in my veins
Call'd love, which no Physitian can cure;
Have mercy on a Maid, whose simple youth—

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: How your example, fairest, teacheth me
A ceremonious Idolatry!
By all the joy of love, I love thee better,
Than I or any man can tell another;
And will express the mercy which thou crav'st,
I will forbear to marry thee: consider
Thou art Natures heir in feature, and thy parents,
In fair Inheritances; rise with these thoughts,
And look on me; but with a womans eye,
A decaid fellow, void of means and spirit.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Of spirit?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Yes, could I tamely live,
Forget my Fathers bloud, wait, and make legs,
Stain my best breeches, with the servile drops
That fall from others draughts.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: This vizard wherewith thou wouldst hide thy spirit,
Is perspective, to shew it plainlier.
This undervalue of thy life, is but
Because I should not buy thee, what more speaks
Greatness of man, than valiant patience,
That shrinks not under his fates strongest strokes?
These Roman deaths, as falling on a sword,
Opening of veins, with poison quenching thirst,
(Which we erroneously do stile the deeds
Of the heroick and magnanimous man)
Was dead-ey'd cowardize, and white-cheek'd fear,
Who doubting tyranny; and fainting under
Fortunes false Lottery, desperately run
To death, for dread of death; that soul's most stout,
That bearing all mischance, dares last it out;
Will you perform your word, and marry me,
When I shall call you to't?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: I'faith I will.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Who's this alights here?

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: With leave, fair creature, are you the Lady Mistriss of the house?

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Her servant, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: I pray then favour me, to inform your Lady, and Duke Orleans wife,
A business of import awaits 'em here,
And craves for speedy answer.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Are you in post, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: No, I am in Satin; Lady; I would you would be in post.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: I will return, Sweet.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Honest friend, do you belong to the house? I pray be covered.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Yes Sir, I do.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Ha, dream'st thou Longaville? sure 'tis not he: Sir I should know you.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: So should I you, but that I am asham'd.
But though thou know'st me, prethee Longaville,
Mock not my poverty, pray remember your self;
Shows it not strangely for thy cloaths to stand
Without a Hat to mine? mock me no more.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: The—embroider me all over, Sir,
If ever I began to mock you yet.
The—on me, why should I wear Velvet
And Silver Lace?—I will tear it off.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Why Mad-man?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Put on my Hat? yes, when I am hang'd I will:
—I could break my head.
For holding eyes that knew not you at first:
But time and fortune run your courses with him,
He'll laugh and storm you, when you shew most hate.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: You're a fair Mounsieur.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Do you mock me, Lady?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Your business, Sir, I mean.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Regard your self good Mounsieur Longueville.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: You are too negligent of your self and place,
Cover your head sweet Mounsieur.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Mistake me not fair Ladies,
'Tis not to you, nor you, that I stand bare.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: Nay sweet dear Mounsieur, let it not be to us then.

speeches.speaker: La Poop.
verse: —A compliment.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: And—of manners.
Pray hide your head, your gallants use to do't.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: And you your foreheads, why you needful accessary rascals,
That cannot live without your mutual knaveries,
More than a Bawd, a Pandor, or a Whore
From one another; how dare you suspect
That I stand bare to you? what make you here?
Shift your house, Lady of 'em, for I know 'em,
They come to steal Napkins, and your Spoons;
Look to your Silver-bodkin, (Gentlewoman)

'Tis a dead
~tensil, and Page 'ware your pockets;
My reverence is unto this man, my Master,
Whom you, with protestations, and oaths
As high as Heaven, as deep as Hell, which would
Deceive the wisest man of honest nature,
Have cozen'd and abus'd; but I may meet you,
And beat you one with th' other.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Peace, no more.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Not a word, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: I am something thick of hearing; what said he?

speeches.speaker: La poop.
verse: I hear him, but regard him not.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Nor I, I am never angry fasting.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: My love keeps back my duty, noblest Lady;
If Husband or brother merit love from you,
Prevent their dangers, this hour brings to trial
Their hereto sleeping hates; by this time each
Within a yard is of the others heart,
And met to prove their causes and their spirits
With their impartial swords points; haste and save,
Or never meet them more, but at the grave.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Oh my distracted heart, that my wrackt honor
Should for a Brothers, or a Husbands life, through thy undoing, die.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Amiens engag'd; if he miscarry all my hopes and joys,
I now confess it loudly, are undone:
Caroch, and haste, one minute may betray
A life more worth than all time can repay.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Hump: Monsieur Laverdine pursues this boy extreamly, Captain, what will you do?

speeches.speaker: La p.
prose: Any thing but follow to this Land-service; I am a Sea-Captain you know, and to offer to part 'em, without we could do't like Watermen with long stave, a quarter of a mile off, might be dangerous.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Why then let's retire and pray for 'em, I am resolv'd to stop your intent; abus'd more than we have been we cannot be, without they fall to flat beating on's.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: And that were unkindly done i'^aith.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: But you are the troulesomest Ass that e'er I met with; retire, you smell like a womans chamber, that's newly up, before she have pinsht her vapours in with her cloaths.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: I will haunt thee like thy Grandames Ghost, thou shalt never rest for me.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: Well, I perceive 'tis vain to conceal a secret from you: believe it Sir, indeed I am a woman.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Why la; I knew't, this Propheti^al tongue o^ mine never sail'd me; my mother was half a wi^h, never any thing that she forespake, but came to pass: a woman? how happy am I? now we may lawfully come together without fear of hanging; sweet wench, be gracious, in honourable sort I woe, no otherwise.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: Faith, the truth is, I have loved you long.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: See, see.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: But durst not open it.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: — I think so.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: But briefly, when you bring it to the test, if there be not one Gentleman in this house, w^l ch^llenge more interest in me, than you can, I am at your di^posure.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: Oh Fortunatus, I envy thee not
For Cap, or pouch, this day I'll prove my Fortune,

In which your Lady doth ele^
^r Husband,
Who will he Amiens, 'twill save my wedding dinner,
Povera, La Poop, and Malicor^: if all sail,
I will turn Citizen, a beauteous wife
Is the Horn-book to the richest Tradesmans life.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Here's a good even piece of ground my Lords:
Will you fix here?

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Yes, any where; Lacquey, take off my spurs;
Upon a bridge, a rail, but my swords breadth upon a battlement.
I'll fight this quarrel.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: O' the Ropes, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Upon a Line.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: So all our Countrey Duels are carried, like a firework on a thred.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Go now, stay with the horses, and, do you hear?
Upon your lives, till some of us come to you,
Dare not to look this way.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Except you see strangers or others that by chance or purpose are like to interrupt us.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Then give warning.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Who takes a sword? the advantage is so small,
As he that doubts, hath the free leave to choose.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Come, give me any, and search me; 'tis not
The ground, weapon, or seconds that can make
Odds in those fatal trials: but the cause.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Most true, and, but it is no time to wish
When men are come to do, I would desire
The cause 'twixt us were other than it is;
But where the right is, there prevail our Swords.
And if my Sister have out-liv'd her honor,
I do not pray I may out-live her shame.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Your Sister Amiens, is a whore, at once.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: You oft have spoke that sence to me before,
But never in ths language Orleance;
And when you spoke it fair, and first, I told you
That it was possible you might be abus'd:
B^t now, since you forget your manners, you shall find,
If I transgress my custom, you do lye,
And are a villain, which I had rather yet
My sword had prov'd, than I been forc'd to speak:
Nay, give us leave, and since you stand so haughtily
And highly on your cause, let you and I,
Without engaging these two Gentlemen, singly determine it.
prose: 〈1 page duplicate〉
〈1 page duplicate〉

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: My Lord, you'll pardon us.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: I trust your Lordships may not do us that affront.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: As how?

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: We kiss your Lordships hand, and come to serve you here with swords.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: My Lord, we understand our selves.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: We have had the honor to be call'd unto the busin^ss, and we must not now quit it on terms.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Not terms of reason?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: No, no treason for the quitting of our calling.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: True, if I be call'd to't I must ask no reason.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Nor hear none neither, which is less:
^t is a favour, if my throat be cut,
Your Lordship does me; which I never can,
Nor must have hope how to requite: what noise?
What cry is that my Lord upon your guard?
So treachery is a foot.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Oh here they are:
My Lord (dear Lady help me) help me all;
I have so woful interest in both,
I know not which to fear for most: and yet
I must prefer my Lord. Dear brother,
You are too understanding, and too noble
To be offended, when I know my duty,
Though scarce my tears will let me so to do it.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Out-loathed strumpet.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Oh my dearest Lord,
If words could on me cast the name of whore,
I then were worthy to be loath'd; but know,
Your unkindness cannot make me wicked;
And therefore should less use that power upon me.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Was this your Art to make these Actors come,
To make this interlude? withdraw, cold man,
And if thy spirit be not frozen up,
Give me one stroke yet at thee for my vengeance.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Thou shalt have strokes, and strokes, thou glorious man,
Till thou breath'st thinner air than that thou talkest.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: My Lord, Count Amiens.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Princely Husband.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Whore.
You wrong her, impudent Lord; oh that I had the bulk
Of those dull men; look how they stand, and no man
Will revenge an innocent Lady.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: You hinder it Madam.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: I would hinder you; is there none else to kill him?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Kill him, Madam? have you learn'd that bad language? oh repent,
And be the motive, rather both kill me.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Then dye my infamy.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Hold bloody man.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Art thou there Basilisk?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose:
To strike thee dead, but tha^
^y fate deserves some weightier hand.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Sweet my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: Oh here's a plot; you bring your champions with you; the adultress with the adulterer: Out-howling—

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Good my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: Are you her Graces countenancer, Lady, the receiver to the poor vicious couple.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Sweet my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Sweet rascal, didst not thou tell me, false fellow,
This Montague here was murdered?

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: I did so; but he was falser, and a worthless Lord,
Like thy foul self that would have had it so.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Orleance 'tis true, and shall be prov'd upon thee.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Thy malice Duke, and this thy wicked nature, are all as visible as thou; but I born to contemn thy injuries, do know, that though thy greatness may corrupt a Jury, and make a Judge afraid, and carry out a world of evils with thy Title: yet thou art not quiet at home, thou bearest about thee that, that doth charge thee, and condemn thee too. The thing that grieves me more, and doth indeed displease me, is, to think that so much baseness stands here to have encountred so much honor: Pardon me my Lord, what late my passion spake, when you provok'd my innocence.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: Yes, do, oh: flattery becomes him better than the suit he wears; give him a new one, Amiens.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Orleance, 'tis here no time nor place, to jest or rail
Poorly with you, but I will find a time to
Whisper you forth to this, or some fit place,
As s^all not hold a second interruption.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: I hope your Lordships honor, and your life
Are destined unto higher hazards; this is of
A meaner arm.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Yes faith, or none.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: He is not fit to fall by an honest Sword,
A Prince and lye!

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: And slander, and hire men
To publish the false rumours he hath made.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: And stick 'em on his friends, and innocents.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: And practice against their lives after their fames.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: In men that are the matter of all lewdness,
Bawds, Thieves, and Cheaters, it were monstrous.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: But in a man of bloud, how more conspicuous?

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Can this be?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: They do slander him.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Hang them, a pair of railing hangbies.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: How? stand Orleance; stay, give me my Pistols boy,
Hinder me not, by—
I will kill him

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Oh, stay his fury,

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Longueville, my friend.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Not for my self, my Lord, but for mankind,
And all that have an interest to virtue,
Or title unto innocence.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Why hear me.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: For justice sake.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: That cannot be.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: To punish his wives, your honor, and my Lords wrongs here, whom I must ever call so; for your loves I'll swear I'll sacrifice—

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Longueville, I did not think you a murtherer before.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: I care not what you thought me.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: By—If thou attempt
His life, thy own is forfeit.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Foolish frantick man, the murder will be of us, not him.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Oh Heaven.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: We could have kill'd him, but we would not take
The justice out of fates.—
Singe but a hair of him, thou diest.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: No matter, shoot.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Villain.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: My Lord, your Sister is slain.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Biancha?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Oh hapless, and most wretched chance.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Standst thou looking upon the mischief thou hast made?
Thou godless man, feeding thy blood-shot eyes
With the red spectacle, and art not turn'd to stone
With horror? Hence, and take the wings of thy black
Infamy, to carry thee beyond the shoot of looks,
Or sound of curses, which will pursue thee still:
Thou hast out-fled all but thy guilt.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Oh wish it off again, for I am crack'd
Under the burden, and my heart will break.
How heavy guilt is, when men come to feel?
If you could know the mountain I sustain
With horror, you would each take off your part,
And more, to ease me: I cannot stand,
Forgive where I have wrong'd, I pray.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Look to him Montague.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: My Lords and Gentlemen, the Lady is well, but for fear,
Unless that have shot her;
I have the worst on't, that needs would venture
Upon a trick had like to ha' cost my guts:
Look to her, she'll be well, it was but Powder
I charg'd with, thinking that a guilty man
Would have been frighted sooner; but I'm glad
He's come at last.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: How is Byancha? well?

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Lives she? see Sister, doth she breathe?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Oh Gentlemen, think you I can breathe,
That am restored to the hate^ul sense
Of feeling in me my dear husbands death?
Oh no, I live not; life was that I left;
And what you have call'd me to is death indeed:
I cannot weep so fast as he doth bleed.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Pardon me, Madam, he is well.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Ha' my Husband.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: I cannot speak whether my joy or shame
Be greater, but I thank the Heavens for both.
Oh look not black upon me, all my friends,
To whom I will be reconcil'd, or grow unto
This earth, till I have wept a trench
That shall be great enough to be my grave,
And I will think them too most manly tears,
If they do move your pities: it is true,
Man should do nothing that he should repent;
But if he have, and say that he is sorry,
It is a worse fault, if he be not truly.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: My Lord, such sorrow cannot be suspected:
Here take your honoured wife, and joyn your hands.
—She hath married you again:
And Gentlemen, I do invite you all,
This night to take my house, where on the morrow,
To heighten more the reconciling feast,
I'll make my self a Husband and a guest.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: WEll now I am sure you are mine.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: I am sure I am glad
I have one to own then; you'll find me honest
As these days go, enough; poor without question,
Which beggars hold a virtue; give me meat, and I
Shall do my work, else knock my shooes off,
And turn me out again.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: You are a merry fellow.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: I have no great cause.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Yes, thy love to me.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: That's as we make our game.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Why, you repent then?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Faith no, worse than I am I cannot be;
Much better I expect not: I shall love you,
And when you bid me go to bed, obey,
Lie still or move as you shall minister;
Keep a four-Nobles Nag, and a Jack
Merling, learn to love Ale, and play at Two-hand Irish,
And there's then all I aim at.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Nay sweet fellow, I'll make it something better.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: If you do, you'll make me worse:
Now I am poor, and willing to do well,
Hold me in that course; of all the Kings creatures,
I hate his coin, keep me from that, and save me;
For if you chance out of your housewivery
To leave a hundred pound or two, bestow it
In Plumb-broth e'r I know it, else I take it;
Seek out a hundred men that want this money,
Share it among 'em, they'll cry noble Montague,
And so I stand again at livery.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: You have pretty fancies, Sir, but married once,
This charity will fall home to your self.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: I would it would, I am afraid my looseness
^s yet scarce stopt, though it have nought to work on
But the meer air of what I have had.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Pretty.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: I wonder sweet heart why you'll marry me,
I can see nothing in my self deserves it,
Unless the handsome wearing of a band,
For that's my stock now, or a pair of garters;
Necessity will not let me loose.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: I see Sir, a great deal more, a handsome man, a Husband,
To make a right good woman truly happy.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Lord, where are my eyes, either you are foolish
As wenches once a year are, or far worse,
Extreamly virtuous, can you love a poor man
That relies on cold meat, and cast stockings,
One only suit to his back, which now is m^wing?
But what will be the next coat will pose Tristram.
If I should leavy from my friends a fortune:
I could not raise ten groats to pay the Priest now.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: I'll do that duty; 'tis not means nor money
Makes me pursue your love; were your mind bankrupt,
I would never love you.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Peace wench, here's my Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Nay, never shrink i'th' wetting, for my presence;
D'ye find her willing Montague?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Willing Madam?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: How dainty you make of it, do not I know
You two love one another?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Certain Madam, I think ye'ave revelations of these matters:
Your Ladyship cannot tell me when I kist her.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: But she can, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: But she will not Madam;
For when they talk once, 'tis like Fairy-Money,
They get no more close kisses.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Thou art wanton.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Heaven knows I need not, yet I would be lusty:
But—my Provender scarce pricks me.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: It shall be mended Montague, I am glad you are grown so merry.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: So am I too Madam.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: You two will make a pretty handsome Consort.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Yes Madam, if my Fiddle fail me not.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Your Fiddle? why your Fiddle? I warrant thou meanest madly:

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Can you blame me? alas I am in love.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: 'Tis very well, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: How long have you been thus?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: How thus in love?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: You are very quick, Sir: no, I mean thus pleasant.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: —Ever since I was poor.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: A little wealth would change you then?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Yes Lady, into another suit, but never more
Into another man: I'll bar that mainly,
The wealth I get hence-forward shall be charm'd
For ever hurting me, I'll spend it fasting:
As I live noble Lady, there is nothing
I have found directly, cures the melancholy,
But want and wedlock; when I had store of money,
I simper'd sometime, and spoke wondrous wise,
But never laught out-right; now I am empty,
My heart sounds like a Bell, and strikes at both sides.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: You are finely temper'd, Montague.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Pardon Lady, if any way my free mirth have offended.
'Twas meant to please you: if it prove too saucy,
Give it a frown, and I am ever silenc'd.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: I like it passing well; pray follow it:
This is my day of choice, and shall be yours too,
'Twere pity to delay ye: call to the Steward,
And tell him 'tis my pleasure he should give you
Five hundred Crowns: make your self handsome Montague,
Let none wear better cloaths, 'tis for my credit;
But pray be merry still.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: If I be not, and make a fool of twice as many hundreds,
Clap me in Canvas, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: I am strangely glad, I have found the mystery
Of this disguised boy out: I ever trusted
It was a woman; and how happily
I have found it so; and for my self, I am sure,
One that would offer me a thousand pound now
(And that's a pretty sum to make one stagger)
In ready Gold for this concealment, could not
Buy my hope of her, she's a dainty wench,
And such a one I find I want extreamly,
To bring me into credit: beauty does it.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Say we should all meach here, and stay the Feast, now, what can the worst be? we have plaid the knaves, that's without question.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: True, and as I take it, this is the first truth
We told these ten years, and for any thing
I know, may be the last: but grant we are knaves,
Both base and beastly knaves—

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Say so then.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: Well.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: And likewise let it be considered, we have wrong'd,
And most maliciously, this Gentlewoman
We cast to stay with, what must we expect now?

speeches.speaker: Mal,
verse: I, there's the point, we would expect good eating.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: I know we would, but we may find good beating.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: You say true Gentlemen, and by—
Though I love meat as well as any man,
I care not what he be, if a eat a Gods name;
Such a crab-sauce to my meat will turn my pallate.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: There's all the hazard, for the frozen Montague
Has now got spring again, and warmth in him,
And without doubt, dares beat us terribly.
For not to mint the matter, we are cowards,
And have, and shall be beaten, when men please
To call us into cudgeling.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: I feel we are very prone that way.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: The sons of Adam.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: Now, here then rests the state o'th' question;
Whether we yield our bodies for a dinner
To a sound dog-whip? for I promise ye,
If men be given to correction,
We can expect no less; or quietly
Take a hard Egg or two, and ten mile hence
Bait in a ditch, this we may do securely;
For, to stay hereabout will be all one,
If once our moral mischiefs come in memory.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: But pray ye hear me, is not this the day
The Virgin Lady doth elect her Husband?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: The dinner is to that end.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Very well then, say we all stay, and say we all scape this whipping, and be well entertained, and one of us carry the Lady.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: 'Tis a seemly saying, I must confess, but if we stay, how fitly
We may apply it to our selves (i'th' end)
Will ask a Christian fear; I cannot see,
If I say true, what special ornaments
Of Art or Nature, (lay aside our lying
Whoring and drinking, which are no great virtues)
We are endued withal, to win this Lady.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Yet Women go not by the best parts ever; that I have found directly.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: Why should we fear then? they choose men
As they feed; sometimes they settle
Upon a White broth'd face, a sweet smooth gallant,
And him they make an end of in a night;
Sometimes a Goose, sometimes a grosser meat,
A rump of Beef will serve 'em at some season,
And fill their bellies too, though without doubt
They are great devourers: Stock-fish is a dish,
If it be well drest, for the tuffness sake
Will make the proud'st of 'em long and leap for't.
They'll run mad for a Pudding, e'r they'll starve,

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: For my own part I care not, come what can come,
If I be whipt, why so be it; if cudgell'd,
I hope I shall out-live it, I am sure
'Tis not the hundredth time I have been serv'd so,
And yet I thank Heaven I am here.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Here's resolution.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: A little patience, and a rotten Apple
Cures twenty worse diseases; what say you, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: Marry I say Sir, if I had been acquainted
With lamming in my youth, as you have been
With whipping, and such benefits of nature,
I should do better: as I am, I'll venture,
And if it be my luck to have the Lady,
I'll use my fortune modestly; if beaten,
You shall not hear a word, one I am sure of,
And if the worst fall, she shall be my Physick.
Lets go then, and a merry wind be with us.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Captain, your shooes are old, pray put 'em off,
And let one fling 'em after us; be bold, Sirs,
And howsoever our fortune falls, lets bear
An equal burden; if there be an odd lash,
We'll part it afterwards.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: I am arm'd at all points.

prose: Then my Lady will have a bedfellow to night.
So she says; Heaven! what a dainty arm-full shall he enjoy, that has the launching of her, what a fight she'll make.
I marry boys, there will be sport indeed, there will be grapling, she has a murderer lies in her prow, I am afraid will fright his main Mast, Robin.
Who dost thou think shall have her of thy conscience, thou art a wise man?
If she go the old way, the way of lot, the longest cut sweeps all without question.
She has lost a friend of me else; what think ye of the Courtier?
Hang him Hedge-hog: h'as nothing in him but a piece of Euphues, and twenty dozen of twelve penny ribond, all about him, he is but one Pedlers shop of Gloves and Garters, pick-teeth and pomander.
The Courtier, marry God bless her Steven, she is not mad yet, she knows that trindle-tail too well, he's crest-fall'n, and pin-buttock't, with leaping Landresses.
The Merchant, sure she will not be so base to have him.
I hope so Robin, he'll sell us all to the Moors to make Mummy; nor the Captain.
Who Potgun? that's a sweet youth indeed, will he stay, think ye?

Yes, without question, and have halfe din'd too, e'r the Grace be done; he's good for nothing in the world but eating, lying and sleeping; what other men devour in drink, he takes in potage, they say h'as been at Sea, a Herring-fishing, for without doubt he dares not hale an Eel-boat, i'th' way of War.
I think so, they would beat him off with Butter.

When he brings in a prize, unless it be Cockles, or C^llis sand to scour with, I'll renounce my Five Mark a year, and all the hidden Art I have in carving, to teach young Birds to whistle Walsingham; leave him to the Lime-Boats; now, what think you of the brave Amiens?
That's a thought indeed.
I marry, there's a person fit to feed upon a dish so dainty, and he'll do't I warrant him i'th' nick boys, has a body world without end.
And such a one my Lady will make no little of; but is not Montague married to day?
Yes faith, honest Montague must have his bout too.
He's as good a lad as ever turn'd a trencher; must we leave him?
He's too good for us, Steven, I'll give him health to his good luck to night i'th' old Beaker, and it shall be Sack too.
I must have a Garter; and boys I have bespoke a Posset, some body shall give me thanks fort, 'tas a few toys in't will rase commotions in a bed, lad.
Away; my Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Seat your selves noble Lords and Gentlemen,
You know your places; many royal welcomes
I give your Grace; how lovely shews this change?
My house is honor'd in this reconcilement.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Thus Madam must you do, my Lady now shall see
You made a Woman;
And give you some short lessons for your voyage.
Take her instructions Lady, she knows much.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: This becomes you, Sir.

speeches.speaker: La^
verse: My Lord must have his Will.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: 'Tis all I can do now, sweet-heart, fair Lady;
This to your happy choice, brother Amiens,
You are the man I mean it to.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: I'll pledge you.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: And with my heart.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: With all my love I take it.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
prose: Noble Lords, I am proud ye have done this day, so much content, and me such estimation, that this hour (In this poor house) shall be a league for ever, For so I know ye mean it.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: I do Lady.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: And I my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
verse: Y'ave done a work of honor.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Give me the Cup, where this health stops, let
That man be either very sick, or very simple;
Or I am very angry; Sir, to you;
Madam, methinks this Gentleman might sit too;
He would become the best on's.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: Pray sit down, Sir, I know the Lady of the Feast expects not this day so much old custom.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Sit down Montague; nay, never blush for the matter.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Noble Madam, I have too reasons rgainst it, and I dare not; duty to you first, as you are my Lady, and I your poorest servant; next the custom of this days ceremony.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: As you are my servant, I may command you then.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: To my life, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Sit down, and here, I'll have it so.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: Sit down man, never refuse so fair a Ladies offer.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: It is your pleasure, Madam, not my pride,
And I obey; I'll pledge ye now my Lord, Monsieur Longaville.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: I thank you, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: This to my Lady, and her fair choice to day, and happiness.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: 'Tis a fair health, I'll pledge you though I sink for't.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
prose: Montague you are too modest; come, I'll add a little more wine t'yee, 'twill make you merry, this to the good I wish. —

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Honour'd Lady, I shall forget my self with this great bounty.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
prose: You shall not Sir, give him some Vine,

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: By Heaven you are a worthy woman, and that Man is blest can come near such a Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lami.
prose: Such a blessing wet weather washes.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: At all, I will not go a lip less, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: 'Tis well cast, Sir,

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: If Montague get more Wine, we are all like to hear on't.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: I do not like that sitting there.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Nor I, methinks he looks lik a Judge.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: Now have I a kind of grudging of a beating on me, I fear my hot sit:

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Drink apace, there's nothing allays a cudgel like it.

speeches.speaker: Lami.
prose: Montague, now I'll put my choice to you; who do you hold in all this honor'd company, a Husband sit to enjoy thy Lady? speak directly.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Shall I speak, Madam?

speeches.speaker: Lami.
prose: Montague you shall.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Then as I have a soul, I'll speak my conscience,
Give me more Wine, in vino veritas,
Here's to my self, and Montague have a care.

speeches.speaker: Lami.
verse: Speak to th' cause.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Yes Madam, first I'll begin to thee.

speeches.speaker: Lav,
verse: Have at us.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: Now for a Psalm of mercy.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: You good Monsieur, you that belye the noble name of Courtier, and think your claim good here, hold up your hand; your Worship is endited here, for a vain glorious fool.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: Good, oh Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: For one whose wit
Lies in a ten pound wastcoat; yet not warm;
Ye have travell'd like a Fidler to make faces,
And brought home nothing but a case of tooth-picks.
You would be married and no less than Ladies,
And of the best sort can serve you; thou Silk-worm,
What hast thou in thee to deserve this woman?
Name but the poorest piece of man, good manners,
There's nothing sound about thee, saith, th'ast none,
It lies pawn'd at thy Silk-man's, for so much Lace;
Thy credit with his wife cannot redeem it,
Thy cloaths are all the soul thou hast, for so
Thou sav'st them handsome for the next great tilting,
Let who will take the t'other, thou wert never christen'd
(Upon my conscience) but in Barbers water;
Thou art never out o'th' Bason, thou art rotten,
And if thou dar'st tell truth, thou wilt confess it;
—Thy skin
Looks of a Chesnut colour, greaz'd with Amber,
All women that on earth do dwell, thou lov'st,
Yet none that understand, love thee again,
But those that love the Spittle; get thee home
Poor painted Butter-flie, the Summers past;
Go sweat, and eat dry Mutton, thou may'st live
To do so well yet; a bruis'd Chamber-Maid
May fall upon thee, and advance thy follies.
You have your sentence; now it follows Captain,
I treat of you.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: Pray Heaven I may deserve it.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Beshrew my heart, he speaks plain.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: That's plain dealing.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: You are a rascal Captain.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: A fine Calling.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: A Water-coward:

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: He would make a pretty stuff.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: May I speak freely, Madam?

speeches.speaker: Lami.
verse: Here's none ties you.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Why shouldst thou dare come hither with a thought
To find a wife here fit for thee? are all
Thy single money whores that fed on Carrots,
And fill'd the high Grass with familiars
Fall'n off to Footmen; prethee tell me truly,
For now I know thou dar'st not lie, couldst thou not
Wish thy self beaten well with all thy heart now,
And out of pain? say that I broke a rib,
Or cut thy nose off, wer't not merciful for this ambition?

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: Do your pleasure, Sir, beggars must not be choosers.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: He longs for beating.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: But that I have nobler thoughts possess my soul,
Than such brown Bisket, such a piece of Dog-fish,
Such a most maungy Mackril eater as thou art,
That dares do nothing that belongs to th' Sea,
But spue, and catch Rats, and fear men of War,
Though thou hast nothing in the world to loose
A boord thee, but one piece of Beef, one Musket
Without a cock for peace sake, and a Pitch-barrel,
I'll tell thee, if my time were not more pretious
Than thus to loose it, I would rattle thee,
It may be beat thee, and thy pure fellow,
The Merchant there of Catskins, till my words,
Or blows, or both, made ye two branded wretches
To all the world hereafter; you would fain to
Venture your Bils of lading for this Lady;
What would you give now for her? some five frayl
Of rotten Figs, good Godson, would you not, Sir?
Or a Parter that speaks High Dutch? can all thou ever saw'st
Of thine own fraughts from Sea, or cosenage
(At which thou art as expert as the Devil)
Nay, sell thy soul for wealth to, as thou wilt do,
Forfeit thy friends, and raise a mint of Money,
Make thee dream all these double, could procure
A kiss from this good Lady? canst thou hope
She would lye with such a nook of Hell as thou art,
And hatch young Merchant-furies? oh ye dog-bolts!
That fear no Hell but Dunkirk, I shall see you
Serve in a lowsy Lime-boat, e'r I dye,
For mouldy Cheese and Butter, Billingsgate
Would not endure, or bring in rotten Pippins
To cure blew eyes, and swear they came from China.

speeches.speaker: Lami.
verse: Vex 'em no more, alas they shake:

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Down quickly on your marrow-bones, and thank this Lady.
I would not leave you thus else, there are blankets,
And such delights for such knaves; but fear still;
'Twill be revenge enough to keep you waking.
Ye have no mind of marriage, ha'ye?

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: Surely no great mind now.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Nor you.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Nor I, I take it.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Two eager suitors.

speeches.speaker: Lov.
verse: Troth 'tis wondrous hot, Heaven bless us from him.

speeches.speaker: Lami.
verse: You have told me Montague
Who are not fit to have me, let me know
The man you would point out for me

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: There he sits; my Lord of Amieus, Madam, is my choice, he's noble every way, and worthy a wife with all the dowries of—

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Do you speak Sir, out of your friendship to me?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Yes my Lord, and out of truth, for I could never flatter.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: I would not say how much I owe you for it,
For that were but a promise, but I'll thank ye,
As now I find you, in despite of fortune,
A fair and noble Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Lami.
verse: My Lords, I must confess the choice this man hath made
Is every way a great one, if not too great,
And no way to be slighted: yet because
We love to have our own eyes sometimes new,
Give me a little liberty to see,
How I could fit my self, if I were put to't.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Madam we must.

speeches.speaker: Lami.
verse: Are ye all agreed?

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
verse: We be.

speeches.speaker: Lami.
verse: Then as I am a Maid, I shall choose here.
Montague I must have thee.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Why Madam, I have learnt to suffer more
Than you can (out of pity) mock me with this way especially.

speeches.speaker: Lami.
verse: Thou think'st I jest now;
But by the love I bear thee, I will have thee.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: If you could be so weak to love a fall'n man,
He must deserve more than I ever can,
Or ever shall (dear Lady;) look but this way
Upon that Lord, and you will tell the then
Your eyes are no true choosers of good men.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Do you love him truly?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
prose: Yes my Lord, I will obey him truly, for I'll marry him, and justly think he that has so well serv'd me with his obedience, being born to greatness, must use me nobly of necessity, when I shall serve him.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: 'Twere a deep sin to cross ye, noble Montague,
I wish ye all content, and am as happy
In my friends good as it were meerly mine.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Your Lordship does ill to give up your right;
I am not capable of this great goodness,
There sits my wife that holds my troth.

speeches.speaker: Cha.
prose: I'll end all, I wooed you for my Lady, and now give up my Title, alas poor wench, my aims are lower fat.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: How's this sweet-heart?

speeches.speaker: Lami.
verse: Sweet-heart 'tis so, the drift was mine to hide
My purpose till it struck home.

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
verse: Give you joy.

speeches.speaker: Lami.
prose: Prethee leave wondring, by this kiss I'll have thee.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Then by this kiss, and this, I'll ever serve ye.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: This Gentleman and I Sir, must needs hope once more to follow ye.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: As friends and fellows, never as servants more.

speeches.speaker: Long. Dub.
verse: You make us happy.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: Friend Montague, ye have taught me so much honor, I have found a fault in my self, but thus I'll purge my conscience of it, the late Land I took by false play, from you, with as much contrition, and entireness of affection to this most happy day again, I render; be master of your own, forget my malice, and make me worthy of your love, L. Montague.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: You have won me and honor to your name.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Since your Lordship has begun good deeds, we'll follow; good Sir forgive us, we are now those men fear you for goodness sake; those sums of money unjustly we detain from you, on your pardon shall be restor'd again, and we your servants.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: You are very forward Sir, it seems you have money, I pray you lay out, I'll pay you, or pray for you, as the Sea-works.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: Their pennance Sir, I'll undertake, so please ye
To grant me one concealment.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: A right Courtier, still a begging.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: What is it Sir?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: A Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: In my gift?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: Yes Sir, in yours.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Why, bring her forth, and take her.

speeches.speaker: Lami.
verse: What wench would he have?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Any wench I think.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: This is the Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: 'Tis my Page, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: No Sir, I am a poor disguis'd Lady,
That like a Page have followed you full long for love godwot.

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
verse: A Lady—Laverdine yes, yes, 'tis a Lady.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: It may be so, and yet we have lain together,
But by my troth I never found her, Lady.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: Why wore you boys cloaths?

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: I'll tell you, Madam,
I took example by two or three Plays, that me thought
Concerned me.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Why made you not me acquainted with it?

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: Indeed Sir, I knew it not my self,
Until this Gentleman open'd my dull eyes,
And by perswasion made me see it.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Could his power in words make such a change?

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: Yes, as truly woman as your self, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: Why, but hark you, are not you a woman?

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: If hands and face make it not evident, you shall see more.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Breeches, breeches, Laverdine.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: 'Tis not enough, women may wear those cases.
Search further Courtier.

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
verse: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: Oh thou fresh-water Gudgeon, wouldst thou come
To point of Marriage with an Ignoramus?
Thou shouldst have had her Urin to the Doctors,
The foolishest Physitian could have made plain
The liquid Epicaene, a blind man by the hand
Could have discovered the ring from the stone.
Boy, come, to Sea with me, I'll teach thee to climb,
And come down by the Rope, nay to eat Rats.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: I shall devour my Master before the prison then,
Sir, I have began my Trade.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Trade? to the City, child, a flat-cap will become thee.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Gentlemen, I beseech you molest your selves no further.
For his pre^erment it is determin'd.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: I am much ashamed, and if my cheek
Gives not satisfaction, break my head.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Your shame's enough, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Montague, much joy attend thy marriage-bed;
By thy example of true goodness, envy is exil'd,
And to all honest men that truth intend,
I wish good luck, fair fate be still thy friend.

plays.play_title: THE MASQUE of the Gentlemen OF GRAYS-INNE and the INNER-TEMPLE; Performed before the KING in the Banqueting-House in White-Hall, at the Marriage of the Illustrious Frederick and Elizabeth, Prince and Princess Palatine of the Rhine:

segments.head: THE MASQUE of the Gentlemen OF GRAYS-INNE and the INNER-TEMPLE; Performed before the KING in the Banqueting-House in White-Hall, at the Marriage of the Illustrious Frederick and Elizabeth, Prince and Princess Palatine of the Rhine:

speeches.speaker: Mercury.
verse: STay Light loot Iris, for thou striv'st in vain,
My wings are nimbler than thy feet.

speeches.speaker: Iris.
verse: Away,
Dissembling Mercury, my messages
Ask honest haste; not like those want on ones,
Your thundering Father sends,

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Stay foolish Maid,
Or I will take my rise upon a hill,
When I perceive thee seated in a cloud,
In all the painted glory, that thou hast,
And never cease to clap my willing wing,
Till I catch hold on thy discolour'd Bow,
And shiver it beyond the angry power
Of your mad Mistriss to make up again.

speeches.speaker: Iris,
verse: Hermes forbear, Juno will chide and strike;
Is great Jove jealous that that I am imploy'd
On her Love-errands? she did never yet
Claspe weak mortality in her white arms,
As he has often done; I only come
To celebrate the long wish'd Nuptials
Here in Olympia, which are now perform'd
Betwixt two goodly Rivers, that have mixt
Their gentle winding waves, and are to grow
Into a thousand streams, great as themselves.
I need not name them, for the sound is loud
In Heaven and Earth, and I am sent from her
The Queen of marriage, that was present here,
And smil'd to see them joyn, and hath not chid
Since it was done. Good Hermes let me goe.

speeches.speaker: Merc.
verse: Nay, you must stay, Jove's message is the same;
Whose eyes are lightning, and whose voice is thunder,
Whose breath is airy wind; he will, who knows
How to be first in Earth, as well as Heaven.

speeches.speaker: Iris.
verse: But what hath he to do with Nuptial rites?
Let him sit pleas'd upon his Starry throne,
And fright poor mortals with his Thunder-bolts,
Leaving to us the mutual darts of eyes.

speeches.speaker: Merc.
verse: Alas, when ever offer'd, he t'abridge
Your Ladies power, but only now, in these,
Whose match concerns the general government?
Hath not each God a part in these high joyes?
And shall not he the King of gods presume
Without proud Juno's licence? let her know,

That when enamour'd Jove
^ gave her power
To link soft hearts in undissolving bands,
He then foresaw, and to himself reserv'd
The honor of this marriage: thou shalt stand
Still as a Rock, while I to bless this Feast
Will summon up with mine all-charming rod
The Nymphs of Fountains, from whose watry locks,
(Hung with the dew of blessing and increase)
The greedy Rivers take their nourishment,
Yea Nymphs, who bathing in your loved Springs,
Beheld these Rivers in their infancy,
And joy'd to see them, when their circled heads
Refresh'd the Air, and spread the ground with Flowers;
Rise from your Wells, and with your nimble feet
Perform that office to this happy pair,
Which in these Plains you to Alpheus did,
When passing hence, through many Seas unmixt,
He gain'd the favour of his Arethuse.

speeches.speaker: Iris.
verse: Is Hermes grown a Lover? by what power
Unknown to us, calls he the Maids?

speeches.speaker: Merc.
verse: Presumptuous Iris, I could make thee dance,
Till thou forgetst thy Ladies messages,
And rann'st back crying to her; thou shalt know
My power is more, only my breath, and this
Shall move fix'd Stars, and force the Firmament
To yield the Hyades, who govern showers,
And dewy clouds, in whose dispersed drops
Thou form'st the shape of thy deceitful Bow.
Year Maids, who yearly at appointed times
Advance with kindly tears, the gentle floods,
Discend, and pour your blessing on these streams,
Which rolling down from Heaven-aspiring hills,
And now united in the fruitful vales,
Bear all before them, ravish'd with their joy,
And swell in glory, till they know no bounds.

speeches.speaker: Iris.
verse: Great Wit and Power hath Hermes to contrive
A lively dance, which of one sex consists.

speeches.speaker: M^rc.
verse: Alas poor Iris! Venus hath in store
A secret ambush of her winged boys,
Who lurking long within these pleasant groves,
First stuck these Lovers with their equal darts;
Those Cupids shall come forth, and joyn with these,
To honor that which they themselves began.
Behold the Statues which wild Vulcan plac'd
Under the Altar of Olympian Jove,
And gave to them an artificial life:
See how they move, drawn by this Heavenly joy,
Like the wild Trees, which followed Orpheus Harp.

speeches.speaker: Merc.
verse: And what will Juno's Iris do for her?

speeches.speaker: Iris.
verse: Just match this shew, or mine inventions fall,
Had it been worthier, I would have invok'd
The blazing Comets, Clouds, and falling Stars,
And all my kindred, Meteors of the air,
To have excell'd it; but I now must strive
To imitate confusion; therefore thou
Delightful Flora; if thou ever feltst
Increase of sweetness in those blooming Plants,
On which the horns of my fair Bow decline,
Send hither all that rural company,
Which deck the May-games with their clownish sports;
Juno will have it so.

speeches.speaker: Merc.
verse: Iris, we strive
Like winds at liberty, who should do worst
E'r we return. If Juno be the Queen
Of Marriages, let her give happy way
To what is done in honor of the State
She governs.

speeches.speaker: Iris.
verse: Hermes, so it may be done
Meerly in honor of the State, and those
That now have prov'd it; not to satisfy
The lust of Jupiter, in having thanks
More than his Juno; if thy Snaky rod
Have power to search the Heaven, or sound the Sea,
Or call together all the ends of earth,
To bring thee any thing that may do grace
To us, and these, do it, we shall be pleas'd.

speeches.speaker: Merc.
verse: Then know that from the mouth of Jove himself,
Whose words have wings, and need not to be born,
I took a message, and I bore it through
A thousand yielding clouds, and never staid
Till his high Will was done: the Olympian games,
Which long had slept, at these wish'd Nuptials,
He pleas'd to have renew'd, and all his Knights
Are gather'd hither, who within their Tents
Rest on this hill, upon whose rising head
Behold Joves Altar, and his blessed Priests
Moving about it; come you Holy men,
And with your voices draw these youths along,
That till Joves Musick call them to their games.
Their active sports may give a blest content
To those, for whom they are again begun.
Shake off your heavy trance,
and leap into a dance,
Such as no mortals use to tread,
fit only for Apollo
To play to, for the Moon to lead,
And all the Stars to follow,
On blessed youths, for Jove doth pause,
Laying aside his graver Laws
For this device:
And at the wedding such a pair,
Each dance is taken for a prayer,
Each Song a Sacrifice.

Single.
More pleasing were these sweet delights,
If Ladies mov'd as well as Knights;
Run every one of you and catch
A Nymph, in honor of his match;
And whisper boldly in her ear,

Jove will but laugh, if you forswear.

All.
And this days sins he doth resolve,
That we his Priests should all absolve.
You should stay longer if we durst,
Away, alas! that he that first
Gave time wild wings to fly away,
H'as now no power to make him stay.
And though these games must needs be plaid,
I would these pair, when they are laid,
And not a creature nigh'em,
Might catch his sithe, as he doth pass,
And clip his wings, and break his glass,
And keep him ever by'em.
Peace and silence be the guide
To the Man, and to the Bride:
If there be a joy yet new
In marriage, let it fall on you,
That all the world may wonder:
If we should stay, we should do worse,
And turn our blessings to a curse.
By keeping you asunder.

plays.play_title: FOUR PLAYS OR Moral Representations IN ONE.

segments.head: FOUR PLAYS OR Moral Representations IN ONE.

speeches.speaker: Frig.
prose: AWay with those bald-pated Rascals there, their wits are bound up in Vellom, they are not currant here. Down with those City-Gentlemen, &c. Out with those — I say, and in with their wives at the back door. Worship and place, I am weary of ye, ye lye on my shoulders lik a load of Gold on an Asses back. A man in Authority, is but as a candle in the wind, sooner wasted or blown out, than under a bushel. How now, what's the matter?
Who are you, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Rin.
prose: Who am I, Sir? why, do y' not know me?

speeches.speaker: Frig.
prose: No by my — do I not.

speeches.speaker: Rin.
prose: I am sure we din'd together to day.

speeches.speaker: Frig.
prose: That's all one: as I din'd with you in the City, and as you paid for my dinner there, I do know you, and am beholding to you: But as my mind is since transmigrated into my office, and as you come to Court to have me pay you again, and be beholding to me, I know you not, I know you not.

speeches.speaker: Rin.
prose: Nay, but look ye, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Frig.
prose: Pardon me: If you had been my bed-fellow these seven years, and lent me money to buy my place, I must not transgress principles: This very talking with you, is an ill example.

speeches.speaker: Rin.
prose: Pish, you are too punctual a Courtier, Sir: why, I am a Courtier too, yet never understood the place or name to be so infectious to humanity and manners, as to cast a man into a burning pride and arrogance, for which there is no cure. I am a Courtier, and yet I will know my friends, I tell you.

speeches.speaker: Frig.
prose: And I tell you, you will thrive accordingly, I warrant you.

speeches.speaker: Rin.
prose: But hark ye, Signior Frigozo, you shall first understand, I have no friends with me to trouble you,

speeches.speaker: Frig.
prose: Humh: That's a good motive.

speeches.speaker: Rin.
prose: Not to borrow money of you.

speeches.speaker: Frig.
prose: That's an excellent motive.

speeches.speaker: Rin.
prose: No my sweet Don, nor to ask what you owe me.

speeches.speaker: Frig.
prose: Why, that is the very motive of motives, why I ought and will know thee: and if I had not wound thee up to this promise, I would not have known thee these fifteen years, no more than the errantst, or most founder'd Castillian that followed our new Queens Carriages a-foot.

speeches.speaker: Rin.
prose: Nor for any thing, dear Don, but that you would place me conveniently to see the Play to night.

speeches.speaker: Frig.
prose: That shall I, Signior Rinaldo: but would you had come sooner: you see how full the Scaffolds are, there is scant room for a Lovers thought here. Gentlewomen sit close for shame: Has none of ye a little corner for this Gentleman? I'll place ye, fear not. And how did our brave King of Portugal, Emanuel, bear himself to day? You saw the solemnity of the marriage.

speeches.speaker: Rin.
prose: Why, like a fit Husband for so gracious and excellent a Princess, as his worthy mate Isabella, the King of Castiles Daughter doth in her very external linaments, mixture of colours, and joyning Dove like behaviour assure her self to be. And I protest (my dear Don) seriously, I can sing prophetically nothing but blessed Hymns, and happy occasions to this sacred union of Portugal and Castile, which have so wisely and mutually conjoyned two such virtuous and beautiful Princes as these are; and in all opinion like to multiply to their very last minute.

speeches.speaker: Frig.
prose: The King is entring: Signior, hover here about, and as soon as the Train is set; clap into me, we'll stand near the State. If you have any Creditors here, they shall renew bonds a Twelvemonth on such a sight: but to touch the pomel of the King's Chair in the sight of a Citizen, is better security for a thousand double Duckets, than three of the best Merchants in Lisbon. Besides, Signior, we will censure, not only the King in the Play here, that Reigns his two hours; but the King himself, that is to rule his life time: Take my counsel: I have one word to say to this noble Assembly, and I am for you.

speeches.speaker: Rin.
prose: Your method shall govern me.

speeches.speaker: Frig.
verse: Prologues are bad Huishers before the wise;
Why may not then an Huisher Prologize?
Here's a fair sight, and were ye oftner seen
Thus gather'd here, 'twould please our King and Queen
~pon my conscience, ye are welcome all
To Lisbon, and the Court of Portugal;
Where your fair eyes shall feed on no worse sights
Than preparations made for Kings delights.
We wish to men content, the manliest treasure,
And to the Women, their own wish'd for pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: Fair fountain of my life, from whose pure streams
The propagation of two Kingdoms flowes,
Never contention rise in eithers brest,
But contestation whose love shall be best.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Majestick Ocean, that with plenty feeds
Me, thy poor tributary Rivolet,
Sun of my beauty, that with radiant beams
Dost gild, and dance upon these humble streams,
Curst be my birth-hour, and my ending day,
When back your love-floods I forget to pay:
Or if this brest of mine, your crystall brook,
Ever take other form in, other look
But yours, or ere produce unto your grace
A strange reflection, or anothers face,
But be your love-book clasp'd, open'd to none
But you, nor hold a storie, but your own;
A water fix'd, that ebbs nor floods pursue,
Frozen to all, onely dissolv'd to you.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: O, who shall tel the sweetness of our love
To future times, and not be thought to lye?
I look through this hour like a perspective,
And far off see millions of prosperous seeds,
That our reciprocall affection breeds.
Thus my white rib, close in my brest with me,
Which nought shall tear hence, but mortalitie.

speeches.speaker: Lords.
verse: Be Kingdoms blest in you, you blest in them.

speeches.speaker: Frig.
verse: Whist, Seignior; my strong imagination shews me
Love (me thinks) bathing in milk, and wine in her cheeks:
O! how she clips him, like a plant of Ivie.

speeches.speaker: Rin.
prose: I; Could not you be content to be an Owl in such an ivie-bush, or one of the Oaks of the City to be so clipt?

speeches.speaker: Frig.
prose: Equivocal Don, though I like the clipping well, I could not be content either to be your Owl, or your Ox of the City. The Play begins.

speeches.speaker: Poet Prologue.
verse: Low at your sacred feet our poor Muse layes
Her, and her thunder-fearless virdant Bayes.
Four severall Triumphs to your Princely eyes,
Of Honor, Love, Death, and Time do rise
From our approaching subject, which we move
Towards you with fear, since that a sweeter Love,
A brighter Honor, purer Chastitie
March in your brests this day triumphantly,
Then our weak Scenes can show: then how dare we
Present like Apes and Zanies, things that be
Exemplifi'd in you, but that we know,
We ne'r crav'd grace, which you did not bestow?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: What means proud Sophocles?

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: To go even with Martius,
And not to follow him like his Officer:
I never waited yet on any man.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Why poor Athenian Duke, thou art my slave,
My blows have conquerd thee.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Thy slave? proud Martius,
Cato thy countrey-man (whose constancie,
Of all the Romans, I did honor most)
Rip'd himself twice to avoid slavery,
Making himself his own Anatomie.
But look thee Martius, not a vein runs here
From head to foot, but Sophocles would unseame, and
Like a spring garden shoot his scornfull blood
Into their eyes, durst come to tread on him:
As for thy blows, they did conquer me:
Seven Battailes have I met thee face to face,
And given thee blow for blow, and wound for wound,
And till thou taught'st me, knew not to retire;
Thy sword was then as bold, thy arm as strong;
Thy blows the Martius, cannot conquer me.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: What is it then?

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Fortune.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Why, yet in that
Thou art the worse man, and must follow him.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Young Sir, you erre: If Fortune could be call'd
Or his, or your's, or mine, in good or evill
For any certain space, thou hadst spoke truth:
But she but jests with man, and in mischance
Abhors all constancie, flowting him still
With some small touch of good, or seeming good
Midst of his mischief: which vicissitude
Makes him strait doff his armour, and his fence
He had prepar'd before, to break her strokes.
So from the very Zenith of her wheel,
When she has dandled some choice favorite,
Given him his boons in women, honor, wealth,
And all the various delecacies of earth;
That the fool scorns the gods in his excess,
She whirls, and leaves him at th' Antipodes.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Art sure we have taken him? Is this Sophocles?
His fettred arms say no; his free soul, I.
This Athens nurseth Arts, as well as Arms.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Nor glory Martius, in this day of thine,
'Tis behind yesterday, but before to morrow:
Who knows what Fortune then will do with thee?
She never yet could make the better man,
The better chance she has: the man that's best
She still contends with, and doth favor least.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Me thinks a graver thunder then the skies
Breaks from his lips; I am amaz'd to hear,
And Athens words, more then her swords doth fear.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Martius, slave Sophocles, couldst thou acquire
(And did thy Roman gods so love thy prayers.
And solemn sacrifice, to grant thy suit)
To gather all the valour of the Caesars
Thy Predecessors, and what is to come,
And by their influence sling it on thee now,
Thou couldst not make my mind go less, not pare
With all their swords one virtue from my soul:
How am I vassall'd then? Make such thy slaves,
As dare not keep their goodness past their graves.
Know General, we two are chances on
The die of Fate; now thrown, thy six is up,
And my poor one beneath thee, next the throw
May set me upmost, and cast thee below.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Yet will I trie thee more: Calamitie
Is mans true touchstone: Listen insolent Prince,
That dar'st contemn the Master of thy life,
Which I will force here 'fore thy City walls
With barbarous crueltie, and call thy wife
To see it, and then after send her —

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: And then demolish Athens to the ground,
Depopulate her, fright away her fame,
And leave succession neither stone nor name.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Dost thou deride me?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Kneel, ask Martius
For mercy, Sophocles, and live happy still.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Kneel, and ask mercie? (Roman) art a god?
I never kneel'd, or begg'd of any else.
Thou art a fool, and I will loose no more
Instructions on thee: now I find thy eares
Are foolish, like thy tongue. My Dorigen?
Oh! must she see me bound?

speeches.speaker: 1. Cap.
verse: There's the first sigh
He breath'd since he was born, I think.

speeches.speaker: 2. Cap.
verse: Forbear,
All but the Lady his wife.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: How my heart chides
The manacles of my hands, that let them not
Embrace my Dorigen.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Turn but thy face.
And ask thy life of Martius thus, and thou
(With thy fair wife) shalt live; Athens shall stand,
And all her priviledges augmented be.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: 'Twere better Athens perish'd, and my wife
Which (Romans) I do know a worthie one,
Then Sophocles should shrink of Sophocles,
Commit profane Idolatry, by giving
The reverence due to gods to thee blown man.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Rough, stubborn Cynick.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Thou art rougher far,
And of a couser wale, fuller of pride,
Less temperate to bear prosperity.
Thou seest my meer neglect hath rais'd in thee
A storm more boystrous then the Oceans,
My virtue, Patience, makes thee vitious.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Why, fair-ey'd Lady, do you kneel?

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: Great Generall,
Victorious, godlike Martius, your poor handmaid
Kneels, for her husband will not cannot: speaks
Thus humbly, that he may not. Listen Roman,
Thou whose advanced front doth speak thee Roman
